en: O Maker of Night, your rays are surely fashioned from fragments of young *ketaka* flowers;
for that reason, their exceedingly pale luster pricks our bodies as if with thorns.

As her new husband hurriedly snatched away her silken garment, he impetuously embraced his newly wedded bride, whose lovely breasts were concealed by the crossed arms of her slender limbs and whose conch-shell bracelets were shattered.
Behold the majesty of the cold season: even the waters, white as snow, have assumed the guise of congealed skin as if out of fear of the chill, like a silken garment.
The hips of the deer-eyed women were concealed by silken garments, and their breasts by bodices;
yet their waists, being incessantly drunk in by the glances of their lovers, seemed to grow even more slender.
Having intensely tasted the honey of the lotus with his rays as hands, the sun,
as if overcome by intoxication and desiring to go to the earth, bore a crimson body.
At the end of the day, even the sun assumed a form tawny with the ripening of its heat;
who else here would not undergo transformation when his body is enveloped by the terrifying darkness?
The first [type of debt] is equal to a share, the middle is equal to the labor [expended], and the highest is equal to the profit;
or it may be the seizure of whatever is obtained, or equal to the deposit.
Even a small portion of the doctrines taught by the wicked may bring about the destruction of others,
just as even a tiny fragment of a tiger's claw can lead to the loss of life.
With his shoulders held steady and bent, his neck free from exertion,
and his face maintaining a composure that casts aside all distortions, he possessed the serene splendor of the moon.

I meditate upon the Enchanter of the World, who rests at the foot of the Kalpa tree; he wears a left earring that hangs over his shoulder, his creeper-like brows are slightly raised, his soft lips are somewhat pursed, and his eyes are cast sidelong. With joy, he fills his flute with fingers like tremulous sprouts, standing gracefully in the three-fold bend (tribhaṅga) posture.

May the Lord of Rādhā protect you—he whose charming sound begins with the gentle breath issuing from his pair of bimba-red lips as they rest upon the flute held against his cheek; he whose mass of necklaces trembles slightly with his smiles, and whose multitude of fingers—each with its own mouth—bends, moves, and rises.
Approaching her, Hari struck with water from his cupped palms that fawn-eyed woman who was hiding her ear with one shoulder, her chest with her chin, and her eye with both hands.
Victorious is the name of Hari, the auspiciousness of the world, which, like the sun over the ocean of darkness, destroys all the sins of every living being by its mere utterance.
A flower-laden earth free of thorns, a courtesan who is not one's own mother, and the glory of sovereignty devoid of a minister— these are enjoyed by libertines and servants.
How can there be a flower garland around one who has no neck? How can there be the scent of incense without a nose?
How can there be song and dance in the ear of one who has no ears? And how can there be prostration at the feet of one who has no feet?
We know that even for Maheśa, life would be fruitless without an *akaparddaka*;
for it is by wearing a mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭaka*) upon his head that he becomes *kapardī*.

"O proud woman, remove my lotus-feet from your head; do not show me honor out of season. O slender one, if you have gone to another's lover, then I shall touch both your breasts and his two genitals."
This gaze of yours, pitiless and showing no mercy with its distressed mind, pursues you from behind even as you turn your face away— like the Ganges following Bhagīratha.
Lack of compassion, engaging in conflict without cause, seizing the wealth of others, violating the wives of others,
and intolerance toward one's own kin and relatives— these are indeed the innate characteristics of the wicked-minded.

"O pitiless one, O ocean of false speech, release my hem! 'Your affection for me was perfectly well-known to me'—who here, O blessed lady, could have reported you, with tears flowing incessantly, emaciated, and stripped of ornaments, were it not for Sleep?"

Why did you redden your eyes, why did you clasp your sprout-like hands, and why did you engage in a quarrel out of anger, O connoisseur of flavors? Those who are bitten by fate do not perceive what is beneficial.
Fate, intent on the destruction of the cosmic egg, left nothing remaining for his ears;
upon hearing the delightful story of Rāma, whose head does not tremble?

Alas! Having been deprived of its rudders by enemies whose limbs were struck by arrows that did not even reach their ears, the ocean of worldly existence has been crossed in battle after sinking it, once a breach had been made in the sun’s boat.
That which ought not to be done must not be done, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
that which ought to be done must certainly be done, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
Like an unchaste woman, craving impels a person toward things that ought not to be done;
yet shame protects that very person from all evils, like a mother.
For beings who are inactive, there would indeed be no means of subsistence whatsoever;
therefore, one should resort to that very [means] and never let it fail in any way.

One should not allow these to dwell in one's house: one who is habitually inactive, a glutton, one hated by the world, one full of deceit, one who is cruel, one ignorant of place and time, and one with an unpleasing appearance.
Adorned with a digit of the stainless moon, that youthful woman of the west shines like the forehead of Śambhu as he sits absorbed in meditation at twilight.
What beauty can there be in the presence of the stainless one for one who is stained by the blemish of time?
The moon desires to run toward the young dawn, as if to hide its spot.
May the dark-complexioned beloved, stainless, bristling with joy, full of affection, and having cast off her bodice, fall upon your chest; may the sword-blade fall upon the head of the enemy.
Spotless, firm, pure, well-furnished, and endowed with excellent qualities;
born of a noble lineage and captivating to the heart—your sword is truly worthy of you.
One who has not distinguished between his own nature and that of others perceives even his own fault as residing in another;
like one standing on a boat, he considers those on the shore to be moving, even though they are motionless.
Since this heart-pleasing, sin-destroying, and non-trivial Kali age has passed away,
my delight here rests with the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, the bestower of bliss who crushed the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
As the sage— whose majesty was vast with the power of his unclouded ascetic heat, who was a treasury of fame, and who was inflated by unfounded pride— rushed forward in anger,
[the prince’s] hand, due to his pride in his newly acquired skill in archery, throbbed impetuously for action, yet simultaneously trembled for the act of clasping the sage’s feet.
Incapable of moving his own limbs like a bird in a cage,
not breathing and remembering his former state, what indeed does he experience within the womb?
Through the lightness of their intellect, men suddenly undertake actions and suddenly suffer decline; they perform both good and evil deeds and achieve greatness through such fickleness of mind.
If any man should obtain some object even by chance, people consider that to be through luck (*haṭha*), for it was not the result of anyone's effort.
O noble elephant, why do you suddenly strike the tree by the roadside like one mad, and why do you tear up the pond filled with blooming lotuses with the blows of your trunk?
Only then shall we recognize your incomparable display of strength, O best of elephants, if you touch the mane of even a sleeping lion cub.
O friend, as I was walking along a certain path toward the bank of the Yamunā, I suddenly beheld this youth whose body is dark like a fresh rain-cloud.
I do not know what he did with a mere glance, but since then my mind has become so restless that it no longer attends to any domestic duties whatsoever.
They become angry quite suddenly and are appeased without cause; such is the character of the wicked, like a shifting cloud.
If this slender-limbed woman laughs all of a sudden again,
surely the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma) reigns supreme over her.
O passionate one, all of a sudden your face, with its sprout-like lower lip quivering,
bears clusters of drops of perspiration that possess the luster of pearls.
The world recoils from one who, out of anger, speaks excessively and repeatedly for no apparent reason, as if from a fire emitting sparks.
One who suddenly hates food served since birth, or for whom there is no longer a relish for condiments, should be abandoned like a king who is ill.
Even by Brahmā himself, it is impossible to bring peace to the mind of a husband who rages without cause and a woman who is attached to another.

The quarters of the sky were gazed upon by flocks of cranes whose hearts were seized by an unseasonable resolve for celebration, and by circles of peacocks performing sudden, sharp dances— all darkened by the dust raised by the night of your vast army as it surged forth, overflowing with its fresh and abundant force.
For those sudden, unexpected blows from weapons that pierce the vital organs—
those deep strikes of intense grief— non-thinking alone is the great medicine.
With hands busily adjusting their garments when their breasts have suddenly slipped out, with breasts raised by the binding of arms lifted in feigned yawns,
and with mutual laughter produced through deceitful coming and going— all these courtesans, alas, steal away the hearts of the world!
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire.
The body of one who desires a woman who does not desire him is consumed with distress; but for one who desires a woman who desires him, there arises beautiful joy.
He who desires those who do not desire him, who hates those who love him,
and who hates one who is powerful— him they call a person of deluded mind.
Neither physical form nor lineage is the cause [of greatness]; rather, action shines among both the great and the lowly.
For this very form, which was previously held in contempt, has now attained even greater honor.
Grammar is not the cause; even the sound of a lute string is not the cause.
The three Vedas are not the cause; in that matter, rice grains are the cause.
Who indeed does not feel fear toward a wicked person who manifests groundless anger and is cruel,
whose harsh speech— like the venom of a great serpent— is always present in his mouth and is exceedingly difficult to endure?
O lord of men, that king who becomes angry with Brahmins without cause is like one who,
incited by pride in his strength, seizes a black cobra by the head.

One should not drink that which causes intoxication, for fear of performing what ought not to be done, because of the avoidance of duties, and because of the disclosure of secret counsels at the improper time.
The prohibition of improper actions and the promotion of those that are proper; the giving away of what should be given and the non-retention of what should not be given.
For men are seen who, having repeatedly committed what should not be done, remain destitute; yet other people are seen who, though established in unrighteousness, are endowed with wealth.
Having exhausted all improper acts and even having committed the acquisition of sin,
for whom is that body truly stable, when it is maintained only for the sake of another's welfare?
Whether true or false, popular rumor—whether it be so or otherwise—destroys the greatness of those of lofty station;
for even the sun, though proven by the scales and having clearly dispelled all darkness, does not possess such brilliance when it has entered the sign of Virgo.
One should never engage in wandering at improper times, in discordant assemblies, or in the company of bad friends;
behold the bird sleeping in the lotus grove, pierced by an arrow released from a bow.
That heart-stealing moonlight of her face belongs to the moon that is an unseasonal cloud;
it is perpetually drunk by the cakora-birds of poets, yet it never wanes.
Through verses on untimely clouds that seemed as if composed by himself,
the eminent poet Kādambarīrāma was born as a master of the dramatic art.
Seeing the solar disc covered by unseasonable clouds,
the pair of *cakravāka* birds cries out, fearing the onset of night.

There is no one equal to the Creator who, by averting untimely death, bestows life and physical well-being upon embodied beings; how could there be anyone superior? In this world, no gift excels the gift of life.
Untimely death is trust; for by trusting, one comes to ruin. He in whom one places trust lives, while the other is dead.
A fortress is said to suffer from calamity when it is ill-timed, unassailable by force, too small, led by a foolish or addicted commander, unguarded, or defended by cowardly soldiers.
One who engages in battle at an improper time is slain by one who fights at the right time,
just as a crow whose light has been extinguished is killed by an owl in the middle of the night.
An undertaking commenced at an improper time does not lead to success;
that very same undertaking, when commenced at the proper time, leads to great success.
If it thunders out of season, or if there should be a foul day,
they declare that the target struck by the first arrow is unfit for study.
Wandering about with nothing at all, you will experience happiness;
for one who possesses nothing indeed sleeps in peace and likewise rises in peace.
He weighed possessionlessness and kingship on a scale;
for one who has conquered the self, possessionlessness was superior even to kingship.
For one who possesses nothing, who is self-controlled, tranquil, and even-minded,
whose mind is contented with me— for such a person, all directions are filled with happiness.
For one who possesses nothing, who is pure, and who has arisen completely [from all bonds],
as I survey the three worlds, I perceive no equal.
Men who possess nothing are seen to live long lives,
while those born into prosperous families perish like moths.
Beholding, touching, and so forth, those who accomplish nothing, whose virtues and actions have been drawn away by the wretched, and who have departed from existence for the sake of evil.
And living beings will also speak of your undying infamy;
for one who has been highly esteemed, infamy is worse than death.
If the ill-repute of any being whatsoever is sung in the world,
he surely falls to the lowest worlds for as long as that sound is proclaimed.
Disrepute is censured by the gods, while fame is honored in the worlds;
indeed, for the sake of fame, all great-souled beings undertake their endeavors.
Woman is the cause of ill repute; woman is the cause of enmity;
woman is the cause of saṃsāra; therefore, one should avoid woman.
O sweet-voiced one, place me—who am filled with unrestrained longing yet lack a throat—momentarily upon the neck of her whose neck is like a conch-shell; remove this pain of my throat.
Beholding the city of Kubera’s son never brings about the birth of a son on earth;
therefore, for the sake of that remedy, worship the eye of Nala, the husband of Damayantī.
Even those who do not commit evil deeds may perish through association with the wicked due to their reliance on sinners,
just as fish in a dragon's lake are destroyed by the sins of others.
Long-lived people witness the rise of those born of low families into noble lineages, the decline of those of noble birth, and both unions and separations.
Whether of low birth or high birth, he who does not transgress the bounds of propriety,
who regards righteousness, and who is gentle and self-controlled, is superior to hundreds of those of noble lineage.
A man of low birth, by nature, when he attains rare sovereignty due to the destruction of virtuous men, becomes arrogant and turns into an enemy.
Even if he is of low birth or even a fool, whoever serves a king here—
even if he lacks honor— he is honored everywhere.
A king fallen into a low family, yet possessing a wise son,
regards the world as mere straw upon the acquisition of wealth when he was previously destitute.
The cloud takes up an abundance of water from the ocean and scatters it; even though he is the presiding lord of giving, this is no cause for wonder.
Blessed is that cloud which scatters its water in the form of pearls, so that its fame dances upon the slopes of the breasts of the wives of kings.
Even without beginning to pluck his beard, placing his palms against the region of his chin as a sign of resolve, casting a most affectionate and tremulous glance upon the young women,
and disregarding his peers in the assembly by asserting "I am a prince," he spreads his charm in his youth while looking at his arms and chest.

With their mouths beginning to form unformed morsels and their eyes closed in fear, these rows of deer stand for a moment with their necks slightly turned; looking repeatedly toward the sky with faces drenched in tears, they cause the water of their eyes to fall incessantly from the tips of their antlers.
Know that one who is ungrateful, ignoble, long-simmering in anger, and dishonest—these four are outcastes by birth; the fifth would be one born as such by nature.
What is the use of the title "King of Kings" for those whose greatness lies in their refusal to give?
The wise do not honor Maheśvara as the protector of treasures.
The hand of a man who does not cut down the rising power of his enemies, and whose actions regarding the protection of those who have sought refuge are fruitless,
is indeed useless, serving only the purpose of scratching.
It is better indeed never to have felt love than to have experienced love that has been broken;
for one whose eyes have been plucked out suffers in a way that one born blind does not.
"O friend, we understand that the face of your beloved young woman, having taken on the form of Bimbasāra, has become the clear light of the world-system.
No, no! This is merely your delusion, my friend; in truth, you must recognize it as a vessel of white poison."
There is no acquisition of what has not been done, nor is there destruction of what has been done;
yet this world, for no other reason, has been made a slave by you, O Craving.
Having encountered a king who has not disciplined his soul and is devoted to unrighteousness,
even prosperous kingdoms and cities perish.
Even when men make no effort, the fruit of actions performed in another life— whether auspicious or inauspicious— comes to them, ordained by destiny.
Death indeed drags one away even while tasks remain unaccomplished;
therefore, one should be devoted to righteousness while still young, for life is without certainty.
No one, even if great, is honored if they have not caused harm;
men worship the *nāgas*, but not Tārkṣya, the slayer of *nāgas*.
Even when the loss of life is imminent, that which ought not to be done must never be done;
nor should that which ought to be done be abandoned—this is the eternal law.
Impelled by the words of women, a man considers what is undone to be done, what is inaccessible to be easy to reach, and what is inedible to be edible.
In this worthless and burnt-out cycle of existence, the essence is the fawn-eyed woman, whose gait is languid with grace and who possesses the flavor of unfeigned love.
Their sexual union was marked by natural grace, required no sequence of learned arts, and was beautiful in its undivided unity of limbs.
He who, remaining idle in this world, enjoys the fruit of action without having performed it himself,
incurs censure and generally becomes an object of hatred.
That king who seeks victory without first securing the defense of his own territory is like a man who attempts to walk while wearing his turban as an undergarment.
Without causing distress to others, without resorting to the servility of the wicked,
and without abandoning the path of the virtuous— even that which is very little is much.
What is the use of that fortune which comes without human effort and belongs to the luckless?
Even a deer eats grass brought to it by fate.
He who, without performing human effort, relies solely upon fate,
labors in vain, like a woman who has obtained an impotent husband.
Without playfully placing one's foot upon the lofty heads of enemies,
how could fame, being without support, ascend to the heavens?
If Fortune does not take refuge in a man who is free from meanness, free from deceit, steady, disciplined, undaunted, wise, and brave,
then Fortune herself is indeed deceived.

May the fortune of the skull-bearer (Kapālin), who possesses compassion in his heart— whose breasts are full, whose waist is slender, whose eyes are wide, whose hips are broad, and whose lower lip is ruddy— be revealed.
Not slender at the hips, thin at the waist, and high upon the breasts;
with eyes exceedingly long—this very life of mine approaches.
One who delights in dwelling in the forest, always subsisting on uncultivated roots and fruits,
and performs the *śrāddha* rite day after day— he is called a brahmin sage (*ṛṣi*).
Does the peacock not speak? Is the osprey not clever? Or is the parrot mute? And he [the cuckoo], though possessing a sweet voice, is he one whose song is impaired?
Since you have obtained through countless merits this sweetness of the cuckoo and this profound dignity, why are you so stubborn that you do not sing beautifully here for a long time?
This eyebrow, flowerless yet the bowstring of the God of Love, a banner of grace without silk,
and a dancer upon the stage of the forehead, follows the gaze even without kohl.
Because buttermilk is not a constituent part of the ritual, it was not offered by Śatakratu;
since the meaning of the statement is that what is not given [as an offering] does not belong to Śakra, buttermilk is difficult for him to obtain.
Knowing that it was not for the sake of the ritual, Śakra did not offer it in the past;
because of the scriptural principle that "one must not give what has not been given," buttermilk was difficult for Śakra to obtain.
An undertaking of action that proceeds without sequence and without the proper means does not succeed, just as [the products] curd, ghee, and milk do not come from the cow of a Śabara.
Those ascetics who are themselves prone to anger yet teach others to be free from anger are like those destitute of wealth who instruct others in alchemy for the sake of riches.
One who is free from anger is superior to those who are angry; likewise, one who is patient is superior to one who is impatient.
Humans are superior to non-humans, and in the same way, the wise man is superior to the ignorant.
Free from anger, truthful in speech, non-injurious toward living beings,
free from envy, and of virtuous conduct, one shall attain a long life.
O Indra among kings, he who is free from anger, devoted to truth, firm in his vows,
and who treats all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
Absence of anger, dispassion, mastery over the senses, forbearance, compassion, tranquility, and being beloved by the people;
being a donor free from greed and removing fear and sorrow—these are the marks of knowledge and the characteristics of fearlessness.
When anger arises toward one who is free from anger, it leads to total destruction;
by the wrath of Rāghava, the lord of rivers and streams was bound.
One should conquer anger with non-anger; one should conquer the wicked with goodness;
one should conquer the miser with generosity, and the untruthful with truth.
Adorning his hair with vernal flowers of undimmed luster, the lotus-eyed one sports within the groves, O you with eyes like those of a wagtail.
Your hands have not yet rested from the work of our mansion; what can we say? You are the foremost of connoisseurs, for this water-jar cannot endure further delay.
I have drunk with tenderness alone, during the festivals of love, that lower lip of my beloved—tempting as the unblemished young sprout of a tree.
O bee, if you bite it, I shall cause you to be imprisoned within the interior of a lotus.
For those possessed of merit, that which was intended appears as if untroubled by affliction, already accomplished;
but for those lacking merit, it flies away—behold the pigeons!

For Pārtha, whose brow was knit with intense rage at the slaughter of Abhimanyu committed by the enemy of the Kṣatriyas, and who was fainting with inner grief because he had not yet avenged his foe—his glances, heavy with shame, fall upon his bow drenched in teardrops; the cries "Alas, my son! quiver within him but do not emerge from his mouth.
When two lovers have made their fortune the stake for a game of dice, and victory or defeat has ensued—
here, if Manmatha knows, let him say which of them wins or even who is defeated.
"Since you are the master in the act of seizing the lower lip won at dice, tell me, who are you to interrupt this?"— thus she spoke with her creeper-like brows arched in feigned anger,
while her hand, moist with perspiration,
pressed against her budding cheek.
In retaliation for that [debt], the lovely-eyed girl has brought me under the power of hunger, even though it was not won by me at dice.
He who, though incapable, exerts himself in an action while maintaining a sense of self-sufficiency, indeed becomes an object of ridicule and faces a danger to his life.
Knowing the turning of the rosary, holding the *kuśa* grass seat,
and adorned with a girdle, this assembly of wicked people is worthy of salutation, like the goddess Brāhmī.
Intolerance, the abandonment of shame, the destruction of prosperity, the decay of Dharma,
covetousness, and lack of wisdom— all these proceed from greed.
Intolerant, untruthful in his promises, an adulterer, and a doer of cruel deeds—
he is cooked in the very hells, being burned by his own karma.
Those two syllables— "na asti," "na asti"— which were practiced in the past,
have now appeared in their opposite form as "dehi," "dehī."
"O friend, what can we say of the youth who possesses syllables, kindness, ornaments, and graceful conduct? No, no, friend, it is not of his poetic composition."
"Viṣṇu himself declared, 'Among letters, I am the letter *a*';
yet that very one has truly been made insignificant by you through your mere appearance."
Let the syllables be examined; what is the use of a grand display of clothing?
Is Śambhu not omniscient even though he is devoid of clothing?
Those men by whom these various letters are understood are like oxen,
though they are devoid of hooves and horns.
The syllables are uniform, rounded, and dense;
they cling to one another like the jar-like breasts of a young woman.
When were the eyelashes ever lost? Indeed, it is the hairs of the head that fall away;
for calamities befall only those whose nature is to grow.
Her ears are not pressed down by her dark-spotted eyes;
I suspect it is as if they are overcome by fear of the noose-like golden earrings.
But one whose karmic bonds are not yet exhausted, having recognized that death has arrived,
attains the state of a yogin again by recollecting [the teachings] at the time of the end after speaking them.
Alas, even the gods, as if powerless, fear a wicked person who possesses undiminished wealth, who is treacherous, and who is free from the fear of both the desirable and the undesirable.
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
likewise, a field without seed becomes merely a barren wasteland.
Through addiction to dice, hunting, women, drinking, idle wandering,
and sleep, a king quickly perishes.
This addiction to dice, this dense passion in the heart, and this face overflowing with intoxication from wine—
even though the lotus is likewise the supreme abode of beauty, it is indeed wretchedness that makes these things ill-fated.

He who, having well-prepared fish with walnuts, ginger, black pepper, fresh ginger, pomegranate rind, coriander, salt, and oil, places them upon a bed of very cold white rice, that man of meritorious deeds attains the world of Brahmā.
One may perform [the rite] even on a day when the lunar mansion is not suitable for shaving, provided it is joined with the days of Mercury or the Moon;
however, one should not perform it even when the lunar day and lunar mansion are auspicious if they are joined with the days of Saturn or Mars.
An *akṣauhiṇī* army may slay the enemy, or it may itself be slain by him;
but a Brahmin who knows the mantras slays all enemies in an instant.

O friend, in the bower, the darkness—beautiful like a dark blue veil—embraces every limb of the fair-eyed women as they hasten to meet their lovers: it casts collyrium upon their eyes, clusters of *tāpiñcha* blossoms upon their ears, a wreath of dark lotuses upon their heads, and musk-leaf patterns upon their breasts.

The charming collyrium on her eyes, the sapphire anklets on her feet, the blue garment upon her limbs, and the distinct application of musk on her cheeks— all that was once practiced out of love for her has now become a darkness that obstructs the sight of others, even in the mere arrangement of her attire, for she belongs to the class of unchaste women.

Satisfying the pair of eyes with her soft and delicate form, the nose with the divine fragrance issuing from her mouth and the breath, and the ears with her charming speech; likewise, she delights the tongue with her flavor—just as the lotus-face bestows pleasure upon the five senses, no other goddess grants such bliss to lovers as this young woman.

The woman who was the protector of the rice crop plucked a blue lotus from her eye with resentment, thinking it an adversary; yet she bore that very same flower upon her head once more—for the enmity of the high-minded is firm toward their opponents, not toward those they have conquered.
Behold this illustrious lord of the earth, whose mandala is unbroken;
unlike the moon, he has never suffered a deficiency in his digits.
Even a whole betel nut that is powdered and devoid of flavor,
or a leaf fallen upon the ground, would take away the fortune even of Śakra himself.
Your power remains unimpaired, yet you have not accepted comparison as a means of knowledge, nor does the method of quibble exist for you;
what then is this adherence to the system of logic on your part, when you are untouched by doubt and error?
That very hand of the sage, beneath which the ocean was cut off in the hollows of its short mountain joints, is indeed [that hand] below the Vindhya mountain.
For the wise who perceive everything clearly through the eyes of a friend and their own hearts, our eyes—though situated so close by—are not subtle witnesses; they are merely ornaments for the face.
Alas, among all birds that roam at their own will,
O parrot, your confinement within a cage is the fruit of your sweet songs.
We worship that single-tusked Gajanana, who is the sun to the lotus-face of the unborn goddess, and who bestows manifold boons upon his devotees day and night.
O Sundara, by means of your conduct— which is indifferent even to its own immeasurable virtues—
you have made her, who has no other refuge, turn back like a ship caught in a whirlpool.
Disregarding my elders, fickle in his begging, always a guest at the edge of my feet, ignorant of decorum, bewildered, unable to wait for the right time, and greedy for pleasure—
my beloved plunges me into shame, heedlessly ignoring my feigned anger, the blows of my hands, and my tears of bashfulness.
The birth of these noble beings, who are like dense suns among men, was brought about for the sake of helping others; they disregard their own fatigue and remain engaged in the affairs of others.
Now, that which is done by one of unreckonable fame, who has abandoned all established conduct, and who is ungrateful—
that deception of yours toward a friend who is affectionate, well-wishing, and full of passion— is not fitting.
Lack of inquiry, excessive faith, and satisfaction with a mere semblance of knowledge—
these three qualities of a disciple arise from the good fortune of a foolish teacher.
Indeed, suffering does not arise from the humiliation of those who have no recourse;
for the most part, aśoka trees put forth sprouts when kicked by the feet.
One should remove the poison of the Vyantara spirits with universal medicines;
incense made from *devī*, *sahā*, and *picchakaṇḍana* removes that same poison.
Generally, a person incurs the need for penance by approaching one who should not be approached;
however, that which is unapproachable—namely, fame—attains purification everywhere.
The man who approaches those women who should not be approached, or who serves those who should not be served,
embraces death just as a female mule conceives a fetus.
Those who regard even their lives as mere grass for the sake of forbidden objects, who cast fear and shame behind them,
and whose entire possessions have been consumed by courtesans— such people are his attendants.
Inaccessible to mantras, beyond the reach even of physicians by their natural remedies, incurable by the essence of nectar, and dense with most extraordinary beginnings—
clearly this wicked person was created by Fate, who possesses matured intellect, as a disease of a fundamentally hostile nature intended to delude the world.

Those who are like Agastya in drying up the ocean of ghee, like the thunderbolt in splitting the mountain of Vaṭaka, and who are like a forest fire to the grove of the Śākāvalī—only they are true Bhaṭṭas; all others are merely soldiers.
"When the ocean, having been swallowed by Agasti in the hollow of his hand, was submerged within the bounds of its shore while he took the form of a vehicle, the gods then sang thus."
Like Agastya, whose sword shone as it bent over the mountains [or kings],
he too made the ocean of battle strange by causing headless trunks to dance.
Due to the curse of the sage Agastya, Nahuṣa, who was seated upon the celestial chariot of Brahmā,
fell from great bliss and became a serpent.
How much of the ocean was drunk and how much was left by Agastya?
O hero, what did you do to the host of your enemies in battle?
The one who plunges into the waters of the Gaṅgā, where the crows are like dark clouds;
he who has abandoned all worldly attachments, whose marks are like the sky, who moves through the air like a bird, and who is free from the bonds of existence.
The Rohita fish, though it moves through unfathomable waters, does not undergo such transformation;
whereas the Śapharī fish flutters about in a mere mouthful of water.
Kings have unfathomable hearts and are as difficult to approach as wells;
if there were not virtuous intermediaries like water-carriers, how could one obtain their livelihood?
Of what use is that water of the salt-ocean, however unfathomable it may be?
It is better for men to have even knee-deep water that cuts through their thirst.
In this lovely house,
she spends her days— alas, O Śiva, Śiva!— painting Lord Śiva’s crescent moon, lofty serpents, and even the entire circle of Rāhu upon the windowsills, in the groves, and upon the roof of the home.
Both the man devoid of merit and the heap of virtues have fallen, by fate, into the mouths of the wicked;
one spreads out like oil upon water, while the other becomes as solid as ghee.
Let the world call him "light," yet I consider him truly weighty,
for he manifests a life solely dedicated to virtue even toward those who have caused him burning pain.
Shaking her mass of hair, which is adorned with the fragrant smoke of aloe-wood and from which flower garlands have fallen with their tips curled, the passionate woman—
possessing heavy hips, a deep navel, and a slender waist— casts off her bed-chamber garment at dawn, radiant with the beauty of love.
Even for one who is not a guru, the praise of him spreads far his virtues;
even when cast into the fire, the agallochum emits its virtues in the guise of fragrance.
That king is the best of monarchs whose citizens and rural subjects do not conceal their wealth, and who understands both right policy and its opposite.
"Is this a face with its filaments of teeth revealed by an unrestrained laugh, or is it a blooming lotus?"—
thus did the women, after a long time, recognize their friend who had been lost within the forest of lotuses.
Just as a heap of cotton is instantly destroyed upon reaching fire,
so too is every sin destroyed by the water of the Gaṅgā alone.
The man who kindles himself like a small spark of fire,
as he grows, swallows even a vast accumulation.
Fire, when sprinkled with clarified butter, grows from a small spark; and a single seed becomes many thousands.
Having observed that both decline and increase can be vast, one should not despise even a small amount of wealth.
A woman is like a fire-pit, and a man is like a jar of ghee;
whose mind would not be shaken by union with another's wife?
A woman is like a pot of fire; a man is like a pot of ghee. When these two are joined together, who can feel secure?
I feel no pain from being burned by fire, nor from being cut, nor from being ground;
that which is a great suffering for me is being weighed together with a *guñjā* seed.
The arsonist, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the stealer of land or wife— these six are indeed considered assailants (ātatāyin).
By means of fire, ashes, a pillar, or by people,
and by a path other than the main entrance, no fault regarding the row is incurred.
Fire, water, women, fools, serpents, and royal families—
these six must always be approached with great caution, for they can take one's life instantly.
Fire is the preceptor of the twice-born; the king is the preceptor of the social orders;
the husband is the preceptor of women of noble family; and the guest is the preceptor of everyone.
Fire burns with heat; the sun burns with its rays;
a king burns with his rod of punishment; a Brahmin should burn with ascetic fervor.
Fire is the deity of the twice-born; for sages, the deity resides in the heart; for those of small intellect, the deity is in images; but for those who see with equanimity, the deity is everywhere.
For Agni is all the deities, and gold has that as its essence;
therefore, by one who gives gold, all the deities are given.
One does not obtain that fruit by means of various sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, which one obtains by traveling to a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
Fire is the heat within the world; it remains hidden in pieces of wood and does not consume that wood as long as it is not ignited by other means.
Indeed, when that very fire, having been produced by friction from pieces of wood, blazes up,
it then quickly consumes both those sticks and the rest of the forest with its heat.
In the very same way, those born of noble lineage, possessing a brilliance like that of fire,
though patient and without outward display, lie hidden like fire within wood.
One should not approach the sacred fire, one's home, a field, a pregnant woman, the elderly, or children with empty hands; nor should one approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands.
"The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple staff, and smearing oneself with ashes—
Bṛhaspati says these are merely the livelihood of those devoid of intelligence and manly effort."
The Vedas have the Agnihotra sacrifice as their fruit; sacred learning has character and conduct as its fruit;
wives have pleasure and sons as their fruit; and wealth has giving and enjoyment as its fruit.
The Agnihotra sacrifice, Vedic study, giving, and all other ritual acts reach futility for that person whose word is without cause.
For Brahmins, the God resides in the Agnihotra fires; for the wise, in the heart;
for those of small intellect, in images; and for those who have realized the Self, everywhere.
Just as there is no cause other than the unseen (adṛṣṭa) for the separation and conjunction of fire with wood,
so too the cause of the union and separation of a living being from the body is difficult to discern.
For those who perform rituals, Hari is the god in the fire; for the wise, he is the god in heaven; for those of small intellect, he is in images; and for yogins, he is in the heart.
That which is consumed by fire, submerged in water, or seized by thieves and kings—
all that they call a gift, provided one does not speak of impotence.
O best of the twice-born, just as cotton placed in a fire is completely consumed by smoke,
so too is all the sin of one who has immersed himself in the Gaṅgā utterly destroyed.
When a person has been cast into the fire, their own performed karma follows them;
therefore, a person should diligently accumulate merit little by little.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
You perceive the form of fire before you like a female cakravāka bird perceiving the moon; you burn like a lotus plant by the chilling breeze, trembling violently.
You somehow sustain your life-breaths with effort as they depart like piercing arrows; O fair-limbed one, by what has this transformation of love been produced within you?

Having gained the world's confidence through the establishment of the sacred fires, through sacrifice, by wearing saffron robes, and by carrying matted hair and deerskins, one should then plunder it like a wolf.
The shadow of a tree at dawn, a fire of straw, service to the lowly, water on a cloth,
a courtesan’s passion, and affection for a rogue— all these are like bubbles.
In front, behind, in the middle, on the sides, and all around,
he shines like a flash of lightning, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
The four Vedas are before me, and behind me is a bow with an arrow;
I am capable of both, whether by means of a curse or by means of an arrow.
With the left foot forward and the right foot slightly bent,
one should assume the *ālīḍha* stance, with the two hands spread at a distance of two cubits.
Clinging with his exceedingly tawny, soft rays to the trees upon the highest peaks,
has the Sun entered the thicket of the western mountain, or the ocean, or the earth?

O beloved, for you there was no ear-ornament that could not be grasped, no decoration suited to your neck, no bright collyrium for your eyes to behold their own subtlety, and no momentary rite of perfuming for your face; rather, you were the very Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) fashioned by the transformative rites of good fortune (*saubhāgyapratikarma*).
These women, endowed with every virtue, should not be seized by the hair;
they are like creepers growing in a grove, who do not deserve to have their tender shoots torn away.
At the beginning of this world, someone was created by someone else at some point; this cycle of existence consists of the descent of childhood, youth, the burden of old age, and so forth.
Let the child hold it in high regard as something rare and attained; let the youth enjoy it; but what does the old man see when he turns away, as if cast out from it?
Before him is a pack of wicked dogs, fierce as they lick the savory taste of raw flesh; behind him is a hunter, intent on slaughter, with a sharpened arrow in hand, never leaving his footprints.
On all sides blazes a forest fire, and a smoke-wind obscures his vision. Alas, alas! O deer, terrified and fleeing in all directions, to whom shall you go for refuge?
"Go ahead, O cowherd girls, taking the milk-pots; the cows will soon yield their milk, and then this Rādhā will follow slowly.
May that Lord Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda by a divine cause, whose heart is thus concealed under a pretext and who makes the cow-station secluded, steal away all inauspiciousness from you.

If there is song before you, charming poets at your side, the tinkling of playful bracelets behind you from the chowrie-bearers, and all this—then indulge in the relish of worldly pleasures; but if not, O mind, enter at once into the thought-free state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

At midday on paths where water-stations have ceased their service, travelers drink from the wells whose waters are heated at the surface yet intensely cool at the bottom; they stir them repeatedly with their arms until the waves, scattered with fragments of floating young *śaivala* moss, become turbid from the agitation caused by buffaloes plunging in after being released from the plow.
"Before us stands this lion of fierce form, arrogant with rage; behind us comes the violent wind from the earth scorched by a formidable forest fire.
What shall we do? Shall we suddenly abandon these young elephants and flee? O, how can we go? Thus the female elephant, her eyes narrowed in distress, ponders in her agitation.
Before her is Kāma himself, holding his bow and arrows; behind her is the haste born from the suspicion that the moon has already risen;
and on all sides is the darkness, its power expanding at the end of the day—is this maiden truly alone on the path as she goes to meet her beloved?
For those whose destruction has already begun, silence is the supreme virtue;
nevertheless, this is said out of a sense of solidarity with those devoted to their lord.
By those very praises with which the Master was brought to the pit of calamity,
he cannot at all be rescued once they have subsequently fallen into silence.
Having seen at the beginning a man who lives off buffaloes, in the middle a husband of a low-caste woman,
and at the end a usurer, the ancestors have departed in despair.
In front, these clouds move like the dust of the chariot as they are pulverized; the whirling of the wheels creates the appearance of another set of spokes within the gaps between them.
Upon the head of the horse, the chowrie appears motionless as if fixed in a painting, while the banner-cloth, held level at the tip of its staff, flutters at its edge due to the wind of speed.
First there is lightness, and afterwards even greatness cannot conceal it;
for it is not by his magnitude that those who know the ten incarnations call Trivikrama "Vāmana."
With the mango trees losing their fruit as clusters of scattered *kurabaka* blossoms fall at their tips,
the youth of the season, facing its transformation, excites the heart with longing.
In front is a hunter holding an arrow in his hand; at her side is a net; behind her fire burns intensely;
nearby are dogs; with her gait slowed by pregnancy and her feet obstructed by fawns, the doe, overcome with anxiety, says to the deer, "What shall I do? Where shall I go?"

Whose mind is not now filled with longing by the clusters of betel-nut trees— trees made beautiful by fruits that are marked at the tip with dark spots like tilaka ornaments, which in the middle are as pale-red as ripe paṭola gourds, slightly brownish at the base, and on the stalks are thick, rough, and the color of a parrot’s breast?
When the maiden Agresarī is in front and the Tāra syllable follows behind her like an arrow-feather, then the supreme Siddhi shall be attained; for Durgā is seen as excellent even at the outset.
At the forefront stands the *kuravaka* flower, pale-red like a woman’s fingernail; on two sides stands the young *aśoka*, beautiful with its burgeoning passion and ready to burst open.

O friend, the beauty of spring stands between them—on the mango tree, the fresh cluster of blossoms is tawny at its tips with slightly clinging specks of pollen, situated midway between childhood and youth.

Foremost among those possessing liberation when engaged in practice, yet relegated to the background regarding mantras; like a master cook who has entered the kitchen solely to satisfy the mind of the chef;

devoted to high status, yet delighting in the company of commoners; showing respect for morsels of food, yet with a mind entirely stirred by various groups of faithful devotees—Bhadroṭṭama shines resplendent.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.
It brings about the impossible and certainly renders the well-constructed unstable in an instant;
it creates this world with all its moving and unmoving beings—alas, such is my conviction, that Fate is powerful indeed.
Fate alone brings together that which was never meant to be joined and shatters even that which was well-constructed;
it unites those very things that a man does not even think of.
The world disregards a king, even if he be of noble birth, if he is like an unpolished ruby or an elephant that is not in rut— provided he lacks valor.
Some suspected it to be a mark on the ocean; others thought it was mud; some declared it to be a deer, and others that it was the reflection of the earth.
But I believe that which appears in the moon, dark as a fragment of split sapphire, is the blinding darkness itself, terrified of the sun, now visible as it stays within the moon's belly.

Victory to the breasts of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, which, while being grasped by the hand of the smiling Hara, caused her son Bāhuleya— confused by the suspicion that he was a Gajāsya (elephant-faced child) nestled in his lap— to snatch away their garments.
What person indeed has not been deluded by scribes who act according to their own whims, with their irregular markings and the curved lines resembling the tresses of a deceptive woman?
During the diversions of the wrestlers, as well as at other festivals and the like,
during the activities of the inner apartments, and while devoted to the worship of the gods;
The moon has the deer placed upon its mark and bears the sign of a deer;
the lion is the lord of beasts who has ruthlessly scattered the herds of deer.
When the mango tree has sprouted, put forth new leaves, formed buds, and blossomed,
so too has Madana sprouted, put forth new leaves, formed buds, and blossomed.
Having placed his head upon the lap of Akṣa, the lord of the monkey host and slayer of Rāvaṇa, and having sportively laid the remainder of his body upon the skin of the golden deer,

he now sits with his ear lent to your younger brother’s words, watching with the corner of his eye the sharp arrow— capable of destroying the race of demons— that has been prepared with care by Lakṣmaṇa.

With eyes devoid of blinking even from afar, a fish gazes intently at a lotus that has grown large within its embrace; a lotus whose every limb is cradled by its childhood state, whose petals are fully opened and turned upward by the intense pressure of the Goddess’s embrace, and which is being incessantly drunk in by bees that have reached their goal and remain motionless.
By placing a zero among the digits, there is an increase by tenfold;
therefore, one should specifically understand that the movement of digits is from right to left.
Ghee, honey, and the fat of the *kiṭika* and *kuṅga* deer, mixed with water decocted from *aṅkolla*,
should be sprinkled upon the trees.
Human flesh that has been boiled in *aṅkola* decoction, steamed, and mixed with goat’s milk and oil-cake should be placed at the root of a mango tree.
A lotus root bulb, treated with *aṅkolla* oil and kept in cow dung,
bears flowers when placed in a jar filled with sleet-water and mud.
A seed that has been infused with *aṅkolla* oil and the fat of a pig or a porpoise sprouts immediately when planted in the ground and sprinkled with water from a hailstone.
Fish-poison is destroyed by fumigation with *aṅkola* leaves or by means of barley meal mixed with hair and smeared with pungent oil.
A fine powder of the marrow of *aṅkolla* seeds is prescribed;
having properly prepared that powder, one should saturate it with sesame oil.
The limbs have wasted away, the head is grey and bald, and the mouth is toothless; though he holds a trembling staff adorned in his hand, even then he does not abandon the morsel of hope.
Her limbs are drenched with sandalwood paste and clinging to lotus stalks; this fever, like a curse, is repeatedly skilled at parching her and shaking her friends.
Her breaths, which once gleamed with the luster of closed pearl necklaces, now rend her fine Chinese silks; that fever of hers has arisen, its great onset marked by the intense pain of burning.
Limbs pale as sandalwood, tender as new shoots and reddened by betel; eyes with collyrium washed away, yet clouded by the spray from water-jets;
hair fragrant with inner flowers and still damp; and a garment so clear and thin—these bestow their loveliness upon beautiful women at the arrival of the afternoon in summer.
If one clearly mounts the right limb and descends with the left, it should be known as causing loss; however, by the reverse, it bestows gain.
On whichever limb a mark resembling a *damana* leaf is perceived,
one should know that it is the *damana-vajra*, sharp-edged and of great virtue.
That which is recognized as a limb (*aṅga*), endowed with many knots,
difficult to obtain and of great value, is called the *granthivajraka*.
"It is a worldly saying that a collection of ornaments adorns the body;
yet these limbs have produced an indescribable beauty for those very ornaments."

May that archer grant us security—he by whom his own body was made into a chariot, his pair of eyes into the wheels, his own garment into the essential equipment for the work of a chariot, and his breaths into horses; he who made his own prowess into a bow, his ornament into a bowstring, and his left side into an arrow.
Is this courtyard not the dwelling place of the lion who sports in the blood of rows of rutting elephants;
would a great elephant abandon the sallakī tree with its shimmering, youthful sprouts of play?
For the steadfast man who has made his vow, the courtyard is the altar, the earth is the sacrificial pit, the ocean is a mere stream, the netherworld is dry land, and Mount Sumeru is an anthill.
One who is free from defects of the limbs, has practiced the four paths,
and knows the *kulaka* and other instruments, is considered a skilled musician (*vādaka*) who brings delight.
When one's own virtues are concealed, as are the limbs of women, then they become objects of longing; for such qualities are indeed extremely rare.
With women between each woman and Mādhava between each Mādhava—
in this manner arranged in a circle, the son of Devakī stood in the center and played the flute.
Then, the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) as taught by Śiva should be performed by the teacher for the disciple who desires spiritual success; it destroys sin and dispels obstacles.
A son is born from the major and minor limbs and is also born from the heart;
therefore, he is dearer to a mother than any other kinsman, because of his inherent dearness.
Then, through the division of major and minor limbs, the physical mass is produced;
it is covered by skin, and the seven constituent elements (dhātus) arise in proper succession.
In the past, I was delighted when women pressed limb against limb and flesh against flesh; that was merely the manifestation of delusion.
No other woman could bring pleasure to my limbs, which are tormented by love, even with the touch of her hand;
they do not respond to the rays of the sun, just as a night-lily does not bloom at the beams of the moon.

Endowed with the [proper] limbs, having mastered the weapons, and performing the ritual procedures correctly, one who discerns the accomplished (*siddha*), the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*), and so forth, is not afflicted by the weapons of enemies.
In the same way, through contact with the limbs, the soul partakes of the material qualities;
though it is overwhelmed by egoism, that imperishable one remains distinct even from them.

O illustrious Nijām, at the sound of your great war-drums, the Aṅgas have their limbs broken as they reach new dwellings; the Kaliṅgas and Tailaṅgas set their minds on bathing in the celestial Gaṅgā; the Vaṅgas have their bodies shattered; the Lāṭas have perspiring foreheads; and the Colas become restless with heavy breathing as they flee on foot.
When her silk garment was pulled from her body, she hurriedly concealed her breasts with both arms; when the cloth at her hips was drawn away, she pressed her two thighs together below.
While my eyes were fixed upon the base of her navel, she—her limbs bowed with shame—struck the lamp with the blue lotus from her ear, its flame flickering in the wind of her breath.
The pulling of her limbs causes pain at the marks of his nails upon her jar-like breasts; her yawning causes distress as her lip is bitten by his teeth.
As she departs, the region of her hips suffers from the rows of his nail-marks; thus, the violence of her nocturnal union reaches its peak of intensity at dawn.
When the enemy has reached limb by limb, what can the retinue do?
When the moon is swallowed by Rāhu, what can the stars do?
Without knowing the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, how can there be a determination of their functional capacity?
Behold: by a mere *ṭiṭṭibha* bird, the ocean was thrown into agitation.
When the lord of her life asked, "O charming one, whence comes this extreme thinness of your limbs? Why this trembling? And why is your face so pale on the cheeks?
the slender girl replied, "All of this is due to my nature," and turning away with a sigh, she released a flood of tears that spread across the space between her eyelashes.
"Why do you pointlessly weary your limbs, which are as delicate as *śirīṣa* flowers?
Here is your servant who shall provide for you whatever flowers you desire."

Limb dusted grey with sandalwood powder, the sprout-like lower lip beautiful with the tint of betel, eyes with clear collyrium, and a very thin garment—this is the full array of ornaments for beloved women. All else is superfluous.
O golden-limbed one, if you were to purchase the lives of men by giving them your limbs, that would be fitting; but it is not right to contract even a corner of your lotus-eyes.
Those men whose limbs, mental acuity, physical strength, and teeth gradually decay,
yet whose sense faculties remain entirely intact, should be known as long-lived.

Kāma caused the limbs of the young women to possess the languid grace of sleepiness, their speech to be somewhat indolent with intoxication, and their glances to be slanted by the knitting of their brows.

"May the fire of separation from my beloved consume my limbs; may he who dwells in my heart protect them. With this hope, the moon-faced woman drenches the region of her heart with hot streams of tears like rainwater.
The limbs of the charmingly languid women have become slack and helpless; their breasts tremble with the agitation of sighs as they sleep with effort, and their brows are drooping.

Moreover, when the curiosity for swinging has ceased, Love has taken up residence upon the faces of these fair-browed women, where the tresses of their hair are disheveled and moistened by drops of perspiration.

May Mañjuśrī be remembered—he who possesses the splendor of a cluster of blue lotuses joined together and strung upon the shimmering thread of his crest-mark, garlanded by swarms of bees falling toward him at the rays of light overflowing with the fragrance of his limbs; he who is jagged with the garlands of light-rays shooting upward from the tips of his toenails, as if worshipped by showers of flower-clusters released by the gods.

If Mars is in the east at the time of departure, there is gain; if the Moon or Saturn is there, there is the acquisition of wealth from the south. If Mercury or Jupiter are there, there is success in western undertakings; and if the Sun or Venus are there, there is the acquisition of wealth from the north.
If a dog is seen urinating upon charcoal, a trident, a stone, straw, hair, a spread-out mat of grass,
a hide, or a corpse, it portends the ruin of one's undertakings and misfortunes such as poverty and death.
A woman is like glowing coals, and a man is like a jar of clarified butter;
those who are attached to her are melted away, while those who remain steadfast stand firm in their station.
A woman is like glowing coals, and a man is like a jar of clarified butter;
O Brahmin, one should never stand near her.
In the interiors of pleasure-houses glowing with embers, upon couches covered with layers of cotton down,
and against the warm, rounded breasts of beloved women, the frosty pride of winter was laid to rest.
In this summer, the earth seems studded with embers, the sky is made terrifying by the rays of the sun, and the wind scatters fierce fires of chaff on all sides;
even the waters of the rivers scorch the very nails, and the quarters of the horizon seem to blaze, so that the entire world exists as if ignited by a fresh fire.
If powdered charcoal of the *śāka* tree is administered with ghee for three days, diarrhea is destroyed; furthermore, by abstaining from water for those three days, it is cured.
The row of bees clinging to her limbs takes on the luster of lotus stalks; the pearl of her nose-ornament plunges into the path of sapphires due to the breath of her sighs.
Even this sandalwood paste applied to her breasts momentarily assumes the nature of a lamp-flame, while the water from a shower vanishes upon the palm of her hand like water fallen on heated iron.
Whether you accept [this] or disregard it, we shall conquer the worlds by the mere words, "We are your servants.
For is it not indeed easy, O Mother of the Universe, to cause the crowns of the servants of the wielder of the fierce rod to bow down, by this much alone?

May that eastern radiance—the fame born from the burning away of the masses of the best of Asuras who were like a torrent of intoxicated darkness—always, always shatter my misfortune; she whose beauty all the hosts of mountains accept as being made of heated gold, and who puts far away the vast pride of the golden mountain (Meru) which has been turned into a mere city.
O Lord, as you soar gracefully upward, this jeweled Mālyavat mountain, embracing your nectar-like radiance within its shadow,
will display a beauty more exquisitely charming than even that of the moon— beauty produced by you, the primordial deity, who creates the lunar orb from your own mind.
Just as a virtuous man who has accepted endurance, is disciplined, and is intent on his final goal triumphs,
so does Śrī Rāma, the best of kings, triumph.
Why do you wish to protect those virtues in vain, even while enduring this injury that has been accepted?
Because of their stainless nature, these very virtues will reveal themselves to you quite clearly.
His scholarship is occupied with the futility of finger-snap counting and various disputes;
his lips are restless with muttering prayers, yet he pretends to be absorbed in meditation among the crowds in the city streets.
Deceiving his beloveds by evading their threatening gestures with sprout-like fingertips, their glances curved with the knitting of brows, and their repeated binding with girdles, he departed.
On the fingers of the fawn-eyed maiden,
the row of rings shines like a series of fine targets pierced by the arrows of the five-arrowed god of love.
As if grasping the mass of darkness with its rays like a cluster of hair with fingers,
the moon seems to kiss the face of the night, whose lotus-eyes are closed in buds.
In the fifth month, the fingers [are formed]; in the sixth month, the eyes and the abdomen;
in the seventh month, movement; and in the eighth month, the eyes.
Your fingers were the young shoots, the luster of your nails the flowers;
your arms were the creepers—you, the beauty of spring, have come before our very eyes.

O angry one, why do you weep in silence, repeatedly wiping away your tears with the tip of your fingernail? You will weep much more loudly when, having reached the height of pride through the words of a slanderer's advice, your beloved becomes weary of conciliation and adopts an attitude of indifference toward you.
O traveler, this clever woman at the water-station is not only skilled at pouring out water through a spout by pressing down with the tip of her finger to make the stream very thin;
but you too, O wayfarer, with eyes fixed upward and motionless, know how to drink the water by slowly parting your lips with a hand whose fingers are spread apart.
That which is recited with the fingertips, that which is recited while skipping over the *meru* bead,
and that which is recited with a distracted mind— these three kinds of recitation shall be fruitless.

"Who strikes the door with his finger, O crooked one? Is Mādhava not Spring? Is the Discus-bearer not a potter? Is the Lord of Serpents not a double-tongued snake? I am not the crusher of terrible serpents; am I not the Lord of Birds? Am I not Hari? Am I not the Lord of Monkeys?"—may that Discus-handed One, who was thus conquered by the retorts of the cowherd girls, protect you!
Holding the letter *Gā* at the nose with the thumb and forefinger, one should bend it while reciting this mantra; thus, cattle, horses, and other animals will become submissive.
Has the moon, defeated by her face and cleansed of its stain, fallen at her feet under the guise of the nails of her big toes?
When the tip of the index finger is well-positioned at the base of the thumb nail,
that should be known as the *matsarī* [mudrā], used for piercing the target in archery.

O friend, the cowherd milks the cow with his toes bent in the sequence of the big toes, his lower half of the foot resting upon the ground; repeatedly striking the gnats with both elbows, he makes the sound of the stream falling into the mouth of the jar—held fast by the mechanism of his two lowered knees—delightful to the ear.
When the tip of the index finger is placed upon the tip of the thumb,
it should be known as the Kākatuṇḍī mudrā, employed for subtle objects of focus.
On the big toe, the instep, the knee, the hip, the navel, the chest, the breast, the armpit, the throat, the cheek, the lip, the eye, the forehead, and the head—

according to the division of the white and non-white [sides]— one should observe the positions of the God of Love (Anaṅga) on the limbs of the deer-eyed women as he moves upward and downward through both fortnights, starting from the left foot.
Having obtained a ruby the size of a thumb's belly, which is easy to carry and of supreme value, what purpose does a connoisseur not achieve with it?
Is some limb of hers being sought to conquer the trembling leaf?
For if it were not distinct from other leaves, how could her trembling arise from fear?
The body without a limb, the face without eyes, the kingdom without justice, food without salt,
and indeed life devoid of dharma— none of these shine, just as the night does not gleam without the moon.
The fire of love’s fever resides in her limbs; the gesture of meditation is in her eyes; her life-breath is in her throat; her cheek rests long upon her sprout-like hand;
the lute is on her shoulder; sandalwood paste is on the region of her breasts; and silence is in her speech—thus everything remains in its place, yet her heart is nowhere except with you.
With limb against limb— the slender by the slender, the intensely heated by the heated, the tearful by the tearful, the longing by the longing,
and the one breathing hot sighs by the one sighing even more heavily— he, his path blocked by hostile fate, enters into you through his thoughts, though he remains far away.
What talk can there be of meeting limb-to-limb through the arrogance of the trunk and so forth? If even the scent of the lordly scent-elephant is sufficient, what other elephants are there?
We therefore revere that mark of Hari’s which must be conquered; for even hearing the report, "The Śarabha born from her womb is itself victorious," he was not marked [by fear].
Squareness of the limbs, even feet, and hands in the *latākara* position—
this is said to be the general characteristic at the commencement of all dances.
O you who are foremost among the limbs [of the body], dwelling in the midst of the twice-born, and ever intent on the aiming of arrows—
O connoisseur of the essence of rasa, abandon praise of men like Karṇa, for it is devoid of the flavor of steadfast love.
She repeatedly adorns her limbs with ornaments; she suspects even a passing leaf to be you; she prepares her bed and meditates for a long time.
Though thus occupied with hundreds of playful fancies regarding her attire, her preparations for the couch, and her mental projections, this fair-limbed woman will not pass the night without you.
With her exceedingly delicate limbs, she strikes down the splendor of flowers;
meanwhile, the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) shatters my life-breaths with his volleys of arrows.
The true meaning is indicated by the limbs through their internalized expressions; the placement of the feet follows the tempo (*laya*), and there is absorption in the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*).
The soft gesture (*abhinaya*) originates from the branches [of the body], and in the following of its variations, one emotion displaces another from its object; that alone is the bond of passion.
May the staff-like leg of Hari, raised upward during the subduing of Bali,
be for your joy— the stalk of the lotus that serves as the seat of Brahmā.
Having left behind her flower-bed, soft and fragrant along with its sprouts, she desired the earth with its fresh shoots;
and finding great restlessness there, she wished to come to your lap, which is so pleasant and cool to her.

The gaze of the deer-eyed woman was steady, innocent, and upturned; her glorious chest was not heaving; her gait was unbroken yet full of subtle intent; and her eyebrows moved without a fixed aim, revealing an inner longing directed toward something unknown.
The Lord Bādarāyaṇa is Brahmā, who does not have four faces; he is Hari, who does not have two arms; and he is Śambhu, who does not have an eye in his forehead.

The eye, though motionless, seems as if it were moving; the chest, though natural, seems as if it were heaving; even that body, though not itself such, now appears as if it were otherwise—thus the fair-browed one triumphs.
To whom does immovable prosperity belong, and who has the lord of the earth as a friend?
To whom is the body stable, and who has a beautiful woman under his control?
To whom indeed is wealth stable? To whom in this world is a king truly a friend?
To whom is a courtesan most submissive? And to whom here does even the body remain constant?
Inconceivable is this deception by fate, that the lotus-eyed woman,
having herself taken the hand of her aged husband and placed it upon her pair of breasts, sleeps while sighing.
Just as inconceivable sufferings come upon embodied beings, so too do pleasures; I believe that in this matter, destiny prevails.

What is there that a being dwelling in existence does not obtain—this inconceivable, most unbearable threefold suffering accumulated through sin, residing within the four states of rebirth? Even while taking up and casting off this body, which is a mine of misery in this world, he nevertheless does not extend his powerful renunciation toward evil.
Inconceivable are the paths of those who possess great majesty; for the radiance that issued from the eye of the Enemy of Andhaka left the God of Love as nothing more than a mere tale.
But the light that was born again from the eye of the Sage Atri—alas! by that very light, these three worlds were spread forth as consisting entirely of the God of Love.

Since the state of being established in the Supreme Self occurs without delay, a wise person should therefore exert effort; fie upon the subduing of desire that only occasionally pleases the self with hardship!
One should, without delay, perform a service for one who has helped oneself, whether that service be great or small;
for the wise, there is no attachment here to such distinctions.
An enemy who has recently ascended the throne is easy to uproot, because his roots have not yet taken hold among the subjects; he is like a tree that is loose because it was newly planted.
Having soon reflected upon the great loss of others and his own contrary situation,
the wise man disregards the prospect of his own decline and acts otherwise to counteract it.
O friend, it seems to me that the days pass away in vain; for one who has taken refuge in the dark fortnight, separation from the breasts of a beloved woman is truly desirable.
That circle of sandalwood paste, which had been kissed by the lotus-like face of Nala,
has become a certain splendor resting upon the moon, acting as a companion to its stars and taking its place within the lunar orb.
Even insentient things generally adhere to friendship;
milk diminishes from its own increase, and even more so when water is added to it.
Prosperity attends someone who remains inactive and sits still;
yet another, though performing actions, does not attain what is to be gained.
Just as flowers and fruits,
though not urged on, do not bypass their own proper time, so too does karma performed in the past.
Upon this beloved full-orbed moon, which possesses clear radiance, brings delight, and is filled with nectar—
did the Creator, after reflecting in his mind, apply a drop of collyrium in order to remove the sight of all people?
Beholding the wives of the virtuous with a friendly disposition is free from deceit.

In the summer, deer-eyed women whose hands are moist with the sap of pure sandalwood, shower-houses, flowers, and moonlight; gentle breezes, fragrant blossoms, and the clean rooftops of mansions increase both intoxication and passion.

Who else besides the Lord of Avanti is so devoted to the eloquent utterances of great poets— utterances as full of aesthetic flavor as young lotus stalks to a swan, or as fresh honey-tree blossoms to a bee?

O dear Muralī, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, may my heart be free from flaw, may my eloquence be complete, and may my pride be extinguished; O friend, I grant you this constant blessing, that during the day you show compassion toward me.
She has shed unrestrained tears for her kinsmen, entrusted her anxieties to her elders, bestowed all her wretchedness upon her attendants, and placed her fevered distress upon her friends.
Today or tomorrow she will attain ultimate peace; now she suffers only from her sighs. Be confident: she has shared the sorrow born of separation with you.

May the body of the Enemy of Smara protect you—his form intermingled with that of his beloved, whose girdle was not loosened, who did not receive a firm embrace, who had no kiss, and who did not behold the beauty of his face; a body that seemed to have established a friendship between the states of separation and union.

It is truly a marvel that these lotuses do not suddenly close their buds upon reaching the touch of her hands— hands which grant a certain indescribable beauty to the eyes as they descend from the weight of her flowing breasts, bestowing a joy like a continuous rain of undiminished nectar-drops, and which belong to a body as radiant as the moon.
This is indivisible, this is unburnable, this is indeed unmoistenable and un-dryable;
it is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
O River of the feet of Acyuta, O Garland of Mālatī flowers upon the crest of the moon-crested Lord!
At the time of surrendering my body to you, let not my greenness (or my virtue) be taken away by the one who takes it.
Due to the power of devotion to Acyuta, equanimity arises here through association with Him;
that delight increases from such pleasure—this is not at all surprising.
Through the medicine of uttering the names Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda, all diseases perish; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
By contact with my body, this Pampā lake became nothing but mud every day;
yet every night it was filled again by waters flowing from the south.
From this [lotus] was born the Blessed One, the Creator, who has established his station upon the heads of the nectar-drinkers; and this lotus is the abode of steadfastness for the goddess Śrī.
Therefore, O Moon, that you harbor a persistent enmity toward this lotus—which is worthy of praise throughout the expanse of the world—is nothing but a delusion of dull-wittedness.
O Moon, this night has become something else entirely—a forest of lunar splendor filled with vast and restless waves;
for this orb of the earth, together with its mountains, rivers, and directions, has been submerged in whiteness.

O slender one, why did Kāma not make the cool-natured moss in the ocean into your hair? For what reason does he carry it so curved upon his head, if this moon, the face of yours, were not its sibling?
A man is as good as unborn, dead, or even a blade of grass,
so long as he does not recover with his arrows the fame that has been snatched away by his enemies.
Those heroes who are unshakable by the masses and never turn their backs in battle display their wondrous forms to others through their lack of passion.
A wise person should contemplate knowledge and wealth as if they were free from old age and death;
one should practice the Dharma as if seized by the hair by Death itself.
One should chew like a goat, bathe like an elephant,
enter a village like a king, and travel like a thief.
Who knows your true nature— you who take birth though unborn, who destroy your enemies though devoid of effort, and who remain awake though appearing to sleep?

The sun releases from the prison of the lotuses the bee who, in constant association with clusters of shimmering lotuses, drinks the nectar to his heart's content; for a compassionate person does not regard faults as a wicked man would.
He was being attended at his feet by the dust raised from the constant trampling of the riverbanks,
as if by the minds of the people who had arrived with the power of *aṇimā* to study the excellence of his speed.

Day by day, this most eminent king, whose splendor was like that of the sun, attained a rising glory as he passed his time, accompanied by a poet and a wise scholar who, through constant practice, shared in his joy with delight.
You constantly ascend that long and distant flight of stairs of her imagination;
yet he, for his part, sheds even more tears because, through meditation upon you, he has attained a state of identity with you.
If a lord of the earth, out of delusion, should slay his subjects as if they were goats, he experiences satisfaction only once; it never occurs a second time.

While creating you— [a body] with a nipple on the neck of a goat, a camel’s tail, hair in the armpits, and a pair of testicles— Brahmā, though foremost among the most eminent, did not become worthy of worship at the beginning of the Sāyaṇa and Māyaṇa lineages.
Although her mass of dust was bestowed by the goat-footed one (Aja), although she was bound with passion by the skull-bearer (Śiva),
and although she has fallen ever lower and lower from there, the Gaṅgā— despite her association with the wicked— purifies the worlds forever.

Rolled in a mire of cumin and dust of black pepper, their contact with my tongue and lips produced by their pungency and heat; their bodies smeared with abundant oil and not yet extinguished [of the fire], these few fried *kavayi* fish were immediately roasted and devoured by me.
Among the unborn, the dead, and the foolish, the first two are better than the last;
for while the first two cause suffering but once, the last causes it at every step.
Between those who are unborn, dead, or foolish, it is better to have children who are dead or unborn;
