for while the former cause only slight suffering, the fool burns [the family] for as long as he lives.

If you have not quickly gone away somewhere after enjoying that princess— who has hairless limbs, exceedingly beautiful body, and who is like a creeper of the erotic sentiment— then there will surely be a downfall of calamity upon you.
Like the dust raised by a goat, like the powder from a broom by people,
or like the shadow cast by a lamp or a bedstead, a person without wealth is abandoned.
If some offense should occur through ignorance, they say that it must certainly be forgiven after having investigated it thoroughly through examination.
A certain city woman, unaware that her breast-cloth was half-blown away by the wind as she longed for a glimpse of him,
presented before the moving traveler the auspicious offering of a water-pot formed by her own bosom.
Not knowing its majesty, the moth falls into the fierce fire; that fish also, out of ignorance, swallows the meat attached to the hook.
Even though we here understand [the danger], alas, we do not abandon these desires, which are entangled in a web of calamities—how profound is the power of delusion!
The urine of a goat, its dung, and likewise the excrement of a pig,
when applied as a paste, destroys the *budbuda* poison arising from *maṇḍalīkṣveḍa*.

From this mountain of your lineage were born Amṛta, Śaśin, Lakṣmī, and others, who were protected by Indra; they have now reached you, O Ocean, the eastern Yamunā of that family. Why then do you now shatter our ears with your thundering roars?
A battle between goats, a śrāddha for a sage, clouds gathering at dawn,
a quarrel between husband and wife, and a minor undertaking amidst many preparations.
The dust from a goat, the dust from a donkey, as well as the dust from a broom,
and the shadow cast by a lamp or a bed— these would take away even the splendor of Śakra.
Sexual intercourse on the new moon or full moon days, eating in a cremation ground or in a monastery,
and gazing at the eyes of a woman in her menses destroy merits performed during the daytime.
One should completely avoid these impurities: the dust from goats, sheep, donkeys, camels, cats, and mice; for they are all sinful.
The mouth of the goat and the horse is pure; cows are pure from their backs;
Brāhmaṇas are pure from their feet; and women are pure in every respect.
By the grace of the lion, the female deer roams the forest without fear;
by approaching Rāma, Vibhīṣaṇa obtained the kingdom in Laṅkā.
For one whose senses are unsubdued, there can be no fruit from mere outward conduct; it serves only to exhaust the body, like the ornaments of an unfortunate man.
Without having conquered the earth including its oceans, without having performed various sacrifices,
and without having bestowed wealth upon those who ask for it, how could I become a king?
Was that lotus-stalk, beautiful with its whorls and auspicious navel, held by his two tender arms?
Or does it lie there, threadless, submerged in the thick mud of his personified infamy?
Anger is the indigestion of austerity; egoism is the indigestion of knowledge;
disparaging others is the indigestion of ritual action; and cholera is the indigestion of food.
Water is medicine when food is undigested; water bestows strength when food is digested.
Water is like nectar during a meal, and it removes poison at the end of a meal.
Through the gift of fearlessness, one becomes invincible, fortunate, gentle, generous, an enjoyer of pleasures, a treasury of fame, long-lived, and free from disease.
A citron tree, through the application of goat, sheep, pig, and *viḍviḍaṅga* dung, as well as fermenting agent (*kiṇva*),
and being repeatedly sprinkled with water turbid with horse urine, constantly bears a great abundance of fruit.
It is better to eat even fruits and vegetables at home with a spirit free from wretchedness, having earned them by one's own effort and without depending on anyone else.
Karmic actions smear the ignorant, but they do not smear the knower;
it is as if only the tongue alone is smeared by the ghee, while the hand remains untouched.
An ignorant person is easily pleased; one who possesses specialized knowledge is more easily pleased still;
but even Brahmā cannot delight a man who is puffed up by a mere fragment of knowledge.
Out of ignorance or out of affection, a king might wear a glass trinket as a crest-jewel upon his head; yet he would not thereby possess a jewel of priceless value.
The ignorant man, the faithless one, and the one whose mind is full of doubt perish;
for the doubting soul, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness.
I am indeed ignorant and dull-witted; I am not capable of composing charming words of flattery by which I might become an object of your compassion.
However, having taken this cry of distress from one who is helpless, pitiable, and suffering into your ears, please quickly place your foot upon my head, for I am unfortunate.
In the three worlds, gods, humans, and nāgas— who, like diseases, are seen day and night engaged in activities whose timing is unknown—
are indeed all impoverished in wisdom.
No one whose family and character are unknown should be granted lodging;
for it was through the fault of a cat that the vulture Jaradgava was killed.
Monkeys show affection even toward one whose family and character are unknown;
they do not weep for their own sake, whereas other people weep for others.
Those who do not know place or time, who have restless mouths, and who are like cripples even when leaping—
such fools, like young birds, are devoured by cunning cats.

Allies who have formed a coalition with the enemy should be divided by those who know the enemy's faults, using double agents who conceal their own defects and who deliver explicit messages from the enemy.
Those of vain intentions even seek the existence of that woman who surrenders her very self for a portion of wealth to men whose names and castes are unknown.

Those who harbor pride in the path of poetry while remaining ignorant of the secret seal of true scholarship are like those who, without having studied the mantras of Garuḍa, attempt to taste the hālāhala poison.
Of what use is the wealth of an astrologer in this world, which is subject to constant destruction by the faults of unknown thieves and the like, and serves only as a cause for ridicule?
Let speech, whose greatness is unknown and which is intoxicated with aesthetic flavor, praise Śiva. Where can a transgression of propriety be found among women due to an excess of passion?
O Moon, you alone are righteous-souled; who else but you still protects today a motherless, fatherless, and friendless infant, having taken him upon your lap?
He who enters another's kingdom without knowing the size of the enemy's supplies, the strength of their water sources, or the state of their crops, does not return again to his own kingdom.

One should avoid from afar those quack physicians who do not know the true nature of the scriptures but are devoted solely to the mere letter of the texts, just as one avoids the snares of Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
The fortress of that lord of the earth into which unknown men enter will undoubtedly be entered swiftly by his enemies.
"Why do you stand there in vain with your eyes closed as if unaware? You are clearly recognized by this simple girl through her limbs that bristle with visible horripilation!
"O fool, let go of her! Do you not see her face drenched in a flowing stream of tears? When her friend spoke thus, the young man released her and impulsively threw his arms around her neck.

Whose heart would not be captivated by the face of that fair-bodied woman—a lotus of wonder for the three worlds, whose moon-like splendor is unknown to defeat; with shimmering, tremulous eyes darkened as if with collyrium, brows like wandering vines, a tilaka-mark of musk, and forehead-leaf of sandalwood; beautiful with lips like the bandhūka flower, it is the nectar of speech that deludes gods and sages.
If separation were not the cause, then ignorance would not be the cause;
as the days pass by, why does sorrow increase rather than depart?
Ignorance is indeed more grievous than anger and all other evils;
for by it the world is shrouded, such that it does not discern what is beneficial or harmful.
Ignorance is its fruit, and unrighteousness (adharma) is proclaimed as its sap;
it grows by the water of mental states, and lack of faith (aśraddhā) is its beloved season.
Salutation to that glorious Guru, who, with the collyrium-stick of knowledge, has opened the eye that was closed by the darkness of ignorance.
This suffering that is experienced arises from ignorance;
ignorance, which arises from greed, increases further as it grows.
In this disease of existence, ignorance is the primary cause; birth itself is the prodromal symptom; wandering in saṃsāra is the ripening of the illness; and ultimate peace is the medicine.
The human donkey is fast asleep within the thicket of the rain of ignorance;
who is capable of awakening him, even with hundreds of drums of wisdom?
Enveloped by ignorance in childhood, deluded by pride in youth, and with limbs failing in old age— when will a person ever attain well-being?
Whether through ignorance or even through knowledge, he by whom a rose-apple tree has been planted is always joined with the dharma of an ascetic, even while dwelling at home.
He who, out of ignorance, performs a śrāddha ceremony devoid of the formal recitation (abhiśravaṇa) becomes a destroyer of the śrāddha; the ancestors depart disappointed.
Whatever has been poorly spoken or uttered by me, whether through ignorance or even knowingly,
that should be forgiven by you both, having made your minds supremely intent on affection for me.
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, having performed a censurable action,
one who seeks liberation from it should not perform it a second time.
O rogue, if this Sītā has been stolen from our sight out of ignorance or through the impetuosity of your power, let her be released now into the hands of the Son of the Wind;
otherwise, surrounded by your sons, you shall go to the city of Death, its quarters covered by canopies of blood spurting from the wounds inflicted by the multitude of arrows discharged by Lakṣmaṇa.
Blinded by ignorance, friendless, and devoured by demons disguised as senses, I have been cast by wicked internal foes into the deep pit of the great darkness of delusion;
O Great Lord, do not abandon me who am crying out, having come for refuge, deprived of fortitude, and the abode of all calamities—console me with your compassionate glance and relieve my terror.
Through ignorance one goes to hell, and likewise through ignorance to an evil rebirth;
through ignorance one incurs affliction, and likewise sinks into calamities.
For ignorant kings, the honor [bestowed] after the festival of his golden consecration was merely the praise of the connoisseur, His Majesty Yuvarangabhūpa;

for the clever youths, it was a pretext for gazing upon the moon-faced woman who knows the essence, rather than the empire of enjoying women who lack the discernment between the essential and the trivial.
For these ignorant men who incessantly indulge in worldly speech, their vow of silence during ritual acts is reduced to nothing more than the mere recitation of mantras.
Alas! For such men here, whose entire time is spent recording the income and expenditure of villages, this Brahminhood has become something entirely different from what it once was through tradition.
O rogue, what was gained by you through this wicked conduct in leading me—who was already distressed, turned away from you out of ignorance, and humiliated—into this state of misfortune?
Behold your chest, reddened by the cosmetic paste rubbed off against the breasts of my beloved, now marked by the impressions of your braid, mottled with the mud of dirt and oil.
When consciousness is obscured by ignorance, what can karma accomplish?
When the eye is impaired by darkness, what can one see even by opening the mouth wide?
The world is shrouded by ignorance and does not shine forth due to stinginess;
through greed one abandons friends, and because of attachment one does not go to heaven.
The world is shrouded by ignorance and brought under the sway of greed;
ruined by many attachments, it does not go to heaven because of that.
Struck solely by ignorance in childhood, intent on the household in youth,
and afflicted by anxiety for his children in old age, he is bound again by his actions.
Afflicted by ignorance in childhood, struck by passion in youth, and distressed by thoughts of a wife in old age— when and what can a person ever do?
The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish.
Neither this world nor the next exists, nor is there happiness, for one whose mind is consumed by doubt.
The ignorant cross to the other shore; the wise, having understood, sink quickly.
Tell me, O Kalāvati, what is this manner of yours, like a river of glances from your eyes?

Those who merely memorize texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely memorize; those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely retain; and those who act with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge.

Among the ignorant he is ignorant; among the virtuous, he is virtuous; among the learned, he is learned; among the wretched, he is wretched; among the happy, he is happy; among those possessed of enjoyments, he has the nature of one who enjoys; he is a knower among the wise;
among young women, he is a youth; among the eloquent, he is a knower of truth. Blessed is that man in this world who, among the ascetics, is an ascetic.
This ignorant and lowly creature,
impelled by the Lord, goes either to heaven or indeed into the pit, according to its own pleasure and pain.
The ignorant man does not give away wealth for fear of becoming poor again;
yet even the wise man gives away wealth for fear of becoming poor again.
Even the ignorant attains knowledge of that [subject] gradually; even a mountain is ground to powder;
even an arrow reaches the great target—behold the manifestation of practice!
The ignorant one is indeed a child; he who imparts the mantra is the father.
For they call the ignorant one a "child," but the one who imparts the mantra, a "father."
Whether one is ignorant, or possesses perverted knowledge, or harbors doubt, if such a person performs an action that contradicts what is seen or unseen, the teacher is his protector.
But when doubt and error have been removed and correct knowledge has arisen, if the king does not punish the man for his contrary conduct, then this ruin of the subjects has arrived.
The night is passing away, this darkness is rising up, and the earth is shimmering with light;
therefore, do not abandon what has been said, but compose a mind that is devoted to the appropriate.

I take refuge in the rising sun, which bears the luster of the breasts of a Gurjara woman— reddened with saffron and veiled by the hem of her garment— and which appears as if colored by the masses of passion in the eyes of a ruddy goose.
A preparation consisting of the powders of *añjana*, *mustā*, and *uśīra*, together with *nāgakośātakī*, *āmalaka*,
and *kataka* fruit, should be placed in the well.
Poison dwells perpetually in the eyes of women under the guise of collyrium;
otherwise, how could young men be struck down even by its slight falling?
Having observed the depletion of collyrium and the accumulation of an anthill,
one should make each day fruitful through acts of giving, study, and virtuous deeds.
One who desires prosperity should speak with joined palms, with oaths, with conciliatory words, and by bowing the head; indeed, the shedding of tears should also be performed.

Joining the palms in reverence, taking an oath, speaking conciliatory words, saluting with the head at the feet, and creating hope— these are the single means that should be employed by one who desires prosperity.
The world offered its salutation with joined palms and was colored by joy without even reaching exhaustion;
O friend, even a very brief dwelling in the twilight is for the sake of happiness alone.
The flowers held in the hollowed palms perfume both hands;
oh, how uniform is the conduct of the *sumanas* (wellspring of joy) in both the left and the right!

In her cupped hands, the woman with tremulous eyes held water that was dappled by the reflection of her own face; though she took it again and again, she was too timid to pour it over her beloved, fearing it might be a shimmering fish.
While wandering through the entire world, I have seen this marvel:
that even Kubera, O delighter of the eyes, avoids contact with the fierce.

With the loud *caṭaccaṭat* sound of the clashing bows of the horses in the moving camps, the shell of the earth clearly bursts asunder; while its own lord, the King, turns away out of a grand display of curiosity, alas, this circle of the world is falling into deep, gaping fissures!
By wandering through the great forest, a well-trodden path is gradually formed;
likewise, knowledge arises from the study of the Vedas, and even the crossing of mountains is accomplished by degrees.
O you who are blind by day, whether you wander about in a terrifying manner with the cries of birds, or shriek harsh words,
or look upon us with cruelty— do not come to that supreme city of ours unless you are self-restrained.
"My dear, what is a forest generally like when it is difficult to traverse?
And what kind of beloved woman extends the festival of amorous pleasure for her lover?"
In the forest, the flowers of the trees; relatives who are far away; and a beloved woman in the form of a painting—these do not endure for long.

At the end of the age, O King, the countryside will have its thorns in the form of lawsuits, crossroads will have their thorns in the form of jackals, and women will have their thorns in the form of hair.
Aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, and likewise garimā;
prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva—these are the eight siddhis.
The subtle pleasure known as *surata* arises for a husband and wife lying on their sides,
when their bodies have become closely pressed together through tight embraces.
Even by entering through a slight vulnerability, a more powerful enemy may utterly submerge the kingdom, just as water sinks a ship.
Not even a tiny bit of wealth should be surrendered by you when I have made it known as the truth:
wealth is the foremost of lives, and the loss of life is the abandonment of wealth.
That which is small at first becomes great later when it is associated with the noble; with the ignoble, it is the opposite. Do as you wish.
From both small and great treatises,
a skillful person should extract the essence from everywhere, just as a bee gathers nectar from flowers.
Just as even a hair’s tip of a thorn causes pain when it enters the body,
so too the mind, when joined with even the slightest [affliction], brings about cyclic existence.

Indeed, not even an atom serves as an ornament for his chest; yet you partake of this very abundance. In this lovely lake, who among the lordly elephants—plunged in exhaustion from incessantly drinking the water—have not sunk down?
Even a minute gem is capable of saving the lives of those who have swallowed poison; even a young lion cub, out of rage, challenges elephants.
Even a tiny fire arising from the trunk of a tree consumes the forest; the innate splendor of those who are great by nature does not depend upon physical stature.
Even a minute association with the wicked destroys widespread virtue;
it undergoes a transformation of its qualities, just as milk does through contact with buttermilk.
Even a minute internal conflict arising from the provocation of subjects destroys a lord;
for fire born from the friction of the tips of tree branches consumes an entire mountain.
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being;
free from desire and with the purity of his elements, he beholds that majesty of the Self.
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest are the waist and the hips of my beloved;
and so too is the sacred thread of my beloved, supremely pure and reddened by cosmetic unguents.
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, present in union and separation during the day of a woman—
having touched this supreme and most sacred sacrificial thread, O friend, I tell you this truth.
O King, may that pleasure which you felt while scratching your scrotum be followed by the suffering of your enemies immediately after their [own] scratching.
Let the egg-born creatures dwell in the lotuses, the Janārdanas in the oceans, and the blue-throated serpents on the mountains; let them not be disturbed by that [act].
A horse born from two hairy testicles is considered not beneficial;
one should avoid one that has a black or blue belly, mouth, and tail.
A purely black horse is censurable, whereas one that is entirely white is honored.
Even a tiny good deed leads to great merit for the great, while even a great one leads to great harm for the wicked;
even a blade of grass serves as milk for cows, yet even milk serves as poison for serpents.
Therefore, a poet should be diligent and possess a resolute intellect until he has mastered the meanings of names;
once the meaning is established otherwise, he should not strive further, considering the labor involved therein.
Henceforth, O subduer of enemies, I shall proclaim the supreme characteristics of the sword, fashioned from the bones of Daityas produced from the primary body.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of arrows:
one should avoid an arrow that is too thick, too thin, over-ripe, grown in poor soil, or one that has a defective knot or is split.
"Beyond this point, this path is inaccessible; let it be rested upon"—as if to say this, her two earrings came to her ears.
Therefore, under an auspicious lunar mansion and on a favorable day, one who is pure should take the medicine according to the prescribed rite, while recollecting the goddess Suprabhā.
The mantra: Oṃ, homage to Suprabhā.
Therefore, the mind should not be placed upon the swing of doubt regarding this work,
*Cīracintāmaṇi*, even in its occasional imperfections.
Therefore, one should act with careful consideration, especially regarding association in private; for in those whose hearts are unknown, friendship thus turns into enmity.
Therefore, with a steady mind, one should set out on an auspicious day,
recollecting the goddess Kṣemaṅkarī and observing favorable omens.
Therefore, I desire to bring Pārvatī for the sake of procreating a son,
just as a sacrificer brings the fire-drill wood for the production of the consumer of the oblation.
For this very reason, the virtuous do not desire association with the good;
for there is no remedy for a mind severed by the sword of separation from them.
Those dull-witted ones who are determined to grasp the sweet fruit without standing on the bank [of the river] become merely vessels for grief, affliction, and disease.
"You do not know reality and you are a fool; you are difficult to satisfy, insatiable, and like a fire.
You do not understand what is easily obtained, nor do you understand what is difficult to obtain."
For those who are skillful can show even what is untrue as true,
just as people skilled in the art of painting depict depressions and elevations on a level surface.
Various phenomena are seen that are unreal yet appear real, and real yet appear unreal;
therefore, it is proper to investigate them.
What anger can there be when that which is not true is spoken as such?
And what anger can there be even when the truth is spoken, since it remains as it is even when not spoken?
"O young girl, you are afflicted by a lingering fever; for your well-being, I consider this fasting to be necessary.
O Lord of Physicians, give me the [alchemical] essence, for I am not capable of the fast prescribed by you."
Beholding that cloudless new cloud raised as a weapon by the slender-limbed one,
she released against him the appropriate weapon of sighs under the guise of long-drawn breaths.
Her voice is a lute without strings; her pair of breasts are water-pots for the neck; her eye is a petal of a blue lotus from the forest; her thigh is a plantain tree without leaves;
her creeper-like arm is without joints; and her face is a moon free from blemish. Thus, her youth constructs a world that is the very opposite of the natural order.
Adorned with the moon, kindling the god of love, and shimmering with stars—
whom does that youthful woman not fill with joy?

Homage to the Blessed One in his haste as he mounts the king of birds, which has not accepted the jeweled sandals offered by the hand extended by the vigilant army commander, while the inner apartments look on in astonishment, and which is devoid of any riding equipment, amidst the trumpeting of the finest elephants.

May the one who wears a forest garland— whose beauty is comparable to the flax flower, who dwells at the foot of a kadamba tree by the Yamunā, and who delights in the dalliances of the young cowherd wives— bestow auspicious blessings.
Those who, upon seeing the sky resembling the flax flower at the onset of the rainy season,
continue to live even in separation, for them no fear exists.
He acquired stable wealth that could not be seized by the hands of thieves, was not subject to the commands of a king, and was not liable to division among heirs.
But for a king who is the opposite of this— lacking self-control—
his fame in the world is diminished like a drop of ghee upon water.
Therefore, a king who knows the treatises on polity, being discerning and capable, is able to conquer even the entire earth through an eightfold intelligence.

The Aśoka tree struck one royal lady with its leafy hand while she gathered flowers; by that very act of striking, the sword-blade in the form of a row of bees was drawn away by the God of Love for the purpose of cutting it down.
How is it that people rejoice by relying upon a firefly of knowledge— which is exceedingly turbid, fleeting, momentarily flashing, and incapable of fulfilling desires?
When an enemy, with a highly agitated mind, acts as the cause for the production of anger and undergoes various forms of transformation—
uttering loud words that are harsh, unpleasant to hear, and so forth— they describe that state of being defiled by such mental agitation as "patience."
Even when highly provoked, virtuous people become gentle through the application of skillful means, but base people do not; there is a method for melting even hard gold, but none for grass.
Among humans who are excessively dark or excessively fair, excessively stout or excessively emaciated,
or excessively tall or excessively short, offspring generally do not exist.
Having moved beyond the outer corner of her eye, as if through the exertion of traveling all the way to the path of her ear, her pupils became tremulously unsteady;
now, at the moment her beloved arrived, a flood of tears of joy fell from Rādhā like a stream of water.
But that man who reflects upon a matter only after it has already passed, that task will not be accomplished for him; indeed, he is ruined by his own reflection.
The time has passed, which was once graced by the fragrance of hundreds of well-performed deeds; the pure dharmas have lost their delicate luster, like the filaments of a fresh lotus.
The essence of the discourse of wise men has mostly withered away, and this world has become joyless, as if its festival has already departed.
The time that was so delightful with the enjoyment of playful women has passed; we are weary from wandering for a very long time here on this path of worldly existence.
Now, upon the bank of the celestial river, we offer our prayers with loud cries of "Śiva, Śiva, Śiva! uttered through deep sighs.
The past has passed away, and the future has not yet arrived;
the delusion regarding present happiness is the same for both the wealthy and the poor.
Wealth acquired through excessive hardship, pleasure gained through excessive greed,
and a livelihood that involves harming others— these are never found among the virtuous.
Do not set your mind upon those goals that are achieved through excessive suffering, by the transgression of dharma, or by bowing down before an enemy.
Steadfastness of mind in the face of extreme suffering and likewise endurance in due order—
these two are known by the wise as the superior causes for the victory and success of armies.
I beheld the great ocean of consciousness belonging to the Great Beings— extremely deep, untroubled, imperturbable, its further shore unseen and impossible to cross, and teeming with dense waves.
In a king who is exceedingly profound like a well, virtuous ministers act as jars to bring about the desired success for people who are sinking in suffering.
An exceedingly unfaithful wife, a neighbor who is an extreme thief, a daughter whose conduct is blind [to virtue], a daughter-in-law who is a child-widow,
and furthermore, a friendship that is excessively deceitful.
Subjugation of all beings, as well as fear of enemies, physical illness, and the eightfold suffering of men.

When will the fragrant spring, possessing the lovely luster of budding flowers and the brilliance of the exceedingly beautiful moon, follow [the summer], acting as the banner for the sport of the flower-arrowed god?
O gold, if after a very long time you wish to abandon these drosses that have clung to you,
you will suffer the feverish pain of being struck by sharp hammers and your weight will vanish.
One should not make [an image] that is excessively worn out, uncooked, or likewise handled by kinsmen; nor one that is burnt or cracked, nor one with hands [protruding] on the outside or the inside.
One lives exceedingly well by means of wealth; one lives happily by means of knowledge;
one lives somewhat by means of a craft; but without work, one does not live at all.

One who is excessively dark, has a goat-like odor, a voice like a crow, and a short beard; who is sinful, timid, and evil-minded—such a person should be known as a Piśāca with the characteristics of a donkey.
Excessive craving should not be indulged in, yet one should not abandon craving altogether;
for one who is overcome by excessive craving, a crest of flame appears upon the head. Even a king of great majesty, if addicted to drink, does not accomplish his goals.
Even the submarine fire, though drinking incessantly, is not able to burn even a blade of grass.
Kumudvatī obtained from the descendant of Kakutstha a son named Atithi,
just as consciousness attains clarity from the final watch of the night.
Indeed, a guest is worthy of honor even if they are an ordinary person, by one who possesses discernment.
If a guest stands at the door and a man receives water for him,
that water is like drinking liquor, and the food is like eating beef.
When a guest departs from a householder having been honored,
the wise declare that there is no higher duty than that.
The wise say that when a guest is honored by one who meditates upon his welfare in their mind, that merit is not equaled even by a hundred sacrifices.
To those of the various social classes, hospitality should be extended according to their capacity and in due order.
A guest must not be turned away even in the evening, at least with kind words, a place on the ground, or water.
A guest, a child, a wife, a mother, and likewise a father—
these five are to be supported by the householder, as well as others according to his own ability.
A guest, a child, a king, and likewise a wife—these do not know whether [something] exists or does not exist; they say again and again, "Give! Give!"
A guest, a child, women, and likewise a king—
these four, and the son-in-law as the fifth, do not know of one's wealth.
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he transfers his own misdeeds to that person and departs taking away their merit.
A guest and a slanderer—these two are my kinsmen. The slanderer shall take away my sin; the guest is the bridge to heaven.
The virtuous praise a householder for providing common food to all guests, servants, and kinsmen alike.
Where there is no hospitality for guests, no association with virtuous people, and no abiding in the praise of one's own self— that is a deception of the householder’s stage of life.
Lanka was destroyed by excessive pride, and the Kauravas by excessive arrogance; Bali was bound because of excessive generosity—everything done to an extreme is utterly censurable.
Prosperity does not come to those who are excessively courteous, who are apprehensive at every step,
and who fear the censure of others.
Karna was destroyed by excessive generosity, Suyodhana by excessive greed, and the Ten-necked one by excessive lust; therefore, one should avoid excess in all things.
Bali was bound because of excessive giving; Suyodhana perished through pride; Rāvaṇa was destroyed by greed. One should avoid all of these to the extreme.
Bali was bound because of excessive giving; Suyodhana because of excessive pride;
and the Ten-necked One (Rāvaṇa) because of excessive lust—for indeed, excess is censured in every case.
Bali was bound because of excessive generosity; the Kauravas [were destroyed] because of excessive pride; Sītā was abducted because of excessive beauty; everything in excess is utterly censurable.
Alas! Due to the fault of his excessively long life, his fame was eclipsed by Vyāsa;
who would not say that he was none other than Guṇāḍhya, having entered another birth?
Those exhausted by a very long journey seek out cool shade, and once cooled, they depart again; what lamentation can there be for this?
I consider strength to be superior to righteousness; from strength, righteousness proceeds.
Righteousness is established upon strength, just as all moving creatures depend upon the earth.
One who speaks excessively low words, who reviles others merely upon seeing them,
and who converses with the base— such a person is indeed wicked and deceitful.
When curdled milk,
free from whey, has been well-matured in a vessel smeared with very ripe kapittha fruit, it becomes like the orb of the moon.
O Wind, you scatter waves of musk fragrance in the city of the vulgar— fragrance followed by thick clouds of smoke, which destroys the fever in the hearts of connoisseurs.
Victorious is this certain creation of the Self-born, possessing an attire of supreme wonder!
What desire could not be fulfilled by her, were it not for the protector who casts glances of hostility?
Excessively embracing silence, having abandoned garlands, ointments, and bathing,
with shame cast far away, she was like a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) who has composed a literary work.
Due to excessive familiarity, contempt generally arises even toward an excellent object;
the people living in Prayāga perform their ablutions in a mere well.
From excessive familiarity comes contempt; from constant visiting comes a lack of respect. In Malaya, the wife of a Bhilla makes the sandalwood tree into fuel.

The statement that "disrespect arises from excessive familiarity" appears to be false; for even in this beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is so thoroughly familiar, no disrespect ever arises.
O King, impatience— like a woman who has missed the proper time for conception, who torments her own body and senses,
and who is like a common woman— is not fit to deprive you of the attainment of the right path.
Unable to endure that excessively yellow streak of darkness,
this lamp seems to slowly vomit it out under the guise of soot.
O fair-limbed one, who would this gaze not enchant— so highly honored, capable of transcending what is heard,
and like the established doctrine of the Jina accompanied by its latent impressions?
The rogue utters words that are exceedingly thin and extremely limited in syllables;
yet in reality, he carries a heart fashioned as if from *kālakūṭa* poison.

One should abandon even a wife who has borne ten sons if she is excessively fierce, cooks many things for others, is quarrelsome, is herself a thief, sows the seeds of abuse, and frequents the houses of others.
One who is exceedingly fierce, a partaker of much suffering, quarrelsome, and one who frequents the houses of others;
one who herself reviles her husband and is a thief—one should abandon such a wife even if she has ten sons.

The night is exceedingly advanced, the lamp with its thick flame burns bright, and my beloved is supremely skilled in the amorous rites begun out of love; yet, O friend, he made love very, very slowly, his body overcome by shame, because this bed was as noisy with its creaking as an enemy.

By means of his son Vāsa, who possessed a defiled disposition, he took the lives of the exceedingly powerful sons of Bali and Karṇa, even though they had come to him in trust and sought refuge with him.
The elephant of youth, intoxicated and the mount of King Madana, has its feet bound by the chains of excessive modesty;
with the trunk of the line of body hair, it drinks the waters from the lake known as the navel-circle, where the jar-like breasts are revealed.
Subjects do not serve a king who is excessively timid, weak-willed, procrastinating, negligent, and overcome by vices and sensual pleasures.
Even that grove, with its mountain of exceedingly fragrant sandalwood,
its trees filled with lovely creepers bearing clusters of blossoms, and its swarms of bees humming sweetly with intoxication, made even the ascetics suffer from the pangs of love.
The intellect of the wicked becomes exceedingly skillful when it must perform an extremely foul deed;
for the vision of owls attains its form only in the darkness.
The sun nourishes its excessive brilliance through its possession of the day;
the moon, too, attains its greatness when embraced by the night.
Excessive pride destroys the prosperity of a man of little intelligence;
a maiden is defiled by pregnancy, and a twice-born man by residing at home.
Even one's own kinsmen will destroy a king who is arrogant, ungraspable, self-conceited,
and prone to anger when he falls into calamity.
Exceedingly soft, more delightful than fresh butter or moonlight, rich in flavor from tasting abundant and playful nectar,
and uniquely worthy of the fortune of every graceful enjoyment— whose cheeks do these sacrificial oblations (*haviṣya*) shine upon in the guise of [puffed] cheeks?
Even when held with excessive effort, a wicked person makes a harsh, grating sound,
just as a half-filled water jar does even when carried upon the head.
In poetry that is exceedingly beautiful, a malicious person seeks out only faults;
for indeed, a swarm of flies hovers only over a wound on a most beautiful body.
Daśagrīva was slain through excessive passion, Suyodhana through excessive greed, and Karṇa through excessive generosity; indeed, excess is censured in every respect.
A certain person of noble birth excels his father by his own conduct:
the jar drinks only a limited amount of water, yet the one born from the jar (Agastya) drank the ocean.
I worship you alone, whose skill is stirred by the exceedingly beautiful elephant-hide,
for when you are well-disposed toward me, even that which is adverse immediately becomes a source of satisfaction.
Sītā was exceedingly beautiful, Rāvaṇa was excessively proud, and Rāma was extremely powerful; yet Laṅkā has come to destruction.
Sītā was carried off because of excessive beauty; Rāvaṇa [fell] through excessive pride;
Bali was bound because of excessive generosity—for indeed, excess is censured in every case.
Sītā was indeed ruined by excessive beauty, Rāvaṇa by excessive pride, and Bali by excessive giving; therefore, one should avoid excess in all things.
Excessive greed should not be practiced; rather, one should act with moderation. Through the fault born of excessive greed, the jackal met his death.
Excessive greed should not be practiced, yet one should not abandon greed entirely;
for one who is overcome by excessive greed, a wheel spins upon the head.
I pay homage to the enemy of Mura, who lies supine, whose hands and feet are exceedingly red, who bears a beautiful tilaka of gorocana, and who forcibly overturned the cart.
For those addicted to excessive greed, calamity is never far off; life perishes through avarice, just as a fish’s life ends at the sight of bait.
One should endure insults and never harbor pride in any way.
When provoked to anger, one should speak kindly; when reviled, one should speak words of goodwill.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, relying upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
O lord of men, excessive speech, excessive pride, likewise lack of generosity, anger, excessive curiosity, and treachery toward friends— these are the six.
These very swords are sharp; they cut short the lives of embodied beings.
It is these that slay men, not Death—may prosperity be yours.
By him who has passed through youth— which is exceedingly deep and difficult to traverse— without censure,
what fruit has not been obtained in this birth, which is a mere storehouse of faults?
Victorious is the Sun, who brings joy through the freedom from fatigue afforded by his journey along the exceedingly vast path of the sky,
and who causes the lotus-pools to bloom with fragrance wafted by the wind.
Victorious is Hara, who, in private, repeatedly stroking with his hands Lakṣmī’s exceedingly full pair of breasts, seems as if searching for his own heart, which had been stolen by them.
One whose vision is directed toward exceedingly clear and infinite objects is not satiated by a sweet glance; one whose desire is intensified is not satiated by the sight of a morning lotus bud.
Excessive rain, drought, locusts, rats, parrots,
disrespect, punishment, foreign armies, and thieves.
The abandonment of the king’s army and favorites, and the affliction of pestilence and disease,
as well as the death of livestock and illness, are said to be the calamities of the kingdom.
Excessive expenditure, lack of foresight, acquisition through unrighteous means, and the embezzlement of funds kept at a distance are said to constitute the calamities of the treasury.
This *kadamba* tree is in full bloom, and the breeze carries the fragrance of clusters of *modaka* flowers;
look, the sky is thick with clouds, yet my beloved has not returned—alas, my misfortune!
Madana, having exhausted all his arrows made of flowers,
clearly made her an even greater target by discharging even his fruits, placing them as a pair of breastplates upon her chest.
Excessive purity or impurity, excessive censure or praise,
and excessive conduct or lack of conduct— these six are the characteristics of a fool.
With breasts that are her very loose supports now drooping, with hair like blooming white kāśa flowers,
and with the flow of the waters of her past beauty having passed away, the rainy season has reached old age under the guise of autumn.
For those excessively greedy for accumulation, wealth becomes the cause of [suffering] for another;
it is gathered with effort by some, yet the honey is drunk by others.
Those who have attained excessive excellence must fear a fall even more;
the very highest peaks of Mount Meru were struck down by Śakra’s thunderbolt.
The ruin of the very virtuous, the exaltation of the ranks of the wicked,
and the loss of the youth’s bosom— is this not the handiwork of Fate?
Even when treated with great honor, the treacherous never abandon their innate nature;
indeed, was not the moon held upon his head by Maheśvara himself while remaining forever crooked?
The giving away of wealth is an act of extreme audacity, exceedingly difficult to perform, and most wonderful;
yet one who gives even his own body does not give so much as a fraction of that wealth.
The ministers recognized him as an extremely reckless hero, the teachers knew him as disciplined, and the women of the inner apartments perceived him as a rogue.
The sun, with its rays possessing dense hues, acts like safflower blossoms upon the single branch of the *spandana* tree, which is adorned with leaves that have been brought down.
That which is recited for the purpose of well-guarding past gains, for the attainment of future gains,
and for liberation from those fallen into calamity— that indeed is the supreme mantra.
When the yogi perceives past and future objects, as well as those that are distant or concealed,
it is then known as *saṃvit*.
Having understood that those entities which have passed, those yet to come, and those existing in the present are all fashioned by time, you ought not to abandon your composure.
The suffering of the cold has passed and the particles of warmth spread slowly; the days expand and even the sun slows its chariot.
Released from the mass of snow, the moon shines intensely; yet the activity of the arrows of the flower-bowed god is not obstructed.
Having bypassed his kinsmen and disregarded his friends, the fault lies with the disciple who approaches the teacher;
for there is no fault whatsoever on the part of the father or the mother who gives their young child to the guru.

If indeed destruction were not immediate, who would not strive for prosperity through evil deeds, when even in this very world there is seen the indication of the ripening of intense misfortune regarding the workings of the next life, which transcend the senses?
Exceedingly harsh and rigid, filled with predatory beasts,
difficult to approach and treacherous, they are like sovereign mountains.
O lord of the earth, this earth is indeed exceedingly dear to you,
since even though she is lifeless, you have abandoned me and are now embracing her with your limbs.
One should certainly not prescribe fasting for those who are extremely weak;
for whatever benefits are said to result from fasting, those same benefits are obtained through a light diet.

A jackal howling in the south during the night bestows extreme happiness and auspiciousness; however, if it howls in the east at the break of day, one should appoint another person as the city magistrate.

I bow to the son of the Wind, whose power and splendor are incomparable, whose body resembles a mountain of gold, who is a fire to the forest of demons, the foremost among the wise, a treasury of all virtues, the sovereign of the monkeys, and the messenger of the noble Lord of the Raghus.
The wives of others lead to ruin that man who is dissatisfied with his own wife, who is fickle, whose senses are restless, and whose intellect is characterized by deceit.
Lack of satisfaction, the destruction of past favors, disrespect, the recounting of misdeeds,
and the forgetting of one's name during the course of conversation— these are the characteristics of a person who has become disaffected.
Not only is this mountain of sunrise illuminated for a moment by the sun, the source of cool light;
rather, all these mountains seem to bear crests fashioned from clusters of blossoming bandhūka flowers by the mass of his fresh rays.
Fire that falls upon a place devoid of grass extinguishes itself;
likewise, one who lacks forbearance brings faults upon others and upon himself as well.
Where the earth is grassy where there should be no grass, and devoid of grass where there is grass, in that place a vein is indicated; or else, one should declare that wealth is there.
What indeed could be more painful than this, even in the hells?
That the lowest man is unable to do what is pleasing for one who is dear to him.
Therefore, a bow that measures its own strength is auspicious;
the bow of the gods is the most excellent, while that which is less than that belongs to humans.
For this reason, the scripture is studied; renown arises among the worlds.
A person possessed of renown is honored in this world and in the next.
Therefore, nothing else in this world is found to be more laughable than when a wicked person himself calls a virtuous person "wicked."

The serpent, afflicted by hunger, desires to eat the mouse of Gaṇapati; the peacock of the enemy of Krauñca [Skanda] desires that serpent; and even the lion of the Mountain’s Daughter [Pārvatī] desires the elephant-faced one.
Since such a gathering of dependents occurs even in the house of Śambhu, how could it not happen for others? Therefore, that is indeed his true nature.

Translucent white silken garments, pure honey, fragrant and clear camphor dust, gazelle-eyed women bearing breasts moistened with sandalwood paste, cooling showers, *pāṭala* trees, and garlands of jasmine— O Creator, this creation of yours would have been in vain had it not been for the summer.
I consider this nature of the mindless one to be most extraordinary:
that even when being assisted, it neither rejoices nor dissolves.
Let one practice the elixir of immortality to the utmost, let one speak pleasant words, let one reach the far shore of the ocean, let one ascend the mountain of the gods;
let one enter the netherworld, let one traverse the quarters, or let one wander through foreign lands—even so, a living being is not spared by Death when it is intent on striking.
A dog that is constantly intent on excessive scratching and always causes discord among men is inauspicious;
however, if a dog lies down with its paws raised, it bestows success in the undertaking of a task for one who knows the proper procedure.
He was utterly black while you are stainless; he was a dwarf while you are lofty in every way.
Since he was Janārdana, you are the one devoted to compassion; O Hero, how can Viṣṇu be a comparison for you?
Excessive anger, harsh speech, poverty, enmity toward one's own kin,
association with the low-born, and service to those of base lineage— these are the marks on the body of those who dwell in hell.
In this world, while a method for binding the exceedingly fickle mercury is well known,
there is no such method whatsoever for the mind of a woman.
When the eyes of a horse are extremely wide open, well-knit, and not turbid— praiseworthy, honey-colored, with dark pupils— [then it is auspicious].
Due to their extreme length and because of their extraordinary smoothness,
the thighs of the fair-browed woman cannot be contained by any comparison whatsoever.

Driven by greed, an ignorant mortal enters a forest that is filled with extremely terrifying wild beasts, difficult to traverse, and inaccessible even to the minds of those who sustain worldly existence; it is infested with thieves, yet such a person never performs a righteous deed.
One who is exceedingly intelligent attains one of these three:
a short life, poverty, or childlessness; of this there is no doubt.
Can even the virtuous endure the torment of excessive churning when they are restrained by moral bounds?
Did not even the ocean, the mine of jewels, after offering Lakṣmī, the nectar-rayed moon, and ambrosia, finally vomit forth poison?
That which is absolutely non-existent for the noble ones is an unexamined activity;
therefore, all their perfections increase constantly.
When fate is utterly adverse and human effort is rendered futile,
for a wise man who has become poor, what happiness is there other than the forest?

Those trees born from seeds separated by an extreme distance, whose growth was delayed even by their species, and who were brought together somewhere by a curious Fate—those trees do not part with their qualities until death; they are harsher even than wood, for they have never been made one with others through a multitude of virtues.

O Sandalwood tree, whose nature is truly auspicious due to your extreme coolness, there is indeed no tree equal to you; yet, because of your association with hideous double-tongued serpents, you are indistinguishable from a poisonous tree even to those seeking shade.
That which is the long-term transformation within the absolutely pure consciousness alone—that would be the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta); one established in that does not grieve again.
The days, with their fortunate suns, are pleasant to the touch at midday, allowing for the movement of extreme ease; yet they are unfortunate in terms of shade and water.
For those whose limbs are utterly motionless, who seek pleasure through physical exertion,
and whose eyes are shrouded by delusive cognition, even a blow feels like pleasure.

Upon the vast pedestal of the exceedingly lofty eastern mountain, the five-arrowed god (Kāma) surely fashioned his own flaming *liṅga* under the guise of the moon; for, out of pride, it scatters sparks in the form of the stars and masses of smoke rising high in rivalry with Hara, so that by its vast splendors he might burn all the eminent sages who are devoted to Śarva.
The sprouts of her feet serve as the prima facie arguments for an unprecedented passion, and her pair of lotuses serves as counter-examples.
Excessive drinking of water, sitting on hard seats, depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), suppression of natural urges,
sleeping during the day, and staying awake at night— by these six, diseases take up residence in men.
Diseases arise from drinking too much water, and likewise, disorders result from drinking too little;
therefore, a person should drink water frequently and in small amounts to increase the digestive fire.
From excessive drinking of water, from irregular eating, from sleeping during the day and staying awake at night,
and from the suppression of urine and feces— through these six modes, diseases arise.
Food is not properly digested from drinking excessive water, yet that same fault arises from not drinking water at all;
therefore, for the sake of increasing the digestive fire, a person should drink water frequently, though not in large quantities.

What is the use of that speech which, though utterly devoid of all other virtues, manifests extreme crookedness and is meaningless— speech defiled by its own unapproachability, like the flick of a dog's tail?
Life is exceedingly short, and sins are utterly sweet to the taste in the moment; therefore, practice that which looks toward the long-enduring world beyond.
The virtuous possessing very meager wealth, a man born into a low family despite being desirable, and prosperity for one of ignoble birth— these are the three blunders of the Creator.
One should not be overly persistent, nor should one speak with obstinacy; for as much as one exerts oneself, so much does the burden become like a heavy woolen blanket.
O Great Lord of the Earth, why is it that you do not recognize this king as a worthy object of your favor—he whose expansion of victory was won with ease?
By his conduct, which is devoted to the subjugation of rival demons, in whom does he not evoke the thought that he is Jīmūtavāhana himself?
Having made the study of the twice-born fruitful through the comprehension of its meaning by means of great reverence,
this well-known authority of yours as a Mīmāṃsaka and others is intended to protect the non-trivial sacrifices.
I do not know at all what that gold of love was which you placed upon me with such great affection;

Excessive devotion is shown toward wives and brothers, yet not toward mother, father, or [other] siblings;
fools are appointed to authority while sons are separated from them—thus do people behold the wonders of the Kali age.
Where there is excessive courtesy devoid of any cause or motive,
one should entertain suspicion, for it will bring unhappiness in the end.

He who, with four arms that were exceedingly long, capable of restraining the arrogant, divine in their splendor, and consisting of unfailing means— arms which were ever the abode of the play of Lakṣmī— sustained this world as Śauri does with his four arms.
One should not, through excessive exertion, cause oneself to rise too high;
for just as a fall leads to suffering, so too an exalted state does not produce happiness.
Prosperity does not approach, out of fear, one who is excessively noble-minded, excessively generous, excessively brave, excessively devoted to vows, or who is conceited in his wisdom.
She does not dwell among those who possess excessive virtues, nor among those who are utterly devoid of virtue;
she does not desire virtues, nor does she take delight in the absence of them.
Like a mad cow that is blind, Fortune (Śrī) settles only here and there.
For who indeed would be able to transgress the splendor of the twice-born, which is a weapon more virulent than a venomous serpent and has conquered the fire of universal destruction?
Land that is too near leads to ruin, while land situated too far away does not yield fruit;
therefore, O best of kings, land should be acquired and granted [to a recipient].
Those who are too close lead to destruction, while those who are far away do not yield fruit;
kings, fire, teachers, and women should be served with moderation.

O King, if you do not become angry when addressed with hyperbole, and if you do not consider it a falsehood, then we shall speak for the sake of proclaiming your wondrous fame: whose tongue does not itch to say that all the oceans have been dried up by the rows of flames from the fire of your youthful majesty, and subsequently refilled by the tears from the eyes of the wives of your enemies?

Her chest is a fortress of exceedingly high mountain-like breasts; her navel is a deep abyss; her body is a formidable forest, dense with the creepers of trembling arms and tangled with the thickets of her rows of body hair.
There, the hunter Pañcaśara (the Five-Arrowed One) hurls his exceedingly sharp shafts of sidelong glances. Tell me, O deer of my mind: where will you now go for refuge?

Desiring the respect of high-minded men, he does not speak in the assembly of kings in a manner that is excessively loud, excessively low, vulgar, improper, or irrelevant.
When both the minister and the king have risen too high, Fortune stands waiting with her feet planted;
yet, being of a feminine nature and unable to bear the weight of these two, she abandons one of them.

With the splendor of their bodies graced by waving yak-tail fans, kings traverse the earth through the power of merit, accompanied by vast multitudes of troops— elephants, horses, infantry, and chariots— that stir up the dust, made variegated by rows of exceedingly high, uplifted, and white banners.
Possessing softness through her exceedingly radiant limbs, bestowing strength, and skilled in the arousal of passion;

fortune— even for great kings— ascends to a state of uncertainty.
When planted among these most exalted assemblies by those who have performed meritorious deeds,
even a mere act of veneration becomes a tree with a hundred branches.

May Lokeśvara protect you—he who, on the glorious Mount Potalaka, resounds with the echoes of deep caverns; who is encircled by the splendor of his own dense mass of light; and who resembles a mass of ice caught within the waves of the Milk Ocean agitated by Mount Mandara as it whirled with extreme speed, firm form, and a thunderous roar.
The earth has been raised up, the host of enemies crushed, and the royal fortune of Bali embraced by this powerful youth;

The chest has exceedingly high breasts, the eyes are very long, the brows are exceedingly curved, and the speech is even more so;

If a cloud, though exceedingly high with its waters, does not satisfy the cātakas,
what will it do later when its entire wealth has been carried away by the wind?
With exceedingly abundant means, as if with four arms,
this king alone embraces sovereign fortune for a very long time and rejoices intensely, like Hari.

O fawn-eyed one, if you are pleased by this arm joined with the most radiant secret [of love], by this face that is a twin to the autumnal moon, and by this speech as lovely as the nourishment of nectar, then from where could there be any summer heat?

The earth is excessively hot, as if afflicted by fever from the rays of the sun, its essence having been drunk up; the trees are like those stricken by consumption, their shade stolen away by the refuge of forest fires.
The mountains, with their caves gaping wide like uplifted mouths, seem to cry out in distress; this world, its heart destroyed by the ripening heat of the sun, has fallen as if into a swoon.
One who desires more than food that is very hot and mixed with ghee, than a garment that is free from holes,
and than the state of not being a servant to others, falls downward.
The night that passes away does not return;
like the full Yamunā flowing into the ocean, the sea of water, it simply goes forth.

Here, in this month of Caitra, the winds from the Malaya mountain— blowing with the grace of serpents, enchanting the minds of lovers, and scattering the fire within the hearts of those who dwell far away— blow without ceasing.

Here, I recognize King Veṅkaṭapati as being exceedingly handsome like the god of love, possessing divine splendor like the enemy of the Dānavas (Viṣṇu), and endowed with steadfastness like the king of mountains (Himavat).

This crow, acting as sandalwood for the rows of flames from the fire of the pain of separation from my lover, has therefore been placed by him in a golden cage because of that very quality.

Here, this attire shines for a long time upon the women of Gauḍa— women whose breasts are adorned with necklaces of fresh sandalwood paste, whose upper arms are clearly revealed by garments kissing their parting lines, and who enjoy the luxuries of life upon grounds as beautiful as stalks of young *dūrvā* grass.
MSS_0724-1 Here, while the noble one was obstructing the world with his effort to sustain the roar of Kharadūṣaṇa and Triśiras, you, startled, momentarily restrained the warrior.

Standing here, having torn off all the flesh of the corpse with his hard nails— his fingers smeared with brain matter from the terrifying, gaping hollows of his naked sinews— that hungry ghost,

Let compassion be the duty of the Lords, while for a servant, such service is his own duty.
Right here in this very lake it was born, and right here it blossomed profusely with lotuses;

Here, O friend, you were somehow painted by her own hand upon this picture-board with lines trembling from her shaking hands, in order to dispel the pain of her longing;
you were gazed upon by her with eyes clouded by tears, hurriedly honored with mango-sprouts, bowed down with her head, and then concealed among her friends under the pretext of love.

In that village—where ominous clouds had gathered, where the minister was absent, and which was pervaded by a sky as empty as the void; where bold actions suited to one's own nature were appropriate—it expanded in such a way that the people could not distinguish between the mud flowing in the streets and the extremely pure, clear waters within themselves, nor even between the currents of the floodwaters.
In this garden, I have seen a creeper with five sprouts;
on every single sprout, there is a copper-colored cluster of blossoms.
Haste in all undertakings is not desirable; haste is the destroyer of tasks.
By a fool acting in haste, a peacock was turned into a crow.
Then the flame arising from the third eye of Kālāgnirudra burns all that, because it is the Nirvāṇa of Brahman.

Now, by what impelled does this man commit sin,
O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force?

know that it is a great devourer, a great sinner, and the enemy here in this world.
Just as fire is covered by smoke and a mirror by dust,
and just as an embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so too is this [Self] covered by that.

Now, cuckoo, maintain silence; even in this season of clouds, the ground is slippery. The *kuṭaja* and *kadamba* trees are in full bloom, and with the frog as the speaker, what opportunity is there for you?
Now, the *dhūka* bird’s cry on the left is auspicious for one setting out on a journey;
on the right it portends death, for its appearance is somewhat inauspicious.

Now, those who know this do not grieve here over what is eternal or what is impermanent;

acts as a messenger for the awakening of the night-lilies, and brings heavy sorrow to the female cakravāka birds.

Moreover, even when other beings are prosperous while one's own power is diminished, one should still feel joy; for loss results from hatred.

immediately thereafter, the *kadamba* trees, his followers, seemed to don armor under the guise of their intoxicated bees.
Then, one should whisper this mantra into the ear and likewise touch the sting twenty-one times for the pacification of the venom of a scorpion.
Then, a certain light, the dust of the army of the God of Love, shone forth before us—
the old age of darkness, the bitter food of the cakora bird, and the flame of the forest fire for the groves where unchaste women sport.

the youths— sluggish with wine and love— reclined upon the beds together with their wives.
Now, a king should not allow himself to be broken even in the face of any calamity;
for if his mind were shattered, he would no longer conduct himself like one who is whole.

one should dry it for five days and then fumigate it with clarified butter mixed with *viḍaṅga*.
By means of Brahmins who know the true principles of the Atharva rites, whose senses are conquered,
and who are experts in the application of mantras and tantras, one may uproot enemies from afar.

incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
He who desires the fruits of his own well-performed deeds does not take anything that is not given; in him dwells the series of auspicious merits like a female swan in a lotus.
Misfortune stays far away from him as night does from the sun, and the divine Fortune of heaven attends him as knowledge does a disciplined student.
Through the fault of taking what is not given one becomes poor; through the fault of poverty one commits evil deeds.
Due to evil deeds one inevitably goes to hell, becoming poor once again and remaining an evildoer yet again.
Having squandered wealth that was long protected by not being enjoyed through theft,
miserly people go to their destruction in their own home, just like mice.
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the rules,
and consorting with another's wife— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action].
Shame arises that she was not given; the mind is distressed that she was given.
Placed between duty and affection, mothers are indeed miserable.
May we, who resort to the porch at the gate of wicked lords out of a longing for food, wear away this body—the means for achieving liberation from rebirth—through old age; Om, salutations to Śiva!

O lady of graceful limbs, those arrows which are cooled by Madana upon the broad slabs of moonstone assume the appearance of sparks from the fire produced when they are struck against the streaks of lightning.
Indeed, Rambhā became devoid of pride, Lakṣmī was embarrassed, and Ghṛtācī had her face covered with her garment out of shame;
oh, even Aparṇā, though of dull complexion, becomes radiant upon hearing even a single portion of her virtues!
O goldsmith, take this [gold] and rub it on a touchstone, or burn it with fire, or break it with iron;
do not compare me, O worker in gold, with *guñjā* seeds!
"Having taken it, why do you bite my lower lip thinking it is a bimba fruit? O fickle one, despair of ripe jambu fruits!
Thus another woman, her lip wounded by the teeth of her lover, spoke loudly to the parrot as she perceived him had reached the doorway.
Having come from the unseen, he has gone again to the unseen; neither he knew you, nor did you know him. Being who you are, for whom do you grieve?
Having emerged from the unseen, they have again gone to the unseen;
they are not yours, nor are you theirs—what cause for lamentation is there in that?

When she is not seen, we long for the mere sight of her; when seen, our sole desire is the taste of an embrace; and once embraced, O long-eyed one, we pray for the non-differentiation of our two bodies.
Due to their lack of courtesy, wicked people are exceedingly fierce like storms;
such rulers strive even to reject their own elders.
"An ungenerous man may be a renouncer, while a generous man is both a giver and a renouncer. Having understood this through one's own intelligence, one should give wealth again and again.
A man who does not give departs leaving his wealth behind;
I consider the giver to be truly wretched, for even in death he does not release his concern for wealth.

I spoke of you—who are no giver yet the best of givers, devoid of conduct yet the discipliner of all, deformed yet rich in beauty, devoid of victory yet victorious over the world, of low birth yet noble—as one under the sway of hope; thus, O speaker of falsehood, the charge of lying rests indeed upon me, the liar.
Failure to give arises from a defect in one's lineage; poverty from a defect in one's karma;
madness from a defect in the mother; and folly from a defect in the father.
The words of a poet never touch the heart of one who is stingy;
they are like the amorous gestures of young women directed toward an elderly man, leading only to his distress.
A slight gift and a small amount of anger may be endured;
however, a complete gift is one's true nature, while its cessation is a cause for enmity.
For one who is undisciplined and untrained, yet falsely conceited as a scholar, virtues do not lead to excellence, just as they do not for an actor who has not conquered his own self.
That five-arrowed god, who was formerly consumed by the eye-dweller of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva),
does not now burn you while residing in your eye, for he has not yet attained the fulfillment of his vow through the purification of their enmity.

An oblation offered when the fire is not aflame is a failed sacrifice; eating without a witness is a failure; a daughter who must be supported by others is a failure; and cooking for one's own sake alone is a failure.
Love, having assailed the young woman for no long time, becomes bold only within her mind; it remains foolishly confined to her body.
She fears the surrender of her body; though she desires that pleasure when depicted in a painting, O beloved, being bewildered by his words and her replies, she does not look him in the face.
Failing to delight her beloved with the juices extracted from the ripe mango fruits she so loves,
this young woman merely causes him torment, like the beauty of the summer heat.
By those who lack foresight, who are cruel and deluded by the arrows of the senses,
actions are performed while laughing, but they are experienced while weeping.

Not procrastinating, mindful, knowing the proper time, and learned in the treatises on ethics; wise, perceiving the long-term consequences—such a minister is well-suited for close attendance upon a king.
To whom is a kingdom without fortresses not a source of humiliation for an enemy? A king without fortresses and without refuge is like a man fallen from his ship.
That fool who abandons his wife when she has been lost or fallen into misfortune will, for seven births, attain womanhood; of this there is no doubt.
He who abandons a wife who is neither unfaithful nor fallen during her youth shall,
at the end of his life, attain womanhood and barrenness.
The sacred ford is not one that requires traveling far; austerity is not the subduing of the body;
bathing is not produced by water; it is the lotus-feet of the Mother.
Before him, rows of wagtails were seen skipping;
sighing, he smiled at the playful movements of his beloved’s eyes.
For actions whose merits and defects are unseen and which remain unperformed,
their desired fruit does not arise without an intermediate action.
This throat of my beloved has never before been seen in the three worlds,
since from it the emergence of the sound of the lute is perceived.
"This which we have never seen before is now being seen by us:
poison has been drunk by the venomous serpents, and the wives of travelers have fainted."
Taking with them things never seen before and unexpected—
both desired and undesired by men— the nights pass away.
Many companions never seen before all become submissive to one who is established in his position;
but for one who is deprived of wealth and fallen from his station, even his own kin become enemies in due time.
It is fitting for a blind man who has never seen the distortion of a face to beg;
alas, what great misery it is that even one with eyes must beg!
When the lord of the day had departed with his functions unseen, when the moon had become nothing but a remnant of its glory, and when the host of planets had lost their luster,
the world became so blind at the onset of the rainy season that these fireflies alone were counted as skillful in the darkness.
When unseen, there is longing to see; when seen, there is fear of separation.
Your face can be obtained neither by not seeing it nor by seeing it.

Having reflected repeatedly with my intellect upon that speech which is ill-timed, inappropriate for the occasion, unbeneficial for the future, unpleasant, and brings about one's own humiliation— I understand that such speech is indeed like the *hālāhala* poison.
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients, and which is offered without respect or with contempt— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
For one who stays in an improper place is slain even by a very minor enemy;
even a tiny crocodile in the water can drag away the lord of the waters.
O twice-born one, they could make a non-deity into a deity, and a deity into a non-deity;
they could even create world-protectors and other worlds.
If you abandon her in the forest, whether out of fault or no fault, who could say of you, O Lord of the Three Worlds, whether it is ill-fortune or good fortune?
My cruel heart remembers this: that for your sake, O ornament of your lineage, she did not even consider her own self in the wilderness.
Clothes are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self of living beings is purified by non-violence; and the intellect is purified by knowledge.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
He whose fathomless ocean of wonderful compassion was increased by Akṣapāda, who is untouched by darkness and is a stainless treasury of arts.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatra from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
their all-pervading heat subsides within their own respective sources.
Regarding the omen for fighting on this very day, one that is contrary to the Yākrika is unfavorable;
however, if the battle is to take place on another day, an omen pertaining to departure is auspicious.
Today Sarasvatī has become a constant stream, ever-supporting and ever-refuge;
all scholars have been adorned now that King Bhoja has gone to the earth.

When the moon-crested Lord said, "From this day forward, O lady of bowed limbs, I am your slave, purchased by your ascetic penances," she immediately cast off the exhaustion born of her observances; for hardship, when met with its fruit, restores one to newness.
O messenger, it is truly true that today is Bhaumavāra (Tuesday), which is inappropriate for you;
nevertheless, you must go, for one who is distressed does not wait for the right time.
O lady with beautiful eyes, today my life has become fruitful through this state of being devoted to love;
since you have come to my abode, welcome to you, O fair-thighed one—please be seated.
Even today, because of the noose of the quality of truthfulness established by you, neither Bali nor Vindhya is able to move; such a noose as that cannot be cast off even by a wise man like yourself.
Today the cold prevails and the wind blows;
the man without a wife suffers from the chill, yet he who has warm breasts dances with joy.
When the sound "He is traveling away today" reached the borders of her ears, O fair-browed one,
a sudden delusion that it was a great serpent arose within the flower-garland she had just woven with her own hands.
O beautiful one, today Mādhava, eager for dalliance in the bower on the bank of the Yamunā,
captivates my heart as he plays his flute again and again.
O virtuous one, today the host of celestial nymphs sings your fame, bright as the moon, with great fervor; meanwhile, the moon will attain a state free from blemish and pride.
Tell me, my lord: once its longing for mouthfuls of grass has been abandoned due to the joy of hearing this song, how many more days will the deer in the moon's lap continue to exist?
O traveler, did you not see him today—the householder who went out from here at dawn to bring back his mother, who had gone far away due to causeless anger—having sneezed at midday?
With his body shattered by lameness and decrepitude, does he not appear almost like a mere skeleton? Stay for a moment and tell me.

Even now, I think of her, fair as a garland of golden campaka flowers, with a face like a full-blown lotus and a slender line of body hair; she who has just risen from sleep, her limbs languid and overwhelmed by passion, like a sacred lore lost through negligence.
