Even now, I remember that beloved, who was the foremost and peerless model among all beautiful women on the face of the earth due to the loveliness of her every limb; she was a vessel for drinking the finest essence of the sentiment of love in dramatic poetry, yet she was tormented by the arrows of the flower-armed god.

Even now, I contemplate her— her gait surpassing that of a royal swan, the luster of her braided hair outshining the rays of a peacock's plumage, her eyes rolling with the intoxication of passion like those of a *cakora* bird, and her throat equal to that of the sweet-voiced cuckoo.

Even now, I think of her— her eyes as tremulous as those of a frightened doe at the mere sound of my words "departure," her speech faltering, her eyes clouded by trickling tears, and her face bowed down by heavy grief.

Even now, I remember her in private— her mass of hair with its tresses loosened, her garland slipped away, her lower lip sweet with the nectar of her smile, and her pearl necklace resting beautifully upon the pair of her full, high breasts as she cast tremulous glances.

Even now, I remember her with great intensity: how she came to that dwelling while I was away, wandering about at night; how she went there and sat down with a certain smile, her eyes flickering, having met with her friend.

Even today, no one in this world is able to describe her, for she has no equal; she is my chosen bride. Indeed, were there a man who had seen the form of two such similar women, he alone—and no other—might be capable of it.

Even now, I remember her as she stood there, though being honored; I, longing to see her hips, pulled at the hem of her garment from one side, while she repeatedly drew it back, her fresh face shrinking with modesty.

Even now, I see her again and again casting her gaze toward me— her neck suddenly bent, her lotus-like hand placed upon the curve of her hip, and the mass of her thick hair shimmering against the side of her garment.

Even now, I think of her in the white chamber, where the darkness has been dispelled by the mass of rays from rows of jewel-lamps; as she makes an effort to meet me in secret, yet her eyes are distressed with shame and fear at the sight of me face to face.

Even now, I remember that mark of a fingernail upon the circle of her breast, which was given by me while I was intoxicated by drinking the honey of her mouth; it remains awake, guards it, and watches over it on all sides with many hairs standing erect in thrill.
Even now, I truly do not know whether she is the consort of the Lord who has fallen by a curse, or the Fortune of Indra, or perhaps the Fortune of Kṛṣṇa;
or was she created right here for the enchantment of the world, or out of a desire to behold that jewel among young women?
Even now, I drink from the face of that moon-faced woman, whose youthful beauty remains fresh and who is weary from the weight of her high,
swelling breasts, pressing her with my two arms as an intoxicated bee drinks at will from a lotus.

Even now, I do not forget her— her waist like a slender sacrificial altar, her pair of jar-like breasts filled with lofty nectar, her limbs adorned with various wonderful ornaments— as she rises from sleep at night or by day.

Even now, I remember her, her limbs unable to endure the exhaustion of love-making, with rows of curls falling upon her pale cheeks; she who bore within her the weight of a secret sin, and whose tender vine-like arms were cast around my neck.

Even now, I remember her—reddened by wine during our lovemaking, possessing a playful smile, slender of frame, with tremulous and long eyes; her body anointed with saffron paste and musk, and her mouth filled with camphor and betel nut.

I remember many times how, even now, she would suddenly pretend to be asleep upon seeing me approaching the door with a quiet face; when I touched her gently, her slender body would bristle with horripilation and the surface of her cheeks would blossom wide.

Even now, I think of that princess, the crest-jewel of kings, whose eyes roll languidly with the intoxication of full youth— like a maiden of the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, gods, Kinnaras, or Nāgas who has fallen from heaven, alas!

Even now, if I might once more behold at the close of day that beloved one with eyes like those of a young fawn, bearing a pair of jar-like breasts filled with nectar, I would renounce the pleasures of heaven, liberation, and the realm of kings.

Even now, O people, I reflect upon that daughter of the king, who was fashioned as the sole vessel for the affection of the most beautiful women; I think, "This fire of separation from her cannot be endured by me."
Even now, I repeatedly recall that fair-toothed woman as she rebuked me with words harsh with anger for my very first lapse in passion,
and as she moved me about with the rhythmic play of her hips during our lovemaking.

Even now I remember her, that young girl bashful from our first encounter, as I sat upon the low stool with passion; she was warding off the flickering lamp—its flame trembling from the hissing sound—with the blue lotus from her ear.
Even now, I see her— her deer-like face drinking from my own, her neck-looped by the vine of her arms as she covers my chest with her breasts, her playful eyes slightly closed.

Even now, I remember her lying upon the pleasure-couch at the end of the night, within the inner chamber, wearing nothing but her victory banner of passion, her limbs— like the spreading arrows of the bodiless god— clinging tightly to my own body.

Even now, for the sake of pacifying the torment of my mind, I remember her— the slender one whose limbs are languid like the pure river of my vision, whose beloved body is inlaid with fragments of sandalwood, and who is a constant treasury of joy for my heart.

Even now, I remember her with my mind—her who, while I was hidden near the door, cast her eyes along my path and placed her hand upon her face; she whose heart was slightly stirred by the soft, low murmurs of my name marked upon the ground.

Even now, I remember that beautiful woman weeping—her speech restrained even as she repeatedly uttered words revealing her inner state toward me, her offender; her throat choked with heavy and conflicting tears, and her lower lip parched by her sighs.

Even now, I remember her intensely— how she would provoke my anger when I approached, how she would walk away, come back, turn around, stand up, sit upon the edge of the couch, or lie down upon the bed.
Even now I remember that smile of hers, which torments me— a glance sweet as nectar, most excellent,
exceedingly powerful, full of sexual passion, yet crooked and well-behaved, and possessing the grace of a tranquil, slow, and perfectly even intoxication.

Even now, I remember her with intense longing— as she, with her beautiful eyes closed upon me, was addressed by her friends saying, "Tell us, who is this?", and as she replied with a smile, "Mother, I do not know," while the planes of her cheeks blossomed with joy.

Even now, I remember her on the couch— her body emitting a pervasive fragrance arising from the scent of musk mixed with smooth sandalwood paste, and her eyes beautiful with pairs of lashes clinging together as they kissed one another’s lips.

Even now, I remember her— her eyes filled with tears, sighing deeply, overwhelmed by anxiety, with her face slightly bowed, not speaking to me even as I bid farewell with my reddened fingertips held near her face.
Even now, I see again that lotus-eyed woman, exhausted by the weight of her full breasts;
pressing her face with my two arms, I drink from it as unrestrainedly as a mad bee drinks from a lotus.
Even now, if I were to see again that lady with eyes as long as her ears, her slender frame fevered by the long separation,
then embracing her firmly with my limbs, I would not open my eyes nor would I let her go.
Even now, seeing her looking into a mirror in private— clearly my very image as I remained hidden behind her—
I behold her trembling, utterly bewildered, overwhelmed with shame, yet filled with joy and having conquered the god of love.

Even now, in private, I remember her with eyes tremulous from applied collyrium, with a mass of hair thick with many flowers, with the luster of teeth like pearls mingled with vermilion, and wearing golden bracelets.

Even now, in private, I remember her— her tremulous eyes smeared with collyrium, her mass of hair thick with many flowers, the luster of her teeth like pearls mingled with vermilion, and her golden bracelets fastened upon her arms.

Even now, with an unwavering mind, I contemplate that young woman who was attentive to me and was the hope of my life;
she whose essence was the burden of fresh youth enjoyed by no other, so that she alone may be my refuge even in another birth.
Even now, I remember her—disregarding my transgression as I fell at her feet, suddenly pulling away from me the hem of her garment, and speaking harshly in anger, "No! No! as she moved away.

Even now, I constantly meditate in my mind upon her of auspicious limbs, who lay well-reclined upon a bed previously rubbed by me without shame for the sake of the festival of love— she whose face was radiant and whose nose was adorned with a blossoming campaka flower, ever humming softly.
Even now, I see her wandering here and there, before me, behind me, within and without, all around—
her face resembling a full-blown golden lotus, with her eyes cast askance.
Even now, I think of her in the grove, attended by her maidservants, having arrived for the festival of love— she who,
out of fear of the people standing nearby, would glance at me with apprehension, turning her eyes away at every moment.

Even now, I constantly remember her, beautiful with necklaces on both sides and wearing a bodice radiant with vāsantī flowers, her lovely face like the orb of the full moon at its most pleasing, and her grace forever surpassing the speed of beauty itself.
Even now, I meditate upon her as she raises her two breasts, her line of body hair marked by three folds at her waist,
her arms swaying as she arches her limbs, feigning to show me the hollow of her navel.
Even now, this upper garment remains before my eyes; she began to pick it up again as it had slipped from the slope of her breasts.
Upon hearing my words, "Your eye, your eye," that long-eyed woman then offered a slight smile.
Even now, the maiden of Praise remains difficult to restrain in her maidenhood;
she does not take pleasure in us, nor do those who are unworthy please her.

Even now my mind runs away; what can I do? Even though I am with my friends in this most lovely bedchamber, let my time pass in the delightful play of embracing my beloved’s limbs, playful laughter, and various dances.
Even now, the splendor of the lion’s mane does not flash, nor does his roar resound within the depths of the caves;
nevertheless, in the forests, intoxicated elephants still behold the path of the lord of beasts with hearts full of fear.
Even now, her face—possessing the radiant beauty of the stainless autumnal moon—would steal away the heart of even a sage, let alone mine.
If I were to obtain that nectar-filled face, drinking from it incessantly while kissing it, my mind would be tormented with longing.
Even now the fire of Hara’s wrath blazes within you like the submarine fire in the ocean;
otherwise, O Manmatha, how could you, who are nothing but ashes for those like me, remain so hot?
Even now, it is said, Hara swallows the Kālakūṭa poison; the Tortoise bears the earth upon his back;
and the ocean carries the unbearable submarine fire; those who have undertaken a task protect it to the end.

Even now, I meditate in my heart upon my mistress, who is as delightful as the god of love; she whose canopy of creeper-arcs is shaken by the breeze, who is the source of delight for my life, who possesses the beauty of the eight-petaled lotus of the five-arrowed god, and who has a beautiful altar-like waist.

Even now, my heart burns day and night because I no longer see before me, at every step, the face of my beloved, which was as beautiful as the full moon, whose loveliness surpassed Rati, and which shattered the pride of Kāma.
Even now, those sweet and meaningful words of hers— which were not meaningless—
uttered by that fair-limbed girl as her eyes were closed in sleep and she was languid with passion, resonate in my heart in some inexplicable way.
Even today, those vast compositions of his, whose splendor shines forth and delight the entire world, have not yet been fully produced;
how then could this famous Gopāladatta, born of a lineage of doubly pure gurus, fail to be a worthy object of comparison?

Even now, as I am being led away from the bedchamber by those resembling the messengers of Yama with their irresistible and terrifying hands—what various things did she not do for my sake? My mind is tormented by the fact that it is impossible to describe them all.
Even now, my mind, wondrously leaving the gods behind, moves away by force; what can I do?
Though I know that at this time of death it is every moment, my intellect remains firm, thinking, "She is lovely," "She is most dear," and "She is mine."
Even now, the moon repeatedly creates his own reflection and enjoys it;
yet he is not able to create a likeness of that beloved with her long eyes by means of her face.
Even though her ears are not adorned with swaying earrings, her arms do not possess jingling bracelets, and her neck is not graced by a captivating necklace or armlets—nevertheless, look!
We perceive that the entire world becomes dear to this lotus-eyed woman through the majesty of her body, which manifests the splendor of ornaments even without them.
Even now, that river of my mind remains ever present, its vast nature shimmering with waves of horripilation;
she who has the luster of the filaments of the *kādambara* flower, that beloved royal swan, tells me of the exhaustion of her limbs as I gaze upon her wounds.

O beautiful one, even now my heart, having kissed the orb of your moon-like face which has captured a pair of lotuses as its prisoners, spreads the bliss born from union with you; yet, devoid of compassion, my discernment still harbors enmity toward it.

"Curse this pride that still desires to dwell in the hearts of women, as treacherous and difficult as mountains of breasts!"—as if red with rage at these words, the moon, stretching out its hands (rays) from afar, instantly draws his sword: the swarm of bees emerging from the buds of the blooming night-lilies.
Even now, they have not been understood in their true nature by Hari, Hara, and the other immortals;
for both courtesans and the illusions of saṃsāra are full of delusion, confusion, and great infatuation.
Even now, O son, the day has passed for your cruel father;
the path is shrouded in darkness. Come, my dear child, let us go to rest.

Even now, I remember my beloved, whose hands are red with fresh *aśoka* shoots, whose nipples are kissed by clusters of pearls, whose pale cheeks are flushed with an inner smile, and who possesses the graceful gait of a pure swan.

Even now, I constantly remember my beloved’s face at the conclusion of our lovemaking— its beautiful eyes half-closed and trembling, radiant with the luster of sighs released at that moment, and bristling with drops of perspiration.
Even now I live only for the enjoyment of sexual union with my excellent bride, and not by any other means for even a single moment.
Therefore, O brothers, I entreat you that death alone may bring peace to my suffering; pray, cut it off quickly!

Even now, I do not forget her face— its teeth like blooming jasmine, its wide eyes cast askance, and its beauty having utterly conquered the moon— just as a grateful man does not forget a good deed done for him by one who has helped him.

Even now, I behold her face— the vessel of blooming lotuses for eyes, possessing a luster equal to the full autumnal moon, with cheeks pale from the slight flush of passion rising at the memory of him, and graced by the sweet, charming humming of bees.
Even now, alas, though this world is filled with hundreds of thousands of beauties, each possessing a preeminent excellence over the others,
it is my thought in my heart that her form cannot be compared even by those others, nor can it be by me.
Even now, on the battlefields, the female *piśācas* dance to the clanging of skull-drums tossed by the flickering hands of intoxicated young *yātudhānas*;
they sing his glories aloud through vast resonances made manifest from the hollows of the frontal globes of elephants agitated by fierce winds.

Now that the spring has ended, the evening breezes, fragrant with fresh jasmine, generally cause a sense of weariness in the deer-eyed women as they recline upon the palace rooftops; these winds quickly dry the sandalwood paste from their breasts, which were once so intensely sensitive to touch.
Today the waters will fall everywhere upon the earth; today the heat of the world shall be quenched; today the people, longing for the harvest, will exert themselves in their fields.
O Cloud, at your rising, the peacocks—sportive in every direction, their crests shaded by the parasols of their flickering tail-feathers—will dance.

From this day forward, with my lotus-like hands placed upon the stalks of my formidable bow, I shall not open my crimson eyes so long as the earth is not made fragrant by the masses of pollen falling from jasmine garlands that slip from the crowns of enemy kings split open by the tips of my arrows.
From this day forward, my dear one, I shall never again become a vessel for pride, which is like poison; I shall not even utter the name of that deceitful-minded man in brief.
Without him, how could the night—whose loud laughter is the clear moonlight—not pass for me? Or how could a single day, clouded by rain, not seem like the rainy season?

Thinking, "Today the meal for my children was prepared with difficulty; how indeed will it be tomorrow?", the wife of a poor man, her cheeks stained by the falling of tears, does not wish for the end of the night.

"Today this task, tomorrow that, and likewise this from the year before last, and that from two years ago"—O friend, where can you find such a moment when your mind constantly thinks thus without distraction?
Is there even a single moment when the forest fire of the creeping vine of your flourishing desires will not burn, and you will remember the Wielder of the Staff?
In the beginning, the lords always bear fruit for the bards and singers like wish-fulfilling trees;
but for the virtuous, they yield something merely through their speech, like camphor offered for a lamp at evening.
In this boundless cycle of existence, some depart at dawn, others during the day’s expansion, and still others later; who indeed remains, for all must surely grieve?
Perform today itself that which is for your welfare; let not this time pass you by.
For death indeed drags one away while one's duties remain unaccomplished.
Do this very day what is for your welfare; being old, what will you do? For when things have turned upside down, even one's own limbs become a burden.

O beloved of the flower-arrowed god, since this wretched body has been reduced by you today to the likeness of the crescent moon that has just risen on the first day of the lunar fortnight, tell me: when the night has passed and morning comes, where will you discharge your volley of arrows?

"Stay right this day, or tomorrow, or the day after, or three or four days hence—at evening, by day, in the morning, in the forenoon, or in the afternoon—even for a moment; you have departed, but come back again!"—in this way, alas, the generous donors in the capital utterly frustrate the crowds of supplicants every single day, who are unaware of the excessive and manifold workings of such deception.
Those embodied beings who this very day laughed, sang, and played—this very day they are no longer seen; behold the workings of Time!
Now, the breeze from the sandalwood mountain pursues the desire to bathe in the snows of the Himālayas, as if distressed by the serpent’s bite while resting upon the lap of the mountain;
moreover, beholding the buds at the tops of the succulent *rasāla* trees, the sweet and exultant cries of the cuckoos—"kuhū, kuhū"—emerge out of joy.
"O friend, today in the courtyard of the garden-house, I raised this foot—red with lac and with its tinkling anklet—in the ritual for the longing of the *aśoka* tree.
Just then, what shall I say? He, skilled in amorous play, emerged from the interior of the bower and, arriving unobserved, suddenly honored me by touching my head with his own."

In various places, the cuckoo recites the *sāmidhenī* verses, as it were, to offer up the lives of travelers into the sacrificial fire of Love; these verses consist of cries that are sweeter than the taste of biting into the tips of mango sprouts shaken by the Malaya breeze at its first awakening.

The lord of the earth beheld that garden, which—with its creepers bent low under the weight of unopened buds and with the sky obscured by the gloom of pollen drifting from them—was the assembly hall of King Spring, the divine God of Love; it was a peerless hall of sacrifice for the bees and a single pavilion for travelers.
Those kings who witnessed the dragging of the locks of hair of Drupada’s daughter, or who permitted it in their minds out of delusion—
of all those, the middle son of Pāṇḍu offers the fuel of their lineage as oblations into the fire of his wrath on the sacrificial ground of battle with two or three *huṃkāra* mantras.

At the base of the quarters, the darkness possesses the luster of a heap of collyrium and is like a mass of clouds; above, it resembles a canopy of sapphire; on the shore of the ocean, it is like a coating of mud; and beneath the shade of the *tamāla* branches, the darkness slowly rises in the evening, conforming to the love of the beloved women going to meet their lovers.
"Does the wind carry away the peak of the mountain?"—thus questioned by the innocent wives of the Siddhas, who looked upward with startled eyes at his soaring prowess;
from this place, rich in succulent *nicula* trees, fly upward toward the north through the sky, avoiding on your path the arrogant thrusts of the massive trunks of the elephants of the quarters.
Among purities, non-malice is the foremost; among specific vows and observances, lack of fickleness;
among unpleasant things, backbiting; and among cruel deeds, the destruction of one's livelihood.
Absence of malice toward all beings in action, thought, and speech,
as well as kindness and generosity, is the eternal dharma of the virtuous.
O King, having made a pact of non-aggression in the presence of the sages, Hari subsequently slew Namuci with the foam of the waters.
Having made a pact of non-aggression, Śakra severed the head of Namuci; for that is considered by him to be the eternal conduct toward an enemy.
That very bull, by whom she was led over mountains, through ancient caves, along narrow riverbanks, and over uneven ground—she whom he, though young and strong, bore as a second burden;
even now, though old and emaciated, he alone is capable of bearing that difficult load, for he cannot be pulled by many other bulls joined together with cart-poles.
This swelling pride of the young woman's face arises from beholding her own peerless beauty in the world, bringing her joy; it is not merely a smile.
My eye shall not look upon anything else; my mind shall not close its eyes to anything else; my hand shall not touch anything else—what will all this do for me today?
One should make the mind tender with flowers, delicate and free from hatred;
for through the fault of hatred, there occurred the destruction of both gods and demons.
That non-duality which is compatible with both pleasure and pain in all conditions, wherein the heart finds its rest, whose essence cannot be taken away by old age,
and which abides in the matured essence of affection when the veil has been removed by time— blessed indeed is that good man who somehow attains even a single instance of it.
O slender one, elevating the singular bliss of non-duality and causing the entire world to be forgotten,
you shine like the discourse on the Vedānta tenets, which proclaims the self-luminous nature inherent in liberation.
We bow even to those young children who are adept at proclaiming non-duality; yet, as for those who speak of duality, we place our left foot upon their heads.
A lion, having placed his own cubs within his heart, strokes them with intense affection and, with great fervor, tears apart the temples of intoxicated elephants—the very seat of agitation.
Fortune never abandons one who is endowed with a mind free from duality, who is heroic, steadfast, and wise,
just as rays never leave the sun.
That the ocean casts down a jewel while it carries a blade of grass upon its crest is the fault of that very sea; for it is a jewel a jewel, and grass grass.
On a certain festival day, a king— whose majesty was intensely manifest and who, in many ways, eclipsed all his subjects— might become overwhelmed by fear of a serpent.
Those who are miserly cast their wealth downward when they desire to go there; but the virtuous, desiring that highest state, bestow it upon teachers, holy places, and the like.
Looking downward with its head turned and tilted to both sides, moving slowly through the sky in a smooth circular path due to the steadiness of its wings, the blue jay—
skilled in seizing prey— suddenly swoops down from above at a swift diagonal angle and pounces with its feet and beak moving rapidly.
"What do you see down there, O girl? What has fallen upon the ground?
"O fool, do you not realize that the pearl of youth has passed away?"
Adhaḥpuṣpī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, lajjālu, girikarṇikā,
nīlinī, sahadevā, and likewise putramārjārikā.
On a day of the Sun, the *jaṭā* of all [plants] beginning with *viṣṇukrāntā* should be gathered;
when bound upon the arm or applied as a paste to the body, it acts as a warder-off of floods of weapons.
Śambhu lies below, having placed your foot upon his heart; the lotus-born Brahmā has taken the position of a gatekeeper at the outer door;
and Indra meets with failure in his own petition—yet even so, there is both shame and fear in my mind that "I might become your servant."
When the woman lies below and the lover lies above,
that well-known sexual union should be known as the one beloved by the simple folk of the villages.
O beautiful one, life itself is indeed wealth; knowledge is half-wealth; grain is great wealth;
but learning, austerity, and fame—these, O fair lady, are supreme wealth.
Even those householders who possess no wealth are truly blessed,
for their homes are masters over the most excellent water, grass, and ground fit for the noble Arhats.
Those without wealth desire wealth; four-footed creatures desire speech;
human beings desire heaven; and the gods desire liberation.
One who desires wealth but lacks wealth cannot acquire it even while seeking it; wealth is bound by means of wealth, just as great elephants are captured by means of elephants.
Even one who is penniless and desirous of giving, when arriving at the house of the wealthy, is thought of as a beggar; alas, what a curse is poverty for embodied beings!
"Having become wealthy, this man, being intoxicated with pride, might not remember me.
Thinking thus, the Compassionate One surely did not bestow abundant wealth upon me.
A violent onset of suffering afflicts the inferior person more intensely than it does the superior;
the sensation of cold quickly reaches the two feet, but not the eyes.
Association with inferior friends and bad companions, the fear of separation from loved ones, poverty,
ill repute, and indeed defeat by the world— such is the fruit of the tree of evil.
The intentions of debtors, those who live off corpses, those who eat at funeral feasts, and wicked kings do not succeed; it is because of this that the world endures.
The base desire strife; the mediocre desire peace;
the superior desire honor, for honor is indeed the wealth of the great.
The base desire wealth; those of middle quality desire both wealth and honor;
the superior desire honor alone, for honor is indeed the wealth of the great.
Prosperity that has fallen into the hands of the base is of no use for anyone’s enjoyment,
like the shadow of a mango tree fallen upon the mud.

One who performs the rite for the mother alone is the lowest; one who performs the rite for the element (dhātu) alone is middling; one who performs the rite for both the element and the mother is proclaimed as the highest.
The inferior [practitioner] should be a knower of the characteristics; the middling should practice according to the characteristics;
the superior is proclaimed as one who is fully endowed with both the characteristics and the object characterized.
Because the fruit called *bimba* is indeed inferior (*adhara*) to this [lip],
the word "lower lip" (*adharabimba*)— which denotes her lip— is thus appropriately derived through its etymological connection.
Her lower lip has the hue of a young sprout, her arms resemble tender branches,
and youth, as alluring as a flower, has blossomed upon her limbs.
"O charming girl, this lower lip of yours is a priceless ruby;
even though it is scarred, for what purpose is this hand of yours placed here so pointlessly?"

The luster of her lower lip, surpassing young shoots; the beauty of her face, eclipsing the splendor of the moon; and the incomparable body of that fair-browed woman—these do not seem to be the work of this Creator.
Placing lip upon lip, throat upon throat, arm upon arm, and heart upon heart, and firmly pressing the waist against the waist— oh,
what a fortunate man is he who, with impetuous force, makes his way through the night of this winter season, leading the thighs and feet of the lotus-eyed woman step by step!

May Kṛṣṇa—whose form is languid with love, who smiles while his body is covered in hidden horripilation—protect you; he who, crying "I am but a child," was quickly placed upon the chest of the cowherd women as they hurriedly pressed their lips to his lips, their necks to his neck, their eyes to his eyes, and their foreheads to his forehead with tender words.
The nectar of her lower lip—of this there is no doubt—is sweeter than honey; the fruit of the grape, with its clear juice, is even more sweet.
Yet let a person who knows other flavors, remaining impartial, say once again if there is anything else here that is as delicious as the lip of a beloved.
Only one who relishes the flavor of experience can discern the sweetness of the lower lip, the firmness of the breasts, the sharpness of the eyes, and the ripeness of poetry.
Let my mouth be guilty for drinking the nectar of her lower lip; but what offense has my head committed that it does not obtain to kiss her feet?
This sound of Hari’s playful flute, preeminent in the sweetness of nectar from the lower lip,
extensively spread great joy in the minds of the deer-eyed women, the fawns, and the sages alike.
By the nectar of her lower lip, bile is destroyed; by the pair of her breasts, wind;
and by incessant sexual union, phlegm—the body of the woman thus pacifies the three humors.
Although the whiteness of the teeth of the long-lashed-eyed woman was concealed by the redness resulting from contact with her lower lip,
it regained its luster once again through her white smile, as if it had grown new wings.
O messenger, by your lower lip— which possesses height, is pressed by a serpent,
and is red as Mount Mandara— my mind has been agitated like the ocean.

The fresh betel-stain upon the lower lip, the brilliant collyrium in the eyes, and the fine silk garment—these are the ornaments of women; any other ornament serves only to mar the beauty of their limbs.
A drop on your lower lip, a string of jewels on your throat, and a hare’s leap upon your pair of breasts—
these, O Ketakī, indicate that your lover is a scholar of the science of the Flower-Armed God (Kāma).
Is this sweet Sarasvatī not indeed the flow of Maṇikarṇikā at her lower lip?
Does a beautiful braid not appear upon her head? How then is she not the Queen of Tīrthas, O fawn-eyed one?
I perpetually bow to the Conqueror of Kaṃsa, who holds a flute placed beneath his chin, who has fashioned a crest-ornament from a campaka flower, and whose left shoulder is slightly bent.
This lower lip of the tremulous-eyed woman steals away the luster of the *bandhujīva* flower;
alas, what wonder is there that it also steals away the luster of the lives of others?
Whirls on the lower lip, the nose, the cheeks, and likewise the chin;
or on the scrotum, the navel, the sacrum, and the belly—these are exceedingly censured.
This lower lip of the deer-eyed woman shines upon the surface of her nose like a ruby fallen from the center of a golden tube.
O Pārtha, that intellect which, enveloped by darkness, perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and regards all things in a perverted manner— that intellect is tāmasī.
If I should embrace this confusion of the worlds by adopting unrighteousness under the guise of righteousness— abandoning what is auspicious and devoid of the prescribed rules of action—
that would be unrighteous for a Kṣatriya, namely, to die of disease at home.
But that death which may occur in battle is his eternal duty.
Unrighteousness is its nectar, which becomes sweet through its intense excesses;
and by whatever fruits it bears, the tree of greed becomes truly fruitful.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys one's reputation and ruins one's fame;
it also prevents one from attaining heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it entirely.
Unjust punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the world;
however, for a king, righteous punishment brings about heaven, fame, and victory.
One should remain indifferent even toward a circle of friends if they are joined with unrighteousness and malice;
however, for a circle of friends who possess self-control, one should sacrifice even one's own life.

The prohibition of unrighteousness, conduct according to the path of justice, and the practice of mutual assistance between those who help and those who are helped— this is the proper conduct of a lord of the earth.
O Lord, having perceived unrighteousness elsewhere upon this earth as a cause of agitation and as something defiled,
your white fame spreads in all directions as if out of anger to expel it.
Fools who delight in unrighteousness and are intent upon the animal realm,
having entered a miserable womb, do not find happiness.
"O wise ones, do not fruitlessly perform rituals that establish unrighteousness; do not commit violence against living beings; through the censure of the Vedas, practice only compassion.
O Lord Buddha, kinsman of pure awakening, having thus enlightened the Creator and established the Vedic injunction [of non-violence], abide within us.
But, my dear, great demerit would accrue to that lord of the earth who takes a sixth part as tax and yet does not protect [his subjects] like his own children.
Wealth acquired through unrighteousness remains for only a short time;
thereafter, it perishes along with its roots, as one must contend with rivals.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two dies or incurs enmity.
One prospers by unrighteous means for a time, and thereafter sees auspicious things;
then one conquers one's rivals, but finally perishes together with one's very roots.
In unrighteous acts, his passion turns sweet through its overflowing;
and by such fruits as these, the tree of greed bears its fruit.
Others of small intelligence seize the wealth accumulated through unrighteousness,
under the pretext of being those with whom one should share meals, just as leeches take away water.

He who performs rites for the sake of the afterlife with wealth acquired through unrighteous means does not enjoy the fruit of that action after death, because of the illicit acquisition of that wealth.
O timid one, for heroes who have never been defeated and who do not retreat in battles,
the endurance of an insult is worse than death.
When the target is well-ascertained on level ground, one should strike with a firm impact by employing an upward posture, even when the aim is at a great distance below.
He does not go to the regions below the earth; he is not attached to all women nor to anything else;
he is not born among the classes of intermediate deities (*vyantara*), nor among the celestial beings of the *bhāvana* or *jyotiṣka* realms, for his inclination is toward the sublime.
This hide, perforated at the bottom and filled with foul odors, is soaked with urine for his sake; O King, do not slay the Brahmins.

"He burned Laṅkā for us; he crossed the ocean of salt water; he brought from the son of Sumitrā that most excellent medicinal herb which removes all pain"—remembering this again and again as Hanumān is inscribed upon the walls of your enemy's city, the enraged host of Rākṣasas bites their teeth.
At that time, his foot was placed upon lotuses; where, then, could there be even a trace of compassion for a mere sprout?
Even the autumnal lord of the full-moon night did not attain the status of being a servant to his face.
One should avoid from afar those who are unrighteous, cruel, and those whose faults have been observed, as well as those who have been expelled and those who have come from abroad.
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood,
and who always delights in violence— this person does not prosper in happiness here.
A son may excel his father in beauty, learning, and prowess;
yet one who remains in the station acquired by his father is likewise called a *subrahmaṇya*.

O fair-limbed one, tell me, whose consecration as the crown prince of the sport of King Smara does this pair of cheeks clearly manifest— cheeks that possess a pallor fading away through the friction of the playful act of sleeping upon the surface of the gaming board?
Chapter 1095-1: Debt, pregnancy, the fourth [state], and mating with a dog;
1095-2: In their arrival there is supreme happiness, but in their departure they are the cause of suffering.
Regarding the empowerments of authority, listen to the words concerning the drum:
"Bound and struck by the staff, you shall become empty just as we are."
How can there be any refutation of one who is endowed with authority?
O King, a favor done for the base is like a mark impressed upon the sands.
Enough with the wicked, who are exceedingly haughty, possessed of extreme cruelty, who repeatedly crush the feet of herds of wandering cattle, and who,
despite the abundance of crops endowed with many qualities established by fate, are harsh by nature and devoid of sweetness.
In this world, the many stars that share in sovereignty over the sky display their lordship like lamps in every house;
and in every direction there are shimmering young fireflies—when the sun has been eclipsed, was it not for these that people looked?
Do not despise the wise who have realized the ultimate truth; Fortune, as light as a blade of grass, cannot obstruct them.
A lotus fiber cannot serve as a barrier for elephants whose temples are dark with fresh streaks of rut.
Alas! One who has attained greatness in the world of men sinks all the more if he is negligent;
a lordly elephant, massive as the peak of a great mountain, sinks deeply because he is heavy, not because he is made of wood.
Having understood her heart to be such,
we perceive the aversion of her breasts— which have cast off softness— as being entirely consistent with their proper nature.
Numerous stars shine forth upon attainment, and lamps find their place of honor in every house;
young fireflies are blooming in every direction—when this sun has risen, what indeed was not seen by the world?
Having swiftly reached its mark, the arrow comes to rest;
yet, due to the steadiness of its pursuit, it cannot be deceived.

Ah! This golden vine upon the threshold, this autumn moon reclining upon a lotus, and this row of pearls upon the beak of a wagtail—by whose noble birth and ascetic merits have these come to fruition?

Worship that Brahman whose long lotus-like eyes were the sole object of Lakṣmaṇa’s gaze, whose beautiful thighs resembled blooming blue lotuses, and who dwelt in a hut within the five-peaked mountain.
Even a cowherd from a small village might become eloquent;
but in an assembly of the best men of the city, whose mouth would utter a single syllable?
O beloved woman with the gait of an elephant, as you approach like a flash of lightning,
I know not how many good deeds must have been performed by that man, who is like a rain-cloud.

Bound by the garland with the words, "O Queen, go to her abode as her most beloved," the youth was unable to move even a single step; for what indeed does not rob those filled with trepidation of their power?
At nightfall, having been somehow forcibly laid down near her beloved by her elders,
the lotus-eyed woman touches him apprehensively, wondering what will happen.
That lamp which at the onset of night bore a deep crimson hue as if intensely blended with the color of thick lac,
now at dawn, its glow extinguished by drinking [the oil], truly possesses a paleness like that of a throbbing lower lip whose redness has been drained away.
Having experienced the state of being without anxiety while dwelling happily in the hunter’s house during the night,
this pair of ruddy geese, free from grief, rejoices at the gift of their lives.
O Noble One, please step upon these sandals adorned with gold with your two feet.
For these two shall provide for the welfare and security of the entire world.
"O bees on the jasmine buds, you have been excessively soiled by the pollen of the cloves!"— thus,
with its blossoms, the kunda creeper suddenly laughed aloud before them, as the bees were startled by the falling petals.
O mango tree, in this glorious garden you are the foremost among the clusters of sprouts; in this world, your branch is the dispeller of fatigue for the auspicious;
your display of blossoms is for the joy [of all], and your fruit is for the satisfaction of living beings. Therefore, O mango, the flock of cuckoos resorts to you by the hundreds.
For when beings are weak, they desire a firm foundation in this saṃsāra, which is as unstable for all living creatures as a drop of water on a blade of grass.

O you who have mastered the art of evading the arrows of the five-arrowed god, if you now enter my heart from without, let it not fear the shafts of Smara once it has entered the true casket of my very self.

Once one has mastered the sciences and childhood has passed, and when the captivating youth endowed with the vigor of wealth has arrived, one should enjoy the hips of playful women; thereafter, for that purpose, one should enjoy the slopes of the mountains.
By protecting his subjects in accordance with dharma, a king receives a sixth share of the merit derived from the study, the performance of austerities, and the good deeds of those subjects.
How is it that he, who does not enjoy the sixth part [of the produce], does not protect the subjects?
By means of the four conditions—study, comprehension, practice, and propagation—he established fourteenfoldness among the fourteen sciences; I myself do not know why he did so.
If one has studied the Mahābhāṣya, then that Padamañjarī is useless;
if one has not studied the Mahābhāṣya, then that Padamañjarī is useless.
Having studied the four Vedas and the treatises on Dharma many times over, one who does not know the supreme reality is like a ladle that knows not the flavors of the food it stirs.
Having studied the four Vedas and mastered the eighteen Smṛtis, oh,
what a fruitlessness of labor it is if even one's own self is not realized!
Having studied political science, for what reason is he— who is not seen to be endowed with prudence and who is ignorant of it— appointed to the office of minister?
Having studied the Vedas, having fully maintained the sacred fires, having performed sacrifices, and having protected his subjects,
a Kṣatriya whose inner self has been purified by weapons when slain in battle for the sake of cows and Brahmins attains heaven.

Having studied the entirety of the sacred scriptures and having performed severe austerity, if you desire the fruit of those two—namely, gain, honor, and the like—you, being empty-minded, cut away only the spreading foliage of the tree; how can you hope to obtain its ripe, delicious fruit?
By studying this according to the scriptures, an excellent man comes to know [the truth].
Renowned for his instruction in the Dharma, he [discerned] what ought and ought not to be done, and what is auspicious and inauspicious.
Men study, understand, and repeatedly become dispassionate;
yet they do not turn back from the state of inequality forever.
A Brāhmaṇa should study, or perform sacrifice, or give gifts, or indeed go to the chief sacred fords;
he may also teach, or officiate at sacrifices for those entitled to do so, or accept gifts that are known to be lawful.
Likewise, a Kṣatriya, having diligently protected his subjects according to dharma, having offered gifts,
performed sacrifices, studied all the Vedas, and taken a wife, should dwell in his home as a doer of meritorious deeds.
A Vaiśya, having studied the Vedas, accumulating wealth through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade, protecting it with vigilance,
doing what is pleasing to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, and being of virtuous character and a doer of meritorious deeds, should dwell in his home.

He should perform service and pay homage to the Brāhmaṇas; he must not study, for sacrifice is forbidden to him. Constantly striving for prosperity and remaining free from indolence throughout the day—this is remembered as the ancient dharma of the Śūdra.

One who is lacking in self-control, one who is harsh, one who is arrogant, one who is poorly dressed, and one who has come uninvited— these five are not to be honored, even if they are equal to Bṛhaspati himself.
You repeatedly press against the jar-like full breasts of the restless-eyed maiden; you gradually take hold of her pair of thighs, so charming with their beauty;
embraced by her arms, you joyfully experience the art of being struck by her hands—reveal for what ascetic merit this fruit of the lute-neck is yours!
O lady whose limbs are languid with the weight of heavy amorous confusion, why do you now persist in churning the curd?
O pot-breasted one, Murāri’s soft, sweet flute-song yearns for you in the bower.
May that Lord of Lakṣmī, the Leader, who is free from all transformations, protect you— he by whom the harmful couple were saved even though they had been swallowed by the king of bees.

I remember the amorous gesture of that fair-eyed woman before me: her bodice-band slipping and not being held fast, her gaze cast askance with a stolen look, her laughter manifest, and the orb of her face upturned.

If the plantain tree were afflicted by the parching heat of a desert salt-flat, it might then experience that same agony as her pair of thighs, which were set ablaze by the God of Love during their separation.
Having descended into the depths and become stained by the mud, the lotus stalks—
though possessed of virtue— are pulled up by fishermen devoid of merit, revealed only by their own sprouts.
Looking downward, devoid of compassion, intent on achieving his own self-interest,
deceitful, and falsely disciplined— such is the twice-born who practices the "heron-vow" (bakavrata).
For one who looks further and further down, how can greatness not increase? But those who look higher and higher, all become impoverished.
When the pomegranate, having performed most intense and great penance with its face turned downward in order to attain equality with a woman’s breast,
did not obtain it, it then clearly split open in its heart under the guise of ripeness.
By this serpent of the female organ, which is difficult to cure, whose single fang is turned downward and flows with poison and semen, the world has been bitten.
That sword whose characteristic marks are visible in the lower half but are not seen at all in the upper half is inferior; it brings fear to the lords of the earth.
If the lower half of the sword-blade has one color and the upper half has a different color, it is a sword characterized by a mixture of colors; such a sword increases the fear of kings.

Because of the downward placement of the lotus and sprouts upon the heads of all sovereign rulers, was this foot marked by the Creator with an upward line so that it might be known: "In former times, this [foot] was above"?
In the study of the Vedas, association with friends, entering [a new home], journeys, marriages, and giving gifts—
in all such auspicious undertakings, the wind that travels with the Moon is recommended.

I take refuge in that Supreme Brahman—the eternal, auspicious reality which is free from the multitude of misfortunes; which has cast off the darkness of superimposition; which is unprecedented; which is to be grasped by those possessing the intellect directed toward the ultimate goal; which is the locus of the human goals of life; which is indicated by its specific characteristics as found in the Vedas; which is devoid of anything yet to be accomplished; which shines forth as the universal manifestation at the end of the sacred tradition; which is not contradicted by anything; and which is Truth, Knowledge, and devoid of all that is useless.
He has taken possession of this hermitage, which is open to the enjoyment of all; yet, through his practice of protection, he too accumulates ascetic merit every day.
Even for him, who is self-controlled, the holy sound "Muni" reaches heaven, sung by pairs of celestial bards; it is only that it is preceded by the word "King."
They teach the scriptures, treat scholars as mere straw,
and cause them to forget their own lineage— all for five or six cowries held in their hands.

Tell me, whose wealth and virtue shall I destroy—of you, who have been taught political science even by Uśanas, yet employ passion as a spy against your enemies; for I am like a swollen flood that sweeps away both banks of the Sindhu river?
"O mosquito, by whom have you been taught this meanness here,
that you cause pain to the very ear upon which you alight?"

Having spread out the sacrificial grass upon the altar of the battlefield, and having offered as oblations the flesh of the enemy, the *caru* of blood, and the *havis* of his head marked with the *svastika*,
he— renowned as the fire of majesty— was swiftly enshrined in the *āhavanīya* fire-altar of the assembly hall by the illustrious one who had formed the four oceans into a water-offering cup.
Those lofty golden pedestals upon which they sat were such that they resembled the peaks of Mount Trikūṭa when traversed by a lion.
We say that your two breasts, no longer finding room within the great heart of your friend whom you have occupied, have emerged outside.

In that battle, which was as difficult to enter as the end of an aeon due to the masses of enemy troops and the dense ranks of arrows, and where fear was instilled by neighing horses ridden by mounted warriors, and where the thundering, snorting, and fiercely powerful herds of rutting elephants roared— there, even though the king himself was a captive who ought to be slain, he was able to provide fodder for the sake of saving their lives.
If a female jackal, having occupied a peaceful quarter, howls on the left side of a man, she certainly bestows the gain of wealth;
however, if she howls on the right, she causes the loss of wealth.
He who, having mounted his bull, moves gracefully through courtyards as radiant as pearls—he alone is honored in my heart, with Gaurī resting upon his left side.

Where in this world does this flood of fame not remain awake? It is a collection of slender bodies as fit for the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa—the remnant of the moon on the head of the Destroyer of Smara—as to fill them; it is the means by which the sage’s cup was spared from the terror of the Ocean of Milk; it is a manifold manifestation of his form.
He studies, he dances, he cuts, he measures, he praises, he buys, he kills, he sows, he piles up, he fears;
he steals, he sings, he gratifies, he carries, he splits, out of greed he sews, he bargains, and he begs.
He who does not acquire the eternal Dharma by means of this unstable body that perishes moment by moment— that person of deluded mind is to be pitied.
For he who does not exert himself in the practice of austerity while the body is still unstable,
that fool suffers later, having gone after death to his own destination.

A woman whose body is weary from travel, one suffering from a new fever, one with limbs relaxed from dancing, or one who has recently given birth—these grant pleasure in sexual union; likewise, one six months pregnant does so as well.

A woman is renowned for her excellence in the act of reunion after separation, when appeased after being angry, during her fertile period, in a first encounter, under the influence of wine, or when passion is at its height. These are the occasions upon which women become the very seat of erotic delight.
In an assembly of connoisseurs, poetry—intent on grasping the meaning through its sequence of words—delights the heart or perhaps not the ear; it is like an anklet during a time of play.
A traveler is to be known as a guest, as is a Śrotriya who has mastered the Vedas;
these two are to be honored by a householder who desires the world of Brahman.
On every stage of the journey, on every path, the shade of trees is resorted to by travelers;
rare indeed is that particular tree which a traveler, having reached home, remembers.
On every stage of the journey, the traveler—simple-minded and addicted to seeking refuge in heights—should have respectfully disregarded from afar the fruit-laden trees that bend low;
for what can be said of the palm tree, which, when the weary wayfarer approaches its base seeking sweet shade and fruit, does not even provide utility with its fallen leaves?

MSS_1168-1 "If this traveler’s wife, distressed by separation from her husband, should give up her life while remembering him on his journey, alas, whose great sin would that become? MSS_1168-2 While the traveler was thus reflecting in his heart, a cuckoo perched upon the top of a tree repeatedly cried out loudly, "You! You! many times.
"O tree, even now the birds that dwell upon you fill your root-hollows with their tears and cry out at evening for a moment along with their entire flocks;
since even these living beings bear such grief on your account, you have not truly departed, O tree, but continue to exist for a long time through your own fame."
Alas, during the winter season, winds that are like the fierce arrows of a cruel executioner enter the bodies of travelers, causing them great distress.
Yet these very same winds instantly bind upon the heads of beautiful women—whether fortunate or even unfortunate—the diadem of their good fortune, loosened by the intense embrace of their lovers.
How many of these forest rivers block the paths, how many pierce the firm embankments, how many inundate the fields, and how many uproot the trees?
These wild streams on this earth have their power of water lost in an instant; as for that ocean which is the refuge of all, however, it is not known where it is.
On this path, where cuckoos warble like those intoxicated by the wine of nectar-drops, I suspect that travelers have avoided obstructing the road out of fear of inauspiciousness;
for this humming swarm of bees, like a cluster of tinkling bells, is surely the mark of a *caṇḍāla* inherited from Spring for the sin of murdering wayfarers’ wives.

O Creator, if you feel no shame in always providing these things for me— my feet for the fatigue of travel, my wife for separation, my speech for begging, and my body for old age— is it not also sheer exhaustion?
One who does not honor with devotion a guest who is weary from the road, unknown, and afflicted by hunger and thirst— him they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
If a kinsman were to stand firm against misfortune, alert as one at the head of a path, he would be worthy of restraining [one from evil];
but let people who know their duty remain silent regarding the matter, and let them follow the path of their own desire with joy.
For embodied beings, old age is the passage of time; for mountains, water is old age.
For women, lack of sexual union is old age; for the mind, the arrow of harsh words is old age.
Travel is old age for humans, while lack of travel is old age for horses;
celibacy is old age for women, while sexual intercourse is old age for horses.

Having traversed the long path through the wandering of the worlds, my chariot, which possesses but a single wheel, is unable to proceed; "I must reach it again tomorrow"—with such a heavy burden of anxiety fixed in his mind, the sun now stands upon the western mountain, having drawn forth the clear row of golden rays remaining from the twilight, as if leading the circle of the quarters back to their starting point.
O leader of the herd, if the path were not mired in the mud of attachment, then how could this quality of yours as a bearer of the burden be manifested?
The wise indeed enter the enemy's house through a non-door;
how can a battle proceed without first having initiated an assault?
May she who is sound by nature— though her form here is beyond syllables, yet flows through the fifty letters filled with the water of nectar,
scattering the mass of the Vedic injunctions within the intermediate space—
protect me on all sides.

Friendship with those who do not know how to read, conversation with them, and service to a bad master; embracing women with heavy breasts—these three alone constitute manifest suffering on this earth.
The same man, when his beard has not yet sprouted, is like milk enriched with sugar; the same man, once his beard has grown, is like salt water mixed with buttermilk;
and the same man, with a white beard, causes distress like burnt guggulu resin—such are the three moods that women with deer-like eyes experience toward their beloveds.
"The bodiless one conquers the universe with five flower-arrows"—this is indeed improbable; or rather, the powers of things are manifold.
In order to soothe his fever of desire, let the lotuses of the celestial river, repeatedly tormented by him during every spring, rather prefer to bear their passion for the cold season.
Behold this banner of victory upon my head, grey with the dust of passion;
now we have triumphed, and your arrows are rendered powerless.
Seeing Śambhu’s head bowed low at the feet of Bhavānī as he was overwhelmed by the arrows of the bodiless god of love,
a certain female ant moving at his feet began to kiss the orb of the moon.
When will he, embraced by that slender-limbed woman with waves of side-glances that serve as the auspicious chamber for the bodiless god of love, attain the fulfillment of his purpose?
The flickering movements of her sidelong glances, which serve as the auspicious ground for the god of love,
repeatedly produce a continuous stream of inner torment within young men.
Whose afflictions would not be dispelled by her two breasts, which, covered by her sprout-like hands, are like two jars for the commencement of the auspicious rites of the bodiless God of Love?
Her hips are the pedestal for the stage of love, a golden throne of passion,
a concentrated mass of the very essence of beauty.
The limbs of that slender-limbed woman, resembling the stage of the God of Love and assuming various graceful gestures,
suddenly cause the hearts of young men to abandon all other thoughts and become tranquil.

May that certain cowherd boy flash forth in my mind this very moment— he whose beautiful garment-hem is flickering with the skillful grace of amorous passion, whose cheeks are radiant with the luster of swaying shark-shaped earrings, and who yearns for the rāsa dance of the multitude of radiant city-women from Vraja.

O sinless one, O ever-blissful one, you who are united with the touch of her whose body is bowed; she, possessing a beautiful form, is accompanied by various anxieties arising from the assault of the bodiless god of love.
O lady of curved limbs, the arrival of the clouds brings the weapons of the bodiless god to a sharp edge, like a blacksmith;
for amidst the rain-clouds, which possess the luster of soot-stained coals, the crest of lightning blazes forth.
For those who have renounced desire, whose bodies are fit for inference [of their inner state],
and who maintain the purity of sacred bathing places, the smearing of holy ashes is their ornament.
May that Kāma of wondrous deeds, by whom the three worlds were conquered through his union with the powerless Anaṅga, grant you the fulfillment of all desires.
This bodiless one will surely reproach his bodilessness today,
since he has not obtained the festival of the touch of your hand.
O beautiful one, your gaze is dark without being anointed with collyrium; your brow is curved without being bent; and this lower lip of yours is rosy without being stained with rouge.
The wandering about with her reddish feet, accompanied by the non-subtle resonance of jeweled girdles and the incessant tinkling of lovely anklets, produces causeless longing.

Here, the earth, washed with refined gold, imitates water from which the clouds have not long departed and in which many bubbles have long since subsided, as it is strewn with scattered fragments of diamonds.
Carrying a mass of gold that possesses no superior excellence, you greatly delight my heart;
however, tell me, for whose benefit is this wealth of yours?
Not too loosely, for they possess bold strength through their masculine nature, the Malaya breezes have entered the face of the lotus and emerged with force;
having taken something from the mouth of the lotus plant and brought it forth at the junction of dawn, they have caused their wives to eat fresh food.

O fair-browed one, this night of three watches, which previously seemed to me as if multiplied a hundredfold while my desire remained unfulfilled, would pass in that same manner if it were spent in union with you; thus I would be successful.
Just as a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas is not entitled to participate in a *śrāddha* ceremony,
so too one who has not heard of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) is not entitled to hear the secret counsel (*mantra*).
He who, without having studied his own treatise, seeks to speak on another’s treatise,
is like one who counts the footprints of a snake that has long since departed into the water in the darkness of night.
Many who possess the intellect of cattle, having not studied the treatises on statecraft,
desire to speak with boldness once they have been admitted into the inner circle of counsel.
My doctrine, whose depth cannot be fathomed even by those of immense intellectual power, and whose ultimate reality has not been seen even by those of great application,
will— finding no worthy recipient in this world— undergo decay within its own body, like the water of the ocean.

Those who are unacquainted with the paths of poetry, whose gait is sluggish in the depths of the sciences, who lack the knowledge of the nuances of speech, who are mute regarding the virtues of others, and who have never practiced service in the assemblies of the learned— how indeed could they serve as whetstones for the itching of others' eloquence?
"Infinite indeed is my wealth, though I possess nothing at all;
even when Mithilā is in flames, nothing of mine is burned."
When the fourfold group beginning with infinite anger arises, and likewise when the impurity of the threefold false belief arises,
the poison of persistent false belief— which causes endless saṃsāra for embodied beings— takes root.
Endowed with infinite renown, pure in being, and possessed of the power of wisdom, he—
whose resolve is firm through learning and vision— enjoys manifold pleasures.
The central portion of this [earth], it is said, was fashioned by the Creator after grasping the infinite reality;
it is exceedingly subtle, perceivable only by the vision of yogis, and fortified by the power of stability in the qualities of existence and consciousness.
Salutations to the one who possesses infinite names, the ordainer of all forms, the one expressed by all mantras, the sole lord of the universe.
The poet’s composition, consisting of an infinite arrangement of words and full of aesthetic flavor,
[shines] if a wise man is nearby and not a base person in front.
The science of grammar is indeed boundless, while life is short and obstacles are many;
therefore, one should cultivate that which is essential, just as swans extract milk from the midst of water.
For Him, from whom an endless stream of jewels originates, even snow has not become a destroyer of his splendor;
for a single defect is submerged when there is a collection of virtues, like the spot on the moon amidst its rays.
Immediately after the enemy, one should station the one who serves the enemy; immediately after the enemy, the friend; and beyond those two, the neutral party.
Deprived of infinite splendor and tormented by misfortune,
she laments her state of being alive, like a heroine who has lost her husband.
The scriptures are endless, the branches of knowledge are many, time is short, and obstacles are numerous;
therefore, one should cultivate that which is essential, just as a swan extracts milk from the midst of water.
"The fame of this king, who is a friend to the night-lotuses of poets, is infinite; this triple world is but a trifle.

Therefore, how could it possibly contain him?"—this doubt of yours is in vain. Consider for a moment the surface of a mirror: is the reflection of the Lord of Poets not clearly manifest there, however vast that surface may be?
In this entire world, crowded with a multitude of beings born in endless succession,
if there are but three or four among those skilled in weaponry and scripture who are as capable as I;
This breeze, born in the Malaya forests and possessing a splendor never trodden by others, drinks up the sweat-water that is the wealth enjoyed by the dolphin of Love;
then, through contact with the intense passion of the embraces of the beloveds of Vidarbha, it causes their limbs to be covered with double the usual horripilation.

This form of yours, which surpasses all other beauty, does not deserve such humiliation in your father’s house, O fair-browed one. No one can lay a hand upon you; for who would stretch out a hand toward the needle-like jewel of a serpent?
Is this waist of hers, whose body is lovely with a splendor unique to no other,
the middle region of the three worlds where the rows of hearts of all living beings reside under the guise of the three folds?

Why did the swarm of bees not resort to the *campaka* tree, which possesses an abundance of exceedingly brilliant flowers endowed with a fragrance unique to no other? How can those of foul nature find delight in that which is fragrant?

He who was celebrated on the face of the earth as a "Giver" (Tyāgin) because of his unique and peerless nature became the supreme target for the arrows of Love, which rushed toward him in a frantic scramble for precedence.
Worship the Bhāgavata love with the state of having no other object of focus.
For humans, what measure does "love" have, if they have attained love for the Lord?
To those people who worship Me, thinking of no other,
and who are ever devoted, I provide both acquisition and preservation.
Even if one who has served as a cloud with a mind not dependent on anything else does not pour down rain,
I consider that to be the fault of the cātaka bird alone.
Independent of the words of the guru, it completely shatters all knots;
may this innate power of discernment (*vimarśa-śakti*), which reveals the supreme secret, be victorious!
Not understanding the meaning of the scriptures, men of beastly intellect,
having been admitted into the inner circle of mantras, desire to speak out of sheer audacity.
A king who is ignorant of virtues is not followed by his servants,
even if he is wealthy, of noble birth, or has inherited the throne through lineage.
One should practice in three ways with the mind: non-covetousness regarding the property of others, benevolence toward all sentient beings, and the conviction that there is a fruit for actions.

O friend bee, your state is indeed auspicious— you who do not desire the pollen-anointing on the lotus-like playful feet of Śrī, who do not wish to drink the stream of ichor from the elephant of the gods, and who have abandoned attachment to the fragrance of the flowers of the thirty [deities], for you are content.
What is the use of that dull-witted learning which, its enthusiasm destroyed by lack of practice, is overcome by others and, due to its stupidity, produces only shame?
Knowledge destroyed by lack of practice is ruined; one who opposes the king is ruined;
a sacred ford for the sake of livelihood is ruined; and a vow for the sake of livelihood is ruined.
Through the lack of practice in the sciences, through lack of association with the wise,
and through the failure to restrain the senses, calamity arises for men.
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of proper conduct,
laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins.
Knowledge is destroyed by lack of practice; women are ruined by constant laughter;
a field is ruined by bad seed; and kings are ruined by the faults of their servants.
The rain of nectar falling from the ears, Sarasvatī, the birthplace of poetic grace,
and the Vaidarbha style— these arise for the learned as the guarantors for the attainment of the beauty of words.
If one sees lightning flashing in a cloudless sky toward the southern direction,
or if there is a rainbow at night, one's life remains for only two or three months.
In this world, it is fitting for a man to possess valor that does not yield to the haughty, wealth acquired by his own arms, and a wife whose beauty is well-suited to him.
Otherwise, what use is this form [of yours] even...
O beloved, there is no such anguish as when you are visible yet unattainable, being out of the path of one's eyes;
a sun-crystal stone merely withers at night, but blazes in the day.
Both misfortune and fortune come to men through destiny;
under its influence, a person performs actions that yield auspicious or inauspicious fruits.
By her— who has been enjoyed by another, who dwells upon the earth, and who is detached—
does not your harem surpass the bodies of the wives of Mahendra?
By her, who moves so slowly due to the weight of her broad hips,
even as she passes by another path, my heart has been struck.
By this limit of your beauty, which has awakened my latent impressions (*saṃskāra*),
that woman of pure smiles has today ascended to my memory, even though she was seen long ago.
By means of this table of contents, these pearls have been described by me;
for each single one is radiant, so what need is there to speak of their entire collection?
O Ocean, why do you surge with billows because of this abundance of jewels?
Your wretched favorites carry water during the rains.
A union with her, who is so ardently desired by the gods, will not be easily obtained by you,
just as the light of the moon cannot reach a lily covered by thick clouds at the arrival of the rainy season.
Then, through that very despondency, her royal splendor withered away like a lotus pond by cold water— just as prosperity perishes through misconduct and high-mindedness through wretchedness.
O lady of faultless limbs, as these two breasts of yours expand, there is no sufficient space within the interval of your vine-like arms.
Discipline belongs to that person whose rule it follows;
even a policy correctly applied becomes a bad policy for one who lacks fortune.

"Your priceless beauty surpasses the world, you are enveloped in waves of sweetness, your fragrance spreads in every direction, and you possess a singular devotion to the essence of flavor—thus, O mango tree (*rasāla*), we have indeed resolved out of affection for you. Who could have known that you were thus afflicted by bitter insects?"
Even a priceless ruby requires a setting of gold;
for the wise, women, and creepers do not shine when they lack a support.
To whom does this graceful woman not instill longing, being a ground for a treasury of priceless beauty?
I know that the flower-armed god, acting as her guard, does not sleep for even a moment, lacking trust in her.
Even priceless jewels are easily obtained through wealth; however, not even a single moment of one whose life has passed away can be regained, even for ten million jewels.
He who does not indulge in purposeless wandering from his home, in association with the wicked, in violating another's wife,
in hypocrisy, theft, slander, or the drinking of intoxicants— he is always happy.
O son, by renouncing everything, one flies up without agitation from this ocean of saṃsāra, which is a house for the crocodiles of misfortune.
Perceiving what is harmful as beneficial, and what is beneficial as harmful,
the fool who is led astray by the senses considers great suffering to be happiness.
Non-benefits appear in the form of benefits, and benefits in the form of non-benefits;
for indeed, for some, even the loss of wealth results in true benefit.
For misfortunes take the form of benefits, and benefits take the form of misfortunes;
these lead to destruction for one who is dependent on fate, yet such a person finds it pleasing.
Wealth that is not used for the satisfaction of those in need, a mind that is not a mirror for meditative concentration,
and a body that does not resort to the true ford— these will meet with lamentation in the end.
Because men do not desire them and out of fear of their kinsmen,
women— who are otherwise unrestrained— remain within the bounds of propriety toward their husbands.
They do not desire a husband who is devoted to what is harmful and averse to what is beneficial,
just as women do not desire a eunuch as their spouse.
Even that which is harmful arises in the form of what is beneficial, and likewise, that which is beneficial assumes the form of what is harmful;
it arises for the sake of destruction. Therefore, one should examine what has been said.
O Mādhava, even though you were unadorned, you always forcibly captivated my heart;
how much more so now that you are adorned with her nail-scratches?
Fire serves to destroy cold; the Gāruḍa [mantra] serves to destroy poison;
discernment serves to destroy suffering; and a wicked mind serves to destroy everything.
Anala was born from water, and Kārttikeya likewise from fire;
for who is able to determine the hidden birth of the great?

First, the orb of the moon shines in the sky with the hue of a cluster of *analasa* and *javā* flowers; then it takes on the glow of the cheeks of intoxicated Yavana women; then it becomes honey-tawny; then it possesses the luster of a mirror of fresh gold; and finally, it appears like a young *tagara* flower.
O fortunate one, you surely know the science for arresting the breath;
otherwise, how could you dwell within my heart, which is scorched by the fire of the arrows of Love?
Alas, how many have gone before us to the city of Yama, prattling incessantly, with eyes fixed and mouths agape?
If it is so that they have passed away, why do we not carry our own welfare in our hearts? Alas, we have been brought to ruin by delusion born from the poison of sensory objects.
It allays the no small torment born of love; likewise, it dispels the pervasive cold on a winter night in the Himalayas.
Thus, victorious is that certain warmth born from the dense, jar-like breasts of women meeting in the festival of their lovers’ embrace.

O beautiful one, this body of yours—motionless from the delusion of the heavy burden of no small anxiety, and causing trepidation merely by being gazed upon—is adorned with its own natural beauty alone; alas, what indeed is it?
Because of his great power and preeminence, other kings become his retinue, just as other notes accompany the primary note of a musical scale.
Just as even a mere drop of *vāruṇī* liquor renders what is blameless into something blameworthy,
so too a disciple perishes by associating with a teacher whose purpose is contrary to the Dharma.

The intellect is like his speech, and his conduct is like his intellect— utterly pure fame is like his conduct— for the expanse of his wealth was rippled by hands holding water-drops from his incessant distribution of gold.

His body, though emaciated, bears a core of vital strength; it is marked by the harsh sound of incessantly twanging the bowstring, is resilient against the rays of the sun, and remains untainted by even a drop of sweat.
Due to its muscular development, this slender frame is not easily perceived, like a mountain-dwelling elephant.
With her rosary formed by the continuous drops of water falling from her eyes,
the young woman in separation mutters your name as if chanting the mantra of the Conqueror of Death.
O powerless one, whom does this face of yours not torment— this face resting upon the palm of your hand, its painted leaf-designs erased by the drops of water incessantly falling from your eyes?
The words of the great ones, whose stainless minds are ever-vigilant in benefiting others,
flash forth like medicines that instantly dispel the harshness of suffering.

The young sprout, possessing an incessant juice, accustomed to being nibbled by fingernails, and cherished by the lover who partook of passion, withered instantly and pitilessly when bitten by his bride.
And that well-spoken word which is uttered at an inappropriate time becomes an object of laughter,
like the recitation of the Vedas during the act of love by bold women in private.
For one whose mind is unsettled, there is no happiness among people nor in the forest;
among people, association causes burning, while in the forest, it is the avoidance of attachment that burns.
Even the favor shown toward those with unsettled minds is terrifying;
it is said that a snake kills its offspring out of affection, not out of enmity.
Is Time indifferent because he is powerless, or is he a great connoisseur because he is entreated by the wise?
Though he consumes everything, Time does not obscure the well-spoken verses of poets.
Nothing is gained by grief, and the body is only tormented;
enemies rejoice, so do not set your mind on sorrow.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, who fails to protect his subjects, and who is a devourer of them, is destined for a downward path.
O Sarasvatī, among the treasuries of knowledge, this treasury of yours is unprecedented: that which is inexhaustible undergoes expenditure, while that which is spent becomes vastly expanded.
On a sandy path where the oxen are exhausted by the weight of their heavy burden,
this charioteer remembers his leader, whose neck is strained by the effort of lifting that heavy load.
Free from envy, possessed of perfected wisdom, and always performing auspicious deeds,
one attains happiness without hardship and shines everywhere.
Anasūyā (freedom from envy), forbearance, tranquility, contentment, and pleasant speech; the renunciation of desire and anger—these are the manifestations of the conduct of the disciplined.
