Absence of malice, straightforwardness, purity, contentment, pleasant speech, self-control, truthfulness, and lack of exertion for worldly gain— these do not belong to those of evil nature.
This is the manifestation of that splendor whose essence has not yet set,
by which even a fragment of stone makes the entire earth seem of little value.
Those who have not attained the human state, who are devoid of the touch of forbearance,
and who oppose the former gods, are not served by the awakened ones.
The moon, accompanied by a pair of lotus petals, has been seized in the upper half by the most crooked of darknesses;
now it incessantly pours forth nectar that produces total delusion—is this a series of portents arisen to bring about the destruction of the world? Tell me!

By means of the innocent gestures and words of her dear companions, this auspicious girl neither succeeds nor desists in bringing about the union of the Pāñcālī couple; she merely causes her cheeks to bristle with buds of horripilation.
Unattracted by sense objects and having reached the further shore of the sciences,
he, who delighted in dharma, attained old age without the infirmity of physical decay.
Foreseeing a future danger, the mouse, who was an expert in the treatises on statecraft (*nītiśāstra*),
made a hundred-mouthed burrow and dwelt there.
He who prepares for the future prospers; he who does not prepare for the future grieves.
While living in the forest, I have reached old age, yet never once was the sound of a cave even heard by me.
For one should indeed understand what is yet to come and whatever task stands before one;
however, due to a deficiency in intelligence, one should not let any purpose pass by.
But he who rejoices after having entertained thoughts concerning the future incurs contempt,
just like the brahmin who broke the vessel.
The man who desires to engage in anxious thoughts regarding the future lies pale upon the ground, just like the father of Somaśarman.
Both the one who provides for the future and the one who possesses presence of mind thrive in happiness; the procrastinator perishes.
Fortune attends upon that man who provides for the future, who is vigilant, free from anger, steadfast in his undertakings, and undaunted.
And kings should provide for the future within their realm.
Furthermore, the traditional scripture (āgama) must also be followed; in this way, no fault arises.
A wise man who desires what is auspicious and anticipates misfortune should take measures for the future.
One who is intent on future acquisitions, violent, evil-minded, and lacking in learning;
one who has squandered what was acquired, and who is fond of drinking liquor, gambling, women, and hunting.
A lord of wealth who employs himself in a task that is too great is deprived of his prosperity.
A flower never smelled, a sprout uncut by fingernails, a gem unperforated, honey whose flavor is yet untasted,
and like the unbroken fruit of merits— this faultless form, I know not what enjoyer Fate will bring before him here.
Though he possesses no sunshade, he is seen here as if surrounded on all sides by white parasols;
though he has no fly-whisk, he is always being fanned by some extraordinary person with a playful yak-tail fan.
Even a successful union between two who are free from illness and longing does not bring me pleasure;
rather, for two who are equally in love but have lost all hope of attaining one another, even the destruction of the body is better.
One who lacks self-control and hates right policy increases the prosperity of his enemies;
even after attaining great sovereignty, he perishes along with it.
The king is the refuge for all who are protectorless, the poor, children, the elderly, ascetics, and those oppressed by injustice.
He who is the protector of the helpless, the refuge for those without refuge, the guide for the distressed, the fearlessness for the frightened, and the support for the weary;
he who is a friend, a kinsman, a master, a shelter, a benefactor, a noble teacher, a father, a mother, and a brother—he is the true man, and he is the king in this world.
He who protects the helpless and the sick like his own children,
having been authorized by his teacher, earns the title of a physician.
A wise man intent on honor and striving for stable prosperity should leave no remnant of fire,
no remnant of debt, and no remnant of an enemy.
The mind does not engage in service marred by disrespect, a marriage devoid of love,
or a friendship dependent upon a motive.
MSS_1320-1 Through his disregard for the world, his grief increased as he was subject to the words of his father’s beloved;
MSS_1320-2 the son of Uttānapāda, having propitiated Viṣṇu, the refuge of the worlds, attained the supreme station.
A man who incurs expenditure without taking in income, who has no companions yet is fond of battle,
who is afflicted by illness and eats all things indiscriminately, perishes quickly.

O noble ones, since this person’s intellect is dependent upon either the stream of the series of causes in the beginningless succession of one's own nature, or upon the Lord, how can such a person be subject to censure?
Even without being commanded by the king, he who strives for the destruction of anything seen to be harmful to him is worthy of service by monarchs.

Disregarding propriety and paying no heed to immense shame, those who—agitated by the wicked hope for a mere fragment of wealth—must gaze upon the faces of the rich, their brows contorted by the fever of false pride; fie on this belly that is so difficult to fill!
A king, even when utterly impoverished, should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor should he, even when prosperous, relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be.
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death.
That craving of men, which is without beginning or end and resides within the body,
destroys them once it has arisen, like a fire not born from a womb.
To those who have not accumulated merit, this mother of the fruit that has shaken off all dust is difficult to attain;
yet for you, this perfection of seeing her is equal to a rain from a cloudless sky.
The lack of traditional study is the impurity of the Vedas; the absence of vows is the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa.
The Vāhīkas are the impurity of the earth; untruthfulness is the impurity of a man.
Those without a leader perish; those with many leaders perish;
those led by women perish; and those led by children perish.
One should not dwell where there is no leader; one should not dwell where there are many leaders.
One should not dwell where a woman is the leader; one should not dwell where a fool is the leader.
One who mismanages income and expenditure, is without a protector, is fond of quarreling,
is afflicted by illness, and eats all things— a man such as this perishes quickly.
The waist of the fair-browed maiden was slender without effort, her two eyes were tremulous without apprehension, and her body was enchanting even without ornaments— at that age.
"Which region was brought today by you to the state of a forest abandoned by spring?
Because it has received a rendezvous with you, even its name is no longer fit to be heard by these people."
The means, having been properly distinguished and honored with their correct application by him, have been made to bear fruit incessantly—
like successes in wealth that, having grown in the future, come together as if in competition.
In every direction and in every region, on water and on land,
beings are incessantly born and die like bubbles upon the water.

The wives of your enemies, seeking to travel to many foreign lands, reproach the heavy autumnal rains with averted glances; for the onset of their journey is blocked by the waters of the rivers swollen by hundreds of incessant streams of tears flowing from their eyes.

That resolve of the slender-limbed one— which was not prompted by outward action, which involved a supreme outpouring of tears, which concealed inner anguish, and which was swallowed up within her heart— that resolve, as it turns toward me, a sinner, with limbs slackened by despair, utterly uproots this very heart of mine.
Some things exist as unconditioned, such as the Tathāgatas;
even human effort applied toward them would be rendered fruitless.
The non-commencement of undertakings is the first characteristic of intelligence;
the carrying through to completion of what has been commenced is the second characteristic of intelligence.

In this world of Brahmā, who else but me is the poet capable of composing or proclaiming such a bold literary work— without having propitiated Kālī, without having relished the Gauḍī style, and without [the mastery of] mantra and tantra, save for the theft of words?
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, longevity, and the attainment of heaven;
it is non-meritorious and despised by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty,
and a disposition toward inaction reveal in this world that a man is born from a defiled womb.
O traveler, this golden jambu sprout upon your ear is indeed a great thorn in the hearts of these ignoble village women;
did you not become a Buddha wandering for alms throughout the city? O traveler, you must not harbor such resentment toward me again.
O gentle one, may you forgive me for this ignoble conduct practiced by a young girl;
for even a swan is worthy of veneration due to his divine nature, just as the Fish-incarnation is venerable because it bears the Śrīvatsa mark.
Misfortunes quickly come upon one who behaves ignobly, lacks wisdom, is envious, and is unrighteous, as well as one who is foul-mouthed and prone to anger.
Association with one who is ignoble and ungrateful is not fitting for me;
relatives always desire even the ruin of their own kin.
A man who spends without regard for his means, one who is helpless, fond of quarreling,
and afflicted in all his undertakings, perishes quickly.
O simple one, why have you now suddenly displayed such pride, disregarding the consequences of love and showing no regard for your friends?
For you have drawn these embers toward yourself with your own hand—embers whose flames blaze like the fire of universal destruction; enough now with this weeping in the wilderness!
Time passes irreversibly; that has gone to waste, and those various conditions, distressed by the onset of hundreds of calamities, were endured without being reckoned.
How much more shall we say? Alas, what indeed was not done for our own benefit, yet we have resolved once again upon that very same [futile course].
Even when her mind is not won over, craving surely runs toward everyone; yet she obtains no fruit at all, like an aged woman in love.
One who is not eager for sense objects enjoys the fruit that is free from turbidity;
one who is eager perishes there through the grief of having gained the world.
It is a marvel that the wind-bird remains within the cage of the nine unobstructed gates; what need is there to speak of its departure from that?
In former times, women were unconfined within their own castes and common to all, because every person was free from enmity.
O dear one, blessed are those who do not witness the ruin of their country or the destruction of their family when a region is struck by drought and the crops have perished.
Not relying on the merit of giving, nor relying on the merit of the Vedas,
those seeking liberation wander here in this world, completely free from passion and hatred.
A king should not harbor contempt for a proud preceptor who has lost his patronage;
indeed, Marutta cast out his preceptor because of Saṃvarta.
Disregard for objects that possess desired qualities when they are presented; thick pride even when an insult is offered; the display of elaborate gestures in anger;
striking with both feet; and the binding of the beloved’s feet with her girdle—this is *vibboka* (feigned indifference), which only a fortunate man experiences.
May your enemies fall like the breasts of noble women, consumed by the premature widowhood of their youth, never having tasted the pleasure of enjoyment.
What is the use of that barren gift which is given without being tasted, without being sold, without being taken, and without being desired, and which provides no benefit?

One who maintains no sacred fires despite possessing a hundred cows, one who does not perform sacrifices despite possessing a thousand cows, a drinker of liquor, the husband of a low-caste woman, a slayer of a Brahmin, and one who violates the teacher’s bed— [these are equal].
One who accepts gifts from the unworthy, a thief, and one who performs sacrifices for those who are contemptible—
these may abandon one another without fault, because their actions are determined by their mutual association with such defilement.
He enters uninvited and speaks much when unasked;
this lowest of men, with a deluded mind, places his trust in those who are vigilant.
Coming uninvited, speaking without being asked,
disparaging others, and praising oneself— these four are the characteristics of the minor [offenses].
For one who enters uninvited, is looked upon with angry eyes,
and sits down of his own accord, death is better than a meal.
Unsolicited, they come of their own accord, greedy for the taste of flavors;
like flies, beggars do not leave even when driven away.
He who enters uninvited and speaks much when unasked,
that fool considers himself a favorite of the king.
Entering without being invited, speaking without being asked,
praising oneself, and disparaging others— these four are the characteristics of a minor offense.
Just as sufferings come upon embodied beings here even against their will, so too do pleasures; therefore, I consider there to be no benefit whatsoever in the wretchedness of anxiety.
They say that the ill-repute of others does not leave the interior of their homes;
yet poets say that your fame, though wandering freely through the three worlds, is indeed virtuous.
Even if they are unwilling, children should be made to practice discipline through the study of knowledge with great effort, just as health is attained through medicine.
Even if he is unwilling in his mind, even if he is staying in a foreign land,
a person is led by the wind arising from his own karma to wherever that fruit awaits.
Through lack of religious fervor, through improper marriages, through the neglect of the Veda,
and through the transgression of dharma, noble families fall into ignobility.

Having reflected thus— that this world is impermanent, a refuge-less place beset by birth, death, and disease, and embraced by the competitive striving for false objects— the virtuous, whose minds are stainless and whose intellects are fixed on the Dharma, have undertaken asceticism to bring about its cessation, following the faultless path of the Jinas.
Youth, beauty, life, the accumulation of wealth, sovereignty, and dwelling with loved ones are impermanent; a wise person should not be greedy for these.
The exposition on impermanence, the mockery of sense objects and so forth, the narration of remorse, and likewise the conduct of Time;
O Impermanence, though you are censured by the world, you are now worthy of homage,
for through your influence you bring about even the impermanence of sufferings.
One who has fixed their mind on impermanence grieves over a withered garland; but one whose intellect is fixed on permanence grieves over a broken vessel.
Those who know that things are impermanent do not come into being, yet they do so;
however, those by whom [the truth] is thus realized never come into being at all.
For the sake of protecting this impermanent body, which consists entirely of defects and is foul-smelling, I truly do not commit any evil.
Bodies are impermanent, and worldly prosperity is never eternal;
death is always present, so one must practice the accumulation of Dharma.
In this impermanent saṃsāra, where the company of loved ones is as fleeting as a wheel’s rotation,
a brother, a mother, a father, and a friend are merely encountered by chance upon the path.
Since victory is seen to be impermanent for two combatants,
and likewise defeat in battle, one should therefore avoid war.
Sleepless is the bad dream; falling from a tree onto a mountain slope is free of old age; trembling is devoid of darkness;

the moment of terror is unassailed by pain; the process of imprisonment is without shackles; death for living beings is full of life; and the pleasure of relying on a sovereign is [but] a taste of the earth.
The man who eats betel nut without first placing a leaf in his mouth will suffer poverty for seven lifetimes, and in the end, he shall have no abode with Viṣṇu.
Not criticizing the actions of others, protecting one's own duty,
compassion toward the miserable, and sweet speech in all circumstances.
One should be helpful to a constant friend even at the cost of one's own life;
when such a friend arrives at one's home, one should embrace them, give according to one's ability, and practice forbearance.
Maintaining close bonds with kinsmen, acting with integrity toward virtuous people,
and conforming to their wishes— such is the conduct of great-souled men.
Mortals blame even the blameless and praise highly even the unworthy; for the sake of their own wealth, what indeed will they not do?
This binding of her upper garment, fastened without a knot and without cause,
and this sudden, gentle smile— these two seem to cast aside her childhood.
Let this treasure simply decay within the depths of the mine, unobserved;
let it not suffer depreciation in value once it has come within the range of vision of merchants.
Having gazed with curiosity throughout the entire night upon the tireless and incessant amorous dalliances of the impassioned,
this flame of the lamp— devoid of clear light and appearing as if drowsy— now flickers as if it were an eye.
I remember your lotus-like infant face, with its unpredictable bursts of crying and smiles, its few shining, tender buds of teeth, and its charming, faltering, and incoherent prattle.
For what the wise say regarding those who are not appointed to the office of ministers is true:
these women are the ultimate stages of affection, flowing with the liquid of passion.

How could a wise person resort to wickedness— which lacks the excellence of asceticism, is devoid of fruit, and is abandoned by the virtuous— just as one would avoid a false woman who bears the name of a "wicked" (khala) man?
Not looking is itself a tender glance; jesting conversation is itself silence; even disdain is itself an application of effort—for love is indeed perceived, even when it is concealed.

The Primal Being, the Lord, having taken up— without destroying— the rain-cloud (which is unexhausted and impossible to extinguish), the ocean (the treasury of waters which is not solid), the wish-fulfilling gem (which is not inert), and the celestial tree (the tree of the gods), and likewise the cow Surabhi (who does not behave like a beast), He has made human beings those whose sole self-interest is the welfare of others.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, tell me: how can one speak of him as a "man" when his indignation is appeased by the mere failure of his enemies to conquer him?
The word "man" (puruṣa), which refers merely to the biological genus, has been used here;
yet he who is praiseworthy because of the qualities he has accepted is described with wonder.
He is a true man, indeed, whose very name— even his enemies— rejoice in pronouncing, as it were, when they hear it in an assembly, for it seems to swallow up their vital energies with its majesty.
How can your heart be so hard toward a form that is soft and deserves tender enjoyment, like the stalk of a *śirīṣa* flower?
The web of words of a eloquent speaker who has not investigated his task is in vain,
like the display of an archer whose arrow has missed the mark.
Inexpressible, undifferentiated, unlimited, and immutable—
the love of the virtuous is like Brahman, cutting away the very root of suffering.
Indeed, the birth of a son who relies on a bad person— being unliberated, dull-witted, and averse to the next world— is for the sake of hell and not for a happy rebirth.
Perseverance is the root of prosperity; my beak is like iron.
The days and nights are long; why does the ocean not dry up?
Perseverance is the root of prosperity, of the destruction of suffering, and of happiness. One who is undaunted becomes great and enjoys ultimate bliss.
Perseverance is the root of prosperity; perseverance is the highest happiness;
for perseverance is that which constantly impels one toward all goals.
For perseverance is that which constantly impels one toward all goals;
it makes whatever action a living being performs bear fruit.
O Wind, the entire universe breathes by your impulse and immediately withers in distress at your departure;
you are the body of the Supreme Lord, for which reason it is not fitting for you to accept as equal that which is fragrant and that which is foul.
How can we compare, even by a fraction, your face— which is ever-delighting to the eyes and gladdened by its loveliness—
to a lotus that sheds its beauty at night?
Just as the incessant trumpeting of elephants is heard in the forest,
I suspect that the lion who used to devour the young of lordly elephants no longer lives there.
Even though the god whose banner is the sea-monster constantly inflicts pain upon my mind, he is nevertheless dear to me,
provided that he strikes with reference to her who has eyes like those of a wine-jar.

Speech that is undetermined, by those who fear definitive conclusion and whose sole purpose is the pleasure of idle chatter, becomes an object of ridicule in the world when it fails to correspond with its intended result.
If a suitor, though endowed with beauty, is undesirable to the maiden,
a man seeking his own welfare should not give his daughter to him.
An earthquake occurring at both twilights brings misfortune to kings;
likewise, a preternatural glow in the quarters (digdāha), due to its yellow color, is another great omen of ill for monarchs.
He who does not fear the union with the undesired, the separation from the beloved, the insults of others, a life destitute of wealth,
or the continuous succession of calamities throughout many births— he alone fears austerity.
Due to union with the undesired and separation from the beloved,
human beings of little intelligence are afflicted by mental sufferings.
Even upon obtaining what is desired instead of the undesired, no auspicious outcome arises;
for where there is contact with poison, even that nectar leads to death.
For the wise, even an action that is not yet completed, when endowed with the proper method,
bring about its fruit— just like a great general.
If my listeners are free from envy, I shall speak; yet, one should fear much more from one's own side than from a powerful adversary.
For even when overcome by darkness, those possessing light shine by their own power for a short while, but never while the Maker of Day is present.
A king should be free from envy, protect his wives, be pure, and be without cruelty;
he should not indulge excessively in women, and he should eat what is wholesome, not what is unwholesome.
Free from envy, he should protect his wife; he should be generous, speak kindly, be gentle, and sweet-spoken toward women, yet he should not fall under their control.
Though powerless over her body, my heart has been placed under its own control by her,
as if deposited there by sighs discernible through the trembling of her breasts.
This person is not his own master over his existence or non-existence, like a wooden doll strung upon a thread;
he is indeed under the control of the Creator’s decree. Therefore, speak, for I am ready to listen.
When it is impossible to imitate, to deny, to surpass, or even to look upon the Lord of Splendors, friendship toward him is permissible only as a concession.
Of the needle, the wicked person and the good person act as its front and rear parts respectively;
the one creates a hole, while the virtuous other closes it up.
For one who has a compatible wife, heaven exists indeed in this very world; for one with an incompatible wife, it is hell—of this there is no doubt.

My speech is favorable, worthy of being sought, non-contradictory, beneficial, pleasant to hear, and endowed with the secrets of the scriptures; yet he turns a deaf ear to it—where is the god of love, and where is the gathering of virtues?
The ill-behaved flower-arrowed god [Kāma] leads the minds of men whose passion is deeply rooted even for favorable city-dames toward those who are unworthy vessels.
Indeed, what kind of king would not be victorious if fate acts in his favor? Yet, how was it that Jānakī, though separated from her husband and dwelling in the forest, experienced joy?
Through the arising of merit, a man obtains a wife who is compliant, pure-limbed, of noble birth, skillful, endowed with excellent character, and possessing the five auspicious marks.
Always favorable, ever-contented, skillful, virtuous, and discerning—
endowed with these very qualities, she is undoubtedly like the goddess Śrī herself in female form.
A gift should be given when fortune is favorable, for Hari will fulfill one's desires; a gift should be given even when fortune is adverse, for Hari will take away everything anyway.
When the Ordainer is favorable, even from the undesirable, the desirable arises without delay;
having drunk even poison, Śambhu attained at that very moment the state of being the Conqueror of Death.

Hari effortlessly subdues even those elephants with fierce trunks, whose temples are adorned by rut-fluid resembling massive boulders and who resound with the dense humming of swarms of bees wandering about; in the three worlds, it is their splendor alone that is weighty, not their deformed appearance.

O King, while your powerful fame travels alone to the ten directions, being guarded by you moment after moment, this Goddess of Fortune—who is daily bestowed upon supplicants—certainly never leaves your side; that these two should be thus is truly a great marvel.

A king whose dependents are satisfied by his constant attentiveness, who speaks sweetly, and whose subjects are devoted to his conduct; who is thoroughly skilled in the treatises of the most trustworthy experts—such a ruler remains radiant for a long time.
If it is not possible to follow the entire path of the virtuous, one should follow at least a small portion of it; one who remains on the path does not come to grief.
Having followed the deceased as far as the edge of the cremation ground, the kinsmen,
relatives, and friends here turn back after casting the man into the fire.
"Have mercy on these children; the forest region for sporting in the waters of the Śabara river has been overstepped. Abandon this timidity; before you lies the compassionate ascetic grove."
In the matter of bestowing grace, there is a great difference between the Goddess and the Mother:
the Mother binds one with a firm bond, while the Goddess cuts it asunder.
Only through the grace of the gods does a human being cast off his human state and attain divinity;
for how could iron, even when touched by an alchemical elixir, be expected to possess the resonance of gold?
Even during the eclipse of Rāhu, the star Tārā follows the moon; the creeper does not fall to the ground from the forest tree;
and the female elephant does not abandon the lordly elephant even when stuck in the mud. Let her walk and let her practice dharma, for women have their husbands as their masters.
Undertaking unsuitable actions, conflict with one's own kin, rivalry with the powerful,
and placing trust in women— these are the four doors of death.
A man who constantly desires fruits he is unaccustomed to is always restrained by fate;
at the time when the grapes ripen, the mouths of crows become parched.
Whether an action is improper or proper—what distinction is there for the Blessed One? Let devotion alone be most firm.
The venomous serpent pours forth poison, while the moon sheds thick nectar; yet the Great Lord bears both of them without distinction.
An unbecoming act indeed was performed by Paśupati when he severed the head of Brahmā;
yet his hand was not cut off, so that he may continue to write this illegible script.
If a person of virtue is employed by a deceitful-minded master in an unaccustomed task,
his virtues do not diminish thereby, just as those of a crest-jewel set upon the foot [of a king].
The limbs should not be raised or lowered, nor should they be moving; the feet should be steady, and the hips, elbows, head, shoulders, and ears should all be held in a state of symmetry.
Those conversant with the science of dance declare that grace consists in the beautiful repose of the limbs, the elevation of the chest, and a poise perfected through practice.
Not left over by the gods, not torn apart by Rāhu’s teeth, untouched by a dark spot, and certainly not eclipsed by the sun;
not swallowed by the new moons, nor surpassed by the face of a young woman—what is this lord of the arts (the moon) that rises upon this golden creeper?
Then the quarters echoed with the divine sound of kettledrums, and beauty was spread across the sky by the falling of celestial flowers;
the ocean, its arms in the form of restless waves at the shore, embraced the quivering earth as if to speak what was dear to her.
One who does not abandon the state of friendship toward friends or even enemies, and who remains equanimous, should be regarded as "bhavya" (worthy) and addressed with the word "namaḥ" (homage).
Just as a figure remains uncarved in clay or in wood,
and just as letters remain in a mass of ink, so does the Supreme abide within creation.
O you of unsurpassed majesty, whose power is concealed even from others,
and who are a friend to us despite our unworthiness— your glories are unprecedented.
In the absence of exertion, there is certain ruin of both what has been attained and what is yet to come;
through exertion, one obtains the fruit and achieves the fulfillment of one's goals.
O dear one, may your friends, together with the virtuous, live depending upon you—
just as all beings depend on the rain-cloud, or as birds depend on a tree laden with sweet fruit.
Without the proper placement of words according to the sūtras, lacking good commentary and a sound foundation,
our science of polity appears like the science of grammar when it is devoid of its introductory manual (Aṣṭādhyāyī).
The tufts of hair on his shoulders have not yet emerged; the sprouts of his claws are not very distinct; the budding of his teeth is slight in his mouth; and his roar is soft.
Although the cub of the lion-lord has not yet performed any action characteristic of his lineage, the great scent of his rut removes the blindness of the elephants.
"O friend, you indeed weep excessively every day with a loud voice; why do you subject yourself to such reproach in vain?
This heart of mine, having melted from contact with the coals of the bodiless Love, pours forth water externally; O steadfast one, these are not tears."
O Śiva, Śiva! Day by day your vine-like body trembles more and more, and yet the stream of tears does not leave the corners of your eyes.
Tell me, tell me, O lady of delicate limbs, who is this for whose sake your cheek no longer abandons its pervasive paleness?
Who, possessing a cultivated intellect, would act contrary to one who daily practices what is favorable?
The blue-throated Śiva bears upon his head the moon, which has allayed the burning in his throat caused by the poison.

Victorious is that certain lordly elephant of the forest on the banks of the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā), who is devoted to his herd year after year, who attracts the bees intoxicated by the fresh fragrance of the clusters of lotuses, who has tasted the sweet lotus-nectar, and who is a profound knower of the depths.
Separation, however long it may last, can be endured through the firmness gained by daily practice;
yet even a moment's obstacle to an imminent reunion is difficult to bear.
As the bridegroom approached her body, the mirror— which bore the heavy image of the leader—
was somehow not dropped from the hand of the bride, though it trembled under the excessive weight.
The essence of the meaning of words, though not explicitly proclaimed by sounds, delights through its manifestation as a clear aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), but not when that flavor is laid bare;
just as the swelling breasts of women captivate when partially veiled by silken garments fluttering in the breeze, but not so when their form is fully exposed.
The playful dalliance of love, which is a gathering for those heavy with affection, a source of excellence for the wine of the mouth, the first guest of the thoughts of the trusting,
and the occasion for the speech of immodesty toward women, has long been proclaimed as the sole teacher of intoxicating charm.
Though bashful, she does not entreat her husband, nor does she say anything to her circle of friends;
yet, as the Malaya breeze blows forth, the newlywed bride bears for a long time an inner void.

Having not accepted his conciliation, the woman feigned sleep and turned away; then, at dawn, hearing the loud cry of a cock, she somehow turned over and, as if blinded by sleep, embraced her lord with her eyes still closed like buds.
Why was the lover, as he fell at the feet of the proud woman whose own feet were stained with red lac,
instantly spurned by her?
Actions performed without the proper means, and those which are done perversely, become corrupted, like sacrificial offerings prepared by those who are impure.
The fortunes of kings, while they neglect the rising power of their enemies through indolence,
depart before long as if out of fear of public reproach.
Without fasting for three nights, without visiting sacred fords,
and without giving gold and cows, one is born indeed as a poor man.
In a composition characterized by alliteration, where could there be an equal to Gonandana?
For his very name is true to its meaning, in that it speaks of his own beauty.
Action that is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for consequences, loss, injury, or one's own human capacity, is said to be tāmasa.
Having carefully considered the consequences, the ripening of his actions,
and his own capacity for exertion, a wise person should either act or refrain from acting.
One should examine the consequences in undertakings that have consequences;
having deliberated, one should act, and not proceed with impulsive haste.
The moon of his face surely approached this great-souled one’s experience,
causing his mind— which was previously as still as the water of the great ocean— to become agitated and tremulous with longing waves.
Experience [the world], give away your wealth, honor those worthy of respect, and serve the virtuous;
for fortune is as flickering as the flame of a lamp tossed by an exceedingly harsh wind.
O fortunate young women, enjoy to your heart's content the pleasures of sporting at the edge of the flower-garland bower;
but for me, a sudden raid by the bees—the thieves of the garden—falls upon the site of this flower-grove.

Experiencing the seasonal festival like a swing, even though she was capable, the woman’s creeper-like arm became as if made of water when grasping the rope of another seat out of a desire to seize her lover’s neck.
By Dhananjaya, who possessed great power and was a master of the bow, that bow— being firm and unerring—
bowed down even while being pressed by his own strength, like a virtuous friend who yields under pressure despite his own distress.
The bees, intent on their constant coming and going near the long ponds where they have previously experienced such delights, announce that the buds of the lotus plants are now hidden by the waters.

The world, established in its experienced state of existence, desires pleasure and delights in it; therefore, I know that in this cycle of birth and death, liberation is achieved only through the conquest of passion.
It is experienced in this world that one who is weak, having been bound by those who are more powerful lords, must be dragged away like a powerless sacrificial animal at a ritual.

As if intending to bring along the mass of darkness that had remained silent, the women going to meet their lovers set their eyes upon every direction, those eyes whose collyrium had sprouted with beauty;
veiled in black cloths with the hue of smoke from the fire of passion, they departed for their beloveds with limbs adorned with ornaments that made no sound.
O beloved of the cuckoo, having abandoned the mango tree— which is full of nectar-like fragrance and enveloped in ever-new, beautiful blossoms—
how can your mind harbor such pride toward the fruitless pippala tree?
Māra reflected: "How indeed could she, though renowned for her supreme delight in passion, remain devoted to her husband?
Why was he, who committed the sin of killing such a helpless young wife, abandoned even by that beloved?"
What person possessed of discernment would resolve upon following [her husband] in death— a practice belonging to the nature of women—
having abandoned the vow of taking up the staff, which is the means for liberation from saṃsāra?
The variegated beauty of the rain-cloud, which wears a circle of bows and whose garment is overspread by the canopy of light from various gem-studded earrings, followed [the king],
stealing away the pride of Balarāma’s own body.
Followed by his own people yet carried away by others, the body of this man— who,
though holding office, is like a corpse— is neither heard nor seen by that one of evil intellect.
Even if, by some stroke of fate, she does not follow her husband, she must nevertheless preserve her virtue; for through the breach of virtue, she falls into ruin.
About to follow after the daughter of the Sage, his progress suddenly checked by decorum,
he returned again as if he had already gone, even though he did not move from his place.
Devoted to the slaughter of bandits in battle, he should exert his prowess;
for him, there is no other duty whatsoever than the eradication of bandits.
Women who are attached to those who have turned away from them, who are both humble and haughty, who are passionate toward those who are dispassionate,
who are addicted to deceitful speech, and who harbor doubts regarding true integrity.
But when he is devoted, joyful, and contented, the lord of the earth,
the protector of the land, conquers the earth even with a small army of his own.
Even when won over by virtues, subjects do not submit without the use of force;
even when held upon one's lap, the lute does not sound its sweet, melodious notes unless it is struck.
Delight the king, and never, even knowing his faults, provoke the subjects to anger; remaining embraced by a firm foundation through affection for these two, abide in your established position.
People feel affection when one's virtues are praised in their absence, and living beings do not fear [the practitioner]; this is the supreme sign of success.
The twilight is full of passion, and the day stands before it;
oh, how strange is the course of fate, for even so, there is no union.

The courtesan of the western quarter drove away the sun from his abode in the sky— even though he possessed a body that was full of passion for her eyes and brought comfort by dispelling heat— just as one casts out a man who has lost all his wealth.
With her limbs seized by a fierce separation from you that moves with passion,
she is like the slender-bodied Gaurī, who was left with only half her form remaining by the enemy of Tripura.
I perceive the stain upon the Lord of the Lunar Mansions as his hair-braid loosened from kissing the face of the night, as he hastens toward her out of passion, having leaped across the ocean.
Affection for women is in vain, and likewise pride in women is in vain; "I am always dear to her," and "she is always dear to me."
"O well, this is indeed worthy of you, who are concealed by a deceptive facade;
for it is through your delusion regarding the true path that he has been caused to fall."
Having obtained association with one who is suitable, everyone rejoices;
just as the sun, the treasury of light, does during the day, so too does the moon, the maker of night, at night.
By that convention, the ointments, the flowers, the women who had become indignant toward their husbands, and the flames of the lamps simultaneously awakened the long-slumbering god of love.
One should subdue a powerful person by conciliation, a wicked person by opposition,
and an enemy of equal strength either through diplomacy or by force.
In every forest, upon the lovely lower lips of the forest-row brides— lips possessing the intense passion of a fresh flush—
the rows of petals of blooming *bāṇa* flowers shone forth intensely, like the playful glances of beautiful-eyed women.
Beholding Rāma following the forest retreat, shedding tears, and appearing withered like a garland of joyless lotuses,
even the day felt the heat within from the sun’s rays, and the night too bore dew-drops like tears.

Day after day, following the forests and the mountains, seeing Rāma exceedingly dejected and devoid of rest because he could not behold Sītā—then this mountain, though composed of thunderbolts, did not split in two; and the earth, though capable of enduring everything, did not crack asunder.
O Lord of the Gods, since you yourself dance before me while playing the musical instrument, [I am filled with joy].
And since your wing is worshipped by the Immovable One (Śiva), you, O peacock, are supremely blessed.
Whoever is an adversary king capable of crushing him— who is struck down at every moment like the surging waves of the ocean— may he seize his fortune.
In the MSS_1513-1, the woman whose husband has gone abroad is described as being full of longing, yet not distinguished by many different states;
whereas in the MSS_1513-2, the woman whose husband is returning from a foreign land is likewise described as being simply joyful.
By instructing through Dharma, through legal procedure, through established custom,
and by means of the fourth, justice, he shall conquer the earth bounded by the four quarters.
May my heart rest upon the goddess of the Kadamba tree, who frequents the groves of thickets, whose hips are adorned with a yellow garment, and who delights in the sweet warbling of the flute.
He who, with a mind devoid of discernment, grieves for one who has departed or died,
is like one who builds a dam after the water has already flowed away, or casts a net after a snake has already gone its way.
What is the use of that parrot-like knowledge which, devoid of actual practice, merely pleases the world through rote recitation alone?
That which has been performed by the gods and that which has been performed by the sages should not be performed by men; rather, one should perform the action prescribed for them.
He who does not disclose a secret regarding tasks that have been undertaken attains success therein, just as the monkey did in the midst of the water.
A lowly person, like a bee whose eyes are blinded by the scent of ichor, follows the elephant's cheek even when struck by its ear; such a base individual does not take account of the insult.
Follow the shore of the lake; why harbor enmity here toward yourself? O proud *cātaka* bird, drink a few drops of water!
For the ancient rain-cloud has been driven away by the winds of dissolution, while this new cloud mercilessly releases its mass of hailstones.
If an unmarried girl enters the house of one who has not yet performed the marriage rite,
his ancestors fall from heaven, even though they were established there by those meritorious deeds.
O Hero, this horse of yours, possessing unflagging speed and peerless, as if ashamed of its shadow and other steeds,
shrouds the Lord of Day with the dust raised by its hooves.
Crookedness, dishonesty, meanness, and fickle-mindedness—
those faults which exist in men toward their friends are considered virtues in courtesans.
Falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, backbiting directed toward the king,
and the persistent speaking of falsehoods against one's teacher are equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Falsehood, flattery, and the acquisition of wealth—this is a great combination;
truth and learning—this combination brings about poverty.
"O Hero, how can those women who say that falsehood is truth, and likewise that truth is falsehood, be protected by men in this world?"
Untruthfulness, rashness, deceit, foolishness, excessive greed,
impurity, and mercilessness are the faults inherent in the nature of women.
Skill in falsehood, cruelty, a mind that insults the virtuous, a disposition toward impropriety, deceit regarding dharma, and even the cheating of one's own teachers;
speech that is charming and sweet when face-to-face but changes when out of sight—these are the manifesting glories of the Great King of the Kali Age.
This is a falsehood, a complete falsehood: that the moon is born from the ocean. Surely this ignoble one has emerged from the *kālakūṭa* poison;
for otherwise, tell me, friend, how could there be in him this power of delusion, which is cruel and capable of burning the heart, yet so sweet?

"When one is untruthful, when dharma has been destroyed, or when one does not wish to listen to what is unpleasant—then neither the pleasant nor the beneficial should be spoken; those who do so are censured by the virtuous."
Having gathered together in a multitude of embodied beings, variegated by many destinies and crowded with the distinctions of various births, and intent upon manifold and diverse activities,
this host of living beings— enjoying the fruits of various karmas acquired in the past and assuming diverse bodies— constantly wanders like an actor upon the stage of birth.
One whose mantra is practiced with many different states of mind becomes detested by practitioners of mantra;
because of his lack of mental stability, he is neglected by them in the performance of rites.
The sins accumulated over many births of men perish by merely bathing in the Gaṅgā; they immediately become a vessel for merit.
What purity is there for one who licks honey that arises from the slaughter of many living beings, which is the leavings of barbarians, defiled by impurity, and placed in a vessel smeared with filth?
For this body, which is corrupted by manifold defects, there is one great virtue:
that it follows exactly the way in which one conducts it.
He who, being attached to its flavor, declares that honey— which is corrupted by many defects— is free from those defects, is an ocean of untruth whose intellect has perished.
Having discerned with a disciplined mind the stain of falsehood along with its defects in various ways,
those fortunate ones who fear the suffering of existence abandon it and resort to the Jaina doctrine, which brings about happiness.

That knowledge by which all reality is perceived as endowed with qualities through manifold methods— knowledge distinguished by the division of the sensory and the non-sensory— is proclaimed by the Lords of Jinas for the benefit [of beings].
For indeed, accumulated over many existences, these unions and separations with the pleasant and unpleasant, as well as misfortunes and successes, are fashioned here by karma;
they always occur for embodied beings in all these states of existence as they sink in the ocean of birth, where old age and death are the waves.

O beautiful lady, this embodied being, driven by the power of deeds accumulated in the past, wanders incessantly through the womb of a woman within this cycle of existence— born from manifold impurities, always teeming with swarms of worms, filled with various and intense pains, censured by the wise, and difficult to endure amidst the perils of calamity.
A certain person of manifold and evil nature, displaying a false guise of asceticism, possessed a variegated character and was prone to the quarrels of monkeys.
He who has won many battles and enters into a treaty,
his enemies quickly come under his control through his majesty.
That which is separated by many kingdoms is cast aside and does not fight;
for that which has the thorn of an enemy within is like one with an internal thorn and is not fit for battle.
Bearing many-colored words like the lightning of speech, may she,
with her radiant qualities, always abide among those who are unerring and ever devoted to the essence.
I bow my head to this ocean-like assembly, a unique and inviolable sacred ford of the teachers, filled with many jewels of learned men and delightful with the waves of logic and the Vedas.
Many treatises must be known, yet time is short and obstacles are many;
therefore, one should cultivate that which is essential, just as a swan extracts milk from the midst of water.
He who does not possess this scripture— which cuts through manifold doubts, reveals hidden truths, and is the eye for all— is indeed blind.
O beloved, behold at the edge of the forest the lovely lotus-face of a woman playing a multi-holed wind instrument, which delights both the eyes and the ears.
The musical instrument with many holes, which is beautiful and known as "Rishi," and which is always to be worshipped by the Wielder of the Discus— he who knows this is a wise man.
There are many hooded serpents intent on devouring frogs;
indeed, this Śeṣa alone is capable of supporting the earth.
"O friend, my husband is endowed with many qualities of a leader; if he alone were to become my lover, my life would be fruitful."
"O auspicious lady, for what reason do you wither your body—so tender as a lotus stalk—with this vow? Why do you seek to propitiate that servant who, longing for your favor, already awaits it?"
Such is my joy when my limbs are touched by this sprout of a noble family; what ineffable bliss would it produce in the heart of that fortunate man from whose body he has grown?
What is not sufficient for this purpose: the total avoidance of meat?
For even when one's own limb is lacerated by a mere blade of grass, it causes intense pain.
O slender-limbed one, by means of these two breasts, which are marked by the arrangement of two jars and which emerge like a youthful elephant, you have become like a pond rippling with waves.
O Aśoka tree, if you are not immediately graced by this foot— tender as a fresh lotus and resonant with the tinkling of jeweled anklets— you bear in vain a longing shared by all amorous women.
By him, while your son was fast asleep in the middle of the forest,
his head was struck off with a sword by raising [the blade] to the topknot with his hand.
With this essential form and with your five flower-arrows,
deluding both men and women, bring about the eternal creation.

O noble lady, because you accept and cultivate this Dharma alone— having turned your mind away from the objects of wealth and desire— the Dharma today appears to me as the preeminent essence of the three goals of life.
By this [puruṣa], a person takes on and relinquishes bodies;
by this, one experiences joy, sorrow, fear, suffering, and happiness.
By this, one becomes preeminent and the members of the assembly are liberated;
for where the one deserving of censure is censured, the sin goes to the perpetrator.
Having reflected upon that which, by means of this mortal body, bestows happiness in both worlds, one should perform it; otherwise, action is to be abandoned.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, do you perhaps find pleasure in the mind of this youth, the king,
to sport together in the succession of gardens shaken by the breezes from the waves of the Siprā?
A person whose garments and ornaments have been perfumed with this king of formulations,
and whose body has been incensed, brings the three worlds under his control.
With his splendor increased by this yoga, and not yielding his own station to another,
he practiced the conduct of the sages while bearing his weapons, through recitation, fasting, and ritual ablutions.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, the stars surely shimmer as fragments of counter-weights to complete the deficiency of the moon, which was defeated in the scales by your face.
O messenger, by this lower [state] which is free from passion, like a Buddha,
emptiness has been declared to you without artifice regarding all things.

By this [king], the state of having fulfilled all desires was achieved; the wish-granting cow and the celestial tree, whose purposes were already attained, reached the pinnacle of their generosity by mutually providing water for irrigation and fresh shoots for consumption.
O slender one, along with this youth of yours, Indra’s love for you has reached its highest peak— indestructible like the string of the flower-arrowed god reaching the tip of his bow.
I shall dwell together with him on the shores of the ocean, rustling with groves of palm trees,
where the drops of perspiration are dispelled by breezes carrying the fragrance of clove blossoms brought from other islands.
By this, indeed, it is accomplished; this is my own prowess as well.
Knowing this, he who should act accordingly—his intentions will be fruitful.
In this very manner, three auspicious marks resting on the neck are favorable; likewise, the pair of curls on the forehead, resembling the moon and the sun, bring about prosperity.
Lack of sovereignty, thirst, a wife, farming on a road, and farming in a field—these three; a pendulous belly, and witnesses—these five are misfortunes that do not cease.
Apart from impropriety (*anaucitya*), there is no other cause for the disruption of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Indeed, adherence to well-known propriety is the supreme secret (*upaniṣad*) of rasa.
That passion which consists of improper attachment to maidens and the wives of others is indeed the foremost of the six internal enemies of the lords of the earth.
That man who does not abandon virtuous conduct, even if it is bitter within and slight in weight,
becomes immediately venerable to the whole world, like a mustard seed.
Human love is always observed to be bitter within;
only divine love does not leave us with frustrated hopes.
Having contracted the tongue and inserted it into the cavity between the inner skull-bones,
one should drink the nectar with the Khecarī-mudrā, while fixing the gaze upon the space between the eyebrows.
Because it is the locus of the affection of the couple— the very essence of their inner faculties—
this singular knot of bliss is called "offspring."

Even in the presence of their elders and attendants, those skilled in the ways of unchaste women recognize the transformation of their inner hearts by means of a glance sweet with the sidelong movement of a knitted brow.
Even a straw effigy, though devoid of an internal organ, was honored by the master of the field as being capable of warding off deer.
O dull-witted lord of the ocean, you bear within yourself a certain, subtle shimmer of pearls; yet from afar, you display only the vomiting of salt water.
That conch shell, indeed harsh and bearing crookedness within,
should be highly esteemed only when it emits a "hum" sound while being blown.

O frail one, that fortunate youth by whom your face was drunk—its throat cooing inwardly as it cried out again and again, "Release me!"; its eyes rolling; its cheeks mostly smiling; its bimba-like lower lip dripping with nectar; its sprout-like fingertips waving; and its creeper-like brows dancing—that youth, indeed, am I.
Some trees possess fragrance within, some in their leaves, some likewise in their sprouts, some in their roots, some in their bark, some in their fruit, and others in their flowers.
Yet, nowhere was any tree seen that bore such complete and pervasive fragrance in every limb as you, O sandalwood tree, who have been made into a mass of excellence.
Even when the heart of a virtuous person is stained by internal anger due to the wicked deeds of others, auspicious words alone emerge from his outward actions in their true meaning.
Even when the interior of the ocean is parched by the extremely fierce flames of the submarine fire, its waves constantly manifest, yielding pearls.
Women are cruel within but gentle-faced, with unfathomable hearts;
they are like food prepared with poison—poisonous within but pleasant on the outside.

May Murajit, who has devoured the vast vessel of the universe with a row of tongues in the form of the flames of rising internal wrath, whose deep roar resounds within the womb of the cavernous earth,
and who possesses the form of a proud lion— may he protect you, making the sky appear as if filled with smokeless smoke by the circles of radiance from his mass of hair!

I know that, having heard of your passion for the splendor of giving and your heroism, the ocean—bearing as it were internal grief—rolls incessantly; and the golden mountain, remaining as if in meditation, does not flow [with its streams]. One fears the striking of the churning-stick, while the other fears the blows of the thunderbolt.
He who does not hold counsel with those who move within the inner apartments,
nor with the king's wives, shall become a favorite of the monarch.
The superintendent of the harem and the treasury, as well as those dismissed by enemy envoys,
shall not enter into association with the king except by the sovereign's command.

Having established the regulations for the women of the harem and guarding against lapses at every step, I, now afflicted by old age, follow the king’s entire conduct through the administration of justice.
In battle you act as the protector of the inner apartments; toward the citizens you behave like a son; Fortune always acts as a mistress to you.
O Lord of the Earth, beheld by your beloved women as if they were seeing the moon, you traverse this world with the gait of Indra.
One should appoint someone equal to a father in the inner apartments and someone equal to a mother in the kitchen;
one should entrust the cattle to those equal to oneself and personally attend to the cultivation of the fields.
May those of noble intellect, desiring internal illumination and wishing to discern the existent from the non-existent, increase their affection for this lamp of well-spoken verses.
Where is there any thought of blossoming for a campaka tree whose roots are being scorched by the sands of a parched desert?
Generally, for those dwelling in an unsuitable place, the highest good is merely the preservation of one's own life.
O wise one, alas, by whatever sequence the breast of young women— which bears the mark of youth— is agitated within,
these two breasts, having relied upon that very rule, rise up and suddenly strike from their split center.
Exuding a parching dryness within their bodies as if vomiting blood through the oozing wounds inflicted by insects,
the trees— soiled by the loss of their shade and submerged in calamity— seem to have set out to go toward the cremation ground.
For those whose minds possess inner contentment, there is prosperity at every step; for those whose minds are inwardly defiled, happiness is difficult to find even in a dream.

He does not veil his eyes with tears of inner satisfaction so that he may hear [the praises] with them; nor, his body hairless, does he produce a row of horripilation—the very root of bliss—upon his limbs;
nor, fearing a collapse of the earth, does he nod his head. Thus we do not know how the Lord of Serpents manifests his joy while listening to his glories.
O bull among elephants, whose limbs are scorched by the intense heat of the fire of separation arising from within, abandon your grief!
Who is capable of wiping away the letters written by the Creator’s own hand upon the tablet of the forehead?
Though she meets him within, she departs outside; though touched, she offers embraces;
and having given her lip, she weeps only dryly—she who is thus unattainable even through ascetic penance because of her playful charms.
What can assistance do for those who lack inner substance?
Even if it stands upon Mount Malaya, a bamboo reed remains a bamboo reed and never becomes sandalwood.
Instruction does not take root in those who are devoid of inner substance;
through association with the Malaya mountain, a bamboo stalk does not become sandalwood.
A kingdom is sustained by ministers who possess inner substance, who are not crooked, who are very affectionate, and who have been well-tested, just as a mansion is supported by sturdy pillars.
Even one who possesses inner substance surely departs along with his state of being a petitioner;
otherwise, by whom could the greatness of embodied beings in that condition be perceived?
Concealing even their longing for the commencement of love-making within,
the couple recognizes one another merely by the flickering of their eyes.
Even a pearl, though situated within, unblemished, well-rounded, and exceedingly beautiful, meets with bondage if it is internally perforated.

May the head of Dhūrjaṭi—whose interior has taken in the waters of the Gaṅgā, which possess the redness of rows of jewel-sprouts moving with great freedom, and which shines like a sprout upon the hoods of the lord of serpents—be for the prosperity of those setting out on the journey to the city of liberation; it serves as a full jar uniquely capable of quelling all obstacles.
The end-maker (Death) stands as the oppressor of the living being who is beset by continuous calamities;
thus, a person worthy of liberation, recognizing that existence is to be abandoned, rises up from it.
The Ender, the Destroyer, Death, the netherworld, the submarine fire, the razor’s edge, poison, the serpent, and fire—all these are on one side; women are on the other.
O southern breeze, by giving yourself to the one who accepts the golden vine-like body of my beloved, alas, you are giving away my very life; why then are you not "southern" (generous) in this?
And at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone, he attains My state; there is no doubt about this.
"For at the time of their end, living beings become deluded"—such is the ancient Vedic revelation;
by acting thus toward the world, the king has made that revelation manifest before his very eyes.
For even Death awaits the time of death for living beings;
however, there is no fixed rule regarding the time for the creditor.
How small a difference do the wise say there is between the *Raghuvaṃśa* and the *Kirātārjunīya*?
The wise say that the difference between the *Raghuvaṃśa* and the *Kirātārjunīya* is precisely this much.
The slender-limbed maiden has embraced a youthfulness full of grace, which is the inner soul of the god of love and the tutelary deity of the erotic sentiment.
For those who are the king’s intimate attendants, who are deceitful and seize the property of others, generally become his servants; he should protect these subjects from them.
To pacify the darkness of obstacles, we meditate upon that certain portly radiance— tranquil, purifying, and of inconceivable majesty—
which is a man in body and an elephant in face.
A wicked person whose impurities are internal is not purified even by hundreds of ritual baths at sacred fords,
just as a vessel that has held liquor is not cleansed even when it has been burnt.
That series of flames from the fire of passion which has entered within—how can it be suppressed here by applications of sandalwood paste?
That application of paste upon a potter’s kiln serves only for its own heating, and not for the alleviation of heat.
What is the use of internal qualities if even two or three witnesses for them are rare?
That quality of song is truly such that it captivates even the deer wandering in the forest.
If Hari is within, what is the use of penance? If Hari is not within, what is the use of penance?
If Hari is both within and without, what is the use of penance? If Hari is neither within nor without, what is the use of penance?
Having fashioned a great sword— deeply set in its hilt, devoid of visible markings, broad, thick in the middle,
with a massive blade and an exceedingly sharp edge— for the purpose of cleaving the chest of the Rākṣasa, the King of the Gods was filled with great joy.
The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of a composition that fails to reveal its hidden meanings and lacks clarity,
just like that of a river, does not bring delight to those who possess the sense of taste.

He leads them into the inner chamber, causing their hair to stand on end through his touch and making their mouths emit sighs; he leaves the city women with wounds upon their lips—is this a lover, or rather is it this winter wind?
Having seen Kṛṣṇa as a thief inside the house, one woman went to her mother after locking the door;
seeing him there as well, bound with a rope to a mortar, she stood motionless.

As the husband entered with his form concealed within the water for the sake of the pleasure of embracing the young woman, the purity of the waters became an obstacle; for the clarity of reservoirs is indeed useless [when it hinders what is desired].
Though concealing her hardness with her own translucent luster, she, through her innate sweetness,
spreads a delicious flavor among those who know how to taste it, like white sugar enveloped by its own qualities.
"O King, it is said that one who is inwardly corrupt yet outwardly patient causes all manner of misfortune;
Śakuni and Śakaṭāra are the two examples seen in this regard."
Those who conceal their own virtues remain in the hearts of others;
it is they alone who provide the complete meaning for a garland of flowers.

Within the heart of the ascetic, who is fond of peace, there shines the inner light—the light of the Self—which is dense with blossoming bliss, wherein the vital breath is restrained within the internal channels and has transcended the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
This light appears as if manifested under the guise of the clearly visible third eye on the forehead of the Lord whose crest is the crescent moon, illuminating the entire universe.
Cursed be the life of that man who, burning with inner fire yet powerless against his enemies, merely continues his lineage.

I repeatedly remember her half-glances, as she was unable to say anything appropriate due to a succession of internal, heavy indignations, while the circles of her breasts quivered with indistinct *hūṃ* sounds.
Having declared before the inner circle of this king of beasts that I am his servant, how can I now make myself light?
Do they not know how the quarters of the sky have been filled with pearls shed from the frontal globes of elephants torn open by my claws?
This speech of yours, naturally graceful yet hidden within its inner meaning,
is as difficult to discern through mere outward transformation as wine laced with poison.
The dull-witted person dwells within the dull-witted, like a deer within the cool-rayed moon; but he who is not dull-witted, even when entered by the dull-witted, emerges from it as if from the sun.
Having entered [the service] of a master, the wise should by all means seek a special distinction;
for who indeed would not simply fill his own belly?

The mountain streams produce great delight, with elephants submerged within them, their sprouting roots trampled by young elephants; they are fragrant on all sides, their waves shimmering from the breath of intoxicated buffaloes; and their banks, bordered by thickly shaded marshy grounds, provide a place for herds of deer to sleep upon rocks cooled by the spray of water.

Until midnight, the nights—during which pairs of *kokila* birds on the riverbanks call out to one another with throats strained by long, drawn-out cries born of inner passion—are passed with difficulty;
meanwhile, the grounds near the village are noisy with swarms of jackals awakened by the cold, and the nights are stretched thin with the anxieties of the wives of travelers.
Who has not been deceived by a wicked person, who is foul within but pleasing on the outside, like the fruit of the mahākāla tree?
Through association with those who are inwardly corrupt, even one who is learned becomes defiled;
just as the ear, through contact with the eye, has become the abode of crookedness.
When her pair of eyes—soiled within, crooked, flickering, and gliding to the very tips of the ears—is beheld, as well as a wicked person, how can there be happiness?

In the presence of her husband, the young woman maintains a compliance bound by heavy virtues, though she is moist with the inner sentiment of passion; she possesses a harsh outward appearance, like a leather water-skin.

May the sound of the flute of the enemy of Kaṃsa destroy your misfortunes— the sound which causes the falling of the mandāra flowers swaying from the heads of the inner-moheras as they reel, which is the great mantra for the paralysis, attraction, pride, and joy of the deer-eyed women, and which is the downfall of the irresistible calamities and sorrows of the gods who were being tormented by the arrogant demons.

The ocean, constantly rolling within its depths those countless drops that were seized by the clouds and brought back as circles of waves, clearly brings those water-drops to the state of pearl-jewels; for generally, even one who is insignificant is honored by masters when he arrives having been received with respect by another.
Like a house with a serpent hidden within, like a forest containing a fierce lion, or like a lake filled with crocodiles despite being graced by the shade of lovely lotuses— so too,
the minds of kings, inhabited for a long time by base and ignoble men who are treacherous in slandering the noble, are entered with difficulty and trepidation.
As the fire of suffering, which has been latent within me, is about to blaze forth fiercely today,
delusion first envelops me like a rising column of smoke.
If a female cat or a bitch dwells within the royal palace,
does the elephant become less significant for that reason even though it is bound outside?
O mango tree, you harbor bitterness within while assuming sweetness in your outward appearance; O deceptive tree, it is only right that you have been cast out by the people.

May the Blessed One, the Supreme Primordial God, the self-born Great Poet of the drama of erotic love, grant us well-being— he who, knowing the sentiments and emotions of the three worlds both within and without, causes all multitudes of embodied beings to dance.
This wicked man, imagining himself to be a scholar within, displays his spite toward these pearls of well-spoken verses;
indeed, this bumblebee seeks out a wound on the limbs of passionate women that are otherwise sources of all delight.
If a female cat or a bitch enters the royal palace,
why is the lordly elephant standing outside deprived of his purpose?
For these women are full of poison within, yet charming on the outside;
by whom were they fashioned, having the appearance of *guñjā* berries?
The three worlds dwell within Viṣṇu; he too lies upon the lord of serpents; that serpent also rests on a single portion of the ocean; and Agastya once swallowed even that ocean in a single mouthful.
Yet, O King Nṛsiṃha, this [ocean] now plays the role of a mere firefly in the sky of your fame, and this ear-lotus of yours shines as a sight to be beheld.
Now that the moon has vanished, that very same night-lily, its beauty now only a memory, no longer delights my sight;
surely the sorrows produced by the departure of a beloved are exceedingly difficult for a weak woman to bear.
There are many holes within and many thorns on the outside; how could the fibers of the lotus stalk not be fragile?
This excessive attachment, acquired through the internal hollows of wicked lineages and difficult to abandon, would not lead to the attainment of auspicious results for one's own family;
rather, it leads to the destruction of those whose bodies are entangled in the garlands of flames from the fire produced by mutual friction caused by the winds of summer.
Within you there is that blazing fire, and on all sides are terrifying, formidable sea-monsters;
alas, O Ocean, since your body is thus full of peril, how can you be resorted to?

The streams of tears from these lotus-eyed ones emerge, their surfaces rippling as they first touch the inner lids, then slightly swelling as they gather at the tips of her lashes, and finally scattering into droplets; in this gradual progression, they perfectly manifest the anguish of her heart through their own increasing weight.
For the destruction of internal darkness, verbal cognition is useless;
indeed, darkness does not perish by merely talking about a lamp.
For all living beings tormented by internal thirst, this world consists of a forest fire; that which is within them is situated without.
When the mass of rays emitted by the moon, having reached near and far, abandoned its curvature,
the edge of the horizon shone as if breathing forth, due to the cessation of the burden of darkness that had issued from it.

Your eye possesses whiteness at its tip and blackness in its center; by possessing this dual nature, it has entered into a conflict with your ear. Thus, you have attained the state of Kurukṣetra itself, embodying the conflict between Karṇa, Arjuna, and Kṛṣṇa. O young woman, the mere attainment of you is reckoned as the supreme blessing.
The wise find delight in extremes; they do not find delight in the middle. They say that reaching an extreme is happiness, while the interval between the two extremes is suffering.
Before [death], one should remember Viṣṇu, the bestower of contentment and the destroyer of calamities;
Bhīṣma, lying upon his bed of arrows, remembered the one whose banner bears Garuḍa.
No end to this collection of wonders is seen anywhere;
for as much liberation as we attain from the boundaries of the petty ego-sense,
so many wonders become manifest to us.
There is no end to thirst; contentment is the supreme happiness.
Therefore, the wise regard contentment alone as true wealth in this world.
Even a man of the lowest caste is worthy of honor if he possesses abundant wealth; conversely, even one born in the family of Brahmā is treated with contempt if he is destitute.
When even an outcaste serves as a witness in a legal dispute, an ordeal is not appropriate there;
how much less so in the case of forest deities?
Even when reduced to its final state, the great one does not abandon his own qualities due to their purity;
nor does a conch shell relinquish its whiteness even after being swallowed and released by a peacock.
With the sky resounded by the noise of her many swaying ornaments—mostly large skulls, thigh-bones, and armlets jingling harshly as they are strung with entrails;
her body terrifying with the weight of her dangling breasts, which are formidable due to the thick mass of blood-slime she has drunk and then vomited; she runs about, arrogant with pride.

With her mass of hair tossed upward by the gusts of wind from the wings of vultures greedy for the flesh on her lips— vultures that scatter the banks of clouds by the weight of her breasts moving like a garland of entrails— she approaches from afar, having opened her mouth with a terrifying, loud laugh, while the throngs of Siddha women flee in terror from the path of the stars.

Having fashioned auspicious amulets from intestines, wearing visible crests made from the red lotuses of women’s hands, and suddenly fastening garlands of heart-lotuses, these female Piśācas— rejoicing, smeared with the saffron-paste of blood, and joined by their lovers— drink the wine of marrow-fat from skull-cups.

With his forefeet bound by his own entrails during the moments when his fainting fit subsides, his wounded limbs covered with weapons yet under his own control, and suppressing the bristling of his hair;
uplifting his own broken men and fiercely threatening the enemy warriors, this blessed man, the very abode of the Goddess of Victory, acts as a banner upon the great pillar of battle.
Having suddenly shaken off his fetters and violently unseated even his own charioteer, he has now emerged with a mind enraged by hearing the cries of the terrified horses;
tearing up hundreds of tree branches in the onset of his fury and snorting at the elephants in the stable, this wild elephant approaches here in haste—let the people be on their guard!
If blinding darkness oppresses you, O lotus-eyed one, the sole thread of the world,
then make the son of Vasudeva— whose conduct is nectar and who is supremely pure— your friend.
Seeing him blind, impoverished, and separated from his beloved, the Lord said, "Choose one boon.
He did not choose eyes, nor wealth, nor a wife; he chose the sight of his son, who was as beautiful as a royal umbrella—thus he spoke.
Just as the arrows of sidelong glances from playful women become fruitless upon reaching a blind husband,
so too the defects of the weekday do not prevail at night for Mars, the Sun, and Saturn.
He alone is blind who is devoid of sacred learning; he alone is a rogue who fails to provide for those in need;
he alone is dead who possesses no fame; and he alone is pitiable whose mind is not fixed on righteousness.
One should be blind at the time of blindness and likewise resort to deafness;
one should make a bow out of grass and sleep the sleep of a deer.
One should subdue an enemy who has come under one's control by means such as conciliation;
however, one should not show him compassion simply because he has sought refuge.
A truly great virtuous wife does not abandon her husband even if he is blind, humpbacked, afflicted with leprosy in his limbs, tormented by disease, or fallen into calamity.
The blind man, the hunchback, and the princess with three breasts—
all three achieved their goals through improper means while the karmic result stood directly before them.
The blind man, the hunchback, and the three-breasted princess—
even these attain success as long as Fortune favors a man.
A blind man, a hunchback, and a princess with three breasts—
when the Lord of the World is favorable, even these opposites become well-matched.
O beloved, because the world constantly and excessively devours the poison of darkness that causes great delusion,
the belly of the Lord of Herbs (the Moon) became bright yet possessed the luster of collyrium.
The sprout of darkness was born and grew without delay,
like the son of Hiḍimbā while she was sporting with Bhīma.
Resorting to blindness at the time of blindness and deafness at the time of deafness,
the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), who dwells in the navel of the illustrious Keśava, is their friend.
Between these two types of blindness, the blindness of being blinded by sense objects is the greater;
one who is blind in his eyes does not perceive, but one who is blinded by sense objects perceives nothing at all.
Like a blind man with a mirror, or like one whose hearing is destroyed by something beneficial,
he who is tormented by suffering and grief neither sees nor hears.
The path belongs to the blind, the path belongs to the deaf, the path belongs to women, and the path belongs to the bearer of burdens;
the path belongs to the king when he has not met with a Brahmin, but when he has met with a Brahmin, the path belongs to the Brahmin alone.

O Lord of Gods, grant the support of Your hand to me, a wretched man who am blind and whose great wealth of discernment has been stolen by the powerful thieves known as the senses, and who have been cast into the deep pit of the darkness of delusion.
