Like the blind, they do not perceive what is appropriate or inappropriate, what is beneficial or harmful;
they travel by that very same path along which kings are led.
Like the blind, the deaf, the mute, or those possessed by delusion,
like the lame— virtuous men dwell in the assembly of a king who does not favor them.
The assembly of kings becomes blind when devoid of learned men, mute when abandoned by poets,
and deaf when lacking singers.
I blind the world; I deafen it; I lead the wise and sentient to a state of insentience.
By this, the intelligent man does not perceive what ought to be done, nor does he hear what is beneficial, and even though he has studied, he cannot apply his learning.
We who sacrifice like beasts are sinking into blinding darkness;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a dharma higher than non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).
Even though he follows a path described by others and is to be served by others,
the king sustains himself through the affection of his people, which is unimpeded by his royal status.
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception, devours the matter like a blind man eating fish along with their bones.
Whether he be blind, deaf, afflicted with leprosy, or even of the lowest caste, let him accept that maiden along with the hundred thousand; he shall become a traveler to foreign lands.
For a king who is devoid of the scriptures is indeed blind;
one who is blind sees by means of his spies, but one bereft of the scriptures does not see at all.
Moving slowly due to the exertion of rubbing against the soles of feet and the slopes of full breasts, setting in motion the beautiful, heavy braids of the Dravidian women;
smelling the lotus-faces of the Siṃhalī women and kissing the cheeks of the Keralī women, the southern winds blow gently, carrying the fragrance of the Malaya mountains.
The food resembles a heap of *kiṃśuka* flowers; it is accompanied by nets of stones, smoky, and full of odors; the entire network [of vessels] is broken, as are the ivory pillars.
The clarified butter is very far away, there is no salt, the sound of the *tintriṇī* fruit is not heard, and indeed, my friend, there is no mention of edible foods—such is the meal I describe.
One should give food to a guest with faith, for that indeed bestows heaven; by giving a prastha of barley meal while accompanied by his family, a man went to the celestial realm.

Just as the most wretched commoners are led astray by each successive [claim] that "food is wealth" or "the earth is wealth," so too even those of pure intellect are deluded by this unstable foundation with each successive [claim] that "the earth is space" or "the sky is the abode of Brahmā."
There is no food, there is no water, and there is no chewing of betel;
in the mansions there is great excitement, yet [only] the beating of dry leather.

In your great house, for the satisfaction of Rāmacandra, the hosts of Brahmins partake of food: rice with pearls and gold, soups possessing the qualities of liquid gold, various fragrant vegetables mixed with fruits and molasses, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), clarified butter, curd, very firm cakes of many kinds, and whatever else is fit to be eaten.
Food has been ordained by the Creator as the sustenance for mortals;
disregarding that, a wise person should not pray for anything else at all.
Having sprinkled the food with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should sprinkle it around clockwise in the evening with the mantras "Truth, you... and "Righteousness, you...".

For food is the life-breath of living beings, but I am the refuge for those in distress; dharma is the wealth of men after death, while the virtuous are the protection for those fearing danger in this world.
Whether born from food or somehow born from fatigue on this earth,
this very sleep belongs to all people in the world.
The giver of food, the protector from fear, the giver of a daughter in marriage, the progenitor, and the one who performs the initiation ceremony— these five are remembered as fathers.
The gift of food is a great gift, but the gift of knowledge is even greater;
through food there is satisfaction for a moment, but through knowledge it lasts for as long as one lives.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of food;
by food is this entire world, both moving and unmoving, sustained.
When food burns, one should remove the flesh; when water burns, the blood;
when desire burns, the eyes. Sleeplessness is a cause of disease.
O Bhārata, the giver of food, the giver of water, and the physician who treats the sick— these three go to heaven even without performing a sacrifice.
One should protect food and drink from poison, especially that of a sovereign; for his security and well-being depend upon them, as do dharma and all other virtues which are rooted therein.
There, one should worship the Guru with food, drink, and the like, as well as with garments, ornaments, and decorations, and with various perfumes and garlands.
In that very same stomach where food and drink, as well as whatever is eaten, are digested,
why indeed would the embryo not also be digested?
Upon the destruction of food, the five elements in the body perish;
all beings on the surface of the earth originate from food.
Food is the root of strength for men, and life itself is rooted in strength;
therefore, a skilled physician should protect strength with diligent effort.
"Go quickly and give fine garments, gold, and various kinds of jewels to the brahmins on the riverbank."
A sacrifice lacking food burns the kingdom; one lacking mantras burns the officiating priests;
and one lacking gifts burns the patron. There is no enemy equal to such a sacrifice.
Flour is eight times more [nourishing] than grain; milk is eight times more than flour;
meat is eight times more than milk; and ghee is eight times more than meat.

A crow whose mouth is always full of grains and other foods, fruits, flowers, meat, fish, and so forth, brings success in one's desired aims upon being merely seen; it portends the enjoyment of delicious food and joy.
Even if it is constantly shaking food, excrement, fire, or cow dung in its mouth,
or even if it is being gazed upon from the left or the right, the bull certainly fulfills one's desires.
This crow, whose mouth is filled with food, excrement, flesh, and the like, bestows desired fruits;
it is auspicious for the accomplishment of mantras and other rites, for the acquisition of wealth by merchants and others, and for ceremonies such as marriage.
The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; he incriminates the one who eats with his food;
and the thief, when released by the king, transfers his guilt to the one who makes false claims during the confusion of the inquiry.

The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king.
From food all beings come into existence; from rain comes the production of food;
from sacrifice comes rain; and sacrifice originates from action.
From food arise both the red and the white; upon this the *jīva* is established.
The sense organs and the intellect are constantly satisfied by food.
"In the absence of food there is death; food comes from rice, rice from rain, and rain from austerity"—saying this, let him practice that austerity for the sake of immortality.
If one eats grain, even a body the size of an atom can be purified through ascetic penances;
but if one eats meat, even a body as large as the king of mountains cannot be purified because of its magnitude.
By food this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is sustained;
from food life-breath arises—this is perceptible, there is no doubt.
In food and drink, betel, fruit, flowers, and ornaments;
in clothing, ointments, incense, beds, and seats.
"Go quickly to another forest with haste; eat wild fruit, O blessed one! A glorious abode shines for you; do not perform such a base act.
O young elephant, do not enter this grove! I speak words of truth: you surely know that the lion, the crusher of the pride of lordly elephants, is sleeping here."
Having fixed one man in their hearts, they beckon another with their glances;
they discharge the flow of their passion toward one, yet desire another with their bodies.
Who else but you has been restrained by monkeys or men within the salt ocean? Who else has been drunk up by a single Brahmin using merely the hollow of his cupped hands?
Speaking thus, this lake constructed near the city vies intensely with the ocean through its loud laughter in the form of masses of foam descending with a sound like the roar of massive clouds.
One person performs the action, yet the scribe becomes defiled;
through the involvement with the female and male organs, the nose is cut off.
Let that other fire of the pot-born sage Agastya remain; it is his internal digestive fire which, when meditated upon, appears like the submarine fire (vāḍava) consuming fine silk.
That venerable belly is the ocean where schools of fish, sea-monsters, and crocodiles dwell, and where the sky, its interior unfilled, revolves with a roar along its western flank.
Thinking "it is another," she quickly raised her eye without any constraint;
but perceiving me, she became startled, covered her face, and bit her tongue slightly.

One who is deluded regarding the actions of others, yet is skilled in the actions of oneself— see how such a person does not understand anything other than suckling at the breast, just like an infant.
They constantly practiced two things that ought to be avoided at other times:
those women displayed boldness toward their husbands in private, while the others showed mercilessness toward the weak.
Sin committed in another field is destroyed in a field of merit;
sin committed in a field of merit will become as indelible as adamantine glue.
O simple one, turn your face away for a moment; this moon is composed of mere digits.
May he never, by transferring the impurity from his cheeks, bring about their equality.
If, out of fear that the loss of honor would lead to others seeking to harm one's own interests, this constitutes a lack of policy;
for even Śrīdhara, desiring prosperity for Bali, assumed the form of a dwarf to maintain his dignity.
A person thinks of one task with a pure mind day and night, yet the Creator ordains another, just as a master; it cannot be held back.
Thinking that the Creator of the universe might swallow the worlds fashioned elsewhere,
has she perhaps contracted her womb and placed it within the space between her two feet?
Except for Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā, and except for Hanumān,
the entire world was deluded by a hide as small as a doe’s hoof-print.
Having spent the night elsewhere, the sun arrived with its body intensely red, as if it had come to another woman;
seeing him at dawn, this lotus-pond became as if angry, its eyes—the blooming *hallaka* lilies—turning deep crimson.
"Friends, you gather flowers elsewhere while I remain here;
for I am not able to wander far. Be gracious, for I offer this salutation with joined palms."
"Is he going elsewhere? What talk can there be of that? Nor does he have such a friend who would not desire me and yet fail to come—alas, alas! What manner of course is this of Fate?
Thus, her heart swallowed up by these manifold fancies, the young woman tosses about within her chamber at night and finds no sleep.
For objects conceived in one way by wise men, O dear one, turn out quite differently through fate;
such is my conviction.
Things perceived in one way by the sages who have seen the Vedas turn out otherwise,
like the gusts of the wind.
In one way a beloved wife is embraced, and in another way a daughter with the same feeling;
thus the activity of the mind differs even toward objects that are otherwise identical.
This one who was our object has become otherwise for us, acting in a different way;
that which was to be performed by us has been performed by the Gandharvas.
The Vedic scriptures are one way, and the scholarly wisdom derived from them is another;
that peaceful state is one thing, yet people suffer in quite another way.
Otherwise, a wise person seeks his goal with an intellect pregnant with the teachings of the scriptures;
yet, like a master, he performs his past karma in a different manner.
Human desires are conceived in one way by a person,
but the courses of actions, their existence being ordained by destiny, turn out otherwise.
O fortunate one, as has been declared regarding the nature of things, she thinks of her son in one way and her husband in another, even though they are both equally real.
For people think of various things in one way,
yet the Lord creates and transforms them in quite another way.
For the friendship of one whose inner self is pure is of one kind,
whereas the speech of one whose mind is struck by deceit proceeds in quite another way.

"I am someone else; I have not asked you for anything, so let me drink from your lip just this once"—saying this with a whispering, plaintive voice, he tasted her [lip] with a forceful manner that involved pressing and crushing.
Something else was spoken previously, yet something else, inferior and flawed, was given instead; what is the use of such a fraudulent gift?
At other times, forbearance is the ornament of a man, just as modesty is for a woman; likewise, valor is the ornament in the face of humiliation, just as boldness is during sexual dalliances.

Without considering the sin of taking what belongs to another, the merciless gambler, devoid of consciousness, seizes that which is like his own life; because of this, he undergoes suffering for a long time.
He who suffers through the suffering of others and rejoices through the joy of others—
he alone is the Lord of the worlds, Hari, assuming a human form.
One being is unrestrained, while another is constrained by the scriptures;
for how can there be coexistence between light and darkness?
It is not tenable that one thing is sown and another is produced;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth.

How could he, dull-witted by his own lack of boldness, proclaim his own virtue as if it were the fault of another? It is said that he indeed acts out of necessity; fie on this state of supplication, which breaks the dam of the wise!
Another type, known as the *gopucchaka*, should be understood as being made of pure wood;
its mouth is to be pierced with an iron ring measuring three finger-breadths.
One should not, out of pride, desire a virtuous woman who has previously belonged to another.
Desiring virtuous women, Mahādeva became a eunuch in the Dāruka forest.
What indeed is the use of even the beauty of one who, upon encountering the prowess of another, does not attain firmness, like that of an ornament made of lac?
Fortune resorts to one man and then to another, and the earth likewise;
but Fame alone is a devoted wife to men, never going to anyone else.

Though she had drunk much wine, she was not intoxicated, for her mind was suspicious of her husband whose heart was fixed on another woman; indeed, the tranquility of the mind is the cause of true intoxication.
In youth, a mortal is deluded by one kind of intellect;
in middle age, he is deluded by another, and in old age, he finds pleasure in yet another form of thought.
That horse whose head is of one color and its tail of another,
or which is of various colors on its tail or its head, is censured.
By the substitution of other letters and by concealing the marks of composition,
a poet-thief is recognized among the virtuous even when his work remains unnamed.

Who in this world longs for another's wife? What is inaccessible by foot? Which element resides in the teeth? What is prayed for day and night by all men? Having seen a lotus-faced beloved woman in his own city, the King of the Yavanas suddenly asked his friend with great respect: "What is this that bites the banks of the Yamunā river? The answers are: *anyastrī* (another's wife), *pṛthivī* (the earth), *dantāḥ* (teeth), *jalam* (water), and *yārānadīdaṃśamā* (the biting of the Yamunā river). One who has acquired heat from another is base and generally difficult to endure;
even the sun does not burn as much as a mass of heated sand.
Even at other times, separation from a beloved causes torment;
how much more so on days when the clouds thunder with incessant and deep rumbling?
But when another is being sent forth, he who springs forward first,
saying "What shall I do?", he shall dwell in the royal residence.
The slanderer reaches the ear of one person and snatches away the life of another like an arrow;
he burns the heart even when he is merely stuck in the foot like a thorn.
"O enemy of Madana, show your favor by granting another limb; I am not able to bear the celestial river on my head, nor can I perform prostrations during the twilight.
Having spoken thus, as Umā—pierced by anger—began to tear apart her own body, may Śambhu’s arm, drawn by the forceful touch of her jar-like breasts as he restrained her, protect you.

He engages in even greater dalliance with other women; therefore, O lady of abundant beauty, do not fall into despair. Wherever the bee may drink the nectar, he never forgets the lotus plant nonetheless.

The mental activity of the learned is one thing, entirely consisting of the welfare of the world; their composition of strings of words is something else entirely; and their supermundane character, which touches the hearts of the afflicted, is far beyond the reach of all mere speech.

With the wretched spirits (*pretaraṅka*) afflicted by the calamity of their hearts being agitated by the seizing of others, crying out as they grasped the tips of corpses whose hideous, loose flesh was falling away from their mouths;

and with all those [demons] moving about, their mouths wide open in the joy of devouring meteors, their radiance clearly manifest as they converged for a moment, the cremation ground appeared as if it were another sky.
By planting other trees as well that are useful for their fruits and flowers,
a person obtains the merit equivalent to the gift of a thousand jewel-cows.
Any other useless thought destroys strength and vigor;
it shall destroy all happiness and manifest the loss of beauty.

Other treatises are merely for diversion; once they have been acquired, nothing further is gained by them. However, medical science, astrology, and the practice of mantras bring conviction at every step.

Other treatises are merely for diversion during times when one has attained leisure, and they provide nothing of substance; whereas medical science, astrology, and the study of mantras bring conviction at every step.
Just as a virtuous person feels deep distress when speaking ill of others,
so too does a wicked person feel satisfaction when slandering others.
The pair of your thighs, which are incomparable and yet compared to one another, and your odd-numbered limbs—O slender-limbed one, these are but the wax of the honey of your facial luster;
and the male cuckoo, intoxicated with passion, proclaims the scale of the notes of your speech, deluded by the hope that there is nothing beyond the reach of practice.
Another woman, her body exhausted by the fatigue of unrestrained lovemaking, her lotus-eyes bloodshot from staying awake all night,
and the mass of her hair disheveled and tangled against the edge of the bed, falls asleep as she is warmed by the gentle rays of the sun.

Seeing her body enjoyed by her beloved, she is filled with joy; having fashioned a beautiful luster upon her lips, her limbs marked by nail-scratches, her eyes curved and adorned by long, dark, and lovely locks of hair hanging down, she puts on her bodice.
O *mālatī*, you are more fortunate than all other wild creepers,
for this honey-bee indeed sports here by your side alone, ever joyful.
Having encountered various and particular states of wealth, men who are discontented become deluded; the wise, however, attain contentment.
What is the use of that base science by which unreason is led to the status of reason through bold assertion,
and reason is led to the status of unreason out of greed?
That king who constantly lives by means of unjust taxes and enjoyments indeed falls from his position among the worlds solely due to the loss of their affection.
An effort is made in vain to acquire wealth through unjust means;
for those who are greedy, their riches surely contract due to the shrinking of truth.

"All people say that even a religious act performed with wealth acquired through unjust means is hypocritical; noble persons declare that the very same act is sincere when performed with wealth earned through righteous means."
The gift-dharma performed with wealth acquired through unjust means does not protect the doer from great fear.
Another [reason] is that you have now taken up that most excellent and honorable garment and are showing it again to me, your dear and dearest friend, for my pleasure and not for my anger.
This is the conduct of every virtuous person; it has been heard from the elders of old that generally, upon attaining one's own preeminence, one shows it with joy to all friends.
Wealth acquired through unjust means remains for ten years;
when the eleventh year arrives, it perishes along with its very roots.
Wealth acquired through unjust means is called "corruption of wealth" (arthadūṣaṇa). Its characteristics are giving to the unworthy and seizing the property of the worthy.

When you accepted water for the sake of another, which gods— fearing that their own gift of water would be surpassed— did not lament for Mount Sumeru as their own domain, their faces filled with mutual dejection?
Abandoning their husbands' homes, disregarding family disgrace and public reproach,
women whose hearts are stained by passion go to the ends of the earth, clinging to men.

Other beautiful women, having long become exhausted by the fatigue of amorous play, their slender bodies made limp, and distressed by their broad thighs and breasts which were bristling with excitement, apply ointments.
"Is there no other woman in the house? Who is this bride who goes at night to the edge of the pond during the rainy season? O mother, O mistress of the house, are you well despite my condition?
This bracelet is broken, the water-jar is shattered, my body is scarred by thorns, and that wretched snake has been trampled; it is a great pity that he did not bite me."
Where is that other young woman whom you have mastered, she for whom such a grip of pride would vanish now that her beloved has come within the range of her vision?
As for us, however, whose souls are hardened by the embrace of hundreds of fierce men, how could there be any trepidation in the embrace of such an unacquainted man?
That lake is different, O swan, where you were seen by sages with their charming faces as you swallowed the rice-grains placed as offerings upon the steps of the shore;
but here in this pond of the hunters' hamlet, what indeed will not be plotted by these hunters, who hide themselves within the clusters of lotuses, for the purpose of binding a simpleton like you?
O bee, divert your restless mind for now toward other flowering creepers that can endure being crushed;
why do you pointlessly torment the fresh jasmine bud, a tender blossom that has not yet released its pollen and is out of season?

Fortunate are those other lands that are the Rohaṇa mountains for the jewels of virtue; truly, the clay from which he was fashioned is of another kind, and the materials by which this youth was created by the Creator are indeed unique.
For when he is seen, weapons fall from the palms of his enemies who possess glorious beauty, and garments fall from the hips of women whose minds are infatuated.
Different are those forest regions of the Malaya mountains where clear, flowing waterfalls exist, and the thirst of embodied beings is quenched by the mere sight of them.
This desert, however, is occupied by harsh crows; these are but vast, shimmering mirages. O deer, this is not water—depart from here!
Holding no small measure of the quality of nectar, adorned with blossoming, shimmering lotuses,
and enjoyed by her lovers together with the lake, the wine brought redness to the eyes of the young women.
Neither too low nor too high, exceedingly broad, bearing the splendor of mountains, and resembling streaks of lightning with their lines of golden ore;

raining down dust as if pouring forth water, these clouds in the form of elephants—whose dark bodies are like that of the serpent Kāliya and whose weapons are the streaks of minerals upon their tusks—brought peace at that time.
And many other passions have arisen in the world due to specific regions, such as Māra and others; they are remembered as the teachers of those [passions].
If other common people commit many evils,
should even a preeminent person act in their wake?
"O brother Cātaka, those other clouds that bring water and quench thirst—why do you exhaust yourself with useless clamor? Rest!
This is merely an autumnal cloud, white as kāśa grass, its belly empty of water; it thunders excessively, yet it does not release even a single drop."
O cloud, those other birds, afflicted by thirst, run about you on all sides; they plunge with eager devotion into the waters of ponds, wells, tanks, and the ocean.
Yet even now you do not recognize me, the young *cātaka*, who—though my throat is parched—desires no other, approaches no other, praises no other, and meditates upon no other.
Those other bees that lick flowers abandon even a blooming lotus when terrified by the tips of its petals trembling in the play of the wind;
yet this is some other warrior bee who, enduring the blows from [the elephant's] ears, has sported in the ichor flowing from the temples of a herd of elephants.
Even when one's own flesh is being cut by another, one suffers; yet, nevertheless, one consumes the flesh of others as if it were delicious.
There are many other virtuous ones in this world, O necklace, yet you alone stand preeminent among the virtuous;
for you dwell eternally upon the breasts of deer-eyed women, and neither your circular form nor your purity has ever been marred.
Alas, there are many other bodies of water adorned with lotuses and encircled by rows of swans;
yet, alas, this is the profound and singular obsession of the cātaka bird, that it longs only for a rain-shower from Indra’s cloud.
This perfection of form is one thing, and this stream of cleverness is another;
this lotus-petal-eyed woman is no ordinary creation of the Creator.
O dear one, for that person who does not contemplate the misdeeds of others as he would his own,
the arrival of evil does not occur due to the absence of its cause.
Whoever inflicts suffering upon others through action, mind, or speech,
that seed ripens for him as abundant and unwholesome fruit in his next birth.
O King, behold with your intellect how the friends and wealth of other men as well perish; observe the calamity that befalls human beings.
The friendship formed for the sake of some purpose by men toward women is merely a mockery of their needs, just as the affection shown by bees toward flowers is for their own benefit.

For other seasons bring suffering to the women going to meet their lovers by means of days whose darkness is dispelled by the rays of the sun; but this winter, with its thousand-rayed lord [the sun] obstructed by frost, grants them pleasure even during the days.
Through conflict with others, we are one hundred and five;
through mutual conflict, we are five and they are one hundred.
Having eaten from these vessels that were defiled by the leftovers of others, why did these kings feel no shame, or why did they not even consider the matter of purity?
Another enjoys the wealth of one who has gone to the realm of the departed; the birds and the fire consume the elements of the body.
Enveloped by merit and by evil, this person goes to the next world accompanied by these two alone.
For those who have harbored mutual enmity, the consequence reaches their sons and grandsons;
but when their sons and grandsons are destroyed, they themselves go to the next world.
As they bit each other’s lips, embraced one another, scratched each other with sharp nails, and kissed one another;
as they practiced ever-new boldness in lovemaking with eager longing—even when the five-arrowed god of love was exhausted, the passion of the lovers did not diminish.
Where one speaks after relying on mutual opinions,
yet there is no excellence in reaching a consensus— that counsel is called the lowest.
The enmity created between those who once lived together becomes softened through cohabitation;
it does not remain fresh, like water standing upon a lotus leaf.
For those bound by the snares of affection and the reality of mutual secret conduct,
death brings about their severance, or for the steadfast, it brings about their final discernment.
The secret shared among the wise is a hundred thousandfold, for their powers are equal;
yet for young women intent on mutual embrace, there is no such pleasure as that of a lover.
Placing upon your two hands—whose fingers are joined together and reddened—the face that is empty of resolve, its petal-like lower lip trembling with sighs;
with the corners of your eyes closed and shedding tears, whom do you remember daily, so wretchedly, whether he be praiseworthy or blameworthy, yet bound to you by firm friendship?
I believe that for only those fortunate few who have seen one another, who possess similar beauty, passion, lineage, and age, does union come to pass.
For two youths whose bodies were covered in horripilation due to the intensity of their mutual, manifest passion, whose limbs grew thin from the unbearable exhaustion of longing,
and who by chance for a moment obtained independence from their elders at night— the festive rite of their rare union became something that could not be told to others.
O Lord, the mutual estrangement of brothers or friends brings about their end by force;
for enemies, O God, it produces joy—of this there is no doubt.
The two pale breasts of the lotus-eyed woman, pressing against each other,
had grown so large that not even a space as thin as a lotus fiber could be found between them, which was dark at their base.
O you two who are under the sway of mutual passion, let this circle of friends depart so as not to interrupt your unrestrained dalliance;
for how could Madana be truly intoxicating if he did not cause one to cast off one's garment or provoke a battle with teeth and nails?
They know a woman who possesses the characteristics of more than one [class] to be *saṃkīrṇakā* (mixed);
they call her *kevalā* (pure) who is endowed with her own [specific] marks alone.
"Her pair of eyes was surely created by the Creator to be constantly engaged in beholding each other's beauty;
thus, the nose was fashioned between them as an obstacle to that vision."
The female deer and the leader of the deer herd, joined together by their mutual fear of the falling rain,
were so deeply deluded by the pleasure produced by that close contact that they felt no pain from the falling spray of the water-bearing cloud.
The opinions of the mind are always mutually contradictory; however,
when ignorance has ceased and higher knowledge exists,
all its constituent parts become complete and fulfill one another.

He who sustains all beings—by means of serpents who, having entered them, feed on their mutual breath; by his attendants who feast upon external creatures; by the joyful Nandin and the multitude of grasses;
and by his wives and sons nourished by the food of alms—he alone is my Lord and my deity; any other is not even mentioned by name.
Now, by the power of their mutual union, let the minds of both you and him shine forth with blossoming delight,
like a pair of atoms forming a dyad at the beginning of creation, intent upon fashioning once more the body of the Mind-born God.
The signs of her prior affection for you were revealed by her friends, who looked at one another with mingled glances;
and there was also the clever speech of her nurse’s daughter, who said, "Who knows what belongs to whom?"

In the pleasure-chamber, during their incessant amorous sports, the couple shines forth, their mutual passion heightened by the luster of their thick, interlocking teeth; their eyes wide with joy and half-closed in intense delight, they momentarily cast aside all restraint.
Through mutual support and through mutual reliance,
kinsmen flourish together, just as lotuses do in a lake.

Those who are divided from one another, whose internal cohesion is broken, do not fight; likewise, those who have retreated and are separated by the territory of another king, even if capable, do not fight.

Because they neither constrain nor overwhelm one another, the days of spring captivate the heart; their heat and cold are neither harsh nor dull, the red splendor of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees and the emergence of fresh leaves on mangoes appear, and their pure radiance is enhanced by breezes wafting the fragrance of blooming lotuses, while people are filled with the intoxication of joy.

When the great elements have utterly dissolved into one another as if out of fear at the end of the eon, that single tree alone expands with its mass of trunks; O Lord, having placed the three worlds within its belly, it remains there like a child, languid from the playful sport of sporting in the water, resting upon the tip of its branch.
Mutual fidelity until death—
this should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief.

If there were not a powerful bolt of shame—mocking the very pillars of fortitude—that barred their way in the courtyard, then surely those two would have embraced like two lordly elephants; for they had already cast glances at one another that produced intoxication, their inner hearts touched by hundreds of mutual gestures, and they were both bewildered by the impact of the arrows of the Mind-born God.
Holding her two hands upturned above, with their fingers like petals interlaced so as to form a steady, knotted lattice,
she— by means of her pair of uplifted arms, which resemble the arches of a festive gateway and are propped high by the weight of her yawn— proclaims the festival of the entrance of the God of Love.

The sons of Pāṇḍu are skilled at moving about within the waters of the singular ocean of battle—a sea where foot-soldiers stride with valor over chariots submerged in a mire of blood, fat, flesh, and brains from elephants split by mutual blows; where headless trunks dance to the auspicious and inauspicious songs of Śiva as they revel in the pleasure of feasting on copious draughts of gore.
Making his face bow down, noisy with the sound of teeth clashing against one another, closing his tear-filled eyes, and scratching himself while covered in horripilation;
crying out "Alas! Alas! most cruelly as he speaks, and stretching out his arms for a moment—the traveler, his beard singed by the flames, seems to drink the sacred fire itself.
Touching one another’s temples with their trunks,
their tails held high and curved, others with upturned heads met together from all sides and fought, making the distinct sound of their tusks.
A woman who is defiled by the enjoyment of another, one who is proud in her youth, one who is joyful,
one who is proud of her beauty, and one whose mind is entirely dependent on love— these are unmarried women.
Even another person, bound by thirst for its virtues, strives to water the sandalwood tree of noble form;
but for this śākhoṭaka tree, which is devoid of merit, even the great-minded cloud is its only refuge.
For one person does not eat the fruit of the action performed by another; rather, the doer himself is the one who experiences pleasure and pain.
Whatever action has been performed by him, he alone experiences that; there is no destruction of what has been done.
"I favored my beloved by bestowing myself upon him at night"— this friend of mine, though speaking falsely, does not yet deceive her companions.
The heart of those who have inherited learning by lineage, those who possess inherited prosperity by lineage, and of wise lords, is not defiled.
One who understands the meaning of things, is brave, patient, and not harsh; one who possesses auspicious intelligence and splendor—he is proclaimed as "Bhadra" (the Auspicious One).
O Lord, if you were to seek out supplicants with effort every day, they would perhaps only manage to entreat you after searching for a long time;

yet this [ordinary] wish-fulfilling gem, which grants only what is thought of upon being obtained, would shatter upon seeing you, who bestows more than was even imagined. It is not a mere stone at all.
The investigation of the sciences, the protection of the virtuous castes and stages of life,
the mastery of weapons and treatises, and training in the methods of warfare.
The winds blow favorably from behind, the sun and the birds fly at his back, and the clouds follow him; victory in battle belongs to such a person.
In the sallakī forest, a lioness— afflicted by the heavy burden of her mature pregnancy— seeks out the ground of the earth drenched with the rut-fluid of an elephant blinded by intoxication.
While drinking water and gazing affectionately at the keeper of the water-station, he thought of Agastya; she too thought of the four oceans.
"Let there be no fear in your heart that I am an injurer;
my sword never desires to strike those who have turned away from me."
The virtuous provide assistance even during a time of harm;
does a tree not protect with its shade even the one who is cutting it down?
A virtuous person should be content even with harm received from the wicked;
it is no loss for one not to be bitten when encircled by a serpent.
If anger is directed toward one who does harm, why should anger not arise toward anger itself— that cruel thing which robs one of virtue, wealth, pleasure, liberation, life, and reputation?
If you feel anger toward one who harms you, why do you not feel anger toward anger itself, which forcibly obstructs dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa?
That lowest of men who places his trust in one who has done him harm does not live long, just like one who is helpless and weak.
Never think of evil toward those who do you harm;
they will fall by themselves, like trees growing on a riverbank.
If a friend should do harm, or fail to provide assistance when one is in need, one should utterly destroy that ally who, having been trusted, has come within one's very grasp.
Even while doing harm, one generally obtains a great reward from a superior person;
the ocean satisfies the Aurva fire even as it consumes it.
Having done harm to one who is powerful, one should not feel secure thinking, "I am far away";
for these [enemies] fall upon the negligent like the swooping of hawks.
Having done harm to an intelligent person, one should not feel secure thinking, "I am far away";
for the arms of an intelligent person are long, with which he strikes back when he has been harmed.

When childhood has departed, youth is intent on arriving, and both innocence and cleverness have grown fond of embracing one another— then that supreme secret of the five-arrowed god, which has not yet been touched by any other age, triumphs in the body of this lotus-eyed maiden.
If uncooked, it leads to ruin; if over-matured, it becomes harsh. If rubbed by kinsmen, it brings agitation and quarrels with one's relatives.
Even an unripe mango fruit will soften quickly if it is constantly held in the sun while being smeared with a paste of jaggery and ginger.
Water does not remain in an unbaked jar, fine flour does not stay in a mortar,
and indeed, news never remains in the hearts of women.
At dawn, a certain woman, her pride and passion departed, having pressed the tips of her breasts firmly against her husband’s embrace;
beholding her own body enjoyed by her beloved, she laughs as she moves from the bedchamber to another dwelling.
With the dust and its transformations gone, the light of the stars obscured by thick layers of clouds,
and bearing the weight of hanging rain-clouds, this rainy season is like an aged woman.
Those of unstained intellect, pure and possessing the virtuous disposition of the mind,
emit a sound that is the lifeblood of the Vedas and the locus of the nine aesthetic sentiments.
Desiring first to withdraw, he should pacify his own army;
then, having bypassed them by means of a sacrificial session, he himself should take the initiative.
Lacking a garment, deceitful, with a luster like that of snow or a waning moon, renowned as a beast, and delighting in the wives of others—
O King, you are equal to the Spring, not Hara, not Hari, not Hara, not Hari, not Hari.
Those men who place their trust in women and in royal fortune are, in my view, unwise;
for both royal fortunes and women perform the slithering movements of serpent maidens.
Whether a friend be unlearned or even learned, if he lacks self-control, [the state is lost]; since the kingdom has its root in counsel, therefore one must keep counsel well-guarded.
With rays that were clear because free from frost, which dispelled the fatigue of amorous union,
the moon sharpened the flower-bowed god whose banner is marked by the sea-monster.
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure depend upon the wife; likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent on her.
Even cruel men would abandon such a mother for the sake of a wife— she who would even sacrifice her own life for the sake of seeing her offspring.

A female boar generally gives birth to ten offspring; yet there has never been, nor will there ever be, another in this world capable of bearing the burden of the earth, who—having placed his foot upon the circle of the hoods of the lord of serpents—lifts up the earth as it sinks within the ocean.

Because of that great calamity which befell my offspring, I am gripped by a sharp and piercing grief that wounds my heart; for this intense, continuous, and acute anguish does not cease, even after a long time, as it cuts through my vital organs like a saw.
Even though it had accumulated, he never proceeded by a wrong path;
for the salt ocean flows out only through the mouth of a river when it has increased.
He who, through improper conduct, causes himself to sink down from his yoga by following base people— even if he possesses noble lineage— he shall fall.
Just as the sick have a longing for unwholesome enjoyments, just as those in extreme poverty long for wealth,
and just as the wicked long to cause pain to others, so do women long for the festival of illicit sexual pleasure.
Those who live off others declare that indifference toward the future arises from greed; prosperity does not come to one who listens to what is pleasing from them.
The uprooting of indolence, of food that has been eaten, of a loose tooth,
and of a wicked minister brings happiness.

And all around the kings, within the space between their ranks, there fell chariots with golden rims whirling rapidly, bearing banners and clothed in the fluttering flags of the dust raised by the earth as it was bent by the swift winds of their speed.
He who is without feet yet travels far, who possesses syllables yet is not a scholar,
who is without a mouth yet speaks clearly— he who knows this is a wise man.
For one who is ruined and despised lives a life of suffering;
such a life, being utterly cast down, is just like death itself.

"O King, remove this great delusion with this sword of yours! Tell me, how and where was this wondrous trickery learned, such that by repeatedly drinking the blood of his enemy—red as the juice of safflower—he instantly vomits forth fame white as the flow from the Ocean of Milk?"
The circle of cheeks of the fair-eyed woman appeared pale as a honey-scented *madhūka* flower,
yet due to being covered with thinness, it seemed to have become sunken as if by the floating droplets of her shed tears.
He who, relying on a very firm resolve, desires to recover a wealth that was taken away by one acting with poor policy— that is the vow of a man of noble character.
O bee, having set your foot upon the flower of a celestial tree, which has surpassed all other fragrances— if you now desire to go even to another flower, then you are truly blessed.
One who desires to rise must first remove the darkness consisting of anger from before the mind with wisdom;
for even the sun does not rise by its own radiance until it has pierced the darkness created by night.
Placing dishonor before him and casting pride behind him, a wise man should secure his own interest; for the ruin of one's purpose is indeed folly.
For those women for whom there is disrespect from their husbands, harshness from the circle of elders, and poverty at home,
which lead to the destruction of their virtue, there arises through excessive passion an attachment to another man.
Through disrespect, ascetic power increases; through honor, ascetic power wanes.
A Brahmin who is honored and worshipped departs like a cow that has been milked dry.
One should bring to pacification through honor that [anger] which has arisen from an insult; or else, in the case of anger born of pride, one should employ conciliation first, or even prostration.
Even when insulted, a man of noble birth does not speak harshly to another due to his natural courtesy;
for a sandalwood tree from the Malaya mountains does not exude pus even when struck by an axe.
Like rain without the rising of clouds, or fruit without visible flowers,
your appearance has occurred to me quite unexpectedly.

When she was pushed away by her angry lover, the deer-eyed woman feigned anger and glared at him; though he stood there feeling pained even while perceiving her ruse, the other [lover] remained as if thwarted by an ill omen.
As the deer-eyed women now departed from the place of their rendezvous,
there occurred a transformation not only of their garments but also of their minds.
How can there be a sense of friendship toward objects that depart by their very nature for the miserly?
For them, even the sacrifice of life is easy at the time of such departure—alas!
In that city, which possessed the splendor of the western ocean and shone with the brilliance of Indra, hundreds of ships—resembling herds of rutting elephants—crushed it;
thus, the sky, filled with masses of clouds like a host of dark blue lotuses, became equal to the ocean, as the ocean was equal to the sky.
Alas, O Karīra tree! How can you remain so steadfast, providing benefit with your fruits and flowers, while dwelling alone in this desert region abandoned by the multitude of other trees?
Like a tree, even a great enemy— when fanned by the wind of internal dissension and having its mass of roots gradually decayed and disordered— is easy for a patient person to uproot.
"Ask what offense I, who have listened to your words,
have committed, that the lute should speak so harshly to me and the sweet-voiced cuckoo so cruelly?"
But those who have offended yet remain very affectionate, he should win over with loving words, honor, and gifts;
and others, as appropriate, by means of sowing dissension or punishment.
"We hear no fault in you, nor has anything untrue been spoken by you.
Thus addressed as "O Gopī," may Kṛṣṇa, remaining silent, purify you all.
That is the fault of destiny, and not of the ministers;
for even a task well-executed with effort may perish through the stroke of fate.
O Hari, you who are the vessel for a thousand offenses, I have fallen into the belly of the terrifying ocean of existence;
I am helpless and have come to you for refuge—out of pure compassion, make me your own.
And he should inflict punishment upon the wicked in accordance with their offense;
he should cause those who are wealthy to tremble with fines, and the poor with execution and imprisonment.
O woman with curly hair, why do you brandish this raised punishment against me, a transgressor? You increase your own amorous play, yet you are angry with your servant here.
"I am indeed an offender; be gracious, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, and desist from your indignation.
How indeed can a blameless servant be treated with anger by one who is worthy of his service?"
The *aśoka* tree, no longer dependent on others, endures the kicks from the feet of lotus-eyed women;
the *bakula* tree, fragrant with the breath of women's mouths, acts like one who has drunk wine.
Even when guilty of an offense, a long-serving official remains fearless;
disregarding his master, he acts without restraint.
"The fact that 'I have committed no offense' is not a cause for confidence;
for even those possessed of virtues may have fear of cruel men."
"O beloved, if you consider that an offense has been committed by me,
why do you not press down and crush my breasts, which are as high as mountain peaks?"
To the trees that seemed to beckon them with their branch-like fingers, gently swayed by the cool afternoon breeze,
the flocks of birds offered their cries as if calling for their nests.
One who desires not to abandon oneself should display to courtesans wealth that is constantly useful and constitutes one's own essence.
A king who, out of greed, disregards what ought to be considered and pursues the deception of others without examination,
is helplessly destroyed like a bird whose wings have been shaken off.

Enough with these people who have not studied the science of logic (*tarka*), whose definitions and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) remain unexamined, who have not grasped the true nature of the meaning of categories (*padārtha*), and whose nets of victorious reasoning remain unsubdued.
One should not act without having examined; one should act only after thorough examination.
Later regret arises, just as it did for the Brahmin woman regarding the mongoose.

The authors of the *Kāmaśāstra* have pointed out that a man who possesses visible wealth is approachable even if he is not wealthy, but not otherwise; so what talk can there be of one whose fortune has vanished?
"O King, this is Aparṇā wandering through the forest wearing garments of bark; this on the mountain peak is Śiva, matted-haired and naked.
O ornament of the earth, as the husband and wife of their enemy meet for a moment in this confusion, their prostrations to one another become "Śiva, Śiva! (Alas, what a pity!)—thus they cry out.
It is my conviction that only the Aparṇā creeper is to be cultivated by the wise;
for by her, even the ancient Sthāṇu produces the fruit of immortality.
What fraction of infinite time is a hundred years? How can one whose maximum lifespan is merely that much afford to sleep?
The circle of her friends, distressed because their arms are too short, fastens the girdle upon her hips with great difficulty.
In your extensive discourse— free from error, pure, captivating to the heart, and a locus of auspiciousness— your stainless intelligence is clearly perceived, as if in a mirror.
The conduct of one who fears no censure, who is indifferent to virtues and faults,
and who follows an evil course— alas, his behavior is as difficult to discern as that of Fate!
Whatever leads to censure, whatever causes loss of confidence,
and whatever leads to rebirth in hell— how could a wise person ever practice such things?
The daughters of the mountain, accustomed to turning in their father’s lap without fear, have now moved forward to approach their husband;
out of affection for them, this river seems to weep along with them through the piteous cry of the birds.
A king whose wealth is based on what is not the sacred teaching does not attain prosperity;
moreover, all that wealth of his perishes in an improper manner.
Having encountered Lavaṇa who was without his trident, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa besieged him;
for victory belongs to those who strike at the weak point when facing their foe.
With a mind free from grief, favor your wife with offerings for the deceased;
for it is said that the tears of kinsmen, when shed in great profusion, burn the departed spirit.
A mantra is said to be excellent when it causes no regret, bestows the desired fruit in its proper sequence, does not require a long time, and is pleasing to the heart.
The Gaṇas withdrew from the battle as if they could no longer see Īśāna;
for in times of distress, the mind, inflamed by agitation, indeed becomes bewildered.
By those who do not perceive objects of great relish and lack discrimination regarding what is sweet,
what else is there to be known beyond food, like blind oxen led by kings?
In that place where a talkative lapwing nearby shrieks harshly, it is only fitting for the royal swan to either depart or remain silent.
The deer-eyed woman does not move from my sight, this night does not pass away, and sleep does not come;
even Love strikes those who are already suffering—alas, calamities indeed multiply before one!
Move aside, O Earth! O oceans, withdraw your waters! O mountains, bow down!
May that cosmic struggle within the belly of the dwarf Hari protect you all.
Depart far away, O bee, even from this *ketakī* flower though it be rich in fragrance;
for here there is no gain of even a drop of honey, only a face made grey with dust.
"Move away, my friend, far from this serpent-like woman who is naturally treacherous, bearing the hood of her coquettish charms and possessing the fiery poison of her sidelong glances.
One bitten by an ordinary snake can be treated with medicines, but those possessed of wisdom abandon one who has been swallowed by the serpent of a fickle woman."
"Remove the camphor, keep the necklace far away, what is the use of lotuses?
Enough, enough with the lotus-stalks, O friend!"—thus the young woman speaks day and night.
A fortress provided with an exit is called such by those who know statecraft;
a fortress devoid of an exit is merely a prison under the guise of a fortress.
The monkeys spread out stones, for they indeed strike down the Rākṣasas;
the monkeys perform their task—the crooked course of Time.
Just as the sun shines within the sky after having dispelled the intense darkness,
so too does one sprinkled with the water of the Gaṅgā shine after having dispelled all evil.
This certain thief Kṛṣṇa steals my mind— he who is the thief of the sins of those who bow before him, the thief of Pūtanā’s life-breath,
the thief of the bracelets and garments of the young cowherd girls, and the thief of the eyes and hearts of the virtuous who behold him.
I do not know how begging robs one of greatness, nor do I fail to realize that it produces profound shame;
nevertheless, tell me, that generous man—who day after day the fire dwelling within the vessel of my belly compels me to beg from—[is he still so?]

You always captivate the minds of men by means of your exceedingly great accumulation of virtues; yet you do not become manifold-minded [in response]. Or rather, who would disclose the property stolen from another?

O friend, this rash act was committed by you out of greed against one whose kinsmen have been cast aside; why then, O dear one, do you now adopt such a course devoid of compassion toward this innocent man?

Leaving behind the sandalwood groves at his own leisure, this wind rises here, skilled in the sequence of a royal raid by the God of Love, for the purpose of plundering the pride of the women of Lāṭa.
He who, having stolen the wealth of another, performs a religious duty with it, that donor goes to hell; the fruit of that merit belongs to the one whose wealth it was.
For that person who was concealing his own restlessness, the God of Love brought about this state;
and both the night, which witnessed the suffering of his wakefulness, and the bed, as soft as the moon, became aware of it.
They honor the ocean with its waters and awaken the sun with a lamp;
yet can those two ever be fully satisfied by them? For the high-souled ones are pleased by devotion alone.
Even the flow of the Ganges water, upon reaching the ocean, inevitably becomes of that same taste; knowing this, a wise person should not resort to anything of an impure nature.
It was once dissolved in the depths of water, momentarily acquainted with the essence of sandalwood, and took light steps upon lotus stalks, necklaces, and the like, as well as upon the moon;
it rested for a moment in the shade of a grove of fresh plantain trees, but now its supreme coolness dwells only in the embrace of my beloved’s neck.
During your sporting in the waters, may the rising spray of droplets floating upon the water create the illusion of a pearl necklace;
may that spray, born from the waves and sounding like the *sāra* and *vasāra* notes, break against the slopes of your two firm, full, and high breasts.
"Friend, wipe away the juice of the *bhujaṅgavallī* from your cheek; cast off this bodice whose fastenings have come undone from your breasts;
cover the tooth-marks on your lip with lac—tell the group of women and the elders that you will go thus. Thus she spoke. How will you go?
Having first dispelled all the dense masses of clouds on every side, as well as the sootiness arising from the thick smoke of darkness,
that autumnal moon— the artisan— then whitens the mansion of the world with his rays moistened by an abundance of nectar for the delight of the Lord of Rati.
Her eyes tremble at the corners, her speech consists of sweet and modulated syllables, her gait is slow with the weight of grace, and her face is exceedingly lovely;
thus, as these qualities manifest spontaneously through the natural playfulness of the fawn-eyed one’s limbs, the arousal of passion, though it has taken root there, is not even perceived.
In the city of Ekaśilā, by means of side-long glances preceded by pretexts,
young men are fettered at every step along every street by those with gazes like a doe's, even though they have committed no offense.

O fortunate one, he who has come to you— his eyes rippling as they meet at the outer corners, his brows dancing with playful arches, and his body clothed in the spreading mantle of horripilation— is here.
O slender-limbed one, this serpent at your outer corner of the eye is extraordinary;
merely being seen, it induces a swoon even in the wise.
The wise man should measure the length from the outer corner of the eye to the base of the tail horizontally; he should measure the height from the tip of the hoof to the hump.
Where no worthy recipient exists, even an unworthy person attains the status of a worthy recipient; in this land, where there is no tree, even the castor-oil plant passes for a tree.
One should never practice bestowing [gifts] upon unworthy recipients, which is censured by the virtuous;
for what else could result from such bestowal upon the unworthy than the depletion of the treasury?
The notion of worthiness in one who is unworthy, and the notion of unworthiness in one who is worthy—
such a thought arises in the donor in the form of a lingering debt.
A woman takes pleasure in an unworthy man; Indra pours rain upon the mountain;
Fortune resorts to the wicked; and the wise man is generally destitute.
The unification of the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths and the cessation of urine and feces occur through the constant practice of *mūlabandha*; even an old man becomes young again.
Furthermore, impelled by the downward breath (apāna) which has the form of Time,
one who exhales and inhales blows while muttering "haṃsa" day and night.

If at any time love for the refuge of valor arises in the mind—one that has its beloved’s purpose fulfilled by her grasping with respect all human sentiments through a smile that rises clearly from being veiled by dense sinlessness—then alone is this entire life fruitful; such is the nature of the Great Soul.
Those who are free from evil and born of noble lineage honor their own benefactors; this is generally the case for kings, yet one who appears virtuous is often viewed with suspicion.

O wonder, by Autumn all this world has been brought, as it were, to discipline: she who teaches the waters their proper place when they have overflowed; who bestows upon the rice stalks a graceful bending when the grain has ripened; and who takes away the fierce pride of the peacocks like a potent poison.
In this world, human life is beset by misfortune; prosperity is fraught with calamity; pleasure born of the senses is transitory; and fortunes are fickle.
Women, whose eyes are tremulous, become like juices drained by old age. And yet, alas, people do not take delight in supreme austerity!

The wise, employing the methods of political science, display as if shimmering before them both the calamity born from the manifestation of misfortune and the success born from the manifestation of skillful means.

In former times the Sage drank [the ocean] up, and again it was brought back by the one who established the bounds [of morality]; in former times it was crossed by the Monkey, and again it was burned by the enemy of Laṅkā;
it was churned by the enemy of Mura, and again it was bound by the enemy of Laṅkā. O Lord of the Earth, where indeed is the ocean of your fame, and where is that [primordial] ocean?

"The ocean is shoreless; the path of the sandbanks extends for hundreds of yojanas; the way in the sky is indeed without support, and the ten directions are empty"—thinking thus, this parrot, having wandered and wandered only a few steps in the sky, falls once again upon the tree of virtue.

O wonder! Your mature glories wander upon the shores of the boundless ocean, on the Himalayas, on the Mālaya range, on the exceedingly rugged and difficult-to-climb Rohaṇa mountain, on the great mountain of the immortals, and in the deep caves of Mandara; yet they do not fall.

O compassionate Guru, tell me this out of mercy: what refuge is there for me as I am sinking in the midst of the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra? [There is] the long boat that is the lotus-feet of the Lord of the Universe.
In the shoreless ocean of poetry, the poet alone is the Lord of Creatures;
for in whatever way he wills, so does this entire universe transform.
Why does the Lord of Śrī lie hidden upon the serpent in the shoreless ocean, so thick with crocodiles and sharks, as if out of fear?
Or rather, let it be so; for who, being surpassed by all in fortune, could dwell without fear while his body is embraced by Śrī?
Spending their days and nights in endless labors for the sake of food, they never perform their ablutions or the twilight rites at the proper time;
abandoning their own traditional duties, these many born of the twice-born lineage live on by becoming village accountants—alas, how they barely survive!
Eating a cow's horn is useless and detrimental to one's lifespan;
the teeth are worn down, yet no flavor is obtained.

Even the Gopālagītās— which, though devoid of meaning and joined with what is contrary [to truth], yet possess the character of being a compendium of the Vyāsa [Purāṇas]— are included within the Vedas and other such scriptures.

By those [travelers], the journey was made pleasant through their own desire which kissed you alone— desire that cast aside the use of excellent provisions for the road, and which quenched both hunger and thirst with its most delicious sweetness.
Why do you place a playful lotus in your hand, which has been cast aside from your broad face?
Why do you apply a necklace to your heart, from which all ornaments have been banished by tears flowing there?
Like a lover abandoned by women at dawn, the full moon touches the shade of the honey-bee umbrella;
this sun, a thief of the beauty of the clusters of *aśoka* flowers used as ear-ornaments for the women of the East, now reaches the eastern mountain.

Casting aside the enmity arising from the abduction of Lakṣmī and disregarding the churning of that mountain, the great ocean gave refuge to Hari; for the conduct of those with steady intellects is free from envy.
Even the surging of the great ocean’s wave, stirred by the wind at the end of an aeon, can be restrained; but the flow of a heart that is full of passion cannot.
Even if a man who serves a king were a coward or a base person,
nevertheless, that individual does not suffer humiliation from the people.
Even if a base man who is a coward should become a servant of a king,
he obtains from the world a reward such that even a virtuous man does not obtain even a fraction of it.
Even a base man can be a companion on the road who ensures one's safety; by having a crab as his second, a man’s life was preserved.
Even that which is the time of time depends upon time;
therefore, Time is the lord of the world, for it is capable of both creating and destroying the worlds.
Moreover, those who are excessively proud meet with immediate destruction for the sake of fame;
they do not desire even an infinite lifespan if it is mixed with infamy.
The mind of a woman is as fickle as the tip of an elephant's ear, as the leaf of a peepal tree,
and as the flickering of lightning.
Moreover, sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass are easily obtained for your ritual purposes, and there is water sufficient for the requirements of your ablutions.
Furthermore, you are engaging in asceticism according to your own capacity; for the body is indeed the primary instrument for the practice of dharma.
Even for one who has committed a terrible offense, if he stands firm by resorting to dharma,
that fault is indeed concealed, just as a mountain is covered by dark clouds.
Moreover, we see people performing actions that yield no fruit;
for otherwise, they would not know how to maintain their livelihood in this world by any means whatsoever.
Even the wish-fulfilling gem requires the exertion of thought;
yet I consider this wonder wrought by the Noble Lady to have been accomplished without even being thought of.
Even if one of very wicked conduct worships me with undivided devotion,
he should be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved.
Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners,
you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone.
Moreover, in this pair of children, there is clearly present here that various corresponding skill of Janaka’s daughter which can be inferred through expertise;
indeed, it is as if the face of my beloved, possessing the splendor of a fresh hundred-petaled lotus, has once again come within the range of my eyes.
Even a cloud, having brought droplets of water from the ocean from afar, is born;
whereas one who brings even a hundred jars from nearby is merely a thief of water.
Furthermore, as the two rivers of luster flowing from her body reach a state of unfathomable depth,
both of her breasts truly become the swimming-pitchers for both Love and Youth.
Even though the young trees seem to emit heat, even though the night scorches and this wind burns the waters of the lakes—
even in such a terrifying summer, there is no fear for those possessed of merit who have obtained the circle of their wives’ breasts smeared with sandalwood paste.
Moreover, he did not take as his mark with an arrow the peacock with its beautiful plumage as it sprang up from near the horse;
for his mind had suddenly gone to the mass of hair of his beloved, which was strewn with variegated garlands and whose tresses were loosened by amorous play.
"Alas! If even a treasury of light were to fall [from the sky], what would sexual union matter to us?"—thus thinking, the *kokila* birds are separated from their mates.
O night-lily, you have indeed established a bond of kinship with the moon in vain;
public scandal has spread everywhere, and alas, no union has ever actually taken place.
Alas, that very female bee who never once set foot upon the Bakula tree out of longing for its blossoming buds,
now suddenly follows after the Badarī tree when fate has become adverse.
Even this sun, the jewel of the day, having been tormented by masses of cold during the night, now sleeps at dawn, embracing his own wife firmly with his arms;
since he rises again with limbs so languid, why indeed should this lovely woman—the night—not be long?
Even when held fast by both arms and bound in manifold ways by skillful men with ropes,
Fortune— slippery as the waters of the ocean at the time of their birth— escapes in an instant, as it were.
O frogs, do you croak so unrestrained because you have been brought to a state of golden luster by these fresh floods of water?
Alas, this is soon to perish; rather, that former purchase of yours within the limits of the pit will long remain an object of pity.
Would that such a superior man might be seen upon this earth, by whom wealthy men with faces swollen with pride have never been looked upon.
Who that is an ordinary person would dare to disregard him who constantly bears within his heart the splendor of eternal bliss as his sovereign power?
Even if studied most thoroughly, [learning] leads only to the sorrow of people— like a jewel situated upon the hood of a serpent— if the mind of a man has ascended to the state of ill-discipline.
Moreover, even for one who has renounced enjoyments, by observing the objects residing within his own mind,
association with the crooked (the wicked) may arise for the sake of non-existence (destruction).
The lord of the earth should also punish five hundred persons deserving of punishment;
in their absence, he should punish five scribes or a single goldsmith.
Even five hundred heroes may crush a vast army;
or else, five, six, or seven who do not retreat may achieve victory.
A wise person should protect their life even at the cost of sons or wives;
for as long as these exist, everything can be obtained again by embodied beings.

Even a human-authored treatise should be accepted if it conveys sound reasoning; conversely, anything else should be rejected even if it is of divine origin. One who adheres solely to what is logical must cultivate this discernment.
Even those fortunes that are as fickle as the sidelong glances of bold women remain for a long time with kings through the employment of wise ministers.
O Mother, for those who have suddenly abandoned even a vast kingdom like a blade of grass to take refuge on your bank, where the *vānīra* reeds sway,
and who drink this nectar-sweet water to their heart's content, their joy mocks the very path of *nirvāṇa*.
Even when war has broken out, he should regard his servants— though as dear as his own life, protected, and cherished— as if they were dry fuel.
Even if she has many sons, is endowed with virtues, and possesses a circle of kinsmen, that woman is to be pitied; for a woman deprived of her husband is a wretched person.
Moreover, how else could this [work], which is certainly superior even to the bliss of Brahman and other such states,
have captivated the minds of Nārada and the others?
Even after committing the murder of a Brahmin, one is purified by performing penance; however, by performing even half of that penance, one who betrays a friend is never purified in any way.
Even though an embrace was offered by the raising of her creeper-like arms, and even though well-spoken words were heard during the playful conversation of her dear companions—
yet the sidelong glance of this girl, fresh with the shame of her recent marriage, turning languidly upward despite her effort to lift her face, creates a great festival of joy.
O Garuḍa, it is only fitting for you, whose mount slays the Dānavas, that you strike down even those among the serpents who wear jewels, yet not others who are your enemies.
Whether it be a brother, a son worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle, there is no one who,
having deviated from his own duty, is not subject to punishment by the king.
Even if one has become dull-witted or has perished upon seeing the beloved,
for living beings, the force of suffering generally becomes even greater.
Even death would come to her while the moon shines; what talk can there be of any other state?
Alas, how can the burning of her body, intense with the fever of the god of the uneven arrows, now find peace?
Even having attained human birth, those who do not become wise are better off as mere animals, since they do not engage in transgression.
Moreover, by means of gentleness, the wise man constantly subdues his enemy by contracting his body,
just as a creeper destroys a great tree.
How many virtuous people are there who, while finding joy in their own playful expressions, also find satisfaction in the eloquent sayings of others?
Does the mango tree, whose basin is already filled by the flow of its own abundant nectar, not desire the watering from the water of a jar?

He indeed was the emperor of the royal lineage of śarabhas, before whom even the lord of beasts— his prowess manifested by splitting the frontal globes of the king of elephants— fled far away with eyes trembling in fear.
Even when addressed with gentle words, he is always obtainable and ever vigilant;
there is no servant equal to Dharma, for he runs forth at the slightest command.
Even a wise man, even a hero, even one as firm as Mount Meru— even such a supreme among men, craving alone can reduce to the state of a blade of grass in the blink of an eye.
Even a task that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone;
how much more so is a kingdom of great prosperity, especially when undertaken without assistance?
Contentment is the supreme happiness— greater even than sovereignty, greater than heaven, greater than the moon, greater than Mādhava, and greater than the touch of a beloved’s breast.
Alas, I am not even able to describe the anguish of that large-eyed woman before you;
for, O Śiva, Śiva, my tongue does not strive even with effort, as if fearing its own combustion.
O ornament of the Raghus, even if it possesses graceful qualities, is adorned with ornaments, and is golden, speech is not auspicious at all— just like a beautiful woman— if it is bereft of you.
If they are truly jewels, they endure even being rubbed by a diamond and even being trampled underfoot, out of their longing for virtue.
Or rather, O mustard seed, you are now destined to rival the great banyan tree, you who were once a mere handful of greens on a fertile plot;
for we have heard that in the past, the Lord—within whose single petal the entire universe played in the hollow of his belly—slept as a child at the time of cosmic dissolution.
Even after remaining for a hundred years, a courtesan who is always feigning passion flees from those free from attachment, like a female parrot hissing in fear.
O Smara, even after fashioning your swift arrows from flowers, the Creator did not attain satisfaction;
for he bestowed only five upon you, yet even by restraining them, alas, the world has been shattered by them.
Moreover, even an enemy who is fierce in his valor can be overcome through sowing dissension;
therefore, a seeker of victory should employ the strategy of creating division among his enemies.
If he knows even the six syllables and desires to instruct Śitikaṇṭha,
or if he possesses merely clothing and food, that rogue surpasses even the Giver of Wealth.
Even the autumnal moonlight, through its difficult ascetic penances, might attain a likeness to her;
yet it does not captivate my mind as does the smile of that woman with eyes as lovely as those of a wagtail.
Even those who are skilled in the scriptures but devoid of worldly conduct—
all of them become objects of ridicule, just like those foolish scholars.
Moreover, these two things, though each is suitable for the application of very cooling remedies, are simply unbearable when occurring simultaneously:
the season of the matured rays of the sun, and separation from one's beloved.
Even though his arms were as thick as elephant pillars, he was unable to support her, who was languid from the weight of her hips, for he was paralyzed by the thrill of contact with her body.
Even sandalwood trees, which are pure, fragrant, cool, and capable of allaying distress,
become terrifying through association with serpents.
Wise men should cultivate friends who are endowed with fullness; even the lord of rivers, though completely full, awaits the rising of the moon.

Between the belly and the noble person, there is only a difference in outward appearance: the belly is constantly filled yet remains empty through its discharging, while the noble person is constantly empty yet appears full through his giving.
Alas, even for clouds that fulfill the hopes of those established on the path of truth,
the conduct of Agastya is a cause of their defilement.
Will that day ever come when my gaze, like a female bee, shall drink the nectar from the blooming lotus-face of my beloved;
and thereafter, through limbs that are the companions of love and are rendered playful by a succession of soft and affectionate words, I too shall experience union with her?
Even the speech of the All-Knowing One does not shine upon a listener devoid of awakening;
is not the adornment of a wife fruitless for a husband who has lost his sight?
Even when living together, there is no union between the good and the wicked, just as a lotus and water remain separate;
yet even when dwelling far apart, the affection of the virtuous remains like that of the night-lotus and the moon.
Even the entire earth, bounded by the oceans, must be searched;
for there is not even a space the size of a cubit that is devoid of those skilled in astrology.
O fortunate one, whenever the moon beholds your beautiful face, alas,
it immediately withers and hides its own face within the clouds.
Even if he should sit like a pillar, withering away and overcome by hunger,
a wise man should never seek his livelihood from one who is devoid of self-restraint.
Even a treacherous enemy who has slain his father might, being enticed by the lure of wealth,
go and surrender himself to the enemy by establishing a state of trust.
These men have even slept through their own dreams so as not to perceive another's wife as me;
how could those who are themselves pilots across the ocean of evil paths touch such a woman, even with their hearts, once they have recognized her for what she is?
"Even the most insignificant matter of a lord of the earth must not be spoken of in the midst of an assembly," so Bṛhaspati declared.
Even one who speaks even a very small untruth in the presence of kings or gods will certainly meet with destruction, even if he is their preceptor.

O cuckoo, whatever benefit for others must be performed—whether by means of all one's own possessions, or by any wealth that can be repaid, or even by protection of one's life—that very thing comes to you today from this sound; therefore, you must somehow cast aside your laziness regarding this sound, even for a moment.
Desiring victory, one should march against the enemies without afflicting one's own army;
for the enemy host is easily overcome when it is exhausted by long marches.
The world was enchanting: its geese were neither yellowed nor intoxicated, the sky was stainless without being wiped clean, and the water was pure without being clarified.
Childlessness is better for you than a son devoid of virtue; for even while living, such an undisciplined son is as good as dead—of this there is no doubt.
For one who has no son, there is no destination, nor indeed is there heaven;
therefore, having seen the face of a son, one may afterwards become an ascetic.
The house of one without a son is empty; the quarters are empty for one without kinsmen;
the heart of a fool is empty; but poverty is the emptiness of all things.
