The house of one who has no son is pitiable; a kingdom without a king is pitiable;
subjects deprived of food are pitiable; and sexual union that results in no offspring is pitiable.
Someone makes a petitioner— who is incapable of returning the favor— into one who does not return,
whose purpose is not to be returned, and who is exempt from returning.
The mass of clouds was nourished by those rays which sustain the world; the moon, who satisfies the assembly of many wise men, was made to wax full.
Beholding that sun, the destroyer of blinding darkness, you blaze forth; alas, you even possess the nature of a sun-stone—what can we do?

Let the Daughter of the Mountain Lord remain unworshipped; what is the use of the partiality of the Mind-born God? For if there exists a messenger skilled in eloquent speech, the husband is but a slave at the feet of his wives.
If a guest departs from one's house unhonored and sighing in distress,
the ancestors, together with the deities, turn their faces away and depart.
Where those unworthy of worship are worshipped, and where there is disrespect for those worthy of worship, three things prevail there: famine, death, and fear.
Where those unworthy of worship are worshipped and those worthy of worship are not honored,
a terrible punishment ordained by fate falls instantly upon you.
One should certainly not die before one's time is complete, nor should one live on once it is fulfilled;
therefore, one must maintain fortitude and strike down the enemy host.
O you of restless eyes, you have practiced an unprecedented form of theft; even from afar, you steal the hearts of men who are wide awake even by day.

Victorious is that reality of Sarasvatī known as the "poet-sahr̥daya," which reveals a novel object without the aid of causal factors, transforms the world— which is otherwise like a stone— into something substantial through the weight of its own aesthetic flavor (rasa), and gradually illumines it with the beauty of the unfolding of fame and renown.
A certain unprecedented fire of anger exists in both the virtuous man and the wicked man:
in the one it is extinguished by affection, while in the other it increases even when restrained.
O Bhāratī, this treasury of yours is quite extraordinary:
it increases through expenditure and diminishes through accumulation.
An unprecedented path has been shown to me by that slender-limbed woman,
by which passion alone increases even as I contemplate yoga.
O deluded one, release me, even though I am a Caṇḍāla by my unprecedented deeds;
you have clung to a poison tree of bitter fruit, mistaking it for sandalwood.
Upon reaching an unprecedented region, at the consecration of a crown prince,
or upon the birth of a son, the release of prisoners is ordained.
Then, gladdening the quarters with an unprecedentedly sweet fragrance, there arrived bees, resonant with their humming and adorned with crests upon their heads.
O King, by his form— which was as if unprecedented and longing for union at that very moment— and by the side-glances of the Goddess of Victory, he was seen.
A previously unknown row of serpents, dwelling within the holes of the mouths of the wicked,
bites one person at the root of the ear and robs another of his life.
For the well-spoken words of the great indeed bestow unprecedented joy, take refuge in the highest state, and utterly dispel delusion.
"One who has never done it before must not perform an action censured in the world;
but for one who has done it before, abandoning it is a great dharma—so says the sacred tradition."
From where have you learned this unprecedented science of archery?
For while the flood of arrows comes from one direction, the string goes to the other end of the world.
An unprecedented fire is seen upon the orb of the beloved’s breasts;
from afar it burns the body, yet when clinging to the body, it is most cooling.
An unprecedented aesthetic flavor shines forth from the nectar-fruit of speech; though the act of savoring it is common to all, the poet alone is the true connoisseur of its sweetness.

O lovely one, this unprecedented lamp of your face shines for a long time; O fair-limbed one, it produces an intense darkness for those who look upon it. Alas, beneath it lies this mass of fragrant smoke-like curls, the mere report of which sets people ablaze like moths.
This is an unprecedented science of archery belonging to the great-souled Manmatha;
having left the body uninjured, it pierces the mind within.

O Śiva, this is an unprecedented path of Your sovereignty: O Lord of the world, for those who bow down with devotion to Your pair of feet, it is not merely that their accumulated evil is destroyed; indeed, all previously acquired merit also instantly vanishes away.
"O lotus-eyed one, this beloved has never been seen by me before;
he who understands the difference between us is a wise man, of this there is no doubt."
O best of the Raghus, I questioned my sons, wife, and others; they said to me:
"All that sin is yours alone, while we are merely partakers of its fruit."
One who does not wish for another's downfall should not speak to them unless asked;
this alone is the duty of the virtuous, while the opposite is considered the way of the wicked.
But a man who says something in the royal assembly without being asked not only incurs dishonor, but also ridicule.
A wise minister should not speak unless asked;
he should not instruct one who does not inquire, for this is a great act of rashness.
Even without being asked, a minister should say something here;
but when questioned, he must especially speak what is beneficial for the lord of the earth.
A foolish person who, being unasked and not an authority, speaks here in the presence of the king,
receives not only dishonor but also ridicule.
The knowledge of a fool arises from mental reflection even without inquiry;
an incomplete object produces sound, but a complete jar does not.
They have no regard for affection, nor for a worthy recipient, nor for their own circumstances; always devoted to the welfare of the world, these supreme ones are like jewel-lamps.
"This dejection that we have escaped our enemies is fruitless; rather, it is proper to constantly devise a remedy against them.
When the enemy of the Dānavas was defeated by Jarāsaṃdha along with the wielder of the plow, did not his dear friend, the son of the Wind, slay him afterwards?"
Depart from my heart, or else show yourself on my left;
the sorrow of longing for a separation that is not yet distant is difficult to endure through such suffering.
Even those who perceive all ornaments do not, when they are connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*),
ever regard ornamentation as such in a poem full of sentiment.
O you of sharp intellect, is your teacher well—he who is the foremost among the seers who composed mantras?
For from him you have obtained complete knowledge, just as the world receives consciousness from the sun.
By bestowing wealth, a king pacifies even excessive misfortune;
yet by not bestowing it, he renders that wealth useless and loses it along with his very life.
Though exceedingly high, it is level with the ground; though a king, he is no king.
His life exists for the sake of honor; when that honor is lost, he does not live.
Even for the omnipresent Lord who does not initiate action,
objects produced by others become his qualities, just as words [become attributes] of space.
Even those who are not won over by their own attachment to results bow down;
the trees of the lineage of the virtuous are grasped even by children.
Enough with many sons who, though well-nourished, are ill-behaved;
the hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, beginning with Duryodhana, serve as the illustration.
Even when desired, they are not obtained; and even when abandoned, they do not leave.
Like latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in this world, women are solely intent on deluding.
Though you have given pain that was impossible for the inner self to bear,
the tears of the Vāhīka women flow with great force down their cheeks.
O auspicious lady, a species of gem produced from a mine does not deserve to be joined with unrefined gold.
A wicked man, rejoicing at the misfortunes of others, does not even consider his own destruction;
indeed, when his head is lost, the headless trunk often dances on the front lines of battle.
Even a time of adversity brings praise to the virtuous; even the period of affliction caused by Rāhu’s assault upon the moon is beautiful.

Thinking first that it was his beloved—even when it is a lotus pond with closed blossoms, or a *vāsantī* creeper with shimmering sprouts, or his own reflection fallen upon the wall of a palace—he embraces it with affection, overwhelmed by horripilation, perspiration, and trembling; yet, realizing "it is not she," he does not faint again from the subsequent sorrow.
That king whose fortitude does not fail even when faced with a formidable and fierce enemy does not suffer defeat.
Even one who has ascended to a high position must never insult those worthy of honor;
Nahuṣa, having attained the status of Śakra, fell from his position due to his contempt for Agastya.
One should extract the essence from everywhere— just as one might find gold among stones— even from the ravings of a madman or the crawling of an infant.
O dear one, when an objective cannot be attained even by the three means,
the wise say that it is the time for the employment of valor.
O auspicious lady, may there be well-being for you in the encounter of lovers upon the path of unrestrained passion, which is the very essence of your art that conquers the world;
O fair-faced one, may your playful charms—those abodes of amorous sport, rich in enthusiasm, and full of mature vigor—remain ever blessed.
Behold these two born of the same lineage, one possessing fullness and the other insignificance:
the bowstring and the bow; one has become a subordinate quality, while the other is the master.
This world consists of night; that night consists of sleep; that sleep consists of dreams; and that dream consists of the deer-eyed one.
She, my beloved, consists of pride; and where am I but one who consists of flattering gestures? O Saṃkalpa, whose sole purpose is to fulfill such desires, salutations to you!
Even though trees standing in the forest may touch a fire,
those who are guilty do not remain unpunished when they have been seized by the king’s fault.
Even when great longing arises for the petitions of their beloveds, these maidens are resistant; though they desire the pleasure of union, they are timid in offering their own bodies.
Indeed, it is not by Love alone that they are afflicted, for having found an opening, they—having cast off all restraint—afflict even the Mind-born God himself.
Displaying wheels in the guise of their unmanifest circular breasts,
these secret yoginīs of the practice of Love captivate the heart.
Even one who is capable suffers contempt from people if their power is not manifested;
fire dwelling within wood may be stepped over, but not when it is blazing.
The learning of one who lacks confidence, the wealth of a miser,
and the strength of arms of a coward— these three are useless on this earth.
Some poets, lacking confidence in their choice of words, are the cause of their mothers' affection;
they are talkative like children.
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating.
A guest who arrives at sunset, brought by the setting sun, is one from whom householders must not turn away.
By honoring him, householders attain the state of divinity.
One should not suddenly engage in harmful actions without first considering one's own welfare;
for even the Three-eyed God (Śiva) met his destruction when the nectar-rayed moon was placed upon his head.
When the listener is unawakened, the speaker's words go to waste,
just as the beauty of women with tremulous eyes is lost upon a husband who lacks sight.
For those who are without support and those who take refuge in what is not the Dharma,
Gaṅgā here is their support, their refuge, their bliss, and their armor.
Scriptural treatises are not directly perceptible; there is only dispute regarding them.
But the science of astronomy (*jyotiṣa*) is directly perceptible, where the moon and the sun are the witnesses.
In this ocean that is the refuge of all, whose power and majesty are beyond measure, dwelling is the fruit of no small austerity; yet there is one great defect:
even a mere shell here utterly desires to rival priceless jewels that are otherwise so difficult to obtain, driven solely by the circumstance of sharing the same abode.
One who does not give, though wealthy; one who is poor, yet high-minded;
and one who is unlearned, yet arrogant—they call such a person a fool of mind.
As a night without a lamp, as a sky without the sun,
so a king without an astrologer wanders like a blind man upon a path.
One who is not prominent may become prominent if he serves a king;
likewise, even one who is prominent may become insignificant if he is devoid of service.
In the light of the morning sun, a slender woman, unable to cover her single thigh with her small hands,
pulled at her silken garment with agitated hands as it slipped away from her beloved.
That king who is heedful, all-knowing, and has conquered his senses;
who is grateful and virtuous in character—that king endures for a long time.
Even when a man is heedful and intent upon beneficial actions,
fate, delighting in the wrong path, causes him to act quite otherwise.
You must practice heedfulness while residing with the king;
we live by the fortune of your very body.
The hearts of the young wives— unpleasant due to their husband’s offense, blazing with anger, and having summoned fortitude—
were as if washed clean, as if pacified, or as if melted away by the streams of honey-wine.
Lack of faith, failure to provide support, the seizing of one's rightful share,
procrastination, and the absence of remedy— these are the causes of disenchantment.
Constantly causing earache with irrelevant praises, he speaks of his own poverty and displays only his tattered clothing;
moving like a shadow, neither in front, nor at the sides, nor behind, the penniless man inflicts distress upon the wealthy, as difficult to cure as a chronic disease.
How could he not be a source of wonder—he who was extraordinary, in whom dwelt compassion and gratitude;
in whom resided prosperity, a splendor blazing with virtuous qualities, righteousness, modesty, humility, and valor?
Although my heart has been captivated by the most wondrous manifestations of his extraordinary conduct, which is beyond the ordinary, I still remain unconvinced;
for this is some being in the form of a heroic child, yet composed of the very essence of immeasurable power.
The prowess of this extraordinary one, who is intoxicated by battle, cannot be restrained by the power of weapons;
for the growth of an enemy, even if small, whose nature is like a disease, leads to great harm.
What virtue can there be in one who is both unwise and cowardly, even if he is devoted? And what fruit can come from one who possesses wisdom and prowess but lacks devotion?

Those servants in whom wisdom, prowess, and devotion are united possess the qualities for prosperity; they are the king’s true wives, both in times of success and in times of adversity, while others are not.
O Bhārata, even Bṛhaspati, if he speaks at an improper time, incurs contempt for his intelligence and suffers humiliation.
Even Bṛhaspati, were he to speak at an improper time,
would incur a loss of mental acuity and eternal disgrace.
That fool who laughs out of his own whim at an improper time shall incur perpetual contempt for his intelligence in the assembly.

For two youths who have not yet attained the pleasure of dalliance, whose reconciliation is blocked by excessive pride, and who have suddenly become angry with one another in private— though they long for each other’s first conciliation, their inner states, betraying a desire for favor, destroy their sleep.

Just as this fragrant young sandalwood branch, its blossoms yet to appear, is so entwined by a serpent that it cannot even be touched by those who desire it; so too is she, though her beauty is like the bloom of flowers not yet reached, obstructed by a serpent.

How can that hero, the friend of Vikrama, be described—he who, while offering his own severed head into the fire during a sacrifice, his other heads having become bowed and silent out of anger at their not yet being cut off, himself uttered the mantra and performed the renunciation of his self with the words, "I am not he"? He was Paṅktimukha.
A woman who has not yet reached her youth is for neither desire nor peace;
when she reaches her sixteenth year, even a female donkey acts like an Apsaras.

In this scene, a female friend who has not yet attained union with her beloved performs a playful imitation of her lord of life before her, with the intention of diverting her own mind through conversation,
costume, gestures, laughter, boastfulness, and other such means.
Just as one does not think of an unattainable object of desire, why is it that one does not likewise refrain from thinking about the Dharma?
Even when neither is obtained, one brings fear while the other bestows auspiciousness.

Since she rendered the death of the Lord of Daityas impossible by means of a spear— [a weapon] that does not require an arrow to reach its mark, that is indifferent to the sword and the thunderbolt, that is free from the fear of distance, that surpasses the discus, and that is an axe even when out of sight— let Pārvatī protect the three worlds, which have been made healthy and free of thorns by her, who is as formidable as the joint of her own toe.
The lack of authority in the Vedas and the transgression of the scriptures,
as well as the failure to find stability in all matters— this is the destruction of the self.
In this world, the restraint of a person— consisting of not desiring, not touching, and not even looking— should be practiced for the sake of abandoning passion.
Just as suffering occurs without being sought, so too does happiness come to a living being of its own accord; everything is constrained by destiny.
One should not speak what is unpleasant, nor should one conflict with anyone;
one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose, for the failure of one's purpose is indeed foolishness.
A wise person should avoid from afar that which is unpleasant, as well as malice toward others, another's wife, unrighteousness, and falsehood.
One should do what is pleasing to him who has done what is displeasing;
he who was once displeasing will soon become pleasing if he performs what is pleasing.
Men who have been addressed with unpleasant words strive to speak twice as much that is unpleasant;
therefore, one who does not wish to hear what is unpleasant should not speak what is unpleasant.
In various places, the earth was adorned by those who were impoverished of harsh speech, rich in pleasant words, content with their own wives, and refrained from censuring others.
Even when burned by the coals of unpleasant words, a noble person does not speak what is disagreeable;
does aloeswood, even while being consumed by fire, ever abandon its natural fragrance?
Where there is a speaker and a listener of even unpleasant words that are not contrary to future consequences, there prosperity delights to dwell.
Even when performing disagreeable acts, the wise, whose efforts are exerted for their own sake, are not found out, just as cuckoos are not discovered by crows.
Even when doing what is unpleasant or speaking harshly,
a beloved person truly gladdens the heart in all circumstances.
He who remains dear even while doing what is unpleasant is indeed truly dear;
for whom could there be disregard for fire, even when it has consumed the essence of one's house?
Those who speak words that are unpleasant yet beneficial to people here on earth are declared to be true friends; others are merely bearers of the name.
Those who are unpleasant will not exist; those who are dear to me will not exist; I myself will not exist, and everything will not exist.
Living together with those who are unpleasant, separation from those who are dear, and association with the wicked— this is the suffering of those who live for a long time.
What would be gained by those who are unable to endure afflictions, even if they were to crush their enemies? The desire for victory is fitting only for those who are capable of uprooting them.
"Even one who is unpleasant may be beneficial," such is the instruction of the elders;
by abiding by the instruction of the elders, one attains favorability.
A man should not forcibly desire a woman who is displeased, ill, pregnant, observing a vow, menstruating, or unwilling.
Stones float upon the waters; humans slay Rākṣasas;
monkeys perform heroic deeds—such is the crooked course of Time.
One should not look at one's own reflection in water, nor plunge into a swift current; one should not board a doubtful boat, nor cross a river by means of one's arms alone.
An ancestral offering made to an unworthy recipient is fruitless; wealth that is not given to those who ask is fruitless;
youth is fruitless for one who lacks self-restraint; and sacred learning is fruitless for one who is ill-behaved.
Even a tree that bears no fruit provides cool shade;
even a kinsman devoid of virtue is better than a stranger, for he remains a stranger indeed.
A wise person should not undertake tasks that are fruitless, those with disastrous consequences, those where the profit and loss are equal, or those that are impossible to accomplish.
Affection gives rise to kinship even among those who are not kin;
conversely, kinship is lost even among those who are kin if they lack knowledge of the world.
The weak man who, deluded by pride, advances against a powerful enemy for the sake of battle, will turn back like an elephant with broken tusks.
[May there be] no destruction by kings through hunting of fish that devour their own weak kin, of birds that damage the trees of their own nests,
or of deer that feed on blameless grass.
Protect this weak woman who has been brought to this state by the powerful god of love;
for the birth of those of noble lineage serves to rescue others fallen into calamity.
That Manmatha is he by whose mere glance even women, though lacking strength, having resorted to his assistance, overcome the lords of heroes.

May the Supreme Lord, who possesses a form enriched by the beauty of a woman, who is endowed with a garland of protective beads and the prostrations of the immortals, whose face is manifested through the five stages (*pañcakrama*), and who is beginningless, protect us again and again.
"You ought to forgive the fault of this woman, who is weak and lacking in intelligence;
for the virtuous always practice forgiveness toward the faults of a fool."
Where a woman is powerful, a child is the ruler, and a minister is illiterate—no, no! In such a place, there is no hope for wealth, and even the hope for life becomes difficult to maintain.
If there were even one person in the three worlds who was devoted solely to women,
then how else could the moon, sandalwood, and other such things be considered unpleasant?
How could a weak woman endure the flow of the essence of passion from him of such firm power,
were it not for the support provided by a love equal to that of Madana?
The playful men experienced new embraces with their very eyes upon the women;
for even at a time when the world was empty due to the news of the wind-god’s arrival, passion remained fully awakened.
O fool, the reproach against women with deer-like eyes is indeed in vain; for by the casting of their glances, the world is made to reel like an actor.
O frail one, while you were striving in the water, your facial expression was not equaled by the lotus;
for how could the lotus, though it is the king of the twice-born, possess the status of the first caste when it has been so severely suppressed by the outcaste moon?
O King, you are weak and do not possess the splendor of victory; do not fly at the multitudes of your adversaries! Where can a mass of fire perish when it has begun to receive falling drops of water?
Her eyebrows do not delight the childish, nor is her gait slow like that of a swan; her glance is not unsteady, and compassion has not arisen in her heart.
Her speech is certainly not a guest upon the path of nectar; nevertheless, her body brings the minds of young men—who are already shattered by the arrows of the God of Love—into a state of delusion.
Even those who are ignorant and immobile have attained the supreme state by some means;
they are celebrated by the people as "ministers," like medicinal pills possessing the power of policy.

How could there even be any fitness for you, whose mind has been shaped by the ignorant, to contend with the sons of Pṛthā? Indeed, a guñjā berry, though surrounded by monkeys, does not attain the heat of fire.
Like courtesans for the sake of gaining wealth,
the foolish have repeatedly adorned themselves and made their own selves instruments for the benefit of others.
And one should forgive offenders who act out of ignorance;
for indeed, wisdom is not easily attained by a person in every circumstance.
But if they should claim that something produced by the Buddha was not produced by him,
one should punish those wicked and dishonest men for their offense, even if it is a minor one.
One who desires their own welfare should not act according to their own whims toward powerful persons without first understanding their minds and gaining their confidence.
"Did she not perceive my modest gestures, or did she disregard them?"— with such thoughts,
the young man’s mind was cut down by the arrow of the girl's glance as she turned back to look with affection at those who had followed behind.
From you arose the lotus, and from that lotus-born Brahmā came this cosmic egg; furthermore, the entire universe—both the moving and the unmoving, as well as everything else—has you as its root.
Thus, O Water, fie upon you! Like a thief, you depart secretly through the openings of the nets, while the helpless creatures who have taken refuge in you and rely solely on you are bound.
One should specify the year, solstice, season, month, fortnight, and day as the deadline for the task;
for in this world, every omen grasped by one who lacks a fixed deadline becomes unreliable.
When the jar of the year was pierced by the lightning-creeper-sword,
drops of water as large as clear pearls fell down.

O King, I believe that the submarine fire was conceived by lightning through its repeated contact with the clouds as they traveled together across the ocean, desiring to seize the water; by that fire, in due course, was born Your Majesty’s majesty-fire, which, though drenched by the tears from the eyes of the wives of Your enemies, only grows stronger.
If poverty should arise from friendship with the ocean, that is merely a blemish upon the ocean itself; it is no blemish upon the one who offers friendship.

Just as the ocean is not satiated by thousands of rivers, nor as a fire is by abundant fuel brought to it, even so the living soul is never satisfied with all sensory objects; having reflected thus, Cārudhiṣaṇa renounced the objects of the senses.

O deer, if you were not disregarded by the ocean at that time, why would you now, with upturned beak, beg for drops of water vomited by the clouds? Such shameless baseness is appropriate for you; how then can we understand, and by what quality, that you are celebrated among the proud?
The ocean holds jewels beneath it, or it holds grass upon its surface;
this is indeed the fault of the ocean alone—that it regards a jewel as a jewel and grass as grass.
The waters of the ocean, which conceal the vast expanse of the world and the depths of the netherworld (pātāla),
indeed possess many means in the form of ships capable of crossing them.
But if, by some stroke of fate, this ocean were to become empty, who then would be capable even of looking into its cavernous abyss?
Like fish sinking into the ocean, like serpents entering the crevices of the earth, like birds leaping over mountains, or like monkeys wandering somewhere in the forest—

O King, Indra among protectors of the earth, the lords of the land have fled in all directions, their vision obscured by the mass of dust shaken up by the array of your advancing and incomparable army.
And he said: "O Blessed One, even for great elephants, such an action is difficult to perform;
I cannot bring myself to approve of this futile behavior of a young elephant."

One who constantly eats forbidden food in the house of a woman with fine garments and a drinker of liquor becomes a leper; the lord of wealth suffers from these defects born of the nature of the prostitute.
The bow-vines, whose middles could be grasped by the fist, were forcibly dragged by those arrogant in their youth; though their integrity was unbroken, they cried out loudly.
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge,
charity, self-control, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness;
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of backbiting,
compassion for all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness.
O Bhārata, splendor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and lack of excessive pride— these belong to one born with a divine nature.
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, and even harshness,
as well as ignorance— these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demonic nature.
The divine nature is deemed to lead to liberation, while the demonic nature leads to bondage.
The sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings—
for him, too, there is no fear from any beings anywhere.
We have heard it said that for one who, devoted to compassion, grants fearlessness to all beings, all beings grant fearlessness to him in return.
For one who is devoted to compassion and grants fearlessness to all beings,
there is no exhaustion whatsoever once they are liberated from the body.
O King, we declare that your wife, the sword-blade, who possesses the beauty of a blue lotus petal and reclines upon the chest of the enemy, grants fearlessness—indeed, absolute fearlessness.
She has given birth to a noble daughter, Fame, who is easily obtained through the proper time; and she too wanders through the entire world as if blinded by passion, in order to delight her.
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is perpetually characterized by the gift of fearlessness as its fee.
Only for the giver of fearlessness is there a very great fruit;
indeed, no gift equal to the gift of life is found throughout the three worlds.
Alas, that very luster which formerly belonged to her limbs— now covered in fresh sprouts— is currently engaged in a contest with the *dūrvā* grass over the emaciation caused by her separation.
An incapable soul, even while reciting the words of the Jina, does not discharge the poison of delusion;
just as a fierce serpent, though drinking sweet milk mixed with sugar, does not relinquish its venom.
The Sindhu river was transformed by its blood-water, which resembled the clouds of twilight;
it was by that river that the people, having been deprived of their vision, became intent on blood in the dust while attempting to fight.
Since there is no human being in the absence of existence, therefore existence is the cause everywhere;
purify the mind with effort—what is the use of other external purifications?
In the absence of silk thread, the sinew of a deer is desired;
or else, for the sake of its strength, the sinews of a buffalo or a cow may be taken.
Those who, having abandoned the faults of pride and contempt, approach the virtuous;
and who dispel the fatigue of those who have come to their own homes with hospitable attentions.
Established in the praiseworthy position of housewife to a husband of noble lineage, you will be occupied every moment by duties heavy with his responsibilities;
and having soon given birth to a purifying son, like the eastern quarter giving birth to the sun, you, my child, shall no longer take account of the grief born of separation from me.
Bringing distress to noble people, spreading intense heat,
and causing a burning sensation, the summer days have arrived upon the earth for its torment, like wicked men who have come into one's sight.
Then the sun, as if unable to endure the intensity of its own heat,
descended toward the western mountain in order to ascend the waters of the western ocean.

The lotus-eyed Nalinī closed her eyes, which had been unblinking for a long time due to the intense heat of the sun and were weary from fixed attention; as she did so, the swarms of bees falling away became like tears of water.
When a cloud is fully prepared to give water on all sides,
whether that falling rain is abundant or small is considered to depend upon the vessel.
When a painting arises without a wall, an expansive wall is seen;
oh, how wondrous is this illusion! Yet the snout is broken and submerged in stone.
By oppressing living beings,
one who acquires fleeting fortunes becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is the receptacle for rivers.
Having then spoken those unpleasant words, Śiśupāla has fallen into a state of supreme resentment;
with his mind set against you, he seeks to pay homage to you while you are filled with wrath.
"Death pursues me with a raised mallet;
O lotus-eyed one, protect me, a miserable man who has come to you for refuge!"
One who covets the property of others finds no joy either in this world or in the next;
therefore, one who desires constant happiness should always abandon covetousness.
The hands were skilled in gesture, the feet possessed the grace of budding shoots,
the limbs delighted the stage, and the dance was characterized by masculine vigor and rhythmic symmetry.
The mango creeper, its sprouts shaken by the Malaya breeze as if striving to master the art of dramatic gesture,
intoxicated the hearts even of those who had conquered the god of love with its blossoming buds.
The circular ornaments upon the breasts of the women, newly displayed as their garments slipped away,
increased the fever of love in the hearts of their rivals even further.
A *śirīṣa* flower on the ear vying with a fresh blade of *kuśa* grass, a garment of *kuravaka* flowers, and a garland of *pāṭala* blossoms around the neck—
such is the indescribable attire of the beautiful women that shines forth at the close of day, moistened by the spray of their delicate, fresh water.

O young woman, the beauty of your youth— your sprout-like lower lip, which vies with the fresh javā flower and whose interior is suffused with the luster of the blossoming flowers of your smile— spreads the splendor of an elegant ornament as it incessantly attracts the swarms of bees that are the eyes of young men.

O fortunate one, for this fawn-eyed woman, by the power of fate, upon the falling of the thunderbolt of separation from you, the fresh lotus stalks, tender sprouts, and coils of lotus fibers have become a mass of forest fires.
Eager for the delight of fresh lotuses and fearful of separation from the budding night-lilies, this bee wanders in the interval; it takes refuge neither with the day-lotus nor with the night-lily.

I praise a certain Being who is dark as the fresh sky or the tamāla tree, who is attainable through meditation by yogins within the inner chamber of the heart; whose copper-hued eyes are delighted by fresh butter, whose joyful face rivals the beauty of a blooming lotus, and who is sought by those in yoga.
May the charming body of Murāri—glistening with fresh butter, imbued with the color of milk, and sprinkled with drops of curd;
possessing a luster like a cluster of *tāpiccha* blossoms that dispel the world's distress, and adorned with a fresh peacock feather—grant you your heart’s desire.
The mango creeper, with its girdle of fresh sprouts, having performed an auspicious bath in the extremely cool dew-water,
appeared like a beloved woman in her menses, now facing toward the fruit.

Her cheek, adorned with a fresh row of horripilation, speaks of a heart swinging with concealed joy; O fair-toothed one, by whose great merits does this restless wandering of the eye toward the God of Love occur so repeatedly?
With its fresh seal of ripening, its small well-like navel, its loose and expansive skin, and its protective rind like a flame,
the orange shines forth, having entirely dispelled its greenness by a crimson hue manifested through the sequence of its transformation.
Upon this earth, which possesses the splendor of fresh young grass, the victorious cowherds attained an extraordinary radiance;
like jewels cast down during the course of amorous play upon a bed of blue water-lilies, they appeared beside the girl with her most charming eyes.
The fire of dried cow-dung has lost its savor for the anger of newlywed brides; the frosty wind has become cruel with its embrace of unfaithful folk;
the radiance of the sun is now dull like the command of one whose wealth has vanished; and the moon bears the likeness of the face of a woman separated from her lover.

May that certain Ganges, the garland of *mālatī* flowers upon the head of Viṣṇu—the lotus-footed one who is a fresh creeper of poison for the God of Love—victory’s banner and the destroyer of the stain of the Kali age, purify us; may she be the victory-banner of the Goddess of Liberation. May she purify us!
In this world, there is no one who has not been deceived by the humble conduct of new servants, the words of guests, the lamentations of wanton women, and the multitude of speeches from rogues.
May that Nārāyaṇa— who, together with Satyabhāmā, mounts Garuḍa accompanied by chowries— be ever victorious, he who is directly worshipped by the gods.
Both the ocean and you are unfathomable and do not overstep their bounds;
yet he is like the color of collyrium, while you possess the luster of gold.
Even toward objects that are not distinct, the activity of the mind differs:
a son thinks of the breast in one way, and a husband in another.
This *cātaka* bird flies toward the clouds, hears their thunder, endures the hailstones, and withstands the waves of lightning;
it fans its wings and utters its cry even when only a few drops of water are offered.
He who, having understood the intention of his master, performs all tasks without weariness—
one who speaks what is beneficial, is devoted, noble, and knows one's capacity— is indeed to be cherished like one's own self.
But that servant who, having been instructed, does not respect the command, or who, when being exhorted,
speaks in opposition out of pride in his own wisdom— he of such a kind should be abandoned with all haste.
She reveals what is pleasing according to their intentions;
oh, how the earth belongs to kings of such great power!
Homage to that Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing desired aims, and who cuts through all obstacles.

Though the wind from the kadamba trees overwhelmed his mind and the cries of the peacocks were sweet with passion, Jishnu did not waver from his steadfastness, just as an ordinary person might; for indeed, it is not easy to break the concentration of the great.
Even when overcome, one should never abandon the resolve for one's own success;
even with his limbs destroyed, Rāhu repeatedly swallows his two enemies.
He who stands at the gate of kings even when overcome and disregarded enjoys the fortune of kings; he is never one possessed by pride.
Surpassing the seasonal splendor of the creepers by the excellence of its honey-scent,
that celestial garland rested comfortably upon the tips of the broad breasts of the king’s beloved.
Having surpassed the established state of the virtuous and having bestowed his splendor upon those born of dull matter,
how could that sun— the cause of distress to the world— not fall into the ocean?
You are the bestower of desired fruits, and you are the wish-fulfilling tree; yet we shall point out a certain manifest distinction here:
O Lord, how can the celestial tree compare to your gift, which is mixed with sweet speech, affection, and honor?

O Blessed One, you who are worshipped by the Supreme Lord, the conqueror of Bala, and by those who have mastered the series of mantras for the attainment of desired fruits; O enemy of Madana, daughter of the Lord of all the mountains, I pay homage to you!
Making repeated, desired gestures with her limbs, raising high her pair of breasts that betrayed their fullness,
her slender body revealed her longing under the guise of fatigue, as her vine-like arms swayed.

This belly-pot, so difficult to fill, brings about a mockery: it is exceedingly clever at splitting the knot of one's cherished great pride; it is the brilliant moonlight that causes the lotus-cluster of one's weighty virtues to wither; and it is the axe that cuts down the sprawling creeper of modesty.
Even when presented with desired objects, the slender maiden shows disregard due to her profound pride;
even when the beloved stumbles, she restrains him rather than striking him—this indeed is *bibboka* (affected indifference).
For all desired success comes to a person through human effort;
even that which you call "fate" (daiva) is simply a quality of the person known by the name of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
Having consecrated with mantras according to the rules of purification, the powder produced from *hastikarṇa* enriched with clarified butter—
any man who consumes it shall indeed become long-lived, even if his conduct is unrestrained.
Those men whose wealth is self-respect live long;
for those devoid of self-respect, what is the use of wealth or of life?
For one whose wealth is pride and who seeks enduring fame through fleeting lives,
prosperity— fickle as the play of lightning— is surely but a secondary consequence.
The activities of men possessed by pride, who do not recognize their own true strength,
appear like those of the blind, ending only in a fall.
O Brahmin, for those possessed of self-conceit who discern between what is appropriate and inappropriate,
it is fitting that they do not disclose their sufferings, which must necessarily be experienced.
For a high-minded man possessed of self-respect who desires to ascend to a lofty and beloved station,
his own manly effort is considered the proper support, capable of averting any downfall.
That which, through the state of being possessed by conceit and with its continuous flow of aesthetic relish (rasa),
brings delight to all the senses, is called *kāma* by the wise.
Enemies destroy a king who is conceited, deluded, self-important, deceitful, and prone to anger when he falls into calamity.
When her beloved approached and spoke to her many times, the deer-eyed woman remained silent with her face cast down;
then, as it were by force, she was gazed upon by him with a playful, flickering look in such a way that I believe her very glance transgressed the bounds of hearing.
One should fear those who are exceedingly sweet when facing one but who revile from behind, those of immoral conduct,
and those who are enemies disguised as friends with inner corruption.
Let victory or even heaven wait for one who has been struck down while facing the enemy;
there is indeed the exceedingly pleasant hearing of the acclaim from both armies.
The cheek of young women— its decorative leaf-patterns unwashed by the perspiration from their foreheads dripping down toward them,
and its luster dimmed like a crushed moon— proclaims their role as the active lovers.

With their forearms like clusters of tree shoots— fallen forward due to the excellence of their qualities and possessing a radiant pride that had conquered arrogance— the women were forcibly brought to a state of bending.
Do not say anything at all as you approach me face-to-face amidst this swarm of bees;
lest they, having caught the fragrance of your lotus-face which is sweet with honey, should alight upon you even more heavily.
When the cavities of the sky are made to blossom by the sound of volleys of arrows coming head-on,
there is someone who is truly rare and supreme when prepared both for giving and for battle.
When I was facing her, her gaze was withdrawn; her smile arose under some other pretext; thus, with her conduct restrained by decorum, she neither revealed nor concealed her passion.
When a portion of another woman’s garment covering her hips was suddenly carried away by a strong wind,
the sight of her thighs exposed in her startled confusion filled even her rivals with amazement.
"This tawny one approaches us, thirsting for our eyes"—thus did the women with shapely hips lament;
yet he whom she gazes upon constantly did not realize this, for even he does not reach a state of satiety.
Insomnia afflicts one who is prosecuted by a powerful person, one whose means of subsistence are meager,
one whose wealth has been stolen, a lustful man, and a thief.
One who is attacked by a powerful foe while stationed in a fortress should exert effort and call upon one even more powerful than that foe for the sake of his own liberation.
When one under attack perceives no way out for oneself,
then the wise man, while fighting, dies together with his enemy.
Since an aggressor who possesses power does not desist without having achieved his goal,
no other form of peace exists for him except through tribute.
O slender-waisted one, by fixing your attachment on what is merely delightful and being indifferent to various gains,
you are mocked by the ranks of clever courtesans.
Seeking success, one should resort to a place that is distinguished, stable, meritorious, renowned, and frequented by the virtuous— just as one would approach the praiseworthy Lord of the Vindhyas.

The enemy of Smara (Śiva) endured even the misconduct of the Pāṇḍava son, who—though desiring the means for valor and glory that are difficult for enemy armies to attain—had come into his lap; just as a father, in childhood, endures the impropriety of a beloved only son.
A wise man certainly does not desire prosperity if it is devoid of fame;
for who in this world would sacrifice a long-lasting benefit for the sake of a momentary object?
The worlds, trembling with their respective fears as they enter the saw-like cycle of existence, long for the Lotus-born One to create sons for the wives of the destitute.
The destruction of even Sunda and Upasunda, who both desired the supreme charms of Tilottamā,
is cited as an example resulting from their mutual rivalry.

O fawn-eyed one, why do the wise here vainly long for the sweetness of your lip? Since your lip surpasses the nectar of the gods, it is for that reason that [the gods' nectar] has become inferior (adhara).
O Moon, if you desire once more to behold the beauty of the fawn-eyed one’s face, plunge again into the ocean and wash away your spot;
then, having purified your orb, make it fragrant with *pārijāta* blossoms. Otherwise, tell me: where is her face, and where are you?
O Gaurī, deity of the Vidyādharas, I bow at your feet— you who grant boons exceeding even those desired, who remove the suffering of those who prostrate before you, and who are the worthy refuge.
He who, observing the rules, rains down the seeds of ritual with the water of discernment,
always presides over an action rich in fruit, just as the world dwells in the autumn season.
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves their elders, four things increase: lifespan, wisdom, fame, and strength.
One should salute an elder and offer him a seat;
one should wait upon him with palms joined in reverence and follow behind him when he departs.
Just as the virtuous attain peace by honoring those who are senior,
so too does a fool find satisfaction by reviling the good.
Beholding the women who had completed their adornments, with hands clutching their garments as they slipped down from their hips,
the rows of palaces seemed to break into a loud, manifest roar of laughter through the echoes of drums reverberating against the walls.
One who is under a curse does not attain success even when engaged in meritorious deeds; Renukā, though intent on following her husband, became a slayer of people.
People look upon one standing nearby who is poor as if they were looking at a criminal condemned to death;
poverty is a calamity in this world—who would dare to praise it?

This mass of *lodhra* pollen arose, obscuring the directions with a brilliance as white as the dust raised by an agitated army; it appeared like the god of love (*Smara*) intending to march his host through the worlds.
With his head still moist from the consecration, the king, looking toward his kingdom, must select his companions; for there, the kingdom is firmly established.
Even that which is a very small task is difficult for a single man to accomplish without assistance; how much more so a kingdom of great prosperity?
Constantly intent on pursuing [her lovers] onto the great paths of battle mired in blood,
this wretched royal fortune casts a stain upon the hearts of those who enjoy the earth, as if her feet were already set there.
"O beautiful one, let there be no doubt in you that it is improper for women to go forth to meet their lovers;
did not even the river Gaṅgā herself, for a moment, become a garland upon the matted locks of Śambhu?"

This essence of amorous pursuit of a slender-limbed maiden has never been seen or heard of elsewhere; for even a snake she would have repelled from her feet, mistaking its thick girdle for her own anklet.
O lotus-eyed one, if you desire to go on a secret tryst,
proceed toward your beloved with great care, having carefully covered your face.
Alas! How does this unrestrained Love strike Mādhava, whose body is so delicate?
Like a virulent and malignant fever striking a young elephant, it will soon become cruel through the transformations of its deformities.
Though attacked, she turned her back on the assault; though her bodily charms were manifest, she did not display them; and unable to act as a man upon you, the enemy's army was like a newlywed bride.
Even on nights made thick with darkness by clouds that roar incessantly and loudly,
women going to meet their lovers proceed out of passion, their paths revealed by the flashes of lightning.

Although his body was already hot, it found no relief from the breezes moistened by water and cooled by drops of sandalwood juice— breezes as gentle as the sighs of the captive wives of the Lord of the Gods— as it did from the frequent blasts of hot air.
Exert yourself with steadfastness in the constant and firm desire to protect yourself; through such perseverance, success will surely be attained.
The attainment of desired fruits, contentment,
and cherished excellent fortunes arise through eating together with two, three, or many others.
Having finally attained her long-desired object after a great length of time, she shone with her hopes fulfilled;
in the arising of the pleasure of love, that woman shone, having cast away all fear and being free from base desires.
When not even a single moment has passed without hundreds of kings having enjoyed it, what great esteem can there be for the acquisition of this earth by rulers?
Yet, regarding even a fraction of a portion—a mere fragment of its part—these dull-witted lords, instead of feeling despondency, actually feel joy.

The *āmalaka* fruit is wholesome when eaten on an empty stomach, but the *badarī* fruit is wholesome after one has already eaten; the *kapittha* fruit is wholesome at all times, whereas the *kadalī* fruit is never wholesome.
For indeed, thieves carry off the wealth of those who neither enjoy it nor give it away,
just as forest-dwellers take all the honey of bees.
"Is it something unprecedented that shall happen to me, or is it all the suffering innate to me?
But, O Lord, for those who have come to you for refuge, defeat is not worthy of you."
Having falsely imputed a hostile desire that is unattainable by force, O King, you seek to obtain it;
for even in one who understands, the mind becomes utterly deluded regarding ruin when it is gripped by wickedness.
The eastern quarter became tawny like a master alchemist after consuming gold; the moon lost its luster like a wise man in a vulgar assembly.
In an instant, the stars faded away like kings who have ceased their efforts; the lamps no longer shone, like the virtues of those devoid of wealth.
The moon dwelt together with the ocean and was the abode of virtues; it spread its fame as the fruit of the eyes.
How is it that the son of a lioness torments even him with his full-grown fangs? Does the tongue of a slanderer ever truly taste the flavor of virtues?
When the three worlds were pervaded by cold,
the breasts on the laps of slender-limbed women became sources of wondrous heat, serving as the seat for the splendor of the god of love.
They should fight without distinction and protect one another;
whatever is weak in the army should be placed in the center of the battle array.
Whether bees remain within the interior of a night-lotus or depart from it toward its rival, the day-lotus,
there is an inexhaustible continuity of service rendered by the virtuous to both themselves and others— a service made sweet by its lack of self-interest.
Impenetrable, free from arrogance, steady, truthful, pleasant to behold,
deeply learned, knowing the proper time, having mastered the texts, and understanding the application of wealth and action.
For those of lofty mind, prosperity is blessed with enjoyment, their lineage is brightened by freedom from wretchedness,
and their learning is clear of pride.
It would have been better to touch two venomous serpents— glittering with jewels, coiled, and having just shed their skins— than to touch the breasts of one's wife.

Noble women do not suddenly approach a king, even one with whom they share a long-standing intimacy, if he is anointed [with unguents], has gone into private, is distracted, or is conversing with another.

Like one who has bathed seeing one smeared with oil, like the pure seeing the impure, like the awakened seeing the sleeping, and like one whose movement is free seeing one bound by women— I perceive people here as being attached to pleasure.
"O King, because of your sage-like impulsiveness, you struck down the deer that was the possession of another;
yet he forgave it, for ignorance indeed conceals the fault of those who act with negligence."
Those who are insiders have gone outside, and those who are outsiders have gone inside;
by these means men meet their end, just as King Kacadruma did.

I entreat you, O source of my very life: depart now while your longing is still fresh, before the scandal of the people reaches the ears of my beloved that I am still alive while she stands within the range of his sidelong glances.
Having been entreated with prostrations, the Goddess herself entered their residence separately from them;
she also recited words that were life-restoring and indicated the imminent reunion with their beloveds.
The ways of the scriptures have been clearly mastered, the further shore of the ocean of true poetry has been reached, and the dawn of renown has been attained in the assembly of the virtuous.

Now, for me who am weary of the world, there is indeed no other path; my inclination desires nothing but to lead this age-appropriate life upon the banks of the celestial river, free from all wretchedness.

Even though you have practiced walking upon the surface of your hips, this gait of yours is weary with fatigue; your glances are cast inward, their vision sparse as the lashes of your eyes are slightly knit together.
Therefore, I think that some beloved has been secretly held within your heart today; otherwise, how could these sighs of yours have become so doubled?
Even regarding a matter long practiced, there is the pretense of ignorance; indifference toward purity and impurity; the revolving of fragmented words of memory;
and the repeated recounting of the discharge of debts—this is some unprecedented method of hypocritical souls, generally employed for the purpose of deceiving wretched, wicked masters.
Having practiced the conquest of the vital breaths and explained all the Śaiva Saṃhitās,
at the time of death, his life-breaths departed like the sound of a drum.

Having mastered the Veda, having mastered the prior system (Mīmāṃsā), having observed the various conducts of the learned, and having acquired abundant wealth through teaching and other means— O Mother, how could those who are lazy perform their duties?
O friend, after we had mastered the skill of the Love-bite and attended upon our female preceptors, we vied with one another even in private regarding the secret doctrines of the art of love.
Suddenly, that dialectician of passion—who was filled with trembling, horripilation, and thick sweat on his limbs—was rendered speechless and defeated by me.
"Having first practiced [the Vedas], then having reached home and obtained great wealth, having sacrificed with sacrifices and fathered sons, one should renounce at the end of one's life"—
whoever proclaims this here, whether Manu or Yājñavalkya, for me that duration of time is as long as the measure of my lifespan.
When even the wind, as it approaches, is instantly swallowed by one with a gaping mouth, a terrifying form, and a naturally crooked nature, harboring unfeigned enmity—
what kind of talk of friendship can there be for people like me with such a wicked and cruel serpent, with whom we are generally so well-acquainted?
O King, well-spoken speech of various kinds brings about prosperity;
that very same speech, if ill-spoken, results in misfortune.
Practice produces skill in actions correctly;
it is practiced according to the prescribed rule until a fawn-eyed woman is created.
Knowledge has practice as its cause; prosperity follows merit;
fame follows generosity; and intelligence follows one's past actions.
O lady, knowledge devoid of practice, royal splendors lacking effort,
and passionate women in finery are all objects of ridicule.
The study of the Vedas is the punishment for negligence; fasting is the punishment for fever;
devotion to Viṣṇu is the punishment for Yama; and a virtuous state is the punishment for enemies.
"From this place, where there is a dense grove of mango trees in full bloom, let your wife—the young bride who is now separated from you—be led quickly to some village devoid of trees.
For soon before us will come days that resound with the warbling of flocks of cuckoos, days skilled in snatching away the very life of the womenfolk on the road."
Through practice, however, one whose mind has become steady becomes one whose vital energy is drawn upward;
such a yogi, consisting of supreme bliss, is freed from old age and death.
Knowledge is sustained by practice; a family is sustained by conduct;
a noble person is known by their virtues; and anger is perceived by the eyes.
Knowledge is maintained through practice; a family is maintained through virtuous conduct;
friends are maintained through good qualities; and anger is restrained by the eye.
Knowledge follows from practice; intellect follows from action;
fortune follows from effort; and the fruit follows from destiny.
Through practice the mind becomes steady; through practice the movement of the vital breath ceases.
Indeed, through practice supreme bliss is attained, and through practice the vision of the Self is realized.
For by practice there is the transition to another [state], by practice there is the assumption of another form;
by practice there is the power of exiting the body, and by practice the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
For human beings, attachment arises from habituation, not from the actual excellence of an object;
for even though there is an accumulation of flesh, the breasts lead to passion, but the buttocks do not.
For practice brings about skill in actions;
indeed, even a drop of water does not create a hollow in a stone merely by falling upon it once.
"You have not been sprinkled by the waters of the clouds, for in the midst of the sky you are intensely like the wing-tip of a blue jay;
this face of yours is false, for it has become lusterless like a winter lotus."
Rising when the householder approaches, showing humility during his conversation, fixing one's gaze upon his feet, attending to him while he sits, and personally serving him;
sleeping only after he has slept, and leaving the bed before him—O daughter, such is the traditional doctrine of dharma for a virtuous wife as taught by the ancients.

The earth has been uplifted, the chests of enemies crushed, and the royal fortune of Bali made a mere plaything by this powerful youth; all that the Ancient Puruṣa accomplished over three lifetimes has been achieved by him in a single birth.

Who would deny that those śallakī sprouts are fond of being seized in rising mouthfuls, and that lake is capable of enduring their splashing—since it is there that this lordly elephant, separated from his mate, rests his weary trunk upon his pillar-like tusks and sighs so deeply? But you, O Lord, are that Vindhya mountain itself.
With her pair of breasts uplifted and her long eyes tremulous, she stands at the doorway for the great festival of his arrival;
she effortlessly provides the auspicious preparations consisting of full water-jars, fresh lotuses, and festoons for the archway.
With the radiance from the nails of their upraised big toes, as if emitting passion with every step they took,
those two feet brought to the earth the unstable splendor of land-lotuses.
Even a slight act toward those who are exalted may later produce great provocation among enemies;
therefore, observing this with vigilance, one should proceed without destroying what is visible for the sake of the invisible.
Raised in front and sinking behind due to the weight of her hips,
a fresh line of footprints is seen in the white sand at this doorway.

O forest fire, even when the clouds have risen— clouds that captivate the world with their universal and singular affection— it is your own fault alone that these trees do not engage in the graceful dance of exuberant joy.
The upward-pointing luster of her deer-like eyes, with its sprouts of toenails,
shone forth like a row of arrow-feathers belonging to the five-arrowed god, as if doubled by the pride of her own beauty.
You are elevated and filled with waters; thus these birds, parched with thirst, entreat you.
O cloud, this is the time for your service to others; where are you now, and where are they, amidst the onset of the fierce wind?
Daily consumed by the virtuous through their coming and going,
and wasting away upon reaching the company of wretched people, riches seem as if they fall asleep.
The saffron leaf-designs upon the bodies of the fawn-eyed women, from whom sandalwood paste has been removed,
shine forth like the rays of the sun that have arrived to protect their lotus-like hands and feet.
By desiring more than lukewarm food with ghee, than a tattered garment,
and than not being a servant to others, one falls downward.
Having approached and been entreated by me, this shameless man cast aside his own modesty and suddenly severed my hope with the weapon of refusal.
The shadow of clouds, the friendship of the wicked, and the earth at the edge of the ocean—
these, as well as youth and wealth, perish with very little effort.
The shadow of a cloud, the affection of the wicked, new crops, women,
youth, and wealth— all these are to be enjoyed for only a short time.
The shadow of a cloud, the friendship of the wicked, the passion of a courtesan, riches,
and the favor of kings— these five are considered to be fickle.
The shadow of clouds, fire from grass, affection for a wicked person, water on dry land,
the passion of a courtesan, and a bad friend— these six are like bubbles.
The shadow of a cloud, fire from grass, and whatever happiness depends on another—
these, as well as detachment toward the ignorant, quickly perish.
Rows of clouds, making the quarters resound with the rumbling of thunder, flood the circle of the earth on all sides with torrents of rain.
It is therefore fitting that my friend bears abundant moisture; yet, O Lord, that you are devoid of moisture is a source of wonder to me.
Even when the cloud desires to give cooling water like a flower from the sky, it is rejected by the traveler who turns his face away;
indeed, with the mere touch of the small bird’s beak, the dense mass of clouds begins to fade.
A mass of clouds ends with the constellation Viśākhā; youth ends with childbirth;
sovereignty ends with hell; and likewise, dignity ends with begging.
The eyes of a deer lack the play of eyebrows and are untouched by the flush of passion;
yet this pair of your eyes is adorned with those very qualities.
Having drunk the beloved words of his mistress, he sank up to his neck in nectar;
yet that sweetness which is relished even in the mouth of an enemy cannot be measured when it comes from the mouth of one who is dear.
The beautiful tree-dwelling maiden delighted the mind with her smile-like luster of fresh jasmine,
which was enriched by the fragrance of honey and joined with her bud-like lower lip.
When the mind has become free of mental activity (amanaska), the exhaustion of karmas occurs;
just as when a painted cloth is burned, the collection of paintings is consumed by fire.
There is no syllable that is not a mantra; there is no root that is not a medicine; there is no person who is unworthy; it is only the one who applies them who is difficult to find.
There is no syllable that is not a mantra; there is no root that is not a medicine. There is no earth that is without wealth, yet indeed, the traditional scriptures (āmnāyas) are difficult to obtain.
Striking the mountains with the extremely forceful tips of their excellent arrows,
those heroes bearing variegated bows shine like clouds.

This indescribable ball-play of the fair-browed girl captivates the mind: her graceful steps are accompanied by the resonant tinkling of heavy jeweled anklets; her girdle jingles and her radiant pearl necklace sways; and it is made especially vocal by the row of shimmering bracelets.
An army camp (skandhāvāra) endowed with such characteristics as being accompanied by a steady and intoxicated elephant force and the rising of fresh reinforcements is highly praised.
At the festival of her birth, the world experienced a flow of intense bliss that suspended all other activities, as if it had drunk nectar.

When will the mass of fuel that is our bondage to worldly existence be turned to charcoal by the waves of the celestial river, variegated with the waters of the Yamunā, for us who bear upon our heads the two lotus-feet of the Moon-crested Lord— feet that bestow inexhaustible bliss and dissolve heavy suffering and misfortune?
He thought that the pollen within the flowers, which blinds those separated from their lovers,
was like the ashes from the body of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva) adhering to the arrows previously discharged by Smara against him.
For the bee whose every desire is fully satisfied by enjoying the fragrance of the flowers of the celestial wish-fulfilling trees,
this pursuit of other flowers is a great mockery.

I bow to the eastern quarter of Indra, which is delightful with gardens and meadows moistened by the nectar-water of the moon scraped away by the horns of deer who raise their necks to listen to the songs of celestial maidens; and which is fragrant with the flow of ichor-streams falling from the temples of the elephant of the Lord of the Gods.
A certain wave of sweetness from the wine-like mouths of the Apsarases, a wave of the arts of grace— the succession of sounds from Murāri’s flute makes my mind tremble.
Drowned out by the sound of the *ḍamaruka* drum of Amaruka’s poetry,
no other erotic utterance enters the ear-cavities of the fortunate.
The gods did not drink the nectar from the ocean, nor did Hara swallow the fierce *hālāhala* poison;
rather, both of these were placed by Fate within the speech of the wicked—one on the outside, the other within.
The gods have departed, the bees have flown away, and even the lotus-eyed women have gone;
when prosperity has vanished, everything indeed departs, for only fame remains certain to the lake.
Whether they be immortals or mortals, sentient or insentient,
it is by placing generosity foremost that they are praised throughout the three worlds.
Like a duty requiring forbearance cast aside by one who cannot endure it, like pleasant and beneficial speech rejected by one intoxicated with pride,
or like human prowess repelled by a superior destiny, the strength of Jiṣṇu, once cast down, shone no more.
For men seized by impatience, whose minds are scorched by resentment, conflict arises through mutual injury.

Ah, the intoxicating charms of this fair-limbed woman captivate the mind— charms belonging to her whose cheeks possess the lovely luster of pure lotus stalks, whose eyes are like trembling, playful, blue lotuses in full bloom, and who bears the splendor of hands as red as blossoming *aśoka* flowers.
Refecting repeatedly on all sides upon the surfaces of the young women’s cheeks— which were like spotless mirrors—
the mass of the moon’s rays, which illuminated the quarters of the sky even more intensely, spread forth with great density.
Stainless, without flaw, free from cruelty, and exceedingly beautiful;
neither to be given away nor to be received—oh, knowledge is the great treasure!
A minister should indeed be brave and skilled in warfare;
yet even from such a person, the king must fear—behold the precarious nature of sovereignty!
The minister, the kingdom, the fortresses, the treasury, and the army as the fifth—
these are declared by those who know it to be the constituent elements of one seeking victory.
The constituent elements of the state, beginning with the ministers and ending with the allies, are called the kingdom;
yet, compared to all the calamities of the kingdom, the calamity of the monarch is more serious.

The power of punishment rests with the minister; the administration of discipline depends on punishment. The treasury and the kingdom depend on the king, while peace and its opposite depend on the envoy.

For a king who acts according to his desires and has taken to a wrong path must be restrained in every way by the virtuous; yet you, though you ought to be restrained, are not being restrained by them.
The minister and the crown prince are the two arms of the lord of the earth;
the counselor is indeed his eye, for if he is divided from them, even the destruction of those [others] follows.
The wise have declared that non-miserliness is generosity, and restraint within the Dharma;
one who is constantly established in truth shall become free from envy.
For one who has been honored and for whom the fulfillment of his purpose through honor has been secured will indeed fight;
but not one who is excessively humiliated, whose fire of anger is blazing intensely.
If a non-human being should enter into the interior of a yogin,
the concentration on wind and fire shall utterly consume it while it remains within the body.
Even though you are immeasurable, by means of your qualities such as generosity and honor,
you make all these people who depend upon you equal to yourself.
One should always conduct oneself with sincerity alone and never with deceit;
being ever well-restrained, one should recognize the deceit employed by the enemy.
On the new moon day, the eighth day, the full moon day, and the fourteenth day,
a twice-born *snātaka* should always remain celibate, even during the period favorable for conception.

O bird, that immeasurable honey—the story of Him—which has been made a guest in my ears by people, serves as a kindling verse for awakening the fire of passion; fie on me, who possesses such lack of fortitude!
O Lord who bestows joy, you are immeasurable through the excellences attained by those who have reached you;
you are measured by the fame of the virtuous, yet you are unfriendly toward the wicked.
Even an object of immeasurable merit becomes censured by a single fault, like garlic, which is esteemed for all its medicinal virtues yet is ruined by its pungent odor.
Its origin is from a mine of immeasurable luster, and its excellence is that of a supremely pure great gem;
furthermore, its application as a crown or a ring for the toes is the domain of the artisan’s craft.
One who makes an enemy of a friend, hates and harms a friend,
and undertakes wicked actions— they are called one of deluded mind.
A man struck by fate makes an enemy his friend, hates and harms his friend,
perceives evil as good, and regards sin as auspicious.
He who makes an enemy his friend, or hates and harms a friend—
his friends perish, and his enemies likewise are destroyed.
One should never release an enemy, even if he speaks with compassion;
one should not feel pity for him, but should strike down the one who has previously done harm.
Even if he is an enemy, if one who is wretched comes seeking refuge,
he who shows him favor in his time of distress is indeed the best of men.
For these enemies are immeasurable, devoid of faith, and extremely cruel;
desiring to kill, they administer poison under the pretext of medicinal roots.
When a friend who has risen from the calamity of an enemy becomes alienated,
that [friend] is successfully won over by the enemy himself through the accomplishment of the enemy's own ruin.
Engaged in the destruction of enemies and devoted to the gathering of friends,
the king who enjoys the fruits of the three aims of life is united with righteousness.
Having attained advancement from an enemy, one should not trust in the thought, "I have risen.
For by attaining such advancement, one may perish like an insect inside a cloak.
One should even make those who are not friends into friends if they bring about prosperity; one should abandon even those who are friends if they persist in what is harmful.
Trust in an enemy, Soma-juice in the skull of a dog-cooker, the waters of the Ganges in a potsherd, and goodness in the lap of a circle of villains;
sacred learning in one whose conduct is ruined, and Vedic scripture in one who has not been initiated—these abandon their self-evident purity and instead yield contrary results.
An enemy must not be released, even if he speaks piteously at great length;
one should feel no compassion for him, but should rather slay the wrongdoer.
An enemy becomes a friend, and even a friend may become hostile; for due to the application of circumstances, the course of affairs always follows that very path.
Let these swans, who break the sprouts of the first lotus stalks, be bound in prison with fetters made of thick lotus fibers;
let the young cuckoos, sweet with intoxication, be driven away from the newly blossoming forest of spring creepers that cuts through their inner buds.

These winds from the slopes of the Malaya mountains— moving through the bowers of sandalwood trees cooled by the spray of water dancing upon the cascades near the banks, thick with the fragrance of the mountain’s embrace, and beloved by the forest peacocks— disturb my mind.
O oil-presser, these sesame seeds have surely been brought by you to this state through affection;
had there been hatred toward them, I truly do not know what you might have done.
These seven masses of water, appearing like sweet drinks mixed with curd,
are the cage for the royal swan of your fame throughout the three worlds.
All these people standing before you are fast asleep; do not let go of your anklet, for you shall walk with ease.
Even as Śrīpati walks, he will take refuge at your feet, O Hari, and this shall be your renown.
These rice plants, supported by broad stalks and turned golden by the ripening of their fruit,
bend down as if to smell the blooming blue lotus in the water of the embankment, its presence betrayed by its fragrance.

O cloud, what fruit do you gain by being sprinkled with these [waters], since even these trees require water from wells? It is surely fitting that this young *cātaka* bird should find joy, for even in the summer heat, he desires no water other than yours.
In his house, they ate these until their throats were full:
sugar-candy crushed as if by a stream of snow, and curds produced from the milk of a Vaṣkayaṇī cow—like mud dredged from a pool of nectar.

These clouds, clinging to the slopes of mountains difficult to ascend, appear like us—doomed and their efforts rendered futile; and these countless rivers, whose vast forms and splendors have become fruitless within, reach their end upon their own ground, just as my internal activities have come to naught despite their great display.
These *śirīṣa* blossoms, used as ear-ornaments by women sporting in the water, fall into the current of the river; tossing about and clinging to the moss, they deceive the fish.
When these living beings, who endure for only a few moments, pass away, what cause is there here for the wise to feel distress?
In an instant they are born, and in an instant they go to destruction; not even these things such as the divine mountain or the ocean remain forever.
For the sake of these lives, which are like water droplets upon a lotus leaf, what have we not undertaken, our discernment having dissolved?
For, before the wealthy whose minds are unconscious with the intoxication of wealth, we—shameless as we are—have even committed the sin of recounting our own virtues.
We have not even heard the names of these [lotuses] who possess the splendor of Mañjuśrī’s beautiful face; where indeed could they be, those whose nature is like the moon?
Yet, this pair of eyes of yours, reddened at the corners as if out of anger that a blue lotus dares to move about near me, may it protect you!
The expansive circle of these very breasts is truly beautiful,
for even kings, upon approaching them, tremble and pay tribute with their hands.
If, due to the delusion of these people who dwell upon the peaks of the mountain kings, or through misfortune, an emerald has not been valued by some;
even so, once it has fallen upon the street, what does it not do? For it makes the very quarters of the sky appear as if they were smeared with waves of its own unfolding blue luster.
In every forest, these bees have come together with many blossoms that are open and as lovely as the affection of a lover;
their thirst never ceases anywhere for the lotus, yet these honey-drinkers drink its nectar freely until their bellies are full.
The humming of these bees, which have ascended into the openings of the blossoms, spreads like the fever of separation for the wives of travelers;
the sprout of the rows of trees is as impassioned as the mind of a youth, and the pollen of the flowers falls like the arrow of the God of Love.
O lake, through your acquaintance with these masses of rays from the hot-rayed sun, let it not be that your natural state has become sharp and harsh;
for these wicked ones, casting aside those who depend on even a few drops of water, bring about an indescribable desiccation within you as they pass by.
These bees, driven by the wind that stirs up the pollen of the lotuses and carries away the drops of nectar,
