are unable to determine their course, just as those who have committed evil deeds cannot discern their destination when calamities approach.
For these companions of mine are departing further and further away, their faces veiled by the hem of my garment;
even a stranger is a kinsman to one who is well-situated, but no one is a friend to one who is in distress.
For these trees, adorned with fruits and flowers and entwined by firm, motionless creepers,
protected by the guards at the king’s command, attain a state of bliss like men together with their wives.

These bees, addicted to the sport of hovering, drink honey at will all around the *palāśa* trees, and people are intoxicated; yet this cuckoo bites into a fresh mango—when this [mango] splits open the very core of my vitals, what kind of coincidence is this?
O cloud, abandon this delay; what is the use of these deep and sweet rumblings? Release your water at once with a crashing roar!
Alas, look at the condition of this tree, its body entangled in the mass of flames from the forest fire flickering due to the encounter with the pitiless wind!

Do you see this Devadāru tree before you? It has been adopted as a son by the one whose banner bears the bull, for it is the connoisseur of the flavor of the milk that flows from the golden-pot breasts of Skanda’s mother.

The playful gestures of the celestial nymphs— glances cast with laughter and girdles partially revealed under pretexts— were not enough to unsettle him, who had already conceived the suspicion that he was Indra.
May people adorn their own bodies— unreleased from the ocean of saṃsāra—
with the pearl-like jewels of liberation from Maṇikarṇī and Tāmraparṇī.

Victorious are the rays of the cool-rayed moon, possessing the luster of unblemished white lotuses, touching the beauty of shimmering foam, possessing the grace of flocks of swans, bearing the playful appearance of small fish, and kissing the multitude of waves of the Mandākinī on the trembling crest of the Lord of Girijā.
A well, even if it lacks a seal, is better; for what is the use of that ocean wherein travelers on the road drink only sweet water?
By this desert well, whose surrounding ground is made slippery by the tears from the eyes of weeping travelers, who indeed has not been deceived?
By Hari, who had suddenly and forcefully engaged in water-sports in the Yamunā, this doe-eyed woman— possessing the full burden of fresh youth— was swiftly embraced and held.
With this very same fortunate ash from the body of my beloved, which has stained her breasts,
I shall lay my body upon the fire as if upon a bed of fresh sprouts.
"O friend, by this very path Hari, who charms the mind, has come and gone today; alas, being terrified of wicked people and thus ruined, I did not see him for a long time."
In this monastery garden, delightful with its trees, the branches clearly seem to dance through the production of various new songs by the humming bees.
O best of birds, O parrot, who else but you could be a knower of the sequence of words and syllables filled with supreme bliss? Why then do you weary yourself?
In this mass of darkness, dense as thick, solid black iron, filling the impenetrable hollows of the trees in this garden—how is it that today our feet have somehow been placed before it?
For there is no difference between the closing and the opening of our eyes—not even for a moment! Not at all! Not at all!

In this garden, while this wicked bird, the crow, warbles most harshly at every moment, O friend parrot, fix all your speech within your heart; for the multitude of virtues belonging to those who possess merit is not diminished by silence.
When the five-arrowed god, desiring to conquer the three worlds, kisses in secret the face of Night— the daughter of Atri and his companion—
the night-lotuses assume a state of turbidity through the falling of bees, as if out of the blazing onset of jealous anger.
When that rain-cloud has donned its armor and practiced several *kakāra* sounds— which produce double *repha*s at their ends—
that intoxicated gallinule, with its broad neck quivering, moves forward, its high-pitched notes rising gradually and becoming increasingly slow and sweet.
In this cycle of existence, when one has discerned what is essential and what is worthless, then the excellence of knowledge reaches its fruition for those who possess learning;
this occurs when the days pass by on the banks of the Mandākinī, which resound with the continuous warbling of sweet-sounding swans.
In this lake of the nectar of beauty belonging to the fawn-eyed one, Smara—surely scorched by Śarva—has fallen upon her broad hips;
for this crest of smoke, the first omen of the embers of his limbs, transforms into the form of the line of hair within the hollow of her navel.

The Lord, pleased with this thief who had conquered the fear of death, granted him ten crores of gold pieces for the sake of his two upper feet— enough to scar the mountains with the tips of their teeth— and also eight lordly elephants whose rutting cries delighted the bees.
In the plundering of his enemies' fortresses, his two arms certainly acquired the length and bulk of a bolt;
and there, by the splendor of his chest, he attained the impenetrable expansion of the swinging panels of a city gate.
Then, indeed, in order to conquer that steadfast hero, the audacious Smara, equipping his bowstring with arrows,
cast even the fame he had earned by conquering the three worlds into jeopardy.
It is no novelty that his fortune has been stolen by her eye;
I do not know, however, whether the blue lotus clinging to her ear is telling him so.
The science of this man, like the triple Veda made extensive by the excellence of its constituent parts, became eighteenfold through the dancing on the tip of his tongue,
as if desiring to conquer the distinct glories of victory over the eighteen islands.
O young woman, during this transit of the sun upon the ship of your youth, the god of love stands as the donor on the banks of the river of your triple folds.
O friend, these two breasts of yours are well-fashioned golden jars; tell me, O gazelle-eyed one, to whom shall they become a great gift?
Her loveliness makes my mind long for her limbs, though they are exceedingly soft; it considers the Creator’s fickleness and the hardness of his hand.
The thought that she occupies a place in the heart was surely first conceived by the Lotus-born Brahmā; this auspicious woman must have been fashioned solely by accumulated merits.

I perceive that when the season of frost has begun through the ichor flowing from the ocean-like elephants of this king’s advancing army, let not the soldiers of rival monarchs tremble within; let not the lotus-face of his bride wither; and let that not become a day of ill omen for them.
These ages pass away; this moment will not remain. How much longer shall I endure? For death does not yet exist for me.
Clearly, he is no longer my beloved, nor has my mind abandoned him within; yet neither that [mind] nor the vital breaths of the body [remain].
It is not a fool who understands that among men whose minds are inflamed by anger,
conflict arises even as they seek to assist one another.
Having pierced through the masses of clouds as lotus-stalk needles pierce through the mud,
streams of water fall from the sky like tears shed because of the moon’s calamity.
"How much is this pair of golden *tulākoṭis* to me, who am priceless?"—
thus, from anger, the pair of feet of the deer-eyed woman became as red as copper.
The moon scatters nectar, while the serpent spews forth poison;
the virtuous man speaks only of merit, whereas the wicked man reveals only faults.
Both immortality and death are established within the body;
one encounters death through delusion, and one attains immortality through truth.
Nectar is in the orb of her lower lip; nectar is in her speech; nectar is even in her glance.
Her jar-like breasts are filled with nectar; truly, she is a creation of an entirely different order.
Amṛta is difficult for men to obtain, and likewise water for the gods;
a son is difficult for fathers to obtain, and buttermilk is difficult for Śakra to obtain.
That which the wise offer as the oblation called *amṛta* into the flames of their mantra-tongues is nothing but the splendor of describing the ocean agitated by Mount Mandara.
O Vidyā, those who have taken refuge in you partake of the supreme nectar;
alas, others, however, suffer as they wander here and there through saṃsāra.
Nectar is fire in the winter; nectar is a meal of milk;
nectar is a virtuous wife; nectar is the speech of a child.
Amṛta is fire in the cold season; amṛta is the sight of a beloved;
amṛta is honor from the king; amṛta is a meal of milk.
Amrita is fire in the cold season; amrita is the speech of a child;
amrita is one's own beloved wife; and amrita is respect for one's master.
Nectar is fire in the cold season; nectar is honor shown to one's master;
nectar is a virtuous wife; nectar is milk warm from the udder.
A virtuous wife is nectar; the speech of children is nectar.
Honor from the king is nectar; food given with respect is nectar.
If a cloud, having repeatedly drunk the waters of the ocean of nectar, were to scatter hailstones shaped like stars upon a ground of crystal,
then only might the harsh words of the eloquent— those which constantly emit a flow of nectar— be compared to them for even a moment.
Having heard the speech of the deer-eyed woman, which excels in the sweetness of the flow of nectar, the sweet-voiced cuckoo,
her throat becoming hoarse from repeated practice, utters its "kuhū" cry.
The Lord of Herbs, with his rays spreading everywhere, acting as a liquid nectar for the lotus-eyed women,
removed the poison from their bodies that was intensely burning them.
O beautiful one, your moon-like face— a lovely treasury of nectar that eternally turns back all suffering— blooms on every side with the radiance of your gentle smile.

In the stone-like slopes of the hips of slender-limbed women— where the girdle-bells act as the drum of security amidst their nectar-sweet tinkling, and which are variegated by the spray of water-drops from the beauty of the waves of their triple folds— the God of Love, his prowess consumed by the mass of flames from the fire of the Three-Eyed One’s eye, wallows.
Nectar is nectar—of this there is no doubt—and even honey is not otherwise; the mango fruit, too, is exceedingly sweet with its clear juice.
Yet let a person who knows other flavors, remaining impartial, say once more if there is anything else here that is sweeter than the lip of a beloved.
Those of celebrated intellect may call nectar "nectar," the moon "the moon," pleasure "pleasure," and likewise honey "honey";
yet, O beloved, if there is no joy without the fragrant touch of a beautiful woman, then I declare that their entire collection is incomplete.
Nectar is nectar, the moon is the moon, likewise the lotus is a lotus, Rati is Rati, Kāma is Kāma, and honey is honey;
generally, these things do not share in mutual confusion. How then does this woman possess a beauty that embodies the essence of them all?

Victorious is the white-rayed moon: the water-basin for the nectar-filled mango-tree of the bodiless Love; the skull-bowl of the Kapalika that is Time; the whetstone for the arrows of the fish-bannered god; and the mirror for the celestial damsels of the city of the immortals.
When the ocean exists— having delivered the gods from death by bestowing a spreading flow of nectar-like essence—
whose heart on earth would still yearn for wretched summer ponds?
How is it that the moon— the essence of the nectar of flavor, the entirety of the Makara-bannered god’s beauty,
and the bringer of delight to the eyes of all people— has risen during the day?
O clever parrot, prepare food and drink with the playful grace of your nectar-like speech for those whose minds are deluded;
let this cuckoo, whose throat is like nectar and who is untouched by the suffering and sin of serving others, enjoy the forest groves.
O slender one, if this body of mine were sprinkled with nectar by your wondrous glances, would you not whiten my lower lip,
which is already fairer than moonbeams, and redden my eyes, which are already redder than the dawn?
The moon is considered by name to be the one whose rays drip with nectar;
yet this other entity, whose rays drip with poison, is something entirely different.
A certain twice-born man, remembering a dark cloud dripping with nectar,
no longer looks upon a mere pool or even the vast ocean when he suffers from thirst.
What is the use of streams of nectar capable of washing the body,
when there is the embrace of a long-lost friend, which is beyond all price?
By whom were women created? They are like jars of nectar, like heaps of happiness, and like treasuries of delight.
The knower of yoga should find satisfaction in insult as if it were nectar;
the twice-born man should always loathe honor as if it were poison.
A twice-born man should indeed be satisfied with contempt as if it were nectar;
for he who is held in contempt sleeps in happiness, while he who holds others in contempt perishes.
Within the belly of the great ocean, growth was born from the rays of the moon;
they say that the pearls of its necklace remove the heat from the heart even as they merely touch it.
While this moon of your face exists— whose nature is nectar, which hates the lotuses, and whose pupils are moist— what need is there for another moon?
There is no nectar other than yours from which the enemy of Tripura has eagerly drawn [his power];
for it is by supporting that [nectar] with the surface of his head that he survives, even while holding the Hālāhala poison.
Out of affection, this person longs for an embrace from you, whose firm body is as smooth as a cloud filled with nectar.
Satisfaction never arises for those who drink the nectar [of wealth];
like cattle in a forest, they seek ever new [grass].
One should say "May it become nectar" when [something] has been drunk, eaten, or sneezed;
and at the moment of yawning, together with a snap of the fingers, may there be long life and bliss.
Lifeless, her breath departed, with a wound inside her that acted like a thorn,
she remained motionless and unbound, like a doe beside a deer standing still in a trap.
In his poetic vision of the nectar of immortality, he is beautiful and a benefactor to all people;
like Garuḍa, this poet is worthy of honor, composing verses such as the Indravajrā.
Having produced clay from gold dust churned from the nectar of immortality and placed it upon his navel-wheel,
the potter of the flower-arrowed god fashioned the two jar-like breasts with the stalk of his new line of body hair.
In this body, which is filled with impurities, swarming with webs of worms, naturally foul-smelling, devoid of purity,
and a vessel for urine and excrement, fools take delight, while the wise turn away.

You are immeasurable, yet you measure the worlds; you are free from desire, yet you fulfill all prayers; you are unconquered, yet you are the ultimate victor; you are unmanifest, yet you are the cause of all that is manifest.
This earth, the bearer of wealth, belongs to Amoghakrodhaharṣa, who personally supervises his duties and possesses a treasury that inspires confidence.
Lightning during the day is never in vain; thunder at night is never in vain;
the speech of the sages is never in vain; and the sight of the gods is never in vain.
The ornament of Brahmins is that which is neither made of pearls nor gold;
it is that by which a portion is offered to the deities and the ancestors.
As her beloved’s hand removed her garment, the constant jingling of the woman’s waistband and bracelets was like the repeated clashing of hands in a quarrel, as if to prevent it.
The sky is veiled by a steady stream of water; clearly, this cloud has appeared on all sides.
As the rainy season feels some shame, the eyes of the sun and the moon have been closed.
The sky is to be traversed by a mere leap, and even the earth is covered by a single step of a dwarf;
even the ocean is to be crossed by a boat—what then could be equal to the minds of the virtuous?

"Remove your garment, O charming girl; let the state of being 'clothed by the directions' attain its full manifestation upon the moon-like orb of your fingernails on the breast-mountain of the river of love known as the pearl necklace."

May that fire from the eye of Hara protect you—the fire which burnt the garment of the enemy of the waters (the moon) in the sky, the leaf of the enemy of the mountains (the sun), and the yellow lotus of the multitude of serpents; and whose son was born from the wife of the lotus-born one (Brahmā).
The day, a lover to the lovely night, gave her his lap most generously; then, having contracted himself, he remained there of his own accord.
Now the boar of darkness plunges into the forest of the sky;
on its bristles, the drops of water from the stars shine as they cling to it.
Having observed the darkness desiring to cling to the very edge of the sky,
it then approached the bodies [of beings] and surely departed out of shame, as it were.

O traveler, when the sky is filled with clouds hanging low with the weight of water, when the mountain slopes are beautiful with intoxicated peacocks, and when the Kadamba trees— the abodes of flowers— are in full bloom, what recourse is there for you in this delay?
"Mother, you are weary; stay! I shall churn the milk. Having grasped the churning rod, Hari—the Lord—stood there. Vasuki, with a dejected face, stood ready;
Lakshmi looked on with indignation; the host of gods with joy; and Rahu with rising fear. May that infant cowherd Hari grant you auspiciousness.
"Mother is angry; O Father, let this Gaṅgā who is held upon your head be released! "O wise Ṣaṇmukha, tell me, what other refuge is there for her who has long remained upon my head?
Under the influence of an outburst of anger, he gave the answer with all his mouths: "The ocean, the water-holder, the receptacle of waters, the reservoir of waters, the vessel of waters."
The mother is not pleased with me nor with my daughter-in-law; she, too, is not pleased with her mother nor with me.
I, as well, am not pleased with her nor with her [mother]. Tell me, O King, whose fault is this?
Seeing his mother carrying the vessel of water for the guest-offering from afar, that crowd of people retreated in confusion;
for hundreds of ordinary folk are indeed struck with alarm at the sight of a Noble One, just as the blind masses flee from the light of the moon.
In him, wherein the multitude of excellent qualities of both mother and father is manifested, that entire form, that very luster, appears as if reflected;
that same speech, that same innate modesty, that same power of merit, and that same abode of praise and dwelling place of happiness—by him alone has the father truly become a son.
That mother Sarasvatī, who possesses sons, offers him aesthetic delights through various forms of flattery; yet he, unrestrained, has treated her with contempt through his playful antics.
Seeing those who cause afflictions and diseases through the wicked vices of their tongues and produce bad offspring, she buries her own wealth here and there, making herself appear destitute.

"Mother, the elderly woman, sleeps here; here lies my father, the foremost among those advanced in years; and here is the maidservant Kumbhadāsī, her body exhausted by the toil of all the household chores. In this [house], I alone am a sinner, for my lord of life has been away for several days. Thus did a young woman speak her desire to the traveler, under the pretext of such speech.
A lotus born in water has never been seen to produce water from itself;
yet now, the opposite has occurred, for the Gaṅgā has issued forth from Your lotus feet.
The lotus has sunk into the water; the moon has taken refuge in the sky out of fear.
Now, who is the adversary against whom your face is crimson with anger?
How can it be said falsely that a cloud, having taken its place in the sky and filled the ocean with a flood of water, lacks the power to fill even a cow’s footprint?
Surely, this mass of ashes from the submarine fire has emerged from the ocean in the guise of the moon;
for its thirst is indeed not quenched by the rivers of tears from the eyes of women whose lovers have been unfaithful.
"Is this my mother? This is not my mother, for her half-face has a beard as harsh and brown as a donkey's. Is this my father? This is not my father, for I have never seen a breast upon his chest.
"Who is she? Who is he? What is this? Is it a young woman, or a man, or could it be a third entity? May Guha, who recoils in apprehension upon beholding the form of Śambhu, protect you all.

O Rājyapāla, when you have departed, the world abandons its very nature: water suddenly turns to mud, liquid mud becomes dust, dust becomes like mist at the horizon through the winds from the flapping of elephants' ears, mountains become lowlands, level ground becomes uneven, and inhabited places become desolate.
Water, jars, lotuses, chowries, ewers, gold, silver,
fruits, betel, excellent garments, wine, fish, clarified butter, and food.

How do these rainy nights pass away—nights that are terrifying with the deep rumbling of clouds heavy with water, which have begun to seize the very life of young women separated from their lovers by the weight of the frogs' croaking; nights where masses of darkness are bristling with lightning, and whose power to uproot steadfastness is bound to a roar of profound depth?
A lotus rises high by the measure of the water;
a servant becomes proud when his master is powerful.
One should drink eight handfuls of water before the sun has risen;
having destroyed wind, bile, and phlegm, one shall live happily for a hundred years.
A dam is breached by water, and likewise a mantra is ruined if it is not protected;
affection is destroyed by backbiting, and a coward is undone by his own words.
A fire whose crest can be measured by a handful is extinguished by water;
yet once it has grown large, it is seen to be fanned into flame by those very waters when they are heated from below.
In the waters of the Yamunā, that son of Devakī, having brought his boat to a standstill,
looks with a smile upon the face of the cowherd girl who is distressed by the loss of her boat.
The element of water, the element of earth, the element of air, the element of fire, and the element of space—
these five, together with the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), circulate within the pair of channels of living beings.
Water is the strength of aquatic creatures; a fortress is the strength of those dwelling in fortresses;
their own territory is the strength of beasts of prey and the like; for kings, the army is the supreme strength.

Then, as she— her body as delicate as the interior of a lotus— melted into my embrace thick with the first flush of passion, I believe my beloved entered my heart through the very channels of the wounds made by the falling arrows of Love.

In these ponds as vast as the ocean, young men have gathered with women whose eyes are as long as lotus petals; there, they are struck by the curved side-glances of those women, which are like the arrows of the God of Love.

O cuckoo, whether it be a cluster of lotuses, a grove of *ketaka* flowers, a multitude of *kunda*, a mass of night-lilies, a group of jasmine, a heap of *campaka*, or a collection of *jāti* blossoms—if these do not show you respect, do not grieve in vain; for somewhere, at some time, there will surely be someone who will recognize your merit.

In the palace of the lotus-eyed woman who had made an appointment with her lover, as her heart’s lord tarried long and she fell into a deep sleep of delusion, a doe—mistaking the clear network of rays from her beautiful jewel for water swirling in the pool of her navel—drinks it and is filled with wonder. Even though the sun is obscured by thick clouds, it causes the lotuses to bloom; even though the cloud is far away, it makes the touch of the breasts exceedingly cool against the heat.
There exists some unimpaired power in great beings by virtue of which, through their majesty, even the most distant tasks proceed freely and without restraint—how wonderful!
An enraged Creator may utterly destroy the swan’s dwelling in the playful groves of lotus plants;
yet he is not capable of robbing it of its renowned fame for skill in distinguishing milk from water.

Hearing the thundering of the clouds, the curious elephant, endowed with great speed, immediately abandons his dwelling in the mountain caves and comes forth; yet at that very moment, hearing the fierce sound of a thunderbolt, the steadfast lord of beasts springs up in wrath toward it, having surpassed it with his own roar.

Salutations to that Fate, who, through his mere will, causes the ocean to become dry land and dry land to become the ocean; who makes a mound of dust into a mountain and Mount Meru into a speck of clay; who turns grass into a thunderbolt and the thunderbolt into the frailty of grass; and who brings fire to coolness and ice to the state of a consuming flame—to Him, who is addicted to the wondrous sport of His own playful whimsy.

The fame born of his sword brings about, on all sides, the splendor of a sandalwood unguent—fame that resembles the waters of the Gaṅgā as they issue from the feet of Hari, which possess the luster of pearls cast up by the ocean; it possesses the radiance of the slough shed by a serpent shimmering with the beauty of the foam of the Yamunā; and it is as lovely as a garland of flowers falling amidst the tresses of a Karṇāṭaka woman.

Like a garland of unfading flowers, borne upon the heads of hundreds of kings from the shores of the four oceans— whose inner waters are agitated by schools of darting dolphins and whose coastal forests are dark with the young shoots of *tamāla* trees— that very garland, now faltering upon me alone, proclaims your sovereignty adorned with humility.
Alas! How many conchs are there not here in the world that have been born from the very ocean, which these mendicants carry about from house to house for their livelihood?

Yet, the glorious *pāñcajanya* is unique; acting as a swan upon the lap of the lotus-like breasts of Hari and Hara, by its immeasurable sounds, the fetuses of the wives of the foremost demons are made to fall away.
Even though the ocean’s water-machines and temples are in motion, the heat breaks apart the dense embrace of Śrī and Nārāyaṇa as they sleep;
moreover, the cruel rays of the sun crush the moon—whose beauty is reduced to a mere skeleton upon the frying-pan-like surface of the heated sky—as one would a crisp cake.
Enveloped within by the flickering flames of the submarine fire of the ocean, these clouds clearly drank the turbid waters out of delusion and thirst;
otherwise, how could the clouds—possessing the luster of half-extinguished charcoal—be scorched under the guise of the rings of Indra’s bow flashing across the horizon?
We praise that Maināka, who sports within the ocean, who bears his fame through qualities that remain hidden, and who possesses wings beyond the reach of the pride of Indra;
he who, when the son of the Wind-god was near exhaustion on his path across the ocean as he sought to reach the far shore of the world of gods, men, and the netherworld, dispelled his weariness.

O Great Sage, when Uccaiḥśravas and the other jewels had been forcibly seized from the ocean— that singular mass of unsurpassed virtues— even that water which you drew out as a consolation was drunk by you, devoid of compassion.
Even water, by its flowing nature, suddenly becomes as hard as stone when it freezes; and a stone, when the intensity of moisture increases, yields and flows with liquidity.
When time’s power proceeds with unimpeded impetuosity, its sovereignty is wondrous; for in this world, whose path is fashioned by the Creator’s power, what natural state remains constant?
Beholding the cātakas eager to catch drops of water, and pointing out the cranes as they form into rows by counting them,
the Siddhas, upon encountering you at the time of thundering, will honor you with trembling embraces from their beloved companions in a state of joyful agitation.

O buffalo, enjoy this lake for a long time according to your desire; do not cause this forest and the pond to dance [in destruction] through such wicked behavior, for by this, your own intention is utterly ruined while the pond becomes free from impurity.
This very script, characterized by the curvature of a parrot’s beak, which was once engraved upon your jar-like breasts due to their close embrace with water, has not been erased;
furthermore, desiring to conceal this garland of stars—the frontal lobes of Airāvata—from the flowers, you plunge fruitlessly into the clear waters of the lake that is the sky.
In the palm groves at midnight, as the clouds vomit forth water, the elephants— standing silently with their ear-fans stilled,
eyes half-closed, and trunks resting on the tips of their tusks— hear the sound of the falling torrents.

O Lord, you are like the ocean, a dwelling place for living beings, yet you are not Mandara, the mountain that churned them; you are like Sumeru by your auspicious nature, yet you are not the mountain that is the refuge of the gods.

You possess the shade [of virtue], yet you are not the Kalpa-tree, which is entwined with difficult-to-traverse creepers. Nevertheless, the deluded intellects of poets attempt to place you on an equal footing with those.

O fortunate one, when you were far away during those nights as white as the moon of a Caṇḍāla, there appeared upon her a lotus for her face, the moon for her eye, the ocean for her body, and the transformation of the flower-bowed god of love.
Having bathed in the water of the pond filled with lotuses, a passionate woman,
endowed with devotion and desiring the fortune of flowers, offers them.
O lotus-eyed one, by whom have the feet of Śambhu been worshipped,
that you reveal the intent of Madana with a trembling face to him?

The lightning became a source of trembling for the minds of travelers and beautiful women: it was the garment of the enemy of the serpents (Viṣṇu) as he draws water; the dwelling of the mountain of darkness (the moon); the divine herb of the night; the playful campaka-bow of Kandarpa (Kāma); a cluster of blossoms on the creeper of the rainy season; and a streak of gold drawn upon the touchstone of the sky, shimmering with light.
"A garland of unfading lotuses was placed around Rāma’s neck by Sītā"—
O wise ones, you wander in vain here, even though the verb is present before your very eyes.

What difference is there between heaven—which possesses unfading garlands, ornaments, and garments; which is a temple of delight for excellent women; and which is attended by the festival of perpetual light—and wealth?

O Protector of the Earth, upon the mass of hair of these fawn-eyed women, [the rays] act as unfading clusters of blossoms; at the borders of their parting lines, they act as vermilion; on the walls of their cheeks, they act as the glow of blending *maireya* wine;
near the corners of their eyes, they rest as the radiance of intense jealousy; and upon their bimba-like lips, they act as the lac-dye of the rising sun.
"May there be unfadingness and a divine abundance of fragrance in flowers through contact with your limbs;
for I have not seen anything else comparable to a flower that is so effective in producing both spiritual merit and worldly pleasure."
Unfading, strong, and brave, always following like a shadow—
truthful, gentle, and self-controlled— he may dwell in the king's residence.

This mountain, fashioned of gold, rising higher than all other peaks, the abode of the thousand-eyed Indra, and having suddenly attained a rise in fortune—O young woman, ward off even slightly the beautiful hem of your garment shimmering over your breasts; let this bearer of the earth abandon his pride.
"This one is blind, this is Venus, this one has uneven feet, this is the son of the Sun; this is Rāhu with his mangled body, and this is the cool-rayed Moon with diminished splendor.
Ignorant even of the fact that these [planets] have their own fixed karma as the fruit of their own actions, people lament, "We are seized by the host of planets!"
"Is this desire innate or acquired by you?"—
thus, as if to ask, the gaze of the fair-browed women takes refuge in their ears.

Indeed, this lord of light, the playful lover of the fresh lotus-stalks, now shines forth; and as he is seen, the saffron-paste leaf-designs on the breasts of the lotus-eyed women—now reversed in their position upon the chests of their lovers—cause those breasts to thrill with horripilation.
And this fire of desire, with its flame of passion and fuel of affection,
is that in which the youth and wealth of men are offered as oblations.
"O Moon, this birth from the moonlight, distressed by your face, has entered the cave of the sky; even there, it is being crushed by this most solid [darkness].

Thus, as his strength gradually fails due to the excess of terror, the Creator, afflicted by the disease of decay, pities him in his wretched state; for vulnerability is indeed the root cause of suffering.
Due to the jolting of her chariot, one shoulder was pressed against the other;
in this body, that alone is truly functional, while the rest of the limbs are merely a burden to the earth.
This stream of tears, as if broken from a string of pearls, spreads across the earth in droplets that have become shattered fragments;
though the inner agitation is suppressed, it is inferred by others through the quivering of the lips and nostrils, and the heart is swollen with its weight.
O young girl, whose mind does this lower lip of yours— shining like coral and resembling a desert path— not agitate with thirst?
This sweet-toned voice is the treasure of the three registers;
it is as if three lines were inscribed upon her throat.

Nala, who surpassed the wish-granting tree (Kalpapādapa), did not make false the divine inscription on the foreheads of supplicants— which proclaims, "This man shall become poor"— by rendering that very poverty itself destitute.
This is the summary of the messenger's purpose: words are restricted to their respective objects; the motive is the production of action—how much more could be said?
O intoxicated elephant, this young bee, wandering far and its mind distressed by intense thirst, has alighted upon your temple.
You too should abandon this addiction to swinging on your thick, flapping ears; let him first satisfy his thirst at his own will.
This leopard licks his beloved again and again with the tip of his tongue;
being licked by his own dear mate, he experiences great joy.
"This is the continuous downpour, this is the lightning, this is the burning hailstone, that is the thunderclap, and that is the chorus of croaking frogs"—
with these thoughts, the slender-bodied woman, fallen into the power of death, repeatedly fans the fire of passion spread through every limb by the heaving of her heavy sighs.

O friend, do you not perceive from his conduct—which is sweet with deceptive modesty—that this man is a rogue? O naturally simple one, look at how he bears upon his cheek this mark, imbued with the deep red of lac-dye, which betrays the events that occurred but a short while ago.
"This one is my own, that one is a stranger"—such is the calculation of those with small minds; but for those of noble conduct, the entire earth is but a single family.
"This is the moon born from the eye of Atri"—what kind of delusion is this for those whose minds are dependent on a familiarity with mere intellectual learning?
Indeed, he who is the vessel of nectar was born from the eye of the Flower-Bowed God (Kāmadeva), which was made glossy by the sprinkling of the nectar-essence of Rati’s bimba-like lips.
This cloth has fallen into a state of threadbare poverty; indeed, this cloth is adorned with hundreds of holes.
This cloth cannot be worn as a garment; indeed, this cloth shines only when folded away.
This cloth was an ornament for my father’s body; its youth was enjoyed by my grandfather and his predecessors.
Now it shall adorn my sons and grandsons; for my part, I wear it now merely like a flower.
Seated upon this lotus throne, the cakravāka bird shines resplendent,
like the Lord Creator at the beginning of an eon, desiring to bring forth all living beings.
O lotus-eyed one, this is the time for the acquisition of wealth, suited as it is to the splendor and fortune of these full, swelling breasts.
Is this the lord of the full-moon night standing before us? Or is it the mirror of the Night-bride?
For her reflection is perceived within it under the guise of the lunar spot.
Regarding this worldly condition wherein "this one is the master" and "this one is the servant," it is the fruit of the favor or the disfavour of Śrī that prevails therein.
"O Brahmin, I do not perceive 'this is my kinsman' or 'this is another,' nor 'this is mine' or 'that belongs to someone else'; by that [realization], I live free from affliction."
This sun, its radiance dimmed, desires to go toward the setting;
thus it informs men of the prosperity that arises from falling.
This bed of lotus petals burns my limbs;
indeed, it is only fitting that it be composed of fire, acting as a substitute for the actual flame.
"Is this the sun? But he is accompanied by only seven horses. Is it fire? Yet it does not spread in all directions.
Is it Death himself? But he is mounted upon a buffalo. Having gazed at you for a long time on the battlefield, your adversaries entertain such doubts.

This bee-like play upon the lotus-faces of fair-browed women, this deer at the station of their breasts, this peacock in the grace of their broad hips— this royal swan upon the sandy banks of the river of the three folds, filled with the splendor of lovely luster, does not long sport as the intoxication of youth rises.
"Here comes the deer; the lion flees from the deer.
Therefore, flee with speed by means of very swift steps!"

Now that the powerful Meghavyūha, our adversary, has retreated, on the riverbank where the sands form steps through the gradual receding of the floodwaters, a clear flock of wagtails moves steadily, as if laughing incessantly with joy at the onset of autumn.
This composition of mine, sweet with the cleverness of its lucid words and shimmering with its rhythmic structure, is barren in the heart of another but finds its fulfillment in the heart of a poet;
yet the sidelong glance of a fair-eyed woman, falling from the corners of her slightly opened eyes upon a youth, though devoid of substance, brings him an indescribable joy.
Thinking, "This ocean is a mine of jewels," I served it in the hope of wealth;
let alone the wealth, my mouth was filled with salty waters.
"How will this mango tree—the sole abode of my good deeds, its basin shimmering with garlands of young shoots—be the giver of joy to me, a noble woman? Thus she lamented, her face bathed in tears.
This is the bower by the Revā, perfectly suited for the service of the flower-arrowed god; this is the breeze, bearing the fragrance of cardamom bursting forth from the coastal forests;
this is the blessed rainy season, skillful in the arrangement of fresh clouds—O friend, my heart is under the sway of Love and seeks to do something indescribable.

This expansive bosom of the dark-complexioned maiden—encircled by a halo of rays from her shimmering pearl necklace, acting as a friend to the God of Love—is capable of eclipsing the splendor of the full moon; its covering of thick, dark blue silk has slipped away, revealing a surface made beautiful by a smooth application of glowing saffron paste.
Whether it carries the Creator or the goddess Sarasvatī,
both wings of this royal swan are appropriately stainless.
Thinking, "This is the sole abode of waters" and "This is a mine of jewels," we have resorted to the ocean with minds agitated by craving.
Who could have known that the Sage would, in an instant, drink it up—along with its gasping whales and sea-monsters—into the hollow of his own cupped palms?
"O auspicious lady, tell me, of what youth is this the ripened fruit— a succession of blessings—
such that this descent of a necklace, with its clear streams flowing from the corners of his eyes, occurs even without the presence of a string?"
"This village is deserted; yonder temple has fallen; before us lies a dried-up pond, and here is a tree with withered branches.
We too are travelers whose fortunes have reached a state of utter exhaustion. This common meeting, though bitter, delights my heart."
This very time has now arrived for those who live under Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son;
I must enter there, not sparing even my own life.
"Here stands he who is eager for union with you; yet you fear him, O timid one, because you might receive his rejection.
Does a suitor obtain fortune or not? How could that which is difficult for Fortune to attain ever become desired?"
This is that Śaṅkara, whose self-restraint is celebrated throughout the three worlds; now, distressed by separation, he bears his beloved in his own body.
"By him we have surely been conquered"—thus laughing, the God of Love triumphs, striking his beloved’s hand with his own.
This is that hand which draws up the girdle, presses upon the full breasts, touches the navel, thighs, and hips, and loosens the knot of the lower garment.
This prince will hold all the treatises in his heart and proclaim them among the wise; he will be a source of power for his enemies and a benefactor to his friends.
O crest-jewel of the army, with sword grasped in hand upon the field of battle, why do you flee, O kings of the enemy, so greedy for life?
Why must you dwell today in mountain caves? Are the blue-lotus-eyed women of the Vidyādhara cities not dear to your hearts?
"Let the people say that this one who dwells here in the waking lotus grove, dark and glossy, is a humming bee;
but I suspect that it is the enemy of Mura, having assumed the guise of a bee, who has approached to delight Lakṣmī, who is addicted to dwelling within the hollows of the lotuses."
This is the very nature of the great-souled ones, that they are inclined by their own essence toward dispelling the toil of others;
indeed, it is said that this moon itself protects the earth scorched by the harsh rays of the sun.
One should not conceptualize in this way: "This is for my own sake" or "This is for the sake of another.
The wise do not perceive self and other as separate from one another.
One should apply oneself to the welfare of others and exert oneself in one's own duty.
For this lord of light, having scorched the worlds with his intense brilliance, has now set; indeed,
the prosperities that arise merely from the power of those who torment others do not endure for long.
For this body of the embodied being consists of substance, cognition, and activity;
it is described as the cause of various afflictions and torments for the embodied one.
For this is the first passion that delights all people;
since it has no second, how could it be the fifth?
Like water droplets falling upon a heated iron ball, virtues, even when bestowed, are not seen for a moment in the hearts of the wicked.
Since those trees that have not been planted according to the rules lack both beauty and desirability, I shall therefore describe the method for planting trees as it has been prescribed.
What is given during the solstices, the equinoxes, the six *aśītimukha* periods,
and during lunar and solar eclipses, becomes inexhaustible.
This lower lip of the deer-eyed woman, possessing unimpaired and lovely splendor, challenges the brilliance of coral,
rubies, and other such gems.
This very state of being sprouts already draws the eyes of the world toward her breasts; how will their beauty be when they have reached the condition of mutual compression?

This [mountain] bears slopes where the quarters of the sky have reached maturity— slopes that are exceedingly ancient, heavily burdened, obstructed by massive, hanging breasts, and perpetually inaccessible to living beings.
"Alas! Having respectfully drunk the honey of another creeper, this bee now comes to drink my nectar.
O *mallikā*, do not harbor such despondency in your heart; indeed, tell me, what discernment can there be in the minds of those who drink honey?

This sun also gathers its rays from the treetops— which act as a chorus for the warbling of intoxicated female sparrows— rays that are as tawny as the ears of a female donkey and whose edges are frayed by spreading, wool-like darkness.
This moon also shines forth beautifully upon the head of Indra’s beloved like a full vessel;
the sun, too, throbs within the midst of the ocean like a copper plate to announce the time for the expedition of Madana’s victory.

This mountain, with its lofty peaks dark as a fresh cloud, where the cries of peahens—loud with passion—are joined by the calls of peacocks; where the trees are lush with nests variegated by birds; and which possesses massive crags—bestows delight upon my eyes.

This leader is a treasury of nectar and even among medicinal herbs; the moon, though possessed of a body made of nectar and endowed with splendor, becomes devoid of rays upon reaching the orb of the sun. Who, when entering another’s house, does not fall into insignificance?

This leader of medicinal herbs, a treasury of nectar, followed by Śatabhiṣaj and serving as the crest-jewel upon the head of Śambhu—yet consumption does not abandon this moon; for by whom can the ripening of destiny be overcome?
Hearing the distant drumbeat of the rival elephant, this enemy-warrior, Arimudgara, wipes his eyes clouded with rut,
raises the bars of his trunk, disregards the goad, and— with ears like long sprouts stiffened by rage— rushes with speed into the king’s inner quarters.
Having surely incurred the sin of murdering the wives of ascetics, this man is being cast down from heaven,
while the sky is made even more starry by the multitude of sparks flying up as they burst against the stone of the dark night.

This chariot, with its rim drenched by spray as it passes above the clouds whose bellies are pregnant with water, betokens its presence by the *cātaka* birds emerging from the hollows of the clouds and by the tawny horses anointed with the brilliance of lightning.
If the submarine fire were not in its midst, would this mass of tongues, lightless yet spreading and vast, not blaze?
And would the ocean, whose substance is repeatedly increased by the waters of rivers, not inundate even the three worlds?
This is the time for the lake to constantly assist those in need with its waters;
moreover, this water will soon become easily accessible upon the rising of the clouds.
This is the opportunity to be of assistance while this prosperity, which is as fickle as nature, still endures; for when misfortune has arisen, where will there ever be another occasion to help?
This cycle of existence appears delightful through its unexamined beauty;
yet, for those who possess the vision of ultimate reality, there is nothing here whatsoever that is truly delightful.
This very sun— the lamp of the courtyard of the sky, the crest-jewel of the flickering serpent of Time,
momentarily mimicking the form of the submarine fire— falls distressed into the ocean.

"Is this the Blessed One, or is it Pāṇḍava? Is he mounted by the silent sage who bears the moon on his crest, or by the Unborn One, or perhaps by Jiṣṇu? Thus did the Gaṇas become bewildered by the force of their speed.
Ah, this lion of the night-rangers has suddenly arisen from his rest in the mountain cave;
he is crimson, as if drenched by the profusion of blood gushing forth from the splitting of the frontal globes of the elephant of darkness.
This Self is itself directly a great ocean of the jewels of virtues;
it is omniscient, all-seeing, universal, the supreme abode, and stainless.
This Malaya breeze, which causes the tender sprouts of the mature sandalwood trees to sway, produces joy for everyone.
This moon-like face, with its glow reddened by intoxication,
rivals the moon that has put on the crimson hue of its rising.
This foolish bee here, having abandoned the clusters of mango blossoms,
follows after the crooked, sapless, and pithless branch of a *śākhoṭaka* tree.

Here rises the full moon, red as the stream of blood from the ears of a deer pierced by the claws of the lion of the Eastern Mountain; its rays are like thorns of grief for the female cuckoo, and it is to be drunk in mouthfuls by the eyes of the women of Indra’s city.
Here rises the moon, washing the universe with its radiance, white as camphor in the sky of perfected purity;
it shines as if the world were situated within a cage of pure lotus stalks, by means of its rays that rival straight rods of silver.
This moon rises from the depths of the waters of the ocean, shining with rays formidable with drops of nectar;
it is like the face of the Mother of the Universe, casually upturned while she reclines upon the palace-like chest of the serpent-bed.
Here rises the sun, the breaker of the seal of the lotus ponds; the young mandāra flower of the forest groves on the mountain of sunrise;
the kinsman of the pairs of cakravāka birds distressed by separation; piercing the darkness with a hue as copper-red as the cheek of an angry monkey.

O slender-limbed one, this moon—charming as the sky is reddened by the rays of the rising mountain and its crimson hues—is approaching like a star in the heavens to pay homage; why do you not cast your eyes upon it?

Having grasped his hand upon the summit of Mount Udaya, the Lord of Day offered the rays of the moon as oblations into the fire of the dawn’s rays. What, then, did the daughter of Pūruhitu—the quarter of the East—do with the stars as her parched grain?
What kind of similarity is there between this risen moon and the face of a woman?
To whom does the perception of blue and other colors manifest through direct perception?
This lake, its dark waters approached by the glances of black antelopes, shines with a face like a full-blown blue lotus;
it resounds with the sweet trumpeting of water-elephants whose temples are rubbed against the high, jar-like breasts of the women of the water.

O friend, this breeze blows at dawn, crushing the dense beads of perspiration upon the high, full breasts of sleepless Dravidian women; refined by the fragrance of the oozing sap of sandalwood trees, it carries the remnants of what has been enjoyed by female serpents.
On one hand, this separation from my beloved, suddenly inflicted upon me, is exceedingly difficult for me to bear;
on the other, the days are bound to become delightful due to the rising of fresh clouds and the absence of scorching heat.
The cognition that "this is one" and "I am one" does not exist for me when they are joined;
rather, attachment alone prevails there, like the blending of turmeric and lime powder.
This alone is the supreme dharma, this indeed is the highest austerity:
where there is service to the husband, that is the cause of heaven for women.
One should not perform that action by which ill repute is acquired, by which a downward rebirth occurs, or by which one falls away from one's own welfare.
Violating another's wife brings ill repute and shortens one's lifespan;
it causes the destruction of wealth, is terrible, and leads to the further rebirth of evil.

In this world, which is difficult to look upon due to infamy, there is no abiding place for anger except death. In this world, which is difficult to look upon due to infamy, there is no abiding place for anger except death.

Chewing chickpeas, pulling the jewel from the hood of a serpent with one's hand, lifting a mountain, leaping across the ocean with one's feet, awakening a sleeping lion, and touching a sharpened sword—all these things might perhaps happen; but the acquisition of wealth from a rogue never does.
One should pierce iron with a crow-beak [tool], hide with a needle-mouth [tool], and likewise pierce a lump of clay and a jar with a needle-mouth [tool].
Entreat with every possible means one who does not ask and who is sinking; compassion is the supreme dharma, for that which is given to one who asks is the highest virtue.
Fate, unrestrained, bestows happiness upon men even when unasked, yet does not grant it when requested;
indeed, it may even seize away their entire possession.
The Mountain was unable to make the God of Gods accept his daughter, as she had not been asked for;
for a virtuous man, out of fear of rejecting a request, maintains neutrality even regarding a desired object.
Obtained by me without being asked for, and having been sent by me, it has gone back again;
it has gone to where it came from—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
They beg for what should not be begged for, they consume what is unfit to be eaten, and they ruin affairs through bribes and deceptions.
Families that are deficient in sacred mantras perish quickly through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, as well as through atheism regarding ritual actions.
O cruel one! Fame is indeed dear to you; but is there no infamy more terrible than this?
Tell me, O Lord, what happened to that fawn-eyed woman in the forest? Alas, how can you possibly think so?
"O beloved, look at the cloud! "No, no, you wicked woman! You are too virtuous for such a thing.
"No, no! Look at my breast; remove the bodice from my chest!"
O virtuous Mālatī, do the bees still live without you?
If they indeed live, let them live; for their life is but a mere semblance of living.
O doe, have you come to this city of hunters by mistake, thinking it a grove of asceticism?
Here you do not see parrots prattling such things as "tear," "kill," "devour," or "drink."
O doe, with the prowess of a horse, abandon this forest and make a swift departure;
for here in the woods roam leaders whose arrows are red with the blood of fragrant [deer].
O Kāverī, noisy with the waves of ill-conduct that uproot the very foundation of the lineage of noble families,
you shall before long become as worthless as the mud and remnants of food left by cranes.
O friends, let not the elephant of pride in the greatness of your intellect become base in your minds; for where humility has been bound, there victory resides.
If this [elephant], puffed up with anger, abandons humility due to intoxication, will it not then throw the entire camp into total turmoil?
O King of the Deaf, you indeed strike this parrot with a probe out of delusion;
let him compose nectar-filled speech incessantly, or let him remain silent before the entire assembly.
Alas! Truly, the ripening of past deeds is indeed harsh for living beings. Those very heads that once shone upon the head of Hara—alas, alas!—now roll about as the feet of vultures.
O startled and innocent *cātaka* bird, why do you run fruitlessly with your neck outstretched across the desert?
This is a *tāpiccha* tree enveloped by a forest fire in the summer heat; it is not a cloud charged with lightning.
O timid female cakora bird, shield your family with the fold of your wings!
Much of the night has passed; how much remains? The darkness has vanished and the moon has risen.
O Cātaka bird, if the wind causes even a single drop of water to slip from the cloud into the hollow of your beak, you alone are the unfortunate one;
the cloud is truly successful as the giver of life.
O mind, O you who possess but a fragment of wealth, how greedy you are out of natural affection! Yet even so, separation from that [wealth] remains inevitable, even for Śiva himself.
O bird of the mind, you have become weary from wandering in the forest of sensory objects;
if you desire rest, dwell for a long time upon the wish-fulfilling tree of Śiva.
O cloud, if you do not give even a few drops of water to the cātaka bird,
then before long he will become one to whom you must offer a final handful of water.
"O musk, you have been abandoned by the vulgar out of suspicion that you are mere mud! Enough with this grief; are there no kings upon the face of the earth?"
O beloved, drinking again and again from your face, the roaring god of love— alas!—
smites us wretched ones even in the darkness, making us smile.
O blooming lotus, let the bees hum sweetly as they lick the flowing nectar of yours;
yet, in every direction, this other kinsman, the wind, remains indifferent and reveals your fragrance to all.
O Lord, moist with compassion for the wretched! O Lord of Mathurā, when will you be seen? My heart, distressed by not seeing you, my beloved, wanders about; what am I to do?
O simple one with a downcast face, why do you despair at the thundering of the wicked?
Even slander against the Son of Devakī, who stands as an obstacle to us, is overcome by our lofty austerities.
O child Lavangi, by what misdeed have you been made to bloom at the door of a plowman, that your clusters of blossoms,
covered in dust, should roll about everywhere within the limits of his courtyard?
O messenger, you alone are my friend; Love is slaying me with his sharp arrows.
Bring that beloved here quickly, otherwise the departure of life will be easy.

O son of Nanda, look with compassion upon me, your servant, who has fallen into the treacherous ocean of worldly existence, and regard me as a mere speck of dust resting at the base of your lotus feet.

O female bird, in this grove of *lavaṅga* creepers, drink the honey after driving away the bees; for in this forest teeming with forest-dwellers, there is no distinction between what is pleasant and unpleasant for the virtuous.
O friend, last year the Malaya breezes blew and the cuckoos sang; yet my mind was not agitated by passion as it has been this year, though all was in vain.
O cakora birds, drink the water of moonlight with your throats upraised and your flickering beaks extended in succession;
for it is not devoid of splendor, and thus it becomes the cause of saving the lives of those distressed by separation from their beloveds.
O musk deer, alas! Do not indulge in such great pride because of your fragrance, which stands at the pinnacle of all perfumes;
for by that very scent, you deprive your own father—hidden in a mountain cave and utterly wretched—of his life.
O lotus, dripping with nectar, I believe that your fortune alone is such that even when you are covered in flowers, the aged and pure swan does not abandon you.
O Madana, were you not burnt by the Lord out of anger? Or did you, O fool, not experience the suffering of separation from Rati?
Since you yourself do not know the pain of others, you torment me with showers of arrows that are useless and unworthy, now that I am separated from the lotus-eyed woman.
O beloved Manmathacūtamañjarī, with eyes as long as your ears, where are you going after stealing my heart? Why does this kingdom remain here without a king?
O, does this young cakora bird of mine not become a disciple of that sage who drinks the ocean?
And for him who has studied how to swallow the sea, what difference is there between drinking the rays of the moon and drinking mere droplets?
O sandalwood, of what words could this greatness be an object?
For you nourish with your outpourings of fragrance even the serpent that vomits poison.

O Mālatī, you who have surpassed the blooming lotus—the abode of the wind—by the excellence of your fragrance! In this world, I consider you alone to be the object of the bee’s pursuit for drinking honey.
O fawn-eyed one, this mark of the beloved’s teeth upon your sprout-like lower lip is not merely that;
is it not rather a mystical diagram (*yantra*) of the yogi Smara, inscribed with the mantra-syllables that enchant the world?
O Ocean, if you do not harbor anger toward us, we shall say something to you:
though the waters were released by the cloud who sought them from you, O Great One, you did not abandon them.
O Smara, you who have transgressed all bounds, remember, remember the fire of Hara!
It is improper for you to burn again this person already consumed by the agony of separation.
O fair-thighed one, you who have extinguished the lamp of Love— if you have indeed passed from the range of my sight,
tell me, how will you depart from my heart, which is pinned by the arrows of the peerless archer?
O timid one, abandon this firm embrace; let go of your lover, for you are afraid of a new union.
The dawn is breaking, O fair-limbed one, and the cockerels are now crowing.
O Moon, ask the Moon: from whom did you clearly learn this generosity in burning?
Was it from the poison that withered Śiva’s throat, or, O dull-witted one, from the submarine fire in the ocean?
O fowler, I join my palms in supplication to you; what other means of livelihood do you have here? Why, by killing these parrots, do you render this forest devoid of Sarasvatī?
O Smara, grant me your sight this very moment; Mādhava here is yearning for you.
Indeed, while men's affection for beloveds may be unstable, it is certainly not fickle toward a friend.
O Pārvatī, be gracious! I, Śiva, have prostrated myself at your feet.
How indeed can you call me "Śiva" (the Auspicious One), when I am clothed in the bloody hide of an elephant?
"O friend, quickly prepare a cool breeze with plantain leaves; O companion, swiftly smear my body with excellent camphor;
O beloved, arrange a bed with fresh lotus petals"—such words, it is said, clearly circulate in the house of that lord.
"O friend, is it night or is it day? Is that the moon or is it the sun? Does Kāma flash before me, or is it my beloved?
Thus, at every moment, the mistress of my life, distressed by separation from her lord, speaks repeatedly and very softly to her friend standing nearby.

"O friend, does a fault arise from a kiss? Or perhaps from an embrace of the breasts? Or what of love-making? Tell me the truth!"—when her lord spoke thus, the deer-eyed woman, looking at the lamp, alas, alas, alas! was submerged in an ocean of shame.
"O friend, my lord of life has gone to another land; therefore, the flower-arrowed god intensely pierces my body with his shafts.
Make such an effort quickly that he of keen intellect may soon return here to ward off the affliction of Love."

"O friend, do you not know that a husband who is like a friend is praiseworthy? O companion, how was it that even you did not realize that a paramour who is like an over-familiar friend is praiseworthy?"
O lotus, this bee has now come to your presence at evening, having abandoned the mango blossom out of greed for its incomparable nectar; yet it is improper that he should now seal your mouth.
O simple one, these words of instruction will enter within your ears only so long as my heart has not yet taken its place within yours.

"O slender-limbed one, quickly ascend the couch and bind my neck with the creeper of your arms!"—when her lord spoke thus, the deer-eyed woman, looking at the lamp, alas, alas, alas! was submerged in an ocean of shame.
O beautiful one, thinking your face to be the eternal full moon, the storehouse of nectar,
alas, this [moon] falls perpetually into the midst of the ocean.
O beautiful one, look now! The sun is reaching the peak of the western mountain;
the night, matted with a mass of darkness, is approaching. Perform all the arts of love.
O tremulous-eyed one, alas, having been told this news by my kinsmen today— news like a stroke of lightning— you will undoubtedly behold all ten directions as empty, with their faces turned away.
O charming girl, with these lives held in your hands like balls, how much longer do you wish to play at this endless game?
O Hāralatā, restrain this agitation caused by the burning of your body by the *huṃkāra* of Śiva;
for a love born of true devotion is not found among courtesans.
O heart, have compassion for me and maintain your fortitude without that fawn-eyed woman;
whether this happens suddenly with a "tat" sound or it bursts forth immediately—this is what has been said, for there is no other way.
They speak much that is improper and lie down anywhere at all;
with their limbs cast about naked, they are like drunkards overcome by old age.
Whether what has been said by the ignorant lord is improper or proper, one should always praise him, even if he is dull-witted;
yet, wishing to be free from attachment, one should somehow simulate indifference in the assembly, and when the king is satisfied, one should discuss one's own affairs as if in secret.
What is improper for a master is proper for a servant, and what is proper for a base person is a reproach;
nectar was death for Rāhu, while poison became the ornament of Śaṅkara.
One who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, and lazy; one who is despondent and procrastinating—such a doer is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Men avoid from afar a ruler who conducts himself improperly, who is difficult to behold, and who lacks self-control,
just as elephants avoid the mud of a river.

What could be more improper than this: that the dust of funeral ashes shall leave its mark upon these two breasts of yours, the very seat of yellow sandalwood, which are so easily accessible even to the three-eyed Lord Śiva?
Fools do not purchase liberation with even ten thousand or a million ordinary enjoyments, nor do they buy it with five or six *bilva* leaves.
By causing blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting,
a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death.
O leader of the flock of parrots, you are spending these hundreds of days in vain upon the trunk of this tree out of an impetuous hope for fruit.
When the *kiṃśuka* tree first puts forth its blossoms, its face becomes dark; at that very moment, it was recognized that any acquaintance with fruit is unattainable from it.
Ah! Who is this blessed woman, standing at the window of the white palace, awakening the god of uneven arrows with the tinkling of her anklets?
She who was previously made emaciated by sleeplessness and mercilessly pierced day and night by the showers of arrows from the flower-bowed god when her lord of life had departed.
Ah! Who is this who, from the surface of the window of her playfully white mansion, awakens the Flower-Bowed God with the tinkling of her anklets?
Oh, how the pair of her eyes shines, transcending the path of hearing; how then shall Madana not conquer the three worlds with his smiling face?
O pillar of the pleasure-chamber, what meritorious deed have you performed,
that the proud woman, having left her beloved on the couch, embraces you instead?
Ah, who knows this? For the company of her own husband does not delight the hearts of women as much as the company of another man.
Even though she has been enjoyed by him at will throughout the entire day, the lotus plant closes her eyes (the lotuses) at the touch of the moon's rays produced during the night.
"Ah! Who is this old man, the master of the house? Is he your father? "No, he is not my husband; rather, he is blind and moreover deaf.
"Hum! I am weary today and wish to sleep right here in this inner chamber. Where shall I go in the night? Indeed, I shall sleep here where there are no biting insects or mosquitoes."

O you who are the support for the lotus-eyes of the daughter of the ocean! Quench me quickly with those eyes that delight the three worlds—eyes which surpass the blazing fire that consumes the body of Śiva, distressed by the weight of his fever, and which eclipse the pride of the rising splendor of the morning lotuses.
O palmyra tree, feel ashamed; you do not shine on account of your great height, for you have neither fruit nor shade, and your surrounding bark is indeed hard.
Blessed, blessed is this simple plantain tree with its beautiful leaves; I consider it to bring happiness to others by its nectar-like fruit.
Ah! By good fortune, my acquaintance with the household-demoness has vanished; through the reversal of delusion, the mind now flickers slightly toward Brahman.
Even the transformation of the senses appears as if dissolved from their objects; nevertheless, the knower of the field yearns again and again for the forest.
Ah! My mind, which has wandered far astray upon the perilous forest paths of the sense-objects, has now been brought to rest by itself;

it is now immersed in that ocean of supreme bliss where all transformations have fallen away through discernment, an ocean that is free from whirlpools, eternal, and characterized by unwavering stillness.
O friend, O blue-necked one, tell me where are those sages today, whose supreme delight your noble play used to spread?
There they are in the distance—cruel Śabaras with feathered arrows, who, having suddenly heard this sound, hasten to kill you! Alas!

O jewel upon the crowns of the circle of kings! Alas, by the flame of your majesty, which is possessed of the intense heat of the splendor of your arms, the fame of your enemies—acting as manifest mercury—burst forth from the furnace of its smelting; thus, under the guise of stars, it has scattered upon the surface of the sky.
O bearer of waters, hide the other quarters and leave this region; here dwells the Sage born from a jar.
When his anger rises, even that ocean will not remain for you, since you display your prowess here only by drinking water again and again.
O bee, alas, do not indulge in this vain despondency of mind, distracted as you are by frequenting hundreds of creepers during the season of frost!
Right here before you, with the arrival of the month of blossoming flowers, this fresh cluster of mango blossoms is bursting forth like a stream of honey.
Ah, my tongue has remained indifferent toward both of those things which are of little utility:
the prolixity of speech when the subject is weighty, and the brevity of speech when the purpose is trivial; for eloquence consists indeed in speech that is both measured and substantial.
O Mother! Seeing your face, has Rāhu, trembling with thirst, taken up residence here under the guise of your hair, mistaking it for the moon?
Or does he, O young woman who is the destroyer of Kandarpa, thus seek to devour the tongue once more, using the streak of vermilion as a pretext?

"O mother! Father! Where has he gone?"—when the enemy's child asked this question here in the cave-dwelling while his own mother remained hidden, she quickly covered his mouth with her tear-filled hand and, sighing deeply, O Śiva, Śiva, answered him only with her eyes.
O pearl, jewel among gems! Spread forth and illuminate the palaces of the lords of the earth; make your own virtues bear fruit.
Why do you waste yourself in vain here within the hollow of a mere oyster shell? This ocean is vast and deep; who here would ever value you?
O Lord Darpanārāyaṇa, if you desire to besiege the city of your enemy, then heed my words:
train your troop of horses in the skill of crossing the surging river of tears from the eyes of the wives of the hostile king’s citizens.
O King, when my wife heard the words [of the executioners] loudly on the road, she, with a distressed face, carefully covered her infant’s ears;
that she did so with eyes full of tears while I had failed in every remedy—that remains a thorn in my heart, and you alone are fit to extract it.
O swans of the lake, do not narrow the space of your own dwelling upon seeing the birds moving in the sky;
for these are the deer belonging to those who observe vows honored by the world, who are free from desire, and for whom even the oceans are as mere blades of grass.
O mass of waters, do not harbor pride on account of this meager wealth of a few drops; for the wise are indeed free from arrogance.
Alas! Have you not been seen within the hollow of the palm of Lopāmudrā’s husband, amidst the throng of wriggling aquatic creatures?
O Ocean, mass of waters! Out of fear of the wielder of the thunderbolt’s wrath, this son of the Lord of Mountains has approached you out of love for your wings.
If, however, this submarine fire dwelling within you should blaze up and wither his every limb, then who would be his refuge?
O moon-lotus, you have vainly cultivated a sense of kinship with the moon;
public scandal has spread everywhere, and alas, our union was never truly realized.

"O friend, the moon is setting, yet your obstinacy does not diminish; the darkness forcibly persists, and your mind has not cast away even a trace of resentment. Dawn has appeared, yet there is not the slightest rise of compassion in you; the night is indeed passing away—do not leave your lover despondent."
Ah, heaven! For those traveling abroad, heaven would be but a journey of a few days, were it not for the lofty jar-like breasts of the deer-eyed woman.
Travel provisions are sought without asking, both roots and fruits are easily obtained, there is water at every place, and on every path there are trees for rest.
O cloud! Alas, why do you vainly discharge a torrent of water into the ocean, which has already surpassed the mountains of the world with its play?
Instead, provide these trees with water; they are exhausted by the devouring of the fierce, blazing flames of fire on all sides.
I experienced a sensation born of non-yoga; this intoxication was not for my benefit.
Even from a fault, a lightening of that fault arises, just as the attenuation of sin occurs through the power of ignorance.
Even one who is worthy may incur wickedness by carrying an unsuitable object;
by carrying the sword given by Indra for the sake of protection, the hunter became a sage.
Ayodhyā has become a wilderness, abandoned by both my father and my brother;
like one afflicted by thirst following a river whose waters have run dry, I am running after it.
"Noble lady, you who act so rashly, what is the use of your pacing back and forth? With the heavy burden of your pair of breasts, you will break with a crash."

One who is not impassioned does not experience pleasure; one who is not impassioned does not suffer pain. Indeed, it is the impassioned person alone who is always the locus of both pains and pleasures.

That which is unprotected remains by the protection of fate; that which is well-guarded perishes when struck by fate. Even one abandoned in the forest without a protector lives, while one who exerts every effort at home does not live.
Truth that is unprotected may be protected by destiny itself;
however, that which has been destroyed by destiny—no protection for it is seen.
Those women who, though confined at home by trustworthy male guardians,
protect themselves by their own efforts, are truly well-protected.
They say that a king who fails to protect his subjects, yet takes a sixth part of their produce as tax,
is one who carries away the entire impurity of the whole world.
Whatever sin the subjects commit when they are not protected,
half of that belongs to the king, because he receives taxes from them.
The forest is protected from the lion; therefore, the lion is well-protected. Thus, through mutual assistance, friendship is established upon that basis.

The forests have been abandoned by the deer, the mountain caves by the lions, the quarters of the sky by the elephants, and the waters by the beds of lotuses—all of these surpassed in beauty by the eyes, waists, breasts, and faces of beloved women. Now that the self-respect of the virtuous has withered, there remains for them only death or departure to distant lands.
And the deer, nurtured by her offering handfuls of wild seeds, placed such trust in her that she,
out of curiosity, would measure her own eyes against theirs before her friends.
Wailing has been performed in the wilderness; the corpse of a dead man has been massaged with unguents; a lotus has been planted on dry land and watered for a long time in barren soil;
a dog's tail has been bent down; whispered incantations have been made into the ears of the deaf; and the face of the blind has been adorned—all this was done because a foolish person was served.
The fire entered the village of wild forest deer;
the smoke ascended to the sky as if to seize the deer in the lap of the moon.

Where is this vast forest, and where is the deer wearing a golden thread? Where is this pearl necklace, and where is that bird? Where is this frail woman, and where is that jewel of a maiden belonging to the graceful lord of serpents? And where are we? The Creator is secretly causing his own mysterious intention to sprout forth in some inexplicable way.
Flowering trees in the forest and kinsmen living far away— what is the use of that which does not stand by one at the time of need, even if it be abundant?
Discontent comes upon me, not sleep; my mind counts his virtues, not his faults;
the night slips away, yet the hope for union does not; my body wastes away, but my passion does not.
The darkness born of youth obstructs the vision of the young; it cannot be dispelled by the light of jewels, nor can it be warded off even by the rays of the sun.
For even enemies certainly become friends to one who wields the rod of punishment;
indeed, a king who relies primarily on the rod enjoys the earth by means of his conquest.
For even enemies should be allied with when there is great importance in the matter at hand;
for, O gods, those who have reached the path of worldly purpose act like the snake and the mouse.
An ointment made from the leaves of the *aralu* tree removes diseases of the mouth caused by bovine afflictions;
lye derived from the *gonāsa* plant destroys long-standing pustules.
Beholding this lotus, charming with its sporting khañjana bird,
I recall her beautiful face with its tremulous eyes.
From Mount Mandara, a breeze arrives here slowly, thick with the nectar of clusters of lotuses,
and enveloped by a torrent of fragrance from the tresses of the most excellent fair-toothed women, exhausted at the end of their lovemaking.
He has delighted among the lotuses and the kunda flowers by the turn of time;
O mango tree, know this: this honey-bee belongs to you alone.
Having seen the sun's orb without rays and fire garlanded with flames,
a man does not live beyond eleven months.
For even speech that is devoid of flavor shines when uttered at the proper occasion;
it brings joy to all hearts, like the giving of a blessing during a tax collection.

It is better for those who appreciate aesthetic flavor (rasika) to engage in a quarrel with those who do not than to converse with those who lack such appreciation; it is better to have one's feet kicked by a woman with breasts like *likuca* fruits than to embrace one whose breasts hang down like those of an old cow.
In a world of living beings without a king, the weak are oppressed by those who are stronger, and no one here possesses mastery over their own wealth.
Since this world would be without a king, therefore let a king be established;
having provided long-term protection for the kingdom, the king shall attain heaven.
In kingdoms without a king, dharma does not indeed endure; they harm one another, so shame on the state of anarchy in every respect!
For when this world was without a king and everything fled in fear from all sides,
the Lord created a king for the protection of all this.
Desiring to embrace those slain by their enemies while fighting in battle, and having heard the sound of the war-trumpets,
the celestial courtesans prepared their long-abandoned ornaments, appropriate for their first reunion with them.
With eyes wide open at the sight of his enemy’s prowess,
and with arms formidable as a sword, he acts like the wielder of the thousand weapons.
As the Creator fashioned the tresses of the curly-haired maiden,
