the line of new body hair shone like the track of a drop of black pigment fallen from the tip of the moving brush.
Hospitality is a duty to be performed even toward an enemy who has come to one's house;
a tree does not withdraw its shade even from one who has come to cut it down.
The dull-witted person who does not recognize an enemy, a friend, a neutral party, one who is indifferent, an elder, or a teacher, perishes in every respect.
Through living with an enemy, through eating poison,
and through intimacy with a wicked person, one meets with death.
The fault of having come from afar is caused by dwelling with an enemy; because it shares the nature of living with a serpent, it is corrupted by constant agitation.
Like a silk-cotton tree produced from eating the seed of a *plakṣa* tree, or like a pigeon [produced] from a [silk-cotton tree],
it constantly causes distress and brings fear even later on.
One must never place trust in a friend who belongs to the faction of one's enemies, even if that person knows one's secrets and speaks kindly— even if they were Bṛhaspati himself in person.
It is the policy of a master that when enemies have been conquered or rendered powerless, their servants must inform him;
O Śambhu, I have been conquered by the objects of the senses—now perform that which is praiseworthy.
With his body wounded by the blows of enemies, yet accompanied by his charioteer, horses, and footmen, he—
ever generous in giving away his wealth— shines with steadfastness as the ornament of the earth.
An enemy becomes a friend, and even a friend may become hostile;
since the human mind is unstable, who indeed can place their trust in it?
"O dear one, this is indeed the group of six enemies; it has six steps.
By cutting even one of them, lame the bee-like Fortune."
O Great King, listen as I describe to you those signs of impending death,
by the observation of which the knower of yoga recognizes his own mortality.

One should recognize as the most unfortunate among people that person who wounds the vitals with harsh and rough speech, piercing men with the thorns of words, and who carries in his mouth the very goddess of misfortune, Nirṛti.
Without the night there is no moonlight, and without the moon there is only great darkness;
without both of these, the stirrings of love do not shine forth for the two lovers.
When the sky was cleared of stars by the webs of the sun’s crimson rays, and the cool breeze blew gently at dawn,
the orb of the moon hung upon the slope of the western mountain as the multitude of young women released their lips from their lovers’ mouths.
I recognize this twilight as the jewel of heaven that performs the marriage rite, offering the stars as parched grain into the fire of the sun’s crimson rays.
Like her, that very jewel causes a delusion of fire from afar; who, being eager, would not look upon its hand with curiosity?
With the tips of her hands and feet charming like rows of reddish lotuses, and with eyes like blue lotuses blackened by a thick swarm of bees,
the newly born morning twilight follows the night like a daughter, speaking through the cries of the birds.

With her tender lotus-feet slipping upon the hard surface of the earth, Janaki walks suddenly stumbling; O Earth, at the places where she sets her feet, abandon your hardness, for Janaki is going to the forest.

"O slender-limbed one, let your face eclipse the beauty of the moon with its reddened eyes, its knitting brows, and its slightly quivering lips! Enough with these conciliations; O high-minded lady, let this anger of yours increase! May Śiva, embraced by the Goddess when she spoke thus, be for your welfare.
O young girl, your lower lip utterly surpasses even the reddish coral tree and the exceedingly tender sprout,
owing to its excellence in sweetness.
By means of garments that surpassed the glow of the dawn, by barley sprouts that had found their place upon their ears, and by the warbling of cuckoos—
the forces of Love have rendered the graceful men single-mindedly devoted to women.
Coloring all the mountains and forests with its glow, repeatedly causing distress to travelers,
the mass of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees bore the splendor of a forest fire.
O young woman, your eyes are reddened and your lover’s face is darkened;
O friend, her face is cast down, yet within it the fire of passion blazes.
At the time of sunrise, one obtains the fruit within ten days;
at the time of releasing the cows, it is held that the fruit is obtained immediately.
This fourteenth [digit] is indeed appropriate here for Arundhatī, Kāmapuraṃdhrī, Lakṣmī, the consort of the enemy of Jambha (Indra), and the nine Mothers,
since it is the invisible power that pervades both ankles.
One who does not become angry when another reviles him finds the merit of the other's good deed;
whereas the one who forgives but nevertheless remains angry merely wipes away his own misdeed.
Whether he be formless or handsome, wealthy or destitute of property,
ill-behaved or endowed with virtue— a husband is the supreme deity for women.
O fish of the mind, you now wander at will in the waters of youth; do you not see the ocean of young women?
There, the fisherman Manobhū (the God of Love) repeatedly casts a net of body-hairs, equipped with the twin pumpkins of her breasts, using the thread of passion as his line.
O Daiva, let desire for wealth and the like, which depends on you, depart; but who in this world has the right to take away my conduct, which depends on me?
"MSS_2882-1: You are the deceitful messengers of Yama, formidable in your deceptive forms; announce me to Yama, for you have no authority over me.
MSS_2882-2: And as for me, I have been drinking the honey-sweet nectar dripping from the pair of lotus feet of Śivasundarī; do you not know this, you wretches?"

O blue lotus, adorned by a swan, with trembling petals, refuge for the swarms of bees that serve as ornaments for Rāma’s hand, dispeller of the shame of Love’s dalliance, subduer of the lives of those separated from their beloveds—O friend, I am distressed; loosen my delusion and tell me, where is she whose face is like the moon?
Chant the name of Hari, the abode of security, at every moment;
for when the breath flows outward, what confidence can there be?
The hub is held together by the spokes, and the spokes are established upon the hub;
in this same way, the wheel of livelihood proceeds between master and servant.
The lotus grove wept bitterly through the bees; it closed its eyes and trembled at the waves of water; and the faces of the night-lilies were shattered.
Seeing this intense grief of the *koka* birds separated from their mates in the lake during the night, what indeed can the virtuous not do when distressed by the calamity of others?
The root of *arka* and *karpāsa*, when drunk with water, overcomes poison. By means of an errhine (*nasya*) of *paṭola* root, even one bitten by a deadly serpent survives.

A certain woman with tremulous eyes was seen, like a goddess of Love, bearing a body as beautiful as a red mirror; she eclipsed the sun’s shadow with her lightning-like flash of nectar, deeply immersed within a vast circle of supreme splendor resembling a wheel.
O trees, what is the use of your accumulation of fruit, what use to you are your fresh blossoms, or your vast abundance of great creepers, or your extensive lineage?
For not a single one among those who once existed remains in the family today, under whose shade travelers sit and satisfy themselves with fruit.
In this forest, some are *arka* trees, some are *akṣa* trees, some are *dalakṣmāruha* trees, some are *nimba* trees, and some are cruel *karīra* shrubs.
But there is no mango tree here, O friend, which is adorned by swarms of bees clustering around it, heavy with nectar, and where the cuckoo spreads its nectar for the ears.

O timid one, the austerities of the red lotus— consisting of its standing in water while facing the sun— have now borne fruit, since you, with this foot whose passion is veiled by lac-dye, bring about its humiliation.

The ocean is the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), the lunar disc is the *śrī-candana* paste, the stars are the rice grains, the sky is the *bilva* leaf, the celestial river is the incense, and the sun is the lamp.

The planets are the five fruits, and moreover, the quarters of the sky are the betel-leaf; O Lord of the World, Meru itself is the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) in the worship of You, the Lord of Fame, the Master of Yoga.
Having offered the *arghya* to the god Bhāskara with a concentrated mind, he should then,
having adorned his body and observed the proper conduct, [proceed] according to the mantra.

Disregarding the king who was crying out, "The water-offering! The water-offering!", the elder brother of Bharata fixed his gaze, with its pupils wide and fierce, upon that direction where the flames of the fire of the Kshatriyas' wrath were rising.
Through the ascetic power of the priest, through the excellence of the worship,
and because of the beauty of the images, the God attains presence therein.
We constantly worship the Lord of the Gaṇas, yet we kill hundreds of mice; we meditate on Bhairava in our hearts, yet we drive away dogs.
We bow to the Lord of Beings, yet we subdue hundreds of spirits. For the virtue of one does not cover even the great faults of another.
By throwing a flower with the thought "I am worshipping," a person is liberated; yet by scattering that very same flower with the thought "I am piercing [him]," the God of Love was reduced to ashes.
Thus, he who delights solely in internal states and is indifferent to external things—he is my Lord and my deity; any other is not even mentioned by name.

Not far from the forest fire, which licks the sky with its terrifying garlands of flames, these cruel smoke-eagles (*dhūmyāṭa*) wander from branch to branch in their own haunts; flying up again and again, their movement slowed by the joy of devouring moths, they shriek further and further ahead, grey and difficult to discern due to the falling of abundant soot.

May the childhood utterances of Śaktidhara bring you auspiciousness—utterances that, while he tore open the flaming caverns of Vāsuki’s mouths and touched his fangs variegated with poison with his forefinger as he counted them, were a disordered sequence of numbers: "One, three, nine, eight, seven, six."

He who perceives a stone in Viṣṇu worthy of worship, a human being in his guru, the notion of caste in a Vaiṣṇava, or the idea of mere water in the water at the feet of Viṣṇu—which washes away the impurities of the Kali age—and he who perceives the name of Śrī Viṣṇu, the mantra that destroys all defilement, as a mere common sound; or he who regards Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, as equal to others—he is a denizen of hell.
A man should always acquire knowledge and wealth as if he were immortal;
yet, as if seized by the hair by death, he should practice dharma.
It is better to eat even fruits and vegetables at home with a noble spirit, having earned them by one's own effort and relying on no one else.
For one who constantly eats in another's house and is treated with contempt, even food that is well-prepared is not beneficial; therefore, this is the discernment of the virtuous.
O charming one, we consider that Kurukṣetra, where Arjuna, united with Kṛṣṇa, pursued Karṇa, to be the Eye.
Arjuna, Phalguna, Pārtha, Kirīṭin, Śvetavāhana,
Bībhatsu, Vijayin, Kṛṣṇa, Savyasācin, and Dhanañjaya.
"These are Arjuna's arrows; these are not Śikhaṇḍin's arrows.
My limbs are failing me, like bullocks in the month of Māgha."
Arjuna has two vows: neither dejection nor flight.
Life protects the vital organs; life provides food.
O lady of excellent hips, [fight] at the end of Arjuna; O lady of beautiful face, [fight] at the end of Bhīma.
One must fight with the Pāṇḍavas, but Dhanañjaya is to be protected.
When a person strives for wealth by threatening those who ought to be avoided, he perishes quickly; who in this world has not been deceived by prosperity that was accumulated over a long time?
Fie on wealth, which creates many enemies for men; fie on kingship, which is fearful and full of anxiety!
Fie on heaven, where there is the cycle of returning once more; and fie, fie on this body, which is the abode of disease!
He who, having attained great wealth, knowledge, or even sovereign power,
conducts himself without arrogance, is called a wise man.
One who possesses assistants alone is capable of attaining an objective that involves obstacles;
even one with sight does not see a visible object in the dark without a lamp.
Wealth, pleasure, virtue, and liberation— all these belong to a person only so long as the fire of the stomach does not cause affliction.
Let there be no wealth, happiness, or even fame in this world; let there be only misfortune—nevertheless, the steadfast, adhering to their own vow, undertake their tasks with great effort.
For indeed, what is considered wealth by some men may become a source of harm;
and a man who is not devoted to the excellence of true wealth does not find the highest good.
A slanderer does not cause such pain when seizing upon one's wealth as he does with his bitter cries;
a mosquito causes more pain by buzzing in the ear than by sucking blood.

One who knows the meaning and can dispel doubt is superior to that; one who performs his own duty is superior to him; one who is free from attachment is greater than him; and one who does not milk (exploit) his own dharma for personal gain is even greater.
O son of Kuntī, one who desires the highest good must indeed relinquish wealth, just as one sows seed; let there be no doubt in you regarding this.
He who abandons both material wealth and dharma to pursue only desire will swiftly meet with such a calamity, just like King Daśaratha.
A wise person should not disclose the loss of wealth, mental anguish, misconduct within the home, deception, or humiliation.
A wise person should never offer a rebuttal to a king, a sovereign, a child, an elder, one superior in asceticism, a learned man, a woman, a fool, or to one's gurus.
In this world, those two—the one who asks about the meaning and the one who provides it—are easily found in every house;
however, the man who is both a donor and a respondent is rare upon the earth.
Having encountered a difficult-to-cross calamity that threatens the destruction of wealth and life, one whose fear is imminent does not recognize his own prosperity and longs only for his life.
But once he has emerged from that, he enters yet another calamity for the sake of wealth; for one of inferior intellect, both life and wealth are a mutual wager.
Who would consider her to be truly devoted, she who, out of love for wealth, gives herself to one who does not love her,
and who feels no affection even for her own body?

Constantly contemplate what is beneficial and what is harmful; it is true that not even a trace of happiness arises from the former. Even for those who possess wealth, there is fear even of their own sons; this is the established rule everywhere.
The performance of what is meaningful and the avoidance of what is meaningless; the collection of taxes according to justice and the personal remission of them.
He who, without understanding the reasoning behind a matter, forms an intention toward what is auspicious—
whether toward a friend or even an enemy— his mind is likewise wavering.
One should indeed request favors from friends whether wealth exists or not;
for it is only by not requesting that one comes to know the worth or worthlessness of friends.

A minister of peace and war should be appointed by the king— one who is devoted to the protection of wealth, who knows how to distinguish between what ought and ought not to be done, and who is skilled in political strategy.
Those who possess wealth are praised, while those deprived of it are censured;
if this is so even in the case of sacred scriptures, what is so extraordinary about embodied beings?
What virtue is there in one who possesses wealth yet does not give it to those in need?
Wealth has but one course: either its distribution as a gift, or else its transformation into misfortunes.
In this world, only one who possesses wealth is honored by friends and kinsmen;
but a man devoid of wealth, even while living, is like one who is dead.
In this world, even a man of low birth who possesses wealth is most highly honored;
whereas one who is destitute is despised, even if his lineage is equal to that of the moon.
Some have declared that wealth must be protected by all means;
how then was it not protected by Hariścandra when given to the son of Kuśika?
Dharma, however, has been protected by all— even at the cost of their own bodies—
by kings such as Śibi and by brahmins headed by Dadhīci.
For the attainment of wealth leads indeed to delusion and great sorrow;
therefore, one who seeks the highest good should abandon the pursuit of wealth from afar as something worthless.
Seeking refuge is recorded as being of two kinds: for the purpose of accomplishing one's objectives while being oppressed by enemies, and for the purpose of gaining renown among the virtuous.

One who desires the supreme accomplishment of one's goals should practice Dharma from the very beginning; for wealth does not depart from Dharma, just as immortality does not depart from the heavenly world.
The ascertainment of the truth is seen through inquiry and beneficial instruction;
it is not attained by bathing, nor by giving gifts, nor even by hundreds of breath-restraints.
A person is the slave of wealth, and that [wealth] never belongs to anyone;
for everyone in all the three worlds is intent upon its acquisition.
"Man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is the slave of no one;
this is the truth, O Great King. I am bound by wealth on behalf of the Kauravas."

The root of wealth is natural disposition and policy; the root of dharma is compassion and sincerity; the root of desire is wealth, physical beauty, and youth; and the root of liberation is indeed the cessation of all worldly aims.
He should employ her in the collection of wealth and in its expenditure,
as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.
The constant pursuit of wealth, the observance of rules, knowledge of action,
the relinquishment of one's position, alertness, freedom from agitation, and mistrust toward women.
In the acquisition, preservation, expenditure,
loss, and enjoyment of wealth, men experience effort, fear, anxiety, and delusion.
Who would despair in the acquisition of wealth that is full of misfortune,
unless it were to provide a feast for the eyes through beloved but wicked people who are content with it?
The acquisition of wealth is difficult; its arrival at home is difficult;
but its distribution among kinsmen once it has arrived brings happiness.
Having acquired wealth, one who is unfortunate does not enjoy it,
just as the fool Somilaka did upon reaching the great forest.
There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, as well as in its preservation and its depletion;
there is suffering in its loss and suffering in its expenditure, and people even kill for the sake of wealth.
Even a word devoid of meaning, if it is sweet, brings pleasure to the world;
the lute, the flute, the drum, and so forth, serve as our examples in this regard.
He who perceives that objects of value in this world are difficult to obtain, while afflictions are easy to encounter,
and that there is indeed suffering for the sake of one's family— he is liberated.
Give away wealth to worthy recipients, obtain sons born of desire, and do what is pleasing to those you love; for the king hastens toward victory.
Indeed, for those who understand [the nature of things], abundant riches are truly a source of great suffering;
yet even when lacking such wealth, they constantly delude those who lack discernment.
Wealth is like the dust at one’s feet; youth is like the rush of a mountain river; human existence is as fickle and unstable as a drop of water; and life is like foam.
He who, with a steady mind, does not practice the Dharma—which unlocks the bolt of heaven—is later struck by remorse and consumed by the fire of grief when he has grown old.
Objects are by their very nature common to all;
for those who abandon the sense of "mine" regarding them, great fame arises.

May that fear which belongs to the poet— who composes words while his mind is drawn toward the meaning, whose very self is attentive to the sounds, who performs the operations of joining, cutting, arranging, and exiting [the verse],
and who looks about repeatedly with apprehension, thinking "Let no one here catch me"— may that fear belong to your enemies.
O King, the acquisition of wealth, constant health, a beloved wife who speaks kindly,
a submissive son, and knowledge that brings profit— these six are the pleasures of the world of the living.
Wealth remains behind in the house, and kinsmen remain at the cremation ground;
however, both good deeds and evil deeds follow one who departs.
For those distressed by wealth, there is neither friend nor kinsman; for those distressed by passion, there is neither fear nor shame;
for those distressed by learning, there is neither happiness nor sleep; for those distressed by hunger, there is neither body nor vigor.
Knowledge flees from wealth like a mouse from a cat;
let one understand the purpose as a crane does, and conquer the enemy like a lion.
Wealth is suffering to abandon, and even when protected, it brings no happiness;
it is acquired with great hardship, so one should not worry about its loss.
O lord of men, from wealth come dharma, pleasure, and even heaven;
for without wealth, the very sustenance of the world does not succeed.
One fallen from wealth should go on a pilgrimage; one fallen from truth shall indeed go to the Raurava hell.
One fallen from yoga should resort to steadfastness in truth; one fallen from his kingdom should resort to hunting.
Even a mind that has reached a certainty regarding what is beneficial or harmful does not shine;
for messengers who consider themselves wise ruin their own undertakings.
Having thoroughly determined what is beneficial and what is harmful, one should indeed apply oneself with resolve;
one should gather [the former] on account of its qualities, but abandon [the latter] on account of its defects.
Wealth does not exist, yet evil desire does not leave me; my wayward mind finds pleasure in renunciation.
Begging brings humiliation, and there is sin in taking one's own life; let the vital breaths depart of their own accord—what is the use of lamentation?
If wealth did not exist, we would abandon the Dharma; for how many kinds of bodily afflictions must one endure to accomplish that Dharma which is achieved solely through wealth?
If the body becomes exhausted, what loss of Dharma occurs thereby? Having directed our minds toward the auspicious state even once, let us accomplish our goal.
MSS_2968-1 There will be the loss of surplus wealth by the king or by a thief. MSS_2968-2 Indeed, if one eats excessively of food, there may be vomiting or purging.
One who does not carry out his duties, who acts according to his whims, and who is boastful,
perishes quickly even after having obtained the entire earth.
The acquisition, increase, and protection of wealth must be attended to;
for even Mount Sumeru diminishes if it is consumed without being replenished.
There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the protection of what has been acquired;
there is suffering in its loss and suffering in its expenditure—fie on wealth, which is a refuge of misery!
Wealth must be acquired, increased, and likewise protected;
for even the Himalayas waste away if consumed without being replenished.
"You rule over riches, and we too rule over words; thus, while you are a hero in this regard, our skill is inexhaustible in the task of quelling the fever of pride in eloquent speakers.

Those blinded by wealth serve you, while those desiring to hear me do so for the sake of destroying the impurities of their intellect. O King, if you have no regard for me, then my devotion to you is all the more absolute; therefore, I am departing."
He who is a master of wealth but not a master of his senses,
indeed falls from his mastery because of his lack of mastery over the senses.
Misfortunes come to the negligent man who pursues wealth;
therefore, let the man of means always remain vigilant on the path.

We praise the Youthful One, who with a heart full of tenderness honors the repeated expressions of meaning from the beauties of Vraja and their unartificial, eloquent words by means of the tips of his ears.
Some pursue wealth like misers; others indeed adorn it like courtesans; and some, like alchemists, extract essences from it.
But only a few poets here, through incalculable merits, become creators of words that shed the essence of meaning and ornament and touch upon praise.
One should speak of matters of substance, but not of virtues in those who lack them, nor of one's own;
one should not take from the virtuous, nor should one rely upon a wicked person.
When fortune rises for a living being, objects of value enter him of their own accord by the hundreds,
coming from all directions like birds returning to their tree at evening.
But when cognition appears as if it were direct perception despite the absence of an object,
one should recognize that as a dream or a city of the Gandharvas.

In the absence of meaning there is softness, and when the meaning is abundant there is firmness; generally, neither softness of meaning nor [firmness] exists in a single place, whether in a verse or in common worldly usage.
For one who seeks wealth, the words uttered by Śrī Harṣa are indeed pleasing;
however, when it comes to the fortune of poetic inspiration (sārasvata-saubhāgya), their opposite is well known.
Seeking wealth, intent upon the worship of deities and upon dreams and omens,
she constantly goes to the house of the astrologer to inquire about the positions of the planets.
This world of living beings, seeking its own interests, approaches one who is blazing with prosperity;
yet a calf abandons its mother when her milk has failed and she can no longer provide sustenance.
This world of living beings, seeking only material wealth, frequents even the cremation ground;
having abandoned its own progenitor, it flees far away if he is destitute.
If this foolish person, seeking worldly objects,
were to endure those hardships even for a hundredth part of the time while seeking liberation, he would attain liberation.
Whatever hardships a wretched person endures when seeking wealth— if one who seeks the Dharma endures those very same things, they will no longer be a vessel for suffering.
Even when great wealth is at stake, one should not abandon the private recitation of the Veda;
by the abandonment of such recitation, noble families fall into a state of ignobility.
How can we praise the skill of those who discourse on the treatises in extracting meanings—
even from indeclinables— in their thousands?

Wealth laughs at one whose mind is devoid of the habit of giving; the earth laughs at the man who says, "This land is mine"; paramours laugh at one who dotes upon his children; and Death laughs at a king who is a coward on the field of battle.
One who is impoverished, one who is diseased, a fool, one living abroad, and a servant of others—
these five, though alive, are as dead and are partakers of suffering.
Desire, renunciation of wealth, independence, and knowledge of what is appropriate—
a man should resort to a patron who possesses these five qualities.
Even though his request was made manifest, the Lord did not grant the fruit; on the contrary, the son of Daśaratha, acting with hostility and contrary conduct, was joined with that maiden.
How can the proud ten-faced lord of the world tolerate the excellence of another, the ruin of his own honor and fame, and the possession of that jewel among women?
The satisfaction that arises for a seeker through the prompt giving of what they desire is not produced by a large gift given with delay.
O Lord, the piteous gaze of supplicants, having fallen but once upon your face,
never again looks toward the face of another while remaining in that same state.

He who does not turn his back on supplicants, on his circle of friends, or on his enemies—that father, by virtue of him, has truly performed his duty as a father; his son is a true son, and his mother is a mother who has given birth to a hero.
He who, having promised his hope to those who have come to him in need and to those who have previously rendered him assistance,
fails to fulfill it, is the lowest of men in this world.
When she is intent on praise, he who desires her composes poetry and recites it; when she is ready to offer hymns, he praises her.
But afterwards, when she says, "I am going," he falls silent and closes his eyes.

To one who requests, not only wealth like a mere blade of grass, but even life itself should be bestowed; thus says the rule for the gift of material goods, which is skilled in expression, that even water should be given like *kuśa* grass.

The speech of those who seek wealth, scorched by the flames of hunger, reaches out to someone; yet we do not understand for what purpose they bestow that wealth upon one who does not even quench their thirst.
Though faced with millions of plaintiffs and defendants, your mind never turned away from them;
it was only the wives of others who caused you to turn your face aside.
A noble-minded person should eat only what remains after those who seek food have eaten;
Śveta, having eaten what was left over by a seeker, became a consumer of his own flesh.

For those who seek, heaps of gold, glowing like lamps, have been bestowed; in debate, the arrogant words of the horned disputants (the learned) have been refuted by the declarations of the scriptures.
Kings have been uprooted and replanted as if playing with dice; whatever remains to be done has been accomplished. If there is a petitioner, we stand ready even for that, should fate so ordain.
He who shows no aversion toward either those who seek his help or those who are his enemies— such a person,
noble-minded, ever tranquil, and grateful, is someone rare indeed.

While this [king] exists, who bestows such excessive charity, let that Kalpavṛkṣa tree remain somehow bent over under the pretext of the weight of its fruit, which increases as it is plucked by supplicants.
But how can the Jewel Mountain (Ratnācala) remain—exalted by the rise of its wealth of jewels that are never spent, yet thick with the shame of the ill-repute for shunning the throngs of beggars?

One who desires wealth experiences wretchedness; one who has acquired wealth feels pride and discontent; and one whose wealth is lost is filled with sorrow. But the man free from longing dwells in happiness.

O Lakṣmaṇa, those who know the treatises on statecraft and those skilled in seeking gain declare that when one who desires something proceeds without hesitation toward whatever purpose he seeks to achieve, that is what is called "gain" (artha).

One who desires gains insignificance; one who is arrogant meets with a fall; one overcome by passion incurs a stigma; a greedy man suffers ill-repute; one who breaks his promise faces humiliation; a wicked man delights in the faults of others; one who is destitute encounters deception; one who is distracted suffers agitation; one overwhelmed by grief falls into despair; one of foul speech meets with unpopularity; and one enslaved by gambling repeatedly meets with misfortune.

What is the use of wealth that has fallen into the hands of a miser? What is the use of beauty devoid of virtue and prowess? What is the use of a friend who turns his back at the time of misfortune? What is the use of knowledge that is full of deceit and excessive envy?
But when a man is deprived of wealth and has become untouchable,
all his kinsmen abandon him, just as the vital breaths leave a dead being.
This kingdom, protected by wealth, returns wealth once again;
yet a king devoted solely to wealth loses both in an instant.
For all the activities of a man of small intelligence who is deprived of wealth are cut short, like small streams in the summer heat.
A man devoid of wealth is abandoned by friends and kinsmen;
deprived of worldly activities and food, he is lusterless like one whose life has departed.
For what is the use of even that object which is associated with misfortune?
Who indeed would take the jewel from the crest of a serpent?
Dharma is acquired through wealth, and wealth is acquired through dharma;
for these two are mutually dependent, serving as the means for the production of each other.
The constant preoccupation with objects and the senses, which causes men to deny all true objects,
leads one who has fallen away from knowledge and discernment to enter into the state of the primary [ignorance].
When one's own purpose has been perceived and the faults of others have been proclaimed,
one should make oneself virtuous, desiring the conduct of moral discipline.
For from objects that have been distinguished and gathered from here and there,
all activities proceed, like rivers from mountains.
Having obtained my heart's desire regarding material objects, my mind now forms improper attachments toward women and wealth;
and being delayed both in maintaining honor and in performing one's duties—fie upon a man’s lineage and his poverty!

Diseases do not afflict one who makes no effort toward unattainable objects, who always shows respect for those things that can be achieved through means, and who has conquered the senses, provided that fate is not adverse at that time.
For even when an object does not exist, the cycle of transmigration does not cease for one who dwells upon sense-objects,
just as one experiences the arrival of misfortune in a dream.
"O auspicious lady, having gratified my mother's mind—which has long been troubled by many anxieties—with various gifts, I shall satisfy her all at once; otherwise, how could we gain entrance here?"
Wealth is acquired through wealth, just as great elephants are captured by means of elephants; for one who possesses no wealth cannot engage in trade with mere desire.
A man devoid of wealth, even while living, is like one who is dead;
he whose mind turns away from the acquisition of dharma, wealth, and knowledge is likewise.
The meaning of words, whether concealed or partially revealed, attains its true beauty like the breasts of a Marahatta woman:
it is not too exposed like the breast of an Andhra woman, nor is it too hidden like the breast of a Gurjari woman.
Let not the gods, their modesty stolen away by the intense longing for wealth, trample upon this ancient heap of jewels; rather, I am distressed as I contemplate that most perilous state:

O Ocean, when the mountain at the base of the shore collapses under the violent impact of the mass of immense and surging waves churned by Mount Mandara, there arises a deafening roar from the falling multitude of peaks.

Wealth is the goal of men, a husband for women, the rainy season for rivers, and the king of seasons for trees; likewise, a king who practices his own dharma brings back youth that has passed away again and again for his subjects.
No wealth whatsoever has been accumulated, no knowledge whatsoever has been acquired,
no austerity whatsoever has been practiced, and yet my entire life has passed away.
Wealth, indeed, is the life of people and the entirety of their manifold activities;
yet in this world, singers with throats like goats—exceedingly cunning—seize even that away.
He who possesses the knowledge of the accumulation of wealth is a wise man;
birds resort to a lake that is filled with water.
One who is skilled in acquiring wealth should always be of a patient disposition;
even if he is learned, he should not meddle in the affairs of others.
If even wealth were to be achieved through wealth, what would be the status of virtue and pleasure?
Wealth is the root of the entire world; misfortune is the opposite of wealth.
An object that approaches even without a formal request, however small it may be, should not be disregarded by the wise;
I believe that gift of affection bestowed by the venerable Ordainer deserves to be highly esteemed.
The heat of wealth, indulgence by one's father, association with groups of libertines, self-conceit, youth, residence in the city, fickleness of mind, and study of the science of love;
likewise, music, the night, the moon, intoxication from wine, and rivalry with competitors—all these assist courtesans in seizing the wealth of those who are infatuated.
If there is meaning, yet no purity of words; or if that exists, yet no style; or if that exists, whence comes the composition?
If even that exists, yet no novel or crooked turn of expression—alas, this poetry is useless without rasa, and oh, how profound it is!
For a maiden is indeed another's property; having sent her away today to her husband, my inner self has become exceedingly clear, as if a deposit had been returned to me.
For one who has lost his purpose, the goal is attained without effort;
O Noble One, enthusiasm is powerful, and there is no strength greater than enthusiasm.
A well-spoken word endowed with propriety of meaning shines through its ornamentation,
just as a fawn-eyed woman is graced by a necklace resting upon her full breasts.

"O Mother, one half of Śambhu is compassion itself, free from all blemish; the other half is the totality of all other virtues combined"—thus, O Mother, the secret has now been revealed to me as I behold this half of Īśvara which is composed of you.
O Mother, half of Tripura has been conquered by your smile; it must likewise be so accomplished by the other half.
O Janani, I contemplate that smile of yours as the means for the pacification of the three cities (Tripura) in their subtle causal form and their gross nature.

May his body protect you during the performance of the twilight rites—a body in which one half of the lip quivers from the power of recitation while the other half trembles from rising anger; one hand is placed upon the head to offer salutation while the other is raised to strike;
one eye is closed in meditation while the other, wide open, watches with intent; thus, his form displays an equal desire and reluctance toward the same action.

O Lord, half of Śiva was taken by the enemy of the Dānavas and half by the Daughter of the Mountain; thus, in the absence of the Destroyer of Cities upon the surface of the earth, the Gaṅgā went to the ocean, the crescent moon to the sky, the lord of serpents to the earth’s surface, while you attained omniscience and sovereignty, but for me, there is only the wandering for alms.

Having spent half the night in the embrace of impetuous amorous play, he—overcome by an unbearable thirst born from the exhaustion of passion and devoted to wine—is on the secluded roof of his palace; yet, unfortunate as he is, he does not drink the autumnal water from his pitcher, which flows in clear, pure streams mingled with moonlight, while his beloved, weary from their union, lets her creeper-like arms slip loose.
Half her mind is bound by love and the other half relies on bashfulness; thus her lotus-eye is fixed upon the face of her beloved while the other is directed toward the window.
Having placed one foot on the couch and the other on the ground, the frail woman is unable either to remain standing or to move at the time of dawn.
A wife is half of a man; a wife is the best of friends. A wife is the root of the three aims of life; a wife is the companion for one who is dying.
Half of ignorance perishes through association with the virtuous;
a fourth part through the meanings of the scriptures, and a fourth part through one's own effort.

O Goddess, you have assumed this body possessing the characteristics of both female and male in order to demonstrate that in this triple world of moving and unmoving beings, half consists of women and half of men; therefore, you are known as one whose body is the three worlds.
One should arrange the battle arrays (vyūha) in this manner: the crescent moon, the wheel, the wagon, the sea-monster, the lotus, the row, and the cluster.
The three-syllable word for "woman" has a shape like a half-moon;
he who knows that it begins with the letter *na* and ends with the letter *ri* is a wise man.
The four-syllable name of the male, joined with a half-moon,
beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *la*— the wise man knows this here.
If a sword naturally possesses the shape of a half-moon,
it destroys even thousands of defects, just as the moon dispels the darkness.
A bow measuring four and a half cubits is proclaimed to be the best;
that divine bow should be known as the one formerly wielded by Śaṅkara.
How exceedingly beautiful is the jeweled cup, half-filled with wine, belonging to the young woman,
as it is filled by the mass of radiance from her lips, which have become even more crimson by her kisses?
He forcibly drags a lion cub away from its mother, who has her nipple half-sucked and whose mane is disheveled by his wrestling.
In the Ardhapuruṣa region, there is a fish and a stone resembling a pigeon;
the soil there is blue, and for a long time there is abundant water.
If lines are seen situated on the half of the chest of a horse,
its death is predicted upon reaching the tenth year.

Having joyfully gathered much flesh from corpses after they were half-burnt at the funeral pyres, and having exceeded his capacity for eating, that hungry ghost— his body now withered and dry, yet bound by veins that stand out even more clearly—
threatens with a crooked and harsh gaze the jackals who, greedy for food, repeatedly pounce upon him, striking them with fragments of bone dried by the extraction of marrow.

With her eyes half-closed and their pupils flickering, she, languid from the fatigue of lovemaking, held them fixed for a moment; yet even that was not enough to satisfy her lover as he gazed upon her.
Out of weariness, she directed her husband for a moment toward the fanning of the palm-leaf fan;
for a beloved who is the very deity of one's existence causes even the Creator to act with such agitation.
At midnight, at the half-point of the day, when the moon was half-full and the sun was half-set,
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the dark lunar month, Sītā was carried away by Rāvaṇa.
When tasks are only half-accomplished, he who reveals his own secret will meet his end, just as the crane did because of the crab.
Inviting the five-arrowed god with a half-smile, casting aside half of the hem of her garment halfway along the path,
and turning back with half of her eye-arrow, the young woman made the youth only half-and-half.
A horse that is deficient by half a cubit (ardhahasta) is considered middling;
one that is deficient by a full cubit (hasta) from that is known as inferior.
May the form of Purāri, whose body consists of half-woman and half-man, bestow prosperity upon you— just as a boat does for one seeking wealth—
since the other half, from the excessive weight of his love, sank into the ocean of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa).

O Lord of the Earth, if your fame were not born from your acts of giving and the like, it would not reach the feet of Śaṅkara—those feet which possess the splendor of a shining white moon as they rest upon the lap of his former consort Kīrti, whose feet are placed upon the head of the world-elephant that has been turned into Mount Kailāsa; feet that are all-pervading and imperishable.
Fearing the exertion of even the tip of a tongue half a finger in circumference,
the ignorant perform actions that produce affliction for all their limbs.
The half-strung girdle of a certain woman, slipping at every ill-placed step as she rose in haste,
then had only the thread remaining fastened to the base of her big toe.
Those twice-born ones by whom the Vedas have been only half-studied, and who eat the food of Śūdras—what will they accomplish? They are like serpents deprived of their venom.
Even if Śakra were to place Śacī upon half his throne and clothe her in armor for battle against the celestial elephant, who—
save for that Daśakandhara who delights solely in reckless daring— could endure the edge of that steadfast one’s sword?
Who would not consider the day to have the form of Ardhanārīśvara, being dark as a rain-cloud in one half and tawny with sunlight in the other?
"You have come filled with fear when my speech was only half-finished; why is your voice faltering? This is no time for such chatter—let this story rest.
Speak what is at hand! Now, through the mouths of my friends, a great satisfaction has already been gathered within my ears by these abundant syllables and words."
With her half-emerged womb-cavity, soft and copper-colored like the palm of a plantain tree,
she drinks the torrential rain with her cupped hands, as if suffering from the fever of summer heat.

May the luster of Viṣṇu’s teeth protect you—white with the abundant radiance of droplets of milk—as he drinks from one breast while his eyes are half-closed, and as he repeatedly wipes the other breast, still smeared with freshly flowing milk, with his hand; and as his mother fondles him with her fingers, his face breaks into a recurring smile.
Every day, the young woman casts her eyes upon the path of her beloved;
she places garlands of lotuses there as if to make the road soft.
Noble-minded people offer their very lives to one who asks for them, but never a bow to an enemy; nor do they ever give the answer "it does not exist" to a friend.

When her lover called out the name of another young woman while offering her wine, she cast off even her intoxication; yet the other woman, though not drinking the wine, became intoxicated upon seeing it.
O you whose banner is Garuḍa, O mind, these cows were first entrusted to you out of affection as if they were young calves; now, being destitute of wealth, this fee is being given.

Having approached from nearby as if out of pride, thinking "This is that very best of rivers," and desiring to lift up the Yamunā with the force of his anger, he raised his plowshare; this was the cause of [the river's] safety.

For the one marked by the palm tree (Kṛṣṇa), whose heart was overcome by the taste of the [river's] water, his upper garment slipped from his shoulder; his feet were cast askance, then followed a great turning, a quick rising, and a rushing forward.

Alas, why is this profound treasure of the preeminent poet being unveiled before those ill-taught people who find pleasure in the proliferation of modern speech? What conscious person indeed would here offer musk in the presence of a village assembly whose mouths are captivated by the heavy scent of mud? It is all in vain.

May that unprecedented Sthāṇu protect you—he whose five branches bend downward, who possesses a shimmering mass of matted locks above, and who, though eternally leafless, removes the threefold affliction of those who take refuge in him;

he who, having received the sprinkling of waters from the celestial river upon his head where the knots of hair are bound with young shoots, bears fruit in the form of hundreds of desired rewards for those possessed of devotion.
He who merely decorates a verse is a parrot, not one of middle rank; he who makes a verse sufficient is indeed a parrot, not one of middle rank.
For old age adorns kings, ministers, physicians, and ascetics;
yet it mocks courtesans, wrestlers, singers, and servants.

Victorious is your life, O lovely crest-jewel, which is praiseworthy in every way as it savors the activities of the lotus-hand of that deer-eyed woman— activities which are the essence of great merit— as she turns her face askance with a hissing sigh while experiencing intense pain from adorning her ears.
His ornament is a skull that inspires dread; his attendant is Bhṛṅgin, whose limbs are withered; and his sole wealth is a single, aged bull.
Such is the condition even of Śiva, the teacher of all the gods, when fate stands crooked upon his head; what then are we?
Viṣṇu is fond of ornaments; Śiva is fond of streams of water;
the Sun is fond of salutations; and the Brāhmaṇa is fond of food.
Indeed, there are certain accomplished poets who bear ornaments, possess stylistic grace, excel in aesthetic flavor,
and have their identities clearly defined by technical characteristics.
For forgiveness is indeed an ornament for women and for men as well; that which is difficult to perform has been practiced by you, especially among the gods.
"O daughters, such as is your forbearance toward one another without distinction—
O little daughters, forbearance is charity, forbearance is sacrifice, and forbearance is truth."
Forgiveness is fame; forgiveness is dharma; the world is established upon forgiveness.
Though adorned with precious jewels worth ten million gold pieces and with elephants, horses, and mounts,
one does not obtain life for even the blink of an eye when seized by Time with its crest-lock.
Peacocks are adorned by their cries, which are reddened with passion;
likewise, the learned are exceedingly adorned by speech endowed with the quality of sweetness.
For those ascetics endowed with the power of adornment, the power of forbearance is supreme;
it is a stream of water for the forest fire of malice, and in this very world, forbearance is the pacification of misfortune.
Enough with talk of the third heaven; what is the use of universal sovereignty? Let even the splendor of liberation remain far away.
Within the depths of the groves on the banks of the daughter of Mount Kalinda, my mind is captivated solely by that luster, dark as a fresh tamāla tree.
These virtues, headed by discernment, were indeed sufficient to restrain Nala’s fickleness;
yet Smara creates one who is truly unobstructed (Aniruddha) even in the presence of Rati—for such is the very nature of creation.
Enough with possession here, for possession is fraught with fault;
indeed, the silkworm is bound by its own cocoon.
Enough of speaking at length to one who disregards beneficial words;
he incurs harm from such a person, just as Sūcīmukha did from the monkey.
Enough with much talk; wherever you find attachment, right there lie the rows of forest fires of your suffering.

Enough, O wise and dear one, of transgressing my request; even after making various protests regarding what must be done, you will surely stumble from the path of glory arising from the state of being obedient, which is free from the play of wicked talk.
Enough with delay, for it is time to hasten; indeed, deliberation is appropriate only for a task that can endure patience.
Sharp intuition, like the instruction of a guru, never waits for the arrival of the right moment.
Enough with this dispute; let him remain exactly as you have heard him to be, in every respect.
My mind is fixed here, its sole essence being devotion; the conduct of desire does not regard what is said.
Enough of staying in this cemetery, crowded with vultures and jackals, abounding in skeletons, terrible, and terrifying to all living beings.
But no one who has come under the power of time has ever returned to life;
whether beloved or hateful, such is the destiny of all living beings.
His body cracked by the mass of snow, brought to an end by his encounter with Phālguna,
and having intensely desired the path of fire, the high-souled Bhīṣma became equal to Māgha.

O fair-faced one, who indeed would not revere your sweet face—which is drunk by the darkness of your curls, graced by the splendor of your beautiful smile, and born together with the treasury of nectar? Alas! How could they fail to honor it?
Tresses of hair and wicked people alike are borne upon the heads of timid folk;
even amidst the highest honors, they manifest their crookedness.

The man who has achieved his purpose beholds the spray of water on the tresses of those women eager for the new clouds, appearing as the luster of scented powder on their locks and as drops of perspiration on the planes of their cheeks.
Just as lac-dye is red, so too is the man full of passion;
yet, once his essence has been extracted, he too is cast down at the base of the foot.
Just as a man, having squeezed out red lac-dye, is himself made red by women,
so too is he forcibly cast down at their feet once he has been made red with passion.
Wandering through the dance floors with the fullness of her breasts unobserved,
the lotus-eyed woman cannot be targeted even by the arrows of Smara.

This circle of the earth is traversed by your horses, who are like the side-long glances of noble women—unobserved in their coming and going, yet momentarily cooled by conciliation; who are like the playful anger of lovers—well-rounded, smooth, and elevated; and who are like the breasts of gazelle-eyed maidens—perfectly formed, supple, and high.
Misfortune enters that man who lies down in idleness;
having obtained the fruit without doubt, the skillful man enjoys prosperity.
The heaviness of the belly has gone to the breasts, and the flickering of the feet has gone to the eyes;
O friend, behold my bodily transformation—youth has arrived through this exchange.
The girdles, resplendent with rows of heavy jewels, completely obstructing the surrounding space and resting upon the terrain of their hips, do not leave them for a long time.
Observing that whatever is lofty among the mountains is unassailable, let not the great fall from their superior state of affection; for by what means could their loftiness be surpassed?
Indeed, for all here, the fruit born of karma is truly insurmountable; calamity is a servant of karma and does not pierce the heart.
That which the ignorant, out of pride in their wealth, perform as a forceful mockery produces instead a deep and supreme anguish within.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired,
increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
Just as a worm that has never experienced the taste of milk or other such things perceives the bitter juice of the *nimba* tree— which arises from that same source—
as a source of flavor, so too one who has not seen the elixir of the words of the Lord of Jinas regards false doctrines as an elixir.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired by means of force; one should protect what has been acquired through vigilance;
one should increase what has been protected through growth; and one should bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
One should seek what has not been obtained through righteous means; what has been obtained, one should protect with effort;
what has been protected, one should increase through prudent policy; and what has been increased, one should bestow upon worthy recipients.
The desire to obtain what has not yet been obtained by righteous means, the increase of what has been obtained, and the formal bestowal of that which has increased upon a worthy recipient.
One who has not received his due reward yet is greedy, one who is proud yet has been insulted,
one who is angry yet has been provoked, and likewise one who is afraid yet has been threatened.
One should break these four types [of adversaries] by means of desired objects of pleasure;
one should bring them to proper pacification within both the opposing faction and one's own faction.
O Lord, let these piteous words of one who cannot find entry within and cries out loudly from outside be taken to heart through Your compassion.
Alas, people full of passion long for what they have not yet obtained; once it is obtained, they become dispassionate.
In winter they desire heat, and then, in summer, they desire cold once again.
Even without obtaining wealth from the king, those who have taken refuge [in him] attain prosperity;
behold the dark-blue forest tree standing near a great lake.
Whether they fail to obtain it or do obtain it, the wise do not grieve;
they do not commit an act of immediate retribution, nor do they covet life or wealth.
In the field of the sky, the stars, with their flickering luster,
received the radiance of the seeds of frost as they displayed their fresh sprouts.
One who desires to attain what is unattainable, one who seeks to know reality for a long time,
or one who wishes to conquer— having cast aside shame, a great clamor must be made.
Such is the fate of a person who desires to obtain what cannot be obtained:
there is mental anguish over things not acquired, and that which has been accumulated perishes.
For the sake of attaining what has not been attained and for the increase of what has been attained, and for the purpose of providing a worthy place of pilgrimage,
you should indeed settle a Brahmin who is illustrious, learned in the Vedas, wise, and deeply erudite.
"Enough with this excessive fickleness! Because of its resemblance to a dream or an illusion, and because of the bitterness of its ultimate transformation, such is the nature of union with a woman.
Even if we contemplate this truth a hundred times over, the inner self still does not forget the fawn-eyed one.
Enough, then, with many words; rather, compose a work that binds the hearts of the world, wherein all that has never before been gathered together is now contained in one place.
O brother, because of the delusion that your dull-witted arm-staff is an ornament,
this venomous serpent does not release its grip on your bite.
Enough of taking it otherwise; indeed, O wise lady, this was not uttered by me out of malice.
Generally, those of equal learning are prone to envy toward one another's fame.
Enough with these other reproaches and recounted transgressions;
one should do what is beneficial for oneself—what is skillful and appropriate.
Enough with speaking words that are unpleasant; why have you not remained here with speech of beautiful meaning? Even though the word "nectar" exists, why indeed is water called "poison"?
Enough with these coils raised in front of us; enough with the whirling circles that dazzle the eyes; enough with these incessant outbursts of roars; enough with these showers of venom!
O serpents, why this unbridled fury? Are we not, in truth, merely the reciters of praise for the blessed Tārkṣya?
Enough, enough with the name of that pitiless one; that very same story has returned, and that time has passed once more.
Speak, speak, O messenger! Even the reply of an enemy must be respected.
Enough, enough of this excessive rashness! O lady, quickly release this noose of a creeper.
O mistress of my life, place the noose of your arms around my neck for a moment, so that even my departing life may be restrained.

"Enough, enough with this excessive growth! Stay still, O pitiless one; do you not see that this waist of the girl with thighs like a young elephant's trunk is breaking?"—thus urged by the command of her heavy hips, the line of hair on the dark-eyed maiden seems to climb upward toward her pair of breasts as if to speak.
"Enough, enough! There is no remedy for this first sorrow of separation for the mistress of my life who has departed after being followed [by me].
Thus she cried out, as if restrained by her girdle before she could fall at his feet, saying, "It is better that the lover's journey proceed immediately."

Enough, enough with this effort to dispel the sins of living beings; for that voice which cries "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa!"—if there is devotion to Mukunda dense with bliss, the Fortune of the Sovereignty of Liberation rolls at his lotus feet.
Enough of this! The beggar, whose own interest is known and who is attentive to the needs of the creditor, has a mind agitated by greed; he calls the moon a sparrow and the sparrow the moon.
Enough with the Primeval Boar; let us praise Vaṭudāsa, the supreme one, by whom the world was uplifted without his face being contorted.
A wise person should sustain their life with water or grass as necessary;
however, an unrefined person of ordinary nature should not be shown such affection.
She possesses a pair of feet with a non-graceful gait and thick, curved toes; she has a short, stout neck;
her mass of hair is tawny; she is of cruel disposition and exceedingly corpulent; she smells of the rut-fluid of an elephant; and she is neither marked nor unmarked upon her own body.
The *hastinī* woman eats twice as much pungent and astringent food, is devoid of shame, and has large, quivering lips; she is difficult to satisfy through sexual union.
She has abundant hair even on the exterior, yet her vaginal opening is extremely wide within; such a woman speaks with a faltering voice.
A ruler of men should abandon a servant who is lazy, talkative, stubborn, cruel, addicted to vices, deceitful, discontented, and disloyal.
Upon hearing your name, O slender-waisted one, the body becomes languid, the silk garment slackens, the mind becomes restless, the cheek turns pale, the eyes startled, and the breasts tremble.
Lassitude from the exhaustion of valor, the failure of strategic efforts,
and being overwhelmed by decline, loss, exile, and toil.
One should win over a coward, a fool, a woman, a child, a righteous person, a wicked man, a beast,
one who is preeminent in friendliness, and one of virtuous intent through conciliation.
Neglected by city women with their languid vine-like arms, and no longer a guest in the *damana* shrubs of the palaces,
the spring breeze wanders through the midst of your enemy's city and wastes away, swallowed by an aged python.

Her languidly sweet and tender gaze has become heavy; her lip, once as lovely as a young sprout, now bears its natural color without the aid of betel; the three folds of her waist can only be inferred by their lines; as if gathering together in one place, these naturally beautiful features have been transformed by pregnancy into something indescribable.

I remember the song she sang from within, accompanied for a moment by the humming of a bee wandering inside her blue-lotus ear, as I stood with my heart agitated upon beholding her face with its languidly half-closed eyes, while she herself had fallen into a state of silence.
The glance of that woman, like a virulent poison, utterly exhausts the body, causes the mind to wander, spreads intense fever, and repeatedly brings about delusion.

There, placing upon my chest those limbs of yours— charming yet languid and trembling from the exhaustion of the journey’s end, receiving massage through my firm embraces, and as frail as crushed lotus stalks— you fell into sleep.

O charming girl, tell me, who is this fortunate man that you gaze upon today with eyes that roll languidly, moist with love, repeatedly half-closed, momentarily turned toward him, trembling with shyness, and averted by winking— as if vomiting forth the secret intention of your heart?

Victorious is that great and blessed lotus-face, which possesses a languid, playful, charming, and tender smile; which is perspiring from the act of devouring the beauties of Vraja; whose youthful lips are bathed in a smile as red as the entirety of the dawn's moonlight; and whose splendor intoxicates the ranks of victorious fawn-eyed maidens.

I became the recipient of various glances—those languidly playful, with trembling creeper-like brows; softly closed like buds, then expanded at the corners; slightly contracted upon the falling of each successive gaze.
Whence can the indolent have knowledge? Whence can the ignorant have wealth? Whence can the poor have friends? Whence can one without friends have happiness?
Even one's own mother turns her face away at the time of giving [in marriage] from a son who is indolent, of little merit, devoid of spiritual detachment, and undisciplined in self.
One should never protect those who are lazy nor those who are ungrateful;
the virtues of even an enemy are desirable, while the vices of even a friend are not.
I long to behold that woman lying beside me, her lotus-like eyes languid and reddened, wearing a single garment grey from use, and beautiful with her braided hair loosely disheveled.
With their slender bodies languid from intoxication, the fair-eyed women slowly returned toward their own homes,
their eyes— like outstretched cupped hands— overflowing with the flood of Mādhava’s nectar they had hastily drunk.
The lazy, the dull-witted, the one who seeks only pleasure, the one afflicted by disease,
the嗜睡者 (sleepy), and the lustful— these six are devoid of the scriptures.
One should not eat a round-shaped bottle gourd, nor an eggplant resembling a jasmine flower, nor lentils with their husks, even at the cost of one's life.

The seed of a gourd and the seed of a *trapusa* cucumber, sprinkled with its own water and applied according to the prescribed rite using ointments and other remedies, shall destroy even poison originating from Takṣaka.
Indeed, due to the lack of men, out of fear of their attendants,
and also from the dread of execution or imprisonment, they protect themselves.
My beloved has hair as lovely as a swarm of bees, is full of fragrance, brings delight, and is slender; her hands are as delicate as young sprouts, and she speaks with a voice as sweet as a cuckoo.
O lady of firm breasts, whom does your face not strike down— that face with its locks of hair dark as bees, with eyes possessing the luster of lotuses, and with the radiance of the moon?
O breeze, you scatter in the city of the common folk a wave of musk fragrance that follows swarms of bees and dispels the fever in the hearts of the connoisseurs.
Marked by bees, charming like drops of collyrium, which settled in rows upon the flowers,
the *tilaka* tree truly did not fail to beautify the forest glade, just as a forehead mark adorns a woman.
How can that noble youth, who for a long time sported within the lotus-bud of the celestial river,
now find delight in the desert where trees have perished, having been brought under the power of the decree of separation by fate?
Fragrance follows the wind; prosperity follows the abundance of virtuous conduct;
water follows the downward slope; and the intellect follows what is written by fate.
This bee, once dwelling amidst the petals of the lotus and languid with intoxication from the nectar of the lotus pond,
has by the power of fate arrived in a foreign land and now prizes the juice of the *kuṭaja* flower.
Whether it be a lotus, a deer, or an eye— whatever appears there, whether it be a lotus, the moon, or the face of this deer-eyed woman.

In the spring, the creepers shine like women: with their clusters of blossoms they are like curls of hair, with their breasts they are like [the fullness of] the season, and with their sprouts they are instantly like hands.
Your existence is indeed false, and my existence is likewise false;
though experienced, it is unreal in nature, just like one's own death in a dream.
If the middle part [of her body] has a false form and her hair bears the shape of breasts,
why should the beauty of the lap of this lotus-eyed woman not rival the beauty of a hand?

Victorious is this moon-like face of the fair-limbed maiden, wherein the mass of rays from her teeth—white as crystal during the onset of a yawn—is set within a halo held by her two creeper-like arms raised under the pretext of binding her thick braid that had been loosened; it thus eclipses the earth of the deer-marked moon, which has slipped away.
In the expanse of the flowering forests, the breeze— possessing the majesty of a mass of matted locks fashioned from garlands of *alīna* bees,
and displaying a coating of ash formed by the pollen of flowers— moves slowly, slow as a wandering mendicant intent on gathering blossoms.
What indeed is the greatness of the great, whose treasury of being is undiminished,
if they do not instantly sever the suffering of another upon hearing of it?
One who desires happiness should cultivate friendship with those free from greed, engage in conversation with the wise, and associate with the most excellent.
Non-greed is the supreme wealth; non-violence is the supreme austerity;
freedom from deceit is the supreme knowledge for the wise, being beyond reproach.
For a few days, the hairless face of young men possesses the splendor of the full moon;
but once the vast web of a beard has grown, it bears a resemblance to a lotus submerged in moss.
O Lord, by whom are you not praised— you who have illuminated the three worlds with your extraordinary great light, and who are a pearl-jewel from a noble lineage?
Freedom from greed, health, lack of harshness, a pleasant fragrance, scanty urine and excrement,
radiance, clarity, and gentleness of voice— these are indeed the first signs of the onset of yoga.
Having acquired even a small amount of wealth, a base person quickly becomes arrogant;
like a frog on the surface of a lotus leaf, he considers himself a wielder of the royal scepter.

O Daitya, the strength born of pride is slight, whereas the strength born of freedom from anger is firm; you have been slain by the faults arising from pride, for you spoke words of forgiveness only after abandoning them.
The Creator, without even considering that the space he had fashioned was so small,
has brought about this very expansion of your breasts.
One should accomplish what is to be achieved with the least effort by means of the simplest method;
just as Gautama circumambulated the earth to reach Ahalyā, he instead wandered around Kapilā.
A water-pot with little water that keeps leaking, cows yielding little milk,
one who possesses little knowledge yet is full of pride, and one who is ill-favored yet highly active.
In the service of a minor lord, the only purpose is mere material enjoyment; his favor is as worthless as the price of a goat, and his punishment is a threat to one's life.
One should not despise even a minor enemy who is arrogant because of his strength;
by Rāma, though he was but a child, another Rāma was slain through the abandonment of compassion for a Brahmin.
Generally, one who possesses but a mere fragment of learning displays his power of speech with great arrogance;
for it is the poor actor alone who excessively mimics a drama in every respect.
Even one who possesses little substance, if out of delusion he desires to expand it,
that person of evil intellect later grieves, just like the coconut tree.
He who speaks that which is certain and pleasing with few syllables is indeed an eloquent speaker; he who speaks much that is devoid of substance is a mere chatterer.
Even a collection of very small things can accomplish a great task;
by blades of grass that have attained the state of a rope, even intoxicated elephants are bound.

A base person destroys even a minor offender who has come close by, but not a distant enemy, even one who has committed no wrong; a dog bites a stone that comes near its mouth, yet that fierce beast does not bite the one who abandoned it long ago, even though he stands far off.
Whether the army be small or large,
the certainty that the host of warriors is filled with joy is said to be the sole sign of victory.
Even small virtues become magnified in persons endowed with many qualities,
just as the rays of the moon falling upon the peaks of the White Mountain at night.
Having encountered a small support, even something great becomes small,
just as a lordly elephant, though mountain-like in size, does when reflected in a mirror.

Where even a slight stumble leads to a fall, where rising up again is achieved only with great difficulty, and where the process of entry through the door—dense with a canopy of cane creepers—is arduous;
O deer, why have you, seeking some special gain, abandoned the delightful forest lands and needlessly worn down your hooves by dwelling on the mountain slopes?
For the very small, misfortune arises from abandoning their place of residence, but for the great, it never does;
from the ocean of jewels, excellent gems emerge, yet frogs find their way onto the heads of kings.
It is well known that a jar is filled with even a very small amount of water;
behold the Brahmanic splendor, for he who was born from a jar drank up the ocean!
One who has few desires, is steadfast, and wise, always following like a shadow—when commanded, he should not hesitate; such a person may dwell in the king's residence.
Excessive expenditure occurs through mere extravagance and not through propriety,
just as one might spread out one's feet while covered by a worn-out garment.
Even with a very small means, if it is well-loved, there is purpose;
with the mouth of a beloved woman aided by her two lips, the world is conquered.
For in this world, someone attains fame through even a very small quality;
an elephant is called "karin" by a single trunk, but the sun is not so called even by a thousand.

Even if the gift bestowed by the king is small, or even if it has merely been promised to be given, one should rise and offer a blessing; or, depending on the propriety of the assembly, one may do so while remaining seated.
Even when slight harm is done, one who out of delusion does not attain peace— such association with the base, cruel, and undisciplined,
a wise man, having observed it carefully with his intellect, should avoid from afar.
O young girl, at such a tender age, how could there be a falling of your breasts?
O fool, do mountains not fall when they are dug into from below?
For even a minor enemy, if his prowess increases excessively,
devours one from close at hand, just as an anthill growing from its roots consumes a tree.
A king who has fallen from his lineage, a wise son of a fool,
and a poor man who has acquired wealth— these all regard the world as if it were mere straw.
"The space within the hearts of well-behaved women is not [easily accessible];
as if for this reason, the Creator fashioned her breasts outside [of her heart] with such perfect roundness."
I understand that the name of this tree is "Aśoka" (Sorrowless) because it is appropriate for one whose self is distressed by the ripening of fruit to be otherwise "Śoka" (Sorrowful).
The lord of the stars, whose beloved rise is complete,
having passed beyond the eastern quarter, undergoes his setting.
The horse's shanks should be straight, free from fleshiness, and very beautiful;
the hock-joint should be even, well-knit, and devoid of knots or sores.
One of deluded mind perceives the loss of a loved one as a dart driven into the heart;
but one of steady intellect considers that very same event as having been extracted by way of a gateway to virtue.
O Anaṅga, having perceived that your beloved kinsman’s body has been turned into a mere tale, the moon— his rising rendered fruitless—
will painfully waste away even as the dark fortnight passes.
In the presence of her beloved, silence was speech; not looking was indeed gazing;
and the covering of her limbs with the hem of her garment was the surrendering of those very limbs.

The forests, filled with the gathering and enjoyment of wild beasts and frequented by predatory animals, spoke out all around the Sage; and the hearts of the women were overwhelmed by a rising sense of trepidation.

Having abandoned the creepers whose flowers had been gathered, the swarms of bees alighted upon the young women adorned with delicate garlands; for among those of a dark nature, lack of familiarity is not the primary cause.
Gathering flowers for offerings, skilled in sweeping the altar, and bringing water for her observances as well as sacrificial grass,
that woman of beautiful hair, her fatigue restrained by the rays of the moon upon his head, attended upon Giriśa every day.
"O playful lady, I have now been conquered by the loveliness of your eyes"— thus, as if bowing down out of shame,
the blue lotus at her ear whispered into her ear through the humming of bees.
That which is given with contempt, as well as that which is given without faith,
the sages who speak the truth call the lowest form of giving.
One should not give to anyone out of contempt or even in jest;
an act performed with contempt destroys the giver—of this there is no doubt.
When Bala laughed loudly out of contempt, his circle of teeth gleaming with radiance,
he instantly restored his own body’s natural luster, even though it had been turned crimson by his wrath.
Even when despised by the wicked, a virtue does not become a fault;
for the fragrance of the *campaka* flower does not turn foul because of the bee's disdain.
Through thousands of insults, the faults regarding wealth become even more grievous; and whatever fraction of happiness exists in wealth, that too is produced by sufferings.
Who is capable of reconciling love that has been shattered by contempt?
A split pearl does not join back together even when smeared with lac.
O twice-born ones, the incarnations of Hari, the treasury of beings, are indeed innumerable;
just as thousands of small streams may flow from a single lake.

May the wise, with virtuous intent, here establish that Dharma which protects the entire world like a revered father, which burns away the mass of evil like fire consumes a heap of fuel, which bestows the bliss of Śiva, and which slays the enemy that is saṃsāra.
May the row of Savitṛ’s horses protect you— shining with Aruṇa as its central leader,
and appearing like a single emerald vine of the Fortune of the Sky, draped with high, swelling clouds for breasts.
For the wicked, who are like wild buffaloes striving to search out the mud of faults,
their desires become frustrated within the celestial river of the speech of the lords of poets.

One who proceeds upon the path free from fault and leads other people along it without longing—that teacher should be served by one who desires their own welfare; for such a teacher, being able to cross over themselves, is capable of ferrying others across as well.
Having inspired confidence in his enemy through attentiveness, silence, saffron robes, matted hair, and deerskins, one should pounce upon him like a wolf.
Ascertain with focused attention that which is the foremost among all phenomena;
dedicate your mind to Govinda, the root of intense bliss.

Perceiving the gravity of the task at hand, the densest of darkness did not cause fear; nor did the breasts of the fair-limbed maiden cause trembling in the path of their fine line of body hair when her lover approached.
O guardian of the water-shed, be gracious so that the wives of travelers may live until the appointed day;
hide your breasts, those mountains upon whose paths it is difficult to pass.
The day of the appointed limit has arrived; either this sun is setting for my body’s separation, or it is the end of my own life, O friends.
Therefore, enough with these fruitless bonds of hope! Be gracious, let there be salutation to you; O heart, suddenly burst open like a pomegranate at the time of its ripening.
"This is the appointed day; he has not come here—why? Grant me this moment, O friend, let my eyes behold this audacity before me!
Here I am, I who have set ablaze the very heavens with my rising flames; I shall fall upon the moonlight with limbs anointed with sandalwood paste."
That you have shown me contempt is surely due to the power of my own evil deeds;
for if a *cātaka* bird receives no water from a cloud, who can find fault with the rain-cloud?
Disregard the man destitute of wealth; bestow your respect upon the man of abundant fortune.
For, O charming girl, the creation of such beauty as yours is intended for the attainment of wealth by those like me.
Even when their pride has been shaken by prostrations and they feel remorse in their hearts,
