high-minded women conceal their shame through the secret entreaties of their lovers.
Having been cast off by our enemies and reduced to a state similar to that of deer,
we feel ashamed even before one another, let alone before our fellow inhabitants.
Pay heed for a moment, O brother who knows the true nature of things; contemplate our words.
In the final state, when it shines forth in the mind, existence is like a silent dream.
At the appointed time, at the close of day, that beautiful woman stood at the door of the house with her eyes fixed upon it; then, seeing that I had arrived, her face blossomed with joy.
In this world, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be killed, nor anything unapproachable, nor anything that cannot be done by those possessed of intelligence; therefore, I shall employ her here.
Brahmins, cows, women, children, and kinsmen are not to be killed; nor are those whose food one eats, nor those who have come for refuge.

"O friend, it is clearly understood that your mind is afflicted by love, since it cannot be overcome by the rays of the moon nor cured by sandalwood water, but is instead tormented by the heat of your own body."
A Brahmin, a child, a woman, an ascetic, and one afflicted by disease are not to be slain;
nor are those whose food has been eaten, nor those who have come for refuge.
A Brahmin, a child, a woman, an ascetic, and one afflicted by disease are not to be killed;
however, for a grave offense, it is ordained that they be marked with physical disfigurement.
Because she stood before him with her moon-like face cast down, as if desiring a screen out of timidity, she captivated his heart all the more; clearly, in women, modesty itself is the true ornament.
Go quickly with bowed heads along the path like bulls whose eyes are struck by rain;
for my eye, which loves dignity in the assembly, is indeed timid at the sight of people of noble birth.
As her lover bent down and embraced her firmly, his chest pressed against her two sunken breasts,
the young woman was made to resound with the tinkling of the small bells on her waist-belt as it shifted at that moment.
O crane, you place both your feet very slowly upon the ground;
you do not look for prey nor do you speak, but you resort to the water; therefore, O crane, you are white.
Avanti, the crest-jewel of the Maukharis, honored his lord with poetry;
and Bāṇa, the poet whose eloquent speech was imbued with exquisite knowledge, became his disciple.
This lord of Avanti, with his uplifted arms, broad chest, and slender, rounded waist,
shines as if he had been carefully carved by Tvaṣṭṛ after mounting him on a lathe, like the sun itself.

May those lords of sages who are equal to Janaka, whose conduct toward the fourfold assembly is irreproachable, and who have crushed the eightfold pride within their own bodies— may they, my gurus, bring an end to my cyclic existence.
One should make each day fruitful through dharma, pleasure, and wealth;
for when that day has passed, one's life is diminished by it.
Embodied beings submit of their own accord to one whose anger is never in vain and who destroys calamities;
but for a creature devoid of indignation and lacking heartfelt affection, no one feels respect or even enmity.
Wealth that is given out of contempt or without faith is like seed sown in barren soil; it is as good as not sown at all.
Noble persons extinguish the fire of anger— kindled by the friction-stick of insults and its flames increased by the fuel of harsh speech— with jars of the water of wisdom.
Through great humiliation by the great, or through excessive joy, anger, and wonder, ascetic merits come to ruin, just as fame is destroyed by very wicked conduct.
That army, having been abandoned and its leaders having fled, is not fit for battle;
however, that hereditary force of the fathers and grandfathers, though enraged, is capable when conciliated.
Those who are merely poets are *avayas*; those who are merely wise are *kīras*. Those who are both heroes and learned poets are *vīras*; but one who merely despises them is a *gavaya*.
When the limbs of that body are reflected in one another, possessing incomparable and stainless luster,
who in this world— even one of great discernment— could clearly determine, "This is this [limb] and that is that"?
Supporting the station of Viṣṇu, drawing the eyes of people toward itself, and possessing incomparable movement—
even an object made of leaves attains the state of a bird through the conjunction of its qualities.
A wise person should not practice loving-kindness toward those who are arrogant, foolish, fierce, and reckless, nor likewise toward those who have abandoned the Dharma.
The clouds increase the pride of the bodiless Love-god, yet they diminish the merit of the Dharma with their spray tossed up by the wind.

Even a mere glance brings happiness to one whose eyes are as beautiful and tremulous as blue lotus petals; how much more so, then, the impetuous embrace of that slender woman, radiant with the luster of her moving locks?
We bow down to the grove of Vṛndāvana, which is like a mass of emeralds, gazed upon, rejoiced in, and embraced with passion by the women.
Beholding the vault of heaven veiled by fresh clouds that caused circles of peacocks to dance,
a woman traveling toward a *vañjula* bower— adorned by her beloved even during the day— entered it with delight.
Having looked at her breasts adorned with *guñjā* berries and clasped them, the distressed wife of the hunter sighed and wept; for what reason?
For those whose senses and minds are not under control, ritual action is like the bathing of an elephant;
knowledge without action is like ornaments on an ugly person—it is merely a burden.
O fair-limbed one, the fire of your anger will surely be extinguished after a long time, and your face, having attained its own natural splendor, will abandon its grief.
But as for these days of mine passing empty of your company, there can be no return of them; my heart is tormented by this thought.
All human beings here must inevitably go to their death;
indeed, when a matter is inevitable, no grief should be felt in this world.
A son necessarily follows the conduct of his father;
for a *ketaka* tree does not produce the fruit of an *āmalakī*.
One must certainly protect the lives of living beings to the best of one's ability.
Destruction, being an inevitable occurrence, is established by its very nature;
for this very time was previously non-existent for you.
Even for the Great One, events that are destined to occur inevitably come to pass:
the nakedness of the Blue-throated One (Śiva) and the reclining upon the great serpent of Hari (Viṣṇu).
If there were a remedy for things that are inevitably destined to happen,
then Nala, Rāma, and Yudhiṣṭhira would not have been afflicted by sufferings.

Objects of the senses must inevitably depart, even after one has dwelt among them for a very long time; what difference is there in their departure, then, that people do not abandon them of their own accord?
For when they depart by their own power, they cause incomparable anguish to the mind; yet when these are abandoned voluntarily, they bestow the infinite bliss of tranquility.
The doer of an evil deed inevitably reaps its fruit when the time arrives, just as a tree bears its seasonal blossoms.
The cātaka bird sustains its life only by means of inevitable causes;
though it fears the rejection of its prayer, it does not beg even from Śakra.
When the time of death arrives for great-souled beings, their life-breaths must inevitably depart;
yet if some benefit to others can be accomplished at that moment, then even death is like immortality.

One should certainly undertake an enterprise that is certain to succeed, rich in great fruit, free from procrastination, and auspicious in its outcome; however, one should never engage in that which involves the fault of depletion.

In whatever direction the Creator’s desire runs— unrestrained by the constraints of those who are destined for liberation— the mind of a person, being utterly devoid of self-control, follows it like a blade of grass carried by a whirlwind.
Prosperities inevitably come under the control of the wise through the power of the pincers of skillful means;
for when applied according to rule, the result for kings becomes magnificent for the sake of accomplishing their objectives.
O dear one, the sense faculties must necessarily function within their own respective domains;
however, the wise person should avoid any fierce passion that arises therein.
The fruit of actions must necessarily be experienced until they are exhausted;
an action that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
One must inevitably experience the results of the deeds one has performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
there is no exhaustion of performed karma even in hundreds of millions of eons.
The partridge sustains its life with drops of dew;
fearing the pain of a rejected request, it does not even beg of fate.
Whatever is recited at the appropriate time attains the status of well-spoken words;
even the harsh cry of a blue jay becomes auspicious at the moment of departure.
Everything recited at the appropriate moment attains the status of well-spoken words, even if it is poorly composed;
even coarse food becomes exceedingly delicious to one who is hungry.
Speech uttered on the appropriate occasion shines even for men if it is devoid of a multitude of virtues;
at the time of love-making, the loss of ornaments becomes an ornament for women.
Seizing that opportunity, those women— whose radiant forms were naturally brilliant—
then set their feet upon the ground, bestowing the very wealth of their grace upon the ladies.
Laughter has ceased; joyous sport has been abandoned; smiles, illuminated by passion, have vanished.
The women are no longer intoxicated; their delight is destroyed. No benefit for the city has been accomplished, nor was any desired goal achieved.
All times are proclaimed suitable for launching a sudden assault against one who is in distress or who is possessed of vulnerabilities.
Out of fear of a sudden assault,
a king should always strike down his enemy whose soldiers are exhausted from staying awake, who has slept during the day, and who is overwhelmed by drowsiness.
"O King, it is the state that is honored among embodied beings, not the body itself;
thus Rāma, who was once a forest-dweller, has now attained kingship."
The city women, advanced in years, scattered parched grain over him,
just as the waves of milk scatter droplets stirred up by Mount Mandara over Acyuta.
Headlong into blind darkness shall fall the sinner who,
when questioned regarding the determination of the Dharma, speaks falsely in response to the inquiry.
Your enemies will utter many unspeakable words, reviling your power; what indeed could be more painful than that?
That king, whose reputation for standing at the forefront of those who have conquered their senses was well-known,
felt ashamed as the unrestrained prowess of the enemy of Śambara gradually became manifest there.
Just as a householder, through the sense of "mine" attached to sons, fields, and so forth, suffers extreme distress, so too did the sapharī fish suffer extreme distress in the water of the pond.
O Daughter of the Mountain, this is not a blemish that has acquired boldness upon the body of the moon, whose luster is now mature;
rather, I think it is the Night, the beloved of the Moon, who, exhausted from lovemaking, lies deeply upon his chest, which is cooled by the flow of trickling nectar.
Having gained familiarity with the coastal lands of the ocean through its great length, this mountain shines with dark-hued waters that form its girdle;
it appears as if the Vindhya range has been seized by the ocean by the hair in a rage, because the ocean failed to obey the command of Agastya.

Or what is it that you have attained? For that which exists even within the single path of your mind—wherein even the darkness of the intellect is dispelled—that Brahman is indeed attainable by those who are straightforward.
Desire those goals which are attainable, never those that are unattainable;
experiencing what is present, do not grieve for what has not yet come.
When a dog turns its left side and scratches its back,
on that very day it will certainly go to the abode of Death, overcome by disease.
When the pit has been filled with fine soil free of gravel, it should be cleared out;
once the excavation, measuring half a bow in depth, has been sprinkled with water, one should plant a tree.
A banana tree and a milky-treed species are to be planted after placing cow dung at the base.
If not exercised, they perish even when capable of performing all tasks;
through excessive exercise, they become emaciated and their limbs become afflicted by disease.
The ignoble person excessively oppresses the virtuous man, even though he remains unchanged;
what has the lotus done here to the frost that it constantly consumes it?

When, during journeys, the goddess Durgā is seen on the left— untransformed, making earthy sounds, well-situated, and making auspicious gestures— she carries one across all difficulties as soon as she is beheld.
Relying upon immutability, these birds carry away my net equally;
when they come together and fall into mutual dispute, then they shall come under my control.
Salt, cooked food, curd, milk, honey, oil, and ghee;
sesame seeds, meat, roots, fruits, vegetables, red cloth, all types of perfumes, and molasses—these are not to be sold.
O You who abide with two distinct forms joined together by an incomparable cause, though You are without physical body;
for no one else in the worlds is seen to possess such loveliness while wearing seemingly contradictory dress and ornaments.
To offer arguments to one who does not investigate is like threshing chaff; O King, a favor done for base people is like urinating on sand.
An action performed without deliberation cuts into one's vital organs;
by the forceful abduction of Sītā, Rāvaṇa’s fortunes have passed away.
He who desires to conquer his ministers without first conquering himself, or who desires to conquer his enemies while his ministers remain unconquered, is powerless and comes to ruin.
The speech of even the Lord of Speech, if its continuity is not understood,
goes to utter fruitlessness, like the effort of one who acts contrary to policy.
Though overcome by one who acted without her knowledge while she was wearing my garment,
she shines like the crescent moon veiled by an autumn cloud.
What difference is there between a master who does not discern distinctions, who robs all of his brilliance, and the darkness that is devoid of discrimination?
The cognition of what is not yet known, the ascertainment of what has been known, the constant initiation of actions, and the seeing of the conclusion of what has been undertaken.
The cognition of what is not yet known, the ascertainment of what has been known,
the cutting away of doubt regarding a twofold meaning, and the observation of the remainder.
Unrecognized and unattached, she has been defiled by my garment;
yet she appears like a crescent moon veiled by an autumn cloud.
If the supreme reality is not understood, the study of the scriptures is fruitless;
even if the supreme reality is understood, the study of the scriptures is fruitless.
A sword worn without being recognized destroys one's auspicious prosperity;
when recognized, O Lord, it bestows all sovereignty.
Therefore, I shall describe their qualities as they have been taught by the preeminent sages.
Due to the lack of discernment on the part of the king, his retinue becomes devoid of wisdom; because of their predominance, wise men do not remain in his presence.
When the kingdom is abandoned by the wise, policy indeed ceases to be virtuous; once policy is lost, the entire lineage, including the king, perishes helplessly.
For he who, not understanding the fruit, pursues only the action,
will grieve at the time of its fruition, like one who waters the *kiṃśuka* tree [expecting fruit].
One who demonstrates one's own capability without recognizing the capability of another incurs ridicule; this mountain here is exactly like that.
O Lord of the Earth, you—who possess a glory celebrated for its excellence in expanding the path of unerring desires—are like the celestial wish-fulfilling tree; to whom are you not desirable?

Nevertheless, my heart runs toward a definitive conclusion because of its lack of satiety; for the excellence of specific qualities in those things to be accomplished is not sufficient to bring about certainty with ease.
An unrefined husband who is the leader of mature women,
and a meager fortune for those virtuous and generous men— these are sources of suffering.
Unrefined, hardened by toil, a dull-witted Brahmin who finds women difficult to obtain— a youth—
has approached me at night under the guise of a lover, as if seized by an untimely death.
There is no fault in those who have attained residence in this land and are unaware of other virtues;
for even those who possess saffron under their own control hold blue in high esteem.
Even when its virtues are unknown, the speech of a true poet pours forth a stream of honey into the ears;
for even before its fragrance is perceived, a garland of *mālatī* flowers captivates the eye.
One who has not known supreme bliss says that sense objects alone are delightful; he for whom ghee has never been seen anywhere considers sesame oil alone to be sweet.
The mind-born god, whose own sensations are unknown, is surely always thus bodiless;
for if he indeed possessed a body, he certainly would not cause pain to another's body.
Those from whose mouths speech issues forth without distinguishing between the letter *śa* and *sa*,
their difference between anus and mouth can only be inferred by their teeth.
Some dull-witted person here has declared that liberation is some indeterminate entity devoid of qualities, in which pleasure and pain are unknown;
but in my opinion, liberation is indeed the loosening of the girdle of a woman whose eyes are sweet with intoxication and rolling with the bloom of youth.
One who, being eager for conflict, does not know his own strength and that of the enemy,
goes to destruction like a moth flying headlong into a fire.
Life without knowledge is empty; if one is without kinsmen, the quarters are empty;
a house without a son is empty; but poverty is the emptiness of all things.
An ignorant man is to be pitied; a childless couple is to be pitied;
subjects who do not provide sustenance are to be pitied; and a kingdom without a king is to be pitied.
Who, other than the Self, would be able to liberate one from the bondage of the fetters of ignorance, desire, karma, and so forth, even in hundreds of millions of aeons?
Knowledge destroys ignorance; meditative cultivation destroys worldly existence;
generosity destroys poverty; and ethical discipline destroys miserable rebirths.
Through the destruction of the seed of ignorance, he, by means of the vision of the Seers,
has encompassed both past and future times within the present.
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is a great deity, just as fire is a great deity.
For in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
Even an unlearned king attains supreme prosperity by serving those advanced in knowledge, just as a tree situated near water thrives.
Why does anger arise in men toward a person who cannot be controlled? And what is the point of anger even toward one who is obedient, since their life is dependent upon him?
An unmanageable servant, deceitful friends, a stingy master,
and a wife devoid of discipline— these four are headaches.
Although the study of knowledge serves to pacify ignorance—the source of all lack of discipline—it leads instead to the increase of wickedness when practiced by those who are naturally crooked.
While this light from the jewels on the hoods of venomous serpents is capable of destroying the darkness of those who fear snakes, it only causes their fear to intensify.
For enemies lead one who delights in lack of discipline into their power against his will unless they are treated with respect;
however, one who has taken refuge in the treasure of learning and discipline never suffers defeat, even if he is physically weak.
But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable.
Sātavāhana made his treasury imperishable and refined with well-spoken words of pure origin, as if with jewels.
How can a son who is undisciplined not be like fire by nature? But how can a son who is disciplined not be the best of men?
Knowledge belonging to one who is undisciplined does not endure for long,
just like a string of jewels tied around the neck of a monkey.
An undisciplined servant, a stingy king, deceitful friends,
and an ill-mannered wife— these four are headaches.
Surely even Madana was initially rendered invisible by the darkness,
since he drew his bow only when that abode of unrighteousness had risen and revealed the quarters of the sky.
The sky shone, its stars indistinguishable, the orb of the moon unseen, and the sun having set; its heat subsided and it was free from darkness.
Indeed, for one devoid of merit, the very absence of faults is his only virtue.

O wretched youth of little merit! Upon what have you relied for this youth of yours, which possesses limbs that are ungraceful to behold, yet feature clearly defined faces and breasts? These are the limbs of vulgar women.
Without reflection, he desires the delight of sense objects through the slaughter of his enemies;
for that is not the method for the destruction of existence. Where is the bow, and where is the path to liberation?
The speech of the virtuous who tirelessly perform the welfare of others is nectar through its exceeding sweetness;
moreover, their mind is an ocean, and their fame is the moonlight of the stainless autumnal moon.
One woman, weary from gathering flowers without ceasing, leaned against the side of the tree with her creeper-like arms resting there,
her full and closely-set breasts pressed against the chest of her beloved.
These lords of the earth, standing amidst thousands of unrestrained young women as if their vows of manhood were dissolving, are exceedingly timid at every step and perceive danger from all sides.
I go for refuge to the Lord Śeṣa, who tirelessly and without fatigue supports the surface of the earth, whose face shines with a gentle smile, and who bestows joy upon the world.

This pleasure-pool bestows delight upon the eyes; it is a house for bees where they drink honey incessantly, a bower for the gathering of royal swans, and a mansion with many wide halls for the lotus-dwelling Lakṣmī.
As she playfully splashed this water incessantly with her two hands raised like blossoming lotuses,
it was as if she were offering a guest-offering (*arghya*) to those who had become targets for the arrows of Love, and bestowing the very essence of the joys of childhood play.

The wind at dawn, having scattered the pollen of *mālatī* flowers over the women’s limbs— which have become incapable of bearing the fatigue born of incessant amorous play— kindles once again the fire of passion by means of those very particles.
The cloud, with its dense coils,
envelops the pair of intoxicated eyes— trembling with extreme fear— of the young vine-like woman who offers her pleasure while her female doves coo incessantly.
May the body of the Self-born One protect us— his body-hair bristling with the joy of creating beautiful forms, as if covered by the thick filaments clinging from his constant contact with the lotus.
This delightful season, which causes the constant blooming of lotuses, brings joy to all bees and cuckoos, and stirs the longing of the world, has now arrived.
The pride of your enemies was seen in their incessant brandishing of swords, their frequent frowns, threats, and roars; yet that pride vanished somewhere in an instant upon seeing you.
By the clouds releasing water in an excessive, dense mass of incessant streams,
the turbidity has been entirely wiped away from the hearts of proud women.

With her cheeks drenched by a continuous flood of falling tears, she offered no other message to you; rather, O traveler, as your beloved meditated on something within her mind for a moment, she cast her gaze upon a fresh sprout of compassion—alas! Thirsty female bees plunge into the river of nectar that flows through the forest's edge, its sandy banks composed of dense pollen, reaching up to the knees of young female cuckoos.

O fortunate one, alas! By means of the incessant streams of her tears and the floods of her sighs, heated by the flames of the fire of love, the ground before that slender-limbed woman seems to be made both muddy and dusty, as if these two were competing with one another.
As the young woman walked along with him, one of her breasts, covered in dense horripilation,
repeatedly struck and rebounded against the surface of her lover’s chest, assuming the playful grace of a bouncing ball at every step.

The winter season, with its sparse frost-drops, attained a merit never before experienced for so long: the forests of *phalinī* trees were in full bloom, and the winds carried the fragrance of blossoming *kunda* flowers.
I bow to Gaṇapati, the Lord of Desire, who possesses a continuous flow of ichor, whose cheeks are frequented by swarms of bees, and who bestows desired fruits.

May the elephant-faced one— who washes his temples with incessant streams of ichor, who is the refuge for all, whose body is encircled by the best of serpents, who is worshipped by the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and others, and who is expert in destroying the darkness of obstacles for the people of the three worlds— grant you constant auspiciousness.
He seemed as if bound by a dense cord of white lotuses, bathed by an overflowing stream of milk,
swallowed whole by his wide-open eyes, and forcibly sprinkled by a thick cloud of nectar.
Victorious is the elephant-faced one, upon whose temples the swarms of bees settle as the ichor flows incessantly,
appearing like a row of newly sprouted facial hair.
With dense and restless clouds, and forest breezes fragrant with *kuṭaja*, *arjuna*, and *nīpa* flowers—alas, this season has arrived; the wives of travelers have perished.
That man who would lead one who is unopposed and dwelling in happiness onto the path of suffering will undoubtedly be miserable in birth after birth.
The abdomen is unprotruding, well-rounded, and highly praised;
the back is not too long, level, and slightly arched, which is auspicious.
When a rite is accomplished without delay, the practitioners of mantras attain fame;
when there is delay, they acquire wealth by proclaiming the abundance of their ritual activity.
Breasts that are indistinct and stiff are seen as like those of the wealthy;
those that are distinct and drooping are despised as being like those of the poor.

Where the king possesses a mind devoid of discernment, where the minister turns his neck away from those possessed of virtue, and where the wicked are powerful— how can there be any opportunity for the virtuous there?
Like lack of discernment and futile exertion leading to ruin, like greed and attachment relying upon one another,
and like misconduct and negligence leading a seeker of victory to his downfall— those two arrows brought him to his end.
Let the pair of breasts, lacking discrimination, indeed destroy the three worlds;
yet it is improper for them to kill a person who is dear to their ears and eyes.
When a king lacks discrimination, the virtues of the virtuous perish,
just as the swelling breasts of a faithful wife wither when her beloved is fond of living abroad.
He who places his hope for prosperity in a king lacking discrimination does so at his own ruin,
thinking, "I shall attain success through this man."
Lack of discernment is indeed the supreme source of all calamities;
one devoid of discernment in this world is nothing but a beast—of this there is no doubt.
A gaze from the corners of the eyes that was indistinct and unsteady, speech that was unclear and trembling with fear, and a touch amidst the throngs of people—
those very same states of being which I observed at the onset of your love were seen by me as hard-hearted when you were becoming detached.
O beautiful-faced one, how have you come to extinction, you who were a lamp-flame in my home— possessing an undiminished wick and vessel, fresh cotton, and abundant oil?
Born of an impure lineage, living by the offering of my body, and acting with deceit— where am I, a woman who lives by her beauty, and where are you, whose birth and virtues are praiseworthy?
Like an unceasing wind, this perseverance generates a continuous fire that, through its constancy, shatters even the great mountain ranges;
it brings forth in all undertakings a firm resolve that, until its completion, secures for one in this world a harvest of results whose splendor is inconceivable at every moment.
One should carry the burden without rest, endure cold and heat, and always remain contented; thus one should learn three things from the donkey.
How will you travel alone along this path through the wilderness of darkness— a journey without rest, without provisions, without support, and without a guide?
Even a man who is a preeminent master of deceit is as blind as one before a woman when he does not trust her;
is not even a crow, though skilled in every branch of training, deceived by female cuckoos?
All women—whether low, high, or middling—are untrustworthy;
whoever places his trust in them is consumed by remorse.
One should always remain distrustful, employing both peace and war,
while relying on the strategy of double-dealing against a powerful and wicked enemy.
Salutations to you, O Hiraṇya, who cause distrust, who are the cause of great sins, and who bring about discord between father and son!
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison.
Poison kills but one person, whereas the property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons.
One who is non-deceptive, skillful, grateful, wise,
and upright gains a retinue even if his treasury is completely exhausted.
Generosity consists in non-deception and not transgressing one’s commitment;
it causes beings to turn back [from evil], as does speech that is rightly directed.
Even if not dismissed, the wise man should move about together with everyone;
he may also enter [the presence] uninvited at other times by the command of his master.
One should not forget a favor received and should not practice ingratitude;
for by killing his benefactor, the Brahmin Nāḍījaṅgha fell to the lower realms.
Even one who is not himself a hero may conquer his enemies with the assistance of a heroic army;
for those devoid of the support of an army, the goddess of victory remains elusive.
Humility destroys misconduct; valor destroys misfortune;
forbearance certainly destroys anger; and right conduct destroys ill fortune.
One should abandon a country where no livelihood is possible; one should abandon a livelihood that is fraught with calamity;
one should abandon a deceitful friend; and one should abandon wealth that threatens one's life.
Servants abandon a master who provides no livelihood, bees a tree that has no flowers,
and swans a lake that has no water— even if they have dwelt there for a long time.
For the lowest classes, there is fear of losing their livelihood; for those in the middle, fear of death;
but for the highest mortals, the supreme fear is dishonor.
One should assist, according to one's ability, those afflicted by loss of livelihood, disease, or grief;
one should always regard even insects and ants as one does oneself.
Having observed himself to be devoid of merit, he desires others likewise; yet this does not bear fruit, for if he does not lament, he cries out, "There are no virtuous people here!
He then strives to wipe them away, to curse them, or to despise them—oh, how delightful is this desire to conquer the virtuous, ordained by Fate for such a base man!

May the weaving of cloths by the one whose banner bears the lord of birds protect us— cloths that require no calculation of the activity of the shuttle, that possess the touch of the fourth state (*turiya*), that involve no repeated effort in joining a multitude of unspun threads, and which are solely intent on removing the calamity of the distressed Draupadi.
One who delights in error perceives the reality characterized by existence and non-existence without distinguishing between them;
like a madman acting by chance, such a person lacks consciousness and turns their back on the words of the Victors.
Even if a person should master the treatises in particular and perform various ascetic practices with devotion,
if their mind is still attached to what is not the ultimate reality, they will not enjoy the unimpeded bliss of liberation.
I know her to be faultless; however, public scandal is considered by me to be powerful. For the shadow of the earth has been attributed as a stain upon the pure moon by the people.
I recognize your strength; therefore, I shall indeed appoint you, who are like my own self, to this weighty task.
Just as Śeṣa is commanded by Kṛṣṇa to bear his body, having regard for his nature as a mountain.
O best of the twice-born, I consider myself purified by two things alone:
by the descent of the Gaṅgā upon my head and by the water from the washing of your feet.
I know that your beloved has been deceived by the intoxication of his own good fortune;
for he does not long make his own face the target of her eyes, which look so skillfully and possess such curved lashes.
I understand that these white rows of swans are the flickering chaff of the fame of your beauty;
having flown up, it is fitting that they have fallen and now float about the fullness of rivers and ponds.
A Brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava is lost; a Śrāddha ceremony without a sacrificial fee is lost;
a field where the Veda is not honored is lost; and a family lacking proper conduct is lost.
Having worshipped the unmanifest syllable (*akṣara*) and realized his own [attainment of] the perfected phonemes, a certain person considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose;
yet we have achieved our purpose through this very state of insensibility born from the intense joy arising from the sudden, graceful throbbing of the *tribhaṅga* posture.
O Bhārata, beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, and indeed unmanifest again in their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
Even for a wealthy man who possesses inexhaustible riches, there may be thousands of kinsmen as long as he remains in his position;
but for one whose wealth has fallen away, even a relative will not show their face.
That which is imperishable undergoes decay, and that which is perishable expands extensively;
O Bhāratī, an unprecedented treasury of yours is thus beheld.
For Fortune does not desire to embrace one who is lacking in resolve, slothful, dependent on fate, and acting with rashness— just as a young woman does not wish to embrace an aged husband.
Even the serenity of one whose mind is unsettled is terrifying;
but one whose self is settled and serene causes no fear, even when angry.
For those whose conduct is unstable, whose eye of sacred revelation is undifferentiated,
and whose enjoyments are acquired through unrighteousness— even a blessing is appropriate for their harm.
For in battle, victory and defeat are seen to be unstable.
Studying the *avyākaraṇa*, crossing a river in a broken boat,
and taking medicine mixed with unwholesome food— these three are better left undone than performed.
The displacement of others is indeed the characteristic sign of the future accomplishment of one's task.

O tongue, if you are a knower of flavors, then speak the name "Kṛṣṇa," which bestows an ineffable and supreme joy when immersed within the heart, which utterly removes the mass of inner darkness, and which pours forth a sweetness esteemed even above grapes and other fruits.

O Mother, by what eye shall I behold even once that lotus-foot of Yours— which is naturally beautiful, unsurpassed, immeasurable, extraordinary, and the supreme auspiciousness— were it but revealed by You, moist with compassion?
By fashioning her, who was naturally beautiful, with graceful discernment,
the Creator prepared a poison-smeared arrow for the God of Love.
May that moon protect you— whose naturally curved form mimics the play of the strung bow of Cupid,
and whose two tips are licked by the rays of the jewels from the king of serpents bound within his matted locks.

May Devakī protect you—she whose feet were reddened by the rows of flame-tips from the crest-jewels of the celestial realm; she who, when the Friend of the World entered her womb to remove the burden of the earth, experienced a longing for the sounds of weapons clashing at the head of the battle against kings of unrestrained arms—sounds terrifying with the snapping of bones and heavy with the impact of their blows.

May the Man-Lion protect you—he who is as fair as saffron from the gushing streams of blood flowing from the chest of Indra’s enemy, torn open by the tips of his strides and his cruel, great claws that possess the essence of a thunderbolt;

he who wears a garland of blue lotuses formed by rows of clouds caught in the tips of his quivering mane; he whose crest-jewels are the sun and the moon; he who displays an incomparable play of amorous adornment.

May the leader of the Gaṇas protect you—he who dances, imitating the elephants of the quarters as they whirl about with faces upturned in play while the earth rotates from the impact of his stamping feet;
and by whose wind from the tip of his uplifted trunk, the circle of stars is repeatedly drawn in and cast out, as if practicing the sport of scattering droplets of spray.
May Vāmana protect you— he in whose reflection within the Kaustubha gem the three worlds appeared as if they were his own belly, gazing upon him with curiosity.
A body free from disease, a most devoted wife, a home of renowned wealth, and sharpened knowledge;
a praiseworthy lineage, a capable end at the time of death, and the power resulting from the glance of one’s mother—these are your riches.

O Great King, drink this anger—which is not born of disease, yet is bitter, a headache, followed by evil, harsh, sharp, and fierce; which the virtuous must drink, but the wicked do not—and thus be at peace.
With a body free from disease and a mind free from affliction,
fulfilling the hopes of those who seek your aid, may you live for a hundred autumns.
The man who desires to exert effort toward matters that do not concern him meets his own destruction, just like the monkey who pulled out the wedge.

Delighting in inactivity during the spring, fond of sexual union in the summer, and attached to the waters of small ponds while loathing the water of deep wells; fond of pungent, sour, and hot foods in autumn, gluttonous in winter, and sluggish with sleep in the cold season—may your enemies, their bodies wasting away through their own faults, perish.
"A cow cannot be protected without a staff"—even a simple cowherd understands this; how much more so the king?
They say that silence is better than speech; speaking the truth is the second best;
speaking what is pleasant is the third; and speaking what is righteous is the fourth.
Now that the winter has arrived, it has come to act as a teacher of the "sītkāra" (the whistling sound of pleasure) for women whose nature is currently unrefined.
When the listener is uneducated, the eloquence of men is useless;
when the husband is sightless, the beauty of women is useless.
Even for you who are without vows, dharma must indeed be practiced from time to time;
for even a bull that has become a threshing-post continues to eat mouthfuls of grass while wandering about.
A virtuous man who is perpetually incapable, an ugly woman devoted to her husband,
a sick person who is devoted to the gods, and indigent students of sacred knowledge.

A thief who is powerless is virtuous; an ugly woman who is devoted to her husband is virtuous; a sick man who is a devotee of the gods is virtuous; and an old courtesan who practices asceticism is virtuous.
But one who is incapable, a virtuous person, a celibate student, or one who is destitute; one who is diseased, a devotee of the gods, or an aged woman faithful to her husband—[these may perform it].
Those wicked people who, being powerless, boast of their own strength,
become objects of ridicule in the presence of the great alone.
Cruelty toward the weak, harshness toward those who are fierce, steadfastness toward those who commit grave sins, deceitful intent, and verbal brutality— such is the "heroism" of the base.
Those who are powerless against a strong enemy should either flee or take refuge in a fortress; there can be no other course for them.
He who, being powerless, constantly practices patience even toward those who do him harm, is certainly like a serpent deprived of its fangs.

Since a powerful man exercises forbearance here when he has the capacity to act, he is one of virtuous conduct; such a man, possessing splendor and desiring to conquer both worlds, is truly victorious.
Unable to endure the sight of him, as one with weak eyes cannot bear the sight of the thousand-rayed sun,
Kauśika entered the interior of a cave on the Golden Mountain and spent his days there in fear.
A wise person should not undertake what is impossible, nor should they ever perform what ought not to be done;
they should never speak untruth, nor should they indulge in sloth.
A wise person should not undertake what is impossible, nor should they ever cause an improper act to be done;
rather, one should live according to the Dharma as it pertains to one's region and according to the proper time.
"O King, it is indeed impossible to suddenly discern the inner disposition of another;
observe closely their skill through those songs that reveal their internal nature."
For those whose conduct involves undertakings that are impossible to accomplish, what fruit can there be other than affliction? How could one who attempts to taste the sky ever take a mouthful?
One whose mind is free from apprehension, who is self-composed, and not deceitful, does not slink about;
nor is his speech wicked. Therefore, there is no doubt in this matter.
One should be wary of those who inspire no suspicion, and entirely wary of those who do inspire suspicion;
for danger arising even from one who is not suspected cuts away the very root.
One should suspect even that which is not to be suspected, and one should always suspect what is already suspected;
for fear born from what is suspected cuts away even one's very roots.

If Fortune does not take refuge in a man who is free from deceit, lack of greed, and crookedness, who is generous, affectionate, and a connoisseur of excellence, then Fortune herself is indeed the one deceived.

One whose heart is free from deceit, who is grateful, compassionate, and established on the path of the virtuous; who refrains from slandering others and delights in pure conduct—he indeed is a noble person.
"Food is mine, clothing is mine, my wife is mine, my circle of kinsmen is mine"—
the wolf of Time kills the man who makes such claims as "mine."
For one who has not sought food, clothing, or shelter in Kāśī,
Kāśī is equal to Kīkaṭa, and even the Gaṅgā flows as a bed of glowing coals.
By being grateful for even a mere morsel of food from his teacher, one who is not treacherous does not equal even a dog;
for friendship with a wicked person does not flourish, no matter how much one benefits him, just as a creeper does not grow in the sky.
Just as all the sense faculties depend upon food, so too do all effects depend [upon it];
for this reason, wealth is said to be the means for accomplishing everything.
Through eating and eating in childhood, through voracious desire in youth,
and through the failure of health in the remainder of life, the lifespan of men is clearly wasted away.
The forest trees, acting as a source of joy for those who have no refuge and providing them with beautiful shelter,
are like the unprotected hearts of the wicked, or like a newly acquired kingdom yet to be conquered and enjoyed.
While the Lord of Sindhu reigns supreme— having instantly destroyed his enemies with fierce, burning, and harsh glances that scorch like the flames of hell—
we hold in little regard the Pāṇḍava, who once set the Khāṇḍava forest ablaze with the dancing tongues of fire from the missiles discharged by his own bow, the Gāṇḍīva.
Having killed a man unarmed, a person is reborn as a donkey;
and one who commits the murder of a woman or kills a child is born as a worm.
"Human flesh, unpurified by weapons, unadulterated, and prepared from the limbs of a man, is being sold; take it, take it!"
Beholding this world-palace devoured by the flames of an unextinguished fire, and the pleasure born of desire as flickering as a face distorted by a violent wind;
seeing the condition of worldly existence as unstable as the moon reflected in water, O people, truly abandon forever your intoxication with sense objects.
With internal thirst unappeased by the contact with the salt-water of wealth, their bodies deprived of luster by long-term consumption of tasteless and parched food;
sleepless and with a weak digestive fire due to fear of kings, water, thieves, and fire—the misery of the miserly is clearly even greater than the misery of poverty itself.
All this is impermanent when reflected upon, O Bhārata;
the world is like a plantain tree, for its equal does not exist.
But that king who collects taxes while failing to punish thieves,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is excluded from heaven.
A king who lacks the eye of the treatises is called blind;
it is better to be blind than to have eyes while having the true path cast aside by arrogance.
The speech of those who are ignorant of the treatises, who are unacquainted with the science of polity (*arthaśāstra*), yet desire vast prosperity, should not be acted upon as beneficial.
For those who have not trained in poetry, the study of the sciences is useless;
for one who has not been initiated, what is the use of sacrifices such as the Vājapeya?

The bee’s movement in the flower-cup is no longer relaxed; these trees, so dear to the eye, are no longer adorned with buds; and this blossom is not yet opening. And yet, the knot of pride in the hearts of those fawn-eyed women loosens of its own accord.
Not loosening her grip around his neck, she firmly embraced him with her broad breast;
her hair standing on end with thrill, she repeatedly entwined one of her husband’s arms softly and tenderly with her own.
A headless torso should be fashioned on the forehead of a slayer of a Brahmin;
he must be rendered unfit for social intercourse—this is the instruction of Manu.
The thief must go before the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me."
O King, he who instructs one who is not a disciple, he who worships what is empty,
and he who associates with a miser— they are called those of deluded mind.
In Māgha, the deer and the bed; in Phālguna, the beasts and the birds;
in Caitra, all aquatic creatures; and in Vaiśākha, men and monkeys.
Bathing in water that is not cold, drinking milk, and excellent women—
these, O humans, are wholesome for you, as is food that is unctuous and warm.
May we eat alms; may we wear robes made of rags; may we sleep upon the surface of the earth—what need have we for lords?
Lacking virtue, transgressing the bounds of propriety, and constantly indulging in sexual intercourse,
they become short-lived in this world and likewise destined for rebirth in hell.

One should avoid sexual union with another's wife, for it is an abode of impurity, the destruction of prosperity, the manifestation of infamy, the source of diseases, the crusher of merit, and the shaker of steadfastness.
How is it that the king is not a deity— he by whose word a man becomes impure when he was pure, and who instantly becomes pure even when he was impure?
Upon seeing something impure, shedding tears, quarreling, coughing or gasping,
walking along a road, anointing the body, sneezing, or during jesting, one should perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśet).
When a king is of impure nature, the people do not feel affection for him;
just as a swan, when in the company of vultures, may behave like one.
A woman remains impure as long as the fetus (the "dart") has not been released;
once that dart has emerged, she is then purified by her menses.
Indeed, women are the abodes of all impurities and are contemptible;
they never maintain purity and likewise consume such food.
Even in this degenerate age, those who are vigilant regarding their own duty daily perform services for the wise;
nourished by many people and bound by their vows, they abandon even their own physical comfort and extend their service to the king.
When misfortune arises for people, their intelligence perishes and no protection exists;
even friends become enemies, and even nectar turns into deadly poison.
Even when not listening, the lord of the earth should be made to understand by his ministers,
just as Vidura caused the son of Ambikā to realize this for the sake of destroying his own faults.
He who, though appearing disagreeable even to all those with eyes and ears,
is the cause of joy for Vinatā— he is the man who is the delight of the worthy.

Like the day for lotuses, wealth constantly produces a blossoming splendor for people— a splendor worthy of a great festival of enthusiasm for the arrival of friends that illuminates and dispels every fault.
The slayer of the entire army of the Lord of Laṅkā, whose sole practice is service at the feet of Śrī Rāma,
the protector of people struck by manifold sufferings— this Hanumān shall be the bringer of happiness to you.

May the playful scattering of water droplets from the trunk of the elephant-faced one bring you joy— droplets that are as capable as consecrated mantra-syllables at warding off every obstacle in all directions.

Wearing ornaments of spring flowers— wherein the *padmarāga* gems were put to shame by the *aśoka*, the *karṇikāra* trees were eclipsed by the luster of gold, and the *sinduvāra* blossoms were fashioned into strings of pearls.

O bee, why are you afflicted with grief at the *aśoka* tree? Why is your mind so agitated even at the *bakula*, and why do you find no joy in the *kunda* along with the *sahakāra* trees? If you place your trust here in the *kusumbha*, there is no doubt that, because of its hundreds of thorns, your body will be mangled and ruined.
The one who should not grieve grieves for that which is worthy of grief, or why is that which is worthy of grief not grieved for?
And who here is to be grieved for by whom, in this body that is like a bubble?
You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom;
the wise do not grieve for the dead or for the living.
Those beings here are not to be grieved for; the fool who grieves for them obtains sorrow upon sorrow and pursues two misfortunes.
The wise man who is destitute is not to be pitied; he whose kinsmen are learned is not to be pitied.
A widow is not to be pitied if she is well-established with sons and grandsons.
He who eats, he who prepares, he who kills, he who gives, he who receives, and he who consents—these six are all to be censured here; they wander endlessly in the forest of saṃsāra.
He who eats meat performs the act of consenting to the slaughter of living beings;
that wretched person thereby incurs sins, and from them the creature goes to a cycle of existence that has no end.
The sinful man who, seeing that one provides food and clothing,
does not feel indignation, is considered the lowest of men.
Eat, drink, chew, stay awake, lie down, or stand;
even once during the day, reflect that this bondage of the body is but temporary.
One should subdue iron with stone, and likewise stone with iron;
one should subdue the Mlecchas with Mlecchas, just as one gathers wood-apples with wood-apples held in the hand.
To the left of an *aśmātaka* tree, either a jujube tree (*badarī*) or the abode of a snake is seen;
at a distance of three and a half men to the north of it, there is water.
A man may, by means of an expedient, digest even stone or iron;
but there is no expedient whatsoever by which the property of a Brahmin can be digested.
Even a stone that examines the essence of one's virtues deserves the desire to fall into fire, just as it is fitting for gold.
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given in charity, or performed as austerity without faith, O Pārtha, is said to be "unreal"; it yields no fruit either after death or in this world.
From that arise lack of faith, false views, delusion, and the three kinds of suffering,
as well as mental distress regarding unsuitable objects and attachment to them.
That which is unbelievable should not be spoken, even if it were something directly perceived; for example, "the singing of monkeys" or likewise, "a stone floats."
Having untied her chest, where the tight pressure on her breasts—whose hardness remains unyielding—had formed distinct circular elevations and whose bodice was clinging there;
and having loosened that braid which hung from her left breast by disarranging its knot with the tips of her fingernails while pressing down upon the seat with her foot; she now relaxes it.
By his very nature, Dharma wandered upon the earth even as a single-footed being through the course of time, swiftly clinging to the rows of sacrificial posts that had been erected without weariness.

Formerly, the daughter of Gādhi, having slightly fashioned the celestial Gaṅgā as if it were a pearl necklace, caused it to sport in the heavens through the swaying of the silken banners on his palaces; she who had brought about the play of new celestial rites by obstructing them with the multitude of the faces of the gods, whose mouths were never-ceasingly purified by the recitation of the Vedas and from which issued abundant hymns of praise.
Lack of weariness sustains one's kin; alas, that which is lost is perishable.
A lame man is not led along the path by another lame man on his shoulder.
The horse was heard by the kings, whose sleep had momentarily vanished as they ate the *harītaka* fruit before them;
bringing joy to those who heard it, the horse produced a sound from its teeth, mingled with the tinkling of small bells dangling from the tip of its neck.
Under the guise of tears, from the beautiful-eyed woman whose eyes were clouded by the smoke of the sacrificial fire,
a flood of the water of her loveliness seems to flow away, unable to find a place upon her body.

O beautiful lady, Acyuta endures the prattling of the wicked as if it were unheard, the clouding of the moon-like face of his guru as if it were unseen, and his own humiliation as if it were of no account— all for your sake.
One who is unlearned yet arrogant, poor yet high-minded,
and who seeks wealth without performing work is called a fool by the wise.
Having prepared water for the feet with her tears and offered the seat of her heart, the beloved woman embraced her lover when he had arrived.
One should not offer a horse, nor an elephant, nor a tiger, nor indeed anything else; one should offer the sacrifice of a goat’s son, for the deity is a slayer of the weak.
One should avoid from afar a bathed horse, an intoxicated elephant, a bull overcome by lust, and a Śūdra who has acquired the knowledge of letters.
A horse, a weapon, a treatise, a lute, speech, a man, and a woman—
these become either unworthy or worthy depending on the particular person they encounter.
One should avoid from afar a sleeping horse, an intoxicated elephant, cows that have recently calved, and a king who has entered his inner apartments.
The wise one, having ground thirty palas of aśvagandhā into powder,
should make it an equal portion with the powder of vṛddhadāruka.
There is no one more senseless than he who maintains a firm hope for life, which is comparable to a drop of water clinging to the tip of a trembling leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
One who plants one *aśvattha*, one *picumanda*, one *nyagrodha*, ten *ciñciṇīkas*,
three each of *kapittha*, *bilva*, and *āmalaka*, and five mango trees, shall not see hell.
Who indeed among men would be able to describe the greatness of the Aśvattha tree,
wherein misfortune (*alakṣmī*) resides in the sun, yet abundant fortune (*lakṣmī*) dwells in the moon?
Aśvatthāman, Bali, Vyāsa, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa,
Kṛpa, and Paraśurāma— these seven are the long-lived ones.
Yudhiṣṭhira spoke the false word in battle, "Aśvatthāman is slain";
having committed a sin, he subsequently fell into remorse. One should feel regret after having done an evil deed.
The back of a horse, the shoulder of an elephant, and the breasts of women;
likewise, the tooth-stick and a weapon—the more massive they are, the greater the pleasure they afford.
The praise of horses is renowned, followed by the science of archery (dhanurveda);
then there is another, the science of music (gāndharvaśāstra), as well as the Ayurveda of trees.
The horse-leap, the thundering of Indra, the mind of women, and the fortune of a man;
likewise, drought and excessive rain—the god does not know these, much less a human being.

A female jackal that howls in the midst of horses, creating a display of battle, is auspicious; a jackal possessing the seven musical notes is to be accepted, whereas those with many sounds are fruitless.
When a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale,
those who know the Vedas understand that truth outweighed them.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
having weighed them, I see that truth alone outweighs them.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
I do not know if one might obtain even half of this truth.
O King, having placed the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices on one side of a scale and truth on the other, it is weighed; truth possesses greater weight.
Even one who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices does not attain that state which is attained by my devotees.
One should avoid from afar a horse-drawn carriage, an elephant in rut, cows that have recently calved, and likewise a female slave within the inner apartments.
When honey-bees enter the horse-stable and construct a honeycomb within it, the horses will certainly die.
Speed is the characteristic of a horse; rut is the characteristic of an elephant;
cleverness is the characteristic of a woman; and diligence is the characteristic of a man.
In horses, banners, children, courtesans,
and the garments of jesters, fickleness is the supreme ornament.
Horses, elephants, multitudes of chariots, perfected mantras, and favorable deities—
these they say are the means for kings, by which this superior intelligence of mine is produced.
He who has horses has victory; he who has horses has the earth;
he who has horses has fame; he who has horses has gold.
Drinking milk while mounted on a horse, sexual intercourse while mounted on an elephant,
being massaged while in a palanquin, and eating while walking on foot— these are [prohibited].
Upon seeing an ascetic mounted on a horse, a menstruating woman mounted on a bedstead,
or a widow with her hair loose, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
The horses number four koṭis, eleven lakṣas,
thirty-seven thousand, and four hundred.
Then, seventy more are enumerated and declared as foot-soldiers;
they amount to sixty million, eight million, and five additional [thousand].
Sixty-two thousand, four hundred,
and fifty— this is reckoned by the wise as the number of great *akṣauhiṇīs*.
Aśvinī, Anurādhā, Revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Mūla, Punarvasu,
Puṣya, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Hasta are said to be the most auspicious for setting out on a journey.
Aśvinī gives birth to a calf, and Kāmadhenu to a horse;
likewise, the ocean produces fire—just as the king is, so are his subjects.
The absolute affection that exists between a horse and its rider, between a mongoose and a venomous snake, and between a cat and mice—

that very same affection is to be recognized as the innate nature of the class of courtesans toward men driven by desire, when their wealth has dwindled, when their kinsmen have failed them, and when public scandal has become firm.
Speed resides in the horse, endurance in the bull, luster in the gem, and forbearance in the king;
grace and emotion reside in the courtesan, and a sweet voice in the singer.
Generosity is found in the wealthy, valor in the soldier, abundance of milk in cows,
self-restraint in ascetics, and eloquence in the learned.
Impartiality toward the members of the assembly, truthfulness in speech toward witnesses, single-minded devotion toward servants, and well-meaning speech toward ministers;
Silence is an ornament for fools, and devotion to one's husband is an ornament for women; yet these very qualities become great disfigurements when applied to the opposite groups.

Traveling by horses is called "travel," while traveling with women is called "sport" (*līlā*). That which is eaten for the sake of meat is simply "eaten," whereas that which is eaten without travel or sport is called "eaten for [mere] sustenance."
The eight mountain ranges, the seven oceans, Brahmā, Indra, the Sun, and Rudra—neither you, nor I, nor this world exist; even so, for what purpose is grief made?
The divine womb is eightfold, the animal womb is fivefold, and the human womb is singlefold; these are the fourteen types of beings.
Having eight feet, four ears, two faces, and likewise two mouths, this terrible being recites at the king’s gate; he is neither a god nor a rākṣasa.
The eighth is the *brahmarandhra*, which indicates supreme liberation;
by meditating upon it as having the appearance of a needle’s point and the form of smoke, one is liberated.
That should be known as Jālandhara, which bestows liberation upon those whose minds are dissolved [in meditation].
The eighth day, the new moon, the fourteenth day,
and the full moon until midday are to be avoided for all ritual activities.
The eighth lunar day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth destroys the pupil;
the new moon destroys fearlessness; and the first day of the lunar fortnight destroys the study of the texts.
Whether on the eighth or the twelfth day, he who cooks vegetables in his own home without relying on bad friends— what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Having kept the difficult-to-attain perfections far away by the firm striking of the practice of the eightfold yoga,
and now attaining the desired discriminative discernment, he— this crest-jewel of those whose wealth is meditative concentration— is liberated.
The wise have declared that the measure of the wind is eight finger-breadths,
and the principle of fire is said to be four finger-breadths in measure.
Likewise, eighteen [finger-breadths] are for the middle [size], and fourteen for the inferior;
the hoof of the best horse is said by the wise to be seven finger-breadths.
In the eighteen Purāṇas, there are two sayings of Vyāsa:
"Benefiting others leads to merit; causing pain to others leads to sin."
Even the eighteen Smṛtis declare that punishment indeed belongs to him who is at fault;
O deer-eyed one, why then is your own head shaved at the base of the navel?
A king arises from a portion of the eight world-protectors;
therefore, he surpasses all beings in his splendor.

Seated upon an unsurpassed throne in the center of his palace, performing the affairs of men together with eight ministers skilled in statecraft and upright judges—is this Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a king and joined by the guardians of the quarters, protecting the world? To whom among those possessed of even slight delusion does this Mādhava not produce such a misconception?

The eight limbs of yoga are: restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (tanmaya).
O Bhārata, these eight are the very cream of joy;
when they are present, they are seen to be truly blissful.
Reunion with friends, the arrival of great wealth,
an embrace from one's son, and sexual union.
At the proper time, there is pleasant speech; among one's own groups, there is deference;
there is the attainment of what is desired, and honor in the assembly of people.
The one hundred and eight verses as spoken by Cāṇakya,
by the mere knowledge of which the wisdom of men increases.
Eight qualities illuminate a person: wisdom, noble birth, self-control, learning, valor, moderation in speech, giving according to one's ability, and gratitude.
These eight do not destroy a vow: water, roots, fruits, milk, sacrificial oblation, what is desired by a Brahmin, the word of a teacher, and medicine.
O King, these eight things in the world of men are indicators of the heavenly world:
four of them are practiced by the virtuous, and four of them the virtuous practice themselves.
Sacrifice, charity, study, and austerity—these four are practiced by the virtuous;
self-restraint, truthfulness, straightforwardness, and compassion—these four the good pursue.
There are eight preliminary signs of a man who is about to perish:
first, he hates Brahmins, and he enters into conflict with Brahmins.
He seizes the property of Brahmins and seeks to kill Brahmins;
he delights in reviling them and does not rejoice in their praise.
One who does not remember these [obligations] when duties arise, and who becomes envious when entreated—
having understood these faults through his intelligence, a wise man should avoid them.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should the king take taxes from his kingdom; for that is the constant vow of the sun.
When eight divine beings are seen on all sides,
the wise call that a divine affliction, like madness.

May Keśava protect you—he who, in the form of a boar, playfully uproots the earth-lotus: whose petals are the eight directions, whose vast sheath is the golden mountain [Meru], whose lovely mass of filaments is the rays of the sun, whose bees are the rows of clouds, whose stalk is the great serpent Śeṣa, and which extends sportively across the ocean.
Eight crores of gold, ninety-three *tulās* of pearls, fifty elephants intoxicated by the scent of honey and agitated with fury,
ten thousand horses skilled in all maneuvers, and a hundred courtesans— let this dowry given by King Pāṇḍya be presented to the bard.
One should conquer desire through the absence of volitional construction, anger by abandoning desire,
greed by discerning the true nature of gain and loss, and fear by reflecting upon reality.
That which proceeds here unexpectedly, without even being intended, and which turns back what has already been begun— that indeed is the work of destiny.
Although he possesses countless flowers, he gives only five for the sake of the arrows of the Mind-born God;
perceiving such miserliness, as it were, the wives of Spring seized his entire fortune.
Innumerable are those who know the faults of others, and some few indeed are those who know their own virtues;
yet, if there are five or six, they are those who themselves know their own faults.
With her pair of eyebrows— unsteady, arrogant, flickering, crooked, and soiled— she oppresses this entire world, just as a wicked person does with his own nature.
Furthermore, hear what the fruit is for a mantra that is not [properly] grasped:
one attains only the goal that is not deficient in terms of both Dharma and desire.
Through the non-accumulation of new karma and the exhaustion of that previously acquired,
one incurs bondage to a physical body again and again.
For a dissatisfied Brahmin, his splendor, learning, austerity,
and fame flow away through the restlessness of the senses, and even his knowledge is scattered.
The twice-born are ruined by lack of contentment, while kings are ruined by excessive contentment; courtesans are ruined by modesty, and noble women are ruined by shamelessness.
Those who are discontented, those fallen from their positions, those degraded from their honors,
those who have been dismissed by themselves, and those who have been harmed by others— [these are the types of servants].
Even the Lord of the Gods, if he were not content, would repeatedly seek to attain worlds;
yet even one who possesses nothing, if he is content, sleeps with all his limbs free from feverish distress.
Discontent is the supreme suffering; contentment is the supreme happiness.
Therefore, a person seeking happiness should always remain contented.
"Discontent is the supreme sin," said the Blessed Lord Hari.
Greed is the seed of this sin, and delusion is indeed its root;
untruth is its trunk, and its great branches are very extensive.
The foolish are intent on discontent, while the wise attain contentment;
there is no end to discontent, but satisfaction is the supreme happiness.
Lack of contentment leads only to unhappiness, and from greed comes the delusion of the senses; consequently, one’s wisdom perishes, just as knowledge is lost when devoid of practice.
Because of failing to abandon evildoers, the innocent are touched by equal punishment due to being mixed with them;
just as the wet is burned by the dry because of being mixed with it, one should therefore not form an alliance with the wicked.
One who, blinded by pride, does not act with circumspection, will be utterly destroyed even by an equal;
like a pot of unbaked clay, he would not remain standing if he were truly powerful.
One should speak with a mind free from doubt, like the juice of sugarcane;
for he who speaks with agitation is struck by the arrow of his own words.
When one's own success is lacking, the supreme gain is the disclosure of secrets;
likewise, liberation from calamity—these are the three fruits of a friend.
How can one who is unaccomplished be a kinsman? How can one who lacks endurance be a master? How can one who does not know the self be a wise man? And how can one who is dissatisfied be happy?
For a person who does not accomplish any purpose through their genus, action, or quality,
birth serves merely as a designation, like a proper name (*yadṛcchāśabda*).
One who has not yet reached puberty is *gaurī*; once puberty has been reached, she is *rohiṇī*.
A girl without secondary sexual characteristics is a *kanyā*, and one lacking breasts is a *nagnikā*.
The birth of a golden deer is impossible; nevertheless, Rāma was lured by the deer.
Generally, when the time of calamity has arrived, even the intellects of men become clouded.
Shame arises for one's own self through the praise of qualities that do not exist; who is not ridiculed for saying that the *karṇikāra* flower is fragrant?
One should not speak of what is impossible, even if it is seen directly:
a stone floats upon the water, and a monkey sings a song.
One should not speak that which is unfit for speech; if you do speak it, it is so because it causes agitation in others and does not result in a virtuous fruit for oneself.

Then she attained that age which follows childhood— a natural adornment for her slender frame, an intoxicant not called wine that serves as the cause of passion, and a weapon of Love distinct from his flowery arrows.
One who is incorruptible, pure, skillful, an examiner of prepared food,
and a connoisseur of the qualities of cooks is appointed as the superintendent of the kitchen.
The wealth of a miser is common to others because he does not enjoy it;
the connection that "this belongs to him" is only realized with pain when it is lost.
Absence of agitation, lack of shame, contempt for the opponent,
laughter, and praise of the king— these five are the causes of victory.
Who, being disapproved by you, has entered the path of liberation out of fear of the afflictions of rebirth?
Let him remain bound for a long time by the clever side-long glances of beautiful women, with their eyebrows gracefully arched.
In the absence of honor, there is an increase in austerity; from honor, there is the depletion of austerity.
Through being worshipped, merit is lost; through being censured, one attains a good rebirth.
Not looking directly at one another is itself a form of consent, even if it is a refusal;
the very sealing of words with silence is the only path for these nine women.
O lord of men, one who does not share, who is evil-minded, ungrateful, and shameless— such a person is the lowest of men in the world and should be avoided.
The undertakings of one who lacks self-restraint, even when they have been specifically attained,
will undoubtedly perish like a leaking boat in the ocean.
For a king whose counsel has been leaked due to a lack of restraint,
his prosperity does not endure, just as water does not remain in a jar that has a single crack.

Without doubt, this noble mind of mine yearns for her, as she is worthy of being taken by a warrior; for the inclinations of the hearts of the virtuous are the authority regarding matters that are subjects of uncertainty.
Without a doubt, the collyrium applied by the women to ward off the redness at the corners of their eyes was surely placed there;
for even when that was washed away by the water, the redness dispelled the whiteness from their eyes, yet it did not remove their beauty.
Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain;
but by practice, O son of Kuntī, and by dispassion, it is brought under control.
Know for certain that everything will bear fruit in due time;
maintain your fortitude with confidence, and all shall become right.
Bringing the pollen of forest trees— whose blossoms were not yet fully formed, whose filaments were scattered by the stumbling of bees agitated by the swarms,
and whose stamens were in full bloom— the wind caused the buds to open for the sake of the young women.
O lotus-faced one, with glances from your unblinking eyes and words charming with smiles and jests, tell me this: for how many more days is Murāri to be thus deceived?

Not fully beheld by the eyes, modesty, the departure of impurity, extreme paleness, and despondency—these various things became their ornament; for the bodiless god (Ananga) has the power to adorn women.

Time and again, a deer, though overcome by exhaustion, pursues with wide-open eyes the vanishing mirage; it does not realize that this is illusory water. Struck by the desire for water, the mind of those blinded by craving indeed turns away from discernment.
I have repeatedly understood from the Vedic revelation that negation is not limited by a temporal boundary;
for it leads one to that supreme, uninterrupted bliss which is of the nature of the indivisible reality.
Repeatedly, by that swift wielder of the bow who led at the head of Indra on a single chariot,
the dust of battle rising toward the sun was suppressed by the blood of the enemies of the gods.
Though defeated in battle more than once, Hari remained fearful of the son of Brihadratha; therefore, having made the water his fortress, he dwelt there—for even a conquered enemy is to be feared.
One should not repeatedly express hope; one should pray to the deity but only once.
Nālāyanī obtained five husbands by invoking [the deity] again and again.
As he propitiates the three groups without attachment, distinguishing them according to their respective needs with impartial devotion,
the triad does not obstruct one another, as if it had entered into friendship through its affection for his virtues.
Through the fault of attachment to the unattached, there arises a delusion of the intellect regarding what is real;
by indulging for even a single night, one undergoes the mockery of a wooden bell.
An evil person, through association with those who associate with the virtuous, accomplishes here even that which is difficult to achieve;
a female ant, having climbed onto the head of Śambhu by taking refuge on his flowers, kisses the orb of the moon.
A king should not hastily grant a boon out of affection to an unworthy person;
by granting a boon to the Asura Bhasmasura, the Lord met his end through the fruit of that act.
If wicked people could indeed be countered by noble ones with sweet words,
then what effort would there be even to bind the ocean with the pollen of *ketakī* flowers?
Through association with the wicked, the virtuous fall into misconduct;
just as sweet, cool water becomes heated upon reaching fire.
For one who is blinded by the intoxication of wealth, poverty is the supreme collyrium;
a poor man regards all beings through the analogy of his own condition.
The rejection of what is non-existent and the concealment of what is existent; the avoidance of unreal harms and unrighteous acts.
If those who lack virtue possess a sense of righteousness, it becomes a cause of torment for the virtuous;
it is like the breaking of a fast by a hungry tiger through the slaughter of livestock.
Lust is the harboring of the wicked, and anger is the suppression of the virtuous;
both are considered to be extreme calamities due to the abundance of their faults.
When even the existence of non-existent things is not logically tenable, alas,
then the hope for the fulfillment of one's purpose from them is like a serpent’s desire to lick nectar.
Through the fault of association with the wicked, even a virtuous mind falls into delusion;
like a piece of wood suspended from a reed that is carried away by staying for just one night.
Through the fault of associating with the wicked, the virtuous undergo transformation;
through his attachment to Duryodhana, Bhīṣma went to the cattle-raiding expedition.
Abandoning the company of the wicked, one should cultivate the company of the virtuous;
through the fault of associating with the wicked, Māṇḍavya met his death upon a stake.
The innate nature of the wicked, though concealed by some cause,
arises together with its fruit, just as the latent potentiality of seeds arises along with their fruit.
The riches of the wicked exist for the enjoyment of the wicked;
though the neem tree is laden with fruit, it is enjoyed only by crows.
Who does not go to the lowest state through association with the wicked?
Even milk in the hand of a female liquor-seller is called "wine."
Likewise, there is the description of the conduct of unchaste women, as well as the description of spring and other seasons,
the description of summer and others, and likewise the description of the rainy season and so forth.
An unchaste woman becomes modest; alkaline water becomes cool;
a hypocrite becomes discerning; and a rogue becomes a sweet-spoken person.
Even that which is non-existent may possess qualities, while those of virtuous conduct may arise from the wicked;
the lotus rises from the mud, yet worms also emerge from the lotus.
Whether describing one's own qualities when they are non-existent or even when they do exist, even Śakra would fall into ridicule; how much more so an ordinary person?
One who delights in what is non-existent, who is unsteady, who is enterprising, and who is a seeker of sensual objects—
