that rajasic person, among humans, attains birth after death.
One who accepts gifts from the wicked goes to the downward-facing hell;
that man who eats delicious food alone goes to the river of pus.
O King of kings, one should neither utter nor even contemplate these four verbal faults: idle chatter, harshness, slander, and falsehood.
In this world, unfaithful women are constantly honored by their lovers; they do not respect their husbands when those husbands have fallen into misfortune.
Untruthfulness, cruelty, ingratitude, fear, negligence, laziness, despondency,
vain pride, procrastination, and likewise addiction to women, gambling, and the like, are the destructions of prosperity.
Untruth is rooted in a lack of conviction, a fortress for the flourishing of evil tendencies,
a primary cause of calamity, powerful in its deception of others, and something from which the wise have turned away once it has committed an offense.
All this is known to be untrue; the claim that you acted improperly is a false fabrication. This constant concealment of your heart is merely a sequence of wicked and fickle behavior.
Young women are untruthful in character, deformed, and always difficult to grasp at heart;
they harbor evil intentions and lose their passion in a mere moment.
We have heard that neither the gods nor the ancestors accept offerings from one who is false to his word, fickle, and of unsteady mind.
The merchant is the root of untruth; beautiful women are its branches;
the scribes are its leaves and flowers; and gamblers are its fruits.
Various phenomena are seen that appear real though unreal, and appear unreal though real; therefore, critical investigation is appropriate.
Speech that is untrue or slanderous is destroyed;
a mantra recited with doubt is destroyed; and a recitation performed with a distracted mind is destroyed.
If the quality of self-restraint is absent, a weapon is warded off with both hands;
yet even this course is not secure, nor is any other found anywhere.
Prostitutes, devoid of truth, live by means of untruth alone; these women perish through truth, just as women of good family perish through liquor.
Through the fault of association with the wicked, even the virtuous sink downward;
through the defect of darkness, even a level path appears uneven.
Even one who knows what is virtuous, through association with the wicked, has his mind attached to sense objects and suddenly meets with destruction, like a deer infatuated by song.
A request made by the great to those who are unworthy does not lead to their humiliation when it is for the sake of a friend;
even Hari himself became a petitioner before the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra on behalf of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
"O Lord, this is an unrighteous thing for us women that we should abandon our shame and consort with men who are more wicked than ourselves."
A king who is served by the wicked is defiled even though he himself is virtuous; is sandalwood, even if fragrant, to be used when it is entwined by serpents?
The wealth and prosperity of the wicked are enjoyed only by the wicked;
the crows alone eat the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree, and no others.
"O friend, this beloved is not of bad conduct, nor is he devoid of virtues; this pearl necklace has fallen at the base of your feet.
Take it, O charming girl, let it attain the affection of your neck; there is no other means for the pacification of the burning heat in your heart."
When wicked men are occasionally requested by the virtuous for some task,
they consider themselves to be virtuous, even though they are actually devoid of merit.
Those who turn back from the Vedas, being non-existent like atheists,
fall into hell and incur sin.

With unsteady steps, her limbs trembling, and charming with movements faltering from intoxication—where will you go, O fair-thighed one, at the time of love-making? Are you perhaps some elusive forest-dweller?
The uncivilized, the slanderer, the ungrateful, and the long-harboring enemy—
these four are outcastes by their actions, with the outcaste by birth as the fifth.
"O fair-thighed one, what is the use of this incomplete gazing? Look at your beloved without hesitation.
For water drunk from the tip of a blade of kusha grass does not quench thirst, even after a very long time."
This has turned out to be inconsistent, most inconsistent;
alas, alas! Hari looks on with curiosity at the cowherd boy’s notion that he is Hari.
Having abandoned those who are powerless, the capable enjoy [the land];
for kings there is no inheritance; the earth is to be enjoyed by the brave.
Surely my intellect falters at an inopportune time, for this new moon, once it has come into my hand, has vanished;
yet it returns again, and though I restrain it and hide it away, O friend, the face of the moon cannot be seen again.
Even sages, when lacking the means, accumulate wealth; why then would kings—who hold their subjects under the power of their treasury—not do the same?
A virtuous man may be incapable, a student of the Veda may be destitute,
one may be afflicted by disease yet worship the gods, and a wife may be ill-favored yet devoted to her husband.
He by whom the hero Hamīra was limited in battle— limiting those warriors who were greedy for the wealth of incomparable combat—
who indeed would not pay homage to him, that garlanded with rays for seizing the fortune of all the stars of arrogant kṣatriyas?
If those who possess incomparable courage and excellent resolve, and who cause wonder to all the world,
do not achieve their desired goals, the disgrace belongs to the cruel Fate, not to the high-minded man.
"Equality will arise for me in this inequality during our quarrel"—
thinking thus, the proud lion surely flees from the deer.

For those who possess conceit, even a modest degree of wealth is sufficient to arouse intoxication, provided their purpose is not yet fully accomplished and their momentum has been restrained by discipline.
What concern for women can there be for a high-minded man who has not yet achieved his desire for conquest?
Without having traversed the entire world, the sun does not resort to its twilight rest.

Being treated as an equal by those who are unequal, being deprived of honor by those who are his equals, and being appointed to tasks beyond his capacity— for these three reasons, a servant abandons his master.
For knowledge, even when applied by those most skilled, if it is improperly employed,
remains unknown despite being perceived, or is known yet not put into practice.
A man who is alone and without assistance does not reach the completion of his task;
even a grain of rice, when deprived of its husk, does not sprout.
What can even a powerful and majestic person accomplish if he is without allies?
In the past, Rāma burnt Laṅkā through the assistance of Sugrīva.
What can one do, even if capable and radiant, if left without assistance?
A fire fallen in a windless place extinguishes itself.
Even if capable, one who is without assistance is not able to accomplish a task;
even when deprived of their husks, grains of rice do not sprout.
"Without a companion and seeking help, he must surely have meditated upon me while being tormented by the sharp arrows of Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and the others."
No undertakings whatsoever reach completion for one who is without assistance;
therefore, in all matters, a companion is the king’s essential recourse.
What can a spirited person do if he is without allies or lacks the necessary power?
Like fire falling upon a place devoid of grass, he is extinguished by himself.
Those born in Videha should be known as lacking companions yet possessing great power;
those born in the land of Aṅga are fierce, with skillful hands and likewise very firm.
The earth, with its circles of dust raised by unbearable winds and scorched by the heat of the fierce sun,
cannot even be looked upon by travelers whose minds are consumed by the fire of separation from their beloveds.
O Greed, you have endured things that were unbearable and heard words that were unpleasant;
you have stood at the doorways of others' houses—now, attain cessation.
Those who lack means and are destitute of wealth, yet possess intelligence and are esteemed by their friends,
quickly accomplish their tasks— just like the crow, the tortoise, the deer, and the mouse.
A man is indeed good or bad by his very birth; wickedness does not come from association, nor does goodness belong to anyone through it.
When the association between a gem and a serpent—both produced at birth—is fully established, the gem does not touch the faults of the snake, nor does the snake touch the virtues of the gem.
One should understand that the unwholesome is not to be pursued, nor is the wholesome to be accumulated;
rather, with diligence, accumulate merit, for death is certain.
A wise person should not undertake what is impossible to accomplish, nor should they ever cause an improper act to be done;
they should never speak untruth, nor should they ever consume what is unfit to be eaten.
Having perceived an enemy to be incurable, one should cause a division within that enemy's lineage,
[targeting] one who is capable and desires the kingdom, just as Rāma did with Vibhīṣaṇa.
The wicked serpent-like person, though incurable by virtuous mantras, emits the intense poison of his speech and maintains a double-tongued mouth.
Just as a physician, having diagnosed an incurable disorder in embodied beings, endures it with his hand raised for surgery, so too does the king endure [the malady] with the sword in hand.
The successful attainment of one who is not yet won, the pleasing of one who has been won,
and the proper enjoyment of one who is impassioned— this is the purpose of the science of love.

I do not know what is appropriate: whether to praise or rather to censure that Creator who, having fashioned you of priceless creation and graceful form, yet abandons his passion for creation even after producing you—a creation unique in its mention, alas, struck by a lack of flavor.
How can you resolve to make this world essence-less, to rob the three realms of their jewels, to leave the world without light, to leave kinsmen with death as their only refuge,
to render the God of Love devoid of pride, to make the creation of human eyes fruitless, and to turn the entire world into a withered forest?
Saṃsāra is essence-less, like the pith of a succulent plantain tree; this life is as flickering and unstable as a flash of shimmering lightning.
This youth is like the rush of a river descending from a mountain; yet, alas, what audacity it is that the mind of men still runs toward sense objects!
Substance is everywhere insubstantial; the collection of substance is found in speech.
He by whom that speech is set in motion has lost his merit.
In this essence-less cycle of existence, the essence is the deer-eyed woman;
for her sake they desire wealth, yet when she is abandoned, what is the use of that wealth?
"Thinking, 'In this essence-less saṃsāra, the woman with shapely hips is the very essence,' Śambhu indeed took his beloved into half of his own body."
These sense objects are indeed essence-less, or perhaps they are distasteful due to their lack of detachment; let them be loathed, or rather, let it be said that they are the abode of every fault.
Nevertheless, for those whose minds are fixed upon the inner reality, an indescribable and exceedingly powerful majesty belonging to them throbs within the heart.
In this truly essence-less cycle of existence, the essence is indeed the father-in-law’s mansion;
for Hari reclines in the Ocean of Milk, and Śiva reclines on the Himalayas.
In this truly essence-less cycle of existence, the essence is indeed the father-in-law’s mansion;
for Hara sleeps on the Himalayas, and Viṣṇu sleeps in the great ocean.
In this truly essence-less cycle of existence, these four things alone are the essence:
dwelling in Kāśī, association with the virtuous, the waters of the Gaṅgā, and service to Śambhu.
In this essence-less cycle of existence, embodied beings harbor a delusion of happiness,
like children’s mistaken belief that they are drinking milk when they are actually sucking on their own thumb.
Alas, in this essence-less cycle of existence, the union with loved ones that occurs for embodied beings through the power of karma becomes heart-rending when they are separated.
In this essence-less saṃsāra, where royal pleasures have a bitter ripening like poison and are swallowed up by Death, and where the strength of life is inherently fickle;
alas, those of dull intellect—whose hearts are struck by the mirage of sense-objects—steal away their own lives with these fleeting breaths in a body that is certain to perish.
In this essence-less saṃsāra, which provides refuge for the wise, how many poets—each following their own inclinations—do not strive at will in the composition of poetry?
But rare indeed is that simple person who produces or speaks words that are smooth as milk and sweet in their construction.
Lacking substance, devoid of virtue, and crooked, yet endowed with a variegated form,
the rainbow soon met its downfall, just like a wicked person.
Scholarship acquired through negligence, sexual union purchased by means of money,
and a meal dependent on others— these three are the mockeries of men.
Despised by the lotus pond with utter disdain, this rice stalk, though bowing its head,
becomes parched and turns pale along with the water, as if scorched by the god of love.
Although he had not been initiated, he mastered the Vedas from his teacher;
for a crystal, being pure by its very nature, does not require further refinement.

O fair-faced one, from where has this moon of yours been obtained—devoid of the touch of blemish, with its full digits eternally complete and free from stain; possessing above it a pair of quivering, blooming, fresh lotuses for ears, and a shimmering conch for a neck, and a multitude of bees for its playful locks?
"O friend, I am made of iron, while this cruel lover of mine is a mere stone;
know that among attractors, liquefiers, and kissers, he is not even one—a mere magnet."
Having ascended the mountain of sunrise, this radiant king with his crimson orb captivates the hearts of the world with his gentle rays.
This is the auspicious conch of the flower-bowed god for his conquest of the world, arising from the overflowing ocean of the mine of beauty.
Gradually revealing its digits— one, two, three, and so forth— in the gentle radiance of a fresh lotus-stalk sprout,
the moon rises as if in secret, fearing the sidelong glances of housewives whose eyes are inflamed by the fire of separation from their beloveds.
Why did the Lord not first distinguish between your sword, arrows, armor, and bow before making his request?
Or rather, if you possess the power, then begging is already accomplished; for those who possess power, taking what they desire by themselves is not a fault.
The sword-seller, the ink-maker, the temple-priest, the village-priest,
the washerman, and the cook— these six Brahmins are of Śūdra origin.
A horse with four black hooves and dark-knotted legs that discharges a forceful stream of urine near its forefeet,
which has a moving bit in its teeth, a girth-like hump on its shoulders like a cock, and thighs as hard as a *kiṭivara*, is a horse capable of traveling great distances.
O Lord, even if Śāradā were to take ink equal to the Black Mountain in the vessel of the ocean, use the branch of the best of celestial trees as a pen, and the earth as paper,
and write for all eternity, she would still not reach the end of Your virtues.
Having perceived the beauty of the dark eyes of his beloveds in the blue lotuses, the sound of their tinkling golden girdles in the cries of intoxicated swans,
and the lovely splendor of their lips in the *bandhujīva* flowers, the traveler now weeps with a bewildered heart.

At the sight of his enemy’s prowess, he became terrifying with a sword-blade like a black serpent; his movements were swift due to a mind agitated by a restless longing for blood; his body was covered in horripilation, and the luster of his cheeks [faded].
The fresh ketakī flower, entwined by a young black serpent,
shines like the fallen tusk of an elephant adorned with an iron ring.
Even when consumed by a single Asura, this poison does not become pure;
yet, though it has been drunk by the gods until its destruction, this moon rises again of its own accord from the ocean, fresh and new.
Clad in black garments and garlands, like a cloud thick with the essence of aloe-wood, bathed in musk and ink, you yourself have become the night.
Go forth happily; O slender one, do not let the gleam of your teeth shine forth, or else release your breath, which would be like the dense emergence of fluttering bees.
Dark-natured, well-armored,
and displaying its fickleness, her brow’s flickering movement acts like a villain, crooked as a serpent.
Punishment is declared by the wise to be instruction for those who have not yet attained realization;
one should administer that punishment through reason alone, for punishment meted out with reason is praised.
He who perceives the edge of a sword, poison, and fire as equal to a garland, nectar, and snow— that one is called a yogi by the wise.
A single *kārṣāpaṇa* coin purchased by walking on the edge of a sword is better than the entire earth,
bounded by the oceans, if it is pointed out to one by another's brow (as a gift).
O Lord, how did Fortune come upon you on the path of the sword’s edge, slippery with the blood of enemies, and how did Renown depart?
This sword-blade of yours, having conquered the entire circle of kings,
shines forth like the terrifying tongue of Time quivering at the dissolution of the world to devour the earth.
Thinking, "May our women not have a parting in their hair without sindūra," those enemies avoid the sword from afar in battle.
Though he was aided by nothing more than a sword and had overcome a vast number of enemies,
this man of great fortitude felt no pride, unlike other trivial people.
Paśupati, though dense with passion, sewed Umā onto his own body while remaining hidden; the lotus-born Brahmā went to his daughter along with the cowherd girls;
and at whose command even this world is subservient to the fawn-eyed women—who could possibly bring him under control? Alas! The burden of the God of Love is formidable.
Whether it be suffering or happiness, alas, these embodied beings inevitably experience it at the time when their karmas ripen.
Therefore, if an astrologer were to declare this very thing beforehand, tell me: what would be the point of that in the end?
Conversing with those who are not suffering, disclosing secrets,
and providing deliverance from calamity— these are the three fruits of friendship.

Having abandoned his own impure body through the contemplation of the foul, the knower of yoga indeed enters the pure body of another by means of the light of knowledge. Oh, how great is your skill! You enter the heart clearly to see it through the subtle apertures of the eyes, yet you manifest your activity even outside.

Overcome by the intoxication of liquor, he commits the slaughter of the innocent; through his lack of self-restraint, he utters unbearable and false speech; he even covets the wives and wealth of others—what indeed will he not do?
By that wise man, who understood the deception of scribes through the efforts devised by the Asuras,
the jewel-filled earth was well protected.

O King, like Raghu—who was equal in prowess to his own kinsmen skilled in the battle with the Asuras and whose bows were braced with adamant—he too has exhausted his treasury through sacrifice; therefore, become a vessel for radiant virtues in this world.
How can there be satisfaction in the enjoyments of humans for one who was not satisfied by the enjoyments of the lords of asuras, suras, and men?
Would he who did not become free from thirst by drinking the waters of the ocean ever be satisfied by drinking water resting on the tip of a blade of grass?
Would not the preceptor of the sons of Diti have deprived even the darkness—though it was devoid of Asuras and had arisen from the Sun—of its life-breaths when it fell into calamity, like Kaca?
He would have done so, were it not for his fear of violating the vow of silence during the twilight hours, as he recites the life-restoring spell that dwells within his throat.
While still in the womb, Prahlāda was instructed by Nārada, who had been sent by the Asuras;
he became the foremost among those who know reality. One should always listen to beneficial instruction.
She, whose face is like the full moon, is difficult to obtain; and this, moreover, is some strange working of the bodiless god of love:
for when desired successes seem to be within reach, the mind attains a sense of fulfillment all at once.
Whether one has enemies or friends, whether one possesses foes or allies,
whether one is wise or devoid of wisdom— it is by destiny that one obtains happiness.
Having approached a young woman who is not pierced by a needle [of desire] yet speaks like one mature, the lover says at dawn: "Alas, what a tragedy! I have been robbed!"
When the needle cannot pass through the darkness of the sky due to the mass of raindrops falling— mistaken for thunder by those who consider themselves wise—
the golden and lovely flash of lightning brings both joy and despondency to the fair-eyed women walking at their own pace along the path.
The *aśoka* tree immediately produced flowers along with sprouts starting from its very trunk;
it no longer tolerated the touch of beautiful women’s feet adorned with jingling anklets.
She gave birth to Maināka, who is to be enjoyed by Naga maidens and who maintains friendship with the ocean;
he remained unaware of the wounds from the thunderbolt even when the enemy of Vṛtra, the cutter of wings, was enraged.
A man who is envious, malicious, cruel, and a creator of enmity,
by practicing evil, soon encounters great hardship.
Prosperity is seized from its makers by their friends and ministers alike, even when they have previously exerted themselves with various means, if they are overcome by envy.
O observer of noble vows, know that if prosperity should arise in a mind possessed by envy, it is like the contact of wind with a fire of chaff.
Envy is one-footed death; excessive speech is the slayer of prosperity;
lack of service, haste, and self-praise are the three enemies of knowledge.
Having observed the withering of the branches of a fruit-bearing tree due to its lack of nourishment and its ultimate exhaustion,
one should sprinkle it with ghee that has been boiled for exactly seven days, along with a decoction of *viḍaṅga* and milk.
Affection for one who is not a servant, giving gifts, and speaking with kindness—these are the signs of one who is devoted; even toward a fault, they perceive only a collection of virtues.
Fortunate is the life of someone who has not waited at the gate of a lord, who has not experienced the pain of separation, and who has never uttered the words of a coward.

May the Destroyer of Smara grant you joy— he who, unable to endure the asceticism that flared up at that moment with its innate intensity, yet being a connoisseur of the confidential conversations of the Mountain’s Daughter,
was simultaneously assailed by both haste and slackness upon removing his disguise as a false young Brahmin.
He has become a true follower of the Sugata, since he would bring about my very state of being without support;
O friend, what else can your beloved be but momentary, selfless, utterly empty, and worthy of veneration?
Perched in a cool mountain cave, this dove, skilled in the amorous flatteries of Love, coos sweetly and fans his beloved— whose limbs are languid from the heat— with the fold of his wings.
If you cultivate that goodness which is appropriate for the state of mind [of a seeker], then all else is in vain; alas, why do you waste your time in this saṃsāra?
You repeatedly experience worldly pleasure with weariness after a long time; therefore, I believe that supreme bliss arises from renunciation.
The moon is as if non-existent, and the sun is as if departed somewhere; the host of planets and stars in the sky is as if erased after being drawn.
Whether it be day or night—both having their distinctions obliterated by these dense, massed clouds—what is this most terrible resolve that has been undertaken?
If this moon, possessing a coppery luster upon the peak of the mountain of sunrise, should become like the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) stumbling in intoxication,
then even this darkness— which steals the brilliance of fresh tamāla leaves— will fall away like his swaying garment.

It brings misfortune; yet that house becomes a wonderful abode for the enjoyment of supreme bliss, made of abundant gold. Seated upon his couch, he experiences the crossing of the ocean of worldly existence whenever you, O Mother, extend either your grace or your wrath.
With its beautiful filaments kissed by the breeze, led by the bright orb of the moon,
and gazed upon by the eyes of women distressed by separation from their lovers, the spring season has arrived like Hanumān.
Dwelling not far from the abode of Mahākāla, the moon-crested Lord,
he indeed enjoys the evenings with his beloveds even during the dark fortnight, as if they were filled with moonlight.
This wind from the sky, scented by the ichor of Mahendra’s elephant and cooled by its contact with the waves of the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā),
drinks the drops of sweat rising on your face at the dawn of the day’s youth.
This lord of Mahendra and the great ocean, whose strength is equal to Mount Mahendra,
appears as if Mahendra himself were marching before him on his expeditions under the guise of the elephants of his flowing army.
Even if a composition is radiant with the excellence of aesthetic flavor and propriety,
it is not fit for the designation of "poetry" if it does not possess the power of a mantra to expel the unbearable seizure of hatred, even in a wicked person.
This youth, though still a child, is now possessed of learning; having departed from his home, he has arrived here with a face like the full autumn moon.
When he is present in the light of day, the city seems as if its windows were filled with blue lotuses by the side-long glances of women trembling with passion.
Does he not desire to establish this Mukunda within his own self in order to expand this daring for battle for the sake of supreme welfare?
What could be greater than this for crossing the ocean of existence, what else here is the cause for the path of happiness in this worldly cycle?
Having surveyed the interior of the forest, this maker of night, with his clearly visible rays like scattered manes,
has emerged from the mountain of sunrise like a lion that has seized a motionless deer.
For that moon, having granted space to the darkness,
now sets with its lofty peak remaining like the sharp tip of the tusk of a wild elephant submerged in water.
For this woman, who delights in the physical struggle of love and is bold in private, will not allow her lover, when he has gone to a secluded place,
to take his pleasure with another— even with an enemy— unless the dawn, that enemy, is about to rise before him.
For the sun sets quickly, as if in fear, having been glared at with anger by those playful women, afflicted by passion and eager for their assignations, their lips quivering.

When the sun, which bore away the world's burden, had set through the power of time, and the moon of Kālidāsa had become dim, this world shone no more; it was now illuminated by the jewel of Bāṇa’s lamp of Nirvāṇa.
When the sun had set, the eastern quarter fashioned a lump of milk-rice as the moon;
meanwhile, the dark spot moved within it like a crow upon the sacrificial grass of the sky.
When the sun, their husband, has set, even the lotus plants take delight after placing the bee within the interior of their bud; what wonder is there, then, that the deer-eyed women do the same?
When the lord of day has set, the lotus plant, under the guise of bees,
swallows a pellet of kālakūṭa poison for its own destruction.
Even when the pitcher-born Agastya, his own enemy, had set, the ocean underwent contraction but did not rejoice;
for this is indeed fitting for the great, who have amazed the world with the quality of their profundity, even upon the destruction of an enemy.
When the sun has set, neither Saturn nor Mercury can dispel the darkness;
yet a son endowed with virtues does not shine merely by his father's qualities—he shines by his own merit.
The sun, the sole kinsman of the lotus groves, has set; no one can transgress what is ordained by fate.
O Cakravāka, take courage and abandon your grief; the steadfast cross over adversity, but not those of dejected mind.
When their lord, the sun—the source of light for the eyes of the world—has set, the quarters of the sky perform the virtuous deed appropriate for women by dissolving their radiance into the fire;
I believe these directions now wear the black antelope skin of darkness, as soft as the throat of a wagtail, as if desiring to practice ascetic penances.

May liberation set, wherein the devotions to Hari cannot be accomplished by the body; may our worldly existence increase boundlessly, through the arising of whose grace there are prostrations at the head of the illustrious Puruṣottama, the name of Śrī Rāma upon the face, and in the region of the heart the beautiful form of the Joy of the Yadus, dark as a rain-cloud.
Even as it was setting, the sun, though situated upon the peak of the western mountain, attained its splendor;
for generally, the virtuous, disregarding their own self-interest, cultivate others even when they themselves are swallowed by calamity.
The sun, having set and thus brought an end to the veil of darkness, has not yet reached the base of the peak of the Eastern Mountain, which is like a deer’s crest-jewel.
Therefore, O young firefly, this time of yours consists of but a few moments; let your light shine again and again—what delay is there?
"O moon-faced one, the moon is setting; now abandon your pride. What is the use of this vain anger, O lady with arched brows? These stars are falling from the sky.
Thus instructing you, as he slowly raises his foot from the ground, this cock, seeing that the night has waned, crows out its naturally charming song.
Having first swallowed the sun with its rays eclipsed by its beak, and then cast down both wings upon the Malaya mountain and the Himalayas,
the crane subsequently produces the lunar orb as a clearly visible egg from its upraised tail-feathers under the guise of the rising light of the eastern quarter.
Clouds moisten the earth with their waters without regard for any return favor or even their own self-interest; these living beings survive because of them.
But when an astrologer speaks that single word, "There will be rain," the entire world feels as if it has been purchased, and my very vitals begin to reel.
Free from arrogance, he should honor those worthy of respect and serve his gurus without deceit; he should worship the gods without hypocrisy and desire prosperity that is not ignoble.
One should directly perceive their lack of arrogance, their lack of fickleness, their non-committal toward enmities, as well as their nobility or even their meanness.

They say that an envoy endowed with eight qualities is one who is unyielding, not faint-hearted, not dilatory, compassionate, gentle, not to be led astray by others, free from disease by nature, and possessed of noble speech.

The western quarter was like the goddess Vāruṇī, appearing as if she were wearing a shimmering copper-red garment resting upon her full breasts— the spreading rays of the sun— cast across her head as it set.
With her attachment to sense objects extinguished, her lotus-like eyes half-closed, and breathing softly,
she constantly meditates upon something imperceptible, like one devoted to yoga.
When the moon had set, the night-lily, exceedingly distressed by passion,
took a bee into her mouth as poison— even though it was right before her face, she was deterred only by the sound of its wings.

Falling here and there along the path in a disoriented state, vomiting profusely, warding off flies from his face with both hands while uttering insults in a stammering voice, and surrounded by many restless children—this great man, intoxicated and of loathsome appearance, passes to the right; for a moment, cast your gaze upon him, for he is coming this way, drunk.

Bringing her straight lock of hair—acting as a screen for her vision and trembling in the disordered wind—up to her ear with her hand, the traveler’s wife gazes up at the path of her beloved; when the sun has set, her hopes severed, she slowly returns to her dwelling, longing for the sight of him in a dream.

Having cast off her saffron body-unguent, the sky—once bearing rows of reed-stalks like the waves of a stream of feathers moving in a confused and rapid succession—is now pitiable, its beauty concealed by contact with the faded garment of darkness; yet, due to its recent separation from the sun, it does not cease to burn the eyes.

When the sun had approached the side of the eight mountain peaks, the bees— like spies dispatched by the darkness of night— wandered for a long time upon the grounds where they move, wondering whether the cool-rayed moon had risen or not.
The Kaula of Time seems to lead the bull of the sky somewhere for the sake of spiritual attainment, marked by the friction of the orb of the sun resting upon the summit of the eight mountains.
When the sun has risen facing the west, when the moon is in its full orb,
when Mercury is in the ascendant, and when Ketu has both risen and set— [these are the times for departure].

In the evening, the splendor of heaven appeared like a pair of bronze cymbals held in the hands of Śiva as he danced at twilight— resembling the sun’s orb hanging down from the eight directions and the full moon emerging from the crest of the Eastern Mountain.

Cows with eyes that are dark-red and rough, or those with eyes like those of a mouse, do not bring good fortune; nor do those with trembling or flattened horns, or those whose color resembles that of a donkey.
There exists an unmanifest cause, all-pervading, both transcendent and immanent;
though difficult to grasp even due to its proximity, it is characterized by the form of the universe.
There is a certain blind man from birth who sings with slightly faltering steps;
upon hearing even a little of it, what woman does not become one whose heart is shaken?
There is a neck but no head; there are two arms but they are devoid of hands. There is neither Rāma capable of abducting Sītā, nor is there Rāvaṇa.
There is water in the great ocean, yet it is salty; what can be done with that?
Better is even a small well, where people drink until their very throats are quenched.
He who has a son under his control, as well as a servant and likewise a wife,
and who possesses contentment in the absence of these, dwells in heaven even while on this earth.
There is fear, there is curiosity, there is bashfulness, and there is longing;
such is this indescribable state of young girls toward a lover, consisting of many moods.
Although there is water adorned with lotuses everywhere,
the mind of the swan does not rejoice except at Lake Mānasa.

There is the Lord, the Master of the entire world, whose chest is marked with the seal of the makara-patterned leaf-designs from the breasts of Śrī; he is the moonrise for the lotus-faces of the wives of Madhu.

When he assumed the body of a boar for sport, upon the tip of his tusk—white as the new moon—the earth shone like a single musta-grass root uprooted from the bed of the basin of the dissolution-ocean.
There is a mountain made of gold; there is a realm free from the burden of hunger and thirst; there are oceans that are mines of milk and ghee; there are trees that grant all desires.
What is to be achieved for us by hearing of such wonders? For those tormented by hunger, what is seen is right here. O wise one, direct all your effort toward that very place.
Is there any sweet fruit upon it? Or is there even a bud fit to be smelled? Let that be; is there at least a leaf fit to be eaten? Alas!
If even such a wretched tree as the *pippala* is to be served by men, then tell me, before whom should one weep over this miserable lack of autonomy ordained by Fate?
One should practice agriculture with the thought "it exists"; one should engage in trade with the thought "it exists or it does not exist";
one should repay a debt with the thought "it does not exist"; and one should commit a daring act with the thought "I am not."
Let it be that Agastya eclipsed the greatness of Jahnu; what talk can there be of that child who was not satiated even by swallowing the entire universe?

May there be well-being for you from the Lord of Wealth, who dwells upon Mount Kailāsa; whose moon-like ornament, Śrīkaṇṭha, wanders day and night like moonlight, creating the illusion of a lunar glow; where Rambhā, though distracted by separation, assumes the guise of a courtesan through the very pallor of her body, as if to begin a pursuit of Nalakūbara.
If Śivā stands in the western direction, she brings fear from the armies of enemies;
if she stands in the direction of Kubera (the north), she brings auspiciousness, but if she stands at the edge of a village, she causes it to become desolate.
Our mind— filled with no small wonder, having forgotten all former events, and shattered by the fever of a newly arisen fear—
attains a state variegated by joy and sorrow, its delusion momentarily broken and then reassembled.

Under the guise of the discs of the sun and moon lingering upon the eastern and western mountains, this twilight has arrived like some woman who for a moment places lotuses upon her ears and scatters flowers in the form of stars.

The discs of the sun and the moon situated on the mountain of setting appeared like a pair of spectacles resting on the nose of the golden mountain, as if to read the letters of the stars for the day that had reached the stage of extreme old age.
With the quarters of the sky bent over by the orb of the sun placed upon his pillow,
the traveler of the day lies upon the bed of the firmament, wearing the mantle of darkness.
It is said that in this very ocean there is that nectar, and right there is the Hālāhala poison; on this very Malaya mountain there are sandalwood trees, and right there are the wind-eating serpents.

Whatever object is noble and found nearby, that same thing is difficult for men to obtain; the Creator has placed what is to be attained upon the tip of the tongue, in the palm of the hand, and upon the forehead.
Even today, the surface of the earth extends as far as the moats of the four oceans, and here and there, kings remain devoted to assemblies of connoisseurs.
If one among them should be indifferent, another may be full of respect; and if the Goddess of Speech dwells within his lotus-like mouth, what person indeed could be considered wretched?
There is an incurable blemish upon the pair of breasts, which,
due to the transparency of the bodices, no longer remains within the realm of concealment.
In the northern direction, there exists the king of mountains named Himālaya, whose nature is divine;
plunging into the eastern and western oceans, he stands like a measuring rod for the earth.
There is one subtle world that you are able to perceive,
wherein you may behold the objects of the art of painting, as well as the variegated and moving forms within those paintings.
And from that very source, a flash of inspiration generally arises for artists regarding all possible types of dramas and narratives that can be composed.
A cloud indeed exists upon the peaks of mountains or shines in the sky;
even when shattered by the winds, does it ever descend to the subterranean realm?
There certainly exists a forest distressed by a fierce wildfire, where the entire world is overcome by intense heat and the rivers are utterly devoid of water.
O shameless Parjanya, why do you roar so much, threatening the wives of travelers? Do people anywhere ever regard you as a true cloud?
Having discharged his entire arsenal during the first attempt, alas,
when the Flower-Armed One again made an effort to slay the frail woman, her very body alone became both his target and his quiver.
Whether it be a weapon, a woman, a dwarf, a mortal, an animal, or something else entirely, by the power of destiny it may happen as it will; yet one should never abandon human effort.

While this father of mine, my preceptor of all masters of the bow, stands as the commander of the army like a submarine fire within the ocean of the enemy forces licked by the flames of his weapons—O Karna, enough with your agitation;
go, O Kṛpa, leave the battlefield; abandon your fear of the son of Hṛdika; while my father bears the burden of battle with his bow as his only companion, what room is there for fear?
In the tumultuous practice of the discharge of missiles, even though he was surrounded by the armies of the Gaṇas, the Kumāra was indeed conquered by me.
Yet, having embraced me with such favor, my venerable Guru, who is fond of virtuous qualities, bestowed this [weapon] upon me.

In the midst of the battle, where heads were severed by the clashing of missiles, helmets, and weapons, where rivers of blood flowed for a moment, where weapons rang out, and where armor was shattered by the force of arrows—
at that front of the fray, when the principal army had been broken, that Lord of Kosala, mounted upon a rutting elephant, was slain by Rumaṇvat alone with hundreds of shafts after being challenged.
The trees fashioned as missiles by the Lord of Monkeys wither away, suffering the calamity of a forest fire caused by the friction against the chest of Rāvaṇa;
and the mountain peak uprooted and hurled forth becomes like a mass of mud from the waters of its own springs, crushed by the grasp of the King of Laṅkā’s hand.

He made his weapons blades of grass toward one who wronged his beloved; he made the bow of the enemy of Smara a mere blade of grass; even a stone became a woman to the sage; and the sandals themselves became a noble lady.
Even the great ocean became a small stream, the monkeys became warriors, and the descendant of Pulastya became a mere gnat; yet you, O Blessed One, became a human being.

O hero, by you—who have reduced Rāvaṇa to the state of a crab in a whirlpool—this infamy has been wiped away: that the son of Rāvaṇa, by the discharge of his flood of missiles, had made even Indra a partaker of ill-repute, his power of arm restrained by the curse of Gautama. Ah, the quality of being a true son remains ever vigilant as a healing herb that extracts the arrowhead.
Even if the method for grasping the syllables of the scriptures occurs through thousands of births, and even if there is an initial understanding of their meaning,
how could one cross over the oceans of difficult prima facie arguments— dense with the waves of conceptual constructions devised by wicked disputants?

Adorned with ornaments that do not suit her, her speech faltering and lacking clarity, like the composition of some bad poet, the woman— blinded by intoxication— was mocked by the people and quickly departed from her own home.

The misplaced attachment of the Lord of Passion (*Ratipati*), the violation of propriety for *rati*, the futility of fresh youth, a certain sprout of blemish upon love, the disregard for good fortune, the lack of virtue in the essence of beauty’s splendor, and a mockery of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)—what more can be said? It is the mere ostentation of passion for a courtesan.
One who is intent upon what is impossible is generally a fool, not a wise man;
for who other than a child would wish to grasp the shimmering reflection of the moon in water?
When the Goddess of Speech is brought to waste by those of ruined intellect in an improper place, she leads to reproach, defeat, great suffering, or sin.
But when expended by the virtuous in a fitting place, she serves for their renown, prosperity, the peace of mind, the benefit of others, and ultimately, the attainment of liberation.
When I was in an improper place crowded with people, as my girdle slightly slipped and my fluttering waist-cloth fell down below the navel,
that fortunate hand was the one granted an opportunity by the deer-eyed girl, whose vine-like limbs were trembling with fear and agitation in that state.
A horse struck at an improper place may incur many defects;
those defects persist for as long as that horse lives.
The wise follow those fools who are intent upon the improper and satisfied with the improper,
just as parents follow their playing children.
Enveloped by his splendor, he, being constantly followed [by his attendants], inflicts various punishments— whether out of place or in the right place, and whether provoked or not.

The forest region at the edge of the woods was seen by travelers as if filled with the bones of the dead by the blossoming *palāśa* trees with their jasmine-like buds; as if strewn with heaps of charcoal by the hovering bees;
as if possessing the glow of embers by the light from the red eyes of the male cuckoos; and as if still containing the remnants of a conflagration by those who had lost their lives there.
There is no bone, there is no head, and there is an arm without fingers;
there are no two feet, yet it tightly embraces the body of its own accord.
In this world, life is unstable; youth and wealth are unstable;
sons, wives, and the like are unstable; but Dharma and fame—these two are stable.
Family ties are unstable; learning is always contentious;
pride leads only to delusion; and wealth is truly a transitory death.
Unstable, multicolored, devoid of virtue, eternally crooked, and difficult to grasp—
the rainbow of the lord of gods in the rainy season is perceived like the mind of a young woman.
One should perform steadfast deeds with this unstable body;
for the vital breaths will inevitably depart, like guests leaving.
O King, your fame shines like bone, like curd, like a conch shell, and likewise like a crane; furthermore, it resembles the teeth of a renunciant.
Wealth resides in the bones, pleasure in the flesh, enjoyments in the skin, and women in the eyes;
movement is in the gait, command in the voice, and everything is established in the vital essence (*sattva*).
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement.
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent.
Just as a tree on a riverbank [is swept away], or as a bird leaves one tree for another,
so too, by abandoning this body, one is released from the crocodile of suffering.
The bones, marrow, and semen are considered the three portions derived from the father;
the blood, body hair, and flesh are considered the portions derived from the mother.
"Bone! Bone! Deer-skin! Deer-skin! Ashes! Ashes! Moon! Moon! Ganges! Ganges! Serpent!
Serpent!"—may these agitated cries of the Gaṇas as they busily prepare the collection of ornaments, garments, and requisites protect you, O Śiva, who are intent upon the commencement of the dance.
One who eats without having bathed eats filth; one who does not recite prayers eats pus;
one who eats without offering oblations eats poison; and one who does not give gifts consumes poison.

Having entered into association with those who are untouchable in this world, having endured blows from sticks and even undergone the binding of drums, you reveal your fault right upon every street; by doing so, you manifest your own aversion to the world.

Let him be untouchable, let him be filthy, let him have no fixed diet, and let him be surrounded by more than a hundred other formidable defects; what loss is there in that? He eats whatever food is available, having invited his own kinsmen to join him. Reflect upon this: who then is truly fortunate and meritorious—one who suffers from hunger, or he who does so?

O fair-faced one, when the day is untouched by the fear of Rāhu and the night is equal [in length], when it is far from the shadow of blemish and free from the terror of eclipses, when its splendors are fully accumulated, its fragrance is heart-stealing,

it is devoid of the veil of clouds, it is difficult to find even upon the surface of the earth, and it bestows delight upon all the world— even then, O lovely-faced one, the moon possesses but a mere fraction of the likeness of your face.
Our ancestors, desiring to see the horse stolen by the Lord of the Gods, pierced the earth with their countless forces and expanded the ocean;
if he should command the mountains for the sake of honoring you, O bird of hidden wings, do not reject a friend’s fitting request even if you are not weary.
"O you who perform auspicious rites at the time of our departure, why do you weep, my dearest? Tell me the reason for it.
O lord of my life, the water of my eyes has flowed away like smoke from the intense heat of the fire of separation."
By the measure of our faith in the Lord,
may the grace of the Master be able to accomplish the task, and likewise provide us with assistance.
"Indeed, sandalwood has been granted as a dwelling place for our enemies, the wind-eaters (serpents)";
as if out of anger at this, the breeze from the fan dried up the sandalwood applied to her body.
"My enemy, the darkness, is indeed being conquered by this moon; for he has followed the face of the fawn-eyed woman under the guise of her mass of hair.
Having heard this, the cool-rayed moon, his pride shattered, immediately arrived in the form of a garland of *mālatī* flowers to perform service.

"O King of Kings, O Sovereign! Thinking thus—that this water of ours who live by it must be drunk by the throngs of excellent horses, resulting in the satisfaction of those whose minds are red with the blood of enemies and the destruction of their husbands—the fish weeps at your victorious expedition festival, the fly laughs, and the wives of your enemies brood in sorrow."
Although the history of our supreme mistress should remain untold, O Lord, I shall speak of it, for it constitutes a certain unpleasant reproach against you.
O illustrious King Rāma, that very sword-blade which you grasped with such reverence by the hand on the battlefield was seen by me rolling upon the heart of another.
"Alas! In our realm, the hand of the King is first laid upon the regions of Kāñcī, Kuntala, and Madhyadeśa, which possess abundant wealth, while abandoning [our own lands].
Seeing this, the breasts of the lotus-eyed women became dark-faced with grief; for even one who is lowly cannot endure such humiliation, so how much less those who are so exalted?
Our *vadarī* grove and the *badarī* tree are in your courtyard;
because of our connection through Vādarāyaṇa, you are you and we are we.
"This alone is our vow: that this vigil within the bower must be observed, and this guest, Madana, must be gratified with the honey from your lips.
Let hundreds of swords fall upon my head, or let my own head be severed; O daughter, the path of your family must not be transgressed by you even in the slightest degree."
"Friend, our garments are not beautiful, our necklace is not radiant, our gait is not coquettish, our laughter is not haughty, nor is there any intoxication at all.
Yet even other people say, 'Her beloved, though handsome, does not cast his gaze elsewhere. By this much alone, we consider the whole world to be in a state of distress."
Our very limbs have been offered as merchandise, a treasury of great wealth;
why do these parasites, the sons of slave-girls, devour them through their addiction?
This heart of ours has been occupied by you for a long time;
now let it be adorned on the outside by you, as the Fortune [Śrī] adorns the chest of the enemy of Mura.
"O Kandarpa, since you, having become our very source of life, now strike us down— alas!— may that state of being bodiless (anaṅga) of yours be eternal and perpetual!"

At this very moment, our roar— arising from thousands of deep and auspicious mṛdaṅga drums and imitating the thundering of clouds scattered by the wind— strikes away the capacity to perceive any other sound.
"Alas! After this, who in our family will perform the funeral offerings as prescribed by the scriptures?
Surely my ancestors drink only the water left over from washing tears, poured by me who am now deprived of offspring."

For those like us who are surely devoid of merit, this treasury of jewel-like virtues—though present—is neither for our own use nor for the use of others; it is perceived as if non-existent, bearing the seal of poverty.

Know us to be different from sesame seeds, which, when struck by the fierce fire of the pestle, suddenly abandon their oil and turn into mere dregs under even slight pressure; we are not such as those.
O sister of Kālakūṭa, O abode of Lakṣmī, do not involve us even in a dream; O Mother, these afflictions repeatedly torment us by becoming diseases.
For the eye does not look upon its desired objects, nor does the ear hear in this way; it is better that the vital breaths depart, rather than that words go out.

O friend, who indeed would abandon us, who possess such wondrous forms and have long followed behind you? Or rather, if you must abandon us—alas, what a pity!—then this loss is yours alone, O best of peacocks; for our place shall once again be upon the head of a king.

Having well considered us—whose wealth is self-restraint—and your own high lineage, as well as this woman’s spontaneous outpouring of affection toward you despite the absence of kinsmen, she should be regarded by you among your wives with equal treatment. Beyond that, it is a matter of fortune; indeed, nothing further should be said to her by the relatives of the bride.

Previously, we reckoned that you had not been enjoyed by any men; thus, our heart moved with desire toward you, thinking you were mature and possessed of self-respect. Shame on you! Now, as you extend your embrace to the crowd of profligates, you are accessible to everyone like a courtesan; you must be cast off by us.

With our heads bowed low and trembling with smiles, we have praised your hand, the supreme lord of the scattering of pearls, which is intent on recovering the Vedas and purified by the waters of charity.
But forgive us, O ornament of the earth; for what indeed is not perceived by poets? Even that fish was clearly seen, hidden as it was, in your very hand.
Wandering over this earth bounded by the four oceans, we have not seen any person of distinguished character whose virtues are free from flaw,
before whom one might speak for a moment or even half a moment of the sorrows or joys long accumulated in the heart, and find relief by sighing.
Above this world and below that one, there exists a great darkness;
indeed, it is a source of great delusion for the senses. Understand this well, O King, lest it should overcome you.
When this moon of serene luster, possessing the brilliance of a blooming *kunda* flower, has reached the eastern sky and you, my beloved, have gone but a short distance away,
her sigh acts like a *kairava* bud, her face acts like a lotus, her passion acts like the ocean of milk, and even her glance instantly acts like a moonstone.

O beloved, this garland of blue water-lilies, though well-fastened and closely joined, does not bear its own natural beauty upon this head of yours, which is so richly adorned with lapis lazuli, crystal, and gold.
In this vast world, there is no object whatsoever created by the Creator that can repay the kindness of a mother, who is affectionate without cause.
In this inert world, who indeed could be a vessel for misfortune—a great-eared elephant? Yet he, the very elephant, has crushed even that bee which had approached him; what more can be said of him?
In this great ocean, which is turbulent with the mighty waves of old age, death, and mortality,
men who cross over by means of the boat of merit and well-performed deeds reach the shore and attain fearless happiness.
In this immeasurable Self, which cannot be grasped, what yoga could possibly prevail?
Who would be capable of leaping across it, except for the god Maheśvara?

O Moon, for what purpose do you perform this sacrifice of ten million unchaste women, casting aside all compassion, toward this circle of light that for long has resembled the lotus-stalks dripping from the trunks of lordly elephants?
At this time, however, whatever is appropriate should now be performed;
for they do not grieve over what has passed, since what has passed is indeed simply gone.

In this bower, even without a breeze moving, something surely exists; "Let us go and see!"—as the group of children followed, trembling with fear, may the friend of Rādhā, the enemy of Kaiṭabha, delight you as he sports, emitting loud, fierce roars like those of a powerful lion.
In these waters, agitated by the tossing of crooked waves,
how could a bridge made of handfuls of sand ever become a cause for laughter?
In this pleasure grove, where the breeze is fragrant, where the women sport, where swarms of bees hum, where the *bakula* trees are vast, and which is crowded with warbling female cuckoos;
where there is the scent of blossoming new *pāṭala* flowers and it is thick with *mallī* blooms—if even a single *mālatī* has not blossomed, is spring not delightful nevertheless?
While he is intent on this world-conquest, the Earth—the wife of the enemy kings—trembles with a state of *sāttvika* emotion, thinking, "May this man remain my husband.
Facing him in battle, the rival kings who are about to ascend to heaven perceive their own path through the sun to be nothing but a dark hole.

In this wretched time, devoid of the distinction between night and day, when the expanse of the sky is hemmed in on all sides by clouds arrayed like ramparts, let the rays of the sun indeed not spread forth; yet, by the mere presence of that radiant one, the beds of lotuses continue to blossom even now.
In this [scene], the hand of the Goddess— whose eyes were tremulous with fear and upon whom auspicious great herbs had been placed— was playfully grasped by the wielder of the Pināka bow,
whose own hand was adorned with a bracelet of sloughing serpents, while her hand trembled violently.

When this Lord, the Moon—the master of the night, the cause of joy for the quarters of the three worlds, the remover of the pallor from the faces of the directions, and a treasury of the essence of nectar—has risen, what does it matter if your lotus-face is eclipsed? For the entire world sings the eternal glory of this jewel that adorns the crest of the Lord [Śiva].
In this lineage, no child devoid of virtue is born;
for how could a glass trinket be produced from a mine of rubies?
O crow, while this lion—who is enraged by the roar of these masses of clouds and who watches the sky—looks on, do not become agitated; eat the fragments of flesh from corpses upon the treetops.

This lion, whose claws are like thunderbolts sharpened by contact with the frontal globes of rutting elephants, has no desire for this, for his mouthful is whitened by pearls dropped while he was intent on devouring [his prey].

In this [forest], the column of smoke from the forest fire—slightly curved, spread out, somewhat interrupted, and bent; its splendor gathered with a certain grace, both massed and rising; dark as the shoulder of a young buffalo—gliding freely through the sky, creates fleeting leaf-patterns.
In this human lifespan, which is harsh with mutual hatred,
only sweet speech brings about and bestows friendship.

In this darkness created by scattered powdered incense, this world of serpents—with its crested hoods raised like peaks—is seen through the faint networks of light from jeweled ornaments; it seems to make me remember Pātāla today.
O beautiful one, because the gaze of the god of love is generally fixed upon this naturally lovely form of yours,
your waist diminishes at every moment.

In this circle of the earth, a person’s greatness arises through fortune; for there is indeed no cause for it other than luck—neither diligent effort nor any personal merit. For the world offers a grand oblation to the crow that feeds on impurities, yet alas, it does not offer one to the pure swan that is devoted to a diet of pearls.
In this desert, what more need be said that is beyond the reach of words? O traveler, do not abandon your state of being ever compassionate toward those who seek refuge.
You have seen this expanse of sand, its surface ablaze, which you mistook for a mere drop of water due to your longing for it.

In this vast and boundless wheel of time, there are indeed only a few fortunate ones, foremost among them the Śuka-yogins, who, being of perfectly pure nature, have dissolved into the pair of your feet; we perceive them as your own nails.
In this cauldron consisting of great delusion, Time cooks all beings with the sun as fire, with day and night as fuel, and with the months and seasons as the stirring ladle; such is the report.
"In this festival of the year, my daughter, you must not remain without food during the celebration of Kāmadeva; therefore, let something now be placed in your mouth.
When the old woman had spoken thus, the traveler's wife somehow managed to swallow a morsel of food that day, while her tears washed it away with their falling streams.
In this spring, men cannot endure separation from their wives nor the disease of consumption;
let the proud women, anointed with the luster of musk-paste, enjoy themselves.
O friend, O wish-fulfilling gem, in this world where jewels abound so greatly, do not become a mere stone; do not become a jewel!
For nowadays, such gems prevail in the world whose only ornament is their skill in grasping a blade of grass.
Thinking, "Misfortune has occurred while this was present," fools who desire auspiciousness avoid a powerful lord who serves those in calamity.

Another man, his mind agitated with longing, set out, his heart trembling at the sound of loud trumpets, conceiving the joy that "I am the mother of a hero" regarding the mother, or "I am the wife of a hero" regarding the wife.

"I am the daughter of a hero and the beloved wife of a noble hero; now, by means of heart-gladdening battles, become the mother of a hero"—thus did a certain mother speak, preceded by the offering of a forehead mark and unbroken grains of rice.

Why would kings not pay tribute to him, since his very sword served as the guarantor in that matter? When by fate they do not pay it, then his lack of mercy is for the sake of seizing his own sword by the hand.
The infamies of this lord of the earth— numbered by a count exceeding a *parārdha*, appearing like darkness perceived by the eye of wisdom—
are indeed sung in the eighth musical note by a multitude of mute children born from the wombs of barren women on the shore of the milk-ocean of female tortoises.
Even when its body is split apart, the sandalwood tree does not relinquish its own fragrance; even when crushed by sugarcane presses, the sugarcane does not lose its sweetness.
Just as gold remains beneficial and does not change when it is cut, rubbed, or heated, so too a virtuous person does not undergo transformation even when struck down by the wicked.
For the sake of this wretched belly, what will the wise not do?
They make the Goddess of Speech dance like a female monkey from house to house.
The fire born from his fierce staff-like arms, surpassing the fierce rays of the sun and possessing immense majesty,
having consumed the forest of *palāśa* trees that are his rival kings, inflicts a great conflagration upon the mature quarters of the horizon.
In the marches of this king who possesses complete power, the dust raised by the leading horses causes the setting of the sprouting rays of light from the crest-jewels of the subordinate chieftains.
For this illustrious King Bhoja, two things alone were very difficult to obtain:
iron for the shackles of his enemies, and copper for his edicts.
How has this beautiful complexion met such a terrible ruin? And how has this sweetness of the face been scorched by fire?
I think that when this woman with tremulous eyes has come within the range of his vision,
the very arrows of the five-arrowed god become his enemies.

O cloud, if the *cātaka* birds do not obtain drops of water during this monsoon, what is the harm? You proceed with the thought, "In the coming monsoon, I shall give twice as much. Yet these very birds are perishing this very day; if even one of their noble kin survives, that alone would suffice for us—of this we have no doubt.
In her, I perceive even the sages were deluded, for the great Bhṛgu took refuge upon the mountain of her breasts;
Nārada, whose face brings joy, resorted to her thighs; and Vyāsa, fit for the composition of the Mahābhārata, dwelt there.
Did that God of Love display a new science of arranging her physical form in this world,
since he dwells upon her— the very limit of loveliness— who has attained full expansion through contact with every limb?
O friend cuckoo, what indeed is the use of your soft warbling in this land inhabited by deaf people?
For these wretched creatures, ignorant of the arts, perceive you—who are indistinguishable from them in color—as nothing but a crow.
Did her tresses and the peacock’s plumage fall into disagreement regarding their beauty?
Was it for this reason that he honored the former with these flowers, while he rebuked the latter by striking it with a crescent-shaped arrow?
Her gaze, emerging clearly from behind the curtain torn by her fingernails,
flows like a stream of nectar, pure as it passes through the cloth.
Indeed, that sprout which attained childhood through the power of its intense rivalry with her hand—
how could it not be called a *pravāla* (a coral branch), since it even now displays pride in its similarity to her lower lip?
By her ear-ornament, every other decoration has been surpassed;
likewise, her ear-pendant shines exceedingly.
Of this beloved’s form, which surpasses all comparison,
only its own clear reflection resting in a mirror could possibly attain similarity.
Having gazed with reverence upon her face— the lovely abode where desire dwells— and having determined it to be the beautiful moon descended to earth as her beloved,
I think that the radiant Rohiṇī, unable to bear separation from him, has taken up residence in his presence under the guise of the pearl in her nose.
The fresh pearl resting at the tip of the nose of this lotus-eyed woman shines with the brilliant whiteness of the moon,
like an egg laid by a royal swan upon a blooming white lotus in the Mānasa lake on Mount Kailāsa.
Indeed, because of the reflection of jasmine and *kadamba* flowers bound in her hair,
this eulogy of the God of Love is inscribed in silver letters upon the golden tablet of her back.
We understand that the sprouts of trees acquired their designation as "pallavas" (sprouts) because, in comparison with the great beauty of her feet, they possess only a minute fraction of it.
Her breast marked by the prints of her pale-red fingernails, her eyes clouded with sleep, the redness of her lips washed away, her hair disheveled and its garland fallen,
and the knot of her girdle slightly loosened— by these arrows of Love buried in my sight at dawn, it is a marvel that my mind remains pinned fast.
As she sits upon the seat, he performs an oil massage for her— she whose hips gleam,
whose braid sways, and whose heavy breasts dance.
O merciless one, in this heart of yours, which is occupied by full breasts, there is not even a tiny fraction of space; where then shall you hold us?
Desirous of quickly wiping away the curse of Bhṛṅgī and Gopana placed upon her hair, which is repeatedly entreated by bees,
this self-restrained woman longs to seize with her hand— its soft luster like that of a heated iron ball under the guise of a dot of vermilion— the circle of her own hair-parting.
The lovely Creator fashioned her breath with the sweet Malaya breeze,
formed her limbs with flowers, and made her voice with the fifth note of the cuckoo.
The mass of her hair, possessing a single type of similarity to its own side (sapakṣaikavidha), rightly took up residence upon her face;
for by it, even the plumage of peacocks—though situated on their wings and adorned with many moon-like spots—was utterly surpassed.
In the creation of this [form], was the Creator the moon of lovely luster? Or was it Love himself, whose sole essence is passion? Or perhaps the month that brings forth flowers?
For how could the ancient sage, dulled by the study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from the objects of the senses, have been capable of fashioning this heart-stealing beauty?
In the creation of this woman, alas, the Creator is not even conceivable; neither is the god of the flower-bow, nor is Spring, and the Lord Brahmā is far removed.
This is my opinion: she is some sort of nectar that has arisen spontaneously, which was preserved by the Ocean after it had given the Goddess Śrī to Hari while being churned by Mount Mandara.
Upon this intoxicating-eyed woman, a charming tilaka-mark made from the paste of fresh, fragrant saffron shines;
it appears like a second heart of mine, clinging to her lovely lotus-face which is suffused with passion.

We have been captivated at every step by this ball-play of hers, whose moon-like face shines with the beauty of its mark (tilaka) washed away by drops of perspiration; she speaks repeatedly during the game of counting the forceful strikes, while her eyes follow the rhythmic sequence of the falling and rising of the ball, alluring us with the graceful charm of her vigorous *tāṇḍava* dance.
In its lap, the fortune of the whetstone shines flickeringly like a streak of gold; the Sudarśana discus, heavy with the downpour of its edge, gazes upon the world.
With a body possessing the luster of collyrium and wearing yellow garments, this cloud is the form of Hari, with its forest-garland raised up and its circle of crests lifted high.

In this lake of her body—where the arms are lotus-stalks, the face a lotus, the eyes and brows bees, and the waters of exquisite youth are muddied with musk—the elephant of the mind has approached and quickly sunk, out of rage at the crushing of the frontal globes of the rival elephants that are her breasts; how shall it emerge from there and depart?

O camel, if this thorn were not a mere fragment of the face of this [elephant], with its leaves unshattered, where would it be suitable for you? It would be fit for the creeper of the wish-fulfilling tree, possessing sprouts that have the luster of pure coral.
By the practice of this excellent treatise, the disciple shall become omniscient with a radiant and beautiful intellect;
even one who is already learned will come to understand, without doubt, the goals of wealth, pleasure, virtue, and liberation through its cultivation.
Defeated by the mass of her hair, which was so enchanting in form,
the yaks and peacocks took up residence in the forest as if out of shame.
Is this some unprecedented second moon, free from all blemish,
or perhaps it was surely extracted by the Makara-bannered God after churning the ocean of her navel with the Mandara mountain of her breasts, joined together by the rope of the line of hair?
Surely the Creator, having filled her face with the moonlight, left nothing remaining;
that which was released here has become solidified and shines in the guise of the pearl at the tip of her nose, appearing like a drop of nectar.

It seems that the lotus and the moon, having requested it from her father, the water, and from her friend, the mirror, occasionally wear the reflection of the beauty of her face as a borrowed ornament.
May this face not possess the fullness of the full moon, having surpassed it in greatness;
for its forehead is indeed a third part that bears the crescent-shaped mark of a brow, like the half-moon.
By her face, which has stolen the beauty of the lotuses,
sleep was destroyed among people at night, just as it is by the moon for the night-lilies.

Having been defeated by her face alone—which possesses the luster of the wrath of saffron meeting it—the moon, our constant rival, is surely being forcibly bound; thus the halo remains as a tethering rope.
On her moon-like face, this lower lip is a fitting reflection of the bimba fruit;
or rather, its beauty resides in coral, whereas the beauty of that fruit is found in trees.
Let these medicinal herbs blaze; let even the insects emit light; let the jewels on the hoods of serpents open wide; let the sprouts of lamps play.
Indeed, you yourselves must be questioned if there exists anyone capable of providing a handhold for the world when it is submerged in the ocean of dense darkness after the sun has set.
When the eighteen branches of knowledge were divided and the two Vedas each held nine of them,
was the deep furrow carved within his ears not itself a new and ever-fresh numeral nine?

When the darkness was dispelled from the front and across by the cool-rayed moon through her face, that very same darkness now exists behind her, bound up under the guise of her clearly shimmering, curling locks.
O King, when the arrow of this enemy and your own shaft fall together in battle, neither produces a whistling sound nor do they experience trembling;
yet it is not fitting that there should be no distinction between them once released, for it is a marvel that one of them pierces a friend while the other pierces an enemy.
The sandalwood leaf-design fashioned upon her forehead by her friends appears like a bandage over the wound of Cupid’s arrow upon the pale, emaciated walls of her cheeks.
Whether youth or childhood has taken its place in her body,
no one can discern her true nature, just like that of a Kāpālika ascetic.
In the balance of her form, when Kāma, full of curiosity, weighs childhood against youth— gold— the needle of her waist does not incline toward the latter.
If this woman with deer-like eyes possesses a row of curls, what need is there for swarms of bees? If she has beauty in her tremulous eyes, what use are the weapons of the God of Love?
If she has full breasts, what pleasure is there in a golden lotus bud? Therefore, I believe she is some kind of illusion created by the Mind-born One to delude the world.
If her gait possesses such grace, enough with the pride of the swan; if her speech is so sweet, let the cuckoos observe a vow of silence;
if the softness of her limbs is such that Mālatī is but like a stone; and if her radiance is like that of Kamalā—what more need be said? Let her simply don the saffron robe.
His sword is a serpent drawn from the hollow of its own scabbard, its dark luster shimmering and its curved movements unfolding with a trembling grace to the terror of those kings;
for what king indeed has not assumed the role of a snake-charmer by placing the joints of his own fingers upon this blade, which is like a great medicinal creeper of mastery?
Her leanness in the waist, the fullness of her breasts, the flickering movement of her eyes, and the gradual, rounded swelling of her thighs all possess a harmonious symmetry.
Smeared with the oozing of her body, that hero whose banner bears the fish-mark released a most beautiful flag under the pretext of a saffron streak, in order to conquer the world.
Upon her body, which served as the stage for the dance of separation, the stage-manager Cupid scattered handfuls of flowers in the form of drops of perspiration;
then, with the sweet jingling of his girdle-string trembling with great convulsions, he recited the benedictory verse (*nāndī*).
On this wall, though it is perfectly level, her two breasts appear as if protruding, her navel as if indented, and her folds of skin appear unevenly raised;
and in her form, this softness is manifest—she of a tender nature gazes at the moon of my face with long-lasting affection, and speaks as if with a smile.
Having bestowed upon us this protection from the evils of separation, you, O fortunate one, depart at your own will; alas, do you not consider that this brings us terror?
What indeed can we do during these talkative days with the songs of the cuckoos proceeding in the fifth note, and during the moonlit nights when we are left without refuge?
Even for this single body, the fragments of bone born together with it will go their separate ways; how much more so, then, for any other beloved person?

O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, has the Creator perhaps fashioned this forest of lotuses merely for the purpose of performing the lustration ceremony for this very face of yours, by which the God of Love has been restored to life?

"The creation of this lotus for your hand is my preliminary sketch for the sake of this very creation"—thus said the Creator to the deer-eyed girl; what need is there for that sketch when she herself is present?
Since there was nothing in the three worlds that could rival the beauty of this belly,
three folds shone upon the fair-toothed woman like the lines used for counting.
Is this the fame of this lord of the earth, ready for a dual reign with the full moon—fame that extinguishes the pride of the white splendor of Mount Śarva, radiant in every limb;
is it the reflection of a conch shell, or perhaps a manifestation of the beauty of autumnal rain-cloud banks, or a complete restatement of the waters of the Ocean of Milk?
A tear at the corner of the eye acts like the wealth of a miser; a choked voice in the throat acts like a bee resting within the lap of a sleeping lotus;

the cry of "Alas! in the heart acts like the longing desire of a noble-born woman separated from her lover; and the fever of separation from Vaidehī acts like the heat of the sun upon the Lord of the Raghus.
Fie on our eyes, which act like ears to incessantly shed tears;
for that youthfulness of his, which ought to be seen, has already been fully beheld by the women of Vraja.
Tossed about in the whirlpools of the flowing stream of blood, wallowing in the mire of flesh, and feasting on the tips of white lotus-stalks in the form of the breaking of thick joints of bone—
may the claws of the illusory lion Śauri protect you, those rājahaṃsas who took their place in the lake-like hollow of the chest of the Daitya, embracing the throbbing, crimson lotus-heart of Viṣṇu.
If the Lord of Creatures had not fashioned this body with its flesh separated from the skin by a layer so thin as the edge of a petal of a fresh blue lotus,
who could have prevented, or how could one have warded off, the vultures, crows, and wolves as they fell upon his limbs to seize mouthfuls of raw, dripping, and oozing flesh?
Women must be kept under dependence by their own men day and night; for when they become attached to sensual objects, they must be firmly established under one's own control.
It is a time when the cuckoos are forbidden from their studies at the commencement of the sacrifice of Love; it is an intercalary month for sleep and some inexplicable famine for the bees;

it is a season of pestilence for the Malaya breezes eager for their journey; and it is the executioner for the wives of travelers—a certain calamitous time that has uprooted the very foundations of the frost.
