O egoism, go elsewhere; O sin, do not remain here, for you are no ground for my pride. O slanderer, depart!
O anger, seek another place; for in the hearts of those whose minds are focused on nothing else, there shines this Lord Hari, the Master of the three worlds.
The ego says to the intellect: "Do not awaken this one who is asleep. When supreme bliss has arisen, there is neither you, nor I, nor indeed the world.

The meritorious one, joyfully laughing as his son speaks words like a lure—asking his mother, "Who am I? Who is my mother? And who is the one most beloved by you?"—smells the crown of that child's head while being questioned by his father.
Abandon the sense of "I-making," the perception of limits, and likewise the ignorance within consciousness;
by doing so, may there arise for you some incomparable and wondrous realization.
"O Indra among kings, both you and I are protectors of the world;
yet, O King, I am a *bahuvrīhi* compound, while you are a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*."
Both I and Devanandin, with our intellects as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, have not reached the further shore of the ocean of words; how much less so others whose intellects are dull?
"I am so slender and exceedingly delicate that I am not yet able to bear the weight of these two breasts"—
as if for this very purpose, her waist develops the three folds of skin to support them.
"O Great King, I do not perceive you as my father;
Rāghava is my brother, my protector, my kinsman, and my father."
Summoned by him with the words, "I have something to tell you," I sat nearby in a secluded place and, because of my simple heart, was attentive.
Then, as he whispered something near my ear, having smelled my face and taken hold of my braided hair, O friend, he drank the nectar of my lower lip.
If I were not to exist, these people would fall into evil states of mind, for they would be without support.
Therefore, if I myself were to join others with sin, would shame not indeed be appropriate for me?
I am not even able to restrain the tears born from my eyes;
yet Rāma, afflicted by separation from Sītā, bound the lord of rivers.
I am perishing through pride; do not engage in quarreling out of pride. Having come into conflict with one's beloved, O lovely one, one suffers no further torment.
The transcendence of the sense of "I" is by no means easy to achieve in any way whatsoever.
Once the sense of "I" has been conquered in the consciousness pertaining to the material elements,
it nevertheless manifests before us again, even more expanded, within the internal consciousness.
"‘I’ and ‘mine’ are indeed the seed of existence; ‘not mine’ and ‘not I’ are the pacification of the seed of existence.
When the seed is destroyed, whence can there be birth? Like a fire without fuel, it attains peace."
"I have come from the kitchen; hell has been prepared for you. I have eaten meat and such things; know me, O crane, to be terrible."

The cuckoo here gazes upon another fruit-bearing tree in order to dispel the false sense of equality that the mango tree has instilled in it— a sense based on the fact that its own flock of birds has been surpassed by the fifth note of the clever cuckoo, which vibrates through the intense vows of passion aroused in the women of excellent complexion who are full of youthful pride.
To me, Dhāriṇī is like the wheel of my chariot, like my dear companion;
without her permission, our union is as impossible as that of night and day.
Having said, "I am your protector," the king who does not protect them should be struck down by his subjects acting in concert, like a mad dog afflicted with disease.
"I have always been like their very life to the kings, yet this monarch regards me as no more than a blade of grass"—
as if to tell its own weariness to the ears of supplicants, gold took up residence within their ears.
For he who, being of such evil intellect, considers himself approved by the king,
should be known as a bull devoid of horns.
Day by day one must reflect: "What good deed have I done today?
Have I given a gift, or caused another to give, or even offered assistance through my speech?"
Day after day, living beings depart for the final abode;
that those who remain desire permanence—what could be more wonderful than this?
Day after day, Prajāpati indeed creates living beings;
yet even today he does not create a single one who does not despise a petitioner.
Who would despise one who begs day after day, like a teacher,
and who performs a daily cleansing, just as one polishes a mirror?
Day after day, it is not even possible for one to know the errors of one's own negligence;
how then can there be the power to know entirely by which path each person among the subjects is proceeding?
I too am a poet, and others as well; nevertheless, a great difference must be recognized between us.
Even though there is identity between the letters *ra* and *la*, does a young elephant (*kalabha*) therefore become like the trunk of an elephant (*karabha*)?
I am Nīlakaṇṭha; indeed, I am pleased with you by your mere sound alone.
O cloud, I do not beg for my life from you like a *cātaka* bird.
When the rainy season of the nectar-like talk of mature women spreads forth, repeatedly proclaiming a festival of love and characterized by a competitive zeal of "I first, I first," a young girl—
her hair standing on end and her budding breasts slightly emerging— slowly circles her trembling gaze around the region of her chest.
O traveler, like me, the fortune of this day is wretched; like you, the road is devoid of the company of other wayfarers.
This too is a foreign land, and that place where you are destined to go is likewise strange. O you whose form is as sweet as love, why are you in such a hurry for no purpose?
The empty forest is like me; the waters have become as diminished as we;
and the days are long and scorching, just like our sighs.

"I am one who has attained learning here, a knower of all fine arts, and the sole lord of wealth endowed with beauty and charm"—thus harboring heavy pride, why does this person suffer? Within the span of a few days, all of this will become nothing at all.
O Noble One, although I remain here, I am yours; and although you dwell there, you are mine. A mere union of bodies is not a true union; only a union of hearts is a true union.
I am alone; there is no one for me, nor do I belong to anyone else.
I do not see him to whom I belong, for he does not exist, nor do I see anyone who belongs to me.
O beloved, having come by the path of the sun, I shall once again become one who rests upon your lap,
before you are enticed away from heaven by the clever celestial nymphs.
"I alone am the teacher of the most cruel things"—O Hālāhala, my dear, do not be so arrogant;
for are there not many words of the wicked in this world that resemble yours?

The thought, "I alone am strong, and there is no other," brings about the downfall of men; for how many on this earth have not been conquered by those who are more powerful, having become arrogant through their own strength?
"Only I am esteemed by the king"—thus everyone among the subjects thought;
like the ocean toward hundreds of rivers, he met with no disrespect from anyone.
A man who, having taken the property of another, dwells in comfort,
is suspicious of everything like a thief who has entered a forest of wild beasts.
Just as a person, intent on staying awake day and night, undergoes exhaustion out of desire for sense objects,
so too, if one exerts oneself in austerity, why does one not enjoy for even a moment that purifying and infinite bliss?

When the lover asked her, "Is it day or night? by placing his hand—alternately warm and cold—upon her breast, the clever woman, out of modesty, seemed to reject his question by placing her finger upon her lower lip, which was as sweet as the twilight.
During the time of Ahalyā’s dalliance, there were two hundred Kāmas;
with his eyes pierced by those five arrows, the Thousand-eyed One fell into blindness.
The handless among those with hands, the footless among the four-footed,
and the insignificant among the great— therein lies the life of the living.
Alas! A man who is intoxicated by liquor treats a king like a servant and a servant like a lord; he regards the ocean, the storehouse of waters, as a mere well, and the well as a waterless pit.
Ah! Why now do you vainly bind this ear-ornament of ivory, O you who act improperly? For your trembling-browed self, the curve of the ear is indeed the noose of Kālasarpa, the eye of the world.
Alas! Where indeed is the householder well? Bound and cast into the ocean of saṃsāra, he somehow obtains a boat, yet by means of that very boat he sinks utterly.
Alas, O fierce wind! What a cruel deed have you committed?
For the very water that falls here into the hollow of the cātaka’s beak has been turned back by you.
Alas! The eyes, like those of a person with false views, are deprived of true vision; the pair of ears, like a wicked son, does not hear what is spoken.
The two feet falter on the path like people overwhelmed by intoxication; when the body is worn out by old age, its luster fades away like a neglected wife.
Alas! Immersed in the ever-new delights of the manifold world of body and home due to innate delusion, I have attained a female form;
thus, infatuated by continuous pleasure, I do not, alas, remember within myself what is beneficial or harmful for my own welfare.
Days end in sunset, and nights end in sunrise;
the end of pleasure is always pain, and the end of pain is always pleasure.
Without letting the time pass for his obedient servants, the king should provide them with a livelihood in accordance with their respective duties.
Unassailable, standing at the center of all, and bearing the luster of gold,
one who is exceedingly lofty attains the fitness for being honored by the virtuous with circumambulation.
By means of the armor of forbearance alone— which is unassailable by others at any time and cannot be stripped away by anyone— the self-restrained person conquers everything.
One should not wake seven who are sleeping: a snake, a king, a tiger, an elderly person, a child, another's dog, and a fool.
The instruction regarding the welfare of living beings must be carried out through non-violence alone;
and one who desires dharma should employ speech that is both sweet and gentle.
Non-violence is the abode of dharma; longing is the source of suffering. Renunciation of attachment is the state of liberation; the practice of yoga is the state of purity.
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; non-violence is the supreme goal.
Non-violence is the supreme joy; non-violence is the supreme state.
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; likewise, non-violence is the supreme self-restraint.
Non-violence is the supreme gift; non-violence is the supreme austerity.
Non-violence is the supreme sacrifice; likewise, non-violence is the supreme strength.
Non-violence is the supreme friend; non-violence is the supreme happiness.
Non-violence is the supreme truth; non-violence is the supreme sacred learning.
Non-violence is indeed the supreme dharma; non-violence alone is the highest austerity;
non-violence is the supreme gift—thus the sages have always said.
Since dharma is preceded by non-violence and is devoted to the welfare of all,
one should therefore protect even lice, bedbugs, gadflies, and the like.
Non-violence is the first flower; the second is the restraint of the senses;
the third is compassion as a flower; and the fourth is the flower of generosity.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, renunciation, and the avoidance of sexual intercourse—
in these five precepts, all dharmas are established.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession;
constant reflection upon what is desirable and undesirable—this is proclaimed as *yama*.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Manu declared this to be the summary of the Dharma for the four social orders.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses,
generosity, self-control, compassion, and patience are the means for accomplishing the Dharma for all.
Non-violence, truthful speech, compassion toward all living beings,
tranquility, and giving according to one’s ability— this is the supreme dharma of the householder.
Non-violence, truthful speech, and straightforwardness toward all beings,
as well as patience and heedfulness— he who possesses these shall be happy.
Non-violence, truthfulness of speech, kindness, self-restraint, and compassion—
the wise know this to be austerity, not the emaciation of the body.
Non-violence, speech that is pleasant and true, truthfulness, purity, compassion,
and forbearance are said to be the common dharma for those belonging to the [four] castes as well as for those bearing [ascetic] marks.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and possessionlessness— these,
free from hatred for kings, are declared by the sages to be the true worthy recipient.
The austerity of one who practices non-violence is inexhaustible; the non-violent person always performs sacrifice.
Being non-violent toward all beings, he is like a mother and like a father.
Those men who, out of audacity, speak of what is harmful as if it were beneficial,
should be regarded as excluded from counsel and treated as spoilers of the task.

What difference is there between a beast and that man-beast whose intellect is devoid of discernment regarding what is beneficial and harmful, who is excluded from the many scriptural traditions, and whose sole desire is merely to fill his belly?
Preventing one from what is harmful, encouraging engagement in what is beneficial,
and not abandoning one in times of misfortune— these are the three characteristics of a friend.

O you who have been endowed with discipline by him, where else could there be another so virtuous and free from pride— one who, though lacking self-respect, fearing what is harmful, and excessively abandoning all fear, was not an atheist?
The entire host of serpents is the domain for those who hold the views of snake-charmers;
yet the breath from his mouth stands as no charioteer for the fire of universal destruction.
Preventing one from what is harmful, encouraging engagement in what is beneficial,
and not abandoning one in times of calamity— this is the threefold characteristic of a friend.
The person of small intellect, perceiving what is harmful as beneficial, disregards the counsel of his ministers;
being impulsive, he rushes forward too hastily and only then awakens when struck by the sword of his enemy.
Those who are full of essence naturally desire the welfare of others even when it is harmful;
for even when pressed, the sugarcane stalk yields only its juice.
While the army of the Rākṣasas, victorious over the immortals, has made the mountains themselves its weapons by fashioning them into fortresses,
how indeed does the host of monkeys— devastating the sprouts of the trees and creepers in their pleasure gardens— fare upon the field of battle?

I bow to him who has the serpent as his ornament yet grants fearlessness; who, though possessing the deadly *hālāhala* poison, is eternal; who, though clothed in the directions of space, is the Lord of all; that one who bears the moon upon his crest.
A house devoid of gold and female slaves, lacking milk products, and possessing a disagreeable wife is another way of life for hell.
"Ah, ah!"—let other people be filled with such agitation and become somewhat terrified;
for the food of the Lord of Birds is simply the lovely stalks of fresh lotus fibers.
In this region, the serpent king is Puruṣa; the *dhātrī* plant is smoky-colored and the stone has the hue of *kulattha* beans.
The *māhendrī* vein flows here, and its water is always frothy.

May the Ganges, who falls upon the head of our beloved father— who is honored by his friends, sons, daughters, wives, and fathers-in-law, and whose banner is the giver of life to the slayer of Hara’s son (Kārttikeya), who was beloved by Ahiripu (Śiva) and connected to his own beloved— purify us.

He who always avoids association with people as one would a snake, and who, having renounced desire and being free from passion, regards women as mere filth and the objects of the senses as poison that leads to an evil end— he, the Paramahaṃsa, conquers and attains the state of liberation.
The snake, the cat, the son-in-law, the ewe with her lambs,
and fifthly, the nephew— these do not perceive their own good fortune.
At the appropriate time, for the sake of the king, for his own interest, together with those who are dear and beneficial to him,
and for the sake of others at the proper place and time, he should speak that which is consistent with dharma and artha.
Whose body is encircled by bracelets and armlets formed from the lords of serpents;
whose deeds bring joy to Śiva and Nandin; and who has destroyed the pride of Kandarpa.
I bow to the Lord, the companion of Pārvatī, who bears the mark of the bull as his emblem, whose eyes are like fire and the sun, and who is the embodiment of all auspiciousness.

Do not harbor in your mind the thought that Death has no regard for time—he who, like poison, draws up the lords of serpents from the netherworld after submerging them; he who, having ascended to heaven, devours the hosts of gods including Indra; and by whom the kings of Raghu’s lineage were conquered after they had wandered again and again over the earth.
O you whose hearts are not captivated by worldly things, I speak the truth—listen! Having now gone to the forest, let your dwelling be made among the deer.
In this Kali age, which abounds in the rise of the wicked and destroys the conduct of the virtuous, this is no time for such as you to remain in homes.
There is no remedy for that partiality which is without cause;
for it is a thread composed of affection that sews together all internal beings.
A king should never frown without cause;
he who protects his servants according to dharma should not do so without fault.
Fearing virtues as if from a snake, sweet foods as if from poison,
and women as if from ogresses, he acquires knowledge.
Oh, what an impropriety! Though your heart is pure, it has been treated as if impure;
a mark has been branded upon me by your sharp-pointed nails, as if by villains.
"Oh! How great am I! Homage to me, since I have been beheld by this young woman, whose wide eyes are as tremulous as a frightened deer!"
Alas! Even for snakes, licking [the hand] must surely be a source of suffering, for service to a king brings such miseries.
One who is bitten by a snake meets death alone; but one who is "bitten" by a king perishes along with his kinsmen and friends.
Oh, for many days the fame of the son of Yaśas is sung, sweet at every step like a stream of nectar, and cool as sandalwood and the moon day after day; it is not marred by the age of Kali.
Oh, how great was the power of the days that reached even toward her who was tormented by love during the arrival of winter;
and even at the height of the summer season, the masses of fat were borne by the nights.
Alas! Who that is a teacher could endure the disconnected and harsh words of those intoxicated by power, who are like those intoxicated with pride?
Oh, how does this boundless thing called snow manifest? Even while the thousand-rayed sun is still shining, a white expanse of darkness spreads abroad.
Oh, who could possibly describe the greatness of gold?
How strange it is that, due to the similarity of name, even the thorn-apple (dhattūra) bestows intoxication!
Oh, how subtle is this certain progression of Time, its movement imperceptible,
by the ripening and transformation of which everything undergoes a change of form!
Oh, some indescribable, pure flower of your fame has blossomed,
of which this young moon, dripping with nectar, is the outer sprout!
Oh, the mind of the wicked, possessed of crooked intellects, is difficult to grasp!
One thing is in their speech, another in their throat, and something else entirely resides within the hollow of their lips.
"Oh! By whom was such a cruel intellect fashioned for you?
Intellect is heard to consist of the three qualities (guṇas), but never anywhere is it said to be made of wood."
Oh, how strange is this method of killing employed by the serpent-like rogue:
he bites the ear of one person, yet another is deprived of life!
Oh, how perverse is the method of slaying employed by this serpent of a rogue:
he whispers into the ear of one, yet another is deprived of life!
Ah! Virtues, gentleness, learning, and birth in a noble family—all these do not shine for one who is submerged in the ocean of poverty.
Ah! For the sake of attaining virtues, men strive in many ways;
for their sake even pearls have their mouths broken—what then to say of others?
Alas, this world would be like darkness and nothing at all would be discernible,
if there were no king in the world to distinguish between the righteous and the unrighteous.
Oh, how wondrous is the conduct of people who are utterly devoid of delusion! It is not fit to describe it;
for there is one thing in the mouth and another sentiment in the heart—neither a god nor a human can know this.
Oh, how exceedingly powerful is destiny, since even without that Great-Souled One,
it bestows victory upon a base faction that is possessed of incapacity!
Oh, how the courtesan of craving, who deludes all people, is clever! She robs the innocent and the helpless of their wealth of tranquility.
With the side-glances of her beloved—expert at initiating calamity, with pupils tremulous and difficult to endure, like fraudulent dice that are deceitfully crooked—the gambler of passion [deceives].
Oh, what generosity! Oh, what vigor! Oh, what unbroken fortitude! Hariścandra is the exemplar of those who are noble, heroic, and steadfast.

Oh, you possess a divine eye, for even that beloved wife of yours transfers her form—ungraspable by other eyes—into young women. Otherwise, how could you alone see before you her likeness, as if she were made of images, while others see only ordinary women?
Alas, what suffering! Alas, great suffering! Alas, what suffering is poverty! And therein, even more, the abundance of children and wife brings excessive misery.
Alas! Behold the world’s delusion, which leads to such miserable ends and bestows the suffering of saṃsāra;
for people disregard austerity—which is easily accomplished through the mere preparation of food—and instead cause themselves further misery.
Alas, how endless is the thirst for enjoyment in saṃsāra, by which even the gods are carried away; they do not fear impropriety or ill repute.
Alas! Through association with the wicked, there is a loss of honor at every step;
fire, through contact with iron, is struck down by hammers.
Oh, what a great difference there is between a wicked person and a serpent!
The one bites the ear, while the other is deprived of life.
Alas, what wretchedness! Alas, what misery, that a mortal should not benefit [others] through his own kinsmen, who belong to another, are momentary, and serve no purpose for himself!
Alas! One who is blinded by the intoxication of wealth does not see, even though he sees;
if he were to see what is beneficial for himself, he would undoubtedly see it.
Oh, how great is the cleverness of riches when they dwell happily in the house of a miser!
They neither reach the state of being given away nor the state of being enjoyed; yet they spread a certain supreme tranquility.
Oh, how great is the skill of the high-souled Manmatha with his bow!
Having left the body uninjured, he pierces the mind within.
Oh! First the Creator fashioned recklessness, and after that, women;
for there is nothing difficult for them to accomplish here, owing to their very nature.
Oh, the audacity of the wicked who revile blameless women, while prattling "Stop, thief! like thieves themselves who are stealing!
Oh, how full of pride is the behavior of the moon, the king of stars!
When waning, it becomes crooked; when full, it is perfectly round.
Alas, how painful is constant wandering! More painful than that is living in another's house. Service to base people is more painful still, and poverty is even more painful than that.
Oh, how wonderful! Mountains are bound together by threads produced from lotuses;
by that ignorance which does not exist, everyone has been brought under control.
"Aha! The lake is clearly full; there is no doubt about this, since everyone rolls about in you and bathes whenever they can."
Oh, how similar is the nature of phlegm and the wicked person!
Both reach a state of agitation through sweet things and find pacification through bitter ones.
Oh, how great is the skill of the wicked in concealing their misdeeds,
such that even while burning like a smokeless fire of chaff, they remain unperceived!
Oh, the power of the Goddess of Speech,
that Mātaṅgadivākara became a courtier of Śrī Harṣa, equal to Bāṇa and Mayūra!
Oh, how negligent is the Blessed Lord Prajāpati! This deer-eyed woman, with her slender waist, has been fashioned;
if she were to be broken by the wind through negligence, how would he ever be able to create such a thing again?
Alas! Though a fool and unlearned, a wicked man becomes a scholar through his merits;
he is like Śeṣa in proclaiming his own virtues, yet a master of speech in censuring others.
Alas! What great misery! This world is indeed perverse:
that for which the virtuous man feels shame is that by which the wicked man finds satisfaction.
Oh, how wondrous are the deeds of the great-souled!
They regard fortune as a blade of grass, yet they bow under its weight.
Alas! This assembly has been brought low by its members through their silence;
for the virtuous either speak the truth or do not enter the assembly at all.

Alas! This is the supreme ignobility of the Lord of Rivers, that he has suddenly attained a state of total identity with those useless, dull stones—which have long possessed the quality of being well-polished—that have arrived from elsewhere and gained a footing there, while they incessantly wear away his jewels of radiant luster with their powerful force.
Oh, what a discharge of arrows by King Smara in the autumn!
Is this not that very Lord of Light who has now entered the zodiac sign of Virgo?
Oh, I have witnessed the devotion to Brahmanas of the God who is the Friend of Brahmanas,
in that even the poorest man has embraced Fortune while she rests upon his chest!
Oh, how great a resemblance there is between a drum and a wicked person!
For as long as they remain within their mouths, both indeed speak sweetly.
"Oh, wife! Oh, son! Oh, self! Oh, happiness!
Oh, mother! Oh, brother! Behold how one is deluded by illusion!"
Oh, among the islands and regions of this earth with its seven oceans, this is the most meritorious,
wherein the people sing of the auspicious deeds of Murāri as he descends in his incarnations!
Ah! This is the arrogance born of pride among these worthless and evil-souled Kauravas; they claim that their sovereignty over the earth was produced by Time alone.
Oh, how great and wondrous is this: by the course of time, so difficult to overcome, the shoe indeed seeks to ascend the head adorned with a crown!
Oh, how extraordinary is the greatness of the great! Even in times of calamity, they continue to assist others;
for even when fallen into the midst of Rāhu, the moon bestows a store of merit.
Oh, how the prowess of great men surpasses all others!
By Rāma, Śambhu’s Ājagava bow was broken like a lotus stalk.

Alas, the snare of illusion! Once the deer of the heart has fallen therein, it is not able to rise up again by any means whatsoever, unless its cutter—the mouse of self-knowledge brought forth by the words of the Supreme Guru—appears with the various, firm, and sharp teeth of sound reasoning.
Oh, the power of Viṣṇu’s illusion! This world is bound by affection.
Where is the material body, which is non-self, and where is the Self, which is beyond primordial nature?
To whom do husbands, sons, and the like belong? Delusion alone is indeed the cause.
Oh, what great fortune is mine! For the speech of Bhavabhūti, when placed upon the vessel of my own words, reflects back its own lightness.
The Goddess of Speech, the Blessed One, immediately bestows the sweetness of the nectar from the lotus buds gathered in the ears for the sake of perfect fulfillment.
Oh, what delusion of men in this world! Birth is indeed considered auspicious, for it supposedly conquers even old age, death, and disease;
yet, though born from another, these very beings undergo hundreds of calamities, and having themselves given birth to sons, she [the mother] consigns those children to slaughter.
Oh, what delusion belongs to this wretched crow,
that it should wriggle and dance before the peacock and the swan!
Oh, how excellent is the birth of those upon whom all living beings depend for their livelihood,
and from whom seekers never turn away with empty hands, just as they do not from a virtuous person!

Oh! Out of fear for the spreading expansion of the fame of the fierce rays of the fresh majesty of the crest-jewel of the Raghus, the Lord of the Gods has quickly fled to the clouds; Lakṣmī serves the lotus, and even the moon, the cool-rayed one, constantly sinks into the ocean.
In this world consisting of day and night, Death, moving about in the form of old age,
devours living beings just as a serpent swallows the wind.
Days and nights pass for all living beings here,
swiftly exhausting their lifespans, just as the sun's rays dry up water in the summer heat.
The sun divides the day and night for both humans and gods:
night is for the sleep of beings, and the day is for the performance of actions.
Oh, what beauty! Oh, what beauty! Oh, what a face! Oh, what a face!
Oh, what a waist! Oh, what a waist! Of this woman with eyes like a deer's.
O Creator, alas, you are exceedingly childish, you who strive for that which is inconsistent with your own creation!
If another dies while yet another lives, then you yourself must surely be the ultimate opposite of a creator.
If there is indeed a sequence here between death and birth for embodied beings, let that be due to their own past actions;
yet you yourself cut asunder this very bond of affection which you created for the sake of increasing your own creation.
Alas! By that wretched Creator, even separation from our loved ones has not been spared for us, like that of the *rathāṅga* birds, for which there is neither a limit nor the possession of wings.
O King, oh, how vast is the interior of the three worlds,
since even the mass of your fame, though impossible to contain, finds room within it!
Alas, women who are rejected after being loved are worse than poison!
Alas, kings who do not perceive the truth are unfit to be served by the virtuous!
Oh, how wondrous is this saṃsāra! What can be said?
Even a virtue may become a cause of affliction when one rests upon the thorny stalk.
Oh, the bitterness of saṃsāra! Women are the cause of that bitterness; fortune is as fickle as a swing, and the body is a dwelling place for the expansion of diseases.
Ah! This harlot of cyclic existence is intent on inflaming passion and the like;
having produced aesthetic flavor for all, she ultimately brings about a sense of distaste.
Oh, what association with the virtuous in this world—what evil would it not destroy?
Or what happiness would it not bestow upon men of meritorious deeds?
Oh, how profound and steady is the mind of these noble ones, as deep as the ocean,
who, despite having produced an incomparable distinction, do not utter it!
Oh, how natural love shines forth even from afar!
The moon brings delight to the pair of eyes of the cakora bird.
Oh, how remarkably similar is the behavior of the end of a balance scale and that of a wicked person:
with the slightest thing they rise, and with the slightest thing they sink.
Ah! The instigation by women is like a whirlwind for men whose souls are overwhelmed by passion; it causes agitation in the depths of their hearts just as a gale disturbs lakes.

Oh! What a steadfast youth must be your beloved, who, since your ear-lotuses have long since withered away, has remained indifferent to these matted locks hanging down with loosened bonds, as tawny as the tips of ripened *kalama* rice, upon your cheek.
Oh, what steadfastness these virtuous ones possess toward the laws of nature! They do not abandon what they have promised, even in the face of great hardship.
For instance, does the Lord of Tortoises—even when his shell is crushed by the weight of the earth-mother bent under the burden of your army—ever move his own body?

Alas! How much I have sinned against my long life, that such unpleasant words as these must be spoken by me. Blessed indeed are those friends who have passed away without ever witnessing defeat in this world.

Whether it be a snake or a necklace, a powerful enemy or a friend, a jewel or a clod of earth, a bed of flowers or a stone, a blade of grass or a woman—may my days pass with an equal eye toward all these, as I utter "Śiva, Śiva, Śiva! while dwelling in some sacred forest.
O noble elephant, three or four times a day you bathe yourself with water drawn from lotus leaves; you eat the most pure and tender leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
You roam in sacred forests and do not enter a village even once. O elephant, if even a modicum of knowledge were to arise within you, even the Brahman-sages would not be your equals.
During the day people desire the sun, and at night they desire the one whose splendor is nectar;
likewise, during both day and night, subjects desire a king who possesses virtuous qualities.
During the day, the sun burns the skin when grown strong; the flower-bowed god (Kāma) burns when carried by a powerful wind.
Day and night, moreover, there is a difference within: there is concealment for the sun, but not for the beloved.

Āṃ! O King, it is known: you alone constantly sustain the entire earth; the lords of mountains themselves are a burden difficult to bear, and by them, on the contrary, [the earth] would sink downward. In lifting her up, no one other than you—such as Varāha and the like—is capable; the skill in the act of supporting even animals is not within the scope of their power.

Alas, what a tragedy! O young deer, having developed a faith in the hermitage of the perfected ones through your affinity for the forest-dweller’s life, how have you now arrived at this village—the very mouth of death?
Here, fierce outcasts fill the moats with streams of blood flowing from their sport of slaughtering many tens of millions of deer.
Alas, what a tragedy! By those whose hearts are devoid of discernment, it was brought into contact with them and sold along with *badara* jujubes upon the ground at the edge of a wretched village.

It lay there until, in the presence of a face both deceitful and utterly dull, it was cast away with a sound of disgust. Does a person devoid of merit know the value of virtue? Therefore, the pearl weeps.
Alas, what a tragedy! Even the learned, though they are refined, are possessed by the fickleness of wealth;
they teach the Vedas only after receiving a monthly fee for a long time.
"Alas! For what reason is this mind of the virtuous as difficult to fill as the ocean?"—as if in anger at this thought, the Creator filled it with the sufferings of others.
"Āḥ! You do not cook, you sinner! How can your father be a sinner, O slut? Why do you prattle? Is your own mother a slut, and your sister as well?
Get out of this house quickly; this is not your home! Alas, alas, my lord! Give me death today; it is the rise of fortune for the paramour!"

Ah! May I become a vessel for those various amorous gestures of the fair-browed one—gestures which expand with a love that is natural and profound, which possess a sense of bashfulness, which cause all the channels of the senses to throb with joy, and whose glances overflow with the intentions hidden within her heart.
Ah! May the night-lotuses blossom everywhere, and may the cakora birds, their bellies full, drink their fill of the moonlight's thick porridge;
for that lamp which awakens the multitude of day-lotuses has now reached the base of the western mountain.

O Sītā, that face of yours which once possessed the radiant beauty of a smile that caused the destruction of your wandering kinsmen, who were bewildered by the weight of your pride in your husband— now,
at this very moment, Rāvaṇa forcibly makes it drenched with tears falling from eyes upturned in terror as he violently pulls back your mass of hair.
There,

it is said, the Blessed One, whose navel is a lotus, lies for a long time being worshipped with hymns by the four-faced Brahmā, who dwells within that navel-lotus and whose sides, back, and belly remain indistinguishable even though his head is visible up to his neck.
With the hem of her bodice tucked up to her neck, a smile suggested merely by the gestures of her fingers upon her chest, languid are her doll-play games;
with sidelong glances, the transfer of clever sayings through speech—such is this indescribable sequence of her play that grows ever more frequent as her childhood wanes.
Shaking the clusters of rice stalks bent down by the weight of their fruit, causing the excellent trees bowed with blossoms to dance,
and stirring the lotus pond filled with blooming lilies, the wind forcibly agitates the hearts of young men.

The wind unleashed at the time of the end of the aeon followed the prowess of him who, with great energy that shook the mountains and utterly surpassed the three oceans with ease, shattered the compact masses and struck down the haughty.
The hearts of the high-minded women were shaken by breezes scented with blossoming mango trees,
and distressed by the songs of the intoxicated cuckoo and the humming of bees, both so pleasing to the ear.
A source of wickedness does not arise as a cause for a living being;
yet the Kālakūṭa poison, though born from the ocean of nectar, is the taker of life for all creatures.
He is a mine of all scriptures, like the ocean is of jewels;
we, being envious, are not satisfied with his virtues.
The treasury originates from mines; from the treasury, the power of the rod is produced.
Through both the treasury and the power of the rod, the earth—adorned by the treasury—is attained.
With grey hair reaching his ears, dark-complexioned, and eighty-five years of age,
the aged Droṇa moved about in battle as if he were sixteen years old.
O Mother, this line fashioned with black collyrium shines upon the region of your outer corner of the eye, extending as far as the ear;
it appears like a continuous row of moss, following the path of your ever-emerging flood of compassion.
O Smara, why do you, harboring resentment, strike me alone with your bow and arrow drawn back as far as your ear?
Discharge your arrows repeatedly at that fawn-eyed woman; let her be the one tormented by love, and do not be the tormentor yourself.
Listen to this discourse, having accepted it, so that someone may come to know the heart of the Vedas;
for even him, may this delusion of duality—earned through hundreds of bonds of countless births—dissolve within a few hundred lifetimes.
Listen, O lotus-eyed one, to this reproach on earth:
the moon is compared by common folk to your face.

O charming girl, it is merely the casting of your eyes—reaching as far as your ears and stealing the luster of blue water-lilies—that captivates my heart; why this agitation? You have simply shown the base of your arms, marked by the scratches of fingernails and covered in dust, under the pretext of binding your loosened tresses.

She, whose tinkling anklets rang loudly as she moved, heard those sounds spreading forth, which were like the resonance of King Pradyumna’s advancing chariot; though she was angry, that noble woman quickly went toward her beloved.
Hearing the terrible thundering of the clouds at their gathering,
the young woman, as if her modesty were shaken away, embraces her beloved in trepidation.
Hearing the roar of the lion, which is like the thundering of clouds, elephants flee to other forests, afflicted by fear;
yet right there, a boar—a treasure-house of prowess—dwells with his own kind, arrogant and free from fear.
Having heard the words of Jayadeva, which bring joy to Govinda, let the ignorant long for Kālidāsa; we, however, do not.
The sounds of conversation from the village of the Son of the Sun (Yama) are being heard, and the noose of Time is surely and slowly closing around my neck;
the vital breaths, agitated by the desire to depart, are bidding farewell, yet even now the mind does not turn away from the objects of the senses.
O King, who here does not shake their heads upon hearing your fame?
Otherwise, the Creator, fearing the collapse of the earth, would have fashioned ears for the Lord of Serpents.
Having heard this, she said to me: "O friend, blessed are those hard-hearted young women who can endure the intensity of the fire of long separation from their beloveds."
Having heard these words of the citizens, I have concluded this:
let the gods and even the goddesses remain; the supreme Nārāyaṇa alone is to be served.
Having heard the completion of the verse recited by the courtesan in the assembly,
King Bhoja, who was of noble character and who immediately perceived in his heart that Kālidāsa had died, was truly the supreme connoisseur of human sentiment on earth.

Having heard of the activities in the great ocean of battle, the mental transformation of those whose hearts were captivated by the pleasure of the assembly causes horripilation on their limbs, a radiance in their eyes, an indescribable luster upon their faces, and a throbbing in their arms.

Having heard the sound of the fresh clouds, which acts as the drum for the coronation of the Youthful God of Love and provides a deep resonance like that of a mṛdaṅga for the flocks of dancing peacocks,
the Earth— thrilled as it were with horripilation under the guise of the opening petals of fresh blue kandalī sprouts— bore aloft banners in the form of mushrooms.
Having heard the praise of the mango fruit, the coconut became water; likewise, the jackfruit became mostly thorny, and the cucumber split in two.

The plantain fruit remains with its face turned downward, and alas, the grapefruit has become small and dark, while the rose-apple has reached a state of blackness—all this, indeed, due to the fault of envy here.
The waists of the women seemed to bend low, as if completely overwhelmed by their own breasts, which were so exceedingly high that they appeared to draw them upward despite being extremely slender.
Whose heart do these creepers not captivate—
creepers adorned with young shoots, resembling young women here, covered with flower-arrows?

O illustrious Lord, how can that king of horses come within the range of words such as mine—[a horse] who seems to draw the earth toward himself, to vomit forth his hooves, to abandon his hindquarters, to take possession of the sky, to drink in the quarters, and to be impatient with the shadows; who seems to touch the earth as if it were a heap of glowing coals, and to consume the wind?
In the Kaiśika-vyāya, one should draw [the bow] and not move the topknot;
the front and back [hands] should be made equal, with the shoulders level and the hands steady.

Victorious is this poem, which is sweet and clear-minded, whose nature is made weighty by its own virtues, and which arises from no small merit through its adornment with the lotus-feet of the Lord of Vast Strides (Viṣṇu).

May the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch bring you joy—a sound that is charmingly noble and majestic, whose sweetness unfolds from the breeze sweetened by the moon-like face of Murāri (Viṣṇu) until the end of the aeon;
it effortlessly surpasses the power of Meghanāda’s roar, inflicts pain upon Kumbhakarṇa, and traverses the ten directions of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
O cloud, even if you were to rain down thousands of torrents every single day until the end of the eon, who within the unfathomable belly of the ocean could perceive your exhaustion?
O cloud, if you release your water upon the peaks of mountains for even a moment, do not your glories spread forth under the guise of mountain cascades and rivers?
Having prepared her couch, which was like the luster of the moonstone, and having tied up her betel leaves filled with celestial flowers, she,
casting the corners of her eyes toward the doorway, caused the mind of the Son of Manas to tremble with wonder.
From dawn until midnight, we are occupied for the sake of our bellies;
yet we never find contentment, whereas those who are peaceful dwell in happiness.
While her friends, though wise, were feigning ignorance with sudden smiles upon their faces,
that fawn-eyed woman, practicing a concealment of her affection, fixed her lotus-like eyes motionlessly upon that very spot even after her beloved had departed.
Entering the palaces of kings— which are like the underworld— for those who desire [wealth],
they obtain no fruit other than that of a downward descent, just like serpents that subsist on air.

When there is a desire for a higher state, the mind should maintain its focus on the task with the thought "I am the Self"; one should not hold such a collection of mental states within another state of mind.
To prevent imbalance, you should seek its cause within yourself alone and not elsewhere; this is always most conducive to your supreme welfare.
For kings who conceal their true intentions while rising to conquer enemy forces, who contemplate statecraft amidst the tangled branches of hundreds of tasks both performed and unperformed,
who follow the counsel of ministers yet remain suspicious of everything, and who dwell in an ocean of suffering— only the embrace of a beloved wife provides even a fragment of happiness.
O Swan! Your form is the ancestral home of loveliness, your gait is languid with grace, your association is with lotus-pools, and your cry is transcendent in its sweetness;
yet, although you possess such a great abundance of virtues, O noble bird, I cannot endure this agitation of yours in this quarrel with the base *madgu* ducks.
That captivating form, that majesty, that splendor, that youth, that radiance, and that rise of fortune and good luck which causes the whole world to marvel—
each one of these, in the task of detailed description, would require someone possessing two thousand tongues, like the Lord of Serpents, to be capable of it.
Having taken the words of the messenger who had arrived to summon the practitioner of mantras,
and having first established them as authoritative, he then performed the consecration there with the mantra.
Even this uncertainty—"this form is terrible; there is fear from this"—regarding the form of Śiva, though it be most terrifying, leads only to auspiciousness.
But the transformation of one's mental state is a humiliation for the intellect;
it is like the loss of hope for one who desires, or like another form of death.
Blessed are those who, having fulfilled their desires through mere mental images,
never hear the piteous cries of supplicants anywhere.
Even though he was like Kandarpa himself in his physical form, dress, and charm,
who indeed has not been deceived after attaining union with those women?
Even when one's outward appearance is being concealed, it cannot be hidden;
for it forcibly reveals the internal state of men.
Even a lover deeply enamored should maintain the outward appearance of restraint; for one who is openly passionate meets with contempt, and how can one who is despised be beloved?
His wisdom was consistent with his outward form; his learning was consistent with his wisdom;
his undertakings were consistent with his learning; and his compassion was consistent with his undertakings.
The lowly camel, with its neck arched and held askance, feels shame at those very same physical forms, conversations, and enjoyments for which other people feel ashamed.

O Lord, may even the host of your enemies become just like you— devoid of the initial letter [A]— possessing beauty undiminished by its form, free from destruction, partaking in the splendor of yoga, valiant, equal to the universe, with a preeminent form and the playful movement of eyes like lotuses, possessing fame that fulfills various desires, composed of the essence of bliss, and having bodies mounted upon elephants.
By one's appearance, as well as by one's gait, gestures, and speech,
and also by changes in the eyes and face, the hidden mind is known.
A young monkey vies with a man in appearance, a mule with a horse, a tiger with a chariot, a gayal with a cow, and a dog with a lion;
and even a crow competes with a cuckoo for its dark plumage. Though they are thus bound by a persistent desire for rivalry, they do not attain even a fraction of that bird’s multitude of virtues.

In appearance he is the moon, in voice the cuckoo, in kissing the turtle-dove, in gait the swan, and in the crushing of passion during dalliance the elephant; since my husband is thus served by all the qualities praised by young women, there would be no fault in the thought that "my married husband is surpassed," were it not for this: [The verse continues: "In appearance he is the moon, in voice the cuckoo, in kissing the turtle-dove, in gait the swan, and in the crushing of passion during dalliance the elephant; since my husband is thus served by all the qualities praised by young women, there would be no fault in the thought that 'my married husband is surpassed,' were it not for this. (Note: The provided text fragment contains a repetition of the first half of the verse. The full intended meaning is that while his husband possesses these virtues, he lacks one essential quality—namely, the ability to provide for his wife's basic needs—which makes the comparison with other husbands flawed.)
By their very appearance alone, wise people discern the intentions of others,
just as bees perceive the presence of a ketaki flower within its bud by its fragrance.

Madana is seen in his form; the Guru is present in the skill of composing fine poetry; and even in the six languages, a passion for them is observed. Alas, having abandoned the blissful union with their own lords of life, women do not live [otherwise]; how then can this daughter practice the arts in his presence?
By means of facial expressions, gestures, gait, physical movements, and speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived.

The clever are not able to understand the crooked speech through its outward forms, nor is it the custom of the group of virtuous matrons to reveal their own inner intentions through words. In this village, the youths are dull-witted, their minds destroyed by the literal meaning of what is said; therefore, let this fever of passion—which has the travelers who have reached the wise as its limit—be endured.
Your form is not pleasing to the eyes; your cawing is like a thorn to the ears; your mouth is a loathsome distortion; and this gaze of yours clings to the very hour of Death.
You dwell upon a wretched tree used for common folk's play and enchantment. O miserable crow, why is it that you have taken possession of a golden palace?
In the sacrificial pit of the sky, where lightning serves as the fire, the fish-bannered god performs a fire-offering;
his thundering is indeed the recitation of mantras for the purpose of exorcising those women separated from their lovers.

How can this body attain purity through that water which falls from the sky and reaches the midst of rivers and the like, yet remains smeared with impurities stirred up by its own flow, and is filled with various kinds of filth from the earth?
The heads of the Lord of Laṅkā, together with their hair, fell from the region of the sky;
for a moment they shone like fruits hanging from the basket of a tall tree in the heavens.
Practicing the concentration on space (ākāśa-dhāraṇā), one certainly conquers death;
whether situated anywhere at all, one enjoys ultimate happiness.
O Space, spread forth; O Directions, extend; O Earth, become vast! You have witnessed the unfolding of the glory of the primordial kings.
Through the expansion of the mass of fame of the illustrious King Muddāphara Shāh, the universe shall ascend to the state of a pomegranate split open by the swelling of its seed.
Fix your gaze upon that moon-like beauty, who is a royal swan plunging into the lake of the minds of women,
a great elephant for the lotus-stalk of passion for women, and the initiating preceptor for the tradition of the Lord of Pleasure as he is being inhaled by his consorts.
Let the sky fly up, or let it go to the ends of the quarters; let it enter the ocean, or let it remain as it pleases.
For men who have performed good and evil deeds in other births, the connection with the fruits of their karma does not leave them, just like a shadow.
O Goddess, men stand with one foot placed upon the edge of the terrace of the celestial chariot, supporting themselves with their hands on pairs of golden staffs;
out of curiosity, they gaze at their own bodies as they are tossed by the waves.
O lotus-eyed one, behold the autumnal orb of the moon risen like a white lotus in the pond of the sky, a whetstone for the arrows of the God of Love, and the ball of the lady Twilight.

I truly believe that the moon, which bears a resemblance to the dark expanse of the sky or a mass of clouds, and which possesses an unprecedented beauty through the locks of hair placed upon its head—that very face of my beloved—is what you feel as joy in your heart upon seeing. O Jñānaśānti, the great ones call that [joy] the exceedingly sharp sword for cutting away the seeds of rebirth in the world of Rāma.

Having ascended the palace of the sky, the moon— whose splendor is like that of the son of Lalitā and who is surrounded by his harem of stars— casts, as it were, a desirable cosmetic upon the limbs of the women who are the quarters of the horizon, under the guise of moonlight, gladdening all the world.
In the palace of the sky, this Night, full of longing, seems to worship with the jewels of the stars that lofty Śiva-liṅga, dark as a tamāla tree, resting upon the moon-slab.
Just as water fallen from the sky flows toward the ocean,
so do all salutations to the gods go toward Keśava.
O friend, this pearl— having fallen from the sky, long remaining in the midst of the ocean, and later beset by the suffering born of the painful holes in its body—
attains the state of being your nose-ornament while performing severe penance upon the pair of eyes of your young fawn-eyed girl, in comparison with your bimba-red lip.

We consider these to be the merits of young lovers: dancing in the sky, the sweet sound of anklets upon a pair of lotuses, warbling melodiously on the moon, celebrating a festival of drinking nectar from a sprout, being humiliated by the nails on the mountain of heaven (Meru), pulling the moon by its rays, and the tinkling of girdles upon the plantain-like thighs of Rambhā.

Look at the sky! These are not dense masses of clouds; they are chests filled with fiery powder. Above them, under the guise of rainbows, these are banners. These are lightning-flashes, appearing like the light of glowing wicks falling from the openings of mechanical tubes. I believe this is the army of Māra, shimmering to crush the pride-fortress of the proud woman.
I weighed poverty and sovereignty on a scale;
poverty, being superior in virtue, outweighed even sovereignty.
Possessionlessness is happiness in this world; it is wholesome, auspicious, and free from ailment.
It is indeed without enemies, difficult for others to attain, yet easily obtained by the virtuous.
Possessionlessness, perfect contentment, freedom from desire, and lack of restlessness—
these they call the supreme good for one who knows the self and has conquered the mind.
Neglected by his wife due to extreme familiarity with her lack of possessions, fearing everyone because he does not follow the ways of kings,
staying at home, foolish and indolent, and sharing the nature of a tortoise in a well— what does such a man know of the affairs of the world, and what happiness does he enjoy?
Between the state of nothingness and kingship, there is this very great distinction:
for the wealthy man is perpetually anxious, as if he had entered the jaws of death.
A king shines when surrounded by a retinue, never when he is solitary;
those who desire his solitude are considered his enemies.
Then, with his toes slightly curled and the beauty of his eyes somewhat cast down,
he scratched the golden footstool with his foot, the luster of whose nails spread obliquely across its surface.

This is the bed of the fair-limbed maiden: one leg drawn up, the upper thigh slightly covered and the other half-thigh concealed, her abdomen heaving with the movement of her sighs and her navel clearly visible.
When both thighs are contracted and the two knees touch the ground,
they call this the *dardurakrama* stance, used for firm piercing.

Having clenched her impure hand against my head, the courtesan, purifying it step by step with drops of consecrated water, struck me with a loud cry and a resounding "thut"; alas, Viṣṇuśarman weeps, crying out, "Alas, alas! I am ruined!"
When her fingertips are bent for scratching with the nails, she gazes with a knitting of the brows; when there is a firm embrace, she utters the words, "Ah! Ah! Let go! Let go!
When her hair is pulled, she closes her eyes, and when struck, she has tearful eyes; thus the young woman assumes various states in the drama of Love.
With his back arched, his raised face and tail-tip quivering, one eye fixed inside the house out of fear, and both ears motionless;
with a mouth made terrifying by bared fangs and gaping corners of the mouth smeared with saliva; and with a throat swollen from the suppression of his breath, the dog springs upon the cat.
Desiring to instruct even children in the turning away from the path of great calamity,
the ascetics— who have conquered birth and death through the power of yoga— cultivate excellent conduct.
Confused by the cries of flocks of birds in flight, and with the glow of dawn not yet risen,
the end of the day— pale as the horses of the sun— attained a likeness to the beginning of the day.
In this vast and alas, delusive cycle of existence, the essence is the fawn-eyed woman, whose gait is languid with grace and who is full of the nectar of affection for physical beauty.
A slight trace of form reveals its characteristic,
like the lunar disk when it is afflicted by a great eclipse.
Dragged by his topknot, scratched with fingernails, touched on the surface of his cheek, and struck on his head with flower-garlands as he moved gracefully along the path in every direction—
may the waves of laughter from Viṣṇu, who bore the playful grace of the Vāmana disguise at the sacrifice of the Daityas while being thus mocked by the courtesans, protect you.
With his sword drawn, as he moved about in the midst of battle, that lord was seen by the enemy army to be like the God of Death himself.

Then, as the women swam through the waters of that great ocean of passion with their slender vine-like bodies drawn along by the outstretched, fluttering wings of their arms, the water was agitated by the massive boulder-like mounds of their breasts.

Drawn by the *cakravāka* birds with their sidelong glances and rejected by wanton women, the sun does not set quickly, but dwells within the interval between the awakening of the lotuses and the onset of sleep.
In the bedchamber, the maidservant, having offered the sprouting evening lamp whose wicks are saturated with abundant sesame oil, laughs as she is glared at in anger by the young bride.

This mantra consisting of the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa effects the attraction of great-souled ones whose minds are prepared, the eradication of sins, and brings the fortune of liberation under its control—a state easily accessible even to untutored people down to the lowest outcaste. It requires neither initiation, nor sacrificial fees, nor preliminary ritual service; this mantra bears fruit by its very touch, like a liquid essence.
O fortunate one, by whom has your lotus-stalk-like arm— naturally delicate and with its bracelets broken by the force of his pull— been grasped, as if it were the very kingdom of Love?
O illustrious Lord Rāmacandra, when you drew your sword— which resembled the tongue of the king of serpents from its scabbard— into the houses of your adversaries, wild buffaloes,
yaks, tigers, tree-dwelling spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, jackals, boars, locusts, rhinoceroses, bears, and Bhilla tribesmen suddenly began to enter them.
When the Lord of the Raghus drew his bow in battle, his left hand spoke to the right: "In matters of giving, taking, and fine dining, you are always positioned in front; why then do you act thus?

The other, however, replied with desire: "I have no fear in questioning the Lord of the World, nor in severing the row of Rāvaṇa’s heads. May he who would grant such [a boon] bestow auspiciousness upon you.

When the bow was drawn in battle, the left hand addressed the right: "O right hand, it is improper for you—who perform great acts such as eating and giving alms—to go behind. Then the right hand replied swiftly: "Shall I ask Raghava whether I should quickly shatter the multitude of Ravana's heads?"
When the hem of her garment was pulled, Rukmiṇī cast down her eyes, dark as blue lotuses, out of bashfulness; she gazed at her own beautiful, golden-hued breasts that were pressed together.
Then Kṛṣṇa, embracing her as she stood with her face bowed—her beauty enhanced by the grace of a slight smile, as if thinking "this is some young mango sprout"—may he protect us.
Just as elephants sunk in the mud are pulled out by great elephants themselves,
so too must great men who have fallen into calamity be rescued by other great beings.

Having first pulled my mass of hair with a slow grip and pressed her face against my face, he—of beautiful throat—clung to my neck; then, having again pressed his limbs firmly against my breasts, he clung to my hips and fell at my feet. "Such a lover as that is mine," [she said]. "O girl, shame has vanished! No, no, you crooked one, is a bodice a cause for shame?"
One who restrains a friend from an improper act by seizing them by the hair becomes beyond reproach by anyone, having exerted effort to the best of one's ability.
Even when provoked, one born of noble family does not speak what should not be said; it is said that sugar-cane, even when crushed, yields only sweetness.
A base person, even when served with hundreds of virtues, speaks such words in jest as would be unspeakable in a quarrel.
How could these lords of the quarters have escaped from him, who, since his childhood, has rendered the earth devoid of heroes by conquering them in battle?
It is known within that those eight entered into a portion of his body; for the sword of Kṣatriyas does not prevail over one who has bowed down in submission.
Alas! From my youth, through service at the feet of my guru, I acquired great proficiency and a firm devotion to the knowledge of Brahman;
yet how has this very skill turned out to be merely a means for passing the time for kings who listen to stories night after night for the sake of sleep?
My cries are equal to your thunders, my tears to your unceasing torrents of rain, and the flames of grief born from our separation to the flickering of your lightning.
Within me is your beloved’s face, while the moon is yours; thus our condition is the same. O friend cloud, why then are you intent solely on burning me incessantly?

Whether there be weeping, crying, or striking the face—who could have a heart moistened by such things? Or what fruit is there in it? O Mother, before you—she whose mind melts with compassion and who is the sovereign mistress of the worlds—I shall speak of my distress.
O tiger among kings, that which is eaten by Brahmins who have been approached when their kinsmen are impoverished, or even by cows, is superior to the Rājasūya sacrifice.
That man in this world, upon whose staff-like arm the circle of enemies shines once it has been subdued, attains the fame of being "Vaikuṇṭha."
Overcome by time, every living being is led to the next world under the power of the noose of karma; what lamentation can there be in that?
O Bhārata, attacking again and again, those pitiless ones will enjoy the wives and the wealth of the virtuous, even while they weep.
Having stepped upon the foremost shoulder of Aja and then ascended fearlessly to his head,
those proud ones, moving with playful ease along a superhuman path, ascended to heaven with comfort.
Having stepped upon one leg with the tip of his trunk and lifting the other leg high with his hand,
that elephant of cruel nature tore some man asunder through the middle like a piece of wood, making a bone-crushing sound.

O cloud, who indeed would not envy such a vow as yours: dwelling on high upon the heads of lofty mountains; taking water even from the ocean for the sake of soothing the world's distress; casting a long shadow across the vast expanse of the naturally great sky; and binding yourself in such a grand form?

Overpowered by wrinkles and violently assailed by grey hair, old age has rendered this body of mine powerless and lusterless due to the loosening of its joints; behold it as nothing but a skeleton worn out by age, reduced to a mere vessel of skin made harsh and terrifying by its thick veins.
The lady of the quarters (the sky), previously assailed with impetuosity by the soldiers and defiled by the dust of the atmosphere,
roared deeply with the dense echoes of the kettledrums' sounds, as if out of intense indignation.
My inner self is beset by enemies such as pride, envy, and the like; my body is pierced by hundreds of ailments, wrinkles, and grey hair;
and my home is surrounded by creditors in the form of wives and sons—O Mother, how can there be peace for my mind?
While the lands from the Bridge to the Golden Mountain were overrun by Yavanas, while the host of kings had fled, and while the pitiless Nārāyaṇa slept;
even during the Kali age when obstacles flow unchecked, it is indeed a single world-transcending being who forcibly protects the Vedic path here and there, free from thorns.
As if crushed by a great rock, as if cursed by Durvāsas, alas, as if constantly sealed with lac, as if rendered unconscious by poisons,
or as if bound by ropes of leather— when the mouth of a wicked man is pierced by an iron rod, his tongue appears powerless to speak of the virtues of others.
While her childhood has been overtaken by fresh youth at the command of the fish-bannered god, the young girl’s pair of eyes has entered the two ears along with the pair of her eyebrows;
the pair of her breasts has emerged high here together with the orb of her hips; and the waist, having been confined and bound on all sides by the three folds, assumes a state of emaciation.
Let the wretched crows themselves trample upon that very mango tree and shriek with harsh "repha" sounds, claiming, "This is our young one too!
O cuckoo, where else can you go? Even this much must be endured; to whom can this be reported now that spring has already passed away?
When reviled, one should not revile in return;
for the anger of one who endures it consumes the reviler and takes away his merit.
Even when reviled, he does not resort to anger nor speak abusively; though exalted by qualities such as heroism and fortitude, he does not succumb to pride.
Even when constantly beset by calamity, he does not fall into despondency—it is after discerning him through the intellect of reality that the virtuous call him a "good man" in this world.
In this world, there is no friend equal to one who reproaches you,
for such a person takes upon themselves your misdeeds and gives their own good deeds to you.
Abusing others, calling out to them, running about the circle, and weeping,
the boy drives the cattle that have descended upon the crops with his staff.
Through abuse and slander, the ignorant harm the wise;
the speaker takes on the evil, while the one who forgives is liberated.
He is not pained by abuse, nor is he cheered when addressed with clever words; he is not distressed by foul odors, nor does he rejoice equally in pleasant scents.
He is not enamored by a jewel of a woman, nor does he feel aversion toward the bathing of the dead. Resplendent in his equanimity, this certain lord of yogis is truly victorious.
The lotuses, O charming one, challenge the beauty of your face;
for what is difficult for those who possess both a treasury and an army?
"You rebuke Karṇa with your eye, yet Bali was bound by you in three ways at his waist; O fair-limbed one, you feel ashamed to give even your body, though you have surpassed all generous givers."
The sky, its beauty departed as it was filled with smoke rising in flames and its quarters obscured by swarms of serpents swooping down, assumed the appearance of a city besieged by enemies.

The splendor of the chowries has been eclipsed, the grace of the *pauṇḍarīka* flower forcibly snatched away, the *vīrakambu* pearl necklace concealed, and the neck-ornament turned into a mere burden; the radiance of laughter has vanished, the heap of flowers has been reduced to some degree of humiliation, and the fame of rival kings—white as the moon—is utterly obscured by his own glories.
O King, because you are enraged, the rival kings who have been challenged tremble and do not display their various great weapons in battle.
With their crowns bowed low from afar before you, they merely project rainbows upon the earth with the clusters of jewels from their various diadems.
Trembling with the playful curiosity of tossing, kicking, leaping, and seizing her hair,
she did not even hear the teaching that for women, the husband is also a guru.
One should never utter words of reproach toward him;
rather, one should speak what is agreeable and pleasing to him in the assembly of people.
A rat attempts to scale Mount Kailāsa; a crow, craving the flesh of Garuḍa, agitates the base of Takṣaka’s tail;

a restless frog, desiring to kill the serpent, wishes to reach the far shore of the great devouring ocean. Generally, one whose downfall is imminent and who performs mean deeds does not remember what is appropriate.
Then, having uttered the name of one who has been bitten by a rat, one should cast the dust from the road far away;
for that person, happiness will quickly arise.
What indeed have rogues learned from rats, and what have rats learned from rogues?
For those whose only activity other than digging up the houses of others does not exist.
The rat desires to steal the ash-smeared thread; the serpent likewise seeks the mouse; the peacock seeks the serpent; the lion seeks the bull; and the Gaṅgā likewise seeks the moon.
O Lord, hear how such suffering must be endured day and night—how can this be borne? May these piteous words, intended to awaken Śambhu to his own true state, protect you.
He who engages in conversation with one who hunts for sport, who causes useless suffering, who is a fool,
or who is addicted to vices, meets with defeat.
By the practice of hunting, wealth comes under the control of men;
one man impels the subjects like a hunter, while another slays them like deer.
The poetic body, composed of verse, possessing the qualities of figures of speech, verbal roots, grammatical inflections, euphonic combinations, and the skillful arrangement of nouns and verbs,
remains here unbroken even for those preeminent poets who have ascended to heaven.
When he was named "the Grandfather," she laughed; at "the Skull-bearer," she trembled; at "the Preceptor," she turned away; and at "the Consumer," her timidity was revealed.
At "the Lord of Paulomī," she felt resentment; then, bowed down with shame by Śrī, she offered that handful of flowers while saying, "May this Supreme Person protect you."
Delighting in tales, he always goes to hear meritorious books;
yet, as if bitten by black snakes, he flees from the duties of giving.
The treasurers, filled with joy, sing its names which nourish delightful meanings;
however, by your merits, you have now attained here this very abode of bliss known as the mango tree.
If there is no collision on the road between those coming empty-handed and those going with full loads,
then that lake is in vain.
By him who came without looking back, as if seeking a mere cowrie shell,
I have been robbed— by him who was unable to carry even the cloth covering my hips.
A festival shines when it is approaching, but not in the same way once it has passed; the rising of the moon glows at evening, but not so at dawn.
The beauty of the faces of the quarters of the sky, turned pale by the dust raised by the armies of the kings as they approached,
clearly revealed their appearance as befitting the state of being widowed by the loss of their husbands.
The honey-bees come, cover [the hive] with their wings, and then again they look upon it and smell it; yet they do not themselves consume even a single drop of what they have begun to gather.
But another, fortunate one, having approached fearlessly and driving them far away, enjoys this [honey] at his own will, tasting it over and over as if it were gathered by himself.
As they were arriving, indicated by the one who had led them toward the house, [the friend asked]:
"O friend, which among these should be honored first—is it the crow, or is it the camel?"
"Come, come! Prepare my excellent horse! Bring it to me quickly! Where is my sword? Hand me the scimitar! What with the bow?

Why, friend, has he already entered?"—such was the dialogue heard among the enemies as they woke from their agitation upon seeing you in their dream within the dense forest of the mountain, their eyes filled with alarm.

"I am coming back instantly, my dearest, having gone to perform a small task; meanwhile, you stay right here in this beautiful, secluded house," he said, O friend. But that deceiver departed, and the entire night during which she remained there has passed for me; yet, though he is exceedingly crooked, he has still not returned.
A wise man, knowing that war has arrived, should bring it to peace through strategic means;
for since victory is uncertain, he should not rush headlong into it.
Hearing from the people that her husband has arrived, the deer-eyed woman comes to the threshold in startled haste;
when will she cool my eyes like the moonlight?
All the Pāṇḍavas arrived there at the instigation of Duryodhana;
to him [they gave] a cow, gold, and various kinds of jewels.
The emaciation of one whose character is marked by the expenditure of what has been acquired is exceedingly beautiful;
the second moon is worthy of worship, not the full moon.
He who has come and gone, and having gone, has come back again—
that fool, lacking both ears and a heart, met his destruction right there.

When their beloveds had arrived and departed countless times, and the fair-browed women desired to win them back, the opportunity for wine presented itself in their hearts, which were now filled with remorse.
That lake is unsurpassed, wherein there is no collision of jars on the path— whether they are arriving incomplete, or departing already full.
When the flower-bowed god of love arrived, the *koka* bird of the slender maiden’s breasts emerged from her mind;
as he stood there, the lotus-eyed girl was suddenly startled by the *khañjana* bird.

Having arrived, he was appeased by his friends with prostrations; when that rogue, having gained access, began to freely massage her limbs while remaining hidden at the side of the bed, she recognized him by the touch.
Thinking it was her friend, she slowly pressed her own breast against him, saying "Are you weary?", and with eyes closed, she joyfully embraced him.

O slender-limbed one, behold how the thousand-rayed sun, having spent the night somewhere else, now arrives at dawn and gently propitiates this lotus— whose limbs are distressed by separation— with a prostration of his rays.

Having now arrived through its grace, this autumn season smiles slightly under the guise of blooming white water-lilies; having dispelled the obstruction of the clouds as if it were anger, it brings delight to the faces of the women who are the quarters of the sky.

Behold! Having arrived swiftly, the sun, having caused the sky to blaze and manifesting a vivid twilight glow through his falling rays, seems to propitiate the western quarter like a passionate woman, perceiving her as if she were angry.
Having arrived from somewhere, having made the expanse of the sky his own, and having led even these [luminaries] headed by the moon to the place where existence and non-existence are observed;
having somehow caused the world to blaze forth, let the beloved Lord of Days go to his setting, or enter the ocean, or perhaps wander around Mount Meru.

In the case of a bird that has arrived from elsewhere or one that wanders about, all crows are considered equal; however, among those, the *kāka* (crow) should always be understood as the *kākola* (raven) when it concerns a bird born of the field (*kṣetraja*).
Having investigated the import, export, storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he should regulate their purchase and sale.
O Mistress Jaimini-yoginī, whose form is the investigation of the scriptures, who has trained in thousands of legal treatises against opposing views— this heart of mine is devoted to you.
The hells, such as Raurava and others, are heard of only from scripture;
however, the wise know that for the destitute, the state of being a mere object of sensory experience is itself a hell manifest to the senses.
For the master always strives for the sake of the sacred tradition and for its preservation; in nourishing his family, he is like a thief in all other respects.
Those states that are destined to arise within me will come;
I am to be followed by them, for they have no other course.
Whatever meaning is established through both scripture and reasoning should be accepted after examination, like gold; why resort to grasping with partiality?
In the case of one who has four [fingers] on the entry-side and five and a half on the exit-side,
their fortunes, though exceedingly vast and extensive, do not endure for long.
Title-deed is superior to possession, except in the case of what has come down through a prior succession;
even in the case of a title-deed, it possesses no strength whatsoever where there is not even the slightest possession.
Amplifying the twang of his bowstring— which causes a fever in the ears of herds of elephants trumpeting from mountain thickets— and which is swollen by the deep resonance of drums,
the hero makes the earth appear as if strewn with the remnants of food from the gaping mouths of the satiated, terrifying Kāla, amidst heaps of swaying, horrific heads and trunks.
Remembering the offense committed against his father by the Kṣatriyas, the hero of the Bhṛgu lineage, whose nature was one of constant indignation from the moment of his conception,
severed even his enemies of life with his axe alone.
O Moon-crested Lord, you know us to be intent on taking refuge at your lotus feet—from the womb, from the heads of our family elders, and even from the four-faced Brahmā.
Yet, O Master, you have declared that *māyā* does not act toward those intent on seeking refuge; this being so, O God, you alone are the authority regarding what is appropriate in this matter.
