When the destroyer of Kaiṭabha, having offended her, made an effort in anger to turn the navel-lotus of Śrī into a weapon for the purpose of striking him,

may the speech-activities of the ancient Sage— which at that moment were intent on protecting the helpless— protect you, as she herself was bewildered by fear caused by the uprooting of her own dwelling.
An arsonist, a betrayer of friends, a fowler, a village priest,
and those who sell *soma*— these fall into the Rudhirāndha hell.
With her beautiful braid reaching down to her ankles, this young girl, a golden-bodied creeper,
shines like the campaka-flower bow-vine of the Mind-born God, who has conquered the earth after drawing back his string.

He whose powerful warrior-elephants are skilled in the *āgneyāstra* weapon and expert at agitating the enemy, and who serve as fuel for the thick flames of the fire of his mature majesty— this very King of Bāṅgāla, whose wrath is swiftly fulfilled by the multitude of hands extended from the eastern ocean, is a sprout of fame sung by the people of the three worlds.

The dawn approaches as if from the direction of Agni; the days seem to shrink away from the cold; even when parched with thirst, the slender flame of fire carries no heat but rather wipes away the suffering of the chill.
Upon the bed, where the firm knot of the embrace has been loosened by excessive passion, the dull-witted wind finds a crack for entry and forces the couple apart.
If there is a well in the south-eastern corner of a village or a city,
it constantly causes fear and, for the most part, brings about fire accompanied by human violence.
In the southeast, there is gain from those who live by fire, from young women, and from excellent minerals;
in the south, there is food consisting of mung beans and horse gram, and association with musicians.
Reciting mantras, he strikes [the drum] and falls into laughter;
he blames [others] for faults and brings about the destruction of their livelihood.
Like a condemned man being led to execution who encounters death at every step,
for a living being, death draws closer day by day.

May the slow and languid movements of the intoxicated Balarāma protect you—he whose body reels, whose soft speech falters, whose garments hang slightly loose, whose helpless arms rest upon Revatī, and whose copper-hued eyes shine;
he whose garland of lotus stalks is bitten by swarms of bees blinded by the intoxication of his breath’s fragrance.
Her lotus-eye, with its thick lashes, rolls about; it surpasses the moon with the whiteness of its glow at the corners, and its pupil is dark and clear like a moving, flawless sapphire.

Homage to that Kalkin, who— wielding a sword in his hand and filled with righteous wrath because people were deluded and had transgressed the true path by smelling, hearing, looking at, tasting flavors, and so forth, as well as by their longing for kisses and their raining down of poisonous words upon the head— forcibly severed the heads of the wicked.

The lotus was smelled by her beloved; the fair-eyed woman smiled and withdrew it, offering her face instead. A nail-mark was placed upon the ball of her amorous play, while she hissed and concealed her breasts.
A garland of *campaka* flowers was laid upon her chest as she stood with arms outstretched, her hair standing on end and her eyes closed; though the lovers were far apart, their passion was full.
Smelled, licked, crushed by fierce claws, chewed, and cast upon the ground in anger because it had lost its luster—do not feel distress over this, O ruby!
It is precisely for your own good that you were suddenly pulverized by a monkey with a stone, out of a desire to ascertain the quality of your inner substance.
Birth is seized by death; radiant youth passes away through old age; contentment is swallowed by the desire for wealth; the happiness of tranquility by the amorous dalliances of mature women;
virtues by envious people; forest lands by serpents; kings by wicked men; and even prosperity is carried off by instability—what indeed is not devoured by something?
Having sniffed the surface of the earth, its hooves having drawn up the dust, the horse gathers all its legs together; as its knees bend in succession, its body is released from tension.
Out of a desire to remove the itch from the back and sides, it rolls its body two or three times; then, rising quickly and remaining still for a moment, it shakes its body from head to tail.
Having merely smelled the book, the fortunate ones stand saying, "We know it all";
yet even though we listen a hundred times, alas, we do not know—futile as we are!

Having smelled the unrestrained breath of the women—a kinsman of blameless fragrance born of exertion—the forest flowers were filled with longing for the bees; for who, desiring distinction, takes account of propriety?
Sniffing the scent again and again, displaying his rows of teeth with a distorted mouth, and running while letting out repeated cries, the donkey—

his sexual pleasure doubled by the kicks of the she-donkey who had pulled him back with force— is finally dismounted in a state of confusion after a long time, his desires thwarted as he was dragged along.
Alas, how can we describe the present state of that once lofty peak of the Vindhya mountains?
There, where seven sages sat in ascetic penance, that very place is now, they say, the dwelling of flesh-eating demons.

Having rinsed her mouth with the waters of the lower Sindhu river, she— her eyes rolling— worships the five-arrowed god upon the chest of that fortunate man, which has been cleansed by the mass of her braided hair, made radiant by the saffron paste trickling from her cheeks as they are bathed in perspiration, and adorned with a garland of pearls falling profusely at the sound of the mantra of her girdle.
I do not know why a wicked person acts so rashly toward matters that are beyond even the reach of the mind; yet I do know this: it is not out of any inherent cruelty that he touches the heart.
By harboring enmity toward many people, even those few who remain trustworthy will perish;
thus, the king, having lost their confidence, abandoned his deceased minister.
And one should practice the entire course of amorous conduct prescribed in the *Kāmasūtra*, which is irreproachable,
in accordance with place, time, strength, and capacity, and without contradicting the medical treatises or established conventions.
Does not even the grey crescent of the moon, with its radiant rays surpassing the luster of the sun,
captivate the eye?
He practices right conduct and abandons pride; he takes recourse in dispassion and desires to perform austerities that cause the lofty arrogance born of worldly association to dissolve.
Yet, when his head of happiness has fallen due to reversals brought about by fate, a person who has been ruined generally attains a pliability like iron melted by heat.
Conduct reveals one's family; speech reveals one's country;
agitation reveals affection; and the body reveals one's diet.
Conduct reveals one’s lineage; the body reveals one’s food;
speech reveals one’s learning; and the eyes reveal one’s affection.
Indeed, right conduct must be practiced even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
through right conduct the body is purified, just as cloth is cleansed by alkaline water.
Conduct is the supreme dharma; conduct is the supreme austerity;
conduct is the supreme knowledge—what is not accomplished through conduct?
Conduct is the supreme dharma, as declared in the Śrutis and the Smṛtis;
therefore, a twice-born man who possesses self-control should always be constantly devoted to it.
"Proper conduct is the supreme dharma for all; this is certain.
One whose soul is overwhelmed by deficient conduct perishes both in this world and after death."
Proper conduct is the first duty for men; it is a great bringer of welfare, resulting in supreme fame in this world and the highest happiness in the next.
That cane staff which I, with attentive care, had taken up as a matter of protocol within the inner apartments of the king,
has now, after much time has passed, become my support for my faltering steps on this journey.

What praise can there be here for those like you, who have been purified by the stream of right conduct, whose minds are intent on the worship of Rādhā’s husband, and who are adorned by the loftiness of knowledge and discernment?
Dharma, which originates from right conduct, is the great bringer of welfare for human beings;
it brings supreme fame in this world and the highest happiness in the next.
For the king is the instigator of conduct; indeed, he is the cause of this time.
If time were the authority, why would there be dharma among those who act?
Casting aside indolence, practice for a long time the conduct appropriate to your birth;
this alone is the means of winning the affection of the world and the way to propitiate Hari.
Dharma arises from right conduct; from Dharma the Vedas have emerged;
from the Vedas sacrifices are produced; and by means of sacrifices the gods are established.
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct, even if they have been studied together with the six auxiliary sciences;
at the time of death, the sacred hymns abandon him, just as birds with grown wings leave their nest.

But for a Brahmin devoid of proper conduct, even the Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs and all the sacrifices—what pleasure are they capable of producing? They are like beautiful wives to a blind man.
From right conduct dharma arises; from right conduct wealth arises;
through right conduct one attains prosperity; right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas;
however, one who is endowed with right conduct is declared to be a partaker of the full fruit.
Through right conduct one obtains dharma; through right conduct one obtains wealth;
through right conduct one attains prosperity; right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, the desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct one obtains prosperity;
through right conduct a person attains fame both in this world and after death.
Proper conduct ends with dwelling in a village; sovereignty for women ends with the household;
the glory of kings ends with a Brahmin’s curse; and spiritual luster ends with its fruit.
The teacher should possess seven [planets] in the yoga; Bhārgava (Venus) should possess four;
a warrior should possess two, and an astrologer should possess one.
For the wise teacher indeed follows the world itself in all activities; therefore, an investigator should follow that very world in matters concerning worldly affairs.
Having invited the preceptor on an auspicious day, one who is pure should fashion a pair of dogs out of flour and worship them;
then, for the satisfaction of Bhaṣaṇa, one should feed them with milk and give [portions] to virgins, children, and kinsmen.
The teacher, the father, the mother, and an elder brother must not be treated with contempt, even by one who is distressed; this is especially true for a Brahmin.
Teachers and kings are of similar character; for them there is neither intimacy nor friendship.
Even service long accumulated with great effort they destroy when enraged, as clouds disperse the dust.
The preceptor should bestow the bow upon a well-examined Brāhmaṇa;
it is not given to one who is greedy, deceitful, ungrateful, or dull-witted.
Service to the teacher, discernment regarding the meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures,
the performance of those prescribed duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech.
Avoiding the sight of, and contact with, women; perceiving the self as being one with all beings;
renouncing possessions; and wearing worn-out saffron robes.
The restraint of the senses from their objects, the avoidance of sloth and laziness, the thorough examination of the body, and the perception of evil in worldly activities.
Purity of *sattva* through the absence of *rajas* and *tamas*, freedom from desire, and tranquility—
purified by these means, he indeed becomes fit for immortality.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the brother is the embodiment of Indra; and the mother is the very body of the Earth.
Compassion is his sister, Dharma is his very self,
the guest is Agni personified, and all living beings are his own body.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is the embodiment of the Earth; and one’s own brother is the embodiment of oneself.

The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master of the world of Prajāpati; the guest is the lord of the world of Indra; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods.

The two teachers, Droṇa and Bhūriśravas, who were filled with the power of arrows; Droṇa’s son, Aśvatthāman, who was his equal; and Bhīṣma, the father of his father—in archery, Karṇa, Duryodhana, and the others are not their equals.

Thus, while the hearts of the Kauravas were agitated by thoughts of how he might be slain, the son of Pāṇḍu, the enemy of Khāṇḍava, stands victorious in the assembly, possessing pillar-like arms that shine with splendor.
Accumulating day after day manifest sequences of monasteries, capturing even the heart of Arundhatī with the moist beauty of his gentle smile,
and extending that priceless state which is praiseworthy for the eyes of the Unborn One— the sovereignty of the breasts of the beauties of Vraja unfolds as bliss.
O twice-born ones, unwholesome karma that has been practiced leads to the experience of its results;
for does a snake with its neck encircled ever depart without having bitten?
Kissed with joy by the best of lovers, the lovely chin of that passionate woman shines like a bud in the midst of a beautiful pair of lotuses of the erotic sentiment, appearing like a bee.
Having kissed her bimba-like lower lip, embraced her creeper-like body, and touched the curve of her cheek,
the lover took sandalwood paste in his hand and startled the lotus-eyed woman.

O Mother, remembering day after day your limbs—the auspiciousness of the world—from the crest to the feet, I am tossed by successive waves of the ocean of bliss; thus, I do not take account of the days that have passed.
When the earth and light are shrouded, there remain only these two: the mind, which is immeasurable by the activity of the god of love, and the self; for others, darkness is the tenth substance.

Now, even the names of time, space, and direction have been cast aside at the onset of the rains; the only substance is water, its quality is the roar of clouds, and its action is the movement of water.
"Why do you cover your sprout-like lower lip with a cloth, O charming girl?
It is only when wounded that the lips and breasts of a hero shine so beautifully."

Who on earth does not marvel at this Lord of Mountains, who stands having ascended the earth with his lofty and vast peaks, whose garment of the quarters is spread wide, and upon whose summit the tip of the moon’s cool rays slips away?

Having covered this great cloth of flowers with masses of new clouds that possess the hue of agallochum smoke and resemble the necks of domestic pigeons swirling within, he seems to be perfuming his own limbs.
Having plucked a fresh kadamba blossom from her beloved— a great sign of the rainy season that brought an end to his expeditions— the wives of his enemies,
overjoyed, kissed it, placed it upon their eyes, set it upon their hearts, somehow fixed it in their hair-partings, and finally made it an ear-ornament.

Only that one enemy of Kaiṭabha— who previously had his fortune snatched away from right here and was sleeping here itself in the bliss of confidence— truly knows the great-mindedness of the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters.

I believe the world was protected by that act of his body being offered to the enemy of serpents—a deed which, by its very nature, severed the birds' longing for the taste of devouring the circles of snakes.
For if the earth had been swallowed by Garuḍa, where would there be a support? Where would the oceans be, where the mountains, and where these guardians of the quarters?
When Fortune departed like the water from a coconut fruit,
she emerged like a wood-apple fruit swallowed by an elephant.
Whether from birth until death, a crow may practice asceticism or perform penance;
yet it will not produce even a single sweet warble like the lovely song of the cuckoo.
From birth until death, let a crow practice asceticism or perform penance;
yet what can it do? It can only utter a single cry like a peacock or sing the fifth note like a cuckoo.
That the bee *milinda*, who has roamed at will through the groves of wish-fulfilling trees since birth, should have approached the *kuṭaja* tree out of curiosity—
this very result is most fitting for that action, in that he has now attained equality with honey-bees.
O dust of base birth, tell me truly: have you performed even the slightest act of virtue since your birth?
You have been raised up for this very purpose by that wicked one who has fire as his charioteer; therefore, fulfill it and defile this entire world!
From birth until now, those various actions of yours, delightful with their excellence at every moment,
and those charming and sweet endearments— now remembered, they burn my body and tear my heart asunder.
The word of that person who has not learned deceit since birth is authoritative for people; let those who study the deception of others as "knowledge" indeed be the ones whose speech is trustworthy.
From birth, there has been no other supreme friend for me than this poverty that persists as if innate;
yet, O Lord, disregarding my own immediate destruction, you have swiftly made me rich with the wealth of merit through taking refuge in you.

O lotus-faced one, it is improper that you alone should drink the funeral water offered by your kinsmen, when you have lived with me since birth and even drank from my mother’s breast together with me.
From birth, his devotion was fixed [on the Sun], and having no other protector, he was appointed to the task of charioteer due to his skill;
yet even Varuṇa has not obtained the two feet from the Sun even to this day—for indeed, desired things do not come to pass without merits.

A lifelong celibate, whose fame for victory over the circle of kings was concealed by the rows of scars from the bowstring shining upon the stone-pillar-like arms of his enemies; sharpening his arrows upon the surface of his chest, hardened by the calluses of wounds from thick weapons; the son of Jamadagni has arrived, eager for the hunt of wild elephants in the forest that is the assembly of the kṣatriyas.

May the son of Vāyu grant you long-lasting welfare—he who has been a celibate since birth; who is like the great fire of time to the entire host of his enemies; who is the end of the eon yet the creator of the eon; whose body possesses the luster of a golden monkey; who moves at will and bestows all desires; who is beloved and a kinsman to the enemy of Kāma (Śiva); who is the ornament of the monkey clan; who is wrathful yet possesses tender limbs; and who is the messenger of the son of Kauśalyā.
Due to her consumption of poison from birth, the girl has been turned into poison;
she kills by touch, exhalation, and so forth, but this is the method for testing her.

O slender-waisted one, who in former times, persevering from birth and propitiating the flower-armed god with hundreds of sacrifices, performed the abandonment of the body at the pilgrimage site of Prayāga—
for whose sake, O friend, you gaze along the path with necks turned toward the intervals where the falling tears of your trembling eyes, like lotus stalks, spill forth?
Crookedness is innate to both the villain and the plow;
of these two, only patience is capable of enduring the insults of the fool.
Even a friend who has been served since birth and nurtured with gifts and honors may at that moment turn into an enemy because of harsh words;
for it is impossible to extract the thorn of sarcastic speech from the mind.
These trees that have stood here since their birth are uprooted from your banks; these waves, though fragile as a moment, are driven to the highest heights.
Within you lies a collection of stones, yet on the outside even the fragrant trees are falling away. O brother Śoṇa, there is no one who does not laugh at the ruin of your prosperity.
"Even though this stalk has accompanied it since birth, the lotus turns its face away from it;
for such is generally the way of those possessed of fortune toward those who are full of virtues."

From birth, he is nothing but darkness; his friendship is crookedness; from his mouth issues forth speech that destroys entire villages; and for the most part, his refuge is the tree of a cremation ground.
Fie, O Creator! Why was that same filthy and cruel owl created? Or rather, why was a lifespan lasting until the end of the aeon assigned to him by you as something fixed?
His arms reach down to his knees; he has a neck like a conch shell, is strong, and possesses four canine teeth.
He is a treasure-house of fortune, broad-chested, eats light and sweet food, and has eyes like lotus petals.
The army of King Coḍa became like a fierce forest fire of moving form in that great forest crowded with horse-deer and filled with rutting elephants as its sturdy trees.

Their livelihood consists of the art of feigned affection; there is no fault in their lack of virtue, nor does widowhood trouble them, because they have reversed the distinction between the good and the bad. In doing whatever they please, the theft of others' property causes them no shame, nor is there any fear of the king—alas, how happily courtesans live!
For great-souled ones, their affections last only as long as life, their anger is momentary, and their renunciations are free from attachment.
Affection lasts until the end of life, while anger is momentary; moreover, the renunciations of great-souled ones are free from attachment and never cease.
Since both affection and aversion serve to destroy one's livelihood,
how indeed could those two ever exist toward anyone?
A king should be like the rain-cloud, providing the means of subsistence for all living beings;
those who find no livelihood abandon him, just as birds desert a dried-up lake.
He who lives off one state while depending upon another finds no security from it, just as a virtuous wife finds none from a paramour.

O King, O protector of the earth, O subduer of enemy clans, when the earth is rent asunder by the playful stamping of the sharp hooves of your rows of horses in battle, the fire of the netherworld (Pātāla) would surely consume the entire universe, were it not for the streams of tears from the eyes of the wives of rival kings, which, like torrents of rain, would swiftly extinguish it.

Having received the command of King Manmatha, the sovereign of the mind, this illustrious merchant named Spring, bold and free from hesitation, frequents the forest groves where fallen leaves serve as carpets; there, with the songs of cuckoos as his invitations to the great public of wandering bees, he carries on his trade with the wealth of floral nectar.
I am her obedient servant, enduring both her blows and her insults; yet she, though cool with virtue, does not even know how to speak anything other than what is pleasing.
Command, a plaintive tone, a request, a rebuke, laughter, and even feigned weeping—
meditating upon such mastery in the art of lovemaking, I am not yet satiated with her.
Command, fame, protection of the Brahmins, charity, enjoyment, and the preservation of friends—
if these six qualities do not manifest in them, what purpose is there in their seeking refuge with a king?
The authority of kings is their majesty, and that is established in their speech;
whatever they may say, whether it be false or true, that is the law for those engaged in legal proceedings.
"You will give the command; you will place it upon the head of your beloved—why do you hasten?
O charming girl who scorns the improper time, do not let our love have its sprout broken."
A king should not tolerate even his own sons if they disobey his commands;
what indeed is the difference between a living king and a king depicted in a painting?
Disobedience to the commands of kings, disrespect toward Brahmins,
sleeping separately from one's wife, and killing without the use of weapons— these are [the punishments].
Having received a great command and swiftly completed the excavation of the enemies' foundations, he— having regained the favor of his countenance,
his appearance being applauded with loud joy— the fortunate one bows at the lotus feet of his lords.
Sovereignty has as its fruit merely the power of command; asceticism has as its fruit celibacy;
knowledge has as its fruit mere understanding; and wealth has as its fruit giving and enjoyment.
Placing the command of the Sage upon your head, O Vindhya mountain, remain still; for you who desire such a lofty position, this [command] must never again be transgressed by you.
What hardship could there even be in the mere contact of your cheek as he swallows you—he who drank the ocean that provided a dwelling place for Maināka and other mountains?

Victorious is that illustrious Rājanārāyaṇa, whose majesty is universally esteemed: by whom commands have been placed upon the crowns of kings, fear and affliction in the hearts of the wicked, and love among the virtuous; by whom incomparable fame has been bestowed everywhere in all directions; by whom the entire kingdom has been made free of thorns and the prosperity of enemies destroyed.
That power which exists at the head of all beings in the form of a command is to be known as the power of the Lord (prabhu-śakti), arising from the greatness of its sovereign influence.

His command is cherished by the crest-jewel of Śakra; the scriptures are his new eyes; his devotion is fixed upon the wielder of the Pināka bow, the Lord of Beings; his abode is the divine city of Laṅkā;
his birth is in the lineage of Brahmā—oh, such a suitor as this is not easily found! Yet, were he not Rāvaṇa, for where indeed can all virtues be found everywhere?
He who abandons a wife who is obedient, skillful, the mother of heroes, sweet-spoken,
and free from visible faults, shall go to an inexhaustible hell.
Is she the command of the enemy of Śambara, which cannot be transgressed; or is she desire personified, come under the sway of my eyes?
Does she approach the market for some other purpose, or does she bring a message from that lotus-eyed one?
The cultivation of poetry produces clarity in worldly transactions, supreme rectitude of intellect,
and even independence within the technical treatises.

Though you serve as a maidservant on the courtyard grounds of kings—filled with elephants, horses, and foot soldiers—and though your body is bent over a *śāṭī* garment while holding a fresh betel-roll in your mouth;

yet, O moon to the mass of matted hair intensely reddened by the row of jewels upon their crowns, you who possess the splendor of a rutting elephant smeared with sandalwood paste, worship Śiva, who is praised by the young wives of the gods.
Even though that speech of a poet may spread, sporting at the outset with great ostentation, it nevertheless does not provide delight to the minds of the wise,

so long as there is no aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— resounding with the tinkling of abundant and beautiful qualities and ornaments, and following in the wake of a downpour of the essence of flowing, shimmering nectar.
Even when remembered with the enthusiasm inspired by wealthy patrons dwelling in one’s heart,
the tongue feels as if it is being pulled inward and does not proceed toward poetry.
What is the use of giving for one who is wealthy? What is the use of food for one who is well-fed? What is the use of the moon to one who is cold? What is the use of clouds at the onset of winter?
O bull of the Bharatas, the food of the wealthy consists primarily of meat, that of the middle class is dominated by dairy products, and that of the poor consists mostly of oil.
The receipt of offerings from wealthy men and the slippery path leading to their dwellings—
these two things disturb the minds of the twice-born who follow the royal camp.
Whether wealthy or poor, suffering or happy,
blameless or flawed— a friend is the supreme refuge.
One should indeed kill an approaching assassin without hesitation;
by that very act of killing, one is delivered from the hell resulting from that evil deed.
One may strike down even one who has mastered the Vedānta if he approaches as an assassin intent on killing; by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.
With their sharp tips reaching from afar and swiftly spreading the sound of their feathered edges in all directions,
they first drank the blood of the soldiers' lifeless bodies, and afterwards, it was drunk by the multitudes of arrows.
To those ignorant of the heat of the sun, even the thousand-rayed sun becomes like the moon;
and to those possessed by passion, the mark of the moon appears as a spot with the luster of a fragment of sapphire.
If a tree is unable to endure the heat, becomes pale, loses its branches repeatedly,
and bears fruit out of season, it is of a pitta-nature and is emaciated.

In the heat of the sun, together with his mate, the bird who was separated from her during the night could not endure the rays of the moon; for when the mind is afflicted by grief, everything becomes unbearable.
O Destroyer of Mura, for the sake of speed across the ocean, I take hold of your boat; you make this non-bargain here, for there is no trust in a professional boatman.
O Goddess, I am pale and wish to remove with my head this coppery hue produced by lac upon your feet;
yet, O compassionate one, I would be able to remove the redness born of the eclipse of anger from the orb of your moon-like face only if you were so moved by pity.
The rays of the sun are copper-red; the trees possess young leaves and bark; and the creepers are graced with the fragrance and beauty of flowers resembling stars.
In this season, the southern breeze blows, fragrant with the masses of pollen falling from the mango trees shaken by the path of bees intoxicated by spring.
As the arrow was swiftly drawn from the corner of the eye of the one possessed by wrath, who shone with a coppery luster,
a stream gushing forth from the frontal globe of the elephant-king appeared, as it were, like a flow of blood.

I behold that visible splendor, beautiful with the gentle movement of His lotus feet, amidst the women of Vraja who have become radiant with the overflowing divine pastimes recounted in song; they are bathed in the nectar-like play of the waves of light from His copper-hued, long eyes, and He gazes with a slightly smiling moon-like face adorned with drops of perspiration.

May Hari protect you—he who, while frightening his beloved who was angered by the words, "Fie! Who knows the mind of a woman?", was touched by her eyes which at that moment became tremulous with fear; for her eyes were copper-red, her heavy breasts heaved, her breath did not cease, and her face was bristling with drops of perspiration, yet no cause for this could be discerned.
The lips, when worshipped, are slightly copper-colored, licking, and soft-skinned;
the tongue is red and slender, and a red palate is praised.

Just as a glance cast upon a beloved at the first breaking forth of youth does not allow any other person standing in the midst of the assembly to attain its full attention, so too [is the case here].
One should provide hospitality for Brahmins in one's home every day;
in the hospitality of Rantideva, there were a hundred cows for each *madhuparka* offering.
A knower of yoga who has accomplished his purpose should never go to a guest-offering, a funeral rite, a sacrifice, a procession for the gods, a festival, or among a great crowd.
Where can there be sleep for one who is ill, for one who is terrified, or for one who is indignant; nor for one who is brooding over wealth, or again, for one who is filled with desire?
Taking wealth from the sick and fleeing from the dead—this is the "medical skill" of a physician; a physician is not the master of life.
When one is ill, the physician is a father; when one has recovered, he is a kinsman. Once the disease has departed and health is restored, the physician becomes a protector.
There is no restrictive rule for one who is ill, nor for a child, nor likewise for an old man; and for one who delights in the conduct of others—this is the eternal dharma.
Fearing it might be a fish, the timid woman with tremulous eyes, desiring to release the water she had repeatedly taken up,
let fall from her cupped hands the water which was marked by the reflection of her own eyes.
When she was unable to cover her breasts with her sprout-like arms because her garment had been snatched away, I immediately fastened it around her chest as an upper cloth.
But when his hand reached her hips, the god of love—who is heavy with the weight of fainting—then rescued me as I was sinking into an ocean of shame.
O King, when the emerald *sīmantaratna* has been taken, the golden ear-leaf (*tāṭaṅka*) stolen, the girdle (*mekhalā*) snatched away, and the pair of jeweled anklets (*maṇitulākoṭi*) suddenly seized;

then, in the forest, the *śabaras* do not take away the necklace of the fleeing deer-eyed wives of your enemies—mistaking it for a string of *guñjā* berries because of the red glow of their bimba-like lips.
One's own duty is a great task, not merely that of another;
through the failure to fulfill one's own duty, a person falls into the well.
Driven by the god of love, women act according to their own will;
they do not feel burned even as they walk upon scorching-hot sands.
One does not perceive one's own faults, yet sees the faults of others;
if one perceives the faults of others, one does not see one's own faults.
O Fire, you may indeed burn the lineage that is the source of your own birth;
but alas, O Fire, why do you burn even these who are standing right here before you?
Having projected the afflictions caused by his children and others upon himself, the fool-minded man,
though unable to remedy them, grieves excessively in old age.
One who knows the Self, is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has conquered the senses,
performs dharma, and is learned in the Vedas and sciences— such a person of sattvic nature attains birth as a deity.
Self-knowledge, diligent application, endurance, and constancy in dharma—
he who is not drawn away from these goals is indeed called wise.
Knowledge of the self, lack of exertion, forbearance, constancy in dharma,
guarded speech, and generosity— these, O Bhārata, do not exist among the lowest classes.
One who knows the Self is blessed because of his father and grandfather; a base man attains renown through his mother's side and his mother.
One who does not know the reality of the self creates much elaboration;
he alone goes to his destruction, like the water inside a coconut shell.
O Brahmin, it is not possible for embodied beings to eat the flesh of their own bodies;
tell me what is appropriate, from which satisfaction may arise.
All people, by their own faults, bring themselves to the mouth of suffering;
I believe there was some misdeed of yours for which this atonement has been made.
From hatred of oneself comes death; from hatred of others, the loss of wealth;
from hatred of the king, ruin; and from hatred of a Brahmin, the destruction of the family.
If you do not desire for others those things that are disagreeable to yourself,
then turn your mind away from doing what is disagreeable to others.
A person does not find pleasure in themselves through another, nor indeed through themselves alone; for I perceive that you, whose desires remain unfulfilled, have a face clouded with anxiety.
Having observed his own power, he who proceeds with pride and enthusiasm may slay even many enemies alone, just as Bhārgava did to the Kṣatriyas.
In defending oneself, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, and in coming to the aid of women and Brahmins, one who kills in accordance with dharma incurs no guilt.
Your arm, which brings glory to you and causes the majesty of yourself and others to flourish, strikes fear into both your enemies and your friends, O King.
He who, having observed the relative strength and weakness of himself and others,
does not perceive any difference between them, is held in contempt by his enemies.
One who is fickle toward his own self cannot exist; how then could he exist for others?
Therefore, a fickle person undoubtedly destroys all undertakings.
The supreme king perceives faults in both himself and his subjects;
he first restrains himself, and thereafter his servants and then his subjects.
One should seek the self by means of the self, with the mind, intellect, and senses restrained;
for the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
When one's self is joined with what is harmful, the mind enters into evil;
having performed that defiled action, one is cast into great affliction.
One who desires long life should not utter his own name, nor the name of his teacher, nor the name of one who is extremely wretched, nor the names of his eldest child or his wife.
Suffering is created by oneself; happiness is created by oneself.
Beginning from the time one lies in the womb, that which was produced in previous bodies is experienced.
Through its own destruction, it does not rise; through its hole, it becomes full once more. Do you not see the water-pot sinking again and again?
One should eliminate an enemy by means of an enemy who has been brought under one's own control,
just as one removes a thorn stuck in the foot with another thorn held in the hand.
Self-reproach and self-praise, as well as the reproach of others and the praise of others—
these four kinds of conduct are not practiced by the noble ones.
Virtues attend upon oneself, prosperity arises, and calamities cease;
since this results in manifold fruits, why indeed should one not seek the company of the noble?

Being yourself an expert in discerning virtues and faults regarding matters to be done, do you not know? That nevertheless you do not consult your elders—this is the reason why this sequence [of events] has occurred.
For a person, especially, the self alone is one’s own teacher,
since it is through direct perception and inference that one attains the highest good.
Neither father nor mother remains for the sake of one's own companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—only Dharma remains.

One who, without knowing his own strength, desires that which is unattainable and devoid of both dharma and artha because of his pursuit of inaction (naiṣkarmya), is called "foolish-minded" in this world.
One who desires his own prosperity, or one who is being oppressed by another,
should indeed initiate hostilities if he is endowed with the advantages of place, time, and strength.
Parrots and mynas are bound because of the faults of their own mouths;
cranes are not bound therein—for silence is the means to accomplish all goals.
"She is half of one's self"—this is the Vedic teaching; she protects one's wealth, progeny, body, worldly affairs, dharma, heaven, the sages, and the ancestors.
Where is that bird-thief who brought about his own destruction, by whom this first act of theft was committed in the very house of the protector?
Acting as if he were undergoing a transformation of his own self, he should bestow what is desired;
like water, he should break through mountain-like enemies while remaining unobserved.
O brother, if you indeed desire to wander upon the path to the eternal city, then provide yourself with every means of protection by donning the armor of self-restraint.
Otherwise, the thieves of the senses will forcibly seize the jewel of discernment from your mind, having pierced it with hundreds of sharp-pointed, flashing spears of anxiety.
One does not have as much trust even in oneself as one has in the virtuous;
therefore, everyone desires friendship especially with the virtuous.
How truly fitting it was for this king—who had elevated his own virtues—that he spared the other limbs of his enemies;
for while his arrows, effective in battle, shattered limb after limb, they did not strike the heart that harbored great pride, nor the shoulder that failed to bow.
The dual policy of counsel regarding ministers, which leads only to the destruction of one's own side and the rise of the enemy's side, cannot lead to prosperity in this world.
He who abandons his own side and takes delight in the factions of others is destroyed by his enemies, like the foolish blue-colored jackal.
One's own father and brothers, as well as one's wife, sons, and enemies;
likewise the daughter-in-law, mother-in-law, co-wife, sister-in-law, and brother-in-law.
Renowned for the virtues of his own self, his father, and his mother, he was the most excellent of the excellent;
he was celebrated for the qualities born of himself, as well as those derived separately from his paternal and maternal lines.
He who possesses within himself these three— firm self-realization and dispassion—
is alone the leader of all subjects, for he is the locus of all the virtues of the wise.
Self-praise is death, as is the disparagement of others;
nevertheless, O descendant of Kakutstha, I shall speak: there is no monkey equal to me.
The world honors that man who praises himself, who is wicked, audacious, and prone to reviling others, and who wields the rod of punishment everywhere.

Self-conceit and the pursuit of pleasure, especially the conceit of being a teacher, lead to ruin; the conceit of superiority over others leads to destruction, and the mind set on women brings about total dissolution.

Through the perception of [the deity] as oneself, one becomes happy; through the perception of [the deity] as a guru, especially so. Through the perception of [the deity] as many, there would be destruction; through the perception of [the deity] as a woman, there would be dissolution.
A man whose own wealth is exhausted who is supported by the property of a woman is, in effect, a woman; and a woman who supports herself is, in effect, a man.
A wise person must always first ensure their own protection;
for it is said that the livelihood of those who depend on a king is like [dwelling] in fire.
Fire may burn only a single part of the body, or it may pass on to others;
but the king may either destroy [the offender] along with his sons and wife, or he may spare him.
For those who protect themselves through their treatises and act with thorough discernment,
no calamities arising from their own faults shall befall them.
Delighting in oneself, extreme deceitfulness, abandoning virtuous people and kinsmen, placing trust in an enemy, devotion to a woman— censure of such a person will surely follow.
Even when they cry out in competition with the peacocks,
do these wretched crows know how to produce the *kekā* call?
One should always look upon even a worm or an ant as one's own self;
one should not do to others what is disagreeable to oneself.
He who looks upon all beings as himself, upon the property of others as a clod of earth,
and upon the wives of others as his own mother— he truly sees.
For those of peaceful mind who see all beings as themselves,
seeing everything as non-different from their own self— who is the giver, and what is given?
Having abandoned one's own group, if one takes refuge in another group,
one goes to ruin by oneself, just as a king does through unrighteousness.
Those who, having abandoned their own group, take delight in the groups of others—I weep for them like a traveler; yet they do not weep for themselves.
Those who abandon their own group and take delight in the groups of others—
all of them perish, just like King Kukardama.
But one who possesses self-mastery, even if his territory is small, being endowed with the excellence of his constituent elements and skilled in policy,
surely conquers the entire earth and does not decline.
For one who has sold his soul, who is impotent, whose mind is ever suspicious,
and who is constantly tormented by separation from what is dear— what happiness can there be for such a beast of a servant?
That knower of the Self, though partaking in enjoyments day and night with her, incurred no sin;
for the one-pointed absorption in sense objects, once brought forth, does not stain one whose mind has been purified by knowledge.
Having obtained a king who is perfectly endowed with the qualities of self-perfection and who acts with propriety,
the world prospers like that of Mahendra.
Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride, they perform sacrifices under the guise of religion, yet out of hypocrisy and contrary to scriptural injunctions.
A kinsman is like a friend, being the protector of one's self, wife, wealth, and secrets;
Kubera is the giver of wealth, and Yama is the one who wields the excellent rod of punishment.
A friend who provides refuge for one's self, wife, wealth, and secrets during times of need is declared to be the highest; others are classified as friends of three, two, or one word [respectively].
Those men who do not speak falsehoods here— whether for their own sake or for the sake of others, or likewise out of playful jest— are destined for heaven.
Both the self and the body—these two are like friends;
yet, having abandoned the body as a friend, the self certainly departs.

Why, O self, do you vainly exert yourself for hundreds of births with the intent of acquiring wealth? Fortune comes to the home of the lame man by the will of fate, even though he has traversed the earth.
These various ways in which the root of human effort is destroyed—expelled by some, yet stubbornly clinging to the lazy—cause a delusion of the mind at every step for the simple-minded.
The self must always be conquered by the king, and thereafter his enemies;
for how can a king who has not conquered himself defeat his foes?
The wise say that a son is produced by the self through the self;
therefore, a man should look upon his wife as a mother and the son’s mother as his own mother.
For mortals whose bodies are under their own control and who sleep their own sleep,
even poor food serves as a means to immortality.

Having conquered that host of senses— which acts like a boar to lead the self astray onto a wrong path, which acts like a black serpent when the life-force of discernment between what ought and ought not to be done is destroyed, and which acts like a flashing axe in the act of hacking away at the grove of the trees of merit— be one who seeks auspiciousness.
Meditating with a vision that is eternally non-differentiated upon both himself and the entire world as consisting of the space of consciousness, the yogi attains the supreme goal.
He protects both himself and the other from great fear;
by not returning anger to one who is angry, he is the healer of both.
Fleeing in battle, one destroys both oneself and the enemy;
in flight, there is the loss of wealth, expenditure, ill-repute, and infamy.
Having observed both oneself and others, the wise person should exert themselves;
for this alone is true discernment: the knowledge of both self and other.
One who causes suffering to himself, to his religious duties, to his children and wife,
and to the deities, guests, and servants, is known as a miser.
One should not despise oneself on account of former failures; until death one should seek prosperity, nor should one consider it unattainable.
Having diligently disciplined the self through various restraints, the wise attain Dharma; happiness is not obtained from pleasure.

Fools indeed abandon that Self, which is supreme, unimpeded, and the object of knowledge that cannot be reached even by a multitude of means of valid cognition, even though it is revealed through the gaze of the Guru;
instead, they strive to understand it within the five measured sheaths, like those who have lost their elephant yet search for it by reaching their hands into other jars.
First, the king should establish himself in discipline;
then his sons, then his ministers, then his servants, and finally the subjects.
First, the king should establish himself in discipline;
then his ministers, then his servants, then his sons, and finally his subjects.
One should constantly cultivate oneself through wisdom and discipline;
then, when dying, there will be no regret.

They declare that the self, the counselor, the envoy, the words of the ministers, the sequence [of action], and the outward appearance as the sixth— this much constitutes the determination of counsel.
The self, the minister, the messenger, the secret, the sequence of the three ablutions,
and the outward appearance— they declare these six to be the determination of counsel.
One should always protect oneself, even at the cost of one's wife and wealth;
for a wife may be acquired again, wealth may be acquired again, but the body cannot be acquired again and again.
A king should protect himself by every means, and he should protect the earth;
for the wise say that all this has its root in oneself.
The wise one, having made himself steady and the target likewise steady, should pierce it in three ways; he is called a "steady-piercer."
The self, O Bhārata, is a river with sacred fords; truth is its water, fortitude its banks, and self-restraint its waves.
One who performs meritorious deeds is purified by bathing in it, for the self is eternally pure, being as water is always water.
The self is a river whose holy bathing places are self-restraint, whose water is truth, and which is endowed with virtue and concentration.
One who performs meritorious deeds bathes in it and purifies himself; the inner self is not purified by mere water.
For those who know the essence of the bliss of the Self, the study of treatises is quite enough;
for cakes must be eaten—what need is there to count their holes?
Grieve for yourself; why do you grieve for another? For your life is wasting away, whether you remain still or move about.

A man possessed by anger slays himself or another, abandons righteousness, commits evil, and rejects what is proper; he fails to honor those worthy of honor and utters censurable speech—indeed, what is there that such a man will not do?
Let the ocean dry up its very self, or let it drench the cosmic egg with its waves;
indeed, there is never any loss nor any gain for the cātaka bird, whose livelihood depends solely on the clouds.
For a person reveals himself through his own deeds, whether auspicious or inauspicious, performed according to his character and conduct;
likewise, even if his family lineage has perished, a person makes it manifest once again through his own actions.
You know yourself by yourself; you create yourself by yourself;
and by your own creative power, you dissolve back into yourself alone.
Beholding her own radiant form in the mirror’s surface, the large-eyed woman became hurried for Hara’s arrival; for the purpose of women’s attire is indeed the sight of their beloved.
He who first conquers himself by means of self-discipline will then not vainly seek to conquer his ministers and enemies.
First, one should desire for oneself alone to be endowed with virtues; once one is perfected in virtue, one may then examine others.
This self is not mine, nor is the entire earth mine;
with the understanding that "as it is for me, so it is for others," I have no distress.
The self, through effort, presides over the mind for the sake of objects;
from the conjunction of the self and the mind, activity arises.
Do not say that the infinite, indivisible, and singular bliss called the Self is equal to the pleasure produced by rituals such as sacrifices;
for to think so is like comparing a potter’s pit to a mine of jewels.
The self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*) are called the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by those who know that science;
from these two, together with effort, volition (*saṃkalpa*) arises.
The self, the intellect, the sense organs, and their objects are called the external instruments;
its accomplishment is proclaimed to be through volition and determination.
For both of these instruments are traditionally held to follow immediately upon effort;
therefore, by restraining effort, one should cultivate the state of being without mind.
When a collection of virtues depends upon oneself, the lack of such virtues is a matter for reproach;
but when wealth depends upon fate, what indeed is there for men to be blamed for?
This Self has entered into the self, residing in the heart, exceedingly subtle and to be grasped by an unwavering mind through constant application.
Since whatever one contemplates, that one attains identity with—it is for this reason that young women have gone to their beloveds.
For one who does not have self-control, how can there be control over other people? Having brought oneself under control, one holds the three worlds under control.
"One must protect oneself with great effort, for success in battle is fickle.
Having all accepted these words of their master, those of great prowess [prepared themselves].

Those who delight in the Self, whose pleasure is established in unwavering meditative absorption, whose knots of darkness are severed by the overflow of knowledge, and who are devoted to pure being— how can this one, blinded by delusion, know that ancient God whom they behold as something beyond both darkness and light?
In this world of living beings, what man does not live for his own sake?
Only he who lives for the sake of helping others truly lives.
He who kills animals for his own sake will inevitably go to hell; however, one who eats meat after having properly honored the gods and ancestors incurs no fault.
For those who act for their own sake, who have acquired wealth through rightful means, who divide the circle of their friends,
and who have transcended worldly conventions, there is no bondage whatsoever, anywhere.
For an object is dear because it serves the self, not because it is dear in itself;
for the self alone is always the dearest to everyone. Therefore, the self is eternal bliss, and there is never any suffering for it.
For the sake of one's own self, one should abandon one's lineage, as well as kingdom, jewels, and wealth;
indeed, even by relinquishing all possessions, one should protect oneself by means of the self.
He by whom the self is indeed restrained—that restrainer is preeminent.

If it is accepted that devotion (*bhakti*) is the bond of feeling (*bhāvabandha*) which one extends toward You after having correctly realized that the Self is the same for all worlds, then our desired goal is accomplished; let the qualifier be superfluous, and let the qualified term alone suffice for us.
The self unites with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with its own object; such is this rapid sequence.
This indeed is the conjunction of the mind—what is there that is inaccessible to it? Wherever the mind goes, there the self has gone.
Having first reflected that the self exists as the support of all worlds, one should subsequently engage in the investigation of reality; for painting can only exist when there is a wall.
For all who have taken a wife, the wife is indeed their very self.
On ground that is uneven, he places his own foot before him; fearing her fatigue, he plucks flowers from the tree with his own hand.
Moreover, on a bed fashioned of deerskin, Śiva sleeps, holding his beloved—who is languid with the weight of inner love—upon his own limbs.

Father’s very self has been born as Cupid, who is likewise endowed with four arms; for are not her two ear-lobes the strings upon the bows of his eyebrows, and are not her flattened ears portions of the bamboo bark?
The Self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the Self.
For the Self indeed produces the connection with karma for these embodied beings.

"The self alone is the burden"—thus, what limbs could that indolent person who places it upon you employ for the sake of surrender? For here, in this attainment of trust characterized by its own unique definition, this very [surrender] is the entirety of the possessor of limbs (the body).
If the self itself does not restrain itself from harmful things, who else is there to act for one's welfare? Therefore, the self must restrain itself.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self. Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self;
the self alone is the witness of the self, both for what has been done and for what has not been done.
Self-exaltation and the defeat of others—this much constitutes policy; by embracing this duality, the wise attain the status of masters of speech.
Men who are clever at benefiting themselves do not take account of the hardships of living in the teacher's house;
for how great indeed is the pain of piercing the ear when it is to be adorned with an ear-ornament?
That man who indeed treats all beings as he himself,
who has laid aside the rod of punishment and conquered his anger, prospers in happiness after death.
He who, by comparison with himself, considers an evil person to be a speaker of truth,
is himself deceived by that very person, just as the Brahmins were by the goat.
O Arjuna, he who, by means of the analogy of his own self, sees equality everywhere—
whether it be pleasure or pain— that yogi is considered supreme.
Constantly acquiring the arts correctly day by day, the lord of the earth increases like the moon moving through the bright fortnight.
A man gains respect in the royal assembly through wealth,
just as a brave warrior gains victory in battle against his enemies through valor.
"O friend, you who possess qualities worthy of honor have been placed upon the head by that great one;
yet this fault of yours—your wavering—is like that of a banner atop a palace."
Just as one praises a wealthy person with devotion out of a desire for wealth, if one were to praise the Creator of the Universe in that same way, who would not be liberated from bondage?

One should always win over the world through respect, sincerity, valor, generosity, and learning; by rising to greet others and approaching them, by speaking with a joyful smile, and by performing acts of service with a pure intention.
From the moment she was seen, that beauty of the world of the gods entered my heart,
having made a path for herself by the unfailing flight of the arrow of the god whose banner is the sea-monster.
How could he not have given this lunar orb as a mirror, the golden mountain as a palace, and the sun as a lamp to the mendicant, just as he gave the earth?
We know that the descendant of Bhṛgu, his lotus-eyes overflowing with the waters of joy sprouting from his desire to give, did not perceive any of that at all.
One should take what is to be taken and not give what is to be given; one should speak pleasant words that are meaningless.
One should make a hope appear timely and join the time with an obstacle.
Even when a flower is merely glanced at once, her fingertips turn crimson; even by the mere report of dyeing her feet with lac, the soles of her feet suddenly become red;
even the memory of anointing her limbs brings extreme distress; alas, for this woman of unsteady gaze, everything else—even the fragrance of her hair—becomes a burden.
He who, acting with haste, performs the taking from the quiver, as well as the aiming, drawing, and releasing of the arrow,
will achieve swiftness in aiming through the power of constant practice.
Some [plants] remove the torment of poison through their taking up, drinking, or application as a paste;
yet a certain medicinal creeper, remaining right there in the assembly, brings one back to life.
Taking what is not given causes displeasure, while giving causes pleasure;
at the proper time, the practice of bestowing desired objects is highly praised.
Having taken taxes from the wealthy, you rain [wealth] even upon the Kīkaṭas;
like a rain-cloud, having drunk water from the oceans, you pour it out upon the dry lands.
Salutations to him of the uneven gaze, who, taking up the immovable bow and making the string unimpaired, shattered the target with a variegated arrow that never misses.
Having taken up his staff, this mendicant Sun wanders through all directions;
now, as if plunging into the ocean, he has donned the saffron robes of the twilight clouds at evening.
O fortunate one, by giving you your garment while taking back no small amount of wealth,
the innocent washerwoman’s wife has been rendered penniless in just a few days.
If, having taken a leaf, a dog quickly goes ahead of the traveler carrying fresh *dūrvā* grass or fresh cow dung,
it certainly foretells royal favor.
Having taken up the masses of fame belonging to your adversaries within the crucible of the universe, and blowing them with your own intensely joyful fires of splendor without hindrance,
you have obtained— purified as if by such a process of smelting— the salt-free, brilliant fame of those preeminent in virtue, which is both concentrated and most exalted.

"O hunter, having taken all the flesh from my limbs except for my breasts, release me; grant me this favor. My young ones are perishing, unable to take mouthfuls of grass, as they are intent only on looking for my path."
Carrying the fragrance of *vakula* flowers and blinding the bees at every step,
this wind, purifying the waters of the Kāverī, approaches very slowly.
Having taken water from all around the mouths of rivers, what has this wicked ocean actually achieved?
It has merely rendered it salty, offered it as a libation into the submarine fire, and deposited it within the hollow depths of the netherworld.
That cloud which takes up water only to discard it again from whence it came is the foremost among the dull-witted;
but he who seeks to receive back that very same water he has emitted is the Lord of Rivers, a merchant-leader beyond reproach.
Even taking the property of a Brahmin, one may destroy those who strike at the kingdom;
indeed, having taken the bones of Dadhīci, Śakra slew the Daityas.

Having repeatedly picked up pearls, mistaking them for fire-crystals, and then picking up clusters of rubies, mistaking them for smoke, the Bhilla women—eager for the fragrance of their own lotus-like faces—began to cook them again and again with great haste in the enemy cities. What can we say of the flood of fame of that King Malla Śāha, which has whitened the entire earth?

Taking the sun-cup filled with nectar in her hand, which had the luster of a red lotus, and looking at it again, Indrāṇī cast the dark shadow of the sky upon it in anger; yet, thinking "it was given to the attendants without being purified," people praise that moon, white as it is released from her hand, saying, "It is nectar."
In the beginning my work was unformed; in the middle it was well-formed for me;
again it became disjoined, yet may he be the Lord who joins it together again and again.
At first you sprouted, then at every step you were covered with leaves; seeing you now laden with blossoms shimmering with fragrance, I am truly delighted.
But what shall I say when you have borne fruit so quickly? Alas, O *kimpāka*! Once again, your burden of thorns agitates me everywhere—what more can I say?

At first, her eyes—whose forms were smeared with a mass of collyrium—are now being treated by the fawn-eyed maiden as if they were the shafts of the god of love’s arrows: first heated by the fire of separation fanned by the breath of her sighs, and then immediately quenched with the water of her tears. She performs, at will, the act of mixing for the Lord whose mind is the field of passion.

May that association with the ignoble—which at the beginning is adorned with the beauty of hypocritical flattery and courtesy, which in the middle is honored by various flower-like words that bear no fruit, and which at the end is foul, loathsome, and stained by backbiting, lack of discipline, and contempt—remain far from you; for it is produced for the sake of false dharma and wealth.
First, the water from the vessel used for the ritual observances of the Primordial Grandfather; then, the purifying water from the feet of the Blessed One reclining upon the serpent;
and further, this daughter of the great seer Jahnu, the divine Bhāgīrathī, who adorns the matted locks of Śambhu and destroys all impurity—she is now seen.
First one should examine the lifespan, and afterwards the supreme physical marks;
for what purpose are the marks of men who are devoid of long life?
Those who, having first abandoned their duties, later seek to have them performed,
become objects of ridicule in the world, just like those who stole the onions.
First of all, rows of banners with staffs shimmering atop the heads of lordly elephants; behind them, a procession of royal tuskers supported by exceedingly fierce warriors;
then a dense mass of chariots marked by upraised standards; and following that, a line of horses triumphs on all sides together with the soldiers.
From the very beginning, a person should act in accordance with what is appropriate,
so that they do not later become joined with regret over a matter already past.
I pay homage to the two primordial poets, the four-faced one and the one born from the anthill— the lotus-born and the earth-born—
between whom there is no difference whatsoever, despite their distinct roles as the creator of the world and the creator of worldly renown.
Salutations to Him who brings about the beginning and the end of embodied beings, who is imperishable,
who always supports the earth below, and who stands even above Brahman.
The *āditāla* is *jayanta*, endowed with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
With words consisting of eleven syllables, it is supreme for increasing longevity.
That in which there is exactly one short syllable (*laghu*) is called *āditāla*.
The sun, the moon, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Indra, and others are not able to conquer those senses which cause such extreme suffering;
those who subdue these powerful and most difficult-to-conquer senses are the truly strong ones in this world.
May the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, as well as Rāhu and Ketu,
always bestow upon you wealth, grain, prosperity, long life, health, and auspiciousness.
The sun and the moon, wind and fire, heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama;
day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of a man.
Life is diminished day by day by the rising and setting of the sun; time is not perceived amidst activities heavy with the burden of many tasks.
Having seen birth, old age, misfortune, and death, the world does not feel terror; having drunk the intoxicating wine of negligence consisting of delusion, it has become like one who is insane.
For those who offer salutations to Āditya day after day,
poverty shall not arise throughout thousands of future births.
The rising of the sun, song, betel, the discourse of Sarasvatī,
a beloved wife, and a good friend— these are wonders that occur day by day.

"Are these ten suns that cause fear at the dissolution of the world? Or are they circles of meteors risen to burn the three worlds?"—thus thinking, the terrified hosts of gods drank in the sight of the hand of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow as he assumed the body of Narasiṃha; may those claws of his, red with the blood gushing from the chest of the arrogant Asura as it was torn open, protect you.

May the light of Sarasvatī—the light that shines more constantly than the sun, flows with nectar more than the moon, is the ornament of the three worlds more than a gem, and consumes darkness more than fire; which illuminates the universe more than the eyes and brings bliss to the heart more than the Supreme Brahman—be for the satisfaction of the world.
May all the planets beginning with the Sun, as well as the lunar mansions and the zodiac signs,
grant you eternal longevity, for whomsoever this birth chart is intended.
Just as all the planets, beginning with the Sun, are satisfied by gifts,
the son-in-law— the tenth planet— is not satisfied even by the gift of one's entire possessions.
Darkness was created for the sun; the summer’s scorching heat for the clouds;
and the fatigue of the road for the tree that provides relief to the weary traveler.
"O fools, this sun remains; show affection and do not fear!
The moment is multiform, and perhaps he may yet live."
May that Primordial Fish be victorious, who, with the waters exhaled by his very breath,
created the ocean in the sky and the sky within the great ocean.
Goodness exists toward a virtuous person from the beginning, through the middle, and to the end, but not toward another kind of person;
gold does not undergo a change of nature through cutting, heating, rubbing, or hammering.
I bow to Hari, who is without beginning, middle, or end, who is devoid of the ten states, who is ancient, who is without a second, and who resembles my own garment.
It does not undergo any transformation in its beginning, middle, or end;
for this very reason, kings gather together those of noble birth.
The reflection of the glory of the first kings, having found its mirror in literature, does not vanish of its own accord even in their absence; behold!
With forests of *kiṃśuka* trees everywhere bowed down with blossoms, shaken by the wind like blazing fires,
this earth now that the spring season has arrived shines like a newlywed bride clad in crimson silk.
It would be better for me to be bitten by a serpent—long, flickering, moving in a crooked course, radiant, a yogi, and possessing the luster of a blue lotus—than to be gazed upon by her eye.
For when one is bitten by a snake, there are physicians in every direction; but for me, who have been gazed upon by the eyes of this lovely-eyed girl, there is neither physician nor medicine.
From afar, her gaze was fixed upon the traveler; though the darkness deepened and the day’s light vanished, hope blossomed within the heart of that fawn-eyed woman and did not turn back.
Her body—its neck bent, its long hair falling from her withered vine-like arms—was carried by her circle of dear friends like a lifeless corpse.
May Lord Śaṅkara protect you— he who, out of respect for the angry Bhavānī, is habituated to binding her hands with a rosary and other such gestures during playful quarrels and the like.
Embraces marked by nail-scratches and kisses with the heavy impact of teeth— thus,
even in matters of love-making, desire alone is perverse, its fame built upon the very quality of extreme delicacy.

Having watched the path of her beloved as far as the range of her vision, the traveler’s wife grew despondent; when the paths were deserted at the close of day and darkness was creeping forth, she took a single step toward her home with sorrow. At that moment, fearing "he might have arrived," she turned her neck repeatedly and looked back again.
When that which is to be received, that which is to be given, and the duty that ought to be performed are not carried out quickly, Time drinks up their essence.

I know that after the Lord had long rendered the world destitute of any talk of beauty by burning the body of the Flower-Armed God, he finally took pity upon the world once again through the craftsmanship of your limbs.
First one should examine the family, then the learning, then the age; then character, wealth, and physical form; and finally, one should arrange the marriage regarding the country.
O friend, is that woman— who first takes one's hand and later ascends the region of the hips and waist,
bestowing the pleasure of caressing with the tips of her nails— not indeed a leprosy?
In the case of the virtuous, old age first arises in the mind and then in the body;
for the non-virtuous, however, it arises in the body and never in the mind.
Just as a shadow, though initially very long in the east, becomes much shorter thereafter,
so too should friendliness toward the wicked, though initially extensive, become much more limited.
First, one should establish affection through secondary suffixes (taddhita); immediately thereafter, one should establish affection through verbal suffixes (kṛt).
Having engaged in a discussion of shared principles, one who remains impartial should accomplish the welfare [of others].
In the beginning slender, then broad in the middle, and spreading wider at every step,
the friendships of the virtuous proceed like rivers— never turning back.
First one should examine the groom, then his wealth, and then his family;
if there is some defect in the groom, what is the use of wealth or family?

At first, while engaged in their occupations, they are like Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera; they are exceedingly arrogant, intoxicated by pride, swollen with vanity, intent on humiliating others, and extremely cruel.

But when fallen from those occupations, their feet bound by the fetters of the elephant-stable and tormented by clubs, they become exceedingly gentle—like sages devoted to tranquility and self-restraint—with long beards and dejected faces.
At first, however, [their actions] are very slow, and in the middle, they are of moderate intensity.
Beforehand, those who act with affection and associate with the highest of men.
Associations with the wicked are pleasant at first, but bitter in the middle, and lead to enmity in the end.
At first she shows herself bowing down, then as she moves she assumes an elevated posture;
though compliant, the sow yields only meager fruit after a long time.

Who on this earth, while properly investigating through hundreds of right and wrong methods the authority regarding the Dharma at the outset, its various types of injunctions and their exhaustiveness, the application, the sequence of prior and subsequent sections, the many kinds of extended application (*atideśa*) and analogical reasoning (*ūha*), as well as sublation (*bādha*), the common framework (*tantra*), and incidental application (*prasaṅga*), can— distinct from the Mīmāṃsakas— diligently protect the Veda?
First is the salutation, followed by words of aspiration;
then comes the praise of well-spoken verses, and thereafter the eulogy of the poet and his poetry.
First humble, then arrogant, and harsh at the time of business,
but humble again once the task is accomplished— the merchant is like a penis.
At first humble, yet crooked again, intent on their own interests;
at the conclusion of their work they are once more crooked—such are the followers of Kāṇva, destroyers of life.
At first, one should not show favor to those who do not seek it; or if it has been granted, it must be nurtured every day.
To lift someone up only to cast them down brings shame; for one already standing on the ground, there is no fear of falling.
At first she neither desires nor abandons talk of love, languid and mixed with bashfulness; in the middle, she is devoid of shame; at the conclusion, her face is bowed down with modesty.
She performs a representation through manifold emotions, and being full of respect, she follows the nature of the man with various gestures, both weary and otherwise.
At first, this mango tree was adorned with variegated leaves; then it was marked with charming blossoms; and later, when the glossy fruits began to emerge, I watered it on all sides with rich juices.
Yet, solely through the power of fate, this very king of trees has been made to reel by the collisions of the flanks of wild elephants intoxicated by rut.

May the glance of Pārvatī at the auspicious marriage ceremony bring you welfare— a glance first tinged with love, eager for the movements of Hara’s face, then slowly rolling from the weight of shyness under the pretext of emitting smoke, and finally meeting her husband's gaze while agitated by a sudden turn away.
At the outset, the one who has made a wager and the one who is wagering should understand the underlying cause;
then, having deliberated on both sides, one should proceed according to what is deemed best.
First, the bathing garment, necklace, forehead mark, collyrium for the eyes, earrings, nose-jewel, jasmine garland, tinkling anklets,
foot-ornaments, sandalwood paste applied to the body, clusters of gems, small necklaces, tiny bells, betel, hand-bangles, and cleverness— these are the sixteen elements of erotic adornment.
First, the mother, the wife of the guru, the wife of a brāhmaṇa, the wife of a king,
a cow, a nurse, and likewise the earth— these seven are remembered as mothers.
At first, raised high by the heavy grasp of pride, and later reduced to thinness by the weight of remorse, she has been brought to extreme insignificance;
now, by following those dwelling within her lap, the shade of the tree clings to this earth as if it were a beloved mistress, embracing her with all her limbs.

First, there is the mention of the abode of aquatic creatures, followed by references to the ocean and its shores; then the description of the ocean of milk, the mention of rivers, and the accounts of the Ganges.
First red, then again red, and in the middle intensely radiant;
I take refuge in that visible one, whose power is difficult to behold, who is the seer himself.
"O restless-eyed one, at the beginning it is said that 'a certain king' was a monarch;
yet he was neither truly eternal nor even a king."
At the outset, she destroys beauty, makes one emaciated, and annihilates desire; she causes the dulling of wisdom, the exhaustion of ascetic merit, and the uprooting of dharma.
She causes division between son, brother, and wife, and cuts away the sprout of modesty. That hunger, the mother of all vices and the destroyer of life, torments me.
At first, she destroys beauty, makes one emaciated, and cuts away the sprouts of desire; she causes division between sons, friends, and wives, and severs the sprouts of pride.
She dulls passion, causes the wasting of ascetic merit, and uproots righteousness. Now, that hunger—which generates every disease and snatches away life—afflicts me.
In the beginning it causes shame, in the middle it brings contempt, and at the end it is empty;
tell me, is there anything at all that remains well-established in association with the wicked?
First, poverty is better than wealth;
likewise, first walking on foot is better than traveling in a vehicle. This is always conducive to happiness, while the opposite leads to suffering.
At first, having spread out their legs, lowered their necks, raised their faces, and struck repeatedly,
the calves drink from the teat with minds at ease as they lick the hindquarters of the udder while their mother turns her face away.
At first motionless with wonder, then trembling with trepidation, then bowed with shame for a moment, and then expanding with the desire to see;
drawn back by the sense of innate nobility yet impelled forward by love, the gaze of the fawn-eyed woman reached her beloved with great difficulty.
In the beginning she is a courtesan, then a servant, and later she becomes a procuress;
when all her means are exhausted, an old woman becomes devoted to her husband.
