"He who, in his infancy, was supported by the hand of the fire Hālāhala, who established a firm friendship with the light from Śambhu’s forehead, and who, having grown mature,
was taken into the inner circle even by Rāhu through the poison of his mouth— that very moon, thinking 'He scorches me with his rays,' has now approached me."
First was anger, then passion, thirdly the separation from you, fourthly the words of the female messenger for the sake of pacification, and fifthly the cool-rayed moon;
thus, O young girl, seeking only you as the fruit without end, alas, alas, she now serves five fires like a female ascetic.
This was the first moment of the Kali age, when the multitude of *bahūdaka* and *haṃsa* ascetics had been eclipsed;
for on that day, a one-eyed twice-born man was summoned with great respect to the presence of my father for his austerities, and alas, he was honored at every house.
With a mind fixed on the immediate present, they are fearless, thinking "tomorrow is far off";
lacking discernment, these all-devouring ones do not perceive the field of karma.
The first and last, as well as those beginning with and ending with them, and the two middle ones,
are the sons of Fire, Moon, Wind, and Varuṇa, possessing splendor equal to that of the Pitṛs.
Among these, each subsequent element acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever of them occupies a particular position in the sequence is traditionally held to possess that many qualities.

Victorious is the Sun, the seed of the universe and the elixir of Soma— the god who is the moon of the eastern mountain, the churner of the ocean of passion for the female *cakora* birds of darkness, the life-giver to the lotus, the crest-jewel of the king of mountains in Indra’s quarter, the director of Vedic rites, and the full oblation of fire to the grief of the night-lily.
When the first crowing of the cock reached her ears, the woman, having awakened, quickly glanced slightly toward the direction of Indra through the window;
then, impelled by fear yet restrained by love for her beloved, the unchaste woman repeatedly performed the acts of rising and reclining slowly upon the bed.

May he who is named Hema bestow prosperity—he whose body, when deprived of its beginning, is invisible in the water; when deprived of its middle, is to be described upon the earth; and when deprived of its end, resounds [as a bell].

On the first day of our separation, she bound her hair into a single braid, casting aside her wreath; at the end of the curse, when my grief has dissolved, that same braid—now as hard as stone—must be untwisted by me with my hand, as she repeatedly brushes it from the curve of her cheek with a finger whose nail is slightly marred by the touch.
In the first watch there shall be Śaṅkha, in the second Mahāśaṅkha;
in the third watch Padma, and in the fourth Mahāpadma.
May this manual, joined with a few initial verses composed by me as well as other [verses], be a bestower of joy upon virtuous people.
First is Adhruva, then Maṇṭha, Pratimaṇṭha, and Niḥsāruka;
then Aḍatāla, followed by Rāga and Ekatālī, which are thus recognized.

O Rāma, the first letter of your name, though situated at the end of a consonant group, bestows infinite and peerless fruit; the second, though belonging to the third class of consonants, produces liberation by its power; and the fourth, traveling as a guest upon the ear, grants the four aims of human life to those possessed of discernment—do not these few letters of your name spread wonder throughout the world?
"O King, all these monarchs have arrived from as far as the furthest islands; this maiden possesses a radiance as soft as gold, and she is the supreme prize of glory.
Alas, this great bow—neither drawn, nor notched, nor bent, nor raised from its place by anyone—leaves the surface of the earth devoid of heroes."
Mount Mandara derives joy from its limbs, which are scarred by the rows of marks left by the clusters of diamond-points on the armlets of the slayer of Danu’s son;
yet we now know that this mountain must have been even taller before the churning of the ocean, for its roots were worn away by the friction against the back of the supporting tortoise.
One who is unrighteous, miserly, averse to virtue, harsh in speech,
and of many minds— tell me, does such a person enjoy prosperity through human effort or through fate?

O lotus-eyed one, if you, who are full of false pride, think that I am angry with an innocent man, then let the lords indeed be angry; for before masters, it is generally easy to maintain the purity of one's own intentions.
But if you think thus, O proud woman, then consider: what woman other than you has ever been meditated upon by me as eternally dwelling within my mind on a painted canvas?

This entire world, from the Creator down to the smallest insect, possesses sight; yet this divine eye, unattainable by others, exists in both [the former and the latter], being supreme and difficult to endure:

in the plowshare of the Lord of Beings (Śiva), it is ever-vigilant in destroying the minor afflictions of the God of Love; and in the arrow of King Ballāla, the lord of the earth, it crushes the pride of rival kings.
Placing the lotus-stalk of her tender hand in sport, she conversed with her circle of friends;
then, with a gentle smile and a sidelong glance at me, that girl with eyes like those of a cakora bird swallowed my heart whole.
Having placed the churning stick into the milk-pot, the cowherd girl, her vine-like arms weary,
attributes the failure to obtain the *pārijāta* tree to a fault in fate.
Having quickly placed himself near [the fish] to inspire confidence through his calm demeanor, this crane—a master in the deceptive art—repeatedly desires to seize each individual minnow;
momentarily casting his eyes in all directions to signal indifference, and occasionally touching his body with his beak, he practices profound stillness.

O fools, why do you sink into this ocean of existence while carrying such a great burden on your heads in vain? Having placed the entire burden at the feet of your Mother, cross over this [ocean] with confidence, for it is like a mere puddle.
The foundation is said to be the *kanda*, and the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is the place of birth;
the navel is called *maṇipūra*, and one should pierce the heart as the *anāhata*.

The bases for its arising are the heart, the throat, the palate, the two nostrils, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of the head; concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is practiced in these ten locations.

The earth exists for the sake of providing a foundation, space for the purpose of granting room, and the sky for the sake of visibility; the sun exists for the purpose of accomplishing the manifestation of its own greatness, and there are certain other qualities as well.
Since this group of benefactors is ever-present and exceedingly difficult to abandon, how can the hearts of the great-minded ever cast off the stain of wretchedness and shame?

O Mother, as I mutter you— who consist of wisdom, whose body is the seed-syllable, and who are a wave of the nectar of abundant compassion— fixed in three ways upon the support of the heart and the region of the crest-lock, may my limbs thrill with horripilation through mouthfuls of the water of insight, which tastes the unimpeded nectar of my own non-duality.
Fearing that the nectar of her lower lip might spill due to its excessive fullness,
the Creator fashioned her chin as a support, providing it with sandalwood paste.
Emaciated by longing, with one side of her body pressed against the bed of separation— resembling the slender crescent of the moon remaining at the eastern horizon—
I saw her passing that very night, which had been spent like a single moment in the company of my desires, now made long by the heat of tears of separation.
For what person indeed would perform an act devoid of Dharma for the sake of this body, which is overwhelmed by mental and physical afflictions and destined to perish today or tomorrow?
Health is utterly uprooted by hundreds of mental and physical ailments; where prosperity flies away like a bird and calamities stand as if with their doors wide open;
and whatever is born, being inevitably and swiftly rendered helpless, death makes its own—what indeed is there that has been created by unrestrained Fate which is truly stable?
An elephant with its mane shaken off; a horse with sharp horns;
this castor plant is heavy and solid; the khadira tree is devoid of pith.
As her lotus-like hand shook with perspiration and her contrary words were hidden by a smile,
the lover, leaving the lower lip of the large-eyed maiden, drank for a long time only her refusal.
Until the smoke [of death] turns back, friends depart along with kinsmen;
therefore, perform that well-done deed which must be undertaken together with you.
Out of fear of the elephant-driver’s goad, the pair of frontal globes on the elephants became a pair of breasts upon the hearts of the women;
even there, they remained split by the wounds of their lovers’ nails—never otherwise than as it was inscribed by the Creator.
In the clash with the elephants, the heads of the elephant-riders, though severed by sharp discuses with razor-sharp edges,
fell only after a long time, their hair caught upon the tips of the talons of hawks.
The winds—friends to the forest fires swollen and raging, scattering heaps of hot dust; echoing with the heat of uneven sighs released by travelers scorched by the road;
and fierce as they rush swiftly into the cavernous mouths of pythons tormented by thirst—seem to threaten with frowns of their brows the soot of the parched wastelands.
Beholding the face of that fawn-eyed maiden, veiled by her trembling locks,
I remember a lotus covered by a swarm of wandering bees.
In ancient times, Śambhu danced, as did Govinda the performer of the *rāsa*;
even Brahmā fell into the state of a beast—by women, who has not been mocked?
O fair-toothed one, if there is impropriety on my part in biting you mercilessly with my teeth, then let that enmity be cleared by you; tell me, why do you not bite my lower lip?
Having beheld the wondrous faces of the fawn-eyed women upon this earth,
the moon rises very slowly, as if hidden within the mass of clouds out of shame.
The tilaka mark, which had been affectionately applied to the cheek— the moon of her face marked by the hare—
was washed away by the tears from the eyes of that tremulous-eyed beloved when her lover broke the appointed time.
The faces of the young women blossomed; their bodies bristled with excitement as they faced their lovers; their hearts became moist with emotion, and their anger flickered within their words.
This moon, causing the joy of the night-lotuses and other flowers to bud forth,
traverses the expanse of the sky just as Hanumān leaped across the ocean.

O Moon, by your rising, the cluster of night-lotuses has been brought to joy, the ocean has been made to swell, the heat of the sun-stone has been quelled, and the quarters of the sky have been adorned;
the three worlds have been refreshed by you—though the lotus’s exclusive attainment of light was ordained by fate, you are not to be blamed for this either.
While the beloved was sprinkling water from his hands upon the face of Śyāmā, bestowing bliss upon her,
the face of the other woman— though not sprinkled at all— became drenched with no small amount of perspiration as she grew envious.
The lotus born from the feet of the glorious Ādivarāha repeatedly spreads bliss for the wise and causes ear-aches for his enemies;
he is a true kinsman, an ocean of virtues, a staff for the blind, and a protector of the path of Dharma; yet even the right arm of the illustrious Lakṣmaṇasena is harsh when it comes to punishment.
Joyful dwellings, wise sons, a non-slanderous wife, virtuous friends, abundant wealth, devotion to one’s own wife, servants who obey commands,
hospitality, daily worship of Śiva, sweet food and drink in the home, and constant attendance upon the assembly of the righteous— blessed indeed is the householder’s stage of life.
O bee, you have come here having abandoned the lotuses that are drenched with the nectar of the bliss-bud;
therefore, O friend of fragrance, you must act in such a way that the bumblebee does not become an object of ridicule.

Alas, the cowherd women—veritable heaps of merit—having drawn near that single bulb of bliss, the essence of all the Vedas, the lamp of the inner self, difficult to cross, and dark as collyrium; having embraced him with their full breasts at will, they have attained their goal.
Bringing joy, dispelling the pride of the fever of passion, resembling the delightful essence of nectar,
spreading love, and imitating supreme prosperity— does not this transformative [glance] steal away the hearts of fair-browed women?
O Ānanda, withdraw your heart from this place; O wise one, consider where you must remain with fortitude. O connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, do not depart so agitated!
I behold her face, with its pair of eyes as tremulous as the fluttering wings of bees humming around a cluster of red lotuses.
The cool, refreshing tears born of joy broke through the warm tears born of grief for those two,
like the flow from the Himalayas descending into the waters of the Gaṅgā and Sarayū heated by the summer sun.
In the city of Ānandatāṇḍava, in the house of a Dravidian, there is a wondrous vessel of clarified butter equal to the wife of Vasiṣṭha;
there, a ladle dances like a flash of lightning, and the perfected one beholds the stream [of ghee] through the power of yoga.
May my mind rest in that state which is the abode of bliss, whose sole essence is consciousness, and which is non-dual— even though it is beyond the range of perception—
yet which, as it were, comes within the range of those dear friends such as the Kumāras who abide in the assembly of the virtuous.
For one whose tears of joy and horripilation are subject to his own will, what need is there for other means of accomplishment? All kings are his servants.
O lotus-petal-eyed one, you bestow this abundant joy upon me;
yet it is by you alone that this separation has been brought about, which torments my body all the more.

I bow to the autumn lotus that is the foot of Heramba— a lotus whose nectar is pure bliss, whose fragrance is infinite, whose bees are the most steadfast lords of yogis, which is free from all bonds, and which blossoms solely by the rays of the sun that is the Vedānta.
May we perceive within ourselves this form of his, which bestows bliss upon those with long eyes, which is dark-blue, with its neck gracefully curved as it holds the flute,
extending from the feet to the crown of the head, and which is embraced by a flood of nectar.

Alas, I remember those repeated comings and goings of yours at my neck— the embraces of that lovely-eyed one, which kindled the fever of passion mingled with bliss and were steeped in the essence of deep affection.
May the Blessed Lord Nṛsiṃha purify you, who bears upon the surface of his lap Lakṣmī, whose eyes are dazed with bliss;
by the mere grace of whose glance the moon-like face of Kamalā became free from the stain of the hare-mark.
This association with the wicked is indeed a forest fire to the deer of bliss, an elephant of pride to the tree of ethical conduct,
and a great wind to the lamp of wisdom.
Who on this earth exceedingly gladdens only the virtuous?
Who awakens the lotuses and destroys the darkness?
He who brings joy to sentient beings with auspicious and gentle speech will be censured in the world if he conceals the words of others.

I take refuge in that radiant Sun, the bringer of the end of calamities, who delights the groves of lotuses with his incense-like rays, repeatedly agitates the night-lilies, and bathes all the worlds on every side with his splendor.

O slender-waisted one, do you utter such a mantra or possess some such medicine that gladdens, intoxicates, and yet causes despondency in the minds of young men at the mere sight of you? Or is this simply the natural power of your eyes?
When served with skillful means, they bring joy; otherwise, they destroy.
By their very nature, they are difficult to understand; therefore, courtesans are like poison.

That anxiety regarding her news, which you have never abandoned for even a moment—the sole abode that binds together your mind characterized by extreme restlessness like an ocean of bliss—now causes you weariness; shame, shame upon us!

May the lotus-foot of Ambikā— upon which the garland cast off by Purandara, beautiful with joy, was forcibly placed upon the head of the demon Mahiṣāsura, and which is enchanting with the tinkling of lovely anklets— bring me victory.

May the eyes of Śambhu protect you—eyes that were first motionless with bliss during his meditations; then languid with the playful charms of Gaurī’s face; then bewildered for a moment, then struck with wonder, and then smiling at his own transformation; then cruel when the Mind-born God drew his bow, then narrowed with pity when he was consumed by the fire, and finally tremulous with tears at the weeping of his beloved.
A stream of joy for the self, an internal ointment of nectar for the eyes, the spreading of affection, the flower of the tree of love, the grace of sexual delight,

and a tethering post for the elephant of the heart wandering through the forests of sense objects— a son, the very essence of worldly existence, is obtained here by a husband and wife through their past merit.

“Why do you stand there in vain with your pair of eyes closed in bliss? You have been discovered by this innocent girl through her limbs that are clearly trembling and bristling with thrills! “Fool, let go of her! Do you not see her face washed by falling tears? When my friend spoke thus, I released her and impetuously threw my arms around her neck.
You have been seen by me for joy, for wonder, or even for sorrow; but now, how can there be even a thirst for you in my eyes?
I am no longer within the range of the pleasure of your company; so what is the use of these vain words? Let the bow stretch in that hand which is renowned for subduing the son of Jamadagni.
May this well-spoken work of mine, delightful with its various chapters interspersed with distinct manuals, bring great joy to the virtuous.
"Tears of joy have welled up in me simply upon seeing this girl;
my eye has been irritated by flower pollen stirred up by the wind."
She who weeps excessively when joyful, or laughs excessively when distressed;
she who is attached yet detached, dispassionate yet passionate—such a woman indeed has a mind that is difficult to discern.

May that Madhupuruṣa (the Enemy of Mura), who lifted up Mount Govardhana, purify you— he who was gazed upon for a long time with joy by Ānanda and Yaśodā, with affection by the cowherd women, with apprehension by Indra (the Foe of Bala), with flowers by the Siddhas, with agitation by the Earth, with envy by the cowherd boys, with compassion by the citizens, and with smiles by the gods.
My eyes, overwhelmed by a flood of rising tears, are unable to look upon you; my arms, trembling and distressed by perspiration, are powerless for an embrace;

my voice falters with syllables and words stammering from agitation; and my mind is wavering in its great distress—it is true that even this long-awaited union with my beloved now feels like a separation.

The eye of the deer-eyed woman steals the heart—this very eye, which smiles slightly through the contact with waves of bliss; whose lashes are closely joined; which is inclined toward the outpouring of love; whose bright pupils are smooth and moistened as they roll; and whose creeper-like brows are curved by the weight of internal thought. This is it.
How many creepers do not shine, their sprouts bending under the weight of clusters and filled with pollen?
Yet the distinction between them regarding fragrance, honey, and softness is indeed known only by the bee.
With your face bowed and your countenance concealed, you gaze into my heart; O fair-faced one, how might my onset of pride become fruitful?
For in whichever direction I turn my face out of pride, there appears the son of Nanda, dark as a water-laden cloud.
Even the young deer, eager to devour rows of tender *kalama* rice, brings a young traveler here, as if leading his own self to this place.

When the girl with the arched brows plunged into the lake up to her navel, the pair of her swelling breasts were seized by the hands of the water's waves; for how can there be any restraint over those who have once been touched?
Bending down the branch laden with fruit, one should pluck it ripe by ripe;
for this is the undertaking of wise men in this world, being intent upon the fruit.
Like a net for fish or a cage for a bird,
a beautiful-eyed woman is a binding snare for the fool, containing every kind of trap.

O Śrī Rāma, this role which I have brought before you like an actor—which has endured for as long as the sky, space, the zeros, the ether, the oceans, and the Vasus until now—has been performed for your pleasure.
Since you are now pleased by my performance, grant me what I have requested; otherwise, tell me when I might ever again be honored by you with such a role.
Brought somehow to the bedchamber by her circles of dear friends under some pretext— like a doe startled by a painting— with streams of tears flowing from her eyes,
her face choked with sobs, her hands waving, her two feet cast down, and her tresses tossing in every direction, the new bride is enjoyed through good fortune.

O arrow-maker, what is the use of these arrows brought here that are worthy of praise? Do you not see before you this famous village of common folk, where even the village headman speaks of "the sickle" and "the bowl," composes hymns for the goad, and takes delight in the plough?

A sandalwood tree born on Mount Malaya was brought here and planted upon a bed of jewels; drenched with nectar and nurtured with care day after day, it began to perfume the entire earth with its abundance of fragrance—yet on that very same day, by the power of fate, it was pulverized by a thunderbolt.
Even when one's wealth is exhausted, it can be brought back by means of the body;
however, the body, once exhausted, is incapable of bringing back wealth.
This pair of lotus-like breasts of my beloved, with their blue-tipped nipples as bees and the single line of hair rising between them as a broad stalk,
speaks as it were of a great treasure situated below the navel, high and closely joined.
Removing with his sprout-like hands the clear cloak of darkness from the eastern quarter, the moon—his passion undiminished—now follows the direction of Indra;
and bearing, as it were, musk-paste clinging to her breasts upon his body, he affectionately embraces this night whose stars are just beginning to bloom.
One who desires happiness should act in accordance with destiny; for that which is adverse is difficult to overcome, like going against the current of a river.
Compassion, forbearance, truthfulness, non-violence, self-restraint, uprightness,
affection, serenity, sweetness, and gentleness are the ten *yamas*.
Compassion is the supreme dharma; forbearance is the supreme strength;
self-knowledge is the supreme knowledge; there is nothing higher than truth.
Compassion is considered the supreme duty for all living beings;
therefore, a king should protect the wretched with compassion.
Compassion, kindness, sacred learning, virtuous conduct, self-restraint, and tranquility—
these six qualities adorn Raghava, the supreme among men.

"Has my dear friend not gone to bring him back? Is he afraid of a serpent? Or is the Lord of her life angry and speaking words of refusal?"—thus, under the pretext of the falling pollen from the golden *ketakī* flower on her ear, some newly wedded girl with a lotus-like face sheds tears from her eyes.

To manifest the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in its entirety, even that which is internal, as if it were external, the speech of a true poet is like a glass jar; these three things alone know how to do so constantly.
Whether within or without, that king who never wavers when commanded shall dwell in the royal residence.

One should protect outsiders from those within, and insiders from outsiders; one should always protect outsiders from other outsiders, and one's own people from their own kin—protecting all from everyone at all times.
I remember the braid of my beloved as she acted the part of the man, which, through her movements and my own body,
clung to me like a whip-cord as she practiced the instructions for sexual union.
O young elephant, shaking the rows of karañja trees in the mountain groves, you did not heed anyone through your prowess;
why then, with the mere flicker of the corners of your eyes, do you abandon your life before the lion?

Swinging her body on a swing, the large-eyed maiden with limbs like golden rods stood in the midst of the sky; she was not perceived by the people, appearing like a celestial goddess, beautiful in every form.

O virtuous one, you incessantly swing in your lap the sun of the sky, the host of stars, the moon, and other radiant splendors such as the brilliant lightning; yet it is a marvel that even so, you do not abandon the blindness within.

Do you remember her, with her hair swaying in her movements, the sound of whose girdle and cluster of tiny bells tinkled, as she acted the part of the man, like a staff marked by the fly-whisk of Love?
The status of being an Āndhra, the Āndhra language, and the diligent study of the Prābhākara school— even there, the Yājuṣī Śākhā is not the fruit of meager austerity.
The Andhra woman is uniquely skilled in binding affection; the Lata woman is beloved by the clever; the Karnata woman is adept in the arts of sexual pleasure; the Cola woman is pure;
the Abhira woman delights in the role of the man; the Gurjara woman is possessed of modesty; the Kashmiri woman is eager for lovemaking; and the Maharashtri woman is bold in the act of union.
The king, endowed with discipline, should deliberate upon Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārtā, and Daṇḍanīti, through those who are learned in them and engaged in their practice.

Logic (*ānvīkṣikī*), the three Vedas (*trayī*), commerce and agriculture (*vārtā*), and the eternal science of government (*daṇḍanīti*)—these four sciences alone are the causes for the stability of the world. ...
Through logic comes the knowledge of the self; through the three Vedas, the establishment of dharma and adharma.
In the science of economics (vārtā), one considers profit and loss; in the science of government (daṇḍanīti), one considers policy and its opposite.
Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, and Vārtā are declared to be the true sciences; for even they are not truly sciences when Daṇḍanīti (the science of government) is in disorder.
When the science of government (daṇḍanīti) properly rests upon a leader, then the remaining sciences are properly cultivated by those who possess knowledge. ...
Logic (ānvīkṣikī) is the science of the self (ātmavidyā), because it consists in the investigation of pleasure and pain.
Perceiving reality through that [wisdom], one casts off both joy and sorrow.
Logic, the three Vedas, economics, and the eternal science of government—
these four branches of knowledge a king should always study.
In Ānvīkṣikī, the science of logic (tarkaśāstra) and Vedānta and the like are established;
in the Trayī, dharma and adharma, as well as desire and its absence, are established.
Through the knowledge of the self derived from *ānvīkṣikī*, one casts off both joy and sorrow;
by abiding according to rule in the three Vedas, one attains both worlds.
Water is the first purifier on earth, and the mantras are the supreme purifier of waters;
and of those [mantras] belonging to the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas, the great seers declare that grammar is the purifier.
For those submerged in the blazing flames and carried away by the waves of calamity,
there is surely no way at all to cross over without the words of the elders.
But when a time of calamity has arrived, he who remains a friend is indeed a true friend;
yet when a time of prosperity has arrived, even a wicked person may become a friend.
In times of adversity, death indeed does not come to men;
one should exert effort in those arts that are useful during times of distress.
Thus, Arjuna (Kirīṭin) took up the profession of dancing in the palace of Virāṭa.
In times of calamity, one must rely upon the balance of one's allies and one's own manliness; in the absence of calamity, everyone acts as a friend, and everyone exerts their own prowess.
Those who have fallen into transgression and have no elders as their teachers are objects of pity for their kinsmen; though living here, they are equal to the dead.
Not all those born into a great family possess the steadfast intellect capable of rescuing others from calamity;
indeed, in the Vindhya forests, trees are rare that can withstand the scraping of an elephant's tusk-like mace.
In times of adversity, what is the use of despondency? In times of prosperity, what is the use of pride?
That which is destined to happen will surely happen; this is the certainty of karmic actions.
Men of wise intellect are not bewildered even in times of calamity;
yet the world is afflicted by the two kinds of suffering arising from the mind and the body.

One should recognize a friend in times of calamity, a hero in battle, and one who is pure in private; likewise, one should know a wife when wealth has perished, and a guest who is dear even in a time of famine.
The wise call him a learned man who, undeluded in times of adversity and possessed of fortitude, correctly undertakes those actions that must necessarily be performed.
For the power of the great is manifested only in times of adversity, not in prosperity;
the fragrance of agallochum is not present before it is cast into the fire as it is once it has fallen therein.
"We shall cross over this calamity; you should speak with reason:
'Sirs, you are my friends; there is no state of servitude among you.'"
If a master should fall into calamity while his servant looks on,
that servant, though his own life remains intact, shall go to hell.
Calamities come for a moment, and prosperity likewise for a moment;
birth and death each last but a moment—O Sage, what indeed is not momentary?
Calamities belong to the great, and prosperity belongs only to the great; for other men, there are neither calamities nor prosperities.
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; for how could calamities befall those who possess prosperity?
Fortune is sometimes fickle, and what has been accumulated may perish.
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
Lack of restraint over the senses is said to be the path to calamities;
their conquest is the path to prosperity. Go by whichever way you desire.
At the time of calamity, one should act resolutely and not waver;
and if unable to fight, one should retreat together with the ministers.
Again and again, I bow down to Śrī Rāma, the remover of calamities, the bestower of all prosperity, and the delight of the world.
Seeing the onset of calamities, the self-controlled man should not become despondent;
and having attained extensive prosperity, he should not become overjoyed.
When calamities are descending, even that which is beneficial becomes a cause [of harm];
for the mother's own leg becomes a tethering post for the calf when it is being bound.
Behold, because of the lack of restraint over the senses, those who stand upon the path of calamity abandon the path of prosperity, which they do not desire.
The examination of a friend occurs in times of adversity; the examination of a hero takes place on the field of battle;
the examination of lineage is seen in one's conduct; and the examination of a woman is revealed in a man who has lost his wealth.
I consider that man to be truly born again who, having returned the favor to both— him who helped him in times of distress and him who mocked him in adverse circumstances— does so once more.
Calamities befall only the great, and prosperity belongs only to the great;
the moon wanes and waxes, but the stars never do.
O fool blinded by wealth, why do you laugh at one who has fallen into calamity? What is surprising in this—that fortune is not permanent?
Do you not see how the buckets on the wheel of a water-drawing machine become empty, and then, having been filled, become empty once again?
Indeed, when fallen into adversity, a noble-minded universal monarch displays a magnanimity never shown before;
even black aloe-wood, when placed in the midst of fire, manifests a world-surpassing fragrance in every direction.
For those seized by the crocodile of calamity, there may be elders but no wise men;
for those who have no liberators, peace is not found.
For one who has been bitten by the serpent of calamity and is always devoid of mantras,
the medicinal herbs of the words of the elders truly render him free from poison.
Even in the face of a terminal calamity, one must never proceed by an improper course;
for even Rāhu, though drinking the nectar, died because he did so in an improper manner.
In times of calamity, when one has gone astray, or when the time for action has passed,
one who seeks the welfare of others should speak wholesome words even if unasked.
Seeing that he has met with misfortune, one should never feel distressed;
indeed, this very time for his uprooting has been signaled by fate.
With words faltering from distress and the roots of my thighs trembling,
a union with old age has occurred for me, as if with a newlywed bride.
O Rāmacandra, who are affectionate toward those in distress, the sole kinsman of the world’s people, the wise one who is a lotus-pool for the swans that are scholars—
may your fame be sipped for a thousand autumns by the cakora-birds of the virtuous, who are deprived of their birth and other rites.
The wise should act as stainless friends toward one who has fallen into misfortune;
for no one here who is devoid of friends can cross over calamity.
I have fallen [into distress]; I am one who seeks refuge at all times and in all conditions.
O Blessed One, I have taken refuge in you; protect me, who have come to you for shelter.
Indeed, young women have calamity as their very root; for that reason, their partiality—which is as transient as the breaking of waves upon the water—is a source of contempt for them.
Even so, O friend, our beloved is not able to cast aside her lotus-face, which is as enchanting as the orb of the full autumn moon.
Until the learned are satisfied, I do not consider the knowledge of performance to be successful; for even among those who are highly trained, the mind lacks confidence in itself.
As the elephant’s body was severed from its base and it fell face-down toward the ground without support,
the pair of its own tusks, having attained their full length, served as its prop.

Oh, how sweet is the face of Murāri—its lower lip pale-red, its tremulous eyes unsteady, filled with fragrance and a wondrous flood of luster; it enchants the memory of the astonished nectar [of immortality], its mouth slightly closed.

With his rays, pale-red as they first sprout forth, this very Lord of Days bestows upon the ears of the beautiful celestial damsels sporting on the eastern mountain the beauty of a fresh leaf from the Kalpa tree.
"Until the taking of the hand in marriage, I have been an intimate companion ever at the neck of the Lord; I am called Kamalā by all as the beloved of Hari, and he too is called Mādhava.
I do not grieve because of that, for my sons and their hosts, as well as the followers of the Son of Padmā, constantly sing this with the lute on the Vīṇā in order to ward off mental anguish."
Pale, plump, firm, round, and exceedingly beautiful— why is this [fruit] pulled so intensely with their hands even by the elderly, full of longing?
My hair has turned grey, three wrinkles have appeared on my cheeks, and my row of teeth has fallen out; yet I feel no despondency.
But when young women with eyes like a doe's see me on the road and are intent on crying "Father!", that indeed is a thunderbolt falling upon me.
The earth becomes pale and the stone takes on the color of cow's milk;
at a height of half a man, a mouse appears in the line of sight, resembling a water-lily.

Having understood that the pleasure derived from the objects of the five senses is delightful only at first sight, that it causes lack of satisfaction, that it is like the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree which is poisonous when ripened, and that it is neither eternal nor free from abundant faults, those possessing the wisdom of the ultimate goal renounce it.
O you who seek pleasure only in the immediate moment, why do you wish to sow the seed of the lotus in this pond?
O ignorant one, the Kali age has arrived; this world is ungrateful, and it will destroy the very beauty of your face by remaining here.
Where indeed is there not beauty that lasts only for a moment?
But a person adorned with ultimate realization is difficult to find.
For the consequence of unions with loved ones, which are pleasant at first sight,
is indeed as terrible as that of unwholesome foods.
Scorched by the summer heat, the elephant plunges into water as deep as the underworld; yet, even when reduced to mere skin and bone, he does not touch the water of a puddle anywhere.

With their hindquarters broadened by thighs swollen with fullness, the herd of white cows wanders through the outskirts of the villages— lands green with newly sprouted crops— during nights that smile with the intense radiance of the moon, while the heavy, deep-sounding bells, like thick, swaying blankets, jingle amidst the clusters of bells.
The young cow, from the effort of bearing the weight of her full udders, and the king, from the heaviness of his body,
both graced the path on their return from the penance grove with their graceful gaits.

Behold the ocean of milk— the single vast white lotus of the lake that is the triple world— its stalk Śeṣa, its petals the thousands of shimmering waves, and its nectar being repeatedly drunk by the clouds acting as bees.

These five arrows, with their feathers to their very tips, have sunk simultaneously into my heart; by them, along with those very arrows, this body of mine has been consumed by the fire of separation.
Alas, O Kāma! You are now weaponless and can no longer conquer people; let me alone be miserable, while the entire world lives in happiness.

O pomegranate tree! Having inspired confidence in all people through the beauty of your blossoming flowers, you have increased your own growth here only so long as this [tree] did not reach a state capable of being enjoyed by others. Once it attained that state, your heart split in two upon realizing its condition; for that very reason, you are worthy of praise.

Let the Daughter of the Mountain Lord be worshipped alone; what need is there for the partiality of the Mind-born God? If there is a messenger skilled in eloquent speech, the Lord would fall at the feet of his brides.
The Creator fashioned this pair of cheeks as a pair of sweetmeat cakes for the sake of an offering to the God of Love;
they shine, exceedingly beautiful with their lovely hollows, filled with great affection.
This entire sphere of the universe, filled to the brim with the deepest, most intense darkness,
shines like a casket of black collyrium.
The stainless moon, though full of its digits, enters the mouth of Rāhu; the rain-cloud, though thick with water, is shattered by the force of the wind;
the excellent fruit-bearing tree, though mature, is consumed by a forest fire; and you, though having become the crest-jewel of the world, have fallen under the power of death.
Desiring a beautiful complexion, she goes with her beloved even as his hair becomes increasingly grey;
though he constantly casts off the state of having flower-like eyes, his lover draws him close with her very glance as he undergoes the process of aging.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness, so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
"May this reservoir of water be filled once more with shimmering waters, its waves teeming with schools of sapharī fish, and may we behold its lotuses blooming again"—
with such a hope, his heart bound by hundreds of threads of longing, the weary-minded, aged crane wastes away day and night on the shore of the lake dried up by the scorching sun.
From the lordly mountain in the east, whose peaks are moistened by the ichor flowing from Indra’s elephants, to the western ocean whose waters are drunk by the navel of Varuṇa’s bride;
from Mount Meru to the Setu, those kingless monarchs who have no other refuge have worshipped his feet, their garlands of flowers falling as they bow their heads to touch the surface of the earth.
The Malaya breezes take leave of the sandalwood trees, comfort the approaching creepers, and converse with the long-acquainted cascades of the Malaya mountains;
having stayed today in the dwellings of Dravidian women, they make their preparations to depart tomorrow at dawn.
Take leave of your friend, pay homage to your elders, and rejoice with the wives of your kinsmen; O charming one with eyes fixed upon the banks of the Kāverī, why do you distress yourself?
O fair-browed one, the Godāvarī itself lies nearby, its caverns jagged by the Tamāla trees on its slopes, which bend down embraced by cardamom creepers from the surrounding groves.

“You have been bid farewell; the travelers have departed, O slender-limbed one. I am going, and you should not grieve, knowing that our reunion will occur in just a few days. Hearing these words of her beloved, the charming girl suddenly acted in such a way that she caused her lover to experience the intense suffering of a sudden, premature separation.
"You have been bid farewell; the beauty of the day causes my weak heart to ache. Come, O Cakravākī, embrace me and pass this night alone.
He is not attached to another woman, nor is he angry, nor has he lost his affection; rather, being dependent on fate and lacking autonomy, I must leave you here."
The birds have taken to the path of the sky on all sides, and the bees take refuge in the mango buds;
the lake is shrinking, and alas, O Lord, to what state shall the wretched fish resort?
Water, cloth, sesame seeds, oil, or likewise perfume with barley—
just as these acquire qualities through the perfuming of flowers, so too do qualities arise from association.
O cloud, water is liberated; in some places it is merely water, in some nothing at all, and in others poison.
Since you have been liberated and become pearls wherever they are released, why are you now turned away from that very place?
Performing the *āpośana* rite, sitting [in a specific manner], and likewise anointing oneself with oil— these,
when done by one's own hand, destroy longevity, prosperity, and sons.
But he who should chew his food without first performing the *āpośana* rite— Manu has declared that such chewed food is impure.
If, disregarding the words of the authoritative one, one acts out of pride, and that results in the opposite of the desired fruit, what lamentation can there be in that?
And for one who is authoritative, there must be someone authoritative for him;
for even a well-guarded secret counsel is disclosed by a succession of authorities.
One who is devoted to it should protect the mantra of the lineage of the trustworthy and the most trustworthy;
for a mantra that is not protected shatters the succession of the trustworthy.
Even when facing his own destruction, a wicked person does not take into account the suffering and misfortune of others;
indeed, at the front of battle, a headless torso often dances even while losing a thousand followers.
From the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, within a body defiled by the impurities of the Kali age,
even the water of the Gaṅgā is as futile as a handful of darbha grass poured into a jar of liquor.

O Cloud, we know that there is no one else in this world who wakes up every day to drench the cātaka bird— who has been swallowed by intense thirst since dawn, scorched by fierce rays of the sun, distressed by the loss of life, and paralyzed by the weight of anxiety— with a stream of smooth nectar.
If a dog, its shoulder-blade bristling with bound-on artificial manes, were placed upon the position of the deer’s enemy,
how could it produce the roar of the lord of deer, who is intent on splitting the temples of intoxicated elephants?
"How has the sun departed now, leaving me after I entreated him with my hands joined like a closed lotus bud?"—
as if thinking thus through the internal humming of bees, the lotus plant, having found sleep at night, fell into a dream.

O Lord, at the front of the battle, your very self has appeared before you under the guise of the shadow of your own sword, with his forehead marked by a furrowed brow of terrifying frown and his lower lip trembling as he turns his face away from the enemy.
Though her mass of stones is oppressed by the burden of tightly bound, harsh rays,
and though she is crushed by feet, sugar here remains sweet even when ground to powder.
All human beings are bound by the constraints of two types of action: destiny (*daiva*) and personal effort (*pauruṣa*); there is nothing superior to these two.

Having bound my two arms and been driven far from the interior of the house during the night when all people were fast asleep, he approached and gently touched my feet; yet, out of extreme fear, I looked upon him with a smile even as he was bold in our lovemaking.

Upon the surface of the slender-limbed maiden’s cheeks, which resemble the edge of a golden stone, her beauty— exceeding the orb of her moon-like face and performing the role of an ear-ornament for the blooming campaka buds— seems to dance, laugh, surge forth intensely, and quiver.
"From childhood on, this husband of mine has known the true nature of this world; yet when you arrived at the center of the earth, even that husband of yours became renowned.
An old woman does not dwell in his house, for he remains here for a very long time with steadfastness"—O King Rāma, as if out of such envy, your fame has reached the ends of the quarters.
O Wind, since childhood you have many times enjoyed the lotus-stalk leaf with her, and likewise spent time in private with respectful amorous talk;
now, with the caresses that swing the heart and the pressing against the breasts of those fawn-eyed women, how can your mind rejoice in sporting again without me?

How could the hand of that lion ever stretch forward even in a state of extreme distress— to snatch away the life of a rabbit tumbling into a pit— when it has been accustomed since childhood to pearls as warm as the blood dripping from the hollows of the temples of rut-maddened elephants it has torn open?

Since childhood, the daughters of the gods in the abodes of the best of deities have desired as their husband one whose name is sung by kinnarīs, heard in their ears as it is set to verses extolled by the preceptor of the immortals, who possesses the pure qualities of unparalleled valor enriched by the magnificence of his generosity, and who is the sole essence of all enjoyments; thus they worship the feet of the consorts of Hari and Hara.
"From childhood, this son of yours was led by me alone to the highest pinnacle of excellence; now he feels ashamed even at our conversation.
Thus, as if distressed by his own fame, the aged multitude of your virtues has taken hold of you and departed for the ascetic groves upon the shore of the ocean.

May that Jina protect you—he before whom neither the Māras, the foremost of whose arrows are the arms of women with the luster of the tips of raised circular ornaments, their chests armored, hot with passion, wounded, crushing the hearts of adversaries, and harsh; nor the breasts of the wives of Māra—with their garments cast aside, bearing the weight of visible forms—experienced any agitation.
From Brahmā down to a mere worm, this entire world is bound together by the union of male and female;
what shame is there in this, wherein even the four-faced Lord was led astray by a young woman through greed?
The beloved’s gaze— unflickering at its tips, possessing many virtues, and granting long-lasting relish—
draws my mind away, just as a fishhook line drags out a fish from a lake.
O friend, her body is an ornament for ornaments, a special refinement of the act of adorning, and even a counter-comparison for every comparison.
A night devoid of the moon never truly shines, nor does the moon, when separated from the night, possess its splendor.
What is the reason for this? It is because these two have been joined in an unbroken embrace, born together month after month.
Before us, this darkness appears exceedingly grey, bearing within it the weight of a few shimmering stars;
it is like the smoke of the white-rayed fire about to blaze forth, followed by sparks, as it seeks to consume the forest of those separated from their lovers.
This young girl shines with her limbs bristling from the touch of my hand,
like a young mango creeper with its buds opening upon contact with the fresh spring.
The line of hair on the large-eyed woman shines like a trail of smoke from the fire of passion situated within the cavity of her navel, as delicate as a swarming cluster of moving bees.

The lovely splendor of this gazelle-eyed woman shines forth through the manifold excellence of her beauty; moreover, her braid is like a row of shimmering locks of hair, resembling a string of beautiful emeralds.

O Protector of the Earth, the entire sky appears as if possessing two moons; the elephant-headed god has three tusks; the flood of the Gaṅgā shines forth in four ways; the lordly elephant has five gleaming tusks; he with six faces (or seven faces) manifests, and likewise the six qualities become seven in number—I suspect that the world, O King, is perceived as if it were new through the form of your fame.

By means of the *ābhicārika* oblations and mantras that accomplish the six rites (*ṣatkarma*), through fierce diagrams (*yantra*) for drawing, and by means of whispered recitation (*upāṃśujapa*) and so forth, one accomplishes the six rites.
By the mere presence [of another], like a mirror, a virtuous person quickly reflects— whether colored or uncolored— their own clarity.
I praise that ancient Person, the son of the Ābhīra woman, whose tiny bells are tinkling upward; whose hands and feet are slightly copper-hued;
who is beautiful with anklets, whose lips are ruddy, and whose eyes are like lotuses; who is non-dual, consisting of pure consciousness, without beginning, and without end.
"O Mādhava, why do you not fear taking the hand of an Ābhīra woman? What would you say?
"What suspicion could the lord of a hamlet feel regarding the grasping of the hand of the beloved of a cowherd?"
The speech of Ābhīras and others is known as *apabhraṃśa* in poetic works; however, in the technical treatises (*śāstra*), everything other than *saṃskṛta* is declared to be *apabhraṃśa*.
With her bud-like fingers curved as she applies them to her mass of hair, her mind fixed on the excellence of the binding, she casts a vacant gaze;
with the silk garment slipping from her breasts raised by the lifting of her arms, the young bride binds her topknot, beautiful with the base of her arms drawn back in modesty.

Having embraced the eastern quarter (the direction of Indra) and firmly clasped the northern quarter (the direction of Kubera) with his rays, and having kissed the day-lotus while simultaneously delighting the night-lotus, this Lord of Night—possessing a supreme luster even now—triumphs; yet, as if out of sudden anger, the clever host of stars has vanished everywhere.
The expanse of your breasts is vast and exceedingly great; the radiant pearl necklace, though it possesses many flowers as its arrows, remains within you, fixed by your majesty.
This Bali likewise dwells within your belly, which shines with a clear luster; yet Vindhyāvalī exists there through the transformation of her body hairs brought about by youth.

Adorned with the grace of effort, possessing the excellence of jar-like breasts, and sweet with internal transformations, the glances and limbs of noble women— betraying the god of love— torment the minds even of those who are firm-souled.
The first section should be the "Ābhoga," and the second the "Uccakhaṇḍaka";
since both are marked with the same name, this is the characteristic of the middle [section].
At the close of day, these villages— enjoying some leisure, their outskirts sprouting with ripened rice and threshing floors,
and girdled by circles of smoke from cow-dung fires glowing with the weight of frost— now captivate the heart.
With the playful movement of her eyes directed with effort, and her form bearing the agitation caused by the turning of her hips,
he churned her heart— the ocean of his own restless longing— swiftly and without interval.
It would be better to touch two venomous serpents— coiled, hooded, and having just shed their skins at that very moment— than to touch the breasts of the slender maiden.
In the *ābhoga* there should be one foot, and the second should be somewhat higher;
marked with the name of the Lord, this is the characteristic of the *kaniṣṭha*.
Protecting against internal danger, one should well-guard against external danger;
for danger born from within immediately cuts away the very root.
The beauty of those two elephant-ivory temples is taken away by these two breasts, for while those two have their pearls hidden out of fear, these two possess ornaments of manifest pearls.
The physician who can recognize a tumor as being unripe, ripening, or fully ripe—he alone is a true doctor; all others are merely those who subsist like thieves.
Shaking the lotuses whose pollen was stirred and knotted together, and which were swarming with intoxicated bees,
the breeze— cool as the waves of the celestial river— brought relief from the fever of his beloveds.
With their warbling, so pleasant to the ear, the cuckoos seem to ask with compassion whether the pain of love can be endured;
meanwhile, the southern breeze, fragrant with mango blossoms, has been employed by Spring like a thickly-palmed hand upon my body.
Dwelling by a river until midday, performing worship of the deities in an assembly,
and always wearing clean clothing— this is the life of hypocrisy.
With cries of "Hail! and shouts of victory, with the humming sounds of the syllable *huṃ* on every step, and with spontaneous exclamations of "Well done!", the singer interrupts his song.
At the beginning, the fragrant breeze addressed you; the fruit given in front was called the "bitter thorn.
Your mouth was broken and you were turned away from the presence of the parrots—the kings—therefore, O jackfruit tree, this fame belongs to you alone.
Brahmins rejoice in invitations, cows rejoice in fresh grass, and women rejoice in the enthusiasm of their husbands; but I, O Kṛṣṇa, rejoice in battle.
Having addressed you, O Lord, with that [oath], I shall justify its futility;
for an oath, even if true and sworn before the gods, has a harsh consequence.
This is the churning vessel, the ocean of milk; this is the churning staff, Vāsuki; and this is the mountain used for churning.
Now, at this very moment, it is the occasion for the gods and demons to scratch the itching of their arms, which have become heavy with pride.
Kings, having observed deformities in those afflicted by disease, pain, enemies, fear, hunger, and the like,
destroy their followers even when they have attained prosperity, out of shame and dread.
Even until death, these wretched crows continue to caw in competition with the peacocks; do they truly know how to produce the *kekā* cry?
Pressing her beloved’s sindūra tilaka with her hands upon a lovely lotus bud, the young woman applied a musk tilaka.

Today in my dream, my friend— who acts so secretly— pressed his hands against my hips, disheveled my braided hair, crushed my pair of breasts, and drank from my bimba-like lips before being held back.
From indignation, passion immediately arises as a blazing fire in the mind;
it is then allowed to increase even toward that man who is hateful to women.
The dosha, located in the stomach (āmāśaya), destroys the digestive fire and obstructs the channels; because it thus produces fever, one should practice fasting (laṅghana).
Her closing eye takes on the likeness of a fresh blue lotus; even her limbs, companions to the new jasmine, have assumed a languor.
Her lower lip, throbbing from speech, bears a resemblance to a swaying sprout, and the teardrops born of joy possess the luster of pearls.
That which produces a continuous consciousness of the essence of divine love for those with eyes closed—
this alone, mutually experienced by couples, is the honored fulfillment of desire.

Constantly recollecting her— her eyes with pupils rolling languidly as they close, her vine-like arms slackened by the loosening of the neck-tying embrace, and the roundness of her cheeks covered with droplets of perspiration— I find no peace within.
The pearls fastened upon the hearts of the deer-eyed women were seized by the Bhilla plunderers; the flesh was snatched from their temples by night-stalking demons, yet not the blood.

O King of Lions, you have become the foremost among those who split the frontal globes of lordly elephants; elsewhere, everything is merely a means to an end, whereas your fame alone remains in your hand.
With their tresses made fragrant by loose flowers, their heavy breasts weary from laughing with strings of pearls,
and their long, lashed eyes white with the beauty of their beloveds, young women approach men by force through the power of merit.
The two lingas of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), located at the sacred ford above his navel, which are to be worshipped by those desiring happiness in this world and the next—
imbued with the crescent moon held upon the tips of his beloved’s sprout-like fingers— for whose wise person in this world would they not bring joy for a long time?
In some places the grassy ground has been uprooted from its very base, and in others it has been cut; the creepers have been bent down by the gathering of flowers, their tips gently pulled aside.
These trees bear the scars of bark previously stripped away, while these other plants still exude sap from their recent felling for sacrificial fuel.

Scorched by the summer heat of passion, I grasp her lovely hand with my own— its lotus-stalk-like arms tender yet bristling from the roots, its petal-like fingers moist— as an elephant seizes a reddish lotus from a lake.

Victorious for all time is this attire of the women of Kuntala: the forehead marked by a mass of curly locks and beautiful top-knots falling from the roots, and the waist-belt tightened within the folds of the garment.
From their roots, the *aśoka* trees, copper-red like the hue of coral and bearing clusters of flowers along with new sprouts,
cause the hearts of those in the bloom of youth to be filled with sorrow when they gaze upon them.
O noble black aloe tree, whose playful fragrance is praised throughout the entire world from root to tip, where else is there a blessed one like you?
Yet I grieve even so, seeing you joined in intimacy with serpents who are solely intent on destroying the lives of the travelers passing by your path.
O *burbūra* tree, your body is covered with thorns from root to tip, you produce scentless flowers, your shade does not relieve fatigue, and you bear no fruit to satisfy one emaciated by hunger.
Let that be as it is; alas, you merely exist to provide a fence for the protection of other fruit-bearing trees, devoid of any association with the virtuous.
From the base of the Jewel Mountain encircled by the Malaya range, down to the shore of the ocean—let all those who are skilled in composing poetry speak without hesitation:
who else besides me is fortunate enough to occupy the position of a master over speech that possesses the sweetness of a flowing stream of smooth nectar emerging from the heart of a grape?
When his arm was sewn from the root to the tip with a long arrow, and his fist was clenched like a frog’s,
the leather shield slipped from the hand of no one else— not even when unbearable pain struck him and his fortitude failed.
Until death, there is truly no end to desires; this has been realized by me today:
the mind of one who is intent on attachment to desires never becomes attached to the ultimate truth.
As if trampling the mud at the edge of the lake like darkness, their feet entangled with foam as if with clusters of stars out of grief for their mate;

pursued by ruddy geese whose beaks greedily snap at exposed lotus stalks, these cakravāka birds appear like the crescent moon itself, captured as a prisoner by the Creator on account of the pain of separation.
That the sighs are crushed by the heaving and trembling of her breasts; that the perception of external objects is severed from internal meditation;
and that the tears are obstructed by the movement of raising the eyelashes—O fierce woman, these very states of being announce a grief that has shattered her heart.

By touching the waves of their folds on all sides with hands whose outstretched fingers were trembling, those who desired the waists of the fair-browed women perceived through experience that they were indeed "measurable by a fist."
Repeatedly touching the circle of her breasts, repeatedly kissing the region of her cheeks, and clutching her neck with hands agitated by excitement,
a mosquito— intoxicated by the winds from the clouds— is buzzing something right at the ear of your enemy’s wives as they sleep in the dense thickets of the mountain river.

Having adorned the circle of the earth from Mount Meru to Mount Malaya with the camphor of your fame, may you, who are composed of virtues, attain eternal auspiciousness; victory and long life to you as long as the sun endures!
Bestowing fragrance upon beds of night-lotuses, calamity upon day-lotuses, the fire of time upon the arrows of the five-arrowed god, intense coolness and pungency upon moonstones,
dejection upon the faces of proud women, discipline within the hearts of fair-browed maidens, and increase within the oceans— the divine lover of the night rises.

Upon the faces of the playful women— whose moving lips were scented with fragrance, whose slightly bloodshot eyes were reddened by sleep, and whose decorative leaf-patterns on their foreheads had been rubbed away— it was the lingering intoxication that established their beauty.

It is no wonder that the Goddess of Fortune dwells in a lotus, which is turned tawny by the pollen swaying in the breeze from the wings of bees drawn there by its fragrance; for that lotus is beautiful by its very nature.

But this is truly marvelous: that she resides for a long time upon your sharp, quivering blade—drenched in the blood from the throats of your enemies—even while being a woman, remaining joyful therein.

O friend, at the close of day, I have been distressed by that intoxicated *kesara* flower falling before me—fragrant, laden with honey, greyish-pale, and fluttering about in a restless whirl; for what indeed is not done by a lover when he is drunk?
In gardens and forests, there exist other trees as well that produce fruits fragrant, very succulent, soft, and sweet;
however, O *mālūra*, the glory of bearing fruit belongs to you alone throughout the circle of the quarters, for these fruits of yours are the abodes of the beauty of the breasts of youthful women.
Smeared with the fragrance of *kadamba* buds and shoots that pervades the entire sky, skilled in providing the prologue for the dance of flocks of peacocks swelling with joy,
and having wiped away the sweat of travelers with the first drops of water from the clouds, the wind blows slowly— a formidable herald of the gathering storm.

By your fragrances you have made the winds fulfilled; by the splendor of your sprouts, the deer; by your bark, the ascetics; by your flowers, the bees; by your fruits, the birds afflicted by the heat;

and by your trunks, the scent-elephants—all have been rendered successful by you alone. Therefore, you are capable of benefiting the entire world, while other trees are merely those whose calamities have been averted by you.
O Sandalwood tree, drawn from afar in every direction by your fragrances, we have come here in person to behold you, the very embodiment of Lakṣmī.
What do we see, O fortunate one? A wild beast is playing right in your lap! May it be well with you; let us go—release us, for we must depart.
The final word of the sacred traditions is: "Singing, modes, pleasures, and fears;
enjoyment, disease, joy, and delusion—[all these are found] in an unsafe place, whereas one should desire meditation in a secure place."
The study of the Vedas is like weeping in a forest; daily vows of austerity are merely marks for cutting away fat; all rites of public charity are like offerings poured upon ashes.
Even the plunging into sacred bathing places is like an elephant’s bath—unless it includes the praise of his two lotus feet. Victorious is that Lord Nārāyaṇa!
In the Vedas, in the Smṛti scriptures, and in worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit.
He who, having cut down a mango tree with an axe, should tend to a neem tree,
and even water it with milk— it would never become sweet for him.
O mango tree, although those days have passed when you were abundant with flowers, fragrance, and fruit—alas! even now, by your mere shade, you dispel the intense heat of people.

Are these mango trees, their heads bowed under the weight of fruit, so beautiful? Are these plantain trees, providing cool shade and fragrance? Are these champaka trees in full bloom, sweet with scent? No, O fool! These are merely *śamī* bushes, half-grown after being licked by fierce, unrestrained camels. Why do you wander in vain in this windless desert, only to die in vain?
O fair-limbed one, this mango sprout, possessing a reddish-dark luster, has emerged from the bone;
it shines, having risen upward as if from the shell of a young tortoise.

May that slender-bodied Spring, the conqueror of the world, bestow upon you manifold blessings— he whose excellent arrows are the lovely clusters of mango blossoms, whose bow is the beautiful *kiṃśuka* flower, whose bowstring is the swarm of bees, whose spotless umbrella is the white moon, whose intoxicated elephant is the Malaya breeze, and whose bards are the cuckoos.
Perched upon a blossoming mango tree, the cuckoo uttered its sweet song,
like a female messenger drawing the hearts of lovers toward her.

With mango trees there is security; with *bhallātaka* trees, danger; and likewise with *pīlu* trees, good health. With *khadira* and *śamī* trees there is famine; with *arjuna* trees, auspicious rain.
Copper is purified by sour gruel; bell-metal is purified by ashes;
a woman is purified by her menses; and a river is pure by its current.
One should observe income and make expenditures; one's expenditure should be less than one's income.
By incurring expenditure when there is no income, even Kubera would perish.
Does the child Smara cast away for play the wind-clothed discus of the moon, which is bound by long, white rays and smeared with the ink-like luster of its spot?
With his long fingers, he was an extra ornament upon the slender waists of the fair-browed women;
upon their broad hips, his hand found contact with its entire palm, for it was a lover’s touch.
One should examine future undertakings and their immediate consequences, as well as the virtues and faults of all past actions, according to their true nature.
Like a future age already destroyed, like a command that has been repudiated, like a quarter of the sky ablaze at the wrong time, or like a worship that has been desecrated.
One who knows the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who understands the remaining consequences of past actions, is not overcome by enemies.
Whatever may be pleasant in its taste both for the future and for the present, that alone one should do; one should not practice what is hated by the world.
A man who recognizes the recompense in the future, who possesses firm resolve in the present,
and who understands the remaining tasks from the past, is not deprived of his goals.
In the future, the wise man shall conquer hope by abandoning attachment to wealth; he shall conquer affection through the contemplation of impermanence, and hunger through the practice of yoga.
At all points of income, he should appoint trustworthy and tested officials;
through them, he should collect wealth, just as the sun draws up water with its rays.
Constant knowledge of income and expenditure, that which is not hot, the cutting away of doubt, and constant knowledge of that— these are the threefold fruit for ministers.

They should be employed in income and expenditure, in the preparation of food, in the maintenance of household utensils, in purification, and in the performance of fire rituals; this is remembered as the protection of women.
He whose income and expenditure are well-balanced, whose spies are concealed and whose counsel is secret,
and who never speaks unpleasantly to his ministers— he rules the earth as far as the ocean's edge.
She does not provoke a quarrel as she did before when her garment slips; she does not arch her brows or bite her lip when her hair is seized.
She offers her limbs of her own accord and is no longer resistant to a forceful embrace; yet, this slender woman has now learned another way to express her anger.

Let someone perform even the most arduous labor; what more could he experience here, O Mother, than that which is experienced by one who dwells happily within the borders of Bhāratavarṣa, having merely moved a short distance north from here?
One who manages his expenditures by spending only a fourth part of his income,
even if his oil lamp never runs dry, will behold prosperity for a long time.
One should carry out the work of expenditure with one-fourth of the income;
for he who maintains a lamp with abundant oil beholds prosperity for a long time.

When you spoke sweetly, "A thief has come to your house at an unaccustomed hour; you are to be punished," my heart was bound even more firmly by the guise of your arms—while the lamp flickered and you wore a garland of jasmine flowers dripping with drops of honey.
"Friend, your beloved has returned after a long absence from his journey; his body is emaciated, scorched by the fire of separation from you.
Immediately satisfy him by offering the touch of your own tender limbs; why do you stand thus with your face turned away?"
The Lord of the Night-lotuses has arrived; the Wind-god, the Lord of All, is victorious; the Bee roars like Bhairava; and the Lord of Life does not depart from my side.
O slender-waisted one, how can this incurable disease of man—this physician with flower-arrows and his faultless festival—remain in your heart when these elixirs of perfection are present?
A learned disputant has come into your presence, whose virtues are stainless; for in this age of disease, he is a remover of ailments who possesses the refined essence of poetry.
O treasury of all virtues, I do not know the remedy for the disease of poverty; yet that remedy has been devised even for one as powerful as the illustrious King Arjunendra.
The rains have arrived, O friend, in which even the day is longer than the year;
in every direction the waves of water rise, and so too do the waves of longing in my heart for the lord of my life.
A line of clouds, embraced by lightning, has arrived with impetuosity; everywhere around the mountains, the rows of serpents are dancing noisily.
Even so, alas, my husband has now departed for another land. O friend, how and before whom can I now express that sorrow?
The honeyed night has arrived; if, however, my lord does not return, let my life-breaths depart into the fire, and may I pray for rebirth.
May the hunter be for the binding of the cuckoo, Rāhu for the eclipse of the moon, the radiance of Śiva’s eye for Kandarpa, and I myself be the god of love for the Lord of my life.
The sweet night has arrived, this night whose song is as pleasing as that of a sweet woman;
O Smara, the tree of love has sprouted within the slender-waisted woman with full breasts.

"Night is coming; the forest fire of great separation will break out. O slender-limbed one, you must not suddenly allow agitation to arise in your mind, O you who are called 'Chariot-Wheel' (Cakravāka).
Having thus conversed for a long time with the female cakravāka in a voice choked and faltering by tears, he—his mind filled with anxiety and turned away from all diversion—alas, censures fate.

Śrī Rādhikā had come to the forest of the Lord of Love, and by a stroke of fate, Hari also arrived there; even his clever servant came along with him. Saying to Hari, "I shall quickly see the dance of the peacocks within the interior of the mountain caves," he slowly returned home.
"You have arrived; cast off this heavy trembling. Have you been seen by anyone? Cast off this blue bodice; let the midnight breeze take away your sweat.

Thus, with a throat faltering from inner fear, the newly unfaithful woman—who had repeatedly said "I am leaving" as she trembled upon becoming a guest of the bed—is embraced at her will by the fortunate man.

"This arrival of flowers has come with blossoming blooms; this autumn, marked by the moon as its tilaka, has arrived"—at these words, people indeed rejoice greatly; yet my mind falls into despair, thinking, "This life of mine is passing away."
She comes and goes, she causes weariness, and like another female bee, she steals away my honey;
you alone are the presiding deity of my mind, as Śrī is to the lotus.
Coming and going, it plunges again into the water; it shakes the lotus shoots and flaps its wings.
Like one driven mad, the cakravāka bird, distressed by separation from its beloved, wanders and coos very softly in the night.

The lotus-lover [the moon] swiftly brings fortune to her eyes; this armor [her breasts] attains a state fit for enjoyment; through her cleverness, she extends her companionship with speech; yet the face of this charming girl cannot endure the primary splendor of the moon.
He approaches with faltering steps, accompanied by a change of facial color;
his forehead is covered in sweat, and he speaks words with great stammering.
A man who has committed evil always looks downward with a trembling gaze;
therefore, he should be carefully recognized by the wise through these signs.
If a dog approaches joyfully toward one, playing and rolling about in front,
then there will certainly be a great acquisition of wealth and grain for travelers at that time.
Let other women come or go, let them cause weariness, or let them take away my honey;
you alone are the presiding deity of my mind, just as Śrī is to the lotus.
If he disappears upon arrival, or if seen again is intent on other business; if his face is smiling when speaking but dejected during talk of his own hardships;
if he desires to dwell within the inner apartments; if he constantly claims to be ill; and if he is intent on proclaiming the faults of the servants—one should not go to such a person's house.
When her beloved arrived after a day passed with difficulty through hundreds of longings, and while the dull-witted attendants were engaged in a lengthy conversation as she entered the bedchamber,
the slender-limbed woman, saying "I have been bitten," quickly shook off her silken garment and, with a mind eager for love, extinguished the lamp.
When her beloved returned after crossing the impassability of the desert lands, the mistress fixed upon his face a gaze tremulous with tears of joy;
then, having offered him mouthfuls of *pīlu*, *śamī*, and *karīra* fruits, she respectfully wiped with the hem of her own garment the dust clinging to the mass of the young camel’s mane.
If your beloved has arrived with impetuosity, you have not risen to meet her for long; nor have you firmly embraced her, with the slopes of your rounded, uplifted breasts pressed close;
nor, having embraced her, have you supported her with your arms or addressed her with words moist with love. Alas, O simple girl, you are destroyed by your own wanton misdeeds!
When the petitioner desired by the breaker of the Gotra arrived, Karṇa released his earring; indeed, the pair of eyes of Bhūriśravas was fixed upon him as the weapon of Kāma.
Let this very heart of the leader of the Kurus be bestowed upon him; let the essence of delight born of asceticism not be lost for the sake of Pārtha.
When her beloved had come within the range of her hearing at the moment of his departure, the innocent girl, standing at the edge of the bed, gazed long and intently at his face;
then, with a deep sigh, she pressed her own face—washed by tears flowing from a heart heavy with intense grief—against her husband’s chest and wept silently.
Night has indeed arrived; the quarters of the sky are strewn with the rays of the lord of night, and in their homes, beautiful women adorn their limbs with clusters of ornaments.
O innocent one, you do not cast away your pride even now due to your anger; alas, alas! Your body, thinner even than a young lotus stalk, is wasting away.

"Night has indeed arrived, spreading wakefulness in the minds of the deer-eyed women; how shall this pride of mine now remain unassailed in my heart?"—while the lotus-eyed one was thus engaged in deliberation and reflection, the orb of the moon, as beautiful as the parasol of King Kāma, shone forth.
"Your beloved has arrived"—at these words she did not immediately believe them; though her lover had come before her eyes, the fair-faced woman still thought it was her own delusion.
Even as his arms embraced her neck, her heart remained empty, and she suspected it was but a dream; how could this slender-waisted woman ever fully trust in the return of her beloved?

Hearing his mother suddenly cry out, "Your father has arrived!", the child—covered in dust and abandoning the pleasures of play already begun with his companions—approaches with a smiling face from afar, stretching out his two graceful arms; he comes before one who is not fortunate, crying out "gharghara" with supreme joy.
The forest-garlanded one has arrived; the householder has arrived with his friends.
Remember, my friend, the rule of Pāṇini: "In the case of a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails."
A man devoted to dharma should spend one-third of his income;
indeed, this alone is wisdom: that expenditure be small compared to income.
Seeing a virtuous person approaching, one should rejoice and show him respect;
for when the virtuous are honored, they strive even more for one's prosperity.
Seeing her husband approaching while she was devouring everything entirely,
she was abandoned by her own sons, as well as by her kinsmen and relatives.
Seeing Hari approaching at the city gate, Bhāmā— alone in her devotion before the line of women—
concealed the signs of her passion, such as the bristling of her hair and trembling, as she bowed down before him.
