Distressed travelers of the summer heat arrive in haste at the banks of deep rivers and at the roots of trees; this is their primary purpose.
That they should be perfumed with flowers, protected by dense shade, and fanned by gentle breezes—this is the purpose of the trees.
Where these immeasurable rivers come, dwell for long, and likewise flow forth as they please;
where, even though many jewels have been carried away by the gods, that which remains is as it was before—may he, the sole ground of immortality, be victorious!
Days come and go incessantly; they do not distinguish between cool water and harsh heat. Alas, we do not know for whom these days will bring what.

Surely these wives of mine, now clinging to their beds like creditors, appear like serpents at the very moment my life departs. My palace now seems like a prison cell; my mind cannot remain there for even a moment, nor for half a moment.
As their own young wives returned from the forest,
the amorous women, seeing a peacock in front of them who was fearfully preoccupied with the heavy burden of another peahen's tail feathers, believed that men were inherently insincere.
As if from the power of the touch of the foot of the approaching splendor of day, a cluster of fresh buds unfolds upon the celestial *aśoka* tree;
spreading the grace of a fresh ear-ornament for the fawn-eyed women of the quarters, this mass of rays from the rising young sun shines forth.
As she applied the line of collyrium to her long eyes,
the hand of the female attendant reached the outer corner of the eye only after resting there for a long time.
O hound of the hunter, your essence consists of exertion and the harming of others;
having driven you away, this deer shall now be divided among others.
Wealth, which is obtained through hundreds of hardships and is dearer even than life, has only one true destination: giving; all other uses are but calamities.
Through pride, a mortal encounters exhaustion, grief, fear, and suffering, his appearance and character becoming objects of reproach by all people;
knowing that pride destroys virtues such as knowledge, compassion, self-restraint, and modesty, one whose intellect is pure does not fall under the sway of arrogance.
With her vine-like arms slackened by exertion, her cheeks flushed with an exceeding smile, and her tresses half-concealed by swarms of bees hovering near her trembling outer corners,
the innocent girl intoxicates [the beholder] as she places the hem of her garment over her chest— though it were already uncovered— as her fine cloth, soaked by perspiration, reveals her breasts.
With their lotus-eyes unopened from exhaustion, and their breasts heavy with the weight of fatigue and making soft sounds as they heaved,
those groups of women moved forward toward the water with great difficulty, their trembling feet placed firmly upon the ground.
Disregarding its own exhaustion and not counting even the slightest gain, the cloud, taking refuge in nothing but its fame, pours forth water everywhere.
Therefore, let the world either utilize this with effort to increase the donor’s eternal glory, or, out of folly, let it neglect and destroy it; in any case, the world is the judge.
Having come to a noble cow who has been milked by many and drunk from by her calf,
would even a well-trained cowherd be able to milk her with effort?
"O beloved, O radiance consisting of my very end, when will you come?"—
having been asked this by her whose face was like the moon, she covered her face with her garment.
It is possible that you will go and return when the end of your life has not yet arrived; once you have returned, those very pleasures shall become manifest to us even now.
However, it is not fully determined what this heart—unaware of the experience of separation—will do when you have departed at once.

"I shall come to you again after the watch has passed, my dear," saying this, the lotus-eyed beloved departed in haste for the assembly. When she had gone somewhere and was making a tinkling sound, I repeatedly looked along the path, wondering if she had returned; thus, I found not even a trace of the pleasure of sleep that night.
Lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death—
these five are indeed created for the embodied being while still dwelling in the womb.
Life is as fickle as a wave; the glory of youth lasts but a few days; wealth is like a mere mental construction; and the floods of sensual enjoyment flicker like lightning in the rainy season.
Even that embrace of beloved women, so cherished, does not endure for long. Therefore, fix your minds upon Brahman in order to cross to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
When asked about one's lifespan, astrologers should declare it to be long;
for those who are alive hold life in high regard, whereas once dead, whom will they ask again?
The transgression of a great person destroys a man's lifespan, prosperity, fame, virtue, the higher worlds, and even his blessings; it strikes down all that is auspicious.
Longevity, prosperity, fame, sovereignty, and whatever blessings a person may desire—
these indeed come to pass at that time, even for one who does not wish for them, just as their opposites do.
Foods that increase longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy; which are savory, unctuous, substantial, and pleasing to the heart—these are dear to those of sattvic nature.
O beautiful one, youth is the essence of life, the season is the essence of the year,
and the taste of the nectar of the flavor of erotic enjoyment is the essence of existence.
The subjects face fivefold fear: from officials, from thieves, from enemies, from those favored by the king, and from the greed of the lord of the earth.
Among weapons, the bow is the best; among seats, the earth;
among fruits, the mango tree; and among gods, Maheśvara.
Longevity is found in ghee and molasses; diseases are always present in pungent and burning foods;
health is found in bitter and acrid things; strength is found in black gram and milk.

Victorious is the hero, the Lord of Kaliṅga: the personified trust of kings who bow before him; a festival for the eyes of deer-eyed women; the supreme radiance of fame; bliss incarnate; the very life of the Goddess of Heroism; and the abode of Dharma itself.

A mind whose inner core is moistened with compassion makes one’s lifespan longer, one’s body more excellent, one’s lineage more venerable, one’s wealth more abundant, one’s strength greater, and one’s sovereignty more exalted; it makes health free from interruption, one’s renown in the three worlds more extensive, and the ocean of saṃsāra easier to cross.
Life perishes even as one watches; youth wastes away day by day; days that have passed do not return; Time is the devourer of the world.
Fortune is as fickle as the breaking of waves upon the water, and life is as fleeting as lightning. Therefore, O Giver of Refuge, protect me now, for I have come to you for shelter.
Knowing that life is as fragile as the breaking of water-waves, they lived happily; perceiving wealth to be perishable like a dream, they constantly remained attached to enjoyments;

and thinking youth to be like a pillar of clouds, they embraced women with passion—by these very things, people here are bound to the flavor of worldly existence, though it is by these same things that one is liberated.
May there be long life and abundant strength; may there be happiness and auspiciousness; may there be vast renown for you.
May there be prosperity, a mind intent on the Dharma, the destruction of enemies, the increase of progeny, and the fulfillment of all desired goals.
Those who desire long life, fame, strength, wealth, and pleasant things must first propitiate their father; for the father is indeed a great deity.
The line of life is comparable to a lamp flickering in the wind; this prosperity is as fickle as the glance of a passionate woman swaying under the influence of intoxication;
and separation from beloved ones burns the heart intensely within. Therefore, we have taken refuge in this ever-pure, tranquil Brahman.
The lifespan of humans is limited to one hundred years; half of that is spent at night, and half of the remaining half is further divided between childhood and old age.

What remains is passed in the company of illness and the pain of separation, or consumed by service and other such labors. When life is as flickering as a wave upon the water, from where can there be happiness for living beings?
The lifespan of humans is limited to one hundred years; half of that is taken away by night, and of the remaining half, some is lost to old age and some to childhood.
Some is destroyed by diseases, separations, sorrows, deaths, and the pleasures of serving kings. What remains is as flickering as a wave; where, then, is the moment of true happiness for men?
Knowing that life is as unstable as the wind, strength and youth as flickering as the bow of Indra, wealth as transient as the waves of a mountain river,
youth as tremulous as a flapping elephant’s ear, and the body as riddled with disease— realizing all this, always practice the stainless Dharma which is eternally steadfast.
Life is like a lotus leaf shaken by the wind; what else can be said? Prosperity is but a companion to the fleeting splendor of the champaka flower, and Death wanders at will.
Why do you wander in this darkness? Go to Prayāga! There, the divine celestial river on earth will repeatedly wash away your sins.
As life passes away through the journey of days, months, and years, the rows of dust kicked up by the hooves of the wild boar of Death advance along the paths.
Thinking, "Our childhood has barely been transcended," "We are standing at the threshold of youth," and "We are clearly not yet devoid of our prime," those who are prone to indolence rejoice.
Life-span, wealth, domestic secrets, counsel, sexual intercourse, medicine,
contempt, asceticism, and giving— these nine things should be guarded with great effort.
One should well conceal these nine things: one's lifespan, wealth, domestic secrets, counsel, sexual conduct, medicine, gifts, honors, and insults.
For wealthy men who desire the cause of the increase or decrease of their lifespan and its excellence, that which has emerged from Time is the desired wealth beyond even life itself.
One who has practiced Āyurveda, whose appearance is pleasing to all,
and who is endowed with noble conduct and virtues— such a person is designated as a physician.
Many physicians are seen who, though studying Āyurveda thoroughly along with its ancillary branches, are themselves overwhelmed by diseases.
Not even a single moment of life can be obtained for ten million gold pieces;
if that moment is spent in vain, what loss could be greater than that?
Not even a single moment of life can be obtained for ten million gold pieces;
homage to that beast among men by whom it is spent in vain!
Not even a single moment of life can be obtained for all the jewels in the world;
that it is led away in vain—this is a very great negligence.
The venerable one should eat facing the east; if he is wealthy, he should face the south; if he desires fame, he should face the west, but never facing the north.
A wise person in this world should protect their lifespan in every way;
even one endowed with only slight virtues, by living, beholds auspicious things.
Life is as fleeting as lightning and this body is perishable; no one knows when death will swallow them up.
O best of the twice-born, follow the path to liberation this very day; for does the new moon not appear even before the end of the month?
How much of your life remains, and how much of that youth? Even here, half has been swallowed by the nature of night, wherein you have no attachment.
How many moments remain? If there is anger even toward that which arises from love, consider it futile; O Cakravākī, what birth would be better for you, and who will tell you what is beneficial?

O hero among men, may your life increase evermore like the nights of winter; may you always be one who increases the joy of the world like the sun in winter. May you always be one who increases the fear of your enemies like the waters of winter; and may your foes likewise constantly go to their destruction like the lotus in winter.
Lifespans are momentary, and youth is generally beset by old age; unions end in separation, and enjoyments perish in an instant.
Even though people know all this world as it truly is, it is a marvel that they—minds filled with heavy pride—both become angry and intoxicated.
The Creator drew a very long line of life upon her hand,
as well as a hope for the fulfillment of the mind-born god’s pride in his prowess.
He should always be free from shame regarding income and expenditure;
he should not constantly conceal himself with garments and other coverings that are tight or secretive.
Having obtained as his ally in battle Kṛṣṇagati, who is the night of doom for the kṣatriyas,
he regards the sharp edge of Rāma’s axe as having the strength of a blue lotus petal.
When the face turns reddish or the tongue turns dark,
then the wise person should know that death is near for himself.
May he, whose long eyes are slightly reddened and who is enchanting to the sight, possessing a body as graceful as ten million gods of love;
may he, the sovereign of the citizens of the city of Vrindavana forest, dwell today within the lotus of my heart.
With its reddish streaks and flowers containing water within,
this young kandalī plant reminds me, with tears welling up inside from anger, of her eyes.
The lotus pond is bristling with reddish sprouts; the night is no longer long; the light of the sky-jewel, slightly released from its frost, has begun to shine forth boldly;
and these days are arriving—laden with the fragrance of mango blossoms, made resonant by cuckoos, and piercing the very vitals of young women separated from their lovers.

O gentle one, the wind— gently drinking the fresh honey of the slightly reddened lotuses, wandering gracefully through the groves of night-blooming water-lilies that have awakened at the hour of dusk,
and moistened by the ichor of wild elephants in the forest— will serve you while proclaiming a competitive rivalry among the various fragrances.

Upon her eyes, which possess flower-arrows reddened with lac, the great blue sapphire-like dark luster of glossy collyrium rests; upon her ear-ornaments of saffron-red *karṇikāra* flowers, it bears the appearance of fresh drops of musk-paste like a blossoming tilaka-mark; thus the swarm of bees possesses the most charming beauty of the Spring Goddess’s forehead.
The trees, with their fresh sprouts reddened by dawn, provide a festival for the eyes; now this southern breeze, fragrant with sweetness, approaches shaking them.
As soon as it embraces him, this world is driven to madness, its mind becoming turbid with the intense desire for play that manifests according to the rite.

Forest-dwellers should perform [the rites] together with their own kind; caravan-travelers with other caravan-travelers; soldiers with soldiers alone; and even in a village, those who dwell in both [forest and village] should do so with each other.
Since the gods took the serpent into their own hands when they began the churning of the ocean,
it was only fitting that its result should have become the very poison that is so dangerous.

Is it a garland fashioned from the tender sprouts of the *ketakī*, or perhaps a long succession of camphor, or else a streak of sandalwood paste? Is it a stream of celestial nectar, or a rain consisting of snow? How can the play of your eyes be described? It is the very form of the five-arrowed god of love.
The Creator, out of the extreme weakness caused by your separation, has not yet fashioned this bow of the fish-bannered god into a complete weapon.
Therefore, O Lord, even now, please be gracious and cast upon her a glance that distills the nectar of love; let it become even the tinkling of the bowstring for the Lord of Rati.
When the Creator began to fashion this [face], which rivals the face of his beloved, it clearly rained down a mass of rays that had been present since his own birth;
yet, as the Lord of Rohiṇī (the Moon) was self-sacrificing and the lotus on the couch was extremely distressed by its closing, the Creator’s artistry in that regard remained unmanifested.
When the drum was struck, while the elders remained seated upon their thrones, and when the water-jar—its mouth bent down by being lifted onto my shoulder and tilted—was overflowing with water;
when I was summoned and dismissed by the King, the people were amazed at my composure. "If a son carries out his father's word, what cause for wonder is there in that? they said.
The ignorant undertake only small tasks and become distracted by their desires;
those of perfected intellect undertake great undertakings and remain undisturbed.
A man should undertake his work without neglecting his own human effort; for the accomplishment of an action is established upon both destiny and human exertion.
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings.
Those petty kings who undertake even a great task become universal monarchs and are born as vessels of prosperity.
Heavy at its beginning and gradually wasting away, light at first and later increasing—
friendship between the wicked and the virtuous is like the shadow of the day, divided into its forenoon and afternoon halves.
Delight in undertaking [tasks], lack of fortitude, embracing what is not a virtuous deed, and the constant pursuit of sense objects— these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa).
Associations with the wicked are delightful at the outset, but bitter in their aftermath; they generally end in enmity.

Near a fire of dried cow-dung, travelers have spent the three watches of the night with great difficulty— sitting amidst heaps of straw arranged at a distance, overcome by cold winds entering through the gaps in their tattered rags, hunched with knees drawn close together like dogs, as the nights were made twice as long by the inner, irrepressible suffering.

O you who move with soft grace due to the weight of your height, that excellent tree over there, which with its own flowers seems to entreat your locks of hair for an ornament until the end of time, repeatedly beckons you with the warbling of cuckoos; let us go there.
"Have you worshipped some deity with blue lotuses that the moon has performed penance? Or what fortune of golden splendors is unfolding here?
Or has some favorable fate smiled upon her today, since even these [limbs] of hers, possessing the beauty of young sprouts, bear comparison to her smiling eyes?"

That you were worshipped by the crowns of [twenty] heads adorned with the crescent of the moon, that your twenty arms are friends to the sun, and that the growth of your majesty overcomes the world—all that was rendered as false by your lifting of Mount Kailāsa; for, assuming the playful role of a thief, you have stolen our lotus-eyed lady from behind our backs.
Whichever deity one propitiates, one should declare that to be superior;
one should never diminish them, but rather encourage their service.
Those courtesans who possess a supreme longing merely to await the love of one who seeks them— verily, they are goddesses of fortune, worthy of being honored by the wise.
For kings, when propitiated and served like gods, bestow favors upon their devotees; in the opposite case, they destroy them.
For kings, when propitiated by virtue and served with diligent efforts, become well-disposed; in the opposite case, they become enraged.
Whether he is honored or even offended, a wicked person always inflicts harm;
whether carried on the head or standing at the soles of the feet, a venomous serpent will certainly bite.
"The husband alone is to be honored, and service to his two feet is her vow. "By whom, O friend, have you been taught such evil inclinations toward setting out on a wrong path?
What is the use of beauty if the minds of young men do not sink into it, and what is the use of teachers skilled in the secret methods of the hidden god of love, if their fame does not endure?"
Having propitiated the gods with nectar itself, the Ocean of Milk, alas, bestowed poison upon the Great God;
for it is certain that the very nature of reservoirs of water is such that they yield good water to the lowly and bad water to the exalted.
"Having propitiated the king and obtained wealth from him, we shall surely enjoy constant pleasures"—
with such a hope, the time of men whose minds are deluded by the Kali age passes away until the very limit of death.
When a king is being propitiated with effort, he is indeed propitiated; what is there to marvel at in that?
But this is an unprecedented and extraordinary image, which, when served, turns into an enemy.
The master of the grove is surely devoid of solitude; the flavors are indeed sapless; the ten directions have been made harsh by the winds; and the fierce heat of the sun is unbearable.

Thus, O cloud, even when every cause for the destruction of this *campaka* tree in the desert was present, you have somehow appeared, sprinkling it with nectar, as if manifested by the Creator himself.
O cloud, you who have drunk away the fierce heat with the clusters of sprouts that serve as ornaments for the grove—bring an end to this forest fire of the tree that is no longer heavy with fruit.

O you who are timid toward those who help you, we say to you: though its wealth of water is nearly exhausted, this tree, even when burnt, will cause the quarters of the sky to overflow with fragrance as it perishes.
The arrowhead with a mouth like a garden-gate, the razor-edged, the cow-tail-shaped, the half-moon,
the needle-mouthed, the broad-headed, the calf-tooth, and the double-broad-headed.
The *karṇika* and the *kākatuṇḍa*, as well as many other fruits of various forms, grow in many different regions.
One should pierce the shield with the arrowhead shaped like a garden-gate, the bow with the razor-sharp tip,
the armor with the needle-pointed tip, and the head with the crescent-shaped blade.
The heart should be pierced with a *bhallā* arrow; the string and the shaft with two *bhallas*;
iron with a *kākatuṇḍa*; and the target with a *gopucchaka*.

If liberation were to be attained through gardens, palaces, excellent horses, noble elephants, songs, diversions, musical instruments, the most charming pride of youth, and throngs of fair-browed women— then why, alas, have these skilled men abandoned all of this to go to the forest to perform austerities that grant the bliss of liberation?
"O elephant, why do you go mad, exultant with pride increased by an inner surge of joy, thinking, 'This entire grove has been destroyed by me, the irresistible and powerful one'?
O friend, every year a fever of the summer heat shall befall you; even then, you ought to consider properly what remedy to apply."
One who is about to undertake [an action] must first conduct a thorough investigation endowed with the power of mantras.
The power of mantras is weightier than the strength of arms; Śakra conquered the asuras through the power of mantras.
A subordinate who desires to properly serve a lord should cultivate himself through knowledge, discipline, the arts, and other such qualities.
For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once established in yoga, tranquility is said to be the means.
Having ascended far, disregarding fierce afflictions and revealing yourself,
you carry me away, O fair-limbed one, like a sail-cloth catching the wind for a ship.
Having first mounted the horses of the senses that have been brought under control,
and having conquered those internal enemies such as desire, anger, and the like,
the king should first conquer his own self in order to achieve victory over other adversaries.
For how can one who has not conquered himself and is powerless bring others under his control?
Having ascended the mountain peak, the Lord of Night stands before you with his rays raised upward, as if to retaliate, for he has had the entirety of his beauty stolen away by your face.
Having ascended this moonstone terrace of the pleasure mountain, this peacock,
with its beautiful and shimmering tail-feathers, dances.
Even that which arises from oneself becomes something to be avoided by the pure, like one who has fallen after having climbed high;
such was the water that, having carried away the blue lotuses fallen from the ears of the young women, cast them onto the shore along with its waves.
Sprinkled by the sweat-drops falling from the foreheads of the mounted kings, their spirits soaring with the thrill of the thundering drums and the twanging of bows;
with the surface of the earth trembling beneath them, their hooves flashing, their manes waving and tossing, and their eyes rolling as they move slowly—the throngs of horses dance in every direction.
Behold this certain slender form of loveliness in the bloom of youth— a forest deity bearing a lotus-face rich in sweetness, with the playful charm of fresh bamboo shoots upon her lips.

For one who has ascended the funeral pyre, the embrace of a beloved woman striving to follow him in death, the drinking of the juice of red sugarcane, and the fragrance of garlands and bracelets from which the breath has departed— when memory is utterly destroyed by a violent great delusion, such is the auspicious majesty of the nature of things for one who is mindless.
A horse with its rider mounted brings about the accomplishment of wealth and desired thoughts;
for all people, the sight of amorous play at the beginning [of an undertaking] leads to the attainment of enjoyment.

May the waves of Hari’s speech— which, while he was in the midst of his rising youth, wandered through various assemblies and desired to express with great secrecy the various thoughts in his mind toward those women— though they surged forth with speed in a state of indistinct syllables due to the weight of shame, now turn back toward you for your own benefit.
Mounted upon the excellent elephant of the Malaya breeze, accompanied by his attendants of amorous play, and drunk in by the eyes of the flower-like young women of the new creepers,
King Spring wandered through the forest city amidst the sounds of the *bherī* drums of the humming bees that swarmed together with the playful warbling of the cuckoos.

When the parrot, perched upon the bamboo pole on the roof-terrace of his master’s house, was seized by the cruel jaws of a wicked cat and cried out even once, though softly, "Ganga!", he attained half the throne of the Lord of the Immortals; yet who can truly know the one who merely touches or even contemplates the waters of the triple-streamed Ganges?

O King, may Aśvinī grant you long-lasting health; may Śiva, Keśava, the Moon, the Sun, and the gods bestow constant joy and prosperity upon you. May Brahmā and all the other deities, as well as Gaurī and the Mothers, bring about, perform, do, cause to be done, and ensure that everything is auspicious and protective for you.
Health, supreme bliss, happiness, and even enthusiasm—
all these, as well as sovereignty and the enjoyment of loved ones, are entirely without purpose without [the Dharma].
One should desire health from the Sun, prosperity from Fire,
knowledge from Maheśvara, and liberation from Janārdana.
One should seek health from the Sun, wealth from Fire,
knowledge from Maheśvara, and liberation from Janārdana.
Good health, learning, friendship with the virtuous, birth in a noble family,
and self-mastery— these constitute great sovereignty for men, even in the absence of wealth.
For one who has performed meritorious deeds, there shall always be health, good fortune, wealth, leadership, joy, victory, and the attainment of their desires in this world.
Health, intelligence, discipline, diligence, and passion for the treatise—these five internal qualities lead to success in study.
Furthermore, the teacher, the books, a dwelling place, assistants, and a good ear—these five external factors cause study to flourish.

Health, freedom from debt, not living abroad, association with virtuous people, a livelihood based on one's own efforts, and dwelling without fear— these, O King, are the six happinesses of the world of the living.
The fortune of health comes to one afflicted by a bilious fever who partakes of a decoction of *reṇukā*;
do not be like Ratnakalā, O dear one, who, tormented by love, was pacified from her anger by her friends.

To mount his excellent state elephant, to carry away a beautiful maiden, to enjoy the pleasure that has arrived, and to adorn his body with jewels—the one by whom the Hālāhala poison was quelled so that the nectar-eating gods might prepare for these things is my lord and deity; any other is not even known by name.
"Why do you vainly attribute this to me? Surely I am not ignorant of your lap;
it is not right to say that I remained there for a divine thousand years."
Placed upon the broad slope of the young woman’s hips, firmly grasped by her vine-like arms around the neck, and pressed tightly against her lofty,
full breasts— this jar enjoys the fruits of the fire that burns dried cow-dung.
Even when abundant virtues are attributed to them by those honored in the world, they themselves do not honor [those virtues] here;
surely the statues of the gods serve as the illustration for this.
Though placed upon a stone with the mantra,
"May you become like stone," she merely laughed at the sight of her lover's face during the occasion of their wedding.
Just as a stone is raised to the peak of a mountain with great effort,
yet falls down easily, so too is the self [elevated or cast down] by virtue and vice.
Mounting bulls, elephants, palaces, mountain peaks, and trees;
being smeared with excrement, seeing blood, encountering the dead, and sexual intercourse with forbidden women in dreams are auspicious.

O lady with limbs as beautiful as golden ketaka flowers, there stands a mountain— shaken by the ocean— that appears ready for your ascent, its body adorned with rows of rays that resemble hundreds of steps worn smooth by the friction of the coils of the lord of serpents.
Let him climb to the peak of a mountain, cross the ocean, or go to the netherworld;
yet the skull marked with the lines written by fate bears fruit, not the king.
It climbs the trees, enters the chasms, vies with the mountains, stretches toward the sky, and tosses about on the surface of the earth;
it hides within the bowers of the forest, wanders inside the hollows, groans, and clings to the creepers—what is there that the fire in the forest does not do when driven by the wind?
The unskilled mount comfortable seats; those who enjoy such things consume betel and the like; actors and parasites eat [their fill], as do elephants and other beasts;

even sparrows and the like dwell in his palace. Such a person is not a fit object for praise; rather, he alone is worthy of praise in this world, the virtuous man who bestows upon the people whatever they desire.
With rows of water-streams hanging down to the earth like ascending creepers,
the sky appears like a banyan tree, shining with leaves as dark as rain clouds.
Uprightness, compassion, self-restraint, and control of the senses—
Manu declared this to be the common duty for all four social orders.
O Lord, always practice straightforwardness toward your sons;
having attained supreme fame in this world, you will obtain heaven after death.
O fair-faced one, straightforwardness is the fourth, and indeed the fifth quality is dharma itself; thereafter, sweetness is proclaimed as the sixth.
Honesty is the crown jewel of those whose ornaments are purity; humility is the crest-jewel of those who wear the finest gems.
Gambling is the ruin of those with evil vices; being conquered by women is the fate of those who are like demons haunting the coastal marshes.
The initiation maintained by us with sincerity toward the supreme deity—
may there be liberation from those exceedingly human afflictions.
Those of evil intellect, deeming a man endowed with uprightness and modesty because of his honesty to be powerless, treat him with contempt.

May that Blessed One protect the world from misfortune—He who, as the elephant devoted to rescuing the distressed, uttered the words "The cause of the burning and so forth" through the mouth of the crocodile Cakradhara; He at whose pillar the sound of hand-clapping arose, which reached even the ear of the gods, and who cried out "Alas, Kṛṣṇa! in an inexhaustible manner.

Those who are afflicted by suffering, those in need of protection, and those in miserable states are said to be, in that order, worthy recipients for the compassionate; however, in their absence, one who possesses virtuous qualities is also such a recipient.

Those sounds characterized by distressed, hurried tones, or those that are broken, piteous, discordant, feeble, or fierce, are censurable; whereas auspicious sounds are those that are joyful, full, firm, and peaceful.
O Soul within the universe, though You see me as I bow in distress, O All-pervading Lord, You do not perceive me; though You hear me, You do not listen.
Indeed, by the power of my ill fortune, even You—the ocean of compassion for that [Kumbha]—have now been swallowed up by him.
The afflicted bow to the gods; the sick perform austerities;
the destitute desire to give gifts; and an aged woman is devoted to her husband.
By whom was this jewel created— the two syllables "mitra" (friend)— which connects the suffering of those in distress and serves as the cause for the repose of affection?
The Supreme Lord, who severs the suffering of living beings afflicted here in this world,
though possessing two arms, is devoid of the conch, discus, and mace.
She who is distressed when her husband is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away on a journey,
and who dies when he dies— that woman is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
A gift given to those in distress, the worship of an empty linga,
and the performance of funeral rites for a destitute deceased person yield the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.

O King, that gift which is given with faith by one filled with compassion to Brahmins who are in distress becomes infinite and boundless; that which is not given to the twice-born cannot be recovered.
There is no one else as afflicted as I, and no one else more devoted to compassion than you. Our union is indeed equal; O Lord, why do you not protect me?
Whether he be distressed or terrified, an enemy who has come for refuge must be protected by one of self-restraint, even at the cost of his own life.
If a dog is seen in front with a raw bone in its mouth, it brings good fortune;
however, if it carries a dry hide or a completely parched bone, it brings about death.
O fair-limbed one, having cast off this garment though it was still moist from your breasts and hips,
the sun’s rays drink it up as if to reach you who are now situated in the sky.

May the assembly at the descent of Śambhu’s dance purify you—where Ambikā bends the fresh garland hanging from her lotus-face down to her knees; where Nandin arranges the crescent moon in its proper place and binds his matted locks with the lord of serpents; where Kāla fastens the skin, and Kālarātri brings the skull-bowl into the hand of Śambhu, each member of the retinue engaged in their separate tasks.
With the breeze from her face, she fans her foot which is moist with lac;
now, for the first time, an opportunity for my service has been granted to me.
O bull of the Bharatas, the wise take delight in noble deeds, perform rites that bring prosperity, and do not find fault with what is beneficial.
For women who are censured by noble people and whose nature manifests as nothing but evil, their only merit is this: that they may enjoy union with their beloved without restraint.
Knowing that this conduct is eternally cherished by the noble ones,
the virtuous, while acting for the sake of others, do not look for any recompense.
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and compassion; constant magnanimity and the arising of the qualities of equanimity.
Nobility is the fourth, and indeed the fifth is the quality of righteousness;
the sixth is virtuous conduct, firmness is the seventh, and courage is the eighth.
Having obtained human birth— endowed with the noble land, lineage, form, strength, longevity, intelligence, and kinship—
he who, being dull-witted, does not perform the deeds of Dharma, is like one who abandons his ship once he has reached the ocean.
Noble son, father, mother, brother, son, and likewise daughter-in-law,
each enjoying their own merits, experience their respective fortunes.
O bull among men, it is the wife alone who attains the fortune of her husband.

By whom was this severe penance performed on the banks of the Muralā, undertaking the noble and limbless great vow (*āryānaṅga-mahāvrata*) and breaking its fast with the winds of the Vindhya mountains,
so that his secret lips— drunk like wine, scented by the deep and soft sighs of her who is weary from the fatigue of passion— are consumed with the moonlight of his laughter as a side-dish?
My noble wife is indeed fickle of speech, yet my conduct toward her is such that she is skillful in household duties and likewise suffers when she is afflicted by pain.
Engaged in noble deeds or again in sinful ones,
the Lord moves pervading all beings, yet he is not perceived as such.
"O Dhanañjaya, they say that noble deeds are easy for a noble person to perform;
however, ignoble deeds are exceedingly difficult for a noble person to perform in this world."

Blessed are those who carry their sons upon their laps— the children who possess bud-like teeth, whose speech proceeds charmingly with indistinct syllables through causeless smiles, and who are fond of resting in their father's embrace— and who become soiled by the dust of those children's limbs.

From the ocean, marked by the rippling waves of milk from the breasts of the women of Laṅkā’s lord, up to the northern mountain whose rocky slopes are difficult to traverse due to the rows of waves of the celestial Gaṅgā;

from the eastern mountain where the sun and moon are submerged, which knows the movements of the amorous play of the Asura women, down to the ocean of Pracetasa—let there be some hero before me, if indeed such a one exists!
She speaks like a female cuckoo, she gazes like a doe, she moves like a female swan;
she flashes like a streak of lightning and tastes sweet like a digit of the moon.
Speak as you wish, O gambler; what is improper for you? This friend of yours, O fortunate one, is a mere beggar for life, bearing the very mark of her female nature.

In the month of Madhu, women— with golden girdles dangling, necklaces clinging to their breasts, and slender bodies made limp by the pride of Kandarpa— forcibly steal the hearts of men with the sweet warbling of cuckoos and the humming of bees.
I take refuge in the lotus feet of Heramba, the support of the world;
by the touch of whose dust the oceans of obstacles instantly dry up.
Having leaned at will against a small branch near the edge of the courtyard garden for the entire day, her bracelets reduced to mere remnants serving as armlets—
what will that young woman say today, with her tear-filled face, upon seeing the path of me, whose mind is deluded by fate and whose appointed time has been cut short?

I imagine that near the mango tree by the edge of the courtyard pond— tree which is beautified by clusters of blossoms and by female bees humming as they swarm after the thick pollen— the young woman, having covered her body with a fragment of her upper garment, weeps, her rising sighs causing her breasts to tremble as she stifles the throbbing sound in her throat.
When the water remaining in the basin does not dry up, one should know that it is undigested; such a person should not be given water.

Be lazy regarding evil deeds; be cruel, wrathful, and harsh in striking others; indulge in greed and delusion regarding worldly objects, but maintain vigilance in meditation upon Hari. Become dull-witted when speaking ill of others, and harbor malice toward those who remember [the Lord]. O mind, in this way all these faults shall become virtues for you.
First comes laziness, followed by the onset of affliction from disease;
negligence is the mind's failure to remain steady when there is a point of doubt.
Laziness, intoxication, delusion, restlessness, socializing,
stubbornness, arrogance, and likewise a lack of generosity— these seven are indeed considered to be the constant faults of those seeking knowledge.
If laziness did not exist as a calamity in this world, who would not be wealthy or highly learned?
Because of laziness, this earth, extending to the edge of the oceans, is filled with human cattle and the destitute.
Laziness, devotion to women, illness, attachment to one's birthplace,
lack of contentment, and cowardice— these six are obstacles to greatness.

O Mother Lakṣmī, by the power of your grace, even faults become virtues: laziness attains steadiness, fickleness resorts to diligence, muteness expands into measured speech, and foolishness becomes straightforwardness; and the absence of discrimination between the worthy and unworthy recipient bestows a noble nature.
Laziness takes away wisdom, wealth, lifespan, fame, and strength;
that person in whom this laziness resides is a mine of all defects.
For laziness is the great enemy residing within the bodies of men;
there is no kinsman equal to diligence, by practicing which one does not come to grief.
Even laziness, having assumed the form of a lion, yawns with pride;
alas, even effort is thwarted by one who is cursed by fate!
Due to laziness, even a person who has good companions does not attain success;
he is like a ball moistened with water that, though struck by the tips of the hands, remains on the ground.
Knowledge is destroyed by laziness; women are lost when they fall into the hands of others; a field is ruined by insufficient seed; and an army is destroyed when it is without a leader.

O King, your arm shines forth: it is the hitching post for the elephant of victory, a stone bridge across the ocean of calamity, the eastern mountain for the fierce-rayed sword, and the playful pillow of royal fortune; it is Mount Mandara in the sport of churning the nectar-ocean of battle, and the bestower of widowhood upon the wives of your heroic enemies.
As if out of anger at being used as hitching posts, these rows of trees are being felled by the elephants with repeated "kṛta-cit-kṛta" roars, accompanied by the crackling sound of snapping branches.

When this elephant of youth is intent on departing, having uprooted the hitching post called "comfort," the breasts of women fall as if out of fear of being crushed by the fleeing herd of lustful men.
An elephant is held by its tethering post; a horse is held by its reins;
a woman is held by her heart. If this [heart] does not exist, then depart.
The cuckoo does not utter its song, the parrots do not make their steady sounds, the sweet-voiced birds do not speak, and the peacocks do not warble;
with the sky’s surface shrouded by a cloudless, gloomy day, the sound of bees is far away, and only the crows, with their harsh *keṅkṛta* cries, cause a fever in the ears.
Her speech is accompanied by the moonlight of a smile; her gaze is radiant with joy; her brow is consecrated for the sacrifice of dance; her step upon level ground is yet wavering;

her desire for ornaments is momentary; she is bound not by the pursuit of debate but by the laws of intoxication; and in this slender maiden, a passion consisting mostly of the honeyed wine of love manifests itself as a field of manifold transformations.
Having heard the buzzing of the swarm of bees, the innocent girl becomes frightened; looking at her face, she abandons the mirror.
Afflicted by the pain of love, she does not even sigh softly—O King, is this perhaps out of fear of the wind from the moon-like faces of the *kīra* birds?
She who converses about improper acts or herself speaks of something [unseemly],
and who does not go to bed, she too has not yet conceived desire.
Through conversation, through the touch of the body, through association, through eating together,
through sharing a seat, a bed, or a vehicle, sin is transmitted among men.
The play of her eyebrows thins out her conversation; her hips, slightly sunken at the waist, loosen the knot of her girdle with their expansive curve as they cast glances with her shimmering arms.
Her chest, with its swelling sides and rising peaks of breasts, surely appears as the youth of the fawn-eyed girl has been touched by the tip of the bow of the God of Love within.

Some [women] delight others with sweet conversations, others with smiling glances, still others with playful gestures radiant with the god of love, some with clever conduct, others with fresh [manners], and yet others with the quivering of their eyebrows; thus do these fair-eyed women please [their lovers], yet I think their minds are otherwise inclined.
"O Āli, O Kapālinī, O Jaṭilā! Enough of your persistent entreaties regarding your husband;
Gaurī repeatedly proclaims from her mouth, even though it is difficult to bear, that he has gone to Hara."
"O friend, prepare before me a lamp of kārpaṭika-cloth, [saying] 'It is the orb of the moon'—
for by this well-known [object], my eye has indeed been quickly covered by a pale ball of darkness."
She embraces one man and delights another with her speech; she gazes playfully at one and weeps for the sake of another; she makes oaths to one and chooses another;

she sleeps with one while, having fallen into a state of exhaustion, she thinks of yet another. By what cruel fate was this deceitful woman created—of wicked conduct and a bringer of harm to the world?

Having heard that he embraced the cowherd girl and placed her arm upon his own with a desire for dalliance, I conclude that the power of the bodiless god (Aṅga) is irresistible within embodied beings.
Let the practices of embracing, drinking the nectar of the lips, and pressing against the chest remain far from you;
O fawn-eyed one, by merely being gazed upon by the casts of your flickering glances, we have achieved our life's purpose.
They embrace the sandalwood trees, they cling to the forest edges, and they take leave of the long-familiar torrents of the Malaya streams;
having stayed today within the midst of the Dravidian women, the Malaya breezes prepare to set forth tomorrow morning and make their presence felt.
Embracing the earth as if to appease it for being torn by their own hooves,
these horses appear, due to their speed, as if their feet have vanished from their mouths.
Embracing her limbs of exceeding fragrance, kissing her bimba-like lips that are rosy-red, beholding the slope of her breasts, listening to the cries of the swans,
gazing incessantly at her long eyes, and savoring the juice of the clove-flower— such a fortunate man considers himself to possess the supreme bliss of the union of all seasons within a young maiden.
Embracing the limbs of the fair-eyed women most fervently, kissing their faces, and creating a variegated beauty with the marks of his nails upon their breasts, thighs, hips, and necks;
drinking the nectar of their bimba-red lips and loosening the knot of their garments through the play of his hands, he sported at will, intent on the most daring amorous dalliances.
She embraces him, entreats him, kisses him, gazes upon him, strokes him, and clings to him;
she looks toward his side, her heart pierced by the state of love, and with an empty interior, she remembers everything done in their dalliance.
O bee, you embrace the lovely *lavaṅgī* creeper and you kiss the lotus in succession; yet why is it that you strike that mango vine so excessively with your feet?
Your Honor has been embraced there by the Goddess of Victory in the afterlife;
now, placing upon your ear this venerable succession of blessings, please show us mercy.
Embraced by others, they stumble even on level ground;
the wealthy speak indistinctly, like those who have drunk wine.

Having embraced the eastern quarter, favored the southern, and gazed upon the northern, the thousand-rayed sun, though resting at twilight, fell into the ocean; thus shines forth the fruit of his union with Vāruṇī.
In this life, the only fruit for young men is that they awaken their sleeping beloved in secret, as she embraces them with sweet moans and languidly opening eyes.
In a beautiful palace that bestows eternal bliss, the fawn-eyed woman, whose breasts are like the frontal lobes of an elephant, embraces her beloved.
O you whose ears are friends to the *karṇikāra* flower, your cheeks shine with the grace of *āli* and *pālī*;
they are like two mirrors fashioned of gold for the lotus-born Brahmā and the five-arrowed god of love to behold Rati.
O friend, out of foolishness, let no offering ever be given to this crow;
for he is indeed the sole cause of well-being for the young cuckoos.
The *ālirdivya* is said to be a medicinal herb covered with fine thorns;
by drinking water produced from its root-fiber, a living being is freed from poisons.

Having for a long time experienced the embrace of her own limbs as her body’s every part moved with the trembling lotus petals stirred by her friend, and having made the cluster of fresh lotuses rustle, the young woman finally regains consciousness with great difficulty; slowly opening the corners of her eyes, she gazes upon the world as empty, her heart itself being utterly vacant.
Led into the interior of the bower by her companions through oaths and many deceptions, she looked upon it and found it empty; agitated, she neither departed nor remained.
Instead, the newly wedded lotus-eyed maiden, out of anger, cast her glances toward the vicinity of the bower—glances that touched upon the wondrous display of the swarms of bees.
Something was whispered by her friends, and even that path was gazed upon; the five-arrowed god of love was somehow worshipped with flowers once he had been placed slightly within my heart.
O beloved, if you thus resort to such piteous compassion toward me, then, O Lord of my life, all this powerful hostility toward me is surely the work of Fate.
In the rows of lotuses, a young girl, repeatedly lamenting my conversation with the impetuosity of play,
suddenly attained a splendor like lightning upon hearing my voice from afar.

"I shall paint a picture in the sky, weave the firmament with lotus fibers, bring back gold seen in a dream, and bind a rampart with snow"—even when such things are clearly stated, only one of dull intellect understands them as true; yet the king who, out of shame, does not speak thus is one whose maturity has vanished and is utterly deceived.
In solitude, she drew her own likeness with a graceful line; filled with many fancies, she formed numerous mental images.
She envisioned another Creator and undertook rigorous vows; how much more did the Creator, intent upon his task, not accomplish in the process of fashioning you?
O proud woman, though you turn your face away from me like the light of day at any given moment and do not remain to my south,
even so, like a shadow, you alone take away my heat.

His eyes fixed in a stare as he hears the intense clamor from the doorway—filled with a flood of people rushing about in terror, crying out great cries of fear like women startled by a flash of light—he is struck by blows from clods of earth by those with mouths exceedingly loud, shouting, "Seize a stick! Seize a staff! Terrified and finding no hole in the house, the snake moves from corner to corner.
By giving light, a person becomes possessed of vision and endowed with radiance;
having given those [lights], one should not harm them, nor take them away, nor destroy them.
One who steals a lamp will become blind, dwelling in the darkness with little luster;
one who offers a lamp shines like a garland of lamps in the heavenly world.
As a certain woman was suddenly rushing toward the path of light,
her mass of hair— its garlands already disgorged from being untied— was not even noticed as she tried to bind it, for her hand was already occupied.
She gazes upon the path, for it is said he has come to give her [the gift];
she carefully braids her hair, provided she has not been captivated by others.
The traveler gazes at the cloud, dark blue with its fresh burden of water near the palace,
suspecting it to be a column of smoke rising from the funeral pyre prepared by his beloved.

A lord of the earth who observes the movements of his enemies through spies and envoys endowed with the qualities of wisdom remains distinct from those people who are devoid of vision and share the same nature as the blind.
There are indeed many luminous bodies such as the sun and others;
yet it is only the moon that is truly skilled in the task of melting stone.
My vision, though wide with light, has been suddenly severed by the onset of darkness;
even when opened, it is as if closed by gloom.
From the very limits of the world, your function—whose activity dispels the darkness—is considered by us equal in effort to that of the Sun;
for while this lord of the luminaries remains for a moment in the midst of the sky, you too, during the sixth part of the day, act according to your own will over these subjects.

By whose power beings attain a happy rebirth as far as light reaches, that [darkness] spreads the illusion of a serpent within the lineage through the power of the attachment to false views. A certain flash of lightning—skilled at instantly destroying the venomous gaze in some serpents—would swiftly destroy even those very serpents with its momentary brilliance.

The sky is suddenly filled with an untimely storm, which is watched by the domestic peacocks with outspread tails, while the swans, longing to depart, turn away with distracted minds; this tempest simultaneously obstructs both the atmosphere and the heart of one who yearns for his beloved.
As the quarters of the sky are being overspread by exceedingly crimson rays that momentarily eclipse the splendor of the stars, and as the dawn of the sun is soon to be anticipated,
I believe that the thick darkness, as if out of fear, is withdrawing into the inner corners of the huts of closing blue lotuses under the guise of bees.

Behold! Having transcended childhood, as he turns toward youth, his lovely form—charming with a manifest passion anointed upon the surface of his tender cheeks—spreads a rippling wave upon the shore of the erotic sentiment.
Beholding the risen moon, this world is whitened by the moonlight, which is as if a succession of atoms spreading in all directions from the ocean whose jars [of water] are tossed by surging waves.
Beholding your mass of hair, which is constantly worthy of being perfumed with flowers,
Kāma turns his own quiver over and touches it apprehensively.
Having looked [at him], having well wiped her hands and eyes, having risen from the bed and put on her ornaments,
having kissed her beloved and donned her garment— she who departs thus, full of shame, pains the heart.
When the proud woman stood with her face like the moon bent down, modestly drawing her garment over her beloved,
it was surely because she beheld the very footstep of pride as it swiftly took flight.
O beautiful one, beholding your face with its gentle smile, the bees rejoice slowly, mistaking it for a lotus;
moreover, O dark-eyed one, the cakora birds flutter their beaks for a long time, in the delusion that it is the moon.
O friend, since you have become emaciated by remembering their glances, their words, and their secrets— which are as sweet as nectar—
why are you not distressed when you remember that the bodies of those deer-eyed women are merely vessels for flesh, blood, and excrement?
Having reflected upon these words, his inner self was delighted as if it had entered supreme bliss;
for generally, things that are destined to come to pass become enchanting when contemplated.
Having churned all the scriptures and the most excellent Purāṇas,
and having reflected upon them, the virtuous show compassion toward all living beings.
Having churned all the scriptures and reflected upon them again and again, this one conclusion is well-established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times.

May that face of the slender maiden protect you for a long time—her row of unswaying *āmala* fruits disheveled, her earrings swaying, her forehead-mark slightly blurred by fine networks of perspiration, and her eyes languid at the close of lovemaking during the reversal of sexual positions; what need is there for deities such as Hari, Hara, and Brahmā?
Bees, restless with longing, gather to seize the flower-garlands from her hair; an indescribable luster spreads across her cheeks from the betel held within her mouth;
her limbs are anointed with fragrant unguents, and her very mode of adornment is a process of perfuming. Such is the singular attire of the lotus-eyed maiden that it brings bliss to the eyes.
Perceiving the blood-red kandalī flower trembling from the touch of a bee,
the traveler on the road remembers the playful gesture of his beloved’s threatening finger.

When the Creator fashioned her face alone, the entire treasury of his luster was exhausted; for even though his craftsmanship in creating the fathomless world was not diminished by a whit, she remained with only a slight residue of body.
Was she then fashioned from masses of blinding darkness, which were easily obtained because the entirety of his orb of light had been spent?
By its power, there shall be no fear of snakes for a year;
and for one who drinks the snout of a snake ground with water, there is no fear.
"Let the objectives for my sake be accomplished by the two chief warriors among us"—
when such a wager is established, that is a treaty mediated through another person.
As if bowed down out of humility, with the lotus of his face slightly brightened by a sweet smile,
and with both hands placed upon his lap, he offered a respectful salutation when looked upon by the king.
As if slightly bent by her breasts, wearing a garment with the hue of the rising sun,
she was like a moving, leafy creeper bowed down by a full cluster of blossoms.

I remember her reclining on the bed, her locks of hair disheveled, one arm resting upon her breasts that trembled with her sighs, her garment loosened, and her body rendered helpless by the passion of love.
That horse which has a whorl of hair on its hump is called *kakudī*;
however, a horse joined with only one testicle is designated as *ekāṇḍa*.
A whirlpool of doubts, an abode of immodesty, a city of rash acts, a repository of faults, a field consisting of a hundred deceits, a source of mistrust;

an obstacle to the gate of heaven, the gateway to the city of hell, a casket of all illusions, a mechanical device of woman—by whom was this created? It is a noose for the world of living beings, composed of both poison and nectar.
When the whirlpool of knowledge becomes agitated like a whirlpool in water, the mind is said to have been caught in a whirlpool; that is called an affliction (*upasarga*).
Your navel is a whirlpool, your eyes are blue lotuses, and your bracelets are the waves; therefore, you are a pond of the waters of beauty.

The beauty of whirlpools arose from the loveliness of their sunken navels; the graceful movements of waves from their eyebrows; and the pairs of ruddy geese from their breasts—these were the comparisons for the limbs of those playful women, standing as if not far removed from them.
The horses, possessing auspicious curls, endowed with conch-like shells that yield good fortune, and filled with the jewels of the gods,
shone intensely as they covered the earth, rushing forward like oceans surging with waves.
Bearing the beauty of a libation with her whirlpools white as foam,
the river Surasā, whose waters are made resonant by song, sings of the auspicious reunion with her beloved.

Having wrapped her neck with her garment and firmly bound the pair of jar-like breasts, that beautiful woman approaches slowly toward Sundarī, carrying an oil vessel balanced upon the tip of her hand.
He who repeatedly recites the mantra and maintains it with effort—
should the mantra be maintained without effort and thus become agitated, it would burn like fire.
[The first speaker] says: "O arrogant one, you claim that no one other than us has been praised as the abode of Love on this earth; this is true.

[The second speaker] replies: "Ho! This is false. How is it, you fool, that you have not composed hundreds of poetic hymns for the Lord of Kuntala? Shame on you! You are merely a different form of Manu himself."

The morning breeze blows freely, fragrant with blossoming priyaṅgu flowers under the guise of frosty spray, scattering hidden flashes of fire across the lotus ponds; it delights in the joy of beholding the abundance of kunda flowers and is capable of making the bristling hairs on the cheeks of the florist’s young bride endure.
The dwelling is the scene of amorous passion; by one's side are beloved women languid with grace; at the ear is the sweet warbling of the female cuckoo; the vine-bower is in full bloom;
there are gatherings with a few excellent poets; the rays of the moon are charming; and here in the month of Caitra, variegated garlands bring delight to the hearts of some.
Make your dwelling either in the waters of the Gaṅgā, which wash away all sins,
or in the captivating and enchanting space between the breasts of a young woman.
"O Lord, in this lodging there are no clever people anywhere, nor is there even the fitness for the enjoyment of sleep; the straw mattress has fallen apart, and here before us is this lightning.

And here is a cloud rising up. When the traveler was told this by the fair-toothed woman—"If you have such a desire, then stay for the night"—he remained there, utterly bewildered and with the fear of the God of Love destroyed.
The birds, eager for their dwellings, are departing from the trees with sweet cries; this timid cakravāka, fearing the impending separation from his beloved, cries out all the more piteously.
The bees rush toward the thicket of lotuses, the owl feels great joy, and the sun, turning crimson, kisses the western mountain.
The dwelling acts like a forest; even the garland of her dear friends acts like a snare; even the heat, through her sighing, acts like a mass of flames from a forest fire.
Alas! In separation from you, she too, O woe, takes on the form of a doe; and how is it that even Kandarpa acts like Yama, performing his *śārdūlavikrīḍita* dance?

From the Vindhya mountains to the Himālayas, having achieved victory through the course of his pilgrimage to sacred sites, the Lord Bīsaladeva—king of Śākambharī—triumphs in the world; he strikes at kings who stand with necks upraised, yet is gracious toward those whose necks are bowed, and has once again made Āryāvarta true to its name by exterminating the Mlecchas.
The age of women, in which childhood has passed away,
manifests itself together with the various delusions of love-intoxication in men.
Manifesting first, it causes the heart of the beloved to breathe a sigh of relief,
like a flash of lightning appearing before the rain for a young peacock scorched by the heat.

How can I now perform even the slightest service with words for that Guru, who does not heed even the most subtle cause on the day of his manifestation, who does not diminish through the commission of offenses, and who does not increase through prostrations; he who reveals the nectar and destroys the tree of suffering for the three worlds?
I worship Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who manifested himself in four forms, was surrounded by monkeys, and destroyed the army of the Rākṣasas.
Let there be no doubt regarding the utterances of those Brahmins in whom the light has appeared;
for auspicious fortune is infused in their speech, and they do not speak words whose meaning is corrupted.

At the onset of pregnancy, O fair-browed one, her face has acquired a pale complexion, the surface of her cheeks has grown thin, her eyes have become languid from constant exertion, and her body is charmingly devoid of vigor; her face has darkened, her pair of breasts has swollen, and her waist—naturally high—is now transformed into something entirely captivating. Alas! How wonderful this transformation at the arrival of the embryo!
When the sun was rising from the eastern mountain, these trees of the grove, their passion suddenly awakened, seemed to hasten far ahead with the shadows of their leaves;
yet when his orb was cast toward the edge of the western mountain, they turned back. For servants who serve a master generally abandon him once his prosperity has departed.
Like the night being freed from darkness when the moon has appeared, or like the flame of a nocturnal fire whose smoke has mostly vanished,
this slender-bodied woman is seen within her delusion as if almost liberated— like the Ganges regaining its clarity after the turbidity caused by falling onto its banks.
Manifested in this material world through the form of supreme beauty, that Blessed One, whose essence is knowledge, shines in the mental realm;
He blazes clearly as the vital breaths in the universe, and His body appears manifest through the gateway of love in the world of the heart.

During those days, her body was such that the tips of her breasts were clouded with pallor, the complexion of her face was as white as the petals of the lavalī flower, and her eyes were solely languid.
From the time of your marriage, whether at home or in the forest, in childhood and thereafter in youth,
this arm of Rāma— never resorted to by another as a cause for sleep— is your pillow.
With deer entering the courtyards of the huts, young trees succulent from the watering of their roots,
and the sacrificial cows for the fire entering [the sheds], the hermitages, with their fires kindled, possess a radiant splendor.
She manifests no affection, she binds herself with no passion for pleasure;
though assiduous, her desire is faint, for that loving woman is in love with another.

Does this sun of fierce rays rise in the sky, as if manifesting with ever-fresh devotion a passion that pervades every limb for the lotus-pond fainting from long separation; or rather, does it display a crimson hue born of hatred and rage toward the darkness that blinds the three worlds?
Alas, the evil-minded do not remain silent when they perceive the virtues displayed by others; rather, it is out of malice that they seek to disparage them, not out of affection.
It is said that even the Kirātas listen to the warbling of the cuckoo only to string their seven-stringed lutes.
As if possessed by a profound sorrow directed toward that [suffering],
and endowed with supreme compassion, he should uplift the distressed.
If that deer-eyed woman covers the golden mountain of her breasts with the hem of her garment, it comes out again even more; for being lofty, it cannot endure being treated with contempt.
As the darkness of dust, having expanded in battle, covered the path of vision,
a stream of blood— born from the weapons-wounded horses, elephants, and heroes— became like the rising sun.

At the conclusion of our amorous play, I suddenly beheld her as she covered her hips with the hem of her silk garment; her hand was busily engaged in binding her tresses, which had become disheveled during the sport;
her breasts were adorned with nail-marks made visible by half-drawn breaths; and at the end of her infatuation, her face was bowed down from the memory of her own boldness.
Knowledge is veiled by this eternal enemy of the wise, O son of Kuntī— by desire, which takes form at will and is like an insatiable fire.
Even though they were completely covered by the pair of full breasts of the women,
the hearts of the impassioned lovers were grasped here and there by hands that felt them out.
Blinded by the intoxication of their own splendor, they make secret signals with one another; standing by their sides, others laugh at will like children, madmen, or demons.
To express our gratitude toward the Lord,
there is no better path than to proceed in silence with contentment.
"Tell me what is unknown, or what remains unsaid that ought to be spoken; for this [silence] is not enough to allay my inner anguish.
"Something is being said—listen to it! "Be gracious, O Mother, daughter of the Pāṇḍya king Malayadhvaja!"
She trembles, wanders, creeps along, and falls into a swoon; she gazes at her beloved and coos most piteously.
When the sun has indeed set, the female cakravāka bird suffers a death even while alive—separation from her dear one.
Fearing my prostration, she respectfully covers her feet with the hem of her garment; under some pretext, she conceals her laughter as it approaches; she does not look clearly at me;
when I speak, she offers contrary words and converses with her friend—let alone her overflowing affection, even the pride of this slender girl is lovely in its manifestation.
He who has made hope his slave is a slave to all embodied beings;
but for him by whom hope has been enslaved, the entire world acts as his servant.
One should make hope subject to time, and join time with obstacles;
one should declare the obstacle by means of its signs, and the sign also by means of its cause.

Are there not quarters of the earth covered with clusters of golden flower-buds? Is there no region on the surface of the earth adorned by those worthy of service who rain down the nectar of benevolence? Are there not paths filled with those praised for their long-standing delight in hospitable conduct? Yet, here dwell those whose virtues are concealed, having been deluded by time.
Dwarf the quarters with your pride; terrify all the excessively noisy, loud-crying peacocks with your roars; drive away the sweet-voiced swans.
Swiftly attack the circle of the sun and utterly ruin the good path, O glorious cloud, until this wind brings it to some state of distress.
It fulfills all hopes, bestows prosperity, removes the heat of the three worlds, provides a sprinkling of genuine nectar, and extends supreme joy;
yet by this cloud-like Time, who forcibly and for long has driven away that full King, the world has become nothing but a mass of intense darkness.

Who would not bow to that praiseworthy Sun, who, having shattered the darknesses, illuminates the quarters and bestows insight upon the eyes; who is desired for his manifold virtues, whose wandering about never tires him in acts of service to others, and who is wise?
Let the moon please the quarters of the sky, let him nourish the cakora birds, and let him spread joy at will among the night-lotuses;
yet he alone, the deer, shares a sorrow and a happiness equal to that of entering the tooth-marks of the fiercely voracious Rāhu.

Smearing the quarters of the sky, which were soiled by the coating of deep darkness, with rays as white as nectar; creating a flood of camphor and fashioning the surface of the earth into a single floor of moonstone—the moon rises, its luster comparable to the pale shade of autumnal ripeness. Behold!
This hope is a bottomless pit, difficult to fill; by whom can it be filled?
For even when great things are cast into it as fillers, it is only further dug out.
This bottomless pit of hope, which had cast down the three worlds,
was leveled by the virtuous— aho!— by repeatedly rescuing those situated therein.
For every living being there is a pit of desire, in which the entire world is like a mere atom;
for whom does anything come to pass, and to what extent? Thus, the pursuit of sense objects is in vain.
Seized by desire, they become impaired; shorn of shame, they cast aside their virtues and self-respect.
Like the intoxicated, they wander about with lost consciousness, their natures fickle, crying out, "Give me!"
Mounting the horse of hope, the beggar runs constantly;
yet he feels neither pain nor fatigue, nor does his speed ever diminish.
Hope destroys fortitude; Death destroys prosperity; anger destroys fortune; miserliness destroys fame;
failure to protect destroys livestock, O King; but a single enraged Brahmin destroys the entire kingdom.

The river called Hope has desire for its water, is turbulent with waves of craving, possesses crocodiles of passion, and has birds of discursive thought; it destroys the tree of fortitude, is difficult to cross due to the whirlpools of delusion, is exceedingly deep, and has high banks of anxiety. May those masters of yoga, whose minds are purified, rejoice having reached its further shore.
Hope is a certain wondrous chain for human beings;
bound by it, they run about, but once released, they stand still wherever they may be.

Hope, certainty, and stability—these, they say, are my women. When might there be happiness among them? That which is the last might accomplish something here; that which is the middle, something in the next world.
But alas, that which is the first accomplishes nothing in either place. Why then do I remain attached to her, who, through her arrogance, daily brings both of those others into disrepute?
Bound by the snares of hope, does a man not dance before his wealthy master? Where can one who is subject to Fate—the wretched actor—ever find happiness?

The mind’s state of self-reliance, characterized by the unwavering bliss of liberation from the snares of desire; the cessation of affection, hatred, dejection, and greed; a mind satisfied with contentment;
constant reflection on impermanence; and detachment even amidst worldly associations—for those whose minds are purified by the sprinkling of wisdom and discernment—this is the path to liberation.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and devoted to desire and anger,
they strive for the sake of sensual enjoyment, accumulating wealth through unjust means.
Bound by hundreds of snares of desire and carrying the weight of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*),
they pass from one body to another, like birds flying from tree to tree.
Those men whose limbs are ensnared by the fetters of desire and who are thus afflicted do not sleep at night at all, due to their constant anxiety over failing to attain those objects.
The demoness of desire whirls me about in all ten directions;
why do you not employ her in your own host of demons to serve you?
Possessed by the demoness of desire,
one bows down, reviles, praises, weeps, or even laughs before anyone whatsoever.
Hope is powerful and painful; freedom from hope is the supreme happiness.
Having turned hope into hopelessness, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace.
O King, hope is powerful; for it is indeed a chain by which those who are bound run about, while those who are released remain still like the lame.
Hope causes the ruin of men and is like an invincible enemy;
therefore, a wise person should abandon hope if they desire eternal happiness.
Running in all directions with a burden of hope, even wandering through various lands brought only suffering, yet it resulted in nothing more than a mere fragment of wealth;

therefore, O hope, abandon your longing for that which binds the world with the noose held in her hand—worship here the Goddess Girīśā, who is the sovereign of many worlds and whose lotus feet are honored by the lords of the cardinal directions.
Alas! Those mortals who are overcome by desire, possessed of great delusion and extreme arrogance, never recognize the suffering caused by insults and the like.
Having generated hope and drawn him in, one should deceive the enemy's minister;
just as the gods, having seized Śāṇḍa and Marka from the Asuras, gave them over to the planets.
Those who are indeed slaves to hope are the slaves of all embodied beings;
but for him by whom hope has been enslaved, the entire world acts as his slave.
Those who are slaves to hope are slaves to the whole world;
but for those whose slave hope is, the world serves as their slave.
Māyā is known as the daughter of Āśā, and Krodha is the son of Asūyā;
Pāpa is the son of Hiṃsā, and the ungrateful man (Kṛtaghna) does not deserve offspring.
Who indeed is able to burn with their mouth the tree of existence, which is entwined by the creepers of hope and has its roots firmly bound by ignorance?
For whom does the creeper of craving, nurtured by the support of hope, not produce fruit in the form of misfortune?
Day after day, the sun, having gained its brilliance, devours the Fish, the Ram, and the Bull.
For one whose mind is overwhelmed by hope, the failure to obtain what was desired is better than its attainment; for through that failure, the longing itself is dispelled and attains attenuation.
However, the joy arising from the acquisition of the desired object violently shatters steadfastness, and like water breaking through a dam, it spreads helplessness with great force.
Dry up the lake of worldly desires through austerity; dwelling within that, nourish [your being] with the mind.
Purify the harshness of bodily affliction, loosen the impurity regarding the Supreme Brahman.
A servant who hopes for blessings for himself from his master is not truly a servant;
nor is a master who, while desiring lordship over his servant, bestows blessings upon him.

O beautiful one seated upon the lotus, I worship you, who have enslaved the Ocean of Milk with the mere luster of your creeper-like limbs as they gather in hope, and who have put to shame the autumnal moon with your gentle smiles.
Any further blessing would be redundant for you, who have already attained all that is most excellent;
may you obtain a son who conforms to your own virtues, one worthy of praise, just as you were to your father.
Hope is indeed the supreme suffering; hopelessness is the supreme happiness.
Having cast off the snare of hope, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace.
Hope is indeed the supreme suffering; freedom from hope is the supreme happiness.
Just as Piṅgalā, having utterly severed her hope for her lover, slept in peace.
Another considered the blessing and the forehead mark bestowed by his mother to be superior even to armor;
for by means of these, he attained a state where his valor alone served as his armor against all warriors in battle.

A woman [is honored] by the mouth of a blessing; a Brahmin, by the mouth of a mantra; a pleasant-spoken person, by being asked about his welfare; and a guest who is a dear friend, by being filled with joy.
A person should always serve with diligence their master, who is the lord of their life and wealth, as if he were an enraged venomous serpent, thinking, "I am not [independent]."
This act of biting the lip by a venomous serpent is not even counted as a misfortune for you;
for it lacks the power to cause pain to your lower lip, which is composed of the essence of nectar.

The face of the woman who had quickly gone to meet her beloved— its cheeks covered with thrills of joy— conquered the unbroken moon by its splendor, [the moon] which possesses the appearance of a decorative leaf-design and a tilaka mark.
Quickly leaping onto the tip of her lover’s hand with a gaze half-closed like a bud,
she cooed sweetly, her voice resonating like the melody from the circle of strings on a lute whose lower strings were struck by a passionate player.
Hanging on, clinging to the single thread of hope, I preserve my life only if there is a fixed limit [to my suffering];
