otherwise, why did Fate—which acts solely for the welfare of the entire world—create this Kālakūṭa poison?

From the lord of mountains, cooled by the showers of spray from the celestial river as it tumbles over the rocks, unto the shores of the southern ocean where the light of many-colored gems flashes forth— there,
kings who have repeatedly approached you, bowing in fear, constantly fill the spaces between the toes of your pair of feet with the radiance of their crest-jewels.
Hope alone is a female demon for men; hope alone is a cluster of poison; hope alone is like stale wine—fie on hope, the source of all evils!
O Mother, this moon, cherished by you with the sense of "mine" since childhood, desiring to discharge its debt to you,
has surely divided itself into many parts and placed them at your feet under the guise of your toenails.
I shall tell a wonder; before whom shall I speak it, or where shall I go? A certain golden creeper has climbed to the very top of my house and is blossoming.
And what do its ripe fruits bear, my friend—such exquisite beauty like that of an orange or a bimba fruit—that upon seeing them, my tender heart falls into a swoon.
O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, it is a marvel regarding your noose-like hands: Śambhu, who is the destroyer of the world's bondage, desires to be bound by you.
It is a marvel that the blessed submarine fire is such, and it is a marvel that the ocean is such, that upon reflecting on their extraordinary deeds, a trembling arises in the heart:

for one, who devours its very support, no satisfaction has arisen despite drinking its waters; yet for the other, the Great-Souled One, there is not even the slightest depletion of water from his body.
It is a marvel how your sword-Rāhu simultaneously effects a total eclipse of both the moon of your enemy’s fame and the sun of his prowess in the sky of battle.
Moreover, O you who are fearless of the next world, at that great festival you, with an unshakable heart, seize all the lands of kings as they abandon them.
O abode of wonders, what is this unprecedented net that you have fashioned with such exceedingly excellent qualities?
For it binds even the flickering minds, though they are formless; that it has entered the ears is indeed unprecedented.
It is a marvel that, due to the proximity of the spotless moon of the lotus-eyed one’s face,
my mind repeatedly undergoes a state of dullness and is maintained in a liquid-like transformation, just as a mountain of natural moonstone is melted by the presence of the moon.

Is this a most wondrous marvel, or is it a delusion of my own mind, that here is a moon even though there is no sky? And yet, surely this is some extraordinary succession of wonders, for here two blue lotuses have blossomed!
Stunned for a moment by wonder, and then with eyes closed in rapture, these glances—releasing streams of nectar like lotus blossoms shaken by the wind;
whose heart do they not captivate? Alas, these gazes, charming with the playful allure of love and directed toward the lovely face of the girl, steal away the mind entirely.
I consider that ocean of milk to be the sole treasure-trove of wonders; for what else could it be, from which the moon—the essence of nectar for the eyes of the world—derived its birth?
It was there that the moon, marked by the waves of the Gaṅgā, fearlessly established its residence even upon the matted locks of Śiva, despite the playful seizing of his hair by the Goddess.
Relatives, together with their kinsmen, turn back at the cemetery;
you must go alone—therefore, perform that deed well.

With its leaves withered and fallen, alas, the beauty of its flowers remains only as a memory; the birds, having lost all hope, have departed in every direction seeking fruit that shall not even sprout.
Yet, with its mass of roots and spreading fibers now exposed in the hollows dried up to the underworld, the desert tree stands silent, meditating nonetheless upon the untimely raincloud.
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, having conquered his senses,
and being weary from the practice of begging and making offerings, one who renounces the world prospers after death.
Whether he be a forest-dweller, a student, a venerable person, or even a great preceptor,
there is no one who stands by his own duty whom the king may not punish.
When twice-born men in their hermitages dispute with one another regarding their duties,
a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to uphold righteousness should not pronounce a judgment between them.
O cloud, this tree, which has taken refuge on the excellent path, is the support for many; let it be watered at the proper time—it should not be neglected because of its distance.
The refuge of all beings and the dwelling place of all birds,
the water-bearing cloud gives a corresponding share to those who depend upon it.
One who desires a refuge should serve a high person, even one difficult to ascend;
for even if he falls from that height, he still remains above those who are base.
By the power of their physical basis, a living being is constantly subject to heaviness or lightness;
alas, elephants as large as mountains in the Vindhya range appear light in a mirror.
This wicked person is a consumer of his own support, black-trailed, and burning; he is indeed like fire. Nevertheless, an offering made into him would be as if offered into ashes.
One should rely upon a sovereign, acquire abundant wealth,
undertake acts of distribution, and bring fame from the ten directions.
The wise, women, and creepers shine only by virtue of their support;
for a highly precious ruby truly glitters when set in gold.
O Bhārata, by failing to provide what has been entrusted and by seizing what has been given, everything that was bestowed since birth is destroyed.
In the maintenance of dependents, in service to one's master, in the practice of dharma,
and in the procreation of a son, there are no substitutes.
Even enemies, when supported by the world, attain prosperity; yet when prosperous, they lead to destruction. Therefore, one should not cause distress to the subjects.
Surely, the moons, seeking the divine state attained through the dissolution of their bodies, take refuge in your feet;
having entrusted the store of their beauty and merit to your face as a friend, they depart toward the sun, divided month by month.
She suspected that lord of rivers, who embraced the earth, roared loudly, possessed great waves in the form of tossing arms,
and was foaming at the mouth, to be afflicted by epilepsy.
Though she embraces me, my body yearns for her embrace; though she is lovely to behold, my eyes long to see her again;
though she dwells within my heart, she enters my very core once more; and though our union is rooted in deep love, my beloved assumes a newness in me every single day.
She who, embraced with passion, seems to melt as if overcome by the bodiless god of love; whose mind is weary of the pretenses of artificial and fierce acts;
and who, when engaged in sexual union, does not distinguish "who is this? or "who am I?"—she is the true beloved and he alone is the true lover; all others are merely husband and wife.
Whether he embraces me, or crushes me while I am devoted to his feet, or strikes my vital organs with his absence—let the city-dweller do as he will;
he alone is the lord of my life, and no other.
Though that enjoyment— consisting of the curiosity of embracing, kissing, and the festival of passion, with love as the stake in a game of dice and Cupid as the guarantor—
is the same whether there be victory or defeat, the hearts of the young couple nevertheless desire only to win.
Only the embrace remained of the women’s passion; only the fragrance remained of the beauty of saffron on their breasts;
even the flower-armed god remained only as his quiver; and the night itself became nothing but its dawn.

After an embrace, after a kiss, after scratching with the fingernails, after the awakening of passion, after agitation, after the commencement of love-making, and after the two lovers have gone elsewhere for some other purpose and met again by mistake— when they recognize each other through conversation, what flavor here, mingled with shame, is not experienced by the couple in the darkness?

May the smiling Ardhanārīśvara protect you—he who says: "Let alone the pleasures of embracing, kissing the bimba-like lips, and conversing with smiles; even this mutual gazing at one another's faces has become difficult to achieve. Since we have thus rendered the arrangement of our single body useless, what kind of mockery of affection is this?"
By averting her gaze with an embrace that clings to her breasts, by looking upon his face while rebuking his lower lip for its thirst for hers,
and by pressing her hand firmly against his hip while holding him fast to her thighs— this clever woman has neither broken her husband’s love nor entirely abandoned her pride.
When the embrace had first been won and the heart-stealing offering of her lower lip followed in due order, as her beloved asked his mistress once more for the stake in the game of love-dice, she—
her cheeks swelling with the expanding essence of deep, hidden agitation— remained silent, placing her hand, moist with perspiration, over the movement of the dice.
In the embrace of her husband, she always desires with her inner soul the conduct of Gaurī within the body of Ardhanārīśvara, as if filled with longing.
At times when sexual enjoyment is unsuitable, the passionate woman remains with her lover at a pond-pavilion, in the house garden, or through the pretext of attending a festival procession.
Even when merely observing the shadow of another or overhearing a slight conversation, she becomes angry with her husband; through such misfortune and the like, she sinks into ruin herself as well.
The distressed old woman, impoverished, drives away her beloved who has come from elsewhere, just as the evening sun in winter dispels the heat.
She regards her husband’s turning away from the bed as if it were a separation;
she views his departure for the temple as if it were a journey abroad.
Due to the flow of excessive affection and the manifestations of intense love,
a woman should follow her beloved like a shadow— whether he is walking or standing still.
When the cause of all-satisfying fulfillment suddenly stood present in the embrace of beautiful women, [the gods] realized that their effort to churn the ocean for nectar was in vain.
Therefore, these wise ones became detached from the world; indeed, they are all truly like those dwelling in heaven—otherwise, how could their renown for lightness be established?
Hide quickly from my vessel of wine before you are seen by my prominent teeth;
for once marked by the circle of my teeth, O Moon, you will not escape the sky out of fear of Rohiṇī.
"Take heart, O mighty-armed one! All calamities that touch living beings in this world, like the force of the wind, come and go in an instant."
Even a crow consoles the sorrowful wife of a traveler;
how can it be said that you, though born from the nectar of the moon, burn her?
One should console the other with soothing words, through the principles of dharma and artha;
then, when he has strayed from the right path, one should strike him at the proper time.
A great abode of confidence, affection, and devotion;
like the excellence of Dharma itself, he was beautiful in embodied form.
O slender-waisted one, just as I was comforted by the recovery of my son, this separation from you has suddenly come upon me;
it is like a flash of lightning striking a tree that has just been relieved of the pain of the sun's heat by the first rain of the clouds.

Having comforted the mountain ranges scorched by the heat of the sun, the forests distressed by fierce forest fires, and having filled hundreds of various rivers and streams, you are now empty; O cloud, that very state is your supreme glory.
In the dark fortnight of Āśvina, on the sixth lunar day, when it is a Tuesday, and there is the Rohiṇī nakṣatra and the Vyatīpāta yoga— then that sixth day, known as Kapilā, bestows infinite merit.
On the day of the Sun during the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should grind the root of the Śirīṣa tree with water and drink it; for such a person, there shall be no fear arising from snakes.
On the full moon days of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Māgha, by offering the *piṇḍas* at Gayā with vacā, ginger, and myrobalan, one becomes meritorious, dispels phlegm, and is freed from debt.

In the month of Āṣāḍha, if rabbits are seen in various places, they grant abundance; however, the sight of a rabbit portends the destruction of quadrupeds and the like, while its acquisition brings success.
In the months of Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa, one should sow seeds and plant [them];
however, some maintain that creepers may be planted at times other than the summer season.
Even when desiring growth until full maturity, one should here seek an alliance with an equal;
for the collision of two unbaked jars inevitably results in their mutual destruction.
O Father, though we have searched this triple world from the very beginning of saṃsāra, nothing like this has ever come within the range of our vision or the path of our hearing—

this which performs the sport of a tethering chain for the elephant of the internal organ, which is intoxicated by the deep-rooted rut of its intense obsession with the female elephants of sensory objects.

O cloud, release your waters profusely for the life of this beautiful sandalwood tree, which delights all; for venomous serpents are coiled in every hollow, the sun’s rays rest upon its crown, and a forest fire, terrifying with its mass of flames, embraces every limb—let your fame expand!
Having herself initiated the act of kissing, she offers an embrace at the edge of the bed without being asked, her thighs trembling as they are pressed between his knees;

enduring his trembling with anger, she conciliates him through the play of love; thus, finding sole delight in mature amorous sport, she draws the heart of her lover toward her by the sheer force of her playful charm.
A hundred kings sit upon the earth; indeed, they are but wells compared to you, who are an ocean.
Do not those various planets shine in the sky? Yet which of them can compare to the sun in weight?

The enraged ocean might swiftly submerge the entire world, including the realm of Satyaloka, within its waters; yet it is not able to extinguish the submarine fire, even though that fire dwells within its own interior, for it seeks to consume him.
From the realm of truth down to the earth, the moonbeams— having exerted themselves by wandering at will—
shed sweat in the form of a ground of melting frost.
Having considered both sitting in wait and marching forth, as well as making peace and waging war,
one should employ the strategies of double-dealing and seeking protection after examining the task at hand.
Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses,
concentration, meditation, and absorption— these are remembered as the six limbs of yoga.
The seat, the restraint of the breath, meditation, and likewise concentration—
know that this tetrad is esteemed in all yogas.
From a seat, from a bed, from a vehicle, from social contact, and even from food—
once committed, evil spreads through these like a drop of oil upon water.
From sharing a seat, a single bed, conversation, or eating together,
sin transfers from men like water from one jar to another.
One should offer a seat, lodging, a bed, escorting, and attendance—
superior service to those who are superior, inferior service to those who are inferior, and equal service to those who are equal.
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of his ability with seats, food, beds, water, or roots and fruits.
That lowest of the twice-born who eats while placing his foot upon his seat,
and he who blows upon his food with his mouth, is equal to one who eats beef.
One should fondle a young girl on a seat, and likewise a young woman on a bed;
and when she has mounted onto the lap of her husband—this, they know, is the threefold fondling.
On seats, in beds, in vehicles, and regarding matters of food and drink—
seeing an opening among those who are heedless, enemies strike at their foes.
On a seat, in bed, or in a vehicle, the internal states of wicked men are especially to be observed; for their inherent nature is most powerful.
O noble cloud, as many as were the tears shed by the cātaka birds,
not even that many drops of water have been released by you.
Day by day, death draws closer to living beings,
like a victim being led step by step to the place of execution.
The water in a pond is on the verge of perishing, and that in wells and such is obtained only with great effort;
O River, you are the foremost among reservoirs of water, for in you the water remains through the ages and is easily accessible.
As she walked along, having passed close by my path, with her head bowed and her face turned back in the course of her movement,
that lotus-eyed woman cast upon me several side-glances, accompanied by a meaningful smile and not too openly displayed.
Behold, at dawn, from the houses of the courtesans, the lights fit for the night’s enjoyment depart like lamps, as the arrival of the day’s beloved is signaled by the approach of his close friends.
A king favors a man who is merely close at hand, even if he is devoid of learning, of low birth, or unacquainted.
For the most part, rulers, women, and climbing vines embrace whoever dwells by their side.
"You are at the threshold of youth; my daughter's youth has likely been wasted by you.
For the youth of women slips away suddenly and unnoticed."
Having been trained with great skill in the service of the king— using playthings, weapons, snakes, and fire— he is now being favored by him.

One should avoid even the timber of those trees that have thorns when near [a dwelling], as they cause fear from enemies; those with milky sap lead to the loss of wealth; and those bearing fruit cause the destruction of one's progeny.
Having repeatedly displayed enjoyments close at hand before me,
craving has led me far away, like a goat lured by a handful of green grass.
When the forest fire has subsided and the clouds are near, a tree fears lightning; when the crocodile’s mouth opens, it fears drowning in the ocean.
For a living being, the process of consuming auspicious food, in its haste to produce sweetness, generates another fear in one whose previous fears have been dispelled.

Clinging with one hand to a nearby *kesara* creeper radiant with flowers, and resting your weary lotus-hand upon the slope of your hip, you close your eyes while tears well up at the corners; whom—whether praiseworthy or blameworthy—is this person remembered by you daily with such firm affection and in such a piteous state?

Leaning with one hand on a nearby *kesara* creeper, radiant with blossoms, and resting her other lotus-hand upon her hip which can no longer bear the weight, O girl with eyes like those of a bewildered deer, lift up your neck and tell me: on this cloudy day, whose path is being gazed upon by you as you raise your feet?
Salutations to Śambhu, who is both near and very far, who is asleep and whose nature is manifest, who is easily attained and yet exceedingly difficult to reach, and who is wondrous.
The wise declare that when an omen is near, the result is near; when it is distant, the result is distant; and when the omen is mixed, the result is likewise mixed.
"Madhurā has arrived; it is the empire of the forest regions"—such wondrous words are heard nearby. Yet, one is not able to know the true nature of the Creator here:
that which was severed by the leaves of the trees has ceased with the emergence of flowers, and that which was withered by the branches is now perceived here once again in visible form.
An anthill is located near the southern side of a Vibhītaka tree;
one should know that there is a vein at a distance of one and a half man-lengths toward the eastern direction.
O Cloud, as many tears as have been shed by Cātaka birds in their supplications,
even so many drops of water have not been released by you.
He whose line of marriage descendants is broken before reaching seventy is surely unlearned;
those women live by spinning and grinding—does a bull give fodder to the cows?
An oil massage on the head on the fourteenth day destroys one's lineage for seven generations;
eating meat on the fifteenth day does so as well, as does engaging in sexual desire on the eighth day.
Those kings who are situated nearby in all four directions, those who are devoted to him,
and others who are progressively weaker in strength— these are his enemies.
The conduct of those libertines, which kindles the god of love in them by directing their unblinking glances toward him, shall now be described.
That very earth which, from the beginning of creation, was awakened and nourished every day by hundreds of flavors, is now, at the time of the end of the eon, consumed by its own rays;

having thus performed some act of destiny that is overwhelmed by its own prior and subsequent contradictions, even that fierce-rayed sun has gone to its setting, its brilliance departed at the close of day.
One who excessively indulges in liquor and sensual pleasures, eats pungent and sour foods, is industrious yet malicious,
is either stout, emaciated, very tall, or dwarfed, or is black or yellow in complexion.

Then the sage reached the penance grove, where offerings had been prepared for him by his circle of disciples; there the trees held their hands joined like folded leaf-cups, and the deer looked up expectantly at his sight.
As these women are intent on splashing water, their pearl necklaces—
though broken— are not noticed as they shatter amidst the spray that rivals pearls and rises upon their breasts.
The vow of these [eyes] is indeed this: that they move before [him], and having gone together with the mind to that place, they turn back again after leaving it.
Having attained a manifest, stainless sword-like moonlight, this pure and lovely autumn season has arrived;
it has uprooted the fierce, dense darkness of the rainy season, like Rāma, who, having slain the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, gathered the bandhujīva flowers.
A time has arrived that is formidable, full of sorrow, and fraught with harm;
therefore, I shall strive in such a way that my connection with the stories of the Illustrious One may continue.
Seized by darkness through the decree of destiny, and desiring once more to depart for its own time,
the great medicinal herbs here bear the position of wives to their husband, the light, remaining unconquered by others.
Having encountered those who are always fearless and ever-ready for battle,
and perceiving them as those whose minds are devoted to the Supreme Self and who perform their duties accordingly— where is there any fear?
Or how can the destruction of one's dignity be attained by resorting to valor? Therefore, a person who fixes their mind upon that [destruction] becomes a vessel for the torment born of the mind.
Having reached the southern quarter, the sun abandons the northern without delay;
for it is generally the women who are *dakṣiṇā* (courtesans) who carry off a man.
"Having suffered defeat in this game where the stakes were set at our mutual pleasure, take back the dice!"—
thus her friends were sent away under the pretext of anger.
Even one whose passion has been subdued, having formed an excessive intimacy with a serpent,
suffers great hardship by wandering about after its coils and ultimately encounters poison.
Let us reach Somanātha and dwell there, where the sand, shining like fine silk, eternally entices one to bathe;
for there, through the experience of the Supreme, he who has forgotten his home now fulfills his daily rites.

Even having reached the great ocean, the submarine fire (Vāḍava) was not quenched by its waters; even the Cātaka bird, having reached a cloud, did not obtain water; and Aruṇa did not attain the feet of the Sun.
Even while dwelling upon the crest of Śaṅkara, the Moon wanes at the end of the fortnight. Generally, even when associated with the virtuous, one obtains a fruit according to one's destiny.
O cuckoo, having reached this mango grove and tasted its fresh blossoms, do not warble thus with the fifth note under the delusion that it is the Nandana garden.
This flock of crows, distressed by the blows of their heavy-headed pecking, will vainly deafen the ears of the noble birds with their harsh cries.
The wise physician should give them water on top of these [medicines];
in this manner he should administer it for two watches of the night, after which he should not cause it to be given to them.
O proud lady, having worshipped the sun with devotion through ascetic heat while it was still heavy with evening moisture, your face has now attained a slight resemblance to the lotus.

How have these nights been passed by those away from home—nights when gentle breezes blow at the onset of the monsoon, when the sky is overspread with clouds, when the quarters of the horizon are glimpsed for a moment during flashes of lightning, and when the moon, stars, and planets are asleep; nights that carry the fragrance of wine produced by kadamba flowers drenched by rain-showers, and where the sounds of frogs spread far and wide as they leap about without restraint?
Due to the heavy rain, it is no longer possible for lovers to go outside from their mansions; therefore, the long-eyed woman embraces her beloved tightly to stifle the shivering caused by the cold.

Through the windows, breezes cooled by spray blow, dispelling the exhaustion from the end of lovemaking; alas, for the fortunate, even a stormy day becomes a beautiful day when one is united with the beloved.

When the downpour has ceased, the fireflies fall shimmering everywhere like the dust of lightning flashes violently ground by the collision of masses of rain clouds; they darken the nights with deepening gloom and touch the minds of travelers’ wives with the suspicion that they are sparks from the continuous flames of the fire of love.
The graceful-limbed woman generally imitates her lover’s sittings, smiles, gestures, glances, speeches, and gait, just as a skilled dancer mimics with agility.

Having sat in solitude, having freed my mind from attachment to sense objects, and having made it motionless, I meditate upon the form of my beloved—the supreme deity—within the lotus of my heart; holding a rosary made of pearl necklaces in my hand, I daily mutter His name in order to attain the fruit of union with Him.
"I shall live as a happy householder"—this was ordained by delusion; through the taking of a wife arose the birth of sons, slaves, kinsmen, friends, and relatives.

For one who experiences the anxieties of maintaining them, humiliations, and reflections on what is improper, what happiness is there? What kind of household life is this? Therefore, I have accepted only misfortune.
"People were once ungrateful, but now they have become destroyers of what is being done"—such a reflection arises in my mind; how will the world come to be?
Until death, she remained patient, self-controlled, and chaste,
longing for that supreme dharma which belongs to women devoted to a single husband.

For an entire kalpa he remained within the waters of the ocean, and for a long time he worshipped the fire from Śiva’s forehead; moreover, month after month, he offered his own body as an oblation into the sacrificial fire-pits.
Thus did the Moon pass his life through such intense austerities; yet would Fate not act with hostility, or rather, does it not desire to erase even that very mark upon him?

My body, which was once made of copper, has now become the color of gold; a multitude of teardrops from my pearl necklace have been fashioned for me as a poor man. My very short life has now been made long, as if it were many kalpas. O Lord, by the power of your grace, what has not been obtained by me? What sorrow remains?
Formerly, you were an ornament for kings upon their crowns and for women upon their heavy tiaras by virtue of your gold;
alas, O emerald, bound by a string along with a fragment of glass, what a state have you now reached on the neck of a Bhilla woman?
In the Kṛta age there was Bali; thereafter, in the Tretā age, there was Paraśurāma of true prowess; and in the Dvāpara age, there was the Lord Dharma.
But now, in the Kali age, there is no donor at all. "By what means, then, shall those who seek gifts live? Having thus resolved, Fate created brokers.
"I see collyrium here in your eyes;
I perceive your form as it will be when arrayed with its future ornaments."

O King, your fame, white as the beloved of Abhra (the cloud), wandering in the sky under the guise of vast autumnal clouds, pervades the celestial realm like a shower of flowers from the Apsarases; it seems, moreover, to spread from heaven to earth under the pretext of snow.

There was a hero whose fame served as sandalwood paste for the entire circle of the earth’s surface, and whose prowess as an archer was loudly sung by the people dwelling on the shores of the seven oceans;

what other man could surpass him, whose moon-like nails were so intensely delighted by the service of the rays of the moon-goddess—the crest-jewels of kings falling simultaneously at his pair of feet?
That seed of pearls which was sown by you upon the battlefield from the frontal globes of the elephants of your enemies has produced this tree of your fame throughout the three worlds:
Śeṣa is its root, the Himalaya its trunk, the ocean filled with milk its basin, the moonlight the spreading branches, the clusters of stars its flowers, and the moon its fruit.
When he was indeed still tender, what could he have said even when struck? Now, O friend, out of his hardened nature, he bellows harsh words like a drum.
He had a brother named Gaṅgādhara, who was like Gaṅgādhara himself;
he bound some wild beasts and released others at his will.

There was a king, a crest-jewel among monarchs, a sovereign of kings, belonging to the lineage of the Gaṅgas; whose footstool was made radiant by the luster of the gems from the multitude of the lofty crowns of prostrate rulers; who, with arms capable of crushing the circle of hostile kings, protected the entire orb of the earth; who bore Lakṣmī upon his chest like the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), and was the lord of speech within his own eloquence.
That little sapling of yours, which was once covered with only three or four leaf-sprouts, sustained solely by the water released from clouds, and which had found its place upon the noble path—
now, after only a few days, through the accumulation of the merit of travelers, it has become one whose ground is overspread by the shade of a mass of branches bending under the weight of fruit.

The bridegroom’s forearm bristled with horripilation and the fingers of the maiden grew moist with perspiration; at that moment, their respective states of being seemed to have been divided equally by the God of Love between the two.

Whether sitting, lying down, standing, moving, dreaming, waking, seeing with eyes open or closed, engaged in worldly affairs, or having entered into silence—I behold her day and night: her gaze agitated with love, her face bright with smiles, her approach slow with modesty, embracing me, and speaking tender, charming words of affection.
If a merchant sitting comfortably in his shop, when requested by the faithful, says "five percent" or "ten percent," this is not surprising for him.
But he who does not abandon that very same fixed price even when the ship is sinking in a tempestuous wind, its waters churning down to the depths of the underworld—that is truly remarkable.
Seated beside his master, gazing at his face with palms joined in reverence,
the clever attendant should accomplish his tasks after having understood the master's disposition.

Seated on the riverbank with her smiling husband, the woman with thighs like plantain stalks— feeling cold and unwilling to descend into the lake— was sprinkled by him as he moved through the water while she shook her hands to display her graceful charms.

May the Blue-Throated One protect you, who effortlessly and playfully swallowed the Kālakūṭa poison in an instant—while Pūṣan was seated [in silence], while the Moon was eclipsed, while the sky was dark, while the Lord of Daityas was full of longing, while Indra fled, while Yama’s luster was faded, and while the Vedic scholar residing in the lotus-cup of Brahmā cried out "Injustice! as the means for peace were sought.

One should fondle the young girl while she is seated, and likewise the young woman while she is reclining; even when she has risen, one should fondle her as she ascends [the bed]. Thus, they know fondling to be of three kinds.

May that *tāṇḍava* dance, which was beheld with longing by those gods, siddhas, and yakṣas who were seated within their own palaces surrounded by beautiful women and whose eyes never blinked; and which was indeed honored by the clouds amidst the sky—clouds that, resembling drums, produced a very gentle sound as they released water like flowers—lead to our welfare.
O Lord, the earth was first your grandmother, and immediately after that your mother; now, for the sake of victory, she has become your wife, girdled by the ocean.
When a full hundred years have passed, she will again become your faultless daughter-in-law. This is indeed fitting for the Lords of the World who are learned in all the scriptures.
It was in my mind that she was not stolen, but dead—that beloved of mine who has passed beyond the range of sight;
for even the moonlight of the autumnal moon, though brilliantly white, appears as thickly dark as gloom to those who are blind.
The Sage Nāgārjuna stated that the one whose boundary is dark-blue and whose minor limb is coiled is named Kṣudravajraka.
Friends and kinsmen turn back at the boundary;
however, one's good and evil deeds follow the person as they go.
O you whose heart was once enamored with King Niśira, the jealous wielder of the thunderbolt, fearing for his own purity at dawn, traveled to the celestial path;
taking you from the depths scorched by the submarine fire of the ocean, he released you outside, where you now shine as the radiant sun in the eastern sky like a heated gold coin.
The demonic lineage is to be disregarded; this mind is to be purified.
The abode of Rāma is to be sought as refuge; by means of his divine play, the ocean of existence is to be crossed.

If I remain at home, I am unable to support my family; if I resort to the forest of sages, which is a means of happiness, thieves plunder me. If I cast my body into a chasm out of fear of hell, I would be committing suicide. O Fate, I do not know what I should do—whether to die or to live!
The faces of all branches of knowledge, as well as those of women, are courted by everyone;
yet, among them, there are perhaps two or three who capture the heart, or perhaps none at all.
Just as the timid women, their hands held by their lovers, could somehow manage to step forward,
those waters, out of eagerness, seemed to hold them within by means of their reflected images.

O blessed *campaka* tree, you have been climbed by young women seeking buds, who embrace you with their creeper-like arms that sway the tips of your branches; and you have borne fruit in the form of their thick, breast-like fruits, which are so well-suited to your own blossoms.

When I suddenly began with my sword Candrahāsa to cut through the forest of neck-stalks up to the shoulders, while the succession of arteries was being severed—if even a single face became tearless, with words faltering from falling tears and eyebrows knit together—then that Blessed One himself is my witness; may he be auspicious to me.
For animals, it lasts until the drinking of milk; for the lowest of men, until the acquisition of a wife;
for those of middling status, until the completion of household duties; and for the best of men, it lasts as long as life itself—like a sacred ford.

As those two attained a state of intense passion during their unions, the inflicting of nail-marks was like the sprinkling of pepper powder upon molasses; though clearly pungent, it was full of desire-inducing charm.

Let it be; what is the use of many words? Acts of benevolence toward others are the essence of this worldly existence, yet that fruit remains unattained by us even in the slightest degree, for fate acts against us.
We are indeed humans, yet our lives have passed away in vain—those for whom the mere filling of their own bellies constitutes some kind of eight great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*).
Let alone the removal of fatigue by the waters of the ocean for those whose minds are scorched by a forest fire;
let this much suffice: that their tongues are not burned up by drops of water, and that their thirst does not double in intensity.
Let alone the practice of deep study; you have not even been touched, let alone embraced, nor have you been brought within the range of my eyes for even a moment.
What can we say of your virtues, O mango tree, which are so rare to others that you repeatedly delight even travelers from afar with your fragrance?
Let this eye of yours remain, which reaches out across the distance; yet even the mind, O Sage of true austerity, has by its own power rendered this ocean—once beyond all hope—a mere mouthful.
You ought to desist with this alone; you will gain no further renown from drinking it up as a single draught, for that would merely be the exhaustion of the supreme treasury of the rain-clouds.

Let that hundred of ponds remain, whose waters were capable only of providing safety for frogs submerged by the terrifying fall of hailstones; we praise that very ocean, within whose womb the mountain range took refuge when all its limbs were crushed by the weapons from the hand of the enraged Śakra, and it bled profusely.
Let alone any other wickedness of women here;
they even kill their own son, whom they have carried in their own womb.
Let my infamy rest for now; rather, let the truth be told:
how indeed was your mind affected upon hearing the sound of the flute of the descendant of Hari?
Let us set aside for now that ancient reputation of Hari, who possesses boundless prowess and whose deeds exceed even the most marvelous undertakings;
for even today, scent-elephants tremble at the mere scent of a lion, though he be old and his limbs incapable of entering the mountain caves and ravines of the Vindhya range.
Let alone the greatness of the ocean—though its fame is dear to the ears even from afar, a person on its shore meets death swiftly through thirst alone.
Therefore, a small lake, a well, or even a pond is better than that ocean, wherein one may drink water at will with the two hands of one's own body.
Let alone the meeting of virtuous people whose excellent fame extends to the ends of the earth; even enmity with them brings about an elevation of extraordinary greatness.

In this world, who would have brought to the ears of the sun and moon—whose splendor is renowned throughout the three worlds—the fact that Rāhu, though bodiless and reduced to a mere head, had become their enemy, were it not for his future destiny?
Let alone your being a fit vessel for the composition of words; let even the possibility of an embrace of your body remain far, far away.
But this much I beg of you with repeated prostrations: as you count your own circle of kinsmen, please grant me, too, some small mark of remembrance.
Let alone those virtuous ones who adorned the entire earth;
even those who now possess a great love for virtue are difficult to find.
Let alone the tasting of the nectar from her lotus-face at a distance; even the desire for such a thing does not arise in my heart regarding the hope of union with her.
Yet, if that lotus-faced one were but once to look upon me with affection—her slender body relaxed by longing—I would consider myself blessed by that alone.
Let alone separation; while embracing my beloved, was not my sweat the lord of rivers, and was not my horripilation the mountain?
Let alone the great reversal seen in the process of other lives; even in this very birth, there is a state of high and low among men:
one who was insignificant becomes vast in a moment, and one who was vast becomes insignificant; a master becomes a servant, and that servant becomes worthy of his master's position.
Let the lunar orb remain; if there is any mention of the beauty of the fair-bodied one’s face, let the blue water-lilies stay somewhere in a corner.

If there is occasion for the eyes, let the sweet sound of the lute remain far off. If it is an introduction to her speech, let there be talk of the fame of her slender waist; salutations to the expanse of the sky!

Let alone liberation, which is accomplished by the power of great awakening and endowed with unimpeded, stainless happiness—even dharma, artha, and kāma do not exist for us without that knowledge; therefore, it must be worshipped.
"Let it be, my friend; today in this auspicious festival, you have placed a *mādhavī* creeper upon me. O beloved, give me its flower—what use have I for it?
It is no small thing that I polish this pearl which you have placed [upon my ear]; let it be burned! Thus, the confusion and agitation of the deer-eyed woman intoxicates her lover.

Let alone her pride or her speaking to her friends; even she, that slender-limbed girl, whose pride in the excellence of her amorous charms was loosened, felt ashamed before me when I reported my own misconduct.
Let it be; better that the betel-nut tree be barren—do not provide it with the longing for fruit; from this very tree, once it has borne fruit, you shall receive nothing but distress.
Let alone placing my trust in friends; even toward that person who knows the very essence of my intention, I am unable to cast my gaze with tears due to shame.
For this world is clever at mocking others and fully capable of discerning subtle gestures. O Mother, to whom shall I go for refuge? The fire of passion has grown old within my heart.
Let alone this sovereignty over the earth, O Lord, which is full of thorns; even the kingship of the three worlds I consider as mere grass.
My heart turns instead toward the mountain forest plateaus, teeming with herds of does sleeping without fear.
The ancient saying that Smara is not visible because he was not accepted by Bhava may well remain;
however, a new argument appears to me: that he is visible because he has taken refuge in your very body, O Śrī.
O good people, let alone other matters, you who are habituated solely to performing service for others— even alas, you weary yourselves over your own virtues when they cause pain to the wicked.
Let alone other worlds; if there were even a desire for sport, she was not restrained by her attendants as she fell into another vice.
O most excellent lake, let alone your water—filled with clusters of lotuses that rival the taste of nectar obtained from the ocean of milk, and adorned with swans as its crest-jewels;
by the touch of the breeze itself, which is made enchanting by the showers of cool spray from your swelling waves, our fevers, parching thirst, and exhaustion have vanished.
If one possesses faith, it is right to bestow all one's wealth upon those who ask; if one lacks faith, then even that [wealth] should be cast away for the sake of pleasure all the more so.
Yet, as for that which is placed in secret by oneself without even touching it—what is the cause within it? We ponder this in silence, but we do not know.
If any serpent does not turn back upon remembering the words of Āstīka,
its head shall split into a hundred pieces like the fruit of the Śiṃśapā tree.
Let the nets be spread along the forest boundaries by those skilled in netting; let the dogs be released from their chains by the hunters into the depths of the wilderness.

Let the grounds be strewn with riders whose horses are loosened by fatigue and who hold nooses in their hands; let the forests be shaken by staff-bearers who roam like Death himself amidst the buffalo herds.

Even upon beds strewn with fresh sprouts and flowers, the young brides— who were ever intent on incessant dalliance— were not granted even a moment’s rest by the night, though it was the giver of moments.
There dwells a certain monk who upholds the ten imperishables;
we ask him for the pair of imperishables beginning with "not mine"—is there anything else?
"Ah! Behold how great is this swan's commitment to contentment; even here in this very lake, his mind does not turn even slightly toward the lotus, the abode of beauty.
Even now he sleeps and does not wake; let us wait for him until that time. At dawn, only those beloved bees are capable of enduring such words.
The three worlds reside within this cave-like belly of Damodara; yet, due to the weight of their own vastness, his glories are unable to fit there.
Having filled that very space, they seem to have emerged through the path of his navel from the Destroyer of Madhu, appearing under the guise of white lotuses and resembling the tusks of an elephant.
The bride, the source of the Creator’s skill in composition and his prowess, stands at the gate; she was forcibly carried away by you from him, O King, while he was terrified by your enemy.
What other task remains to be accomplished here that may now be hoped for? Let a great effort be made, O Lord of Men, for the auspicious ceremony of her marriage.
There is no exquisite beauty here, nor even the slightest fragrance of flowers; nor is there any cleverness regarding the bestowing of nectar—what further skill could there be?
Yet you nourish the lotus petal depicted in the painting with your humming sounds! O bee, alas, how can I describe such greatness as this?
Would that swan, who dwells in Lake Mānasa— the play-vessel of Mṛḍānī where golden lotuses bloom, where he sports with the minds of intoxicated female bees,
and where the masses of young mud are fondly embraced by frogs— would he ever long for a small pool of limited water?
"The moon dwells upon the head of Śambhu in supreme bliss"—such is the mental state of the people of the three worlds;
but alas, who other than the cool-rayed moon himself knows the inner pain of the burning from the fire of his hidden eye?
This ocean, though well-known for its waters being undrinkable even by women and children, is protected from afar precisely because it is unfit for drinking;
does it not further terrify others with successions of waves made formidable by rows of sea-monsters with jagged fangs?
When base enemies have been brought under control by relying on firm resolve,
the greatness of the noble ones becomes manifest through their compassion.

O Mother, having assumed some most cruel disposition in order to discipline even those who have committed the gravest of sins, you seize these flowers in place of arrows; indeed, this severity toward your own children is truly great.
The western quarter of the sky, occupied by twilight that veiled the rows of clouds,
assumed the splendor of the ocean dyed by the radiance of a canopy of coral amidst its waves.
That water of the oblong ponds which, when struck by the fingertips of young women, followed the deep resonance of a drum,
now cries out as it is struck by the horns of wild buffaloes.

If, by the thought that it is no longer a thing of value, one drives away a jewel with the successive waves of the lashed ocean, then even its status as a "treasure-mine" would be destroyed; yet alas, the jewel itself remains something to be worn upon the body.

Thinking, "Does this [collyrium] extend a constant splendor like the shadow cast by the eyes of our young women? What need have we for these? the waters, as if possessing a jealous desire to conceal their own qualities, fled away from the collyriums.
O Cloud, having cast aside your mouth and laughed for a long time with your roars, you rain down upon the other limbs of the cātaka bird;
yet for him, whose neck is stretched out and curved toward the tip of his beak, this results in the loss of life, while for you it is merely a joke.
Covering his entire mouth along with his nostrils with a hand whose fingers are slightly spread apart,
this child produces a charming sound by uttering the syllable "da."
Although this face is devoid of laughter, it is graced by a dance; although her speech is free of jesting, her eyes possess the splendor of red lotuses; yet for a moment, she pauses somewhere.
As she prepares to string a garland, she begins the carving of sea-monsters on her lotus-like breasts; the incense for the evening is seen upon the tresses of the fair-eyed woman.

Her face is considered by some to be the moon; the multitude of men is conquered by her eyes; lightning is surpassed by her luster; and alas, delusion is utterly defeated by her breasts, which bear the gold of water-lilies.

Yet, that body—foul-smelling with leprosy, transformed by tiny worms, and pervaded by the flow of pus, marrow, and blood, swarming with flies—is such that there is no destination in this world more loathsome than it.

If the face of the deer-eyed woman is accompanied by a smile, her eyes are full of playfulness, her forehead is graced by the rising beauty of a dot of vermilion, and her braid is fresh— then what need is there for any other countless ornaments?

Having fashioned this woman— who possesses the glory of the full moon wiped away by her face, who has surpassed the pride of the blue lotus with the beauty of her eyes, and whose radiance surpasses the coral of the *aśoka* tree hidden by her lips—
the Creator himself, I believe, became a poet fierce in his own praise out of the power of joy, having created for the three worlds this drinking fountain of the nectar of sight.

Having made the withered moon pale by the splendor of her face, she holds a ball in her hand; while her face bears a coppery hue mingled with the curiosity of play, I have been made the recipient of her glances—which rival the petals of the black *ketaka* flower held at their tips by bees—and which possess as their sole friend the rippling waves of her long outer corners.
O beautiful one, your facial splendor suppresses the moon; your glance transcends the ear; your curling hair reaches the crown of the head; and you are bound by virtues yet remain liberated.
Since such unruly behavior has been observed in you, a mere woman, I believe that the fish-bannered god of love has become your conqueror and has gone before you.
Casting her arms like a halo around the moon of her face, like the campaka-bow of the Lord of Love, or like lightning from the cloud of her braided hair;

with the folds of her skin becoming distinct, the navel appearing, the waist-knot loosening, and her waist rising slightly as the hem of her garment lifts ever so gently—oh, the lady with jar-like breasts yawns!

May that Umā—the very path of grace for the worlds—stand manifest for our joy: she whose face is the full moon, whose feet possess the majesty of the wish-fulfilling tree, whose body has the luster of gold, and whose skin is itself fresh butter; and in whose eyes there ever shines an unconditioned stream of compassion.
One should cause those who have accumulated [wealth] to discharge it and divert it toward [proper] activities,
so that they do not consume their own wealth or, having consumed it, vomit it out.
One should properly drain out accumulated [faults], like malignant ulcers;
and they, being appointed, should conduct themselves toward the king as if toward a fire.
From the world of the gods down to the city of the serpents, what has not been brought to whiteness by your deeds, which spread the splendor of a new light?
Even for these wives of your enemies, separated from their lovers, it was by those deeds that their ornaments consisting of nail-marks were reduced to a pallid whiteness.
The *mākanda* flower, its lovely drops of sweet nectar tasted at will by beautiful blue lotuses,
brought great joy to the hearts of women through the abundance of its fragrance.
Just as sweet utterances are like one who has tasted the nectar of a beloved’s lip,
the cuckoo does not warble its melodious song until it has experienced the taste of the mango bud.

Who would wish to seize and overcome the fang of Hari, which gleams red from the blood of elephants he has tasted— resembling a digit of the moon reddened by twilight— and which flashes forth from his mouth as it gapes wide in a yawn?

Ah, this forehead of the lotus-eyed one, possessing a noble form, is surely the boundary-line of the parting of the hair for the moon’s orb, as it were released from the mouth of darkness after being tasted!
Alas, you have been tasted out of delusion; indeed, the sweetness of your face was perceived. Yet, like a razor smeared with honey, you know only how to cut the tongue.

O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, may Your name be my constant offering— Your conduct like the taste of a young woman’s lip, Your form like the fresh speech of a maiden, Your beauty like the splendor of a noble bride, and Your fame like the message of a wife long separated from her lover.
Having relished the tender flesh of women separated from their lovers without distinction,
I believe the cloud now spits out their bones under the guise of hailstones.
Having tasted it myself, I say that begging is a great, heart-piercing agony; let no wanderer in *saṃsāra* ever suffer this humiliation.
Behold, brother: it is a playground for the mockery of dignity and old age, a stain upon one's pride, and a miscarriage of the boldness born from the possession of virtues.
O bee, having tasted the honey here, do not become intoxicated by the astringent sprouts of the mango tree that has deceived the cuckoos;
for even while the cuckoo was closest at hand, it was you who were offered such nectar—this is the loss of discrimination on its part, not a virtue in you.
Having tasted the bitter sprout of this mango tree, the young cuckoo, his heart bound by intense affection, spreads its fame across the walls of the quarters;
meanwhile, these bees, having drunk its honey, hum right there—tell me, who can describe the conduct that transcends the path of both the wicked and the virtuous?
"Excellent! This has been well endured by you," said the necklace as it fell from the chest of the beloved, breaking upon his breast;
the shower of pearls fell like a rain of flowers.
If, when struck, a sword produces a sound resembling the cry of a crow,
or if it makes a sound like the syllables "aṃ" or "ā," it should be avoided by the best of men.
That sword upon which a sweet sound arises when struck is worthy of worship by a king, for it is the destroyer of the hosts of his enemies.
Together we shall attain heaven and liberation in due order;
for when the union of husband and wife is harmonious, nothing whatsoever can be adverse.
The cow licks her calf to her heart’s content—his face speckled with droplets from the stream of milk falling as he drinks greedily again and again from his mother’s udder with his head bowed;
his single knee slightly bent, his beautiful tail moving incessantly, ears pricked up, and making the sound of "hum" out of affection for her dear son.

As her lord’s face was kissing her, that fair-toothed woman, manifesting gasps of "sīt" and trembling with a great agitation born of passion, then expressed his state of being the moon without using words.
Even while eating, he is not at ease; even when awake, he does not wake up [to reality];
he says nothing according to his own will; here, even a servant lives [only by serving].
A man should always acquire knowledge and wealth as if he were immortal;
yet, as if seized by the hair by Death itself, he should practice dharma.
O Śrī Nṛsiṃha, protector of the earth, may there be well-being for your arm, which is like Rāhu to the circle of kings who are arrogant in battle.
And those heroes in battles who have renounced their lives for the sake of their master— those men, devoted to their lord and grateful, go to heaven.
In battles, kings who desire to slay one another,
fighting with their utmost strength and not turning their backs, go to heaven.
As for her statement, "I do not delight in anyone other than Nala even with my mind," that was rendered false by the god of love, whose presence in her was inferred from her youth.
That she has ceased all talk regarding food, that there is a seal of silence upon her mouth, that her eyes are closed, that her slender body remains in emaciation,
that she stays in solitude, and that her mind is one-pointedly absorbed in meditation— I believe, O fortunate one, that she performs this intense penance for your sake.
Food consists of fruits and roots according to one's taste; the earth is the bed; bark garments are the clothing; grass, sacrificial fuel, and flowers are the requisites; deer are the sons;
and trees—providing clothing, food, shelter, and enjoyment without restraint—are the friends. What indeed is there for householders in their homes other than suffering?
The cry "kākadī" portends defects in food; "ākuṭāni" is a sound for battle;
"kekedhvani," "iṣṭhā," "kuvatī," and "kikī"—these three indicate the ruin of the city.
Eating, sleeping, fear, and sexual intercourse—these are common to humans and animals alike.
Knowledge is the superior distinction of humans; those devoid of knowledge are equal to animals.
One who knows the Dharma should perform the activities of eating, excretion, and recreation with great restraint;
likewise, speech, mental actions, ascetic penance, wealth, and longevity should be kept most strictly guarded.
Food, drink, betel, perfumes, garlands, fruits, and so forth—
whatever is enjoyed is considered "enjoyment" (bhoga) by the most excellent of the virtuous.

A man who consumes food rejoices in the slaughter of stationary and moving beings; therefore, he too incurs a connection with that evil. Thus [the Sage] spoke, and I shall say something regarding him.

When a variety of easily obtained food exists on this earth, free from sin, why— if there is still greed— do you consume meat after nourishing yourself with various forms of suffering caused by slaughter?
From eating [at improper times], disease arises; from [sleeping] in the womb, one is born cruel;
from [sleeping] on a bed, one becomes unfortunate; and from reciting [the scriptures] while lying down, there is a depletion of life-span.

One should perform blameless work for the sake of food, and that [work] for the sake of sustaining life. Life should be sustained for the sake of the knowledge of reality; reality should be known so that there is no further birth.
One becomes ill through food, and the fetus is destroyed through sexual intercourse;
prosperity is carried away by sleep, and death is certain through anxiety.
A submarine fire regarding food, acting like Kumbhakarṇa when lying down, deaf to instructions, a lion in flight, a jackal in battle,
blind in observing objects, lame in walking, yet clever in lamenting— only by good fortune is such a supreme servant found again.
"Abstention from food, total withdrawal from the entire range of sense objects, the fixing of the eyes upon the tip of the nose, and that which is one-pointedness of mind;
this silence, and this entire universe appearing as empty to you—if you possess these, friend, tell me: are you a yoginī, or are you a woman in the throes of separation?"
One who has cast aside shame regarding food and social conduct may find happiness;
wealth brings about friendship when given in charity, but it becomes a cause for enmity when withheld.

Purity in food, sweetness in voice, dependence on others for a nest, lack of attachment to kin, delight in the forest, and eloquence during the month of Mādhava—why indeed do people abandon this best of cuckoos, who possesses such a multitude of virtues, and instead worship the *khañjana* bird that feeds on worms? Strange indeed is the course of karma!
His food is poison; he has a third eye on his forehead; a skull is in his hand; his garment is an elephant hide; his delight is in ashes; his ornament is the lord of serpents;
his birth is untraceable; his lineage is without witness; and his caste is unknown. How can we serve this master of a host of goblins? We are undone!
Food acts like poison; even a necklace becomes a burden day by day; the moon acts like the fierce sun; and even the gentle breeze acts like a thunderbolt.
My dwelling acts like a forest; the application of sandalwood paste acts like sparks of fire. Alas! Oh, the time of separation from my beloved acts like the time of universal dissolution.
The food of women is said to be twofold, their intelligence fourfold,
their resolve sixfold, and their desire eightfold.

An actor, even though devoid of actual emotion, brings delight to the minds of the audience by means of the perfect accomplishment of the entire performance— including the application, release, and withdrawal [of emotional states].
O King, when your sword was whetted, the hearts of your enemies burst like jars; yet their beloved wives' eyes overflowed with tears—this is a great marvel.
When sweetness had been infused by honey and the movement [of passion] had been brought to full bloom,
the season for the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) among amorous women shone forth as if newly arisen with intensified rapture.
Those who know the Dharma say that truth is indeed the supreme duty;
they say that the protection of ministers is something more subtle than that,
but the protection of oneself is even more subtle than those.
By the oblation, the sun is nourished; from the sun comes rain, and then the plants.
That food, in the form of sap, attains the state of semen.
O fool, summoned from all sides by the vast display of the weight of its branches, why do you run so swiftly with the hope of obtaining the fruit of the *śālmali* tree?
On that very spot, where the heaps of cotton-like fibers from the fruits ready to burst forth are scattered, the paths ahead cannot even be seen by one wandering with eyes closed.
Whether summoned for his consecration or dismissed to the forest,
I did not perceive even the slightest change in his facial expression.
"Having been invited today to my festival, she has come leaving her house empty at night; how will this young bride of noble family go home alone while the servants are intoxicated?
Child, you must take her to her home. Hearing these words of Yaśodā, the sweet, smiling, and languid glances of Rādhā and Mādhava are victorious.

When birds are summoned, the mosquito is not warded off even though it arrives first; a jewel made of grass, whether dwelling in the midst of the ocean or elsewhere, assumes the luster of precious gems;

and even a firefly does not tremble to move among the luminous bodies. Fie upon this insentient commonality, which, like a master who has failed to discern the true nature of things, remains indifferent!
Even when called by his companions and saying "I am coming," even though he has shaken off sleep,
the traveler— even if he is a newcomer— does not abandon his sluggishness at all.
Summoned from the Malaya mountain, the seasonal breeze has begun to blow; on the path, flocks of cuckoos stand nearby, established as masters of song.
Abandoning their jasmine dwellings by their faithful neighbors on all sides, the rows of mango trees, about to blossom, are being swarmed by flights of bees.
Whether summoned or unsummoned, he who stands at the gate of kings indeed enjoys the royal fortune; never does one who is disrespectful do so.

Called by the plowman, yet as if not hearing his words, the peasant stands for a moment with his hair bristling; somehow leaving the windless branch, he approaches the field with arms crossed over his chest, moving with sluggish gait and dejected steps, his lips parted and quivering with gasps and shivers.
Prajāpati considered alms that have been brought forward and offered, even if not requested beforehand, as acceptable even from one who has performed evil deeds.
Wealth acquired and then abandoned produces the mere appearance of happiness;
wealth completely renounced leads to supreme bliss.

Even when brought under one's control and guarded with great effort, friendship with the wicked, a courtesan, and royal fortune— who possesses them, and for how long, can they remain stable when they are inwardly devoid of affection?
Alas, when the three worlds, scorched by the heat of the day, have been consumed by the flames of the sun and those flames have subsided, this remains as ashes; yet this darkness is not such ashes.
May this one gladden you by tearing open the hollows of the Daityas' chests with his harsh, claw-tips,
as if desiring to find within their hearts a second jewel of a son, as dear to them as Prahlāda.
By the turbidification of their own beauty and luster through the faultless, joy-inducing form of her slender body,
the very name "ornaments" became a misnomer for those lotus-eyed women, even though their own radiant splendors were cast aside.
O you who understand questions, what indeed can be the purpose of summoning some tree? Generally, in this Kali age, people do not perform any service for others.
Who, with faded eyes, asks about the full moon? By what does the world suffer such incomparable agony born of thirst?
There is a vast difference in the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth;
nevertheless, even Sarasvatī herself would not be able to describe it.
The tracks of carts, whose essence is crushed sugarcane rinds, bear banners of thick dust; a flock of parrots settles upon the heads of the awned rice stalks, bowed down by the ripening grain.
From the fields, rows of minnows enter the nearby reservoirs through irrigation channels; the clear mud on the riverbanks brings comfort to the sun-baked travelers.
Sugarcane stalks, sesame seeds, Śūdras, a beloved woman, gold, and land; sandalwood, curd, betel, and massage—these increase one's virtues.
Even after consuming sugarcane, water, milk, roots, betel, fruit, or medicine,
one should perform the rites such as bathing and giving gifts.

May the invincible Smara protect the three worlds—he whose bow is sugar-cane, whose arrows are a profusion of flowers, and whose bowstring is a swarm of bees; he who, with a tranquil mind, brings under his command the kings of whom the realms and so forth are the tribute, and by whose arrow-strikes Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, and the others appear as if they have pervaded the entire universe with their faces.
O fair-limbed one, the flow of the sugarcane river, the game of dice, and the grasping of pride—
yet this creeper-like brow of yours brings forth even greater delight when it is bent.

Just as there is a gradual excellence of flavor in every successive joint of a sugar-cane starting from the tip, so too is the friendship of the virtuous; but for those who are the opposite, it is the reverse.
Just as people take the juice of sugarcane and discard the fibrous pulp,
so the wise man takes the essence of the Dharma and abandons the body.
The various products of sugarcane, the insights of poets, the milk of cows, the playful antics of children,
the finest betel leaf, and the side-long glances of young women— alas, O Śakra, these things do not exist in heaven.
Having blazed all day like a seven-flamed coal, the fierce-rayed sun has subsided;
the shining orb of the moon appears like the ashes of that fire, scattering its light across the sky.
The people of Magadha understand by gestures; the people of Kosala understand by glances;
the Kurus and Pañcālas understand when half-speech is uttered; and those of the Deccan understand when everything is spoken.
Messengers who discern the minds of others through gestures, facial expressions, and movements; who are trustworthy, very swift in travel, eloquent, and moderate in speech.
He understands the true meaning of gestures and facial expressions, is skilled in reasoning and refutation,
is brave and learned, yet is neither arrogant nor envious.
One who understands the truth of gestures and physical expressions, who is strong, pleasant to behold,
ever vigilant, and always skillful— he is called a doorkeeper.
Having inferred the ocean of her own passion through his gestures, her appreciation of virtue through her flatteries,
and her devotion through her constant service, she brought him under her increasingly complete sway.
For those birds who, along with their mates, desired inseparability throughout the night, their pairs were nonetheless overtaken by separation; indeed, the decree of time cannot be transgressed.
The proud man desires death, yet he does not go for refuge to his enemies;
for the wise man who has mastered himself, death is simply the destruction of pride.

One who possesses a hundred desires a thousand; one with a thousand strives to acquire ten million; even one endowed with ten million seeks kingship, and alas, even a king aspires to the status of a universal monarch.

One who possesses a hundred desires a thousand; one who possesses a thousand strives for a hundred thousand; from being a lord of a hundred thousand, he seeks a kingdom; and from a kingdom, he strives for heaven.
Some desire residence in the hells, while others do not desire residence in the hells;
for it is better to enter a distinguished hell than the womb, for there is no suffering greater than dwelling in the womb.
Relatives do not constantly desire even their own destruction rather than the prosperity of one of equal lineage; they bow to enemies and endure the increase of their kin with hearts full of anguish.
Sundarapāṇḍya, possessing a mind intent on exaltation, fulfilled his desire by preparing a pair of food-offerings under his own name;
he made the deep belly of the Lord of Raṅga, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, completely full—a filling which would have been difficult to achieve even with all fourteen worlds.
If one desires extensive loving-kindness, one should avoid three things therein:
verbal dispute, involvement in worldly affairs, and speaking ill of their wives.
One who desires to follow the Supreme with clear devotion through the vision of his image,
yet fails to attain union with him, should place [the Lord] within his heart as the supreme treasure.
He who desires to live happily on this earth should go to the king’s auspicious assembly and speak only virtuous words in the council;
being skillful, he should accomplish his business, acquire wealth without hardship, win over the king’s favorites, do good for the people, and never cause harm to anyone.
Of the acts of sacrifice, ritual conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and Vedic study, this indeed is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga.
Sacrifice, study, charity, austerity, truthfulness, fortitude, forbearance,
and freedom from greed— this is remembered as the eightfold path of Dharma.
Among these, the first group of four may be practiced even for the sake of hypocrisy;
however, the latter group of four resides only in the Great-Souled One.

The wind moving through the *iḍā* is considered auspicious for gentle activities; likewise, it is auspicious when moving through the *piṅgalā* for fiery activities; however, its movement through both simultaneously is never favorable.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumṇā, Sarasvatī,
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and Pūṣā are likewise named.
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is considered the tenth;
these ten principal channels (nāḍīs) should be known as the carriers of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The *iḍā* is in the left nostril, while the *piṅgalā* is in the right;
the *suṣumṇā*, having pierced through the palate, extends to the gate of Brahmā (*brahmadvāra*).
If the earth and water elements flow within the *iḍā* [nāḍī],
then the undertaking of stable and gentle activities will lead to success.
Iḍā should be the channel of Soma, and Piṅgalā the channel of the Sun;
Iḍā is gentle and flows on the left, while Piṅgalā is fierce and flows on the right.
On this side is a terrifying flock of crows; on this side is the cry of owls; on this side is a formation of vultures, and on this side is a family of herons.
In this cremation ground, which stands devoid of all virtues and is a desolate wilderness, there are indeed not even two or three birds with melodious voices.
From here the peacock torments me with cries rivaling the thunderbolt; from there Kama strikes at will with his most cruel arrows.
From here the mass of clouds roars with terrifying sounds; O friend, I know not what will indeed happen to me without my lord.
On this side, the vulture of anger displays its own wing; on this side, this female jackal of craving runs forward with mouth agape.
On this side, the cruel demon of passion roams about for a long time—alas! This cycle of existence is a cremation ground; who, having fallen here, can remain in happiness?
O Vaidarbhī, behold these enemies whose weapons can be snatched away even by children; I grant you permission to look at them.
By such martial prowess as this, you—who have already fallen into my hands—are being sought after by them.
In this eastern quarter, the sun, the jewel of the sky, gradually reveals a tiny spark of light that pierces the vitals of the spreading darkness;
here, emerging from her lover skilled in new dalliances, the young bride wipes away the crocodile-patterned musk-designs imprinted upon her breast.

Because of this rejection, she resolved to follow her kinsmen; though her preceptor, who was like a father, cried out repeatedly, "Stay! to his disciple-like pupil, she cast upon me—a cruel man—her gaze, clouded by a flow of tears. That very act burns me like a poisoned dart.
On one side, this moon has brought about the destruction of darkness with its mass of rays, which are arrogant in dispelling the weariness of the clusters of night-lotuses;

on the other side, O friend, the five-arrowed god, whose prowess is most difficult to endure, cannot tolerate the disregard of his command. Therefore, in this situation, the essence of daring is our only refuge.
Here, white with the luster of the moon, here, red with the rays of the sun, and here, dark-hued with darkness whose movement is obstructed within—
this splendor of dawn shines before us like the confluence of the Gaṅgā, the Sun, and the Daughter of Brahmā for the sake of the virtuous who desire to bathe therein.
From here, the light of the sun bestows its ruddy hue upon the eastern quarter; from here, a humming bee rises up toward the lotus pond;
and from here, women emerge, their anklets jingling for a moment as their footsteps falter, weary from the exhaustion of intense lovemaking.
That Daitya, having attained prosperity from this source, does not deserve destruction from this very source;
for even a poison-tree, having been nurtured by oneself, is unfit to be cut down by that same person.
Here sleeps Keśava; here lie the kinsmen of his enemies; and here rest the winged mountains seeking refuge.
And here too is the submarine fire along with all the clouds of universal destruction—oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight is the body of the ocean!

That which is directed outward is called one thing, but that which throbs within the heart is quite another; this conduct, which fails to deliver the restless, stands at the forefront of the unrealities, like the reflection of water.

O Four-faced One, bestow upon me at your will whatever fruits of other sins I may deserve; do not, do not, do not inscribe the presentation of my poetry upon the heads of those who lack aesthetic taste!

Other rākṣasas also fell upon the crores of monkeys,
like dust raised in battle falling into rivers of their own blood.
Others desire wealth; young women desire beauty;

When other means are difficult to employ, a king who applies fierce punishment does not suffer harm in the future and enjoys the abundant fruit of his policy.

at the end of the night, they expand, dispelling the fatigue of the amorous play of lovers in their war of passion, and acting as friends to the fragrance of lotuses opening with yawns.

From here, the moon—thick with nectar and sweet in its transition between the ages of youth and maturity—brings delight with its rays, as if with the shimmering smiles of a young woman’s playful dalliance.

The bridge has its banks shattered here and there by the waters; the earth within is difficult to traverse; and this mountain is thick with mire of snow.
Now that the ritual lustration of elephants and horses has been completed, I know not by which path your enemies have fled.

With hundreds of thousands of silken banners, fluttering here and there in the wind and filling the directions and the sky,
and with their clusters of tinkling golden bells, they sank into the ocean of dust that had risen to the heavens.

Then, as she was fleeing in terror from here, abandoned by the kings who had fled, the beloved forest-dwelling woman was seen by the local forest folk;

Thus, having reflected upon the perishability of all people through their understanding of reality, the wise do not harbor even the slightest grief in their minds— that grief which destroys one's limbs, reputation, and happiness.

they are like the ladies of the inner apartments of monarchs—how much more so, then, other women born of noble families?

and at night, they attained satisfaction through the attentions of courtesans as beautiful as goddesses, sixteen years of age.
