Thus, with his eyes and other limbs transformed, his steadfastness dissolved,
overcome by the seizing demon of Māra, he lost all memory of his former appearance.
When he manifests a desire for dalliance and casts his gaze upon the region of your hips moment by moment,
you shall, as before, suck him dry like a ripe mango until nothing remains.
Thus, even an enemy who has set his heart upon the path [of hostility] attains the state of a good friend;
therefore, one should bring the world under control through the quality of discipline, with the sole exception of a king’s envy.
Thus, he whose purpose is well-calculated, who follows the path of the scriptures, and who, with self-restraint, governs his subjects through the science of punishment—
into him prosperity enters for the sake of non-return, just as rivers flow into the ocean once they have entered its course.
Thus, having witnessed their marriage, their journey together in a single vehicle, and their continuous glances from the corners of their eyes as they looked at one another with apprehension,
the lords of the gods in heaven, dense with joy, gazed on with curiosity and seemed, as it were, to resolve to depart for the celestial realm.
Thus, whatever is destined for a living being in this world by the necessity of prior karma,
that he obtains without effort, even if it be unattainable, as it falls before him.
O virtuous ones, always keeping in your own minds this cycle of existence— which is as treacherous as a provoked serpent and which constantly bestows intense suffering—
abandon the crooked obsession with grasping at possessions, if you wish to taste the nectar of bliss that is free from all that is inauspicious.
O King, even among noble and fortunate women who are truly discerning, the mind wanders here and there toward whatever it pleases; however, women of pure nature are rare indeed.
When her beloved asked this, the young woman, overwhelmed by emotion, somehow suppressed her sobbing and stammering; that she replied only "Nothing" told him more than words could describe.
Thus, by many such means, that ungrateful procuress, devoid of merit, practiced deception upon lustful men;
alas, even the young fawns, constantly witnessing the trapping of deer in the forest, nevertheless enter the concealed snares.
Having observed those impassioned men, clearly inflamed by pride and desire, and ever devoted to the splendor of incessant dalliance,
the night— her hands [the stars] cast down and her moon bent low— then underwent a transformation, as if turning her face downward in shame.
Thus, those of deluded intellect, their minds robbed by departing fortune, act without reflection out of impulsive passion;
out of great pride in the weight of their own power, they enter upon the vow of the moth before the lamp of another’s majesty.
Thus, because the self-possessed king sustains both worlds,
he should therefore properly wield the rod of punishment over his subjects, like a staff-bearer.
Thus, by means of the method of instruction on the conventions of pleasure as shown by the masters of love,
the world of women abandoned the distinction between their own and others' parts, becoming absorbed in the stage of supreme non-duality of Smara.
He who practices these aforementioned royal virtues experiences auspicious things in this world and is glorified in heaven after death.
Thus, regarding kingdom, wife, friends, sons, and his home as mere blades of grass,
the lord of men went to the forest to abandon *prakṛti*, which is stained by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

"O King, who can place their trust in the conduct of a courtesan?"
Thus she speaks to her friends, her eyelashes doubled in density as they close;
she falls into her husband’s lap out of fear of the bee—for timidity is indeed a virtue in women.

Thus speaks another man to his circle of friends out of affection; having waited for a long time for his most beloved, he places his long strides upon the ground as if measuring it, following after her.
May this manual, composed by me with such a structured arrangement, be for the eternal delight of all virtuous people—
a treasury of vast, pure, and shining noble arts, which eclipses the owls of my adversaries.

hunting— like a clever mistress— carried him away through its ever-increasing passion and persistent service.

Thus, for those whose minds are scorched by the heat of the sun of the suffering of *saṃsāra*,
where else can there be happiness for human beings except in the shade of the tree of liberation?

Thus, with my beloved both in her embodied form for a moment and in her bodiless state for the rest of the night, I spent the nights as if they were mere moments and the days as if they were interminable;
by my conduct, which was the reverse of the activities of day and night, I imitated the deeds of the one known as Rathacaraṇa (Cakrāyudha).
Thus, O Goddess, women born of noble families serve their husbands with pure and steadfast conduct, their minds never turning elsewhere; for the husband is indeed the supreme deity of virtuous wives.

Thus, from her clear speech and her respectful regard, as well as from the mockery of the gods' longing for her, she heard his words while sleeping with one cheek and ear resting upon the hollow of his hand; yet, at the same time, those very words remained unheard by her.

Thus, proceeding by the path of policy, the king, being industrious, should practice the purification of his realm;
with his circle purified, he shines brilliantly, delighting his subjects like the autumnal moon.
Thus the king, endowed with discipline and practicing that conduct honored by the lords of men,
ascended to the radiant station of glory, which is as lofty as the peak of a mountain of great jewels.
Immediately after that, he should listen to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
having eaten, he should then enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments.
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will misrepresent me."
From this supreme history, the insights of poets are born,
just as the three worlds are produced from the five elements.

On one side, the Ganges flows with its banks crumbling; on the other, forest lands where rows of trees are scorched by forest fires.
Before me, a lion roars with great speed. Alas! Alas! There is no way out for me except through fate; thus does this young deer lament.
From here the forest fire blazes from the dry land; from here comes a net, tangled and complex; from here this hunter runs, following step by step with his bow bent.
And right ahead stands this python with its mouth wide open. Where can this young deer go, and what can he do, fallen as he is under the power of fate?
There is nothing here, nor anything from beyond; wherever I go, there is nothing.
For when the world is investigated, it is nothing at all; there is nothing whatsoever that exceeds the realization of one's own self-nature.
Falling from this and falling from that, while wearing the garb of one devoted to the supreme solitude,
he shall experience neither the happiness of saṃsāra nor the happiness of liberation.
From this comes death, from this disease, from this calamity, and from this old age;
impermanence, with its four components of equal strength, destroys the world.
From this side, let me repeatedly contemplate the flash of a mass of lightning; from this side, let the many cries of the peacock steal away this pitiless heart.
From this side, let the perverse God of Love strike again and again with his feathered arrows, since you, O tremulous-eyed one, have gone far away from me, my beloved.

On one side is the play of lightning-garlands; on another, the wafting fragrance of the blooming *ketaka* tree; on one side is the thunderous roar of rising clouds; and on another, the sweet, clamorous cries of peacocks at play—how shall these days of separation pass for the long-lashed-eyed women, though they are filled with such intense emotion?
On one side, the rows of groves are marked with the sprouts of mango trees, and from the Malaya breeze comes the sweet warbling of female cuckoos;

For one who thus sifts through the words of the family of poets,

Thus, even when men dwell among those activities that exclude those of powerful character,
and likewise when they find satisfaction in those who possess the wealth of recklessness rather than wisdom, the rulers of the earth become intent on giving gifts.

By means of this present life and by the power of one's own previously performed karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious— every being in this creation, including gods and asuras, shall indeed experience various enjoyments that are eternally in accordance with that [karma].
And thus, even a quality acquired with great effort through destiny when fate is adverse does not merely fail to lead to prosperity; rather, it results in calamity.
For when its root is never altered and is constantly watered with the water of wisdom, the tree of human effort— encircled by the trench of right policy— generally bears fruit.
Thus, ascending the surface of the bed, thus the manner of offering leaves, thus the sequence of words for the couch, and thus the propitiation of the beloved—

even one who is poor in wealth lives, but one who is poor in intellect does not truly live.

"This has been done; this is to be done;
this other thing is half-finished"—while one is thus attached to the pleasure of such striving, Death brings one under his power.
"This is black, O beloved; surely it is black, but what if it is white? Shall we go, or shall we stay? Let there be going, or let there be staying.
That very path of my heart which was followed by him for so long has become something else; O friend, who can truly know men?"
And this, my dear, I tell you as the highest of all things: the meritorious state that is most distinguished.
One should never abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of fear, nor out of greed, even for the sake of one's life.
He who wanders about thirsty, thinking "this is to be known, this is to be known," will not attain what is to be known even in thousands of eons.

This is that bank of the Kālindī; for here, as the cowherd community heard the fame of the slayer of the demon Kaṃsa, their mouths dropped their morsels of food, while in every direction the gopīs incessantly sang it out, their voices rendered soft, high-pitched, and sweet by the affectionate resonance of the flute’s sound.
This is that entire essence of affection, common to both the wealthy and the poor;
it is an ointment for the heart, requiring neither sandalwood nor ushira-root.

This is indeed a marvel: that upon the surface of the earth there is the full moon, free from blemish, and something else shines within it—a sprout, a ruby, a blue lotus petal, the bow of Love, and the sound of playing the lute of the mind; such is the great wonder of her lower lip.
"O lotus-fearing-faced one, tell me who told you this, that you should indeed hold the notion that 'this is a golden bracelet'?
This is that supreme weapon for attacking difficult-to-subdue foes, a discus placed by the God of Love at the base of your lotus-hand out of affection for you."
O bird-catchers, they say that this pair of portents on earth is a source of great fear:
namely, when a crow is seen engaged in copulation, or when one is occasionally white.

O beloved, I long for this lotus-face of yours—whose cheeks steal the luster of a blade of *dūrvā* grass and are sprinkled with a few drops of perspiration, and which is made fragrant by its natural scent of *bakula*; O lovely one, grant me leave to drink from your copper-red lips or else to inhale its fragrance.
In this sky, where the clamor of wandering owls is terrifying and which provides a feast for the eyes of the throngs of night-roaming women, there spreads a thick,
dense darkness— solid as a mass of flesh with a herd of boars wallowing in it, shimmering amidst an abundance of thick mud.
This was not, nor has it arisen; it was not, nor will it be. That very Brahman, whose nature is existence, remains established in this manner.
This Rohaṇa mountain, abandoned by supplicants seeking jewels because of its growth of gem-stalks, will in a few days cover the sky; in vain did the sage Agastya obstruct the Vindhya range.
This most beautiful city of the body of the fawn-eyed women has indeed been forcibly led away by him [Love], having first driven out their childhood.
Fearing his arrival, what has the fish-bannered god done? He has made the two mountains that are her breasts difficult to cross for the river of her triple-fold.
This world, by its very nature subdued by sense objects and greedy for the wives and wealth of others,
remains established upon the eternal path frequented by the virtuous only when it is oppressed by the fear of punishment.
Generally, this is something not previously familiar to the eyes in this world: that a request does not diminish the measure of a man's virtues;
for when the Soul of the Universe entered his own body at the request of Bali, he became dwarfed in stature because his limbs were hidden out of shame.
This is the thunderbolt of Maghavan, with fire inherent in its edge;
the mere remembrance of it is sufficient to cause the miscarriage of the embryos of the Daitya women.
Thinking, "This will take away the pride of the moon, our rival,
on all sides," they offered their own lotuses as a gift to the face of the city woman.
This day, which occurs once in thousands of yugas, has become today;
what then can be said of the limit of death?
"This has been gained, this has been lost; this desire I shall obtain"—while embodied beings are thus reflecting, their lifespan wastes away.
This face is the moon itself, free from its spot; this lower lip is the orb of the sun fully ripened by time;
these eyes are two blue water-lilies whose beauty increases day and night; and this body is an ocean of loveliness, most pleasant to plunge into.
Those for whom it is a firm conviction that "this entire universe is my family," those peaceful and most noble ones— by whom are such virtuous people not to be honored?
This entire world must be protected with a mind diligently applied according to the rules; yet the grief for my beloved withers my life as the heat withers a flower.
Having myself brought about this abandonment, even the diversion of lamentation is no longer easy to find; that I still breathe even now is surely a gain, for to weep is indeed a blessing.
In the midst of this lake of the sky shines a white lotus as bright as the moon,
within which the dark spot appears like a hovering bee.
This body of a person, born of delusion, is perceived as a separate material structure like a house;
just as a person born of water, earth, and fire is transformed and perishes over time.
Just as fire is perceived as distinct within pieces of wood, just as the wind exists separately though it has entered the body,
and just as the all-pervading sky remains unattached, so too is the Supreme Person, the support of all qualities.
This body, with its joints slackened and worn out, will inevitably fall, being difficult to sustain through the process of decay.
Why do you ask for medicine, O fool of wicked mind? Drink the disease-free elixir of Kṛṣṇa!
"Drink this cool water, O travelers; release for a moment the fatigue of the road, doubled by the anxiety born of remembering your beloveds.

With these words, accompanied by wide sidelong glances, gentle and sweet modulations of speech, and smiles, the rows of women guarding the water-stations steal away the progress of young men upon the path.
This wondrous illusion, consisting of one's own kin, body, children, mother, and wife, has surely been fashioned here by someone;
for in this triple world, where, to whom, and how does anyone truly exist as one's own or as another, when embodied beings are subject solely to their own karma?
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this constantly brings renown; and this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss.

For this indeed is the unfailing fruit of a man’s austerity, sacred learning, well-performed sacrifice, and eloquent hymns, as well as of the wisdom bestowed by the Buddha—namely, that which has been determined by the poets: the description of the virtues of the One of Supreme Renown.
For this city of trade and commerce brings both life and fame;
here alone is the remedy for extracting the thorns of mistreatment from one's master.
For the wise declare this to be the mark indicating the excellence of greatness among the great:
that their minds, when confronted with the occurrence of pleasure or pain, do not fall under the sway of elation or despondency.
This is indeed the supreme secret of wit: one should not recite a fine saying before those who merely imagine themselves to be poets;
for such a person not only fails to appreciate it, but actually destroys it by their own clumsy poetic composition.

O lady with intoxicating eyes, if you interpret this heart of mine— which is devoted to no other— as being otherwise, even though it dwells within your own heart, then I, already struck by the arrows of Love, am struck down once again.
This is improper and out of order for men, that even in old age there should be such amorous transformation;
and it is likewise improper that the lives or the sexual pleasures of women are not made to end with the sagging of their breasts.

Before the morning oblation had begun, someone spoke of this sacrificial pit of Indra as glowing with fire at the conclusion of the rite; others said it was a jeweled vessel for his morning consecration; and some called it the orb of the fierce-rayed sun filled with water-like light.

This interval exists for the sake of assistance while this prosperity of the petitioner is still unstable by nature; but when misfortune inevitably arises, where will there be another opportunity to help?
This entire triple world would become blind darkness,
if the light called "Word" did not shine throughout the course of saṃsāra.
O celestial sage, this and another secret concerning all women is that as soon as they see a man who is pleasing to the heart, a woman's womb becomes moistened.
This door is weak, this cage is dilapidated, and the cruel journey of the cat does not cease in this house.
O parrot, remain with your tongue folded; what is the use of your words? The vulgar have no regard for the diversion of your speech.
This is another most wonderful thing: that while being plundered by thousands of young women, there is an increase rather than a decrease in the treasury of your good fortune.

Having cast aside these swarms of bees— the pollen-laden clusters of lotuses— the one devoid of passion turns toward you, O lady with the fresh creepers of her eyebrows bent down by the weight of her breasts which surpass their flower-bunches.
"Look at this incomparable lake, filled with lotuses!
Friend, do not speak; the eyes of women are burning me."
This is the immeasurable nectar; this is that ocean of bliss; and this too, sweet as honey, stirs something within:
that time passes in the dalliances of young women languid with the play of rising passion, as they engage in the exchange of love.
"O friend, this fresh nail-mark upon the slope of your breast belongs to her whose pride remains unfading; let it be concealed with your upper garment."
O Mahādeva, it is truly improper that the wind, which at other times merely stirs the hair of beautiful women, should now—
accompanied by snow— strike those separated from their lovers, who remember the warmth of their youthful breasts.

Every night, this golden bracelet— its gems discolored by the heat within me as I am not cooled by external contact, and its mark from the bowstring’s impact unmarred— is repeatedly slipped down from my wrist by me and pushed back up, as tears spread from the corners of my eyes fall upon it.
Even at first, the five-arrowed god [Kāma] consumes my mind, which is difficult to restrain due to its longing for an object so hard to attain;
how much more so now that the sprouts of the mango trees in the grove have been revealed by the Malaya breezes, which have stripped away their pale leaves?
Hold fast to this unerring [teaching] and ward off harsh words;
for in this world, a man of harsh speech is the sole enemy of all people.
I pray to this ocean of the nectar of compassion, the crest-jewel of the young moon:
"In birth after birth, may my body become a means for the worship of you."
This lunar orb shines in the sky, piercing the continuous darkness and bringing delight to the eyes of beautiful women.
Luring one woman after another with flowers of various trees, saying "This one, this one," the God of Love repeatedly entices them; oh, how he hastens people to sport in secret!
Having reflected that "this and this" must certainly be applied through right action, one who strives should bring it to fulfillment;
he whose common folk have their vulnerabilities closed by sound policy enjoys the three aims of life for a long time, like a lord of the earth.
This face of yours, with its locks of hair slightly disheveled and its speech stilled, pains me like a single lotus sleeping at night, its internal humming of bees having ceased.
Friends, with this in mind, bow down to your own chosen deity;
let the Yamunā be knee-deep, or not, and let there be another boatman.

Her youthful body, covered by a bark garment with a fine knot tied at the region of her hips and concealing the fullness of her breasts, does not display its own natural beauty, like a flower bound within the interior of pale leaves.

Smara, with a sense of curiosity, resorts to the body of this young girl— which, like a bow with a pellet, contains a single bud-like breast nestled within a necklace-string stretched between two walls.
"I shall do this, and from that, this will come"—
death does not wait for such a resolution as this to be formed.
This indeed is the great manifestation of the intoxication of this Kali age:
that my heart's desire has been fulfilled not even through the worship of Rāma.
This alone is the unbarred gate to heaven for kings:
that their own vow and their subjects are both protected.
This indeed is the ultimate folly, devoid of the three means:
that both sides of warriors exert their prowess equally in battles.
This indeed is the great fortitude of the steadfast and the truly ascetic:
that even when encountering obstacles, they are not thwarted by those obstacles.
For this alone is the fruit of birth, this alone is the fruit of life for men:
that their youth passes away in the pleasure of union with women possessing shapely hips.
For this very thing has been determined: from malicious speech comes the encounter with suffering;
for one who digs a pit for another's sake, a fall into a well is certain.
For this alone is true scholarship, and this alone is true cleverness;
this alone is true wisdom—that one's expenditure be as small as possible.
For this alone is true wisdom, this alone is noble birth, and this alone is the supreme dharma: that income be greater than expenditure.

But now I have realized that there is no happiness higher than renunciation;
there is no eye equal to knowledge, and there is no strength equal to the eye.

Now enough of these bamboos, which are friends to the mountains, forests, rivers, and villages, and which have become witnesses to the unrestrained secret dalliances of Śabara couples;
for their riverbanks are now encircled by bamboo shoots whose bark resembles the ears of young goats, dark with bristling hair.
Now let there be many poems upon the surface of the earth;
yet alas, that first poem which was like a mirror [to them all] is indeed gone.
Just now your limbs were washed and unguents applied; O Kṛṣṇa, even now your body is covered in grey dust.
Now the houses of the plowmen are radiant, rejoicing at the first harvest of grain and emitting the fragrance from the pots of fresh rice;
there, young women, their bracelets jingling as they raise their creeper-like arms, grasp, lift, swing, and smoothly wield their pestles.
That lord alone is to be served who, with his own light that sheds nectar,
restores to fullness the circle of the moon-like twice-born that has been diminished by misfortune.
The campaka flower, its interior filled with bees and slightly opening its petals,
was like a golden inkwell prepared by the God of Love for the purpose of writing his edict.
If the *indindira* bee turns its face away from the *maranda*, what indeed is the greatness of honey?
And if the connoisseur does not desire it, what is the excellence of his bimba-like lower lip due to passion?

Once, having laboriously fashioned a blue lotus to serve as a comparison for her two eyes, the Creator perceived their incomparability; thereupon, casting dust upon it, he threw it into the midst of the mud.
I bow to the Joy of the Yadus, who is dark as the petal of a blue lotus, who is the sprout of bliss for Indirā, and who is a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for those who offer him salutations.
This king has a body dark as the blue lotus, while you have a slender frame fair as yellow pigment;
may your union be like that of lightning and a rain-cloud, for the mutual enhancement of your respective splendors.
This space between her lotus-eyes is that of the blue water-lily;
for even the light of the moon does not tolerate one [eye], while the other, called her face, stands having overtaken the moon itself.
O lotus-eyed one, I consider there to be only two remedies for the wounds caused by the falling arrows of your piercing side-glances:
first, the drinking of the nectar of your lips; second, the smearing of the saffron paste from your high, full breasts.

While she who has eyes like blue lotuses and lips like bright coral was wandering in the forest toward a secret tryst, thieves stole all her ornaments; why is it that they did not take away the jewel from her nose?
Having fashioned her eyes with blue lotuses, her face with a lotus, her teeth with jasmine, her lower lip with a fresh sprout,
and her limbs with petals of the *campaka* tree— the Creator, O beloved, how did he fashion her heart out of stone?
Possessing a thick splendor like the interior of a blue lotus, wearing garments resembling a mass of molten gold,
and with a chest adorned by a beautiful pearl necklace— who is this youth who makes the world full of the god of love?

O best of kings, this movement of my mind is always longing to behold you— just as the night-lily longs for the moon, the flock of ruddy geese for the sun, the cātaka birds for the rain-cloud, the swarm of bees for a cluster of flowers, the sweet-throated female cuckoo for the mango tree, and a woman for her husband who has gone abroad.

The Creator fashions the moon—possessing the luster of a circle of broken rice grains, eternally risen, yet at times appearing on the new-moon day as if its body were being ground by the millstone of clouds;

surely, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, he scatters from the sky onto the earth the cooling frost, which is like a delightful flour made from white clouds, providing nourishment everywhere.

The pair of cakravāka birds reviles the moon; the owl [reviles] the treasury of light; one who has lost their appetite for sweet milk [reviles] the virtuous; the sinner [reviles] the wise; the dullard [reviles] the learned;
the wicked man [reviles] one abandoned by all people; and the vulgar man [reviles] the refined. Who, indeed, exists here in this world of Brahmā who is honored by everyone?

O King, your fame and the beloved wives of your enemies both sport with intense, shimmering whiteness: your fame scorns the moon, cannot endure sandalwood paste, does not look upon garlands of jasmine, hates pearl necklaces, abandons white lotuses, and rejects heaps of lotus stalks; meanwhile, your enemies' beloveds scorn the moon, cannot endure sandalwood, do not look upon jasmine garlands, hate pearl necklaces, abandon white lotuses, and reject heaps of lotus stalks—both sporting thus with great whiteness upon the mountains, in the forests, and on the shores of the ocean.
She censures the moon, cannot endure sandalwood, hates the lotus, considers her pearl necklace a burden, and sets her mind not even on a heap of camphor;
she plunges into the celestial Ganges and firmly embraces the snowy mountain—her fame, as if afflicted by the pain of separation, does not rest even for a moment in one place.
A thief reviles the moon; a paramour, the householder; a rogue, the virtuous; an ignoble man, the woman of noble birth; a youth, the aged;
an illiterate man, the learned; a base person, the lord of wealth; one deformed by ugliness, the man radiant with beauty; and an inferior person, the awakened and exalted.
She censures the moon, takes no pleasure in beds of lotus petals or plantain leaves, scatters camphor, and finds no delight in a chamber cooled by showers of snow.
What more need be said? Consumed repeatedly by the fire of separation from you, she sprinkles you—who dwell within her heart—with tears out of fear of the forest fire.
Let people indeed revile the moon, or let the cakravāka birds revile the lotus; yet by this, there is no loss of splendor for the moon, nor any ill-repute.
For its purpose is fulfilled simply by the fact that the world finds joy in it, and that the flocks of cakora birds rest their beaks for a long time within its rays.
O you whose face mocks the beauty of the moon’s orb, it is because they call the moon "one with much grass" (mṛga-tṛṇa) that the deer does not abandon it;
for the power of delusion does not pass away from those animal-like perceptions until the moon's splendor is truly imitated by your countenance.
Perceiving the moon as the sun, mistaking sandalwood for a forest fire, knowing the lotus to be a flaming torch, and regarding her bed of snow as a funeral pyre—
with a mind tormented by necklaces that feel like glowing coals— this wretched woman, abandoned by you, now perceives this entire creation as consisting of nothing but fire.
"Is this the moon? Where is the spot? Is this a lotus? Where has the water gone?"—O gazelle-eyed one, it was only after these playful and charming words that it was finally ascertained to be a face.
The moon shall depart; the splendor of the stars will perish; and the jewel-lamps, having swallowed the darkness, shall no longer remain.
O firefly, the entire world will become blind; even you shall reach your end—this is far off indeed.
O Bhāratī, having abandoned that bird who knows the essence of moonlight, why do you shine within the mouth of a parrot? What delight is there for you here?
If you resort to the former, let this [audience] speak of the distinction between the moonlight and the words of Govindarāja.
O slender-limbed one, your face is perceived by those who contemplate it as if carved from the orb of the moon, or extracted from the heart of a lotus.
Where the banners, shaken by the wind, serve as fans for the sun and the moon, who are weary from their journey across the sky.
O moon-faced one, behold the world scorched by the rays of the sun;
it is like a palm-leaf fan held in the hand of Night, yet deprived of its handle, which she now uses to fan him.
The ocean, born from the direction of Indra, danced with the rows of its waving arms;
the fish-bannered god rejoiced, and the bees attained release from their confinement within the night-lotuses.
O Goddess, you with the face of the moon, eyes like white lotuses, thighs like plantain stalks, and hands and feet as beautiful as lotuses—
you whose loveliness is like the essence of nectar— why do you burn me when you have entered my heart?
"Is it the moon, the moon?"—what is this vain hope? This is merely a drop of water being observed.
Nay, it is the face of the deer-eyed woman that shines forth here, with its dark and tender cheeks.
May that pair—the moon upon the head of Śiva and the curved nail-mark on the breast of the Mountain’s Daughter—grant you prosperity as they mutually emulate one another;
for their correspondence consists of the *praṇava* (Om) which, when the two bodies are unified, is contemplated as the upper door and meditated upon in its true form within the heart.

Where the moon is not censured, where the sweet words of a messenger are not heard, where conversations clouded by tears do not fall, and where the body does not undergo emaciation—where one sleeps embracing one's own wife, who is submissive and compliant—is that love? This is merely the arduous observance of the householder’s vow.

If the moon has not yet appeared upon the crest of the eastern mountain, let it be; nevertheless, these rays of his uproot the mass of darkness even in the outskirts. They pour forth joy for the eyes and perfume the quarters with night-lotuses; yet now, he shall manifest himself upward to reveal his characteristic mark.

The gaze of the deer seems as if smeared with collyrium and dulled; the luster of coral has lost its ruddy glow, as if turned dark; the radiance of gold is as if dimmed; and a touch of harshness has begun to manifest even in the throats of the female cuckoos, like that of the beautiful woman. Alas, before her, the plumage of the peacocks appears as if it were held in contempt.
One who performs a thousand moon-vows for the purification of the body,
and one who drinks the waters of the Gaṅgā— these two may be equal, or they may not be equal.
O Lord of the Earth, the Indus has been surpassed by your fame; the sun by your splendor; Kandarpa by your physical form; and the ocean of nectar by the grace of your speech.
My mind now wavers in doubt as to which of these two—your victory or your generosity that dispels poverty—will truly prevail.

The rising moon, sandalwood, the moon-faced Caitra month, and his own body composed of erotic passion—these are his great wealth; yet I think you cause him torment because of your union with the fire of Śiva.
With a multitude of lunar digits arranged in successive rows,
these arms have been fashioned for the removal of all suffering of children.

O beloved, it is no wonder that you take from the moon its luster, from the elephant in rut its gait, or from the startled deer its eyes—those with their cold rays, those with their sluggish pace, and those with their timid glances.
But this is truly marvelous, O dear one: that you steal away with the mere play of your eyebrows the entire splendor of the bow of Kandarpa, the conqueror of the world.
"Shall I take from the moon, or from Brahmā, or from Indra, or from Yama, or from the Lord of Beings (Śiva) his collection of bone ornaments to give to you?"—
may that Śaṅkara protect you, at whose terrifying utterances during the act of adorning himself, spoken from within the chamber of his ornaments, the gods were struck with fear.
Is she the nectar created by the Creator, preserved from the waning of the moon? Is she the beloved body fashioned by Kāma to steal away the fortitude of Śiva?
Is she a creeper graced by the beauty of the spring of youth and sprinkled with the essence of passion? Or is she a river of loveliness, a Rati attained once more in another birth?
The rays of the moon enter the lotus, while the rays of the sun enter the water-lily;
likewise, his virtues found a place even within those who were his adversaries.

This indescribable play of light veils the world—the light of the moon, who is a sandal-paste mark upon the slopes of the breasts of the young women that are the three watches of night; who is the chowrie of the Fortune of the Sky; who is the bud upon the creeper-like matted locks of the Destroyer of Tripura; who is the crystal palace for King Kandarpa; and who is the pearl from the nose-ornament of Indra.
"O friend, tell me, what evil deed have you committed, that you wander here before him with your face turned away and veiled, as if you were his shadow?"
This [spot], which is like a mere trifle compared to the single digit of the moon that was extracted by Rudra and placed upon his head, appears as a transformation into the form of a dark mark.

O ornament of the earth’s circle, the moon’s mark, the base of the throat of the conqueror of Tripura, the cheeks of the world-elephants—stained with the ink of their rutting ichor—and even now Murāri all appear as if smeared with blackness; tell me, what then has been whitened by your glories?
Her face, with its luster like that of her teeth, is like the moon marked by a drop of sandalwood paste; her earring serves as a whetstone for the sharpening of the arrow-like glances from her eyes;
the pearl necklace upon the hollows of her breasts is like a stream of nectar from her smile; and that sapphire bangle jingling at her lotus-foot is like a swarm of bees.

In the moon, the cakora birds find it blameworthy; for the white lotuses, the night-long vigil at an improper time; for the bees, the lack of association with wine; and for the blue lotuses, excessive languor—in autumn.

Yet, when I behold the constant stream of tears from the eyes of the young women of Vairāka at his frown, I see that the camari deer, whose secret movements are hidden by the cascades of their incessant flow of tears, are the sole standard of comparison for them.
Indra, the ocean with its two eyes, the five-faced one, the lotus-born Brahmā, the sweet-watered Sindhu, Śiva with his white throat, Kāma with his beautiful form,
the winged mountains, and likewise the horses and the tawny Lord of Lakṣmī— all these were seen somewhere, yet none of them were ever given away by the King of the Raghus, nor lost by him himself.
They call Indra "eunuch," the Moon "stained," Mādhava the son of a cowherd, Vyāsa the son of a fisherwoman, the ocean "devoid of essence," and Fire "all-devouring.
They say Vasiṣṭha is the son of a prostitute, and that the Pāṇḍavas were born of other origins—considering such popular sayings, O Lord of Men, tell me: who is without fault?
Indra, his mind agitated, making all the guardians of the quarters in every direction remain vigilant, took the divine army surrounded by the best of gods and, holding the thunderbolt weapon in hand,
stood at the gate of heaven— he whose fierce and powerful drum-beats were struck down by [the enemy's] strength, while being sung of by Kinnarīs with the slopes of their jar-like breasts trembling.
Indra is the foremost among the deities in heaven; the Brahmin among men; the Gaṅgā among rivers;
cows among livestock; grain among riches; and everywhere, the head is the principal part of the body.
In the forests, a spreading succession of indragopaka insects shone intensely,
like a jeweled earring made of rubies fallen from the ear due to the impetuous onset of the rainy season.
The earth shone as if covered with indragopa insects, appearing like drops of blood flowing from hearts pierced by the arrows of the bodiless god of love for those dwelling abroad.
"Indrajit, you are of fierce valor; by your very name you are powerful. Shame, shame upon you! Agitated by fear of us, you fight while concealing your true form."
Soft as an emerald or a parrot’s wing, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, a white lotus, or the moon,
and rivaling molten gold and a blooming campaka flower— such is the earth praised.
"You are Indra, O King; Sundarī is your Śacī; your son is like Jayanta; your palace shines like Vaijayanta; and your elephant is the beloved of Abhramu.
Thus praised at will with such untrue words by those who seek to awaken him, he perceives himself as Hari of manifest prowess—such is to be known the power of the illusory Māyin Hari.
The highly illustrious Asura Vṛtra was slain by Indra’s thunderbolt;
smeared all over with his fat, that [sacrificial ground] is for the purpose of anointing.
The king shall possess sevenfold the qualities of Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, and Pṛthivī.
Taking sovereignty from Indra, majesty from Agni, wrath from Yama, and wealth from Vaiśravaṇa,
as well as valor from Rāma and Janārdana, the body of a king is fashioned.

"Indra and the other guardians of the world, Viṣṇu, Candra, and Sūrya, the Nāgas, Vidyādharas, and all other gods—even those who are hostile—are dear to you. O giver of boons, who is more venerable or more exalted than you?
Having heard these words from his beloved, the ten-faced one spoke these words: "Śūlin, Śambhu, Pinākin, Śiva, Bhava, Paśupati, Śarva, Īśa, and Bharga."

O Mother of the Universe, what has been given by Indra and the others that you bestow upon them a white, auspicious abode, while to me you grant not even a hut made of grass? What offense have I committed against you? Or if, O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, you dispense blessings to all according to their past actions, then of what use is your exalted compassion?
Having extracted the eternal portions of Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka; of Agni and Varuṇa; and also of Candra and Vitteśa.
At the request of Indra, the Four-faced One formerly instructed Bharata in the art of drama for the delight of Mahendra.
Beholding Indra, I relish his face; longing for Ananta, I embrace my beloved today; and yearning for Kārtavīrya, I savor her very presence.
By him who has conquered the sense-faculties, the entire world is conquered;
but he who is overcome by the sense-faculties is defeated everywhere.
Attachment and aversion are established toward the objects of each sense-faculty; one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries.
Day and night, one should apply oneself to the conquest of the senses;
for one who has conquered the senses is able to keep the subjects under control.
A hero is he who conquers his senses; a wise man practices the Dharma.
He should be a speaker of truth, whether or not he is a giver.
But if among all the sense-faculties even a single faculty leaks,
then one’s wisdom flows away from it, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
Through the indulgence of the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by restraining them, one attains perfection.
Through indulgence in the senses and through the non-cultivation of the Dharma, the ignorant and lowest of men go from one evil rebirth to another in saṃsāra.
When the senses have run wild like horses on their paths, one should exercise firmness as a charioteer; through such firmness, one will surely conquer them.
A wise person should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
For when the mind follows after the wandering senses,
it carries away one's wisdom, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters.
Salutations again and again to that Goddess, the presiding power over the senses and over all beings, who is eternally pervasive within all beings.
The non-restraint of the senses is no different from death; conversely, excessive restraint may even cause one's own divine faculties to decline.
Having restrained the senses and being free from attachment and aversion,
one who is equanimous toward pleasure and pain, tranquil, and a knower of reality is called a virtuous person.
They say that the senses are superior; the mind is superior to the senses;
the intellect is superior to the mind; and that which is beyond the intellect is He.
Having made the senses the sacrificial animals and having made the altar consisting of austerity,
and having offered non-violence as the oblation, I perform the sacrifice of the self.
Having previously conquered the senses, you conquered the three worlds;
yet now, as if remembering that enmity, you have been utterly defeated by those very same senses.
The turbulent senses carry away even the mind of an ascetic.
The sense organs, the mind, the vital breath, knowledge, life-span, happiness, fortitude,
retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense.
Effort, form, color, likes and dislikes, existence and non-existence—
all this is born of that [Self] who desires a beginning for what is without beginning.
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat;
through these, it deludes the embodied being by veiling their knowledge.
One who desires to attain greatness should restrain the senses regarding both material objects and spiritual duty;
for when the senses are restrained, the intellect increases like a fire fed by fuel.
Having restrained the senses from their objects, as well as the vital breaths and the mind, one should undertake withdrawal (pratyāhāra) through their complete integration.

Without defiling the senses, the highest good can be attained even in the householder stage of life; therefore, they say that the fourth stage of life is not supported by the logic of non-obstruction.
Just as the internal sense-faculties cause people to fall,
so too do the internal servants in a kingdom who are devoted solely to their own self-interest.
The senses alone constitute all of that which consists of both heaven and hell;
when restrained or unleashed, they lead respectively to heaven and to hell.
One should not become attached out of desire to any of the objects of the senses;
one should also turn back with the mind any excessive attachment toward them.
By those very senses by which even the gods, such as Indra and Candra, were put to shame,
how then could a mortal possibly possess unfading pride?
When the senses operate upon their objects without restraint,
they torment this world, just as the planets torment the stars.
Indra censures his mount; the sun speaks ill of his horses; and the bird of prey strikes down the horse—what is this, born of an excess of fear within the enemy of the serpents?
The wind limps and the host of gods becomes lame out of hatred for your steeds as they gallop with ease toward the battlefield against their foes.
Since Indra is restrained by his many-fold wrath, since Pāvaka is a consumer and Antaka is the destroyer, since Dhanada is devoted to his celestial chariot, and Pāśī is the lord of waters;
since Īśa removes desires, Anila is fickle, and Nairṛta is a Rākṣasa—therefore, O Guardian of the Earth, there is no one else equal to you in virtues.

O Lord whose footstool is adorned by the crest-jewels of sovereign kings, I carry as fuel the fruit of that falsehood— the repeated claim that "You are Indra, you are Yama, you are Varuṇa, you are Agni, you are Brahmā, you are Hara, and you are Hari."

The women of the Kukuras and the Kauravas embraced one another, their bellies held far away from each other by the weight of their breasts, which were as high and firm as the frontal globes of elephants, while their broad cheeks were fully blooming with joy.
If wealthy men are honored at the gate of a king, what is so wonderful about that? Now, they themselves are being placed in the forefront at the gate of the gods.
"How can you abandon this son, who possesses a golden hue, is adorned with ornaments, and provides the ancestral offerings, merely because of the words of a vulture?"
Having contemplated this nostril-cavity of a young woman, which is as delicate as a sesame flower, a person of refined mind attains joy in his heart.
O friend, contemplate instead a serpent with its hood raised, full of the arrogance of its venomous hiss; do not desire it, but abandon the sight of it.
Having abandoned his enemy on the battlefield, the wise Arjuna, broken himself, entered his own refuge;
for he did not realize that one who is arrogant cannot be protected from this place even by a mountain fortress.
Through devotion to one's mother, one attains this world; through devotion to one's father, the middle world;
but through service to the teacher alone, one reaches the world of Brahmā.

One should recognize these as the gestures of one who is enamored: she speaks pleasant words, gives her own wealth, rejoices upon seeing him, is free from anger, and wipes away faults by praising his virtues.
Desiring to protect her from this misfortune, fearing defeat by the enemy, and devoted to his master, he attained freedom from debt to his lord through his own dear life-breaths.

To create this radiant vine of an arm for the lady with arched brows, the Creator must have taken its essence from a lotus stalk that was exclusively beloved for its hardness; otherwise, how could it be so tremulous within?
May this lion among kings rule over us— the earth bounded by the oceans, adorned with the Himavat and Vindhya mountains as its earrings, marked by the single royal parasol.
One should generally cause these to be given only to courtesans;
she will soon relinquish all that enjoyment for herself.
If these lotus-eyed women, who pride themselves on their youth, should lose their luster as their youth fades away, do not abandon them;
for old age wanders the earth plundering the charms of intoxication and grace, and thus one becomes indifferent toward their faces.

These—beauty, status, kinsmen, sons, wealth, wives, daughters, fortune, fame, splendor, joy, intelligence, affection, and fortitude—are as fickle as the eyes of women blinded by passion; alas, what a tragedy that mortals nevertheless intend to pursue these objects of the senses!

These are those rivers along the forest wilderness, their banks scarred by the sharp hooves of musk deer; their waters are covered with lotuses, wherein swans—delighting in the taste of fresh lotus shoots—sportively settle, serving as the sole masters of the art of the young woman’s gait.
These are those lands of the Vindhya mountains, dense with bamboo groves green as parrots, where trees are bent by the tusks of elephants restless in play;
from whose creeper-bowers, near the riverbanks, the breezes blow away the clusters of perspiration-drops from the cheeks of Śabara women exhausted by lovemaking.
These women with tremulous glances, their splendor whirling upon swings, possessing the form of modesty through the luster of saffron and wearing most flickering necklaces,
proclaim with the thick resonance of their rising girdles the sound of victory-bells for the Emperor of the Mind-born God over the three worlds.

These amorous gestures of the fawn-eyed women—possessing the fresh fragrance of the beauty of youth, the precursors to the power of mature lovemaking, and the sureties for the conquests of Love; long-time thieves of the heart and the sole masters of novel transformations—triumph in some ineffable way.
These are lotuses, not water; this is a sandy shore, not a river; this is the sky, not its pervasiveness; these are two clusters of blossoms, not creepers;
this is coral, not the ocean; this is the cool-rayed moon, not the night; this is a cloud, not the rainy season—alas, alas! What a marvelous artistic creation of the Creator!
"These—my wealth, sons, kinsmen, loved ones, body-born [offspring], friends, father, maternal uncles, and so forth—are exceedingly dear to me.
Thus, with a mind destroyed by delusion, one suffers for a long time in the forest of existence; for in this world, who belongs to whom? It is like a handful of sand.

For these horses, their eyes closed in dejection, stumbling repeatedly and rendered helpless, and the elephants, smelling of rut-fluid like the *saptacchada* tree, seem to announce a retreat from the battle.
These two are plantain-stalks; this pair is the frontal globes of a lordly elephant; this is a playful lotus; this is clearly the autumnal moon.

What else is it that the slender-limbed girl perceives within her own body, such that the world regards her as exceedingly beautiful, and remains perpetually as if subservient to her and as if intoxicated?
This Kalāvilāsinī, the skillful one standing nearby, whose eyes are like lotuses and who dispels the sorrow of the mind-born god;
adorned with hair resembling a mass of fresh rain-clouds, she does not cause the fever of the heart to be shattered in any person.
"Is her breast so very beautiful?"— as he looked thus at the heart of the water-bearer, which was covered [by her garment],
her pair of hands, holding the water-pitcher, surely gave a charming answer by means of their movement.
This is Lakṣmī in the home; this is an ambrosial ointment for the eyes; this touch upon the body is like abundant sandalwood paste;
this arm around the neck is a cool and smooth string of pearls—what of hers is not dear, were it not that separation from her is utterly unbearable?
This cow, though bound tightly by you, is unrestrained; for how is it that she does not touch anything other than Vaidarbha, even though it is easily accessible?
She is renowned on earth as fruitful, yet how is she inaccessible to the bulls among poets? And how is it that she yields much nectar, even when milked by many?

This is our only cow; we do not see any other anywhere that yields such an abundance of milk for the purpose of mixing [with grain]. If we tie her by the neck, there is no peace; if we try to hold her with force, there is fear of the cattle-thieves. Therefore, what remedy can prevail in this matter?

This woman, whose gait is like that of a lordly elephant in rut and who always sits upon a variegated lion-throne, is cherished by many beautiful women; yet, by the power of destiny, she alone, though virtuous, now desires offspring.

May this celestial river—the Goddess who, though her nature is consciousness, appears in a manifest form of matter—protect the entire world from calamity day by day; for even a single drop of her water bestows the state of Śambhu, purifying and shaking off every kind of sin.
This was indeed his play: that he mounted upon an aged bull, that he smeared himself with the ashes of funeral pyres, and that he covered his forehead with ornaments;
this was his activity: that he bore fire upon his brow, that he wore a serpent around his neck, and that he swallowed even the *hālāhala* poison.
"Here is your mother arrived, intent upon seeing you,
her two breasts overflowing with the flow of maternal affection."
This night, though possessing a hundred watches, now holds a hundred agonies; from the moon, fire rises on all sides.
Even the breeze of soft sandalwood spreads heat; for when fate is adverse, there is calamity at every step.
But this [earth] is sustained only by those who do not overstep the bounds of propriety, who are well-instructed, self-disciplined,
all-enduring, skilled in means, and free from delusion.
This steadfast woman finds no joy in this Malaya breeze, nor does she delight even in a cluster of lotuses with their graceful nectar;
nor does she become joyful amidst the rows of fresh kunda blossoms. Therefore, what remedy can there be here that might alleviate her suffering?
This village is surrounded on all sides by Bhillas who delight in improper undertakings and are fond of arrows as deadly as poison.
O parrot, spend your time silently upon the trunk of this tree; for here, eloquence is not auspicious—silence alone is your refuge.
This creeper of affection, which has by chance arisen in the soil of the heart, must be protected with such effort— being naturally tender and subject to many perils—
so that the fire of the wicked words of malicious people does not consume it while it is flourishing, nor cause the treasury of friendship to wither away within.
This young girl, newly married, will surely suffer distress upon hearing the truth;
for while she may be firm by nature, the disposition of women is nonetheless timid.
This young girl incessantly casts her eyes toward me—eyes that steal the luster of the blue lotus petal; what does she intend?
Our delusion has passed, and the feverish flames from the impact of Cupid’s war-arrows have been extinguished; yet even so, this poor girl does not desist.
This young creeper has entwined itself around a fresh, very large *śāla* tree with tender sprouts that melt away the heat and provide dense shade;
yet, how indeed can this poor thing perceive the towering serpent within it, whose mere drop of venom would reduce the forest to ashes?

This is some kind of golden creeper that has come within the range of my vision; it is inhabited by female serpents, endowed with many shining flowers, frequented by swarms of bees, adorned with joyful wagtails, bent down by the weight of its two fruits, and made beautiful by fresh sprouts.
Thinking, "While I was away on a journey, she has united with the moon and adorned herself," the sun,
as if out of jealousy, swiftly and in anger stripped away her ornaments of variegated stars.
This proud woman, having held in contempt the lords of the four quarters beginning with Mahendra,
desires to obtain as her husband the wielder of the Pināka bow, who cannot be won by physical beauty due to his subjugation of Madana.

Does this young woman, out of respect for the swarm of bees that has come near her lotus-face under the guise of her hanging tresses, actually bear it with affection? Or does she merely hold it [as an ornament]?
Is this the fame of the moon, the enemy of darkness? Is this his lap, or is it his face? Terrified by his glories that pervade all the worlds, the ink of the night flees away.
By this entry onto the stage, through the mastery of the arts,
and by her skill in deception, she relies upon her proficiency in vocal modulation.
This is the splendor of the longing of the tree of grace; this is the nectar of the milk-ocean of youth;
this is the flash of radiance from the ruby of loveliness; this is a handful of powder for the enchantment of the mind.
This young woman acts as a hunter; her brow acts as a bow;
her side-long glances act as arrows; and my heart acts as a deer.
"This is twilight; alas, I have come from afar from Malaya. Therefore, O compassionate one, I shall spend a single night at your house.
Thus addressed by the breeze, the young mango creeper, newly blossomed, shakes her head and cries out, "No, no, no! indeed.
This is that Kālindī, sweet and glossy as the petals of a blue water-lily, beloved by young water-fowls warbling in the intoxication of passion;
on whose banks, in former times, the days of Murabhid were mostly spent with impetuous longing in the amorous diversions of the cowherd girls.
This is that fickle-eyed woman, the sole abode of the ornament of the three worlds; and this is that wicked-souled man by whom my sister was wronged.
On one side is intense passion, on the other is this heavy fire of anger; and here is this disguise—how can my mind reconcile this? It reels in confusion.
This fair-eyed woman,
with her stainless face that has eclipsed the splendor of the lotus, triumphs over the moon which is marred by its spot.
This is the river Surataraṅgiṇī; here there shall be no meeting of boats, nor any sinking of vessels, O traveler, nor even the arrival of other wayfarers.
Always keeping the pair of large, beautiful jars within your heart, my friend, reach the further shore of the thick nectar when the clouds arrive in full force.
This woman with beautiful breasts, carrying a water-pot upon her head and wearing a lovely garment as red as safflower,
appears as if she is going along after having seized the mental activity of the entire world and placed it within the pot.
This flickering golden creeper was created by the Lotus-born Creator and watered day after day with a flood of the nectar of beauty;
that now this swarm of bees—the line of body hair—suddenly flutters here, I suspect the season for the blossoming of flowers has arrived at last.
Is this the Lakṣmī of the Lord of Heaven, or a daughter of the Yakṣas;
or perhaps, O Pārvatī, is she the very deity of the forest?
For this sleep, hanging over my eyes, seems to creep toward me from the region of my forehead;
it is invisible in form and fickle, like old age which grows by overpowering the strength of human beings.
For this is the first birth, O Lord of the World,
reaching which one is indeed able to save oneself through actions characterized by auspiciousness.

For this earthly nature, which by its very essence tends toward deviation from worldly norms, must be forcibly restrained through discipline; for in the accomplishment of policy, discipline is the precursor.
Thinking, "What indeed will she accomplish later that has not been accomplished by this much age?
the Creator, under the guise of a line of hair, smeared a powder of collyrium upon her face, which was like a mixture of sesame and rice.
You have reached such a state of good fortune that, for her sake, I dispel your fainting fit caused by the affliction of love with these tears from my eyes— she who has exhausted her merit.
"How vast is this world, and how much will it become as we lower our faces?"— thinking thus,
the horse gallops through the courtyard of the sky, as if leaping upward to dance in the performance of its frolic upon the stage of the firmament.

"The earth is only this much, and the vault of the sky is likewise this much; the netherworld extends only this far, and the water within the earth is only this much"—having realized this within the well, this frog, who knows the full extent of his domain, does not cry out with greater force than another, but is merely deluded.
Even upon such an infinitely vast path, only these two or three most ancient virtues reach the count.
Alas, the world is vulgar; not only does it find no satisfaction in them, but—stiffened by pride—it regards even this entire collection as mere straw.
O lake, if even now, despite such an abundance of water, you do not suddenly quench the thirst of those afflicted by it, then alas,
when the summer sun scatters heaps of burning coals all around and you have grown shallow, for whom indeed will you be the protector from that thirst?
"Even with such an abundance of means, you have not performed any virtuous deed"—
as if enraged by this, the Ender (Antaka) violently causes his teeth to fall out.
In this world, there is such an excess of boundless wonder that either Varāha or Rāhu becomes the object of such marvel:
for while one [Varāha] lifted up the submerged earth with the tips of his tusks, the other [Rāhu], though reduced to nothing but his head, swallows his enemy and yet releases him.
In this matter, this path for those who perceive through the lens of ethics has been shown by me in one particular direction;
however, other points should be inferred from the works of Cāṇakya and others, who are repositories of knowledge.
In this matter, there is a certain great and extraordinary hardness of heart among the virtuous:
having rendered assistance, they keep themselves far away from others who might seek a return for that favor.
This girdle, your first companion in private, which lay sleeping with you in your unconsciousness,
does not appear as if it has followed you in death out of grief, for it remains silent as your graceful movements have ceased.
Adorned with ornaments that are pale and wasted due to her physical emaciation, like a young creeper that has put forth flowers yet remains parched within,
this woman of noble form bears the lovely and rising splendor of the great festival of marriage, while simultaneously manifesting a deep-seated anguish of the heart.
This is she, with her tremulous, long eyes and heavy, high, full breasts;
moving slowly under the weight of her broad hips, my beloved who has stolen away my life.
This is not the neck of the deer-eyed woman, but rather the creeper of bliss;
for upon it roll these pearls, whose internal qualities are pure.
This very one, who delights the Dānava Maya, is the birthplace of the conqueror of the Lord of the Thirty-three;
what more need be said? As the wife of the Ten-necked One, she joins her two hands together before you.
May these words, possessing brilliant meaning and endowed with desirable qualities, be pleasing to you as well;
for indeed, the wise, in accepting speech, are indifferent to the particularity of the speaker and are guided solely by its merits.
If this cave-like belly were not a ground for the shattering of pride, already filled to the brim with misfortune,
I could not endure for even a moment the sidelong glances of kings such as yourself.
This day-sleep, appearing before me, robbing me of my composure and causing my eyes to close— I do not know what she says to you, like a rival wife.
Resorting to meditative concentration, she desired to make her own beauty fruitful through ascetic practices;
for otherwise, how could both such love and such a husband be obtained?
O Śeṣa, do not bend your neck, which is burdened by supporting the surface of the earth;
while you alone are suffering, the world of living beings remains forever happy.
By meditating on the bee-meditation of the *ilikā*, one becomes a bee as one meditates;
by meditating on the state of one free from passion, one will certainly become free from passion.
Since the three worlds were conquered by the flower-arrowed god with only three arrows,
these remaining two have been made fruitful by being consecrated upon the lotus-like eyes of his beloved.
He gives what is desired, accepts [what is given], tells of one's business, asks about it, eats together, and causes [others] to eat; this is the sixfold characteristic of a friend.
A tree that has grown in a pit dug out all around and filled with bricks,
being short in stature, indeed bears fruit and flowers at all times.
One should not visit one's beloved wife, a dear friend, a younger son,
an astrologer, or a lord with empty hands.
It is the opinion of the virtuous that even beloved children, wealth, dear friends,
and one's wife are for the sake of liberation from calamity.
For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you the enjoyments you desire;
he who enjoys what is given by them without giving to them in return is truly a thief.
One who performs sacrifices and charitable works should be celebrated throughout the world; such a person shall dwell in heaven.
Following the conduct described by Akūpāra, Indradyumna ascended again to the celestial realm.
Childish play was desired, then the pride of youth, and then the world-weariness of old age;
that too has passed, he too has gone, and even that has vanished—all this is but a dream and an illusion.
Sacrifices have been performed, the best of the twice-born have been gratified with me, and kings, filled with the sentiment of fear, have been brought under my influence.
Yet, despite this, I feel no joy in my heart; for a father of a daughter must always have much to reflect upon.
Like Kubera, the granter of desires, he bestows wealth upon those who seek it;
and people should always revere him with devotion, as disciples revere their teacher.
Whether cherished, or pampered with many good deeds, or embraced, or protected from hundreds of calamities—
an evil person never inspires confidence, just like a snake sleeping in the middle of one's lap.
Having performed the sacrifice of battle with various weapons as its waters,
how can he bathe in this concluding ablution without me, his wife?
O deer, why do you place your trust in her whose eyes tremble with feigned curiosity?
This wife of a hunter, agitated by impetuosity, is lashing her tail against yours.
O young deer, why do you abandon the stalks of rice in this field?
This is merely a deceptive mannequin, fashioned from grass, with arrows of grass and a bow of grass.
What can possibly flash before me here, who have seen the further shore of the ocean of the treatises on policy,
when you stand before me like a lamp-flame never shining in the presence of the sun that has swallowed all darkness?
Indeed, in this world, the uneven ripening of deeds performed in the past manifests among living beings;
those very heads that once shone upon the head of Hara, alas, alas, now roll at the feet of vultures.
O gazelle-eyed one, here the wise man shall first undergo exertion, but thereafter he shall attain great happiness,
just like a newly wedded bride upon union with her beloved.
Here, these rivers have their depths filled with the heavy burden of water; they possess a terrifyingly great velocity due to the whirling of ravines and caves;
and they are made fearsome by a doubled roar as their currents clash against the slopes and ridges of their banks.
In this world, four kinds of giving have been proclaimed by the supreme sages,
after they had examined various scriptures, for the sake of happiness both in this life and the next.
Fearlessness should be granted to those who are afraid, and likewise medicine to the sick;
knowledge should be given to seekers of learning, and food should be given to those afflicted by hunger.
In this very world, women are blessed by the preservation of their virtue;
yet, upon the destruction of their virtue, the world of Yama is most terrible for women.
O Vaiśya, women must always protect their virtue by avoiding association with the wicked; for through virtue alone, women attain the higher realms of heaven—of this there is no doubt.
In this world, in whose mind does the primary concern for the attainment of happiness not reside?
Indeed, all that belongs to him which the Lord of the World, the Sovereign, ordains.
In this world, how many fair-browed women, skilled in the arts of the Lord of Love, do not wander about at midnight?
But for me, cursed by fate, alas, O companion, as I break into a smile, it is the mere radiance of my teeth that acts as a rival.
O Lord, here, by the water from the *kuśa* grass in your lotus-like hand as it falls,
rivers are produced at the doors of those who are far impoverished, by you, the enemy of the two-legged demons.
In this world, let fools travel by hundreds of horses, and let the wise, though devoid of wealth, travel on foot;
for a flight of crows perched upon a mountain peak cannot attain equality with swans standing on a sandbank.
In this world, one encounters suffering from kings and others, and in the next world, from the hells and other realms, due to theft; therefore, the wise should always renounce theft.

In this context, dissolution (*laya*) is said to be suffering; yet dissolution is capable of removing suffering. If dissolution within auspicious suffering is itself suffering, then what can be said of that [other] suffering?
In this world, the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma is desired as the fruit;
therein, artha together with kāma should be examined with the eye of dharma.
For he who, having abandoned the Dharma, regards wealth as the goal of wealth, or sensual pleasure as the goal of obtaining sensual pleasure, is not wise among the Buddhas.
O beautiful one, in this city where movement along every street is charming due to the throngs of lovers, it is my opinion that it is better for me to be protected by a mongoose.
"Who has prepared this secluded bed of young sprouts for the lover in the very heart of this *nicula* thicket?"—
may the glances of Rādhā and Mādhava, variegated with smiles as they hear these words from the circle of women, protect you all.
"If you see this field, I shall sleep for a moment here in this thicket of *nicula* reeds, which abounds in bamboo,"—
thus does a cowherd girl, with a graceful arching of her limbs, suddenly address a handsome young traveler who has sat down right on the path.

O doe, wife of the deer, here the Kirātas—with their bow-vines drawn into circles and their feet silent with stealthy tread—strike you, for you are unaccustomed to my slow and lingering glances; go far away!
Here dwells Meru, the crest-jewel of mountains; here indeed are the seven oceans that bear their heavy burdens.
This incomparable and infinite surface of the earth, capable of supporting the emergence of abundant beings, is the abode of those such as we are.
Here at night, a certain woman, her heart weighed down by the pair of her firm, closely-set jar-like breasts,
and drawn along by the virtues of her lover, crosses the river of darkness.
O emerald, this familiarity with you is for those born blind; it is no credit to you that those who possess sight have been utterly deceived by you.
This outpouring of false defects will merely serve to diminish your virtues in the eyes of wretched merchants, resulting only in infamy.
"Where there is fragrance here, the beauty of spring's honey is not manifest; where the honey is abundant, there is no richness of scent.
Thus disparaging the *maruvaka* flower and losing interest in the *kunda*, the bee desponds as he repeatedly recalls the lotus.
In this world, what creeper here, its form shaken by the breeze, does not unite with the tree?
O friend, do you not remember the festival of love-making with your beloved? For the arrival of the clouds has not been described as a mere natural phenomenon.
Here, the moonlight has become thickened by the radiance of the female cakora birds, which are marked with the beak-prints of those intoxicated with passion;
this light reveals the playful snapping of sprout-like hands by the young women as they prepare couches for the exhaustion of intense lovemaking.
In this world, even one who is small attains some measure of greatness through association with the great;
the deer, having ascended the moon, traverses the expanse of the sky with ease.
In this world, it bestows enjoyment, fame, joy, and great honor in assemblies;
in the next world, it grants a favorable rebirth and the unsurpassed wealth of knowledge.
Here, the lovely tradition of warbling coos resounds from the female bees who have drunk the honey of the jasmine;
here, the blossom-cluster of the *vañjula* tree dances playfully, instructed at every step by the southern breeze.

Here are the forest edges, where the slaughter of the fetuses of pregnant does occurs easily through stumbling upon stone seats scattered by the horns of buffaloes; and where the weapons of Kirāta hunters fall from their hands in terror at the mass of growls from full-grown bears sporting in the caves.
Here, a terrifying roar is raised in every direction by young elephants repeatedly exulting;
and herds of yak-cows shimmer throughout the forest, as do the rays of light from the ground of gold and jewels.
Whatever action is performed here is experienced in the next world;
the fruit of a tree whose root has been watered is seen upon its branches.
Whatever action is performed here, its fruit is experienced right there.
O King, this is known as the land of action, and that is remembered as the land of fruition.
In this world, I have fully experienced the pursuit of the path of Kṛṣṇa, the scion of the Yadu lineage;
now, for my mind intent on attaining that [state], does even the sweetness of desire still hold any appeal?
O bee, in this painted lotus and water-lily, which consist of nothing but the essence of form, there is neither flavor nor fragrance; you wander here in vain.
O you who are thick with passion! Here is a young woman, dark as Rāhu, adorned with curls, playful with the sentiment of love, possessing a lofty gait, and delighting in the arts.
O Great-minded One, that woman whom a man's fathers have given away in this world with water according to the divine law belongs to him even in the state after death.
In this world, even a stranger acts as a kinsman to those who possess wealth;
but for the poor, even their own kin vanish while they are still alive.
In this world, even a stranger becomes like one's own kin to the wealthy;
yet even one's own kin instantly becomes like a wicked person to the poor.
O King, just as this world is ruined for men by poverty,
so too is their birth ruined without the ritual bath in the month of Māgha.

In this banyan tree dwells a yakṣa, where there is apprehension of fear even by day; yet it was beneath that very tree that the young bride was led through nights whose watches were spent in longing for her husband.
"Here he grazed the calves; here our Lord played the flute"—may my day pass on the banks of the Yamunā as I speak these words with tears.
In this world, this earth, adorned by the vastness of many great oceans, carries a pride of self-importance;
yet it does not even reach the entire back of Your Majesty in the form of the Tortoise.
Whether he delivers him from distress in this world, or whether he delivers him after death, in every way a son delivers; therefore he is called "son" by the wise.
Here, the month of Caitra— exceedingly red with the assistance of the abundant blossoms of the blooming Aśoka trees, possessing an intensely affectionate nature,
and ready for the conquest of the three worlds— proclaims the vast friendship of the Flower-Archer (Kāma) toward those who enjoy abundant sovereignty.
"O young deer, here roam the Kirātas, who destroy the freedom of those like you; therefore, do not set your ears to their singing and such."
In this victorious lineage, there was one named Śrī Yaśovigraha, who bathed the entire world with a multitude of streams of glory;
he was a certain hero, skilled in the playful act of extinguishing the fire of the pride of kings arrogant in battle, like a jar of water.
In this world, the ripening of past deeds indeed occurs for living beings in a manner contrary to one's wishes:
where is Janaka’s daughter, where is Rāma’s beloved, and where is residence in the palace of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa?
In this world, a disciple who performs virtuous actions is not to be restrained; however, when he abandons the path through delusion, then the teacher becomes the goad.
Therefore, the virtuous who delight in discipline are always free from the goad; for we are indeed averse to any form of independence that exceeds this.
In this world, who does not hold sandalwood dear when it serves as a relief against the heat of the earth?
For even by applying a mere nasal dot (*anusvāra*), the purpose of the vowel *o* is fulfilled.
For some, [the result] is here but not in the next world; for others, it is in the next world but not here.
For some, it is both here and in the next world; for others, it is neither in the next world nor here.
Here is a troop of hunters equipped with sharp weapons and well-constructed traps; here is a pride of lions leaping with their fierce claws;
here is an insurmountable mountain, here a river of thick mud, and here a blazing fire in the midst of the forest—alas, what a calamity for the lord of elephants!
Whether lying here upon my bed or standing in the midst of my kinsmen,
I must alone endure the agonizing pain of the severing of my vital organs and the like.

Here, the island-rivers flow, proud with waters fragrant from the channels of pollen from rows of *śirīṣa* flowers borne by the wind; they are foamy with the thundering bursts as boulders and mountain peaks split by the jagged peaks, and they are filled with a mass of bubbles.
In this world, the course of worldly affairs proceeds entirely through the grace of speech alone— both that of those who have been instructed by the learned and that of the learned themselves.

In this thick darkness at the onset of the rainy season, the quarters of the sky search all around for the pleasant forms of the sun and the moon by means of streaks of lightning that flash like lamps.

Here flow mountain streams with cool, clear waters, fragrant from the blossoms of *vānīra* reeds and creepers trodden upon by flocks of birds; their many currents are made resonant by stumbling against groves of *jambū* trees darkened by the ripening weight of their fruit.
In this lake, gracefully shaking his beautiful wings, with his body scratched by his slightly trembling bill turned askance,
the impassioned swan follows his mate who has gone ahead, raising his neck-stalk at every step.
O bee, here in this lake, joyfully engage in play with the lotuses, charming with your sweet humming;
