for as long as this *mālatī* flower does not abandon its sleep—sleep from which it derives delight through the incomparable fragrance of its nectar.
In this world, the great trees of noble sons, which bear the fruit of all their possessions,
utterly become fruitless when devoured by the birds that are courtesans.
In this context, the modern Naiyāyikas, intent upon the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅga*), proceed through numerous instances while teaching the universal concomitance (*sāmānyānugama*).
"O Lord, here a thorn remains clearly visible; pull it out slowly with the playful gesture of your fingernails.
With these words as a pretext, a certain woman placed her foot, though it was not pierced by a thorn, upon the surface of his lap.

For here, in the fresh autumn, the swarms of restless bees— bodies white from being sprinkled with the pollen of clusters of blossoms and throats sweet with charming *huṃ* sounds— wander playfully toward the *sinduvāra* tree, which is beautiful with its abundant fragrance and swarm of bees.
For here indeed, "this is sweet song, this is form, this is flavor, this fragrance wafts forth, this is the touch of breasts"—
thus, being whirled about by the senses which have stolen away the ultimate truth, I have been deceived by these five rogues who act against my own welfare.
In this world, many—such as cattle, buffaloes, rams, sons, horses, and the dwellings of the lowly—are happy with only a few blades of grass;
yet for elephants, whose trunks are smeared with the ichor of rut, there is only one [place]: either the forest of the Vindhya mountains or the palace of a king.
In this world, there are many wise ones who, though dwelling here, are constantly grateful and perform acts of service for those who have helped them.

Yet, how few are those virtuous ones, who, through the ripening of their merit, take delight in the welfare of others and feel a natural devotion toward the tasks of others even without any self-interest?

Here, this stream of nectar flowing from the essence of the flood of scriptures, though somewhat circuitous due to its lack of clarity on certain paths, runs toward the hollows of her ears like a channel carved upon the pair of her ear-leaves.
O Ocean, here was born from your jar a certain crest-lock-wearing sage (Agastya), who, though desiring water, was unable to hold even a single mouthful of your waters in his hollowed palm;
why then, having been silenced by the deep and heavy roars of your own praise for your own greatness, do you now, as if enraged, afflict the cavities of our ears?
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here— once he has gone to that place where no medicine exists, what will that sick man do?
In this very world, that which is born capable of establishing beings in their true nature is perceived in one way by those who are steady, and in another way by those who are crooked.
Alas! In this garden, now remaining only by the force of sequence, are these anthills—the playful dwellings of families of serpents.
Those certain trees, naturally majestic, which once filled the sky with waves of fragrance from their abundant clusters of blossoms, have departed.
"How was my birth here brought about by what karma, and where must I go from here?"—
for one whose mind contains no such reflection, how can they become inclined toward the Dharma?
Just as fish, tortoises, and birds nourish their own offspring through glancing, gazing, and touching, so too do those who follow the conduct of the wise.
With her lower lip bitten by her lover's teeth and shaking her hand as if to ward him off, she seems to instruct the God of Love— who has just arisen with joy— to dance before her gaze.
One should perform such a ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by which there will be well-being;
even others shall never cause harm through evil mantras.
When her beloved spoke such words, she closed her eyes for a moment out of joy,
like the night-lotus that closes its petals at dawn after the sweet warbling of the cuckoo, as if from exhaustion due to staying awake all night.
Who indeed would not abandon that person who would forsake a brother fallen into such calamity as this? And whom would he not abandon?
How is it that for one such as you, there is this constant lightness during acts of love?
She displayed the great size of her hips by casting her long garment upon the ground.
It is indeed fitting that kings, when cast by their ministers into such a fire of worldly affairs,
fall into a miserable state.
By such people as these, who are like white crows and who subvert the king's commands,
thousands of the innocent have been slain and continue to be slain.
For whom does every desired happiness of the mind come to pass? Since everything depends upon destiny, one should therefore take refuge in contentment.
Fie on those hypocrites who maintain the family lineage by guarding women out of envy,
yet fail to protect men in the same way, even though the blindness of passion is no different for both.
Agitated by envy alone toward that man of wicked mind,
Prosperity, Fortitude, Memory, and Fame flee from him, even though they were deeply attached to him.
Envy is the root of strife, for forbearance is indeed the root of all prosperity;
through the fault of envy, Janamejaya incurred the curse of a Brahmin.
There is no jealousy toward noble women on the part of the hero, nor is there unrestrained dalliance with the wives of others;
yet these two traits are fully developed in courtesans. Oh, they are the very everything of the God of Love!
For a courtesan becomes angry out of jealousy, loses interest due to excessive attachment,
becomes stubborn from over-indulgence, and is even ruined by her own generosity.
She did not show me her face, beautiful with its lower lip quivering from jealousy, nor did that charming girl utter even a single word of reproach;
yet, though her mental state was tormented by my fresh faults, she expressed her anger by tying the knot of her garment more tightly around her waist.
Food consumed by one possessed of envy, fear, and anger; by one who is greedy; by one afflicted by disease and dejection; or by one filled with malice, does not reach proper digestion.
The stain of envy dwells within the wicked, like venom in virulent serpents.
Burning with jealousy and anger as I contemplate union with my own wife, I find relief through the intense bliss of imagining her hips from which her garment has slipped.
Envy, greed, arrogance, attachment, anger, fear, and recklessness—
the wise have declared these seven to be the causes of lapses in conduct regarding one's duties.
The envious, the contemptuous, the discontented, the wrathful, the constantly suspicious,
and he who lives off the fortune of others— these six are perpetually miserable.

The Lord holds the golden mountain in his hand, and Kubera’s friend dwells upon the silver mountain; yet even so, he must wander for alms. When fate stands over one's head, crooked as it is, whence can there be prosperity?
When omens arise from the northeast, thieves, having entered the village, do not obtain anything;
one afflicted by disease does not survive, and even one who is healthy falls into ill health.
If omens arise from the northeast, especially when the circle of heroes is overrun,
one should flee far away, abandoning the place as if surrounded by enemies.
O proud lady, do not grant favor for even a moment to this lord who is devoted to your feet, even though he is dearer than life itself;
let my husband know the pain of having his desires frustrated even by women like us who bow at his feet.
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
the Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
"The Lord is time, which is difficult to overcome"—this is the truth-bearing Vedic revelation;
for even the intellect of the elderly is led astray by the words of children.
He is the Lord, worshiped by the world; he is the eloquent one with four faces.
He who possesses wealth in this world is indeed the supreme among men.
He alone is heartless Rāhu; he alone is the sluggish Śanaiścara; he alone is the crooked one of evil birth—namely, he who possesses no wealth at all.
The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by His illusory power, as if they were mounted on a machine.
This is the temple of the Lord; for here poison, the bull, and ashes are held in high regard.
But what account can there be here for that which is neither poison, nor the bull, nor ashes?
O bee, why do you fall pointlessly upon this flower, deluded by the thought that it is fit for the possession of a lord?
This worthless sprout of a rogue is devoid of nectar, its only essence being the name "gold."
For one who worships the Lord with pride dissolved and has attained sovereignty, lightness (*laghimā*) becomes manifest; as for heaviness (*garimā*), we simply do not know how it might be.
Service to the Lord involves easily obtained insults and rarely attained exaltation;
long-term attendance is fruitless, and even the discarded offerings lead to hell.
There exists one who, having deprived women of their womanhood, seems to remember his enmity toward the Lord who created this entire world in such a disorderly fashion.
What wonder is there that lords constantly support sycophants?
For it is generally the case that treasures themselves most certainly harbor double-tongued serpents.
The word of the lords is true, and their conduct is likewise in some instances; a wise person should practice that which is consistent with their own words.
This treatise on the lords will likely arouse curiosity,
since the path of policy is demonstrated through the conduct of animals.
From Īśvara was born Rudra, the lord of Umā, consisting of light;
from Rudra was born the primordial Viṣṇu, the protector of the three worlds.
For even a child, if favored by the Lord, attains tranquility;
yet some base person, though old, does not reach peace.
It is not heard in scripture that a poor man should obtain, for the mere price of a *kākiṇī*, that same fruit which lords indeed obtain through abundant giving.
O Lakṣmaṇa, intimacy with a lord does not please me;
for one who has gone there, there is no respect, and for one who has returned, there is the loss of wealth.
Having extracted verses from the *Dhanurveda* spoken by Īśvara and also from the eloquent sayings of Vyāsa, this work has been composed by me in brief.

Blessed is he who enjoys love-making, wherein the breasts tremble slightly, the heavy strike upon the hips is wondrous, the forehead perspires, many laughs are full of flavor, the pain in the feet is discussed,
the chest is repeatedly pressed against him with delight, the lower lip is bitten, and the nails are applied ever so slightly to the region of the hips.

In the springtime, women also make their mansions cool with slight frost and their beautiful hair fragrant with *campaka* flowers; they likewise adorn their breasts with lovely blossoms and pearl necklaces.
The mild [passion] is slightly manifest, while the intense is indicated by horripilation and the like;
that which here causes the limbs to wither through sighing is the most intense.
As soon as the winter had passed, its dullness only slightly remaining, the slender woman—
like a young maiden in her fresh youth— resorted intensely to the pond for a long time with her limbs.
Even when exerting only slight effort, a powerful lion slays even rutting elephants; therefore, one who desires welfare should make peace with him.

O beautiful one, by these very glances of yours—cast with slightly curved rows of lashes and innocent smiles—the entire world now rests within the palm of your hand. Yet, O cruel woman, what more do you desire here, beyond merely pointing out the base of your arm, whose beauty is as difficult to attain as that of the interior of a golden *ketaka* petal covered in dust?
A slight contraction of the nose, a harsh yet pleasant gaze, a trace of a smile, a lack of courtesy due to one's own ignorance, speech full of faults, and a disdainful disregard;

silence, preoccupation with other matters, and a fondness for reciting verses pleasing to others—O Śiva, O Śiva, how many and of what kind must those wicked and envious people be tolerated by you, O Poetry?

Fortunate is he who drinks from the face of the gazelle-eyed woman—her eyes slightly closed due to the force of a stream of charming, playful *sītkāra* sounds; her lower lip washed by the rays of teeth shining through indistinct and agitated cries of passion; her breasts stilled and motionless from intense embracing; and her body rendered helpless by the excess of joy.
With eyes slightly closed, all her limbs relaxed, agitated by exhaustion, gasping for breath, her jeweled girdle loosened and the sound of her throat silenced;
with passion rising like water and skilled in the arts, that shameless beloved woman, at the end of love-making, for a moment fell under the power of her lover due to the force of time.

Who could ever forget that face of the slender-limbed woman which I beheld at the conclusion of our love-making— her pair of tremulous eyes slightly closed, her eyebrows arched, her bitten lower lip betraying the pain [of passion], uttering soft syllables of "No, no," and her pale cheeks moistened with sweat?
Even when it has gained only slight entry, a wicked person causes the severance of affection;
having stirred up agitation, he dances about like a churning-stick.

Consider these *māṣī* creepers, whose foliage is slightly hairy and possesses a hue tinged with brownish-black; their bark is smeared with a greenness like that of the *cakora* bird or a parrot. Bearing fruits that rival the touch of the fingers on the hands of young female monkeys, they possess a beauty made charming by their full maturity.
If, despite exerting himself in various undertakings, he does not obtain wealth, he should undertake fierce austerity; for what is not sown does not sprout.
Through generosity one becomes possessed of enjoyments; through service to the elders, one becomes wise;
and through non-violence, one becomes long-lived—so say the sages.
The pursuit of wealth is not pleasant, and once obtained, anxiety is even greater;
the loss of what has been gained is like death, for it remains uncertain whether one will actually obtain it.
Reproach already spoken and that yet to be spoken, a sidelong glance,
and in some cases the speaking of the truth as it is— these are the sixfold methods of explaining the Tantra.
O fortunate one, I have never uttered harsh words to you, even in jest, for nothing brings such pain; nor have I ever caressed another woman with my speech, having abandoned all others for you alone.
I honor you alone with the weight of faultless ornaments. O you who become angry without cause, tell me: why have you directed this anger toward me?
The wealth of the rich, when mentioned to others, becomes mere bait; when unmentioned, it passes into invisibility;
and in death, it takes on the nature of a thorn within the heart.

O friend, that which was spoken in piteous words, the vast expenditure of wealth that was made, the repeated blows of the thunderbolt of separation that were endured, and the messenger girl who was sent again and again—all this has been forgotten; even as this prayer with joined palms is offered, and while the eyes, washed by tears, gaze upon the sprout-like lower lip of the deer-eyed one.
"I have been spoken to by you; my head has been touched by you with blood"—
having made these oaths, she indeed may be approached again and again.
She departs bashfully as described, she desists out of affection, she glances slightly, she plucks at her hair, she performs a yawn, and she repeatedly composes a verse;
O friend, she goes elsewhere, she cries out harshly, she kisses the boy, she breaks her limbs, she yawns, she laughs, and she asks for a reply.
She reveals the base of her garment, adjusts the cloth over her pair of breasts, scratches the earth with her big toe, and feigns bashfulness with a smiling face;
she bites her sprout-like lower lip with her teeth and speaks quite clearly—by these gestures, the desire of fawn-eyed women is always to be understood here as manifest.
"You say that you did not speak of our lovemaking during the night, O woman with the gait of an elephant, out of malice or perhaps out of shame;
yet that upper garment of your lover, variegated with the marks of betel juice, collyrium, and the wounds from my breasts, proclaims it all to me."
No other speech stirs within her, nor does any other meditation abide; indeed, her eye sees nothing else, nor does her ear hear anything but him.
On the paths, she gazes again and again at the dark [trees] with startled eyes; such is our way in Vṛndāvana—what women have not lived long acquainted with this?
What is the use of so much that has been said, or what is the use of these heavy oaths?
I tell you this very truth: you alone reside within my mind.
Where the preservation of the lives of living beings would occur by speaking a falsehood,
there falsehood becomes truth, and even truth becomes falsehood.
In matters concerning women, at weddings, and likewise in the release of cows,
as well as upon the misfortune of Brahmins, there is no sin in taking oaths.

O you who are pleasing to the eye, your fame—alone—crosses the waters of the ocean filled with fierce crocodiles, wanders in the supportless sky, ascends the inaccessible heights of mountains, and enters the netherworld (pātāla) teeming with swarms of venomous serpents; I believe that the fear of women is merely feigned.
One should resort to severity or mildness after observing the proper occasion;
for the sun does not become fierce without first dispelling the darkness.
"I shall make your pair of breasts, which possess a fierce form and support a necklace of skulls, the crest-jewel for the moon; meanwhile, become naked."

The bee, imprisoned within the hollow of a lotus, suffers extreme dejection through the cries of distress from the *cakravāka* bird; for the intense pain of another, when it strikes the heart of one who is already tender with longing, causes a grief that is neither slackened nor mitigated.

Sinking deep into the fierce grasp [of the enemy], with their drivers shaken by the brandishing of *kuśa* grass and struck by the elephants' trunks, the circles of gods—terrified by the battle and the violent upraising of fresh, stiff trunks—could find no passage anywhere;
for the rutting elephants, having repeatedly beheld the mountains and striking them with the clanging chains on their feet as they moved, shattered the walls of the quarters of that conqueror.
Fearing the injury caused by fierce curses, the Rākṣasa has cast far away those whose purity of complexion is worthy of burning even the sacrificial fire;
yet they behold their own protection through the very splendor of Janaka’s daughter, while the wives of the world-guardians attend upon her as their own confinement.
It is appropriate to conceal these two breasts, which steal the splendor of the golden mountain;
but why conceal the orb of your face, which has eclipsed the circle of the moon?
It is indeed fitting that there be thorns even on a *nāra* jasmine or a *ketakī*; but why, O *kaṇṭakārikā*, do you have thorns when you are devoid of both flavor and fragrance?
O slender one, a bond is indeed fitting for this pair of breasts,
which act as snatchers-away from those who see them in the act of stealing the gold of the hearts of young men.

It is better to reject a suitable request, for many reasons for rejection have indeed been observed; for high-minded women, a formal courtesy devoid of true feeling is not acceptable, even if it exceeds their previous obligations.

Appropriate action does not bring about prosperity for the wise, nor does any other course, for they perceive it as non-existent; thus, with all connection to happiness cast aside, how could the learned man not despair?
Just as scales, though raised by their proper weights and even when a piece of gold is placed before them, suddenly fall back down with their mouths [downward]; so too do manifest women [behave].
Even emaciation is beautiful for one whose nature is accustomed to spending;
the second moon is worthy of worship, not the full moon.
Having attended upon her as is fitting and pleasing, speak your words with constant attention;
for even when a man possesses a bright future, he becomes defiled if his master speaks harshly to him.
Well-spoken words attain beauty through appropriate reflection,
just as the sciences of the wise reach clarity through the realization of the true nature of what is to be known.
When a dog, having climbed to a high place, barks repeatedly while gazing at the sun,
then, before long, abundant rain released from the clouds will fall.
"O dull-witted one, do not, out of pride, enter into rivalry with the Sun, your own father, thinking, 'Just as this tree is tall and yields excellent fruit, so am I.
From afar, all those like you are utterly destroyed by his splendor; for he, a treasury of light and a friend to the virtuous, does not himself desire to cause offense to anyone."
O young woman, your necklace— resting upon the jar-like mounds of your high breasts, its ends clinging to your hips, and resembling a wooden beam spanning across a very deep chasm— stirs my heart.
A Yakṣa who descends from a high place to a low one and moves to the left brings happiness;
likewise, one who goes from a low place to a high place is auspicious even if moving to the right.

Then Dāruka, seeing Śauri—who knew how to utter words—standing on the bank where flocks of birds were warbling, and observing that the mountain was longing to see him, spoke thus to the eager one: "O Uddhava! [or "O Mountain! He addressed him as "Uddhara" (the upholder).
Those who have ascended to a great height must protect themselves with extreme effort;
for a fall resulting from a collapse at such a high elevation is most difficult to endure.
As soon as he has entered, the king alone wards off the manifold miseries of the world, just as the Veda wards off the phenomenal world for us.
Do not make various loud noises, O birds; fly away quickly! O beasts, close your mouths!
Lending their ears, let the connoisseurs experience joy, for this young cuckoo extends its shrill warbling.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding the various high and low unjust practices of former kings,
a wise ruler should act in such a way that they do not fall into disuse.
Births are high and low; as long as actions exist, they do not all go to destruction.
Therefore, O noble ones, strive to uproot the root of action, as long as the disease of the water-binding [head] does not cease from the head.
One who is lowly remains low even when seated on a high throne; he does not become superior.
Does a crow, even while perched atop the pinnacle of a palace, ever act like a Garuḍa?

Desiring to gather the mass of flowers resting on the branches that had first fallen to the ground, the deer-eyed woman placed her foot upon the ashoka tree to climb it; by that very act, the tree blossomed again from its very root.
O young *cātaka* bird, why do you vainly stretch out your neck and beg the cloud? In this mass of water there is only an exceedingly powerful roar; a single drop, however, is far away.
In that place, where even the seeds of *śyāmāka* millet—dropped from the tips of the beaks of female sparrows—were diligently gathered from the houses of Vedic scholars who were destitute of food;
and where, when that donor suddenly appeared, the young women saw heaps of pearls rolling listlessly right there, having fallen from the pearl-ornaments pulled off by the hands of nimble boys.

O King of Kings, it is a marvel that your enemy is like you in this regard: he speaks loudly, brings auspicious news, has conquered the earth with his hands, and is always full of desire; yet he is famous for his conduct toward his ears (or "deafness") rather than his speech, experiences the ripening of various [karmic] fruits, looks only to his treasury, and is intent on recounting many stories to others in the world of merit—whereas we perceive trembling in him.
With a high forehead, tawny tusks, and well-proportioned joints of the shoulders; with fingernails like gems of glossy copper luster and long, rounded, thick trunks;
this noble lord of elephants is brave, his temple-fluid rivaling the fragrance of the *saptacchada* tree, and he wanders along the banks of rivers and dense forests.
One who occupies a high position generally becomes deluded regarding the true nature of things;
even one who has ascended to the peak of a mountain perceives the landscape as level.
One should avoid loud speaking, laughter, spitting, and likewise reviling; one should also avoid yawning, stretching the limbs, and cracking the joints.
Loud spitting, boisterous laughter, shifting from one’s bed or seat, slapping the limbs, yawning, entreating for easily obtained objects;
kissing the circle of children, looking at a female friend when facing her, casting glances while turned away, speaking of virtues, and scratching the ear.

O Moon, as long as splendor is not spread abroad by you— who dispel the darkness of the world— how can that ocean of jewels reach its supreme fullness, even though these various luminaries such as Venus, rising with great heights and exalted rays, assume a false pride here?
May virtuous people, desiring to ascend to the station of the wise who stand on high,
resort to the steps of the well-spoken words of the good.

Loud recitation of scripture, ancient tales, conversing with women, delight in fondling their children, false praise for their maturation, blessings upon sons and brothers, proclaiming one's own auspiciousness and worthiness, and the formal salutation with talk of one's own religious practice— these are the twelve faults of a mendicant.

Loud recitation of scriptures, ancient tales, conversing with women, fondling their children, praising one's own husband, false flattery regarding his wealth, following the instructions of others, the practice of seeking alms by holding out the hand, composing literary works out of pedantry, and the practice of astrology, the Gāruḍa-mantras, and Tantras— these are the twelve faults of a mendicant.
Let the peacock, having climbed a tree on the path, cry out loudly for a long time;
yet when the quality of sound pervades all directions, the conch shell is the proper object of such expectation.
Whatever is recited loudly should be done so even by a man who knows nothing;
fools hold it in high regard, and even the learned may have doubts.
With that [steed], he carried away Uccaiḥśravas, the jewel among horses,
who was as high as Indra’s fame acquired over a long time, as if it were embodied.
Desiring to rise higher and higher, the great man strides forward with firm steps; the base man sinks lower and lower out of fear of falling.
That which flies up high at first but carries a downward bend at the end as it moves along, yields little that is difficult to obtain; whereas that which does so quickly yields much.

May the *tāṇḍava* dances of Śambhu be victorious—dances in which the confluence of the celestial river with his crown is revealed by the ocean as it surges and expands from the falling mass of mountains tossed by the wind of his high, wildly leaping forest-like arms; and in which the falling rain of flowers is intercepted by the multitude of constellations falling in great numbers due to their collision with the tips of his clearly formidable matted locks.

May that fierce infant with an elephant’s face protect you from calamity—he whose half-closed eyes are opened by the melody of a swarm of bees, swollen with intoxication from drinking the abundant ichor trickling from his high and expansive temples;
and whose tip of the trunk is raised aloft to uproot the thickets of trees that are obstacles to his feeding.
If the mediator is unlearned, one should shout loudly that victory must be won;
if he is learned, let partiality be applied right there.
When the ocean was violently churned by that powerful and contemptible fate, casting away its splendor—did it become diminished by this?
Does it lose its depth? Does it fail to nourish the clouds? Does it break its bounds? Or does it fail to protect the submarine fire? No; it remains as it was.
Seeing this tree so high and its fruit so large, the parrot, delighted at the mere sight, abandoned the ripe field of *śāli* rice; that dull-witted one went to that coconut tree.
Having climbed it with a mind eager for food, he made an attempt to break it open; not only was his hope shattered, but his beak was reduced to powder.
O serpent of Time, you spread your terrifying hood here before Lord Paśupati only so long as he remains far off, serving as his ornament;
for as long as Garuḍa maintains silence, somehow suppressing the swelling of his anger out of fear of your insolence.
Niṣāda and Gāndhāra are to be known as high-pitched; Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata as low-pitched; while the remaining notes—Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Pañcama—are to be understood as circumflex (svarita).

Victorious is that Lord with the face of an elephant, the master of the worlds, whose form is a marvel to the three realms; who bears a pair of frontal globes that accompany the two lofty segments of the universe; who is beautiful with broad ear-flaps rivaling the wings of the enemy of the serpent (Garuḍa); whose offspring is the god Śambhu; and whose increasing trunk vies with the body of the lord of serpents.
This wall of inferior hue, adorned here with high rows of great silver and colored like thick plaster,
attains the grace of the forehead of Śiva, which is whitened by ashes and graced by his upward-gazing eyes.
If the mind remains lofty, what does it matter whether there is adversity or prosperity?
When a man's mind is broken, his fortune appears as if submerged in calamities.
This very tree of shade, which was once loudly sung of by flocks of bees whose minds were greedy for honey-drinking, which was built into a nest by birds arriving from distant lands,
and which was resorted to by hundreds of travelers to dispel the exhaustion caused by the heat of summer— now that tree has been crushed by an elephant in its fierce rut.
Having approached this lofty, vast cloud, I have come as your guest, seeking water from your breasts.
Yet, out of shame, I speak these words; for even though my kinsman is far away, my own breasts are also firm.
Even envious people offer praise more highly in public assemblies;
one should not trust the wise in this regard, for that which is called friendship is only what is performed out of sight.
The sun has fallen from the lofty summit of the mountain of the sky like a boulder of red chalk;
by its very fall, as it is shattered to pieces, this streak of dust of twilight rises up here.
Her breasts are high, her waist is exceedingly slender, her navel is deep, and the orb of her hips is most elevated;
O fortunate one, my mind is submerged in the body of this fair-eyed woman, rising and falling with its contours, and does not return to me again.
In this Kali age, when the lineage of the Bull’s feet has been obscured, you have once again fashioned that new line and set the chariot of his foot upon it.
O Lord, having heard this proclaimed by the rays discharged from your weapons as they pierce the sun, Anūru shall abandon Mihira and serve you.
Striking the waters with the blows of the staff-like tips of the leaping fish's tails,
the garden of the world rose up and sank down within the ocean.
A step taken contrary to the scriptures,
or one that rushes headlong into danger, does not cease until it has been swallowed by the jaws of the enemy.
The practice of Dharma is cut off and great unrighteousness prevails;
they say there is fear day and night when the wicked are not restrained.
The tattered garments of the sky-clad Lord [Śiva] surpassed the hundreds of beauties of the fair-browed women whose bodies were adorned with jewel ornaments;

and the wealthy cities of the citizens could not equal the cremation-ground dwelling of the mendicant. Indeed, the lineage of the Sena dynasty was ignorant of how to provide for the poor, for it failed to bestow its fortune upon them.
Like an unfaithful wife distressed by the loss of her refuge, Fortune has departed for another lineage; the subjects, following her lead, have followed her and abandoned their affection.

Even the trusted ones, failing to attain the fruits of their manly efforts, have cast off the burden of duty; what, then, can the best men do? They remain like outcasts, shunned by those who once relied on them.
A discarded water-pot, fallen on the road, was reviled by fools and the dull-witted, yet it was held in the heart by Brahmins who contemplate reality for the sake of awakening to their own Self.
Likewise, one who dances naked, with matted hair, was abandoned as a "fool" by children; yet the young ones laugh at him repeatedly clapping their hands on the crossroads.
Remnants of food, the remains of offerings to Śiva, vomit, a shroud from a corpse,
and that which arises from crow-droppings— these five are exceedingly pure.
One who is impure from eating should not touch the sky, nor should one place [the vessel] at the head of the bed at night;
and by day, one should honor it with the excellence of perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
If a dog lies down having placed its paw at the head of the bed,
it indicates that a beloved person will arrive at that house before long.

With eyes languid and reddened by the flow of tears, with the luster of her lips marred by hot sighs, and with her locks disheveled from the space between her brows; pale and resting quietly upon the surface of her cheek like a tender sprout—O innocent one, for whom has this state of yours ripened as the fruit of ascetic penance?
By what elephant—agitated by its towering trunk, indifferent to all else, and intoxicated—was this world thrown into turmoil?
How was this dull-witted beast brought under control by force, once a young mahout had placed his foot upon its head?
"Annihilation, depletion, oppression, and likewise emaciation—
those who know the science declare these to be the fourfold conduct toward an enemy."
Even that which ought to be cut off, the wise sometimes increase for a time;
for phlegm, when increased by jaggery, eventually comes to total destruction.

With bristling whiskers, a gaping mouth, and corners of the lips licked by the sprout-like tongue, his eyes wandering wildly like those of a bull, and his tail-hair quivering and blazing with horripilation;
tireless in every direction, sometimes hidden away and at other times visible only up to his knees—this painted tiger hastens toward the young fawns of the pleasure-grove deer to seize them.
Excessive height causes fear among people; an abnormality is its long neck; it is cruel, and its birthplace is everywhere the parched desert;
it has a fondness for high and bitter thorns—alas, what misery that such a beast as a camel should receive royal favor and become the recipient of two great titles!
Her pair of breasts, swelling with growth and bound with budding folds at the edges of their circles,
proclaims her chest to be insufficient for its expansion.

Breath is in gasps, the heart is trembling in fragments, silence is the ornament of the jewels, even the exchange of words is performed through gestures, the dusty ground is a comfortable bed, and reconciliations and quarrels occur only in silence, where kissing is devoid of sound—may there be well-being for that secret amorous dalliance; let there be a benediction of salutation to it!
Heaving sighs as their limbs loosen their bonds, agitated by the god of love,
women now become truly longing for their beloveds who are nearby.
Sighing, hiccupping, lying down, yawning, belching, vomiting, gasping, and stretching;
a dog’s mouth half-open and its gaze directed upward—these, along with leftward movements, are praised when occurring during the light of day.
Life-breaths have exhalation as their limit, and that exhalation is itself the wind;
there is nothing more unstable than the wind—that which continues to breathe is truly a marvel.
When the arrow remains lodged in his heart, not even a breath can escape;
how much less so his speech, with its formidable grandeur and rhythmic composition?

"Let him be told everything that needs to be said; O friend, harshness is not proper toward a Lord. Bring him here after having conciliated him; for how can one who causes displeasure be conciliated?"
When one's own vital secrets are being disclosed, one should maintain silence;
however, regarding one's own actions, one should possess deafness, steadfastness, sweetness, and warmth.
O golden *ketakī*, let not your abundance of fragrance unfold while your clusters of bees are blocked by your jagged petals, which have been bewildered by your constant wakefulness.
When jackals emit auspicious southern notes as one passes through a deserted village, they indicate that the desired place is already within reach.
The moon, whose mass of rays is scattered in every direction like coral shoots, emerges as the merit of the night-lotus;
he appears like some royal conch being lifted from the depths of the ocean.

With her face blooming, the slopes of her breasts quivering, her creeper-like brows darting and wandering, her slender body bathed in drops of perspiration, and her modesty slipping away as her hair stands on end—
O charming girl, what fortunate youth is there whose face she now directs those glances, which resemble masses of foam from the great ocean of milk?
The eye is said to be of four kinds: bright, straight, curved, and reddish; its various emotional states (bhāvas) are each distinct.
It is brilliant when meeting a friend, straightforward upon seeing a son,
crooked during sexual union with a lover, and reddish-brown when beholding an enemy.
A base person can by no means endure seeing one who has risen with radiant virtues;
even after burning its own body, a moth destroys the bright flame of a lamp.
If one touches a lamp out of fear that it might be a radiant campaka bud,
what else could possibly happen to him except to be smeared with the black soot?
Abandoned by you, whose radiance is brilliant and who are so affectionate, she no longer shines,
like a lamp-wick with a soiled face when deprived of the flame.
As the king of stars approaches, swiftly casting off the darkness as if it were impurity,
the eastern quarter assumes the beauty of a face bright with the smile of rays, adorned with the quality of clarity.

Casting off their golden girdles with a jingling sound, they fashioned waist-bands from campaka blossoms; they laid aside their pearl necklaces for rows of jasmine buds and their coral ear-ornaments for red aśoka sprouts. Thus, as if carved into their hearts by the arrows of Love, they became the very beloveds of their friends.
Even those who have abandoned the union with bulls are indifferent to the excellence of men at the time of pleasure;
even those who delight in dwelling in darkness are constantly fond of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Between two youths whose pride in their own good fortune has been cast aside and whose requests have become explicit,
yet whose minds remain unperceived by one another, a single glance serves as a messenger sent with a specific mission.
"O child, I do not grieve that I was abandoned by Rāghava out of fear of defiling his lineage;
but when asked, 'Who are you?', alas, I must tell the forest-dwellers [the truth]—why does my heart faint?"

May Lord Śiva protect us—he who, having abandoned the quarters as his garment and donned the most excellent celestial raiment; having long left the cremation ground and taken refuge in the palaces of Kailāsa; having cast off ashes and applied a mass of saffron paste with the essence of sandalwood juice; and who, having performed the marriage with the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, became a householder.

Even this moon, the leader of the host of stars and the sovereign of medicinal herbs, though possessed of a body of nectar and endowed with brilliance, becomes devoid of rays upon reaching the orb of the sun; for who, when entering the abode of another, does not fall into insignificance?
That the lord of the stars (the moon) tormented the lotus-stalk wreath worn by his wife (the sun), and that the night-lily laughed at the sun’s consort (the day-lotus)—
both of these are considered to have been done out of envy for its own splendor, now that the new sun has risen with rays as red as the *karkandhū* fruit.
Is it that the assembly of stars lacks worthiness, or is it the night’s lack of propriety, that they have not beheld here their husband whose mass of rays is so easily counted?
Clearly, the chest of the Moon-lord is made of stone, possessing the luster of shimmering, dark gemstones; for alas, even upon separation from these two, it does not melt quickly.

If that woman— whose face is like the king of stars (the moon), whose hips are like the king of beasts (a lion), and whose slow gait is as majestic as the king of elephants— is placed within one's heart, then where is recitation, where is austerity, and where is delight in meditative concentration?
The broad-winged sun-bird, having risen in the eastern direction and gradually spread its radiance,
now falls with its rays shed from the sky beyond, exhausted upon the western mountain.

In that very lake—where birds flew away, aquatic creatures died, and tortoises sank into the earth; where it repeatedly fainted due to the rolling of large fish upon its broad banks—a cloud out of season arrived and performed such a feat that herds of wild elephants, submerged up to their temples, drink its water.
The arrows of virtue have flown away; the fruits of happiness are scattered far below; the sprouts of the creeper of prosperity have withered on all sides, their fame now but a mere tuft.
Long ago the deer of joy has fled, and the shade of our story has come to its end, for the mighty elephant of Fate has broken the tree of our self-respect.
O young woman, this row of birds flying up from the palace flashes like a Vaijayantī banner tossed and scattered by the wind.
Is this the lunar disc risen from Uḍḍīya, or is it a pair of *khañjarīṭa* birds? Have two blue lotuses abandoned their bud-state to reach full bloom?
Or have these two *cakora* birds become impetuous upon reaching the orb of the moon? Ah, I know! They are the eyes of the girl with the beautiful hips, skillful in the playful movements of a fish.
Uḍḍīyāṇa is always declared by the Guru to be innate (*sahaja*);
one who practices it without sloth shall become young again, even if he is old.
A bird that flies upward and then descends while uttering cries as it prepares to strike portends death for the traveler;
if it does so on the left side, it indicates the death of the enemy.
Alternatively, a path that is grassy, level, and easy to traverse is praised;
likewise, the threefold path is easily cleared, as is one's own sixfold strength.
The bee, its mind overcome by an incomparable nectar, enters the *ketakī* flower, disregarding in its heart the abrasions caused by rubbing against the sharp tips of its formidable thorns.
The garland of clouds excites the flock of peacocks,
and this god whose banner is a sea-monster excites the minds of the youths.
Struck by the sighs of young female *cakravāka* birds agitated by longing, the moon, as it sets forth, attains the likeness of a clear mirror;
and as the sun is summoned by the cries of roosters as if out of pity for the *kokila* birds, the eastern quarter has become the color of freshly polished coral and the hue of the *sautrāmaṇī* wine.
Let your mind be agitated by longing for a thicket of thorns; let it be filled with joy in tasting the sprouts of the *picumanda* tree—what harm is there in that?
But, O camel, how can I endure this unbearable thing of yours: that you are intent on disparaging the tender shoots of the *puṇḍraka* and *kandalī* plants?
The young woman’s mind is filled with longing, she stands far away, and her youth is fresh;
fate is adverse, and desire is an enemy—alas, alas, what a succession of miseries!
For one who longs [for a lover], a female companion who accords with the heart is the best diversion when the tryst is delayed;
she is the most cherished consolation for those afflicted by separation, and a joy that increases the passion of one already enamored.
For one who is longing, conversation regarding sense objects—which follows the heart like a friend and is free from the faults of confusion—is beneficial;
likewise, for women addicted to the passion of play and the infatuation of love, a beloved wife is a source of joy, whereas a co-wife is an obstacle to the pleasure of her lover.
O fair-limbed one, the thief— his hand slipping from the guard of his arm which was slick with sweat from trembling—
prays for your welfare regarding your two breasts, which are like five-fold cloths.
Trembling, with the hem of your garment slipping away in fear, casting your distressed eyes in every direction—
you were not seen by the cruel fire, which, blinded by its own smoke, suddenly consumed you in its ferocity.
Even trembling is full of tremor within his heart; even anxiety is accompanied by anxiety; even sighs breathe forth incessantly; even tears turn into tears.
As the lover dwelling in a foreign land remembers his beloved day and night, sorrows—laden with further sorrow—issue forth from his mind like sprouts from a tree.
Trembling in my heart, my words falter, my mind is restless with agitation, my body grows weary, my eyes are clouded with tears, and my face dries up with anxiety.
O friend, since this is the preliminary array of symptoms for one whose pride has been abandoned by me, there must surely be other women on this earth who hold him in high esteem.

O King, the sound of the morning drum has been drunk in from all sides by the ears of women in the forest thickets, their eyes trembling with agitation; it has been heard for a long time with uplifted ears by herds of elephants, with blossoming joy by peacocks, and with eyes quivering in anger by the playful lions kept in cages.
With ears pricked up, skilled in sudden ferocity, with broad and quivering manes, possessing a fierce form and a gaping mouth, and bearing his stiff, upright tail—
this lion, stationed upon the frontal globes of an elephant trumpeting in a mountain thicket while causing all creatures to shrink in fear, cannot be depicted even in a painting.
Though capable of cutting through and possessing wings for flight,
the bee, out of greed for fragrance, falls into captivity within the lotus.

The more a person of noble character, possessing excellent qualities born of their own lineage, hears of the virtues of another, the more they bow down, just like a well-crafted bow made of good bamboo.
Neither prosperity nor adversity would be permanent;
likewise, due to prior karma, one who is always wealthy might become poor.
An abundance of longing and that respective natural fluidity—this is unconditioned affection; therefore, Gaṅgā is dear to the Lord.

The salt-water ocean has attained the splendor of the surging sea of milk; the gods' power of discrimination has been cast away, such that they wonder which is the Vindhya mountain and which is the father of Gaurī;
even the horses of the sun’s chariot have been turned white, and alas, O King, the moon, whose beauty was once the pride of its neck, has been surpassed by your unrestrained white glories.
These deep, thundering clouds, flashing with lightning and possessing the luster of her curls, cause the young girl to long for him and become distraught.

The peacocks, sluggish with the sleep of night, appear as if carved upon their perches; the turrets, where pigeons are mistaken for smoke issuing from the lattices, are visible; and the elderly attendants of the inner apartments, purified by ritual observances, distribute the glowing lamps at the twilight hour among the places where flower-offerings have been laid.

He cries out, wanders about, weeps, and shrieks repeatedly; he tosses lotuses far away with his beak, plunges into the water, and gazes at the moon—alas, the cakravāka bird, separated from his beloved, suffers thus through the night.
It cries out, sighs, faints, and goes to the bank; from the bank it goes to a tree, and from the foot of the tree it returns again to the pond.
It does not stay in the pond, nor does it remain even upon a fragment of lotus stalk; indeed, during the nights of separation from its mate, the ruddy goose wanders thus.

Let the cranes shriek at every banyan tree, and let even the wretched crows always warble, for they are experts in such clamor; but that other, unique melody—the playful sequence of the sweet warbling from the throats of cuckoos sporting with the skill that thrives upon tasting morsels of mango sprouts—is something entirely different.
Having somehow hacked from a burning corpse a piece of flesh for a hungry ghost to eat— a morsel of meat as if made of fire— the preta,
his belly suddenly searing with pain, runs, leaps, repeatedly falls and rises, looks about, cries out in all directions, crushes his belly with his fist, and beats his head.
Having repeatedly torn away the skin, and having first devoured the flesh— abundant with massive swellings and easily found on parts such as the shoulders, buttocks, and the mass of the back—

the corpse-eater, seizing the tendons, entrails, and eyes, his teeth bared, greedily eats the raw meat remaining on the bones, even that which has settled in the hollows of the hand, without any hesitation.
Having repeatedly cut open even the wombs and hacked them to pieces out of rage for the Kṣatriya lineage, and having slaughtered all the royal dynasts on every side up to twenty-one times—
while my fire of wrath was being stilled by the great joy of the sacrificial libation in the lake filled with their blood— surely my true nature is not unknown to all beings.
The expedition of one who possesses superior strength and vigor, who desires victory and seeks triumph,
and whose subjects are devoted to his virtues, is known as *yāna* (marching).
Just as lines drawn on stone, sand, and water [persist], so is loving-kindness toward superior, middling, and inferior people;
just as lines drawn on stone, sand, and water [disappear], so does enmity toward inferior, middling, and virtuous people respectively.
A wise man immediately seizes upon a bribe, a gift of affection, the stakes of a game, a well-spoken word, a woman, and the first stage of a disease.
Bribe-takers, those who practice fraud, deceivers, gamblers, as well as those who live by giving false directions,
along with fortune-tellers and soothsayers;
Furthermore, high officials who act improperly, physicians,
those skilled in the practice of arts and crafts, and clever courtesans;
One should recognize such individuals as manifest thorns to the world, as well as others who move in disguise— ignoble persons wearing the marks of the noble.
Bribes, rewards, wages, well-spoken words, and portions of stolen property must be accepted at that very moment; otherwise, they cannot be obtained at any other time.

Your stride has surpassed the mountain peaks; your claws are as hard as adamant; your splendor is formidable and your roar is great enough to shatter the mountains. Yet, by a sleepy lion who did not leave his mountain cave out of laziness, all this—the sole means for universal conquest—was gained, but nothing was actually achieved.
The leaf-borne arrows, having passed above the corpses, soared upward into the sky;
surely those embodied life-breaths, though deprived of their bodies by cruel weapons, were still looking back even now.
He who, being self-restrained and esteemed by the learned, should contemplate the Gaṅgā with his mind as his vital breaths depart, shall attain the supreme goal.
This pair of water-jars has been lifted; the girdle has been fastened firmly with great effort; silence has been imposed upon my noisy anklets.
O dear friend, just as I have begun this festival of a secret tryst with impetuosity, the moon—a veritable executioner—casts off the veil of darkness.
Friend, the anklet has been lifted—its mouth filled with wick and silenced; the girdle-string has been cast aside, its jingling sound ceased; it has been tucked within the folds of the silk garment.
The female parrots in their cages have fallen asleep, and the attendants are reeling with sleep. The royal road is empty and the darkness is dense; come, come, let us depart!

That bow of the Lord was lifted up along with the horripilation of Kauśika; it was bent down together with the faces of the kings; it was drawn back simultaneously with the doubtful thoughts of Janaka;
it was suddenly pulled forth together with the mind of Vaidehī; and then it was broken along with the sprout of Bhārgava’s mature arrogance.
O mango bud, as your friend raises her arms and reveals the base of her shoulders,
you shine forth as she pulls you, attaining a position far higher than yours.
Lifted up by their heads, which are held aloft by hands grasping raised white cloths and which have the stars fixed upon them,
the sky clearly falls down on all sides upon its slopes under the guise of the waters of its credible waterfalls.
Even when tossed up by enraged lordly elephants,
the foot-soldiers nonetheless took the lives of those [beasts] with blows from their swords right before their own master.
When the warriors were tossed far off by the elephants and released,
their individual souls attained a divine state in the sky, while their bodies reached the earth.
Having lifted its feet from the sky out of fear of falling, the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird remains there;
who, indeed, does not possess pride here that is imagined by their own mind?
Having tossed back her disheveled mass of curls from her pale cheeks, and having slightly raised her hands for fear that her slipping bracelets might fall,
a certain meritorious man embraces at that moment the frail woman who, with her vine-like body leaning against the doorpost, has fixed her gaze upon the path.
Lifting high with his tusks an enemy elephant that was quivering violently,
he who possessed tusks like plow-poles clearly attained the likeness of a mountain whose rain-clouds are impaled upon its peaks.
The surface of the earth has been dug up in search of hidden treasures; the ores of the mountains have been smelted; the lord of rivers has been crossed; kings have been served with great effort;
and nights have been spent in cremation grounds with a mind intent on the propitiation of mantras. Yet, O Greed, not even a single broken cowrie shell has been obtained by me; now, cease!
I think that the forest of red lotuses at twilight has been uprooted and torn asunder; the wild buffalo named Night, intoxicated, has plunged into the middle of the lake of the sky, lashing its tail.
From that very moment, emerging along with a mass of bubbles that are the stars—both small and large—the terrifying darkness rises up, turbidly pervading the world.

Now that King Hammīra has departed for the abode of the gods, I behold the entire universe as a necklace deprived of its central gem— the temple of Śiva like a sanctuary whose deity has been uprooted, and the sky like the firmament when the sun has vanished behind the western mountain.
Transplanting those that have been uprooted, gathering those in bloom, pruning those that are small, bending down those that are too tall, thinning out those that are too thick,
removing those that are thorny, and protecting those he has planted himself— like a skilled gardener, he who thus manages his kingdom remains there for a long time.

Having uprooted flowers from the garden of the mind, the wise have fashioned them into garlands within the private groves of books; we now attain supreme bliss as the fruit of these poetic trees that have been planted therein.

This young woman is surely the Vārāṇasī of liberation for the minds of people—a river where the three folds of her waist are the tossing waves, and the line of hair upon her body is a garland of *śaivala* moss.
For on the slope of her chest, in place of the restlessness of childhood, two funeral mounds fashioned by the artisan of youth are visible.
With crest-ornaments of peacock feathers upon arms as dark as emerald bracelets; with necklaces of dense sapphire and elaborate facial paintings made of musk;

with the beauty of blue-lotus headdresses and the wearing of dark garments—such is the playful attire of these fawn-eyed women on their way to meet their lovers, now acting as companions to the heavy darkness.

O mango tree, the ornament of the garden, whose sprouts were not even plucked by the fingernails of playful women acting out of the desire for a head-ornament, you have now fallen into the reach of those who build houses.
No lotus shines with such brilliance as her face;
alas, for this reason, the Creator, who knows the proper rites, has fittingly made her two eyes the ornaments for her two ears.
With the moon as his crest-ornament, tossing back the waves along with their serpents, and established in a boundless and vast majesty smeared with the ashes of moonlight;
making the celestial river roar by striking its banks with the tips of his skull-bowls, the ocean laughs loudly at Rudra with a roar of thunder on the path.
It did not dance upon the crest-ornaments of kings, nor was it noticed by spectators; nor did it ever roll with longing upon the slopes of the breasts of playful women.
Alas! By fate, that gem—its size diminished by the friction of rubbing against the necks of sporting serpents—was shattered long ago within the depths of the ocean.
Scorched by the heat, this serpent takes refuge in the shade of the peacock’s crest; abandoning its natural enmity, the peacock goes to the root of the tree.
Afflicted by thirst, the sarika birds beg for water in the bower; and the bees, leaving the lotuses in the heated water, take shelter in the creepers.
The Puṣkara field is the most excellent; the Tārā field is not middling;
Kurukṣetra is inferior, while Prabhāsa is the lowest of the low.
One should win over a superior by prostration, a hero by sowing dissension,
an inferior by small gifts, and one of equal power by valorous deeds.
Misfortunes do not at all overwhelm the supreme person for very long;
the eclipse caused by Rāhu’s seizing may darken the moon for but a moment.
Wealth earned by oneself is the best; that earned by one's father is middling;
wealth belonging to a brother is inferior; and the wealth of a woman is the lowest of the low.
Only the superior person is able to endure the agitation of the afflictions, and not the other;
for it is only a gem that withstands being ground upon a great whetstone, and not a particle of clay.
The best *ṣaṭpada* is said to consist of six lines, the middling likewise of five, and the lowest should consist of four; thus the *dhruvaka*s are of three kinds.
Even one born into a noble family performs service for lowly people;
and a mortal, tormented by the lord of the stomach, speaks base words.
Of an exceedingly youthful nature, with attachment to another body indicated by horripilation and other signs,
and with its manifest conditions clearly present— by whom can such erotic sentiment be restrained?
O Karaṭa, those who relish excellent things are easy to find in this world;
however, you alone are considered by me to be one who relishes things that are corrupted.
Her body, its hips rendered motionless by the embrace of an excellent lover,
is dragged here and there by the gods like Mount Mandara.

O King, Sarasvatī, her garment scorched by the flame arising from the fire of the creditor’s demand for the payment of wealth— which dwells within her heart— does not emerge from her mouth out of shame.
Looking at the face of the creditor, the debtor bows down in shame;
he beholds the tumultuous struggle between life and death.

O you whose sole resort is the most excellent women, like an elephant plunging into the waters of a lake, you seize the courage of your friend by merely touching her with your hand as she is assailed by passion.

The best son acts upon what he has reflected; the middling one carries out what he has been told; the inferior one acts without faith; and the lowest does not act at all on what was uttered by his father.
If one nourishes it at that time, the tree attains supreme satisfaction;
generally, a tree does not flourish by itself without being tended by the feet [of those who care for it].
The anger of the superior lasts for a moment, that of the middling for two watches;
but that of the inferior lasts a day and night—the most wicked man is never released from it.
Even if he belongs to the lowest caste, a guest who has come to the house of even the highest caste must be honored as is appropriate, for the guest embodies all the gods.
Even if he belongs to the lowest caste, one who has come to the house of even the highest caste—
whether a child or an elder— is a venerable guest for everyone.
The best are renowned for their own virtues; the middling, by the virtues of their father;
the inferior, even by those of their maternal uncle; and the lowest of the low, by those of their father-in-law.
Those who [perform the rite] with wealth earned by themselves are the best; those with their father's property are middling;
those with their mother's property are inferior; and those with the property of a woman are the lowest of the low.
Those renowned through themselves are declared the highest; those renowned through their father are middling;
those renowned through their maternal uncle are low; and those renowned through their father-in-law are the lowest of the low.
Because he was born first from the cow, because he upholds the Veda,
and because of his role in this entire creation, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord by virtue of dharma.
The wise should listen to the speech of those who are superior, inferior, or middling;
therein, they should accept that which is beneficial to themselves, just as a king accepts the words of a commoner.
Having discerned actions as superior, inferior, or middling,
the king should assign them to persons who are superior, inferior, or middling.
Knowing that women— who are pure on the outside— associate with both the high and the low, and that their conduct is similar [to all], the Creator designated them by the name "ganā."
This is the nature of the noble: an inability to endure the suffering of others;
even when suffering has come upon oneself, one considers it as being warded off for another's sake.
Trust is never to be found even in the most excellent of women;
the night-lotuses, though beloved by the king, dally with the bees.
Moving only toward those who are superior or equal while avoiding those who are inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains excellence; through the opposite conduct, he reaches the state of a Śūdra.
One who desires his own welfare should serve only the best; when the time is right, he may serve those of middling quality, but he should never serve the base.
One should not cause those endowed with the highest lineage to prosper together with the lowly;
for even one who is emaciated, if he possesses discernment, becomes worthy of seeking refuge.
Those renowned by themselves are the best; those renowned by their fathers are middling;
those renowned by their maternal uncles are inferior; and those renowned by their fathers-in-law are the lowest of the low.
The Tājikas are declared to be the best, as are the Pārasīkas born by the sea;
likewise, the horses born in Kokkaṇa, Akhatalāṇa, and Saurāṣṭra are excellent.
In the case of a superior person, anger lasts for a moment; in the case of a middling person, for two ghaṭikās;
in the case of an inferior person, it lasts for a day and night; and in the case of a caṇḍāla, it ends only with death.
Having observed everything that is supreme among men with great effort, those who are truly discerning should speak of it all, even regarding what has not been previously seen.
In the highest [grade] there is the presence of obstacles; the lowest is a vessel of suffering.
Therefore, because it is suitable for all circumstances, the intermediate is indeed considered the best.
Who does not attain greatness by associating with the most excellent?
Grasses are carried upon the head together with strung flowers.
Associating with the excellent, engaging in conversation with the learned, and maintaining friendship with those free from greed— one who acts thus does not come to grief.
One should remain even in captivity with the best of men— those who are wise and speakers of truth— but never in a kingdom with the lowest of men.
A base person, even when accepted by the noble, remains base and does not become noble;
a dog, even when presided over by Bhairava, never becomes a lion.
One should not desire to perform an action unauthorized by superiors, nor should one act together with them;
for it was because of drinking the nectar with the gods that Rāhu’s head was severed.
One who desires to lead one's family to excellence should always cultivate associations with the most excellent people; one should avoid those who are inferior and even more base.
The superior person should not speak excessively, while the inferior person is a talkative chatterer;
for the resonance produced in bell-metal is not like that which is produced in gold.
Even a man who is of the highest birth, well-born, honored by all the world, and wise—
if he resorts to that state of servitude which a courtesan resorts to, would the virtuous ever resort to her?
Even a superior person may, on occasion, become humble through the act of begging from an inferior;
for Hari begged the ocean for the Kaustubha jewel and other gems.
The best person gives even when not asked; the middling person gives when requested;
but the lowest of the low does not give even when entreated by beggars.

A man is considered superior, middling, inferior, or lowest according to the qualities of his brothers; however, a man whose fortune lies with daughters, wives, or sisters is regarded as the most base of all.
The discourse on alchemy (*rasavāda*) is the best; the discourse on metallurgy (*dhātuvāda*) is middling;
the discourse on mantras (*mantravāda*) is inferior; and false discourse (*mithyāvāda*) is the lowest of the low.
O beautiful one, may the sky become as deep as the majesty of the waves of the Yamunā, whose eyes are like those of a bull in rut and which dispel the pride of the lotus.
To the north of the Madhūka tree is the abode of a snake; to the northwest is water.
Having bypassed five cubits, one should declare [the site] to be seven and a half fathoms in depth.
Having waded through the deep mud and passed beyond the heat of the sun,
the leaders of the forest boar herds emerge from the pond, scattering about like fierce elephants that have just crushed lotus stalks with their tusks.
Each subsequent statement arises from the preceding one,
just as a further seed is produced from a seed endowed with the quality of having been well-sown by rain.
What can we say of the loveliness of the women of the Northern Path,
whose lotus-faces do not wither even amidst the falling of snow?
Another woman, feeling ashamed due to the adjustment of her upper garment, as it were obstructing the path of his gaze,
covered the circle of her breasts with the broad chest of her husband-to-be.
Furthermore, with the five-arrowed god of love as witness, I have given you to my friend; she must not be served by me in secret.
To the north, one should always act in a way that does not oppose the vital breath;
except in battle, one should never aim toward the south.
It is better to be those who live off the king and covet easily accessible fruits,
rather than being the masters of those fruits which ripen only through intense hardships.

May the three lines of the Great Dancer at the end of the aeons— consisting of flames, laughter, and poison— protect you as he suddenly begins his whirling dance, wherein some arms are outstretched, some curled, some with midsections bent by speed, and some cast down, raised up, or contracted in the sequence of the triple symphony (tauryatrika).
Having laid down one creeper-like arm extended toward the west, and having placed the other languidly upon her broad, expansive hips,
she— her waist slender, her curls trembling with her sighs, and her breasts raised askance by the pressure of the bed— sleeps while keeping her waist-knot slightly loosened.
Who that is not a worm would develop an attachment for a woman’s moist wound, which resembles the split belly of a bloated frog lying on its back?

How can the poetic art of those poets—who have established the entire reality of the universe within every single word—be cultivated by the ears of the inexperienced, which are deceived by shallow chatter?

Where can the ocean, the mine of jewels, be grasped by those who perform the wonder of plunging into the ditches of the street, when its glories consist of great mountains submerged at their very edges by the mouths of the lowest of fish?
Having carefully placed the two feet flat upon the thighs,
and likewise the two hands flat between the thighs— this indeed is the lotus posture (padmāsana).
If one has a friend who is ever-present, highly affectionate, and obedient to the movement of one's brow, what is the use of a fickle eye?
If the king relies on wealth in the expectation that it will rescue him from misfortune,
then its utility here is such that the accumulation of riches is inevitably a disease.
Unshaken even at the sight of the violent calamity wrought by Tāṭakā,
he now hesitates when appointed to destroy her, because of his feminine nature.

The marshy regions of the Lāvaṇa and Saindhava rivers were reached by the army’s soldiers— regions where the *ketakī* flowers were parted by the wind blowing through the dense groves of tall palm trees.

May the Yamunā (Kālindī) protect you—she whose mental state is rendered helpless by the excessive drinking of the essence of wine, who possesses the beautiful luster of black aloe-wood uprooted and dragged from the forest, whose nature is to intoxicate the streams, in whom all the fleeing, trembling, and terrified creatures have become prisoners on her islands, and who has made the crocodiles fierce; she who has made the abundance of your accumulated merit blaze forth and has brought an end to your enemies.

The tossing of high locks, the practice of arranging the mass of hair into a braid, the grooming of the teeth, the fastening of the waist-knot, the training in the graceful play of the eyebrows, the sidelong glances, and the transition into clever speech— this indescribable sequence of amorous play in women fades away moment by moment as childhood withers.
"Arise for a single moment, my friend; bear this heavy burden of poverty while I rest from my long-worn exhaustion and enjoy the bliss of death.
When addressed thus by a learned man devoid of wealth, the corpse went to the cremation ground and, realizing that "death is better than the misery of poverty," remained silent.
He rises, bows, inquires after the merchant's welfare, and offers him a seat;
seeing that the man has placed his hand upon the deposit, he engages him in righteous conversation.
"Arise, messenger! Let us go; the watch has passed, yet he has not come.
Even if he were to live beyond this watch, he might still become the lord of her life."

May the body of Lakṣmī purify you—her body which, as she rose at the end of their dalliance, rested one hand upon the lord of serpents for support and held her garment with the other, while a mass of hair fell over her shoulder; and which was then drawn back onto the bed by Śauri, his arms languidly glowing with the redoubled joy of love from that very moment of her renewed beauty.
One who desires their own welfare should not overlook an adversary who is rising up;
for the wise have declared that both are alike: one's approaching illness and an impending enemy.
"Arise! If you desire me alive, bring him here;
though I am unable to go myself, this distance is very great."
Hearing those words, which were like nectar, "Arise, my child," he rose up; having risen, the king saw before him his own cow, dripping with milk like a mother, and not the lion.

"Rise quickly! What power do I have to climb this tree of my youth? "I shall tell you plainly, O innocent one: what is the 'taru' (tree) here? It is the *taraṇi* (the sun); what pleasure is there for me in its name?

"This is merely talk regarding the boat; how could there ever be a conversation between us intended for a union? Thus, with a smiling face, I worship the unconquered Kṛṣṇa, whose speech was conquered by Rādhā.
Arise, arise! Why do you lie there now that this new humiliation has arrived?
Today, indeed, the rays of the sun have entered Lankā without fear.
Beneath a tree, an ox— lightened though it had cast off its burden, yet far more incapable of exertion due to its full satisfaction from the thick mass of grass—
performed rumination with its heavy dewlap moving slowly, while its eyes closed in languid lassitude.

Having crossed over, some first [placed] Kṛṣṇa on the right and later the deer on the left, while others were highly censured; by some Kṛṣṇa alone was placed on the deer, and by others all [the figures] were disregarded.
If, after crossing over, one goes behind and performs an encircling,
for one who is healthy it brings the attainment of an encircling, and for one who is fearful, it removes fear.
Pressed against her two firm and full breasts by Rati with an arm whose hair stands on end from joy,
this glorious Kāma approaches— delighting the worlds and enchanting the eyes, his lotus-eyes rolling with intoxication.
With his eyes fixed upon the peak of Mount Govardhana,
Hari felt no desire for the excellent forest even when it was close at hand.
Alas, high towers, windows, gateways, houses, and wealth acquired by difficult means—
all these become useless for this guest from the funeral pyre, causing him to fall downward in an instant.
A crow, though emaciated, obtains fruit from a tree standing on the peak of Mount Uttara because it possesses wings;
whereas a lion, though capable of tearing open the temples of fierce elephants, receives nothing but leftovers because it is devoid of wings.
Some rivers, by taking refuge on the peaks of lofty mountains, become turbulent with their surging waves;
others, however, being mere trickles of water, do not suffer depletion even when grass and clods of earth fall into them from the clouds.
Indeed, even a crow, possessing wings, can obtain ripe fruit from the top of a lofty mountain tree;
yet, alas, a powerful lion, though fierce in rending elephants, perishes at the foot of that same tree when deprived of his wings.
Descending from Mount Ujjayanta, this very Yamunā—the daughter of Kalinda, possessing the luster of a fresh blue lotus, a garland of pearls, and a line of hair—is here;
at this most meritorious place of pilgrimage where their confluence occurs, the moon surely plunges in under the guise of nail-marks to remove its stain.

With her breasts as mountains, her body hair as trees, her line of hair as creepers, her girdle as a bowstring, the sound of her anklets as the twang of the string, her pearl necklaces as hunting nets, her brow as a bow, her sidelong glances as a wide array of arrows, and her amorous charms as forest fires of passion, the young woman sports with her own qualities as a hunter; thus the deer-like lover is bound.
With the middle of her chest weary from the weight of her high breasts, with flowers falling from her thick,
loosening tresses, and with eyes terrified by the bees circling her lotus-like face— the lovely-eyed girl approaches me very slowly.
This burden of her uplifted breasts, these tremulous eyes, these flickering creeper-like brows, and this sprout of a lip—let them indeed cause distress to those blinded by passion.
But why does that line of hair, inscribed by the Flower-Armed God himself as a string of letters proclaiming her good fortune, cause such excessive torment even though it rests in the very center?
Descending from the circle of her uplifted breasts like a garland of pearls, this line of hair possesses the luster of a fresh lotus stalk; it is indeed the daughter of Kalinda.
This sacred ford, which produces great merit, has been formed here by our union; truly, the moon must be submerged in her heart under the guise of nail-marks to erase its spot.

May Lakṣmī bring you joy at the festival of her marriage—she who, with face bowed under the pretext of modesty, clearly beholds the form of Murāri; she whose pearl necklace glitters above the circle of her uplifted breasts, its luster reflecting the internal shadow of a cluster of sapphires.

The chest is as difficult to cross as the mountain of Utkaṭa, the region of the navel is deeply depressed, and the forest of the body—with its quivering creeper-like arms and dense thicket of bristling hair—is terrifying.
The hunter Pañcaśara (the Five-Arrowed One) hurls his exceedingly sharp arrows of side-long glances; tell me, O deer of my mind, what refuge will you seek now?

From the edge of the bank, their garments fluttering in the wind, the women leaped into the waters with heavy hips and without haste; they fell even more swiftly than the hearts of their beloveds, who perceived danger.
Is it because he has taken refuge on the high peaks of this mountain with its jagged rocks that the banyan tree’s praise is exhausted by mere words?
Is he perhaps a kinsman from a former life, or is it the accumulation of past meritorious deeds, that people find rest upon reaching him even on a path where the branches are harsh and leafless?

Having eaten at will the fruit atop the peak of the tree of prosperity, one has slipped from that place by the power of fate and fallen, without support, into the interior of the pit of poverty—a terrifying belly of the underworld inhabited by serpents of manifold afflictions; it is a marvel if such a person still breathes.
"What is the use of these lofty trees that touch the sky yet bear no fruit? Blessed indeed is that *ulūpaviṭapa* tree standing on the riverbank;
for one who has resolved thus: 'By the power of the surging waves rising from the water, I shall rescue the people drowning, or else I shall drown along with them.'"
One should rise, remain vigilant, and apply oneself to deeds that lead to prosperity, constantly maintaining a mind free from distress with the thought: "It shall come to pass."
In this world, the exertion of even capable men, if devoid of destiny,
is seen to be fruitless despite being properly undertaken.
Exertion, self-restraint, skillfulness, vigilance, fortitude, mindfulness,
and undertaking actions after due deliberation— know these to be the root of worldly existence.
For Bṛhaspati declared that exertion is indeed the root of the duty of kings.
A man steadfast in exertion surpasses those who are merely steadfast in speech;
those who are steadfast in speech wait upon and delight the one who is steadfast in exertion.
O Bhārata, all beings recognize the necessity of exertion;
they experience the visible fruits of their actions, witnessed by the world.
A man who is constantly intent on rising up and searching for the vulnerabilities of others achieves freedom from debt both toward others and toward himself.
For a king who lacks exertion, even if he is always possessed of intelligence,
