shall be overcome by his enemies like a venomless serpent.
Through exertion, the nectar was obtained; through exertion, the asuras were slain.
Through exertion, Mahendra attained preeminence both in heaven and here on earth.
One should increase one's strength through exertion, just as fire is nourished by fuel;
for even a weak person who constantly exerts himself attains prosperity.
When the members of the assembly rise, he rises; when they depart, he follows them.
Even before the king has expressed his opinion, he discerns it and approaches outside to offer his blessing.
The dust raised in battle by the horses was thickened by the rows of chariot wheels and spread wide by the flapping of elephants' ears; in its gradual expansion, it obstructed the sun.
Having raised the serpent-like power (śakti) situated below by means of the root-winds,
one should [unite] that auspicious power which pierces the five wheels within the suṣumnā.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed his purifications and composed himself,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
When the mind of one of dull intellect delights again and again in evils— when there is neither urgency nor peace, and no sense of revulsion while performing censurable deeds—
then why is it that at dawn you do not fear the fierce capital city of Yama, named Raurava, which is like a blazing fire, sharp with the sound of iron wheels and saws?
Rising again and again, one must reflect: "What good deed has been done today?
Having taken away a fragment of my life, the sun will go to its setting."
Rising up again and again, one should reflect: "What good deed has been done today?
Has anything been given, or caused to be given, or has truthful speech been uttered?"
Rising again and again, one must remain vigilant, for a great terror has arrived;
which of these—death, disease, or sorrow—will fall upon me today?
The desires of the poor arise again and again only to dissolve,
like the breasts of noble women consumed by the early loss of their husbands.
Having risen, with his feet spread and tucked upon the tip of his upraised tail-feather, his crest of plumage bristling upward and his eyes slightly opened,
the cock— having shaken off his two wings out of a sense of peace and having craned his neck from afar— crows, causing the loss of pride in the eyes of the fawn-eyed women.
People who seek to achieve their own ends honor others only while they are standing;
for what man would ever pay homage again to one who has fallen, even as he would to an enemy?
Rising with her feet first, the broad-chested woman, while gathering a cluster of flowers from the tree,
shamelessly embraced the neck of her beloved under the pretext of fearing she might break his waist.
The moon, the storehouse of digits, rises at night in order to attain equality with her face;
yet, having been brought to a state of dimness by her shame, it now passes out of sight in the sky.
Restrain the flow of tears from your eyes with their lashes upturned, and by means of composure, bring an end to their persistence;
for on this path where the depressions and elevations of the ground are not discernible, your footsteps will surely become unsteady.
Whether one flies up into the sky, goes down to the surface of the earth,
or runs across the entire world, that which has not been given does not come to one.
Even when birds fly up into the sky or alight upon the earth, they do not obtain what has not been given, despite their efforts.
Leaping up, whirling around, and bowing down, that lotus-eyed woman,
spreading out a hundred flashes like lightning, performed a dance of confusion like a female bee.
Whether they fly up into the sky or enter the subterranean realm,
or wander through all the directions— nothing that has not been given can be obtained.
One should flee from a diseased land afflicted by sickness and famine,
or go elsewhere to dwell, or live there always being honored.
Your origin is the ocean; your form is renowned as the abode of nectar; your rays, white and straight like jasmine creepers, rival strings of pearls;

the night-lily is your beloved; and Cupid, whose essence is passion, is your dear friend. O Moon, what is there here that causes distress? That you exist for my torment is itself the cause of my suffering.
For that which is already perfected by its very origin, what need is there for other purifiers?
Neither the water of sacred fords nor fire deserves to be purified by anything else.
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is fit for becoming Brahman.

His birth was from Jamadagni; that Blessed Lord is the wielder of the Pināka bow and the preceptor [of the world]. As for his valor, it is indeed not within the path of words, for it is made manifest by his deeds.
His renunciation reached its limit in the unfeigned gift of the earth sealed by the seven oceans—what, then, in the Blessed One, a treasury of Kṣatriya and Brahminic asceticism, is not extraordinary?
Born from the sacrificial ground of the gods, the king is a father who speaks the Veda;
his exceedingly serene and radiant form inspires affection for me.

The birth of the Lord of the Maruts on the first day of the Yuga was proclaimed during a festival for the whole world; there was great renown from the recitations of auspicious days (*puṇyāha*), full maturity, and manly prowess.
He shared with the descendant of Kakutstha the same enmity toward rivals and such skill in astrology; by virtue of that quality, the crow was confined in a golden cage.
In Malaya, the abode of the ocean, is the place of origin; the path there is blocked by *rākṣasa*s, and alas, the sea-faring merchants cut down even the sandalwood trees found there.
Yet the *śākhoṭa* and other such trees that stand nearby remain happy. Therefore, I consider those among the family of trees to be truly fortunate who are not fit for utility.

Wherein various multitudes of qualities—both those yet to arise and those already arisen—find their firm foundation; wherein there is neither sublation of prior [rules], nor restrictive injunction, nor the assignment of specific numbers or purposes;
wherein every modification (*ūha*) manifests everywhere, and where even the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is indeed true—this new form of yours now attains the very essence of Mīmāṃsā.

May the forest of matted hair of the Lord of Bhavānī grant you prosperity—hair which appears as if sprouting from the flames of his gaze, blossoming under the rays of the moon, and possessing a mountain-like growth;
for upon its edge, the ancient row of skulls attains the playful beauty of massive, shimmering clusters of foam from the flood of the celestial river swirling around it.
Some paths are treacherous rivers, turbid with many whirlpools;
they violently destroy even those standing on the bank once their embankments have been breached.
Sometimes it goes by a wrong path, sometimes it travels on the right path;
now hot, now cold, it is fickle and flees with fickleness.
Beings like me, who are but insignificant creatures, arise and perish;
how could there be the appearance of such as you, who have girded yourselves for the sake of others?
That which was born into the lineage of the wise, yet abandoned by all; that which has never once been forgotten by the learned, nor ever practiced by the wicked;
and even for such great poverty, into which no one had ever extended a helping hand—that [poverty] has now been cast down as it falls into the flowing stream of the waters of charity.
If one possessed such an intellect as arises when torment has already been produced,
who would not achieve great success?
For a man who has merely fathered a son, heaven is certain;
by the mere birth of a *ṭiṭṭibha* chick, Mandapāla went to the celestial realm.
Indeed, for a human being born here in this world from the very moment of birth,
various kinds of sufferings and pleasures attend them.
If one were to lead him along either of those two paths,
he would not rejoice upon encountering happiness, nor would he be distressed upon encountering suffering.
The horn of a deer that has been born grows as it matures;
like the desire of a man, there is no measure for its growth.
Those aquatic creatures who were born in the lakes of rivers, nourished there for a very long time, and then reached the ocean during the rainy season—
having attained a state of immobility within the family of *timiṃgila* fish in just two or three days, they no longer tolerate even in secret any talk of their own lack of respectability today.
Many clusters of lotuses have arisen upon the surfaces of lakes, which have become the standard of comparison for the faces of women resembling the lord of the night;
yet, in the navel of the enemy of Bhauma (the Earth), there arose that one unique Great Lotus (*mahāpadma*), which became the birthplace of the progenitor of the three worlds.
He who overcomes a calamity that has arisen is truly wise,
just as the lover was denied by the merchant’s wife in her very presence.
And he whose intellect does not falter when difficulties arise overcomes all hardships, just as Gopī did with her two lovers.
O Jar-born One, you are a universal monarch; furthermore, having entered the fire, you performed penance through the exertion of morning ablutions and by drinking water.
When you stand upon the hips of fawn-eyed women with your knees raised, you invade the boundary of their breasts as their vine-like arms cling to your neck out of passion.
Of the blue lotus, the red lotus, the fish, and the white water lily—
though born from the same species— their form and fragrance are each distinct.
The redness of the lotus, the benevolence of the virtuous,
and the lack of compassion in the wicked— these are the three kinds of inherent natures, just as they are.
Like a *utpala* flower with its rays, and like a tree in bloom with its stars,
this moon rises upon the edge of the eastern mountain, possessing a cool shade like a celestial wish-fulfilling tree.
I foresee, my friend, that although you wish to travel swiftly for the sake of my beloved, there will be delay at every mountain fragrant with *kakubha* flowers;

for there, the peacocks, welcoming you with their cries and eyes moist with tears and white-cornered glances, will come out to meet you, so that you will somehow find it difficult to resolve to go quickly.
O King, this portentous event must be investigated here: whether it be Nārāyaṇa or Subhadrā who is falling?
For it is indeed fitting that one supported by a pillar should fall to the earth when his eyes are reeling from the intoxication of *kādambarī* wine.

O friend, the day of summer shines forth, a banner of rising heat for the lord of love, a thunderbolt-strike to the grove of pleasure-creeper vines, and like the time of universal destruction for the wives of travelers— its hopes far removed.
The sun, with its mass of grey rays, rises like a lion with its mane bristling, having opened wide its mouth-like aperture born of portents— terrible to the world— to devour the people.

Just as for those who are healthy, the report that "the earth's foundation has collapsed" leads to calamity, so too in poetry a bad omen portends misfortune, and in dramatic performance it does so for the plays.
Between the one who gives birth and the one who grants the Veda, the father who grants the Veda is more venerable;
for the birth through the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both in this world and after death.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born,
and the daily conduct of worldly life— each of these is directly dependent upon women.
The Malaya breeze generates joy for the world;
indeed, one endowed with courtesy becomes dear to everyone.
This face of yours, resembling a fading lotus, produces sufficient despondency in my mind;
yet, knowing the cause of this, I, sharing your sorrow, desire to become dear to you even at the cost of my own life, O most beloved one.
Causing obstacles to pleasure and robbing lovers of the joy of their mutual conversation,
sleep suddenly and firmly clung to the eyes of those impassioned with desire.
If she was produced by herself, then she is one's own daughter; if by her father, then she is indeed one's sister, Śrī;
and if she has union with another, then she is another's wife. Therefore, the wise are intent on renouncing her.
A wealthy man is obstructed everywhere by artificial faults he has created himself; yet a man without wealth, even if he has committed a thousand offenses, remains a supreme lord.
Having procreated sons and made them free from debt, having provided them with some means of livelihood,
and having settled all his daughters in suitable marriages, he should dwell in the forest, desiring to live like a sage.
Since even the sun, though possessing powerful radiance and pursuing her closely,
is followed by his shadow which extends far away, I believe that she has fashioned this as a fitting likeness of noble lineage.
With tail uplifted, his body swelling with the joy of passion, and his two wings drooping downward as he circles gracefully and repeatedly about by means of spontaneous, leaping movements;
with a warbling cry languid with longing, the sparrow for a moment trembles as he hastens toward his beloved, whose sweet cooing has subsided due to her intense desire for dalliance.

Shaking their tail-feathers and ruffling their wing-quills, making whistling sounds with their movements, and uttering cries as they move their beaks, the peacocks dance repeatedly lifting their feet in the flow of the rhythm;
with the branches of their plumage meeting near their upraised necks, they gaze at the dark cloud-banks that rival the color of their own throats.
The forests are covered in fresh sprouts, the ponds are filled with blossoming lotuses, and the moon is full; yet, by the power of desire, these have become poison to the eyes of the traveler.

Having leapt far up and shaken his wings, looking down with his aim fixed for a moment, he plunges into the midst of the water; who is this fish-eater that, having made the leap, rises up from the water along with a fish?
That very lion who, having leaped up, burst open the frontal globes of rutting elephants and bounded over mountain peaks extending for hundreds of leagues,
now, overcome by inevitable old age and with eyes swollen and bloodshot, licks his paws.
Leaping from the corner of the house, the frogs moved forward a short distance, then approached with slow, winding steps, slightly swaying their necks.
Falling upon the putrid matter with their eyes half-opened in a "micimici" sound, they clear the area of flies with their mouths wide open like crocodiles.
When another’s face was severed from afar by a leaping crescent-moon arrow, his teeth biting his lip in rage,
I feared even more for the headless trunk as it lunged forward with a sword in hand, its neck already severed and its army dissolved in panic.
As Hari rushed swiftly and effortlessly from the peak of the eastern mountain with a great leap, the elephant of darkness was rent asunder by the blows of his high-flaming palm-strokes;
then all those stars fell instantly, crimson like blood poured from its temples, casting wonder upon all who saw them, and appearing like the glowing red hues of twilight.
O Gaurī, whose radiance is as fair as the pollen of the filaments of full-blown lotuses,
may my heart's desire be fulfilled through your grace, O Blessed One!

May the Lord of the Mountain purify you— he who, at the conclusion of their dalliance, was embraced very tightly by Girijā, whose full breasts had their nipples pressed down, and who was swarmed by bees greedy for the fragrance of her lotus-face with its blossoming, wide-open cheeks.
Those with foul faces converse happily with their mouths wide open;
yet it is only a poet who truly understands the labor of another poet.

When will Kṛṣṇa, possessing the lovely splendor of a blossoming *tāpiccha* flower, his lotus-face resting upon his mother’s breast, come within the range of my vision as he moves about, planting the tips of his lotus-feet?

Whose wonder does the graceful *stamāla* tree not inspire— its shimmering bees clinging to full-blown lotuses, its beauty enhanced by clusters of slightly awakened lilies, and its base entwined with various marvelous garlands?
He beheld a stainless lake filled with blossoming lotuses,
like a crystal mirror for the amorous dalliances of the forest goddesses.
Her face was like a full-blown lotus, her eyes like opening blue water-lilies;
her lips were as lovely as the bandhūka flower, and her breasts like clusters of mandāra blossoms.
As delicate as the *śirīṣa* flower, like a song composed of five flowers,
she was fashioned by Smara as the singular arrow capable of conquering the entire world.

May Hari, beheld by the continuous succession of Radha’s sidelong glances— which captivate with the splendor of swarms of bees emerging from the center of a blossoming lotus pond— graciously bestow all your desires and happiness.
O lovely *sahakāra* tree, friend of the *rasāla*, abode of flocks of warbling cuckoos,
act in such a way that the humming and wandering bee, having fixed its thirst upon you, shall not go to other trees such as the *picumanda* or the *karīra*.
The pollen born of lotuses, wafted from that grove of full-blown land-lotuses and whirled about in the sky on all sides by the winds, assumes the splendor of a golden parasol.
The full-blown *navamālikā* flower intoxicates, delighting the sense of smell; the dark cluster of blossoms on the *kiṃśuka* tree has turned greyish-white.
Intoxicated bees gather honey from the pale *kadamba* flowers, while the perspiration, beaded like drops of water, finds its place upon the full, firm breasts of women.

Salutations to that Supreme Person, the ornament of Raghu’s lineage, who possesses a splendor that destroys the cycle of existence; who is as dark as the petals of a full-blown, tender blue lotus; who is the fulfiller of the desires of beautiful women's hearts; whose collection of pure virtues is manifested for the first time; who is the very soul of Rāma; who is a swan in the lake of the minds of the great sages established in yoga; and who possesses vibrating power.

Now those very days have arrived, which bear the splendor of the transition between the departure of summer heat and the onset of rain: days when the eastern gale blows, scented by the blossoming *arjuna* and *sarja* trees; days when rows of clouds, glossy as fragments of sapphire, surge and stumble along; and days when the earth is made fragrant by showers drenching it.

In this garland, the abode of fragrance, which is both lovely and pervasive—filled with full-blown *bakula* flowers, *lavaṅga* buds, *śephālikā* calyxes, clusters of blue lotuses, and *vicikila* blossoms—why do you, O charming *kusumbha*, vainly display your scentless state in its midst? This course of action is by no means fitting for you.

O gentle one, having placed her lute upon a stand or on a soiled garment, my beloved’s sister, desiring to sing a song composed with verses concerning me, somehow manages to tune the strings wet with tears; yet, though she herself repeatedly performs the melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*), she forgets them again and again.
The rivers bear clusters of rose-apple trees with their long, hanging tresses of ripening fruit, their sandy banks marked by the tracks left by hundreds of birds;

and the breeze, its body bristling as it swings upon the waves of the water, stretches its neck in eager longing for the fragrance of the granthiparṇa flowers being chewed by the musk deer on the banks.

O ornament of the illustrious Sena dynasty, our house is like that of your enemy: its roof is collapsed, its plaster is peeling away, its walls are crumbling, its circular ornaments are falling; it swarms with rats and rows of frogs sporting in their playgrounds, while the flapping wings of a multitude of old leather shields begin to emit a hollow *bhāṃ-bhāṃ* sound.
When shall we behold with stainless eyes this ruined marketplace,
where the wish-fulfilling gem and a piece of glass possess inverted qualities of merit and defect?
The mango grove is flourishing with the cries of cuckoos; this [spring] is also flourishing with the Malaya breezes—we have known this even before.

O travelers, why are you so deluded as to think you must be satisfied by that alone? If the god of love still lives, however slight his existence may be, let this parched obsession with life depart from your breaths.
May the hosts of yakṣas—those who possess great swords and axes, and those with terrifying foreheads—be victorious; through them, may you, O Ilāpī, conquer the villages, the cow-pens, and the earth.

When the darkness, possessing the luster of rising streaks of smoke, has pervaded the sky with the stars appearing like faint sparks, the Lord of Day has reached the western quarter; as his beloved lotus plants—now bent down as if in grief with their tongues of bees faltering—he enters the fire of the twilight glow, and the beauty of the day is consumed.
Even for the base, a quarrel is more pleasant than a festival;
having gained even half a cowrie shell, the clever man considers himself highly successful.
Those who possess faith, are self-controlled, wealthy, and perform auspicious deeds go from festival to festival, from heaven to heaven, and from happiness to happiness.
He who stands by one during a festival, in times of calamity, during a famine, in the face of an enemy threat,
at the king’s gate, or in the cremation ground— he is a kinsman.

In a house where all doors are barred by a fondness for clearing them out, they dwell without restraint; their intellects made light by prosperity, they do not realize—due to their unimpeded conduct—the sudden onset of destiny through their own impetuosity.
Driven away from their cheeks by the radiance of smiles, as if shaken off from their breasts by single-strand pearl necklaces,
the darkness— deprived of the pleasure of enjoyment upon their limbs— seizes hold of women in their braided tresses as if out of rage.

Homage to that meritorious Malaya breeze, to whom these languid young women— having pushed back their locks of hair, cast aside the edge of their silk garments, and raised their creeper-like arms— long with their bodies drenched in perspiration.
In the *kanduka* time-measure (*tāla*), there should be energy (*utsāha*) within the comic sentiment (*hāsya-rasa*).
The foot [of the verse] consists of thirteen syllables, which effect the increase of the bamboo lineage;
in the *kanduka* time-measure, there are two short syllables (*laghu*) ending with a pause.

Having performed her rite of adornment at the words of her friends who incited her enthusiasm, the girl, fair as gold, set out for the home of her lord; yet even so, the innocent maiden still bears a heavy trembling in her heart.
O Bhārata, a king endowed with the powers of energy, sovereignty, and counsel should march forth; otherwise, he should do the opposite.
For energetic men, even if weak, will surely slay a powerful enemy when they join together; in this same way, these five [monkeys] shall kill the elephant.
For men who possess enthusiasm do not falter in this world, even when faced with extremely difficult tasks.

Fortune herself approaches that man who possesses a mass of valor and fortitude joined with the power of enthusiasm— one who regards the ocean as no larger than a cow’s footprint and the king of mountains as merely like the crest of an anthill— but not one of feeble spirit.
Due to a lack of energy and power, both an old man and one afflicted by a chronic illness are undoubtedly despised even by their own kin.
Prosperity herself desires to dwell with one who is endowed with enthusiasm, free from procrastination, knowledgeable in the performance of duties, unattached to vices,
heroic, grateful, and firm in friendship.
They say that the three powers of the king consist of energy, majesty, and counsel;
likewise, there are three types of prosperity for oneself, one's friends, and one's allies.
O child, as I behold both your extraordinary energy and your youth,
my mind is simultaneously overcome by joy and sorrow.
Encouraged by the intoxication of all the liquor, the young bride, though still clinging to her modesty as the sun half-risen,
failed to complete her speech before her circle of friends and thereby aroused an especially great curiosity in her husband.
For kings who have lost their enthusiasm, for robbers seeking victory,
and for those distressed by a lack of means, the Caraka bird is always an auspicious omen.

The mass of pearls, released from their breaking threads as they were displaced by her necklace turning in the whirlwind of her vigorous and exuberant dance, clung to the slopes of her breasts; appearing like a continuous stream of nectar-drops falling from the moon of her face, they momentarily took on the beauty of the thick drops of perspiration arising from the exertion of her passion for dancing.
O Noble One, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm.
By the mere initiation of enthusiasm, all prosperities are born.
O Noble One, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For one possessed of enthusiasm, nothing at all in the worlds is difficult to attain.
Zeal is like a friend to one's enemies; laziness is like an enemy to one's friends.
Knowledge is like nectar; women are like poison that resembles nectar.

Intoxicated by the nectar of flowers, embracing at night the blooming *kumudinī*—the beloved queen of the moon—and fearlessly cultivating intimacy with her tender shoots, the breeze quickly departed while gathering all the fragrance of the lotus; yet when dawn arrived, this very wind now flees in every direction out of fear.

On one hand, my arrival here draws me toward this man—who is exalted and a treasury of ascetic power and valor—through my love for the company of the virtuous and my own intoxication with heroic ardor;

on the other hand, this embrace of Vaidehī, which repeatedly causes my consciousness to fade away, checks that impulse from another side, being as blissful and cool as Haricandana sandalwood and the moon.
All living beings would perish if they did not perform action;
likewise, they would not even increase if action were to be fruitless.
Having abandoned your bed of flowers, with the covering for your breasts made of lotus petals,
how will you go out into the heat when your limbs are so delicate that they are easily oppressed?
Abandoning their songs before they were finished, leaving off their graceful dances, and suddenly casting aside their jeweled lutes,
the women of the city, their minds intensely agitated by the curiosity to behold him, ascended to the windows.
Having relinquished their entire essence of water, the clouds— now pure and white in form— abandoned the sky just as yogins cast off the body.
O dear one, kinsmen, friends, and sons turn back and depart,
just as birds leave trees that have neither flowers nor fruit.
He who, with a crooked mind, deceives another by abandoning virtuous conduct,
is himself the one deceived— by his own foolish intellect, which has failed to perform good deeds.

How can this wonder be described— that the lotus-eyed Lord, who for a long time observed the vow of gazing upon the pleasure of the lotus-face of the Ocean-born goddess and slept upon the waters of the sea, has now awakened from his serpent-couch during the festival of the cool-rayed autumnal moon?

Having taken up the jewels of pride cast off by the lotus-eyed women, this mango tree, through the pretext of the sweet warbling of the male cuckoo, spreads forth a declaration of its intent toward the swarms of bees that are like floods of honey-water.
Just as water in a jar that has been brought into contact with fire undergoes agitation,
churning, and heat, so too does it become affected in that very same way.
Just as a bird from the sky takes on the qualities of its material environment, so too does the soul, overcome by the sense of "I," assume the natural qualities;
yet that soul remains immutable even when seemingly divided from them.
This treatise, written with great difficulty, should be preserved with care from water, fire, thieves, and especially from mice.
All seeds are contained in water; all gods are contained in their own Lord;
all happinesses are contained in a wife; and all dharmas consist of compassion.
All seeds are contained in water; all gods are contained in fire;
all forms of happiness are contained in a wife; and all gifts are contained in a brahmin.
Upon speaking with a menstruating woman, one who has fallen from his caste, a barbarian, a *cāṇḍāla*, or others;
upon touching a cat or a mouse; and upon seeing the voiding of feces or urine; [one must perform purification].

That Lakṣmaṇa, who possessed a noble lineage and honored his ancestral line, whose fierce array of pure warriors was formidable, who surpassed the god of love by the perfection of his own form, and who shone with the auspicious marks of a great man; that great king— MSS_6691-1 udagragotāvatagotragauravo mahārajaḥ pūtabhaṭotkaṭacchaṭaḥ / MSS_6691-2 svarūpasampattiparāstamanmathaḥ sa lakṣmaṇo lakṣitalakṣaṇojjvalaḥ //
If a dog barks facing the east at midnight, it portends affliction for the twice-born and the death of cattle;
if it faces the northeast at the end of the night, it indicates the violation of young girls, miscarriages, and fire.

O fierce Agastya’s daughter, these winds blow in the month of Caitra—winds that roll about in the embrace of the surging waves of the Kāverī, terrifying the elephants in exile by the powerful roar of lions with throats like those of the cuckoo; and winds made fragrant by the *hallīsaka* dance of swaying creepers upon the jasmine vines in the playful dalliance of youthful Aśvinī.
May she whose hips are exultant with the shimmering jeweled girdle-bands resounding with upward-sweeping *huṃ* sounds;
who is the object of compassion; who is the source of the consecration of the crest-jewel of liberation; and who is the flame that destroys the world’s suffering—may she be our companion.

He beheld the beauty of the lake—sweet with the humming of swarms of bees summoned by the thick fragrance of lotuses awakened by contact with the rising rays of the sun—and thought: "The family of frogs dwelling in the hollows of the bellies of the blind lives happily, for they are devoted to their food of nectar."

How could that age of the lotus-eyed girl not constantly distress the mind— she whose hips are shaken by the weight of her two upward-turning breasts, who has eclipsed a pair of shimmering blue lotuses with her sparkling eyes, and who displays the arching curve of her eyebrows like the drawn bow of the God of Love?

Let my words, sweet with sweetness, indeed not rise up; nor let my new compositions, so fortunate as to be blessed by you, blossom forth. Yet, if for even a moment I could bring you into my heart under the pretext of praise, then by that alone my soul would surely attain purity.

I consider the lovemaking of the lotus-eyed woman to be blessed— lovemaking accompanied by the sweet tinkling of her girdle blending with the rising sound of her anklets, her bracelets jingling as charmingly as the humming of a swarm of bees, and beads of perspiration falling from her breasts onto the strings of pearls, while her curls sway to and fro.
Raise the corner of your eye so that the swarm of bees may flutter; pour forth the nectar of your speech so that it may embrace the rim of my ears.
O city-dweller, dance your brow so that the God of Love may cast aside his bow; turn your face toward me so that the moon may suffer in comparison.
"Turn your glance upward; compose yourself; here before you, after a long time, has arrived your beloved.
Hearing these words of her lover, her ears bristling with thrills of joy, her dear friend reveals her eyes to us through a feigned doubt.
The ocean is the limit of the earth, yet Hanumān crossed that limitless sky;
thus all things appear to have their bounds, but the discernment of the virtuous alone is one and limitless.
Like jewels from the ocean or rays of light from the sun,
your far-reaching deeds transcend all praises.

The earth is bounded by the ocean, and that reservoir of waters is but a hundred *yojanas* deep; the sun, ever a traveler, measures the extent of the sky—thus, for the most part, all things are closed in by the seal of a manifest limit. Yet, this boundless flash of wisdom belonging to the wise triumphs.
That lord who is known by those who depend on him to be as unshakeable as the ocean—
what other shame could there be than that he is overcome before others?
The conqueror of Kaiṭabha rose from his bed with the luster of a white lotus that had blossomed,
as if by the moon-like face of the daughter of the Nanda king who had first awakened, possessing the brilliance of cool-rayed moonlight.
Having attained its rising and become difficult to behold due to its sharpness,
the sun does not indeed settle at the feet of the earth when it is possessed of pride.
Whose heart would not feel longing for those who, as rulers, attain their rise only through collective effort and meet their end likewise through collective effort?
When the eastern sky has turned pale with the first light and the night follows the peak of the western mountain,
there now triumphs an indescribable splendor in the midst of the heavens, like the waters of the Ganges and the Yamunā mingled together.
Having awakened the lotus-beds from the slopes of the Eastern Mountain with the tips of his exceedingly soft rays and having enjoyed them himself, the Sun—
having become flushed with the blood-like glow of the wrath he felt toward the bees who had soiled him with their departure from those beds— has gone to his setting.

May that Lord bring you joy—He who, stationed upon the crest of the Eastern Mountain, ceaselessly fashions this entire world free from disease while it is stupefied by sleep; He whose mass of spreading rays dispels immeasurable darkness and the violence of poverty.
When the darkness has been driven far away by the rays of the moon hidden behind the eastern mountain,
the face of the goddess whose vehicle is the monkey (Hanumān) captivates me, as if her two eyes were drawing back her disheveled tresses.
This eastern quarter, veiled by the edge of the rising slope, indicates the Lord of Night,
just as a beautiful woman, with her face turned pale, reveals the lover dwelling within her heart.

This moon, the light of cool rays and the southern eye of the world, rises with its slow and deep throat-rhythms, manifesting the humming of bees within the lily buds; he is the one who performs the service of water for the cakorī birds made vocal by passion.

The friend of Rati rises, variegated like lightning; having placed her body beneath a pair of blooming lotuses upon two plantain stalks like new pillars, the sky flashes with lightning, and the two mountains resting in the sky appear on the mountain slopes; the conch shell rests upon the conch shell, and the orb of the moon, the treasury of arts, rests within the conch.
If darkness persists even when the sun has risen, tell me, how can there be any distinction between day and night?
O Blessed One, if karma is indeed insurmountable, what is accomplished by the remembrance of Your feet?
When the moon of childhood has come to rest, the sun of youth rises;
the pair of cakravāka birds that are the breasts meet together upon the river of maidenhood.
The moon rises, white as a mass of fresh butter, striking the beds of night-lotuses with the tips of its rays;
it is the loud laughter bursting from the slopes of the mountain of sunrise, the mirror for the face of the bride that is the night.
Even if the sun were to rise in the western quarter, even if Mount Meru were to shake, even if fire were to turn cold,
and even if a lotus were to bloom upon a rock on a mountain peak— nevertheless, the speech of the virtuous is never redundant.
As the sun rises with its cord of widespread upward rays and the moon sets,
this mountain bears the grace of a lordly elephant attended by two hanging bells.
Indeed, the moon rises—pale as the cheek of a loving woman, surrounded by a host of planets, and serving as a lamp for the royal road;
amidst the mass of darkness, its white rays fall like streams of milk from a cloud that has shed its water.
You should not again place me, who am as tender as the interior of a *bakula* bud, into the hands of one in whose heart there is no shame, no compassion, and not even a trace of fear.
How many times did the eye of the fickle-eyed woman not dart back and forth at the moment of her husband’s rising, as it was being restrained by shame—
just like the mind of a miser at the time of giving?
Let the clouds indeed rise; let night fall; let the rain descend incessantly.
With my heart turned toward my beloved, I do not take any of this into account at all.
Rising, this sun bestows beauty upon the lotuses in order to manifest the fruit of his supernatural powers: the favoring of his friends.
The lord of sūris, Udayaprabha, renowned for the dawning of his genius,
shines forth as the creator of various divine compositions.
While the lord of sūris, Udayaprabha, illumines the earth,
all other scholars everywhere appear as if devoid of luster.
Rising, it utterly dispels the gloom; it brings an end to the seal of sleep and sets all activities in motion.
Alas, alas! This mass of radiant splendor shines forth, performing the severing of the impulse toward unrestrained conduct.
The moon, whose brilliance was once radiant with rising joy when it met me, now falls away;
having gone elsewhere, it shines forth clearly in the eastern quarter like a flash of a woman’s smile, as if she were suddenly manifesting her indignation.

Having reached the peaks of the mountain of sunrise, this young sun, his lotus-like face smiling as he is gazed upon by the lotus-beds, descends from the sky with ease— his soft rays extended and accompanied by the warbling of birds.

While you, Udayasiṃha, the lord of the earth, shine forth, what need is there for the sun or even the moon? For with your own splendor you illuminate the world, and with your own fame you cool it as well.
The thousand-rayed sun has risen; it is time for you to go from sight. When, or whom, do women not overcome with their excessive charms?
Having flown from the mountain of sunrise and wandered throughout the day,
this sun now, at the time of evening twilight, offers its own body as an oblation into the submarine fire.
Among them, the two [asterisms] named Mūla are the rising and setting; those called Dhruva and Nivāsa are the northern and southern;
and those named Prayāṇa and Caraka are the southwestern and northwestern.
The sun is red at its rising, and likewise red at its setting;
so too, great beings maintain the same disposition in both prosperity and adversity.

With his fist, the thumb extended from between the four fingers, he pressed down upon her belly, creating three beautiful folds at its center; thus did he fashion the abdomen of Damayantī, whose waist and back were sunken.
Does some curious person measure Damayantī’s belly with his fist?
For it shines with folds that appear like four fingers held there along with a golden girdle.
Was the moon not held within the belly of the ocean, though as treacherous as the submarine fire?
Even when cast out by him like poison, did not the all-powerful Śiva, the destroyer of Smara, consume it?
The cavity of the belly is a dense thicket where everything that enters dissolves away somewhere;
and there dwells a single serpent who, being wicked, whom does she not cause to lament?
If he had not married out of fear of having to support two bellies,
how could his son still be a youth even today?
O boar, that you fill your belly in this world is seen to be difficult for anyone else to accomplish,
since you eat even excrement and make it delicious.
If this smallness of the belly and this innate heaviness of the heart were not so,
how could there be such laziness regarding its own interest, and how could its mind be so devoted to performing what is beneficial for others?
One should never consume anything merely for the sake of the belly;
for even if its color is the same, a swan does not eat fish like a crane.
Indeed, by virtuous men desiring prosperity in the future, the forehead-slip of another's wife is not to be looked upon, just like the crescent moon on the fourth day.

When her steadfastness was cast aside by her lover who entreated her with devotion, the face of the lady with the arched brows— its eyes closed and its tears warded off by the water from his hands— seized the beauty of her rival’s face as it were.
O friend jackal, you raised your tail high, placed it upon your head covered in matted hair, and devoured morsels of the flesh of an elephant that had perished by chance;
you dwelt for a long time within the empty depths of a cave. What can we do about this, since you have not attained equality with the lion?
"As long as I have my weapon raised, what is the use of other weapons?
Or rather, if something cannot be accomplished by my own weapon, by whom else will it be achieved?"
A generous person of noble conduct is more wretched when asked for alms than a miser;
for one gives away wealth, while the other gives away his very life, and life is more precious than wealth.
To the noble, wealth is as grass; to the hero, death is as grass;
to the dispassionate, a wife is as grass; to the desireless, the entire world is as grass.
O Pārvatī, I see no others more noble than you;
grant me the ruby of devotion to Śrī Rāma, even though it is not to be given away.
When, having worshipped with love Candraśikhara— whose peak is fashioned from noble mandāra flowers— my body adorned with a profusion of horripilation,
shall I honor the Lord with words of praise resonant with the humming of wild bees, exultant and intoxicated by the binding of fragrances?
Though she is indifferent to those who cling to her, yet in their words she is dissolved; though she is overcome by exquisite shame, she is led by the path of piteous entreaties.
Seated in the hearts of poets like the moon, this fresh fish-eyed maiden agitates the minds of even sages.
The Lord who crushed Madana remains indifferent; he has made the common folk his attendants while being intent on the sport of the Kali age within the families of the virtuous.
This river of the gods is now overrun by barbarians on both its banks; tell me, O brother, O doer of good deeds, where can one remain free from fear? Tell me!
An example [is found] in benedictions: "Of those high-minded men, you are the foremost, by whom indignation is cast upon enemies like a thunderbolt upon dry wood."
The words spoken with affection toward his beloved were trusted by the lover;
for when one's song is already known, words uttered even before the person is present truly take root.
The orb of the moon has risen; immediately thereupon, the host of those separated from their lovers has wept, while Madana—the crest-jewel of all women—has rejoiced at his command.
The risen moment resorts to its setting; everything that is created meets with dissolution.
All fruits fall from the tree; every river flows into the ocean.
The thousand-rayed sun, risen and joyful, destroys the darkness with its rays; yet the accumulated gloom expands again and again.
This darkness does not cease, nor does the sun sit idle; for the wise, whose enmity toward it has blossomed, do not remain indifferent under any circumstances.
When the king of the twice-born has risen, in whose heart do joys not find a place?
O lotus, that you wither—alas, alas! Fate is adverse toward you.
When the supreme cognition, which is the source of the scriptures, has arisen, and the natural world of manifold diversity has dissolved away,
who— even a scholar— is capable of saying that the solitary cognition that has suddenly emerged is "this much"?
When you, who bring delight to the eyes, have risen like the moon,
the faces of the enemy's women become like moonstones, raining down incessant drops of water.
O Lord of the Earth, it is a marvel that even when your majesty has risen as the sun, possessing a vast burden of spreading rays,
the masses of infamy belonging to your enemy kings continue to manifest with shimmering intensity.
When the sun has risen, one should fix the target in the west;
and in the afternoon, the target should be placed in the eastern direction.
My mind has been struck by the cries of the cuckoos that have arisen;
O messenger, it is likewise struck by your words and even by the southern breezes.
Even when risen at the edge of the sky amidst a dense mass of frost, the sun does not shine,
like a lamp placed upon the rim of a shallow bowl filled with hardened ghee.
The body of the fair-eyed woman, distressed before her husband with trembling and a sinking heart due to shame,
yet proclaiming an excess of affection, became intensely bewildered as to how to respond.
In the north there is the production of crops, while in the south there is the destruction of the harvest;
for those departing from their homes, the east is auspicious, and the south is favorable for the fields.

A meaning expressed is grasped even by a beast; horses and elephants carry when urged. A wise person infers what has not been spoken; for the fruits of intelligence lie in understanding the intentions of others.
O Bhārata, in whichever army the warriors and mounts are high-spirited,
victory will certainly belong to that side.
Even when words of consolation were uttered, Rādhikā’s pride was not removed;
"Let your pride remain if I were an offender, but even in a dream I am not an offender at all."
Whoever personally plants eight udumbara trees,
or even encourages others to plant them, rejoices in the world of the Moon.
Time, which always devours universes like *udumbara* fruits and strips away all pride— who are we, mere mosquitoes, before it?
A thick mass of clouds has arisen, a flock of peacocks dances, lightning flashes on all sides, and the ketaki-scented breeze blows;
yet, my friend, if he has still not come, I think that now the fish-bannered god holds his bow with its string broken.
First the flower appears, then the fruit; first the rising of the clouds, then the rain. This is the sequence between cause and effect; but in your case, prosperity precedes your grace.
"Which auspicious lunar day (tithi) can be attained by the meritorious, in which the enemy—the moon—does not rise?
To her who lamented thus repeatedly with distress, the cuckoo cried out "Kuhū! Kuhū! as if in response.
The sun rises copper-red and sets copper-red as well;
for the great, there is uniformity in both prosperity and adversity.
Among all twelve kings,
he alone, not abandoning his rising luster, is fit to conquer them just as the sun alone among the Ādityas is fit to do so.
The paths of the moonstone pavements, moist with droplets of the luster of the rising nectar-rayed moon and bearing the thick footprints of red lac,
reveal at every step the backward glances of immodest women, whose movements were suddenly interrupted by the flight of *cakora* birds.
The humming of bees rises like the sound of the bowstring of Smara; the clusters of blossoms on the *kaṅkelli* tree emerge, as treacherous as poison-smeared arrows.
O travelers, look! Now the mango tree unfolds its impurity with vehemence, its sprouts quivering with a web of buds like a messenger of Death.
"O friend, this row of foam rising from the agitation of churning the ocean of milk is described by the ignorant as a garland of stars."

The people gazed insatiably upon the night, in which the darkness was pierced by the risen moon, just as one looks at a newlywed bride whose face is half-revealed by her loosened garment and who is deeply abashed with shame.
In his rising, sitting down, lying down, turning over, and moving about,
my beloved— clinging to my heart like a breath— constantly deludes me.

Just as this sound rises loudly, piercing the path of hearing— exalted by the continuous, impetuous lashing of the lordly elephants of the water roaring within— and making all the interior regions of the mountain caves resonant with echoes, so too does this ocean tide generally approach, encircled by countless, tossing branches of coral.
Roaring, crooked, and violent as you uproot the trees on your banks, do not be so arrogant, O river current, thinking, "I shall agitate the ocean!
If you desire your own existence, wander instead in the deserts or remain right there; for far off lies the submarine fire (*vāḍavāgni*), but here, the great beings swallow you as you enter.
The orb of the moon, resembling the impression left by the pressing of the high and low breasts of a young Hūṇa maiden during the amorous play of coition,
reveals the first foot of Viṣṇu with its foremost rays, which are as pale-white as a mature lotus stalk.

Having taken up the betel-roll and covered her bosom with the hem of her garment, the girl with the arched brows, while drawing off her tight bodice, captivates the mind even of the God of Love himself.
The *udgrāha* may belong to one musical mode (*dhātu*), while the *dhruvaka* belongs to another;
the *melāpaka* may belong to one mode, and the *ābhoga* to another.
Indeed, this fourfold structure is what is proclaimed by the wise as a *rūpaka*.
And the placement [of the syllables] in the first section of the *udgrāha* is considered the *dhruvaka*;
thus, the six-pada *uttama-dhravaka* has been described by the wise.
The *udgrāha* and the *dhruvaka* should come first, followed by the *ābhoga*;
the wise should know that there are three types of *niyama* for the *maṇṭhaka*.

The way she looked with neck uplifted, her body languid with shame as she went before her friends, and that indistinct speech she uttered—O my vital breaths, why have you departed through separation? Why have you adopted such cruelty? If it is right to remain [in life] by remembering that, then alas, you yourselves are my authority!

With neck upturned and eyes fixed, looking here and there as he stood concealed, his wing-tips quivering, the crane moving about the lake suddenly brought the minnow— terrified and bewildered by the mutual trampling of their feet—
into the interior of its belly, having first tossed it upward and sideways with the force blunted by the tip of its open beak.

With necks outstretched, the cavities of their mouths wide open and reddened, their palms fluttering from thirst, and their bodies trembling because they lack wings, the young *śarāri* birds take flight slightly from the ground at dawn; crowding one another on the riverbank, they drink the dewy water trickling through channels formed by hollows in the blades of *vīraṇa* grass.
He whose right eye is opened and then rubbed with the hand by a Yakṣa during his consecration shall,
by his own power, have his lotus-feet gazed upon by a hundred thousand lords of the earth.
When the bird of the vital breath remains within a cage whose nine doors are wide open, that is a marvel; what cause for astonishment is there in its departure?
If, having opened his right eye, he licks his own navel while mounted [on a cloud],
or sleeps wakefully upon the roof of a house, then the cloud will pour forth abundant water.

May that Mukunda—who, when the sheath of the heart-lotus is opened by the art of yoga, is grasped according to one's desire even after a long time by the fortunate; who, possessing a perfectly full form, vibrates incessantly—grant me eternal welfare.

Your hand possesses the beauty of the tender bud of an upturned *kokanada* lotus; its forearm is bristling with thrill from grasping the hair of your beloved; and it bestows honor, gifts, fear, and enjoyment upon your circle of friends, the twice-born, your enemies, and the women of pleasure.
When your staff-like arm, the bow, flashes forth,
the circles of enemies, the orb of the sun, and the breasts of Rambhā all tremble.

As if their intensity were rendered futile by the rays of the fiercely blazing garland of suns, the shadows now gather into a single mass at the roots of the trees; moreover, this lake possesses a false parasol of sunlight created by the flocks of birds flying up in agitation from being splashed by the plunging of the wives of the demon king.

Seeing the multitude of women distressed by separation, the tree, out of compassion, seems to say "Do not, do not" to the flock of cuckoos with its branches violently shaken by the forceful southern wind, as if to restrain their crying out.

May the boisterous laughter of Śambhu as he dances—whose outburst of light from his unrestrained teeth causes the half-moon’s crescent to blossom forth, and which swallows up the spreading darkness that obstructs it—grant you prosperity; its roar is as deep as the rumbling of a mass of rain clouds.
The world became as if breathless and agitated by the trumpeting of herds of elephants in rut, by the excessive neighing of tall horses, and by the rattling of the rims of moving cloud-like chariots.

The darkness, resembling clusters of bees rising from the temples of the wild elephants of the quarters whose ears are flickering, possesses a luster like that of musk; closing up the sky, it shines intensely within the caverns of the directions.

Frightful are these empty quarters at midday, where the slopes of the mountain ridges are thick with the mass of flames from sun-stones playing in the intense contact with the rays of the fierce sun; where lapwings shriek out; and where the cruel glare of the sun's rays, floating upon the heat of the earth, brings to an end the life-span of one’s eyes—fie on them!
That very lion, by whom the elephant—whose trunk was like a wild tree and whose tusks were deep-set—was struck down, now abandons the forest due to the deceptive actions [of others].
Therefore, neither affection nor skill, neither battle nor patience, leads to the exhaustion of the mind; rather, for this treasury of honor, it is better that he takes refuge in the forest.

The breezes from Lake Pampā— honoring the sky with the fragrance of lotus stalks uprooted by wild elephants, enriched by winds from the rows of wings flapping as they are stirred by *kalahaṃsa* geese,
and touching the pride of the thick, low-hanging necks of cranes stretched out in the distance— smear the quarters of the world as if with droplets of liquid camphor.

May the Lord, the director of the drama of the destruction of the three worlds—who, having fashioned a cage encircled by the rows of cloud-poles from which the waters of the celestial river fall through the channels of his matted-hair vines spread wide by the force of his violent whirlwind; and who acts as a swan with the pair of wing-spreads formed by his whirling staff-like arms—protect the universe.

O lotus-eyed one, since you have come from the inner apartments of Karṇa— during a time when the quarters of the sky were devastated by the blinding darkness censured by the unrestrained clouds, and when a tumultuous clamor was raised by fierce warriors kept awake by sentries— I consider the fear felt by women to be merely feigned, for he is like the submarine fire to the ocean waters of his enemies.

O lake, when the onset of the rains brings water even to dry lands— lands tumultuous with the excessive cries of peacocks excited by the swelling of fierce clouds— if you do not protect the wretched shoals of fish that are repeatedly observed out of mutual fear during the terrible summer season, what essence is there in you?

Where has that roar of the great ocean gone—that clamor of the waves which once caused a fever in the ears of travelers whose eyes were blinded by the intense rays of the sun and whose minds were kept awake by clutching at the shore?
And where has it now vanished, as it entered the hollow of the mouthful of water being sipped by the Sage, his mind having transcended all afflictions?

O traveler, in this wilderness—where the interior is turned to ash by the jewels of the sun-gem blazing with the fierce rays of the sun; where dust is scattered and strewn with masses of sparks from a fire fanned on all sides by the wind; and which is afflicted by kings—somewhere on the road, at the tip of a needle belonging to a cloud-army, there is a group of six wells, above them a city, and therein the flow of the Gaṅgā.

Beholding this garden creeper today— like another woman filled with passion— with its unrestrained blossoms, its pale luster, its sudden yawns, and its exhaustion manifested by incessant sighs of breath, I shall surely cause the face of the Queen to take on a glow as crimson as anger.
As her friend was departing on some business, she— her brow curved with feigned anger—
thus seized her ear-ornament so that it fell like a lamp struck out.
When a certain subject already mentioned, such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, is further contemplated in its increased state,
that which is produced from the elements (*dhātu*) and the primary constituents (*mātra*) is called a "subsequent interval" (*pratyantara*).
Though kindled, though lovely with a golden luster, though filled with oil, though well-sighted, though well-turned,
and though adorned by the glow of the breasts within the arms of a beloved woman, the lamp does not abandon its natural sootiness.
Victorious is this sage whose blazing fire digests within his belly the remaining waters of the ocean, which were somehow vomited out as another sea;

moreover, from that very gastric fire, as if by the process of being regurgitated at that moment, the submarine fire (Vāḍava) has emerged once more to go to Yama, having entered the depths of the waters.
This is the region of the Narmadā, where lovers find their pleasure beneath trees made lovely by the golden sands of its secluded banks;
moreover, O slender one, these breezes blow here as companions to amorous play, before whom the God of Love moves with his throat-throbbing anger aroused.
This region of the Narmadā surpasses the beauty of rows of succulent plantains, excels the splendor of forest groves, and evokes the amorous charms of lovely women;
moreover, O slender one, in this place blow those breezes which are friends to love-making, before whom the God of Love moves forth, manifesting sudden anger.
The haughty are capable of uprooting the arrogance of those whose souls are burdened by evil,
just as the power of alkaline substances alone serves to destroy the stains on garments.
As if impelled from both sides by the jar-like breasts pressed against one another,
the bodies of the women— possessing an extreme beauty through their graceful movements— reeled with excessive intoxication.

The continuous cooing of the fawn-eyed women— loud at times, silent at others, and varied— was heard as if it were being cut up, yet it remained entirely unbroken by the sounds of their tinkling girdles and anklets.
One should uplift oneself by means of oneself; one should not let oneself sink down. For oneself alone is one's own friend, and oneself alone is one's own enemy.

It is said that when the sun was deeply submerged there, the celestial women, out of longing, eagerly sought to retrieve the pearls from within the ocean that had been scattered during his impetuous mountain-sports;
having firmly bound them with their rays, he cast them up, and falling through the sky, they assumed the guise of stars.

Where the moon and sun are capable of lifting up the earth, of casting it from the path of the wind, of arresting the wind, of drinking the waters of the ocean, and of pulverizing a mountain—yet even these enter the mouth of Death; what then is the standing room for him? When even a mountain, along with its forests, goes into a subterranean hole, what stability can there be for a mere atom?
O Uddhava, you must by all means report this to Mādhava:
even a mansion of great value would not be equal to a grove on the Yamunā.

Having abandoned the feverish heat of the fire of desire, which is born of excessive faults, and having understood that the distinctions of the limbs of passion for the forest and such are merely mental constructs, women find delight in men.

These steeds carry the chariot through the limits of the sky, their hooves kissing the ground as they gallop with such persistence that the clouds of dust they raise allow one to infer their continuous motion; they bear it amidst a roar as terrible as the sound of the ocean being churned.

This rising column of smoke from the fire of Love, which torments the minds of those separated from their lovers; this row of musk-paste leaf-designs upon the faces of the women of the quarters, which are like a mass of darkness; this extinguished streak of poison from the day’s sacrificial fire; and this line of wandering bees—it all shines forth as the blue lotus of the sky, its stalk shaken by the rays of the sun.
Raising white dust from the depths of the earth, a whirlwind rose up and swirled in the sky,
like an arm lifted by the earth distressed by the heat of summer at the end of the hot season, as if uttering a loud hiss.
She is not fanned with a lotus leaf lest her slender body be agitated; she is not sprinkled with water infused with sandalwood paste for fear that a boil might break out;
fresh sprouts are generally not placed upon her breast lest they cause it to burst under their excessive weight. How, then, can the mental anguish of this delicate-bodied woman be assuaged?
"Her brow might be stirred by the breezes arising from the fluttering of her eyelashes"—
thus does her companion in separation gaze upon her face with unblinking eyes.
Even when their weapons have been drawn, a messenger does not speak otherwise;
those who speak exactly as they were told must not be executed by the ruler of the earth.
Even when weapons have been drawn, even when there has been slaughter among their kinsmen,
and even while uttering harsh words, messengers must not be executed by a king.
As the rays of the moon are being drawn forth, the earth emerges from the ocean of darkness,
with streaks of mud-like shadows clinging here and there.
Look at the rows of jackals, their necks outstretched among the trees filled with the thick darkness of night far from the funeral pyres;
they drink the thick, dripping fat-water from the circles of boiling corpses, which are being watched by the flickering light of torches emerging from the caves of their own mouths.
If even a lion endures being bound tightly and firmly,
then how is it that jackals bear the insignia of kings?
One who follows her husband, speaks like a man, dresses according to the signs of passion,
is not overly fleshy, is fond of wine, and is fickle in every respect.
The breeze, being fanned by lotus leaves, acts as either a relief for the burning of his heart— the dwelling place of her—
or as fuel for the fire of love.

By whom can happiness be found when they have come within the range of this base man— who has exposed every villain, who is utterly reckless, who by fate has obtained wealth while forgetting his previously committed lowly deeds, and who is a hater of virtue?
When the mass of blinding darkness is dispelled by the sun, those bees, charming with excessive honey from both sides, meet their destruction;
having slain the elephant and drunk much blood, the lions vomit out the bees that had been in the lamp-like frontal globes.
Having seen the swelling breasts and face of the fair-eyed woman, and her eyes that strip away the pride of bees,
the elder censures the Creator for being devoid of discernment.
What is this pair of blossoming lotuses, the playthings of King Manobhava (the God of Love)? How indeed could they have been produced from the single stalk of her shimmering line of body hair?
Even this pair of Cakravāka birds is unable to remain before the moon of her face; I perceive them to be the two frontal globes of the elephant of youth submerged in the waters of her loveliness.

O Mother, for those fawn-eyed women whose minds are filled with passion for fresh enjoyments— beautified by the splendor of forms made enchanting by emerging youth— their desired aims do not indeed come to pass when they are deprived of your instruction.

O slender one, may the nectars of the pleasure of your embrace— overflowing with the surging of manifested *sāttvika* emotions and instantly dispelling the pangs of love— manifest once more as my life has returned.

Her chest bears two budding breasts, and her lower lip, possessing the luster of the *madhūka* flower, seems to slightly smear its beauty upon the surface of her cheeks; it is filled with a charming splendor as youth approaches this deer-eyed maiden. Moreover, what more need be said? Her body exists with a lovely radiance, as if it were a fresh drop of the nectar of loveliness manifesting itself.

Adorned with beautiful clusters of blossoms like ear-ornaments, swayed by the blowing breeze, and possessing the luster of leaves and trunks shimmering with the dust of pollen cast forth by the flowers;
with songs rising from the deep-toned, impassioned fifth-note warbling of cuckoos, these trees sport as if celebrating a resurrection of the festival of Love.
O slender one, although that low humming (*kākalī-huṃkṛti*) emerging from the throat-cavity of the sweet-voiced cuckoo is heart-stealing, pouring nectar into the ears, and the sole abode of softness;

nevertheless, O fair one, it is your fifth note—ripened by its transformation, possessing a developed aesthetic flavor favored by the five-arrowed god of love after he was scorched by the three-eyed Shiva—that constitutes the offering of life itself.

Having first emerged as a swelling bud, then gradually attaining the state of a ripe jujube fruit, subsequently assuming the form of a *puṃnāga* flower, rising to the stature of a betel nut, and acquiring the splendor of a wood-apple;
having reached the likeness of a palmyra fruit and attained a graceful beauty, her two breasts now bear the full expansion of shimmering golden jars in the likeness of elephants.
In this pond, whose waters are crowded with swarms of agitated frogs, if there were indeed no other resort for the crane, he might stay;
but you, O royal swan, ought not to remain here, having abandoned lakes fragrant with full-blown lotuses.

Either I must exert myself in a manner befitting no coward, following my father’s path until death on the battlefield; or else, having snatched away the tears from the eyes of my own mother and kinsmen, I must lead them to the eyes of the wives of my enemies.
I would rather enter here into a fire that consumes the world with its rising rows of flames, or into the waters of the ocean teeming with crocodiles and sharks;

or I would enter a fierce battle where many preeminent warriors are struck down by various arrows—never, however, into the midst of the pleasures of women, which are skilled only in producing the infinite sufferings born of hundreds of existences.

Rising at nightfall—the moon who steals the beauty of the young sun—was recognized by his beloved lotus, half-asleep and caressed by his cool rays; overcome with passion and filled with shame, he turned pale as if in haste.
Seeing a raised weapon, one becomes overwhelmed and falls into despair;
terrified for one's life, there is no fear equal to that of death.

O moon-faced one, today you dance the *madraka*— with one hand and foot raised, the second hand gracefully executed, well-bent, sweet with the sounds of flutes, mṛdaṅgas, and other instruments, endowed with various wonderful movements, and manifold in its many forms— with beautiful, clever, and graceful gestures, your steps agitated by playful charm and permeated by refined aesthetic sentiments.
For one who rises up to strike another, who is arrogant and seeking a vulnerability, a fall is certain; rising again will be achieved only with great difficulty.
Indeed, it is not praised to oppose desire when it has already arisen;
how much less so for one who is attached to desire and bound by the pursuit of pleasure?
Wherever the king raises his sword, there alone is the protection of wealth;
one does not grasp the fruit from a tree whose branches are crowded with thorns.
One should exert oneself according to one's ability, but never become attached;
for the success or failure of those things to be accomplished is determined by destiny once they have been performed.
Even when weapons are raised, an envoy speaks not otherwise; for, by virtue of his perpetual immunity from being slain, he is indeed a speaker of the truth.
Even when weapons are raised, one should proclaim the teaching as it has been spoken;
one should discern passion and its absence through the expressions of the eyes, the face, and gestures.
May Kalki Hari— who wields a sword in his upraised hand, who is supremely skilled in destroying the darkness of the Kali age,
and who has arisen at the end of the night of Kali— protect you from all calamity.

May the rays of Kṛṣṇa’s feet protect [us]—rays that are capable of stealing away the splendor of the rising Lord of Stars (the Moon), crimson with thick sindūra, and rivaling the formidable trunk of the illustrious elephant; which possess an intense redness surpassing that of rubies, whose edges are variegated by the rows of the sun’s rays as they bend low from afar, and whose luster is doubled by the deep affection of clusters of guñjā berries.

O fair-limbed one, while your face—charming with the intoxication that surpasses the excellence of rising youth and wine, and a proliferation of eyes as beautiful as bees belonging to the five-arrowed god—is present, the moon remains of dull splendor and its light falters; even the lotus, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, does not attain a smile at night, being devoid of beauty.

Having gazed in every direction with joy at the mango trees, which were filled with the splendor of emerging sprouts and heavy with rising fragrance, the young cuckoo used to warble aloud; yet today, finding those very same trees made noisy by flocks of plundering crows eager for fruit, that same youth has become silent.

By the power of their well-performed merits, the foremost among mortals obtain through true good fortune a beloved woman who—emitting a continuous fragrance, possessing the essence of supreme bliss, warbling with the cooing of a cuckoo, and tender as a garland of flowers—surpasses even the wife of the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāmadeva) in beauty; she bestows upon all the senses their desired pleasure and is cherished within the mind.
When the mind is fixed on the unbearable thinning of its wealth, and the helpless person wanders impetuously down a wrong path, tumbling into a precipice,
alas, for such a creature, a favorable turn of fate— displaying a wound on the back of another’s chest as it falls— brings about the cessation of misfortune.

O friend, do not abandon the young girl, whose eyes are clouded by incessant tears falling from her high breasts, now that the rainy season has arrived—this season in which the peacock spreads its plumage, the frogs croak, the lives of travelers are exhausted, droplets of rain fall, the moon’s light is stolen, and the swans are driven away; a time when the splendor of the sun is swallowed by clouds as dark and formidable as Death himself.

O Lord, in every direction the beauty of its emerging young shoots is formed by the tusks of the elephants of the quarters; in this belly of the netherworld, it grows roots from the exceedingly white hoods of the lord of serpents;
and in this region of the sky, with the clusters of stars as its blossoming flowers, the creeper of your fame bears this fruit—the orb of the moon, moist with nectar.
Bearing a coppery luster through sprouts with the brilliance of rising coral, and assuming the playful sport of indistinct chatter through the sweet warbling of flocks of parrots;
these trees, swaying repeatedly with their masses of branches tossed by the restless Malaya breezes, now seem intoxicated by the onset of spring.

May the mass of matted locks of the bull-bannered Lord protect you— pregnant with the waters of the celestial river clinging to the expansive flash of the lightning-fire from his rising eye, and beautified by the crane-like splendor of the shining moon.
O lotus-heart, blossomed by the rising sun of discernment,
may devotion to the Blessed One enter you as Lakṣmī enters a lotus.
Let there indeed arise many great lights, and let even the moon be sufficient for adorning the circle of the world;
yet none other than the sun rises or sets—that by whose rising there is day, and by whose setting there is night.
May a hundred suns rise; may a hundred moons rise.
Without the words of the wise, the inner darkness does not perish.
The bows, being drawn by the archers with loud cries—harsh, thick, and held high in circular forms—were vigorously twanged;
meanwhile, the elephant-riders struck the heads of the elephants at will.
Rising daily and acting with haste, you dispel the darkness by drawing it away with your rays;
O Mitra, it is fitting that you are thus honored, for you are a man while others are weaklings.
Even as you rose, you destroyed the dense mass of darkness spreading over the world; you placed your footsteps upon the ridges of the pedestals of all the mountain peaks;
you surpassed even the moon and bestowed splendor upon the clusters of lotuses that had attained their beauty—may he live, or let his life be true life, who is like you.

Agitated by greed and disregarding the danger of death, he enters the midst of the ocean, where its swelling tide has risen high and where crocodiles, sea-monsters, and other creatures are utterly terrified by the various waves tossed up by the force of a great rising wind.
With the rows of rays from the rising sun, which resembled a king of the earth, and with the swarms of bees that were like his outstretched arms,
he utterly destroyed the vast accumulation of dense darkness.
A living being exerts effort, yet destiny is the cause in all things;
from the churning of the ocean, Hari obtained Lakṣmī and Hara obtained poison.
For men who exert effort, the fruit comes according to their fortune:
from the churning of the ocean, Hari obtained Lakṣmī, while Hara obtained the poison.
For men who exert effort, the fruit is like the action of a cat:
from birth onwards, a cow does not exist, yet it constantly drinks milk.
Exertion, quarreling, itching, gambling, liquor, other men's wives,
sleep, sexual intercourse, and laziness increase through indulgence.
Exertion, daring, fortitude, strength, intelligence, and valor—
if these six abide in one, even a god is afraid of him.
Through the power of exertion, various arts and skills are seen to flourish;
only the cowardly prattle that "whatever is destined to be, will be."
Another is the narrative titled "Exertion" (Udyama), as well as the miscellaneous narratives;
another is the narrative of the poetic riddle (samasyā), along with the praise of enigmatic puzzles (prahelika) and the like.
One who exerts effort attains success for certain, even if they are unqualified;
Anūru reaches the very end of the sky day after day.
One who exerts effort attains success even if devoid of assistance;
the sun, with its single-wheeled chariot and horseless charioteer, traverses the sky.
O King, without effort, one's desires are not fulfilled;
those who speak thus are cowards—whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass.
O King, without exertion, one's desires are not fulfilled;
for deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion.
For undertakings are accomplished through exertion, not by mere wishes;
indeed, deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion.
In exertion there is no poverty; for one who recites prayers, there is no sin;
through silence there is no quarrel; and for one who remains awake, there is no fear.
Tasks are accomplished through effort alone, not by mere wishes;
for deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion.
From the midst of the lotus pond, the bud of the dark blue lotus emerged,
as if shrinking away from the rivalry of the skillful glances of women.
The joy that flashes forth in the embrace of the celestial nymphs whose bodies are encircled by the splendor of rising loveliness, the weightiness of all sweetnesses found in nectar,
the fragrance in saffron, and the purity in water— O friend, if you desire to behold all of that gathered in one place, then look upon the poetry of Kṛṣṇa.

The circle of friends indeed rises up; the opposing forces indeed sink lower; the glories of fame indeed arrive; and virtuous reputations indeed spread in every direction—by that single path of your sword’s edge, whose moist tip has been revealed by the mere grazing of its point upon the surface, that very path, consisting of every marvel, is victorious!
A garden, moonlight, song, a beloved, play, and conversation with friends—
these are the enjoyments of heaven existing on earth for those who have attained success through their meritorious deeds.

There are pleasure gardens with forest grounds filled with fragrant, flowering trees; mountains with laughing waterfalls and artificial peaks dark as rain clouds; rivers with circles of waves swelling with cranes, serving as bathing places during the heat; and cool, fragrant breezes from the lotus ponds, which, through their contact with spray, become friends to those scorched by the summer sun.

O garden keeper, this is precisely the time for sprinkling water from jars upon this *campaka* tree. Whether it be destroyed by the summer heat or nourished by the rain from the clouds, your labor would be in vain in either case.
The pollen of mango and campaka flowers, stirred up by the garden breeze,
causes the eyes of travelers to well with tears, even though it does not touch them.
No cluster of blossoms has yet burst forth from the mango trees in the gardens;
let an offering of water mixed with sesame seeds be given to the wives of travelers.
The gardens do not always occupy them out of fear of being surpassed; indeed, they do not sit upon the ground as if dreading contact with dust.
Alas, what a pity! For these cuckoos of most venerable form, this state of being "nourished by others" (parapuṣṭatā) is surely the result of some past karma.
In the gardens, there are various methods of feasting; [elsewhere] there is most intense austerity, a loincloth as one’s only covering, fine garments, wandering for alms, and adornment.
Death is imminent and equal to a thunderbolt. Alas, why do the wise abandon that Kāśī and dwell elsewhere?
In the garden, the cuckoo desires to stay out of hope for the nectar of mango buds, for he is both the friend and the minister of the King born of the Mind (Kāma).
However, amidst the cawing of crows, the songs begun by the cuckoos, the *kreṅ-kāra* sounds, and the notes of the fifth scale (*pañcama*), the listener does not perceive the difference between them.
Alas, my exertion comes to naught and sudden dullness overwhelms me; even the sight of my friend is denied me—what more need I say?
That life which once attained the state of being desired by the world has now become useless; that foul day, like a stroke of ill fortune, pains my heart.
Diligence is like an enemy to laziness, which is like a friend;
knowledge is like nectar, while women are like poison.
Exertion, daring, fortitude, intelligence, power, and valor—
against one who possesses these six kinds of enthusiasm, even a god hesitates.
