Diligence, intelligence, fortitude, courage, truthfulness, renunciation, devotion, steadfastness, and dignity;
mastery over the senses, endurance, modesty, and eloquence—these are the preeminent qualities of the self.
For the wise man who does not turn back from exertion and possesses good companions,
prosperity follows him constantly like a shadow, as his constant companion.
Prosperity follows effort; fame follows generosity;
knowledge follows practice; and intellect follows action.
Prosperity comes to the industrious lion among men; "it is to be given by fate," say the cowards.
Overcoming fate, perform manly effort according to your own power; if success is not achieved despite the exertion, what fault is there in that?
The Goddess whose abode is the lotus extends a helping hand to the industrious; the elder sister of Lakṣmī extends a helping hand to those who lack industry.
If success is not found when a task has been performed with diligence, then fate is indeed the authority; yet human effort must always be exerted.
Without exertion, no task whatsoever is accomplished;
indeed, deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion.
As she was massaging him, the king’s gaze fell upon her heart and quickly withdrew,
as if seized by the neck by the crescent-moon-like nail-marks on her breasts, out of enmity toward those separated from their lovers.
Even though it is massaged in many ways and anointed with the essences of sandalwood, agallochum, and other perfumes, the body nevertheless remains foul-smelling; what is the cause of this?
The bees construct a honeycomb within the house to store their honey;
Durgā makes her nest there, and the earthworms would build an anthill.

May Annapūrṇā—who, when her own feet were placed upon the altar at her wedding, was joined by the Moon-crested Lord as he bowed before her, and who was instantly made full of food (Annapūrṇā) by the digit of the Moon;

she who, through the influence of the nectar-like eyes of Śiva and the fire of Śivā, brought to ripeness the unbroken grains of rice offered to her—may she bring fulfillment to the multitude of people who bow before her with various offerings.
People tremble before a man who speaks untruth as if before snakes;
truth is said to be the supreme dharma in the world and the very root of heaven.
Beholding her breasts drenched by the water splashed from the bud-like hands of her beloved, another woman,
out of indignation, repeatedly struck her own bride with the water released from her wide-open pair of eyes.
May the discus of Hari, its crimson stream flowing thick with blood gushing from the severed throat-pits of the haughty lords of the Daitya hosts,
and bearing the splendor of a sky made terrible by the conflagration of the quarters, grant you your heart’s desires.

Let this burden of uplifted breasts, these tremulous eyes, these flickering creeper-like brows, and this leaf of a sprout-lip—exceedingly red—indeed cause pain; but why does that line of body hair, situated in the middle like a row of letters of good fortune written by the Flower-Armed God himself, cause such excessive torment?
Her chest was heavy with the weight of her swelling breasts, yet she did not let her bodice slip; though their union was as it may be, she did not loosen her entire girdle.
"Where indeed might our meeting take place again?"—thinking thus, she did not raise her voice; by this hurried and agitated, fearful lovemaking, we have been utterly deceived.
At dawn, these villages—whose outskirts are filled with gathered heaps of grain, where the clusters of creepers and pods on the thatched huts are white with frost;

where the elders, their reddish beards soiled by continuous trails of cow-dung smoke, stand motionless against the walls seeking shelter from the sun while begging for alms—produce a sense of poignant distress.

For the warding off of distress, for the cutting away of evil, for the attainment of merit, for the drinking of the nectar of hearing, for the maintenance of steadfastness, and for the destruction of some particular affliction—one should repeatedly utter the names: "Puruṣottama, Acyuta, Hari, Govinda, Nārāyaṇa, Śrīvatsāṅka, Mukunda, Kṛṣṇa, Kamalākānta."
One who causes terror to living beings, being cruel and a doer of evil deeds,
does not remain [in power] even if he were the lord of the three worlds.
If one punishes too severely, it causes agitation; if too mildly, one is held in contempt.
Therefore, one should administer punishment according to what is deserved, without partiality.
A king who uses severe punishment causes agitation, while one who uses mild punishment is held in contempt;
therefore, a king who employs appropriate punishment is praised.
The jingling sound of the supreme seal terrifies the poor man,
just as the tinkling of a housewife’s anklets alarms her paramour when she has met with him in secret.
A king who employs harsh punishment causes living beings to tremble;
and living beings, being thus terrified, seek refuge with his enemies.
The wicked rule of that king who causes living beings to tremble quickly results in his being deprived of the lion-throne and reduced to a mere seat of *kuśa* grass.
Even on a path where the frost has turned to solid ice, the Aśvamukhīs do not break their slow gait, though they are pained by their heavy hips and breasts which press against the toes and heels.
Having herself unwrapped the letter, her fingers trembling with joy and perspiration, she saw that the sequence of the writing was blurred and indistinct by the moisture;
"What is this? Am I now destroyed? Such was his state! Alas, this is tears; alas, this is the trembling of my hand!"—saying this, she wept.
Unable to support her golden ornaments, encircled by its companion lotus-stalk fiber,
and burdened by the weight of the glances of a rival wife, the young woman’s arm became exceedingly heavy.
Saying that one who is insignificant will fall with ease even after attaining a high position,
a fragment of stone atop a mountain peak falls downward when shaken by a gentle breeze.
For one whose mind is elevated, fortune is likewise elevated;
for one whose mind is not elevated, fortune is likewise not elevated.
A lofty mansion, a horse of noble breed, honey, curd with sugar, milk,
the night, and the delicate digit of the moon— how can these be obtained when Śiva is not worshipped?
Whom did the heavy burden of breasts of the slender maiden not fill with longing— she who was elevated, possessed of shimmering nipples, and darkened by black aloe-paste?
Even though it is devoid of color, the rainbow attains beauty when situated amidst thick clouds;
for this reason, the wise long to dwell together with the great.
A female osprey with her right wing raised, her mouth full of food, and uttering a royal cry,
when she alights upon a tree, bestows more than what is desired.
A division does not arise among those who are elevated and of noble lineage as long as a woman does not enter their midst, like the edge of an axe.
Due to its state of being high and low, this moonlight on the mountain, mingled with darkness,
shines like the ash applied in various patterns upon a rutting elephant.
The moonlight rests upon the high places, while the night’s darkness is intent on taking refuge in the low;
surely the Creator himself has fashioned the course of virtues and vices according to their own nature.
Though lofty, pure, soft, and capable of removing cold,
and though possessing brilliant inner qualities, one who is destitute of wealth meets with contempt, like a bale of cotton.
The dull-witted servant, his vision blinded by craving, bows down for the sake of advancement; he stands outside to see the master’s house; he squanders his own wealth in the hope of future riches;
he risks his very life in battle merely to survive; and he exhausts himself through the desire for enjoyments—he performs everything that is quite the opposite of what is right.
Victorious is the soft murmuring of a woman for whom pride is her wealth: "Hum! Hum! Let go of me! uttered as her beloved forcibly raises her face by the hair and kisses it.
As she composes her steps, her face with one creeper-like eyebrow raised reveals her passion for me by means of her bristling cheek.

Raising themselves high and repeatedly bending down, their beloveds— whose heaviness of hips had become slackened by the fatigue of the swinging play— reached a state of excellence in the act of *puruṣāyita* (the woman-on-top position) because their exhaustion had been overcome.
Rising again and again toward those very objects, the desires of the poor fall futilely upon their hearts, like the breasts of a widow.

O Śiva, O Śiva! The rainy season has come to an end after bringing joy to the peacocks—those charming creatures with sweet voices and trembling crests—who find delight in the streams of rain from the clouds rising within their uplifted tails; for you, however, it has become like a polished sword, drawn by the autumnal arrows.
The hunter Smara raises the line of body hair, which is like a string of pearls and sinks into the hollow of her navel,
in order to bind the flight of the young birds that are her falling eyes upon the mountains of her breasts.
In this season of new clouds, when bees blinded by intoxication hum as they settle amidst the petals of blossoming *kandala* flowers—
to that hornless bull who wanders abroad even in his dreams, having abandoned his beloved, I offer my salutations.
In the long ponds of the mansions, honey-bees, reddened by the pollen of blossoming *kokanada* lotuses, hum sweetly;
and there shines the orb of the sun, kissing the peak of the mountain of sunrise, with the luster of the petals of a fresh *bandhujīva* flower.

Sleeplessness, a fishy odor, the loss of sprouts, and the presence of ants—these arise from water-induced indigestion due to the peeling of bark; in such a case, medical treatment must be administered to the tree.
The body of the beautiful woman, lovely and charming as a blossoming priyaka flower, shone forth clearly in the lake;
for even a flood of water is not sufficient to obscure those who are endowed with purity.
O Lord of the Earth, today I, remaining sleepless, reflected: "The ten incarnations of Hari have been described and celebrated; why are you not mentioned there as the eleventh?
Though I know that your life-story is beyond the reach of poets' words, O King, I do not begin it out of fear of the poet Vyāsa; for who could speak such a thing?
That path which was formerly led by Bhavabhūti every day after Bāṇa had departed, which was long practiced by Kamalāyudha, and by which Keśaṭa reached his goal—
that very path, purified for a long time by contact with the dust of the feet of the illustrious Vākpatirāja, now fortunately unfolds once more through someone of praiseworthy merit.

The riverbanks, with their forests swaying as they emerge from the water, with successions of drying sandbanks and shallows, and with mud marked by the tracks of swans— these remnants of water in the depths captivate the mind.
Like a sea-monster emerging from the celestial river, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow rushed with speed against the current of the Bāṇa-river and,
with both arms, struck the chest of the three-eyed god, which resembled a slab of gold.
O madman, you harbor enmity toward the jackfruit tree in vain, perceiving it as the rival of the thorny fruit;
the virtuous laugh at you but do not associate with you, and even if they should associate with you, being deluded, they will suddenly cease to do so.
O mad rogue, you have been stationed by the Lord of Piśācas in a place fit for the residence of the young moon;
yet do the night-lotuses bloom, does the darkness depart, does the moonstone melt, or does the ocean swell?
When the Ganas begin their work out of the impetuous intensity of their intoxicated love,
even Brahmā is indeed afraid to place an obstacle in their way.
Having encountered the intoxicated [lover], both Hara and Smara experience boundless joy;
for while the former once took delight in rivalry with him, the latter now surely rejoices in the one who is tormented by the pain of separation.
Whatever verses are uttered by the insane, whatever is spoken by children,
and whatever women speak— there is no transgression in that.
Those whose life-span has come to an end place their trust in madmen, in elephants in rut, in those who drink liquor, in women, and in royal families.
One should never place trust in madmen, in those with arms like elephant trunks, in those with horns, in those with weapons in hand, nor in women or royal families.
By some form of madness, even when a man has at times set out upon a wrong path,
the instruction of a friend immediately turns him back, like a goad for an elephant.

With voices faltering from madness and eyes clouded by intoxication, their true nature lost and their past deeds forgotten— what men indeed do not stumble at every step, reeling from drinking the liquor of sovereign power?
Some bring about madness, while others fall under the power of their enemies;
some enter into servitude for the sake of another's wealth.

This river, bearing the form of a beloved woman—adorned with the bracelets of her unfolding triple folds, possessing a pair of prominent breasts like a rising pair of ruddy geese, and radiant with the lotus of her face—is cruel-minded on all sides; if you do not wish to be submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, then let it be abandoned from afar.

When will there be once again that tasting of her bimba-like lips— her eyes clouded with passion, her body bristling with horripilation, her locks of hair disheveled, her cheeks moist with perspiration, her earrings swaying, her breaths hissing in agitation, her hands raised, her brows slightly knitted and then arched, her bodice shimmering, and her necklace slipping down?

In that union, which was dear to them both, there was no obstacle to the commencement of their lovemaking; for it was hindered only by the rising of horripilation during a tight embrace, by the winking of eyes during playful glances, and by the sipping of the nectar of her lips during jests. Even in the battle of amorous arts, there was no hindrance due to the onset of bliss.

Blossoming from her breast, adorned with a swarm of virtues, free from flaws, and serving as her own ornament, this heart-stealing speech—full of joy at dawn and flickering with a well-disposed mind—attains a soft bed like my own poetry; thus, like a lotus-lady, she embraces the throat of some person whose former merit and austerity have reached their peak.

If Cupid, who is himself nourished by nectar, were to churn the ocean of fresh sugarcane juice using a rope made of threads of ripening molasses and a churning-stick of a mountain of sugar-candy heard within his own gift,
and thereby produce fresh nectar— that nectar would rival the supreme excellence of my tongue and serve as a final feast for my ears.
"O dear friend, your youth is blossoming, and the ways of city-dwellers are treacherous; therefore, from this day forward, you must not suddenly look anyone directly in the face.
As long as the moon and sun endure, you must serve your one husband with exceeding devotion. You must guard your beauty, but you must not give your heart to our words."
At the onset of spring, how many lovely creepers with blossoms fragrant with trickling drops of nectar and tender young shoots are there not in the pleasure grove?
O mango tree, sole treasure of good fortune, adorned as you are with glorious clusters of blossoms, yet the swarm of bees does not rest upon anyone other than you anywhere else.
Driven far away by the spreading radiance of the moon-like beauty of her blossoming face, shattered by the luster of her full breasts, and struck down by the light of her hands—
the darkness, as if out of anger, suddenly seized her hair before it could reach her neck, which is like that of a *kalaviṅka* bird or a plantain tree, while she gazed on with rising curiosity.

How many flowers do not bloom at the rising of the hot-rayed sun? Yet, even with ten million births, this lotus plant cannot repay its debt to those poets who have bestowed upon it such world-renowned fame as "the close friend," "the exceedingly dear one," and "the beloved of the Sun."

"Her blossoms are opening—pluck them with your nails! This garment is being carried away by the wind—cover it with the hem of your silk! They are entering the pleasure grove—frighten them with the tinkling of your bracelets! Such are the secret signals exchanged among her friends, O fortunate one, in their mutual conversation during your absence.

The rays of the sun of intense brilliance emerge at evening—those physicians who perform the incantations for exorcising the night-stalking demons of the lotus groves that have slumbered languidly; those masters who impart the sacred syllable *praṇava* in the form of the humming of swarms of bees arising from the hollow interior of the blooming lotus buds.
A few rays of the moon of nectar are emerging, possessing the soft luster of lotus stalks and acting as if bound by a vow to close the petals of the day-lotuses;
even as the mountains turn white with the morning dews, this ocean of darkness suddenly foams up like a sea agitated by the rising universe.

O brother, tell me where that lovely face of my beloved remains— the face which, while you stood for a moment with your friend Kāntā near her ear-lotuses, those lotuses whose forms could only be discerned from their fragrance alone as their beauty was entirely swallowed by the surging waves of luster from the corners of her opening eyes, and which, being touched by you, uttered a faint humming sound?
O Lord, your hand— dense with the shadows of the lattice of rays from blossoming jewels, resounding with the clatter of its bracelets, and hardened by the sport of slaughtering enemies—
has entered the orb of the fierce-rayed sun with impetuosity, as if to draw back those foes who, having abandoned their lives in battle, have departed upon the path to heaven.

These days are passed by travelers with great difficulty—days during which the fever of their ears is aroused by the sweet warbling of playful cuckoos, while mango blossoms are shaken by bees greedy for the scent of emerging honey; yet these days are sustained by the joy of the essence of union with their beloveds, attained through moments of intense meditation.

O Wind, friend of the fragrance of the thick nectar dripping from the buds of the *kunda* flowers, which are formidable with their opening blossoms—touch that slender maiden whose eyes are slightly trembling; go, go! Come back to me!
Which trees here indeed do not put forth beautiful blossoms appropriate for this season?
Tell me, what longing could there possibly be for one such as this, which has been fashioned exactly like the great Aśoka tree?

This pond was excavated by him—a pond whose surging waves are made resonant by the gusts of wind rising from the wings of flocks of birds sporting within its expanse, which is overflowing with the fragrance of the opening petals of playful blue lotuses;
a pond whose edges are embraced by rows of trees filled with fresh, green foliage, providing relief from the traveler’s distress and bestowing joy upon their eyes.
Her body, radiant with its four-cornered symmetry, became manifest through her fresh youth, like a painting brought to life by a brush, or like a lotus opened by the rays of the sun.

Opening your eyes, you do not look at your friends; though addressed, you give no reply; you do not distinguish between what is appropriate and what is not in this state of yours, having fallen into such emptiness.
O you who have made this cage of your body invisible by means of your life-force, yet still clinging to it slightly—what do you wish to do? Bestow your love upon one who has come from another land.
With your lower lip slightly parted and your half-closed eyes blinking from the fear of the particles of ash, do not stop even this smoke; it is merely a bee following your breath.
With her bodice cast off, she of noble luster is like the sword of the enemy of Śambara drawn from its scabbard;
with the red veil of twilight serving as a covering cloth, she resembles the crescent of the moon embraced by an evening cloud.
O leader of the herd of young śarabhas, what other mountain here is capable of supporting you as you leap from the peak of Mount Meru with an unrestrained stride?

Therefore, O lord of the śṛgāla deer, whose soul is cherished by dense artistic skill, go to that very Lord of Mountains, who is difficult to approach and whose golden moonlight is scattered for your dwelling.
"Abandoning quarrels born of pride, enjoy yourselves united with your beloveds"—
thus, as it were, did the cuckoos address the people with their sweet songs.
Now that they have been released, this entire universe appears as if veiled on all sides by those very shadows;
at its borders the ocean blazes, in the center the jeweled mountain shines, and the earth delights us with its wondrous play of masses of darkness.

Having unyoked themselves and cast aside their own kin like blades of grass—even their lives which are more dear than anything else—the merchants crossed the difficult-to-traverse ocean in their hope for sandalwood. They were turned back by your terrifying breaths; now, O serpent, remain at ease, and you alone have gone to smear yourself with fragrant juices.

If the river of our well-spoken verses should flow into your unfathomable ocean of the heart— by means of those highly precious qualities of yours which bear the weight of universal wonder because they have never been unveiled—
then the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, with its deep resonance pouring forth the thick nectar of all the world’s diverse thoughts, shall blossom forth once more as something unprecedented.
May she, whose navel has uprooted the pillar-base of her tethering post, whose line of body hair is severed and slipping,
and whose high breasts are like the ramparts of slumber for the intoxicated elephant of passion, be our dwelling place.
Having uprooted the white hairs, one should apply [the remedy] at each and every root;
thereafter, the hair grows back black and wondrous.
The wise man should employ this with the previously mentioned method using the milk of a ewe.

Having uprooted the tree of his tethering ground and violently tearing apart the neck-chains, this lordly elephant, a son of the gods, rushes impetuously toward Hari with feet stained by rut-fluid, scattering his starry girth-belt; with blows from his trunk-staff, he shatters the Puṣkarāvartaka and other clouds in the sky, his head shaking wildly.

Seeing the leaf-design of a crocodile wiped away from the border of her breast by the forceful embrace of the best of the Raghus, the daughter of Mithila smiled and said, "Let there be no anger; I shall draw it again.
May that side-glance, reddened by anger, moistened by falling tears, and yet expanded by love, bestowed by the princess of Mithila, grant us prosperity.

The floods of water attained the affection of the young women as they rubbed away their painted leaf-patterns, disheveled the ends of their tresses, clung to their necks, touched their hips, and struck against the regions of their breasts.

O lady of graceful form, I believe that the beauty of the lotus has out of joy clung to your feet because this face of yours— with its splendor surpassing the luster of a blue-lotus petal— has forcibly quelled the pride of that moon’s loveliness, which is the natural enemy of the moon and cannot endure its appearance even for a moment during the night.
For even a superior person returns a favor when wronged, whereas an inferior person acts otherwise;
a middling person seeks equality, while another is solely intent on his own self-interest.
One who is rich in the authority of being a benefactor does not consider his own transgression;
making his past favors a banner, he plunders everything.
To help others, to speak kindly, and to show unsurpassed affection—this is the very nature of the virtuous; by whom was the moon made cool?
A small thing is often as capable of providing assistance as something great;
generally, a well constantly quenches thirst, whereas the ocean does not.
Between one who helps and one who is ungrateful, there is this much difference:
the former immediately forgets what was done, while the latter forgets it only later.
The stable substance of one who benefits others is the effort exerted at that very moment;
what need has a palm-leaf fan for the accumulation of a gentle breeze?
To assist those who have not assisted one, to do kind deeds for others, to remember favors received,
and to uplift those who have fallen— this is the proper conduct for those of noble lineage.
To assist others unobtrusively, to forgive those who are inferior, to give without being asked,
and to win over others through virtues— only a few among hundreds understand how to do these things.
One should form an alliance with a benefactor even if he is an enemy, not with a friend who causes harm;
for benefit and injury are the defining characteristics of these two.
The wise man who rains benefits upon his circle of friends and harm upon his enemies— like a cloud over men— is always desired for his prosperity.
But those who, remembering a favor, are subject to the power of gratitude,
follow the path of their benefactors even if they are insentient.
Following the extinction of the fire, the heated stone is extinguished; following the moon, the moonstone [melts]; and furthermore, following that which is drying up, it dries up as well.
Benefiting others is the supreme dharma; skill in action is the supreme goal;
giving to a worthy recipient is the supreme desire; and freedom from craving is the supreme liberation.
Patience is a most helpful source for the abundant production of the fruit of karma;
there is no means equal to patience for the unfailing destruction of enemies.
One should eliminate an enemy by means of an enemy who has been won over through a favor,
just as one extracts a thorn embedded in the foot with a thorn held in the hand.

The superior person, intent on doing good, returns a favor; the mediocre person does so out of indifference; the base person does not even do that, and by virtue of the favor received, he becomes an enemy.
The virtuous person is by nature constantly intent on benefiting all people;
yet, alas, the rise of such a one incessantly causes deep heartache to the wicked.

One should be intent on benefiting even an enemy who is intent on doing harm; one should remain single-minded in both prosperity and adversity, and one should be envious of the cause, but not of the result.
A friend is characterized by helpfulness, while an enemy is defined by harmfulness.
A person of true virtue extends even greater assistance when fallen into adversity;
in this regard, mercury (*pārada*) in its state of liquefaction (*rasa*) serves as the illustration—whether it has reached a state of fainting or even death.
By whom can a wicked person be won over even with a hundred favors? A virtuous person, however, becomes a seller of his very self through mere honor alone.
Even with a hundred acts of service, even with very extensive gifts,
and even through affectionate fondling, a sister’s son cannot be accepted [as a slave].
For this one whose heart is like stone, for whom benefit and harm alike pass into oblivion, the designation "living" is in vain.
Friendship arises from benefiting others, from signs such as those of beasts and birds,
from fear, from greed in fools, and from the mere sight of the virtuous.
Even without receiving any benefit, a friend quickly stands by one for the sake of their welfare;
one who possesses such a friend accomplishes even difficult goals with ease.
Born for the sake of benefiting others, he is truly well-born even when born amidst enmity;
though himself devoured, the lover of Rohiṇī causes his devourer to swallow nectar.
What is the use of that burdensome learning, accumulated through heaps of written leaves, which provides no benefit to others nor to oneself?
A shameless villain may slay even a great benefactor on a critical occasion;
thus Dhṛṣṭadyumna killed his venerable preceptor, a hero at peace, in the midst of the assembly.
When the water in the field, which had been so beneficial, gradually diminished, the rice plant,
out of compassion, became pale-faced.
O Blessed Earth, how can you support that man who breaks his word and commits evil against one who has been helpful, trusting, and pure-minded?

If one possesses compassion toward a benefactor or one free from envy, what is extraordinary about that? But he whose mind remains compassionate even toward a harmful person who has suddenly committed an offense—he alone is the leader among the virtuous.
What merit is there in being kind toward those who have been kind?
He who is kind toward those who have done him harm is called truly virtuous by the wise.
Gratitude toward a benefactor and ingratitude toward one who has done harm—these two are qualities of the object; for the agent, they would be the opposite.
The high-minded suffer because of the favors they bestow; they cannot endure being shown compassion. Even in times of calamity, they are difficult to propitiate, for they are perpetually sorrowful.
For by helping the base, only harm is produced;
drinking milk for snakes serves only to increase their venom.
A hero, however, is bound by the duty of returning a favor;
one who is ungrateful and fails to repay it strikes at the hearts of virtuous beings.
If the state of being helper and helped exists even at a distance, that indeed is friendship;
look, are the sun and moon close to the night-lotus and the day-lotus?
Much has been done for you there; what more need be said? You have displayed supreme goodness toward me. O friend, by always acting in this very same way, may you remain happy for a hundred autumns.
"There has been great benefit from this"—the wicked have no regard for such things anywhere;
fire, even when held in the hand of the officiant who carries it, still burns.
One should not place trust in a base person even if they have been helpful, thinking, "I am dear to him.
For even when its roots are watered with milk, the neem tree does not become sweet.
By Śrī, Ratna, Abhyā, Hare, Śaśilekhā, and even by the nectar of the enemy of Manasija (Śiva), all the gods were benefited;
otherwise, how could the ocean have remained so burdened with the weight of fame, had it not been for the steadfast one who endured the toil of churning?
Indeed, doing a favor for the wicked becomes the cause of their most grievous offense; for diseases become exceedingly aggravated by the application of favorable treatments.
Out of their boldness in doing good, the virtuous do not even count a loss;
for the flames of a lamp produce their own light by consuming themselves.

Having rendered assistance, great beings endowed with the quality of compassion keep themselves at a distance from others out of a desire for a return favor; indeed, this is a certain kind of hard-heartedness on the part of the noble-minded.
One desiring a desired commencement should quickly act by means of the arrival of an envoy to effect a treaty;
if, however, no treaty is reached, one remains there alone and achieves the elevation of one's own self.
The moon agitated even the lord of the oceans, whose waves were like swift arms embracing the shores; what wonder is there in this that he should overwhelm the assembly of passionate men?
The herds of buffaloes flee in every direction like personified masses of darkness from the forest fire that embraces the wilderness, the glory of the three worlds.
Even a courtesan who has been excessively honored by a man whose wealth is exhausted casts a longing glance at his departing back, even toward his mere undergarment.
The speech of those with deer-like eyes is refined when mingled in the assemblies of the virtuous;
their conduct consists of neither exhaustion nor pride, nor even fear of the crooked Fate.
Courtesy should be practiced toward those persons with whom affection has not yet arisen;
for those toward whom affection has already arisen, courtesy becomes mere hypocrisy.
Even one who knows the rules of etiquette, if he is destitute, what can he accomplish?
He is like a man without a goad mounted upon the head of a rutting elephant.
Those displays of affection and coaxing by the rogue were overlooked because of my friend's words;
now, even if he speaks harshly under the pretext of a quarrel, I shall depart.
With its parts accumulated from pure pollen grains, having attained union with a swarm of bees,
the flower-cluster was perceived to possess a similar beauty to the pearls of a *tilaka* lattice-work.
Even the powerful one becomes incapable when his enemies have grown strong by the force of time;
for the sun, with its rays dulled during the heat of summer, did not become a destroyer of the great snows.
Even by means of persuasion, one who desires peace should give to the powerful;
for Gāndhārī, by not giving, went to his destruction along with his very roots.
One should instigate those who can be instigated and remain aware of their actions;
when fate is favorable, one who desires victory should fight, free from fear.
He has sown dissension among them toward you;
though small, it will quickly inflame them when they are already angry, just as even a tiny spark kindles a great mass of fuel when there is fire.
Sowing dissension, a long siege, a sudden assault, and fierce valor—
these four are declared to be the means for capturing a fort.

Overpowering those kings who were susceptible to subversion, that exceedingly arrogant creator did not tolerate even the humiliation of common folk, much less the royal assembly, which possesses a splendor superior to the world.
When the affection for one's master has been stolen away by subversion, and the primary [minister] seeks refuge with another,
there is no doubt that the fall of the lord of the earth is imminent.

The ocean, like a merchant, constantly subsisted upon the moon— the storehouse of waters— which, descending into the pathways of the clouds, maintained its digits for the sake of its own increase, while itself remaining perpetually in a state of childish simplicity.
A daughter who must be supported is ruined; cooking for one's own sake is ruined;
a sacrifice performed with alms from a Śūdra is ruined; and the wealth of a miser is ruined.
The juice of the fresh betel leaf is unable to bring about the melting of the lower lip of the dark-lotus-eyed woman, as it is being scorched by her sighs, which are heavy with heat.
Knowledge instructs one in the ways of the world, bestows wealth, and delights the mind; it elevates one's greatness, just like service to a wise king.
The virtuous know that instruction to be pure which the teacher imparts;
it does not cause you to turn dark, just as gold does not turn black when placed in fires.
For those men who provide instruction and desire the welfare of others,
no calamity arises either in this world or in the next.
Instruction should not be given to just any person whatsoever;
behold how by a foolish monkey, a well-built house was reduced to ruin.
For instruction given to fools leads only to anger, not to tranquility;
it is like drinking milk for snakes, which results only in poison, not in nectar.
For instruction given to fools leads only to provocation, not to peace;
it is like drinking milk for snakes, which only increases their venom.
The supreme person within this body is called the witness, the consenter, the supporter, the enjoyer, the great lord,
and also the supreme self.
Having been thoroughly tested by means of secret trials, those who strive properly for the attainment of results should,
being full of devotion, examine all his deeds— both those performed and those left undone.
Because one approaches [the king] and is employed, it is therefore known as *upadhā* (a test).
*Upāya* (means) should be understood as *upadhā*; by means of this, one should examine the ministers.
Through purification from the three conditions, what further examination is there for this [Buddha], just as there is for gold?
May those Lords of Sages—who accept alms out of necessity for the body yet remain entirely unopposed by body, speech, and mind;
who are endowed with vows and restraints, have destroyed the proliferation of delusion, and have slain the warrior of anger—grant me liberation.
Whatever path may prove beneficial when danger has approached, that very path should be followed with discerning intelligence, whether it be noble or base.
Why did Arjuna, who is skilled in great weapons and whose arms—resembling elephant trunks—are marked by the scars of bowstrings, not fashion bracelets upon them like a woman?
That which is filled with a vast accumulation of merit brought near, and guarded with diligence,
becomes a refuge in prosperity and adversity, as well as a treasure and a friend.
On the sandy bank of the river, a great palāśa tree— with its single leaf acting as a hand fanned by the wind—
bestows water, like a life-giving draught, upon the trees whose lives have been destroyed by the forest fire.

The sun’s heat now draws forth the drops of sweat from the Dravidian women— drops fragrant with turmeric and pungent with fresh nail-marks— which are set in motion by the swaying of their eyes as they rest like buds upon their cheeks, where the tremulous leaf-like ears are placed.

Due to the influence of the Kali age, these people regard the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and marriage solely as festive occasions, being ignorant of the distinctions between their proper times;
moreover, even when they have reached an age suitable exclusively for the study of the Vedas, they never abandon the practice of recitation, unlike the Yavanas.
I bring ink and this leaf; what shall I write here? To ask "Are you well? would be a lapse in decorum; to say "You" would wound our affection.
To call him "friend" is false; "Lord" is too formal; "King" implies indifference; and "How are you? requires further explanation. Thus, how am I to address the Joy of the Yadus?
The Upaniṣads have been thoroughly drunk in, and even the Gītā has indeed been brought within the path of my intellect;
yet, alas, that moon-faced woman still does not depart from the chamber of my mind.

The bull, with its horns curved, enters the dwelling of the peasant, catching the streams of water from the wind as they blow crosswise; its gate is barred by the yokes placed thereon, and nearby vessels are hurried away by the womenfolk in their agitation.

The lone true person, who has brought the ship of right conduct to its destination and possesses the helmsman of the virtuous, carries many people across the vast waters of the transformations of saṃsāra.
Having brought a *kuḍava* measure of black sesamum seeds, the terrified plowman said to the physician:
"A red disease, resembling the crescent moon, has arisen upon the breast of my daughter-in-law."
O Night, having brought my beloved to me and having removed my burning pride that was unaware of the improper time,
you have set forth like a messenger at the very commencement of our dalliance.
O friend, let that Mandara mountain alone bear the weight of all grandeur— the very mountain upon whose slope the gods, having brought Śrī, suspended her arm high.
A certain man, approaching with haste, suddenly embraced and held fast a bride who had risen up impetuously, as if her pair of breasts were swiftly lifting her toward heaven with their height.

The utterances of those with true poetic sensibility are unfading because they are supported by reasoned arguments, yet they are not rendered trivial by mere formal instructions; their essence is to be realized through personal experience.
Is it not indeed fortunate for me that you, the dispeller of both divine and human calamities, have appeared before me in these seven limbs?
O travelers, as you leave the vicinity of the Godāvarī, look for another path here;
for here, by some woman of ruined hopes, a red Aśoka tree has been made to don the cloak of fresh sprouts rising from the placement of her lotus-like feet.
O best of Rākṣasas, [know] bribery, conciliation, sowing dissension, and the timely display of valor; as well as strategic application, and both policy and its opposite.
Direct your gaze toward the top of the outer wall and consider for a moment: what is this cool-rayed moon, whose deer has vanished from the sky?
It sheds a pure radiance, beloved by the ripening of fresh *lavalī* fruit, followed by the *cakora* birds of the grove who have taken morsels of nectar.
Is this a calamity for the princess, or is it a deluge of moonlight, or perhaps a thunderbolt’s fall?
Enough with her; she alone is indeed my life. Fie on me, or rather, I alone am one who has achieved his purpose!
O Sustainer of the Universe, you alone are capable of drinking up this world overwhelmed by those intoxicated with pride;
for who else but the sun is able to wash away the sky when it is suddenly soiled by the darkness of night?

The youth sleeps with his lotus-like hands placed upon her breasts, having made his own arm a pillow for the face of the lotus-eyed maiden against the curve of her cheek, and having respectfully laid his own thigh upon hers.
Just as a garment that has been worn out, or as a garland that has been crushed,
even so one who has fallen from his kingdom is useless, even if he remains capable.
A courtesan does not weep "Alas, father! Father! even when her father has died, out of fear that the red dye on her lips might be smudged by the moisture of her tears.
Who can gaze upon the sun, that lion among sky-dwellers, who resembles the God of Death, as he runs toward the enjoyment of Mṛgaśiras, having already consumed all the other constellations?
A miserly person never knows how to enjoy [wealth];
even when submerged up to his neck in water, a dog licks it with its tongue.
For those men who are fearful of enjoyment and intent on the accumulation of wealth,
their riches remain in the house for the sake of others, like a jewel of a daughter.
Apart from its being experienced, no destruction of that [karma] exists;
for who is able to alter the bondage of past karma?
Wealth is for enjoyment, and life is that by which wealth is protected;
but for one who has not protected the earth, what is the use of wealth and life?
Through the enjoyment [of the fruits] of past merits as well as of sins,
and likewise through the non-performance of obligatory duties out of a lack of desire, [the body is sustained].
Even when deprived of all enjoyments, one should not let oneself despair;
for even in the state of a Caṇḍāla, O dear one, human birth is difficult to obtain in every respect.
Kalidasa possesses simile; Bharavi, the weightiness of meaning; Dandin, the grace of diction; and in Magha, all three qualities reside.

That which was once the standard of comparison for the ornaments of the playful, by virtue of your own loveliness—that very thing has now reached such a state; yet I do not break asunder, for women are indeed hard-hearted.
The night-bride, her face pale at its edge from the rising of the moon and her body thinned by the spring season,
attained a state of emaciation that was fitting for a woman who had not yet found the bliss of union with her beloved.

Then, with her slender creeper-like arms outstretched and turned sideways, her fingers interlaced above the knot of her braided hair, she cast glances from which the beauty of her left eye-corner, breast, and cheek was revealed; glances whose splendor was such that they were mistaken for garlands of blue lotus petals.

Victorious are certain extraordinary people who, though possessing a cruel nature like the edge of a sword from their preeminent serpentine kin, are within themselves the direct initiating gurus of the grape.
Having taken the lotus from above that was of the same color, you place it in my hand to play with; blessed indeed is Kṛṣṇa, who, having cast aside his pair of lotuses, touched your pair of breasts.
Above, thick clouds form dense masses; across, even the mountains have their peacocks dancing;
the earth, too, is white with *kandala* sprouts—where, O traveler, can you cast your gaze?
Above, thick clouds thunder loudly; far away is my beloved—what has befallen me?
On the Himalayas are divine medicinal herbs, yet a serpent has settled upon my head.
While she was performing a sacrifice with trees grown above her, another man, eager for an embrace due to his skill,
took hold of the charming young bride with both arms, saying, "Take this woman of celebrated, full breasts yourself."
O friend, above that *tāmāla* tree, there is someone with a face like the full orb of the autumn moon;
and there, by his skill upon the flute, he brings even the family honor to its lowest depths.
With its bricks fallen from the upper surface, thin at the top and broad in the middle,
this great house has split like the heart of one who fears union with an unsuitable person.
O my wife, this young girl of mine floats above like a row of swans;
you, however, dwell within my heart, having reached its depths, like a lotus stalk in a lake.
O beautiful woman, this bodice of yours shines like a silken tent pitched over the full breasts of the victorious King Manobhava (the God of Love) as he seeks to conquer Tripura’s enemy (Śiva).
The sun above is cruel, the mountainous ground below is harsh, the wind blows carrying heaps of dust, and the essence of the lake is meager;
alas, why do these travelers not give up their lives at that very moment, were it not for the trees that provide them with the shelter of their leafy canopies?

Due to the expansion of the powerful bows held aloft by the Śāris above, the fierce elephants stationed near the banks, their trunk-staffs extended, are unable to plunge here into the waters of the rivers as they set out to drink; instead, they drink the water from the surface.
When a woman, being on top, delights a man who desires her,
that should be known as the inverted sexual act (*viparīta-rata*), which is dear to all those who seek pleasure.
How can devotion that is superficial and lacks roots within deliver one?
For even thick blue-green moss is never seen to be capable of supporting a heavy load.
The sages obstruct their breaths; they neither eat nor drink.
They are praised by virtuous people—what else do these men place around their necks but a golden chain?
Upon its ridges, the perfected beings (siddhas) who roam above the sun hold their umbrellas downward out of fear of the heat.
Above that, they say there are eight hundred and seventy;
one should specify this very same measure for elephants.
Everyone desires to rise higher and higher above the world;
they strive to that end according to their ability, yet it does not happen in that way.
Having observed the intermixture of colors, the absence of connection with excellence, and the loss of stability,
travelers are struck with alarm upon seeing the rainbow, as if beholding a wretched land.
Gold is tested by a touchstone; a man is declared to be tested by his conduct;
a bull is the test for a cow; but for women, no test exists.
This is a fragment of stone used for breaking up the cow-dung brought by the young students; this is a heap of sacrificial grass;
and even the shelter here, with its thatched roof sagging under these drying fuel-sticks, reveals its dilapidated walls.
The southern breeze arrived— skilled in teaching the young trees of the groves to dance, having engaged in amorous play with the lotus-women,
and expert at shattering the meditative absorption of yogis who are enemies of the god of love.

How will you perform those tasks appropriate for the women of the household, which are unfamiliar to you— you who even find it exhausting to weave a garland from the blossoms of the fresh jasmine in the grove?

When the bees, skilled in following the breezes from the groves, attained the fragrance of the women’s bodies, it was indeed because prosperity stands at the forefront for those who follow the exalted.

Like a grove submerged in the midst of water, the pond—possessing a clarity that reflects [the surroundings]—seems as if filled by a mass of moonbeams; with its waters brought to a state where they may be drawn, it exists for the sake of pleasure.
With the young lotuses of the garden waters, the throat-songs of bees and cuckoos,
and the graceful, intoxicated gait of amorous women, the month of Madhu proclaims its skillful conduct.
Appointed by the king, whether addressed by him or by some other person,
the wise man sits down after observing a seat appropriate to his own station and caste.
One who sits in the midst of an assembly and does not speak words clearly,
or one who would not proclaim the truth— such a person should be avoided from afar.
O King Mānasiṃha, the supreme Apsarases play the lute for the sake of your fame for generosity,
striving most intensely to bow down before it out of a longing for the flowers upon the crests of the celestial trees.
What wonder is there in this, that for those who desire the fruit of wealth from the seed of knowledge—which has tranquility as its fruit—the undertaking becomes fruitless?
For all things have their fixed domains and do not undergo transformation; a grain of rice can never produce a sprout of barley.

May this auspicious day of the festival of lamps— wherein the roar of the clouds has been stilled, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa is set ablaze, and Rāma is made to rejoice— like the *Rāmāyaṇa*, remove your misfortune.
For a hero, splendor alone is his companion; success resides in daring.
Indeed, it is the lion, though his domain is but a deer, who shatters the herds of elephants.
At that moment, the slender web of rays from the cool-rayed moon reached the peaks of the mountain during twilight;
indeed, even at the time of setting, the path of the virtuous remains truly elevated.
It is the consensus of Pāṇini that prefixes (*upasarga*) are used in connection with a verbal action;
yet how is it that your enemy, though devoid of action, is always possessed of a prefix?
Afflictions arise even for the yogi who has perceived the Self;
I shall explain those to you, so listen to me in brief.
In the face of an invasion by another army, during a famine, in the presence of terrifying danger, and when in contact with wicked people— he who flees survives.
When these afflictions have been conquered, the afflictions—
consisting of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas— then arise again for the yogin.

One who appears due to the ripening of ordinary merit, standing before one and touching his own head with his right hand, or one who acts with right-handed gestures— such a maṇḍala is a bestower of the attainment of a maṇḍala.
There is no counteracting a desire that has already presented itself;
how much less so for one who is stained by desire even while liberated from the body?
When a terrible calamity has arrived,
it is proper for wise men to flee, casting aside even their own clothing, in order to protect themselves.
When the life-taking Kṛtānta has arrived, what should a wise person strive to do immediately?
With speech, body, and mind, one should contemplate only the lotus feet of Murāri, which grant happiness and destroy Yama.
When calamity has arrived, the entire inner state of men is measured;
for when the wind blows, no distinction at all appears between a heap of cotton and a mountain.
O Lord, he who creates an obstacle when a marriage, a gift, or a sacrifice is at hand,
is born as a worm after death.
May the bringing of riches, the withdrawal of the entire web of evils,
and the deliverance from saṃsāra— this conduct of the Lord of the Universe, be for your supreme welfare.
Following that, there is the laughter and so forth of the messenger and the heroine;
then, in the erotic sentiment of union (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*), there is the mutual gazing of the two.
The cluster of buds upon the *kiṃśuka* tree, bestowed by the beauty of the departure of winter,
shone like the ornament of nail-marks upon a beloved woman whose modesty has been dispelled by intoxication.
Since a minister who plays with the king in secret acts as the king himself,
he is inevitably treated with constant contempt due to that very familiarity.
Did the line of hair upon the lotus-eyed maiden shine like the path of the beauty of childhood as she departed with fresh youth, shedding a stream of tears mixed with collyrium?
The thousand-rayed sun took up for him a new parasol fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ;
with his crown not far from that silk garment, he shone like the Ganges falling upon his head.
As long as there is no one to receive them from those possessed of merit, virtues—though they be worthy of the three worlds—remain like non-existent things.
Even before he took up residence in the heart of the enemy of the Daityas, was the Kaustubha jewel not already in the ocean? And had there not been some mention of it even then?
Even though constantly associated with limiting adjuncts, an entity does not abandon its own nature;
for even a crow that has been immersed in the ocean of milk since birth remains, they say, black indeed.

Those who betray their preceptor, father, or mother, whether by thought or by deed—their sin is no different from that of foeticide; therefore, there is no other evildoer in the world greater than they.

The preceptor, the physician, the guarantor, the mistress who has been enjoyed, the woman who has recently given birth, and the female messenger— once the task is accomplished, these are like blades of grass.
Ten preceptors are equal to one teacher; a hundred teachers are equal to one father;
but a thousand fathers are surpassed in respect by a mother.
Come back, O travelers, to that lake—the ornament of the path—by reaching which you may sport in its clear waters, your burden of fatigue dispelled;
for from here, toward the salt ocean whose waters are churned by aged crocodiles, retreat is auspicious, but entry is not possible under any circumstances.
And he who gives a pair of sandals to an excellent twice-born man who is a worthy recipient,
he too attains worlds honored by the gods.
Having caught the fragrance brought from afar by the wind, a honeybee has approached this sandalwood tree out of greed for its sweet nectar.
Any further gain would be far off; yet if one should escape the wrath of the serpent dwelling in the tree and live, that alone would be an incomparable gain here.
O dear friend, you shall one day go with curiosity to the banks of the Śiprā, which are matted with trees budding at their edges;
for there, mistaking it for a white snake made of a string of pearls, a peacock grown old in years will scratch his breast with his claw.
A wise person should consider the means of success, but he should also consider the potential for failure;
for while the foolish crane looked on, his children were devoured by mongooses.
Whatever means a servant employs when serving his master,
one who does not understand the immediate context considers that very means to be appropriate for that situation.
He who does not slay a physician skilled in means, one devoted to corrupting his servants,
or a hero desiring sovereignty, is himself destroyed.
He should be skilled in means, skilled in yoga, a knower of reality, and possessed of inspired eloquence;
he should always be devoted to his own duty, averse to the wives of others,
a speaker of truth, a narrator of diverse stories, and one whose speech is forever unimpeded.
That which is presented as a gift to friends, relatives, and kinsmen,
or given out of customary practice on occasions such as marriages, is indeed what is given out of modesty.
One should seek [one's goal] preceded by skillful means and spring forth after observing the right time; for one who knows only the flavor of impetuous valor leads to regret.
Even for one who has resorted to skillful means, wealth perishes if he is negligent;
even while lying in wait, a sleepy hunter does not kill the deer.
Among all means of livelihood, that which arises from trade is the best;
for one is praised as being for the sake of wealth, while any other is fraught with uncertainty.
Expedients, stratagems, and deceptions are said to be mere procrastination;
victory without risk is achieved swiftly through valor alone.
Victory over an enemy achieved through skillful means is not the same as that achieved by weapons; even one of small stature who knows the right means is not overcome by the brave.
For that which can be accomplished by means cannot be accomplished by valor alone;
a female crow killed a black snake by means of a golden thread.
For that which can be accomplished by means cannot be accomplished by mere valor;
an elephant was killed by a jackal while traveling along a path of mud.
I know that those lords of men cannot be conquered even by various means;
if they are merely disregarded, they will become invincible even in one's thoughts.
Through those four well-employed expedients at the proper time, as it were,
the kingdom of King Mailugikṣa became perpetually exalted.
Indeed, the relinquishing of wealth already acquired is its true preservation,
just as the overflow of water from a reservoir is the means of preserving the water stored within it.
This lotus from the navel of Hari, whose majesty is a wonder to all the worlds, is not to be blamed; for destiny prevails everywhere.
For here Brahmā drinks the honey of his own life-span, while the bees again plunder that nectar which is more abundant with sweat and as heartening as immortality.
Just as children afflicted by hunger wait upon their mother,
so do embodied beings here who desire their own welfare wait upon the Gaṅgā.
Then, as if being attended by a tender, unripened lotus stalk to learn its own softness,
the two arms of the fair-toothed maiden shone, joined together with her auspicious bracelets and conch-shell ornaments.

The prosperity of another who has lost his sense of propriety, lacks control over his senses, and is possessed by pride and other vices, is indeed to be viewed with indifference; for it becomes a cause of dispassion and ultimately destroys him root and branch.
An enemy, though neglected and weakened in strength, becomes incurable— just like a disease— due to the fault of negligence on the part of men blinded by pride, even though he was initially curable.
This boastful talk arises from those who are indifferent and dull-witted, who are treated with contempt by resolute beings,
and who are provoked to anger by those blinded by rage.
He should remain indifferent toward what is lost and take back what has been obtained. He should neither over-indulge a child nor a woman, nor should he strike them.
He should gradually engage both of them in the study of knowledge and in household duties.
If one is capable, one should disregard those who obstruct the Dharma;
for such a person is undoubtedly the cause of total destruction.

The pride of kings toward those they disregard is for the sake of achieving their own ends; yet for the high-minded, that same pride is to be maintained even at the cost of disregarding their own lives when it comes to those they favor.
The mongoose, disregarding the thrower of the clod, bites the clod; but the lion, disregarding the arrow, looks toward the shooter of the arrow.
Endowed with both treasury and army, together with his ministers and counselors,
the lord of the circle of states, stationed in a fortress, should carefully deliberate upon the circle of states.

Approaching her, you were at last eager for a firm embrace, your beautiful sandalwood paste long since rubbed away; by suddenly kissing her eyes, you smeared them with collyrium—O beloved, right here your purpose has been fulfilled.
Behold this cloud: it approaches the salt ocean, endures the onset of many winds before it, and undergoes various breakups;
yet, having somehow obtained its waters, it bestows them upon the world—its nature in giving knows no calculation of merit or fault.
The grain attains a loveliness through ripening; the rivers have lost their turbulence and the earth its mud;
now, by these new qualities, the love for the splendor of the monsoon's arrival—which was once steadfast through long acquaintance—is eclipsed.
Though filled with passion by her intoxication, that frail woman has been joined with the essence of wrath by her own sin;
though she has reached a state of being tormented by the bodiless god of love, she is not joined to me today, but is led instead toward further torment.
The moon, with its passion fully aroused, seized the face of the night so that her eyes trembled;
thus, she did not even notice that her entire garment of darkness had slipped away before her out of passion.
Upodakī arrives together with Tintidī the minister;
flee, flee, you wretched vegetarians!
Having fasted on all eleventh days as well as the fourteenth days of the dark fortnight,
and having meditated upon the god Harihara, one attains the supreme state.

O Lord Śrī Rāmacandra, the creeper of your fame has been sown with your virtues and watered by the waters of your charity; having reached the pillar of Mount Meru, it has spread across the quarters and ascended to the vault of the sky.
It has been perfumed by the incense of the sighs of the millions of women who are your rivals, and it has put forth buds in the form of the stars and blossomed with the moon as its flower.
The afflictions, as treacherous as the seeds of poisonous creepers, are sown by men under the guise of what is dear; before long, from them arise sprouts containing the fire of a thunderbolt.
From these, trees of sorrow grow, their thousands of blazing crests slowly burning the body with the heat of a hundred pits of glowing embers.
A field that is repeatedly plowed will itself lose its vitality;
it is no longer fit for cultivation, and the seed sown therein perishes.
O King, just as a fire is not extinguished by drops of oil, so too a mind whose disposition is set on sensual desires does not become dispassionate through excessive indulgence in those very desires.
The wise speak of both as those who rain down according to the occasion for those who have performed their duties:
that destroyer of armies, the lord of wealth, and him who dispels fatigue, born of the lineage of Manu who wields the staff of justice.
The Sage’s view is that one of both natures may become attached to sensual pleasure;
likewise, even Pāṇini, when speaking of the third [nature], says it pertains to liberation.
A virtuous person is likewise able to overcome such a calamity for both [parties],
just as the elephant and the crocodile each escaped their respective misfortunes.
Neither of these two has a desire for their own enjoyment; both accumulate wealth for the sake of others.
Yet, behold the great difference between the miser and the magnanimous!
If there is joy in the union of both, then that is true union;
for indeed, the clapping of hands is not produced by a single hand alone.
For both the fetus and the debt, there is only one course of action:
while laughing, she carries the fetus; weeping, she releases it.
Just as the flight of birds in the sky is accomplished by both wings together,
so too is human effort, when joined with destiny, effective in achieving its fruit.
Just as the flight of a bird in the sky is achieved by means of both wings together,
even so the supreme state is attained through both knowledge and action.
Where both the target and the archer are moving,
that should be known as the "double-moving" (dvayācala) [type of shooting], for it is accomplished through effort alone.
If two separate streams of the waters of the celestial Ganges were to fall from the sky,
they might serve as a comparison for his chest, which is dark as a tamāla tree and adorned with a string of pearls.
Two plantain-stalks stand inverted above two lotuses; above those, a slab of precious stone—what indeed is that?
Then two jars, followed by two young lotus-shoots, and then a kandalī sprout; upon that, two blue lotuses and bees—what on earth is this?
Having surveyed both worlds, the sages themselves created the King, a being of great power, thinking: "This one shall be Dharma."
Both wings are white, he moves through the sky with unimpeded gait, he always eats fish, and he dwells entirely upon the head of Śiva.
O best of men, all the collection of qualities belongs to the crane; however, qualities are to be honored when they are in their proper place, but not when they are devoid of such a place.
I worship Kumāra, who wears golden earrings and a lotus garland, and whose forehead is honored by the soft, lotus-like hand of Umā.
By Gadādhara, the son of Umā’s body, who worships Śaṅkara at every festival,
and the son of Gaurīśa, this certain poetic composition is being composed for the sake of those who appreciate aesthetic flavor (rasajña).
In the Umātilaka tāla, two drutas (short notes) are prescribed as a laghu and a guru;
this is the tāla called Cāra, and it is sung by the learned with that [rhythm].
Beholding Umā, who has the cool-rayed moon as her crest-jewel,
this goddess Bhāratī dances, having taken up the intoxicated Sun.
O Umās, you must strive to attract the mind of Śambhu, which is stilled by self-restraint,
just as a magnet attracts iron.
Both are equally capable of bearing the seed sown by both;
whether it be that form of Śambhu or my own watery form.
Umā is the bride, you are the giver, and we here are the suitors;
Śambhu is the groom—indeed, this arrangement is sufficient for the exaltation of your lineage.
Just as Umā and the Bull-bannered Lord rejoiced at the birth of Śarajanman, and Śacī and Purandara at Jayanta,
so too did the King and the Magadhan queen rejoice with their son, who was their equal and resembled them.

Having made her chest the target for piercing, with her breasts pressed firmly against a jeweled surface, the celestial maidens dwelling in their mansions in the sky call out, "Come here! Seizing her by the arms, they suddenly address her with hurried steps through a side door and carry her away from the front of the battle to the world of the gods by supporting her hands.
One should prescribe that the chest, the back, and the hips are equal to the face;
the two ears are said to be seven finger-breadths, and the palate six finger-breadths.
"Who here supports a chest without breasts? Inform the eater of wind (the serpent). "What do people call one born in a city? And what fruit is compared to the breasts of a cowherd's wife?"
A female serpent directed her own hissing toward her hungry offspring with the breath of her mouth;
even at a time when all was empty of the news of the arrival of the wind, she remained wide awake and fully aroused.

Fortunate are those who drink the honey of the lips of young women whose hair-knots have loosened as they lean against their lovers' chests, whose eyes are half-closed yet slightly opened, and whose cheeks are perspiring from the exhaustion of lovemaking above.
A bright necklace is placed upon your chest, a jingling girdle is fastened upon your firm hips, and your feet are adorned with tinkling jeweled anklets;
O charming girl, if you thus approach your beloved like one striking a drum, why do you gaze toward the quarters of the sky, trembling with excessive fear?

The lord of serpents upon his chest, the fire upon his forehead, the moon upon his head, and the celestial river within his matted locks—O dear friend, what secret of the Destroyer of Cities shall I tell you? Even in private, it is as if in public.
On whose chest was Murabhid firmly embraced? Who in the Nandana grove is perfumed by the nectar of the lotus?

Which meter exists that is composed with syllables as light as mountains, numbering the same as the ocean, yet also heavy? On the chest of Viṣṇu (Murabhid) is Śrī; in the Nandana grove is the *mallikā* jasmine; and there exists the meter called *Sragdharā*, which consists of syllables as light as mountains (*giri*)—seven—and is heavy, numbering the same as the ocean (*arṇava*)—fourteen.
"Your chest is marked by breasts; how can you expect forgiveness from me? Therefore, let the wealth previously promised to me be paid.
Thus, with a wavering heart, the courtesan pulls from her lover’s palm his jingling golden bracelet.
The celestial maidens, fallen under the power of love and dejected in mind, drop their flower ornaments from their loosening hair as they fall from the sky.
The gods sing of him, their faces streaming with the Ganges, that this glance of yours, which shines forth out of compassion, has fallen upon them.
In the battle, they cried out much, they praised, they were greedy for the spoils, they flourished in their joy, and they repeatedly fainted again and again.

The lake of the doe-eyed woman’s navel might be found possessing the lovely form of a pair of breasts like a pair of wheels, or like a row of hair resembling a swarm of bees; it would be as charming as a musical performance with its delightful opening of the two hollows.
Horses born in Uroja, Kīra, and among the Turuṣkas and Raṭṭas; those born in Ṭakka, Saindhava, Madhyadeśa, and likewise those born on the plains.
The youth of this deer-eyed woman, though its fullness has not yet manifested in her chest due to her fresh charms, already agitates these three worlds.
What indeed would be the story if her breasts were already swollen with fullness? Moreover, everything else has already been conquered by the flower-bowed god of love.
Was it because she was blooming with a pair of jars upon her chest, created by youth as a fresh offering,
that the slender girl, having crossed even the river-fortress of bashfulness, entered the heart of Nala?
There is no loftiness in the region of her chest, nor gracefulness in her gait, nor curvature in her speech, nor such tremulousness in her eyebrows;
nevertheless, in the body of this deer-eyed woman, a certain luster of beauty is perceived within, like the radiance of a great gem covered by cloth.
When two months have passed, the chest [is formed]; likewise, the abdomen after three months;
and the hips, as well as the hands and feet, are established after four months.
Some fortunate person beholds the infant, laughing as he fills the hollow of his own mouth with playfully drawn milk from his mother's breasts and then blows upon it into her face.
As her lover loosened the fastenings of his bodice in order to behold the lotus-like breasts upon her chest,
his effort proved fruitless, for his eyes were already clouded with tears of joy.
A broad chest is praised, as are long and elevated armpits which are auspicious;
well-rounded and symmetrical thighs, arms, and hidden knees are highly commended.
Whether it be Urvaśī in her beauty, Rambhā, Tilottamā, Gopālī, or even Menakā— other men's wives must be avoided.

The serpent Śeṣa constantly bears the heavy earth as he dances for the Lord of Beings; moreover, becoming a necklace, he serves as the bed for Viśvaṃbhara. This task is supreme in the three worlds and possible for Śeṣanāga alone; let other large-bodied serpents eat frogs.
While your arm, bearing the scars of the bowstring, supports the entire earth, the Tortoise King’s exhaustion is stilled; he performs some small feat of sport.
Having held a gathering to eat the sprouts of the *lavalī* vines on the sandy banks of the shore, the elephants of the quarters now drink together the waters of the ocean.

O upholder of the earth, heavy as it is, lighten it with your arrows; you who make the paths of heaven—already heavy with the pride of the swarms of serpents—lighter by subduing the hosts of enemies through your valor. Who else but you could make the enemy armies short with the victory banners won by conquering the earth, while making your own unbearable energy visible to others through the fire of your bow that wards off other weapons?
In the interior of a lord of the earth, of a crystal stone, and of a woman’s heart devoid of character,
the influence of another gains entry due to the absence of constant presences.
May Indra cause the earth to produce abundant crops by sending down desired rain; may the foremost of Brahmins duly provide satisfaction to the inhabitants of heaven through their offerings;

and may the association of virtuous people remain firm and ever-increasing until the end of the kalpa. May the unbearable words of malicious folk, which are as hard as adamant, come to a complete and peaceful end.
"O Earth, here this row of trees has a beautiful position at its edge;
it is not fitting to go straight ahead—bend your head slightly."
On this earth, some mountain was held effortlessly with two arms; for that reason, you are constantly celebrated as Govardhana in heaven and on the ground.
I carry you, the upholder of the three worlds, upon the tips of my breasts—yet that is not taken into account. What more need be said, Keśava? Fame is obtained through meritorious deeds.
Just as a mortar stands firmly in the center of an oil-press,
so Mount Meru, the support of all, stands in the center of the terrestrial sphere.
Enveloped by the amnion and covered on the outside by moist membranes,
he remains with his head toward the belly, his back and neck bent.
The braid of the large-eyed woman, hanging down after passing over her calf,
quivers like a creeper of a sword-stalk placed by the Mind-born God upon a sandalwood branch after he had conquered the world.
Let the wise cross over rivers, forests, villages, and mountains as they please; yet, like women going to meet their lovers, they do not themselves voice the internal craving that drives them.
Having transgressed the words of my friend, cast aside all propriety, abandoned shame, and discarded even a trace of my own pride in my good fortune,
I have surely taken only the command of the preceptor Manmatha and sought refuge in you, the crest-jewel of the entire host of lovers.
Wearing a well-woven garland of flowers possessing radiant fragrance,
the king perfumes even others standing at his side.
O you with trembling brows and waveless eyes, why do you contemplate what has passed?
The ripening of love is as unpleasant as that of treacle when it has undergone a slight mishap.
O lady of beautiful limbs, by your wide eye with its arched bow of eyebrows,
which great men— even those as firm as mountains— have not been brought to a state of instability?
This moon, whose mark is uplifted and who showers forth moonlight,
shines like a cart with its axle attached to Kṛṣṇa’s foot, manifesting milk.
In the vicinity of the crescent moon,
the shimmering clusters of stars gleam like drops of nectar falling from the bow held by the flower-armed god of love.

As the young bride was joking with her messenger regarding her beloved and putting on her ornaments, a certain radiance appeared upon her face— was it from the beauty of her attire, or from the news of her lover?

The blossoming of her sprout-like lower lip spreads a full smile; the casting of a sidelong glance from the corner of her eye betokens a daring full of passion. Her stepping onto the couch marks the limit of the extraordinary stage leading toward the path to the chamber of love; yet, once there, her behavior becomes boundless and utterly inverted.

Joy has been brought about by the sound of your cry; confidence was restored by your eating of the auspicious offering; and the obstruction of tears in my pair of eyes has been removed by your movement.
The sun has now set before us; may it be well with you, depart! Let these very breaths of mine, seeking my beloved, follow after you now.
By that Lord, who raised aloft the great cloud of his dark sword-blade and uttered a mature and powerful roar,
the entire blazing majesty of his enemies in the three worlds was extinguished in battle by the waters of its edge.
Let their limbs, which have touched Nala’s body, be made to dance; let their gaze, too, drink in the shadow of Nala.
For even a stone of Rati was made to dance by her husband; yet her hair remained unshaken, for it did not perceive the cutting away [of her joy].
She examines her own mention in his utterances, learns supreme proficiency, composes strings of words, and cultivates familiarity with the path of *dhvani*.
She expands the variety in the art of expression in the presence of Vācaspati; O King, what does the Goddess of Speech not do for the sake of praising your virtues?
The child spoke the words first uttered by his nurse, walked while grasping her finger, and became humble through the instruction of prostration; thus, that infant spread great joy for his father.
Whatever treatise Uśanas knows and whatever Bṛhaspati knows, they are not distinguished from the intellect of women; how, then, are they to be guarded by men?
Uṣaḥkāla, Garga, Śakuna, Bṛhaspati,
Aṅgiras, Manotsāha, Vipravākya, and Janārdana.
Gārgya recited the Uṣas, Bṛhaspati the Śakuna,
Māṇḍavya the Manojaya, and Janārdana the Vipravākya.
At dawn, while the royal parrot began to mimic the expressions of passion, the deer-eyed woman, feeling bashful in the presence of her elders,
concealed [the sound] with the clamor of her jingling bracelets as she clapped her hands under the pretext of a child’s playful dance.
At dawn, near her teacher, the deer-eyed girl carefully covered with her garment the nail-marks made by her lover all around;
when questioned earnestly by her friends, "What is this?", she—alas, alas!—was submerged in an ocean of shame.
At dawn, as her beloved was fastening the earring that had slipped from the edge of her ear during their amorous play,
the beauty of her face— with its playful laughter and the manner of her sidelong, curved glances— was savored by the eyes of the fortunate.
O bashful one, who has not perceived your mastery in the *puruṣāyita* posture, as you turned over at dawn and made your pearl necklace serve as a sacred thread?
At dawn, young bees, having seen in a dream the imperial sovereignty of the lotuses, now inhale the waters of the lake, having abandoned their beds of kunda flowers from the previous kalpa.
At dawn, the wind-thief dwelling on Mount Malaya enters through the lattice-windows, scattering the pollen of blossoming lotuses like a powder of delusion;
having suddenly extinguished the lamps, he steals away from the women the pearls of sweat born of the exhaustion of lovemaking.
Like at dawn, this family wanders here and there for the sake of a belly that has been struck down; carrying its own members about, it roams in every direction.
Alas! Like crows satisfied with nothing more than a single morsel, we have somehow failed to find even a limit to our lives or to our miserable state.
Sarasvatī dances gracefully upon the lotus-face of the Lord of Uṣā,
singing of the weight of the virtues of Kavirāja, the king of poets.
And at the weddings of camels, donkeys sing songs;
they praise one another, saying, "Oh, what beauty! Oh, what a voice!"
One should pour hot water into it; there is no fixed measure for this.
When the vessel has been placed for one fortnight in a warm location by a wise person, it will indeed become *kuṇapa*, which promotes the growth of trees.
In the hot season one should give water; in the cold season, fire;
in the rainy season, a house; and at all times, food.
Warm food, ghee, wine, a young woman, a meal of milk,
and the shade of a pond or a mountain cave— these six increase one's strength.
