Scorched by the heat, the peacock sits in the basin at the foot of the tree during the cold season; the bee, having broken through the tops of the *karṇikāra* buds, settles within them; the *kāraṇḍava* bird, leaving the heated water, resorts to the lotus-pond on the bank; and this parrot in the cage, exhausted from its playroom, begs for water.
I take refuge in that white abode which is fond of heat in the presence of the sun, slightly inclined toward sleep in the cool breeze, repeatedly eager to kiss the face of its wife who is shy,
constantly intent on flying about, lying for a moment upon the bed of the earth, longing for songs, and compassionate toward the wretched.
Just as one who possesses a turban is covered by three garments,
so too is this embodied being enveloped by the qualities of goodness, passion, and darkness.
Those by whom the moon was bowed down sleep during the nights of the cold season, embraced by courtesans whose breasts are warm with passion and whose charms are manifest.
Even the noose-handed Lord, raising his hand, spoke these improper words to him:
"Fame alone is your beloved wife, with her pearl necklace formed from the streams of water poured out in charity."
You have married a dark-skinned Mātaṅga girl whose creeper-like sword you carry;
for this very reason, I believe you have been avoided from afar by others.

O charming girl, though you were wedded even by him who is worshipped by the three worlds, he whose crest is marked by the playful ornament of the young crescent moon—alas, you have in vain gone to the ocean, that storehouse of dullness, which possesses fierce crocodiles, sharp rays of stars, deep chasms, and reaches the very heavens; strange indeed are women!
O Earth, though you are immovable, carry for a long time this one who has married you, even though he clings to your back;
why then do you seek the embrace of the tortoise, whose shell is so hard that it endures everything?

Alas, what a tragedy! That very white bull, who once bore heavy burdens alone upon the most treacherous paths, who never tolerated the sound of another bull in his own stall, and who was the ornament of the herd of cattle—now that he has grown old, his price is being proclaimed for sale.
For just as one who desires milk but cuts off the udder of a cow will not obtain any milk,
so too a kingdom oppressed by improper means does not prosper.
If a man who has not reached twenty-five years of age conceives a child in a woman less than sixteen years old, that fetus perishes while remaining in the womb.
In the deficient [syllables], one should add heavy syllables until all become light;
this is called the *prastāra* by those who know the science of prosody (*chandovicitivedibhiḥ*).
A wise person should somehow cultivate friendliness even toward one who is inferior, insignificant, or even an enemy; for such friendliness does not cease even in times of adversity.

Desirous of bathing in her holy waters to receive a noble stream of affection from the moon and to cast off the profound distress caused by the rays of the sun, the night enters her; yet, for the most part, her water remains darkened by the masses of her own shadows.
The thigh of the deer-eyed woman, with its fluttering hem of her garment,
shines like a golden pillar of victory belonging to Smara, adorned with a banner.
By expanding her faultless pair of thighs, broadening her hips, creating the line of hair, endowing her navel with the beauty of depth,
slimming her waist, making her breasts full, and anointing her face with luster— by all this, the fresh youth of the slender-limbed maiden has somehow brought every limb of hers to full bloom.

The two thighs of the deer-eyed woman are like plantain stalks and young sprouts along with their stems; her hips possess a contour as broad as a stone slab; her chest has the beauty of two frontal globes struck by her breasts; and her face is the companion of the moon.
The two thighs of the deer-eyed woman are like plantain stalks, and her waist is an incomparable altar;
her pair of breasts are golden jars filled with the water of loveliness for the consecration of King Manasija.
The elephant’s trunk was defeated by the two shapely thighs of the slender maiden;
it is fitting that, out of shame, it conceals its own lotus-like face under the pretext of curling itself.

Her hair disheveled by the impetuosity of their play, she who was skilled in the arts of love pressed her face— captivating with its expressive gestures— to the mouth of her beloved, whose eyes were fixed upon the roots of her thighs.
Those very flowers with which these women struck their beloveds— whose eyes were restless upon the roots of their thighs—
they instantly made the name of the God of Love, "Flower-Armed," true to its meaning.
Her thighs are plantain stalks, her eye a lotus, her mass of hair water-weeds, her face the moon, her speech nectar, and her waist a lotus fiber;
her navel is a well, her fold of skin a river, and her hand a tender sprout—if such a woman is not upon one's chest, alas, how can there be any relief from the heat of passion?
Her thighs are like plantain stalks, her arms like creepers, and her breasts like lotuses;
has the Creator fashioned this garden of youth for the amorous play of the God of Love?
Having placed my head upon your thigh, with my fatigue dispelled by the breeze from the moving lotus-fiber fan granted out of compassion,
may I hear the supreme instruction of the Lord right here in this very birth at Maṇikarṇikā.
Seeing a powerful and virtuous person, the base one hates him again and again;
Rāhu devours the healthy moon in the sky.

He gives not even a tuft of wool; there is no scope for carrying or milking him, and there is no satisfaction for his great belly even with many mouthfuls of grass or leaves. Alas, what a pity! How can a sack be loaded upon the peak of his back? "Who would take him for a mere few cowries?"—thus is the elephant mocked by the villagers.
One may infer the weight of that object simply by this: having abandoned it, they go upward; having grasped it, they fall downward.
Those established in *sattva* go upward; those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle;
and those established in the conduct of the lowest quality, the *tamas*-dominated, go downward.
Just as milk cannot be obtained from a cow after the flow of milk has ceased,
so too tribute cannot be obtained from a kingdom that has been oppressed by improper means.
Above is this orb of the moon fashioned like a mass of clouds, while below it are two lofty mountains placed upon a sky variegated by a pond;
furthermore, at the base of the sandbank, two plantain trunks have been planted. Therefore, I believe this is a truly extraordinary creation of the clever Flower-Bowed God.
For the vital breaths of a young man indeed depart when an elder approaches;
he regains them by rising to meet him and by saluting him.
If the grip on the bow is held high and the grip on the string is held low, that released arrow will go far from the target; of this there is no doubt.
The measure of three grains of rice placed vertically is declared to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
indeed, a cubit (hasta) is also defined as being twenty-four finger-breadths.
Then, sighing upwards, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs from the body, having failed to find a stable footing;
driven by time, the individual soul (jīva) follows it as it goes.
One should know that mark on which an upward-pointing, tawny-colored limb is perceived to be a "mongoose-mark"; its touch destroys snakes.
With arms upraised I cry out, yet no one hears me;
from dharma come both wealth and pleasure—why, then, is it not pursued?
One who pierces above the target is the best; one who pierces at the level of the navel is middling;
and he who pierces the target at the level of the feet is considered by me to be the least.
By the descent of the upper power (*ūrdhvaśakti*) and the contraction of the lower power (*adhaḥśakti*),
through the awakening of the middle power (*madhyaśakti*), supreme bliss (*paramaṃ sukham*) is born.
Dogs that howl with their faces turned upward, facing the sun, portend great danger;
for if this occurs at the time of twilight, the inhabitants of that city shall indeed be driven into exile.

Just as a woodcutter, intent on descending, cuts down the trunk of a tree that serves as a support for his ascent, so too does the wielder of the axe [of wisdom] cut away the mountain that is the cause of clinging to the upward path.
Those of expert intellect and wisdom declare that sword to be of middling quality whose characteristic marks are present in the upper half but not in the lower half.
O young cātaka bird, why do you vainly beg the cloud with your neck held aloft? This cloud possesses only an exceedingly powerful thundering; as for even a tiny drop of water, it is far away.
With their mouths upturned and their eyes fixed upon the sun, all those enemies of the gods gathered before him;
then, howling piteously to one another with voices that pierced the very ears, the dogs departed.
The city of Vārāṇasī is a field for the crops of karma that has become saline;
there, liberation is obtained equally by both the outcaste and the scholar.
Just as seed sown in saline fields is indeed fruitless,
so too does any benefit rendered to base persons become like that.
Even upon saline wastelands and in the hollows of waters, waves have been created by you;
yet the drops placed within the boundaries of the fields, O Cloud, constitute your novel policy.

Whether upon saline soil, in a river, in a forest of silk-cotton trees, or even upon sandalwood engulfed by a forest fire, the cloud bestows water equally; may fame arise from such weightiness of virtues.

Devoid of harshness, free from arrogance, lacking in association with the wicked, and light within— though they may be like the syllables of a verse, these enemies become heavy when they reach the end of one's feet.
If there is heat or smoke in a particular soil, water is to be indicated for that pair of men;
and a vein with a great flow of water is to be pointed out.
For the warmth born of wealth brings an increase of vital energy to embodied beings;
how much more so, then, when one enjoys it while endowed with the virtue of renunciation?

O Hero, at the gateway of your enemy’s city during the season of frost, hunters behold this morning the single eye of a bear sleeping nearby— its body curled into a circle as its snout is thrust into its chest—
opening with a blissful gaze born from the process of rousing itself from sleep, appearing like a spark of fire resting upon chaff and ashes.

May that other monkey army—the host of bears of vast luster presided over by their lord; with its wide eyes flashing with terrible fire; having forcibly restrained the high-bowed god whose banner is the fish;

dependent upon Rāma; as pure as white water-lilies; possessing shining dark necks; belonging to the Enemy of Tripura—be the cause for the severing of the ten-faced one’s heads and for your prosperity.
Surrounded by bears, dwelling in the domain of the monkey, generating coolness through the flow of his breeze, delighting the night-lotuses,
and destroying the darkness of night-stalkers— this lord of stars, marked with a broad blue spot, shines forth like a wondrous Cupid.
The three Vedas, known by the names Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, are remembered as the Trayī.
One who abides by the Trayī according to the prescribed rule attains both worlds.
I remember you straightening your arrow as your bow rested upon your lap,
engaged in smiling conversation with Madhu, and casting glances from the corners of your eyes.
Let there be straightness in the bow and its string by virtue of their inherent nature;
however, for the accomplishment of the task, it is precisely their curvature that is praised.
Worship is offered even to one who abandons uprightness to display his skill;
for the Moon, the king of the twice-born, is honored by Maheśa despite his lack of uprightness.
Uprightness, generosity, valor, equanimity toward pleasure and pain,
courtesy, lack of excess, and truthfulness are the qualities of a friend.
That very conduct of his— straightness, silence, and mastery of the Vedas— which was intended to cause supreme harm,
and which appeared exceedingly trustworthy, was indeed a great and deceitful arrow of his.
Those who know the past and possess clear vision declare that the Slayer of Madhu indeed severed the head of Rāhu;
yet they do not say he shattered the head of the one separated from his beloved—how could it be so, if the fire within his belly were not [the moon]?
Whom would the sidelong glance of the tremulous-eyed woman not strike, even though it is slight—a direct fall upon the eyes that strikes the core of the science of love?
Thus, in the midst of the assembly, the clever woman gazes at her lord, the master of her life, with her moon-like face bent down, looking through the space between her eyelashes.
"Place your feet straightly; avoid, my friend, all the conduct of a city-dweller.
Here, the village chief calls you a 'ḍākinī' and punishes you even for a sidelong glance."
The subjects take delight in him who looks upon everything with straightforward eyes as if drinking them in, even when he is seated in silence.
Do not feel affection for an arrow simply because it is straight and feathered; do not feel affection for a wicked person for the same reason.
For generally, one who has abandoned virtue tears the heart with his fruit.
Straight and extended, yet sparse, rising and falling, and curved like the lineage of the Seven Sages in its turnings—
it seemed to mark the boundary of the expanse of the sky, as pure as the belly of a sloughing serpent.
O fool, you perceive this straight and long garland, swaying from the archway above and fallen upon the ground, to be a snake;
yet it is merely a garland that, fluttering in the gentle night breeze, mimics the slight movements of a serpent.

With a straight gaze, a non-excessive smile, and slow movement; with aversion toward jesting, an effort to visit distant holy sites, and a delight in ascetics; whose body indeed has abandoned the desire for pleasure, possessing full yet small and drooping breasts, nursing, and being the sole mistress of a rogue servant—may that widow bring you prosperity!
Straight, firm, well-rounded, radiant with its grasped handle, and born of a noble bamboo—
this staff now supports me as I falter, just as a virtuous wife supports her husband.
If a debt incurred remains unpaid, it causes affliction both in this world and the next;
likewise, an evil deed does not perish without its fruit being experienced or through expiation.
One should not incur debt from a friend, nor should one lend to a friend;
for the creation of debt is known to be a destroyer of affection.
Debt, begging, old age, adultery, theft, poverty, disease, and the remnants of a meal— these eight are proclaimed to be miseries.
A father who incurs debt is an enemy; a mother who is unfaithful is an enemy;
a beautiful wife is an enemy; and an unlearned son is an enemy.
A threefold debt is established for the twice-born from birth;
for men burdened by these debts, life is lived without true living.
That one person alone is truly virtuous who has discharged the three debts and incurred no new ones; such a person prospers in happiness everywhere.
In order to discharge the three debts, while fearing first the violation of the scriptural injunctions,
one faces the manifest fear of the king in order to clear the fourth debt.
A moneylender, an astrologer, a Vedic scholar, and a river with good water—
wherever these are not found, one should not dwell for even a single day.
What is the use of that gift in the Kali age by which one is constantly approached by creditors, kinsmen, and sons seeking to receive diminished returns?
The removal of debt is traditionally held to be superior to the removal of sin;
for while the fire of debt may burn one in the next world, it burns both here and there.
Where there is no creditor, no physician, no learned Vedic scholar, and no river with water, nor a king— there one should not establish a residence.
He who, having cast off the first debt, casts off other debts as well,
and whose firm foundation shines forth— he alone truly dwells in the householder stage of life.
That which is offered through speech, like a debt to be cleared after a long time, brings aversion to constant begging; what is the use of such a gift?
One should not allow a remainder of debt, a remainder of disease, or a remainder of an enemy to persist. When requested by beggars and others, one should not give a harsh reply;
rather, if one is capable, one should perform that task oneself or cause it to be done.
Since a remainder of debt, a remainder of fire, and likewise a remainder of disease will grow again, one should therefore eliminate the remainder entirely.
A remainder of debt, a remainder of fire, and likewise a remainder of an enemy—
if not checked, even a small one will increase again and again.
All those bound by debt—sons, wife, and likewise cattle—come to an end when the debt is paid off; what lamentation can there be in that?
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but by pursuing liberation without having discharged them, one goes downward.
Cattle, wife, sons, and home exist in the form of a debt;
when that debt is extinguished, they come to an end—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
What is the use of wealth to one who is constantly at odds with creditors, whose income is never-ending yet spent on counting it,
who hates giving, who is childless, and who has a weak digestion?
Was the beauty of her two eyes borrowed from the female deer?
For this entire excellence, possessing even greater qualities, was obtained by her from them by force, while they were trembling with fear.
"When a woman remains menstruating, the giving [of her] at her own will is prescribed;
therefore, one should marry her while she is still naked," so said Manu, the son of Svayambhū.
Two months constitute a season (ṛtu), and six months are known as a solstice (ayana). Two solstices make a year; for the gods, this is a day and a night.
The season passes and returns again; the moon, having waned, comes back once more. But the water of rivers that has flowed away never returns, nor does the youth of men.
But that fool-minded man who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; there is no doubt in this matter.
If a woman who has bathed after her menses drinks the root of white kaṇṭārikā with milk,
the birth of a son will certainly occur for her.

One may live by truth, one may live by untruth, one may live by measured speech, or one may live by excessive speech; or one may even live by both truth and untruth, but one must avoid the single mode of life known as the "dog's way."
Without a formal injunction, it is impossible to understand the capacity [of a word];
for an application of meaning made impulsively appears to me as faulty.
That which is protected out of affection even without a specific purpose, and which in turn protects [its friend],
having a relationship established from former times— that is called a constant friend.
Even a very large army, when deprived of its leader,
breaks apart upon encountering battle, like a swarm of ants.
Sacrificial priests, family chaplains, teachers, disciples, relatives, and kinsmen—
all who are endowed with learning and virtuous conduct— are to be honored and revered.
It is no wonder that this foolish Rākṣasa, though possessed of supernatural powers, is so arrogant;
for what indeed is the reason for ignoble beings to follow the path of righteousness?
For men endowed with supernatural powers cannot endure the praise of others.

"Having heard that the *Ṛṣabha* melody is being sung here, we, who have mastered the nuances of musical tones, have arrived. Who knows what this cow-pen is, where such great honor has been bestowed for the sake of the cows' peace?"
Both the sages and the gods indeed regarded truth alone as supreme;
for in this world, the speaker of truth attains the highest state.
Even sages of fierce asceticism, when oppressed by fate,
abandon their rigorous observances and fall away due to desire and anger.
The sages, the Manus, the gods, and the sons of Manu of great prowess— all these,
along with the Prajāpatis, are but portions of Hari himself.
The seers say that the speech of the insane and the arrogant is like that of a Rākṣasa; it is the source of all enmities, for it is indeed the destruction of the world.
"If this sage is a guest, let a seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering, and then the honey-mixture be prepared for this Vedic scholar.
But if he is an enemy who suddenly hates our precious son, then here, in the absence of diplomacy, the bow has its rightful place."
The army of the seers is not dear without the Veda as its companion;
the army of the gods is not dear without a donor; and a lord of the earth is not dear without Viṣṇu.

Neither sages, nor gods, nor great asuras, nor those aged in the three Vedas, nor forest-dwelling munis—none of these can overcome the calamities that befall the world; yet those who know both the higher and the lower do not tremble.
The origins of the sages, of rivers, and of great-souled lineages, as well as the source of women's misconduct, are not to be discovered.
O best of the Bharatas, this supreme secret of the seers—
that the meritorious pilgrimage to sacred fords excels even sacrifices— is hereby declared.
In this holy hermitage of the sage, his mind terrified by the curse,
this lion flees from the deer even when he is wide awake.
O Śrī Rāma, having obtained a golden mountain as an excellent bracelet, the ocean of nectar as a garment, and this circle of the moon, the king of stars, as a fine earring,
your fame— though remaining far away— seeks yet another ornament similar to each of those, like a woman stubborn with pride.
Solitude is indeed one eye, and association with the virtuous is the second;
he who lacks these two will surely fall swiftly into the pit of delusion.
I have seen here one painting that is truly extraordinary—something never before beheld or heard of. What shall I say to whom, or in whose mind might there be conviction regarding it?
Within a single golden frame, the intoxicated elephant of the lake, the moonlight, the moon, the cakora bird, the cakravāka bird, and the yak-tail fly-whisk all appear together in a wondrous display.
Though it is but a single root of life, flickering and constantly causing her pain,
that poor woman carries you within her, just as the nose carries the breath.
One lip quivers from the power of his recitation, while the other throbs with rage; one hand is placed upon his head to offer salutation, while the other is raised to strike that very same head;

one eye is closed in meditation, while the other cannot bear to look at the unbearable [sight]. May that body of the Lord—which, though its parts are thus opposed, remains equal in its intent—protect you at the conclusion of twilight.
Having seen one, having seen a hundred, and even having seen five hundred, one should not practice excessive greed; otherwise, a wheel will spin upon one's head.
Spring nourished both a twice-born man of desirable speech and an intoxicated bee;
for one devoid of noble birth is unable to distinguish between the virtues of the good and the faults of the wicked.

One abode of your splendor is hidden within the *śamī* trees; another is concealed among the mountains under the guise of the light of sun-stones (*sūryopala*); and yet another, well-guarded in the ocean, acts as the submarine fire (*aurva*).

If these splendors have fled to the trees, the mountains, or the waters out of fear of the intense heat produced by the mass of your radiance, which rivals the sun’s rays—then why do kings still remain?

May the three eyes of Śambhu protect you during his time of meditative absorption—the first nearly closed like a bud from the act of meditation; the second languid with the sentiment of love for Pārvatī’s lotus-face and heavy breasts; and the other kindled by the fire of anger at Madana, who had drawn his bow far back.
One name for that which is dull by nature has been robbed of its splendor by her: the moon’s beauty and the luster of the blue lotus; this is likely not false.

Yet, that wretched elephant, intoxicated, does not even know his own gait has been stolen from him; that my heart was stolen by this slender-limbed woman, despite my being fully aware of it, is truly marvelous.

When a king appoints a single minister as the sole authority in the kingdom, pride takes hold of him through delusion; and because of that pride, he becomes indolent. In the heart of one who has become despondent, a longing for independence arises; and through that longing for independence, he then plots against the life of the king.
Victorious is the pair of feet of the Mountain’s Daughter, one resting upon the head of a buffalo and the other bowed to by joyful hosts of gods,
colored with the hue of rubies.
The moon associates with a single friend for a month while it itself undergoes waning;
you, however, by associating with hundreds of friends at every moment, attain increase.
One friend—either a king or an ascetic; one wife—either a beautiful woman or a mountain cave;
one scripture—either the Veda or the spiritual science (adhyātma); one god—either Keśava or the Jina.
A single sign suddenly renders the heart of a woman shattered; how then are those not beasts in whose interior the six signs are hidden?

One part of my mind says, "I shall go," while another part of my heart says, "I shall not go. O beautiful one, you who have stolen the heart of your beloved, it is only fitting that you possess two hearts.
There are many archers who can split a single object into two;
but Māra alone is the true archer who unites those two into one.
The one reality that exists—the essence of the joy and delight of all people—is the entire statement "That art thou" (*tat tvam asi*), which finds its final rest in you alone.

O Lord, the ornament of the earth, having heard of you, one considers nothing else; since you are attained, what further need is there for the investigation of knowledge (*jñāna-mīmāṃsā*) that merely produces the fame of Janaka and others?
Either we shall remain, having brought satisfaction to our minds by enjoying the pleasure of sporting with the lovely, full breasts of an angry beloved;
or else, on the banks of the celestial river’s sandy shores, we shall dwell with concentrated intellects, meditating upon the state of Brahman while seated upon a mat of eight blades of darbha grass.
A single dose of poison kills one person, and by a single weapon one is slain;
but the leaking of counsel destroys a king along with his kingdom and his subjects.
A woman devoted to her husband serves only one man constantly, even though another may please her heart; this is due to the unavailability of other men.
Regarding two things that are both doubtful, they say that when one of them is produced, the cause is their own mantras and so forth; otherwise, they are merely lechers acting without restraint.
Either one performs the worship of Acyuta with flowers gathered by one's own hands and washed in handfuls from the vast waters of the seashore;
or else, one dwells in a palace adorned with a couch graced by lovely jasmine petals, enjoying the essence of amorous play with a beloved whose hips are high and shapely.
A tigress gives birth to a single offspring, while a she-wolf brings forth many cubs;
yet the Uttaras meet their destruction, no matter how much they devour.
An arrow shot by an archer may or may not kill a single person;
but an intention directed by a wise man may destroy even those still in the womb.
An arrow released by an archer may kill one person or may not kill at all;
but the intellect unleashed by an intelligent man can destroy an entire kingdom along with its king.
An arrow released by an archer may kill one person or may not kill anyone at all;
but the counsel of a minister destroys the king along with his kingdom and his subjects.
For one pure eye is innate discernment, and the second is dwelling together with the wise;
he who lacks these two on this earth is blind in reality—tell me, what fault is there in his straying onto the wrong path?
O King Karṇa, do not harbor in vain the anxiety every day as to whom you shall give what, for there are more than a hundred thousand supplicants;
does a celestial wish-granting tree stand before every beggar, or the sun before every lotus, or the moon before every night-lily, or a rain-cloud before every creeper and shrub?
A single coward, when broken, may cause a great army to break; following him who has broken, even the most heroic warriors are shattered.
A certain mountain, exceedingly light, was held effortlessly by Your two arms; thus You are known throughout heaven and earth as the Uplifter of Govardhana.
I always carry You, the bearer of the three worlds, upon the tips of my breasts like a flower. Therefore, O Keśava, what is the use of much talk? Glory is attained through meritorious deeds.
There is one fault in the patient person, and a second is not found:
that people consider him, because he is endowed with patience, to be weak.
This fault of his should not be considered; for forbearance is the supreme strength.
Indeed, forbearance is a virtue for the weak, and an ornament for the powerful.
If there should be even a single wicked person in an assembly, he renders futile all the efforts of the learned.
Alas, does not even a single fly, having stirred its full belly with sweet substances, cause one to vomit?
One who has met with death is born again eightfold;
oh, what a success in trade for the residents of the city of Kāśī!
One should not travel alone on a road, nor sleep in an outer chamber; one should not engage in conversation with people, nor deliberate on matters concerning women, without [proper supervision].
One person commits sins, but the multitude enjoys the fruit;
those who enjoy are released from it, while the doer alone is stained by the fault.
One person protects the world; one person protects his family.
One indeed sinks into hell, while another is honored in heaven.
A single learned son is better than many who lack virtue; one such son delivers the lineage, while others only cause distress.
A single being is born; alone indeed does it perish.
Alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone the fruit of evil deeds.
One man departs for his end, while another, having forcibly seized his wealth, carries it away with great joy;
he does not realize that at his own death it will pass into the treasury of another—fie on this latent desire, which creates a blinding darkness through incomparable delusion!
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight off a hundred; a hundred can fight off ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is constructed.
O King, there is one enemy for a person and no second; it is ignorance, by which enveloped and impelled, he performs terrible and most cruel deeds.

One [of these two] had his vision lost by the rows of dust raised by the hooves of horses galloping on the battlefield; likewise, the other was crushed by the earth sinking under the weight of intoxicated war-elephants triumphant in their world-conquests.

What heroes indeed in the three worlds did not fall into exhaustion because of them? Yet, by this [Buddha], who granted fearlessness through the maxim of the one-eyed and the hunchbacked, both Vāsava and Vāsuki attained liberation.
Who is more cruel than he who, without sharing with his dependents, eats well-prepared food and wears beautiful clothing all alone?

Behold, O Lord, the moon rises in the ocean of the sky—the merchant’s vessel for the expedition of the five-arrowed God of Love; it is now the sole provider of nectar to the city of Indra, the sovereign remedy for the darkness before us, and the wish-fulfilling gem that awakens the night-lotuses, acting as a magical spell to dispel the pride of the deer-eyed women.
He alone truly lives who is a man of taste, even if his own heart is empty, he being Rāhu,
who does not bear that belly— the cause of all meanness— which is so difficult to fill.
He alone among the enemies of the gods is truly majestic— the son of Siṃhikā—
by whom his foes are conquered while remaining nothing more than a mere head.
May he alone protect the worlds— he who, emulating the conduct of Gaurī and the Lord of the Mountain,
shines like the One-Tusked One (Ekadanta), whose single tusk appears as if his wife had been taken away by the half of his body where one part of his face is devoid of teeth.
Intoxication is the one enemy who has taken up residence in the hearts of all people;
possessed by it, a person becomes paralyzed, neither hearing nor seeing.
My one dear friend, who was exceedingly helpful and endowed with virtue—alas, he must be killed on account of a woman; a terrible calamity has befallen me.
There is but one man truly wretched: he whose life-breaths depart along with his final sighs as he cries out, "Alas, my beloved!
Others, however, are merely beasts who cast away their grief for the loss of a lover by abstaining from food and shedding tears born of anxiety, exhaustion, despair, and dejection.
A single moon can by no means suffice to satisfy your two eyes;
therefore, let it be accompanied by Nala’s face as its second moon, so that it may be a source of inexhaustible delight for your gaze.

May that daughter of the mountain king protect you— she who, bearing the state of being half of her beloved, had one breast so high that it went to the very edge of his face as if to ask after his well-being.
"One has remained within, while another has just now reached the other side and is difficult to grasp"—while others were thus asking their mothers, "What shall we do? [the sun rose].
One should not eat delicious food alone, nor should one contemplate matters of wealth alone;
one should not travel the road alone, nor should one stay awake alone among those who are asleep.
In the forest dwells a single proud bird, the cātaka;
either he dies of thirst, or he begs from Indra.
The proud *cātaka* bird alone lives happily;
it seeks a boon from Śakra, yet it does not approach the lowly.
One should practice the Dharma alone; there is no companionship in the Dharma.
Having attained the method by oneself, what will a companion do?
There is only one fault in self-restraint, and no second can be found:
that people consider one who is endowed with patience to be powerless.
But for this fault, O one of great wisdom, there is a very great merit:
through patience, vast worlds are indeed easily attained by the forbearing one.
If a man desires his own welfare, he should not eat alone;
he should take his meal together with two or three kinsmen.
A single object indeed appears in three ways when viewed:
as a corpse by yogis, as a beautiful woman by lovers, and as meat by dogs.
For there is indeed only one supreme Self for all embodied beings;
it is perceived as if manifold by the deluded, just like light or like the sky.
There is this one great fault in your otherwise stainless lineage:
that with each successive birth of sons superior in virtue, you eclipse the glory of your ancestors.
Where there is only a single *laghu* at the beginning, that is called *āditāla*;
by means of this, the *rāsaka* brings delight and provides happiness to the listeners.
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
for everything else indeed perishes along with the body.
Only one radiant ruler of the earth exists for the sake of the world's welfare; many such as these lead to calamity, like the suns at the end of an aeon.
For the single Self of all beings, residing in every being,
is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water.
For a barren woman, there is indeed only one mental sorrow:
the anguish that "I am childless. O son, no other [sorrow] exists for her.
A single gift alone is peace; this indeed is our view. All other varieties of gifts, excluding friendship, are merely forms of dissension.
Even when assigned to a single task, these two do not possess identical dispositions,
just like two fires— one at a wedding and one on a funeral pyre.
Bamboos that grow on the same mountain, though possessing holes and thick with thorns,
are consumed by fire through mutual friction when they rub against virtuous trees.
Even hair, which has dwelt within a single womb, was once glossy and cherished upon the head; yet even that becomes discolored by old age—how much more so for women?

The lunar day (tithi) has one unit of potency, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) has four units, and the ascendant (lagna) has sixty-four units; this is the established conclusion of the science of astrology (jyotiṣatantra).
Though its wheel is single, its driver is impaired, and its horses are uneven,
the radiant sun nonetheless traverses the vault of the sky.
This is not a one-eyed crow, nor is it a serpent seeking its hole;
neither the ocean nor the moon wanes and waxes in this manner.
One with a single-minded focus attains accomplishment; one with a divided mind perishes.
For the arrow-maker does not see the army as it passes by.
That the lords of men enjoy this earth under a single umbrella, that the lords of sages rejoice with delighted minds in the abode of heaven,
and that the foremost of mortals obtain incomparable bliss in nirvāṇa— this is the radiance of the power of pure, solitary generosity alone.
One goat, two sheep, three oxen, five buffaloes,
six horses, and seven elephants— this would take away even the prosperity of Śakra.
On one side are all the sacrifices together with their complete and excellent sacrificial fees;
on the other side is the protection of the life of a living being who is terrified by fear.
On one hand there is the pain of longing, and on the other, the devotion to the taste of maintaining pride;
how can a high-minded woman find peace in this life while guarding both?
On one side is all knowledge, and on the other side is cleverness; for without cleverness, all arts are incomplete.
On one side are all evil deeds, and on the other side is the drinking of intoxicants;
on one side are all acts of giving, and on the other side is celibacy.
O best of men, on one side are the four Vedas, along with their limbs and sub-limbs, in their full detail; and on the other side, indeed, is truth alone.
On one side are the four Vedas and on the other side is the life of celibacy;
on one side are all sins and on the other side is the drinking of intoxicants.
On one side, the host of celestial beauties and Fortune welcome him;
on the other, infamy and the cause of his family’s disgrace flee along with his sin.
No distinction could be perceived even in the greatest of beings who had, as it were, attained oneness;
for all particularities of the worlds were absorbed into him, as if fallen into the sun itself.
On one side the fool counts the days, and on the other side stands the Ender; we do not know whose presence we shall reach first.
If there is dissatisfaction with one [king] on either side, one should resort to another king,
just as a traveler in the heat resorts to one shade after another.
Behold! From a single lamp on the ground, alas, many lamps have appeared;
they are like the rays released by the sun to destroy the darkness, appearing as if they were divine arrows discharged from his bow.
On one side is the orb of the moon risen; on the other is the smiling face of the dark-browed woman;
the female cakora bird flutters its bud-like beak and runs toward both.
On one side is maternal affection, and on the other are millions of virtues;
even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are not able to declare the equality between these two.
O enhancer of the family, whether it be one side of the entire clan or the self alone,
the wise are certain that these are not equal in every respect.
On one side are all the calamities of the subjects, headed by disease and famine;
on the other side is the single greed of the lord of the earth.
On one side was the fear of breaking the Kaula vow; on the other, the dread of losing their cleverness.
Thus, for the agitated women of the Kula, the night passed away in nothing but coming and going.
Finding no pleasure in one place, the bee, as if being shaken off in anger,
respectfully kissed the lotus-face of the lotus-pond— its red petals, fragrant with honey, trembling and reeling from its sighing.

In one place they recite the *Sāman* and the *Yajus*, while in another there is a different Veda; in yet another, the smoke arising from sacrifices is auspicious, as are those who appear like deer though they are fierce.

Elsewhere, the ritual procedures beginning with hospitality are duly performed with water for the feet and other offerings, and the analysis of various scriptures is continuously pursued by well-disciplined students.
In one place there is equality with common folk, and in another there is dependence;
for the sake of Śuka’s contentment, neither the forest nor the city is suitable.
In a single drop of honey, countless living beings are consumed;
for one who would have no compassion for them, therefore, one should not eat honey.
As if recollecting the splendor of betel-leaves that had shared a dwelling with her until their very end,
the radiance of the smiles on the faces of her rivals’ women grew thin.
When many people traveling together in a single caravan experience an identical omen, yet the results that arise are of various kinds, we shall therefore investigate that "swan-like movement."
In one place the waters are split by the rays from crystal banks, while in another the water is shattered by the luster of blue gems;
thus, here the rivers partake of the elegance of the celestial river, possessing the splendor born from the waters of the Yamunā.
On one side the masses of clouds take up water, on another these blazing elephants of the quarters do so, and on yet another the fires issuing from the mouth of the submarine mare;
even with such constant expenditure, it is all the more a marvel that the ocean remains as it was—its stability, its majesty, and its profundity remain exactly the same.
If even when a single creature is killed, a terrible sin arises,
then what can be said of the honey-gatherer who slaughters many minute beings?
Sitting together on the same seat was avoided by rising to meet her from afar; even a sudden embrace was thwarted under the pretext of fetching betel.
No conversation was intermingled as she kept her attendants busy nearby; thus, by means of these polite gestures toward her lover, the clever woman made her anger bear fruit.

When his two beloveds were seated together on one seat, a certain rogue approached from behind and, out of affection, playfully covered the eyes of one of them under the pretext of a great game; then, with his neck turned sideways, he kissed the other, who was thrilled by the emergence of horripilation and perspiration, her cheek-slabs radiant with a suppressed smile.

In this rainy season, the earth and the sky—both filled with the essence of water—have finally attained oneness after a long time; for what pair of woman and man has such unity ever arisen through their shared flavors?
This season is seen where all young men are hidden in union with women; even the youth, though covered by the day, sports embraced by the night somewhere in secret.
I bow to Vināyaka, the leader of the Gaṇas, who has one tusk and three eyes, whose radiance is like a blazing fire, and who has the face of an elephant.
May the son of Śambhu, white with the luster of his single tusk, be for your prosperity—
captivating like a new sprout emerging from the bulbous root of knowledge.
A king should never at one time engage in conflict with many who would strike him down;
even a proud serpent is surely destroyed by many insects.
The teacher who imparts even a single portion [of knowledge] is called an *ṛtvij* (sacrificial priest) and a performer of sacrifice (*yajñakṛt*).
These are to be honored according to their precedence; among them, however, the mother is the most venerable.
In the commissioning of one or two of the five great sins,
he who commits all five does not consider anger and lust even as much as a blade of grass.

That the Lord Sun, seizing and releasing the moon in the sequence of one, two, and three *kalās*, still performs the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance today—this is for the sake of rivaling the fire of the majesty of Your own pillar-like radiant arms; it will not succeed again against this sacrificial animal, the lunar mark, which has been consumed by him in due order.

As if counting the thousand rays of the sun as they set by means of a sequence beginning with one, two, and so forth, the lotus plant closed its thousand petals; now, as if eager to count them, it is gradually opening them once again.
On one or two mango trees, buds have just begun to open; how is it that all these travelers are reeling from whispering it from ear to ear?

Somewhere, the cry of the cuckoo—though heard only by two or three—is clearly audible even to those who had not heard it before; alas, an unbearable cry of "Hā! Hā! spreads in every direction through the houses of women separated from their lovers.
Have one or two wise men perished? Or have two or three friends met their end? And have three or four terrible, great diseases departed?
Enough with seven or eight; even this is no longer desired by our mind. For five or six moments, delight in yourself alone, or rather, when all time has vanished, find joy in the light itself.
In one or two days, the slight unevenness between her breasts will become prominent; in just two or three days, the line of hair will come within the range of vision.
Moreover, O Love, why do you exert such extreme effort to conquer the world with her eyes, when their flickering restlessness has already been achieved in merely three or four days?
With only one or two drops of honey, a bee may indeed fill its belly; yet where are those five or six flowers easily found?
Such a time has ripened that, agitated by a single thirst, whatever flower he approaches, he does so like a miser—may his effort not be frustrated.
A single *dhātu* should consist of two sections; after the *udgrāha*, the third section should be somewhat higher [in pitch], beautified by the *gamaka*.
Where the earth appears uniform, devoid of grass, trees, anthills, and shrubs,
and where a change occurs in that ground, there is water.
Having extracted this single essence from both the world and the Vedas, it is said:
even at the cost of one's life, one must not abandon the righteous path that is relaxed in its adherence to Dharma.
When Brahmins are seated in a single row for a communal meal,
if even one of them should reject the food, all must eat what has become leavings.
"You should remain united with one another, devoted solely to a single wife, and without favoring any particular one; for women are indeed the root of division."
One should not travel alone with a single man, for fear of crows and snakes,
just as the brahmin was restored to life through the grace of a crab.
With a single tail, four legs, a hump, and a hanging dewlap—
he is the offspring of a cow, a bull, who eats fodder with ease.
My heart was made restless by the longing for the lotus-feet of my one beloved;
it yearned to behold the moon-like faces of various women, charming with the full-blown state of their burgeoning passion.

"Reflecting that the suffering caused by the serpent of enemies lasts for only a single lifetime, whereas the suffering born of the mind lasts for hundreds of births— by this noble discernment, the great ones destroy the enemy that is desire in an instant."
Eating once [a day] always brings health; eating twice increases strength. From eating three times, there will be affliction by disease; from eating four times, death is certain.
Even having obtained rightness for but a single moment,
he who does not abandon it crosses the ocean of saṃsāra and attains nirvāṇa.
Even a single good deed performed for the virtuous expands like a drop of oil cast upon water;
yet a hundred favors done for the wicked shrink away like clarified butter on a cold surface.
If a teacher should awaken even a single syllable for a disciple,
there is no object on earth that he could give to become free from his debt to him.
Even a man who might consume but a single drop of honey here will fall into the ocean of existence, strewn with the rain of suffering.

One thing has one supreme effort, while another thing has the quality of shamelessness; the former is constantly dispelled by the ever-warm light, while the latter perpetually rushes toward blinding darkness.

A short vowel is said to have one measure (mātrā), and a long vowel is traditionally held to have two measures. A protracted vowel should be known as having three measures, while a quick vowel would consist of half a measure.
A single venomous serpent kills one person, and one person is slain by a weapon;
however, a brahmin, when provoked to anger, destroys entire kingdoms and even cities.
One heart is pervaded by longing, another is stolen away by my beloved;
how many hearts do I possess that maintain this consciousness?
Having acquired but a single virtue, the bow attained humility; yet that Your Majesty, possessing every virtue, should be so rigid—this is truly a great wonder!
But the Lord assigned only one duty for the Śūdra: service toward these very same social classes, performed without malice.
Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the king’s fire, like the fire of destruction, consumes the entire family along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.
Relying upon one alone, ten human beings live;
without that one, they do not shine, just as numerical digits do not shine without the zero-point.
Having bound only a single *bali* (muscle fold), Hari attained loftiness;
yet by her [the woman's] binding of three *balis*, that very same waist became curved.
Poverty alone indeed afflicts the entire world;
I salute that grammarian who made it neuter.
O lovely-eyed one, adorn this single eye with a line of collyrium,
so that a union of the *khañjana* bird and the lotus may arise within the lunar orb.
O King, that which you do not perceive is the one and only reality, without a second;
it is the truth, the ladder to heaven, like a boat for crossing from this shore to the other.
Having discerned two by means of one, bring three under control by means of four;
having conquered five, known six, and abandoned seven, be happy.
Even one who possesses but a single pure digit attains the status of the Lord of the Mountains;
whereas someone else, having acquired many digits that are defiled, gradually declines.
That which one may obtain through the gaze of a guru alone, or even through two,
cannot be obtained by anyone through three, eight, or even a thousand [other gurus].

Victory to You, who have one tusk, two mothers, are beyond the three qualities, and who, though four-armed, possess five hands; You who are praised by the six-faced one, whose intoxication has the fragrance of the seven-leaved tree, and who are the son of the eight-formed one.
Just as milk is of a single color among cows of many colors, so too,
amidst the diversity of phenomena, the ultimate reality is once again one.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this entire universe was formerly of a single caste;
it was established as the fourfold caste system through the differentiation of actions and occupations.
That sword which is of a single color and endowed with even one auspicious mark should be known as a royal sword that brings prosperity to the king.
Look at the water of a single pond: it attains sweetness in the sugarcane and bitterness in the neem;
so too does food, depending on whether the recipient is a worthy vessel or not.
Water from a single well becomes sweet in the case of a mango tree and bitter in the case of a neem tree, depending on the distinction between a worthy and an unworthy recipient.
Twenty-one hells have been taught by those who have mastered the scriptures;
compared to dwelling in the womb, they do not equal even a sixteenth part [of its suffering].
The *śṛṅgāraka* meter, consisting of twenty-one syllables per quarter,
bestows desire and grants the wishes of men when set to the *turagalīlaka* rhythm.
If a pomegranate seed is sprinkled with the blood of a cock twenty-one times,
it will certainly grow and bear fruit at that very moment.
One should have [the patient] drink water consecrated twenty-one times with the mantra;
when there is vomiting, then death occurs, but if there is no vomiting, he certainly lives.
Even a man who is preeminent in a single branch of learning may become a possessor of much knowledge,
provided he studies the well-spoken words that have indeed been extracted from the scriptures.
Various colored birds, having perched upon a single tree, fly off toward the ten directions at dawn; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Just as various birds gather on a single tree at night and depart toward the ten directions at dawn, so too is the gathering of living beings.
Just as other footprints are absorbed within the footprint of an elephant, so too is the concealment of one's own caste and complexion achieved by relying on a single [exalted] lineage.
Indeed, a horse or even a man dies from a single blow of a weapon;
whereas an elephant can endure a hundred great blows in battles.
If one possesses these qualities— uniformity in conduct, age, learning, birth, adversity, and livelihood— and is upright, such a person may be a friend in association.
If one man in a family is an ancestor who is highly learned,
while another is a fool who commits evil deeds, whose lineage does the family follow?
Among all those traveling together as a single caravan toward that same destination,
for whomsoever the time of death passes first, what cause is there for lamentation?
Those who destroy hundreds of misdeeds with a single good deed are to be served;
but not those whose anger, born from a single fault, destroys hundreds of favors done for them.
One [should know] austerity, two [the meaning of] study, three [the nature of] song, four the crossroads,
five and seven [the types of] agriculture, and battle with many men.
It is a marvel that you, though single, always dwell threefold within the hearts of enemies, the learned, and the fawn-eyed women— causing them respectively distress,
the essence of joy, and passion, through the heat of your valor, your humility, and your grace.
He who, though one, shines forth instantly as the essence of all things—known without obstruction in three ways by yogis, servants, or those most skilled in leading;
that very Mukunda, whose splendor is supreme bliss, has now arrived at Nanda’s settlement and sports in the Vṛndāvana forest together with the hosts of cowherds.
O cuckoo, you must never utter your sweet notes in this thicket;
for fear that you are one of their own kind, the merciless crows might kill you.
O lordly tree of the desert, you alone, adorned with hundreds of spreading branches laden with blooming flowers and uncrushed fruits, may live for a thousand years.

Who, other than one whose nature is pure goodness (*sāttvika*), could have fashioned you—whose intent is righteousness (*dharmāśaya*)—to tirelessly fulfill every need of the multitude of travelers exhausted by fatigue?
In birth and in destruction, you alone carry the consequence of experiencing the fruits of your own actions;
no other is ever a companion in the ordaining of pleasure and pain, for that cluster of branches gathered merely for your own livelihood.
O Lord of Life, we behold the essence of the entire universe concentrated in you alone; the eye of a man of meager merit does not rest upon this dark-hued body of yours.
Who else but you possesses such exceedingly vast delight? Your very glance is nectar—may Hari, who was thus described by both Daityas and sages, protect you in his form that captivates women.
O King, from a single tree come the sacrificial vessels—the *sruk*, the *droṇī*, the *voḍhanī*, and the *pīḍanī*.
O King, understand from me as I speak this: from a single Person are born both the non-existent and the existent.
O brother, our birth occurred together in the clear water of a lake; some days have passed for us right here, while others have been spent elsewhere.
You, O lotus, have obtained the status of a playful ornament for the deer-eyed women, whereas I wallow in the water trampled by the feet of low-born wives.
On a single bed, two spouses lay with their backs turned to one another, suffering in silence; though the conciliation remained in each other’s hearts, both guarded their dignity.
Then, as their glances slowly mingled through the turning of sidelong eyes, the quarrel of pride was broken by a laugh and a sudden embrace around the neck.

On a single bed, while her lover was offering endearments, the innocent girl—having turned away in sudden anger and become dejected because he had not chosen one of her rival women—spurned him out of agitation.
As her beloved remained silent for that moment, she looked back at him again with her neck sharply turned, lest he appear as if he were asleep.
On a single bed, perceiving that one of the two lotus-eyed women was asleep, he craned his neck and saw her whose veil had blossomed open;
then, approaching the other, he brought about the loss of her sleep by flickering the hem of her garment with the movements of his fingers, which were moving stealthily and restlessly.

One day, while wandering about, I somehow obtained a jewel whose value cannot be found even if one possessed the entire earth. By the power of fate, it has now become utterly like common glass. What shall we do? To whom shall we turn for refuge? Where is that friend to whom this might be told?
When even a single day has passed devoid of Dharma,
one’s heart burns for a long time, like that of a person robbed by bandits.

May that glorious Sun, the Great God, protect us—even though he is served for but a moment—He who, at the time of his scorching heat, brings about a process of burning such that the state of night becomes difficult to find; He whose presence as light is known in the world even within a fraction of the sky.
In one and the same family, both a eunuch and a great chariot-warrior are born together,
just as on a single tree there may be branches that bear fruit and branches that do not.
On a single mountain of Malaya, what is the use of those various birds that are of no consequence—the flocks of crows, owls, pigeons, and cuckoos?

If even a single peacock stands nearby and cries out, then the sandalwood tree, having broken the bonds of the swarming serpents, becomes the delight of the minds of all people in this world and worthy of being served.
When one evildoer is brought to his end, the security of many is secured; therefore, the killing of such a person is a source of merit.
When the mind is conquered in even a single domain, the entire world is conquered;
but if that [mind] remains unconquered, not even one's own son is truly subdued.

Even when one head has been struck down, how can there be any pacification of your anger? Rather, the destruction of your heads is seen as a means for your own appeasement—provided it is not at the hands of the enemy.
O Lord of Rākṣasas, because of the multiplicity of your heads, this very fruit is fully obtained by me; as each one is severed, you will come to recognize your own misconduct.

When two [recipients] are equal in the arising of their virtues, what is the point of giving with attachment and aversion by offering a full portion to one and a meager portion to the other? Such a gift is based on discrimination.
Having observed the action of one person, another also performs a censurable deed;
the world follows like a flock, for the world is not concerned with ultimate truth.
Whatever sins fools commit for the sake of a single lifetime,
they produce suffering for themselves throughout thousands of future births.
I consider that single cloud to be truly fortunate,
whose face gazes upon the entire universe, including its mountains and forests.
Before I can reach the end of one suffering, as if reaching the far shore of the ocean, a second has already arrived for me; thus, misfortunes multiply through my vulnerabilities.
O timid one, what burden could your own sin possibly impose upon the Self revealed by the Vedas, who is already submerged in the infinite torment caused by the sins of the entire world?
The creation of the Supreme Lord is one, yet it is divided fourfold at the time of its application:
as Bhavānī for enjoyment, Durgā in battles, Kālī in times of wrath, and Viṣṇu among men.
For by the favor of one person, the entire world becomes gracious;
it is a certainty that when one is agitated, everyone becomes agitated.
How indeed can he who is not even capable of subduing his own single mind conquer the earth bounded by the oceans?

When even the single Mind-born One [Kāma] conquered the world with the side-glances of those weak women, we were indeed deprived of every manner of manifesting the sentiment of wonder; yet that the Sugata, though possessing power, did not even begin to tremble of his eyebrows in order to conquer him along with his forces—that story of his virtues serves only to paralyze us.
For one who lacks the power to give food even to a single guest,
what is the fruit of dwelling in a home filled with manifold afflictions?

The moon rises upon the summit of one mountain and, in due course, sets upon another; of these two, the mountain where it sets is the more praiseworthy. Who does not make of his head-jewel a crest for the rising [sun], yet he who makes it so when it has set is as rare to find as you are, O High-headed One!
Whether for the sake of oneself or another, he who would kill even one among many living beings— his sin in this world shall be equal to that of killing a single person.
O auspicious lady, when many prosper through happiness upon the death of one individual,
there is neither mortal sin nor minor offense in that killing.

The moon, its splendor surpassed by her lotus-face, approached as if to serve her who was made terrifying by the rays of the sun; instantly assuming the guise of a white parasol, it acted like a beloved friend.
That which is born from the treasury of Brahman is not sufficient for even one person;
yet for one whose disposition has been nourished by it, even a small amount brings fulfillment.

Having made his body one with the peerless moon-crested Lord, he abandoned half of himself to Bhavānī, destined for the constant suffering of separation; surely it was by him, having thus divided his limbs, that Viriñci fashioned this slender, delicate creeper-like form, appropriately composed of those very parts.
Austerity is for one alone; study and singing are for two; traveling is for three;
visiting a field is for four; and battle is for many.
One should not travel alone, even if there be a hundred tasks to be done;
by [the presence of] a single cock, a Brahmin was protected.
One should not travel alone, even if there are hundreds of tasks to be done;
by a mere crab, the black cobra was brought down.
In the lord of beasts, who dwells alone in the forest, lacks royal insignia, and is ignorant of the treatises on polity,
yet is exalted by his courage, the words "King" find their fulfillment.
Having found a rare woman alone in a secluded place and intoxicated,
he who, being inexperienced, does not enjoy her but instead requests her through a messenger on another day— [is called a "messenger"].
And he who, having abandoned at that very moment prosperity obtained through impetuosity,
seeks it again on another day through policy— who could be more pitiable than those two?

"Since I am a young woman here all alone, and the master of this house has gone abroad—what do you ask for lodging here? This wretched mother-in-law of mine is both blind and deaf; surely you are a fool, O traveler!"
"This house belongs to me alone; my watchman is blind. Alas, what fear does not arise in my mind here from this thief?
O traveler, had you not been so happily fast asleep through fate’s decree due to your exhaustion, would we not say that this night's lodging was anything but appropriate?"
Alone, having abandoned his home, using only his hands as a bowl and clothed only by the directions, even he is constrained in this world by craving; behold the wonder!
Alone, one should constantly reflect upon what is beneficial for oneself in solitude;
for by reflecting alone, one attains the supreme good.
O Śambhu, when shall I become solitary, free from desire, peaceful, using my hands as a bowl, clad only by the directions, and capable of uprooting all karma?
He who does not respect a teacher who has bestowed upon him even a single syllable will,
after passing through a hundred births as a dog, be born among the Cāṇḍālas.

The Gaṅgā is but one at Prayāga; sandalwood trees exist only on the slopes of the Malaya mountains; pearl necklaces are found only upon the necks of beloved women; the moon is but one in the sky; and likewise, white lotuses grow only in lakes. The Yamunā is but one; black serpents are rare; emerald pendants are unique; and the spot on the moon is but a single swarm of bees. Thus, wherever your fame spreads, it is joined there by the ill-fame of your enemy.
The ritual of the single fire (*ekāgnikarma*) and that which is offered in the three fires (*tretā*),
as well as whatever gift is given within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*), is designated as *iṣṭa*.
O King, one should be single-minded and ever vigilant for vulnerabilities; one should conduct the affairs of the kingdom among rivals while remaining constantly alert.
One-pointedness and resolve are capable of growth like sinews;
through constant practice and application, they become increasingly effective.
Placing one foot upon her lover’s foot and resting the other upon his knee, with her waist gracefully arched, she clasps his neck with both hands;
pressing her full, high breasts firmly against his chest out of passion, the moon-faced girl, her hair standing on end with thrill, kisses the mouth of that most fortunate man.
Sovereignty over the world under a single umbrella, fresh youth, and this lovely body— you,
appearing deluded in your judgment, seem to me to wish to abandon so much for the sake of a trifle.
Considering it improper that there should be only one Gaurī for the eleven Rudras,
O King Rāghava, by your fame all ten directions have been made white (Gaurī).
When Govinda is situated in the eleventh house, all the planets are likewise situated in the eleventh;
what do all the planets—Saturn, Mars, and the Sun—do [then]?
From a quarter consisting of eleven syllables, by increasing one syllable at a time in each successive section (*khaṇḍa*),
there are sixteen *dhruvās* up to twenty-six syllables.

One they enchant with sidelong glances, another with the undulations of their eyebrows, yet another with their smiles, and still another with secret intimacies; oh, who indeed knows the artistry of these women so rich in arts?
Having brought that incomparable one, who resembled the God of Love and was seated upon his couch in a secluded chamber,
as a guest to her eyes, the young girl with eyes like those of a cakora bird bowed her lotus-face in salutation.
Mankind consider that which is called the Abode to be uniquely and utterly peaceful,
the destroyer of the pair of effects known as heat and cold.
For one who is devoted to solitude, firm in his vows, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses,
whose mind is absorbed in internal yoga, and who is eternally non-violent, liberation is certain.
Where is the Creator, dull-witted as he is in the production of singular beauty, and where is this form of hers, so skillful in the loveliness of every limb?
I think that the Fish-bannered God, seeking to save his life out of fear of Maheśvara, has assumed this form of a young woman.
For it is not possible, O dear one, to please everyone exclusively—
whether friend, foe, or neutral party— among all beings, O Bhārata.
"From the forest to the house, even the moon-faced one appears different in solitude; prepare quickly, daughter, let her go to another dwelling on this auspicious day.
Thus repeatedly urged by her mother-in-law who was in a state of agitation, the young bride, seeing the traveler, broke her smile and left that very half-cooked rice.
In a solitary, secluded place, pure and free from disturbances,
one should practice upon a seat made of woolen blankets, deerskins, or cloth.
In a secluded, solitary, delightful, pure, and undisturbed place,
one should practice meditative absorption while seated comfortably on a cushion made of cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass.
Sit comfortably in solitude; let the mind be concentrated on that which is beyond; let the nature of the vital breath be thoroughly examined; let this world be seen as pervaded by it.

Let past karma be dissolved through the power of consciousness, and let no future karma be attached; let the karma already begun be experienced here, and then remain established in the Self that is the Supreme Brahman.
When one person attains liberation, the world attains liberation; when all have attained liberation, there is no longer any doubt.
Adopting such a position as this, those who proceed along this path are able to abide in happiness.
Even a single auspicious Tārā, seated in the fivefold peaceful posture, grants the attainment of one's desires;
when both [postures] are present, the gain is greater, and with three, there is success in royal undertakings.
One mother gives birth to the body; the second mother gives birth to speech.
They say that what is born of speech is even more precious than a biological sibling.
One wife, three sons, two ploughs, and ten cows—
these shall not undergo any change even at the end of the kalpa.
One wife, three sons, two ploughs, ten cows,
and residence in a village with old friends— this is more delightful than even heaven.
One wife is naturally talkative and the second is fickle; his son is the world-conquering, irresistible god of love.
With Śeṣa as his bed, sleeping upon the ocean, and the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa) as his vehicle—remembering again and again the circumstances of his own home, Murāri has become like a piece of wood.

One cheek became like the quiver of the flower-armed god, with the rows of downy hairs clearly visible as its feathered shafts; the other cheek was like a protective amulet for the victor, covered in horripilation.
O Hero, as you beheld that tremulous-eyed maiden—unable to endure the distress of separation that would arise in an instant—and heard the roar of the great battle, [your state was such].
The identity of both is their being a single tree;
the difference between rice and wild millet is discerned by their fruit.
Having mastered a single science, one who has entered an assembly of those possessing many sciences becomes afraid;
where is a multitude of weapons gathered, and where is a man with but a single arrow?
It is well known in the world that enmity among siblings arises solely from a single object of desire;
for instance, there occurred a fierce conflict between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas on account of the earth, which brought about the destruction of the world.
For desire for a single object of enjoyment is the seed of the great tree of enmity,
just as the desire for Tilottamā was for Sunda and Upasunda.
May Bhairava protect you—he who, having made the entire world desolate upon the earth turned into a single ocean, sports with Kālī as his companion, letting out playful, forceful bursts of laughter;
and who, seeing the reflection of his own body in the darkness suddenly pierced by the rays of his fangs, cried out in anger, "Who are you? Who are you? Speak!", yet remains fearless.
If there is a mutual dissension between two neighboring kings who are both friends and enemies,
then one whose policy has matured may, free from fear, launch an attack upon them with ease.

The five arrows of Smara, joined with the letters *e* and *au*, are renowned as the slayers of Hari, Hara, and Brahmā; their targets are, in order, the heart, the breasts, the eyes, the head, and the secret parts.
When these arrows, discharged from his own eye-bow, fall repeatedly upon these vital points, drops of the waters of passion, resembling blazing fire, flow forth from beautiful women.
When two parties set out on a journey toward a single objective,
their combined advance is called a "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), which is a form of alliance (*sandhi*).
Attachment to a single purpose is said to be the characteristic of an enemy; however, one who possesses the qualities of a conqueror is considered a formidable foe.
Under the guise of a single-string necklace of pearls adorning the pair of her lofty breasts,
the exceedingly pure minds of the self-restrained ascetics performed service to them, their internal barriers having been breached by the falling arrows of Kandarpa.
May the eternal abiding of these two gods, who are enemies of the city of the demons and whose limbs possess a beauty like the peaks of mountains of snow and collyrium, lead to your welfare;
they in whom the coils of serpents are disarrayed by the fear of Garuḍa, and in whom the lake of the navel has a lotus sleeping within the sheath of its luster, bright as the crescent moon.
Either a single dugdhikā, a tumbī, a śaṅkhapuṣpī, or a jaṭā worn [on the body],
when placed upon the neck or the teeth, is capable of removing the afflictions caused by bhūtas.

Even those who sit upon a single seat, subsist on water and air, seek liberation, and have renounced all possessions—even they inquire about the movements of the sky-dwellers from an astrologer; how much more so those whose minds are set on worldly gain?
If one is devoid of recitation for a single day, or devoid of the twilight devotions for three days,
or remains without the sacred fire for twelve days, he is undoubtedly a Śūdra.
The emperor among poets named Śrīpāla, who completed this great composition in a single day and was accepted as a kinsman by the illustrious Siddharāja, composed this excellent panegyric.
O Kaunteya, for even a single day, provide abundant water;
O dear one, it delivers seven generations before, seven after, and seven in between.
Content with a single meal a day, always devoted to the six duties,
and approaching his wife only during her fertile period— that Brahmin is called a *dvija*.
Though standing in the midst of her own herd, the female elephant, like one all alone, trumpeted fearfully;
and out of apprehension, she repeatedly nibbled at the base of the male elephant's tusks with her trunk.
By her, whose budding breasts are full and pressed together, all that collection of camphor,
pearl necklaces, yellow sandalwood, moonstones, flowing moss, lotus stalks, ice, and the like has been gathered into my skin as if poured there by squeezing.

Having gathered together within the vessel of the sky the juices of the Lord of Herbs (the moon), which are repeatedly blown from all sides by the breath from the mouths of the blooming lotus-faces of the women that are the day-lotuses;

and having thoroughly and intensely heated them with masses of fire possessing the ruddy luster of kindled wood—thus does the blameless physician, the Sun, perform the alchemical killing (*māraṇa*) of the mercury that is the stars.
The power to effect separation belongs to swans and to wicked people alike, even when water and milk have become one, or when the hearts of friends have merged.
O mind, remember how many deceptions have been committed by these elements when they have dissolved and acted as if clearly united as one.
Therefore, abandon your acquaintance with them and contemplate your own true state; has not your speech been heard—that even a "wise" man would be shattered?
Some are not even noticed when standing in a corner of a hut; for others, even this entire universe is too cramped for their wealth.
Some among them, having fallen into the hands of the executioners, receive the designation of "vessels"; others sing with sweet and passionate melodies accompanied by the lute.
Some, through the power of their association with those [executioners], help cross over what is difficult to cross; yet some among them, their hearts aflame, drink nothing but blood.
Some, having become mendicants with water-pots, bring themselves to the state of worthy vessels; others, clinging to pure bamboo flutes, sing with sweet and passionate melody.
Some, indeed, being strung together with virtues, enable others to cross over what is difficult to traverse; yet among them, some with hearts ablaze drink only blood.
Some depart today at dawn, others later in the day, and still others at different times;
all go into this boundless cycle of existence—whom can anyone mourn, and for what?

A poem lacking a word that produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*), even if it possesses the luster of a priceless gem and is free from even a trace of flaw, does not take root in anyone’s heart; it is like the youth of women devoid of beauty.
Even one who is lowly may attain high standing in the worlds through some single quality;
as an example, the moon, though renowned for its softness and a mine of defects, has attained a lofty position.
The ocean was drunk up in a single mouthful by the pot-born sage Agastya;
therefore, at his rising, the waters cast off their turbidity as if out of fear.
With one hand holding back a lock of hair and with the other raising her chin,
I see her face at the city gate, its ears washed by tears.

O Ketaka flower, if you have been rejected by Maheśvara alone, why do you harbor such grief? Are there not others in this world who truly recognize merit—the gods among men (kings) who carry you upon their heads?
With one [hand] staying below and the other staying above,
the distinction between the giver and the beggar is indicated by the hands alone.
With her own words as her sole dear witness, she quickly conquered the lute; with her gait alone, she surpassed the swan that travels to every house.
With her face, she defeated the moon which delights all without exception; and with her gaze, as if its tip were fixed upon the target, she shatters the pride of the lotuses.
The splendor that a single royal swan bestowed upon a lake could not be matched by a thousand cranes dwelling all around its shores.
Having learned that two lotuses have grown from a single stalk,
lustful men dig at night, thinking there is treasure beneath them.
Just as an entire forest is consumed by fire ignited from a single dry tree,
so too is an entire family destroyed by a wicked son.
One should form an alliance with one [king] and engage in conflict with another, or seek prosperity from all sides after careful deliberation;
thus should one who desires victory employ these policies, knowing the essence of what is beneficial and harmful to oneself.
With one [eye], they speak many words with lips as rosy as a smile; with another, they gaze from here with eyes shining like blossoming night-lotuses;

and with another, they meditate in their minds upon the wondrous splendor of a far-distant noble character. By what means, then, can there be love for these fair-browed women that is truly meaningful in the ultimate sense?
