One who desires prosperity should accomplish the goals of dharma with one part;
with one part, the goal of pleasure; and he should increase the remaining one part.

With one eye, reddened with intense anger, she gazes at the orb of the sun situated in the sky; with her other eye, shimmering with tears, she looks upon her beloved. At the close of day, the female cakravāka bird, fearing separation from her mate, displays two mingled sentiments like a skilled dancer.
By one you have been struck with a blow; by another your husband has been drunk up; by another your brother has been cursed; and by yet another you have been banished from the three worlds.
O Mother, since King Śrīvīra now regards you as a mere blade of grass, O Dweller in the Lotus, do not direct your anger toward me, who am devoted to you solely out of affection for our common birth.
By one you were struck with a kick on the chest; by another you were drunk upon; by another your husband was cursed; by another you were driven out from the three worlds.

By one your house was hidden away; by another it was torn down; and yet another has the nature of a co-wife. Therefore, O Consort of the Enemy of Mura, I believe that you are perpetually separated from the twice-born.
Even by a single person who possesses virtue, is pure by birth, and performs beautiful deeds,
one's entire family is adorned, just as a crown is adorned by a single pearl.
Even by a single virtuous man, endowed with learning and goodness—
a lion among men— a family is illuminated, just as by the moon.
Even with but a single quality, one who possesses excellence becomes an object of longing;
for even though he is dark, the cuckoo is honored by people because of its sweet warbling alone.
Ah, even by a single quality a man may become desirable;
like the moon, which, though it is the source of darkness (the night), is beautiful because it possesses the light of its digits.
By even a single ocean, those clouds have been filled by the millions; yet not even a loss of water as fine as a drop of dew resting on the tip of a blade of kusha grass has occurred in it.
Or rather, through the shifting of fate, the clouds—though they gather together—are unable to produce even a trace of stillness in its dust, for their waters dry up.
Even by a single disciplined son, a family is uplifted;
behold Bhagīratha, who brought down the Ganges to its distant shore.
Even by a single person who is very steadfast and full of enthusiasm toward battle, the entire army becomes enthusiastic; yet when that [single person] is broken, it suffers defeat.
For this very reason, kings desire warriors of great strength; they favor those who are brave, steadfast, and full of zeal, while they avoid those who are cowardly.
Even by a single good son being born, a noble family is illuminated forever,
just as the sky is made radiant by the moon.
Even by a single good son who is endowed with learning and is virtuous,
the entire family is gladdened, just as the night is by the moon.
By even a single good son who is virtuous and endowed with learning,
a family attains brilliance, just as the sky does by means of the moon.
Even with but one good son, a lioness sleeps without fear;
a she-ass carries her burden even with ten sons.
Even by a single well-grown tree, flowering and fragrant,
that entire forest is perfumed, just as a family is by a good son.
For even by a single hero, the surface of the earth is trampled underfoot,
just as it is by the sun with its vast and shimmering radiance.
"O Kṛṣṇa, this Govardhana has been held up by you alone for a long time; you are weary, so rest now for a moment while we all support it.
May Hari, smiling as he ceased when the mass of cowherds raised their arms in this way, yet was slightly distressed by the weight of the mountain as his arm bent, protect you.
For indeed, someone attains renown in the world through a single quality alone;
an elephant is called "karin" because of one trunk, but the sun is not so called even with a thousand.

Having drawn his sword with one hand and breaking with the other the arrow fallen upon his chest, his face adorned by the knitting of his brows, his eyes impetuous, and his lower lip clearly bitten—this preeminent warrior lies there, his body unhurt by the throngs of carnivorous beasts and using a lordly elephant as his pillow; if such is death, what is the use of victory?
One girdle produced no sound, while another resounded repeatedly; one eye met with a slight contact from the thigh, while the other was born of full contact with the thigh.
One passion departed from the heart, while another remained just as it was; externally there was horripilation, while internally a great agitation arose from the excitement of the embrace.
Some say that at the end of the day, the sun enters the ocean; others speak of his departure to another world, and some declare his union with fire.
O dear friend, this is false, for it lacks witness. I believe, rather, that the sun rests upon the hearts of women traveling on the road, whose heat is as intense as his own.
In the speech of some, [well-spoken words] are like those of a parrot; in the hearts of others, they are like those of a mute.
But for yet others, beautiful utterances leap gracefully both in the heart and in the speech.

Some are noble beings who accomplish the welfare of others by abandoning their own self-interest; those who exert themselves for the sake of others without contradicting their own interest are merely ordinary.
But those who destroy the welfare of others for their own sake—these are human rākṣasas. And as for those who destroy the welfare of others pointlessly, we do not know what they are.

If even those who devote themselves to each sense-object individually become guests in the house of Death, what need is there to speak of one who revels in the domain of all five senses? Those of pure intellect and refined minds abandon the objects of the senses.
Even individually, the sense objects—which are like poison—strike down [beings];
how then could one who indulges in all five simultaneously remain secure?
O fortunate one, this tremulous finger, leaping over each young man as if skipping over a cluster of pebbles, comes to rest upon you, just as it would upon Mount Meru.
Each individual sense object, resembling poison, strikes down [the mind] one by one;
how much more so when the five are combined—why indeed would they not destroy it?
When the honey accumulated from each individual flower is gathered,
even that is consumed by groups of bees who are utterly devoid of compassion.
One should join four wings to each individual arrow;
one should have the cutting of the wings performed with a measurement of six finger-breadths.
"O monkey, for each single service rendered by you, I shall give up my life;
we remain indebted for all that remains to be done day after day."

These wealthy patrons excel individually in their respective arts; they are uniquely skilled in recognizing the virtues of others and are proficient in the conduct of masters in all branches of learning.
Yet, alas, they tremble at the mere mention of flowers and words, fearing that their earrings might wear away from rubbing against their heads when those heads are bowed in praise.
Since each single drop of honey is produced from the slaughter of innumerable living beings,
how can a wise person eat honey?
A single poem alone is sufficient for men; it serves for a village, for a horse, for an elephant, and ultimately even for food, clothing, and betel.
For the great, there is but one single state: either fine garments or a patched rag;
either a young woman held by the fingertips or a rosary amidst the waves of the Ganges.
The followers of Uśanas maintain that there is indeed only one science, namely the science of government (daṇḍanīti);
for within it, the undertakings of all sciences are firmly established.
In union, the young woman is one alone; in separation, the entire world consists of her.
Since this separation has actually been beneficial, by whom could it be censured?
There exists that certain digit of the moon, composed entirely of nectar, which is exceedingly priceless;
it is by this alone that the Supreme Lord, who recognizes merit, has placed her upon his crest-jewel, without taking account of the fault of its dark spot.
One meaningful reflection is that which is contemplated for the sake of the Dharma; the second meaningful reflection is that which delights in the Dharma for practitioners of yoga.

May that Lord remove from you the state of darkness for the sake of beholding the path of the righteous—he who, though established in absolute sovereignty, is himself clothed in an animal hide as a fruit of his many devotees; he who, though his body is united with his beloved, stands beyond those ascetics whose minds are free from sense-objects; and he who possesses no pride even while sustaining the entire universe with his eight forms.
The Lord Giriśa is one, yet his attendants are equal to him in both number and favor;
what can we do, for the course of karma is such that Bhṛṅgin withers away while Vināyaka remains stout?
According to those of old, one man is said to belong to his own lineage when he supports his own family;
yet even that same single man becomes many when he is capable of supporting others.
One man of virtuous conduct is victorious; how much more so two who are well-united?
What wonder is it if the world is conquered by the two breasts of a slender-limbed woman?
There is one soul and many bodies; there is one reality and many delusions. There is one knowledge and many heresies. Why do the wise engage in such frivolous debate?
Those born from the same womb and born under the same constellation do not become equal in virtue, just like the jujube and its thorns.
Those who share a single womb but have separate necks, and consume different fruits,
perish if they do not remain united, like the *bhāruṇḍa* birds.
The son of Daśaratha was indeed alone, while the Yātudhānas were by the thousands; yet as many as they were in battle, so many did he perceive himself to be through them.
There is but one God, whether Keśava or Śiva; there is but one friend, whether a king or an ascetic;
there is but one dwelling, whether in a city or in a forest; and there is but one wife, whether a beautiful woman or a mountain cave.
A single quality is the highest good: forbearance; a single thing is the supreme peace: tranquility;
a single thing is the ultimate vision: knowledge; and a single thing brings happiness: non-violence.
Before one [wound] has been healed, another has arisen; this other wound was not even planted.
True indeed is the proverb: "Into the openings of those who are negligent, misfortunes enter in great numbers."
Nineteen women went to the Sarayū river for the purpose of bathing;
twenty returned, while one was devoured by a tiger.
Nineteen women went to the forest to play; twenty returned home, while the one remaining was devoured by a tiger.

There should be one leader, whether a Kṣatriya or a twice-born; one science, whether the science of inquiry (Anvīkṣikī) or the triple Veda (Trayī); one wife, whether born of noble lineage or beloved; and one friend, whether a king or an ascetic.
May he protect us—he who is known as the one at the end, equal to two, three-eyed, praised by the four Vedas, five-faced, the father of the six-faced one, and saluted by the seven seers;

he who possesses eight limbs, is equal to nine, whose dwelling is among the hosts of immortals, who holds the ten directions, who is himself the eleventh, and who, as the twelve-fold soul, cannot be conquered by the rays of the sun.
Even a single prostration made to Kṛṣṇa is equal to the final purificatory bath of ten horse-sacrifices;
one who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth, but he who prostrates to Kṛṣṇa does not return to further existence.
One should serve even a single person who, whenever he is diminished,
makes him new again without distress, just as the sun does for the moon.
Even a single son endowed with virtue is better than a hundred devoid of merit;
a single moon dispels the darkness, whereas thousands of stars cannot.
Even a single son endowed with virtue is better than hundreds of those devoid of merit;
the moon alone is the eye of the world—what need is there for the stars?
Even a single son who possesses virtue is better than a hundred sons devoid of virtue;
a single moon dispels the darkness, whereas thousands of stars cannot.
Alas, even a single Kālidāsa is not surpassed by anyone;
how much less so the triad of Kālidāsas when it comes to the graceful expression of the erotic sentiment!
Though it is but one, this ball appears as if threefold: deeply red from the glow of the beloved’s palm when held there;
pale white with the rays of her toenails upon the ground; and deep blue with the beams of the eyes when situated in the sky.
Let there be even one who is capable of accomplishing every task and preeminent in strength; what is the use of many offspring?
The moon illuminates the expanse of all directions, whereas the host of stars, though risen together, is utterly incapable of doing so.
In whatever city even a single renowned archer may reside,
from that place enemies flee far away, like deer from the lair of a lion.
Even a single lordly elephant, endowed with the qualities of rut and courage, destroys the properly arrayed army of enemies;
for the victory of kings is established upon their elephants. Therefore, a king should always possess a force superior in elephants.
Even a single lion can crush a herd of a thousand elephants;
therefore, viewing oneself as noble as a lion, one should charge forward.
Even a single minister who is intelligent, brave, capable,
and discerning can bring great prosperity to a king or a royal official.
A certain young student, with darbha grass and kuśa tips in his hand, waters the young mango trees in the forest;
thus the mango trees are watered and the ancestors are satisfied—this single act is renowned for accomplishing two purposes.
A wise man who has fallen among many fools will surely be overwhelmed,
like a lotus amidst the waves of a river.
One arrow that pierces the vitals of lovers is the tremulous glance of amorous women; another is the Malaya breeze for those filled with desire;
another is the sounding of lutes and flutes; the fourth is the mango blossom; and the fifth, which is the foremost minister of universal longing, is the cuckoo’s song itself.

Whether you alone or ten of you stand equal to me, with your bows drawn and the sky filled with the twang of bowstrings—therefore, take up your bow along with Lakṣmaṇa and the world-protectors; let there be a battle worthy of this moment.
A single state is always praised for ascetics of purified soul,
but not for those greedy for wealth, nor especially for worldly people such as kings.
One arose from the sandy bank, and another from the lotus; these three were the ancient celestial poets who sported with the Goddess of Speech.
If there are moderns who pride themselves on their eloquence and skill in composing prose and verse, the poet Śākallamalla plays with them all, surpassing them completely.
There was one [poet] from a lotus, another from a riverbank, and yet another from an anthill; all of them are poets and they are my gurus—to them we offer our salutations.
If those who are recent [poets] delight the mind with their compositions in prose and verse, I place my left foot upon their heads, O beloved of the King of Karṇāṭa!
A single frog, having obtained the water of a cow’s hoofprint, cries out repeatedly and loudly in rivalry, "Who is there?
Who is there? But the great ocean, having received the waters of all rivers such as the Gaṅgā and possessing abundant jewels, generally does not harbor even the slightest pride.
My eternal self alone is the enjoyer of pleasure and pain, having the nature of knowledge and vision; nothing else—such as my body, wealth, senses, brothers, wife, or happiness—is truly mine.

All these have arisen from karma, being transient and yielding only suffering. Therefore, O soul, abandon this vain delusion through reflection; take refuge in the path of liberation, which is your own true and unerring welfare.
One ocean alone survives in this world, from which, alas, such vast quantities of water have been gathered that these clouds,
having somehow drunk a mere fraction of it, satisfy even the entire earth for a long time.
The sun alone possesses supreme brilliance; the lion dwelling in the forest is exceedingly brave;
the sky is indeed vast and empty; and the salt ocean is profoundly deep.

There is but one single flavor, the pathetic (karuṇa), which, though appearing as if divided into various distinct forms due to differences in its causes, assumes diverse transformations; just as water assumes the modifications of whirlpools, bubbles, and waves, yet all that is indeed nothing but water.

Among those possessed by passion, Hara shines supreme, for he has taken half the body of his beloved; among those free from passion, the Jina shines supreme, for there is none higher than he who is detached from attachment to women.

As for all other people, they are bewildered by the pervasive venom of the serpent-like arrows of irresistible Love; mocked by desire, they are indeed incapable of either enjoying or renouncing the objects of the senses.
One person reflects upon his purpose; one applies his mind to dharma;
and one performs his duties—him they call the mediocre man.
One [mark] is on the forehead, two on the head, two each on the sides and the flanks, and two are to be known on the chest; however, there is only one during the departure.
Greed alone is the great predator; from greed, evil proceeds.
From that evil comes the acquisition of unrighteousness, and from that, suffering arises.

There was an only son of a wealthy man who had lost his father while still in the prime of youth; there was a scribe in the service of a foolish king; and there was the son of a merchant who vied with the god of love.
The son of a preceptor renowned as a physician to the king’s ministers, who were perpetually afflicted by illness,
was a man of hidden desire who wore matted locks.
Seeking the peace that comes from the doctrine of the neuter, subsisting on fruits, intoxicated,
accompanied by rogues, and unrestrained— such was the prince.
A rustic son of a nurse and a twice-born man, a singer who has attained gain,
a caravan leader who has arrived immediately, and a glorious man devoted to fate.
The fool who blindly follows others, the scholar intoxicated by his own learning,
and the man perpetually drunk— these are the moving wish-fulfilling trees for courtesans.
"I alone, pitiless, snatch away the lives of living beings who place their trust in me"—do not harbor such remorse in your mind, O hunter.
For how many men, whose intentions are hidden, who are enemies of the virtuous and equal to you, do not dwell in the palaces of kings or in pure sacred fields?
One Vaiśya, two Śūdras, and three Brāhmaṇas—
these five who subsist by their learning should not go together on their own.
One Vaiśya, two Śūdras, seven or five Kṣatriyas,
nine women, and three Brāhmaṇas should not go [together].
"I am alone, I am without companion, I am emaciated, and I have no retinue"—
such a thought does not arise even in a dream for the king of beasts.
"You think to yourself, 'I am alone,' yet you do not know the ancient sage dwelling within the heart;
he is the witness of your evil deeds, before whom you commit your transgressions."
O auspicious one, as for this self of yours whom you think of as "I am alone," this sage who observes merit and demerit is eternally situated within your heart.
Hara alone among the gods is a connoisseur of the virtues of his beloved’s lip; the others are fools, for he drank only the poison, perceiving it as equal to nectar.
For one person, having fallen under the power of the noose of Time, commits an evil deed; through that base transgression of his own, the entire family is destroyed.
For a single, excellent wagtail perched upon a lotus petal, when seen, brings about the sovereignty over a fourfold army;
yet I know not what this pair of wagtail-like eyes will do for me within the lotus of your face.
It was wrongly said that "a single fault sinks away amidst a collection of virtues";
for why does singular folly not destroy all the virtues, such as beauty and the rest, of those who possess bodies?
For a single fault sinks away amidst a multitude of virtues, like the spot on the moon amidst its rays;
surely some poet has observed that poverty alone is the destroyer of a heap of virtues.
For a single minister who is wise, brave, self-controlled,
and discerning can bring great prosperity to a king or a prince.

The black buck plays, the boar digs, the leopard puffs with pride, the jackal howls and leaps, and the hare runs with speed; the young elephant, free from fear, playfully tears apart the trees and creepers. Alas, O lion! Without you, what state has come upon this forest today?
Wherever one looks in this bower—whether it be a line of black antelopes, a multitude of rabbits, a thicket of porcupines, or a herd of boars—they find comfort even there.
Alas, what tree indeed remains in this ruined forest that is so tall that a lordly elephant, afflicted by the heat, might dwell within its shade?
Due to the dawning of discernment, there is no longer any longing for the fawn-eyed goddesses; fearing constant downfall, we do not rejoice in heaven even for a moment.
I have no thirst for the enjoyment of other perishable objects, nor even for the celestial river; I desire only meditation upon the feet of Hari on its sandy banks.

The animals here are deer and the like; this assembly consists of Kirātas who do not appreciate merit; there is no wandering about as there is in the city; and the minds of the sages are detached from worldly objects.
We burn the aloe-wood tree from its very roots, perfuming every direction with fragrant smoke at every step—what can we say to anyone? To whom can we explain this?
O black antelope, with eyes closed in heavy pride among herds of female deer, why indeed do you sport in this forest?
Mark this boundary of the earth where Hari sports—a boundary consisting of pearls released from the temples of shattered lordly elephants.
The braid of the gazelle-eyed woman, held in the hollow of her hands as she rose from bed,
shone like a swarm of bees clustering together as they emerge from the calyx of a lotus.
O bee, when women with eyes like a doe’s place you upon the edge of their ear, that alone constitutes the greatness of the fresh *campaka* flower;
if you do not sport there, O bee, it does not diminish the flower in the least, but rather it is your own loss.
Victorious is the braid of the fawn-eyed woman, hanging down her back like a whip of the five-arrowed god for the purpose of threatening young men.

The female deer moves on, having spotted young locusts, desiring to eat the sprouts of grass; the hen-cock, for a long time, guards the buds of the *chatrī* plant, mistaking them for its own tail-feathers; the peacock shakes his head and runs away from afar toward the edge of the forest, eager to swallow a swarm of black insects, thinking them to be venomous snakes.

May the King of the land of Vraja protect us—he who is surrounded on all sides by rows of women whose eyes are like those of young does, whose hips possess the fullness of languid weight, and whose passionate movements have become as still as braided hair; he who diverts the hands of the Lord of Rati with arrows resting in his quiver, and who is the supreme object beyond the reach of words.
The deer, the elephant, the moth, the bee, and the fish as the fifth— these, indeed, are destroyed by sound, touch, form, smell, and taste respectively.
And this is the root of austerity, indeed the very root of austerity:
the constant victory over desire as well as the victory over mental constructs.
The wise one should add four times this amount of oil and four times that amount of *kāñjika* (sour gruel), and then cook the oil.

Why does this city abide in a vow of silence—its crossroads and streets once so peaceful and variegated; where the verses of praise from bards have ceased, the sweet-sounding drums have fallen mute, and the sound of song has been destroyed; where Vedic study has turned away, the playful compositions of great poets have stopped, and the path of debate for learned men has been laid low?
O sinless one, I have thus explained to you the true essence of this treatise;
now another secret is being told, concerning the lack of trust among kings.
This is the very discernment between the insentient and the sentient, and this alone is the skill in purifying the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth;
this is the Śaiva knowledge obtainable through the pinnacle of the scriptures, unto whose pair of feet I have surrendered my self.

Together with a host of spirits summoned by the tumultuous sounds of the *ḍama* and *ḍamaru* drums, I shall gratify the Consort of Bharga with streams of blood, thick with foam and swelling bubbles, rising from the neck-stalks severed by my terrifying sword.
If this nectar called poetry, which issues from the moon-like face of the Lord of Poets, had not been swallowed by serpents,
what would have remained here as a dwelling place for the mental diversion of worldly beings who endure thousands of various miseries?
"‘This is lovely, this is lovely’— with such a thirst for a dwelling,
I think her entire body wanders like a deluded god of love."
In this world, the fruit of desire is this: that two people possess a single mind.
When desire is formed with another's mind, their union is like that of two corpses.
O immortals, this task has been heard by me: steadfastness, tranquility, and adherence to truth and dharma;
having untied every knot of the heart, one should bring both the pleasant and the unpleasant under the control of the self.
"Is this perhaps an ear-ornament? This is a necklace; has some new girdle been fastened by you today? A praiseworthy tilaka has been applied, my dear.

As he touched her limb after limb, the slender woman—her body covered with a multitude of horripilations arising at that moment—was gently released from her pride by the rogue through his very disregard for it.
What is this that even toward a lover, she becomes proud? I think that in the practice of pride there must be some pleasure distinct from [ordinary] aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
A desire for that pleasure constantly awakens in my heart as well; yet, since this husband does not offend me even in my dreams, how can I be angry with him?
O wise one, was this deed— which you have performed and which suppresses the arising of virtue— consistent with what you have heard, appropriate for your vows, or in keeping with your noble lineage?
All the dark forces of the three worlds, having been banished by the cleansing of his fame’s radiance, found rest only in mere stories;
for alas, from this fame-filled king, a weight of infamy was so born that its dark shadow could not even establish itself upon the path of his legend.
Because it vied with her breasts, the balance scale (*dhaṭa*) attained its status as a well-known illustration in the treatises;
and from that craft, the maker of jars and such became famous by the name *kumbhakāra* (potter).

Having done this for me—whether out of friendship for one who has followed the path of an improper request, or out of a sense of compassion for me as one who is distressed—wander through your desired regions, O cloud, with your beauty enhanced by the rainy season; and may you never, even for a moment, suffer separation from the lightning.

This body of the charming moon triumphs as a key that opens the bolted door of the beaks of female cakora birds; it is a thorn in the hearts of the wives of the cuckoo family, yet a fresh sprout for the tree of Love even though it was once burnt, and an unbridled goad for the wild elephant of the beloved’s pride.
This is that poison consisting of sons and wife which is difficult to conquer in this world;
having drunk it, deluded beings are born and they die.
This sky, dark as a cloud, resembles the face of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and Duryodhana, his strength exceedingly arrogant, roars with joy like a peacock.
The cuckoo has departed for its journey like Yudhiṣṭhira, defeated at dice; and the swans have now gone from the forest into a life of concealment like the Pāṇḍavas.
"Where is that face? Where is the honey of those lips? Where are those long side-glances? Where are those tender conversations? And where is that play of the eyebrows, curved like the bow of Love?
Thus, with teeth bared upon the tip of the *khaṭvāṅga* staff and the gentle breeze whistling through it, this skull—a web of delusion—is, alas, a loud mockery of those blinded by passion.

O friend, consider this: the rays of the sun, which grant consolation to the cakravāka birds, which provide the joy of rescue to the world submerged in the ocean of dense darkness, and which are skilled in splashing the water of saffron paste upon the deer-eyed women of the quarters—these rays, bringing forth the beauty of the lotus groves, now blossom forth.

O Cakravāka, consider this: the treasury of light shines forth to comfort the hearts of the cakravākas, to swallow the clusters of stars, to mock the shimmering orb of the moon, to apply saffron powder to the jar-like breasts of the quarters of space, to cause the lotuses to bloom, and to terrify the thickets of hostile night-lilies.
This is but a small portion from his mouth: that fool, hearing from him that a drop of water on a lotus leaf is a pearl, thinks even this to be so;
yet when it is slowly picked up, dissolving at the slight movement of a fingertip, he does not sleep day after day because of the inner grief, crying out, "Where has it flown away? and "It is mine!"

But this burns me: that guests avoid our house because its wealth is exhausted, just as bees, when the season has passed, wander away from an elephant's cheek where the thick, dark paste of ichor has dried up.
This face of yours, with its creeper-like eyebrows and its sprout-like lower lip glowing like a *pāṭala* flower, is the Nandana garden; everything else is merely a forest.

O Lord, tell me, how could these deer-eyed women not meditate upon you alone? Your face possesses the radiant luster of unblemished jasmine; your eyes are indistinguishable from blue lotuses; your lower lip is as red as the *bandhujīva* flower; and the creeper of your brow is like the bow of Kāma, practicing in playfulness.
O lotus-eyed one, why do you bear this grief in vain upon seeing this pair of breasts fallen?
For what wonder is there in this: that one who is rigid, devoid of discernment, a tormentor of people, and excessively haughty, should surely fall?
"This thousand lotus-eyed maidens shines before me; tell me, where shall I fix my two eyes?"—having thus reflected, Acyuta stood with his lotus-like eyes closed and his body covered in horripilation.

This skeleton of Pūtanā is seen, its ancient bony cage thick with joints of sinews and bound all around by black skin; its shanks reach as high as the date-palm tree, and it is making a crushing, wailing sound while nourishing the wolves on all sides with the remnants of human flesh, half-eaten and cast aside in her voracious, unbridled consumption.
O Pracaṇḍī, this stainless form has arisen, staining the vault of the sky and the circle of planets;
it possesses the luster of a mass of fresh jewels scattered from the opening of the casket-like lids of the joined sun and moon.
Having fully understood all this, one should begin the planting of trees,
since from trees comes the accomplishment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

Friends, listen to all these words in brief: this friend of yours is surely the complete fruit of our lives. While she remains, we are entirely free from darkness; but in this separation, she will flicker violently like a lamp in a gale. Therefore, protect her at all costs.
A king who is guided by policy, being diligent, leads all these—beginning with his ministers—to prosperity; however, one who is addicted to vice leads them only to ruin.
O traveler, behold here this great lake, the sole life-sustenance of all who pass by, which is drying up utterly;
O vain cloud, you have blocked its proper course—why then have you swollen this river that flows only to the marketplace?
In marshy ground (anūpa), this should be declared by five men; and in arid land (jāṅgalabhūmi), by these same signs, one should speak by means of eight men.
Corrupted by hatred, he applies his intellect to the sacred scriptures for this purpose:
"By means of disputes, I shall cause the humiliation of the wise."
For this purpose indeed do kings amass wealth;
having protected themselves, they bestow that wealth upon the twice-born.
For it is for this purpose that lords of men rule their kingdoms:
so that in all their undertakings, their minds may meet with no obstruction.
For this purpose, kings gather together those of noble birth;
they do not undergo any change of character in the beginning, middle, or end.
Unable, as it were, to endure the weight of the moonlight that it had inhaled with its sighing,
the night-lily suddenly breaks free from its stalk, releasing the humming of the bees.
This alone is true nobility, this alone is the acquisition of virtue:
that the head is always bowed in humility before the virtuous among the virtuous.
This very same [retribution] should be understood to arise from the destruction of one's own wealth and dharma;
however, that which arises from the destruction of the enemy's territory consists of the oppression of the enemy's domain.
This alone is the supreme valor: the protection of another's life. For one who takes life is not a hero; a hero is one who bestows life upon those who seek it.
O slender-waisted one, this alone is my immeasurable merit that you have become a guest for my eyes;
let alone the glances of my eyes, whose pupils reel with intoxication, O moon-faced one! Let them remain far away.
This alone is the great wonder of past karma in this world:
that the life-span belongs to those who lack self-control, and that prosperity belongs to those who lack discernment.
This indeed is wisdom; this alone is great learning;
this indeed is the supreme gain: that one protects much from very little.
For this alone is true scholarship, and this indeed is true nobility;
this alone is the supreme dharma: that one's expenditures be less than one's income.
This alone is the essence of life, which by its very nature is momentary:
that one remains unrestrained in the company of those who are affectionate, charming, and wise.
This very capacity of objects is perceived through direct perception:
the connection of men with wives, children, and so forth, is based upon wealth.
This very efficacy of the object is perceived through direct perception:
that while those who are living carry a corpse on a palanquin when bound by the aggregates.
This scent-elephant, his body submerged up to the throat in the water out of thirst and turned white by froth that rivals the fame of his playful victories over the elephants of the quarters,

extinguishes the ocean’s grief of separation from the beloved of Abhramu under the guise of vomiting water from his trunk— appearing as if he had four tusks due to the reflection of his own pair of tusks in the water.

To whom did this mass of dust raised by the hooves of the multitude of horses in his vanguard on the battlefields not cause the illusion of smoke from the fire of his unrestrained majesty blazing forth— its fuel being the lineages of his enemies drenched in blood flowing from the wounds of sword-strokes dealt by him— as he observed the burden of that peerless battle during his expedition for world-conquest?

This pair of her budding breasts, swelling in their development at the center yet finding their own boundaries slightly toward the edges, possesses the beauty of a pair of palm trees smeared with saffron by a dancer in the bloom of youth.

Having observed with the strength of his tusks the entire earth embraced by her limbs at the edge of the battlefield— causing the delusion that it was a multitude of moving mountains— King Pṛthu, moving amidst the rows of gods who had descended to witness this fierce battle, again set his mind upon hurling the mountain.
O King, this brings glory to a ruler: that he inflicts a punishment upon a thief that is sweetened by the length of his life, while bestowing long life upon the world;
for by you, he was bound as a thief of the vermilion from the wives of rival kings and cast into prison, where he now acts as a terrifying executioner of his own retribution.
Dhanañjaya should be told this: "Vṛkodara is ever-exerting;
that purpose for which a Kṣatriya woman gives birth—the time for that has now arrived."
For this indeed is the supreme and eternal duty of a noble woman in this world:
that she should act for the welfare of her husband, even at the cost of sacrificing her own life.
The orb of the sun, its rays imitating the color of tawny hair, falls into the western ocean like the severed head of the day that has betrayed the king;
and this celestial night, too, having cast her beloved into the twilight-fire kindled by fierce fuel, remains with only her bones left, under the guise of the stars.
Having attained unsurpassed subtlety of intellect, the knower of yoga, having expanded his mind over all beings, abandons this [world].

Terrified by this [news], the wives of the enemy—spending their days in mountain caves, emerging with young children who were intensely pleading because they mistook the moon for their own play-swans—cried out so much that the reflections of the swan-like moons in their tears seemed to join them; yet they found both solace and despair in the laughter of their sons, who rejoiced at the proximity of those reflected moon-swan images.
This lake, the essence of worldly existence, was fashioned by Bhīmaparākrama; it is dedicated to the skill of eclipsing the story of the Lord of Waters (the Ocean).

Upon beholding its majesty, the wonder of which causes the splendor of the sky to tremble, the earring fallen from the head of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) shines under the guise of the sun reflected in the water.
"O Rādhā, if Mādhava were to behold this skill of ornamentation upon your body while he was present near you, he might indeed maintain his composure even with a fickle mind.
While the artisan was speaking thus, as she remembered Hari, a river of perspiration immediately overwhelmed the pure circle of her decorative leaf-patterns.
This speech of poets plunges into the unfathomable depths of the ocean of the milk of his fame;
this falling of the marks used for counting his virtues wears away the chalk-lines of his rivals' reputations.
This is the supreme secret and this is the highest state;
this is the goal of those who are dispassionate, and this is that which is the supreme Śiva.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on Brahman and who desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king.
Knowing this skill in knowledge and realization as taught by me, he neither censures nor praises; he moves through the world like the sun.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this ordinance;
however, if he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.
This orb of the cool-rayed moon, possessing the luster of a mass of foam kissing the peak of the western mountain,
shines forth as if bearing the smoke of the kindled fire of love throughout the night under the guise of its manifest mark.

This darkness—like the girdle of the boar that swallowed the sky and earth, like the military camp of Smara, the sole hero of the universe, consisting of a herd of elephants blinded by rut, and like the tresses of the dark-complexioned bride—is now being crossed over.
It is a mass of smoke from the great comet appearing amidst the scattered flocks of *cakravāka* birds, serving as a collyrium for the eyes of the throngs of owls.

O bull among kings, as the night departs, this moon—cool-rayed—unfolds with his flood of rays from the lotus-beds what was hidden away, as it were, for the sake of being sown; he reveals the swarm of bees like the very seed of darkness from the source of the lotuses.
Alas! This pair of breasts, with their pale outer edges and dark centers like ripe *tinduka* fruits, is now within reach of the touch of the beautiful hands of the forest-dweller (*pulinda*).
O daughter of the village chief, the herd of elephants, distressed by their plea for safety from the frontal globes (*kumbha*), entreats you: do not cover your pair of breasts with leaves.
Surely her mind has become composed of this very [emotion] and has fallen upon her;
for it does not emerge from the body of that fawn-eyed woman by any means, even through the application of skillful methods.
O proud lady, this is the celestial lake whose golden lotuses have been plucked by Pārvatī for the purpose of worshipping her beloved; from here the river Gaṅgā has issued forth.

From this place, the water is taken by the Citraśikhaṇḍins on the supreme festival day, rendered pure through contact with the dust of the ashes from the bull-bannered Lord’s body as he emerges from his bath.

This region of Mālava shines forth with people who are like sprouts of the jewel of benevolence, abodes of the splendor of prosperity, and the very essence of the erotic sentiment; what more need be said?
For there, having ascended the balconies adorned with various paintings of the pleasure-palaces, lovers spend their days with their beloveds during the rising of the clouds.
This face of my beloved, having surpassed the moon with the radiance of its two cheeks,
now surely seeks to conquer the lotus, which is already reddened by the heat of the sun.

The Creator fashioned this eye through the delusion that it was a blue lotus, her face through the error of mistaking it for a lotus, and her left lip through the confusion of taking it for a *bimba* fruit.
Since even the Creator himself fell into such errors at every limb of her, who is the natural abode of the play of Love, what hope is there for the intellect of those like us?
Having taken some drops of water from this ocean, the clouds then fill the earth, obstructing the sky with their waters;
yet, having obtained from this very source a single water-nymph whose eyes rolled in fear of the impact of Mount Mandara’s peak, the illustrious Acyuta became the sovereign of the three worlds.

How much more illusory than this is the other "magical net" (indrajāla) that is dwelling in a woman’s womb—unstable, with semen dripping, and with various sprouts appearing from every part of the head;
enveloped in succession by all the guises of childhood, youth, and old age, it sees, eats, hears, smells, repeatedly sleeps, and wakes.
From this supreme bliss, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, the individual soul (jīva) is first born; from that, the mind (citta); and from that, the world.
Alas! From this lake, the wise swan—who possesses a mind capable of discerning water from milk—has long since departed on his wings.
And somewhere, the *kāraṇḍava* bird has quietly gone away making sweet sounds; with whom, then, can the young *sārasa* crane, filled with distress, hold conversation?
"From this [ocean], the nectar was obtained by the gods through Indra; from this, the virtuous Uccaiḥśravas [was gained]; and from this, Kṛṣṇa, the sole abode of wondrous valor, obtained Lakṣmī.
Having heard such abundant ancient tales from everyone, we have nevertheless not seen even a single drop of sweet water anywhere in this ocean.

O mind, desist from this deep thicket of sensory objects which is a source of exhaustion; in an instant, attain that peaceful state on the path to the highest good, which is skilled in the task of pacifying all suffering. Abandon your own way of being, as fickle as a wave; do not again indulge in the fragile delight of worldly existence—be at peace now!
O dark-eyed one, knowing from this gift of recognition that I am well, do not become distrustful of me because of rumors;
for they say that affections diminish during separation, yet through lack of enjoyment, their flavor intensifies toward the beloved object until they become a mass of love.

With the hope that "from this flower, which is great by its very nature, a fruit likely even greater, beautiful, sweet, fragrant, and cool, must surely be obtained," the parrot remained there, perceiving the timing of the *śālmali* tree's ripening; yet he saw only the cotton-fiber down emerging from the seam of the fruit's opening.

At the close of day, from the vine-cottages there slowly emerge gazelle-eyed women whose bodies are moist with thick sandalwood paste, whose eyes are reddened by sleep, and who repeatedly yawn under the guise of their soft, swaying, and shimmering vine-like arms; the full expanse of their breasts is bristling with droplets of perspiration.
O elephant, how many years have you not spent at ease and according to your will in this forest lap, which possesses abundant prosperity and where new warmth has been attained?
Fie on you! You were born here at a time when everything was consumed; there is now neither water, nor trees, nor grass—only this forest fire is sporting.

In this spring, which is delightful with the thick pollen shaken down by the fluttering of the wings of swarms of intoxicated bees clinging to creepers stirred by the southern breeze—[in this spring], even a gentle embrace around the neck of mature women, whose bracelets jingle as their arms grow slack from the sweat of passion, causes the heart to languish; how much more so, then, separation?
At this midday hour, even the wind does not stir, as if terrified by the fierce heat while the orb of the sun blazes upon the forehead;
moreover, the shade, though it has moved far away, turns back and huddles beneath the foot of the tree, as if unable to endure the scorching of its rolling upon the heated dust.

Carrying an abundance of water and driven by the agitation of the wind-born current, these great lakes bear a resemblance to the words of Vālmīki, which likewise carry an excellence of meaning and were moved by the speed born of the Wind-god, while being devoid of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Upon this pair of breasts of the deer-eyed woman, possessing a pure and radiant luster, the reflection of the lunar orb appears divided into two;
it is seen as if it were a pair of bronze cymbals raised for the festive dance of the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma), who is trembling with joy at that moment.

In this place, let the regions of unceasing beauty be beheld— regions where great-stalked lotuses tremble, shaken by the wings of mallikākṣa geese warbling with intoxication, appearing amidst the intervals between the falling and rising of teardrops.

In this season, when the clamor of the clouds—augmented by the trumpeting of elephants and worn out by intoxication—bestows a restless stillness upon the mind and swells with the sound of falling rain;
when, resting upon the lap of the quarters, the roar of the water-bearing clouds makes them thunder, I believe even the sky itself, its eyes of sun and moon closed, is falling asleep.
In this region of Maru, where herds of cranes sport amidst the clamor of rolling waves and shoals of fish play fearlessly upon the mud-free banks—
by whom was this vast lake created, its waters so brilliant that they delight the flocks of travelers, with bees humming within the corners of the huts of blossoming lotuses?

Even while he had gone out hunting, with his bow strung, the arrow drawn back to his ear, released from his grip, and fixed upon her body, the doe neither trembled, nor fled, nor moved, nor yearned, nor leaped— because she held her lover under her control with the hope, "This is Love himself."
In this vicinity of the forest path, there stands that one supreme mango tree, marked with the seal of beauty by its burgeoning abundance of fruits, leaves, and flowers;
seeing it, these throngs of travelers run toward it with smiling faces, with great joy arising within them, their longing swelling, and their pace unimpeded.

While your enemy’s sovereign is forming the thought, "I shall dwell happily in this lonely forest where the space is covered by dense trees," he suddenly faints again and again, struck with incomparable terror upon seeing the carcass of a lion fallen there on the ground, pierced by a shaft inscribed with your name.
In this forest, which powerful being has not been commanded by me? To whom have the fruits not been scattered as is fitting for both my wrath and my favor?
Such as I am, today I entreat a mouse for the purpose of severing the cords of my bonds; yet even he pays no heed—why does this wretched heart not shatter into two pieces?

Born into this vast lineage of monkeys, there was a certain singular monkey, preeminent in virtues, a son of the Maruts who is worthy of worship even by the gods. To him, the lord of waters—the ocean—was like a mere pond in a pleasure courtyard; he took delight in leaping into it even when the world trembled from the sudden upheaval of its surging waves.

O frog, in this lake of clear water, be silent indeed with your clamorous outcry that rends the throats of living beings! Day after day, the cries of the swans—responding to the tinkling of the anklets of Goddess Lakṣmī as she moves among the petals of their blossoming eyes—reach out to you.
O lord of my life, although you are now striving to depart for another land during this season of spring, I do not yet feel fear of the heat;
for during the nights, a pure mass of lunar rays spreads in all directions along with the lake breeze, stealing away the fragrance of the essence of night-lotuses.
"In this vine-bower, O slender-limbed one, there is a most beautiful *mālatī* flower not yet gathered by another.
Having said this, a certain rogue took the hand—like a tender sprout—of the innocent-eyed girl and led her away into private.
Pārvatī’s lover bears a single digit of this nectar-rayed moon,
like a row of letters being fashioned month by month.

O snake-charmer, do not thrust your own finger into his mouth out of pride in your mantras; for here indeed lies some serpent, by whose virulent poison a thousand people like you have fallen down, lifeless and consumed.
O dear friend, when my lover was struck on his chest in secret with a lotus leaf,
seeing his smile, I too broke into a laugh.
O Kalāvati, by the power of ill fortune, you have fallen into the house of this plowman, O slender one;
therefore, acquire skill in carrying water-jars and preparing cow-dung for your husband’s subjugation.
Kāśī is the ancestral capital of this lord of the earth and the boat of Dharma for crossing over worldly existence belonging to the Enemy of Smara;
having arrived there, even those whose minds are filled with misfortune cast off their long-accumulated sin and become free from passion.
In this pleasure-lake of King Rativallabha, the fierce-rayed sun of youth is slowly drying up the maidenhood of his young wives;
yet, as the slope of her breasts—though situated within—provides a double obstruction, the row of large fish that are her glances kills the thirst [of the sun] in such water.

Upon the slope of her breasts, which resemble the frontal globes of an elephant and are captivating with rows of pearl necklaces containing *guñjā* seeds like young elephants, this wave has come from afar and fallen; how is it that it has dissolved so swiftly? Or rather, what other thing would not dissolve upon meeting a passionate woman?
I suspect that the pair of lotus-buds of this deer-eyed woman’s breasts does not bloom again because of the white moonlight of her moon-like face;
yet, when her eye-lotus—frequented by the bees of her eyebrows—is in full bloom, it repeatedly casts a great doubt within my heart.
Her chest is bent under the weight of her breasts, the surface of her hips is strewn [with jewels], her waist sinks down, and the edge of her garment clings to the pit of her navel.
O deer of my mind, maintain your composure; for ahead lies the snare of the line of hair. What indeed can be done by Fate for one who suffers from the cycle of wandering in delusion?
The fever of her separation from him cannot be tested by the touch of palms, even by those who are affectionate, for fear of being burned; it is a fire that cooks its own vessel.
While the application of sandalwood and medicinal herbs has been rendered powerless, these jewels of all the pearl necklaces burst open like parched grain, producing a wondrous effect.
If even Śambhu, Brahmā, Purandara, and the rest are not capable of praising this crest-jewel of the three worlds, the performer of all lofty deeds—
then tell me, how could a mere mortal be capable of describing his beauty, when even the Lord of Serpents and the Goddess of Speech herself are dull in that regard?
If people say that this braid of the deer-eyed woman possesses the beauty of a fresh rain-cloud, let them indeed say so;
we, however, declare it to be a female serpent carrying a jewel, who has come here out of a longing for the nectar of her moon-like face.
"Behold this plateau before you, where Hara, while sporting as a Kirāta, was suddenly struck on the crown of his head by Kirīṭin with his bow"—
having heard this wondrous tale on Mount Himavat, the Lord of Subhadrā very slowly made an ornament of his own two powerful arms.
O slender-waisted one, behold this Tāmraparṇī river as it flows into the ocean;
its waters, drawn up by the opened shells of oysters, transform into the form of necklaces upon the expansive breasts of beautiful women.

If I cut these [ropes], what use is life to me, a eunuch? And if they remain as they are, what use are they to the Lord of Cows? If I sit with them stretched out, the people will laugh at me; alas, my labor is in vain—both by the burdens, the ropes, and the testicles!
Shall I bind these locks of yours, dark and curling like a swarm of bees; or shall I place a decorative line of leaf-patterns upon this cheek, sweet and pale as a *madhūka* flower?
Or rather, having loosened the binding of these lotus petals that steal the beauty of blooming buds, shall I fix them upon the breast of this deer of all hearts?
These young women, having been sprayed in their faces by their friends with streams of water squeezed from their hands out of sportiveness,
now emit droplets of water reddened by *cūrṇa* powder through their locks of hair, which fall in straight lines from the tips of their curls.
Even when disheveled by sporting in the water— with hair hanging loose, decorative leaf-patterns fallen away,
and pearl ornaments scattered— the appearance of the women's faces remains truly enchanting.

These women adorn some men with various kinds of ornaments, and again, they deceive other people with false words; indeed, they delight certain excellent men with their intense, mind-stirring gestures. Alas, why do you vainly cause your heart to wander among women? For that [attachment] is truly in vain.
These riverbanks, with their muddy shores where stalks of *nalada* grow and conch shells resound, their waters turbid with *jambāla* mud torn up by circles of sporting crabs;
these lands on the slopes, their edges jagged with sandbanks and their moist earth scattered by the sprays from the gaping mouths of frogs, produce a poignant impression in the heart.
These cowherd girls, with faces and eyes like blossoming lotuses and water-lilies, fair as golden campaka flowers,
dressed in garments of various colors and speaking sweetly, sport about with their hair-tresses strewn with wild flowers.

These lands terrify us: their surface is drenched with the blood of herds of deer torn apart by the playful ferocity of tigers; they resound with the clamor of fierce *kalahas* and *pheraṇḍas*, greedily intent on tasting the earth thus sprinkled; and they are made noisy by the encounter of shameless owls sporting in nests within the hollows of trees encircled by coils of writhing sloughed-off snake-skins.
"Alas, how could these women of the king’s harem, currently burdened by the weight of their pregnancies, possibly endure the flight through the wilderness on foot?"—
having reflected thus with compassion in his mind, O Lion of Vaikuṇṭha, was the miscarriage of those fetuses brought about by the rows of your roars as if they were female companions?
These courtesans— devoid of truth, clinging to fragments of wealth, and dependent on fleeting moments of pleasure— enter the hearts of the thoughtless, sweet as honey to the face.
O fair-limbed one, these friends of yours, situated on Hemakūṭa, behold your face,
which has regained its serenity like the moon released from an eclipse.
By encompassing these forest regions on the slopes of the Snowy Mountains, which possess the exceedingly lovely splendor of Śiva and Śivā, they nourish a festival for the eyes;

there, the celestial trees are made glistening by the flow from the sacrificial ponds of the celestial river, which issues from the cavities caused by the fresh blows of the tusks of the pre-eminent elephants of the leaping enemies of the gods.
These women are intent on their own interests and find delight solely in their own pleasure;
for there is no one dear to them, not even their own son, without regard for his happiness.
Because their heavy hips and breasts made it difficult for them to support themselves,
these young women, unable to swim, were crossing through the water with great effort by using their arms as firm oars, driven by the power of passion.
Even in such an age as this Kali Yuga, there is perhaps one in a hundred who has developed devotion toward the path of the Vedas in this world.
Whatever he may practice, he is a worthy object of praise; for is not even a small pool in a desert something to be celebrated?

Behold these holy hermitages, which possess such splendor that the Brahmins within them roam upon the sacrificial altars, fire-piles, and Vedis, and the trees at their borders are shaded by *vātapramī* deer;
hermitages whose minds, once uplifted and gladdened by faith in the worship of Nārāyaṇa, turn away entirely toward the Supreme, never again seeking the gates of wealthy men or their own wives.
These very bodies, once censured for their fresh youth and indulged with sweet foods, drinks, beds, and seats,
now fall and roll upon the ground, adorned only with necklaces, half-necklaces, and jewel ornaments.
These side-long glances of broad-hipped women, which are the world’s favorites and elixirs for destroying the scars of Love burnt by the fire from Shiva’s eye— whom do they not fill with wonder?
These efforts, which have now arrived at the time [of fruition], have become fruitless due to the exhaustion of my fortune—
like the auspicious rites of the *nīrājana* ceremony for a horse when the battle has already ended.
These improper comings and goings of my exhausted body portend an empty mind;
and these trees on the riverbank proclaim the heat with their sprouts that have withered from being grasped and then cast aside.

O Bāladhavala, having set aside at will these frolics of the restless calves in the courtyard of the cow-pen, place your shoulder to the yoke; for this burden has been released from the shoulders of the former leaders and has now come to be carried by you.
Whoever goes to the assembly after reciting these verses of mine is always honored by the king, just as the True Dharma is honored by hosts of men.
That man who shall practice these twenty steps will conquer all enemies and shall become auspicious.
These streams, resembling molten silver poured forth, fall with speed from the bellies of the clouds;
flashing like the crest of a lamp, they vanish in an instant, falling like the severed fringes of the garment of the sky.
After that, these [defects] never arise for him again.
One should avoid sexual union with effort and protect the *bindu* with great care;
through the loss of the *bindu*, the lifespan is diminished and incapacity arises.
O dear one, when a king honors a man, this single quality forcibly takes hold of all these great qualities; indeed, this one quality outshines them all.
These [senses], when unrestrained, are capable even of bringing about destruction,
like untrained horses that are not under control leading a bad charioteer astray on the road.
Behold, O people: these flowers of fame, born from the *pārijāta* tree of the Lord of Avanti and white as the moon, I now wear as ear-ornaments upon the brides that are the quarters of the sky.
These days, it is said, were spent by the young *cātaka* bird with its life-breath held within the hollow of its throat.
O Cloud, fulfill the desires of that seeker; alas, let there be no neglect toward one who has you as his sole refuge.
These same seven subtle elements always lead to bondage;
however, detachment from the elements beginning with earth (bhū) leads here to liberation.
O one of great intelligence, these splendors that you behold, flickering with parasols and fly-whisks, are but a dream lasting for three or five days.
These streams of arrows issuing from the cloud that is Rāvaṇa shine forth upon reaching Rāma, like torrents of rain falling upon the ocean.
This much can be said by us: that you are virtuous.
But as for the discernment of the mass of jewels within a mine of gems, who are we?
This much is the fulfillment of birth for embodied beings among other embodied beings in this world:
one should always practice only that which is beneficial through one's life, wealth, intellect, and speech.
The fruitfulness of birth consists only in this: that one's livelihood is independent.
Those who have fallen into dependence on others—what life do they possess? They are truly dead.
Indeed, by this much alone, the region of the waist of the blameless lady, which shone as if it were an object of inference,
was subsequently placed upon the lap of Giriśa— a lap that is not to be coveted by any other woman.
By this much alone, you consider yourselves to have achieved your purpose;
indeed, there is truly no further limit to what remains to be done.
Such is the function of the lotus in the lake: that it pierces the water and suddenly emerges outside;
they consider all else—the fragrance, the blossoming, and the abode of Lakṣmī—to be the work of the Sun.
This alone is sufficient for a monk who sleeps in solitude:
no one dies for him, nor does he die for anyone else.
Indeed, for one endowed with the essence of knowledge, this alone is a sufficient fruit:
that he is not deluded in times of adversity, nor is he filled with pride in times of prosperity.

O bee, for so long a time you have sported in the lap of the *kesara* flowers and have constantly delighted the female bees during your wanderings among the lakes. By fate, O honey-drinker, having now fallen upon this forest of *ketakī* plants, you experience this wretched state, pinned fast by their thorns.
This inexhaustible dharma, practiced by those of virtuous fame, is this:
that the self grieves when there is grief for living beings and rejoices when there is joy.
A person is only as great as that in whom a favor done is never lost;
and whatever another might do for him, he should repay it many times over.
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have said; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman."
A person is only such as he who is impatient and intolerant;
one who is patient and free from impatience is neither a woman nor [a man] again and again.
These thirty-two arts, whether held in their sequential order or taken as a whole,
constitute the knowledge of those who possess wisdom and who deceive the cycle of existence.

At this rising of the moon, these wives of the common folk thresh the rice, their necks made beautiful by the tips of their thick, dark, jar-like breasts which sway from the incessant tossing of the pestles; the rows of bracelets on their vine-like arms jingle as they move, and they find pleasure in the sound of their long, drawn-out songs.

Whose mind do these young women not render helpless with their side-long glances, which resemble those of startled, innocent does, while the sound of their tinkling anklets and the jingling of their girdles made of clusters of moving bracelets attract even the female royal swans?
Among these blossoming *ketaki* creepers, you possess a most wonderful beauty,
since the bee, unaware that its own body is being pierced by thorns, begins to serve you alone.

These city women run toward the sun at the end of the day, intent on securing the hem of their garments which slip from their shoulders; they leap up for fear of meeting farmers returning early in the morning, and their fingers are busy with knots to calculate the prices of goods purchased at the market.
O fawn-eyed one, these are the banks of the rivers near the Malaya mountains, the beloved dwelling-place for the practice of archery by the divine Mind-born (Kāma).
Upon these banks, during nights dark with moonlight, female cakora birds drink the pearl-like moonbeams—having swallowed the darkness—with their beaks wide open and their throats quivering.
But these [women], due to their constant lack of compassion and mercilessness,
and especially because of their dull-witted actions, bring disgrace upon the three families.
These women laugh and weep for the sake of their own interests; they inspire confidence in others while themselves placing no trust in them.
Therefore, by a man endowed with noble birth and good character, women should be avoided like little pots at a cremation ground.

O friend, these delightful days have arrived, their sunlight variegated by fragments of clouds forming here and there; they offer hospitality with *darbha* grass mingling with *ketakī* petals, while the minds of the cowherds rejoice at the embrace of the young rice seedlings sprouting at the village edges; and the quarters of the sky are filled with the long-sustained songs of those driving the cattle.
Are these truly trees with clusters of swaying blossoms, or is this a faultless garden grove where these cuckoos dwell?
How strange! Where has that desert region vanished, where my city stood with its manifold splendor of cascading streams? Whence has this suddenly emerged?
These peacock feathers, once cherished daily by the hands of Karnataka women as they pulled them with jingling bracelets, had reached the highest state of prosperity;
yet now, crushed by the razor-edged blades brandished by sinful barbers, they fall all around upon the ground like those who have committed a transgression.
These rays of the cool-rayed moon, grey with the pollen of *ketaka* flowers and worn out by old age, have now reached the shore of the western ocean;
meanwhile, these youthful rays of the sun, honored by the glances of the forest of blooming lotuses, are proclaiming their arrival from the east.

These monsoon winds— possessing the fragrance of *ketaka* thorns, whose faces have been feasted upon under the pretext of being caressed by the tossing tresses of bold city women, and which captivate the hearts of those separated from their lovers with the warbling of swarms of bees rolling in the pollen within the huts of blossoming *kadamba* buds— draw forth the longing of the parted.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, these clouds produce the pain of love in my eyes during my separation from Sītā; even the spray-laden winds cause me intense torment.
This is that very Mālyavat mountain, where forest parrots even today stir the hearts of the sages with such words, refined through an ancient lineage of tradition.
These mountains, composed of masses of moonstone, roar as rivers of water flow from all their limbs, shimmering under the moonlight;
upon their plateaus where fireflies are wakeful with intoxication, the dark *koyaṣṭi* birds perched on *nameru* trees cry out with voices as deep and faltering as clouds.
These are but portions and fractions of the Supreme Person, but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself;
in age after age, they bring joy to the world distressed by the enemies of Indra.
These and many other such practices involving adultery are carried out in various regions, having been instituted by kings.
However, a king devoted to the welfare of the world should not employ these [measures];
rather, having restrained the group of six internal enemies, he thus conquers the earth.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, these and many other faults arise when a king is endowed with excessive mildness and is prone to levity.

And these sons of kings, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the others—heroes equal to Indra, true to their vows, radiant as the sun, and embraced by Keśava—are now seen with begging bowls in hand, following the life of mendicancy like wretches in this world. Who is able to erase the line of karma written upon the forehead by the hand of Fate?
These mango trees are smoking with the dense swarms of bees; these aśoka trees are ablaze with the bursting forth of their sprouts;
even these kiṃśuka branches are turned to glowing coals by their dark buds. Alas, where can I rest my eyes? Everywhere fate is adverse.

These gale-force winds play with the clusters of water-stalls, entangled in the webs of decayed nests, dragging up heaps of dust; they shake the trees where birds sit distressed and helpless as their branches tremble; and they sport by swinging, dancing, tossing, striking, clashing, uprooting, hurling, tossing upward, and whirling the water-stall roofs with effortless ease.
These mountain cascades, whose waters are shattered by impact against the masses of crags like peaks, are smiling with the spray-drops from their swaying chowries;
at their falls, lions roar fiercely on all sides, their throats constricted as they seize the lotus-stalk sprouts falling from the mouths of elephants in the forest thickets.

These are those days, heavy with separation, when the oceans surge with floods, the sky is dark blue with clouds as black as the Vindhya mountains, and the air is fragrant with *nīpa* and *arjuna* flowers;

days during which even the crow becomes distressed, intent on gathering bits of straw from the tips of its beak for a nest, upon seeing its mate weary with the approach of her time to lay eggs and seeking a nesting place.
These are those same days, those very trees, and those same bold women; that is the same mango grove with the song of the cuckoos, and this is that same moonlit night.
That wind is still the southern breeze, and this is that same wind of spring that steals away one's fortitude; yet, alas, O youth, without you, everything today feels like a mere burden of straw.
These monsoon winds, whose course is difficult to resist, strike the vital points of the joints of the clouds and block the quarters with a mass of water-laden dust;
they seize the droplets from the streams of water falling into the cauldron-like belly of the sky, which turns dark blue through the friction of masses of clouds held together by a violent onset.

O cloud, these trees before you in the desert lands—whose leaves have been scorched by the rays of the fierce sun licked by the flames of violent forest fires—are now weary of body; it is not fitting for you to pass them by, disregarding these trees drenched by the ocean tides, as you play with the harsh whirlwinds of ill-nature.

Alas, what a tragedy! These winds, which dwell in the caves of Mount Malaya and serve as teachers in the art of playful dancing upon the clusters of branches of its trees—these kinsmen of the God of Love, resounding with the humming and buzzing of bees intoxicated by mango blossoms—are now spreading forth, slaying the lives of young wives of travelers.
These [beings], such as the full moon and others, whose luster imitates your face, bring me to remembrance and, alas, burn me from within as you flash forth inside me.
You are my mistress; therefore, either leave me or stay—do not, O beloved, continue to crush me with these lowly things that vie with you.
These impoverished children, placing their thin, worn, and filthy rags upon their shoulders, their limbs bristling with horripilation,
engage in quarreling during the cold season for the sake of obtaining a patch of wall dappled by the rays of the shining sun.
By this aged body, bound by strength and having reached a state of contraction,
I have gone only two or three steps with difficulty, like Hari.

O Gold, let these merchants—whose heads are bent low by the recitals of your multitude of virtues—be the heralds of the jewel; for we, however, are the bards of your fame, since they, O King, are made to sit comfortably upon the crowns of monarchs by you, who with an unfading countenance have accepted the pain of burning and cutting [for their sake].

These are the embankments of wild rice, this mountain has abundant flowers and sacrificial fuel, this is the cave, and this is the Goddess, the daughter of Jahnu, where one may lie upon the sands free from fear or danger;

in this wilderness, pure with its clusters of *darbha* and *dūrvā* grass, the Brahmins—staying awake through the night due to the density of the planet’s ill-omened influence—repeat the words of the Smṛtis.
In the midst of the forest, these cuckoos captivate the heart with throat-sounds intensified by their excessive devouring of fresh mango buds;
they appear like the sparks from the charcoal of the god of love’s body, which was once made terrifying by the mass of flames from the fire of Lord Bhūteśa’s eye.

Alas, even on this earth— the very abode of people who witness the spectacle of battle— there was no one left to behold the wonder of the dance commenced by rival warriors whose throats had been severed,
for the world was shrouded in the darkness of the thick columns of dust rising from the surface of the earth as it was pulverized by the hooves of horses galloping with unrestrained speed.
These fifteen misfortunes are considered by men to have their root in [false] wealth;
therefore, one who seeks the highest good should abandon from afar that which is called wealth but is actually misfortune.
Brothers, wives, fathers, and friends alike are divided; those who were once united in affection are instantly made all enemies by a single *kākiṇī*.

For these people, with their passions inflamed, become agitated over even the slightest matter; they quickly abandon those they once vied with and suddenly cast aside their friendship to strike them down.

These breezes from the groves of the Tāpī river blow, having washed away with droplets of water the intense heat of the sighs of travelers' wives clinging to them during their water-sports with the women of Palli;
they resound with the loud noise of high-pitched mṛdaṅga drums begun by the swaying of the trunks of elephants roaming at will.

These winds blow freely from lake to lake, carrying with them the fragrance of *gundra* grass crushed by the tusks of wild boars— fragrances that rival the abundance of sweat upon the slopes of the full breasts of the wives of village chiefs, who are exhausted by intense amorous play.
These winds—highly skilled in the art of dancing for the young trees in the sandalwood groves; bringing forth a shower of cooling droplets from the perspiration of city women sporting on swings;
followed from behind by swarms of bees drawn by their fragrance; serving as swelling fuel for the fire of love; and harboring an ancient enmity toward the wives of travelers.
These holy hermitages shine forth before us, where the redness of fresh sprouts has been drunk up by streaks of fragrant and tender sacrificial smoke;
they are filled with families of deer who stand motionless and intent upon the Sāman chants so beloved by the Vedas.
These excellent trees are for the purpose of cleaning the teeth: twelve finger-breadths long, free of thorns, produced from milky trees, and without blemishes.
These various kinds of grief, as well as lamentation and weeping,
must indeed be avoided by a wise and steadfast person in all circumstances.
These currents of water before us, lovers of the Mekalā daughter [the Narmadā], which touch the very foundations of the underworld and cleave the Vindhya mountains, inspire terror;
for they sportively uproot, dance, strike against, turn back, propel, abandon, seize, hide, move, and toss aside the trees on their banks.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, these clouds distress me who am separated from Jānakī, and these cruel breezes from the Kadamba trees strike my very vitals.
May Hari—who was thus addressed while recounting his separation in a previous birth, and who was watched with jealousy and apprehension by Rādhā as he lay dreaming—grant you happiness.
We here possess but meager wealth; this earth is wretched, and these hundred [servants] are miserable and speak soft, prolix words.
Therefore, brothers—O Śakuni, Pherava, and Sārameya!—approach; alas, let this [earth] shatter in an instant!
"Here we are, and here are these wives; this maiden is the very life of our lineage.
Tell us what business you have here, for there is no concern with external things."
These methods for subduing others are considered fruitless when applied to a wicked person. A wise man should avoid their company; if he is capable, he should overcome them through punishment.
Or else, he may use these very same methods, which are deceptive in nature and assume that same form.
These days have arrived—days that sever love, during which the winds from the western ocean must be endured, bringing the chill of suffering to the breasts of those with lovely eyes;
days in which the God who is the source of passion casts aside his bow made of ancient lotuses and takes up another fashioned from the tips of fresh *kunda* buds.
These clouds scatter water-drops upon men, they do not rain down [the dead]; these mountains vomit forth green grass, they do not vomit up the leaders [of men].
Trees in the three worlds produce fruits, they do not bring forth people. O Creator, I speak in distress; what have you done for the sake of a wanton woman?
These beasts of grammarians, considering themselves wise, waste their own lives in vain with networks of words harsh to the ear;
whereas for us, who constantly describe the sweetness of the beloved’s lips, the connoisseurs here daily increase our prosperity with their blessings.
These [ascetics] dry their robes for a long time in the sky out of fear of deer; they see their water-pots as empty when performing the twilight rites, yet as full;
they beg for fruits from trees using their cupped hands as bowls; and when they approach for the offering of guest-water (*argha*), the creepers suddenly burst into bloom.

Who here has not placed upon their ears these virtues of yours—which are born from the lineage of the autumnal moonlight, brothers of the Ocean of Milk, friends of the serpent Śeṣa, pouring forth the splendor of rows of blooming white lilies; who were playmates with the Moon in childhood, kinsmen of the celestial Ganges, and relatives of the Snowy Mountain?
For the sage who meditates upon each one of these nine wheels,
the accomplishments (siddhis), together with liberation, shall come into his very hands day by day.
Among these, there are the *anukūla* (favourable), the *dakṣiṇa* (courteous), the *dhṛṣṭa* (bold), and the *śaṭha* (crafty).
I shall state the fourfold classification of these, providing one example for each.
