O cloud! While these trees are being devoured by forest fires fanned by the youthful winds, if you do not release water, then do not release it; but for what reason, O merciless one, do you hurl your thunderbolt again?
These village settlements on the saline wastes will captivate the mind, where the scent of continuously parched chickpeas prevails and the shadows are worn by long exposure;
their deep interiors resound with the clatter of heavy water-lifting machines as they are swung by the exuberant hands of young, rustic women in the height of their youth.

These days now incessantly spread unalloyed despondency— days in which the bees are delighted by the fragrance of lotuses on the plains of the forest, while the travelers, fleeing in terror at hearing the cries of the male cuckoos vocalizing from the slopes of the blossoming mango groves, are overwhelmed.
These jasmine buds, shining with radiant luster,
gleam like stars that, fearing the cold, have taken refuge in the jasmine creeper.
"These are the most affectionate"—do not place your trust in such trifles;
even the affection of these Siddhārthas causes tears to fall.
For these elephants, agitated by passion, are quickly bound by women who have their rut indicated by the humming of swarms of bees clinging to their fragrance.
O lotus, although these qualities exist within you, they do not become manifest,
since your calyx is enjoyed by bees while you are the abode of Lakṣmī.
For these living beings, whose nature is consciousness, have been cast into this world by their own mental impressions;
they are forms fashioned from Brahman by the thousands, tens of thousands, and millions.
For these physicians, like unbearable separations following the burning of the body, are as fierce as summer days; with their many cravings, they surely cause one to wither away.
For these clouds, bound by the cords of lightning and rushing at one another like elephants,
draw up the earth with its streams as if with a silver rope, by the command of Śakra.
For these water-fowls, though gathered closely together,
do not plunge into the water, like those lacking courage on the battlefield.
Smeared by these clouds, which resemble the color of crushed tamāla paste, and fanned by the fragrant, cool evening breezes gathering together—
this lightning, longing for union with the cloud, has arrived of her own accord and embraces the sky, as a passionate beloved embraces her lover.
The sky, its sun swallowed by these clouds dark as moist *tāla* leaves, appears as if struck by autumn; the anthills, battered by the downpour, collapse like elephants struck by arrows.
A flash of lightning, fashioned like a golden lamp moving through a palace, is swept away by the clouds like a woman whose weak husband has been driven off.

When the mind is already pierced by these very clouds—dark as lordly elephants, with swollen bellies, thundering, and variegated with lightning and cranes—then why does this crane, its hope destroyed, cry out "Rain! Rain! like a drum for the execution of one whose husband is away? Alas, alas! Of deceitful intellect, it sprinkles salt upon a wound.

This world is adorned by the rays of the moon of cool luster—by the waters of the Jahnu’s daughter (the Gaṅgā) mingled with those of the Yamunā and free from soot; by the eyes of women unstained by collyrium; by lotus stalks unsoiled by mud and smeared with pollen; by necklaces shimmering with flickering sapphires; and by jasmine flowers with bees clinging to them, all swaying like the rays of the moon.
What is the use here of these many born serpents? However, I believe that there is one certain venerable being who prevails as the sole survivor in this world:
Śeṣa, upon whose chest—the mark of which is the saffron paste from the slopes of Gaurī’s full breasts—the play of the garland of necklaces on the breast of Sthāṇu was surpassed.

O sandalwood tree, we shall speak of your fragrance through these southern breezes; for by it, this young honey-bee is drawn from every side—having been snatched from the mango tree, wafted up from the groves of lotuses, drawn from the interior of the *kunda* flower, and pulled from the surface of the temples of wandering elephants, as his heart rejoices.
If these ant-hills are very smooth and surrounded by such mounds,
then there is water three *hasta*s to the north of a man [measured] by four and a half [units].
Whatever has been commanded by these [preceptors], whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
must certainly be performed by those who are fearful, vigilant, and desirous of prosperity.

May these two arms of the Lord of the Raghus—those which sever the desire of the forest of plantain-like necks of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa; which are marked by the dense, crimson stains of the saffron powder from the jar-like breasts of Vaidehī; and which served as the sacrificial posts for the commencement of the noble sacrifice that protects the three worlds—grant you abundant blessings through their great prowess.

Leaving him aside, let the cowherd girls elsewhere close their lotus-eyes near the grove of *tulasī*; but who indeed could find Mukunda, whose dark luster is like a *tulasī* leaf, as he lies hidden within it?
What kind of terror is this, that one might become an animal because of this sin?
For even a water-snake is happy through its own causes of happiness, just like a king.

O charming six-legged bee, having abandoned the lotus— the very seat that satisfies the intense longing for the mass of blossoming drops of its unceasing nectar— why has your mind become attached to this worthless hibiscus flower?
When these have been conquered, everything has been conquered by that high-souled one;
therefore, having remembered this, the lord of the earth should avoid these six defects.
On these days, the teacher should cause the disciple to receive the weapons,
having satisfied the gods with gifts and fire-offerings according to the Vedic injunctions.
All the divine classes of beings, whose connection [to liberation] has been destroyed by these [obstacles],
return again and again due to most terrible afflictions.
Reclining on a bed of castor leaves, her broad hips exuding sweat,
the farmhand’s wife— like a mound of dust gathering together— removes the fever of love.
That sword which is named Mahisha, whose blade appears like the seed of an *eraṇḍa* plant, possesses a luster equal to a dark blue cloud.
Just as there is no use for woodwork with an abundance of castor, jujube, arka, and reeds collected together, so too there is no purpose in employing the ignorant.
The *śuddhasūḍa* is said to consist of eight [melodies]: Elākaraṇa, Ḍhekī, Vartanī, Ḍūmaḍa, Lambha, Rāsa, Ekatālī, and [the eighth].
Thus, at times, living beings— deluded by ignorance within the perils of cyclic existence— wander through hells, heavens, and other various wombs.
Thus, by exercising his capacity for action and restraining himself through his own self,
the king— who knows what is right and wrong— should act for his own welfare.
Let him who knows how to act or speak in such a way, being fond of deceit, do so; let him go about acting and enjoying his own self-interest.
In this way, the evil deed of everyone always bears fruit within oneself;
for whatever seed one sows, that very person reaps its fruit.
Therefore, noble-minded persons do not venture to oppose others;
for this is the established rule of the virtuous vow for those of supreme character.
A wise person should act in this way: he should demonstrate the increase of income and the decrease of expenditure, and he should accomplish the opposite as well.

O Mother, witness of the world, though I have reached this state, I lack the power even to understand what is appropriate for me now, what is the means for this, how this goal is to be accomplished, or what the measure is in this matter; what can I do?
And thus the world says: "Sandalwood is indeed cool;
yet the touch of a son's body exceeds that of sandalwood."

If such is your greatness as a natural state, O lotus stalk, why this dullness? Why is there such inherent crookedness despite your natural straightness? If your root is pure, whence comes this reputation of being "born from mud"? If these are indeed virtues, why are there holes? O friend, we cannot comprehend your true nature.
If you have been created by fate thus, yet are incapable of rendering even the slightest assistance, then do not offer help at all; otherwise, O desert, you would be subject to reproach.

But rather, by creating from afar the illusion of water through clouds, you draw others toward you with affection—even those whose minds are fainting with thirst—and for this reason, you are to be pitied.
In this manner, he should restrain those called thieves— even if they are not thieves— as well as merchants, artisans,
actors, mendicants, impostors, and others, from causing oppression to the country.
Such is the state of worldly people who are dull-witted; what then can be said of women who are so easily deluded? We live solely by the favor of those devoid of intelligence.
Thus old age destroys memory, beauty, and prowess without distinction;
yet the world does not experience spiritual urgency, even while witnessing such a state before its very eyes.
Having understood this, a lord of men should employ servants who are discerning,
of noble birth, endowed with heroism, capable, devoted, and hereditary.
Knowing this, O fortunate ones, a man who possesses discernment should perform that work during the day by which he may sleep happily at night.
Thus, the course of women's minds is indeed difficult to discern— minds that are full of enmity, devoid of reflection, and directed solely toward the base.
Thus, for those beings who have not abandoned their ethical discipline and have conquered anger,
prosperity comes of its own accord, unexpectedly, through mere contentment.
Thus, those of little intelligence become objects of ridicule for the gods in this world;
they do not achieve the accomplishment of their goals, whereas those of sound intelligence are honored.
In this manner, the king should protect the existing wealth consisting of forests, waterways, embankments, and mines, and he should also establish new ones.
O Lord of Men, thus, even a mere fragment of truthful speech never dwells in the heart of a woman except through deception.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should never take pleasure in them, for they are like desolate forests whose journey can only be accomplished by means of a caravan.
Thus, those of little intelligence, who are unable here to perform that [task] in its entirety, do not perform even a fraction of it according to their capacity.
Thus, for those of virtuous nature, only what is auspicious comes to pass as a certainty;
likewise, transgression leads to suffering even for the great.
A woman's touch leads to destruction and becomes a ground for mistrust;
even the favor of saving one's life—what else can be said of them?
Thus, women are by nature fickle, their many evil deeds producing a continuous stream that deprives one of discernment and dispassion;
yet among them, there may be some virtuous woman who adorns a great lineage, like the crescent moon newly appearing in the sky.
Having thus slain the wicked enemy, who was arrogant with pride, in battle,
he gladdened his own brave warriors with the sound of victory-trumpets.
In this way, the fool does not abandon his objects until he is abandoned by those very objects.
In this way, the beast and the fool are equal, for their minds are devoid of discernment.
In this way, one should not form attachment toward sons, grandsons, kinsmen, or relatives, for separation from them is certain.
Thus, wisdom alone is the supreme strength, and not valor;
for by its power, even a lion was slain by a hare.
One should exert such effort regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food,
as well as in standing, grooming, and all forms of ornamentation.
Thus, for everyone, the ritual bears fruit according to the quality of the being;
therefore, one should be a noble being, for prosperity does not choose those devoid of virtue.
Thus, one whose intellect is blinded by wealth wastes away much for the sake of a trifle.

Thus, even alone, a steadfast man— possessing peerless prowess— conquers at the head of battle many enemies who have entered the fray, who are agitated by hatred, and who disregard the true nature of themselves and others, having shattered their core strength and the fever of their pride.
Thus, having understood that which is beyond the intellect and having steadied the self by means of the self,
O mighty-armed one, slay the enemy in the form of desire, who is so difficult to overcome.
Thus do they speak here in this world while standing before the wealthy:
even those of noble birth are seen to act out of a desire for wealth on account of wicked people;
[this is the case] even when a poor man exercises sovereignty upon the earth.
Thus it is in this world, O Lord, for everyone at all times:
everything, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that belongs to a living being has been acquired through their prior karma.
Thus, courtesans are devoted solely to their own self-interest and devoid of genuine affection;
what loss is there for you even in the attainment of your desired objects?
Thus, while ignorance is being superimposed upon the self, the mind is set into action under the power of karma;
as long as there is no love for me, Vāsudeva, one is not released from the bondage of the body.
Thus, a deluded lord understands neither restraint nor favor.
Thus, the folly of the fool and the extreme strangeness of one blinded by self-interest are evident.
In this way, passion born of delusion leads to suffering for whom, if not for those very women? Yet for those who possess discernment, detachment toward them leads to liberation.
Just as you have said, O lady, all these faults are mine; what connection, O lotus-eyed one, could there be with my master?
Here I offer this salutation with joined palms; inflict punishment upon me. For a servant who has committed an offense, what occasion is there for forgiveness?
In this manner, one should apply three coatings on every seventh day;
thereafter, from the time of birth, the hair will become black with the luster of a bumblebee.
Thus one should know this world and the next to be perishable, fashioned by karma,
characterized by equality, excellence, and destruction, just like the realms of those who rule over circles of territory.
Having thus brought oneself under control, one should always have a smiling face;
one should abandon the contraction of the brows, speak first, and be a friend to the world.
When the celestial sage had spoken thus, Pārvatī, standing by her father’s side with her face cast downward,
began counting the petals of her play-lotus.
In this way, discernment and reflection are the very essence; what indeed could be more important for a kingdom?
Having brought such noble elephants from the forest, a king should discipline them like disciples and protect them like his own sons.
Having fixed in his mind whether such a thing will occur or not, he should utter his speech;
once he has consumed the morsel and attained steadiness, his movements and other actions should be observed.
Having thus observed his manifold virtues, which are capable of destroying all enemies in the form of evil,
those of pure awakening never abandon the great worship of knowledge.
Thus, the destruction of enemies by means of the administration of poison,
when carried out by one who has been weakened, is called "the staff of poison" (viṣadaṇḍa).
Thus, having endured the decree of adverse fate, virtuous women protect the wealth of their character even in times of calamity;
guarded by the greatness of their own inner strength, they bring about the welfare of both their husbands and themselves.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
Thus one should perform the three piercings amidst the sounds of conchs and drums;
then, having prostrated before the guru, one should present the bow and arrows.
One should perform this procedure of exertion until success is achieved;
once success in the exertion has been attained, during the rainy season, the bow must not be held in the hand.
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death,
he should constantly perform virtuous deeds through thought, word, and deed.
Thus, there certainly exist here on earth noble women devoted to their husbands;
however, it is not the case that all women are invariably of wicked conduct.
Having thus performed all these duties of his own,
he should protect these subjects, remaining disciplined and vigilant.
Thus, having observed the entire world seized by Death— who possesses irresistible power, who wields a sword that destroys the assembly of all living beings—

the virtuous, whose minds are tranquil and who have taken refuge in the imperial sovereignty of the Lord Jina’s asceticism, take up the multitude of arrows consisting of the excellent Three Jewels in order to cut him down.
Those lords of ascetics who extinguish with the pure waters of contentment the most treacherous fire of the belly, which causes suffering to all people— [they alone are truly wise].
Having thus performed all this, whatever merit has been acquired by me,
by that may I become the pacifier of all the sufferings of all sentient beings.
Having thus deliberated upon all this together with his ministers, the king,
having exercised himself and bathed at midday, should proceed to the inner apartments to eat.
Thus, the knower of yoga must constantly provide protection for the body with all one's being,
since the body is the means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Thus, having realized that Hari consists of all beings, the wise should cultivate unwavering devotion toward all living creatures.
Thus, what wise person, having made common to themselves this body whose origin and dissolution are unmanifest, would kill living beings except for the sake of the wicked?
Thus, by means of this wondrous human prowess, the yogi becomes perfected after having, according to the prescribed rite, deceived Time and the conditioned cycle of existence.

"O fair-browed one, hold your creeper-like arms thus; take this stance; do not bend too high; curve your toes; look at me for a moment!"—may those claps of hand (tālikā) from Śambhu, who dances with his own face as a drum sounding like a rain-cloud, protect you as he strikes them to the rhythm of his dance.
Thus, O Lord, one's own fault, though manifest, is not perceived by the ignorant.
Having thus understood their nature to be born of Prajāpati’s creation,
a man should apply the greatest effort toward their protection.
For thus does a woman act, O King, when she is constrained by jealousy.
For jealousy alone teaches women to avoid contact with other men;
therefore, a wise man should protect a woman by never manifesting that very jealousy.
And a secret must not be disclosed to women in any way whatsoever by a man who desires his own well-being.
Thus, fools whose hearts are ignorant, having created a misconception,
destroy their own interest as well as that of others, and they offer such a reply.
He who, pierced by the arrows of the god of love, performs such various actions that cause him to fall into the ocean of rebirth, finds no happiness here and no happiness in the world beyond.
Thus, an action performed with an unjust mind brings about inauspicious results;
therefore, one should perform it with a just mind, as was done by the crane for the snake.
He who thus observes the mutual shifting of the six measures of statecraft plays at will with kings bound by the chains of his intellect.
Thus, with his mind cast down and shaken by the force of the Flower-Bowed One (Kāma),
why does a person, censured by the world, not incur suffering that is unbearable, endless, and indescribable?
When the world is thus assailed and oppressed by time,
one should take hold of great fortitude and direct the mind toward liberation.
In this way, a minister who has heard little, even if he is of noble birth,
is not capable of examining counsel that is connected with virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
Having thus seen the course of Dharma through right conduct, the sages adopted right conduct as the supreme root of all austerity.
Thus, from the words of the authoritative one, he believed in the manly prowess of Rāghava— even though he wore the side-locks of childhood—
just as one believes in the power to burn inherent in fire, even when it is no larger than a cowherd’s thumb.
"O Ālī, Śaṅkara should be enjoyed in secret once your timidity has been subdued"—
though thus instructed by her friends, she, being distraught, did not remember this when her beloved stood before her.
Thus, why do you, following a conduct contrary to the stage of life, corrupt from birth this self-restraint— which,
though its pleasure rests upon the quality of purity— just as a young black cobra defiles a sandalwood tree?
Thus, even animals of noble birth, O beloved,
do not abandon their master in times of calamity, nor do they fail to rescue a friend from such distress.
But for those born of low birth,
who are fickle-minded, neither affection nor love ever touches their hearts, even at any time.
Thus, for one who gathers merit little by little as it is accumulated, a vast amount is perfected; and in this same way, learning and austerity are perfected as well.
In this very way, she who is endowed with ritual action bestows all good fortune;
he whose wife she may be is a lord of the gods, not a mere mortal.
In this very way, one certainly cannot live with a wicked person; what then need be said of one who is a favorite of the king?
For fire is already difficult to endure at first, how much more so when fanned by a powerful wind?
In the very same way, one should not place trust in those humans who have previously done one harm, just as one would not trust a river whose water has already flowed away.
In this very way, whatever man plants an *aśvattha* tree according to the prescribed rite,
wherever he may go, he shall reach the abode of Hari.
This indeed is the mental anguish of an elephant sunk in the mud:
that his kinsmen look on with suppressed smiles as they attempt to pull him out.

This wind blows favorably upon our limbs, sweet with the fragrance from the faces of the women of Kusumapura who are weary at the end of their play; it prolongs the charming, drowsy warbling of the cranes; it follows the scent of rows of swaying *vicikila* flowers; and it proclaims the grandiose martial titles of Love, as echoed by the bees pursuing its fragrance.

He churns up the mud, breaks the lotus plants, and eats the shoots of *gundrā* grass; he makes the marshy thickets of *mustā* grass uneven and moves toward the waters where the embankments have been washed away.
"He has arrived! He has arrived! "He has entered the dense forest! He is going this way!"—thus pursued by the troops from behind, the boar enters the rugged depths of the forest.
O beautiful one, this elephant, surrounded by its young, plays at the foot of a mountain peak amidst a thicket of trees and shrubs bent low with the weight of blossoms;
hearing the roar of the clouds, he is delighted and, possessing the speed of the wind, once again performs the "falling of bamboo leaves" maneuver.
O lovely-faced one, this moon is united with the trembling orb of the star Yogatārā,
like a bridegroom joined to a maiden at her first initiation who trembles with fear.
This ocean, with its tumultuous display of surging waves, underwent mere agitation;
meanwhile, Love blossomed within the women through the amorous gestures appropriate for his rising.
Alas, this sun, impelled by the fierce force of its ill-regulated punishment, has lost its luster;
for how much longer will it remain suspended in the sky with its rays hanging down, before falling of its own accord?
O lady of beautiful hips, this is indeed the law: submissiveness toward one's father and mother.
Therefore, having transgressed their command, I have no desire to live.
This dharma has been declared by me as the supreme goal for women;
whatever woman does otherwise, she certainly goes to hell.
This crane has suddenly perished; alas, where indeed has his deceit gone?
O Kṛtānta, well done! No one at all is capable of deceiving you in any way.
O Goddess, here is Brahmā upon a lotus, his crest adorned with a digit of the moon; this is Śaṅkara, the destroyer of demons, with his four arms marked by the bow, sword, mace, and discus;
here too is Indra, lord of the thirty gods, mounted upon Airāvata, as well as these other deities; and there these divine women dance in the sky, their anklets jingling upon their moving feet.
"O friend, this moon of stainless radiance is being swallowed by Rāhu;
the clear water is becoming turbid due to the collapsing of the riverbank."
This is the sun, full of splendor; alas, even this glowworm is full of splendor!
This is a mango tree; even this is a śākhoṭaka tree.
This is indeed the supreme duty of kings: the alleviation of the suffering of the afflicted.
Yet, here goes the son of a barren woman, wearing a crown made of sky-flowers, having bathed in the waters of a mirage, and wielding a bow made of a hare’s horn.
This is the clear distinction between fire and the fire of your majesty:
what is scorched by that [ordinary] fire sprouts again, but for that which is scorched by this [fire], there is no further rebirth.
Perched upon the tip of this tree, its orb as bright as the essence of gold,
it seems to drink the waning heat of the afternoon sun from the peacock with its full thighs.
This young bee, intoxicated with passion, passes the nights upon you, O *kunda* jasmine;
yet even so, the unbearable pain of separation from the lotus does not diminish in his heart.
In the sky’s edge of dense darkness, like a dark expanse of water belonging to the Yamunā,
the moon shines like a royal swan with its beak concealed within the fold of its wings.
This deer, scorched by the rays of the sun, has taken refuge in a wretched tree;
like a virtuous man whose fortune is exhausted, he languishes upon reaching a low person.
This is the nature of women: having previously experienced happiness, they become corrupted and even abandon their husbands upon encountering even the slightest misfortune.
This moon has risen, possessing the luster of the tusks of the world-elephants meeting the waters of the celestial river; it bears the grace of falling silver jars.
It acts like a female swan, like a spotless lotus, like a shimmering mass of foam, and like a vast crystal earring; it is the very root of joy for the quarters of the sky.
For this is the primary duty of a consecrated Kṣatriya:
by means of it, O one of great wisdom, the protection of the subjects is possible.

O friend, may there be well-being for these creepers and trees on the banks of the daughter of Mount Kalinda, who were companions to the amorous play of the cowherd women and witnesses to the secret trysts of Rādhā;

now that the union which served as the means for preparing the bed of love has been severed, I know that they are becoming hoary with age through their sprouts, though they still possess a shimmering blue luster.
Their shoots are silken garments, their flowers are pearls, their fruit is coral, their petals are lapis lazuli, their sprouts are emeralds, and their hundreds of branches are gold.

Who are these trees of the world that I, though a forest-dweller, have never known before? They are likely the very essence of the celestial trees; what burden do they pose to me, for I have other concerns?

Who is this woman with such a charming hip-region, overflowing with intoxicating passion? Her curved knitting of the brows resembles the bow of the Bodiless One (Kāma), and her face—with cheeks like the full moon and a lotus-like mouth—is radiant as the moon. With a slender waist, this beautiful woman moves along, her single braid of hair appearing like a staff balanced against her swaying arm.
Who is this lovely woman of fresh youth with a moon-like face walking along the path, her eyes rolling and agitated by sleep, her lips as red as ripe bimba fruit?
With her hair disheveled, torn by nails, and mangled by teeth—who is this Rākṣasa of Lust who has ravished her, playing like a tiger?
This beloved woman walks gracefully, trembling, through the forest thicket concealed by great trees;
"Alas, alas! What is this? I am bewildered and do not know," [he thinks], for she clearly intends to display the playful gait of a female *śarabha* in her anger.
Who is this woman with a face like the full moon, fair as a doe, agitating [the senses], whose gait is like that of a playful lordly elephant or a swan—[her form is]...
/ Her mouth is cooled by the fragrance of her breath from her lower lip, and her speech is soft and delightful; blessed is that man, he truly lives as the best of men, who has such a beloved as this.
Who is this woman who has entered the hall, walking with the grace of a swan, her limbs manifest, her eyes darting, her two hands smeared with saffron and adorned with gold?
With her body bent, carrying many flowers and holding a lute, smiling, and concealing betel in her left hand, she has entered the hall, overcome by passion.
Who is this young woman who, having eaten and drunk, with trembling eyes and garments clinging to her limbs from perspiration, goes forth at dawn like a startled doe, apprehensive on all sides?

By whom has this lotus-face, with its quivering nectar of lips, been drunk as if by a bee? By whom has heaven been enjoyed today? And for whom has the God of Love, struck down by Shiva’s eye, become satisfied?
Who is this woman who bears a moon-like face shimmering with *hāva* and *bhāva*, whose body is as fair as a garland of *campaka* flowers and hangs down with full breasts;
who moves about with the confident grace of a playful doe at her own will—is she a celestial nymph brought down to the surface of the earth by Brahmā?
Whose breasts are firm with the weight of their fullness, yet her waist is slender; who wanders like a startled doe with tremulous eyes, having fled from her terrified herd;

who moves with playful grace, dripping with internal sweat like the ichor falling from the temples of a lordly elephant—seeing this form, dense with the limbs of a beloved, even an old man becomes filled with desire.
Seated upon this flower, though thirsty, this female bee remains devoted to you; she awaits you, for she truly does not drink the nectar without you.
"She has indeed arrived; yet, a hindrance is created for the long-lashed-eyed woman by the weight of her thick, rounded hips.
As if thinking thus, the light movement of the mind went before the gazelle-eyed one as she proceeded toward her beloved, as if to speak these words.
This creeper with its broad clusters of blossoms seeks to surpass you, who are weary from the weight of your full, firm, and swelling breasts.
My dear, let us pluck its clusters so that other creepers shall never again dare to rival them.
"O Hara, O fair-limbed one, which of these is yours? Which one rests upon your head? Is it matted hair? Does a swan resort to matted hair? No, it is the moon; the moon does not dwell in water.
"O innocent one, this is ash; where is the water here? The ash ripples like waves. May that Śaṃkara, who thus conceals the river of the three paths (the Gaṅgā), protect you all.

O beloved, alas, these faults have arisen in you according to the facts during our separation: that you have become a sinner guilty of murdering a woman, and that you have acquired a stigma throughout the three worlds.
O dear one, I swear truly that I shall never again commit such an offense; for the God who subdues the Mind (Kāma) is eager to strike me with his exceedingly sharp arrows once I am abandoned by you.
This Mandākinī— whose banners are the Dharma, whose banks are graced by the presence of Apsarases, who causes sinners to wither away, who is intent upon the fruitfulness of Bhagīratha’s asceticism,

who has mounted her affection upon the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva), who gazes with a sidelong glance from the face of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), and who is a Ḍākinī to the pomp of evil— exists for the joy of the three worlds.

O swan, this lotus pond is covered with foul waters from the side-streets; if you desire to dwell here through ignorance and the lack of compassion of Fate, then let your confidence be placed in flocks of cranes, your modesty among frogs, your kinship with those blind at night, and your wretchedness among rows of lapwings.
Having somehow survived her journey abroad, she has now fallen once again into a state of uncertainty;
for who indeed is able to shut the doors of fate when a living being is facing its final ripening?
In this season fragrant with blossoming *kadamba* and *nīpa* trees, illuminated by the clouds, she—filled with passion, joyful, and her locks wet from water—has come to her lover’s dwelling.
Startled by lightning and the thundering of rain-clouds, yet longing for a sight of you, she stands washing her feet which bear mud clinging to her anklets.
This girl with eyes like blossoming lotuses will be some beloved daughter or granddaughter of Kāma;
for how else could Kāma, merciless toward the ignorant, strike down a youth who gazes upon her for even a moment?
This celestial nymph forcibly draws my mind from my body toward the intermediate state of my father,
just as a female royal swan pulls a lotus fiber from its broken tip.
She is indeed skilled in entering the stage, in the training of the arts, and in modulating her voice; let her not be withheld from speaking.
If this creeper were a playful woman, how could it be? And if it were a streak of lightning, how could it remain upon the earth?
Has the Creator fashioned it as a city for King Manojan (the God of Love), made impassable by the formidable fortress of her heavy breasts?
Walking gracefully and smiling along with her companions,
this exceedingly bold woman of the mountain region shines like a goddess who has eternally attained the bliss of amorous union.
This is that Narmadā, whose waves roll upon the broad rocky slopes in the midst of the Vindhya range, bestowing bliss upon the Śabara women who rest on her banks weary from amorous play;
and whose riverbanks, where sprouting kandalas are trampled by deer, are frequented by Siddhas who have halted there, concealed by beautiful women meeting at the base of the dense rows of trees.
Out of pride regarding your youth, you followed after a man of good family; though your hair was rich with flowers worthy of being cherished, it has been dragged down.
For this, O delighter of the Raghus, is the nature of women since the beginning of creation:
they are devoted to one who is in a state of prosperity, and they abandon one who is in a state of adversity.
For this is my firm vow when I have gone to battle: that my enemies shall not see the flanks of my horses.
In battles where fortune is fickle, my vow remains constant; as for victory or defeat, those depend on what destiny wills.
Among these, the touch of excellent women captivates even the mind of a sage;
therefore, one should enjoy sense objects with vigilance and as is appropriate.
This is surely some woman with eyes like blossoming lotuses, perhaps a certain beloved of Kāma, or his daughter, or even his younger sister;
for how else could Kāma strike down that young man—merciless as he is—at the mere sight of her for a moment?
This indeed is a great shame for a king of virtuous conduct:
that untimely death should touch his subjects.
Among women, she alone is blessed who attains both virtuous conduct and happiness;
for she is devoted to her husband by day, yet becomes unchaste at night.
This so-called "Agnihotrin" maintains cows, yet having sold them, he offers milk and water as his oblation;
though renowned in the worlds as one who approaches his wife only during her season, he goes to a prostitute—even during the day—when she is in her menses.
This Aparṇā is the wife of you, the venerable Jaṭila; Sthāṇu himself is here, as is your son Viśākha.
O Vāmadeva, who in this world would desire fruit from you? For you, the mere sight of whom brings about the destruction of rebirth.
"O daughter of the Sun, this boat is now full of water as it leaps over the slopes of the banks with its lofty waves; there is no fear for Hari even of a blemish.
O beautiful one, do not be hard-hearted today; O Rādhā, we live by your grace. Clearly make the festival of sporting in the mountain valley a reality."
This intoxicated elephant, whose roar is like the sound of the ocean and whose gait is faltering and slow,
hears the thundering of the clouds on the mountain slope and crushes the trees.
I, born from the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain, who am far beyond the reach of the desires of gods and demons,
have arrived here after having made the daughter of the Asura king attain the fruit of exquisite beauty through her union with Aniruddha in a dream.
One should desire many sons who are virtuous and well-versed in sacred learning; for among those gathered together, it may happen that at least one might go to Gayā.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
or performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or sets free a dark-colored bull.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
where stands that banyan tree renowned in the worlds as the "Maker of the Imperishable."
"I thought, 'May he not come back again,' and thus performed an inauspicious act at his departure;
now that very same act is the cause for the master of the house remaining as a mere ruin."
Kings afflicted by love will come from the ends of the earth in numbers beyond counting to enter this sanctuary;
indeed, even by the Creator were fashioned here as many lines upon these lotus-feet as there are fingers on a single hand.

"Your heart's lords will surely come now; O simple ones, do not indulge in various lamentations in vain"—thus did the clouds seem to speak to the lotus-eyed wives of travelers under the guise of their thundering.
"Come here! Go away! Fall down! Stand up! Speak!
Observe silence!"—who has not been deceived by her whose eyes are like those of a startled deer?
"Come here! Go away! Fall down! Stand up! Speak! Observe silence!"—in this manner do the wealthy play with supplicants who are seized by the crocodile of hope.
"Come, let us gather beautiful flowers there among the splendors of the *koca*, *mañju*, and *sumana* trees.
Having thus brought the proud woman alone into a secluded spot under a pretext for a moment, he captivated her.
"Come, O child, you have been designated as alms for the Universal Soul.
The sages are seekers; I have now attained the fruit of being a householder."
"Come, O beautiful woman, look at this spectacle: one whose body is grey with dust and who is naked! She too drank in the lotus-face of her brother; even when told thus, why does she not understand?
"Come, come here; sit upon this seat. Why have you been seen after such a long time? What is the news? You are very weak. Are you well? I am delighted by the sight of you.
Those who thus address their friends who have arrived with such respect—it is always appropriate for them to go to their mansions with a mind free from suspicion.
Come, embrace me; the beauty of the day hastens my heart, and you, O weak one, are weary. O female ruddy goose (*cakravākī*), spend this night alone with me.
I am not attached to another, nor indeed am I angry, nor have I fallen away from love; rather, being subject to fate and lacking self-mastery, I abandon you all at once.
"Come, come! Where have you gone, O Maithilī? A deer has been caught by me; I shall flay its golden skin and place it over your breasts as a fine silken garment.
Do not remain alone in the forests even out of a desire to test my devotion; do not be so simple-minded, for deceitful Rākṣasas roam there, hostile toward me."
Come, come, my child, Raghunandana, Rāmabhadra! I shall kiss you on the head and embrace you for a long time;
or else, I shall carry you upon my heart day and night, or I shall worship your two lotus-like feet.
Called out by the exceedingly sharp cries of peacocks saying "Come, come!", hurriedly embraced with longing as if by a female crane taking flight,
and gazed upon with great agitation by swans who have abandoned their lotuses— the cloud rises, making the quarters of the sky appear as if blackened by collyrium.
In the absence of effort, there is a single result: the non-existence of the fruits of actions.
On the other hand, if there is effort, there is a twofold result: the fruit either comes to be or it does not.
When ministers, having attained unanimity, apply themselves with the eye of insight as seen in the scriptures, that they call the supreme counsel.
When many opinions have been presented by ministers during the determination of a matter,
but they subsequently reach a state of unanimity, that counsel is known as "middling."
Where counsel is discussed by relying on one another's opinions,
yet no consensus is reached, that consultation is said to be the lowest.

"O righteous one, having seen this deer-skin, this hut of *palāśa* leaves, and this black antelope skin before you, why do you wander about seeking alms with the thought that this is a grove of ascetics?
Know this to be the city of the Bhillas, where the gods, stationed here, drink wine accompanied by the meat of buffaloes roasted in forest fires from the horns of cows."
Overwhelmed by the suffering of separation from his beloved, this lover reckons the fire, though it is cold, to be hotter than the rays of the moon.
When the wind enters the lunar channel (nāḍikā) of its own accord,
and when the *potakī* moves to the right, then the entire desired fruit shall be attained.
Bearing her rainbow upon her pale cloud-like breasts, resembling fresh nail-marks, the autumn season,
while pleasing the spotted moon, increased the heat even more than that of the sun.
It is said that a bird belonging to Indra tore at her breasts with its claws,
as if displaying a spirit of rivalry over the marks of her lover's enjoyment.
If, while looking toward the eastern direction, the sun faces a householder within his home,
there shall be fear of the king, fear of thieves, danger from executioners and quarrels, and danger from cattle.

By your glories, O King, all elephants act as Airāvaṇas, all serpents act as Śeṣas, alas, even birds act as swans; all mountains, like blue lotuses, act as white lilies, and they are intent upon becoming Mount Kailāsa.
With his body stained orange by the pollen of lotuses clinging to him from the falling drops of ichor from Airāvaṇa’s face,
his wings shattered by frost driven by a fierce wind, this exhausted bee lies here on the ground, helpless.
While Airāvaṇa keeps his ear-flaps motionless to hear your fame being sung by celestial nymphs, the swarms of bees drink his ichor without obstruction; whose prosperity does your conduct not bring?
A fall toward the northeast is inauspicious; other intermediate directions are auspicious.
They bring joy and nourishment, and bestow success in the performance of surgical operations.
In the northeast, there will be the acquisition of vessels filled with clarified butter and a bull;
such is the fruit for a householder when [the omen] rests upon the roof of the house.
The sovereignty of Nahuṣa, the devotion to the realm of Śambhu possessed by the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), the innate heroism of the Lord of the Raghus, and the profundity of the ocean— if these,
along with the generosity of Bali and Karṇa, were to exist together in one place in this world, only then might there be some slight resemblance to King Śrī Vīra, the crest-jewel of monarchs.
The eye obscured by the darkness of power sees even while looking, yet does not see;
later, it attains clarity through the medicinal ointment of the pill of poverty.
For we have heard that even those who possess sovereign power, wealth, and jewels— even when they remain with an enemy— may indeed be seen to return once more to life.
The most wicked person is one intoxicated by power, even more so than one intoxicated by drinking liquor;
for those maddened by the intoxication of power, no upward path exists.
Among intoxications such as that of drink and the like, the intoxication of power is the most evil;
for one intoxicated by the pride of power does not awaken until he has fallen.
Those who are vigilant, though they may be deceitful or brave and courageous, attend upon those who are intoxicated by the pride of power as well as those intoxicated by the madness of liquor.
For those intoxicated by the pride of power, for the hungry, for those possessed by desire,
and for those deluded by egoism, discernment never arises.
Having obtained sovereignty, which is impermanent, fix your mind on the eternal Dharma;
for even worldly prosperities, along with one's very self, perish in an instant.
For generally, having attained even a small measure of power, a wicked person becomes arrogant;
whereas a virtuous person, having attained very great power, attains tranquility.
May the dust from the lotus feet of Heramba bring us unimpeded sovereignty—
those very particles which bear the splendor of the vermilion powder upon the parting lines of the beautiful women of the Vedas.
Sovereignty, envy, cruelty, intoxication, and lack of discernment—each one of these alone could do what? What need is there to speak of their presence in a fivefold combination?

For even those who possess power are truly destitute if they have failed to offer the wealth of their sovereignty as a voluntary gift to their friends; such men, having surrendered themselves to greed, find their labor in vain and their lives consist of nothing but mere existence.
He in whom the supreme pinnacle of sovereignty is eternally manifested—
he, the giver of wealth, whose arising of qualities is so desirable, would not be envied by anyone?

Goodness of character is the ornament of sovereignty; restraint of speech is that of valor; tranquility is that of knowledge; humility is that of peace; and expenditure upon worthy recipients is that of wealth.

Absence of anger is the ornament of austerity; forgiveness is that of power; and sincerity is that of righteousness. Indeed, for all these, this virtue is the supreme ornament and the cause of everything.
One should never form an alliance with someone on account of their power;
for when they have departed, there is no respect, and when they have arrived, there is a loss of wealth.
In truth, the world serves a lord who is not devoid of power; those who follow him in times of calamity do so with the hope of being established by him once more.
But those virtuous ones like you, who—even at their master’s destruction—bear the burden of his duties with detached devotion due to the attachment formed by past merits, are rare to find.
How can one who possesses forbearance even in prosperity, benevolence even in poverty,
and steadfastness even in calamity be considered a mere mortal?
Whether in vast prosperity or in most terrible calamity,
Fate drags a person along, binding him as if with a rope.
Men practice actions pertaining to this world and the next; however, O auspicious lady, one who is intent upon desire merely attains [the fruits of] those actions.
They strive for worldly gain that merely increases flesh and blood,
while remaining utterly asleep regarding matters pertaining to the next world, being profound nihilists.
When the yogin has always restrained those desires pertaining to this world and the next, which consist of greed and delusion, there shall be for him the attainment of all desires.
The syllable *Oṃ* is the primordial Puruṣa, and the *Vyāhṛtis* are Prakṛti, the woman;
when these two are joined together by the hands, a man should cover them with a cloth.
In whose kingdom the sound of the syllable *oṃ* prevails among the Brahmins,
that king shall indeed be a yogi and will not be afflicted by diseases.

The sound of the cuckoos is the *oṃkāra* of the secret teachings of the flower-armed god; it is the recitation of mantras for the study of Love; it is the fragrant scripture for the rite of rebirth in sexual union;
it is the accomplishment of the goal of attracting the mind; it is the fever for the ears of unchaste women; and it is the nectar-sprinkling for travelers in the mango groves.

Oṃ! Seek the Lord of the House within the true lamp of the syllable Oṃ—subtle and dwelling in solitude—having restrained the door-keeper, the breath that flows incessantly, and the leader of the senses.

For what purpose do you spread a web of words with your speech? Nothing at all is seen [therein]. Behold the Master residing within the body; why do you wander in the darkness of delusion caused by other scriptures?

The digit of the moon shines forth: it is the syllable *Oṃ* for the twice-born god of love; the sprout of a single tusk for the elephant of the sky; the pearl-oyster shell for the pearls of the stars; the goad for the elephant of blinding darkness; the bolt and key for the door of erotic passion; the scissors that cut through the pride of women separated from their lovers; and the nail-marks left upon the twilight-bride.
We worship that lotus-foot of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), whose root is the syllable *Oṃ*, whose sap is the Upaniṣads, whose stalk is the web of logic, whose stem is the cosmic egg,
from which sacrifice spreads as its pollen, whose humming is the Purāṇas, whose dwelling is on the banks of the solitary celestial river, and whose nectar is bliss.
Oṃ, homage to Śambhu, whose single form is the ultimate reality, who is the supreme self, and who appears as the manifold diversity of the unreal through his own will.
Oṃ hraum, obeisance to Śaṅkara at the location of the crest-lock; Oṃ hraum, obeisance to Keśava in the two arms;
Oṃ hraum, obeisance to Brahmā in the center of the navel.
Oṃ hrauṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati at the two shanks.
The seed carried by the flood-wind that sprouts in someone’s field belongs to the owner of the field alone;
the sower of the seed does not receive the fruit.
Indeed, surely the Goddess of Victory does not approach one who lacks vigor or who is without a companion;
for even the Lord Ananga, though he is the friend of the moonbeams, took up his victorious bow.

Surely that blazing tongue, vomiting forth intense inner luster under the guise of flames, shrieked aloud as it surely consumed the fierce vitality of those standing in battle along with their very bodies.
May this syllable *Om*, the supreme Brahman, the mouth of the Vedas, the imperishable,
which alone consists of the three puruṣas, be gracious within the hearts of the virtuous.

In the sky above the lofty heads of the elephants, the garlands of stars appeared like the conflagrations at the end of an eon, arising from the friction of the trees that were their tusks as they were tossed by the winds of rising intoxication.
For the lovers who relished the biting of sprout-like lips,
the turn of wine became a source of heart-felt delight through the goblets of women’s faces, adorned with full-blown blue lotuses of their eyes.

The tip of the lip quivers as the eyes flicker; like a fish in the depths of a well, the flower-adorned braid loosens and must be bound again. As she walks, her breasts move forward and her hips become visible; though her sash is fastened very firmly, it slips away—such are the gestures of women revealing their passion.
Through the proclamation of her husband's good fortune, beauty, humor, virtues, and affection, she attains happiness;
and by gladdening the hearts of her relatives and friends from afar, even when out of sight, she manifests the signs of her desire for sensual pleasures.

O King, when the women with eyes like lotus petals had become exhausted by their efforts— mistaking the king’s lips for bimba fruit, his tresses for ripe *jambū* fruits, and the red gems adorning his ears for pomegranate seeds— they were instantly overcome by thirst and fainted in the desert, as if they were the parrots in the cage of the Gūrjara king.
Propriety is the foremost among things worthy of praise; the application of sandalwood paste and the like is foremost among fragrant ointments;
a maiden is foremost among causes of sorrow; and one devoid of intelligence is foremost among those deserving of compassion.
One whose conduct has fallen away from propriety cannot achieve their own purpose through mere reasoning;
by the very pretext of slaying Bālin, Rāma’s fame was tarnished.
On one side there is propriety alone; on the other, a heap of virtues.
A multitude of virtues, when devoid of propriety, acts like poison.
The harsh beauty of the golden *ketaka* flower was abandoned by its dear petals out of sheer disgust, not because it was trapped in a watery fortress;
nor was its splendor obscured by thorns, but rather by being laden with dust.
The gaze wanders as if filled with longing, and the mind goes somewhere in a state of agitation,
for one who is being separated from a person endowed with virtues and possessed of constant love.
Establishment merely suppresses one's natural zeal, while the duty of protecting what has been acquired causes distress;
sovereignty is not for the removal of fatigue, but rather leads to further exhaustion, like a parasol held in one's own hand with its staff.
You do not reveal the cause of your longing, for logic does not have the singular essence of realizing the truth;
nevertheless, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, I shall make myself the target of these lamentations.
Victorious is the festival for the eyes of a young couple at their first union— eyes that repeatedly close from longing and yet contract again out of bashfulness.

May Gaurī bring you auspiciousness—she who, in her new union with Hara, was hurried along by an eager longing born within her, yet turned back again and again by bashfulness; who was drawn forward once more by the various words of her kinswomen; who, seeing her husband before her, was overcome with the sentiment of trepidation; and who, her hair standing on end with thrill, was embraced by the smiling Śiva.
Magnanimity, courtesy, loathing of evil, and pure understanding—
these are the signs of the attainment of Dharma, as well as being generally beloved by people.

MSS_8248-1 Magnificence known throughout the three worlds, birth from the ocean, dwelling in the Nandana grove, and a fragrance that captivates the hearts of the gods—MSS_8248-2 thus all the qualities of the celestial tree, the preeminent giver, are transcendent; yet it would possess only one quality of discernment if it were capable of fulfilling the requests of the most excellent supplicants.

Generosity is the ornament of the wealthy, propriety that of the virtuous, modesty that of noble women, fine poetry that of the mouth, rut that of the elephant, the male cuckoo that of the forest, the bee that of the lotus, and the artful nail-marks on the cheek of a beloved; O Lord, even you are the ornament upon this circle of the earth.
The indifference of the compassionate and the misfortune of the supplicants are not due to any fault of the mirror,
just as one's own ugliness is not the fault of the mirror.
One may see *audumbara* flowers or a white-colored crow, or see fish-feet in the water; but one does not see that which resides in the heart of a woman.

Your height reaches the level of the towering peaks of Mount Sumeru, and your pervasiveness is determined by the same principle as the vastness of the base of the King of Mountains. Yet, not even for a single young *cātaka* bird does your water suffice for its satisfaction; you are recognized, O cloud, as being like the swollen breasts of a barren woman.
One’s own biological son, one bound by friendship, one inherited through family lineage,
and one protected from calamities— friendship is to be known as fourfold.
For kings abandon even their own biological sons if they act against their interests, yet they accept even strangers if they are capable.
If a man, out of lust, should have sexual intercourse with his own uterine sister, or even with the wife of his younger brother, death is declared to be his punishment.
Like the sons of Aurva, they become exceedingly greedy, possessing an intense thirst for the salt water of even a fragment of wealth;
they would cast away their own bodies like a blade of grass, yet not a fraction of their riches.
Let those afflicted by fever abandon the medicine of foolish physicians,
just as virtuous people avoid a wife who is attached to the company of others.
Among medicines, mantras, and the wisdom of the Great-Souled Buddhas,
there is nothing within this cosmic egg that cannot be accomplished in this world.
Medicines, mantras, constellations, omens,
and planets may be effective during a time of good fortune, but they become fruitless during a time of misfortune.
Medicines, antidotes, knowledge, and the various states of divine power—all these are accomplished through austerity alone; for austerity is indeed their means of attainment.
Even that mortal who, lacking discernment, consumes honey as medicine is born into a miserable womb; how much more so, then, one who is greedy for it?

Then, having gathered from the lowlands, the darkness— having hidden itself for fear of the heat of dawn and being more effective at obscuring the fading luster of the day— slowly rose up toward the level ground.
Likewise, high-souled kings on earth generally maintain heat as well as valor, gentleness, punishment, and graciousness.
Therefore, kings are to be honored and worshipped in all circumstances.

These courtesans inhabit this city; they possess the charming allure of fresh youth that seems to be steaming with passion, appearing like lovely ripples on the ocean of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and they are the victory banners of fame acquired through the delights of amorous play.
O Murāntaka, you who are clever in deception, indulge in pride;
for toward a man who has many favorites, courtesy brings only sorrow.
O serpent, do not spend some time in the depths of a mountain cave playing in vain, you who are arrogant with the swelling venom of *hālāhala*!
O serpent, do not [be so], for it was during the rainy season, when the sky was crowded with rising water-laden clouds, that the peacock reached this state out of a longing to roam the forest.
"Endure this for just a moment, or rather, cast off your garment; here your attendants are awake—shame on you, you are shameless!
Here is my joined palms; extinguish the lamp!"—these words of a beloved woman bring a joy even greater than that of sexual union.
The lotus never forgets you, even when you have gone elsewhere for some time; O swan, sport in the Mānasa lake, and do not ever abandon your friendship with it again.
With the beauty of her hair like a row of humming bees amidst a mass of lotus pollen,
and with the interior of her mouth occupied by learned Brahmins, this venerable lady, a knower of the stars, shines like a river.
Whom do calamities not touch in due time, or who is there in this world who possesses uninterrupted happiness?
Suffering and happiness come by the power of transformation, like the circle of stars revolving in the sky.
"Whom shall we ask, O gods? We dwell in heaven, while you dwell on earth.
Is the essence of poetry sweet, or is the nectar of immortality sweeter?"
To whom can I speak now, or who could possibly believe it?
That the son of the cowherd’s daughter is a Brahmin who is a paramour to the young cowherd women in the forest grove!
Just as a man, while applying himself to his purpose, might fall into a pit if he lets go of one who has lost their sight;
even so, the craving for sense objects among men causes them to fall into the blind well of hell.
Relying on what distinction do you resort to the earth for the sake of your beloved’s splendor?
For you, the reason for your abandonment is exactly the same: she too, as well as this earth, is merely a place for the discharge of waste.
Whom did Kṛṣṇa slay? The Gaṅgā flows coolly for whom? Who are devoted to nourishing their wives? And whom does the cold not afflict, however powerful he may be?

Salutations to you, O Kṛṣṇa! You cause Kaṃsa to perish, you obscure Mura, and likewise you strike down Haṃsa; you bring Bāṇa to ruin, you diminish Baka, and likewise you destroy Pauṇḍra. You humble Bhauma by force, you utterly shatter the pride of Indra (Balabhid), and you protect the distressed multitude of the virtuous who bow before you. Salutations to you!
Tell me, by what means might there be a journey for the enemy of Kaṃsa? Where does one of few desires fix his gaze?
What do the wise declare brings auspiciousness to all? And what, O good man, would you do to remove sorrow from the world?
O Haṃsa, I think: how could your mind take delight in the waters of small channels, when it has been caressed by the waves of the ocean born from the feet of the Enemy of Kaṃsa?
Kaṃsa, Rāvaṇa, Rāma, and King Duryodhana—these four were all great fools; Śālivāhana was the fifth.
Who is able to protect whom at the time of death? When the rope is severed, who can hold up the jar?
In this way, the world shares the same nature as forests; from time to time it is cut down and it grows again.
Which boar would not grunt with a terrible roar here and there? Which elephant would not strive to make this lotus-pool devoid of its blossoms?
And which wild buffaloes would not uproot these forests? For the lion dwells here, bound by the affectionate dalliance of his love for the lioness.
Who creates the sharpness of thorns, or the diverse nature of beasts and birds?
Sweetness in the sugarcane and bitterness in the neem tree—all this is indeed established by its own inherent nature.

Who is the father of Karṇāri? Whose beloved is the daughter of the Mountain King? Who is Tuk? Who knows the gestures of others? From where did Viṣamagu arise? Whose wife is Videhajā? What torments on the day of Bhauma? And who is censurable? The answer to these questions, formed by the middle syllables of each word, bestows the attainment of all goals. The answer is: *kāntābhūtkamalā hareḥ* (The beloved of Hari was Kamalā). 1. Who is the father of Karṇāri (Arjuna)? **Kāntā** (The beloved). 2. Whose beloved is the daughter of the Mountain King (Pārvatī)? **Abhūt** (She was). 3. Who is Tuk? **Kamalā** (Lakṣmī). 4. Who knows the gestures of others? **Hareḥ** (Of Hari). 5. From where did Viṣamagu (the God of Love) arise? **Kamalā** (From the lotus). 6. Whose wife is Videhajā (Sītā)? **Hareḥ** (Of Rāma). 7. What torments on the day of Bhauma (Mars)? **Kamalā** (The lotus). 8. Who is censurable? **Hareḥ** (A rogue). Thus, the answer is: *kāntābhūtkamalā hareḥ*. This phrase brings about the fulfillment of all desires.
Who is a relative to whom? What is obtainable by anyone from another?
Since a living being is born alone and perishes alone.
Therefore, O Rāma, that man who becomes attached to mother and father should be known as one who is like a madman; for no one belongs to anyone else.

Who went to the forest at his father’s command? What does a lover do when he embraces the region of a woman’s neck? And what grows back after being severed by the forceful act of a vulture? Who was the night of destruction for the race of Rākṣasas?
Who hates the moonlight? And who, tormented by separation from Sītā, kisses the face of Rāvaṇa? Rāma; [he] embraces; a sprout; Tārā; [he] hates; and [he] kisses.
"What is the time? Who are my friends? What is the place? What are my expenditures and income? And who am I? What is my power?"—thus one should reflect again and again.
Who could create the entire world? Who could uproot the trees? What is the most prominent among the limbs of the body? Who attains merit in the next world?
What anger and what affection can there be toward courtesans, whose heads are struck down by actors and libertines,
and whose hips and faces are like the stones of a washerman?
What laughs at what? Who laughs at whom? What laughs at whom? The lower lip laughs at the sprout; the two feet laugh at the two swans; and the teeth laugh at the buds of the jasmine.
Who moves through the sky? What is delightful? What is to be recited? What is an ornament?
Who is to be saluted? What is Laṅkā like when shaken by heroic monkeys?
Who moves through the sky? Who makes a sound upon seeing a thief?
What is the enemy of the night-lotuses? And who is the abode of anger?
What shines in the sky?
By whom was the lord of night-stalkers slain? What sinks in the ocean?
Of what nature is the amorous gait of a young woman?
Who indeed is dear to kings? What is a king's letter? What is playful in the waters?
Who is the one who captivates Rāma’s beloved? May that middle syllable of the answer to my question be a word of blessing for you.
Who could be the Indra of the city of the departed, and who could be his servant,
if one were to take the name of Kṛṣṇa— the sole auspiciousness of the world— upon the throne of one's throat?
Who can look even face-to-face at the brilliance of a thousand suns,
when he [the moon] endures the shattering of his orb by the light of the moon?
Who provides the fragrant species of flower? Who indeed makes the sandalwood cool?
Who would pray for the sun when there is already light? In the same way, a virtuous person benefits others through his own nature.
Who is to be honored? One of virtuous conduct. Whom do they call base? One whose conduct has wavered. By what has this world been conquered? By the man who possesses truth and forbearance.
Who is worthy of worship? Who attains the state of a virtuous person?
Where do the wise abide? With whom was a terrible battle fought in the world by the illustrious Śivā?
And what do people always desire?
What do young people meditate upon in their minds? May my answer to this question—the middle syllable of the word—be your blessing.
While this descendant of Puru, the ruler of the earth and chastiser of the ill-behaved, is reigning,
who is it that practices such immodesty toward these innocent daughters of ascetics?
Who produces the pre-dawn wind? Who impels the rain-cloud?
When the month of Śrāvaṇa arrives, the world becomes a single ocean.
What wise person would desire affection from courtesans or from sand?
Or perhaps you are being released by me; such is the very nature of things.
Who, even when entreated, will give even a measure as small as a blade of grass or a husk more than what is written on the surface of the inner forehead in a garland of formidable letters?
Who is sought after by a young woman overwhelmed by passion? Where does the *puṇḍraka* mark shine? How, alas, does life pass away? Where is there a lack of respect?

By what does the lotus shine? What is the fruit of the coconut called? (The answers are: a man, on the forehead, it passes away; in a low-born person, by its fragrance; the outer shell, and the water.)
Who is Śakra? Who is the Creator? And who is that wretched Yama, that they would dare to transgress the command of kings devoted to the vow of truth?
O wise ones, what peace can there be? Why exert yourselves for the sake of pleasing those you love? Once a being has been reduced to ashes, how can there be any returning?
Who will believe the truth? Everyone will judge me;
for in this world, poverty is suspect when it lacks power.
Who possesses such enviable birth that even on the night of the month of Māgha,
this sound of his girdle— prolonged by the wintry breeze— proclaims his good fortune?
Who would be a petitioner for water?
Whom do young women desire as a husband? By what is shame restrained?
How does one behave toward a servant who is nearby? Yavanī.
"Show the language!"—thus [he said]. Regarding the subject matter, when might it be accomplished in Mahārāṣṭra through the skillful composition of eliding the initial and final syllables?
Who could perceive the external misfortune of those whose nature is profound,
unless it were revealed by a foolish child or a servant?
Who here is the self and who is the other? What is one's own and what belongs to another?
For embodied beings, there is no such thing as "self" or "other" apart from the ignorance of clinging to self and other.
He who had no such anxieties as "Who has anointed himself?", "Who is her beloved?", "On whom does she meditate?", or "Whom does she gaze upon?"— he was the one worthy of honor among courtesans.
Who could turn back the mind, which is firmly resolved upon its desired object, or water, which flows toward the low ground?

"O Flower-Armed One, you alone are the one who brings about the destruction of my meditative absorption; even if all the gods were armed with flowers, what of it?"—may that Teacher of yours, the conqueror of Māra in the ten directions, who surely reduced them here to the state of having flowers as their weapons, grant you his own weapon.
If *kakubha* and *karīra* are joined together in one place, or *kakubha* and *bilva*,
then after three cubits there is water at a distance of twenty-one human paces.
The fruit and flower of the *kakubha*, lac, *śrīvāsa* resin, and *guggulu*; the root of white *aparājitā*, along with *viḍaṅga* and mustard seeds.
Suddenly illuminating the faces of the quarters and bringing about an intense agitation for the sake of pleasure,
the moon— born from the eye of Atri— shone forth like another fire to the flower-arrowed god of love.
In every direction, the clouds have performed the highest good by spreading and emitting thunderclaps that pierce the ears and agitate the darkness;
for otherwise, how could that swan—distressed and having abandoned the small ponds—now rejoice in Lake Mānasa, adorned as it is with golden lotuses?
Having wandered from tree to tree and looked again and again, we have not seen any tree equal to this one born on Mount Malaya;
for even when scorched, cut, or rubbed against a stone surface, its accumulated sap spreads an ever-increasing, heart-stealing fragrance.
What is the limited book in the corner? What is the water?
It is the water that is the essence of poetry. What is long, if it is written on palm leaves? And what is the script here? It is the Gauḍīya script.
What is the fragrance, if it is the scent of the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa? What is great? O friend, you prattle too much; listen! By name, it is an ancient fish.
Men who are devoted to anger are born among vultures, eagles, jackals, gadflies, mosquitoes, and serpents.
The feathers of the *kaṅka* crane, swan, hare-eater (*śaśāda*), fish-eater, curlew, peacock,
vulture, and cock are auspicious among these.
Is this *kaṅkelī* tree truly insentient, since it does not offer you its flowers of its own accord?
Or rather, it is a rogue that bows down as if out of a desire to behold the expanse of your high, swelling breasts revealed by your uplifted arms.

May the Discus-Wielder protect you— he who, during his first union with the Daughter of the Ocean in that abode of the bodiless god of love, had his hands occupied with her breasts, her hair-knot, and her chin,
and thus required four additional hands to loosen the tightly bound knot of her waist-cloth.

In the union of love, the god whose banner is the dolphin (Kāma) brings to lovers the seizing of the hair as a favor, the biting with the teeth as an ornament, the smearing of collyrium upon the eyes as a non-deception, the offering of the essence of the mouth as a gratification,
the scratching with the nails as no injury, and the firm pressing as a sport.

Victorious are the amorous gestures of the fawn-eyed women during the encounter of the festival of love—gestures adorned with sighs that imitate the soft humming of bees rendered sluggish by the pressure of their lotus-bud lips as they are seized by the hair. These gestures are kissed with affection overflowing with joy and passion.

When indeed shall I drink from that face of my beloved— its half-bud-like lips turned upward by the grasping of her hair, its large eyes with pupils trembling with shame, and agitated by the pain of her lower lip being forcibly seized?
From the weight of her hair, the weight of her breasts fears; from the weight of her breasts, the weight of her hair fears;
from the weight of both hair and breasts, her hips fear—O moon-faced one, what a marvel this is!
The lunar disc, its markings clearly visible, shines like a skull-bowl belonging to Īśāna, its center blackened by the smoke from the fire of the venomous breath of serpents bound at its base.
The hair is a dwelling for lice; the face is a collection of bones bound together by skin; the breasts are lumps of flesh; even the belly is a jar for excrement and such;
the hips are a machine for discharging filth; and the pair of feet are the pillars supporting it—what is there in all this for the passionate attachment of the great?
With hair half-shorn, with hands smeared with blood, with the slopes of breasts torn by nails, with cheeks shattered by blows from stones, and with foreheads split open;
with throats distorted by the sounds of wailing—this state of the women in the inner apartments grinds the heart within.

I hope that those dwelling in the wilderness suffer no oppression from dogs or any other danger; I hope the partakers of the sacrifice do not fail to consume the oblations due to some impediment to the rites.
Or perhaps a sacrifice with the earth as its sacrificial fee is being performed within, for which reason you have arrived—is this such a transformation of the ascetic power of the Raghu lineage?
I hope that the great forest where you now dwell, surrounded by your friends, is favorable for cattle, free from disease, and abundant in water, grass, and creepers.
Would you prefer a single wise man over a thousand fools?
For a wise man can bring about great ultimate welfare in times of financial or existential crisis.
O gentle one, does your dear companion, the lightning, embrace you; or do the cātaka birds, their faces bright with manifest affection, attend upon you?
Does the eastern breeze delight you with its skillful fanning, spreading beauty in every direction while bearing the mark of the rainbow, the weapon of the Lord of the Gods?
O gentle one, I hope you have resolved to perform this service for my kinsmen; indeed, from your silence, I do not doubt your steadfastness.

For even when silent, you grant water to the *cātaka* birds when entreated; for the very act of fulfilling the desired object of those who seek it is the response given by the virtuous to their supplicants.
I hope that you do not obstruct dharma for the sake of wealth, nor wealth for the sake of dharma,
nor both of them for the sake of pleasure, greed, or desire.
O best of those who are born, O Bharata, you who know the proper time— do you pursue wealth, virtue, and pleasure, dividing them all according to their appropriate seasons?

May King Mīvara arise, spreading his fame—a moon over the ocean of the Kaccha lineage, a unique nectar-rayed luminary; a consumer of the dynasties of his enemies, noble-minded, and a connoisseur of virtues; fond of learning, devoted to policy, wise, and generous.
O lady whose moon-like face is marked by a collyrium tilaka and whose hair is wet with trickling drops of water—
whom among those who are like cotton to the fire of fresh separation must you bring back to life?
O lotus, grant full bloom and abandon your contraction; this bee is wandering about.
Even if no fruit results, he nevertheless spreads his fame with satisfaction.

May Hari, Hara, and Kamalāsana— possessing the luster of collyrium, snow, and gold, and having for their vehicles the eagle, the bull, and the swan, and dwelling upon the ocean, the mountain, and the lotus— grant you prosperity.
Just as the state of being a bracelet cannot exist apart from gold, and the state of being a wave cannot exist apart from water,
so too the world cannot exist apart from the Lord.
Their arms, adorned with beautiful ornaments of fresh pearls, bear bracelets;
and by their broad, mountain-like cheeks, they certainly maintain an inseparable union with colorful paintings.
While feeding upon the thorny Karīra, Khadira, and other shrubs and trees that have a bitter taste,
a female camel may, by the power of fate, obtain a sweet cluster of honey.
O friend, if she were to glance at me even for a moment with but a slight sidelong look, then a dense bliss would surge forth, eclipsing all other objects of sense.
What kind of embrace could there be from that lotus-eyed one, wherein her garment is torn away by her jar-like breasts rising with horripilation?
"O dear friend, in the pleasure-house in the forest, he was drawn away by my sidelong glances; even this pair of breasts turned away under the pretext of gathering flowers.
Seeing the pair of deer engaged in love-making, I laughed softly; yet even so, my beloved does not know anything at all—why is this?"
Her waist can be grasped by a single fist, yet her belly must be embraced by the arms of two men; her breasts dangle like bells as if striving to reach her hips.
Her smile has the resonance of a kettledrum, and even her face inspires fear in her husband; nevertheless, this slut humiliates and torments him.

Whose wife is she whose hips have been shouted over by hundreds of libertines, whose face has been drunk from and abandoned by travelers, and whose breasts have been crushed by thousands? Whose wife is she? Who indeed is her own?
One should contemplate the world as having the form of a human being standing in the vaiśākha posture with hands placed at the hips,
filled with substances whose nature consists of persistence, origination, and dissolution.
The wind-elephant, roaming through the groves at the slopes of the hips,
scents the fragrance of the lion of castor oil and flees.
Wicked people, making harsh sounds and bestowing impurity, revile [the virtuous] excessively like fetters for binding;
but the good, with their sweet voices, captivate the mind at every step like jeweled anklets.
Vāta is provoked by pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes; pitta by pungent, hot, salty, and sour;
and kapha reaches a state of agitation by unctuous, sweet, sour, and salty [tastes], like [the sap] of a tree.
Touched by the mother’s excessive intake of pungent, sharp, hot, salty, alkaline, sour, and other such substances, he experiences pain arising in all his limbs.

Victorious is the sun, who with his rays— though pungent yet possessing a cooling potency that soothes the fever of separation for flocks of harsh-cackling ruddy geese— purifies the mass of eyes in the world, which had been struck by the darkness of ignorance.
The groves of *damanaka* now possess pungent and sweet fragrances; their leaves are carved with decorative patterns, and their stalks are an intense, uniform white.

O mosquito of unawakened intellect, why do you buzz so harshly in the ears of the enemy of elephants? Do you not know that the entire herd of elephants, their frontal globes split by the sharp-pointed saws of his tusks, sank into the hollow of your own throat?
O you whose arrow is the fierce flame of the fire, O five-faced one, dear friend of the Giver of Wealth, O you with Mitra as your eye;
O you who have assumed all conceptual constructions, O great dancer revealed at the end of the aeon—dance forth your grace!
Although there may be a justification for including pungent flavors here because they possess a distinct essence,
