nevertheless, such a mode of presentation is not acceptable to those who know the true nature of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
There was no jeweled girdle upon your hips, no garland upon the circle of your breasts, no collyrium in your eyes, nor indeed any rouge upon your lower lip;
O beautiful one, you have been utterly plundered by your lover, who acts as a companion, in this forest of amorous play against the thief that is Love.
Though you have become a cuckoo with a harsh voice, you are nevertheless praiseworthy for being a perfect protector of the cuckoo’s offspring;
like the moon, which possesses its mark because it brings delight, or like the black musk-deer, which bears musk because it carries fragrance.
Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning are dear to those of a rajasic nature; they bestow suffering, grief, and disease.

Just as when two bitter tamarind fruits have been cooked, their sweet flavor is not perceived even though it is present within them, so too, knowledge is not attained in one whose faculties are unripened.
Whether it be harsh or sweet, speech that is relevant and captivating is pleasing to the mind; even the braying of a donkey on the left during journeys brings joy to the heart.
One who is harsh and has shallow roots is difficult to serve, as is one who is left-handed;
even some who possess a noble lineage are not supported by others.
O young girl with tremulous lotus-eyes, your breasts are firm; O girl with lovely curly hair, your eyes are yours;
O girl with beautiful locks, your hair is yours; O slender-limbed one, it was said falsely that your waist is thin.
May that Dāmodara protect you, whose folds of skin shine forth, creating the appearance of lines as if he were encircled by a very firm rope.
A virtuous person should moisten even the heart of the *kaṭhina* with their gaze;
for the moon causes even the moonstone (*candrakāntopala*) to melt with its own rays.
O hard-hearted one, abandon this anger that destroys happiness; O proud woman, Yama indeed writes down every day as it passes.
This is not fitting while youth remains, for when union is fleeting, it is better, O beautiful one, to enjoy pleasure for as long as there is quarreling.
O hard-hearted one, abandon this delusion based on false rumors; it is not right to bring suffering upon this person with the words of a slanderer.
Or rather, O charming one, is this truly what you have decided today? Having done whatever pleases you, my dear, remain in happiness.
Are those pens with hard, sharp points and likewise with sharp results actually pens, or were they fashioned by mathematicians?
Dwelling in a harsh or inaccessible place, the disclosure of hidden power,
a son in battle, and a quarrel with a courtesan— all these are to be lamented.
The lion, his magnificent mane stained with blood as it falls from the frontal globes of elephants struck by his hard claws,
feels ashamed before the battlefield along with the young deer who, terrified by his deep roar, utter cries of extreme distress as they flee.
His body is dark like the neck of a mature pigeon, with shoulders well-rounded by the hump of the *vṛṣan*;
his gaze is as steady as that of a lion at ease, and his voice is as resonant as a festive drum.
Resonant with the clattering sound produced by its impact against the joints of hardened bones, its momentum momentarily checked by the severing of tough tendons, let this sword—
now free from fear as it sports among masses of flesh as if in mud— immediately scatter your body limb by limb.

Like a grain of ash from the ancient fire that consumed the cities, the crest-jewel of the serpent upon the matted locks of Śiva—whose thick radiance dispels the onset of night—is victorious; it shines like a star brought down by the flood of the celestial river.
You carefully guard grains, chaff, husks, and charcoal,
yet you do not notice the heap of jewels stolen by mice from your treasury.
But for a splintered thorn, a loose tooth,
and a corrupt minister, it is easier to uproot them by their very roots.
Just as people avoid thorns, a pit, and fire,
so do people avoid a man who performs cruel deeds.
Just as a hedge of thorns serves to protect a fruit-bearing tree for the sake of obtaining its fruit,
so too does association with the wicked serve as an obstacle to the company of the virtuous.

O moon among men, this young woman, her body bristling with horripilation and her eyes closing like buds out of modesty, longs for the touch of your hand, just as a night-lily longs for the moonlight.
Even those who undergo some transformation when touched by a mere thorn eat the flesh of an animal cut down by a weapon.
Even when pierced by a mere thorn, great pain arises;
how much more so for one being slain by terrifying weapons such as discuses and swords?
With his feet as if torn by thorns from the western mountain’s lotus-covered slopes,
the friend of the day-lotuses ascended its peak to reach the shore of the ocean.
A thorn and a fragment of wood cause pain in the throat;
a scorpion that has fallen into the condiments pierces the palate.
If there is an exchange between thorny and non-thorny plants, then after digging three men’s depth with three cubits of water, there will be treasure at a depth of three parts.
The *anyokti* on the *kaṇṭārikā* plant has been illustrated; the *anyokti* on the *dhattūra* tree and the sayings regarding grasses are now to be attended to.
O Lord, even the Kālakūṭa poison resting upon the hollow of Your throat is for me a great nectar;
yet even the nectar obtained from elsewhere does not please me if it does not exist as a manifestation of Your body.
Whose self would not ever approach even with life-breaths reaching the throat—
the fool, the despondent, the arrogant, and likewise the ungrateful?
Even when angry, she does not readily embrace her husband despite his efforts;
like a row of bangles, she clings only to his faults.
Like one intoxicated, like one distracted, like one overjoyed, and like one afflicted,
a woman who has reached the fullness of youth cannot be easily attended to.
Bestowing both pleasure and pain, women established in their third stage, youth,
become as difficult to fathom as the ways of saṃsāra itself.
When the embrace around her neck had somehow been loosened, he who considered death itself to be the means to happiness departed;
as he went, his creeper-like arms were released by her bracelets, as if they could no longer hold him back by force.

May Śiva protect you at the conclusion of the aeon, as he withdraws even the forty-nine winds under the guise of the shadow of his throat, the Mandākinī river under the guise of his crest-jewel, the fire of the dissolution under the pretext of his upward-facing eye,
and the serpent-ornaments under the pretext of his playful drinking.

How can that Rāvaṇa be described— he whose smiling face, desiring to kindle the sacrificial fire, caused a contraction of his eyebrows at the serpent on the throat of Śitikaṇṭha (Śiva) so as to provoke its hissing, thereby shattering the radiance of the fire with the mass of blood gushing from the severed neck?
Just as a razor, though made of gold, is certainly not beneficial when it severs the throat,
so too should one who causes harm be abandoned by all, even if they are a kinsman.
Contracting the throat, one should firmly fix [the breath] at the heart by means of will;
this is the Jālandhara Bandha, which prevents the draining of the nectar.

May Dhūrjaṭi bestow happiness upon you— he who bears upon his neck the splendor of the Kālakūṭa poison, its formidable hue resembling a garland of lovely clusters of blue water-lilies, appearing as if soiled by the smoke rising from incense consumed as an offering.
Having attained an embrace of her neck,
this body of mine— fallen away— is comforted as if by a friend who shares the same condition.
With soft arms entwined around his neck and the soles of their feet placed upon his toes,
the beloveds sought from him, as he rose from bed, that kiss which marks the end of the night's conclusion.
The golden throat of that lotus-eyed woman is like some extraordinary conch shell; it displays the water-offering for the King of Love, whose essence is the water of loveliness.
There, three lines manifest his victory over the three worlds—so why would the Creator’s arrangement of the three folds on her waist not be a mere redundancy?
Knowledge that resides in one's throat should always be made manifest by the wise;
that knowledge which remains with the teacher or in a book deceives the fool.
Between her neck, which was made beautiful by her breasts, and her necklace of pearls,
which was perfectly round, there arose a mutual relationship of ornament and the object to be adorned, as each enhanced the beauty of the other.
Just as the wearing of pearl ornaments bestowed beauty upon her neck,
so too did the wearing of pearl ornaments enhance her neck, which was already naturally beautiful.
The vital breaths emerge from the throat together with the syllables of the request;
they enter back through the ear of the donor along with the syllables "I give."
He drinks the blood from the throats of the virtuous, yet he does not consume liquor or meat; he steals the property of Viṣṇu, yet he observes the fast on the twelfth lunar day;
having heard the Sāṃkhya philosophy, he seizes the livelihood of cows and Brahmins—of whom is this wicked hypocrite, the friend of the Kali age, a true ally? He is merely a government official.

O King, even on the desert slopes, the sequence of amorous play among the fair-browed wives of your enemies proceeds as follows: there is the humming within their throats from the exhaustion caused by the sun’s rays; the contraction of the corners of their eyes due to the distress of the dust; the hissing sounds produced by wounds from the tips of sharp *kuśa* grass; and the surging waves of sighs born of fear of the forest-dwellers.

May the Bull, the personified Dharma, protect you—he whose roar from the bells adorning his neck fills the hollow of the universe with a ghaṇa-ghaṇa resonance; whose back is as beautiful and firm as that of the bull Kaṇṭhekāla; who, with his white hump, wipes away the peaks of Mount Kailāsa; and who, standing immovable, shall strip away the thicket of the densest darkness.

May that Kṛṣṇa protect us— he who, as if out of jealousy at the thought, "Who is this that seeks to obtain before my beloveds the auspicious embrace of their necks, the festival of enjoying the fullness of their firm breasts, and the fortune of union with their hips," forcibly took away the collection of silken garments from the Gopīs on the banks of the Yamunā himself.

As the attendants helped the wives of the king’s harem dismount from their horses—their soft creeper-like arms clinging to their necks—they clearly received embraces; yet, due to their purity, they did not kiss the women's cheeks.
Though it clung to her neck, gripped the slope of her hips by the weight of her high breasts, encircled her pair of thighs, and even reached the ramparts of her buttocks,
the moon-faced woman— though momentarily overwhelmed by shame— quickly cast off that golden garment as soon as she realized it was loose-knit and unable to withstand firm pressure.
"O beloved, what is this anklet on your neck? This is an ornament for the foot;
that was a bracelet!"—not understanding such words spoken by the deer-eyed woman, he felt a surge of longing even though he knew the truth.
Dragging a golden chain that remains severed around his neck, having leaped through the gates with a circle of tinkling bells jingling from his playfully moving feet,
causing alarm to the women and followed by horse-grooms in a state of agitation— this monkey, having escaped, enters the king’s palace from the stable.
Hoarseness in the throat, perspiration on the face, discoloration, and trembling—
these very signs that belong to one who is dying are also present in one who is begging.

The *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) mark on the throat should be known as one that always grants desired objects; the *āvarta* (whorl) on the spinal column is remembered as the auspicious one called *sūrya* (the sun).

O merciless one, in her throat is life, in her face your virtues, in her hands her cheeks and breasts, in her mind the fever of separation from you, and from her eyes a flow of tears that never ceases. Everything she possesses now has a support; alas, in this life of hers, what indeed is left for her circle of friends to hold onto? They are utterly without support.
Intoxication from *kodrava* grain resides in the throat; intoxication from betel resides in the heart;
but the intoxication of wealth pervades every limb, even extending to one's sons and wife.
With a necklace of pearls around her neck, pure camphor powder upon the slope of her breasts, thick sandalwood paste on her limbs, and lotus-stalk bracelets encircling her wrists—
this slender woman, wearing two bright silken garments at night, shines like the presiding deity of the moon fallen from the sky as it ascends its zenith.
Having tied a rope around the neck of a man who has died, and taking that rope,
she ties a fragment of it around her own neck and removes the garland from her cheek.
Because the clever Sarasvatī dwells in her throat and plays the lute (*vipañcī*),
that very sound, becoming speech in the mouth of this deer-eyed woman, turns into the essence of nectar for the ear of the listener.
Victorious is that Caṇḍī, at whose feet Candraśikha fell— though he was worthy of her neck— he was cast away by a mere "huṃ" sound, like an arrow of the God of Love.
If that dog scratches its face with its right paw at that time,
then there will be abundant food and edibles for a long time, along with kings and their retinues.
The trees on the banks of the Godāvarī worship her with their own flowers, which have fallen as their stalks loosened by the heat and were shaken by the rubbing of the temples of itching elephants;
meanwhile, the birds scratching in the shade have stripped away the insects' skins from their beaks, and flocks of weary, crowing yellow cocks dwell in their nests upon the trees.
Indeed, when scratching his forehead with his right paw,
Bhaṣaṇa bestows upon him the binding of the excellent turban at the royal consecration, which humbles the circle of rival kings through its splendor.
O Destroyer of Cities, which is more harsh between the request for a mouthful of *hālāhala* poison and your words?
Your single tongue alone is the knower of taste that discerns the relative intensity of the flavor of both.
How many deer do not roam again and again, slaying them on every peak and in every forest?
Yet, as a cause for the diversion of people's minds, a certain unique fragrance manifests in some rare places.
How many deer, arrogant with rut, do not roam from peak to peak and forest to forest? Yet, those excellent deer are rare indeed, for it is their very rut that intoxicates the lords of the earth.
O lotus, how many creepers have not been visited by me, who am fond of wandering bees? Yet, that very same sweet honey which belongs to you is the only one I have fully drunk.
In spring, how many creepers or trees did not become adorned with limbs beautified by fragrant flowers?
Nevertheless, for the delight of young people, it was the mango tree alone that truly shone, laden with the weight of fresh buds.

Some are excessively haughty and full of envy; some are characterized by praising their own words; alas, others have bellies as empty as they are of learning! Therefore, against whom shall my efforts be directed here now?
For several days, trees were found with only their trunks remaining, their old and withered leaves having fallen away entirely;
though their bark was stripped of its contemptible sprouts, they could not even be distinguished by name.
For some days she spent them in your house, longing for union with you; for some days in the forest upon a bed of lotuses, by her voice bringing joy to the female cuckoo.
Neither in the forest nor in the palace does she find delight—she who has surpassed gorocana in her exquisite form;
O abode of compassion, what can be done by her whose lotus eyes are reddened with longing?
"My dear, how could your braid not be unapproachable by its own qualities— because of its excessive blackness from contact with flowers, and because of its possession of many curls?"
How many people are there not on the surface of the earth? Yet my mind remains distressed by separation from them.
How many moons and stars are there not? Yet the lotus plant becomes withered without the sun.

O Sandalwood tree, how many trees on earth are not abodes of fragrant flowers, honey, and excellent fruit? And yet, there are no trees whatsoever that so perfume other trees as you do; such is your supreme fame.

O Supporter of the Earth, how many objects have not been scrutinized by you, or how many rulers of the earth have not been served? Having ascertained your virtues, I have considered my own teacher to be insignificant.
In youth, which lasts but a few days and brings intoxication,
the wicked commit such offenses that their very birth becomes in vain.
O river, though your flood may rise very high and last for only a few days,
the sin of felling the trees on your banks will endure for a long time.
"The Golden Mountain (Meru) shall go to ruin within a few days, its day having come to an end"— thinking thus,
the female ruddy goose rejoices while King Vīrarudradeva abounds in liberality.
In this world, which is agitated by birth, old age, and death and lasts but a few moments,
the spreading fame of poets shines forth as a kinsman for ten million aeons.

Formerly, I was a ruler of only a few towns, difficult to satisfy even at the cost of my body, and I followed delusion by giving away only a little; but now, having attained the Lord of the Three Worlds—who is to be worshipped with wisdom and who bestows his own station—alas, that former expenditure of days pains me.

With a few mango blossoms lovely with their fragrance, the *sinduvāra* flowers slightly opened and their frost thinned, the dewy season arrived— the sole kinsman of the God of Love— foretelling the end of winter and the onset of the fragrant spring.
In spring, how many trees are there everywhere that are budding but not yet in flower? Yet, in the conquest of the world by the Flower-Arrowed One, the mango tree alone is his true ally.

To how many has service not been rendered, or by whom have they not been praised with the wealth of speech? Yet, there was no wise man to whom one who delighted in virtue did not grant even a blade of grass.
But here, this one—like an unseasonal rain-cloud—has utterly extinguished the mass of the flames of suffering for the learned with torrents of golden water.
How many trees are there that do not bear pride? Yet you alone, O mango tree, possess the most excellent fame;
for the bee is the cause here by which it takes the fresh nectar with intense devotion.

How many creepers are there in the forest that are indeed laden with clusters of flowers and covered in new shoots— creepers entwined with the fragrance of *campaka*, sandalwood, *nīpa* groves, and fresh lotus ponds?
O Mālatī, though the bee wandered for a very long time among the flowers, no other was ever encountered by him such that she was held in his heart during the act of drinking honey as you have been.
How many graceful clove creepers, newly sprouted, are there upon the surface of the earth?
How many venerable trees, laden with sweet fragrances, dwell on Mount Malaya?
O Mother of the three worlds, how many eyes, how many skulls, how many skins of leopards and elephants, how many crows, how many serpents, and how many fragments of the moon are there?
And what more—how many are you yourself, since you take up each individual being as they emerge from within the belly of the flood of your waters?
How many horses? How many milch-cows? How many elephants? How many wondrous trees? How many beautiful women who have borne children? How many priceless great jewels?
When the ocean was intent on giving away everything when a certain maiden was born, all that was expended; at the time of the marriage, only the name "marriage" remained.
After a long time, I have somehow, as it were, plunged into the profound and smooth-flowing stream of Kālidāsa’s eloquence.
Somehow, the wholesome instruction instilled in the heart during the day is forgotten at night by the king, as if by a donkey.
When her anger has somehow dissolved like a summer day and her favor has returned, followed by a gradual nightfall,
the moon-like face of the proud woman— dispelling the mass of darkness that was separation with the onset of the moonlight of her smile— shines forth for the man of merit during the act of love.
How can those who have abandoned virtuous conduct sleep peacefully at night,
when their rebirths in the hells are separated from them only by death?
How is it that such a state, which destroys women, is not able to take hold of this woman here, since your hope for her recovery has been frustrated?
Why does the mind not delight in the Dharma, which bestows manifold happiness?
For living beings who fear suffering are, for the most part, possessed of false views.
How was the Sun, such a treasury of splendors, not ashamed to stretch out his feet upon reaching this mere fragment of the cosmic egg?
Why indeed are the Supreme Lords not served with effort—
those who, when satisfied, fulfill one's heart's desires in no time at all?

How is it that you have cast off that hand with its beautiful, tender fingers and plunged into the water? Does one fail to perceive the quality known as insentience? Why was my beloved abandoned by me alone?
How indeed could sons kill their father in any calamity,
or a brother kill his brother, O Saumitri, when one’s own life is at stake?
How could one like me forbid a righteous performance,
or how could he authorize an act whose sole essence is recklessness?

O lotus-eyed one, how indeed did you come to this house while the moon’s rays were shrouded by thick clouds— without heeding the fresh lightning of the rain, O slender-limbed one, appearing as radiant as if possessed of supernatural power?

And how does this slender girl, whose creeper-like limbs are naturally so delicate, endure the exhaustion of passionate lovemaking? Even the scorching sun brings only pleasure to the lotus; when love is intense, what indeed cannot young women endure?
How could he— affectionate toward his beloved wife and compassionate toward her, devoted to secret intimacies and charming conversations,
bound by love for his friends, and his heart attached to the lisping syllables of his children— [be able to leave]?
She remembered her sons, her daughters, her brothers, her sisters, and her wretched parents;
she remembered her charming homes with their abundant furnishings, her ancestral livelihoods, and her flocks of cattle and servants.
O Lord, how can a man attain dharma, artha, or even kāma without a wife? For all three of these are established in her.
In the same way, in the accomplishment of dharma and the other goals, a wife is not capable without her husband; this triad of aims is dependent upon the state of matrimony.
When her beloved whispered, "How is it that this arrow, making a sound as it strikes my chest with its feathers, has been placed there?",
his beloved turned back and, saying "What? What?", released him in agitation and anger.
O charming one, how are your beloved’s eyes? How are they curved? How do they lead to the people's affection, and how do they bring about the people's ruin?
How should a person strive, since their very nature is divided? It is taught that there is a distinction between nectar and poison produced from the same place.
How could a king established in righteousness touch another's wife?
O one of great power, the wives of kings must be protected with special care.
How may I gaze upon this youth, who rises like the friend of the night-lotuses [the moon]?
For even the partial glance of my husband’s sister would bring reproach, just as the fourth day of the bright fortnight does for the moon.

Why do you teach us this path that leads toward worldly desires? Be gracious and instruct your own disciple, Muralī, who has the face of a most wicked person. Alas, alas! O Best of the Yadus, this bold girl transgresses all bounds and carries her heart toward another man; why does she not call out to us?
How is a king to be enlightened? Who is the beloved of Sugrīva?
What do the destitute desire? And what do the wise do?
How can that sun, which is devoid of teeth and has already left the zodiac sign of Pisces, be called "wise" by the learned when it is intent upon devouring Aries?
For the virtuous fulfill one's hopes even without being asked;
indeed, the sun shines at every house even without being requested to do so.

How will that lord of men behold him whom he has never before counted; how will he, whose word is authoritative, hear the words of one who is no man? How will he, when restrained, honored, or even insulted, maintain his indignation toward one who is beyond his reach and barren of power?
Alas, how futile is that wretchedness you have cultivated through the anxiety of livelihood—thinking, "How will it be today? How will it be tomorrow?"—for it only brings about the end of one's life.
When her beloved had somehow regained his composure after a faltering reply, she—emaciated by separation—feigned that he had not heard her words;
then, fearing that her intolerant friend might overhear, she turned her eyes with agitation toward the empty room and sighed again.
Even the Supreme Lord himself would not be capable of fully describing the multitude of glories of your Vṛndāvana forest.
Moreover, it was so greedy for the taste of even its blades of grass and fruits that it took on the state of a calf toward the very lords who consume nectar.
For some reason, that father of mine—pained and fearful—did not prevent my left hand from being seized by the son of Drupada today;
yet, as you pride yourself on the strength of your arms, this foot of his is now placed upon your head: restrain him!
In her dream, somehow familiar with the seal of his embrace,
she touches her beloved at the edge of the bed at dawn while closing her eyes.

"O friend, somehow when I said, 'Go,' out of playful anger, that hard-hearted man left the bed and went away by force. My heart still yearns for him—him who has violently destroyed our love, who is devoid of compassion, and shameless; what can I do?
Indeed, through the union of a fertile field and excellent seed, they bear fruit for the sake of benefiting the world and not for their own sustenance;
for in this world, both the virtuous and the fine rice plants, through the abundance of their harvest, truly assume a state of profound humility.
O Lord of Beasts, if you have merely been inhabited by mean mice who have somehow found a hole within you, why do you harbor such despondency regarding your own prowess?
How could the Śrutis or even the Smṛtis negate an object,
when not even a single word among them moves from its literal meaning?
O King, how can you feel pride because you have seized the fortune of your enemies whose heads were severed by the edge of your sharpened sword?
Surely, even though their lives were taken, did they not carry away your beloved fame to the heavens with their departing limbs?

How can he, whose sense of discrimination is destroyed and whose passion for love is slain, not attain bodilessness— that man who feels no compassion for his wives when they are as tender as plantain leaves while he strikes them?
How is it that this Madana, the dolphin-bannered god who stands upon the foundation of discernment, is not to be revered?
For he strikes with arrows born of flowers the deer-eyed woman whose body is as graceful as a plantain tree.
How is it that in this forest there is not even a single such noble tree, lofty and rich with flowering creepers and fruit?
By the decree of a cursed fate that ordains misery for the world, only the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees flourish here.
"How indeed can you have such an inclination, having been rejected by the sage along with the seasons?
Thus did the summer season, causing the full blossoming of jasmine flowers, seem to smile at the spring.
How does one born as a human enter here into this assembly frequented by the gods,
so that he may drink to his heart's content the refreshing nectar of well-spoken words?
How does a phenomenon arise? How does a phenomenon increase? How is a phenomenon established? And how does a phenomenon perish?
Dharma arises through truth; it increases through compassion and generosity;
it is established through patience; it is destroyed by anger and greed.
How is it that above there shines the plumage of a peacock, beneath it the crescent of the eighth-day moon;
below that, a pair of restless blue lotuses; beneath those, a *tilaka* flower; and from that, a sprout?
"How is it, O beautiful one, that this pair of breasts has fallen? Look down, O fool; even mountains fall when they are undermined."
Tell me, how can hope for my life arise? The winds, vomited by the serpents of Mount Malaya, blow like the messengers of Death.
And indeed, this humming bee at the crest of the lovely mango tree swallows up my very consciousness.

Tell me, dear friend, why does this lord of the Yadus gather *campaka* flowers for the sake of binding them upon his breasts? That trembling in his palm is nothing other than my memory, which has become my rival.
"Tell me, is there any place seen or heard of where this sun never sets? Thus the wretched female cakravāka bird constantly questions the flocks of birds, fearing separation by night.
"Tell me, what is this famous by its species? For how many cowries can it be obtained? Or rather, what is its use?
Thus, at every step, being belittled by a crowd of villagers, alas, the merchant holds the jewel in the palm of his hand and desponds.
O fair-faced one, as if speaking, your eyes have reached the roots of your ears; having turned away from your breasts, look at the ground.
If your pair of lotus-feet should somehow stumble, your exceedingly slender waist might break—but for us, there would be no fault.

"Tell me, how was she given away by Menā? Alas, alas! The daughter of the mountain has been given to an aged Kāpālika!"—may the illustrious Maheśa protect you, who, while this circle of matrons was speaking thus, assumed the guise of a bridegroom for the sake of a mere fragment of his yogic power.
"Tell me, O clever one, where was he seen, how, for how long, what was written by him, what did he say, and when will he come here?"—
thus, conversations about the beloved, though expanded by the outburst of manifold affection, do not come to an end even when the matter is slight.
"I am gazing at you with unblinking eyes; how is it that this has come about merely by beholding your form?
O lady with curly hair, for those who drink the nectar of your lips, the attainment of sexual union is only fitting."
O friend, through stories of various lands and by some means over a long time, my beloved has finally arrived; yet, O friend, half the night has already passed.
Then, just as I became feigning anger out of playful affection, this eastern direction turned crimson like a rival wife who has become truly enraged.
Those who have found aesthetic delight in the stories of poets do not take pleasure in other tales;
musk-deer, whose affection lies with the granthiparṇa flower, do not graze upon common grass.
Having been told the limit of her husband’s lifespan, she counts the days moment by moment;
alas, she survives only by erasing a few of those lines with a flood of tears for her beloved.
I consider a bad son better than a good son who is a source of grief;
a mortal should become weary of the household, for households are a multitude of afflictions.
The pith of the *kadamba* tree wards off the fall of lightning;
there is no fear of a lightning strike when the name of the King of the Gods is invoked.
For even when one whose conduct is firm is treated with contempt, the quality of his fortitude cannot be wiped away;
for even when fire is turned downward, its flames never go below.
One should never beg from these— miserly, abusive, unlearned, born of low stock, disrespectful, arrogant, spitting, hostile, and ungrateful— even when one is deeply distressed.
Wealth acquired by a miser may become the enjoyment of those who are fortunate;
the teeth chew with great difficulty, while the tongue swallows with ease.

Neither the plantain tree, nor the plantain tree; neither the young elephant, nor the young elephant; nor even the trunk of the king of elephants—none of these in the three worlds can bear comparison with this pair of thighs of the fawn-eyed woman.
Like the root of a plantain tree, the Dharma does not grow when it is exposed;
however, when covered, it produces beautiful fruit, like the base of a jackfruit tree.

He who perceives the exceedingly beautiful form of those resembling plantain trees and young elephants has been led by skillful means to firm yoga through the state of being an object for the equipment of the heart.
With her thighs as beautiful as the trunk of a plantain tree and her broad hips encircled by a great girdle of many strings, the young bride appeared like the female elephant of the god of love.
How indeed can the plantain tree attain a resemblance to her shanks?
For coolness is innate to it, whereas there [in her shanks] is conformity with the seasons.
Fire situated in the midst of a grove of plantain trees has its power diminished; what can a virtuous person do when placed among people who lack discernment?
In this fourfold collection of living beings— both stationary and moving— all of which are as insubstantial as the core of a plantain tree and as flickering as a mirage.
When, reclining on a bed of flowers mingled with fragrances in the chamber of my beloved, bearing the pair of my beloved’s breasts upon my chest,
and crying out repeatedly, "O dear one, O charming one, O you with crooked eyes and moon-like face, be gracious!"— then shall I pass my days as if they were but a single moment.

O All-pervading Lord, beyond illusion, primordial, dense with supreme bliss—having suddenly cast aside all worldly exertion and remembering that eternal light which is peaceful and beyond the reach of heart and speech, I shall spend my days as if they were a mere moment, crying out: "Be gracious!"
When, prostrating before Gaṇapati—whose pure and sweet form is like a lotus, and who is beautiful with vermilion flowing from his temples as he rubs them—calling out, "O elephant-faced one!
O son of the illustrious Śambhu! O handsome-faced one! O large-bellied Lord! Be gracious!"—I shall pass my days as if they were a mere moment.
Sometimes even something small is employed for a great task;
why, for the sake of security, would one not disregard long grass and the like in favor of dūrvā grass?
Sometimes armor may be pierced by an iron arrow or a shaft, even after being struck for a hundred years; yet the blessing of a Brahmin is never pierced.

Once, having obtained a small amount of wealth with great difficulty through the service of a lowly man, I buried it in the ground for fear of thieves. Then, while that wealth was there, a rat made a hole in my dwelling and carried it off; when one's past karma is adverse, even wealth that has been acquired does not remain.

May the Lord of the World, my Master, come within the range of my vision—He who sometimes delights in the music of the forests on the banks of the Yamunā; He who is like a bee tasting the lotus-faces of the joyful cowherd women; and whose feet are worshipped by Lakṣmī, Śambhu, Brahmā, Indra, and Gaṇeśa.
Once, in a forest glade, Pāñcālī was addressed many times by Bhīma: "O slender-limbed one, you are weary; sit here for a moment.
Having slowly reached a tree on the bank that offered cool shade, the virtuous lady, filled with joy, embraced her father-in-law before her husband out of desire.
Sometimes a child, whose mind has not yet matured, attains excellence;
elsewhere, even trees with pale leaves are seen blooming beautifully.
Even if, at some time, an undesirable action were to become a means for achieving a desired end,
that which is undesirable cannot, by virtue of being an effect, be an instigator toward an action that is not to be performed.
Sometimes she ascends the lofty palace, and sometimes she returns again to the surface of the earth;
sometimes, placing her face at the lattice window, the newlywed bride gazes at her beloved with bashfulness.

O Blessed One, when shall I become joyful, casting off fear through the restraint of the senses that causes blindness, while following the daily rites on the bank of the Narmadā— where the slopes are curved with spreading young *urvā* grass— in the company of discourses told by Manu and others?
When shall I see Nanda’s son,
Nīpamālaka— the protector of all beings, whose forehead is adorned with a shimmering *tilaka* mark?
O young girl, when shall I become a lover like a bee upon the lotus of your face, which has lower lips for its petals and is adorned with teeth for its filaments?

"O when shall I wash away from the world this firmly rooted rumor of my approaching a maiden?"— as if thinking thus, the sun, having increased its heat, ascended to the zenith as if for the sake of purification.
When, indeed, shall I lift up her face, with its lovely bimba-like lips like a lotus, and drink from it as a sick man drinks an elixir?
Realizing that her beloved was unable to say, "When will our meeting take place? in the midst of the crowd, the frail woman closed her play-lotus.
A wise person should never rely upon one who is merciless yet speaks sweetly,
or one who is hypocritical and intolerant, just as one would avoid poison mixed with molasses.
One should never be severe in punishment nor intent on harsh speech;
for even a wife and a son become distressed by bitter words and excessive punishment.
Even animals come under one's control through gifts and gentle speech.
A courtesan may never be a seeker of virtue, nor indeed a seeker of beauty, nor a seeker of welfare;
she is not even a seeker of knowledge—if you do not believe this, listen to the story of Kayavannaka.

When, in this field of merit, shall I pass my days as if they were a mere moment, holding a rosary of rudrākṣa beads in my hand and dwelling within my tranquil heart upon the auspicious state of Śiva—the state of all-auspiciousness—while crying out:
"O Maheśa! O Śrīkaṇṭha! O Smarahara! O Hara! O Tryambaka! O Śiva! Be gracious!"?
Worshipping in my heart Viṣvaksena, who is praised by the hosts of gods headed by Brahmā, Īśāna, and Indra, and who has conquered the armies of the demons;
crying out, "O Viṣṇu! O Conqueror! O You whose chariot is Garuḍa! O Supporter of the Universe! O Hari! Be gracious!"—I shall pass my days as if they were but a moment.

O Destroyer of Naraka, when shall I, with my mind withdrawn from all external objects, become absorbed in the joy of meditation alone, having settled myself in some bower in the place of darkness, where my delight is spread by the surface of the Ganges— whose tossing garlands of waves serve as a boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence?
When will my body remain, with all sensory pleasures ceased, sustained by alms-food and trembling with water from the Gaṅgā held in my hands?
When will the forest birds, their minds deceived by the delusion that I am a tree trunk, perch upon my shoulders because of the stability of my body through the practice of Brahman?
O fair-limbed one, when has your face ever been the object of my anger for even a moment without cause?
Tell me, how will the night appear when the orb of the moon is clouded by an eclipse out of season?

When, dwelling in Vārāṇasī on the bank of the river of the immortals, wearing a loincloth and placing my joined palms upon my head, shall I spend my days as if they were a mere moment, crying out: "O Lord of Gaurī, O Śambhu, destroyer of Tripura, O Three-eyed One, be gracious!"?

Or when, at Sāketa, on the sandy banks of the pure Sarayū, I shall spend my days as if they were a mere moment, crying out, "O Rāma! O Lord! O Beloved of Janaka’s Daughter! O All-pervading One, be gracious! as I behold Śrī Rāma wandering there accompanied by the daughter of Janaka and Lakṣmaṇa.

When, in the forest of Vṛndāvana, shall we fortunate ones attain satisfaction by beholding with our own eyes the son of Nanda— who resembles a fresh cloud and is surrounded on all sides by cowherd girls as lovely as lightning— our steps faltering from the overflow of love and our bodies trembling?

When, in the forest of Vṛndāvana— blessed by the union with the daughter of the Sun— I shall wander again and again, loudly chanting the surging waves of the life-story of the Lord of Gokula, I, filled with longing, will provide a dense irrigation for the trees with the streams of tears from my eyes.

When, in the forest of Vṛndāvana, upon the pure sandy banks of the Yamunā, I shall pass my days as if they were a mere moment, crying out, "O Kṛṣṇa, my Lord! O All-pervading One who plays the sweet flute! Be gracious! while Govinda wanders there accompanied by Haladhara, Sudāmā, and the others.
When, lying at Maṇikarṇikā, shall I whisper the syllable of the Moon-crested Lord into my ear;
and having attained the seal that removes the seal of delusion, shall I no longer behold the world of conceptual proliferation?

O Lord of Planets, O Śrī Bhānu, O Mihira, O Taraṇi, O Sūrya, O Savitṛ: when shall I pass my days as if in a mere moment, crying out, "Be gracious!"; perceiving that indescribable Vedic splendor which spreads forth like a blooming forest of glorious lotuses?
When shall I release myself, bound within the net of saṃsāra by the ropes of the three qualities, using the probe of devotion to Śiva?

When shall I spend my days as if they were but a single moment, meditating correctly upon that indescribable consort of the Enemy of the Cities, whose conduct is incomparable and who is adorned with variegated ornaments shimmering with clusters of jewels; crying out, "O Śivā! O Durgā! O Kātyāyanī! O Mother, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, be gracious!"?

When indeed is a fool afraid of words? When is a rogue unskilled in any deceptions? For when has any young woman ever been seen by a blind man? Who, then, would feel shame regarding desires in this world?
O descendant of Raghu, when indeed shall I be reunited with the high-souled Bharata,
with the heroic Śatrughna, and with you?

O slender one, your body is golden and fragrant, and O friend, even your lip is sweet like a jewel; yet it becomes a shackle for happiness. The majesty of the Creator who fashioned you is indeed boundless.

Today at dawn, the women stand within their homes like personified Goddesses of Fortune, with faces like golden lotuses— freshly washed by water, with eyes reddish at the corners and resting against the temples, and with locks of hair clinging to their shoulders.
With faces as lovely as golden lotuses and pale cheeks, with breasts moistened by sandalwood paste and adorned with strings of pearls resting upon them, noble women—
bowed by the weight of their breasts— seek to entice the tranquil lords of sages with glances full of passion-born coquetry.
There, the row of golden jars, loosened at midday by the kisses of the sun and the blows of his excessively harsh rays, melts;
yet, sprinkled with drops from the celestial river brought by the fluttering banners of the wind, it regains its firmness.
To him who speaks while adorned with golden earrings, the enemy of Śaka gave ten regions,
including Magadha, Kekaya, Kerala, and Kośala, as well as a hundred elephants whose eyes were languid with rut.
Who possesses such good fortune that upon his beautiful chest there first appears what resembles a golden betel nut, then a lotus bud, and which gradually becomes like a water-pot?
The golden parasol of the Mother produces great wonder,
as it emerges from the head right into the midst of the eyes.
Seeing Rāma united with his beloved, who was as lovely as molten gold,
the young *cātaka* birds in the forest danced, mistaking him for a cloud accompanied by lightning.
Beautiful with a pair of thighs clad in garments as pale as molten gold,
his knees were matted by the spreading lines of radiance from his rising jeweled anklets.

May Rāmacandra, whose body is embraced by Sītā who shines like gold upon a touchstone, and who is beautiful with a complexion dark as a garland of fresh blue water-lilies— like a fresh mass of clouds adorned with lightning— quench my fever from every side.

Victorious is Hari, who, mistaking the reflection of his own dark splendor— shining like a fresh rain cloud— upon the surface of Rādhā’s breast, which is as clear as gold on a touchstone, for the edge of her black garment, repeatedly lifts it up, only to be laughed at by his beloved as she bows her head in shame.

The *asana* trees achieved their purpose not in vain, for with their petals as tawny as broken pieces of gold, beautiful with pollen and reddish filaments, they dispelled the anger of proud women who had been slighted by their lovers.
If a gem fit for a collection of golden ornaments is set in tin, it neither cries out nor fails to shine; rather, the blame falls upon the one who joined them.
Having cast aside the golden deer, he entered his own hut; yet, he did not see his young wife anywhere among the women or elsewhere.
Nevertheless, that hero of the Raghus would not enter the interior of the leaf-hut, being exceedingly afraid lest the thread of hope in his heart be severed.
Buffalo butter, processed until smooth like liquid gold and mixed with the root of *hayagandhā* that has been kept overnight,
should be placed here within a golden fruit from which the seed has been removed; it should first be rubbed thoroughly with cow dung and subsequently smeared with this [mixture].
Indeed, there occurs a penis resembling that of a horse, which is firm and beloved by women.
The five parts of gold, camphor, and the pollen of the *ketakī* flower,
when combined with one's own semen and consumed by a woman, bring her under control.
Having killed the golden deer, Rāma returned to his own hermitage without seeing the daughter of Janaka, who was dearer to him than life itself;
with eyes closed by a steady flood of tears, he did not enter the hut for fear that even the final thread of hope might be severed.

O you who possess such slenderness, why indeed do you offer worship with saffron paste to your breasts— which steal the splendor of the Golden Mountain— when that very act is a bond for your waist that is already subject to emaciation?
Where indeed there is the residence of beautiful women whose breasts surpass the golden mountain,
how is it that the logicians, who claim that the mind is as subtle as an atom, do not feel shame even today?
Thick like the little finger and bent at its forepart—
this shall serve as tooth-cleaning wood in the absence of one, even on a forbidden day;
by twelve mouthfuls of water, purification of the mouth will be achieved.
He conducts himself with impartiality toward all his younger brothers,
as well as toward those who share in the same enjoyments and livelihoods, just as he does toward his own sons.

At that time, the ornaments of the young women shone forth: collyrium for their eyes through the loveliness of their pupils, sandalwood paste for their hearts through the radiance of their smiles, and fresh blue lotuses for their ears through the luster of their side-long glances.
Like the pupil of the eye, like the fragrance of a flower,
right view is said to be the essence of all religious activities.
O evil-minded one, you carry a patched garment that even donkeys find difficult to bear;
what burden will these topknot and sacred thread become for you?
O Pārtha, those foolish men who eat bulbous roots and roots on the day of the Sun-god, the consumer of births, surely go to hell.

We pay homage to the feet of the rogue of the cowherds, whose lotus-like faces are supported by gentle smiles, and who are longed for by the blue-lotus-eyed women who are themselves prisoners to his side-glances itching with passion.
O Kandarpakandalī, mow down the sprout of my anger with your playful glance; may I become a guest seeking refuge at your feet.
Look, be gracious! The orb of the moon, pale as a lavalī fruit, is setting, kissing the crest of the western mountain.
It is a marvel that her mind, its body agitated by the fever of love’s passion, has long been tormented by thoughts of sandalwood, the moon, and lotus ponds.
Yet, overcome by exhaustion, she remains in solitude meditating for a moment only upon you—the coolest of all—and somehow, though wasted away, she breathes for a moment.

Blessed indeed are those men who impetuously embrace the limbs— so exceedingly tender and enchanting— of women whose bodies are possessed by the pride of passion, who have come of their own accord to the chamber of love out of affection.
The creation of celestial chariots for Kandarpadeva, the rows of palaces for Rasapārthiva,
and the sport of swings— the distinctive mark of all seasons for Caitra— shone forth amidst the beautiful-eyed women.

O lustful men! Here, upon the broad slabs of the hips of courtesans—beautified by rows of folds impressed as the surety for their amorous play—and here, by the falling of pairs of vine-like arms gracefully raised in sport, you have played with dice in the form of side-long glances; as a result, poverty alone shall stand as your final reply before you.

I bow to the youthful adolescence of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose splendor of beauty rivals that of Kandarpa, who is the kinsman of the rain-clouds, who is devoted to the playful damsels of the Vṛndāvana forest, and whose attire consists of ornaments; whose lotus-face bears a gentle smile, whose bimba-like lips are touched by sweetness, and who has blossomed with the forest of tender youth.
Kandarpa and Rati, fashioning two crucibles with an application of saffron paste according to the prescribed rite for the preparation of the elixir, extract camphor;
from within, due to the abundance of heat from the passion of young men tormented by the arrows of Love, drops of the elixir emerge here in the guise of pearls from the necklace.

Victorious is this king of the twice-born: the preceptor for the imperial consecration of Kandarpa, the conqueror of the three worlds; one who subsists by gleaning ears of grain from the wives of his enemies; skilled in the sorcery that dispels all darkness; an ascetic on the banks of the river that adorns the crown of the three-eyed God; and initiated into the sacrifice of erotic passion.

May the Jina protect you—he who was saluted by Rati with tears, trembling, and horripilation: she whose passion was intensely aroused because his form was more beautiful than even Kandarpa; whose heart was agitated with fear because he had brought old age upon beautiful women; and who was bowed low by the weight of her faith because his heart could not be pierced even by the arrows of Māra.

May Rāma— who is more beautiful than Kandarpa, who possesses the great splendor of the sun, who is a moon to the lotus-faces of his enemies' wives, who is of immense power and equal to Arjuna in battles,
who is the protector of the world, renowned for his own fame, a donor of joy, a servant of Śaṅkara, endowed with excellent virtues, and supreme in statesmanship— always remain steadfast.
O Lord of the Earth, when the winds out of curiosity recounted those tales of your beauty— tales that treat even Kandarpa, Nalakūbara, and the Moon with contempt—
Urvaśī grew thin, Rati became utterly exhausted, Rohiṇī was struck down, and Rambhā too, burdened by the fever of fierce passion, became as slender as a plantain stalk.
O creeper of the single sword of Kandarpa in this forest, O young sprout of black aloe-wood, why have you climbed here out of delusion? Alas!
May these blows from the axes be endured by those lovely limbs of yours—limbs that have acquired fragrance through embraces and possess the luster of the thick tresses of beautiful city women.
Association with the virtuous causes joy to blossom, censures the gentle breeze, the moon, and sandalwood paste; it diminishes dullness and brings about even great successes.
In the *kandalī* plants, the *kuṭaja* trees, the clusters of *mālatī*, and the fresh *ketakī* blossoms,
as well as in the crests of the peacocks, the arrival of the clouds seems to have been shared out by the honey.
The vital breath (prāṇa), rising from the tip of the bulb (kanda), constantly flows for embodied beings;
having reached the living soul (jīva) situated in the heart, it goes outside and returns.
Like a ball repeatedly thrown against a wall and rebounding,
a fault intended for another usually falls back upon oneself.
Beauty in its trunk, straightness in its leaves, perfection in its color, loveliness in its branches, and succulence in its fruit—whose else possesses such qualities?
O blessed mango tree, support for weary travelers, standing upon the right path, may you live long; well done, well done! You have been fashioned by a wise Creator.
When the rain-cloud pours down, the earth sprouts with *kanda* tubers, the forests bud with new shoots, the creepers blossom, the trees put forth leaves, and the people rejoice;
yet, O brother Cātaka, we do not fully understand what sin you have committed, that not even two or three drops of water fall into the hollow of your beak.
Having abandoned his neck and reached the earth in battle, he laughed at someone,
as if from the separation from that belly which was so difficult to fill and which, it was said, had bent him down for its own fulfillment.
As you went to the earth with your neck bent and your face cast downward,
how is it that shame— indeed, shameless as you are— did not arise, and how did your pride not dissolve?
Having married some maiden whose youth was just dawning, a fool—dragged by the noose of hope for wealth—wanders for a very long time in foreign lands, alas!
Fate, having brought about the loss of youth through their mutual longing for embrace, has thus inflicted a union of grief upon both worlds of a couple who have become shrouded in distress.
Whoever obtains a maiden, an umbrella, ripe fruit, a lamp, food, a great banner,
or a mantra, for him there is the accomplishment of whatever he has desired.
Fire consumes a maiden during her menstrual period; the Moon, upon the appearance of body hair;
and the Gandharvas, at the emergence of breasts. Therefore, she should be given away in marriage even before that.
Even a great man might fall into delusion upon seeing a beautiful maiden;
Vasiṣṭha was infatuated even with Arundhatī, though she was a Caṇḍālī.
A root of *apāmārga* tied with a thread spun by a virgin,
when fastened upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*), swiftly destroys fever of this day.

Thinking that even in this matter some maiden might be the prize, the scion of Raghu drew the bow of Nārāyaṇa; then, fixing an arrow, he made it unfailing by severing the path of Bhārgava, thereby causing the sky to be deprived of the moonlight from the face of Sītā—whose eyes were tremulous with indignation and whose radiance was thick with the rays from the corners of her glances.
A maiden [seeks union] out of mere curiosity; a widow, seeking merely the relief of physical contact; a courtesan, out of desire for wealth; and one's own wife, because no other recourse is possible.
Thus, women desire union with men for various reasons; yet a woman who is the wife of another, being bound by pure affection, is obtained only through great merits.
When the sun has entered Virgo, the ancestors remain in the house;
the city of the departed spirits remains empty there until the appearance of Scorpio.
One should avoid these five gross falsehoods: lying regarding a maiden, a cow, or land; the misappropriation of a deposit; and giving false testimony.

For those who have set out on a journey, it is declared to be auspicious and beneficial to see a maiden, a cow, a conch, a drum, curd, fruit, flowers, a blazing fire, a lordly elephant, a horse, a chariot, a king facing them, a full water-jar, or a banner;
likewise, ground that has not been dug up, a pair of sandals, cooked food, a centenarian, a courtesan, liquor, and meat.
One should give a daughter without property to a suitor who possesses wealth, but one should never reveal even an unknown person to a thief who intends to kill him, even if he is well-guarded.
The daughter was sent out as the most excellent; the bride was brought in as the most excellent.
The food prepared was the most excellent; Dharma is the most excellent day by day.

What difference is there between Himavat and Karṇa— both of whom gave birth to daughters, both of whom attained prowess through their connection with Dhanu (the bow/the mountain), and both of whose valor was dependent upon Dhanañjaya (Arjuna/the fire)?
It is said that fathers honor the trusted kinsmen of their daughter’s husband; yet in this relationship, your worship toward me was quite the opposite.
You have been so ravished by passion as to destroy the very seed of our kinship. In this terrible hell of my living world, shame on the life of a sinner like me!
A maiden chooses beauty; the mother, wealth; the father, learning;
the kinsmen, family lineage; and other people, delicious food.
Those who sell daughters, those who sell liquids [intoxicants],
and those who sell poison— such men go to hell.
O maiden, behold this lord of men, Kanyakubja, whose fame is unimpeded;
by the dust raised from his earth, even the oceans are turned into dry lands.
Indeed, no one recognizes his extensive deceit;
the weaver enjoys the king’s daughter under the guise of Viṣṇu.
Gazing gently at her beloved who was feigning sleep, she desired to drink the honey of his lips at her own will;
yet, her heart drawn back by shame—charming with the intoxication of passion—she stood like a figure in a painting, her lotus-face closed like a bud.
Struck from the mountain peak by the fierce and formidable matted locks of Dhūrjaṭi, who has descended as a dancer from the pinnacle of deceptive acting,
those elephants rise up and move through the supportless sky, stationed in every direction, struck by the blows of his exceedingly harsh trunk.
Skill in deceit, a mind set on malice, a disposition toward insulting the virtuous, a bent for misconduct, dishonesty even toward friends and children,
speech that is falsely sweet yet destructive behind one's back— these are the sovereign powers of the Great King of the Kali Age.

"By some who utters deceitful words, this courtesan—a deceiver of the entire assembly of connoisseurs—has been deceived. Thus does the pleasure-bower laugh, its eyes cast about by hovering bees under the guise of the beauty of its blooming flowers.
Even though deceived by enemies skilled in a hundred deceptions, and though himself adept at practicing deceit, he who fears this worldly existence and does not resort to crookedness through body,
speech, or mind— of that virtuous person they say his conduct is perfectly straightforward and free from impurity.
"Even by means of deception, one should effect the destruction of the enemy; such is the political science of Uśanas.
Furthermore, according to the doctrine of Bṛhaspati, if killing is not possible, imprisonment and other measures are prescribed for the enemy through stratagems."
If, however, through deceit no further activity is undertaken,
then that wooden vessel is no longer fit for cooking.
Kapardin, endowed with sacred ashes, the lord of the world, non-dual and immutable— even he, Bhṛṅgin, withers away severely because of this cursed fate.
"O lovely-eyed one, open the door! My enemy Kāma is following close behind me. O moon-faced one, my body is pierced by his arrows; I have come to you for refuge."
"O lady with tremulous eyes, open the door! The enemy of Kandarpa has come up behind me. Drawing his arrow, he is making me falter; O moon-faced one, I have come to you for refuge."
For him, whose chest was as broad and beautiful as a door-panel and who bore the Goddess of Fortune upon his breast,
there arose a second Lakṣmī that clung to all his limbs and delighted all people.
A skull, the roots of trees, clothing made of rags, and companionship with solitude; equanimity toward all things—this is the characteristic of one who is liberated.
The skull, the offering, the lineage, and likewise the association;
the proposal, the remedy, the union, and the other person.
The unseen man, the commissioned one, the one who seizes upon the bait of the self,
the one who has cut off his livelihood, and likewise the one who corrupts others.
The junction brought about by the *skandhas* is proclaimed as the sixteenth;
thus, those expert in junctions declare the junction to consist of sixteen parts.
The junction of the skull is known as the *vijñepa*; it consists solely of an even seam (*samasaṃdhika*).
That which arises from the act of giving is called an *upahāra*.
Deep within the skull, thin in the hollows of the matted locks, and surging amidst the jewels on the hoods of the crest-serpents;
soft at the edge of the crescent moon as it trembles with force—may the roar of the Gaṅgā upon the head of Hara purify you for a long time.

In a skull, the cat licks the rays of the moon, thinking them to be milk; the elephant gathers them as they pierce through the gaps in the trees, thinking them to be lotus stalks; and at the end of love-making, the woman snatches the garment from the bed, thinking it to be a cloth—alas, the moon, intoxicated by its own radiance, throws this entire world into confusion!
Just as water in a skull, or milk in a dog-skin bag,
[is spoiled] by the defect of its container, so too is sacred learning [corrupted] when it resides in one who lacks virtuous conduct.
How can he, who is bound by skulls, be the lord of the entire universe? This is indeed a most extraordinary arrangement on the part of us ignoble ones:
that while the moon scatters a mass of rays consisting of liquid nectar, the jewel of the poison-bearing serpents—worthless as it is—is found in every hood!
By smearing one's own feet with the root of *kapikacchū*, the immobilization of a man's seed is achieved; this practice has been observed many times.
By rubbing with the root of *kapikacchū* ground in the urine of a goat intoxicated by passion, there is union;
and by the root of *durālabhā*, there is the causing of paralysis.
It is better for a man to subsist on fruits from the base of trees, broken off by the claws and mouths of monkeys,
than to lead a life humiliated by the contortions of faces arrogant with the pride of wealth.
The monkey was intoxicated by the wine of Kāpiśāyana, bitten by a scorpion, and moreover possessed by a piśāca; what can we say of his transformation?
By drinking the milk of a brown cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman,
and by investigating the syllables of the Vedas, that Śūdra shall go to hell.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he who bestows thousands of tawny cows upon Brahmins does not equal one who grants the gift of life to a single being.
The pain arising from the burning by fire of horses with the fat of monkeys comes to an end,
just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Just as a young monkey, having bound its middle, moves toward a high position,
so too, by relying on a protector, one should take refuge in a lofty station.
From her eyelashes it falls upon her cheek; from her cheek, onto the slope of her breast; from her breast, to her waist; and from her waist, to the fresh lotus of her navel.
We do not know what, where, or how much has been undertaken by this drop of tear-water as it wanders across every limb of hers.
Where the fragrance produced by the oozing sap of *sarala* trees, which have been rubbed against by elephants to relieve the itching of their temples, perfumes the mountain ridges.

With his banner the makara-marked ear-ornament on her cheek, the Mind-born God desires to conquer the worlds with his bow; here, at the balcony, the God of Love, accompanied by his two devoted wives, finds delight through the honey of her lower lip.

O slender one, blessed with loveliness, I consider your cheek to be the region known as the North; for in that place, where the curls are gracefully arranged, the beauty of the ear truly shines forth, enchanting the mind.
Alas, her two cheekbones, having become so emaciated,
seem as if they cannot endure one another and have reached such a state of exhaustion that they no longer look at each other.
As the two moons emerging from her cheeks were spreading forth to conquer one another,
the Self-Existent One himself placed a nose between them as a rod of equality to prevent their conflict.

O fair-limbed one, if your hips were covered by a girdle-string that had begun to jingle as it was being fastened without distinction, then your drops of perspiration— mingled with the nectar of the fresh mango buds swaying against your cheeks— might conceal the fatigue from the reversal of sexual positions.

May Heramba, who bears an exceedingly beautiful splendor like that of a moving peacock-feather parasol— [a splendor formed] by swarms of bees that have flown up from his cheeks and, agitated by fear, have gathered in clusters above out of greed for the ichor of rut— may he accomplish the destruction of your sins without obstacle.
When I gently touched her cheeks, which were covered in a mass of blossoming thrills, her lotus-face seemed to blossom with an inner smile;
how could the speech of that lotus-eyed one ever be described—speech that was as sweet as the overflowing juice from bursting grapes?

Gazing repeatedly at Jānakī’s lotus-face— her cheeks, which steal the luster of a young elephant’s tusk, now blooming with the smile of Love and bristling with thrills— and hearing the tumultuous clamor of the night-stalking army, the Lord of the Raghus tightens the knot of his matted locks.
The Enemy of Mura himself, holding a brush in his hand, was intent on painting a line of leaf-designs upon the blossoming cheek of Śrī Rādhā;
yet, with his eyes fixed upon her moon-like face, he stood with trembling arms—victorious is this power of His ever-fresh form!
A row of leaf-designs has been crushed upon your cheek by the pressure of your palm; this nectar-like essence of your lower lip has been drunk away by your sighs.
Tears repeatedly cling to your throat and cause your breast to heave; O you who are devoid of compassion, it is resentment that has become dear to you, not we.
A certain paleness upon the cheek, a flow of tears in the eyes, emaciation in the body, dejection in speech, and the flame of a forest fire in the heart;
disregard for life and a reversal of one's natural state—what else now does this renunciation display toward all objects of the senses?

Seeing upon the cheek of her lotus-eyed beloved the mark of his teeth, and on the face of her own lotus-eyed rival the trace of the nectar from the serpent-creeper fallen from his mouth, the co-wife, her pair of breasts heaving with deep sighs of distress, weeps softly and repeatedly in secret.
The cheeks of the tremulous-eyed one surpass the grace of honeyed blossoms; her breasts shine, as beautiful as the fullness of golden jars.
Her eyes possess the luster of blue lotuses trembling in the wind; we know not whether her speech consists of nectar or of poison.
When a virtuous person carefully discards on the surface of the earth what consists mostly of phlegm, urine, and excrement, ensuring it is free of living beings,
that constitutes the *utsarga-samiti* (the carefulness regarding the disposal of waste).
A headless trunk, resembling a massive iron bar, was seen near the sun;
the great planet Svarbhānu swallowed the sun out of season.
This bow is as hard as the back of a tortoise, while this joy of the Raghus possesses such a tender form;
how can it be strung by him? Alas, father, your wager is cruel!
O King, a minister who gives much away while taking little is like a water-pot; a fool who is impoverished is like a cowrie-shell.
Her ear, the abode of loveliness and adorned with variegated gems,
held the conch-treasure (*śaṅkhanidhi*) at a great distance, as it had produced jewels in its very vicinity.
Wearing a necklace of most desirable pearls, surpassing sandalwood paste with her lovely breath,
having frequented the monasteries of the Pāṇḍyas, this lotus-faced woman offers herself as a gift at my feet.
Taking up any one of the sense-pleasures, which are as hollow as a reed, he remains seated;
yet, even with such excessive pride, he is unable to conquer those men who are free from passion.
In the Vindhya forest, a lion— the terrible embodiment of transformation— was seen by an elephant who had neither swallowed a lotus nor playfully offered water.
O Kamalā, grant me the state of a bee at your stainless lotus-feet;
I desire nothing else, for what song could there be after alms have been received?

The lotus is his palace, pollen is his unguent, honey is his drink, the sweet warbling of beloveds is his song, and the soft filaments are his pillow; for the bee, what royal luxury is there that is not found in the water?
The row of tooth-marks upon the high cheek of the lotus-eyed woman shines like a coral rosary of the god of love,
who desires to bring the youth under his sway by means of silent recitation.

O lotus-eyed one, afflicted by separation from you, she plunged into a lake desiring to bathe amidst the lotuses; alas, alas! Even as her slender-limbed, deer-eyed form was following closely behind, she became submerged in the mud.
In this triple world, what youth does not experience delight upon seeing the lotus-eyed one, so charming with her shimmering jeweled earrings that adorn her ears?
Alas, O fool, when the Creator has prepared to sever the head of the warrior of tranquility, do you not wake up when the noose is cast and the wheel is raised?
Why do you always guard wealth— which is like a drop of water on a lotus petal and as flickering as the tip of a young elephant’s ear— rather than fame, which is more enduring than life itself?
May Kamalā, born from the lotus, dwell upon your lotus-like face; may she rest upon the sprout of your hand;
may the son of Kamalā (Brahmā) delight in your body; and may the Lord of Kamalā (Viṣṇu) reside in your heart every day.

Having abandoned the drinking of lotus-honey, having cast aside the fresh blue lily, and having discarded the naturally beautiful *mālatī* with its intense fragrance—these deceitful bees now suffer in the bitter water of elephants' ichor; for having thus forsaken what is easily obtained, people take pleasure in hardships.
A lotus without water, water-lilies upon a lotus, those upon a golden creeper, and that creeper herself so delicate and lovely— what is this succession of marvels?
O lady with intoxicating eyes, your face is as beautiful as a lotus, your pair of arms is as tender as a lotus stalk,
and your dark tresses are like a swarm of bees.
Her body is as soft as a lotus bud, possessing the fragrance of a full-blown lily; her divine scent pervades the waters of sexual union.
Her eyes resemble those of a startled doe, with reddish corners, and her pair of breasts is priceless, rivaling the beauty of the *śrīphala* fruit.
She possesses a nose like a *tilaka* flower, is ever devoted to the worship of the twice-born, her teachers, and the gods;
she has the luster of a blue water-lily petal, is fair as a *cāmpeya* flower, and bears a parasol of love shaped like the calyx of a blooming lotus.
She walks gently and gracefully like a royal swan; she is slender, with a waist marked by three folds, possessing the voice of a swan, and well-adorned.
She eats food that is soft, pure, and light; she is proud and deeply modest. Fond of white flowers and garments, such a woman is a *padminī*.

O lotus-faced one, just as rivers whose natural flow is obstructed by their banks are beautified while performing the act of warding off [the flood] from all sides, so too are tremulous-eyed women adorned while performing the act of warding off [the gaze] from every direction.

This slender young woman has a lotus-like face and bears a pair of breasts that are plump, elevated, and shaped like jars; she has large eyes with darting glances, bright teeth, and a slender waist. People labor in vain and for naught through passion when they describe her excessively as being unlike others.

May the summer season pass for you in happiness upon the roof of your palace at night, accompanied by your beloveds—amidst waters filled with lotus groves, delightful with the fragrance of *pāṭala* flowers, where the sprinkling of cool water is pleasant, and where the rays of the moon serve as a necklace. May it pass while soft and charming songs are sung.

That is the skill of the Creator: [a river] rich with a succession of lotuses for its waters and sands, possessing lightning-bolts weighed down by the burden of golden jars, with sprouting lotus-stalks as its necklaces and coral, and the moon as its blue water-lilies.
The lotuses, bowed down by ripeness, with fragrant white water-lilies (kahlāra) wafting from their bases,
and their heads shaken by the breeze, generally evoke praise for their exquisite scent.

I bow to Acyuta, who is the cloud for the golden mountain of Kamalā’s breasts, the god of love for the beautiful Ābhīra maiden, and the bee for the lotus grove that is the row of hoods of the serpent Śeṣa upon whom he rests.
O lotus-eyed one, wait a moment while I bind this lovely mass of hair;
today I shall slowly withdraw this pair of eyes that are firmly fixed upon it.
May the hand of Kṛṣṇa, which raises the lotus to his chin and by which his face shines intensely like a mirror with a dark handle, bestow auspiciousness.
"He who used to close our lotuses—the vessels for drinking honey—is now within the range of this adverse fate";
thus, as if with angry bees, she bore a face from which a fragrant and pleasant breeze was wafted.
Let others compare the two lotuses to the faces of the two nectar-ocean-eyed ones; however, where are these two lotuses, and where are those two?
May Kamalā— whose lotus feet are praised by those who sit upon lotuses, whose eyes are like lotuses, who wear the diadem of the enemy of Kamala (Śiva),
and who have mounts that bear lotuses— and who holds a lotus in her hand, grant me well-being.
"O lotus, why do you sully your heart because you are disregarded by swans who lack discernment? May those bumblebees, who are connoisseurs of your ripened nectar, live long in this world."
O lotus, born in pure water, you do not perform conduct befitting that;
for you cast the pure rays of the moon outwards, while the swarm of bees within you remains soiled.
The lotus plant, Malini, cannot endure being frequented by her beloved in his absence;
now that he has been placed within her heart by the spring, she remembers him—the very essence of Rati—day and night.
This bee, who finds delight in the playful arts within the lotus groves and has won over the virtues of the night-lilies,
now falls into the thicket of *ketakī* thorns out of greed for your fragrance.
Your face, with hair like lotus filaments and causing envy to the lotuses,
makes even the lotus itself seem like a mere drawing among those who are intoxicated by beauty.
Kamala rests upon a lotus; Hara rests upon the Himalayas;
and Hari rests in the Ocean of Milk—I suspect it is out of fear of bedbugs.
O bee, as you constantly drink honey from lotus to lotus,
there will undoubtedly be suffering when the moon, the source of faults, rises.
It is heard, but not seen, that lotuses grow from within a lotus;
yet, O young girl, two blue lotuses are seen upon your lotus-face.
Placing a lotus in her own lotus-hand, she who dwells in the lotus fashions a lotus;
from the pair of her lotus-hands, she wards off the lotus with her lotus-hand.

Ah, he in whom intelligence shines constantly like a lotus, and the lotus-like Lakṣmī like intelligence; in whom radiance shines like his body, and his body like radiance; in whom fortitude shines like the earth, and the earth like fortitude.

I bow to the Jina Nemi, the ornament of Mount Girnāra, who possesses the soles of his feet as tender as the interior of a lotus, whose strength of arm is beyond all calculation, and who brings awakening to the three worlds.
Here, the shadows of fair-limbed women hastening toward their lovers are seen at night as if they were flying upward through the moon-white surroundings.
Trembling, perspiration, fatigue, fainting, vertigo, exhaustion, loss of strength,
and diseases such as pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣmā) may arise from sexual intercourse.
The virtuous constantly describe King Kampa as the moon risen from the milk-ocean of music,
the royal swan upon the Mānasa lake of literature, and the stage-manager for the performance on the battlefield.
If the grip on the arrow trembles behind the handgrip of the bow,
while the grip on the bow itself faces forward, then the movement will be to the left.
The monkeys tremble violently; the cattle, goats, and sheep grow thin and cold; and the dog, though cast even for a moment into the hollow of the hearth, does not leave it.
Furthermore, this wretched person, afflicted by the calamity of suffering from the cold, desires—like a tortoise—to withdraw his own limbs into his very body.
The mountains, led by Maināka, tremble out of fear of Indra; the clouds cry out again, and the fires issuing from the mouth of the submarine mare flicker.
O Agastya, born from a jar, let the ocean be released! May it be well with you; for now Hari, slumbering and sinking as he is embraced by Lakṣmī’s lotus-stalk-like arms, is distressed.

"This wind that causes trembling is a thief of the winter season; it robs the trees, will it not take us too?"—as if out of fear at this thought, the grasses upon the ground have become parched and turned utterly pale.
Trembling, frightened, rasped, indistinct, nasalized,
with a voice like a crow’s, produced in the head, and likewise devoid of the proper place of articulation.
"Trembling, you fall at my pair of feet; though struck by the corner of my eye, you are overcome with fear.
Why do you fight with arrows, O dear one? You speak like a coward!"—laughing thus, another man moved forward.

What word is used in the sense of "all over" (abhividhi)? What is the indeclinable (avyaya) here? Where does fluidity (dravatva) reside? What is the form of the first and second case endings for the word *vi*? Call out the sky (*kha*) today! What root (dhātu) means both "motion" and "smell"? What does a beggar ask from the wealthy? Quickly give the answers to these questions: *re bhayyā jalebī khavā*. [The answers are: *sarvataḥ*, *api*, *apsu*, *veḥ dvitīyā ekavacane viṃ*, *kham adya āhvaya*. The root is *gam* (to go). A beggar asks for *bhikṣām*. The answers are: *re*, *bhayyā*, *jalebī*, *khavā*.]
O Lord of the Earth, your enemies, their entire bodies paralyzed by trembling and with drops of sweat trickling down, have acted like women since they were attacked by you.

With blows from whips fallen upon the body and streams of splashing blood; with prison cells, dense shackles, leaping over, and kissing—knowing this to be so, O wise one, desist! Do not apply yourself [to these things]; the pen, its face soiled, hisses into the vicinity of the ear.
