O lady with a neck like a conch-shell, this Saturn-like gait of yours is your foot, and this mass of hair is Rāhu; yet even so, youth has not departed—this is surely the compassion of her heavy breasts.
Let Brahmā play with some woman; you yourselves may dally with celestial women. Let Kali practice asceticism, or let him go to the world of Brahmā for your great pleasure.
"O passionate one, since you have rejected me— who bowed at your feet— due to the offense of my love-making,
I shall cause her to feel such deep remorse that her body will find refuge only in a bed of young shoots."
Taking her hand and gently caressing it, pressing her waist and stroking her thigh,
the rogue removed the knot of the lower garment of that bashful woman and recited the secret doctrine of the mind.
By stretching out its hand— the sun— toward the southern quarter,
it has not only made itself small, but has also shortened the day.
With the clanging sounds produced by the collision of shields, armor, walls,
and swords, the Night of Doom, as she dances, plays a war-lute as it were.
With his feet placed upon the ground purified by water from a ritual vessel, he uttered distorted *huṃ* sounds;
meanwhile, all the joints of his fingers were occupied with the futile recitation of mantras.
When the hero Rāmanātha was clad in battle armor and became terrifying with his sword-staff brandished by his hand,
the right and left eyes of the celestial beauties belonging to the enemy kings ceased to move.

Those who cling to this ocean of existence lie here in the hell of being seized by their own hands; only those who find aesthetic delight therein are worthy of honor—let them consider themselves blessed.

O Lord of Heaven, who holds the Pināka bow in hand; O wielder of the trident, who pierces the hearts of the enemies of the gods; O Śūlapāṇi, whose vehicle is the bull; O you who are intoxicated with pride; O causeless savior of the three worlds, be gracious!

Are small streams to be protected by the ocean— those who are already terrified by frogs made fearful by crows— or are they comparable to mountains that are expert at protecting themselves from the fear of Indra’s thunderbolt strike?
The movement of her hand, like a sprout, as she fans herself with the winnowing basket, causes the rows of eyelashes on her eyes to rise and fall;
and with her pupils fixed upon her hand, that smile-filled glance does not leave my heart for even a moment.
Shaking her sprout-like hands again and again, her girdle hanging low, she throws the remains of her flower garland toward the flame of the lamp;
repeatedly covering her husband’s eyes with a laugh, the slender woman, agitated at the end of lovemaking, is gazed upon again and again for her beauty.

Blessed is that man into whose ears have entered the abundant cries of young wives—“Ah! Ah! No, no! Do not, do not! Let go, let go!”—as they shake their sprout-like hands at the root of their ears during a first-time embrace.
Disregarding the blows from her hands, feet, girdle,
and necklace, the lover, having seized her hair with force, kisses the beloved’s face, whose lips quiver and whose eyes are reddened.
Whether committed by hand or foot, born of the body or born of action, produced by the ears or the eyes, or mental;
whether prescribed or unprescribed—forgive all of this! Victory, victory, O ocean of compassion, Śrī Mahādeva, Śambhu!
Making his hands, feet, nose, and so forth turn red, he first seizes his ears; then, like a tortoise, he withdraws his limbs from the cold and heavy pain.
The man of taste strikes her with his hands and feet upon her limbs, as she, her eyes trembling with anger, provokes him with harsh words; yet he delights in his beloved.
The great ocean becomes a mere handful of water from a cupped hand, and the great earth becomes one's own courtyard;
for men possessed of perseverance, even the depths of the underworld become like their own home.

"O playful lover, you console the woman who is ashamed and suspecting with jealous anger that the marks of nails and teeth on her body were produced by another woman at night; 'Surely you do not remember, for this was given by you yourself when you were intoxicated.'"

O fair-toothed one, just as you are adorned with nail-marks and have your lower lip bitten by teeth, so too is your gait slow due to the weight of your feet; O deer-eyed one, you are the very embodiment of desire.
May that unprecedented web of rays of the fiercely radiant one, which grants the desired objects of those who worship it,
bestow liberation from the bonds of worldly existence upon those who bow down to it.
A medicinal preparation made from the bark of *karañja*, *āragvadha*, *ariṣṭa*, and *saptaparṇa*,
combined with cow's urine, *musta*, and *viḍaṅga*, destroys worms.

When the swarm of bees hovering nearby makes a humming sound out of thirst for the flowing stream of ichor trickling from the elephant's temples, the elephant speaks with shakes of his head: "Do not ward me off, O elephant; give, give more of your gift! For riches are indeed fickle."

The moon, when situated in front [of one], removes the defect of the *karaṇa* and *bhagaṇa*, the defect of the day (*vāra*) and the *saṃkrānti*, the defect of the *kutithi* and *kulika*, the defect of the watch (*yāma*) and half-watch (*yāmārdha*), as well as the defects of Mars, Saturn, and the Sun, and the defects of Rāhu, Ketu, and others— it removes every defect.
Now, as the passionate women adjust their bodices, which are loosened by their trembling hands, the reflected coppery glow of the lamp’s flame creates,
upon the expanse of their breasts, the preliminary sketch for the playful patterns of nail-marks yet to be made.
Her two jar-like breasts, reddened with saffron and embraced by her pair of palms,
resembled the frontal globes of a lordly elephant marked with vermilion, like a garland of stars.
Making [the subjects] pay tribute, the crushing of enemies by kings,
and the further acquisition of land— these constitute the eightfold conduct of a king.

This lion among suns, who has ascended the peak of the mountain that supports the earth and entered the path of vision, has discharged sprouts of pearls under the guise of frost-droplets from the frontal globes of the lordly elephant of darkness, which were rent asunder by his claws.
In the fever of separation from her beloved, the hundred-petaled lotuses known as her hands, feet, face, and eyes released the sun’s heat—
which had long been drunk up by them— under the guise of incessant burning.
With rays difficult to behold, scorching all creatures with its sharp heat,
and with a disc momentarily reddened, the sun is not equal to you.
The tree of energy, with its vast root of the power of wisdom, bears fruit in the form of great sovereign power that is to be grasped by the hand.
Victorious is the goddess Sarasvatī, by whose grace poets of subtle intellect behold the entire surface of the world as clearly as a *karaba-dara* fruit held in the palm of their hand.
"O young camel, why do you wither your little body with such long sighs? Desist, O rogue! For whom, my friend, has ultimate happiness ever arrived?
Eat the sprouts of the *pīlu* tree at ease and abandon your longing for honey; once again, you shall become a vessel for auspicious things."

O beloved of Karabha, why do you cry out in longing because you cannot find that honey, so difficult to obtain, which was once drunk by you while in the forest? Make yourself a fan with the familiar leaves of the *pīlu* tree found in desert lands; for in this entire world, whose attainment of uninterrupted happiness is there?
O beloved of the female camel, that *pīlu* tree which you, greedy for honey, abandoned—its dense shade having vanished—and did not look upon with respect;
even now, with its trembling shoots and newly sprouted buds, it is being enjoyed at ease by other herds of female camels.

O young camel, if by some stroke of fate, while wandering about, you should ever come upon honey from the swarm of bees—desist, desist from it! There is young grass in the forest; those [bees], though sweet at first, will surely cause you to wither in the end.

O camel, alas, you desire to cry out impetuously; indeed, your long and crooked neck shall be your refuge from the fever of hearing [the consequences]. Or rather, exhausted by the movement through the many cavities of the throat, will speech emerge from your mouth? Who knows after some time what will happen to whom?
Resting upon the breast of the mountain of the rising sun, where the garment of the mass of darkness has slipped away,
the nectar-rayed moon kisses the face of the eastern quarter, whose eyes are the blooming night-lotuses.
In every house, the women scattered parched grain and flowers from their hands— which were like lotus buds— withheld from the pair of palms—
upon Priyarathāṅga, as if scattering heaps of pearls released from the opened shells of oysters.
As the two hands vied with one another over the breasts,
the rows of bracelets, repeatedly falling, proclaimed their relative strength and weakness.
When her lover approached, she, who had been sitting without haste, let go of the hem of her garment that was tucked up at her waist;
then she drew it back over her quivering thighs, which resembled golden slabs seen for a moment.
Having wandered about and rested upon the tips of [your] fingernails dug into [the earth], you who are difficult to reach even during the night—
though emaciated like the sun ground down by a water-wheel, you still captivate the gaze of the world.
Even when fondled in the palms, he burns; even when fanned with a whisk, he blazes.
Like a fire that has not been extinguished, the slanderer does not relinquish his heat.
While King Mukundadeva brandishes his sword with his lotus-like hand,
the young women of Amarāvatī begin by fashioning garlands of golden pārijāta flowers.
O Giver of Desires, O King of Tīrthas, your fame— like the Yamunā with its fierce torrent of sword-blades and like a divine river— follows from afar the Sarasvatī of poets.

If the leader of the herd does not move forward, fanning cool spray from his trunk over the forest ground scorched by a fierce fire, then the path will not be easily traversed for the young elephants.
The withering of hands, the casting off of garments, the loss of luster, and the state of being stained by passion—
these conditions arising from association with Vāruṇī are experienced even by the Sun.
Even though it is held in their very hands, these farmers thus sow the seed in the mire of the broad field;
friend, by whom has the emergence of the fruit ever been seen—whether it exists or does not exist?
Having abandoned the water held in his own hand, he longs for that which is in a cloud;
having rejected cooked food, the fool wanders about begging for alms.

When the touch of his hand begins, her broad jar-like breasts bristle with thrill, and from the left half of her body she pours forth the sweat of exertion, easily brought on by the intentions of Love;
thus, the ash-bath of the Lord—though its application of thick smearing was performed again and again—is somehow completed upon her body, and it reigns supreme.

If one were to compare those two breasts, which possess hands with hundreds of millions of fingers ever-active at their tips, then even the entire *śrīphala* fruit would become intoxicated with pride and unable to obtain even a single seed-pod (*vaṭī*) now.
What loss could there be to an elephant from food falling from its trunk?
Yet by that very same food, an ant supports its own family.
That which is brought by hand, brought on a cloth, brought by a woman,
and likewise brought on castor-oil leaves, is not fit for the deities.
Having concealed its rays, having crushed the trees, and having leaped over even the most massive rocks,
another sun, manifested by the power of time, has arisen once again beneath them.
O auspicious one, may your slender form— with its lotus-hand adorned by a rosary of beads and possessing a splendor that surpasses the moon—
cut through the mass of my misdeeds, just as a river with its surging flow of moving water cuts through its own bank.
He whose lotus-hands dispel the intoxication of passion, who delights the hearts of those who take refuge at his feet, whose feet are adorned with sweet-sounding jeweled anklets,
who reveals the essence of the arts, who brings joy to the young women of Vraja, and who eclipses the deep luster of the clouds— he alone is the supreme wealth of my life.
I constantly remember the infant Mukunda, reclining within the hollow of a leaf-cup of the banyan tree, as he places his lotus-foot upon his lotus-face with his lotus-hand.
May this Yamunā water, which removes the misfortunes of people through its form as the formidable Kālī and serves as a boat for crossing over, become a savior and a vessel of salvation.
Seeing the quarters of the sky filled with dust, their mouths noisy with terrifying cries and their garments torn away by the troops,
the sun vanished from somewhere, shrouded by the darkness of that dust amidst the thickets.
A man who, in a dream, is struck with stones by terrifying, hideous, black men with uplifted weapons, shall meet death immediately.
Like the hands to the body, or like the eyelashes to the eyes—one should act for the beloved's sake without deliberation; such a person is called a friend.
"O beloved, it should not even be suspected in your mind that the rays of the moon cause such torment;
rather, it is the heat from my heart, scorched by separation, that reaches you who reside within it."

O restless bee, why do you pointlessly abandon this fresh *campaka* flower, golden-hued as a young elephant, which has taken refuge here among a cluster of soiled lotuses out of a mind puffed up with pride?
O young elephant, abandon your restlessness; move with the discipline of a vow, your face bowed low. The heavy goad above you, as fragile as the tip of a lion’s claw, cannot endure your insolence.

These foothills of the Vindhyas terrify one from all sides with their scarlet paths, where the tips of tree branches have been nibbled and stripped by monkeys; they are further agitated by wild boars startled by the fierce sound of cow-horns blown by a moving army of Śabaras.
"O friend, how is it that you listen with such respect to unrestrained poets who compare your breasts to the weight of two jars of ichor? For women indeed understand things in their reverse."
MSS_8749-1 Karikṛṣṇā, aśvagandhā, and buffalo butter—
MSS_8749-2 through the rubbing of these, supreme enlargement of the penis is produced.
Elephants are indicated by *hastikarṇa* leaves, horses by *aśvakarṇa*;
cattle by *pāṭala* flowers, and goats and sheep by *kadalī* leaves.
O elephant, do not trumpet so loudly; here dwells the lord of beasts in very close proximity. By chance you have not been seen; depart quickly from here to a great distance.
Do you not see before you this mountain slope, whitened by rows of scattered bones of elephants torn apart by his sharp claws?
While the mountain-river breeze blows outside, carrying the fragrance of rutting elephants,
the lioness does not abandon her soft, womb-like dwelling within the cave-house.
When a tree has its roots pinned by the trunks of monkeys crushed by a lordly elephant,
its fruits do not appear for as long as a year, even though it is otherwise fruit-bearing.
"The Lord of the Arts (the Moon), eager for sport, will place his hand in the sky"—
with these words, the Lady Night extinguished the lamp of the Sun.
One should not speak of what one intends to do, but should reveal only what has already been done;
in matters concerning Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, the counsel remains thus unbroken.
Where he shall perform austerities most difficult to practice for the sake of propitiating the Destroyer of the Mountain Lineage—
that mountain of beautiful peaks, this Guhyaka shall lead you there in an instant.
Through the thought, "I shall do it, I shall do it, I shall do it," [the time] was forgotten; "I shall die, I shall die, I shall die."
The statement "I shall certainly do it" makes you at fault even while you are acting;
for the visible and invisible causes of your action are not under your control.
If the elephant repeatedly fills the direction with its roar, what quarter does it cause to tremble? And if it does not cause the female bee to dance;
if it holds fast to the *ketaka* flower, repeatedly honors the crane, and utterly withers the flower-cluster—such is this state devoid of conflict and hostility.
All of that [substance] placed within cow dung for five months becomes liquefied;
one should then extract it all and smear with it.

Piteous words were spoken, shame was cast aside, and tears were shed before him by those women; for such is the extent of the means available to weak women to entreat a beloved who has become enraged during a secret tryst. Indeed, a wicked man afflicts a virtuous person all the more when that person is moved by compassion.
For a thorn pierces what is soft; on what is hard, it merely becomes blunted.
Placing her hand upon the base of her jar-like breasts, the fair-faced woman clearly and repeatedly agitates her necklace;
she whose eyes are like fish and whose lashes are like blue lotus petals, weaving threads, completely bewilders all living beings.
If [the mark] is on the right hand, it removes disease; if on the heart, it bestows the attainment of sovereignty and other blessings;
if on the back, it destroys calamities; and if on the belly, it provides the enjoyment of delicious food.
When a Yakṣa scratches his left hand with his right hand,
he then proclaims universal sovereignty over the earth, enriched by a multitude of abundant elephants.
Though firmly seized by the trunk of an enraged elephant, the hero,
remaining himself unhurt, swiftly took away that very elephant's life with his sword.
In battle, the female elephants of your enemies, struck by your trunk which brings an end to foes,
shine with flowing blood like clouds at twilight.
Taking the gift with his hand, the Sage says this as a sign of his devotion:
"In the bestowing of the fruit desired for both worlds, this right hand of mine has been given."
O you who speak thus with such boldness, desiring to seize the moon with your hand as if it were a mere object of longing—
am I not capable of even hearing that matter with my ears, just as the final letter of the alphabet is incapable of uttering the sound of the Vedas?
O fierce one, when you, full of curiosity, touched with your hand hanging from the window,
that cloud— its circle of lightning flashing forth— seemed to fasten upon itself a second ornament.

One should not touch the cheeks with a hand moistened by water, nor one cheek with the other hand, nor should one touch the eyes; rather, for the sake of prosperity, one should touch the knees when they are to be touched.

The female elephant, who was fond of sharing her own morsel of food, was not summoned; nor was the young calf caressed with a sprout-like trunk out of affection—by that very lord of elephants, who, rushing out of pride and the impetuosity of his desire to conquer a rival elephant, sank in the waters of a lake while fleeing in anger; alas! MSS_8769-1 kareṇurnāhūtā nijakavalabhāgapraṇayinī na cāmṛṣṭaḥ snehāt karakisalayenāpi kalabhaḥ / MSS_8769-2 sa yenāsau darpāt pratigajajigīṣārabhasataḥ krudhā dhāvan magno hradapayasi kaṣṭaṃ karipatiḥ //
Charity in hand, meditation in the heart, silence in speech, and wealth in the home;
a vehicle on the pilgrimage site and knowledge on the mountain—this is the adornment of the great.
Holding a garment in her left hand and a string of pearls in the other, with a wound-mark from her husband’s teeth upon her bimba-red lip,
a withered garland upon her head, and a crescent moon upon her breast— this fawn-eyed woman rising at the end of lovemaking is not worth even the entire world.
Having been held in his hand by the Goddess of Speech with a smile, she was made a traveler on the path of Indra;
thus, she shared the very name "Vāmā" (the Left-handed one), which is common to all women.
Upon the hand of the slender-limbed woman shines a cluster of jingling bracelets,
like a line of snares belonging to the Mind-born God for binding the deer of the mind.
On the roof-terrace at the conclusion of her bath, this charming girl with eyes like those of a doe, holding her braid in her hand,
repeatedly causes the tree of the mind-born god to sprout with a glance resembling the thick waves of the ocean of milk— even though he had been consumed by the fiery luster of Shiva’s eye.
Praiseworthy generosity in the hand, bowing at the feet of the guru upon the head, truthful speech in the mouth, incomparable valor in the victorious arms,
a pure disposition in the heart, and sacred learning acquired by the ears— this is the natural ornament of the great, even without worldly sovereignty.
The Sun, with his own rays, took honey-drops from the clusters of blossoming lotuses and deposited them upon her lotus-face under the guise of perspiration.
One should satisfy a powerful enemy with measured handfuls or villages during the year; for that indeed constitutes a gift appropriate for enemies according to the circumstances.
Time creates everything, for Time alone indeed destroys it;
Time sustains the universe, and this world is dependent upon Time.
The hand, exceedingly red, performs the graceful gesture of striking the lute strings for beautiful women,
and out of jealousy, it performs the striking of the lotus on the ear of the beloved.
Neither the lion, nor the venomous serpent, nor the elephant, nor the king,
nor even an exceedingly enraged and arrogant enemy, inflicts such harm upon embodied beings as does this fierce enemy of false views.
A stainless substratum brings great value even to that which is worthless;
even a tiny drop of water becomes a pearl within a pearl-oyster shell.
If a sow builds a nest upon the ground or gives birth to offspring that are uniform in appearance,
then this entire world will burn in the fire of the rising rays of the sun.
He who commits evil out of ignorance and does not recognize his own capacity for forgiveness, and who harbors hatred toward those of virtuous conduct, incurs the censure of the world.
Whoever, possessing a body, always performs worship with flowers for the Leader of the Jinas at the three times of day,
the splendors of the Lord of the Immortals, the Sovereign of the Earth, the Universal Monarch, and so forth, shall swiftly come under his control.
Even when being honored, a wicked person who is dedicated to the ruin of the world causes terror at every sight, like a snake in one's own home.
Meat produces strength for the sense faculties and from that, the increase of passion;
therefore, having reflected with their intellect upon this lack of propriety, the virtuous abandon meat in three ways.
The prosperity of that king who commits injury against innocent people, even if it be firmly established, meets with destruction along with its very roots.
He who, through his deeds, establishes a meaningful reputation that surpasses all other people,
is not counted as a mere filler when the rank of a superior man arises in assemblies.
What benefit does one derive from respect shown by those devoid of gain? What quality does the moon acquire merely by being borne upon the head of the Lord?
The fortunate person who always practices abstinence from eating at night will certainly have half of their human lifespan spent in the state of fasting.

When being openly rebuked he harbors enmity; he takes pleasure in unwholesome sounds that are pleasant to the ear; devoid of discernment and arrogant regarding himself, alas, this lord is a great calamity for his friends!

Who creates beauty on the forehead of a woman? Who is not beloved when seen? And by whom was she declared [to be] by fate? On which limb, however, is the fire of the Enemy of Cities [Śiva]? [Answer: A dot of vermilion on the widow’s forehead.

The wise one, having exerted effort for the sake of liberation, produces a state of detachment toward cyclic existence, the body, and enjoyments, while maintaining passion for ethical discipline, vows, meditation, austerity, and compassion.
Whatever action a living being performs, he makes that action bear fruit.
This sound of the intoxicated cuckoo causes my mind to long for the mango blossom with ever-increasing longing; yet even this very sound of the cuckoo agitates my mind further.
A wicked son certainly brings misery to his friends and joy to his enemies,
and he inflicts premature old age upon his parents.
Homage to the wicked man, who, like a pestle naturally prone to falling, repeatedly crushes another with his own mouth.
One who makes the sounds *huṃ-huṃ* or *śṛgiti* is neither undesirable nor wicked, since he seeks pleasure;
the sound *cala-cala* leads to quarreling; *kikī* is brilliant; *gururuk* is pacifying.
O son of the Daitya, to whatever extent one makes an acquisition,
to that same extent it inflicts suffering upon his mind.
Let the crow live always in the courtyard and make its noise;
the wise man does not listen to it with pleasure, yet he listens to the song of the cuckoo.
May he produce such affection as that between water and mud;
for when the water is dried up by the sun, the body of mud falls apart.
Though a man skilled in policy may indeed exert his efforts here and there,
the fruit that comes to pass is only that which resides in the mind of Fate.
Even as a lord, I do not commit aggression, being weary with remorse;
even as a poor man, I have no desire for more, and thus I live free from affliction.
"I am doing this," "that has been done by me," "I shall do this"—thus a person is always occupied with the performance and causation of actions;
with a mind devoid of discernment, unable to endure any of the phenomena of existence, and utterly distracted, alas, he does not perceive even time as it passes away in this world.
You make those thoughts firm in the place where delusion has been uprooted;
therefore, through excellent austerity, the ascetic attains a state that is as white as pure light.

Whatever small merit you have ever performed in any way for the sake of your welfare after death—do not let it be wasted through pride, envy, and the like; and do not become a guest in hell because of that.
Shaking her hands, which were like fresh sprouts, as she was supposedly startled by the deep water,
the proud woman obtained an embrace of her lover’s limbs— a joy unblemished by the immodesty that would have been censured among her friends.
O proud lady, do not exert yourself in vain by shaking your hands which resemble fresh sprouts;
for how else could this swarm of bees, having approached them under the suspicion that they are *kalpalatā* creepers, now flee in terror?
Behold this childhood glory, an ambrosia for the eyes: hands that serve as masters in the art of emulating the grace of autumnal lotuses; feet that surpass the first sprouts of the celestial tree;

and eyes that have shattered the pride of the beauty of all three worlds. The Śabara woman gathers the jujube fruit, longing for it to be a pearl; even a crow acts like a swan in the presence of a flock of vultures and owls.
O Protector of the Earth, while the three worlds have been whitened by your fame, Fortune, seeing you dark-complexioned, speaks softly with shame, thinking, "This is Balarāma."
Deceived by others, they utter harsh and unbearable words;
they even perform the cutting off of the ears, nose, and other limbs of a gambler.
How can one who is preoccupied with harsh logic and investigation understand the heart of poetry? Like a rustic man intent on agriculture, he knows nothing of the secrets of a tremulous-eyed woman.
The flight of that arrow which is drawn with a stiff bow by one who has a loose grip is proclaimed to be like the movement of a fish's tail.
Having powdered the roots of *karkoṭikā* and *arka*, along with mustard seeds,
the mantra-practitioner should have them drunk with clarified butter for the pacification of stationary poisons (*sthāvara-kṣveḍa*).
Karna reckoned the eye as his ear; O dear one, your father reckoned your father [as his own]; and he, in turn, reckoned even the prince Śaktyādhāra as being full of cowardice.
The Lord regards the world as if it were his queen; yet even so, virtuous men whose wealth is wisdom display their boldness in making such distinctions.
Karna is present upon every head; what in the three worlds has not been heard by Karna? It is not surprising that even the glances of fawn-eyed women rest upon his ear.
But this alone is a marvel: that he, a flawless orb of excellence, supports the entire circle of the world—the earth girdled by the seven oceans.
The Enemy of Mura is gazed upon by Rādhā, whose cheeks are turned tawny by the mango blossoms placed behind her ears, as she pours forth streams of tears from her eyes.
This unfailing gaze of yours, reaching to your ears, and this spear given by Indra—
neither of these has ever failed to achieve victory, nor have they ever fallen fruitlessly.
With golden palm-leaf ornaments hanging from both ears, and clusters of gems, pearls, and gold suspended at the ends of her braided hair;
with the roots of her breasts and arms covered by a short bodice, and the hem of her lower garment tucked around her hips, she is a woman of Lāṭa.

Just as generous archers, whose excellence lies in arrows that leap over the ear, do not release their shafts in vain when standing in battle, so too [the wise] do not let go of those who have transgressed the ear.
And when afflicted by the poison of flattery, what will a foolish person not do?
He even assumes the guise of a mendicant and drinks liquor from a human skull.
Karṇa gave his ears, Śibi his skin, Jīmūtavāhana his life, and Dadhīci his bones; for there is nothing that cannot be given by the high-souled.
This Karṇāṭa maiden possesses a lovely form, beautiful with the radiance of golden earrings shimmering on her ears, enticing with the sight of her two breasts,
and marked with saffron paste that resembles clusters of *kāleya* buds.
"This ornament belongs to Karṇa, who is an enemy of my future prosperity"—
thinking thus, your gaze mostly avoids the blue lotus on his ear.

The Creator fashioned a second [face] right here for him— who has conquered all things equal to himself, such as his ears, eyes, lips, arms, hands, and feet— out of a sense of agitation caused by the conceit of duality.

With his ears pricked up, his body slightly bent, and his head lowered as he holds his tail—now withered by old age—firmly tucked between his buttocks, the dog sees his rival from afar; with his neck quivering in a sudden burst of rage, his teeth bared like opening jasmine buds, he moves along while letting out a low growl.
Those whose blood appears like vermilion when the tips of their ears are pressed will quickly become carriers [of burdens] and live for a long time.

O Śāh Jallāl ud-Dīn, whose gaze is like a lotus, grant me Karṇāṭa—O you whose generosity is ordained by rites exceeding those of Karṇa—or Lāṭa, O you with a lofty forehead; or Drāviḍa, which is intensely resplendent through the majesty of its ever-moving arm-strength;
or Gurjara, which thunders; or Vaidarbha, where the wombs of the wives of vanquished enemies have been rent asunder; or even a hundred blades of Kuśa grass!
Marked by the tooth-bites of a Karṇāṭī woman, struck by the sharp side-glances of a Mahārāṣṭrī, pressed by the breasts of a mature Andhrī, terrified by the frown of his beloved,
entwined by the arms of a Lāṭī, and threatened by the forefinger of a Malaya woman— this very Rājaśekhara poet now desires Vārāṇasī.
The air is filled with [beings] running here and there, their mouths wide open in a terrifying gape that reaches to their ears and blazes with fire, their fangs formidable as they are set on edge;
with masses of hair, eyes, brows, and beards resembling clusters of lightning, these Ulkāmukhas—with their long, emaciated bodies appearing and disappearing—cover everything with their faces.

At dawn, the great bull somehow reaches the water of the field; his eyes are narrowed for fear of the *kalama* rice, his backbone bent by the blows of the stick from the cowherd woman enraged by his behavior, and his desire to increase his herd thwarted by the fear of the shadows of crows—who, greedy to taste the blood from the wounds inflicted by the horns of his enemies near his ears—seizing him in terror.
Having cast aside the nectar for the ears that is well-spoken, the wicked indeed exert great effort toward fault-finding;
having entered a pleasure grove, a camel looks only for a thicket of thorns.
O crow, enter this mango tree, beautiful with its nectar, yourself, without making a sound that pierces the ears; we consider you to be a cuckoo.
Some things are rendered excellent by the excellence of their location; who would not suspect musk to be mere mud when it is on the forehead of the king of Nepal?
The song of the cuckoo is truly piercing to the ears once her speech is heard; the moon possesses no public charm before the splendor of her face is revealed.
For the deer, closing their eyes is better than gazing upon her eyes; even the golden vine is charming only so long as she is not seen.
On her cheek— roughened by the lodhra decoction applied to her ear and made intensely pale by the application of gorocana—
the sprout of a barley grain, having attained a superior luster, captivated the eyes of all.

"When was her ear-ornament made?"—thus he touched her cheek; "How lovely, oh, what a beautiful bodice!"—thus he placed his hand upon her breast; "Is this natural glow upon her face?"—thus he touched her bimba-like lower lip. By such innocent guile, my desire for the deer-eyed girl was fulfilled without obstacle.
Disregarding the conflict of the elephants' blows upon his ears, this bee of sweet vows persists in his pursuit of the bitter ichor;
when the lotuses have become mere memories, fie on this wretched creature’s addiction to life!
Salutation to that supreme glory which, though undivided, appears divided— like gold in its various ornaments such as the *karṇikā*, or like water in the ocean and other receptacles.
The *karṇikāra* creepers, crowded with blossoming flowers and bees,
shone like rows of lamps with bright flames and black soot.
One bitten by a mad dog should drink a mixture of *karṇikāra* juice, *sauvīra* (sour gruel), the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), honey, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, coriander, molasses, and milk.
Barbed arrows, reed-tipped shafts, and iron bolts can be extracted from the body;
but the arrow of speech cannot be removed, for it lies deep within the heart.
When her ear hears the news of her lover's arrival, she adorns it with golden ornaments; when her eyes do not see him, she applies collyrium to darken them.
Wondering, "Where might my beloved be standing? she touches her chest, which is embraced by her necklace, and spreads a bed of horripilation as a pillow for his heart.
If the prescribed method of adornment— earrings of beautiful chowries and jasmine buds on the ears, a cluster of gems on the neck, a mass of vermilion on the head, and tinkling bells near the flanks—
is obtained by a royal elephant that has been captured and bound, then why is the wild elephant, its body grey with mountain dust, not worthy of honor?

Your whisperer at the ear has a crooked form and his left hand is foremost; yet your other hand remains clenched in a fist. Even so, these arrows of yours reach their target; O archer, that is some truly marvelous skill of yours!
May even those whisperers in the ear— who are always crooked by nature, evil-minded, and who act as enemies without any prior provocation—
be joyful at heart with affection toward me, they whose sharp tongues excel in the exchange of virtues for virtues.
The elaborate deceptions of backbiters do not defile the great-souled anywhere;
the contact with the venom of serpents does not render great lakes undrinkable.
They whisper that into the ear what has been proclaimed throughout the kingdom by the sounds of drums; they speak piteously with bowed bodies because they are full of shame;
they praise that which is uttered even by a debtor, provided it does not strike a vital point—surely those who are repositories of deceit and foolishness are the ones who delight kings.

May the Lord of Beings protect you—he who wears the beauty of earrings in his ears, the makara-patterned leaf-design upon his chest, and fine silk upon his thighs; who bears a serpent and ashes on his left side and a snake-skin on his right; and who, while placing a boundless garland of skulls around his neck, was gazed upon by the Daughter of the Mountain with a raised eyebrow and a face graced by an inner smile.

May there be a palm leaf behind the ear, sandalwood paste on the body, camphor-scented cloth for the garment, a cluster of *ketakī* petals woven into the crest-lock, and a fresh single-string necklace around the neck;

may the splendor of the forest-dwellers’ abode be the dwelling place, the eloquent words of a true poet be the beauty of speech, a piece of betel-nut be in the mouth, and hair disheveled with love stand before me.
Having caused Ghaṭotkaca to be slain by Karṇa through the discharge of Śakra’s spear, [the Pāṇḍavas] saved their lives; one should protect oneself from all sides.
O Cintāmaṇi, abandon the thought, "I have been defeated by Karṇa";
the five celestial trees were conquered, yet there is no suffering because of those five.
The root of the white horse-killer (*śvetaturaṅgaripu*) tied to the ear at sunrise removes all fevers; so too does the root of the white mandāra.

Because the words of her friends were not heeded in her ear, because the advice of her kinsmen was disregarded, and because even as her beloved fell at her feet he was struck with a lotus from her ear—
therefore, the moon acts like a fire, the application of sandalwood paste acts like sparks, the night acts like a hundred kalpas, and even a necklace of lotus fibers acts like a heavy burden.

The minds of women were intensely longing for the rays of the moon— to place them as ear-ornaments, to apply them to their tresses, to wipe away the sweat of amorous fatigue with them, to pour them into drinking cups, to fashion necklaces from them, and to create bracelets from them.

At the onset of summer, fresh adornments delight amorous women: ear-ornaments of *śirīṣa* flowers possessing the playful grace of young female parrots; jasmine necklaces emitting fragrance with their inner threads visible; and lotus stalks with tips as tender as budding sprouts, white as pearls, fashioned into bracelets.

Whose heart would not be moistened with longing by that woman at the conclusion of her bath—her breasts encircled as if by a necklace formed by the water clinging to the tips of her hair tossed back against her ears; her skin bristling with goosebumps from the cold and emitting soft sighs; her eyes, their corners reddened by washed-away collyrium, and the mass of her braided hair dripping with moisture?

O Daughter of the Ocean, your ear-lotuses are your side-long glances; your radiance is your exquisite golden bodice; and your smiles are the pearl necklaces that sport upon the waterfalls of your mountain-like breasts.

Even when your eye has strayed from the *karṇotpala* flower due to your movement, this bee does not leave your face when it closes; why then, O Mother, do you not prevent him today when he is so heedless—even by your hand, which possesses the likeness of a lotus?
If her face were graced even by an ear-lotus conquered by the brilliance of her eyes,
then the doe, having achieved her purpose through that [lotus], would do what with her own eyes?
The beauty of her eyes, spreading to the hollows of her ears, takes on the very essence of loveliness, rendering the lotus-ear-ornament and even the application of lac indifferent;

the moonlight of her smile alone serves as her necklace, and the radiance of her limbs acts as her bodice—for I consider that for this slender maiden, her own physical splendor is now her sole and supreme ornament.
"The ears of these lotus-eyed women have already been surpassed by their lotus-like eyes; now even the region of the forehead must be surpassed by [the nose] which is as radiant as gold.
With a mind agitated by such apprehension, the Creator fashioned a boundary line with masses of collyrium under the guise of thick, creeper-like eyebrows.
Rivals may widen one’s ears, but they can never broaden one’s eyes;
knowledge is acquired through the power of constant practice, yet goodness is not obtained merely by the force of habit.

Those who follow the prescribed rites should perform the salutation of the Jinas with minds overflowing with joy; they should always serve the virtuous ones (sādhus) who are adorned with excellent conduct;
the word of the Jina, which destroys false belief (mithyātva), should be heard day by day; and lay followers (śrāvakas) should constantly take delight in charity and the observance of vows.
"Action must indeed be performed"—this is Manu’s firm resolve; for a person who is entirely devoid of effort surely comes to ruin."
Even when exhorted by kinsmen who are full of affection, a man—even if he be wise—does not do what ought to be done; out of desire, he disregards beneficial and desired counsel.
In this world, no transformation is seen in a person devoid of desire; therefore, it is determined that this [desire] alone is the root of all misfortune.
Protection of those who have come for refuge must be provided by a protector of the earth;
having protected the pigeon from the hawk, Śibi attained fame.
The words of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out by all.
Every day, with a serene mind, one should perform even a small measure of religious duty consisting of vows, observances, and fasting.
For death constantly strikes at the lives of living beings, despite the greatest effort being made.
One should always practice accumulation, but one should not engage in excessive accumulation;
for this jackal, who was habituated to excessive hoarding, was killed by a bow.
That which ought to be done must indeed be done, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
that which ought not to be done must not be done, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
Even in poetry that prioritizes meaning, verbal artistry must be cultivated;
for an elephant does not look beautiful while walking without the ringing sound of its bells.
Friends should be made, both weak and strong;
behold how the lord of tortoises was bound and liberated by a mouse.
One must certainly make friends, both powerful and weak,
just as the herd of elephants bound in the forest was liberated by the mice.
Excessive rashness is always to be condemned when a task must be performed;
through the fault of extreme recklessness, Bhīma fell under the power of a serpent.

One should cultivate a collection of virtues, offer one's own mind in service, listen to the nectar-like words of the Jina’s speech as they truly stand, and bestow wealth acquired through righteous means upon the foremost of ascetics. This is the method that constantly brings about the welfare of the virtuous through their excellent conduct.
Even when one must rely upon a superior person, the result follows according to one's own fortune;
though Vāsuki dwells upon the neck of Nīlakaṇṭha, he remains a consumer of air.
Affection for one's brothers should be cultivated, and their faults should be forgotten;
kinship with one's relatives is beneficial in both worlds.
O cloud, if a benefit for this tree is still to be performed and remains in your heart, then do not let the time pass; drench it with floods of water at the proper season.
When its flowers and fruits have withered, its leaves fallen, and its roots have reached dryness, for whom will you perform a service, and what benefit will you bring? Only your remorse will remain.
The doer, the one who causes it to be done, the one who incites, and the one who approves—
these four share equally in both good and evil deeds.
The one who acts, the one who causes it to be done, and the one who approves—
whether it be good or evil— their fruit is equal.

That arrogant man was the author of the deceits at dice, the one who set fire to the house made of lac, the wind that stripped away Draupadī’s hair and upper garment, and he under whose command the Pāṇḍavas were slaves.

"Where is that Duryodhana—the king who is the elder of a hundred younger brothers beginning with Duḥśāsana, the friend of the King of Aṅga? Tell me, for we have come here not out of anger, but to see him."
No one other than the Three-eyed Lord is capable of accomplishing the victory of Pārtha;
how, then, can that purpose be perceived by those who possess only two eyes?
He who is able to create, to destroy, and to alter this entire world—
leaving aside that Rāma, do not direct your desires toward anyone else in your mind.
Who is capable of doing what is desired or undesired without destiny?
It is only by attributing agency to another that people feel satisfaction or anger.
Having manifested the majesty of the Self like a mire for the sake of the human race for a long time,
and having scorched his own body with the intense heat of the sun, he has departed to the celestial lake.
One should cook the powder of the pulp of cotton seeds with oil;
by means of that, flowers will be produced even for young women whose menses have long since ceased.
With the exception of cotton, ashes, buttermilk, and bones, everything white is auspicious; however, with the exception of cows, horses, elephants, and divine sages, everything black is censured.
Those courtyards of the huts of destitute Vedic scholars, once strewn with heaps of cotton seeds and surrounded by dwellings expanded only by the wind,
now, through your grace, have pearls from the necklaces of young women— snapped during games and battles— falling upon the grounds surrounding their palatial mansions.
Camphor, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, tulasī, and resin derived from the sarja tree;
musta, śilārasa, dhattūra, and likewise aguru.
Śephālī, śatapuṣpā, mustard seeds, *agastura*, jaggery,
as well as rudrajaṭā— one should combine all of these together.
A person whose garments and ornaments are perfumed with this king of medicinal compounds (*yogarāja*), and whose body is likewise incensed, brings the three worlds under his control.
Like camphor, he remains potent among every person even when burnt.
Homage be to that Makarakeṭu (the god of love), whose prowess is irresistible.
I bow to Bhava, who is white as camphor, the incarnation of compassion, the essence of worldly existence, who wears a necklace of lordly serpents,
and who dwells eternally in the lotus of the heart together with Bhavānī.
Bearing white powder of camphor and sandalwood, with every limb smeared with dried sandalwood paste,
she resembles the remaining ashes of the great fire of passion that dwells within and burns her, as if reduced to cinders by the force of its own exhaustion.
As if plunging this earth into a great mist of spray from liquid camphor, as if smearing it with a thick layer of paste from the fresh foam of nectar,
or as if casting it into the interior of a house made of a single clear crystal, this lord of the full-moon night shines forth with unrestrained splendor.
When the orb of the quarters was washed by the flood of light white as camphor dust from the cool-rayed moon,
she appeared upon the ground of his eyes with the elevation of her breasts revealed by the particular arrangement of her playful head-scarf.
Does an onion, even when provided with a basin fashioned from camphor dust, endowed with the beauty of a nourishing treatment prepared from musk,
and being sprinkled with floods of icy water, ever relinquish its former quality?
Does an onion, even when provided with a basin made of camphor powder, its body smeared with musk and saffron,
and being sprinkled from golden jars, ever relinquish its own natural quality?

O you who possess camphor, you who possess the *ketaka* flower, you who possess the autumnal full-moon, you who possess the glorious moon, you who possess sandalwood, you who possess a flood of pure nectar;

O you who possess Mount Kailāsa, you who possess the shimmering, clear waters of the milk-ocean, you who possess the glorious Śambhu—proclaim your glories, O Lord, you who possess the lordly elephant!
Resembling camphor, like liquid nectar, like the smile of the lotus, like swans, like frost, like the Himalayas, like a lake of hailstones,
and like a string of pearls— those glories of his, endowed with the boldness of a gait that traverses the stage of the three worlds, now triumph like the spreading rays of the cool-rayed moon.
When the moon— whose copper-hued luster rivals the brilliance of a pearl-oyster shell in its dispute over the hue of camphor—
is eclipsed by the spreading darkness that hates the king, the female cakravāka bird weeps at the rising of the sun.
O Śrī Rāmacandra, as for the fact that poets compare your fame to a flood of camphor,
we understand this to mean that it would become greyish-white due to the excessive infamy of your enemies.

There are certain many virtues of his that rival camphor, rub against the peaks of the snowy mountains, surpass the essence within the midst of the Ocean of Milk, and outshine the flow of the Gaṅgā; they freely eclipse the luster of yellow sandalwood, emulate the jasmine and the moon, and possess the brilliance of the interior of a lotus bud.
Camphor, bhallātaka, powdered conch-shell, barley-alkali, and realgar—
oil cooked with these and mixed with yellow orpiment instantly causes the hair and body hair to fall out from the roots.
By applying a plaster made from *sehuṇḍa* (Euphorbia) milk mixed with camphor,
a great enlargement of the penis is produced, which brings intense pleasure to women.
A phallus smeared with a juice produced from the seeds of *kaṇṭakārī* mixed with camphor becomes a liquefier for women during sexual union and brings about extreme pleasure.
O camphor, your fragrance is revealed when you are crushed; O sandalwood, your fragrance is revealed when you are ground.
O agallochum, your scent is revealed when you enter the fire; whereas musk is seen to possess its own inherent fragrance.
Like a camphor wick that dispels the heat from the eyes, like a garland of blooming lotuses that is the sole cause of bliss for the throat,
and like a beautiful poem that is a source of wonder to the mind— she shone forth, worthy of being bowed to by women, like a celestial nymph.

The earth, with its seven oceans, has been whitened by your white glories— whiter than camphor, than the night-lotus, than the blossoming jasmine, than the surging waves of the celestial river, than the ketaka flower, than the playful side-glance of a beautiful woman, and even than the crescent moon upon the head of Śiva, from which all stain has long since departed.
Even on a couch strewn with fresh lotus petals that had been sprinkled with camphor-water, where their bodies lay tossing about and their flower-garlands were falling away,
what else could have happened to those two whose eyes were barely opening, other than that state in which sandalwood paste, the moon, and rows of campaka petals seemed like fire?

O slender one, we desire great friendship for this [wind], which turns the sands into camphor, which transforms the mass of sunlight into cool powder, which acts as the wind of a great gale for the breeze of the fan, and which possesses the great audacity of a festival for her who is eager to go on a tryst during the middle of the summer days.

The white rays of the cool-rayed moon act like camphor upon the earth, behave like white water-lilies in the lake with impetuosity, act like the waves of the Gaṅgā in heaven, and everywhere in every direction act like *ketakī* flowers; furthermore, they act like female swans in the atmosphere, like pearls on the necks of those with eyes like lotus petals, and act like oyster shells in the ocean.

If there were some golden creeper growing there, fashioned from camphor as its base, with a basin of saffron and nourished daily by honey-water— the very weapon of the five-arrowed god— then perhaps it might attain even a fraction of the delicate loveliness of this fair-browed maiden.
Was the body of heaven and earth filled with camphor, smeared with sandalwood paste, washed with mercury, or fashioned from crystal stones?
Reflect on this regarding the full moon—the remover of the fatigue of night-lotuses, the initiating preceptor of love, the mirror for the faces of the quarters, and the friend of the cakora bird.
O Lord, alas, even during the day, the interior of the quarters has become as if flooded with camphor, mercury, and streams of nectar by your glories;

thus, Kāma, wearing armor upon his body, placing Mādhava before him as his quiver, and shaking his bow with the thought that it is the rising of the moon, the friend of the night-lotus, hastens forth.
O crusher of enemies, one who has been born must indeed perform action in this world;
for it is the immobile beings, and not other people, who live without action.
One should perform actions that are beneficial to oneself, whether they be harsh or mild;
however, one who is habituated to inaction and possesses nothing is always swallowed up by misfortunes.
Indeed, karma alone is the motivator of all causes;
for it is karma that brings about the results here, whether they be auspicious or most evil.
Upon bodies produced by karma, bodily and mental afflictions fall here like arrows released from firm bows.
Calamities born of karma indeed arise in due time;
however, this is what is truly grievous: that the agent considers himself to be the enemy.
Having attained certainty regarding the self through thorough knowledge, the virtuous one uses the probe of equanimity (*sāmāyika*) to separate karma, which is closely adhered to the soul.
Knowledge of action leads to liberation, and the purpose regarding action consists in one's qualification for it;
therefore, absolute isolation (kaivalya) is attained through the purpose alone, not through isolation itself.
The agent himself experiences the fruition of his action;
this is seen directly in the world, both in what has been done and what has not been done.
From the accumulation of karma arise heaven and hell, as well as liberation and bondage;
through karma a living being is known, just as a new sprout is known from its seed.
They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by sattva;
the fruit of rajas is suffering, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas*, greed;
from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance itself.
The performance of praiseworthy actions brings happiness;
the failure to perform those very same actions results later in great remorse.
Relying precisely upon that which was performed as action in the past and that which was practiced by the virtuous, those who are self-controlled and devoted to tranquility rejoice.
A living being is born through karma and perishes through karma alone;
happiness, suffering, fear, and security are all attained through karma alone.
If there exists some Lord who possesses the form of the fruits of other actions, he too depends upon a creator; for he is not the master of one who is not his creator.
Just as a human being is fashioned by a carpenter into a doll,
so too is one impelled in all actions, having been pulled by the rope of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
A living being is bound by action, but is liberated through knowledge;
therefore, ascetics who see the further shore do not perform ritual action.
The intellect is obstructed by karma, but karma is not obstructed by the intellect;
for even Rāma, though possessed of excellent intellect, pursued the golden deer.

One should practice dharma with effort through deed, mind, and speech; however, one should not practice even that which is consistent with dharma if it does not lead to heaven or is despised by the world.
Whatever one habitually practices through action, mind, or speech, that very thing carries one away; therefore, one should perform what is wholesome.
The supreme sages have declared that non-violence consists in never causing distress to any living being, at any time, through action, mind, or speech.
When there is a complete exhaustion of the fruits of actions— whether desired or evil—
due to the turbidity of the mind's objects, that state is called "destruction" (ghvasti).
The entire world is deluded by the karma of delusion;
blessed are those of great intelligence who, having cast off delusion, practice asceticism.
By whatever means possible here, whether mild or harsh, one should rescue one's own wretched self; once capable, one should practice the Dharma.
Knowledge devoid of action is like a cripple;
by it nothing is attained, nor is anything accomplished.
Thus, action devoid of knowledge is considered equal to that of a blind man;
for him, neither the path nor the goal of the path is perceived at all.
For one who performs the action that ought to be done through deed, mind, and speech,
from that very source the perfect accomplishment of desired goals arises in its entirety.
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone;
you should also perform action, having regard for the maintenance of the world.
What can even auspicious planets do against the preeminence of karma?
Though born under a *lagna* assigned by Vasiṣṭha, Jānakī was still a partaker of suffering.
Whichever lunar day (tithi) encompasses the specific time for a particular rite, one should perform that rite during it;
one should not allow the duration of the rite to be shortened or extended.
For what purpose would intelligence be required for that which is primarily characterized by action?
How could a stone possess intelligence, and from that [intelligence] how could it become a god?
For one must understand action, and one must understand improper action, and one must understand inaction; the way of action is profound.
He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions.
"This is the rule of non-action within action: that they perform various deeds with the desire to abandon their respective consequences.
"True; yet, no new bondage will arise. But what means is there for removing the bondage of the past?"
Unskilled in action, stubborn, foolish, yet imagining themselves to be wise,
these deluded ones speak flattering words with which they eagerly seek to entice others like honeyed speech.
Your entitlement is to action alone; never to its fruits.
Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.

If we were to abandon action, we would surely fall downward; if we were to perform it, we would never cross over saṃsāra. We do not understand by what intention the Vedas have proceeded with the injunctions "one should abandon action" and "one should perform action."
The world is an heir to its actions, characterized by the bonds of karma; just as actions impel one another here, so do we.

Abandoning the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*) and Brahman—which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation—these logicians merely produce some sound that results only in parching their throats.

Perception does not purify, nor do clusters of *pīlu* fruits remove sins; pervasion does not protect, nor does inference preserve, nor does the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) guard one from evil.
Just as parents are the cause for the birth obtained through one's own past actions,
so too are others the cause for the commencement of a kingdom for kings.
Having reached this land of action, one must perform whatever action is auspicious;
for fire, wind, and the moon are partakers of the fruits of actions.
O Brahmin, this world is considered the field of action, while that world is considered the field of fruition;
whatever action is performed here is experienced in the world beyond.
O night-stalker, everyone slays one who performs actions contrary to the world, just as people kill a sharp and wicked snake that has appeared.
Having attained stability as well as tranquility, a person may be able to discern: "What would be the most excellent action for me to perform?"
All the great karmas accumulated in other lifetimes are instantly burnt away in the great fire of consciousness; for can there be any moisture in a great conflagration?

Good and evil deeds bind the agent, who is indeed the *jīva* conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), but not the Supreme Witness who is free from all defects; would one eat a cowherd while the goat is lying down?
Whatever actions in the world are causes of suffering and are shameful,
all of those this living being performs, having fallen under the power of the king that is the belly.
All actions reside in delusion; all sufferings reside in poverty;
all evils reside in the state of theft; and all faults without exception reside in falsehood.
One should observe the reversal of the ripening of karma for men who, while undertaking actions for the sake of destroying suffering and attaining happiness, move in pairs.

He performs undesirable actions, becomes subject to the power of others, and feels no shame before people; he knows not dharma and adharma, abandons the teacher’s family, and serves the base. Though having been wise, of noble birth, renowned for great virtues, and a respected scholar, the embodied being here is seized by him. Drive away that enemy, Madana, who is skilled at inflicting suffering! Live! (Buḥkha-dakṣam! MSS_8943-1 karmāniṣṭaṃ vidhatte bhavati paravaśo lajjate no janānāṃ dharmādharmau na vetti tyajati gurukulaṃ sevate nīcalokam / MSS_8943-2 bhūtvā prājñaḥ kulīnaḥ prathitapṛthuguṇo mānanīyo budho'pi grasto yenātra dehī nuda madanaripuṃ jīva taṃ buḥkhadakṣam // He performs undesirable deeds, becomes dependent on others, and feels no shame before people; he does not distinguish between righteousness and unrighteousness, abandons the teacher's household, and serves the lowly. Having once been wise, well-born, possessed of celebrated and vast virtues, and honored as a learned man, the embodied soul here is devoured by him. Cast out the enemy, Madana; live, [O you] who are skilled in [overcoming] suffering! (Jīva taṃ buḥkhadakṣam!)
Afflicted by the consequences of his own karma, he thus wanders through the wilderness of saṃsāra— which is dense with the darkness of delusion— like a blind man on a treacherous path.
In all cases, the functions of qualities that are beyond perception are to be inferred from their effects;
therefore, one should discern the activity of those whose operations are imperceptible by means of their results.

Actions performed in another birth, whether good or bad, constitute destiny alone at the beginning of a new life, such as birth into a noble family; even the capacity for discipline and excellence after childhood is born of human destiny. Therefore, one should exert effort, just as in the case of agriculture.
When the destruction of sentient beings is imminent due to the transgression of their karma, injustice,
taking the form of justice, seizes hold of the intellect and persists there.
The fruit of human actions depends upon karma, and the intellect follows that karma;
nevertheless, one should be wise, acting only after careful reflection.
Like fire, it burns away the forest of karma; like a mother, it protects one from suffering; like a teacher, it speaks the correct doctrine; and like a master, it sustains one.
A mortal who is skilled in revealing truth and untruth clearly attains that pure, stainless realization through the gift of knowledge.
He who sits restraining the organs of action but continues to dwell upon the objects of the senses with his mind, being deluded in soul, is said to be a hypocrite.
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action without attachment— he is preeminent.
The fire of fasting reduces to ashes in an instant all that fuel of karma accumulated through ignorance in the forest of rebirth.
Relying upon the fuel of karma, the initiate should perform the fire-offering using the oblation of firm, authentic cultivation,
with the fire of the meditation on the Dharma.
In this regard, karma alone is the cause for both a good rebirth and a miserable one;
even in a single moment, it is karma from the past—what person indeed exists who is without action?
For those men who rush about every morning with talk of work, jesting, and worldly creations, and who constantly cry out "Wealth! Wealth!", death has been forgotten.
From the arising of karma comes existence; rooted in existence is the formation of the body.
From the body arise the sense faculties and their objects; and conditioned by those objects, there arise pleasure and pain.
Having accepted through their own reasons that an effect must undoubtedly possess the same nature as its cause,
those wretched ones— who assert that pleasure is the effect of suffering— are destroyed by their own very statement.
If one sneezes while traveling for the purpose of plowing or searching, it portends rain from the clouds;
if a new ornament made of gold or other materials is worn, it leads to the acquisition of ornaments.
He plows, sows, reaps, gambles, sews, purifies, and weaves;
what task does a person of embodied form not perform for the sake of quenching the fire of his belly?

Dragging the hems of their garments with excessive passion, embracing them, seizing their hair, scratching their lips, and crushing their breasts—even before the eyes of the Lord of the Kaliṅga realm, alas, what indeed did the women of the inner apartments not do, like rakes with their branches in a forest? "Fie! What a tragedy! they cried.
O slender-waisted one, neither the digit of the moon free from blemish nor your pair of breasts can surpass you;
therefore, when counting living beings, the name "slender-waisted" does not apply to anything other than you, for it is only you who are free from blemish and possess a slender waist.
The mango tree does not suffer when its own sprout— the weapon of Kāma to be relished by throngs of sweet-voiced cuckoos— is torn out by those who subsist on neem trees.
Another woman, having raised a vain clamor among the ornaments of the earth, reached the corner of her eye; for the third eye of the deer-eyed women descends upon the means of seeing the God of Love.

O dear friend, what can that frail woman do now, who is tormented by the sight of the full moon, the dense groves of lotuses, and the fragrance of campaka flowers, and who is further distressed by the winds that remind her of you?
With a throat filled with cooing sounds and rolling eyes, the pigeon,
desiring dalliance, circles around and kisses his beloved.
O lute with its sweet sound, cease from your tinkling; O friend cuckoo, do not be distressed—the humiliation you suffer was ordained by Brahmā himself.
O nectar, abandon your rivalry; these words of the deer-eyed woman, made delicious by contact with the honey of her lips, are bursting forth in a manner that is somehow most enchanting.
Spreading a web of threads from the moon’s light across the ocean of the sky, the fisherman Kalaṅka,
stationed upon the boat of the moon, hastens toward the western sea, desiring to quickly seize the stars that have become his fish.
Women, exceedingly fickle and shrouded in much dust, like whirlwinds, defile those who tread the path of virtue and utterly humiliate them.
Therefore, those of steadfast character and keen intellect should not be attached to them;
rather, they should practice ethical discipline in order to attain the state of one free from passion.

Even if the lord of the twice-born were free from blemish, devoid of the defect of waning, and eternally liberated from the fear of darkness, I believe that even then he would not possess the splendor of your face.
O beloved, the moon— stained with spots, a source of faults,
and cold— is never capable of rivaling your face.
The solar light, reflecting somewhere in the turbid waters,
spreads its power to dispel darkness and increases in brilliance day by day.
Let this moon, though stained with spots, burn without fear; let sandalwood paste, though entwined by serpents, act as poison;
and let the mind-born god of love himself, though already consumed, bestow intense burning. O Life-Breath of the world, why do you take away my life—is this truly appropriate for you?
Just as the moon is marred by a stain and the salt ocean by its brine,
so too does even a man possessed of knowledge appear tarnished by quarrel.
He who, casting his own wife behind him, takes pleasure in another's woman, incurs unrighteousness and calamities; for him, the fruit [of his action] ripens immediately and constantly.
For a man who is consumed by anxiety over his wife, all learning, moral conduct,
and virtues perish along with his body, like water poured into an unbaked clay pot.
Struck thus by the heavy reproach of his wife— a reversal of his own fame— the heart of the Lord of Vaidehī, already heated like iron struck by a hammer, burst asunder.
Even when some blameworthy action has been performed for the sake of wife, children, and so forth, a person of noble character, being apprehensive, censures it, thinking:
"This deed I have done is condemned by the virtuous."

With breasts upon which her silk garment was slipping due to the weight of her hips and the loosening of her girdle; with a chest where the line of body hair became distinct as the folds of skin vanished; and with a distended belly that appeared elongated and weary.
With her mass of hair hanging down in disarray and her upper arms revealed, one woman,
under the pretext of gathering flowers from the trees, respectfully captivated the mind of her lord.
Wife, self, friends, and wealth become useless here in the mere twinkling of an eye;
since these are repeatedly agitated, the wise man should not engage in excessive strife.
The longing of beautiful-eyed women to grasp their own breasts— exhausted by the distress of being plundered by their husbands— is like the eagerness of the wise to preserve their lost wealth.
O young elephant, never treat with contempt this bee that has come into your presence;
for it is one who must be borne upon the head even by the best of elephants, beautiful in their gift of rut.
What is the use of wealth to a scribe who has seized the entire world with his pen, who is as black as ink,
and who stands on the verge of imprisonment?
The *kalama* tree, its head weighed down by the excessive burden of its fruit,
bent slowly as if to inhale the nearby blue lotus that had emerged from it.
May the chief courtesan, whose voice is sweet and passionate like a black bee, languid with wine upon her couch and full of passion,
wait upon you with the *vaktra* and *aparavaktra* meters.
The *kalamā* rice stalks, bent down by ripening and fragrant with the scent of *kalhāra* lilies smelled at their bases,
generally offer praise for their fragrance as their heads sway in the breeze.
Under the guise of ink-drops emerging from the tip of the pen, with teardrops mixed with collyrium,
Royal Fortune weeps as if exhausted while being plundered by the scribes.

Where young men, having uttered "O lotus, remember me! and placed their lotus-hands upon the reflected faces of their ruby-loving mistresses standing there, became the recipients of silent laughter within the crystal forest.
She compares the likeness of her eyes to lotuses and proclaims the similarity of her speech to the essence of nectar;
tell me, friend, what shall I do? O beloved, the only fault that has arisen there is my own endurance.
Does that tree not always attain fruitfulness and even great abundance of fruit,
for whom no one— even an adversary— is anything other than a partisan when it comes to performing service for others?

Her curved cast of sidelong glances emulates the grace of a garland of blue water-lilies; her lower lip possesses the charm of a tender sprout, and her face bears the splendor of the moon, the treasury of arts.
It makes my bed feel like glowing coals; it sets my limbs ablaze, though they are smeared with sandalwood and cooled by moonlight.
The darkness born of delusion obscures my eyes, and Love, with his many distorted transformations, torments me.
Let that wretched crane practice the graceful gait of a swan in the lake;
how could he ever possess the maturity required for the discernment between water and milk?
"Put on your bracelets, place jasmine flowers in this braid, arrange your garment, and quickly adorn yourself with a pearl necklace.
Apply a paste of musk and leaf-patterns to your cheeks, O companion; your beloved has arrived this morning."
Friend, why do you favor the beautiful science of rhetoric?
Here, observe the mutual exchange of speech and reply, like the frequent falling of weapons upon one another.
With a single digit of the moon before it, the sky— its mass of darkness momentarily thinned out like matted hair—
was not falsely perceived by the people for a moment as the form of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
If even a small portion of this divine life were to be revealed here,
then in that [revelation] too, there would be a vast, radiant, and peaceful illumination.

I perceive her lower lip to be a tender sprout; I suspect her pair of hands to be a lotus; I consider the body of the slender maiden—so uniquely enchanting to the eyes—to be the staff of the Mind-born God.
O beloved, in this amorous dalliance filled with the warbling of sweet-voiced cuckoos and the soft cooing of sweet-throated pigeons, I long to behold your face with its eyes half-closed.

Does the quality of causing the wheel to whirl, produced by its own cause—the stick—reside within the jar? For it is that very quality, manifesting in her high breasts, which creates the illusion of a whirling circle of streams of light.
"May there never be a quarrel"—thinking thus, Śiva and Śivā, who have attained oneness of body, fell into a dispute over my protection, each crying, "I am [the protector]! I am [the protector]!"

Excessive attachment to wealth is like the Vindhya mountains for the young elephants of quarrels, a cremation ground for the vultures of anger, a hole for the serpents of calamity, and the onset of night for the bandits of hatred; it is a forest fire for the grove of merit, a wind for the clouds of gentleness, and frost for the lotuses of the eyes.
Out of shame during their quarrel, the fair-browed woman bent her face down and pulled her bodice over it to conceal the rising of her horripilation;
yet immediately thereafter, the seams of the garment on her breasts suddenly and sharply burst from within, revealing her longing for her beloved.
One who is fond of quarreling, excessively tall, or short; one who is dark, yellow, or greenish;
one with drooping lips, a small nose, and small, flaccid breasts—such a woman is [inauspicious].
Under the sway of liquor, one instigates quarrels by which he here casts away his life;
he abandons virtue, accumulates impurity, loses his wealth, and is held in contempt by people.
MSS_8999-1: From this point forward, there is the lamentation of a woman separated by a quarrel, as well as the instruction of the hero;
MSS_8999-2: the manifestation of sexual enjoyment, the unchaste woman, and the mixed [love]—these constitute the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
MSS_9000-1 Mansions end in quarrels; friendship ends in harsh words. MSS_9000-2 Kingdoms end with bad kings; the fame of men ends with evil deeds.
Fools quarrel over who will be the guarantor for tomorrow morning;
yet on this very night, who can be the guarantor for one's own existence?
I worship that digit of the moon by which my father, the lord of the sea monsters,
having ascended the head of Hara, was established at the summit of the three worlds.
All the *kalās* (portions), including the Prajāpatis, belong to Hari alone;
these are portions of the parts of the Supreme Person (*puṃsaḥ*), but Kṛṣṇa is the Blessed Lord himself.
Great-souled beings, though endowed with a full array of arts, do not turn their backs on one who has helped them, just as peacocks do not turn away from a lake.
The passage of time— consisting of *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, and *muhūrtas*—
moving with such speed that its divisions cannot be perceived, is like the movement of the flame of a lamp.

May the Beloved of the Gopīs be for your prosperity— He whose form is charming with the playful illusion of artistic grace, who is delightful with the sound of his sweet-sounding flute, and who, resting in the heart, agitates the three worlds.

Like a gallant man, the moon—possessing its digits as ornaments, curved, with the glow of its rising hue shimmering like a flushed lip, and possessing a fresh body—kisses the young women whose passion for pride is melting away;
it kisses their firm orb-like hips, their bud-like eyes, their petal-like lips, their cheeks, their necks, and their jar-like breasts.

"O you who possess the status of the lord of the arts, why do you harbor pride, thinking 'I am without a second' after having attained [only] the second? O lady, believe my words: this one here desires to attain the third."
Sent by the night-lily at evening to bring the Lord of the Arts (the moon),
has the bee been embraced with passion in the moon's lap, that it spreads the illusion of being its dark spot?
Fortune arises simply from the acquisition of the arts;
however, their application may or may not be possible, depending upon the place and time.
The Lord of the Arts (the Moon) passionately loves Kāma, whose body is marked by many defects; yet does she not feel attraction for him as well?
Does the lotus plant not find joy even when her beloved, the hot-rayed sun, rises? Generally, the heart of the deer-eyed woman does not take account of faults.
From contact with the moon, the repository of digits, her pupils become clear and radiant;
as she gazes upon the deep blue sky, the night acts like a passionate woman.
This moon, a treasure-house of digits, having personally perceived the form of the sun at the close of day, was instantly filled with passion and touched the lotus;
seeing it closed up due to contact with the hand of another man, his beloveds surely laughed, and for that reason he became pale.
The flocks of peacocks, having endured the arrival of thick clouds, attain beauty;
the charms of the peacocks, whose arrival of thick clouds has been dispelled by the wind, pass away.
A courtesan who is elevated by her arts and endowed with beauty, character,
and virtue receives the title of "gaṇikā" and a place in the assembly of people.
If the moon were to give up its digit, the giver of rays, and the cloud were to give up its stream of rain,
then how would the world survive?
The jewel of the arts is song; the jewel of the sky is the sun; the jewel of the assembly is the learned man; the jewel of the ears is the story of Hari;
the jewel of the night is the moon; the jewel of the bed is the moon-faced woman; and the jewel of the earth is the illustrious Raghunātha, the best of kings—may he be victorious!
For one possessed of artistry, that very art is what subdues worldly existence;
and what is the use of many arts by which only a mere mark is displayed?
