When the moon—possessing artistic grace, dispelling darkness, powerful, rising clearly, and delighting the eyes of people—was present, women going to meet their lovers looked at it with anger; for sometimes even one who is exceedingly handsome becomes ill-favored.
O Kalāvati, you should not cast a flickering glance again and again;
for an arrow, even when lodged, does not cause as much pain as it does when it is moved.
The limit of art is poetry; the limit of all virtues is generosity; the limit of fear is death; the limit of all happiness is a fair-faced woman;

the limit of austerity is liberation; the limit of all undertakings is supporting those who depend on one; the limit of joy for a beloved is the delight of hearing the stories of Hari, which is the limit of all pleasant things to hear.
Art, service, then dharma and wealth, followed by the paths of craving and poverty;
contentment, patience, compassion, detachment, and thereafter praise.
You possess those various arts perfectly since you are the lord of the twice-born, and your brilliance is such, as is your recent birth in the family of the ocean;
what more need we say? You are the crest-jewel of Śiva, yet all that of yours, O Moon, has been rendered fruitless by your spot.
For one distressed by the exhaustion of maintaining a family agitated by the perils of the impurities of the Kali age,
travel abroad is like a representative substitute for the ocean of bliss that comes from detachment from worldly existence.
When one's own mind is defiled by the Kali age, how can the world attain straightforwardness?
While a defect in the eye persists, how could the appearance of two moons ever cease?
Until this very day of the Kali age, even the mind of the sage Agastya is shattered here by her who resembles the crescent of the moon.

Her hips have acquired weight, her waist displays three deep folds, modesty arises in her heart while her long-standing fickleness sinks away; her chest bears budding breasts and her eyes have assumed a slight coquettishness—her body, with childhood gradually slipping away, spreads forth its splendor.

O friend, the moon— measuring the sky with its rays, pressing against the breasts that are the calyxes of crushed lotuses, and gazing with eyes that are blooming blue lilies— renders the night as delightful as a lake.
If one performs beautiful ritual acts while being devoid of passion, how can there be any fruit?
When the lotus-eyed Lord is remembered in the heart, He bestows His grace; therefore, one's exertion becomes fruitful.

Illuminating the interior of the forest on the banks of the Kalinda mountain’s beloved daughter (the Yamunā), always removing the heavy burden of fatigue from the coming and going of living beings on the path,
and enveloped by hundreds of rows of creepers, may that Tamāla tree, endowed with a sweet luster, quickly remove my exhaustion most completely.
Half-submerged in the mass of water from the Yamunā, the cranes cry out loudly with incessant clamor;
I imagine them to be the young colts of the moon, wailing as they are being swallowed by the darkness out of enmity.
When King Kali has arrived, dharma on earth behaves like adharma; alas, adharma is sought by men everywhere as if it were dharma.
Seeing Kali approaching, even the gods dissolve;
what then can be said of the dharma and other virtues dependent upon them, let alone their continued existence?
In one night it becomes a *kalila*, and in five nights a *budbuda*;
in one fortnight it becomes an *aṇḍaka*, and when the month is complete, the head and the trunk are formed.
Having entered the empire of Kali, one need not fear the cycle of rebirth;
for those of us deluded regarding the practice of Dharma, only fear remains.
If water should become turbid, bitter, salty, tasteless, or foul-smelling,
it becomes, by means of this [jewel], pure, flavorful, fragrant, and endowed with other excellent qualities.

O Lord of Kings, your eye—possessing a splendor like that of a white lotus—has suddenly become turbid toward your enemies; and clearly, by its sidelong glances, calamities have fallen upon their bodies.
At present, water everywhere is turbid yet sweet,
just like the deceitful speech of a person who is not upright.
At the end of the Kali age, Rākṣasas will appear in human form;
they will devour men by means of their wealth, not by means of their bodies.
O King, in this Kali age, which is a treasury of faults, there is indeed one great virtue:
by the mere fame of Kṛṣṇa, one who is liberated from bondage shall go to the supreme state.
In this terrible Kali age, one finds no happiness even for two fortnights during a time of conflict;
moreover, neutrality is even censured on all sides—alas, such is the power of the Kali age!
In this degenerate age, when friends are wicked, sons are addicted to evil vices, thieves have multiplied, and the king is greedy— what is the use of wealth?
"In the Kali age, the divine Gaṅgā at Kāśī, the city of the Destroyer of Tripura, is praised and remains worthy of service even for the gods every day.

Thus speaks Vyāsa, the foremost among sages, who is established in well-being through drinking the nectar of the stories of Hari, whose bonds of worldly existence have dissolved, and who possesses incomparable intelligence.
O Maitreya, in the Kali age, people afflicted by heresy will not worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, the Sovereign, and the Creator of all.
In the Kali age, at ten thousand years [remaining], Hari abandons the earth;
for half that time, the waters of the Jāhnavī [remain], and for half of that, the village deities.
In the Kali age, those whose minds are defiled have no authority for dharma other than this:
by constantly chanting with reverence the two syllables "Rā-ma," a living being attains liberation.
May Kalkī, whose radiant splendor blazes forth, remove the impurity of the world; may he be a comet for the destruction of the evils manifested by the destruction of the Vedas.
By him, having raised his sword-blade for a moment like smoke and slain the barbarians who desire defilement, the Kali age was shattered and the Age of Truth (Satyayuga) brought about.

Though you are but one, you are perceived as many: day after day, you are envisioned by the Brahmins as the wish-fulfilling tree of the world; you are long contemplated in the hearts of passionate women as the God of Love; you are meditated upon with love by Śrī as none other than the illustrious Nārāyaṇa; and you are regarded by the lords of the earth as Time itself.
This work has been fashioned from the dust, water, fire, and space belonging to the Kalpataru, the Kāmadogdhrī cow, the Cintāmaṇi gem, Dhanada, and the Śaṅkha jewel.
The wish-fulfilling tree produces only what is imagined; the cow of plenty milks only what is desired;
the thought-gem grants only what is thought of; for the company of the virtuous indeed brings forth everything.
When the Creator, bestowing prosperity upon the wicked, placed wish-fulfilling trees where people have no desires, jewels on Mount Sumeru, and [the waters] in the deep-sea lord of rivers,
he has indeed set a most brilliant lamp within a common clay pot.
The wish-fulfilling trees and the virtuous do not deserve to be placed on an equal footing,
because the former bear fruit only when requested by those in need, whereas the latter bear fruit spontaneously.
Of what use are the wish-fulfilling trees standing on the Golden Mountain, which are rendered useless by their dependence on receiving the favor of others?
Better is the *karīra* tree growing on the desert path, which brings fulfillment to the caravan of travelers.
The wish-fulfilling tree does not know [what to give], nor does Bṛhaspati;
but this Lord of the World both knows and gives.
If even the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) were not to yield fruit at the proper time,
what distinction would there then be between it and other wild trees?
You are the wish-granting tree even to the wish-granting tree, and the jewel even to the greatest of jewels;
you are worthy of worship even by the gods—how much more so for me? What could possibly satisfy you?
That quality by which one provides for one's livelihood and by which one is praised by the virtuous in the assembly—
by that quality, the possessor of virtue should both increase it and protect it.
One should have one's hair, beard, body hair, and nails trimmed one by one;
however, a superior person should not do so with his own teeth or with his own hands.
O woman of unblemished beauty, the moon, filled with eager curiosity, now seems intent on counting the strings of pearl necklaces with its rays shimmering upon the tops of the wish-fulfilling trees.
Life does not endure for an eon, nor is the sovereignty one desires ever attained;
yet the world still performs what ought not to be done—aiming at what, then?

May that certain Kāpālika bestow welfare upon us— he whose cruel sport ends the eon, who brings about the destruction of sacrifices, whose splendor is like jasmine and camphor, who sports on the peak of Kailāsa, who has made himself the lover of the night-lotuses, whose body is beautiful, who is eager to play with skeletons, who has raised a tumultuous roar, whose wife is Kālakālī, and whose throat is as dark as the Yamunā.
Let the winds at the end of the aeon blow, let the oceans become one, and let the twelve suns scorch; for one who is free from the mind, there is no injury.
For those very qualities of stability, clarity, and constancy belong to the great ocean alone, which has leaped over all mountains during the upheaval at the end of an eon.

May the roars protect you—those roars of the wrathful conqueror of Tripura as he wanders at the end of the eon for sport; though he has made all species of living beings guests within the cavity of his own mouth, he finds no satisfaction.
Seeing the walls of the quarters empty, he feels a rage born of the fruitless effort of swallowing his own form, which was previously seen by the ocean of dissolution during the cataclysm.

May the Great Bhairava, who has assumed the role of a fisherman, destroy the delusion of the virtuous—he who, at the end of the aeon, has bound the great skeleton of Śiva (Trivikrama) once his three strides were stilled; who has impaled the flesh of the Primeval Boar upon the claws of the Nṛsiṃha’s hand, which was sewn together with the quivering serpent Śeṣa; and who drags along both the Fish and the Tortoise, who rejoice in their identity as the single universal ocean.
Why is this mind of yours so drenched with the sweat of anxiety over what action might be performed?
For those who behold it, merit alone—drawn from previous existences—leads them through the worlds; what else could it be?
"O companion, what auspicious thing shall I tell you? Previously, in our private moments, you constantly addressed me by the name 'Mistress of the Life of the Enemy of Mura.
Yet here I am; out of fear that my love might be destroyed, even though I have seen the Lord's messenger, I ask nothing at all, being filled with doubt as to whether I have been sent with a message."
O charcoal-maker, brother, what greater blessing could there be for us than this livelihood, that you cut down trees from here and burn them?
But alas, what remedy is there for travelers distressed by sunbeams as fierce as lightning in this shelterless desert wilderness?

"May auspiciousness be envisioned for the flocks of cuckoos; may the desires of the swans be fulfilled; may there be the rising of the full moon; may there be well-being for the blue lotus"—uttering such words of her weeping bride, the lover, who had prepared his equipment for departure, was vehemently restrained by his friend standing nearby, who completed those phrases word by word.

What fault could there be in composing poetry that includes the erotic, heroic, and other sentiments—provided it is based on the auspicious narrative of the Blessed One and is fashioned as an integral part of that very work? For what poet inclined toward composition would not resort to the path observed in the works of Vyāsa, Vālmīki, and the Vedas?
May your auspicious fame spread; may your righteousness ever increase; may your prosperity expand; may your subjects bow down; may the destruction of your enemies occur.
May your speech be consistent; may your body be radiant; may the Lord of Lakṣmī be pleased; may you live for a hundred autumns; and may you be victorious through giving for the sake of long life.
May there be auspiciousness for him who is like a peerless ornament to the flock of cuckoos, by whom the entire world—tormented by the harsh howling of jackals—is comforted with sweet notes;

[notes] which overflow with a flood of bliss born from the experience of the essence of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), shining forth through the awakening of the great sound that has arisen from extreme and constant practice.

May the drawing of the bowstring of the Destroyer of Tripura bring you auspiciousness—those drawstrings which are like creeping vines, upon which the women of the gods and the serpents stand with their joined hands as hammers; which are adorned with garlands of fresh kalpavṛkṣa flowers and serpent-strings tossed about by them; and which cause the eyes of Śiva’s forehead to close from the streams of honey flowing from the lotus-palms of Lakṣmī as she embraces his shaft.

May that ancient jewel of an elephant bring you auspiciousness—he who makes the quarters of the horizon resonant with the clamor of bees sporting in the garlands of restless waves of the ichor-river flowing from his temples; he whose jeweled serpent ornaments, their hoods spread wide in a roar of joy, desire to seize the sprouts of wind arising from his constantly flapping ears.
In the Vīra [rāga], the *dhruvaka* should be auspicious and have Candraśekhara as its name;
therein, words consisting of two syllables are prescribed for the *tripuṭa* meter.
In the rhythmic cycle known as Tripuṭa, there is a pair of short syllables followed by a pair of long syllables.
I pay homage to the Lord Śrījñānanandana, who is a beautiful tree and grove, the Himalayan mountain for the Gaṅgā of sacred learning, and the sun for the lotuses of wisdom.
She who always shares in auspiciousness in every undertaking and increases all good fortune—
such a wife is indeed a goddess, not a mere human being.
May the Boar of Illusion bring us auspiciousness— he in whose every pore and upon the very limits of his bones,
the entire earth appears as he lovingly supports it, like a manifestation of the *sāttvika* emotion known as perspiration.
May the body of Śiva and Śivā bring you auspiciousness— she whose dark-complexioned base of the throat,
even on the side opposite the white one, creates the suspicion that it is the very beginning of the transformation into the daughter of the mountain.
What word here is as lovely as your auspicious speech, O virtuous king? Who else like you brings such complete satisfaction?
Who always possesses a bull-like gait like yours, being excessively supported by prosperity while protecting all living beings? Tell me.
The virtuous person, however, makes their speech fruitful according to their ability;
the deceitful person, out of a desire for gain, wavers between both sides.
The king was devoted to what is auspicious and beneficial, a protector of his teachers' shortcomings,
equanimous in pleasure and pain, and one who never fled from battle.
One who is perfected in family and conduct, wise in the principles of policy and dharma, is likewise honored by the king; such a person is proclaimed as "four-cornered" (caturasra).
O fair-faced one, he by whom you—whose mind is enamored by the luster of your auspicious limbs—are sought after, and for whose sake you prepare even to renounce your life;
that very man, O beautiful one, has his chest pierced by the arrows of the five-arrowed god (Kāma) and his thick breasts pressed at will within the cage of your vine-like arms.
O Lord of universal form, you are the vessel of auspicious splendors; therefore, O God, be gracious and bestow upon me abundantly the preeminent fortune.
O Lord of the world, cast away whatever sin belongs to me who bows before you; grant me every blessing, O Blessed One, for the sake of supreme well-being.

May the name of Rāma—which is a treasure-trove of all that is auspicious, a crusher of the impurities of the Kali age, a purifier among purifiers, and the provisions for the seeker of liberation who has set out immediately for the attainment of the supreme state; which is the sole place of rest for the words of the best of poets, the life-breath of the virtuous, and the seed of the tree of Dharma—bring about your prosperity.
May Gaṇapati grant you auspicious blessings—he, when pleased, causes even Brahmā to shrink back from exercising power over even the most trivial task;
he, through the arising of whose fortune and good luck, made easily attainable by prostrating at his feet, even the sovereignty of the Lord of the Gods enters the lap of a pauper without restraint.

May the coils of the creeping vines upon the garden-trees of the matted locks of the Wielder of the Axe (Śiva)—coils encircled by rows of writhing serpents and glowing with a crimson luster—be for your welfare;
may they be so, as the moon is reddened by the waves of the celestial river (Gaṅgā), which are grey with the pollen falling from the mass of filaments within the blossoming golden lotus buds.
O auspicious lady, having sprinkled your body with sandalwood juices, you should somehow pass these two or three days;
placing you on my lap and embracing you with both arms, I shall turn even the rays of the sun into coolness.
O auspicious lady, it is not fitting to release these pearls that have fallen upon your hand without reflection;
for here, as they roll about, it is merely the radiance produced by your lotus-like hands and your lotus-like eyes that creates the illusion of pearls.
"Truly auspicious is this worldly verse that occurs to me:
'Joy comes to a living man even after a hundred years.'"

May that certain deity named Rāma— whose limit is the splendor of auspiciousness, who is as delightful as a dark rain-cloud, whose dwelling is Sāketa, whose prostrations remove the exhaustion of wandering through the thicket of worldly existence,

who puts even Kāma to shame with his beauty, whose abode is the affectionate side-glances of Janaka’s daughter, whose greatness is renowned in all directions, and who is praised by the gods— bestow well-being upon us.
Always intent on rising at dawn, she was devoted to serving her teacher;
she kept the house well-swept and smeared it with cow dung.

This fragment of the moon—the ornament of the world—acts as a lotus stalk for the celestial river upon the head of the Destroyer of Tripura tossed by the waves; it is a mass of camphor powder and the handle of the wine-vessel for the wife of the Flower-Arrowed God. To whom does it not bring joy within, like a drop of water upon a petal of the sky-lotus belonging to the Lord of the Milk Ocean?
Fortune is as fickle as a surging wave; associations are like dreams;
and youth is like a tuft of cotton tossed about by a whirlwind.
O abode of sea-monsters, do not despise these jewels because of the harsh blows from stones tossed by the surging waves;
was not even Puruṣottama himself made to stretch out his hand in supplication to you for the sake of the Kaustubha gem?
What is the use of those lords of rivers whose waters are unfathomable, surging with waves, yet remain restless and undrinkable?
May this mountain torrent, though its body is worn away, be victorious; for even by its single drop, the thirsty are satisfied.
O Ocean, covering the faces of all directions with waves that pierce the clouds, you roar day and night with your salt water and never rest.
If Fate had made you sweet instead of this abode of terrible crocodiles, I do not know what you would have done—perhaps even more mischievous antics with your own restless movements.
Let this ocean scatter the great mountains with its surging waves, or deafen the quarters of the sky with the sounds arising from the play of its shores, and let it assume vast proportions;
yet what comparison can the ocean, despite its grand display, have with a small lake that cuts through the excessive thirst of travelers whose bodies are scorched by the heat of the sun?
Let poets compose their verses; let the people of the South indeed be full of flavor, even when they have eaten oil.
Yet, the eyes of does, though flickering with their pupils, are not equal to the side-glances of a woman with intoxicating eyes.
The poets such as Kālidāsa and others are poets, and we here are also poets;
for both a mountain and an atom possess the nature of being a real entity (*vastutva*).
Do the poets not see this? Or do the crows not eat it?
What do women not do? What do those who drink liquor not say?
What do poets not see? What do crows not eat? What do drunkards not prattle? And what do women not do?
Poets alone are delighted by the eloquent verses of poets, and no others; for wells do not swell with the beauty of the moon like the great ocean.
Neither the suffering of poverty nor the words of malicious people gnaw at his heart, nor do they cause an itch in his ears,
for he here engages in the contemplation of poetry— which vomits forth honey— while enjoying the fragrance of the assembly of excellent poets.
When the King of Pandits composes poetry, other learned men compose as well;
when the wielder of the Pināka bow dances, other spirits and vetālas dance too.
O poet, tell me: where are they, what are they like, and what is known everywhere as being hard?
Now, leaving aside which ones, does intense heat prevail in the hearts of your enemies' wives?
O Cakora bird, you swallow the rays of the moon; surely you are devouring glowing coals incessantly. What is it that you perceive here as being even more intensely hot than these two?

"Here a lotus stalk has been swallowed; here a water-lily bud has been seen; indeed, here in the heart of a night-lily, cool water has been drunk"—thus does the wretched female *cakravāka* bird lament at night as she wanders along the bank, abandoned by her mate.
The poet composes poems, and the connoisseur tastes their flavor;
the husband knows the firmness of his lover’s breasts, not her father.
The poet composes poems, but the scholar alone knows their sweetness;
even the husband knows the beauty of his wife, not her father.
The poet composes verses, but it is the superior person who cherishes them;
the tree produces flowers, but the wind carries their fragrance.
The poet is her father who nourishes her, the connoisseur is her husband who protects her,
and those possessed of discernment are surely the siblings of the young maiden that is poetry.
The poet produces poems; the virtuous cherish them in their hearts. The ocean produces pearls; the breasts of young women bear them.
What is the use of composing poetry for kings if poets do not obtain their full desires? What is the use of the eyes of deer-eyed women if young men are not beheld by them?
I offer my salutation to Māgha, who causes the jasmine flower of poetry to bloom, who has conquered the heat of the common people, and who has shattered the most formidable evils.
To whose heart, possessed of consciousness, does poetry and the woman not bring delight? For their essence indeed seems to dance everywhere at all times.
The wretched man, devoid of fame, does not hear poetry at all;
what can a eunuch do even when a gazelle-eyed woman stands before him?
The Creator has placed poetry, song, pleasant speech, and truth upon her throat;
under the pretext of marking these with three lines, He has divided the boundaries for their residence.
For those whose hearts have long been completely surrendered to the power of aesthetic relish (*rasa*) through the constant immersion in hearing the unfolding of poetic compositions—
does there not arise for them a delight, or even a passion, for the sweetness emanating from the lips of the celestial damsels nourished by nectar?
Poetic skill, excellent health, great intelligence, being beloved by women, the acquisition of gold,
truthfulness toward all, and honor among one's own kin— these, it is said, are the signs of those who dwell in heaven.
For the power of poetry has descended from heaven to earth like a shower of nectar due to the merit of the noble; the gods have arrived as eager poets to reclaim their own property once more.
Poetic skill in a flower made of gold, fragrance in a golden blossom, generosity in wealth, sweetness in the fruit of a most poisonous tree,
nobility in one of high birth, the application of red dye in musk, scholarship in sovereignty, and human speech in the mouth of a cuckoo— [these are all rare].
The mark produced by a poet’s creative imagination does not become faulty even when applied elsewhere;
for what indeed cannot be achieved by those who have mastered themselves through the accomplishment of their desired goals?
Like a courtesan, the speech of poets— which captivates with its various ornaments— is made a tool for the benefit of others through greed for royal service.
Like the intellect of a poet, abundant in iron (or: full of worldly desire), with its wheel well-fashioned;
like the hour of dawn, accompanied by smokeless fire; like the form of Hara, she shines, laughing.
Salutation to that perpetrator of violence who steals an entire composition, while the poet merely mimics a shadow by taking a single word, a single foot, or even half a verse.
The poet Amaraka, the poet Acala, the poet Abhinanda, and Kālidāsa—
other poets are merely monkeys who possess only the fickleness of their steps.
O tongue, rejoice and expand upon these five or six great excellences of the poet Ravi; why do you falter, being unable to proclaim them all?
Even though the Creator counts them by means of a garland of days, even that Blessed One never finds their end.
The utterances of one devoid of a poet result only in the parching of the throat;
but if a poet is present before one, even a mere father of a clan becomes as a father of the poetic lineage.
Only a poet understands the skill of another poet in the craft of poetry;
only Śeṣa, the serpent king, knows the full extent of the earth's burden.
The poet Bhāradvāja— whose fame remains awake until the end of the world, and who is a connoisseur intent upon the essential practice of the succession of aesthetic flavors (rasas)—
is such that the majesty of his compositions, consisting of abundant bliss, brings about the awakening of the hearts of those who appreciate beauty.
Only those kings whose bodies of fame are thoroughly purified by bathing in the sacred waters of the nectar of the poets' words truly live; all others are dead in vain.
MSS_9118-1 He who is invincible in the science of poetry, like another Rākṣasa; MSS_9118-2 the renowned poet Rākṣasa, who resides in Dakṣiṇa and has attained excellence.
I bow here to Śrī Harṣa, who bestows excellence upon poets by raining down radiant, faultless, and heart-gladdening speech; who utterly subdues the wicked and rivals the very god of joy.
Absence of envy in the hearts of poets, freedom from staining in musk-paste,
lack of saltiness in the ocean, and scholarship in kings.
He who is the teacher of poets, scholars, and the generous, whose wisdom is proficient in various scriptures— that Śivanātha is saluted.
How could there not be pain for the wicked man, whose ears are pierced by the well-spoken words of great poets, which indicate other hidden meanings?
I bow to the mind of poets, wherein the fourteen worlds float like flocks of swans upon the waters of their creative intuition.
O Hero, that you bring about the death of these three—poets’ distress, wandering everywhere, and misfortune—is not at all surprising;
yet, you have rendered the four Vedas ninefold, and you have reduced even a hundred thousand enemy troops, though they were joined by ten million, to nothing.
The pride of poets surely vanished because of the *Vāsavadattā*,
just as the pride of the sons of Pāṇḍu vanished when their spear came within the range of Karṇa's sight.
I bow to Vālmīki, the moon among poets, whose story of Rāma the virtuous gather like cakora birds do the moonlight.
First, the courtyards of the lords of poets were fragrant with the scent of rut from elephants agitated by swarming bees;
later, the glances of King Rudra fell upon them—glances that were companions to the vast waves surging from the Ocean of Milk.
Only those who are treasuries of knowledge rejoice in the diversions of the words of great poets, and no others;
for only moonstones ever melt from the rays of the moon, and never other stones.

To you who remain silent while expressing through limbs that bristle with horripilation the poet’s intention— which lies beyond the reach of words and flashes forth solely within these tender verses— this salutation is made with joined palms.
The sky, struck on all sides by lightnings like golden whips,
seemed to be in pain with the thundering roar within it.
And what man of the kṣatriya caste would abandon direct perception— which is certain— and practice a dharma that is based on the future, characterized by doubt, and lacking definition?

A certain man, bewildered by the stroke of a weapon, having regained consciousness, turned back from the combat despite his friend’s loud cries; he abandoned his life—what then is the pursuit of worldly custom?
Someone whirled a play-lotus, its stalk grasped by both hands, which caused bees to buzz as they struck its trembling petals and gathered a circle of pollen within its interior.
One cloud scatters a painful mass of hailstones; another roars excessively and hurls forth the fire of lightning;
yet another produces a swift wind. Therefore, O bird, understand this first: why do you open your beak toward every single rain-cloud?
A certain person may be the sole friend and vessel of trust for another;
the sun causes the lotus to bloom, yet it causes the night-lily to close.
A certain Yakṣa, having neglected his duty and being overcome by a curse from his master to endure for one year—a curse heavy with separation from his beloved—had his greatness eclipsed;
he made his dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri, where the trees cast cool shade and the waters were sanctified by the baths of Janaka’s daughter.
In one place someone wails, "Alas, alas! My son! upon seeing his excellent child suddenly snatched away and destroyed by the cruel hands of Time;
in another place someone dances, surrounded by male and female dancers—oh, how strange! This path of worldly existence spreads both joy and misery for us.
Someone crosses a very deep great river by means of a log;
he carries that log across, and he is carried across by the log.
Have you ever seen, heard of, or even suspected anyone—
whether on earth or in heaven— for whom death does not exist?
A certain lover, having fallen into poverty, arranged for courtesans to provide hospitality for other men by means of his accumulated wealth.

A certain traveler, afflicted by thirst while journeying on the road during the summer season, asked another traveler with joyful absorption: "Tell me, O wayfarer, where is the flow of the daughter of Jahnu?

To him, that excellent Brahmin, whose mind was agitated, replied with rapid speech: "On the tip of a needle there is a cluster of six wells; above that is a city, and there flows the stream of the Gaṅgā."
When some man hurls harsh words at me, I attain joy by becoming an ornament of forbearance;
yet I fall into grief again, thinking, "Alas, because of me, this poor man has stumbled from his virtuous conduct."
Someone who, having cut down a mango grove, plants *palāśa* trees—
greedy for fruit upon seeing the flowers— will grieve when the time for the fruit arrives.
A certain wicked person may possess beauty due to the excellence of his physical form, yet he bears no true luster,
like dark collyrium applied to the eyes of a woman.
O Saumitri, what man would venture to fight against destiny,
for which no cause other than past action is ever observed?
O son of Sumitrā, what person would venture to fight with destiny,
against whom no means of resistance exists here in this world?
A certain man, his head severed by an enemy’s sword, immediately attained mastery over a celestial chariot;
with a divine maiden clinging to his left side, he beheld his own headless trunk dancing in the midst of battle.
Although his hand remained in its proper place, as if it had overstepped its own position,
he moved one finger— the hollow of which was filled with rays of diamonds— toward his crown.
One is capable of composing speech, while another is able only to hear it; your auspicious intellect causes us wonder in both respects.
For the collection of excellences does not reside in one place: one stone produces gold, while another is capable of testing it.
One person takes a fresh sprout, another takes flowers, and another takes fruits;
yet, during this terrible summer season, there is no one at all to provide water for its root.
One friend is like a garland; one friend is like a balance scale;
one friend is like Mount Meru; and one friend is like the earth.

A certain celestial woman, having fainted after being struck severely, was revived by the cool spray from the elephant's trunk; as she set out, desiring to seize him, she fainted again, her intentions rendered futile.
What noble man would kiss the sprout-like lip of a courtesan, however charming it may be, for it is but a spittoon for the saliva of soldiers, thieves, servants, actors, and libertines?
To King Mīraśāha, who desired to go to Kaśmīra,
King Śāhābuddīna dispatched a messenger with this message:

Why do you, like a young deer, desire to wander with such fearless and restless steps? Desist! This forest is by no means empty; here stands a lion, his magnificent mane radiant with the mass of blood-sprays splashing from the crushing of the leader of an elephant herd.
The soul, turbid with the passions and its mind colored by attachment,
sinks in the ocean of existence consisting of the four states of rebirth, like a shattered boat.
Perform the sacrifice ordained by the wise, using tainted sacrificial animals that destroy virtue, pleasure, and wealth, and which have been neutralized by the mantra of tranquility.
Conduct that has been described as free from passion undergoes corruption when passion increases;
when a person’s passion subsides, then that conduct becomes pure once again.
O messenger, your lower lip speaks words of astringent passion, yet it is devoid of desire; your dwelling place and your throat region are likewise—have you perhaps become a female renunciant?
In the victory over the passions and in the restraint of the senses,
there arises for the self that supreme excellence which shatters the cycle of existence.
For embodied beings afflicted by the objects of the defilements, there is no peace;
yet for those who desist from them, a most wonderful happiness arises.
That in which the renunciation of fermented acids, sensual objects, and solid food is prescribed should be known as *upavāsa* (fasting); the rest they know as *laṅghanaka* (lightening therapy).
One who has eyes moist with compassion does not tolerate the attachment to worldly desires nor the dust of the day;
therefore, sages endowed with right conduct always shake off both the attachment to desires and the dust.
One should view the passions as enemies and sense objects as poison; likewise, the wise have declared that delusion is the supreme disease.
The passions, sense objects, activities, negligence, lack of restraint, as well as false view, and the *ārta* and *raudra* meditations— these are the causes for the inauspicious.

Those who seek liberation must destroy the passions (*kaṣāya*), as well as their concomitants, and the secondary passions (*nokaṣāya*), which have become like a stream obstructing the path to auspiciousness (*śiva*).
Having declared that the recovery of men brought about by decoctions and fasts was actually achieved by his own medicine,
the physician takes away their wealth.
The dull-witted person turns away from what ought to be done, thinking, "Action is painful"; yet no higher good is attained without undertaking bold effort.
Alas, folly is indeed miserable; alas, poverty in youth is indeed miserable;
but more miserable than even the most miserable are dwelling in another's house and living abroad.
Foolishness is indeed painful, and youth is indeed painful;
but living in another's house is even more painful than pain itself.
Alas, the astrologer, the courtesan, the storyteller, the servant, and the physician live a miserable life;
day by day they face death, for their livelihood consists of pleasing strangers.
Alas, misfortune does not arise from external circumstances, nor does it ever emerge from external events that are themselves ineffective;
rather, it truly arises for us from some internal state of being, and it manifests specifically from an internal disposition latent within the vital breath itself.

For a man living here in the forest at all times, there arises not only suffering born of his own body, but even the entire ritual duty toward the gods and ancestors does not shine forth; therefore, one who dwells in the home should contemplate what is for his own welfare.
"Alas, O rash woman! That ascetic, whose body was that of a twice-born, was touched by you on the road with but half a glance; yet he was not recognized by you even from your sacred thread."
Alas, the fire of grief burns within my heart; my two eyes are kept awake by the fever of separation;
and yet this mind of mine wanders everywhere through the vital breaths—even so, O Smara, you desire to steal it away like a thief who steals before one's very eyes.
A livelihood dependent on others is miserable; a dwelling without support is miserable; so too is enterprise without wealth. But poverty is the misery of all miseries.
The pain of piercing is bitter, and the fatigue of constant wearing is bitter;
yet it is an ornament for the ears, and a kundala for the cheek.
Wealth was acquired with great hardship, yet it has vanished somewhere in a moment;
what shall I do, and where shall I go? I am a man of ill fortune upon this earth.
People are difficult to please; they must be won over by the wealth of one's family. Therefore, that inauspicious thing which was spoken is not at all fitting for you.
For it is natural for a fragrant flower to abide upon the head; it is not its destiny to be trampled underfoot.

All the wealth I acquired here with great hardship has been squandered by me on gambling; the knowledge I obtained from my teacher with even greater toil has been employed in worthless praise; and the discipline inherited through my lineage has been bestowed upon a woman with sidelong glances. What can I do, helpless as I am, now that the time for a worthy recipient has drawn near?
What is the purpose of his life, and what is his human endeavor,
when he possesses wealth yet turns away and dismisses a petitioner who has come before him?
Who would blame or erase the pigment from the board of Love? Who is deluded enough to treat a jewel as a thorn? And for whom does a lack of appetite arise toward the nectar of immortality?
Of what avail is the praise of the magnitude of the great gifts of Bali, Karṇa, and Bhārgava, and what is the use of this extensive prologue concerning the white fame of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas?
As long as the son of Vīrasiṃha pours down these golden showers during the rainy season, the cloud, though possessing the luster of collyrium, is no longer a true bearer of rain.
Having placed musk in the navels of the forest deer who feed on grass, Fate rendered them worthy of death;
for if that deluded Creator had placed it at the root of the tongues of all wicked people, it would have been a universal benefit.

O deer, abandon the musk; do not perfume the quarters with your fragrance near the edge of the forest. Let be your fame; alas, even a protector from the strike of the Kirāta’s arrow will be difficult for you to find.
Musk, sandalwood, and saffron are the marks of good fortune for amorous women;
yet on the forehead of a widow, the very act of applying a tilaka with the clay of Prayāga is the mark of good fortune.
O friend, having applied a tilaka of musk at evening, ascend immediately to the top of the palace with a smiling face;
let the night-lotuses attain their full bloom and let the faces of all the quarters radiate great joy.
For those who have happened to go to a marketplace for the purpose of buying or selling musk and other such goods,
the fragrance that has completely adhered to their limbs does not fade even for five or six days.
If I were Fate once more, having extracted the entire quality of fragrance from the eggs of musk deer, I would deposit it within the tongues of the wicked.
From what does musk arise? Who slays hundreds of elephants?
What would a coward do in battle? [The answer is: A lion flees from a deer.
"Is it musk? "No, my dear; is it some other fragrant substance? "Is it something to be drunk?
"Certainly not."
Of what nature is it?
It is the locus of the amorous play of deer-eyed women. Where is it to be worn?
The fullness of the breasts diminishes upon their slopes; thus, the afflicted seller of musk suffers greatly from the insults of the marketplace.
The musk-tilaka upon the space between her eyebrows produces a beauty like the fruit of the five-arrowed god’s bow resting in the middle of his arch.
"O young girl, do not, do not apply the musk tilaka on your forehead!
The moon is waxing today, thinking, 'I shall attain equality [with it].'"
"O young girl, do not, do not apply a musk tilaka on your forehead;
fearing it to be a dark spot, Rāhu will swallow your face."
Adorning a musk tilaka upon the surface of his forehead, the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, a fresh pearl at the tip of his nose, a flute in the palm of his hand, a bracelet on his wrist,
yellow sandalwood paste upon his entire body, and a string of pearls around his neck— the Crown Jewel of the cowherds triumphs, surrounded by the women of the cowherd community.

O child, you yourself act like a rose-apple tree, a drop of water, a lotus, a mire, and a net, in this process of catching the fish of men's minds by means of the musk-tilaka painted upon your forehead, the rounded jewel of your nose, your face with its mass of curled hair, and your gaze perpetually cast forward.

May those splendors of Śrīkaṇṭha’s throat grant you auspiciousness—splendors which, upon the forehead-slate of the Goddess, act as musk-tilakas; which, upon her lotus-face, act as bees; which, upon her head, act as ornaments of fresh tamāla buds; which, upon her ear, act as blooming blue lilies; and which, upon the slope of her breasts, act as applications of black aloe-paste.

May these playful splendors of the neck-luster of the Conqueror of Cities bring auspiciousness to the three worlds: they act as musk-paste upon the forehead of the Goddess; thereafter, they act as collyrium for her eyes; at the edge of her ears, they act as blue lotuses; upon her chest, they act as emerald ornaments; above her navel, they act as a line of body hair; and at her waist, they act as a girdle of sapphires.

The mass of musk-leaf patterns has not fallen from your cheek, my friend; the sandalwood paste on the slope of your breast has not been rubbed away; nor has the collyrium from your eyes been washed off.
The redness of the betel, increased by the chewing, has not faded from your lips. Are you angry, O lady with the gait of a rutting lordly elephant? Or is your husband a mere child?

O King, with the rising of the moon of your fame, musk has acquired whiteness, your locks have turned pale, your blue garment has become white, and a whiteness has arisen in the multitude of gems; darkness has been entirely pacified, and throughout the three worlds, the passion for the audacity of secret trysts has subsided in the deer-eyed women.

O Hero, King Śrī Siṃhabhūpa, while the makara-designs were being fashioned upon the surface of her two cheeks with musk, those skilled [artists] among the enemies of your foes— desiring to inscribe praises of you upon their own chests but finding them too familiar with such work— suddenly felt shame under the guise of the royal insignia (the *māna* mark), as they were rivals to your royal fortune (*rājyalakṣmī*) within their own harems.
"O Moon, what is this delusion of yours? I am the maker of nectar; there is no one distinct from me.
"O fool, do you not indeed see the face of your own beloved woman?"
What pride of valor do you have in fighting when you are mounted upon a single horse? When you are mounted upon [the chariot of] the seven-horsed Sun, your adversaries become as many as those horses.
"Who are you? Know me to be Kṛṣṇa. What is your purpose here?
Why do you place your hand inside the vessel containing fresh butter, suspecting it to be my house?
Is it to remove the ants from there?"
"Are these sleeping girls awakened so that I may discern the gait of my calf?"— may Hari, speaking thus, protect you.
"Who are you? Someone or other? From where do you come?
I am from the shore of the ocean, the abode of jewels."
You have gained nothing but deafness from the roars and injury to your eyes from the sands;
do not be distressed. Do you not consider it praiseworthy, my friend, that you live by resorting to that salt ocean which was so unbearable with the rows of flames from the Aurva-fire?
"Who are you? Who am I? From where have I come? Who is my mother?
Who is my father?"—reflect thus upon everything as being without essence, having abandoned all such deliberations as those concerning a dream.
Who are you, O rogue, among those cowherd women who stand there by chance and do not know love? O Hari, what deception can you have for them?
Alas, this one of wretched hope was indeed ruined by being solely devoted to you; therefore, her love for me will now surely depart along with my life-breaths.
"Who are you? "I am the one in yellow garments.
"Are you speaking falsely? By whom were the garments made yellow? "O innocent one, [it was by] the enemy of Kaṃsa.
"Alas, alas! Where have you seen water that is an enemy to crops?"

May the Lord of Śrī, who at night spoke to the cowherd women with words such as "I am the destroyer of the dance of Malla" and "Why have you destroyed my own dance?"—may he be the unsurpassed source of joy for you.
"Who are you, O Brahmin, who have never been seen before? And where do you dwell?"
The entire creation of Brahmā is yours; who then is your lord?
For you are indeed without a lord. And where is your father?
"I do not even remember my father;
what is it you desire? Shall I give you land measured by three paces?"
May that Vāmana protect you—he who asked Bali, "What is this trifling three-worlds? while [the latter] was filled with pride.
"Who are you, O Brahmin? You are unprecedented; you are a follower of mine."
"I am not without a protector; I am alone.
What desired thing shall I give you? This is the space for walking three paces; how much do you require?"

May the words of Viṣṇu—uttered toward the enemy of the gods with a feigned placement of words, yet appearing as if he were truly devoted to self-restraint—purify us, for they were spoken by him who was utterly deluded in his state of mind, thinking, "The three worlds belong to me, a twice-born."
"Who are you, sir?
"I am Khaleśvara.
"Why do you stay here in this dreadful forest?"

Thinking, "I am to be eaten by tigers and other such predatory beasts," why have you resolved upon this painful course? Let those who eat the flesh of my body— who already intend to consume human flesh— slay all men!
"Who are you, sir?
"I shall tell you: know me to be a wretched Śākhoṭaka tree, cursed by fate. "You speak as if out of world-weariness.
"It is well understood."
Why is this said?
"O traveler, people here serve that banyan tree with their whole being; yet not even its shade performs a service for others, even though it stands upon the path."
"Who are you, sir?
"I am a poet.
"Then why, my friend, have you become so emaciated?"
"Curse this land for not providing food even to one endowed with merit; it is not I who am cursed, but this wicked-minded land!
For as soon as I, hungry and desiring cooked food, resolved to cook, there was no fuel on the Vindhya mountains, no water in the ocean, and no grain upon the surface of the earth."
"Who are you, sir, at night?
"Keśava. "Why do you take pride in your hair, good lady? "I am Śauri."
"What would happen here to a son through virtues residing in his father?
"O moon-faced one, you give me a wheel, but not a jar with a body. May Hari protect you—he who was thus rendered distressed because the cowherd girl withheld her reply.
"Who are you, with red eyes, beak, and feet?
A swan. From where? From Lake Mānasa. What is there?"
There are groves of golden lotuses and water resembling nectar;
there are heaps of jewels, coral, gems, and beryl-groves, and in some places there are even water-dwellers.
And hearing this, the cranes cried out "Hī-hī! in alarm.
"Who are you, monkey,
this carrier of letters to the palace of King Rāma? Where has that Hanumān gone, who previously arrived and utterly consumed the city of Laṅkā?"
Having been beaten and threatened by the monkeys with the words, "The son of Rākṣasa has grown old," that forest deer, overcome with shame and defeat, is no longer known where he has gone.
"Who are you, O man with the spear? Enter the house of physicians; I do not know a doctor."
"O child, the blue-throated tree-spirit does not speak; O deluded one,
utter at least a single cry of 'kekā'!"
"O frail one, the horns have not been seen at all," said Paśupati; may that Lord of Pārvatī, rendered speechless by such a reply from the Daughter of the Mountain, protect you.
"Who are you, O spear-bearer? Seek a physician. "I am Nīlakaṇṭha, my dear; utter a single cry, O Paśupati!"
—When the horns are not seen, O deluded one, how can that post move? It is a post; how does it move?
May the moon-crested Lord, whose words were silenced by the cry "O Lord of my life, go to the forest! from Śivā, protect you.
Why, and upon what arising, does the threefold world become possessed of passion? He who knows this which was stated at the beginning of the verse is a wise man.

Why [should there be doubt]? Who am I, and what indeed are you? What is this phenomenal expansion here? Each one’s own object of knowledge is like the sky, the manifestation of the full reality known as bliss. For those who wander upon the path devoid of the three qualities—dense with the flavor of equanimity, and lacking both external and internal distinctions—what injunction is there, and what prohibition?
"O slender one, why have your limbs now become so thin? Why has this face of yours, once like the luster of a red lotus, become like the moon?
When her beloved asked this, O lotus-faced one, she turned away out of her habitual nature and released a flood of tears with a choked voice.

Why are you here? Where indeed is the face of happiness seen? Where does darkness reside? Where has the smoke-bannered god of love arisen among women? Where have those youths been seen? Where will he go? And where is the fifth [note]? Where is *ṇasakṛt*? Where has *ātsaṃkura* emerged? Where is the arising of the singular flavor of bliss (*ānandaikarasodaya*)? Where is the virtuous woman? Who is the traveler? What is the talk of that?
"O father, why have you come from your home? Tell me, what is the news there?
"It is another young woman. "Tell me, what is the news there?"
"By the Goddess, the God has been defeated— what [is there left] of the bull, the hand-drum, the ash, the serpent-king, and the moon?
When the Lord of the Peacock spoke thus, may the cry of Bhṛṅgirīṭi, born from the agitation caused by the loss of his master’s mendicant ornaments, protect the world for a long time.
"Why are you so weak? her friends asked her;
"when you are present, they would speak to them—tell us the answer."
"Tell me, friend, why have you come from your own abode? Speak of your welfare."
"By your favor, I have seen Subhagā;
you have not seen Subhagā, the wife of your lord."

In her house, the wretched woman—fearful of the moon, the bodiless god of love, the wind, and the cuckoo—is distractedly scratching the ground again and again, imagining Svarbhānu, the three-eyed Śiva, the venomous serpent, and the crow.
"Why do you distress yourself, my dear? We shall return in just a few days; come, place before us the auspicious rites for our departure.
When her beloved spoke thus, the wife sighed, took the auspicious jar in her hand, and filled it with the streams of tears from her eyes.
O Pārvatī, why are you so harsh? This lack of affection is innate for those born of stone; how could it be otherwise?
A man made of ash never possesses affection anywhere.
"O beloved, your anger toward me is fruitless;
what fruit could there be from [anger directed at] a pillar? May Śambhu, thus rendered speechless by the Daughter of the Mountain, protect you for a long time.
Why does the wise man suffer distress through this constant and futile pursuit of objects?
Surely this world is utterly deluded by the illusion of someone.
Why was the human form of Hari—beginningless, middleless, and endless—not described by the sage, the son of Satyavatī, amidst his accounts of the future?
Thus, seeing you—the sun in the sky of battle, occupied with uprooting the thicket of the world’s enemies—the denizens of the heavens are filled with doubt.
"Why is this body of yours today not adorned with excellent golden ornaments? Why have you not accepted garments that are so much more beautiful than before?
O charming one, when I spoke thus to that large-eyed young woman in private, she did not give any reply, but immediately began nothing but weeping.

Why has this eye lost the luster of its collyrium, and why have the decorative patterns on your cheeks faded? O royal swan in the forest of the lotuses of love, why are you so emaciated, so listless, and so soiled?
Why does this moon delight the world with rays containing nectar? Or why does the cloud drench the earth with streams of water?
And why does the sun, revolving again and again, gladden the three worlds? For the minds of the virtuous require no external motive for performing the service of others.
"O messenger, why do you sigh so secretly?
Has the redness been rubbed away from the petal of your lower lip by your hurried turning around?
Is it because of your prayers on my behalf?"
And why is this mass of hair disheveled? Tell me, how could his garment be upon you from plundering his feet,
unless it were for the sake of providing proof for you alone?
O fair-faced one, why are your bracelets broken?
Why is your face devoid of adornment from having fallen on the road at night?
And why is it washed, covered as it was in dust?
"The color on her lip has somehow faded; was it stolen by the winds of your sighs born of distress, or was it taken by me out of greed for her garment?"— thus [I spoke].
Why is there fear here of death? Who is more distinguished than even a blind man who is full of passion?
Who is a hero who has not been pierced by the arrows of the glances of beautiful women?

In what does Murāri lie? Where indeed is there no dwelling for a crow? What is the prohibition for women? In what does passion reside? Where indeed is whiteness found? What is the vocative address for a Śirīṣa tree? What is the vocative case ending for the moon? And what are the vocative endings for Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu? What does a hunter say? Or how did the destruction of the Kuru clan occur? By whom was it done? By Keśava. * *kasmiñchete murāriḥ* (In what does Murāri lie? — *jale* (in water). * *kva na khalu vasatirvāyasī* (Where indeed is there no dwelling for a crow? — *sarvatra* (everywhere). * *ko niṣedhaḥ strīṇām* (What is the prohibition for women? — *niṣedhaḥ* (prohibition). * *rāgas tu kasmin* (In what does passion reside? — *manasi* (in the mind). * *kva nu khalu sitimā* (Where indeed is whiteness found? — *kṣīre* (in milk). * *śairisaṃbodhanam kim* (What is the vocative address for a Śirīṣa tree? — *he śirīṣa* (O Śirīṣa). * *saṃbuddhiḥ kā'himāṃśoḥ* (What is the vocative case ending for the moon? — *he himāṃśo* (O Himāṃśu). * *vidhiharavayasāṃ cāpi saṃbuddhayaḥ kāḥ* (And what are the vocative endings for Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu? — *he vidhe*, *he hare*, *he vaya*. * *brūte lubdhaḥ katham* (What does a hunter say? — *mṛga* (deer). * *vā kurukulahananaṃ kena tat* (Or how did the destruction of the Kuru clan occur? By whom was it done? — *keśavena* (by Keśava). The answer to the sequence of questions is: *jale sarvatra niṣedhaḥ manasi kṣīre he śirīṣa he himāṃśo he vidhe hare vaya mṛga keśavena*. When read as a single sentence, this yields: *jale sarvatra niṣedhamanasi kṣīre he śirīṣa he himāṃśo he vidhe hare vaya mṛga keśavena*. This is a clever wordplay (*prahelikā*) where the individual answers form a coherent, albeit cryptic, statement when combined. The final solution is: *jale sarvatra niṣedhamanasi kṣīre he śirīṣa he himāṃśo he vidhe hare vaya mṛga keśavena*. When read as a continuous phrase, it means: "In water, everywhere, [there is] the prohibition in the mind, in milk, O Śirīṣa, O Moon, O Brahmā, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, [the word] 'deer', by Keśava. The intended meaning of the final line is that the destruction of the Kuru clan was brought about by Keśava (Kṛṣṇa) through his intervention. However, the primary focus of this specific verse is the demonstration of the punning structure. The final answer to the series of questions is: *jale sarvatra niṣedhaḥ manasi kṣīre he śirīṣa he himāṃśo he vidhe hare vaya mṛga keśavena*. When taken as a single syntactic unit, it provides the solution to the puzzle. The final answer is: *jale sarvatra niṣedhamanasi kṣīre he śirīṣa he
When her friends asked, "Why do you wither like a crushed *mālatī* flower?", the bashful young girl, though clearly distressed by the separation, did not speak aloud;
she merely managed, with great effort, to look toward the mango tree in the courtyard, its tips just beginning to burst open with buds, while suppressing the flood of tears in her eyes.
In what action does his capability not shine forth most brightly? Since he is a practitioner of the righteous, let this salutation with joined palms be offered here to him.
When any one doctrine is true, those who abandon all doctrines are ruined;
from that perspective, there is merely futility, but no harm arises from dharma.
Tell me, where do the schools of fish dwell? What calamity does the conceptual mind proclaim? What does the sun do?
And what indeed is that cloud, encircled by streaks of lightning, which causes distress to the wives of travelers?
In what does the enemy of Kaṃsa sleep? What is the lowest conduct of men?
What does a child say to his father? Seeing what does the mind rejoice?
To whom should what be told, and whose mind will find conviction?
The young cowherd girl delights the Supreme Brahman within the bower-cottage.
O Goddess, whose long abode is the chest-slab of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, having saluted you with some feigned intent, we shall say something, provided you do not become angry:
Is this lotus your residence a school of learning? And as for your approaching those who are lower than the low, is this the teaching of the waters?
May Rāma—who, having bestowed the entire earth conquered by his valor upon a certain brāhmaṇa, took delight in finding a dwelling in the ocean through his own majesty—be for your well-being!

People praise his conduct on the battlefield, wherein he placed the circle of kings within the belly of his battle-axe that vomited forth flames capable of wearing down even the banks of the fire of cosmic destruction.

To a certain kinsman among the twice-born, who once petitioned for even a little milk, he—whose very body is the essence of compassion—gave the entire ocean of milk itself. That Lord, who is equal to the wish-granting tree of Śrīvallabha, to nectar, and to the cintāmaṇi gem, is my deity; any other is not even mentioned by name.
To whom, preeminent in compassion, is homage offered even by the gods?
From what—the forest of saṃsāra—should the wise person feel dread?
To whom does a virtuous person give abundant wealth? By what is the world created? Who shines upon the throat of Śambhu? And what is worn by young women in their braided hair?

(1) Whom did the Lord of Gaurī strike with his foot? Who was protected by the Rākṣasas? As one ascends and another descends, provide a single answer for each of these two pairs. (2) [The answers are: *kasmai* (to whom), *kena* (by what), *kāni* (which), *kā* (what), *kam* (whom), *kā* (who), *ārohādavarohataḥ* (from ascent and descent).]
O virtuous one, for what purpose indeed do you exert yourself in acquiring a multitude of virtues? If it is for the adornment of your own self, then listen to my wholesome words:
those very things that captivate the heart by being laden with an abundance of beauty serve as the daily sustenance for this Kali, who has a body as his vehicle.
In whose hand would the Goddess of Fortune not have slipped, slippery from the moisture of the ocean?
Yet she became firmly bound to the heart of Hari, which was made rough by the dust of Bhṛgu’s feet.
O Śambhu, when some creature on the road strikes you with its foot,
the pain from the crushing of your feet causes the enemy of Jambha to yawn.
One should not take anything belonging to anyone else, nor should one utter even a word that pierces the vitals;
one should remember the pair of feet of the Lord of Śrī and cross the ocean of worldly existence with ease.
For someone intent on drinking from the face of his beloved, who was herself intoxicating,
the wine itself, though tasted but once, served instead as a mere momentary relish.
For the intellect of no one of evil mind arises according to their own whim;
whatever kind of action one performs, such is the fruit one experiences.
Whose thirst do you not quench? Who does not drink your water once it has entered within, O lake of the true path, if only the crocodile does not dwell in your lap?
In whose family is there no fault? Who has not been afflicted by disease?
Who has not encountered misfortune? And for whom does happiness endure without end?
To whom is wealth not dear? Whose mind is not captivated by wealth?
However, those greedy for the riches of fame do not desire their goals through evil deeds.
Alas, whose eye was not struck by the terrifying masses of darkness?
Only those women hastening to meet their lovers, already thwarted by the God of Love, did not turn back.
Whose vehicle are those of dull intellect not fit for, who are intent on trivial pursuits and,
out of passion, are unrestrained toward fickle women, even though they delight in tranquility?
O charming one, whose mind would this lower lip of yours not render agitated by thirst? It has the luster of coral and is like a desert path.
In whom is [the god] difficult to attain in the desert? Tell me, who has made his dwelling in the lotus? By what means is Cāmuṇḍā pleased? And tell me, from where have your enemies fallen?
O Great Sage, who is whose mother, who is whose father, and who is whose kinsman? It is through delusion and the loss of mindfulness that living beings become bewildered.
Whose mother is whose? Whose father is whose? Whose wife or even whose son is whose?
For in birth after birth, living beings will have different mothers, fathers, wives, and sons.
Who is not subject to censure? Who does not live by means of some method?
By whom has misfortune not been encountered? And for whom is happiness constant?
Under whose control does the host of living beings abide? Under one who speaks the truth and is disciplined.
Where should one stand? On the righteous path, for the sake of attaining both the seen and the unseen rewards.
Who has never stumbled? Whose every desire has not been fulfilled?
Who possesses constant happiness in this world? Or who indeed has not been thwarted by fate?
To whom do the splendors of heaven belong? To whom on earth belongs the station of Indra?
Whom do the gods hold in high esteem, other than one who dies in battle?
Death in battle is meritorious, as is death at Gayā;
death in the Gaṅgā brings liberation, and death in battle is blissful.
If the minds of men long for the company of celestial women,
then let them die in battle after having brought others to a state of happiness.
If some base individuals should offer criticism against certain words of ours, what loss would that be to us—those who possess celebrated virtues and are lords over millions of poems?
If five or six horses, slower than the wind, are lame and blind, what harm is done to the jewel of the Śeraśāha dynasty, the lord of millions of steeds?
To whom shall I tell this misfortune so that I may be freed from my grief? Who knows the secret essence of the affection between us two?
O moon-faced one, my mind alone knows the truth of our love; for it has followed after you alone for a long time. Therefore, my dear, what am I to do?
To whom has absolute happiness ever come, or suffering that is exclusively constant?
One's condition moves downward and upward like the rim of a wheel.
By whose command does the sun, the seven-horsed one, dispel the darkness of living beings? By whom has the salutation of trees been established on the path for the sake of providing shade?
Or by whom are the fresh rain-clouds entreated for the sake of rain? Indeed, by their very nature, these virtuous ones are ever intent upon performing deeds for the benefit of others.
Whose heart is there that knows nothing of this? For though he gazes upon her, this world remains as if mute toward me; indeed, every person suffers.
It is impossible to show him my body by splitting it in two like a jackfruit; truly, friend, I have surely seen the moon on the fourth lunar day.
Who could possibly feel affection for things that are impermanent, when because of that affection one will not see a loved one again for thousands of lifetimes?

O fish, who in this world—save for the dwellers of heaven—possesses eyes as wide as those that never blink? Having seized even those two with your gaping mouth, O fool, why was this clear hook not seen by you within the baited lump?
No one brings about happiness or suffering for anyone else, setting aside destiny;
yet, in vain, one takes pride, thinking, "I am the slayer of my enemy."
Whoever possesses some excellence attains renown in the world for that reason, for indeed not everyone is omniscient.
Does the *ketakī* bear fruit? Does the jackfruit tree have beautiful flowers? And does even the betel vine possess both flowers and fruit?
One should never proclaim one's own virtues of one's own accord before anyone; however, even if they are insignificant, the virtues of others should be spoken of as being weighty.
O beloved, what lotus could not perpetuate its fragrance before this face of yours,
which never blooms at all unless supported by a single friend?

When the chamberlains saw the body of a certain bride of the inner apartments— motionless as she closed her eyes upon seeing him whom she had long heard called "fortunate," and who had now awakened her passion— they were distressed in mind and filled with fear.

Upon the face of a certain woman, whose decorative leaf-patterns had been washed away, a variegated beauty was spread by the sprouts at the tips of her curls— sprouts that hung down with the weight of water and whose interiors were turned tawny by contact with the filaments of lotuses.
For whom is there destruction through the expansion of the mind? Where is there no fear whatsoever in liberation?
What is the supreme thorn? Is it not one's own foolishness? And who indeed are the venerable teachers to be honored?
"To whom does this mansion belong?
To me alone.
And who are you, O fair-browed one?"
The young woman of Lāṭa said: "Is my very innocent friend at home, or is her husband there?"
Having thus heard these words of the traveler at the close of day—words of hidden meaning—the slender woman shook her head, her clusters of earrings swaying gently.
Whose parents are these, joined together by the fever of desire, who procreate offspring and so forth through the elements such as earth?
For the nihilist whose mind is thus distressed and who finds pleasure in desire—how can there be peace for him, who possesses wealth yet relies on the dharma of evil deeds?
"Whose water-stall is this, young woman?
"O traveler, ours.
"What is being drunk here?"
The milk of cows, or that of buffaloes—O deaf one, this is merely a turn [of service];
how can it be auspicious? Is it Soma, or is it Saturn?
"This is dead;
it is seen below you, O illustrious traveler, beautiful friend. Drink whatever pleases you."
In this worldly existence, which is insipid in its conclusion, short-lived, and of an unsuitable origin, for whom could a longing arise—
were it not for this very assembly for drinking the nectar of the discourse on the recollection of Nārāyaṇa, which serves as a diversion for the mind?
Whose mind delights in wealth merely for its utility? Who does not tremble when standing upon a support the size of a single footstep?
O Malaya breezes, quickly strike him from all sides repeatedly with blows of the *kasara* pestle until he is fragrant; place a heavy chain around him!
Cast the king of passions, the fifth note (*pañcama*), into prison with force, and grind the moon to powder upon a stone slab like flour.
As the moon embraced the night, whose garment of darkness was slipping away due to the arrival of the cool season with its lovely fingertips containing the touch of white lotuses,
the women of the quarters— casting glances at one another, overflowing with love born of long acquaintance— seemed to break into a clear laugh as their joy reached its peak.

Seeing her at midday, scorched by the sun's rays, with the orb of her moon-like face hidden within the hem of her blue garment, the poet remarked: "It seems that Rāhu swallows the moon during the day, even without it being the time of an eclipse."
I bow to the breasts of Gaurī, which appear as if smiling, wondering what state the ascetic Śiva has reached, their faces whitened by the touch of Bhava’s thick embrace.

By means of hundreds of flattering words for some, through excesses of affection for their own daughters for others, and by means of crooked speech for yet other wealthy men, procuring them to their own homes,
and then seizing them under the pretext of fraudulent claims regarding previously given gifts, these procuresses are clearly capable of destroying these men whose conduct is unrefined.

Some have spent a hundred kalpas accumulating their existence, some a hundred yugas, and others likewise a hundred years; yet for certain beings, Time devours them all—whose lifespans are wasting away day by day through their own actions—in but a hundred days. O brother, where is there any skill in this?
It makes some empty and fills others; it leads some to exaltation and again brings others to the state of downfall; it throws some into confusion.
Making known this worldly condition of mutual opposition and alliance, Fate plays, engaged in the manner of the buckets on a well-drawing wheel.
A wise person swiftly undertakes certain matters that require little effort but yield great results, and does not allow such things to be obstructed.
Smara indeed fashioned from bronze the orb of the moon, with its mass of clinging rays;
and he used his own bowstring as the scale for the two who were made equal in their mutual passion.
That sword in which the sound produced when struck by another blade resounds like the tone of bell-metal—
Śiva calls that the best of swords, which increases one's auspicious fortune.
Whom did Hari, in the form of a boar, support? What king desires a woman free from passion? By what is the production of love caused, and by what does the face of a young woman shine?
A crow was placed in a golden cage, an owl was set upon a lotus pond, a dog was appointed to the ancestral offerings, and garlic was offered into the sacrificial fire.
What more need be said? He has accomplished everything for his own great peace by that act of ignorance, whereby a lowly person was elevated to a high station.
The crow is black, the cuckoo is black; what is the difference between the cuckoo and the crow?
When the spring season has arrived, the crow is a crow and the cuckoo is a cuckoo.

The crow, having raised up the cuckoo, causes him to taste the fruit of the mango tree; the osprey, having driven away the royal parrot, enjoys the pomegranate while intent on sport; the owl sleeps happily with his mate upon the branch-tip where the peacock once was—alas, today everything in the forest has turned upside down now that the hawk has gone out of sight!
If a crow obtains a morsel of food in a king’s palace by the strength of its wings, does that bring greatness to it, or has the insignificance of the lion been attained?
For the lion, having attacked the pair of temples of a lordly elephant and torn them open with ease, seizes a choice morsel, yet casts away a multitude of pearls, regarding them as mere cowries.
Among birds, the crow is considered the outcaste; among animals, the donkey;
and among men, anyone who reviles all others is considered the outcaste.
A crow finds no contentment in a lotus grove, nor does a swan in the water of a well; a jackal stays within the cave of a lion, yet a low-born man occupies a noble throne.
A wicked woman never serves a virtuous man, for she is pursued by the base; whatever nature has been ordained for one by the Creator, how can it be prevented?
A crow, a dog, a man of low birth, a cat, and a snake— these,
as well as a woman of low birth, are declared to be equal.
A crow, though naturally fickle, invites both his own kin and strangers when he finds a pure offering;
yet even toward the carcass of an elephant, full of skin, bone, and flesh, a dog—being of a wretched nature—hates and attacks it.
A crow calls out to other crows, but a beggar does not call out to other beggars;
between a crow and a beggar, a crow is better than a beggar.
Crows, roosters, and scribes nourish their own kind;
lions, dogs, brahmins, and elephants destroy their own kind.
Having formed the lips like the beak of a crow, one should drink the air as it is exhorted;
drawing it in with the sound of the syllable *oṃ*, one should fill the interior until it is full.
The matted hair of the *kākajaṅghā* plant, when placed upon the head, induces sleep.
Dog bile extracted during the Puṣya asterism cures epilepsy when used as an ointment.
The juice of *kākajaṅghā* sprinkled into the ear destroys deafness;
its matted root tied to the ear certainly cures eye diseases.
That Fortune, by a chance occurrence like "the crow and the palm fruit," should show affection for even a moment toward one who lacks self-control— that is her feminine fickleness.
Even upon seeing a treasure that has come before him by chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, fate does not take it up itself; it depends upon human effort.
The *kākatuṇḍokti* is one [type of simile], while the *mallikokti* is another, being incomparable;
the *pāṭalokti*, the *padmokti*, and the *padminyukti* are clearly recorded as distinct types.
O crow, having by chance reached this forest bent with fruit, why do you deafen our ears with your harsh clamor of *kreṅkāra* cries?

If you were to maintain silence, how is it that the flashes of the charming glances of beautiful women would not fall upon you, even under the mistaken impression that you are a male cuckoo set out for love-making?
What need is there to speak of his aiming an arrow? For he dispels obstacles from afar by the very sound of his bowstring, as if by a mere "hum" from his bow.
Crow's flesh is likewise leftover and meager; it is weak even in that small amount. What is the use of consuming that by which no satisfaction arises?
One should cook kākamācī and kuṣṭha with cow's buttermilk;
this antidote will certainly destroy the poison of the maṇḍali snake.
The root of the *kākamācī* plant tied to the ear removes nocturnal fever;
held in the hand, the *vṛṣavṛndāka* plant brings victory in gambling.
O Arjuna, you do not perceive that this wretched crow has been worn away;
for it has been submerged in the water that serves as collyrium for the eyes of the wives of your enemies through your valor.
A crow, a woodpecker, a frog, and a blue fly—
these five, together with a cricket, killed an elephant through the use of skillful means.
How many teeth does a crow have? How many palas are there in a ram’s testicle?
How many hairs are on a donkey? Such inquiry is useless.
Even if a crow's beak were adorned with gold, its feet set with rubies,
and each of its wings decorated with the pearls of a lordly elephant, it would still remain a crow and not a royal swan.
A crow's nest facing three of the cardinal directions is praised as a cause for rain;
however, if it is situated in the southern corners, it becomes a cause for famine and death.
What do crows not do? They utter their "kroṅ" cries here and there;
only the parrot, cherished in the hand of a king, speaks truly.
Let the crows obtain the nectar of the blossoms from the mango groves by means of the silk scarves bestowed by their master;
but now that the spring season has arrived, how is it that they do not utter their sweet, melodious warbling in the fifth note, which is like nectar to the ears?
How could there be a distinction between the boundaries of crows and cuckoos if the Creator had not fashioned the auditory canal for each with its own specific ear?
If you desire the bond of affection and long-term cohabitation characteristic of crows, then you too must utter those loathsome, harsh sounds that are so effective at reaching the ears of your kind.

If you do not practice this, let this nectar-like song flow from your throat; or else, having heard it, these [crows] will abandon you as one whose qualities do not conform to those of their own species.
Who is the beloved of the enemy of Kāliya? Furthermore, what is the indeclinable used for "again"?
What is to be worshipped by all the gods? And what among fruits is beautiful?
"Who is that beloved who, having embraced her dearest with both arms, does not abandon her sleep even though the sun has risen?
The flock of crows, like a swarm of bees, made a secret sound as if saying, 'Wake up! Put on your upper garment!'"
"Who is this woman, her limbs oppressed by the fatigue of amorous play, who has fallen asleep embraced by the vine-like arms of her lover?
Let her go to her own home; this is the rising of the sun"—thus do the flocks of crows speak these words of assignation.
What is the wish-granting cow here? What is the thought-gem? And what is the wish-fulfilling tree?
All these in this world are merely synonyms for merit.
Crows dwell happily by the hundreds upon your crown; monkeys and owls reside in your branches and deep hollows; and your foliage is thick with mosquitoes and gadflies.
How many things do you support? You have attained a very stable and pure fame. If travelers do not approach you, what loss is there for you, O King of Trees?
Who is dark? Who is sweet? Who flows coolly? The Gaṅgā.
Whom did Kṛṣṇa slay? Whom does cold not afflict? The powerful one.
Taking greed from a crow, cruelty from Yama, and the capacity for firm striking from a carpenter—
by whom was the scribe fashioned, having taken one syllable from each?
