Crows, wolves, owls, cranes, and frogs, having bowed to you, I beg this very thing of you:
do not make such a clamor; forgive me, for the male cuckoo is warbling its sweet song.
Having placed the leaf and root of *kākī*, along with *sahacara*, the bulb of *ketakī*, and *bhṛṅga* dried in the shade, together with the juice of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) into oil,
and having set it in an iron vessel on the ground for exactly one month, his hair becomes as bright as *kāśa* grass and resembles a swarm of bees through the application of this ointment.
Why do you make such a cry, O rogue, with your limbs hidden in a heap of dried cow-dung in the corner of the house? Go away in vain!
Where today is that skill of yours in mocking the groups of cowherd girls, who are terrified by the thought that the sun might have set?

If the ten-headed Rāvaṇa had not abducted the wife of the descendant of Kakutstha, where would there be the ocean, where the construction of the bridge, and where the victory over Laṅkā after crossing it?
If the enemy had not brought about the defeat of Pārtha, where would there be such ascetic power? Generally, those who possess great pride are led by their enemies to the highest state of excellence.
I believe that the fire of Kakutstha’s prowess, which was extinguished by the dark night-stalkers, has been rekindled by the tawny-faced monkeys.

Those very heads of the descendant of Pulastya, the repository of illusions, which were severed by the descendant of Kakutstha by the hundreds within the precincts of his aerial chariot and caused the dwellers of heaven to tremble—
those same heads now serve to relieve the fatigue of the Lord of Sītā’s bow, swaying like the grand display of play-fans.
What was created by Viṣṇu? Of what kind is that which is praised among women?
What kind of master is not to be served? Who is the slayer of intense darkness?

O child, do not suffer in vain, thinking, "He has adopted a forest life while I, though equal to him, am beset by a crow whose harsh cawing pierces my ears and by the sweet flow of the nectar-like fifth note of the flute. Where, indeed, has such deceit not been practiced upon people by the foolish Creator?
In the crow, blackness is extraordinary; in the swan, whiteness is innate. There is a vast difference in their depth; what more need be said of the distinction in their speech?
O friend, even amidst such differences, where this is observed—"Who indeed are the crows, and who are the young swans?"—salutations to that land!
Purity in a crow, truthfulness in gamblers, patience in a serpent, the subduing of lust in women,
fortitude in a eunuch, and reflection on reality in a drunkard— by whom has a king as a friend ever been seen or heard of?
The notes of a cuckoo raised among crows remain melodious; how could there be harshness in one whose nature is inherently auspicious, even when in the company of the wicked?
Living together with crows, the swan is agitated and suffers;
though he remains as gentle as ever, he is not crooked or wicked like the crows.
With crows you have sought to defeat these peacocks with their variegated plumage—the Pāṇḍavas by means of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having abandoned the lions while hiding among jackals, O lord of men, you will grieve when the time arrives.

O Supreme Goddess, O Bhāgīrathī who flows through the three paths, when shall I behold your form—once ravaged by crows, devoured by dogs, tossed by waves, driven by currents, soiled at its banks, and trampled by jackals; [but now] being fanned by the beautiful breezes from the yak-tail whisks in the hands of celestial maidens?
At Kākodumbarikā, an anthill is seen; there is a vein therein.
At a distance of three and a quarter men [from the anthill], situated toward the western direction, that [vein] flows.

O friend, I bow to that sleepless darkness, to which the raven, the cuckoo, the blue lotus, the rain-cloud, the mud, the enemy of Kaṃsa (Kṛṣṇa), the braid of hair, the slender sword-blade, musk, collyrium, the Yamunā river, the whetstone, the herd of elephants, and the throat-region of the enemy of Kāma (Śiva) all pay tribute.
What rivalry can there truly be for a self-respecting virtuous man with a wicked person— one for whom terrifying speech and the reviling of the good are considered ornaments?
What need is there to mention a wretched man under the sway of the senses who longs for a beautiful woman?
Even she, while looking at him under a pretext with the intent of meditation, touches true knowledge.

What is the use of wealth to one whose body is worn out by old age— wealth which, though desired and yet unobtained, was once fit for enjoyment during the prime of youth, and now acts like a mere burden?
What is surprising in this—that fools tie glass, a gem, and gold upon a single thread?
But the discerning Pāṇini, on a single sūtra, spoke of a dog, a youth, and Indra.
Glass, through contact with gold, acquires an emerald luster;
even a stone attains divinity when well-established by the great.
Just as glass, through contact with gold, acquires an emerald luster,
so too does a fool attain proficiency through proximity to the virtuous.
Due to the defect of ophthalmia (kācakāmala), one may perceive a distortion in the eyes;
the tongue speaks slander, and therein it is said that passion (rāga) resides.
What did Hari create?
What is the nature of one whose intellect is miserly regarding wealth?
What is found in a serpent?
What is the belly of the one born from a jar like?
What is a bride who desires to go like?

What kind of verse is desired by the virtuous? What is the sky like when it is stainless? O Earth, call out: what has arisen that is all-pervading? And what is a lake like at night? [The answers are: *ślokaḥ* (verse), *nirmalam* (stainless), *kṣoṇīm* (Earth), and *sarvagam* (all-pervading).]
How many pieces of glass, adorned with gold, do not nourish the splendor of jewels? Or how many base things do not bear upon their crowns those very same gems, mistaking them for such?

But those which wipe away the darkness from the eyes, and by which the ocean is truly called a "mine of jewels"—alas, those gems are indeed distinct; and among them, those who possess true discernment are likewise distinct.

One woman, having taken flowers with both hands, held them near the feet of Śambhu; desiring to speak of the ill-conduct of the God of Love, she seemed to be casting forth his arrows right before him.

Some women, their beauty of face eclipsed by the moon and covered in dust, mirrored the sky; others, with their inner spirits agitated, bore a lack of luster like the quarters of the horizon consumed by fire;
some moaned like whirlwinds, while others trembled at every step like the earth—thus did the women foretell the inauspiciousness that was to come upon the departure of the kings.
Whether some work has been composed or whether it has been offered to you, not even a single drop of joy arises within my heart.
My ignorance in this matter is known only to myself; yet, O Mother, I place my trust in your nature as the refuge of the wretched.
A certain woman, afflicted by thirst in the summer heat, approached the Gaṅgā which was the color of nectar; taking that water with both hands and gazing at it, she did not drink—what could this be?
Thinking, "Because of the beauty of her hand-like sprouts, they might be mistaken for blood," a certain woman,
moving playfully with unhesitating steps among the female elephants of the harem,
showed contempt for the heavy hips and the weight of the breasts of the king's other women.
Long ago, a certain woman in separation gave water to a *navamālikā* creeper as a means for its growth;
now that the creeper has blossomed, she has somehow become free from her debt to it by offering water in the form of tears during their parting.
A certain golden vine; above it, a stainless moon; within that, a lotus; near it, a sesame flower; close by, a sprout;
and below those two, two beautiful jars that enchant the world. May this [arrangement] grant you prosperity—what need is there for Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and the rest? For the three worlds!
One woman, overcome by a strong man, does not leave her lover even though he is charming;
another spends the day at a drinking party together with her friends.

One woman, like a young tree, has fallen to the ground; though she has blossomed through the acquisition of wealth, she is fruitless because her roots have been severed. Another possesses the splendor of noble birth, yet is barren. One woman is like a plantain tree, beautiful in enjoyment but deprived of the seed of true merit. Yet another is beautiful in every limb, marked by the seeds of merit, like a mango creeper.
A certain young woman, sending a casket to her lover’s dwelling, fearfully drew a serpent upon it by the hand of her maidservant.
Mallinātha, the lord of poets and a master of aesthetic sentiment, asks the noble one regarding the meaning of the lion, the son of the Wind, and the campaka flower depicted there.
A certain woman, her hand resting upon a mirror, adorns her lotus-face in the morning sunlight;
she draws back her lower lip, which has had its essence sipped by her beloved and is marked by the tips of his teeth, and gazes at it.
A certain woman, her limbs tormented by the fire of separation, drew these figures in order to sustain her life:
a serpent upon her arms, the orb of Rāhu upon her heart, and Maheśa made of camphor at her navel.

A certain woman with tremulous eyes, afflicted by the arrows of the god of love when her lover had gone far away, suddenly abandoned her body; oh, how strange, she began to drink the breeze from the Malaya mountains, which was rich in fragrance!
A certain deer-eyed woman, her body covered in the dust of the ground, emerged from the playing field after sporting at ball;
she was like the goddess Lakṣmī, grey with the pollen of filaments, after wandering for a long time in a forest of full-blown lotuses.

O Lord of the Yadus, O Lord of Lakṣmī, what anxiety can I have for my livelihood if Hari is sung of as the sustainer of the universe? Otherwise, why did he create his mother’s breast-milk for the life of Arbhaka? Reflecting thus again and again, I spend all my time solely in the service of your lotus feet.
A certain woman of graceful form, her left hand resting upon her hip and her arm curved like a line,
fashioned for the king an archer’s bow as skillful at discharging arrows as that of the God of Love.
A certain woman, at the command of the elderly women, was here reciting something appropriate for her family;
while she was engaged in sketching trees in a grove, she became bashful when signaled by her companions.
A certain woman, prevented from going outside by her mother, approached a lattice window of the palace to see Hara;
in an instant, her eye appeared like a fish obstructed within a mechanical net.
A certain fawn-eyed woman, unable to reach the end of the night while separated from her beloved,
took up a lute in her hand to sing and, beholding the moon, smiled softly.
In the presence of those whose intellect functions by mistaking glass for a gem and a gem for glass,
not even a servant in name alone will remain.
Those embodied beings for whom glass is a gem and a gem is glass are indeed others; those wise ones are truly wise for whom glass is glass and a gem is a gem.

O golden-limbed one, I shall indeed bear for a moment with my hand those two *likuca* fruits, lovely in their clusters and encased in their husks; grant me your jewel of a lower lip, for I am your slave.
Having stirred it with sour gruel, one should eat it every morning;
by practicing this for six months, one destroys gray hair along with wrinkles.
A man who is devoted to eating milk and rice shall become long-lived.

At the departure of Mānasiṃha, the woman of Kāñcī no longer wears her girdle; the woman of Kerala does not cast a glance upon her bed of pleasure; the noble lady of Āndhra casts far away the vermilion placed in the palm of her hand;
the woman of Saurāṣṭra repeatedly wipes away the redness from her bloodshot eyes; and the woman of Karṇāṭa blackens the ornament on her ear—so it is at his march.

We long for some indescribable erotic delight of a courtesan, whose loveliness of navel is softened by the tinkling of her girdle, whose line of throat is variegated by the cooing of pigeons, and whose eyes are like wandering cakora birds.

This girdle, placed upon her hips, has caused a certain slowness in her gait; this tightly fastened bodice has given fullness to her swelling breasts; and now the pair of earrings on her ears makes the corners of her eyes restless. Alas, what is this sequence of yours toward me, O friend, in the matter of adorning yourself?

O Mother, I meditate upon your entire expanse of hips— the seat that adorns the circular posture of the Enemy of Tripura— whose beauty is enhanced by the contrast with the saffron-colored rags visible beneath the golden garments knotted at your waist.
Women do not adorn their hips with girdles variegated with gold and jewels,
nor do they grace their lotus-feet— which possess the luster of a lotus— with anklets that mimic the cries of swans.

The beauty fashioned by girdles upon their hips and the established presence of jeweled necklaces upon the slopes of their breasts led the broad-hipped women to maintain an unrestrained slenderness in their waists, as if thinking, "We have not yet been adorned."

The binding of the girdle with playful grace, the striking with ear-lotuses, the rebuke through silence born of anger at the interruption of a playful embrace—O angry one, have you suddenly forgotten these things previously customary here, and out of a heavy burden of resentment, departed from my sight with a longing heart? Ah! Having fastened her girdle tightly and bound her tresses firmly with strands of hair, repeatedly removing the necklace from her breasts and shaking off the lotus from her ear;
having cast her bracelets far away, alas, whose neck does that moon-faced woman now forcibly embrace with the binding of her arms amidst a playful laugh?
As he fastens the girdle, he arranges the loose garment of the fair-browed one; as he places the necklace upon her breast, he rests his palm upon her lotus-like bosom;
and while speaking words of endearment, he drinks from her lower lip—what cause for wonder is there in this? But if, while scattering dust into her eyes, you take her wealth, then you are a thief!

O steadfast one, at the boundary of Kāñcī, a certain golden ladder shines; having reached it with some great festive joy of battle, you shall immediately seize the two mountains with your thorn-studded pair of hands and obtain the abundant nectar of the Moon who dwells upon their slopes.
When her beloved asked her attendants at her leisure, "Why is the lovely-eyed girl sleeping again with the hem of her garment fastened so tightly by her girdle?",
she, feigning anger as if thinking, "O mother, she even steals my sleep here," turned over on the bed under the pretext of sleeping and gave him space.
Desiring to create hardness in their lotus-feet as they do in their breasts,
noble women in your cities reproach the Creator.
"O Brahmin, how is it that you have not attained these two—the firmness of the jar-like breasts and the flickering of the eyes—upon our feet?
O Śrī Narasiṃha, thus do the wives of your enemies, intent on fleeing from one another in the forests out of fear of your army, speak as they are pursued by the Lord of the three worlds.

Hardness is ever present in mountains, softness is constant in water, and radiance is in the sun; likewise, enmity resides in the hearts of the wicked, while forgiveness dwells in the hearts of the virtuous.
Hardness was banished from all her limbs and took refuge in the breasts of the slender-limbed woman;
as if out of fear that they too would fall downward, even those two were unable to abandon it.

One-eyed, humpbacked, or lame; deficient in learning or strength, or a dwarf; crippled, blind, impotent, or even with a severed nose; devoid of attendants, unfortunate, and a body afflicted by disease;

having wicked sons and a wicked wife, reviled by one's own kin and attendants, and humiliated in honor—truly, whatever is born here is the result of one's own past deeds; alas, this is how it manifests in the world of the living.
Those one-eyed ones with eyes like lotus petals, those miserly wish-granting trees,
and those cowardly Vikramādityas have come within the range of the poets' vision.
The king should always employ these within the inner apartments: those who are one-eyed, hunchbacked, eunuchs, as well as the elderly and the lame.
One-eyed men, the lame, the hunchbacked, those who have been severely wounded, and the crippled—
these indeed should be appointed by the king for the protection of the inner apartments.
Those who are one-eyed, those with trembling limbs, those who are crippled, as well as the elderly and the lame—
these should always be employed within the inner apartments by the ruler of the earth.
One who is one-eyed, with a gaze fixed on uneven and sunken depths, is capable of producing detachment in those distressed by worldly existence;
yet he does not become dear to the mind of anyone, even when depicted in a painting—how much less so in his actual form?
Her eyes, softened by timidity, a sidelong glance, love, shame, and anger,
turn toward him whom she has obtained through her purpose— neither able to join with him nor yet to let him go.
"Timidity is mere policy; valor is the behavior of a beast of prey.
Therefore, he sought success through the combination of both."
Cowardice is not the cause, nor is sorcery, nor is it supreme deceit; what is it that women possess—a fickleness of mind and body, a honeyed appearance like the moon, and yet such thinness of frame?
O friend, look now: even our own slender hair stands on end, and we, with our husbands newly away, have instantly mocked the wives of travelers whose lords have departed.
Cowardice, ill-breeding, miserliness, and lack of discernment—
poets, who are like servants holding handfuls of rice for them, sweep all these away.
Who is your mother? Who is your son? This cycle of existence is exceedingly diverse.
To whom do you belong, or from where have you come? O brother, reflect upon this.

"Who has been silenced by my thundering? Who has been struck down by the torrents of rain? Who has been driven to madness, distressed by separation? Or who has been stirred by the winds from the Kadamba trees? And who has been led to agitation by the sweet, intoxicated cries of the peacocks? Thus does the cloud, as if with the lamps of lightning, look about among the houses of travelers.

O Kātyāyanī, for what purpose have you entered the deep interior of this forest thicket out of a desire for flowers? Alas, O fair-throated one, look! The cowherd, his anger aroused, beholds the marks of thorns upon the clusters of your breasts.

What beauty is there here in the curve of the hips, which is merely a cavity for the belly filled with excrement? What splendor is there in the pair of jars that are the breasts of women, which are in essence mere lumps of flesh? What radiance is there in the pair of eyes, which are turbid with fluids and filled with phlegm, blood, and the like? What charm is there in the whorls of the navel, which are nothing but pits? Alas, tell me! Who are those deluded ones who praise them?
"Who are you, O lovely one? Are you the Jāhnavī? What business do you have here? Is not this Hara indeed your husband? You surely know the arts of the God of Love."
"Does this husband of yours know [the truth]? "O Lord, this is true;
for how can there be truth among lovers toward their dearest ones? May this dialogue between Hara, Jahnavī, and the Daughter of the Mountain protect you!
"Who are you? "I am the fame of Kuntalamalla.
"Alas! Where are you situated?
"Nowhere. "Tell me, where are those friends of yours? Where are your speech, fortune, and splendors?"
Speech has departed for the mouth of the four-faced Brahmā, Lakṣmī for the chest of Murāri, and the splendor of the lunar orb for the moon; yet even now, my own resting place remains nowhere.
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, dressed in yellow silk,
standing there leaning against the branch of a tree, O blameless lady?"
"Who are you, daughter? O king, you are the wife of a hunter; what is this in your hand?"
"O King, is this emaciation natural? If you will listen with respect, I shall tell you:
on the banks of the rivers that are dear to your enemies, the wives of the Siddhas sing so loudly that the deer, blinded by their songs, do not graze upon the grass; therefore, the meat is meager."
"Who are you? "I am Mādhava’s messenger.
"What do you say?
"O beloved, abandon your pride; that rogue has his mind set on another."

"O friend, He does not abandon even the slightest regard for you"—with such words of mutual affection, Hari, appearing in the guise of a female companion, led the delighted Rādhā to a bower; may he, having revealed his true form and smiling, protect you all.
“Who are you? “I am Mukti. “From where have you come?
Why have you suddenly arrived here? “O Lord, by the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, I have been brought to the state of being your maidservant.
“Stay far away! You are innocent; how could I do anything ignoble to you? From the mere scent of you, the application of sandalwood paste—my own name—would be lost.”
"Who are you, O auspicious one, whose wife are you, or what is the reason for your coming to me?
Speak, considering that the minds of the self-controlled Raghus are naturally averse to the wives of others."
A mass of clouds, a woolen blanket, the breast-slab of a beautiful girl in a Kadamba field,
musk, the fragrance of Ketaka flowers, and the cry of peacocks— these are the sources of joy in the rainy season.
"O friend, is this a bank of clouds at the foot of the *kadamba* tree, or is it a *tamāla* tree, or perhaps the darkness itself?
You do not understand, my friend, that this is the lordly elephant who breaks the creeping vines of the secret vows of the cowherd women."
O scion of Raghu, let a proper blessing be given to you by him through whom the worlds have been made free of thorns;
nevertheless, we pray that your bride may have two sons who are like the two sons of Kaśyapa, together with her own heroic brothers.
O Goddess, what a wretched state would be the world’s lot if it were not for you— terrified by the wrathful and merciless Citragupta—
were you not the one who issues the official decrees that purify the records of Dharmarāja and release beings from the bonds of karma?
What is heaven? What is the abode of Indra? What is the earth?
If all this were never to become perceptible, what would it matter to you, O all-seeing one?
O frog, let those who wander about indeed prattle on; you have understood this perfectly: apart from this supreme pit of embers, what else could possibly be conceived?
In the forest, by the banks of rivers, and even in the caves of mountains,
your enemies shall see you alone before them, resembling the God of Death.
What kind of intellect-deficient and unrefined is the Creator, who did not provide oil for the *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds nor wool for the elephants?
With its brilliance made manifest by contact with the wind, [the fire] considers: "Which places have been burnt, which regions remain exceedingly dense, or what portion of the forest still stands?"
The forest fire, its loud laughter released from the bursting joints of tree-creepers licked by fierce flames, stands upon a dry tree on a rugged mountain peak in the thicket, as if it were watching.
The father-in-law was a *kānīna* (son of an unmarried woman), while the father and his ancestors were *golakas*; their sons, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, were indeed *kuṇḍas*.
These Pāṇḍavas had Drupada’s daughter as their wife, yet their kinsmen were slain in battle; by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the family honored by the world has been brought to a state covered in disgrace.
The Pāṇḍavas themselves are indeed *kuṇḍas*, the sons of Golaka—the grandson of the sage Kānīna, who brought an end to the widowhood of his own kinsmen’ wives.
These five were devoted to a common womb; by praising their virtues, one’s merit becomes inexhaustible and complete, for subtle is the course of Dharma.

May the young women, though harsh, bear upon their hips— fallen there because they were overcome by passion— the lovely flower of Kandarpa, the moon upon the slope of their breasts, the sprout of the tree of love, the wound from the blow of battle on the bed, the banner of the chariot-warrior exhausted in the combat of divine love, the opening of their eyes, the marks of fingernails, and the signs of secret enjoyment.
A beloved poem indeed gains even greater luster through the words of a harsh critic,
just as a heart-pleasing golden ornament becomes more radiant when touched by a set of teeth.
Beholding her beloved with the region of his neck marked by bracelets, she did not utter harsh words out of fear of others;
instead, the fawn-eyed woman, with tears welling in her eyes, cast glances from the corners of her gaze toward the messenger from afar.
Lovely form, youth with graceful playfulness, generosity, dexterity, and speech endowed with conciliation—
having obtained whom all these excellent qualities shine forth, what woman in this world would not seek to win his favor?
The female dove speaks to her beloved in distress: "O Lord, the time of my end has now arrived; the hunter stands below with bow held low and arrow ready, and the hawk circles about.
Thus bitten by the real snake, the hawk was also struck by him with an arrow; both have quickly gone toward the abode of Yama—the ways of destiny are indeed wondrous.
Reflecting upon her beloved, whose union is so difficult to obtain, and hearing that the Lord of Vidarbha has been humbled by his forces,
her heart suffers like a lotus struck by rain-showers after being scorched by the sun, yet it also experiences joy.
Seeing her mate on the riverbank, the peahen displays her pride;
he who knows that the verb is hidden here is a wise man.
Seeing her beloved’s face stained with the red lac from the lotus-feet of a rival woman with long-lashed eyes, she bowed her head and became as if fixed in a painting;
she spoke no harsh word nor did she even sigh hotly, but at dawn the lady presented the mirror from her palm for his auspicious morning greeting.
The beloved one, O dear one, whirling his two eyes with a sidelong glance,
is attended by a fragrant breeze permeated with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra).
The beloved touches her hand, speaks sweet words, gazes at her face, and pushes aside her silk garment;
thus does the newlywed lotus-eyed maiden perceive these very acts of amorous play even in her dreams, fearing they might become reality.
With one hand, the lover playfully pulls the braid from the breast of the deer-eyed woman—
like a dark female serpent from a golden jar— for the sake of purifying her from contact with another woman.
The beloved behaves like the God of Death, his mother is as crooked as fate, and the words of wicked people are like thunderbolts;
these strike every limb of my inner being, yet, O friend, my life-breaths do not depart.
"Since your lover was struck by your foot, why do you seek to appease him after offending that simple girl?
Is such a kick so easily obtained, and is his favor likewise so easy?"
"O daughter, your lover has departed by force; you did not fall at his feet, nor did you stay bound with this girdle by your friend during the secret tryst, nor did you cry out.
What shame is there? You have been robbed! Why these embarrassed smiles? Alas, O wicked girl, do you not know the heart-piercing flames of the fire of separation?"
Like female messengers from their beloveds, copper-red with saffron and hastening toward the evening circle,
the rays of the sun, falling through the lattice-windows of the palaces, were gazed upon with longing by the women.
The redness of her hand, resting upon the lotus in the garden of her home, was surpassed by the brilliance of her lip as it touched the cloud-like darkness of twilight.
Placing upon her head an *utpala* lotus that filled her ear, as if desiring to create a jewel for it, she performed,
before the Mind-born God who was her own beloved’s body, a worship as if to sport with him.
"What did the newlywed bride do upon union with her beloved?"—
even to this question, the limit for providing an answer is the entire lifespan of Brahmā.
"Who is this one, followed by his beloved, with thick shoulders and arrogant with pride, who follows behind the deer— Śambara, in the full bloom of youth?"

Suddenly embraced by his beloved, a certain man with bold hands desired to pull off her silk garment; but with his vision obstructed by her firm breasts, he did not see that the garment had already slipped away.
The women went to the beloved’s house for the sake of pleasure, giving many instructions; for those whose minds have been robbed by the God of Love, even a mistake is generally helpful.
When the pride of the indignant women had been overcome by union with their lovers, and their quarrels had been pacified by the tasting of wine, and when peace had been established between them,
the Bodiless One (Kāma) did not fix an arrow upon his bow.

"O beloved, with eyes as lovely as lotuses, I have heard today from the talk of people that you are indeed going to another land; is this word true?"—when I asked her this, O treasure-house of compassion, she replied with a downcast face; even now, my tongue is not able to utter those words.
"Under the pretext of meditation, he daily desires some beloved woman, because of whom even the sages—purified of all craving—meditate upon Him who is without beginning or end.

May Śambhu, whose body was thus bound by his wife as she seized him by the foot from his lotus posture and pulled him from her lap, protect the universe as he emerged from that state of meditative absorption.
Having called his beloved who lingers somewhere with sweet warbling notes, and having looked repeatedly toward the various quarters of the sky, he then leaves the stage of the earth on foot;
now this peacock dances joyfully, fanning himself with a canopy made of rows of feathers to the sweet sounds of the clouds like the resonance of large drums.
Seeing my beloved engaged in washing her feet, he recited with great effort the words, "In this kingdom is Fortune";
and when offering the betel-roll, he said again, "To the Lord [Devasya tve]"; this son-in-law of yours is dull-witted and a Vedic scholar—what am I to do?
"Let some traveler, if he has the power, pass me by—me whose limbs are languid with the exhaustion of beginning a state of distress due to separation from my beloved.
Thus, at the onset of the flowering season, the God of Love bestowed upon the entire world this Ashoka creeper as if it were a thief.

Are there not lovely mansions belonging to someone, white as the radiance of the moon? Is there not a beloved woman to be enjoyed, her broad hips adorned with a girdle of bells? Or is there not music and the like, which is pleasant to hear and a nectar for the ears that brings happiness? Yet, seeing the entire world as flickering as the wind, the wise practice austerity.
Homage to the flower-bowed god, whose body consists of the side-long glances of beautiful women;
by him even the sapless tree of worldly existence is made to bear fruit and cast its shade.
He whose mind the arrows of a beloved’s sidelong glances do not pierce, whom the heat of the fire of anger does not consume,
and whom the snares of greed for abundant sense objects do not drag away— that steadfast man conquers this entire triple world.

The winds blow, carrying droplets from the Revā river; they have become motionless upon the slopes of the breasts of the broad-hipped women of the Cōḍas, having stolen the pollen of the jasmine flowers in the braided hair of the Kerala women who tremble at their lovers’ embraces; and they are made resonant by the *hūṃ* sounds of young female cuckoos.
May some tree provide sport for beloveds; may another produce great joy for lords with its fruits; may yet another satisfy the world.
But oh, I consider the sandalwood tree alone to be blessed, which swiftly removes the intense torment of worldly existence by the sacrifice of its own body.

Though he is devoted to dalliance with his beloved and though he is a self-controlled ascetic tranquilized by compassion for living beings, when the wielder of the Pināka bow saw Smara with his bow drawn, he became enraged and acted as follows—his face terrifying with a fierce frown that shattered his playfully ascended meditative absorption; even you, Kauśika, he now treats in that very same way with his gaze, out of anger.
A beloved woman, the rising of the moon, and the fifth note of the lute—
these things which delight those who are happy cause pain to those who are suffering.
As if approaching very slowly to massage the beloved women whose eyes were closed from the exhaustion of lovemaking,
the night-ending breeze revealed the scents of flower garlands and the enjoyment of wine within the mansions.
When their hair was forcibly seized by their beloved women in private during love-play, those who were satisfied by the laughter of Smara—
by that love, they slept with their minds full of joy even during the wintry nights, satisfied by that laughter of passion.
A beloved woman bestows passion; passion brings forth incomparable torment that finds no relief;
and that torment leads, alas, to death—yet even so, she alone remains the refuge of men.
The pleasure that arises in a youth from tasting the nectar of a beloved’s lips is but a mere drop compared to the ocean of bliss from tasting the inner science of the self (*adhyātmaśāstra*).
Having partaken of the drinking of the nectar from the lips of a beloved, a wise man does not feel a desire to drink the draught of ambrosia;
for if there were some sweetness therein, alas, truly, O father, would those who are thirsty and hungry ever become so again?
As if out of a thirst for the nectar-like juice of the beloved’s lower lip, the reflection of the moon fell into the vessel of honey;
when the honey was entirely consumed, that reflection vanished, its mental state overcome by shame at being surpassed in beauty by her lotus-face.
"The blue water-lily has been surpassed by the beauty of the eyes of lovely women, and I alone am not surpassed by the luster of their faces"—
singing as if thus out of joy through the humming of bees, the great lotus danced in the water with its trembling ripples.

Upon the breast-paste of their beloveds, which caused horripilation to arise, and upon their faces where the tilaka marks had vanished, the water from pearls became the sweat born of exertion; for even a transformation bestows beauty upon things already lovely.
Now the moon bears the loveliness of the moon-like faces of beautiful women; the rows of sporting *khañjana* birds spread the splendor of the eyes of those with deer-like gazes;
the lotuses rival the fragrance of the sighs of fair-browed maidens; and the female royal swans practice the gait of those with full breasts.
"You are skilled in the passion for lovely women, you are charming, you are my lord, and moreover, you are adorned with fresh youth.
Having spoken thus, the fair-eyed woman sighed and cast her glances, tremulous with tears, upon the face of her beloved.

The half-glances from the eyes of beloved women, the radiance of their faces accompanied by smiles, the playfulness of their brows, the meaningful fragments of speech, the sounds of clapping hands, and laughter that appears and vanishes;
the repeated uncovering of the navel, flanks, and breasts, the touching of girdles, and long sighs of exhaustion—all these indicate a passionate woman struck by the arrows of Love.

A person who understands the proper conduct obtains from courtesans— without even the need for personal affection— their lovely side-long glances, their sweet conversations seasoned with laughter, the incomparable touch of their full hips as they occupy half his seat, and various charming qualities such as the interlacing of hands that reveals their affection.
A younger brother devoted to pleasing his beloved, a son who delights the heart through his discipline, fortune to be enjoyed by celestial nymphs, stainless prosperity, and unadulterated happiness;
honor in the royal court, exceedingly pure fame, assemblies with the learned, and an intense passion for giving—such a delight in the teaching of the Jina may belong to someone through their merit.

O heart, why do you not shatter into a hundred pieces upon remembering at the end of love-making the beloved’s face— pale, sprinkled with beads of sweat born from the exhaustion of the amorous play, its eyes half-closed with pupils trembling?

O beloved, seeing the supreme splendor of the blossoming clusters on the *kuravaka* trees— which possess a radiance rivalling the luster of a beautiful woman's face— whose heart, even if possessed of aesthetic sensitivity, would not be pained by the falling of Cupid’s arrows?

Since these travelers, when touched by the rays of the moon, turn their faces away from tasting the face of their beloved and undergo such unbearable torment, I believe that there is no other source for it than that [moon].
The decorative leaf-patterns were drawn upon the surface of his beloved’s cheek with fingernails; while sporting, he drank from her bimba-like lower lip which had been staked in a game of dice;

the slopes of her breasts, their sandal-paste moistened by perspiration, were embraced with joy; all sense-objects have now been fully enjoyed, and his mind is placed within the auspicious light of the Supreme Self.
The pure rays of her beloved’s blossoming, playful smile serve as the fly-whisk; her breasts, marked with sandalwood paste, are the two golden jars for the consecration;
her lovely hips, radiant as refined gold, are the throne of kings—this is sovereignty, consisting of both victory and defeat, while the remainder is merely the nature of anxiety.
Just as no one else is capable of burning a wilderness without a forest fire, nor can another extinguish a forest fire without a rain-cloud;
and just as no one else is skilled at driving away a rain-cloud without the wind—likewise, what else is capable of destroying the flood of karma except for well-performed merit?

While a most powerful forest fire raged all around the wilderness, a lion, arrogant with pride, by chance fell into the deep cave of a jackal; because the lion did not kill him out of compassion, the jackal now runs about with his tail held high, crying, "I am now the one who grants safety from fear to the lions in this forest!"
Kāntāra, the one called Samara, Vaikuṇṭha, Vāñchita,
Viśāla, and likewise Nanda— these six are the Niḥsāruka.
Just as the fruit of trees in a wilderness is not to be enjoyed by humans,
so too wealth among the ignoble is not to be enjoyed even mentally by the noble.

Those parrots, who usually dwell upon the crests of trees in the wilderness and are generally intent on flight at the sight of people, even they indeed warble the name of Rāma; for association is the cause for the transformation of one's very nature.
In wildernesses, forest fortresses, and difficult calamities, amidst confusion,
and when weapons are raised, those possessed of courage have no fear.

The beloved wife, the sage, the youth, the one who is never separated from his partner, and even Kāmadeva— each bears a luster upon their respective pairs of breasts by means of a radiant jeweled bracelet,
a breast ornament, a necklace, Lord Śiva, the moon, the sea-monster, and the hand.
In the wilderness of dense darkness, we were neither afraid of serpents nor did we take account of the great river;
O young girl, why do you harbor fear? Now that the elephant has been sold, what dispute can there be over the goad?
O Pṛthvīcaṇḍaruci, in the wilderness hostile to water and trees, the daughters of your enemies—with their hair disheveled and eyes agitated—find their every step blocked as they wander;
they douse the fire of your majesty, blazing from the friction of the hem of their tattered rags, with the tears gathered in their cupped palms.

O King, having somehow spotted some food that had fallen amidst the wilderness by the turn of fate, those birds fly up again and again and take refuge once more upon the very tips of the tree branches.
In this way, O Lord of Men, the wives of your enemies on the mountains describe the behavior of the bees before their hungry husbands, mistaking them for *jambu*, *lambīka*, and *kadamba* fruits.
In the wildernesses, with their children supported by their hands, worshipping your path with feet dripping with blood and manifesting their grief with tears from their eyes,
your enemies' wives— who were seen by travelers turning back with faces full of pity and cries of "Alas!"— travel only a quarter of a *yojana* in an entire day.
O Lord of the Earth, having wandered through wildernesses and forests, along the banks of rivers and upon the slopes of mountains, through cities and on the shores of the ocean,
your glories— possessing the luster of the inner sprouts of the *ketaka* flower— now grow, as if weary, in the lovely vicinity of the *kandalī* plants in the Nandana grove.
Even in the wilderness, a man traveling on a journey finds rest; he who has a wife is trustworthy. Therefore, a wife is the ultimate refuge.
Separation from a beloved, humiliation by one's own kin, a remaining debt, service to a wicked king,
and a friend who turns away due to poverty— these five burn the body even without fire.

If the moon were to burn someone who has turned his face away from the embrace of his beloved, that would be understandable, for alas, the Creator fashioned such people precisely to be destroyed by it.
But what a tragedy! That this wind—having gained its power everywhere from the sandalwood forests and having plunged into the celestial Ganges—is now burning this fiercely blazing [fire]!
As I lay with my eyes wide open, longing to hear the stories of the virtues of my beloved and her friends, that beautiful night passed me by;
for sleep, when indulged in, destroys the pleasures born of all the objects of the senses, just as one's own habitual conduct destroys long-term happiness.

Having seized their luster from saffron filaments, their sweetness from grape-wine, the purity of their speech from the Vaidarbha style’s mature refinement, and the softness of their voices from the poetry of the poet—
alas, whom does these fair-browed women of Kashmir not captivate, created by Fate as he grew old and took each of those qualities from its very source?

That the young cakora bird daily drinks with love, using its darting beak, the splendor of the full moon’s orb—which is like a companion to the glow of a ketaki bud—I believe to be the nectar for the eyes of the Lord of Rati; and that this beauty was beheld by him, seeking it, upon the surface of the cheek of his beloved, as he sought to conquer death.
O fair-browed one, who would not hold you in high esteem when you yourself resort to this river of nectar for the eyes, which is surging with waves of loveliness?
The redness of her hand, which was like a lotus situated in the pond of the domestic garden, surpassed the glow of a twilight cloud resting upon the petals of her lips.
From that great Sudarśana, which consists of splendor, is exceedingly pure, and whose time is spent in incessant benefit for the world,
there proceeds forth something even greater than the great, like a lamp from a lamp.

Behold this black aloe-wood (kālāguru), whose luster is a companion to the shade of a blooming blue lotus for fair-browed women; which, even when in its raw state, possesses a fragrance that is a source of joy for many and whose essence is beyond reproach; yet it has been burnt by ignoble, vulgar, and utterly foolish people who, out of a desire for charcoal, destroyed it despite its weighty and excellent qualities.
"O necklace, you who possess a luster that rivals the beauty of a digit of the autumnal moon—the very playground of Fortune—why indeed do you go here to be sold?
Look at this city of the Pulindas before you, where the kings wear garlands of *guñjā* berries upon the hollows of their necks and upon the slopes of their breasts, like the eyes of does."

O sandalwood tree (*śrīkhaṇḍa*), your splendor is a wondrous balm for the eyes, your form is magnificent, your fragrance is great, and your exudation is more refreshing than even the flow of nectar from the moon; yet alas, look, this entire delightful collection of virtues, rare indeed in the world, has been ruined by your association with the serpent worn as an ornament!

O lotus-faced one, your luster belongs to the moon, your eyes to the deer, your arms to the lotus stalk, your gait to the swans, and your breasts to vessels of gold—all these are things belonging to others; O proud beloved, do not take pride in your own beauty, for your only true possession is your sense of self-respect.
The two things that are praised for their lovely fragrance—
the newly blossomed lotus among the waters and her lotus-face upon the land— both surpass the ruby in the splendor of their beauty.
Your luster is a rival to the Golden Mountain; your beauty vies with the breasts of lovely women; in the act of being beheld by kings, your sight comes first;
your fragrance surpasses all others—O citron fruit, what more can we say? If it were not for your hostility toward camphor, every single virtue would reside in you alone.
O lotus, if your beauty is stainless, if you possess virtues, and if your splendor is enduring, do not yet succumb to pride; nevertheless, these autumn days have indeed slipped away.
For now, with your form shattered by contact with droplets of frosty water, you must remain right here in the middle of the lake as nothing more than a mere seed-vessel.
"O beloved, pass however many days you wish with your eyes closed; I shall close my own eyes until the quarters of the sky are no longer empty.
We have arrived, and by the rising fortune of our circle of friends, we shall depart. Tell me, what message do you desire? A handful of water at sacred fords?"

When her beloved had somehow announced his departure, she stood for a moment with bowed head, her limbs tormented by the thought of separation; then, seeing him [return], the charming girl embraced him, crying "When have you come?", and attained great joy.
While her beloved was holding a golden citron in his hand,
the moon-faced woman placed a dot upon the sun depicted on the wall.
When her lover had fastened the edge of her bodice and the rival lamp was burning brightly,
the closing of the eyes of that dark-lotus-eyed woman became her only wing.
While her lover stood gazing at her bodice, Kalāvatī bowed; as he remained there speaking with tender, plaintive words, she restrained his quivering lip.
Then, when her beloved rose and touched her hand during the fresh union of the young couple, Love practiced the art of pacification through the pretext of the tinkling of the girdle.
"O beloved, tell me, why do you go alone to the water-shed?
O lotus-eyed one, your youth itself causes the god of love to sprout intensely within your limbs."
"O beloved, are you angry?
O lord of my life, how could there be anger toward another person? O fair-browed one, who is this 'other'?
It is you yourself."

Having said, "O beloved, I am your slave; who else could I be?", the lover bowed down; then, being raised from the surface of the earth by the slender woman with joy, he was placed upon her breast, which was marked by drops of tears from her eyes.
"O lovely one, why do you look askance while scratching behind your ear? O auspicious lady, tell me freely what I, your servant, should do."
"O beloved, take back this garland of yours; why do you quarrel without cause?
That which you consider to be pure in its first half is indeed true, provided that this [second half] were not so."

"O beloved, you have been released by my mass of merit from the dark cavern of the jaws of Death; therefore, embrace me limb by limb and cut away the heavy burden of the toil spent in acquiring that merit.
Hearing this, the lover gently kissed the lotus-face of the deer-eyed woman—her face slightly bent, smiling, full of joy, and with her eyes half-closed.

When her lover had departed, the unchaste woman awoke suddenly upon hearing the crowing of the rooster; seeing the eastern quarter of Indra’s direction slightly brightening through the lattice window, she—driven by alarm yet restrained by love for her beloved—repeatedly rose and settled back down upon the bed.
In that manner, the deer-eyed woman, her passion aroused during amorous dalliances,
displayed such skill that hundreds of domestic pigeons acted as her pupils, repeatedly imitating her cooing sounds.

When my beloved approached the bed, the knot of my lower garment loosened of its own accord at that very moment; my dress remained slightly upon my hips, held only by the slackened cords of my girdle.

O friend, this much alone do I know; but as for who he was, who I was, what the pleasure was, or how it occurred—in the embrace of his body, even the slightest memory of these things has not remained with me.

"She is lovely," "she has lotus-eyes," "she has broad hips," "she has high, full, and towering breasts," "she has a beautiful lotus-face," "she has fine eyebrows"—seeing a woman who is a visibly impure doll, even a wise man becomes intoxicated, rejoices, delights, and praises her; alas, what a wicked performance of delusion!
O beloved, your nipples upon your breasts, the necklace smiling above them, and your face— reflected therein, O lady of youthful limbs, with the dark luster of a creeping vine—
bind the minds of the three worlds with your gaze, O you who are beautiful in every limb, like a rose-apple fruit, a drop of water, a lotus, a stalk, and a web.

O beloved, a vast forest of lotuses possesses the beauty of your eyes; the moon is an established fact as a counterpart to your face; even the flock of cuckoos imitates your voice; the trunk of the *rambhā* plant shares the luster of your thighs; conch shells resemble the shape of your neck; and peacock feathers are like your hair—so how can you claim to be peerless?
"O beloved, wash my feet," was the request made by her husband;
she did not wash his feet, yet she did not disobey her husband's command.
Sent by her beloved, cherished by her circle of dear friends, and offered to Love by her longing heart, the fresh mango sprout did not leave her hand;

repeatedly stroked, repeatedly gazed upon, repeatedly smelled, repeatedly rolled about, and repeatedly pressed against each of her limbs—what indeed did the deer-eyed girl not do with that mango sprout?
When her lover, charming in his joy, pulled at the edge of the bodice on the slope of his beloved’s breast,
the young woman, with her face bent down, bore another garment in the guise of a slight smile.
O beloved, by these words you appear as if deeply provoked to anger; for who, when their offenses have been spoken, does not burn with remorse?
When her lover, having committed an offense, stood before her turning away, a sudden friendship arose between the lotus and the moon;
for as the fair-eyed woman was unable to utter a word of anger, the pair of blue lotuses received a shower of frost.

When her beloved gazed at her with passion, that woman turned her face away; yet when he, skilled in the entire range of amorous arts, turned his own face back toward her, she looked again and again with eyes swinging in her inner heart of love. Though caught between shame and passion, she became a source of supreme delight to him.
"Beloved, I am going; where? To another land, even from my bed."
"No," [he said]; "What?
Even from my own home? "How far is it? "Just this much.
"Ah! What are you saying? From the city?"

"O beloved, even though I am at peace,"—having heard these words, with a heart overwhelmed by the dense and heavy pain of the sequence of events described, she said: "I do not know; who am I? Where am I? Who is this? Alas, am I one whose time has been destroyed, or am I not?"
In that private chamber, where passion was kindled by the sequence of various amorous acts, the fawn-eyed woman,
moved by intense emotion, uttered some indistinct cry such that her bed was not merely surrounded by a few, but by a multitude of quails warbling in response.
"O beloved, playful, artistic, lotus-eyed one, my mind always delights in you, my most cherished.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, even wise people laugh at me as I speak thus to you with such intense devotion.
When her lover touched her bodice with a transgression, she turned her neck aside and released side-long glances—sprouts of sidelong looks cruel as the arrows of Love, reddened by anger.
Yet, with a meaningful, soft smile like filaments and speech dripping with honey, that fair-browed woman bestowed a certain love, like a wish-fulfilling vine, acting as a great donor.

When her lover approached her side after committing an offense, a certain woman, rebuking him with glances from the corners of her eyes that were curved by the knitting of brows and reddened with anger, looked at him repeatedly;
then, agitated by rage, she struck his forehead—which was marked by the red lac from the lotus-feet of a rival wife—with a playful blue lotus fastened to her girdle.
When my beloved had departed after committing an offense, my dear friend arrived dressed in his clothes; mistaking him for him, I embraced her and, longing for union with him, revealed my secret.
"O simple girl, this is exceedingly difficult to do," he said with a laugh, and having forcibly embraced me, that rogue deceived me today at the onset of nightfall.
When the beloved spring— the treasury of affection— has arrived, having conquered the beauty of the winter season, this forest-goddess, as if paled by the separation from him,
now tears away the ancient leaf-patterns on all sides with the hem of her garment, the wind, in order to create a new and variegated arrangement of foliage for this splendor of the woods.

O beloved, alas, you were previously thought to be very tender; yet, through delusion, you have become utterly hard-hearted toward me on this earth, for even though you see me, you do not acknowledge me.
Therefore, the Creator must have driven two great mountains into your chest under the guise of breasts; for there is no lasting happiness for one who causes suffering to others.
Your lover is known for his skill in jesting; childhood is averse to play, yet this mountain-peak is the crest-jewel of our pastimes, and this house is a delightful spring festival.
Your friends are clever in the arts of amorous discourse; now, at this time of union, whether there be pride or quarrel, when shall there be peace for your heart?
"O moon-faced one, the thought that my beloved will go to a distant land gives rise to supreme anxiety within me; for the moon, though it brings joy to the world, now acts as an enemy.
Moreover, this sweet warbling of the cuckoo provokes lamentation, and alas, the gentle breezes from the pleasure grove utterly steal away my very life-breaths."

O sugarcane, you are lovely, eternally sweet, and overflowing with flavor; moreover, you are the peerless bow of the five-arrowed god of love. Yet, you possess one supreme deficiency: that once consumed, you gradually turn to saplessness.

Alas! In its luster, which possesses the brilliance of gold; in its fragrance, which is to be enjoyed by the fortunate alone; and in its truly noble beauty, there is indeed no flower equal to you. But listen, O *cāmpeya*, there is one fault in you, as it were—a flaw that even those who know the truth have not kissed: you are [ignored] by the bees.
The moon falls into poverty through its own radiance; what essence, then, could possibly exist within blooming blue lotuses?
I do not understand how the Creator’s creation of beauty was stolen by that fawn-eyed woman, for she is utterly beyond belief.
The circles of the breasts of the wives of his enemies, whose eyes were reddened by excessive weeping, appear as if they are once again smeared with saffron due to the loss of their luster.

O lotus-eyed one, though you captivate the heart with your supreme golden luster and purity as you constantly cast your own locks of hair all around, I know that the fire, turbid with anger, has consumed you.
All the twice-born of Kānyakubja, with the exception of those from Māgadha and Mādhura, are renowned as Gauḍas and Drāviḍas; these Kānyakubjas are of great origin.
Who is the wife of Pāṇḍu? What is the ornament of the house? Who is the enemy of Rāma? What is the birth of Agastya?
Who is the son of the Sun? [These are] questions in reverse order: the sons of Kuntī, Rāvaṇa, and Kumbhakarṇa.
A certain woman said this to her beloved: "Accomplish your task in battle so well that the Goddess of Victory and the Lady of the Lord of the World may both be your co-wives."
A certain woman, whose beloved was away from home, was counting the lines drawn on the wall as a limit; while the house was enveloped by a fierce fire, she was led outside in tears by her friend.

Having raised a certain female friend to the position of leader, she went to the house of love-play with her lord of life, holding a lamp in her own hand; wonderful indeed was the instruction of the Lord of Love!

The intoxicated bee, reeling and fragrant with the scent of *kāpiśāyana* wine, settled down to rest upon the lotus-like faces of the women— faces with blossoming eyes— and likewise upon their cups, which were as beautiful as lotuses.
A certain proud woman, her anger quickly cast aside, moved toward the abode of her beloved;
even the wind arriving before her considered it a mitigation of her own insignificance.
A base man is like a dog, solely intent on food;
when caressed, he comes to one's side, and even when driven away, he does not depart.
One beautiful woman reddens the feet of Kāpya with dyed footprints; another shines with ornaments; yet another sings, while still another laughs, wearing a garment marked by waves.

Where one offers joy with floods of affection, and another reaches for swings—whose mind would she not plunge into the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra), she who is herself the very embodiment of that passion?
A certain splendor, joined with the authority of budding flowers, has appeared upon the *aśoka* tree; the mango tree assumes its noble form according to the rites appropriate for the season.
Moreover, the breeze—skilled in introducing the victory of the bodiless Love-god, a friend to the playful grace of young sandalwood vines—glides freely from the mountains of Āṣāḍha.
As those two, dressed in pure white garments, proceeded, a certain indescribable splendor attended them, like that of the moon joined with the star Citrā when freed from the clouds of winter.
Seeing that the lord of her heart had arrived, she rose respectfully from her seat to offer him a chair;
striking the couch with her hand, upon which her bracelets tinkled, she called out to him in a sweet voice.
Who could cause the noble one, the eldest in virtue, to fall from the consecration that has been prepared?
I believe it is by my own merits that Fate has created this opportunity for service.
By what beloved is a noble woman separated? By which son is a household made to rejoice? By what kind of man is the constant binding of birds desired?
What pleasure is there with cats? What pleasure with a king?
What pleasure with courtesans? And what pleasure with beggars?
By what means could I not have been made a merchant for depositing my trust with the newly awakened god of love there?
For no one among the beasts feels shame because some beast does not look askance from anywhere.
What is the ornament of the powerful?
Forgiveness.
What is their humiliation? [The lack of it].
What sorrow is there in anger caused by one's own kin? What is the misery of depending on others?
And who in this world is truly praiseworthy?
Whoever relies [on this],
who abandons death, calamity, and grief?
By whom were those enemies conquered? By the Pāṇḍavas, who remained unrecognized while living in disguise in the city of Virāṭa.
If you wish, place a fire of dried cow dung beneath you and endure an excess of heat through delusion;
until this very day, you have had no right to the sweetness of the lips of those most innocent maidens who have been milked.

Granted, the exceedingly sweet cry of the peacocks has been made harsh to my ears, and even the clouds, though bearing nectar, have for the most part been turned into pourers of poison. This bed, with its rows of emerging new sprouts, acts like a serpent; what is there that has not been made contrary to me by separation from her?
Shake down the wish-granting cow for Mitra and Varuṇa;
through your steadfast gift, may we attain all our desires.
He desires no lotus for sport, he does not rejoice in the outpourings of moonlight, nor does he seek even the playful conversation of deer-eyed women;
sinking during the nights with limbs too frail to endure and listless from his longing for enjoyment, the bewildered Hari suffers in his heart, holding the cowherd girl within his mind.
When the desire of one who longs for pleasure is fulfilled,
then another desire pierces him like an arrow with its thirst.
O Lord of the Earth, it is true that you are renowned in this world as being equal to Kāma himself by virtue of your form alone; yet your mastery of the bow is of a different kind.
For, toward whichever man you release an arrow, the celestial nymphs—casting aside their shame, tearing through their bodices, and filled with longing—run toward him indeed.
A skillful person, with great care, eats even a kingdom that is like a fish trap and full of many thorns,
provided it is accompanied by ripeness and is exceedingly flavorful.
At will, on the banks of rivers, near mountain slopes, and close to the nesting grounds of herds of female buffaloes, the cranes plunge into rows of young grass, eager for mouthfuls of fresh locusts;
meanwhile, in a corner of a field, a flock of pigeons somehow pecks at grains of *kodrava* millet, while being startled by scarecrows made of reeds and straw placed within.

O lordly elephant, you may indeed joyfully drive away the petty wild beasts with sudden leaps of your trunk, making your pair of eyes bloodshot with rage; however, we consider it only when you stand your ground once Lord Hari—his body crimsoned by the blood gushing from the frontal globes of elephants shattered by your effortless play—comes within the range of your vision.
O lord of the earth, he who knows how to properly conquer lust, anger, greed, hypocrisy, and pride, shall truly rule the world.
Abandon desire, anger, fear, greed, hypocrisy, delusion, and likewise pride;
abandon sleep, envy, laziness, and atheism.
Having abandoned desire, anger, greed, and delusion, behold indeed the Self; for who am I?
Those fools who are devoid of self-knowledge are cooked in hell, those deluded ones.
Granted that he is great in virtues, yet by nature he is demonic;
for due to his universal excellence and conduct, he is indeed arrogant in every way.
Granted that people smile when the splendors of Kailāsa are described;
yet, at the moment the means for its attainment are explained, they turn their faces away in aversion.
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died.
Let the winds of the Malaya mountain burn me at will, or let even the moon cast down showers of sparks;
yet my beloved, that jewel of a stainless lineage, is far away—bring him back somehow at once!
Granted that the journey may be long, granted that the path may be great;
even that [journey] ultimately depends entirely upon the grace of the Lord.
The wise call that cow of auspiciousness, *sūnṛtā* (truthful speech), the mother of all blessings; she yields desire at will, drives away misfortune, gives birth to fame, and destroys evil deeds.
Passion indeed produces an unbearable fever that makes the eyes whirl, violently swells the limbs, thighs, hips, cheeks, and heart, and brings about various deformities;
by which friends suffer deeply—what are those ailments like dysentery and the rest compared to it, when youth itself is destined for one's own destruction?
Granted, I beheld all the wives of Rāvaṇa naked;
nevertheless, not the slightest disturbance arose in my mind.
For the mind is indeed the cause for the operation of all the sense faculties;
and its state, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, is well-established within me.
Though she does not look at her beloved even though she intensely desires to see him, and though she does not speak even when addressed, she speaks with great earnestness;
through the interplay of shame and love for her lord of the heart, this young girl bears this charming variety of aesthetic flavor.
O messenger, you know Kāma to be pitiless; you know him to have many favorites;
you know that the quarters of the sky are harsh with mango sprouts—do you not know anything else?

Granted, there may be thousands of other kings; yet they say this earth possesses a true king only because of him. Though crowded with constellations, stars, and planets, the night is radiant only by the light of the moon.
Knowing that desire is supreme, even the god Purandara once lusted after Ahalyā,
the wife of the sage Gautama.
Granted, I do not recall the sage having ever rejected my suit for his daughters;
yet my heart, being deeply distressed, seems to persuade me otherwise.
Betel leaf kindles desire, reveals the beauty of the form, brings about good fortune, and provides fragrance to the mouth;
it bestows vigor, destroys diseases born of phlegm, and likewise produces other such qualities.
With a properly prepared powder, one produces passion; with an excess of betel nut (*pūgaphala*), it brings about the destruction of passion.
An excess of powder causes a foul odor in the mouth, whereas an excess of leaf (*patra*) produces a fine fragrance.
Excessive use of leaves at night is beneficial, while during the day it is said to be fruitful; to act otherwise than this is mere mockery.
Perfumed with *kakkola*, betel nut, *lavalī* fruit, and *pārijāta*, it brings joy through the intoxication of passion.
Granted, you are not seen due to the darkness of the evening, like a flash of lightning hidden within the hollow of a cloud;
yet, O timid one, this fragrance arising from your garlands and the tinkling of your anklets will reveal your presence.
Wise men may indeed relinquish even their dear lives at will,
but they do not desire even great honor from their enemies.

Granted that a beloved is not easily obtained, yet the mind finds consolation in perceiving her feelings; even when the god of love has not achieved his purpose, the mutual longing between the two creates delight.

Granted, let the clusters of lotuses possess deep sounds produced by the friction of swarms of bees greedy for honey; yet, that certain lotus at the navel of the Mountain-Bearer (Viṣṇu), where the Creator himself hums with exceeding sweetness to the ear, is something truly extraordinary.
Granted, let there be rivers on earth well-established, and let their waters be sweet along with oyster shells;
yet, O woman of excellent complexion, apart from this Tāmraparṇī, the wish-granting cow of pearls cannot be found elsewhere.
"By all means, do not desire sensual pleasure; honor even the bull [Śiva] intensely; do not set your mind on wealth, but take refuge in that one art which has the fruit of supreme immortality.

Thus, having made the bull his mount and desiring to bestow instructions for the entire world through his very form, may the Lord—the enemy of Smara, who is himself destitute of possessions yet wears the digit of the nectar-rayed moon as his crest—protect you.
Granted that someone might paint the shape and the form of the sun;
but how could one paint its light, which does not rest upon a wall and has no support?

Granted that deer in the forests live on grass, which is easily obtained without effort; yet they do not display wretchedness before the wealthy. They are indeed called beasts, while we are the wise ones.
Granted, O friend, your body is thrilled with horripilation, your eyes hold tears, your words consist of faltering syllables, and your chest trembles;
it is known, O moon-faced one, that the sweetness of Mukunda’s flute-song makes your heart waver.

Granted, let some of the words of poets in this world be fruitless; yet there remain others that, through their praise of the stories of Madhuripu, are like cows of plenty. Granted, let wealth given to those unlearned in the Vedas be useless; for it is by giving wealth to worthy recipients that a great donor attains true merit.
When poison and sensual objects are compared, poison is better when viewed, for sensual objects are not good when indulged in;
poison destroys only in a single lifetime when drunk, whereas sensual objects cause torment throughout successive births.
"O Mother, is this praise of you: 'Kāma was indeed pacified by Śiva, yet you have made him rise again'?
But for her, who effortlessly brings forth the four aims of human life, that [statement] is merely a figurative expression."
I would gladly dwell in the forest wearing a patched garment woven from withered *palāśa* leaves, sustaining my life even with waters obtained without begging;
yet, I cannot bring myself to utter that wretched and piteous speech—"Give!"—accompanied by trembling limbs, shivering, trepidation, and the internal fever of distress.
Granted, by the favor of the king, a dog might even come to stand upon the head of a lordly elephant;
yet, O wretch, it can never be made to bite you along with him.
Granted that he is dark-bodied, that he soils one’s dwelling, garments, and the like, that he makes the world weep, and that he shatters the assembly of people even in an instant;
yet, O beloved of Svāhā, having given birth to this smoke born of fire—which clings to your very finger on the path for your own natural welfare—were you not ashamed?
Granted that there may be thousands of those who are pre-eminent in aesthetic essence, or granted that there may be those who have taken a vow to the sovereignty of the fragrance of loveliness;
yet we do not dispute this, nor do we speak merely to please you, O Lord—for it is the truth that the culmination of beauty has reached its ultimate limit in you alone.
Granted that every ornament indeed infuses aesthetic flavor (rasa) into the meaning;
nevertheless, it is non-vulgarity alone that primarily bears this burden.
Granted, let the crow dwell happily upon the terrace of a palace that has the divine form of the nectar-like rays of the moon;
yet, can this pigeon ever rival him who is embraced by the neck of the beloved of Śrī Sundarī and silenced by her overflowing, nectar-like cooing?
A wise man may indeed enjoy women or drink in moderation, but he should not indulge in gambling or hunting, for those two are extreme vices.
O fool, you may well become Hari, or become Candra, or even become Hara with the crescent moon upon his crest;
yet you shall not escape becoming fuel for my fire of wrath, its terrible radiance intensified by the destruction of your knowledge.
Desire, by its very loveliness, excessively produces a certain delusion;
like a poison, it suddenly snatches away life through its sweetness.
May Kāma—who dwells at the corners of the eyes of those with lotus-like faces, and who has reduced the people of the three worlds to servitude—arise for your delight;
he whose loveliness, though he was burnt by the enemy of Tripura, has increased all the more, becoming an object of longing for all the world, like the application of collyrium.
Love is enraged; even the moon is striving by force to burn me; and the winds have gathered from the direction of Yama to carry away my life-breaths.
O messenger, those cuckoos with blood-red eyes are urging them on with their warbling; therefore, bring that beloved here quickly, for otherwise there is no protection for me anywhere.
Desire, anger, and greed dwell in the body as thieves; they have stolen the jewel of knowledge. Therefore, be vigilant, be vigilant!
Desire, anger, greed, pride, exhilaration, and likewise arrogance—
these six, which constantly reside within one's own body, must indeed be conquered.
Desire, anger, greed, arrogance, mental pride, and likewise joy— these are indeed the enemies that lead to the destruction of wicked rulers.
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, joy, and likewise pride—one should cast off this group of six; when these are abandoned, O King, a ruler is happy.
Lust, anger, and likewise delusion—these three are great enemies.
As long as these have not been conquered, how can there be happiness for human beings?
Lust, anger, and greed—these thieves dwell within the body; they plunder the entire world. Therefore, be vigilant, be vigilant!
Desire, anger, as well as greed, passion, hatred, and envy; pride, deceit, as well as delusion, amorous longing, and arrogance.
For these are indeed terrible enemies who steal away the entirety of one's dharma;
by them the living soul is made to wander in this cycle of existence which yields manifold sufferings.
Lust, anger, greed, exhilaration, pride, and arrogance—one should cast off this group of six; when these are abandoned, O King, one becomes happy.
Desire, anger, intoxication, pride, greed, and likewise joy—
these must be avoided with diligent effort by a ruler of the earth who acts with reverence.
Having achieved victory over these, the king should then secure the victory over his servants;
having secured victory over his servants, the king should conquer the citizens and the people of the countryside.
Desire should be abandoned by every means; if it cannot be abandoned, it should be directed toward one's own wife, for she alone is the remedy for it.
It is my conviction that desire alone is more important than both wealth and dharma.
This desire is the great enemy; one should resolutely conquer it alone.
Those great-souled ones who have conquered desire have conquered the entire world.
O wise and sinless one, it is ordained that for teachers, as well as for wives and sons who have come into being, there is always the right to act according to their will.
People describe her creeper-like eyebrows as the bow of Love; however, my opinion is otherwise: they are a pair of young bees resting upon her two lotus-eyes.
One seeking knowledge should indeed avoid these eight: desire, anger, greed, the taste for delicacies, amorous play and curiosity, excessive sleep, and overindulgence.
Having fashioned a boat made of steadfastness, cross over the difficult waters of birth— the river whose current consists of desire and anger, and whose waters are the five sense-faculties.
When one is tempted by desire, anger, fear, or other [passions], yet does not succumb to greed;
that power by which one is endowed for the sake of action is known as the power of counsel (*mantraśakti*).
Those who are intoxicated by lust, anger, and pride, and who remain under the control of women,
are not purified by water even through hundreds of baths at sacred fords.
For those ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained,
and who have realized the Self— verily, for them, there is the extinction into Brahman on every side.
Lust, anger, delusion, greed, pride, and arrogance—one should cast off this group of six; when these are abandoned, O King, one is happy.
Desire, anger, and all the rest— intellect, the senses, and egoism—
along with their various qualities and actions, dissolve through the dissolution of the mind.
Tormented day and night by the afflictions of desire, anger, and the like,
this self dwelling within the body is cooked like a medicinal herb in a *puṭapāka* vessel.
O Indra among kings, they know him alone to be a Brāhmaṇa in whom lust, anger, falsehood, malice, greed, delusion, pride, and the like bow down.
Disregarding desire and anger, one should uphold dharma alone;
for dharma, O best of the Bharatas, is the most conducive to the welfare of kings.
Having not conquered desire and anger, what will one do in the forest?
Or, having conquered these two, what will one do in the forest?
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives matters according to righteousness,
his subjects follow him just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
Both desire and anger are two adversaries to self-mastery; having slain the bodiless one (Kāma), what indeed was accomplished by the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva) through his wrath?
May that leader of sages, the Kinsman of the Sun (the Buddha), who pacifies the hundred enemies beginning with Manmatha through patience, grant you prosperity.
That foolish king who pursues wealth while placing desire and anger at the forefront grasps neither dharma nor wealth.
Desire and anger, which are most intoxicating, should be employed as is appropriate:
desire in the protection of subjects, and anger in the destruction of enemies.
Having completely conquered desire and anger, what will he do with forests?
The body is sustained by food; the family is sustained by virtuous conduct.
For desire and anger drag a man away from his goals;
having utterly conquered those two enemies, a king conquers the earth.

Who, like a bee, does not wither before the Lord—who destroys desires, who looks with a crooked eye, who is smeared with worldly prosperity, and who delights in the company of serpents? Do not long for fruit from one who possesses no virtues.
Hunting, gambling, women, and likewise drinking— these four types of vices arising from desire have been declared by those who understand the nature of vice.
O Desire, I know your root; you are born, it is said, from volition.
I shall no longer form volitions toward you; thus, you shall cease to exist, root and all.
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; however, one addicted to those born of anger is deprived even of his own self.
Skilled in the arts of love and adept at appeasing the angry woman,
he becomes somewhat disenchanted with his beloved when she manifests a slight disregard.
Assuming forms at will, raining down weapons, missiles, stones, and water,
as well as darkness, wind, mountains, and clouds— this is indeed superhuman illusion.
Bhīma slew Kīcaka while assuming the form of a woman;
Nala remained concealed for a long time through his divine power of illusion.
The prosperity of those with foolish minds— who are characterized by lust, pride, and the like, and who act without reflection— perishes along with their very lives.
Knowledge possesses the qualities of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), for it yields fruit even out of season;
in foreign lands, knowledge is like a mother, and it is remembered as hidden wealth.
Givers of the wish-fulfilling cow, the earth, and other such gifts are easy to find on this earth;
however, a person in this world who is devoted to compassion for all living beings is rare to find.
Women are the snares for binding the limbs of the bird-like men— spread out by the hunter named Desire for those of deluded minds.

In what form does the one who assumes the shape of a boar bear [the earth]? What kind of woman does the king desire? By whom was that which generates passion created? And by whom does the face of a young woman shine?
