He who, having attained some measure of prosperity, does not strive for its increase,
will find no welfare in his future lives, like a family that consumes its own seeds.
Just as Pāṇḍu was brought down after remembering himself to be addicted to desire,
so too should one turn back from anger, like Anuhāda whose son was slain.
The bond of sensual desire alone is the only fetter; there is no other fetter here.
For one who is liberated from the bond of sensual desire is fit for becoming Brahman.
Fainting at every step from the strike of the arrows of desire,
the hearts of young men are revived by the nectar of the smiles of young women.
Granted that this entire world may be subject to the power of Time;
yet for those who have taken refuge in the Death of Death, what can Time do to us?
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father’s house at his pleasure until death;
yet he must never give her in marriage to one who lacks good qualities.
Relying on insatiable desire, and possessed by hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance,
they embrace false convictions through delusion and proceed with impure observances.
They desire, they become dispassionate, they cause passion, and they abandon; even while dragging away all goals, women are never truly known.
A high-minded person should never desire a trivial object;
rather, he should increase his own magnanimity, power, and fame upon the earth.
The rain-clouds constantly showered down desired boons, the earth was always rich with crops, cows yielded as much milk as one could hold in a jar, and trees were perpetually laden with fruit.
This entire world follows the conduct of desire;
for as is the conduct of kings, so indeed is the conduct of their subjects.

In this forest of birth— which is terrifying with the tiger of desire, the serpent of evil intellect, the nest of the uncontrollable mind, the roaming lioness of illusion, and the bear of greed for worldly objects— those virtuous people who know the truth never find delight, for its borders are strewn with the thorns of attachment to sense-objects.

The wound inflicted by the arrows of the hunter Kāma was not reckoned as such, for you were remembered as the "Life-restorer" (Saṃjīvanī); we were not consumed by the fire of separation, for we were sustained by the hope of union with you.
This day was passed by me through various painted forms created by my own imagination; what more need be said? You truly dwell within my heart—you yourself are the witness to that.
Upon the breast of the fawn-eyed woman, which possessed the power to crush her lover in the act of amorous combat,
a line of perspiration rose up on all sides like a shower of flowers from the flower-bowed god of love.
Victorious is the Lord of the body among ascetics, who desires sovereignty over the universe, the master of the mind, and the ruler of the horses of the senses;
he whose command even the great elements uphold with their heads—whose crest-jewels cast forth rays of light.
He has no desire whatsoever; this is perceived through direct observation.
Through the shared duty of husband and wife, he shall attain the dharma of the three Vedas.
But Kāma, awaiting the opportune moment for his arrows, like a moth desiring to enter the mouth of a flame,
repeatedly touched the bowstring while aiming firmly at Hara in the presence of Umā.
If someone somehow managed to bypass four of the arrows of Love,
they were nonetheless brought under his sway by the fifth weapon, emerging from the mechanical throat of the cuckoo.
The Lord of Light arrived as if to make the fish of heaven his gateway for meeting the King who desired to conquer Kāma.
The beauty of dress, gracefulness, loveliness, excellence of qualities, various kinds of playful gestures, and the knowledge of the hearts of beloved women belong to Kāma.
Others say that the primary cause of desire is Māyā, the great teaching, who is resolute and possesses the playful skill in composing the entire web of phenomenal manifestation;

through association with her, even the Blessed One—who is effortless in the cycle of activities concerning the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe, and who destroys the great delusion within every individual—comes forth as Śrīraṅga.
The inherent nature of desire belonging to anyone cannot be wiped away;
for, O Noble One, it does not dwell long in the abode of those with corrupted minds.

How is it that the slender-bodied, innocent girl was not instantly consumed by that fire of passion, which has been so greatly intensified by the winds of the sighs of women separated from their lovers? O Hari, she now lives because she has been drenched by the heavy streams of water falling from her restless lotus-eyes; therefore, you must bring her back to life.
One afflicted by desire may not obtain the woman he longs for;
Indra, though possessing a body born from a thousand wombs, became [afflicted] due to his pursuit of Ahalyā.
That power by which one is not led astray when being enticed by others out of desire, anger, fear, or greed,
and which is joined with the capacity for action— that is known as the power of counsel (*mantraśakti*).
You weary yourself out of desire; what is this "woman"? It is merely a name for hell—a sack of flesh filled with filth and marrow—so why is it not reviled?
A self-centered nature driven by desire is not praised, yet there is no such thing as a total absence of desire;
for the mastery of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.

"The triple set beginning with desire (*kāma*) alone is the root of all affliction for mortals born of *māyā*"; thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, my Master, who is dear to all living beings and whose radiant crest-jewel shines upon the crowns of the gods. Therefore, that triad must be abandoned with a resolute mind by one who seeks the goals of human life.
Even for a king who lacks other means, the powers consisting of the influence of desire, the support of a faction, and the strength of a family are the causes of success.
Women do not tolerate even a husband who provides them with sensual pleasures, who offers them mental comfort, and who protects them, if he is not supreme.
Having thoroughly mastered the *Kāmānuśāsanaśata*,

let him honor your breasts in private with nail-marks that bear the likeness of the crescent moon on Śiva’s forehead, mingled with the red dye from the saffron paste of the angry Daughter of the Mountain.
A man who follows after desires perishes along with those desires;
by casting off desires, a man shakes off whatever passion (rajas) there may be.
Having cast off sensual desires, a person shakes off whatever passion there may be,
as well as the suffering born of desire and anger, along with shamelessness and lack of delight [in the Dharma].
Whether overcome by desire or by anger, he who acts wrongly toward his own people or others will find that no one becomes his companion.
O King, sensual desires indeed cling to a man as the very root of obstacles to the Dharma;
by first subduing them with fortitude, a man gains blameless praise in the world.
Even the self of a wise man, though restrained, yearns for sensual pleasures;
like a bull confined to a stall, it rushes toward the young grass upon encountering it.
The man who does not enjoy a woman of shapely hips who has come to him of her own accord, afflicted by desire,
will surely go to hell, struck by her sighs.
He who does not approach his own wife when she is afflicted by desire, distressed, and entreats him again and again, is indeed to be regarded as a Cāṇḍāla.
"Afflicted by desire or tormented by the heat"— these ambiguous words the messenger spoke jokingly in order to agitate the young man.
For the sake of desire, the ignorant person acts miserably and encounters suffering such as execution and imprisonment;
for the sake of desire, the wretched world of living beings, miserable with hope, undergoes penance, death, and exhaustion.
One who desires pleasure and wealth should practice dharma from the very beginning;
for neither wealth nor pleasure ever departs from dharma.
Whatever sin one commits by speaking falsely out of lust, greed, fear, anger, or likewise from the testimony of witnesses— that is proclaimed as untruth.

An entrance for those devoid of wealth, an instruction in deceit, a treasury of illusion, and a locus of trickery; may this brothel be an easy entry for those who have no substance, a delightful affliction, and a place of easy access.

Those who are virtuous, relishing the taste of the bliss of tranquility and subsisting on nectar, perceive sensual pleasure— the supreme enjoyment of those possessed by desire— as loathsome, just as swine view the food of humans.
The lower garment of a lover, clinging to the hand of his wife as he delayed the conclusion of their amorous festival,
provoked her resentment by its long threads that remained caught in the loops of her girdle.
By means of these amorous exploits, some fools, though they are beloved, cause themselves to suffer by staying awake at night.
Through association with lustful men and women, a man becomes lustful;
thereafter, in another body, he is born as one characterized by anger, greed, and delusion.
With their curved fingernail-tips, soft with perspiration,
lovers somehow managed to leave marks upon the hard slopes of their beloveds' breasts.
The pleasure that comes from embracing a passionate woman endowed with the bloom of her first youth— her soft, low-toned moans gentle and restrained,
her breasts full and swelling— that pleasure, I am certain, does not exist in the abode of Brahmā.
O traveler of the mind, do not wander through the forest of the beloved's body, which is difficult to traverse due to the mountains of her breasts; for there dwells the thief of passion.
Receiving the turbid glances of amorous women as they opened their eyes,
the cool-rayed moon, having risen very slowly, proceeded toward the sky as if trembling with fear.

The wild boar of passion, intoxicated by desire and arisen from the mud of collyrium in the eyes of longing women, wanders within the forest of the hearts of lovers and uproots the very root of the creeper of pride.
Defeated in its splendor by the faces of amorous women, the moon was indeed unable to shine;
as if out of shame, it submerged itself into cups filled with wine in order to regain its stainless form.
Who has not had sin transferred to them through contact with groups of lustful women?
Alas, out of delusion, the world—its vows emaciated by passion—neither eats nor bathes.
In the mansions of that lover who was accompanied by amorous women, where the sound of mṛdaṅga drums resounded, each succeeding festival—
possessing even greater prosperity than the former— superseded the previous celebration.
Alas, lovers afflicted by the fever of cold on a winter night survive,
protected by the embrace of the breasts of fawn-eyed women.
O traveler of the mind, do not wander through the mountainous terrain of the beloved’s breasts; there, in the thicket of the line of hair, lies the cave of the navel.
Hidden therein is the son of Madhusūdana, and by that thief, O man, you are stripped naked even during the day—what need is there to speak of the night?
The luster of the beloved’s breasts, enhanced by their fullness,
is intent upon utterly conquering the splendor of the peaks of the golden mountain.
What kind of man is dear to a woman whose gait is languid from the weight of her breasts, whose eyes move playfully, and who is the eternal abode of the sole amorous sport of Kandarpa?

From where do your enemies emerge—those whose throat-pits are parched by the exertion of panting—as they seek to live after their elephant hosts have been slaughtered by your sword drawn with effortless ease?
Lustful women, like rivers flowing toward the lowlands, certainly do not hesitate;
for even the wives of a king offer their affection to the Lord of the Cowherds, just as stars belong to the Moon.

A lustful man, overcome by the wounds of desire, first abandons his beloved woman and later enjoys a thousand women without fear. Even for men who are single-mindedly devoted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures in this manner, this enjoyment must be abandoned from within this very body after only a few days.
People will become lustful, stories will be base, and who will find delight in anything?
Having obtained this auspicious day, O seekers of wealth, what riches will you now create?
While her lover is anxious with intense embraces upon their first union,
the courtesan, absorbed in meditation, performs the accounting of the household.
The bee is said to be for the lover, and the mango blossom for the beloved;
likewise, the sprouts of invitation are used, and the wall is prescribed for warding off.
What did Hari lift up when it was stuck in the middle of the ocean? What kind of learning of the scriptures is considered pure?

Do you desire that woman of shapely hips— who, though her character was once disciplined by the hardship of the vow of fidelity to one husband— has now entered your fickle mind through her beauty, and who has cast off all shame to cast her arms around your neck of her own accord?
"Even at their final breath, those who ask, 'What is my destiny? while still pursuing their own self-interest—for the sake of such people as well, the wicked commit evil deeds."
Whence does it come from the clouds? Who is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa? And what is the assembly like?
Whom does the serpent-killer protect? What does autumn cause to blossom?
And what is the destroyer of fortitude?
What does the Lord of the Gaṇas hold in his palm?
Tell me, what is the fickle one?
From ascending and descending, there is one answer for both from those who are skillful.
Driven by desire, the rainy season moved swiftly to conquer the three worlds;
was it as if she were eating the moon’s orb like curd, holding fast to the greenery for the sake of beauty?

May that Lord of Sages protect you—he who was seen remaining unmoved from his seat of yoga, while Māra’s heroes drew their bows with desire amidst the sounding of sharp drums, and the divine host of women gazed with playful glances, charming smiles, yawns, and the raising of eyebrows; while the Siddhas bowed their heads and Vāsava, his body bristling with joy, looked on in wonder.
Could even Kāma not pierce the hearts of young women?
Yet their chests appear as if swollen from the strike of his dull arrows.

When even the mind of the enemy of desire (Kāma) is agitated by the arrows of desire, what can be said of human beings? When the lord of elephants stirs in the monsoon wind, the ocean itself is the only limit for the waves.
Those whose wisdom has been carried away by various desires resort to other deities,
adhering to their respective rules of conduct, constrained by their own innate natures.
Desire, intolerance, liberality, compassion, modesty, trepidation, cruelty, and lack of refinement; hypocrisy, arrogance, then piety, wretchedness, and the disparagement of one's own group.
Betrayal, fear, constant negligence, and intolerance of cold, heat, and rain—
when these occur at the proper time, they certainly and inevitably create obstacles to success.
My heart, scorched by desire, was submerged in the deep lake of her navel—a necklace of great emerald stones—and was swallowed by many serpents;
then a certain banner of the enemy of snakes (Garuḍa), with hands moving through the force of his sport, performed here itself the appropriate counter-measure by destroying them.
The youth of the ignorant, seized by the agitation of passion, ridiculed by rogues for their display of love, and struck down by poverty, leads only to misfortune.
There is no desire in a eunuch; there is no shame in a group of unchaste women; there is no water in mirages; and there is never any constancy in a woman.
There is no righteousness in one who lacks wealth, nor is there any prosperity for one whose soul is intoxicated; and generally, there is not even a drop of affection in the world of courtesans.
The conquest of the earth by kings has as its fruit the successful enjoyment of sensual pleasures; enemies are conquered by self-confidence—what need is there for the glory of political strategy?

The glorious Vīravara, the best of lords of the earth, reigns supreme over all: he is the God of Love to those with beautiful eyes, a treasury for those who follow the path of policy, the Fire of Time to his enemies, the celestial tree for the learned, a preceptor for the virtuous, Pārtha among archers, a pleasure-palace for those belonging to noble lineages, and Karna to those seeking gold.

Which are the Kambojas, who have made their refuge in the mountain-born waters of Kambuja; which are the Sahyakas, dwelling in the marshes of the Sahya forests; which are the Kacchavahas, whose shadows seek out the marshlands; and which are the Kāmarūpas, who are ill-favored?
O jewel of the Nara clan, as you suddenly draw to your ear the bow—held in your lotus-like hand, raised above the back of a tortoise, and drawn back to the tip of your ear—they now listen to Karṇa.
Likewise, one desires rites performed for specific wishes, as well as human objects of desire:
women, the fruit of giving, knowledge, magic, base metals, wealth, and heaven.

The state of divinity, lordship over the immortals, the collection of elixirs (rasāyana), ritual acts, leaping into the air like the wind, performing sacrifices, and likewise entering into water and other elements;
The fruits and the rules for all types of *śrāddha* offerings, as well as those resulting from fasting, works of public utility (*pūrta*), and the worship of deities;
Afflicted by various such karmas, one desires [objects];
the yogi should with effort turn back the mind that functions in this manner.
People perform certain optional rites that grant a limited heaven for a specific number of years and produce an immediate and intense delusion of the mind;
yet they do not know that self-bliss which is unknowable by others and unlimited. Does a seller of salt truly know the supreme value of camphor?
The wise know the renunciation of optional rites to be *saṃnyāsa*;
the discerning call the relinquishment of the fruits of all actions *tyāga*.
Considering the body to be perishable and realizing that life is fleeting, and understanding all enjoyments to be fragile,
O wise ones, apply your virtuous minds to the practice of yoga in order to cross to the further shore of the ocean of existence.
Your trunk is defiled by thorns, you possess no dense shade, whence could there be sprouts? Your flowers have lost their fragrance, and your rows of leaves are not captivating.
What can we say of the ripening of your fruit, for which we feel shame even to mention it? O *śālmali* tree, by what merit have you become a "moon-tree" (*somadruma*)?
The body is accompanied by impending ruin; prosperity is the seat of calamities; meetings end in departures; everything that arises is transitory.

He who, for the sake of desire, seeks worldly activity through the exhaustion of time and what are called "austerities," while failing to examine the defects of saṃsāra, seeks only suffering by means of suffering.
Whatever fruit a man might obtain through great physical hardship,
a woman obtains all of that with ease by honoring her husband.
The Ṛṣikas have severed limbs, while the Guravas strike the vital organs;
the Vāṅgas are fierce and endure being cut, while those born in Śūrpāraka are firm.
Malicious intent of body, speech, and mind, lack of respect,
and the failure to maintain mindfulness are known as transgressions regarding the vow of equanimity (*sāmāyika-vrata*).
The scribe and the thorn share the same fate;
once they have both entered within, all the constituent elements are corrupted by them.
The reason why the intestines were not devoured by the worm residing in his belly— mistaking them for its mother's flesh— is his lack of teeth.
Whether it be stability of body, dexterity of the senses, the prosperity of kinsmen, wealth, or cleverness—what indeed is the strength we possess that we remain so full of self-assurance?
Reflecting on whether this is my final breath or merely the one before the last, how can we endure for even a moment, having forgotten the Lord?
Having deliberated with the mind, one commits evil with the body and speaks falsehood with the tongue; thus, the threefold action is sinful.
One should always abandon the ten paths of unwholesome action: those of three kinds by way of the body, four kinds by way of speech, and three kinds by way of the mind.
Yogis perform action with the body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification.
When the body fails, when phlegm obstructs the throat, when the path of speech is dulled, when the sight is dimmed, when life desires to depart, and when the breath slowly subsides—
may the Beloved of Kātyāyanī come of his own accord out of compassion and whisper into our ears the *tāraka* (the Savior), which delivers one from the fear of the ocean of existence.

The winds blow, making the *kārañja* trees hum as they reveal the seeds within their bellies; they carry away the ripe black berries and the pods situated in their wide cavities; they cast into the sky the buzzing of crickets that deafens the world, while themselves rattling with the jingling sound of clusters of rustling *aśvattha* leaves.
He who neglects a friend who has been ruined by causes and non-causes, or who has fallen into misfortune through causes and non-causes, embraces death.
One becomes dear for a reason, and one becomes hateful for a reason;
this world of living beings seeks only its own interest—no one is dear to anyone by nature.
One becomes a friend for a reason, and one becomes an enemy for a reason;
therefore, a wise person should cultivate friendship here and not enmity.
That king who becomes angry with a servant without cause takes upon himself the madness of poison, as if bitten by a black cobra.
Friends and enemies alike arise solely because of a cause; therefore, one should abandon that cause by which enemies are produced.
The popular notion that the effect is similar to its causes is false;
for from you, who possess pride, has arisen a fame on earth that is free from pride.
Even though their anger was produced by a cause, these women now embrace their beloveds tightly at night under the pretext of the cold.
The rivers, their garlands of waves stirred by the *kāraṇḍava* ducks, their banks crowded with flocks of *kādamba* geese and *sārasa* cranes,
and reddened by the pollen of lotuses, bring joy to the people on all sides with the cries of swans.
"O Mother, do not delay; release my hand, for I am going to Hari.
I cannot bear to remain here while that flute thunders like an impudent messenger."
One becomes dear for a reason, and one becomes hateful for a reason;
this world of living beings seeks only its own interests—no one is dear to anyone by nature.
Woman was created by the Creator as a prison for the continuity of rebirth, a snare in the forest of saṃsāra, and a great pit on the path to heaven for men.
Compassion is the hallmark of meritorious deeds; gratitude is the mark of true men; deceit belongs to those of deluded minds; and ingratitude is the cause for falling into hell.
Since compassion and generosity are observed in you toward your servants,
your mind may well aspire to the lordship of even the three worlds.
O Kinsman of Mankind, you who are the abode of compassion and merit,
O Lord of the Holy Tīrtha Pārśva, grant me your gracious favor, which is the source of happiness.

May those rays from the tips of the toenails of [the Buddha], who bestows fearlessness— rays which are like jasmine flowers upon the stalk of the nectar of compassion, the beauty of a pearl necklace for his consort Wisdom, and the spray tossed up by the surging current of the river of tranquility— meet upon your heads as various garlands fit for the consecration of sovereignty over the world.

I take refuge in the cloud that is Śrī Rāma, who removes the suffering and sins of the entire world; he is the water of the nectar of compassion that brings joy to the *cātaka* birds that are those who have taken shelter in him; he is the rainbow of Viṣṇu that grants boons to the peacocks that are Brahmā, Agni, Indra, and the other gods; and he is beautified by the lightning-flash of the daughter of Janaka, who shines upon his lovely, smiling face.

By means of compassion, the passion for killing was destroyed; by truthfulness, the tendency toward harsh speech; by contentment, the skill in stealing the property of others; and by virtue, the blindness of passion.
By means of renunciation, the grasping at possessions—by those virtuous ones, I believe this entire earth has been clearly purified, even in their youth.
One should conquer self-conceit through compassion, craving through contentment,
sloth through exertion, and discursive thought through certainty.
Roughness in their breasts, tremulousness in their eyes, falsehood in their faces is praised; crookedness in the mass of their hair, dullness in their speech, and stoutness in their hips;

cowardice in their hearts is always said to be present, and the employment of deceit toward their lovers—those fawn-eyed women for whom such a collection of faults is considered a virtue would be dear to beasts.
Harshness, fickleness, discoloration of the skin, violence, restlessness, and folly;
anger, contempt, and suffering—these are the natural qualities of women.

These winds blow, bestowing joys through floods of sweet sandalwood fragrance; they possess the excellence of drawing forth the intense scent from the swaying fresh leaves of the trees in the Kārṇāṭī pleasure-grove, and from the trembling Campaka garlands worn by young Cola women. Carrying the quality of coolness acquired from sporting on the waves of the Godāvarī, they carry delight.

May that Ganges quickly dispel our misfortunes—she by whom this great wonder occurred: when the waters of the Tāmraparṇī, surging with their full weight of waves, mingled with the ocean, the pearls from the golden ear-ornaments of the Karṇāṭa women, upon being touched by mere droplets of those waters, became violently white and began to sport together with the oysters in the sea alongside Śacī.
For one desiring victory and possessing superior prowess, marching against the enemy's territory is recommended in either the month of Kārttika or Caitra, and not at any other time.
He who beholds his lord on the full moon day of Kārttika during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation shall become a wealthy Brahmin, a master of the Vedas, for seven births.
Those who have met with them before desire to behold their form in its entirety;
yet the eyes of these large-eyed women do not fall completely upon their beloveds.
The wise know that miserliness, arrogance, pride, fear, and even agitation— these are the sufferings of embodied beings born of wealth.
A life of miserly conduct toward one's own kin, reviling others, wearing tattered clothes, devotion to low-born people,
excessive anger, and harsh speech— these are the marks of a man who has come from hell.
Fame through meanness,
a collection of virtues through anger, and truth through hypocrisy—
Discipline is tested by hunger, wealth by calamities,
and steadfastness by adversity.
Through negligence, O twice-born one,
a family is destroyed by backbiting,
and discipline by intoxication.
Through misconduct, one's manliness is destroyed; through poverty, one's respect from people; and through possessiveness, one's self-knowledge is lost.
Cotton cloth that has been freed from its frame is pure until it is worn out; silk is pure until it is eaten by moths; woolen cloth is always pure, for wool is purified by the wind.
Even with hundreds of cotton undershirts,
the cold is not dispelled without the embrace of a slender-waisted woman with full breasts.
Her mass of hair is as radiant as a cotton pod, and her breasts embrace the abode of Love;
both her cheeks resemble those of an old goat—nevertheless, this harlot does not relinquish sexual pleasure.
Cotton, medicinal herbs, black grains, salt, eunuchs, bones, oil, fat, mud, charcoal, molasses, snake-skins, dung, and those afflicted by disease;

those who have vomited, the insane, those with matted hair, fuel, grass, those emaciated by hunger, buttermilk and the like; those with shaven heads, those who have smeared themselves [with ashes], those with disheveled hair, the grey-haired, and those wearing saffron robes—these are inauspicious.

What business have you with seeing the faults of others, and what business have you with thinking about others? O one of childish intellect, why do you distress yourself for no reason? Perform your own duty and abandon all concern for others.
Having understood that an action may be either tranquil or intense, the wise person should deliberate upon everything;
when it is tranquil, one should grasp what is tranquil, and when it is intense, one should grasp what is intense.
Having truly considered the task at hand, as well as his own power, place, and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.

Having thoroughly considered the task, those who accomplish it and the like, its expenditure, and its secure completion, the wise man undertakes it; otherwise, he does not do even the slightest thing.
"I shall perform this task according to rule; meanwhile, I will do that other work. Having done this, he thinks, "Today I have performed this; previously, I had that done.
Thus, intent on nourishing his own family, the living being, distracted by activities and devoid of righteous conduct, approaches the grasping hand of Death with a ruined intellect.
Even when one's life-force is powerless,
does a lamp not protect that which has come for refuge, preserving it according to its own nature?
One should appoint a messenger who is distinguished, well-born, and clever; however, one devoid of noble birth and good character will certainly destroy success.
Prakṛti is said to be the cause in the agency of actions;
Puruṣa is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain.
But when the time for action has arrived, one should never disregard these three:
seed, medicine, and food; just as with profit, so it is with purchase.
A servant who indeed requests wealth at a time of need or misfortune must be expelled immediately by kings who are conversant with statesmanship.

The intellect and understanding of a person are deprived by sins when they are appropriate for action; however, by the power of destiny, that same intellect arises for a man in all circumstances as something favorable.
Due to the diversity of the course of action, even one who is lowly may sometimes be sufficient, whereas a great person is never so;
for even for kings, a mirror is made of bell-metal alone, and not of gold.
One who knows the business at hand should be consulted, and not merely someone who is honorable or dear to me;
even a teacher must be served while seated, whereas a beloved’s hips may be enjoyed whenever one desires.
Whatever is caused to be done and whatever is done—whether it be good or bad—is what constitutes "the done.
One should place confidence in that which has been well-done, but one should not trust that which has been ill-done.
An action undertaken by the wise after considering its potential pitfalls is commendable not only in times of prosperity, but even in times of adversity.
O Arjuna, when prescribed action is performed simply because it is one's duty,
abandoning attachment as well as the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
For, because the task at hand is of great importance, one who knows the proper time— even if they are of low status—
should conceal existing faults and speak of virtues even where none exist.
In view of the task at hand, even poison consumed becomes like nectar for all living beings; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

What should and should not be done is not heard by the ignoble, whose intellects have failed due to being unrestrained on wrong paths; even when spoken with words of sound policy, it is not heeded by those who are deaf to reason.

Whether there is something to be done or not to be done, there is never any sense of agency at all; for one who has realized the state of liberation while living, it is like the appearance of a burnt cloth.
Thus, when the body has dissolved, the liberated one remains; for him who walks upon the path beyond the three qualities (guṇas), what rule is there and what prohibition?
Everyone who is satisfied weighs what ought to be done against what ought not to be done; but who, when afflicted by thirst on a desert path, deliberates over whether water is sweet or pure?
Regarding what should and should not be done, the *kākolaka* bird is indeed praised; however, common crows are not to be understood as such, though they may be accepted in the absence of the former.

He who reaches the end of his undertakings through action is wise. The courses of affairs are as crooked as a serpent; the minds of women are fickle; sovereignty is more unstable than a surging wave; and the youth of men runs away. Intentions are as flickering as the eyes of intoxicated women, and death is certain for mortals. O best of the intelligent, reflecting thus, apply your minds to Dharma according to reality.
Even if he is personally devoted to him, a minister who accomplishes his tasks by means of the destruction of wealth should not be neglected by the king; for if neglected, he will crush him.

Those skilled in statecraft who, through conciliation alone, peacefully resolve matters that would otherwise result in the highest fines and corporal punishments and require great effort to accomplish—they are true ministers.
However, those who improperly seek out ventures yielding little fruit and lacking substance by exerting forceful punishment—the sovereign’s fortune is weighed down by their ill-conducted actions.
"You must not show opposition, nor must you go outside this house; and anger, even if provoked for a moment, should last no longer than a prostration.
If you accept these rules for women as being not absolute, then, O rogue, I shall become your beloved—what is the use of persisting in your anger?"
I have spent the day with little difficulty, my longing occupied by various tasks;
but how indeed shall this night, with its long-waiting watches and lack of diversion, be passed?
A jackal following one even while engaged in other tasks is declared to bestow prosperity when it cries out in a peaceful direction;
however, if it howls in a blazing quarter of the sky, it portends great danger.
Generally, a person who has a purpose in view displays great affection;
a liquor-seller seeking wool nourishes his ram with tender grass.
When people, observing the flourishing of the fruit at the commencement of an undertaking,
generally disregard the calculation of its inconsistency [with the effort], they are not to be censured.
One should not completely fulfill the purpose of a crooked person who has sought assistance but whose resources are nearly exhausted;
for such a person, a mine of faults whose pride has increased upon receiving aid, flees far away from his friend.
Like those seeking a goal enduring the long fatigue of a journey, like sold slaves bearing the burden of labor,
or like those afflicted by disease enduring bitter medicine, women endure the house of their husbands with great hardship.
Relatives become friends through various services when one has a purpose to achieve;
wives and sons are easily obtained, but wealth alone is difficult to find in this world.
In this world, one who seeks a purpose relies [upon another] only as long as that purpose has not been accomplished;
once the further shore has been reached, what use is there for the boat?
People resort to one for the sake of their own interests; the ultimate beloved is not [sought].
Seeing the exhaustion of her milk, the calf abandons its mother.
One who has a purpose seeks association; once the purpose is accomplished, there is no association.
Therefore, one should cause all tasks to be performed with something remaining unfinished.
For these two must be accomplished by Time; indeed, Dharma brings about victory and serves as the light for all three worlds.
One should not mock one who is great but incapable of performing his duty;
while laughing at the pot-bellied Gaṇeśa who was unable to dance, the Moon became one who could not be dismissed.
The river Mālinī should be made, with pairs of swans resting upon its sandy banks; on both sides of it, the purifying foothills of the father of Gaurī, where deer are seated;
and beneath a tree from whose branches bark-garments hang, I wish to depict a doe scratching her left eye upon the horn of a black antelope.
One who, when assigned a task, accomplishes even many things provided they do not conflict with the primary task, is worthy of being entrusted with that work.
For there is no single cause that accomplishes even a very small task here;
indeed, he who knows a matter in its many aspects is capable of accomplishing that matter.

In this world, whatever action leads to the censure of one's own dharma through the practice of critical inquiry and debate should not be undertaken; for even if it appears beneficial here, it is not truly auspicious when viewed from the perspective of one’s own discernment.

Even for the sake of some business, a mother-in-law does not tolerate a delay in another's house; when a young man arrives at the home, the sisters-in-law whisper among themselves, harboring suspicions.
Furthermore, the angry sister-in-law threatens her even as she departs through the street. Alas, woe! For deer-eyed women, a husband’s house is generally nothing but a prison.
When a task is difficult to accomplish, people should not exert excessive effort;
if the task is achieved, there is no [further] toil, but if it is not achieved, there is only toil.
A servant in work, a courtesan in pleasure, like a mother at meals,
and a giver of wisdom in times of adversity— such a wife is difficult to find anywhere.
A lord of wealth who employs himself in a great undertaking is deprived of his prosperity; kingdoms where women hold sway and which are shunned by the wise,
being tormented by foolish ministers, wither away like drops of water.
A wife who is a counselor in affairs, a servant in tasks, a mother in meals, and a Rambhā in bed;
who is compliant in dharma, like the earth in forbearance, and possesses the six virtues—such a woman is blessed in this world.

A wife is a counselor in affairs, a servant in tasks, a mother in affection, the earth in forbearance, a partner in dharma, and a courtesan on the bed; through these six roles, a woman uplifts the family.
Even when there is business to attend to, she never goes outside nor looks at another man; she serves her elders and her mother-in-law, emulating even virtuous women.
She places great confidence in her husband, yet when midnight has arrived and all the people are asleep, that moon-faced woman goes out to dally with libertines.
Because one who exerts effort day after day, following the pursuit of the goal, repeatedly attends upon the Supreme Person, there arises from that practice a form of devotion characterized by love.
At the outset, composing even a slight introduction to the plot while desiring its expansion; revealing the extremely profound and hidden fruit of seeds that were contained within;
performing an investigation with the intellect and again withdrawing the mass of actions already set forth—the author of dramas, or one like me, undergoes this very same hardship.

Emaciation born of hunger, eating coarse food, endurance of cold and heat, coarseness of the hair on the head, and sleeping upon the bare ground—these very things, which at home bring about humiliation, lead to exaltation in the forest; for faults themselves become virtues when applied by sages to a worthy state.
If her emaciation is but a single digit of the moon at its first appearance, then her paleness is vast; if her playful lotus-stalks are but dense clouds, then how great is the ocean of her tears!

If her fever is cool, then how much more so is the fire? O Rāma, what more can be described? In her heart there is only the remembrance of you, and in her body, only the residue of its loveliness remains.
O mind, why do you desire to see that very beloved who is so difficult to find— one who, even when merely heard of, brings about emaciation, sleeplessness, and torment?
A farmer, having thoroughly mixed all the seeds, should sow them;
he should discern the actual existence of the seed that has arisen by means of the sprout.
I bow to the one who bears the mark of a garland of skulls, the sole slayer of Andhaka,
the boon-granting Lord, and the teacher of the Flower-Bowed One.

Having fixed the time, one should indeed perform one's duties and never otherwise. One should regard cows and other such beings as oneself; one should regard oneself as being toward wealth and dharma what one is toward them; one should employ food for the accomplishment of [one's goals], and the mother for instruction, and the teacher for [the acquisition of] knowledge.
One who performs an action after observing the proper time succeeds quickly;
one who considers the planetary positions when gambling will not suffer defeat.
In former times, poison rose from the ocean; today, a white poison called the moon emerges.
O friend, if Śiva were to consume this today, alas, he would surely destroy the blackness placed upon his own neck—and my fear as well!

Upon merely beholding his form and body as he drinks up time with the hollow of his hand— the circle of his fingers representing moments and his palms representing days and nights— whose limbs do not grow weary with the thought of their own destruction?
Time performs all actions, and Time alone destroys them;
the fool is merely deluded, thinking "I do" or "I destroy."
Time, acting as a Kirāta hunter, has brought about the slaughter of this day-elephant with its blossoming lotuses;
its twilight is the stream of beautiful blood, and the stars are the pearls from the frontal globes.
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake while others sleep; indeed, Time is difficult to overcome.
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
Time again extinguishes Time itself as it consumes all creatures.
The time that now prevails is the Kali Yuga; truthful men are rare, countries have gone to ruin, and kings have fallen into greed through heavy taxes.
Various bands of thieves plunder the earth, the noble people perish, and fathers do not trust even their own sons; alas, such is the age that prevails!
Time, though its nature is constant movement, behaves as if stationary;
like a fierce wind, it overturns the entire universe in an instant.
Time makes things equal and unequal; Time brings about both contempt and honor. Time makes a man a giver and a beggar.
Time keeps watch while others sleep; indeed, time is difficult to overcome.
Time moves through all beings, unrestrained and impartial.
Time, whose movement is subtle and eternal, is here considered to be twofold:
by way of gross aggregation and by way of subtle internal activity.
Time cleanses all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
All are subject to the power of Time, but Time is not subject to anyone's power.
It is Time alone that, bestowing restraint and favor through Time itself,
enters the intellects of living beings and impels them toward their duties and goals.

O Kālakāla, with a neck as black as the black of time, with a face as black as the black of time; O Kālakāla, as black as a dense cloud, as black as the black of time, as black as the black of time; O Kālakāla, white-black Kālakāla, O Kālakāla of the playful woman, go, O Kālakāla!
The Death of the Kali Age.
O Moon, you still carry the Kālakūṭa poison within you in the guise of your spot; alas!
It is as if, out of fear of it, Rāhu releases you immediately even though you have been swallowed.
In this world, people condemn the *kālakūṭa* poison because by it Śambhu became ageless and immortal;
yet they praise the moon as nectar for women separated from their lovers—truly, discrimination is rare indeed.
There are nine varieties of poison, such as *kālakūṭa* and others;
their medical treatment is now described concisely, preceded by mantras.
To those whose eyes long to gaze upon the face of their beloved, even a moment’s separation from her is equal to death; indeed, even the blinking of an eye becomes an obstacle.
This ketaki flower is lovely in the sequence of time; what hope can there be for it? For as its growth increases, so too does the proliferation of its thorns.

A tree on a riverbank, whose foundation has been shattered by the passage of time and which relies solely upon its own roots, is feared by those who see it falling due to the river's floods; yet, it is precisely through those very floods that have bestowed prosperity upon it that its standing ground gains firmness.
In the course of time, by the power of transformation, things that were previously utterly insignificant indeed become non-trivial;
even a tiny drop of water from a cloud becomes a pearl when it remains for a long time within the hollow of a bamboo reed.
One must not waste time; life passes away day by day.
King Yama observes the various courses of dharma.
What is prosperity? An elevated position.
What is that position? That which is the master’s dignity. What is that dignity? A uniquely weighty status, free from all obstacles.
And what is this state?
It is the conceit of self-adornment and the activity of others; to whom does all this belong?
To the Moon, the crest-jewel of Śrīkaṇṭha.
Bhīmaṭa, the lord of Kālañjara, composed five dramas;
among them, *Svapnadaśānana* attained the status of the king of literary compositions.
Whatever is devoid of personal conviction throughout the three periods of time—
that cannot be clearly declared as "it is thus" by a wise person.
O King, even the supreme seers, though they recount my births and deeds occurring throughout the three periods of time,
do not reach their end.
The unintelligent person who does not grasp a great jewel when it has come into his hands,
seeing it later gone into the hands of another, suffers remorse.
A king should take what is obtained at the proper time and should not disclose his purpose;
day by day, a wise ruler should milk the earth like a cow.
A wise man should recognize these as the signs of a dispassionate lord: the wasting of time, the increase of desires, and the destruction of results.
"Why do you hesitate, thinking, 'This woman is the terrible Kālarātri'? O dear one, strike Tāṭakā in order to save the three worlds!"
You are the Night of Time, the Great Night, and the terrible Night of Delusion;
you are Śrī, you are Īśvarī, you are Hrī, and you are Buddhi, characterized by awakening.
When the rain-cloud pours forth in due season and the king practices righteousness,
such prosperity as this sustains the people in happiness.

O Raghava, if that person whose scholarship has been determined by those who know the proper times does not receive instruction from others, yet remains a knower of that [truth], then destiny is supreme.
If he whose life was determined by those skilled in time to be exceedingly long-lived should live even with his head severed, then fate is supreme.
Seeing the sun falling from the sky, struck by the serpent of Time,
the Mother of the Ancestors seems to run along, taking up the Lord of Herbs.
A king who knows the proper time, a learned Vedic scholar, a river, and a virtuous person as the fifth—
wherever these are not found, one should not make one's dwelling.
Time generally agitates both the learned and the common folk;
if you wish to bring it under control, forbearance alone is the great medicine.
If Time were devoted to compassion; if the Kali age were fond of righteousness today; if the sword were gentle; if the serpent were a giver of contentment;

if fire were exceedingly cool; if the wicked person were a benefactor to all; if poison were to become life-giving; and if even a courtesan were full of passion—[then perhaps the world would be different].
The king is the cause of time for good and evil deeds;
therefore, by means of both righteous exertion and punishment, he should establish his subjects in their own duty.
O Lakṣmaṇa, the power of Time over all beings is truly immense.
Everything that is difficult or even more difficult is under the power of Time alone;
when Time is enraged, how will there be protection for us from Time today?

In those underground chambers, which serve as a locus for perfumes scented by the rising fragrance of black aloe-wood incense, men do not suffer from the harsh winds of the month of Māgha, as they remain sheltered within the warmth of the breasts of dark-complexioned women.
With their limbs anointed with abundant black aloe and sandalwood paste, and their tresses made fragrant with flower ornaments,
women hasten from their parents' homes to their bedchambers at nightfall upon hearing the roar of the clouds.
Even in black aloe wood, despite its own excellence of fragrance, the scent begins through association with another tree;
by the winds that cling to you, this skill of sandalwood attains identity—what multitude of trees does it not thus become?
Kālāgnirudra is in the Ādhāra, and likewise Kuṇḍalinī is the Śakti;
Ānandā is in the Svādhiṣṭhāna together with the Śakti named Kāmā.
Delay your arrival; terrify him with the flashing of your lightning, frighten him greatly with your thunderous roars, and display the blackness of your face.
O cloud, for the sake of testing the mind of this *cātaka* bird who has no other recourse, you may employ all these means here; yet even so, he begs nothing from you beyond that.
If a king does not allow the lapse of time for the payment of livelihood,
his servants will never abandon him, even if they have been rebuked.
For when there is a delay in the payment of food and wages, the employees become resentful toward their master and turn hostile; that is considered a very great calamity.
There is the wasting away of time, the oppression of dharma and artha,
and the provocation of those of virtuous nature due to constant residence within.
The disclosure of secrets, inciting others toward improper actions,
envy, resentment, anger, obstruction, and acts of rashness.
And because of [the consequences] such as those beginning with MSS_9830-1, and that which was previously proclaimed regarding addiction to women (strīvyasana),
therefore a king who desires his kingdom should renounce addiction to women.
From Time the universe sprouts forth, and again Time sets it in motion;
Time has both gross and subtle movements, and its various aspects are thus described.
From Time the seed proceeds; from Time it releases the embryo;
Time generates the son, and Time again shall withdraw him.
From time the seed sprouts; from time the fruit proceeds.
Indeed, time sets the creation in motion, and indeed, time withdraws it again.
O Mother, disregarding the times of the equinoxes, solstices, and transits, as well as when the moon and the sun have set,
may I remember your lotus-feet, which are characterized by bliss and in which all duality has been cast away.
The suitability of the timing for both Rāghava and Arjuna is clearly evident;
when destiny is favorable, even a small action becomes highly fruitful.
A vulture perched upon the roof of a house brings misfortune after some time; however, a wicked person standing near the house brings immediate harm to living beings.
I shall describe the characteristics of the Kālañjara swords, which are capable of bearing great weight. A sword measuring fifty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) is proclaimed to be the best.
If even Kālidāsa, that abode of the arts, were moved by the words of a servant while walking here on the royal road, what shame would there be for others?
May the poetry of Kālidāsa, fresh youth, buffalo curd, milk with sugar, venison,
and a tender young woman be mine in birth after birth.
If the speech of the poet Kālidāsa should ever attain equality in meaning with my words, it would be terrified at every step.
"O Kālindī, speak, O Agastya born from a jar! Why do you take my name, 'Ocean'?
And why do you, Narmadā, address me by the name of my co-wife?"
If that is so, then why do you experience this sootiness?
It is from the tears of the Mālavī women meeting with their collyrium;
what has happened to them?
King Kuntala became enraged.

Having watched his mother depart for the Kālindī, the son of Nanda, with his face beautifully radiant, cast his eyes all around at the cowherd women absorbed in their chores and entered the dairy house within;

there, having broken open the vessels and slowly eating the milk products while exclaiming "Madhu! Madhu!", he quickly returned with a bright smile upon his face—may that son of Nanda bring about auspiciousness.

We worship with true devotion that radiant splendor which alone is steadfast in destroying all sins; it is ever-delighting, for it has captivated the hearts of the women of Vraja with the sound of its flute, and it is joyfully pervaded in every direction by cowherds and boys who shine with the skill of their play in the forests on the dark banks of the Yamunā.
The braid of hair of the heroine Earth shines forth as the Yamunā; her daughter is the Gaṅgā; and here, the collection of her great merits is the water, which is the essence of Sarasvatī.

This braid is distinguished by being endowed with the excellent affection bestowed by the best of the immortals, yet it is devoid of binding—herein lies a wondrous marvel that shines intensely, for it is entirely free from the quality of darkness (or the color black).

May the streams of pure luster from the body of Madhumathana bring us prosperity—streams which were joyfully plunged into by the young female deer, thinking them to be a mass of Kālindī’s lovely waves; which were gazed upon with delighted hearts by the peacocks, thinking them to be a young cloud; and which were gathered as ear-ornaments by the charming cowherd girls, thinking them to be clusters of *tamāla* blossoms.
May that song of Hari protect you— sung with longing by Him who sits in the shade of the *vañjula* groves on the banks of the Yamunā’s waters, savoring His fresh passion for Rādhā,
and which is being listened to by herds of calves who have raised their ears and bent their necks to touch it with their tips, while they gaze at the unfaltering garland of lotuses He wears.

Victorious is the meaningful sound of the flute of Śauri, who, having emerged and seen all directions filled with the water of the Yamunā as young women eager for sport in her waters were scattering their silken garments,
and who has been watching for a long time from a hidden bower on the riverbank where he meets the shore, now causes these women to tremble with agitation.
Victorious is the arm of the Earth, which is the sole root of unbroken world-bliss and whose stability was proclaimed by such deeds as splitting the banks of the Yamunā and the ruin of Hastināpurī;
may that ploughshare of his—whose wrath was vomited forth under the guise of the spray of blood spurting from Muṣṭika’s head when struck by a harsh fist—shatter all that is inauspicious for you!

O King, bearing a pair of jars that embrace the waters of the Yamunā and Narmadā flowing with the ichor of rut, possessing a trunk-like flood of the celestial river extending across the expanse of the sky,

adorned with bells and the sound of "well done," crushing the lotus-stalks of undesired fame, and appearing like a great water-pot amidst the clouds of his mass of glory, he wanders restlessly through the lake of the belly of the world.

May the agitated cries of the enemy of Kaṃsa—“Huṃ! Huṃ! Child, the bow! The bow! The bow!”—heard as he lay sleeping in a bower of *vañjula* creepers on the sandy banks of the Yamunā while a circle of attendants was softly massaging him and engaged in private conversation, protect you.
On the banks of the Kālindī, it was not by me; nor on the slope of the mountain, was it not by me; nor at the foot of the banyan tree, was it not by me.

"Is it not so? I have never seen Kṛṣṇa before in the courtyard of Rādhā’s father!"—may Hari protect you as he laughs in the presence of Yaśodā’s astonished husband, who is filled with fear by the cowherds' words, while departing from his own home.

May Hari protect you—he who, having heard the words of Yaśodā—who was intent on deceiving him with such childishness as, "O Hari, go to the sandy banks of the Kālindī to play with Musalī; meanwhile, drink the milk from Karburikā, for your tuft of hair will grow long"—was delighted and touched his own tuft while the milk was only half-drunk.

May Dāmodara, the Lord of Dvārakā, bring fragrance to the three worlds as he remembers with rising remorse the Kālindī river with its soft current along its banks, the mountain slopes dark with blue lotuses, the caves fragrant with *kadamba* blossoms, and Rādhā, sweet in her first secret tryst.
On the banks of the Kālindī, delightful with the pollen of lotuses crushed by elephants, Kṛṣṇa wanders through the fields at the edge of the cool waters;
there, playfully fickle, he made the lotus buds into ear-ornaments for the young cowherd girls as they sang something most sweet.

O crest-jewel of kings, O ornament of the world, within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), your enemies' ill-fame repeatedly acts like the Yamunā river, like collyrium, like the moon, like a serpent, like the circle of fire, and like the throat of Śiva; it acts like moss, like the cuckoo, and like a mass of great blue clouds.

Is it the dark mass of the Yamunā’s waters, or a swarm of bees upon a cluster of *mālatī* flowers, or perhaps a heap of musk from the navel? The lovely tangle of hair on the moon-faced woman surpasses them all.
Why do you fall into delusion? Alas, this fierce expanse of the poison-bearing serpent is manifest before the world, swallowing it by force so that there is no longer any happiness.

May the throat-pipe of Śambhu’s consort, filling the three worlds with a manifold display of shimmering beauty— as if with masses of Kālindī’s ripples, groves of blue water-lilies, flashes of sapphire, moss, floods of collyrium, the weight of thick darkness, clusters of young clouds, and swarms of musk-deer and cuckoos— alleviate all calamities.
Let the sands of the Kālindī, the evening breezes, and the lovely rays of the moon not merely fail to dispel my fever—why then do they instead intensify it?
For here in the inner apartments, as I listen to the sighs of the women of Vraja who have bitten their lips, those sighs spread forth and utterly shatter the pride of the lovers' good fortune.
How could one search for that serpent who is submerged within the waters of the Yamunā—waters dark as fragments of sapphire on her banks—and who resembles a mass of collyrium or a swarm of bees?

For if the jewels upon his circle of hoods were not radiant like stars, he would not attain eminence through them; indeed, it is by those very qualities that the virtuous rise, yet by those same qualities they fall into calamity.

May the unbroken conciliation of the enemy of Kaṃsa—whose feet were placed upon the footprints of Rādhikā as she departed from the Rasa dance, having abandoned her lover on the banks of the Kālindī while she was angry during their play, and who followed her with eyes clouded by tears—be nourished for you; he, whose hair stood on end as his beloved looked upon him with a gracious glance.
May Kālī, who is the form of the tumultuous roar, the destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, the Heroine,
who is satisfied by the devouring of Śumbha and Niśumbha— may she protect you, O Lord.

May Kapardin bestow welfare upon his servants—he who takes delight in the arts of Kālī’s playful dalliance; who possesses the luster of a jasmine flower; who is like Death itself at the end of an eon; who is the primary root of the narrative-stalk of the sacrifice’s destruction; whose throat is as cruel as a raven’s; who has exhausted the beloveds of Kandarpa with his tumultuous clamor; and whose beauty is overcome by compassion.
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa was intent on seizing the serpent Kālīya on the bank of the Yamunā,
the three worlds were turned upside down as he submerged himself headfirst into the water.
Bestowing upon the quarters the splendor of a paste ground from *kālīyaka* sandalwood, and possessing a radiance shimmering with rays of light,
the dust born of the golden soil beneath the mountain spread abroad, having been dug up by the hooves of the mung-bean-eating horses.

O lotus-faced one, why is the wonder of the golden mountain of your breasts dispelled by black [garments]? What kind of musk ointment is applied to a face that possesses the luster of saffron filaments? Why is a dark-blue bodice placed upon your expansive hips? For what audacious person do you desire such a contrary arrangement of fate?
Causing turbidity in the dull-witted, uprooting the tree of Dharma, distressing the lotus-ponds of ethics, compassion, and patience, swelling the ocean of greed,
breaching the banks of moral boundaries, and driving away the swans of the virtuous mind— does not the swollen flood of the river of possessions cause nothing but affliction as it increases?
Seeing the turbidity of the waters, the swans have slowly flown away; the lotuses, their filaments shattered by the downpours and their luster dimmed, have sunk into the water.
That lake, once a path for the easy descent of all seasons' delights, is now covered with fresh grass; alas, even such a place, though naturally pure, has been ruined by its very growth.
When the wise, observing the turbidity of the moon, say that it is due to its association with me, I do not agree;
I know that his beloved, the Night, resides in his own lap, for she is not stained by blemish.

Do they not eat various kinds of food when it is available at the proper time? Do they not take water, or do they not sleep during the nights? Do they not nourish their own children, and do they not take pleasure with women? What difference is there between those whose intellects have lost the sense of what ought and ought not to be done and the beasts?
Just as a vessel must be emptied from time to time in order to be filled again,
we must prepare ourselves to attain a weighty capacity for receiving; yet,
within our own selves, we experience only emptiness.
At that time, as the horses moved with some difficulty, their own radiance stained the atmosphere;
for those weary steeds, the rain-bearing clouds became like supporting poles amidst the torrents of water.
At that time, when their son had fallen into a swoon, the queens arrived;
for the touch of a mother's hand is indeed like a handful of water to one who is parched.
When a tree bears fruit that provides no benefit at the proper time, its destruction is indeed appropriate out of a sense of shame;
but this is truly marvelous—that the plantain tree, having benefited others with its fruits, should suddenly abandon its own life.
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable.
A man who acts appropriately according to the time and place attains his desires; if two people had already eaten their fill, what would they have gained by eating more food?
The self-possessed man who, having deliberated at the proper time with his ministers regarding virtue, wealth, and pleasure, pursues them in this world shall not encounter misfortune.
By time alone do nights become dark or bright; by time alone does the moon reach its full orb.
Not out of season do trees bear flowers and fruit, nor do rivers flow with the force of the monsoon except in due time.
We know from inquiry that with the passage of time, the world—comprising earth, water, fire, air, space, and the rest—as well as the gods beginning with Brahmā, all go to destruction;
yet we see numerous worlds being incessantly destroyed, and still, in vain, we do not abandon our attachment to this worldly existence which consists of the delusion of *māyā*.
In time, even Mahendra becomes a worm, and a worm may attain the state of Mahendra;
thus, the conceit that "this one is great" and "that one is unstable" is unworthy of finality.
At the proper time, one should make peace with an enemy; at the proper time, one should wage war against a friend.
Relying on the necessity of the task at hand, the wise man makes time pass.
In due time, swift winds blow; in due time, rain comes from the clouds;
in due time, there is water with lotuses and lilies; and in due time, the trees in the forests blossom.
In the season of dark clouds and lightning, which brings joy to the peacocks, I shall tell you a marvel; listen, sirs, to what occurred in this house:
Alas, out of fear that their good fortune might perish, the beloved wife and her husband—both proud lovers—spent the entire night on a single bed as if observing the vow of a traveler.
When food is ready, one who is attentive and desirous of giving should not eat first, but always wait for the guest;
even if that guest does not arrive, the Victors declare in the doctrine of the Lord of Jinas that such a donor has cast off all impurity and rests upon a mass of merit, and is thus preeminent.
In the course of great time, when there is no limit, someone might at some point, in some final birth, attain the goal;
such is the method of establishing the supreme scriptures by leading them toward the meaning of negation through the manner of figurative expressions.
A king who is mild at the appropriate time and severe at the appropriate time,
while having regard for both worlds, shall possess both worlds.
He who is gentle at the proper time and harsh at the proper time indeed attains happiness both in this world and in the next.
He who is mild at the proper time and becomes harsh at the proper time accomplishes his tasks and overcomes his enemies.
If a king is both mild and sharp at the proper time, like the sun,
his rise is brought about by a circle of devoted subjects.
At the appropriate time, having learned the entirety of the king’s anger and subsequent events as they occurred,
he should enter the royal palace slowly, with his body bowed and his garments restrained.
Whether at the proper time or even at an improper time, one who is intent upon the twilight prayers—
whether ignorant or learned— is a Brahmin and my own body.
At this time of the clouds, it is simply not possible to remain without falling;
you are full of longing, O fickle one, but no, no, my friend—the path is slippery.
At this time, amidst a web of lightning flashes and adorned by the dancing of peacocks,
the beloved young moon— desired by all people— is not to be found in the sky.
May the clouds rain continuously in due season; may the earth be enriched with crops; may kings be devoted to the protection of their own dharma; may the Brahmins be filled with the three Vedas;
may the cows, their udders bowed down by sweet milk, be free from calamity day by day; and may the virtuous people, intent on peace, be endowed with goodness.
At the proper time, one should be as patient as a mountain and as intolerant as fire;
one should even carry enemies upon one's shoulders while speaking pleasant words.
At the proper time, one should speak what is beneficial, measured, non-contradictory, and pleasant;
one should be the first to speak, with a cheerful countenance, virtuous conduct, compassion, and gentleness.
At the proper time, a man should always consume food and engage in recreation that are wholesome and moderate; he should eat light food, remain undepressed in spirit, sleep well, and maintain purity.
Who is the mother of the world? What is the foremost part of the body? What does a man do first during sexual union?
Who is the slayer of the Daityas? Tell me in order: who kisses the face of Gaurī? Vāsudeva.
O Brahmin, Hari is declared by the Unborn (Aja) to be ninefold: time, place, action, agent, instrument, effect, scripture, substance, and fruit.

Time, destiny, action, the individual soul, inherent nature, substance, field, vital breath, the self, transformation, their combination, and the continuous flow of the sprouting of seeds—this is Your Māyā; I take refuge in the negation of that.
All those people enjoy their time appropriately; they are eternally joyful, always devoted to truth, and all are dedicated to the Dharma.
Having heard the cry of the kalahamsa, an elixir for the ears, received at the proper time from the sky, the lotus pond,
its flood of water gracefully opened, rose up with reverence.
Time approaches a man but once; having reached him, he who desires time does not indeed obtain it again.
Even the slow-moving python attains success by waiting for its prey that has come within its range at the proper time.
The season is Spring, and this flower-bowed god of love is enraged; the breezes are steady, carrying away the exhaustion of passion;
even this pleasure-grove is charming with its thickets of *vañjula* trees, yet my husband is far away—tell me, what is to be done today?
This time has become a vast tree, from which the worlds arise like *udumbara* fruits, and upon which the falling beings— mosquitoes and *ghuṃdhuma* insects— are perched.
Time passes, life ebbs away, and desires diminish;
yet some good deed has been performed, worthy of being remembered by the virtuous.
"Whether time is the cause of the king, or the king is the cause of time—let there be no such doubt in you; the king is not the cause of time."
Time transforms all things in the world, both auspicious and inauspicious;
Time withdraws all creatures and emits them once again.
Time transforms the cause, and self-interest follows it;
the wise man understands his own interest, and the world follows the wise man.
What is knowledge without poetry? What is prosperity without generosity toward those who seek it? What is dharma without compassion? Who indeed is a king without statesmanship?
What is a son without discipline? What is a woman of noble family without devotion to her husband? What on this earth is to be enjoyed without a beloved woman? And what is birth itself without fame?
What is adverse? The course of fate. What is desirable? A person who appreciates virtue.
What is happiness? A good wife. What is difficult to grasp? A wicked person.
Having reached that Kāverī, which is frequented by hosts of Apsarases,
a man who bathes there, O King, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O beautiful lady, let the Kāverī be seen before you like the braided hair of the Goddess of the Earth; with its betel-nut trees entwined by *nāga* creepers, it seems to teach the art of embracing.
Having drunk her waters, which were once flooded by the hips of Karṇāṭaka women during their baths, they are now carried toward the eastern direction by the luster-filled hollows of her navels.
These breezes from the banks of the Kāverī, akin to the fragrance of camphor pollen,
are like drops of perspiration from the women’s bodies during lovemaking.

O traveler! Alas, the southern breeze blows—a breeze that is the remainder of the pearls once enjoyed by the serpent-wives of the trees growing on the banks of the Kāverī; that is slow due to its swaying against the borders of the garments covering the full breasts of Karṇāṭaka women; and that is restless with the playful dancing of the tilaka-marks in the tresses upon the foreheads of the fickle Lāṭī women; it is the very God of Death to the beloveds of travelers.
Where, for whom, and what kind of longing increases by the spring breeze, which is the kinsman of the fragrance of the lovely lotuses of the Kāverī?

These winds blow—cool from sporting amidst the circle of waves tossing on the waters of the Kāverī, filled with abundant fragrance born from wandering through vast groves of sandalwood, and reaching the breasts of lovely women as they playfully tug at the hem of their garments; yet they act as enemies to those lovers who are most distressed by separation from their beloveds.

May that Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, who reclines upon the coils of the Lord of Serpents at Śrīraṅgam— a place worshipped by the Creator on the auspicious banks of the Kāverī, delightful with its heart-like sandbanks, meritorious, a blessing to the world, situated on the shore of Candra-ambhojavatī, and served by Lakṣmī and the Earth— protect us.
Who is a prostitute? What is this hostility? And what is the glory in battle?
Such is the mindset of fools who wish to waste their lives in vain.
The skilled poet composes the poem; only the connoisseur reveals its true essence. The mine produces the gem, but the craftsman fashions its exquisite beauty.
Let him compose poetry, let him speak refined Sanskrit, or let him master all the arts as they are taught;
yet if he does not understand the worldly conduct appropriate for his station, he is but a fool among the assembly of fools.
I compose poetry, yet I do not compose it very beautifully; though I compose with effort, I do not compose it very beautifully.
O King, whose footstool is adorned by the jewels in the crowns of monarchs—O Sāhasāṅka! I am a poet, I am a weaver, and I am a traveler.
Do you compose poetry because you have no friends who might restrain you when the wind rises? Drink cow’s ghee and enter a windless house; for it is men afflicted by wind who become poets.

Even a poem, though beautiful, does not bring delight to the connoisseur if it is not bound by multiple aesthetic flavors (*rasa*); likewise, sexual union with a fawn-eyed woman does not please if it is not accompanied by the play of love-quarrels.

If poetry is full of rasa, what is the use of nectar? If the face of a deer-eyed woman has cheeks pale with the fever of love, what is the use of the full moon? If there is independence for as long as one lives, why the grandeur of heaven, earth, and the underworld? If the Vaidarbha style is possessed of the full weight of youth, what is the use of even the Goddess of Speech out of affection?
He whose poetry or home shines forth like the sky variegated and radiant with gold—
that Nandana Śrī Kṛṣṇarāma, the poet whose desires are fulfilled, rejoices in the splendor of the kunda flower.

Although poetry that is rich in sentiment brings delight, it does not please the deer-eyed woman unless it is composed with a single, unified flavor; nor does lovemaking bring her joy unless it is free from quarreling.

Poetry leads to fame, to the attainment of wealth, to knowledge of worldly conduct, and to the warding off of misfortune; it provides immediate supreme bliss and, by being equal to a beloved, it serves as a means for instruction.
Poetry is nectar for those who know aesthetic flavor; a beloved woman is nectar for those filled with desire;
wealth is nectar for those possessed by greed; and peace is nectar for renunciants.
One who is merely clever at the elaborate display of poetry composes verse but does not possess its essence;
trees produce fruits, but it is the flock of birds that finds the core.
As long as his words, consisting of poetry, circulate clearly upon the earth,
for that long the poet, having attained the abode of Sarasvatī, rejoices.
The time of the wise passes in the enjoyment of poetry and the sciences;
that of fools, however, passes in vice, sleep, or quarreling.
In poetry, words that possess a friendship with the syllables— being neither harsh nor vulgar— and men who are likewise virtuous, are alone capable of conveying the intended meaning.
In poetry, just as with a mango fruit— whether tender or otherwise—
the flavor differs according to the specific quality of its composition and luster.
Agitated by poetry, she intoxicates; they call her the delightful golden coin. Here, adorned with the crescent moon of Kālī, she is fit for desire.

Formerly, those playful graces of yours, as sweet as the essence of nectar, used to revolve within my mind in the form of poetry; without them, O lady of lovely character, how could our fine poetry ever have been captivating to the heart?
The nectar of poetry, swallowed by the Rāhu of wicked men, would not be obtainable by those of noble mind,
were it not for the excellence of its sharpness, which shines forth through the unfeigned assembly of the virtuous.

Who would not desire as her husband a man from the Deccan who is skilled in poetry, music, and the science of dance, who knows the rules, is capable, generous, and upright— provided that his union with women is characterized by sincerity, as is common among the people of Koṅkaṇa?

Those fools who desire to please a wealthy fool with poetry, a base person with affection, a courtesan with learning, or a deceitful enemy with honesty— their efforts are equal to wailing in the wilderness.
In poetry, one should cultivate the poetic qualities (*guṇas*), yet it is the wicked who find fault with them;
for bandits never set a trap inside the house of a man in dire straits.
Even when a most excellent poem is being repeatedly savored by throngs of connoisseurs, the persistent search for faults is the natural, perverse obsession of those possessed by envy;
even in a lake filled with blooming lotuses and sporting swans, the curlew—with body hunched—seeks only a snail with its beak.

Although indeed there is no benefit whatsoever for the wicked here when an auspicious poem has been composed, I shall nevertheless do this for the sake of the virtuous; for would one discard one's garment out of fear of lice?
Among poetic works, the drama is delightful; within that, the *Śakuntalā*;
within that, the fourth act; and within that, these four verses.

Those who are skilled in extracting the distinct milk of merits from the mass of water that is poetry—wherein merits and faults shine as the sole vessel—are the king-swans of poets, whose minds are as pure as the moon; they know how to effect this distinction through diligent application.
The Vedas are ruined by poems; sons are ruined by sons-in-law;
cattle are ruined by horses; and noble women are ruined by courtesans.
Who is the beloved of Śambhu? What indeed does the moonstone do? What does a serpent do to a beautiful woman’s face?
Who is the Lord of Fortune? What is the difficult riddle? Vāsudeva kisses the face of Gaurī.
Clad in saffron robes, with a face as charming as a blooming lotus, delightful with the sound of intoxicated swans like the tinkling of anklets,
and possessing a slender body as beautiful as ripened rice stalks, the autumn has arrived, lovely in form like a newlywed bride.
The *kāśa* flowers shone like *kāśa* flowers, and the lakes were like lakes;
they stirred the hearts of the youths just as rivers stir other rivers.
The *kāśa* flowers resemble milk; the *saptaparṇa* trees have the color of curd and cream; the moon resembles fresh butter; and in autumn, the moonlight has the luster of buttermilk.

Kāśī is beautifully adorned by rows of pearl-like droplets shimmering from the thick, lofty waves of the incomparable celestial river Ganges; with the sky darkened by swarms of flickering bees, she shines like the beloved of Viśveśvara, her lotus-eyes wide open upon the lake.
