O Lord Śrī Raghunātha, in the city of that Lord of the Rakṣasas who is terrified of you, there is only one conversation among people—namely, the story of fleeing; there is no other talk, not even in a dream, of erotic discourse, tales of curiosity, stories of the arts such as singing, accounts of intoxicated elephants, stories of horses, or discourses on the initiation into archery.
The earth was whitened by *kāśa* grass, the nights by the moon, the waters of the rivers by swans, and the lakes by white lotuses;
the forest edges were made white by *saptacchada* trees bent under the weight of their blossoms, and the groves by *mālatī* jasmine.
Who is the daughter of the mountain? What is pleasing to the eyes? What does a young parrot do with fruits?

Who is the giver of liberation through mere remembrance? And who kisses the face of Gaurī? [The answers are: Śailaputrī, netraramyaṃ (the eye-delighting), śukārbhakaḥ (the young parrot), phalāni (fruits), mokṣasya dātā (the giver of liberation), and vāsudevaḥ (Vāsudeva).
The *koyaṣṭika* bird perches upon the *kāśmarya* tree, its new leaves having emerged; the *pūrṇikā* birds, their beaks touching the pods of the *aśmantaka* on the bank, run toward the water.
On the trunk of the *tiniśa* tree, which is full of hollows, a *dātyūha* bird remains hidden; below it, the wild cocks cry out, echoing the cooing of the young pigeons in the nest among the creepers.
With the regions of her cheeks stained by the mud-paste of Kāśmīra saffron, and with a crest made beautiful by a cluster of *kahlāra* lily buds,
a certain Cola woman approaches the courtyard of the monastery, her breasts like two *āmalaka* fruits resting gracefully upon the palms of her hands.

This darkness, as intensely black as the leaf of the *tamāla* tree, which is bound on all sides by the clusters of light from the women of Kāśmīra— fair of complexion as they go to meet their lovers— spreads like a touchstone for the gold of their love.

O fair one with the luster of liquid saffron from Kashmir, alas, why this excessive attachment to cosmetic ointments for the body? Or rather, O lotus-eyed one, why this great agitation over collyrium for the eyes?
Why is lac applied to feet that are already comparable to the petals of a red *aśoka* tree? A gem does not seek another hue when it is already resplendent with its own radiance.

Adorned with a beautiful tilaka of a crescent moon shining amidst a cluster of saffron pollen, her mass of hair fastened at the nape of her neck, she possesses eyes like the petals of a lotus; she is indeed that goddess Vaiṣṇavī.
The row of fresh nail-marks from her lover, scattered upon the copper-colored sash on the surface of her breasts which are inlaid with Kashmiri paste,
reveals, as it were, the royal edict of youth bestowed by the King of the Flower-Bowed God upon this doe-eyed woman.
As if melted and poured into the lineaments of the limbs of Kashmiri women, where the waves of loveliness ripple, sixteen-carat gold has been set down.
This lunar orb expands, anointing the vault of the sky with saffron, establishing a dual sovereignty over the faces of fair-browed women, and piercing the water-vessels made of moonstone;
it is the very image of that [moon] whose lap is intoxicated by the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass offered as an *arghya* greeting by the city brides of Indra’s capital as they come forth to meet him.
O friend, stay in Kāśī, which is eternally praised by hosts of gods; worship Śrīkaṇṭha, the ocean of compassion who is skillful in the task of protecting his own devotees.
Bathe in the Ganges water that removes all sins, and remember the Lord of Śrī; you shall attain the path of liberation without any hardship when your life comes to its end.
Liberation from death occurs at Kāśī, while liberation from birth occurs at Kamalālaya;
[liberation] comes from the sight of Abhrasaras, and from the remembrance of Aruṇācala.
Cast your body down in Kāśī, or in the house of a dog-cooker; lead me to heaven, or to liberation, or to a lower state.
Show mercy this very day, or in the future—what haste is there for me?
As for wealth, the wealthy man is the judge.

O Lord of Kāśī, one whose mind is fixed on what is unreal does not perceive the form of the Sovereign residing in the heart—He for whom that Śrī was the most beloved, surpassing all other wives at every moment.

Since Your mind has been constantly devoted to Him, Your previous merits are beyond counting, such that even toward the bliss of non-dual Brahman, Your mind feels but slight regard when compared to His worship.
What is praiseworthy for the virtuous?
Forgiveness.
What is contempt? [The lack of it.]
What suffering is there for one supported by his own kin? What is dependence on others? And who in this world is truly praiseworthy?
Who is it that relies [on this]?
What is death and calamity? And who abandons sorrow?
By whom were the enemies conquered? By those who realized this while the Pāṇḍavas remained in disguise in the city of Virāṭa.

The arising of the mind [toward worldly objects] is not destroyed by saffron robes, nor by rules regarding food and the like, nor by dwelling in the forest, nor by exposition, nor even by the burden of the ascetic’s vows;
rather, it is destroyed by even a mere fraction of the undertaking of worshiping the lotus feet of Govinda as he sports upon the banks of the daughter of Mount Kalinda.

O Lord of the Raghus, I do not compare you to these: the wish-granting tree is but wood, Mount Sumeru is a mere mountain, the wish-fulfilling gem is a stone, the sun has scorching rays, and the moon is waning; the ocean is indeed salty, Kāma is bodiless, Bali is the son of Diti, and Nandin is but a beast that wanders at will—to whom can you be likened? To what comparison can you be put?
Wood, even when abandoned by fire, may serve to quell the cold of monkeys; water purifies the fur of monkeys, while fire purifies the skins of deer.
The dispositions of living beings bring about the accomplishment of their tasks according to their nature; in reality, there is no inherent essence in them whatsoever.
Having placed a piece of wood upon the head, one should likewise strike with a piece of wood;
by that means, memory is immediately restored to the yogin whose memory has been lost.
When a pair of wooden balls is thrown far away by those standing high above in front,
one should indeed go behind it, following its tail and mouth before they have reached the ground.
By making [an image] out of wood, stone, or metal,
and by serving it with devotion and faith, one attains accomplishment through the grace of Viṣṇu.
Wood turns into charcoal, and cow dung and the like turn into ashes when cast into fire;
but gold, when cast into fire, attains a state of supreme excellence.
He should remove forest fires and cause wells to be dug; likewise, he should have those wells cleaned that were previously constructed by people seeking water.
Fire is born from wood when it is rubbed; the earth yields water when it is dug.
For men who possess perseverance, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished; all efforts undertaken on the right path bear fruit.
Just as fire produced from wood burns its own source in an instant,
so too the fire of anger born within the body certainly burns that very same body.
O illustrious Kārtavīrya, as your blazing majesty awakens and increases through its attachment to wood [or fuel],
rival kings fall into it by force like moths.
Having tied a horse-hair to a piece of wood and fastened a cowrie shell to it,
he who strikes it while it is being whirled around by the hand is a true archer.
O Subhaṭa, tell me truly: what is awakening? What is the forest like at dawn when the birds have fully awakened?
In what does the world find joy? And what is your victorious [name]? By what kind of being, generally, is happiness found here in this world?

"What is this cycle of existence? What is its cause? Of what kind are you, and what harm has been done to you by it?"—to these questions, O Mother, I am not skilled enough to provide an answer; I only feel a certain inexplicable weariness that persists in this way.
One who suffers from cough, dyspnea, fever, indigestion, grief, thirst, or inflammation of the mouth,
as well as one afflicted by diseases of the head, eyes, heart, or ears, should not [undergo this procedure].
Among some, he dwells for a long time as white; among others, however, he is blue, or tawny, or red, or black—the excellent bull.
Though disregarded by the villagers, with drooping shoulders and ears that do not stand erect, this brindled beast, his body bloated and dependent on others, remains awake within my heart.
For what calamities is excessive greed and blinded intellect not the cause?

Victorious is the lotus, a marvel of diverse conduct, which smiles in friendship with the midday sun— even that fierce heat-rayed one who parches the marshlands and consumes the masses of fresh, charming, and excellent lotus-stalks— yet it finds happiness therein.
In this lake is a lotus pond where a pair of charming buds stands not far apart, and wherein the activity of the rays of the newly risen moon is praiseworthy.

Therefore, having seen this directly before you with its specific details remembered, you should disregard it; O knower of the welfare of the women of Vraja, do not let this excellent time pass in vain.
Even travelers drink water from a mere pond; nowhere else do they find it, for you are salty, O Ocean—and thus this name alone is fitting for you.
Yet these other names of yours are not meaningless, nor do they denote different things: Ambhodhi, Jaladhi, Payonidhi, Udadhi, Vārāṃnidhi, and Vāridhi.
In that very lake, whose waters were once drunk by herds of elephants intoxicated with rut until they sank up to their tusks, and which pervaded the entire world with the surging of its vast waves—
now that its water has been consumed by the fierce rays of the sun, the ground in its center becomes scorched for travelers at every step.
"Alas! To take up water from puddles, rivers, and oceans, as well as from low-lying places—what else could be more contemptible for the proud? Furthermore, even there, one must bow the head.
Having reflected thus and abandoned all longing for them, O Cloud, bearer of rain, the young *cātaka* bird now looks up with reverence, stretching its neck toward you.
O excellent *kāsāra* (lake), adorned with lotuses as your crest-jewels, where the surface of your waves sports with water-drops like pearls—
what ornament is there for you without many cranes and those sweet-voiced swans who are worshipped by kings?
"Who are you? Speak, you thief! Where are you from? Who are you? "I am a city watchman. "What do you say?"
"The two golden jars of the king have been stolen; by whom? By you!
Where are they? They are right here, visible at the edge of your garment! Where?"
When the words "Let the heated iron be licked" were spoken, may You, the yellow-robed one who held the pair of breasts of the cowherd girl, protect us.
One who desires to live in this world should avoid theft from Kāśī, a thief of skins should avoid sleep, and one afflicted by disease should avoid greed of the tongue.
One should consume honey and long pepper (madhupippalī) in cases of cough, dyspnea, consumption, weak digestion, irregular fever, urinary disorders, and difficulty in urination.
What woman is not under the sway of a lover? Who is devoid of the playfulness of the god of love? What dharma is without tranquility? And what happiness belongs to those separated from their beloved?
Who is this woman with a veil, whose bodily beauty is not clearly visible,
standing in the midst of ascetics like a fresh sprout among pale leaves?
"Who am I? the cave says; what is the answer to this question? How is it that you do not understand how it was spoken, and thus, my friend, you treat me with such contempt?
Day and night one should reflect upon the insubstantiality of saṃsāra, and not upon a woman. What should be cherished? Compassion, courtesy, and loving-kindness.
What other creeper can ever equal the creeping vine of a serpent’s arm,
which, even when bitten by teeth, produces a most exquisite beauty upon the face?
